## Volume front matter

### Series title page

*Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, based on the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each individual volume or author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject treated; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any theme may be viewed at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on the individual texts of the books of Scripture, and in which places in their works they did so.*

*The most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others, if one considers the elegance of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection itself—single, methodical, and chronological—which for the first time in our library has gathered together six hundred fragments and short works previously scattered here and there, from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.*

*SECOND SERIES, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the complete courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.*

# PROLEGOMENA TO THE WORKS OF THE VENERABLE BEDE, ANGLO-SAXON PRIEST

[Col. 0009]

## HISTORICAL EULOGY OF THE VENERABLE BEDE, BY DOM JEAN MABILLON

*(From the Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order, vol. III.)*

## I. Bede’s birth, the question of his date, and his monastic profession

[Col. 0009A]

### 1

“The Venerable Bede,” says William, monk of Malmesbury, in book I of *The Kings of England*, chapter 3, “the light of the English Church, born in a remote corner of the world, illuminated all lands with the splendor of his learning.” For Britain—which some call another world, because, surrounded by the Ocean, it was known to few cosmographers—has, in its most remote region, near Scotland, the place of his birth and upbringing. That place belonged to the kingdom of the Northumbrians, which within its boundaries comprised Deira, or the people of York, and Bernicia—that is, the Scots of today—separated from one another by the River Tyne. Almost at the very mouth of the Tyne is seen a village called Girvum, in the vernacular Jarrow, the native soil of the Venerable Bede. There he received the use of the light of day [Col. 0009B] from unknown parents, at the time when Egfrid ruled the Northumbrians. The year must be investigated.

### 2

In the preceding *Life*, Bede is said to have been born in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 677. But this calculation cannot stand. For Bede completed his *History of His People*, composed in five books, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 731, as is marked at the end of book V. In that same year he completed his *Epitome*, as we observe in our manuscript copy, in which the *Epitome* ends with the year 731 in these words:

“In the year 731 Archbishop Berctwald died. In that same year Tatwine was consecrated as the ninth archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, while Ethelbaldo was in the fifteenth year of his reign as king of the Mercians.”

This is the conclusion concerning ecclesiastical history, and so the material found in the printed books [Col. 0009C] concerning events occurring in subsequent years must be regarded as an interpolation. Therefore, in the same year 731, Bede completed his *History* and his *Epitome*. Moreover, he completed the *Epitome* in the fifty-ninth year of his life. For shortly after the words quoted above he writes:

“From the time when I received the priesthood until the fifty-ninth year of my life, I have taken care briefly to note, from the short works of the venerable Fathers, those things concerning Holy Scripture that were necessary for myself and for my brothers …” [Col. 0010A]

If, then, from the year 731 you count backward fifty-nine years of age, you will understand that Bede’s birth must be assigned to the year 673.

### 3

“I was born,” says Bede, “in the territory of the monastery of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, which is at Wearmouth and at Jarrow. When I was seven years old, I was entrusted by my relatives to be educated by the most reverend Abbot Benedict and afterward by Ceolfrith; and from that time I spent the whole period of my life dwelling in that same monastery, and so forth.”

Both monasteries were built by Benedict, or Biscop: Wearmouth in the year 674, in the second indiction and the fourth year of King Egfrid’s reign, at the mouth of the River Wear, as Bede testifies in book I of the *Life of Saint Biscop*, in the second century, under the year 690; hence the name Wearmouth, since *mouth* in English means “mouth” or “estuary. Jarrow, however, was built around the year 680, since the church of Saint Paul at Jarrow was dedicated in the fifteenth year of King Egfrid and the fourth year of Abbot Ceolfrith, its founder, as we noted in the same place.

From this we infer that Bede was entrusted to Biscop not at Jarrow but at the monastery of Wearmouth, although he later remained at Jarrow with Ceolfrith and there completed his earthly life. Certainly, Bede says in the same book, “there was one peace and harmony between the two places, the same continual familiarity and favor,” so that he commonly calls them one monastery, both because of the proximity of the places and especially because of their one and the same government and the mutual agreement and intercourse of the monks. [Col. 0010C]

It has been clearly demonstrated in the observations on the life of Biscop, from Bede’s own words, that the Rule of Saint Benedict prevailed from the beginning in both monasteries. From him we learn that, when Biscop was near death, he instructed his disciples to choose a worthy successor according to the rule of the once-great Abbot Benedict and according to the provisions of his privilege. Abbot Ceolfrith likewise gave this advice when he was about to resign the administration of the monastery. And Alcuin, exhorting the monks of Wearmouth and Jarrow in letter 49 to preserve with the greatest care the observance of the regular life established by Benedict and Ceolfrith, adds:

“Let the Rule of Saint Benedict be expounded in the brothers’ assembly in their own language, so that it may be understood by everyone.”

Since, therefore, Bede spent, as he himself says, the whole period of his life in one or the other of these monasteries, no one can deny that he obeyed Benedictine institutions. Why, however, he is commonly called a priest rather than a monk, we shall explain below, although Saint Boniface the martyr, in letter 9 to Huetbert, abbot of Wearmouth, requests something concerning the short works of “the monk Bede, that most diligent investigator of the Scriptures.”

## II. His activities, especially his study of the Scriptures, and his teachers

[Col. 0011B]

### 4

What Bede did in his monastery he reveals to us in his *Epitome* in these words:

“Spending the whole period of my life from that time in the dwelling of the same monastery, I devoted all my effort to studying the Scriptures. And amid the observances of the regular discipline and the daily responsibility of singing in the church, I always found it delightful either to learn, teach, or write.”

The whole substance of his life, therefore, was meditation on and study of the Scriptures. He devoted to learning, teaching, and writing as much time as remained after the obligations of regular discipline and the divine offices. The more remarkable it is, then, that a man so occupied with so many matters neither neglected the duties of his state, from which he could easily have been excused, nor ceased to learn or write things worthy of the greatest men. [Col. 0011C]

“Bede was a monk,” says Gaufridus Boussardus, “watching day and night with his brothers in unceasing psalmody; and, as though he were never praying, he was always occupied with literary studies. If you consider his life, you will judge that he allowed nothing to literature; if you consider his studies, that he devoted nothing to prayer.”

Thus he writes in his letter to Peter Securibilis concerning the edition of Bede’s commentary on the Apostle, extracted from Augustine’s works.

Would that this pious activity of mind, following Bede’s example, might also spread to many others! After his monastic exercises, his sole concern was to meditate upon the Scriptures, to learn, to teach, and to write.

Nevertheless, the monks of both monasteries were not occupied only with spiritual activities. For, as Bede testifies in Biscop’s *Life*, Biscop, their abbot, “like the other brothers, rejoiced to exercise himself cheerfully and obediently with them in winnowing and threshing, milking sheep and calves, and in the bakery, garden, kitchen, and all the works of the monastery.” [Col. 0011D]

And Bede himself, although perhaps less occupied with external duties, nevertheless did not avoid the work of a secretary and copyist, as we shall see below, no. 8.

### 5

There was no kind of art or discipline in which this man, so eager to learn, did not engage with the greatest diligence. To support this work, he acquired not only Latin but also the Greek language. This is certainly remarkable in a private individual living within the walls of a monastery in the almost most remote regions of Britain.

He directed the entire method of his studies toward the interpretation of Sacred Scripture. To this he devoted his vigils and his nightly labors, so that he might advance so holy and praiseworthy a study both in his own mind and in those of his disciples. At the end of his book *On the Art of Meter*, he addresses his disciple Cuthbert as follows:

“I have taken care to excerpt these things diligently for you, my dearest son and fellow-deacon Gutberht, from the short works of ancient writers. What I had gathered here and there through prolonged labor, I have presented to you in collected form, so that, just as I have striven to instruct you in the divine writings and ecclesiastical statutes, I might also carefully train you in the art of meter, which is not unknown to the divine books. I have also thought it appropriate to append a brief book concerning figures and modes of speech, which the Greeks call *schemata* or *tropes*. And I earnestly entreat your affection to devote yourself to the reading of those writings above all in which we believe that we have eternal life.”

And in his book *On the Figures of Scripture*:

“But so that you may know, dearest son—and so that all who wish to read these things may likewise know—that Holy Scripture surpasses all other writings not only in authority, because it is divine, or in usefulness, because it leads to eternal life, but also in antiquity and in the very arrangement of its expression, I have therefore decided, by collecting examples from Scripture itself, to show that the teachers of eloquence in any age cannot produce any such figures or tropes that did not precede them in Scripture.”

Nor did he regard as beneath him even the smallest matters, provided that they could contribute to understanding Sacred Scripture. Hence he composed a little book *On Finger-Reckoning*, or *On the Method of Counting by the Fingers*. For, he says:

“One must not despise or regard as insignificant the rule which nearly all expositors of Sacred Scripture are shown to have embraced no less than the forms of letters.”

### 6

Bede had several teachers, among them the monk Trumberht, a disciple of Ceadda, bishop of Lichfield. Bede admits in book IV, chapter 3, of his *History* that Trumberht was one of those who instructed him in the Scriptures.

Some say that Trumberht was a disciple of John, bishop of Hexham; more correctly, one would say that he was a disciple of John the Roman archcantor. For Biscop, as Bede testifies both in book IV, chapter 18, of his *History* and in Biscop’s *Life*, introduced into his monastery the order of singing, psalmody, and ministering in the church according to Roman practice. He had requested and received from Pope Agatho John, archcantor of the church of the blessed apostle Peter and abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin, in order to bring this Roman to the English as the future teacher of his monastery in Britain.

When John arrived, he transmitted orally to those learning not only the ecclesiastical practices that he had learned at Rome, but also left behind a considerable amount committed to writing, which to this day is preserved in the library of the same monastery as a memorial.

There is no doubt that Bede heard some teachers among the disciples of Theodore, bishop of Canterbury, and of Abbot Hadrian. Both men were abundantly instructed in sacred and secular letters, and, having gathered a crowd of disciples, daily poured forth streams of saving knowledge to water their hearts. “Thus,” says Bede in book IV, chapter 2, of his *History*, “they even taught their hearers the disciplines of the art of meter, astronomy, and arithmetic amid the volumes of the sacred writings.”

## III. His ordination, teaching, and reverence toward the Fathers

### 7

“In the nineteenth year of my life,” says Bede in his *Epitome*, “I received the diaconate, and in the thirtieth the rank of the priesthood, both through the ministry of the most reverend Bishop John, at the command of Abbot Ceolfrith.”

This was John of Hexham, first made bishop around the year 697, at the beginning of the reign of Aldfrith, king of the Northumbrians, as Bede testifies in book V, chapter 2. Later, after the death of Bosa around the year 704, he became archbishop of York.

“Moreover,” says Bede in book V, chapter 6, “he remained in the episcopate for thirty-three years. After Wilfrid, his own priest, had been ordained bishop of the Church of York, he withdrew to a monastery founded by himself in the forest of Deira.” He eventually died in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 721, in which year we dealt with him.

We assign the year of Bede’s ordination as deacon to the Christian era 691. He attained the rank of priest in the year 702, when John still presided over the see of Hexham, to which the monasteries of Wearmouth and Jarrow seem then to have belonged, before the bishopric of Durham was established.

For, besides the fact that Bede was ordained by John, bishop of Hexham, this is supported by the authority of Bishop Acca over Bede. At Acca’s urging and insistence, Bede undertook many of his nightly labors. Acca presided over the see of Hexham after Wilfrid’s death in 709, as we saw above under that year.

Some may perhaps find it surprising that Bede was ordained a deacon in the nineteenth year of his life, since the canons prescribe the twenty-fifth year. Yet bishops sometimes granted dispensations on account of the holiness of those being ordained, as can be observed in the cases of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, Saint Sequanus, and others.

### 8

“From the time when I received the priesthood,” Bede continues in his *Epitome*, “until the fifty-ninth year of my life, I took care briefly to note in Holy Scripture, for my own necessity and that of my brothers, things drawn from short works, or also to add material according to the form of their meaning and interpretation.”

From this we understand that Bede did not devote himself to writing books before the thirtieth year of his life. In this work he had as his principal encourager and instigator Acca, bishop of Hexham. A letter of his survives, addressed to Bede and placed before Bede’s commentaries on the Gospel of Luke, beginning as follows:

“To the most reverend brother and fellow priest in Christ, Bede the presbyter: Acca sends perpetual greetings in the Lord. I have often suggested to your holy brotherhood, both in writing while absent and in conversation while present, that after your exposition of the Acts of the Apostles you should also deign to write on the Gospel of Luke. You have until now preferred to postpone this rather than undertake it, offering the modest excuse that you were deterred from attempting the work chiefly for two reasons: namely, that the work itself was arduous and that it had already been undertaken by the most holy and learned bishop Ambrose.”

Since Bede replied that he feared he might be thought to be producing something new in criticism of the work of the ancients, Acca meets the objection and adds:

“For I wish that, once by God’s help you have completed the work I request, this letter also be placed at its head, so that it may be known that you were asked to write on Luke for no other reason than fraternal condescension: namely, so that those who, because of the weakness of their understanding, cannot grasp lofty or difficult matters may more easily apprehend them when they are explained in a simpler style.”

And shortly afterward:

“I also believe that through your most vigilant study—for you spend days and nights in continual watchfulness meditating upon the law of God—the Author of light will reveal in certain places what should be understood concerning those matters which they [the Fathers] left untouched. For it is entirely just, and fitting to the moderation of heavenly piety and equity, that you who, having neglected the business of the world altogether, pursue the eternal and true light of wisdom with tireless mind should attain here the fruit of a purer understanding and, in the future, behold with a pure heart the King in his beauty, the very one in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden.”

But since these words seemed to have been spoken too extravagantly in Bede’s honor, as he himself thought, he replies in a humble letter as follows:

“To the most blessed and greatly desired Lord Acca, bishop: Bede, a humble presbyter, sends greetings in the eternal Lord. Truly marvelous, and marvelously true, is the judgment of the distinguished teacher, because love believes all things and hopes all things. In the letters you sent me, you say that you are asking me to write something for you; and while asking, before you have received my consent, you compose the seal of a preface concerning the requested short works as though they had already been obtained and perfectly completed. Before the foundation has been laid, before even the material has been brought, you send the keys with which the entrance is to be secured, as though the building of so great a labor had already been completed. Thus your friendly confidence makes me ashamed not to undertake quickly a work which it presumes should be undertaken quickly and completed even more quickly.”

And after a verse:

“Therefore, as soon as I had read the pages of your most sweet holiness, I submitted myself to the labor of the work imposed upon me. In this work, to pass over the countless restraints of monastic service, I would myself be composer, secretary, and copyist at once.”

Here we see the truly remarkable modesty of so great a man. Worthy as he was of such great matters and occupied with such arduous studies, he did not shrink from the work of a copyist and secretary, nor from the countless restraints of monastic service.

He continues in the same letter:

“I have also appended, where it seemed appropriate, certain things which—as I shall put it in the words of your holiness—the Author of light has revealed to me, as signs of my own labor. Although I am not capable of spending days and nights in continual watchfulness in meditation on the divine law, as you yourself wrote, I do not doubt that I have nevertheless devoted no small amount of effort to the Scriptures.”

At the urging of the same Acca, Bede wrote two books of commentary on the *Hexaemeron*, six books on Samuel, and an exposition of Ezra. The preface to the *Hexaemeron* should therefore be addressed not to Abbot Acca, as in the printed books, but to Bishop Acca, as the manuscripts indicate. In these manuscripts Acca, or Accan, appears without inflection in every case.

### 9

In all his nightly labors Bede was exceedingly devoted to the teaching of the holy Fathers, so that he seems not so much to have forged new works as to have excerpted collections from their monuments. Thus he extracted his commentaries on the *Hexaemeron* from the works of the Fathers Basil, Eustathius, Ambrose, and Augustine.

Thus, after consulting the writings of the venerable Fathers, he produced his more extensive book *On the Reckoning of Time*. He did the same in his book of thirty *Questions*, in which he strove to provide answers by following the footsteps of the Fathers, and in his exposition of the *Song of Songs*, as he himself affirms in the prologue.

Certainly, in his exposition of the Gospel of Luke, he diligently attempted, by gathering from here and there the short works of the Fathers as though they were the most distinguished and worthy craftsmen of so great a task, to examine what Saint Ambrose, what Augustine, what Gregory—the apostle of his own people—what Jerome—the interpreter of sacred history—and what the other Fathers had thought and said concerning the words of Luke.

In his exposition of the Gospel of Mark, he likewise took care to insert here and there whatever he found especially in the writings of the venerable Fathers, asking the reader that, if he judged these short works worthy of transcription, he should preserve through careful writing the notation of the names placed in the margin.

The more unjust, therefore, was Desiderius Erasmus toward this most modest man. In his notes on Mark, chapter 14, Erasmus taunts Bede for concealing—as he supposes—the name of Jerome, when Bede transcribes a passage from Jerome’s commentaries on Matthew into his work on Mark, as though he wished to steal from the writings of the ancients a little glory for a novel composition.

But, as we have seen, the man’s intention was entirely different. Among the Fathers, Augustine above all was Bede’s delight, so much so that he composed a continuous exposition of the Pauline Epistles from the words of that great teacher alone.

He defends himself by Augustine’s authority against certain people who complained that, in his exposition of the Apocalypse, when he reached the four living creatures, he had designated Matthew by the lion and Mark by the man in a new interpretation. Some, on the contrary, assign the man to Matthew, since he begins to write about the Lord as a man, and the lion to Mark, in whom the voice of one crying in the wilderness is heard.

This is how Bede himself replies in the letter to Bishop Acca prefixed to his commentary on Luke:

“As for your statement that some people are troubled by the reason why, in the Apocalypse, I assigned Matthew to the lion and Mark to the man in a new interpretation, whoever they are whom this troubles ought to have observed that I did not say that this was my own new interpretation, but that it had been handed down in the ancient explanation of the Fathers. For I did not arrive at this view on my own, but I recalled that it had been explained in this way by the blessed Augustine—namely, in book I, chapter 6, of *On the Agreement of the Evangelists*—as I shall prove below.”

## IV. Whether Bede was summoned to Rome by Sergius, whether he taught at York, and whom he had as disciples

### 10

Bede gained such esteem for his learning through his writings, even among foreigners, that Pope Sergius himself is said to have summoned him to Rome. William, monk of Malmesbury, produces a letter written by Sergius concerning this matter in book I, chapter 3, of *The Kings of England*, in the following form:

“Sergius, bishop and servant of the servants of God, sends greetings to Celfrith, religious abbot.

“With what words and expressions can we proclaim the mercy of our God and his ineffable providence, and offer worthy thanks for his immense benefits toward us? He brings those placed in darkness and the shadow of death into the light of knowledge.”

And below:

“Know, meanwhile, that we have willingly and cheerfully received the grace of your blessing, which your devoted religious community sent us through the present bearer, just as it was directed by you. Therefore, favoring with the strictest devotion the suitable and worthy requests of your solicitude, we exhort the goodness of your religious devotion, beloved of God, that, since certain matters of ecclesiastical controversy have arisen which need to be made known more fully through examination, we need men trained in letters for consultation, as befits a devoted helper of God to the holy mother, the universal Church. Do not cease to offer obedient devotion to this exhortation of ours. Rather, without any delay, send the religious servant of God, Bede, presbyter of your venerable monastery, without delay to the thresholds of the chief Apostles Peter and Paul, your beloved ones and protectors, and before our humble presence.

“With God’s favor, through your prayers, you may confidently expect him to return successfully to you after, with God’s help, he has completed the desired solemn proceedings concerning the matters mentioned above. For, as we trust, whatever benefit the universal Church may derive from his distinguished gifts will also benefit all those entrusted to you.”

At this point William exclaims:

“So celebrated was Bede’s reputation that Roman greatness needed him to unravel its questions.”

Yet it is sufficiently clear that Bede did not leave his native land, from his own *Epitome*, where he affirms that he spent the entire period of his life from childhood dwelling in his monastery.

There is also some ground for suspicion in the letter mentioned above: first, because Bede can scarcely have been ordained a priest before the death of Pope Sergius, who died in 701; second, because he began to devote himself to writing books from the time when he received the priesthood, and through these works his reputation spread abroad.

Bede was certainly worthy to be consulted by the Roman pontiffs, but it is important to distinguish what is certain from what is uncertain. Baronius correctly infers that Bede never visited the city of Rome from the fact that, in the letter to King Ceolwulf prefixed to his *History*, Bede testifies that he obtained from Nothelm, who had traveled to Rome to visit Pope Gregory II, the materials that he needed to construct the history of his people—not that he himself brought them back from Rome.

One may reply, however, that at the time when Bede went to Rome at Sergius’s command he had not yet begun to think of writing his *History*, and therefore had no concern for the monuments necessary to that undertaking. Nor does the very short time he would have spent on the journey to Rome prevent it from being truly said that he spent the whole period of his life dwelling in his monastery.

Certainly Bede testifies in book II of his *History* that monks from his monastery were sent to Rome during the time of Pope Sergius and obtained from him a privilege.

Whatever the truth may be, the story is fictitious which, as I remember reading both in a certain copy from the monastery of Ursicamp and in Spelman’s *Glossary* under the word “Venerable,” says that Bede traveled to Rome and deciphered an inscription, understood by no one, carved on the Iron Gate in the following form:

“P. P. P. S. S. S. R. R. R. F. F. F.”

He supposedly rendered it as:

“Father of the Fatherland is lost. Salvation has been taken away with him. The kingdom of Rome will fall through iron, flame, and famine.”

By this interpretation, he is said to have earned the name “Venerable” by decree of the Senate and People of Rome.

Nonsense.

### 11

The Venerable Bede spent most of his life in his monastery, where he had almost as many disciples as there were monks—that is, six hundred, for that many religious lived in the communities of Wearmouth and Jarrow. Others also came from different monasteries so that they might advance through his instruction.

There he had as hearers Eusebius, or Huethbert—for he had two names, as is clear from the preface to book IV on Samuel—later abbot of Wearmouth, to whom he dedicated his book *On the Reckoning of Time* and his *Explanation of the Apocalypse*;

Cuthbert, Huethbert’s successor, to whom he dedicated his book *On the Art of Meter*;

Constantine, to whom a short work *On the Division of Numbers* survives;

Nothelm, first a priest of London and later bishop of Canterbury, at whose request he published his book of thirty *Questions* on the books of Kings;

and others whose names are unknown to us.

Nor did he confine himself so entirely within the boundaries of his monastery that he never went outside. Recently his letter to Egbert, archbishop of York, was brought out of the darkness. It is directed against the corrupt morals of his age, and begins by saying:

“I remember that last year, when I stayed with you for several days in your monastery for the sake of reading, you said that this year also, when you came to the same place, you wished to receive me into your conversation for our common love of reading.”

This seems to refer to the monastery of the Church of York, where Egbert was still a monk. He was related to Ceolwulf, king of the Northumbrians, and is said in the *Life of Abbot Alcuin* to have had Bede as his teacher.

For this reason some count Alcuin among Bede’s disciples, since he was educated under the discipline of Egbert, who had already become bishop. Alcuin testifies to this in a certain letter to Charlemagne, a fragment of which William, monk of Malmesbury, reports in book I, chapter 3, of *The Kings of England*. Or perhaps they confuse Albinus Flaccus, or Alcuin, the teacher of Charlemagne, with Abbot Albinus, whom Bede mentions in the prologue to his *Ecclesiastical History*.

## V. Bede’s holiness and modesty

### 12

“As for the holiness of his life,” says William of Malmesbury in book I, chapter 3, of *The Kings of England*, “the unquestionable truth of that saying which the majesty of divine wisdom brought forth for the world prevents anyone from doubting it:

‘Wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins’” (*Wisdom* 1:4).

This does not refer to worldly wisdom, which indiscriminately enters human hearts and by which the worst people, very often placing no limits on themselves until the final day, are seen to be stained by crimes. Rather, it names that wisdom which “will flee from discipline that is feigned” and which separates itself from thoughts that lack understanding—by understanding I mean the understanding both of living well and of speaking well.

The ecclesiastical orator therefore first cleansed his conscience, so that he might then approach the unlocking of the meaning of the mystical writings. For how could a man serve vices who drank in the innermost marrow of the Scriptures and expended all his thoughts on their exposition?

For, as he himself admits in book III of his work on Samuel, even if his expositions brought readers no other benefit, they would be of no small value to him for this reason: while he devoted himself to this task with every effort, he placed behind him the slipperiness of the world and empty thoughts.

Thus purified from vices, he entered the inner regions behind the veil, bringing forth in disciplined speech what he had received within his mind. More will be said below concerning his holiness.

### 13

The man’s modesty is sufficiently indicated by the book of *Revisions* that he himself published on the *Acts of the Apostles*, following the example of the outstanding teacher and bishop Augustine. He did this especially either by adding what had been said too briefly or by correcting what seemed to have been said differently from what he wished.

“In this work,” he says, “we have also taken care briefly to mention certain things which we saw expressed in Greek, or otherwise, or with greater or lesser polish. We have not yet been able to determine whether these were omitted or expressed differently through the negligence of the translator, or whether they were corrupted or omitted through the carelessness of copyists. For I do not dare to suspect that the Greek exemplar itself had been falsified.

“I therefore warn the reader that, wherever we have made such observations, he should read them for the sake of learning, but should not insert them into his own volume as though they were corrected readings, unless perhaps he finds that they had long ago been translated in this form in the Latin codex of his own edition.”

From this disposition of modesty, Bede strove not to express his own opinion in explaining the Scriptures, but to set forth the teachings of the holy Fathers. This has already been demonstrated above in greater detail.

Thus, in his *Revisions* on chapter 2 of the *Acts of the Apostles*, where the tongues of the apostles are discussed, he says:

“I know that I have been criticized by certain people because I said that this passage could be understood in two ways, or rather because I asked how it ought to be understood. I reply briefly that everything whatsoever I have written in the present volume concerning this same passage was not brought forth from my own judgment, but from the words of a holy and altogether irreproachable teacher—namely, Gregory of Nazianzus.”

## VI. Zeal for truth, faith, and purity of morals
### 14.

Yet this man, who loved truth above all, was not so wholly devoted to the authority of his predecessors that he thought everything they had said ought to be affirmed without discrimination. He knew Augustine’s distinguished statement in Letter 19 to Jerome:

> I have learned to defer such fear and honor to those books of Scripture alone that are now called canonical, that I most firmly believe none of their authors made an error in writing. But I read the others in such a way that, however great their holiness and learning may be, I do not therefore regard something as true because they thought so, but because either through those canonical authors or by probable reasoning they have been able to persuade me that it does not depart from the truth.

Bede followed Isidore, bishop of Seville, when in his Commentary on the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 1, he wrote that Simon the Zealot was the same man who, after James the Lord’s brother, governed the Church at Jerusalem and was crowned with martyrdom on the cross under Trajan when he was one hundred and twenty years old. Yet in his Retractations he calls this into question, although he still did not dare firmly to deny it. He adds the following concerning Jerome’s authority:

> In the same work I wrote, following Jerome’s commentary, that Jude, the brother of James, who was also called Thaddaeus, had been sent to Abgar, king of Osroene, as ecclesiastical history has handed down. But afterward, examining the ecclesiastical history more carefully, I discovered that it is not written there that the apostle Thaddaeus, one of the Twelve, was sent to heal the aforesaid king, but that Thaddaeus, one of the Seventy disciples, was sent for this purpose.

Then, in defense of himself, he adds:

> I do not think that an error should be charged against me when, following the authority of great teachers, I believed without hesitation that what I found in their little works ought to be accepted.

And in chapter 8 of the Retractations of the same book he rejects the book On the Dormition of Blessed Mary, written under the name of Melito, bishop of Asia, and exposes the author’s falsehoods:

> I have taken care to mention this because I know that some people, through heedless rashness, give assent to the aforesaid volume against the authority of blessed Luke.

Other testimonies could also be adduced by which we might prove that Bede was not so credulous or so hasty in judgment when writing his History, since he even exercised discrimination and critical judgment in the writings of the Fathers. Read his own preface to the History addressed to King Ceolwulf, in which he declares from which authors he learned the matters he has related.

### 15.

No less was his zeal for the Catholic faith, for whose defense he undertook his exposition of the Song of Songs. Hear his words at the beginning of the first book:

> When, with the help of heavenly grace, I was about to write on the Song of Songs, I first thought that the reader should be warned to read with the greatest caution the works of Julian, bishop of Celana in Campania, which he composed on the same book, lest, through the abundance of his seductive eloquence, he fall into the banquet of harmful doctrine. Rather, as the saying goes, let him gather the cluster of grapes while also avoiding the thorn—that is, let him examine and select the sound meanings in Julian’s statements, and avoid the unsound ones no less carefully. For he is as skilled a rhetorician as he is a fierce opponent, after Pelagius, of the grace of God, as his writings more clearly show, in which he raged against Augustine, the most vigorous defender of that same grace.

And below:

> But in another book, which he wrote to Demetrias, a virgin of Christ, On the Institution of a Virgin, he discloses the same view concerning the power of free will. Some of our people, reading that book attentively, rashly suppose it to be by the holy and Catholic teacher Jerome, failing entirely to see that both the sweetness of its beguiling eloquence and the perversity of its seductive heresy plainly prove that this little work is not his.

Afterward Bede reports and refutes fragments of Julian, as he supposes, truly performing the office of a Catholic teacher, by which he would fortify unwary readers against the deceptively flattering words of a heretic.

It was as a result of this zeal for the Catholic faith that, when he once heard that the stain of a heretical name had been fastened upon him, he shuddered utterly and immediately took up his pen in his own defense. There is an extant letter on this subject to the monk Plewina, recently published by Waraeus, whose opening is as follows:

> Two years ago, dearest brother, a messenger of your holiness came to me. He brought from you the most joyful words of a peaceful greeting, but soon confused them with a grievous addition, namely, that you had heard me sung about among heretics over their cups by wanton rustics.

> I shuddered, I confess, and, pale, asked what heresy they accused me of. He replied that I denied that, in the sixth age of the world, the Lord and Savior had come in the flesh. I therefore began to ask how this was being said: whether they meant that the Lord had not come in the flesh although it was the sixth age; or that, when the Lord came in the flesh, the sixth age had not yet arrived; or certainly that the seventh age had already come, although it is clear by reason that the sixth age could have begun only with his incarnation. I discovered that, whether this or that was being alleged against me, in either case I stood in fellowship with sound faith and ecclesiastical unity.

He then vigorously and forcefully argues his case, and concludes the letter as follows:

> I earnestly ask you to deliver this letter of my vindication to our religious and most learned brother David, so that he may read it before our venerable lord and father, namely Bishop Wilfrid. Since, in that man’s presence and hearing, I was previously attacked with insults through folly, may it now also appear, in his hearing and judgment, how undeservedly I suffered those same insults, and so forth.

This was Wilfrid II, who, after John, the successor of the elder Wilfrid, presided over the see of York from approximately the year 717 to 732.

### 16.

The holiness of conduct that he strove with all his heart to express in himself, he also endeavored, insofar as he could, to revive when it was languishing in others and to repair when it had been violated. Evidence of this is the letter that, as we conjecture, he wrote during his final illness to Ecgberht, who after the younger Wilfrid became archbishop of York. It begins as follows:

> To the most beloved and most reverend bishop Ecgberht, Bede, servant of Christ, sends greetings.

> I remember that last year, when I stayed with you for several days in your monastery for the sake of reading, you said that this year also, when you came to the same place, you wished to receive me into your conversation for our common love of reading. If this could be fulfilled, God willing, there would be no need for me to send these matters to you in writing, since I could speak with you more freely face to face and, in private conversation, suggest whatever I wished or considered necessary.

> But because, as you know, my bodily health intervened and prevented this from happening, I nevertheless took care to do what I could for your affection, out of fraternal devotion, namely, to send by letter what I could not accomplish by coming in person and speaking with you. I ask you by the Lord not to suppose that the words of this letter display the pride of arrogance, but rather to recognize them truly as an act of humble and devout service.

In what follows he urges the bishop to strengthen his sacred office through sacred action and teaching. Above all, he instructs him to restrain himself, in keeping with his episcopal dignity, from idle conversations, slander, and all the other contagions of an undisciplined tongue. Instead, he should occupy both tongue and mind with divine utterances and meditation on Scripture, especially by reading the Epistles of blessed Paul the Apostle to Timothy and Titus, as well as the words of the most holy Pope Gregory, in which he discussed with great care both the life and the vices of rulers, whether in the book of the *Pastoral Rule* or in his homilies on the Gospel.

Furthermore, he should associate with those who serve Christ with faithful devotion.

> I do not say this, he writes, as though I knew that you do otherwise, but because it has become widely reported concerning certain bishops that they serve Christ in such a way that they keep with them no men devoted to any form of religion or continence.

Moreover, since the territories belonging to the governance of his diocese were too extensive for him alone to travel everywhere and to preach the word of God in every village and field, even if he devoted the entire course of the year to it, Bede says that it was entirely necessary for him to enlist many assistants in the sacred work: namely, to ordain and train priests as teachers who would preach the word of God in each settlement, consecrate the heavenly mysteries, and especially perform the rites of holy baptism.

In this preaching to the people, they should strive above all and with every effort to impress upon everyone’s memory the Catholic faith contained in the Apostles’ Creed and the Lord’s Prayer; they should make the uneducated recite these in their own language and diligently sing them.

He further urges him to consecrate more bishops and divide the enormous burden of ecclesiastical government among several men. Finally, he again insists that he provide the people with sufficient teachers of the salutary life, and have them learn, among other things, by which works they may please God most, from which sins they ought to abstain, how often and carefully they should fortify themselves and all that belongs to them with the sign of the Lord’s cross, and how salutary is the daily reception of the Lord’s body and blood for every class of Christians, in accordance with the practice that he knew the Church of Christ diligently observed throughout Italy, Gaul, Africa, Greece, and the entire East.

> This form of religion and God-devoted sanctification, he says, is through the negligence of teachers so far from almost all the laypeople of our province, as though it were something foreign, that those who appear to be more religious among them dare to communicate in the sacred mysteries only at Christmas, Epiphany, and Easter. Yet there are countless innocent persons of the purest conduct—boys and girls, young men and virgins, old men and old women—who, without any scruple of controversy, can communicate in the heavenly mysteries every Sunday, and also on the feasts of the holy apostles and martyrs, just as you yourself have seen done in the holy Roman and apostolic Church. Married people too, if someone shows them the proper measure of continence and instructs them in the virtue of chastity, can and should do the same both lawfully and willingly.

You see whom Bede wishes to be admitted to frequent communion in the holy Eucharist: the innocent and the most chaste, including married people, provided that they observe the prescribed rule of conjugal chastity.

### VII. Bede’s Death, Tomb, and Epitaph; His Declared Holiness; His Relics

### 17.

Bede ended his life on the feast of the Lord’s Ascension, the seventh day before the Kalends of June. For, as the monk Cuthbert testifies in the letter related above, he continued to live until the day of the Lord’s Ascension, that is, the seventh day before the Kalends of June.

Lest anyone say that Bede died on the eve of the feast because the day of the Ascension itself is being excluded, the same letter provides the answer. It says that on Wednesday, after the ninth hour—that is, toward evening—Bede summoned the priests of his monastery, gave them little gifts, and spoke to them.

Certainly, ancient authors were convinced that Bede completed his final day on the very feast of the Ascension. The monk William of Malmesbury says in the passage already cited:

> On the day of the Ascension, when his soul, now weary of the frail use of the body, throbbed with desire to depart, he lay opposite the oratory in which he had been accustomed to pray, with a hair shirt beneath him. With unimpaired understanding and cheerful face, he invited the grace of the Holy Spirit, saying, “O King of glory,” and so forth. When this prayer had ended, he breathed out his spirit.

And Simeon, monk of Durham—or rather Turgot—in Book II, chapter 14, *On the Church of Durham*:

> He died on the seventh day before the Kalends of June at Jarrow and was buried there . . . He passed away on that very solemn day of the Lord’s Ascension.

In what year? Hear the same Turgot:

> In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 735, in the seventh year of Ceolwulf’s reign, and in the eleventh year of Ethelwold’s episcopate, that lamp of the Catholic Church reached the light that had illuminated it, that stream of water springing up into eternal life reached the living God, having died in the fifty-ninth year of his age. From the time when King Oswald and Bishop Aidan established the episcopal see and the habitation of monks on the island of Lindisfarne, it was the 101st year; from the construction of the monastery of the Apostle Peter at Wearmouth, the 72nd; and from the passing of Father Cuthbert, the 69th year.

Turgot correctly gives the year of Bede’s death, but incorrectly gives his age. Bede completed his History in the year 731 of Christ and in the fifty-ninth year of his age; but since he survived until 735, he must be said to have lived sixty-three years.

Thomas Stubbs, a Dominican, assigns the same day and year in his book *On the Acts of the Bishops of York*. And certainly, in the aforementioned year 735, the day of the Lord’s Ascension fell on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, with lunar cycle 11, concurrent 5, epact 23, and the day of the Lord’s Resurrection on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

Accordingly, the author of the *Life of Abbot Alcuin* should be corrected when, following the opinion of some, he asserts that Bede died at the age of ninety in the year 731. There is no doubt that an interpolation has entered Bede’s letter to the priest Wichred concerning the spring equinox according to Anatolius. That letter gives an example from the present year of the Lord’s incarnation 776, a year Bede certainly did not reach, both because he would then have been more than one hundred years old and because Saint Boniface, bishop of Mainz, who suffered martyrdom in 754, praises Bede as already dead in his letters, as we shall see below.

Certainly, if Bede had lived long after 731, he would have extended his History beyond that year. He did not do so, as is clear both from what will be said below in section 29 and from chapter 9 of the *Chronicle of Fontenelle*, written under Louis the Pious:

> The venerable priest Bede brought the ecclesiastical history that he had composed concerning his own people, that is, the English, by a marvelous work up to this year, in which Ragenfred was slain; and not long afterward he departed to the heavenly kingdoms, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June.

In a certain handwritten chronicle of the six ages of the world, likewise written under Louis Augustus, I read these words:

> Charles Martel rules for twenty-seven years. In his twenty-second year Bede, priest of the English, died.

### 18.

“He was buried at Jarrow,” says Turgot, prior of Durham. In Bede’s honor, a portico was consecrated on the northern side of the church of Saint Paul at Jarrow, where it still provides the faithful with a venerable memorial of his name. The place is also shown today where, having a little stone dwelling, he used to sit free from all disturbance, meditate, read, dictate, and write.

The monk William of Malmesbury writes:

> Almost all knowledge of deeds was buried with him until our own times. No English rival of his studies, no follower of his gifts, arose who would pursue the line of the coin that had been neglected. A few whom impartial Jesus loved, though not untrained in letters, spent their entire lives in ungrateful silence; others, barely tasting them with their first lips, cherished an idle leisure. Thus, as one sluggard was always succeeded by a greater sluggard, the fervor of learning languished throughout the whole island for a long time. The verses of his epitaph will provide great testimony to this laziness: they are altogether shameful and unworthy of the mausoleum of so great a man.

> Here the priest Bede rests, buried in the flesh.  
> Grant, Christ, that his soul may rejoice in heaven forever,  
> And grant that he may be drunk from the fountain of wisdom, for which  
> He sighed, rejoicing, with ever-devoted love.

There is also another form of epitaph, not so uncultivated, which we cited above from the Thuane Codex after Cuthbert’s letter.

### 19.

Immediately after his death, Venerable Bede was regarded and called a saint. Saint Boniface repeatedly calls him a lamp of the Church in his letters. Lull, Boniface’s successor, sends a silken garment to the relics of Bede of blessed memory, and calls him blessed Father, as we shall see later.

Benedict, abbot of Aniane and Bede’s near-equal, quotes several verses from the sayings of blessed Bede in chapter 36, section 6, of the *Concordia of Rules*. Alcuin too praises blessed Bede the priest in the preface to his commentary on the Gospel of John and more than once in his books against Felix.

Hildwin, in the letter prefixed to his *Areopagitica* and addressed to Louis Augustus, likewise calls Bede holy and venerable. Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, one century after Bede, twice gives him the epithet “saint,” namely, in the letter in the name of the Council of Tusiacum to Rodulf of Bourges and Froterius of Bordeaux, and in chapter 9 of his book *On Predestination*.

Notker Balbulus praises Saint Bede the priest in his Martyrology on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April. Indeed, an altar was erected to Saint Bede in the monastery of Fulda at the beginning of the ninth century, as Hrabanus Maurus testifies in inscription 39 to the altar of Saint Benedict in the western crypt. Its verse reads:

> Cuthbert, Bede, and Aequitius remain here.

In litanies composed metrically by Hartmann, a monk of Saint Gall, in the same century and published by Canisius in volume V, Saint Bede is listed after Saint Pachomius:

> Pachomius, Bede, Attala, Paphnutius.

Certainly Elfred, a priest of Durham, as Turgot reports in Book III, chapter 7, of the *History of Durham*, knew that Bede the teacher had lived, died, and been buried at the monastery at Jarrow. Every year, when the anniversary of Bede’s death arrived, Elfred used to come there and devote himself to prayers and vigils. That priest was alive under Eadmund, bishop of Durham, who was elected in 1020.

### 20.

This is the same Elfred who secretly stole the relics of Saint Bede and transferred them to Durham. Consequently, when he was repeatedly asked informally by his intimates where the bones of Venerable Bede rested, he was accustomed to reply with certainty concerning the matter:

> No one knows this better than I do. Be firmly convinced, dearest ones, and beyond all doubt certain, that the same chest which preserves the most sacred body of Father Cuthbert also contains the bones of the venerable teacher and monk Bede.

In 1054, when Saint Cuthbert’s incorrupt body was removed from its coffin, it also contained a linen sack holding the bones of Venerable Bede, which had shared lodging with Cuthbert’s body, as we shall see elsewhere in the history of the translation of Saint Cuthbert.

“These bones of Bede,” says Turgot, “separated from the other relics, were found placed in a little wooden chest.” Hugh, bishop of Durham, elected in 1154, constructed a very costly bier, splendidly made of the purest gold and finest silver and adorned with precious stones in marvelous workmanship. In it he placed the bones of the venerable man Bede the priest and monk of Jarrow, together with the relics of many other saints, as is read in the appendix to Turgot.

John Speed, in *The Theatre of Great Britain*, writing about the bishopric of Durham, says that Bede’s marble monument still exists in the western part of Durham Cathedral. Yet in volume I of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, the bones of Venerable Bede, Biscop, Saint Hesterwin, Sigfrid, and Herbert, abbots of Jarrow, are said to be preserved in the church at Glastonbury.

### VIII. Bede’s Various Eulogies, and Why and When He Was Called Venerable

### 21.

Almost no ancient writer mentions Bede without praise. Saint Boniface, bishop of Mainz, commends him in several letters. In Letter 8 to Egbert, archbishop of York, he writes:

> Moreover, may you deign to have some treatises from the little works of Bede the reader copied out and sent to me, whom, as we have recently heard, divine grace has endowed with spiritual understanding and permitted to shine in your province, so that we too may enjoy the lamp that the Lord has granted you.

The same is found in Letter 9 to Huetbert, abbot of the monasteries of Wearmouth and Jarrow. In Letter 85 to the same Egbert he writes:

> Now, desiring this eagerly, we earnestly ask you to take care to send us, for the joy of our sorrow, as you have done before, some portion or spark of the lamp of the Church that the Holy Spirit has caused to shine in your regions—that is, of the treatises that the spiritual priest and investigator of the holy Scriptures, Bede, composed by opening them up. Above all, if it can be done, send something that seems to us suitable, practical, and most useful for our preaching, on the annual Lectionary and the Proverbs of Solomon, since we have heard that he published commentaries on them.

Boniface’s Letter 150 to Cuthbert, abbot and successor of Huetbert, has the same purpose. It is worth observing here that Boniface asks others, not Bede himself, for Bede’s scholarly works, and says that Bede had recently shone in the province of the Northumbrians. Thus there can be no doubt that the aforementioned letters of Boniface were written after Bede’s death.

### 22.

Lull, Boniface’s successor, was moved by no lesser devotion of veneration toward Bede. This is attested by Letter 109 of Lull’s Bonifacian correspondence to Coena, an English bishop:

> I ask you to obtain any of these books and deign to send them to us, books that the priest Bede of blessed memory expounded, for the consolation of our pilgrimage: namely, the four books on the first part of Samuel up to the death of Saul, or the three books on Ezra and Nehemiah, or the four books on the Gospel of Mark.

Gutbert, or Cuthbert, abbot of Wearmouth after Huetbert—the Cuthbert to whom the letter written concerning Bede’s death appears to belong—sent two letters to the same Lull, numbered 89 and 95 among the Bonifacian letters.

In the first, Cuthbert replies to Lull in these words:

> I gratefully received the little gifts of your affection, and all the more gratefully because I learned that you sent them with the deepest devotion: namely, that you intended to send a silken garment to the relics of Bede, our teacher, of blessed memory, in remembrance and veneration of him.

> It seems right to me that the entire English people, in all the provinces wherever they are found, should give thanks to God because he granted them in their nation so remarkable a man, endowed with diverse gifts and so diligent in exercising them, and likewise living in good morals. For I learned by experience, having been trained at his feet, the things that I relate.

And below:

> Now, because you asked for something from the works of the blessed Father, I have prepared for your affection, together with my pupils and according to my ability, what I could: little books composed in verse and prose about the man of God, Cuthbert.

And in Letter 95:

> I have taken care to send, for the consolation of your pilgrimage, the book that Bede, the most illustrious teacher of God’s Church, composed on the building of the temple.

### 23.

Bede is celebrated by many other eulogies from authors both his contemporaries and those of later generations. Alcuin calls him “the most noble teacher, Bede the priest” in Letter 5. The author of the book *On Ecclesiastical Offices* attributed to Alcuin calls him “an outstanding priest and teacher” in the chapter on the Purification. Ratramnus calls him “a priest of the English, a member of Christ who is not reprobate” in chapter 8 of *On the Nativity of Christ*. Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, calls him “a priest of the Church of York and a teacher of the English” in his letter to Pope Alexander II.

Most illustrious of all is the eulogy that the Fathers of the Second Council of Aachen, held in 836, bestowed on Bede, whom they number among the holy Fathers. Thus they speak in the preface to Book III:

> At the end of the preceding little book we remember promising that, at the beginning of this one, insofar as God granted us ability, we would briefly demonstrate from the utterances of the holy Fathers that the temple of the Lord which Solomon built and dedicated to the Lord was a figure of the Catholic Church spread throughout the world, and that King Solomon, its founder, represented Christ. With the Lord’s favor, we are striving to fulfill this promise. Without prejudice to the exposition of the other distinguished holy Fathers on this matter, whose statements are to be set forth below, let us see what Bede, a venerable and admirable teacher in our own times, thought about the frequently mentioned temple in his exposition of the Gospel of John.

Here Bede is called Venerable, an admirable teacher, enrolled among the Fathers and in a certain sense set before them. Paschasius Radbertus, abbot of Corbie, likewise includes Bede’s authority among that of the holy Fathers in his book *On the Eucharist*. Walafrid Strabo, in chapter 25 of his book *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, calls Bede “the Father of the English.”

Finally, Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, as Frodoard reports in Book III, chapter 23, of the *History of Rheims*, asked Bishop John of Cambrai to have Bede’s exposition of the Proverbs of Solomon brought to the synod.

### 24.

I am prompted at this point to note when and for what reason Bede was called “Venerable Bede the priest.” I omit the many fables on this subject. If we believe Trithemius, he was called Venerable while still alive, because, when his homilies were being regularly read in ecclesiastical services during his lifetime, they called him Venerable, since they could not yet call him a saint while he still lived in the flesh. This led to the name Venerable being generally adopted and retaining its authority among everyone down to the present.

Certainly, in the handwritten lectionaries of the monastery of Corbie, copied nearly five hundred years ago, several of Bede’s homilies are assigned the familiar title: “Homily of Venerable Bede the priest.”

Yet our own Menard, in his notes on chapter 36, section 6, of the *Concordia of Rules*, believes that the title “Venerable” is more recent and was not used by Alcuin, the monk of Saint Gall, Odorannus, William of Malmesbury, Florence of Worcester, Henry of Huntingdon, or Roger of Hoveden.

That this surname arose after Bede’s time is sufficiently proved by the silence of authors near his own period. None of those whom I have read so far calls Bede Venerable. In the most ancient Thuane Codex, copied by hand eight hundred years ago and containing all Bede’s homilies, the title everywhere reads: “Homily of Lord Bede.”

Moreover, before Paul Warnefrid, the monk of Monte Cassino, compiled the ecclesiastical Lectionary at the command of Charlemagne, the names of authors whose homilies were recited in divine services were not customarily pronounced beforehand, as Charlemagne states in his letter to Paul. Therefore, even if Bede’s homilies were read in the Church while he was alive, the name “Venerable Bede” was not yet prefixed to them.

From the ninth century onward, however, the name Venerable began to be attributed to Bede. Amalarius, in his books *On the Divine Offices*, frequently calls him “Lord Bede,” but in Book I, chapter 37, he calls him “Venerable Bede the priest.” The same usage appears in Jonah, bishop of Orléans, in Book I, chapters 16 and 17, and Book III, chapters 6 and 7, of *On the Institution of the Laity*, as well as in Usuard’s authentic Martyrology on the Nones of August.

Some add Paschasius Radbertus; but in the cited passage from his book *On the Eucharist*, manuscript codices give a different title, namely: “Bede the priest in his sermon,” omitting the name Venerable.

We may also add the author of the *Chronicle of Fontenelle*, chapters 9 and 16 (15 in the printed editions); Hildwin; Radbod, bishop of Utrecht, in his sermon on Saint Swibert; and Heric, a monk who, in his as yet unpublished book *On the Exposition of Computus*, if I am not mistaken, especially praises books on this subject by “the Venerable man, Lord Bede the priest.” This author was writing his work in the year 980.

There is no doubt that other authors of the same age frequently used the same title, although not all of them did so, just as not everyone in our own age does, even though this honorific designation has long since become customary.

I omit other writers of later times and mention only Alger, a Cluniac monk, who refers to “Venerable Bede the priest” in Book I, chapter 8, of *On the Sacraments*, and Matthew of Westminster, a monk in whose time—he was writing in the middle of the thirteenth century—Bede had long since deserved to be regarded by the universal Church as “the teacher of the English” and “Venerable Father.”

But why, you ask, “priest” rather than “monk,” if he was a monk? Obviously, in former times, as was fitting, the dignity of the priestly rank was held in such esteem that those distinguished by this rank were called priests, with their other titles omitted. Thus Jerome, who also often admits that he was a monk, is commonly called “the priest.”

Indeed, abbots too were called priests—for not all priests were once abbots—because of the dignity of their rank; they were rarely called abbots. This is why Saints Carilefus, Richarius, Gallus, and Walaricus, although endowed with abbatial dignity, are nevertheless regularly called priests in ancient Martyrologies.

### 25.

It will not be irrelevant to observe here that Audoen, in the *Life of Saint Eligius*, attributed the name “Venerable” within a stricter monastic discipline, and specifically to distinguished monks.

Thus Buchinus, converted from paganism, “afterward,” he says, “became Venerable—that is, a monk—and presided over the monastery of Ferrières,” Book I, chapter 10. Thillo, Eligius’s servant in his youth, is said afterward to have led a venerable—that is, monastic—life; and Eligius is said to have honored as lords those who undertook the venerable life of monks.

Ado, bishop of Vienne, speaking in his history of Wilicarius, bishop of that same see, says:

> Having abandoned the episcopate and entered the monastery of the holy martyrs of Agaunum, he led a venerable life.

And in the *Life of Saint Desiderius*, bishop of Cahors, the Scot Arvanus is said to have led a venerable life in the monastery.

Finally, to omit other examples of this kind, Saint Benedict is praised by Gregory the Great as “a man of venerable life.”

### IX. Observations on Bede’s Little Gifts

### 26.

We have deliberately reserved for this separate section some observations both on the little gifts that Bede distributed to the priests of his monastery when he was near death and on certain of his works.

### 27.

As the holy man approached the final period of his life, he said to one of his disciples, Cuthbert, at the ninth hour:

> I have some precious things in my little chest, namely pepper, napkins, and incense. But hurry quickly and bring the priests of our monastery to me, so that I too may distribute to them little gifts such as God has granted.

At that time, if ever, it was customary for friends to give and receive such little gifts as tokens of mutual affection. They did not consider the value of the objects, but the intention.

The letters of Saint Boniface, archbishop, and of others of the same period contain many examples of this kind. Thus, in Letter 5 of the Bonifacian correspondence, Lull sends the abbess Kanebada, a girl of royal blood, three little gifts: frankincense, pepper, and cinnamon.

A certain anonymous writer sends Abbess Eadburh a silver stylus and a portion of storax and cinnamon in Letter 7. Boniface sends Egbert, archbishop of Canterbury, in addition to copies of Saint Gregory’s letters, a corporal, a pallium, and a rough cloth for wiping the feet of God’s servants, as a token of affection, in Letter 8.

He sends Huetbert, abbot of Wearmouth, goat-hair bedding in Letter 9. To the priest Herefrid he sends a portion of incense and a cloth as a blessing and sign of pure affection in Letter 10. To King Ethelwald he sends one hawk, two falcons, two shields, and two spears in Letter 19.

To the aforementioned Egbert he sends two small cups of wine in Letter 85. Cynehard, bishop of Winchester, among other things, sends a scarf, a hood, and a short cloak. Read Letter 148.

We read in the letters of Boniface IV and other Roman pontiffs that they often gave combs, mirrors, and other things of this kind. Fortunatus, too, frequently gives thanks in Book XI of his epigrams for gifts that had been sent. What sort of gifts do you think these were? Things with a pleasant smell, naturally—chestnuts, milk, plums, eggs, and so forth. As he himself says in Epigram 23:

> In a small gift great love is seen.

We also know that Saint Benedict did not forbid gifts in chapter 54 of his Rule, provided that they were neither given nor received without the knowledge of the abbot.

The gift of the miserly monk who brought Saint Hilarion a bundle of green chickpeas is well known, as Jerome testifies.

Therefore Venerable Bede, as a sign of mutual affection and fraternal concord, gave little gifts to his brother priests when he was near death, so that they might remember him in the sacred services, just as Antony left one sheepskin garment to Athanasius and another to Serapion, and a cilicium garment to the brothers in his will.

But why, you ask, incense? We learn from the letter of Gemmulus, a deacon of the Roman Church, to Boniface, numbered 149:

> We have sent through the priest mentioned above a quantity of coczumbri, which you are to offer as incense to the Lord at the morning and evening hours, or while you celebrate the solemnities of Mass, and so forth.

What, finally, were the napkins? As we conjecture, they were thin linen cloths with which the mouth is usually wiped, which Boniface calls *sabana* in Letter 10. That *orarium*, a word otherwise of varied meaning, is often used in this sense is demonstrated by Vossius in Book III, chapter 31, of *On the Faults of Speech*.

### X. Judgment on Bede’s Writings

### 28.

Having said these things by way of digression, we must now come to certain observations that occurred to me while examining Bede’s writings, both those published in print and those written by hand. First, we must discuss the dates of the writings; afterward, the doubtful and spurious works; and finally, the works he left behind.

29. Bede began the third book on Samuel after Abbot Ceolfrith had died, that is, in the year 716, as is clear from the preface to Book III. The Brief Explanation of the First Epistle of John appears to derive from his own studies of Sacred Scripture. Next came the Exposition of the Apocalypse, which he dedicated to his brother Eusebius, or Huetbert, his future abbot—for that Huetbert had two names, and was called Eusebius on account of his love and devotion to study, is clear from the preface to Book III on Samuel. Bede further divided the Book of Revelation into chapters.

After the Apocalypse he commented on the Book of the Acts of the Apostles, at the urging of Acca, bishop of Hagustald; then also on Luke’s Gospel. He explained thirty Questions on the Books of Kings at the request of Nothelm, then a priest of London and later archbishop of Canterbury, whose assistance he used in writing the Ecclesiastical History. Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, requested Bede’s Questions on both Testaments from England, in Letter 62 to Altigis, abbot of York.

Afterward he published the entire Commentary on Samuel. As we have already said, he began its third book in the year 716; but he published the Exposition of Mark many years after he had explained Luke’s Gospel. All this is understood from Bede’s own prefaces to those books.

Furthermore, he composed with great care an Exposition of the Epistles of Paul, and likewise of the Catholic Epistles, from the writings of Saint Augustine; and he completed the book on the six ages of the world in the ninth year of Leo the Isaurian, that is, in the year 724 of Christ. Having completed these works, he published the Ecclesiastical History of his people, which he finished, together with its Epitome, in the year 731. For in the excellent manuscript preserved by us, the aforesaid Epitome does not extend beyond that year, as we noted above.

In the same Epitome Bede provides a catalogue of his writings. Among them is counted the Letter on the Spring Equinox according to Anatolius, and therefore written before the year 731. Accordingly, the example in that letter addressed to the priest Wichred, which refers to the present year 776, is an interpolation by the copyist who was transcribing the letter in that very year and wished to explain Bede’s statement by means of a substituted example.

Finally, he wrote the book of Revisions on the Acts of the Apostles after the year 731, when he was already an old man.

30. Apart from the works of Bede listed in his catalogue, there are few that we can safely attribute to him, with the exception of the letter to Egbert, bishop of York, written thirty years after the death of Aldfrith, king of the Northumbrians—that is, in the year 735, which was Bede’s final year.

If Bede is indeed the author, the Commentaries on John’s Gospel were published by him after the year 731. They appear to be a kind of abridgment of Augustine’s Exposition, with sayings of other Fathers inserted here and there; thus, in chapter 5, when discussing Regulus, the work introduces the words of Gregory the Great.

Certainly Jonas, bishop of Orléans and a contemporary of Louis the Pious, cites several verses from Bede in Book I, chapter 13, of his *On the Instruction of the Laity*. These verses occur in Bede’s twentieth homily on the Gospel and are found in chapter 2 of the aforementioned Commentaries. We therefore suspect that Jonas should be read as referring to the second homily on the Gospel.

Alcuin, moreover, confesses in the preface to his Commentary on John’s Gospel that he took much from the homilies of the blessed priest Bede. In addition, while suffering from his final illness, Bede rendered John’s Gospel into the vernacular, as his disciple Cuthbert testifies in the letter he wrote concerning Bede’s death.

The Expositions on Matthew’s Gospel, the Commentary on the Psalms, the Lives of the Saints—except for the Acts of Saints Felix, Cuthbert, and Anastasius, which Bede acknowledges as his own—the little book *On Offices*, the Commentary on Boethius’ book *On the Trinity*, the *Meditations*, the *Passions*, the *Books on the Elements of Philosophy*, and the book *On Remedies for Sins* must be relegated to the category of doubtful works. Spelmann has already placed the last of these among the spurious works in volume I of the *Anglo-Saxon Councils*, although Regino, in his collection of canons, cites a *Penitential Book of Theodore or Bede* in Book I, chapter 297. Ivo and Gratian likewise quote from Bede’s *Penitential* a chapter concerning a priest who vomits the Eucharist.

I will not, however, omit what I read in the very ancient Thuane Homiliary of Bede, entered by a more recent hand about four hundred years ago:

> “I do not ask for Bede’s book of Expositions on the Gospels; rather, I ask for Bede’s book of Expositions on the Psalms of the Psalter.”

Away with the Letter on Divination concerning Death! How far its ravings are from the mind of a pious man is proved by the letter to the priest Herefrid prefixed to the little book *On Thunder*, which Bede translated into Latin. This is Herefrid, a priest from the kingdom of Mercia, to whom Saint Boniface the martyr’s Letter 10 is extant.

The author of the book *On Divine Offices* was writing after Easter had fallen on 7 April, as is evident from the chapter on that year’s Easter. This did not occur between the year 731, when Bede compiled his catalogue of works, and the year 771.

31. Bede certainly wrote two books of Gospel Homilies, as he himself acknowledges; or, as Saint Boniface’s Letter 9 puts it, an annual lectionary. But it is important to distinguish which of the published homilies belong to Bede and which are spurious. In this way we shall determine the more celebrated days then observed with annual solemnity.

The Thuane Library contains two very ancient manuscripts in which Bede’s homilies are found. In the first, numbered 144 and written eight hundred years ago, thirty-nine homilies are presented in continuous sequence. In the other, numbered 38 and six hundred years old, they are divided into two books, with tables of contents prefixed to each. It is useful here to compare and reproduce both copies. The later manuscript proceeds as follows.

### The Table of Contents of Book I of Bede the Priest’s Homilies, Twenty-Five in Number

1. Homily on the reading of the Holy Gospel according to Luke, “The angel Gabriel was sent.” In the first manuscript: “Homily of the lord Bede.” In both manuscripts it begins, after the Gospel text: “Today’s reading from the holy Gospel commends the beginning of our redemption,” etc., as in the published editions for the feast of the Annunciation of Blessed Mary.

2. Homily on the reading of the Holy Gospel according to Luke, “Mary arose.” In both manuscripts it begins: “The reading from the holy Gospel that you have heard.”

3. Homily on the reading of the Holy Gospel according to Mark, “John was in the desert.” In the earlier manuscript: “Homily of the lord Bede, *On the Advent of the Lord*.” In both it begins: “John, anticipating the coming of the Lord’s preaching,” etc.

4. Homily on the reading of the Holy Gospel according to John, “John bears witness.” It begins: “The forerunner of our Redeemer, bearing witness concerning him,” etc. It is absent from the earlier manuscript.

5. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “When she had been betrothed.” In the earlier manuscript: “Homily of the lord Bede, *On the Vigil of the Lord*.” In both it begins: “The nativity of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who was eternal before the ages,” etc.

6. Homily on the Holy Gospel according to Luke, “The shepherds were speaking.” It begins: “When the Lord had been born in Bethlehem,” etc., as in the published editions. It is absent from the first manuscript, but is cited by Jonas, bishop of Orléans, in Book II, chapter 16, of *On the Instruction of the Laity*.

7. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “In the beginning was the Word.” In the earlier manuscript: “Homily of the blessed lord Bede, *On the Nativity of the Lord*.” In both it begins: “Because [of] the temporal [life] of the Mediator between God and human beings,” etc., as in the published editions.

8. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “Jesus said to Peter, ‘Follow me,’” to be read on the Nativity of Saint John the Evangelist. In both it begins: “The reading from the Holy Gospel that has just been read to us,” etc.

9. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “An angel of the Lord appeared,” *On the Nativity of the Innocents*. In both it begins: “Concerning the precious death of the martyrs of Christ, the Innocents,” etc., as in the published editions.

10. Homily on the Gospel according to Luke, “When the eight days had been completed,” *On the Octave of the Lord*. In both it begins: “The sacred and venerable commemoration of the present feast,” etc., as in the published editions.

Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “An angel of the Lord appeared,” to be read *On the Vigil of the Epiphany*. There is no homily in either copy.

11. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan.” In the earlier manuscript: “Homily of the blessed Bede, on the holy day of the Theophany.” In both it begins: “The reading from the Holy Gospel that we have just heard, brothers,” etc., as in the published editions for the octave day.
