12. Homily on the Gospel according to Luke, “Jesus’ parents went every year.” In the first manuscript: “Homily of Bede, *First Sunday after the Theophany*.” In both it begins: “The reading from the holy Gospel, beloved brothers, has been opened to us,” etc., as in the published editions.

13. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “There was a wedding.” In the first manuscript: “Homily of the blessed Bede, *Second Sunday after the Theophany*.” It begins in both: “That our Lord and Savior was invited to the wedding,” etc.

14. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “John saw Jesus coming toward him.” “Homily of the blessed Bede, *Third Sunday after the Theophany*.” It begins: “John the Baptist and forerunner of the Lord.” This is so in both manuscripts, except that it does not occur in the table of contents of the later one.

15. Homily on the Gospel according to Luke, “When the days had been fulfilled,” to be read *On the Purification of Saint Mary*. In both manuscripts it begins: “The solemnity of today’s celebration,” etc., as in the published editions.

16. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “It was a feast day of the Jews.” It begins: “Today’s reading from the Holy Gospel gives us two miracles of human healing together.” It is absent from the first manuscript.

17. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “Jesus wanted to go into Galilee,” by the blessed Bede, *after the Theophany*. It begins: “From the reading of the Gospel, beloved brothers, we have heard the gracious favor of our Redeemer,” etc. It is absent from the later manuscript.

18. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “The Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father.” In the first manuscript: “Homily of the blessed Bede, *Second Sunday in Lent*.” In both it begins: “Because the Lord and our Redeemer leads his chosen ones, through the labor of this life, to that life which knows no labor,” etc.

19. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “Jesus departed and withdrew into the region of Tyre.” It begins: “In the reading from the Holy Gospel that has just been read to us,” etc. It is absent from the first manuscript and appears in the published editions for the Second Sunday of Lent.

20. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “Jesus went to the Mount of Olives.” In the first copy: “Homily of the blessed Bede, *Third Sunday of Lent, Saturday*.” In both it begins: “The reading from the Holy Gospel before us should be considered with all the greater attentiveness,” etc.

21. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “Jesus went across the Sea of Galilee.” In the first manuscript: “Homily of the blessed Bede, in Lent.” In both it begins: “Those who read correctly the signs and miracles of our Lord and Savior,” etc., as in the published editions for the Fourth Sunday of Lent.

22. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “Jesus went down to Capernaum.” In the first manuscript: “Homily of the blessed Bede, *Monday in Lent*.” In both it begins: “Some are accustomed to be troubled by the fact that at the beginning of this reading,” etc.

23. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “When Jesus had drawn near to Jerusalem.” In the first manuscript: “Homily of the blessed Bede, *On Palm Sunday*.” In both it begins: “The mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who was also about to suffer for the salvation of the human race,” etc., as in the published editions.

24. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “The Passover of the Jews was near.” It begins: “It is customary among the prudent,” etc. It is absent from the first copy. It appears in the published editions.

25. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “Before the feast of Passover.” In the first manuscript: “Homily of the blessed Bede, *On the Lord’s Supper*.” In both it begins: “As the evangelist John was about to write down that memorable mystery of the Lord,” etc., as in the published editions.

In the later manuscript, after the first book of homilies, one reads:

> “The first book of the Homilies, twenty-five in number, is complete.”

Yet in that manuscript only twenty-three homilies are actually present. We supplied the others from the earlier copy. The later manuscript continues.

### The Table of the Readings of the Holy Gospel, Twenty-Four in Book II of the Same Author

1. Homily on the Holy Gospel according to Matthew, “On the evening of the Sabbath.” In the first manuscript: “Homily of the lord Bede, *On the Vigil of Easter*.” In both it begins: “The vigils of this most sacred night,” etc., as in the published editions.

This homily was read at the Vigil—that is, at the morning office—of Easter. Yet in the first manuscript a homily of Saint Gregory, customarily read on the holy day of Easter, is inserted here. Observe the same thing concerning the Vigil of Pentecost below.

2. Homily on the Gospel according to Luke, “Jesus stood in the midst of his disciples.” In the first manuscript: “Homily of the lord Bede, *Tuesday in Easter Week*.” In both it begins: “The Lord and our Redeemer [the glory of] his Resurrection,” etc., as in the published editions.

3. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “The eleven disciples.” In the first manuscript: “Homily of the blessed Bede, *Friday in Easter Week*.” In both it begins: “The Gospel reading, beloved brothers, which we have just heard,” etc., as in the published editions.

4. Homily on the Gospel according to Luke, “On the first day of the week, very early.” It begins: “The reading concerning the Resurrection of our Lord and Redeemer has been recited and opened to us, brothers,” etc. It is absent from the first manuscript and from the published editions.

5. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “A little while, and you will no longer see me.” In the first copy: “Homily of the blessed Bede, *Second Sunday after the Octave of Easter*.” In both it begins: “The joyful promises of our Lord and Savior,” etc., as in the published editions.

6. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “I am going to him who sent me.” In the first manuscript: “Homily of the blessed Bede, *Third Sunday after Holy Easter*.” In both it begins: “As we have heard from the Gospel reading, beloved brothers,” etc., as in the published editions.

7. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “Whatever you ask the Father.” It begins: “It may trouble weak hearers,” etc. It is absent from the first manuscript. It appears in the published editions.

8. Homily on the Gospel according to Luke, “Ask, and it will be given to you.” In the first manuscript: “Homily of the blessed Bede, *On the Greater Litany*.” In both it begins: “Our Lord and Savior leads us to the joys of the heavenly kingdom,” etc. It does not appear in the published editions.

9. Homily on the Gospel according to Luke, “These are the words that I spoke,” to be read *On the Ascension of the Lord*. It begins: “As the Lord was about to ascend into heaven,” etc. It is found in both manuscripts. Another appears in the published editions.

10. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “When the Paraclete comes,” to be read *On the Sunday after the Ascension of the Lord*. It begins: “From many passages of the Holy Gospel we have discovered,” etc. It is found in both manuscripts and in the published editions. Amalarius cites this homily in Book I, chapter 37, and again in Book II, chapter 1, of *On the Offices*.

11. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “If you love me,” *On the Vigil of Pentecost*. It begins: “Because today, beloved brothers, we celebrate the coming of the Holy Spirit,” etc. It is found in both manuscripts and in the published editions.

12. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “There was a man of the Pharisees.” In the first manuscript: “Homily of the blessed Bede, *On the Octave of Pentecost*.” In both it begins: “As you have heard from the reading of the Holy Gospel, beloved brothers,” etc. It appears in the published editions for the feast of the Invention of the Holy Cross, and is cited in the letter that Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, wrote in the name of the Council of Tusey to Rudolph, bishop of Bourges, and Frotarius, bishop of Bordeaux.

13. Homily on the Gospel according to Luke, “There was in the days of Herod,” to be read *On the Vigil of Saint John*. It begins: “Our Lord and Redeemer, who was to come in the flesh,” etc. It is found in both manuscripts and in the published editions.

14. Homily on the Gospel according to Luke, “Elizabeth’s time was fulfilled,” to be read *On the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist*. It begins: “The nativity of the Lord’s forerunner,” etc. It is found in both manuscripts and in the published editions.

15. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “Jesus said to Simon Peter,” to be read *On the Vigil of the Apostles Peter and Paul*. It begins: “The power of perfect love,” etc. It is found in both manuscripts and in the published editions.

16. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “Jesus came into the region of Caesarea,” to be read *On the Feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul*. It begins: “The reading from the Holy Gospel that you have just heard, brothers, is to be considered with all the greater attentiveness,” etc. It is found in both manuscripts and in the published editions.

17. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “Simon Peter said to Jesus: ‘Behold, we have left everything,’” to be read *On the Nativity of Saint Benedict Biscop*. It begins: “When Peter heard from the Lord,” etc., as in the later copy and in the published editions. It is absent from the first manuscript.

18. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “The mother of the sons of Zebedee approached Jesus,” *On the Nativity of Saint James the Apostle*. The first manuscript adds: “James, the brother of the Lord.” In both it begins: “The Lord, creator and redeemer, heals the wounds of our pride,” etc., as in the published editions.

19. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “Jesus departed from the borders of Tyre.” It begins: “That deaf and mute man whom the Lord wondrously healed,” etc., as in the published editions. It is absent from the first manuscript.

20. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “Herod the tetrarch heard,” to be read *On the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist*. It begins: “As we celebrate, beloved brothers, the day of the nativity of blessed John,” etc., as in the published editions. It is absent from the first manuscript.

21. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “The dedication took place,” to be read *On the Dedication of a Church*. In both it begins: “We have heard from the Gospel reading, beloved brothers, that the dedication took place,” etc., as in the published editions. In the later manuscript this homily follows the next one; in the earlier manuscript it precedes it.

22. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “Jesus saw a man sitting at the tax booth,” to be read *On the Nativity of Saint Matthew the Apostle*. In both it begins: “We read the Apostle saying that all have sinned,” etc., as in the published editions.

23. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “John was standing, and two of his disciples,” to be read *On the Nativity of Saint Andrew the Apostle*. In both it begins: “Great and such is the sublimity of divine Scripture,” etc., as in the published editions for the vigil of the feast.

24. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “Jesus wanted to go into Galilee.” It begins: “We have heard from the Gospel reading, beloved brothers, the gracious favor of our Redeemer,” etc. It is absent from the first manuscript because that manuscript is mutilated.

Thus the later manuscript ends:

> “The second book of the Homilies of Bede the priest, twenty-four in number, is complete.”

32. From these facts we understand that the homilies for the Sundays after Trinity, as well as those for the feasts of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, Saint Scholastica, Saint Mary Magdalene, the Transfiguration of the Lord, the Assumption of Blessed Mary, Saint Bartholomew, the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin, Saint Michael, Saint Luke, the Presentation of Blessed Mary, and others for the Common of Martyrs, etc., are either spurious, doubtful, or at least extracted from Bede’s authentic commentaries on Mark and Luke.

Certainly, the homily on Saint Scholastica is attributed to Saint Bertarius, abbot of Cassino, in a Cassinese manuscript. The sermon customarily read on the feast of All Saints is attributed in certain copies to Hrabanus Maurus—whether correctly, I do not know. The fact that the Feast of All Saints was instituted by Pope Gregory III is significant, as is proved by the oldest copies of Usuard and by our own Menard in his edition of Saint Gregory’s *Sacramentary*, p. 184. Yet that sermon bears the style of Bede.

Finally, the sermon attributed to Bede on the verse of the Psalm, “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men,” etc., is certainly not Bede’s, since it cites testimony taken from the *Life of Gregory the Great* written by John the Deacon, who lived a hundred and fifty years after the death of Bede the Venerable.

33. Some believe that Bede’s Expositions on Paul’s Epistles, excerpted from the books of Saint Augustine, should be attributed to a certain Florus, a monk whom Trithemius considers to have been from Saint-Trond. Thus the excellent Corbie copy, divided into two volumes, gives the following title:

> “Expositions of the Epistles of Saint Paul the Apostle, collected from the books of Saint Augustine, the distinguished doctor, by a certain Florus.”

At the end it says:

> “This book was composed—that is, written—by Richer, subprior, and John, his one-eyed scribe, in the year in which the church of Saint John at Corbie was restored and Tours was the second seat of the Roman city, while Pope Alexander III was holding a synod at Tours, in the year 1164, under Louis, king of the Franks; Theodoric, bishop of Amiens; and John, abbot of Corbie.”

Yet the expositions contained in those two volumes are precisely the same as those found in Bede’s Works. They are a genuine production of Bede, both because he himself mentions these expositions in his catalogue of works and because another commentary exists under the name of Florus, composed not only from Augustine’s works but also from those of other Fathers. A manuscript of this kind is preserved by the learned Pierre-François Chifflet, a member of the Society of Jesus. In the same way Claudius Scottus, later bishop of Turin, extracted another commentary on Paul’s Epistles from passages of Augustine and other Fathers.

Nevertheless, the monk Ratbert, in Book 10 of *On the Affairs of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, mentions the *Collections of Florus the Priest from the Volumes of Saint Augustine on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans*; shortly afterward he mentions the *Collections of Florus on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians and on the Epistle to the Hebrews*. Finally, Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, praises Bede’s *Collection on the Apostle* from Augustine’s works in Letter 76.

34. In the published works of Bede, several of his genuine writings are missing, unless I am mistaken. One is the *Explanation of the Song of Habakkuk*, which in our copy, no. 275, begins as follows:

> “The song of the prophet Habakkuk, which you asked to have explained to you, most beloved sister in Christ, chiefly proclaims the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion. Hence, according to the custom of the holy and universal Church, it is solemnly repeated each week at the morning praises on the sixth day of the week, on which that same Passion was completed,” etc.

Also missing is the poem *On the Divine Judgment*, addressed to Bishop Acca, published by Simeon of Durham, a monk, in his *Book of the Deeds of the Kings of England*. It is also attributed to Bede in the Thuane manuscript.

There is likewise the Letter on the Sixth Age of the World to Plegwin, which, together with the *History of the Abbots of the Monasteries of Wearmouth and Jarrow* and the letter to Egbert, bishop of York, was recently published by Waraeus.

Bede’s genuine Martyrology has recently appeared in volume III of the March volume of the Bollandists. It is doubtful, however, whether the Feast of All Saints should have a place in it, since Bede lived only four years after the election of Pope Gregory III, who instituted this solemnity.

Herric, a ninth-century author, cites the words of that Martyrology concerning Saint Lupus, bishop of Troyes, in Book I, chapter 15, of *On the Miracles of Saint Germanus, Bishop of Auxerre*. Amalarius also reports certain passages in Book II, chapter 24, of *On the Divine Offices*. Yet he is mistaken in Book IV, chapters 39 and 41, when citing Bede’s *Life of Saint Cuthbert*. The words he recalls occur in neither of Bede’s works on Saint Cuthbert; they are found instead in the work composed by an anonymous monk of Lindisfarne in three books published in the Bollandist volume for March.

In our very ancient and excellent copy, no. 546, which contains Bede’s work on computation, the following verses of the lord Bede, said to be intended for constructing a sundial, are read with this beginning:

> “What courses of the sun join the months to their appointed seasons—  
> I shall teach you, reader; attend briefly to my song.”

Yet these verses should be attributed not to Bede but to Wandalbert, deacon of Prüm.

The same manuscript also contains several writings on Computation, among them the *Excerpt or Explanation of Computation by Herric the Monk*, composed to elucidate Bede’s commentary. Its Prologue runs as follows:

> “When I had begun to explain in the common language to certain young brothers some rudiments of the calculating art, I wished also to impart something of this not contemptible discipline, as many suppose, to those whom, with the help of divine generosity, I had introduced to some extent into the grammatical art. Inflamed by some unknown desire, they began to insist most earnestly that what I had set forth orally should somehow be published in writing for the benefit of many. I resisted them more stubbornly, since I showed that books on this same subject remained . . . . . especially those of the venerable lord Bede the priest,” etc.

Near the end of the exposition the author indicates that he was writing in the year 980, indiction VIII; therefore he is a different person from Herric, the monk of Auxerre, who lived a full century earlier.

Or was he Helperic, the monk of the monastery of Saint Gall who wrote a book on Computation, according to Trithemius, Book II of *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, chapter 77? See also the poem on Psalm 122 in volume VI of Canisius’s *Ancient Lectures*, p. 619, where it is attributed to Bede the Venerable—if it is worth the trouble.

## The Life of Bede the Venerable, Priest and Monk of Jarrow

Written partly by Cuthbert, his disciple, and partly by another man who lived in the eleventh century.

*(From printed books and the Thuane manuscript.)*

1. There were three Bedes, separated from one another by no great interval of time. The elder Bede, a priest and monk of Lindisfarne, is praised by Bede the Venerable in his *Life of Saint Cuthbert*, chapter 37. Another holy Bede, a monk and contemporary of Charlemagne, is celebrated by the Genoese; we shall discuss him in the following century. Between these two, but more illustrious than either, was Bede the Venerable, priest and monk of Jarrow, called Beda or Bedan by the ancients without inflection of the name. It is his deeds that we undertake to present here.

2. Although Bede the Venerable had many admirers and panegyrists, among the ancients he had no careful biographer. For the *Life* that we present should more properly be called a brief commendation of Bede than a precise and complete narrative. Certainly, in the Cheminion copy it bears this title:

> “A Brief Commemoration of Bede the Venerable, Priest and Monk, Catholic Teacher of the Holy Church and Expositor of the Scriptures.”

At the end it says:

> “Here ends the brief commemoration of Bede the priest, which Antonius, his disciple, published.”

Perhaps “Cuthbert” should be read instead, since Cuthbert was truly Bede’s disciple and, after Huetbert, abbot of Jarrow; Cuthbert’s letter concerning the death of his teacher is reproduced here.

The author who added the other material lived long after Bede, since he mentions Bede’s translation to Durham, which took place during the eleventh century. Edward Maihew, in his *Anglo-Benedictine Martyrology*, cites a certain very ancient anonymous author, from whose manuscript work he reports several fragments that shed little light on Bede’s life.

More substantial material is found in Simeon of Durham the precentor—or rather, Turgot, prior of Durham—in Book II of *On the Church of Durham*, chapters 14 and 15; in William of Malmesbury, Book II, chapter 4, of *On the Kings of England*; and in Matthew of Westminster, a monk, under the year 734. From these and other British writers, together with Bede’s own writings, we shall compose his Eulogy, which we shall append after the following Life in place of a commentary.

Read Edward Maihew under 27 May, and John Capgrave in the *Legend of the Saints of England*.

## The Life of Bede the Venerable, Priest

1. The venerable and God-beloved priest Bede was born in the province of the Northumbrians, in the territory of the monastery of the apostles Peter and Paul, which is at Wearmouth and Jarrow, in the year 677 of the Lord’s Incarnation,

[Note: The year of the Lord’s Incarnation is not expressed here in the Thuane manuscript; but this reading of the printed editions agrees with no. 2, where Bede’s age of eleven is correlated with the year of Saint Cuthbert’s death, which occurred in 687. But see the Eulogy, no. 2.]

which was the second year of Saint Cuthbert’s solitary life.

When he was seven years old, he was entrusted, at the urging of his relatives, for education to the most reverend Abbot Benedict, and afterward to Ceolfrith—that is, in the tenth year after the monastery of Saint Peter the Apostle had been founded, and in the third year after the monastery of Saint Paul had been begun.

These two monasteries had been joined in such peace and harmony, with such common association and fraternal fellowship, that, as Bede himself later describes them, they were regarded as one monastery located in two places. Thus, when mentioning one of them in his history of the English, he says:

> “The monastery of Peter and Paul, which is at the mouth of the River Wear and beside the River Tyne, in the place called Jarrow.”

2. This child, therefore, full of good promise, was diligently imbued with both divine and secular learning, destined in time to become an instrument of the Holy Spirit. When the Spirit illumined his heart, he was to compose many books on the exposition of the New and Old Testaments for the defense of the holy universal Church.

While he was being educated in the Latin language, he also acquired no mediocre knowledge of Greek. For at that time he was devoted to study in the monastery mentioned above, when Archbishop Theodore and Abbot Hadrian—both abundantly learned in sacred and secular letters—had traveled throughout Britain, gathering a company of disciples and daily pouring forth streams of saving knowledge to irrigate their hearts. They even taught their students the disciplines of metrics, astronomy, and arithmetic among the volumes of the sacred writings.

[Note: The words enclosed in parentheses are lacking in the printed books.]

For Bede himself speaks of them in this way, and then adds the following (*History*, Book IV, chapter 2):

> “There is evidence of this in the fact that to this day some of their students survive who know the Latin and Greek languages equally well, as though they were their native languages.”

When Father Cuthbert passed to the heavenly realms, Bede—who would one day become the distinguished author of his life—was then eleven years old and had spent four years in study at the monastery.

3. Thus Bede lived hidden in a remote corner of the world, but after his death he became known throughout every region of the world, living on in all his books. In them he often describes with precision the locations, natures, and qualities of various lands and regions, as though he himself had traveled through them all, although he had been raised from infancy in the monastery and spent his entire life there until the day of his summons. Some, however, wish to assert that he had been in Rome.

Lest anyone suspect that we are saying anything about him other than what is true, it seems appropriate to append his own words concerning himself.

4. “I,” he says, “Bede, servant of Christ and priest of the monastery of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, which is at Wearmouth and Jarrow, was born in the territory of that same monastery. When I was seven years old, I was entrusted by the care of my relatives for education to the most reverend Abbot Benedict, and afterward to Ceolfrith. From that time I spent the whole period of my life in the dwelling of that same monastery, devoting all my effort to the study of the Scriptures. Amid observance of the monastic rule and the daily duty of singing in the church, I always found it a pleasure either to learn, teach, or write.

“In the nineteenth year of my life I received the diaconate, and in the thirtieth the priesthood, both through the ministry of the most reverend Bishop John, by order of Abbot Ceolfrith. From the time when I received the priesthood until the fifty-ninth year of my life, I have taken care to make brief notes, for my own needs and those of my brothers, from the works of the venerable Fathers concerning Sacred Scripture, or to add something to their treatment in accordance with the sense and interpretation of those works.

“On the beginning of Genesis, up to the birth of Isaac and the expulsion of Ishmael, three books. On the tabernacle, its vessels, and the garments of the priests, three books. On the first part of Samuel, that is, up to the death of Saul, four books. On the allegorical exposition of the building of the temple, as also of the other matters, two books. Also, in the Books of Kings, a book of thirty questions. On Solomon’s Proverbs, three books. On Ezra and Nehemiah, three books. On the Song of Songs, six books. On the Song of Habakkuk, one book. On the explanation, allegorically concerning Christ and the Church, of the book of the blessed father Tobit, one book.

“Also, tables of readings for the Pentateuch of Moses, Joshua, and Judges; for the Books of Kings and Chronicles; for the book of the blessed father Job; for Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs; for the prophet Isaiah, and also for Ezra and Nehemiah. On Mark’s Gospel, four books. On Luke’s Gospel, six. Two books of Gospel Homilies.

“On the Apostle, I took care to transcribe in order everything that I found expounded in the works of Saint Augustine. On the Acts of the Apostles, two books. On each of the seven Catholic Epistles, one book. On the Apocalypse of Saint John, three books. Also, tables of readings for the entire New Testament except the Gospel.

“Also, a book of letters to various persons, one of which concerns the six ages of the world; one concerns the stations of the children of Israel; one concerns the saying of Isaiah, ‘And they shall be shut up there in prison, and after many days they shall be visited’; one concerns the calculation of the leap year; and one concerns the equinox according to Anatolius.

“Also, works on the histories of the saints. I transferred into prose the book on the life and passion of Saint Felix the Confessor from the metrical work of Paulinus. I corrected, as far as I could according to the sense, the book on the life and passion of Saint Anastasius, which had been badly translated from Greek and worse revised by some incompetent person. I wrote the Life of the holy father Cuthbert, monk and bishop, first in heroic meter and afterward in plain prose.

“I wrote in two little books the history of the abbots of this monastery, in which I rejoice to serve the supreme goodness: Benedict, Ceolfrith, and Huetbert. I wrote the Ecclesiastical History of our island and people in five books. A Martyrology of the birthdays of the holy martyrs, in which I diligently tried to record, for all those whom I could discover, not only on what day but also by what kind of contest, or under what judge, they conquered the world.

“A book of hymns in various meters or rhythms. A book of epigrams in heroic or elegiac meter. On the Nature of Things and On Times, one book each. Also, a larger book on Times. A book on Orthography arranged according to the order of the alphabet. Also, a book on the art of meter, and another little book added to it on figures and tropes—that is, on the turns and modes of expression with which Sacred Scripture is composed.”

5. After publishing these books with sleepless diligence, he died on the seventh day before the Kalends of June at Jarrow, and was buried there. But after many years his bones were transferred from that place and laid beside the incorrupt body of the most holy Father Cuthbert.

He passed away on the very solemn day of the Lord’s Ascension. We think it best to record his passing in the words of the man whose disciple, Cuthbert by name, was present at it and who wrote to a fellow disciple as follows.

“Cuthbert, your fellow disciple in God, to Cuthwin, beloved collector in Christ, eternal salvation.

“I gladly received the little gift you sent, and with great gratitude read the letter of your devoted learning. In it I found, above all, what I most desired: namely, that you were diligently celebrating Masses and sacred prayers for our beloved father and teacher Bede. Therefore, because of my affection for him, I am pleased to say a few words, insofar as my ability permits, about the manner in which he departed from this world, since I understand that you too desired and requested this.

“He was indeed burdened by a very severe illness, with frequent gasping, though without pain, beginning before the day of the Lord’s Resurrection—that is, for nearly two weeks. Thereafter, cheerful and joyful, giving thanks to almighty God every day and night, indeed at every hour until the day of the Lord’s Ascension—that is, the seventh day before the Kalends of June—he continued to live. Every day he gave lessons to us, his disciples, and spent whatever time of the day remained in singing psalms. He also passed the whole night awake in joy and thanksgiving, except insofar as a little sleep interrupted him. When he awoke, he immediately resumed his customary activities and did not cease giving thanks to God with outstretched hands.

“O truly blessed man! He sang the saying of blessed Paul the Apostle: ‘It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God,’ and many other passages from Holy Scripture, some of which he also spoke in our own language, that is, English, just as he was learned in our songs.

[Note: Simeon of Durham, or Turgot, reports several verses in the Saxon language and renders their meaning as follows: ‘Before the necessary departure, no one is wiser than is required to consider what good or evil he has done, or how he will be judged after his departure—namely, before the soul leaves this place.’ He also sang antiphons and other things, as recorded in the History of Durham, Book II, chapter 15, where this letter—indeed, almost this entire Life—is found.]

“He also sang antiphons according to our custom and his own, one of which was:

> O King of glory, Lord of hosts, who today ascended triumphantly above all the heavens, do not leave us orphans, but send upon us the Spirit of truth promised by the Father. Alleluia.

When he came to the words, ‘Do not leave us orphans,’ he broke into tears and wept bitterly. After an hour he began to repeat what he had started. When we heard him, we mourned with him. At one reading we read; at another we wept; indeed, we always read with tears.

“In such joy we passed the fifty days until the aforementioned day, and he rejoiced greatly and gave thanks to God because he had been found worthy to fall ill in this manner. He cited, and often repeated: ‘God chastises every son whom he receives,’ along with many other passages from Holy Scripture. He also repeated the saying of Saint Ambrose: ‘I have not lived in such a way that I should be ashamed to live among you; nor am I afraid to die, because we have a good Lord.’

“During these days, apart from the lessons we received from him and the singing of psalms, he took care to produce two little works worthy of great remembrance. He translated the Gospel of Saint John into our language for the benefit of the Church, and from the books of Notes by Bishop Isidore he extracted certain passages, saying: ‘I do not want my disciples to read a falsehood and, after my death, labor at it without benefit.’

“When Tuesday before the Lord’s Ascension arrived, he began to suffer more severely from difficulty in breathing, and a slight swelling appeared in his feet. He spent the whole day cheerfully dictating, and sometimes said among other things: ‘Learn quickly; I do not know how long I shall remain, or whether my Maker may take me away after a little while.’

“We thought that he knew his departure well. Thus he remained awake through the night in thanksgiving. At dawn, that is, on Wednesday, he ordered what we had begun to be written out carefully. After this was done, we walked until the third hour, and then went with the relics of the saints, as the custom of that day required.

“One of us remained with him and said: ‘There is still one chapter missing, dearest master. Does it seem difficult to you to be questioned any further?’ But he replied: ‘It is easy. Take your pen, sharpen it, and write quickly.’ The man did so.

“At the ninth hour he said to me:

[Note: In this place Simeon of Durham’s edition has the following: ‘I have some precious things in my little box—namely, pepper, a cloth, and incense. But go, run quickly,’ and so forth.]

“‘Run quickly and bring the priests of our monastery to me, so that I too may distribute to them the little gifts that God has granted me. The rich of this world take care to give gold and silver and every other precious thing; but I, with great love and joy, will give my brothers what God has given me.’

“He addressed each one, warning and entreating them to celebrate Masses and diligently offer prayers for him. They willingly promised to do so. All were grieving and weeping, especially because of what he had said: that they would no longer see his face in this world. Yet they rejoiced because he said: ‘It is time for me to return to him who made me, who created me, who formed me from nothing. I have lived for a long time, and the merciful Judge foresaw my life well. The time of my release is near, because I desire to depart and be with Christ.’

“He said many other things of this kind with joy. He continued through the day until evening. Then the boy mentioned earlier said: ‘There is still one sentence, beloved master, that has not been written down.’ He replied: ‘Write it quickly.’

“After a short while the boy said: ‘Now the sentence has been written.’ He replied: ‘You have spoken the truth well: It is finished. Take my head in your hands, because it gives me great pleasure to sit opposite my holy place, where I used to pray, so that I too, sitting there, may invoke my Father.’

“And so, while singing on the floor of his cell:

[Note: That is, of his little chamber, in which, lying on a hair shirt beneath him, he breathed his last, as the monk William of Malmesbury says below, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June in the year 735. Certainly devout men used to pray in hair shirts.]

> Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit,

when he had named the Holy Spirit, he breathed his last breath from his body and thus departed to the heavenly kingdoms.

“All who witnessed the death of the blessed Father said that they had never seen anyone end his life in such great devotion and tranquility. For, as you have heard, as long as his soul remained in his body, he did not cease, with outstretched hands, giving thanks to the living and true God by saying ‘Glory be to the Father’ and other spiritual words.

“Know, dearest brother, that I could relate many things about him; but the brevity of my speech is caused by the uneducated condition of my tongue.”

[Note: Here Baronius, on the basis of several manuscripts, has the following passage: ‘Nevertheless, with God’s help, I am considering writing more fully about him in due time, recording what I saw with my own eyes and heard with my own ears.’ But these following verses were omitted from the Annals. — Editor.]

> The crystal of his homeland, the star of his flock, the light of his forefathers,  
> Praise of the law, bearer of the law, and its honor, lies here.  
>   
> Beda, devoted to sacred things, an old man in gravity though young in years,  
> Fills the heavens with the incense of his devout mind.  
>   
> He learns, searches out divine things, teaches, and meditates;  
> His concern was to render his vows back to God.  
>   
> The seat of justice, the citadel of virtues, the downfall  
> Of temptation, the sword that plows through slippery flesh.  
>   
> With the holy sword of the word he guards the camp of his brothers,  
> So that the soldier of Christ may not fall when the enemy attacks.  
>   
> In his presence poverty did not invade men’s minds;  
> For those wounded by hunger, there was a joyful pasture.  
>   
> In the Church the nard of this man breathes forth its fragrance,  
> And by its good scent soothes those around it.  
>   
> While this carbuncle is taken away from the blind world,  
> The world, suffering the loss of its gift of light, is left in want.  
>   
> Having laid aside his fleece, he accompanies the heavenly flock,  
> God is the blessed life, the reward of his labor.

## The Life of Bede the Venerable, by a Very Ancient Anonymous Author

*(From the recently published edition of Bede’s Works by Giles of London.)*

Among the Catholic expositors of Holy Scripture who have shone as lights of the world, second only to the apostles, Bede, a priest of sacred learning and a monk of exemplary life, holds a name and rank of outstanding honor. Nor does the holy Church admit him undeservedly among the teachers, whose study, diligence, and purpose in the Holy Scriptures he imitated. As he pursued these things through meditation and writing, he offered, as a true Israelite, a great portion of sacred service for the protection and adornment of the house of God.

For he published not a few volumes explaining the divine utterances, composed with apostolic salt. Established upon the rock of inviolable faith, they will not be shaken by any assault of the gates of hell. Before his death, indeed, since he lived beyond the civilized world on an island in the Ocean, the name of this man lay hidden in obscurity. After his death, however, as Scripture says, when God brings the clouds from the end of the earth, wherever the sound of the apostles has reached, he himself lives in the memory of the faithful through his books; and, set like a lamp upon the lampstand of the Church, he shines upon all who are in the house of God. Thus, with God’s grace cooperating, he illuminated by his writings the mother Church, which had regenerated and enlightened him in Christ Jesus.

Although by the merit of his teaching he sits so exaltedly among the leaders of the Churches and holds a throne of glory among them, crying out with them among all nations and raising the voice of the Gospel like a trumpet, the brilliance of so illustrious a man seems somehow obscured by a cloud of abasement if the Church’s ears pass over in silence where he came from, who he was, what his life was like, or how his life ended—as though such matters were useless or even unworthy to know.

Far from him be any suspicion of this kind, from that vessel of election and instrument of the Holy Spirit whose teaching strengthens faith and whose example of life, once known, kindles the love of faith even more fervently. Planted from his earliest cradle in the house of the Lord, and advancing by grace like a palm tree, he brought forth the flowers of righteousness, continually proclaiming the mercy and truth of God upon the ten-stringed psaltery, joining the harp of good works to the song of words.

Indeed, raised among saints and by saints under monastic discipline, and liberally trained in letters, he pursued the course of his life as a holy man among holy men and as an innocent man among the innocent, striving with all his strength to keep himself unstained by this world. To establish unquestionable proof of this, we have gathered both his own writings about himself and those of others concerning him. As though collecting fragments of limbs from here and there into one bodily structure, we have joined them together in describing the perfect man in Christ.

For the sequence of writings, scattered and interrupted through the volumes of various authors, had broken off the reader’s knowledge of this memorable man. When arranged continuously, as the order of his deeds requires, it presents a clearer understanding of him through the effectiveness of an ordered reading.

Certainly, the difficulty of this undertaking—which the vigorous diligence of the learned readily recognizes—exceeds the strength of us who are unable to contribute anything worthy either in speech or in knowledge. Yet because all things are possible to one who believes, we who believe in the Word—that is, Christ, the power and wisdom of God—will not fail in speech. May his mercy, whom we hope to have as the beginning and end of our work and speech, deign both to precede whatever we are about to say or do by inspiring us and to accompany it by assisting us.

### Here Begins the Life of Bede the Venerable, Priest and Monk of Jarrow

When Christ Jesus, author of human salvation, sent workers of holy preaching into the harvest of the multitude destined to believe, and when the grace of the Gospel was already shining throughout the whole world upon every creature, the province of the Northumbrians too—although almost cut off from the world by its remote position—became a participant in divine knowledge. In the cold region of the north it was kindled by the sacred fire of the Savior.

For the Lord came to cast the fire of the Holy Spirit upon the earth. Since no one can hide from its heat, it penetrates even to the ends of nations and kindles the flames of his love in human hearts, so that those who depart from the old way of life may become a new creation in Christ.

Once faith had been received, a city of the great King was founded there among the unbelieving—who, according to Scripture, are the flanks of that apostate north. In praise of its founder, it proclaimed with the exultation of the whole earth: “Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised in the city of our God.”

To begin with the highest matters, even the kings of that province, once they had recognized the Creator, ruled all the more truly because they rejoiced in serving Christ, the King of the ages, with greater devotion. As future citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, by bearing the burdens of public administration they served Babylon in mere forced labor.

This is attested by the fervent and pious devotion of King Edwin toward religion. It is also attested by the unconquerable constancy of Oswald’s faith. Since he gloried in nothing except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, he triumphed victoriously on the cross over the enemies of the holy cross. After distributing the resources of his kingdom in aid of the poor, he entered heaven to be glorified with a twofold crown, that of mercy and of martyrdom.

In his brother Oswiu, the zeal of the house of God burned fiercely. Whatever weeds the enemy had sown among the good seed of the Gospel through misguided and schismatic men, he cut down with the sickle of Catholic truth and drove completely from his kingdom.

I pass over the diligence of his son Ecgfrith; I omit the counsel and support he gave for the construction of monasteries throughout his kingdom. Writings worthy of belief testify that he was most devout and beloved by God. To pass over other matters, this above all greatly increases his praise: that he had caused the virtuous man and angelic blessed Cuthbert to be advanced to the episcopate.

Happy, and not undeservedly blessed, may I call the condition of that province at that time, whose priests too, exalted in Christ and in the Church, were a great adornment and protection through their life and teaching. Setting aside the bishops of outstanding holiness whom that region had possessed before or afterward, it nurtured as contemporaries the magnificent fathers of its illumination and salvation—I mean Wilfrid, Eata, Cuthbert, and John—illustrious pontiffs of incomparable merit.

Under these twin rulers of the state and the Church, as zeal for sacred religion grew daily, churches and monasteries were freely built everywhere. In them, citizens destined to become saints and members of God’s household gathered together so that they might live spiritually in the flesh. Renouncing both their possessions and themselves, they carried the Savior’s cross in their way of life, and through the fire of heavenly love they burned themselves entirely as a holocaust of most sweet fragrance to the Lord.

Among these men who had sworn themselves into Christ’s army and fought against the world and its prince, Abbot Benedict stood out very conspicuously through his deeds in Christ. He had obtained from the Lord the grace of blessing signified by the evidence of his name.

In order that he might one day enter into the joy of his Lord and multiply the talents entrusted to him, he founded two monasteries which, although distinct, were one through an unbreakable bond of peace and charity. One he established at the mouth of the River Wear, in honor of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles; the other at Jarrow, in honor of Paul, teacher of the nations.

What more need be said? Following the example of the blessed patriarch Abraham, the sons of God who were scattered abroad came out from the land and kinship of the old, worldly life and gathered there in large numbers. To build by their way of life the tower of evangelical perfection, they renounced everything, became voluntary paupers, and followed the poor Christ.

Thus a numerous and noble company of monks quickly grew together in both places. There they learned by experience the pleasant sweetness of that blessed fellowship which the psalm proclaims: how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity.

The religious care of parents also entrusted their offspring, filled with good hope, to Benedict for education in God’s service, so that, formed by sacred instruction, they might forget their own people and their father’s house. Thus, while they were still tender, they could be presented as a living, holy, and God-pleasing sacrifice, and begin to serve the spirit before they were able to know the things of flesh and blood.

One of these children—indeed, the only one among them who was especially distinguished for his good character—was Bede. Already seven years old, he was handed over by his parents to the aforementioned holy man so that he might be prepared solely for the service of the Divinity. He was born in a small village belonging to the territory of Jarrow, through which the ever-flowing River Tyne passes before soon emptying into the Ocean.

According to chronological calculation, the year of his birth is found to be the six hundred and seventy-seventh year of the incarnate Word. This was the seventh year of the reign of Ecgfrith, king of the Transhumbrans, and the fourth year from the founding of the aforementioned monastery of blessed Peter.

At first in that monastery, and afterward in the monastery of the Apostle Paul, his childhood was brought up under the restraints of discipline. Following the example of blessed Samuel, he was dedicated to the Lord and lived as a boy in the temple of God, so that one day he might reveal to peoples the mysteries of God’s words disclosed to him in the ear of his heart.

Yet, so that in his progress of age he might be able to do this, a great intelligence, by the power of his natural talent and with God as its author, shone forth even in his childhood, lest the liberal study to which he had devoted himself prove in him weak or ineffective. After acquiring knowledge of the liberal arts and polishing his intellect through practice and exercise so that it could grasp higher things, he strove to enter into the depths of Holy Scripture and devoted all the strength he possessed to understanding them. To his desire and labor he added prayers, joining the prayer of the Psalmist: “Open my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law.”

Because he asked in faith, without hesitation, he was given by the Father of lights the best gift and perfect gift of wisdom—not the wisdom of this world, which is destroyed, but the wisdom that the Apostle proclaims: the wisdom of God hidden in mysteries.

For the study of continual meditation on the law of the Lord, he received the watchful eye of an exceedingly perceptive understanding. Along with an abundance of sacred books, he also received the proven, diligent, and frequent instruction of teachers learned in ecclesiastical letters. Thus the youth of this memorable man was cultivated by those who planted and watered in hope of good fruit. With God giving the increase, he was prepared as a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, that is, in the Church.

Perhaps someone who does not readily believe these things will reluctantly accept them, since, as even an author of secular eloquence testifies, everyone calmly accepts what he thinks easy for himself to do; whatever exceeds that, he regards as fiction and falsehood.

Who would not be astonished, or even declare it beyond belief, that so many spiritual gifts should abound in a remote corner of the world, so that Holy Scripture was not only read there but its mysteries also explained there for diffusion throughout the breadth of the world? Even if the name of Christ had not been heard there, it would surely not be surprising how far, to speak poetically, Boreas comes when his wing fails.

But faith’s piety will satisfy the doubter. It affirms that the majesty of the almighty Spirit is not stretched out through local distances or confined by narrow boundaries, but is present everywhere and in all things; and that his omnipotence grants the grace of his inspiration wherever he wills: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence?”

Let me therefore briefly say through whose ministry the Holy Spirit breathed the riches of his goodness onto these farthest shores of the Ocean, so that where the people had known nothing except how to utter barbarous cries, there they searched out the wondrous testimonies of the Lord and pronounced all the judgments of God’s mouth upon their lips.

The venerable man Benedict, whose grace and name have been mentioned above, was an industrious provider for his church and frequently returned to Rome. He made the journey there five times for the benefit of his monastery. Among the many ornaments he brought for the adornment of the house of God, he also transported home, as we are told, an immeasurable supply of books of every kind.

Whatever England lacked in ecclesiastical usefulness and adornment, Gaul or Rome offered to this devout merchant, either willingly given by friends or acquired at an agreed price. He also experienced the great generosity of the glorious pontiffs of the Apostolic See, Vitalian and later Agatho, in strengthening the monastery he had built and magnificently adorning the Church.

At the command of Pope Vitalian, he brought Archbishop Theodore and his companion, Abbot Hadrian, to Britain—truly apostolic men and highly suitable ministers of the word of God, sufficiently trained in knowledge of both secular and ecclesiastical philosophy, and in both languages, Greek and Latin.

After traveling throughout the entire island wherever the peoples of the Angles lived, they gathered groups of disciples and caused the daily streams of saving knowledge to flow out for the irrigation of their hearts. They even handed down to their hearers, among the volumes of sacred letters, instruction in metrical art, astronomy, and ecclesiastical computation. Thus anyone who wished to be educated in sacred learning had teachers readily available to instruct him.

This is shown by the fact that many of their disciples survived for a long time afterward, knowing both Latin and Greek as well as the language in which they had been born. Let this be said briefly, lest Bede’s knowledge of Scripture seem incredible in those remote hiding places of the world. For the providence of heavenly teaching had supplied him with both a sufficient store of sacred books and the diligence of distinguished teachers in every branch of knowledge.

At the time when the churches of the Angles were being visited by the aforementioned teachers and, after them, by their disciples, and the studies of both literatures were flourishing, the teachable youth was filled with love of knowledge and trained by vigorous labor in those same studies.

Having acquired knowledge of Latin as fully as of the native language in which he was born, he also attained no small degree of knowledge of Greek. Moreover, he and the church of the apostles in which he lived had as their teacher in reading and singing John, archchanter of the holy Roman Church. Benedict obtained him from Pope Agatho and brought him there for this very purpose.

He also testifies that a certain monk named Tunbert, educated under the instruction of Bishop Ceadda—a truly holy man and one sufficiently trained in Holy Scripture—was his teacher in the sacred writings.

He had many other guides who went before him on the path of Scripture. Living among six hundred fellow soldiers of the holy monastic army—for the aforementioned monastery of the Apostles Peter and Paul is said to have had this number of brothers—he rivaled each one in the better gifts. Whatever any of them had received through spiritual knowledge, he absorbed by learning from each, so that the Lord might intoxicate him with the abundance of his house and give him drink from the torrent of his pleasure.

Thus, like a most prudent bee, eager for a sweetness pleasing to God, he gathered flowers from here and there in the field full of blossoms that the Lord had blessed. By the craft of wisdom, as though making honey, he composed utterances sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.

While he burned with zeal for these studies of sacred philosophy, his years increased, as did the grace of spiritual gifts. Along with the spirit of wisdom and understanding he received the spirit of the fear of the Lord, so that, chastising his body and bringing it into subjection, he might know, according to the Apostle, how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honor.

Thus, while still in his nineteenth year, he was chosen from among the other tribes and assumed as a sacred Levite for the ministry of holy things. Serving at the altar of the Lord, he might have his lot and share with the true Levites of the true sanctuary, the inheritance for which the Psalmist longed with sighing and cried out in his sighing: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance, my hope and my portion in the land of the living.”

Accordingly, as a deacon he solemnly read the Gospel. To make his life correspond to the evangelical reading, he shaped it according to evangelical principles, with the loins of his mind girded and his feet shod in readiness for the Gospel of peace.

When he had reached the age of thirty, the blessed man was earnestly devoted to the study of contemplation. Then, behold, he was brought to the sacred altars at a higher rank, where, together with the sacrifice of a troubled spirit and contrite heart, the Son is daily offered to the Father as a sacrifice of appeasement and reconciliation.

From the time he received the priesthood, he unleashed the sharpness of his natural intellect upon the interpretation of Holy Scripture. Producing many books of Catholic learning, he disgorged through writing and teaching into divine service everything that, by learning, reading, and meditation, he had until then ruminated like a clean animal.

Every day he advanced in mystical understanding, to such an extent that, by grace acting as his teacher, he himself led many of those who had been his guides along the paths of Scripture into the abyss of a deeper understanding. With the inner chambers of the mysteries laid open, he contemplated the Holy of Holies with the eye of a pure heart. The one in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden revealed to him the uncertain and hidden things of his wisdom, so that what he had learned in darkness he might speak in the light, and what he had heard in the ear he might proclaim from the housetops of the Church.

Because he greatly desired to understand, in a lofty sense, the Psalmist’s fiery utterance, he approached as though to the fiery mountain on which the law was written by the finger of God. There, while searching out the hidden things of the sacraments, he entered with Moses, so to speak, into the cloud and darkness.

Our spiritual Israelite freely contemplated with the eye of understanding the radiance of the face of that Moses which carnal Israel could not behold in its understanding of the law, once the veil of ignorance laid over the heart of the unbelieving had been removed. “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” of understanding.

When he had perceived this in the law of perfect freedom, his speech and teaching, according to the Apostle, were not in words taught by human wisdom, but in spiritual words, comparing spiritual things with spiritual. Thus the abyss of the Old Testament calls to the evangelical abyss in the voice of waterfalls—that is, in the voice of the prophets and apostles.

Since the grace of God shone so sublimely in him, fame carried the name of this distinguished man everywhere and poured his excellence in Scripture into the ears of the Church. You would immediately see many acting like the Queen of Sheba, who came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom, because many also came from far away to hear, through his interpreter, the wisdom of the true Solomon—that is, our peacemaker, who made both one.

Some of these clung to him in constant residence and observed him as their authoritative teacher. Others, unable to be present, sent letters asking him to untie difficult questions concerning passages of Scripture and to clarify obscure matters for them.

At the request of some, he also followed in the footsteps of the Fathers and treated certain complete books of divine authority more plainly, explaining them from beginning to end, as the saying goes, from the crown of the head to the last fingernail.

Among other works, he also published six splendid books of exposition on the Gospel of Luke, at the request of the most reverend bishop of Hexham, Acca. His letter urging him to undertake this work begins as follows:

> “Often, both when absent by writing and when present in conversation, I have suggested to your holy brotherhood that, after your Exposition of the Acts of the Apostles, you should also deign to write on the Gospel of Luke. Until now, you have preferred to postpone this with a modest excuse rather than undertake it.”

Later in the letter he writes:

> “Explain blessed Luke in a splendid discourse. Since Saint Ambrose passed over certain matters without discussion because they seemed clear and not worth investigating to a man of such profound learning, take care also to explain these more diligently, after examining the little works of the other Fathers, through your own words or theirs.
>
> “I also believe that, through your most watchful study—for you spend days and nights awake in meditation on the law of the Lord—the Author of light will reveal in some places what ought to be understood concerning matters they left untouched.
>
> “It is entirely just, and fitting to the measure of heavenly piety and equity, that you who, completely neglecting the affairs of the world, pursue with tireless mind the eternal and true light of wisdom should both attain here the broken reflection of a purer understanding and, in the future, contemplate with a pure heart the King in his beauty—the very one in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden.”

Through these words the holy man indicates the sanctity of the teacher whom we ought to venerate, showing that he was free from worldly occupations and always devoted to the business of true and eternal wisdom amid the leisure of contemplation.

Finally, as Bede himself writes about himself, he spent the whole time of his life dwelling in the aforementioned monastery of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. As the preceding account already demonstrates, he devoted himself entirely to meditation on Scripture. Between observance of regular discipline and the daily care of singing in the church, he always found it sweet either to learn, to teach, or to write.

Thus, after completing his books with the greatest devotion through twenty-nine years of irreproachable labor, and as he was about to receive the reward of his holy way of life and pious work in the Church, he groaned beneath the burden of this mortal body, desiring that, once the house of his earthly dwelling had been dissolved, he might be found worthy to possess in heaven a building from God, an eternal house not made with hands.

Therefore, to preserve his memory forever, after listing all the titles of the books he had completed, when the laying aside of his tabernacle was already at hand and he was panting with an incredible ardor of desire toward the fountain of water springing up into eternal life, he composed this little prayer:

> “I beseech you, good Jesus, that, just as in your mercy you have granted me to drink sweetly from the words of your knowledge, so also, in your goodness, you may at some time grant me to reach you, the fountain of all knowledge, and always to appear before your face.”

## Here Begins the Second Little Book

Thus the venerable man’s soul, sighing for God and melted by the fire of holy love, longed for and fainted for the courts of the Lord, so that, seeing the God of gods in Zion, once what is partial had been emptied away, it might grasp what is perfect, and what it had seen here through a mirror in riddles it might see there face to face.

The gracious Divinity was present to the prayers and supplications of his servant. Wishing to crown him with mercy and loving-kindness, and not allowing any stain or wrinkle of sin to remain in him, God chose to cleanse him through the disciplines of pious chastisement, so that, purified in the furnace of a prolonged illness, he might shine like gold purer than the purest in the heavenly Jerusalem, which is built as a city, a radiant ornament.

Suddenly, therefore, he was struck by a grave affliction of constricted breathing, so that his voice became extremely weak and his breath was forced through the difficult passage of his airways. He suffered the distress of this nearly interrupted breathing for many days—about fifty-three—but, so that strength might be perfected in weakness, he gladly gloried with the Apostle in infirmities.

For, except when exhaustion briefly compelled him to sleep, neither the sun by day nor the moon by night saw him cease from praising God. Even then, upon his bed of suffering, he burst into words of exultation and confession:

> “I will confess to you, Lord,” he said, “with an upright heart, because you chastise and discipline me, so that you do not hand me over to death, and so that, having entered the gates of righteousness with the blessed who dwell in your house, I may be found worthy to praise you forever and ever.”

The rushing stream of saving teaching, which customarily gladdens the city of God, that is, the holy Church, did not then cease to flow from his mouth, the channel of living water, even though he was weakened.

Cuthbert, who was faithfully present with other disciples to the sick and dying master, bears witness to this in a letter to his fellow disciple Cuthwin:

> “Every day he read the Holy Scriptures to us, his disciples, and opened their mystical meanings. After the reading, he spent as much of the remaining daylight as there was in singing with the spirit and singing with the mind.
>
> “Instructed by the teaching of blessed David, he praised and invoked the Lord, asking to be saved from his enemies, because the Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth, to fulfill the will of those who fear him, to hear their prayer, and to save them.
>
> “Long before this he had corrected his little works with great care. Now too, although his breath was weak and he was failing incessantly, he repeatedly returned to correct certain very small matters that had been neglected because of the more important occupations of others. He wished that, when he had come to rest from his labors and his place had become peace and his dwelling Zion, not only his thought might not offend the ecclesiastical reader, but neither his expression—whether gaping in its vowels or harsh in its consonants—trouble the teachable grammarian.
>
> “For although, as someone has said, an intellect may be elegant and well trained, and speech may flow smoothly through long practice, nevertheless, unless it has been corrected and polished by the author’s hand, it gives off the odor of negligence.”

Amid these events, the memorable doctor was shaken by ever more violent sighs; and now, destined to live blessedly after death, he was being sharply pressed toward the debt of death, as his spirit was constricted, while a certain fatal swelling had already seized the lower parts of his body. Although this branch, remaining in Christ the vine, had already borne the fruit of the sweetness of fragrance, God the husbandman nevertheless cleanses it by more severe chastisement, so that it may produce more abundant fruit of salvation. But lest he should murmur against the will of his Lord and thus bless God to his face, he consults the sayings of divine speech from the mercy-seat as arguments for hope and rejoicing, such as this:

> “My son, do not be fainthearted under the discipline of God, nor fail when you are rebuked by him. For the Lord disciplines the one whom he loves; he scourges every son whom he receives. For there is no son,” says the Apostle, “who, when he has sinned, is not scourged by his father.”

And again, concerning those predestined to the kingdom of God:

> “He who did not spare his own Son,” he says, “but delivered him up for us all, how will he not also, together with him, graciously give us all things?”

“When this promise is fulfilled,” he said, “what shall we be, what kind of beings shall we be, and what good things shall we receive in that kingdom, since, when Christ died for us, we have already received such a pledge?”

By contrast, he considered nothing more wretched than the prosperity of sinners, who spend their days in good things and in a moment descend to the underworld; who do not share the labor of human beings and are not scourged together with human beings, so that they may be punished eternally with demons. Indeed, because divine severity rejects such people by a deep and just judgment, it releases them without hindrance into the desires of their hearts. Against them, in the person of ruined and despairing Jerusalem, that fearful sentence is uttered by God abandoning her:

> “Let him no longer be angry with you; my zeal has departed from you.”

But those whom he predestined as vessels of mercy he visits with the rod for their iniquities and with blows for their sins. To them he will grant the good of their predestined inheritance, when, as Scripture says, he gives sleep to his beloved.

He also recalled this saying of blessed Ambrose:

> “I have not lived in such a way,” he said, “that I should be ashamed to have lived among you; nor am I afraid to die.”

A brief commendation indeed, but sufficient for a man of perfect conduct. It ought not to be attributed to arrogance that he spoke of himself for the benefit of all who heard, so that they might glorify our Father who is in heaven, since his example could be imitated by everyone. And he said this at nearly the final moment of his life, when praise of virtue does not lift the heart of the person praised into pride, while it kindles the hearers all the more intensely toward the pursuit of virtue, because the condition of the flesh places the necessity of death before their eyes.

Thus the Apostle—who had earlier said, “I am the least of the apostles, and I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God”—when the time of his dissolution was approaching, praised himself, yet in the Lord, so that “whoever glories may glory in the Lord.” He said:

> “I have fought the good fight; I have completed the race; I have kept the faith. From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness.”

By these and similar testimonies of Scripture he had, in a certain sense, made himself a stranger to pain amid his illnesses, since through tears he breathed into the whole company that great multitude of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden from those who fear you but perfected for those who hope in you.

Meanwhile the annual cycle of the seasons began to turn toward the Church’s feast—the day on which the Son of God, powerfully ascending into the heights of heaven, led our captivity captive by his own strength. I mean the day Beda longed for, which would provide him with the end of the passing day and the beginning of what endures forever and ever.

Therefore, as he appeared to know beforehand the hour of his departure, on the day before he passed away he sent word for his disciples to come near, so that whatever uncertainty still remained in their minds they might diligently ask him about it, and, lest forgetfulness erase what they had learned, commit it to writing. The question of the learners was thus mingled with weeping; indeed, the voices of those eager to learn were hindered by sobs. And while excessive grief could not satisfy itself even with tears, it constricted the spirit as it advanced through the very passage of the throat. Nor was this without reason: the loss of such a teacher would mean their eternal deprivation of an equal instruction.

Soon afterward a devoted circle of the brethren stood around him, as he drew near his end. He urged them, forgetting what lay behind and stretching themselves toward what lay ahead, to attain the prize of God’s heavenly calling. He told them, by the example of Joseph, to remember that the cloak of the Egyptian mistress—that is, the restraints of worldly desire, the bonds of secular affairs—must be left behind. By fleeing and overcoming her obscene embraces, they were to bring sinful flesh into servitude and subject the kingdom of Egypt—that is, the realm of vices—to themselves.

He taught them that they could give no other proof that Christ dwelled within them except through the spirit of holy and indivisible charity. Since through communion in the heavenly bread they became one body of Christ, they must not be separated from the unity of that body by a spirit of dissension.

And he said:

> “Oh, my dearest ones, since the time has come for the debt owed to our condition to be paid, I ask you: pray to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, that through him in whom the prince of this world found nothing, he may send an angel of peace to meet me in salvation, so that, surrounded by his protection, I may not be put to shame when I speak with my enemies at the gate. I plainly desire to depart and be with Christ, by whose death I trust that I shall pass from death to life, death itself having been destroyed. But if I have labored for you in any way, if I have borne even the smallest fruit for the Church, I ask you to repay me that kindness: remember me after death there, where Christ is daily both priest and sacrifice of propitiation.”

The compassion stirred in the brothers’ hearts could no longer restrain its tears; joy drew some of them forth, while the greatness of grief drew out others. They rejoiced because they had nurtured one who was now to be brought into heaven; they grieved because they were about to lose in him the light of the Church. But since faith never feels any loss, his departure is not to be mourned; rather, his dwelling with God, to whom all things live, is to be celebrated with joy.

Meanwhile, as he awaited with joy the hour of death—or rather, the entrance into eternal life—there remained something from Scripture about which the disciples needed to hear their master’s judgment. Once he had given it and it had been written down, the scribe said, “It is finished.” He, rejoicing at the word of completion, said more cheerfully:

> “You have spoken well and truly: ‘It is finished.’”

Without delay, he ordered himself to be laid upon the pavement of the little cell in which he had been accustomed to write, dictate, read, and teach. There, with his head raised slightly, he was supported in a reclining position by the hands of his own companions, so that, facing the oratory where he had been accustomed to pray more privately—and whose sight still delighted him—he might adore toward your holy temple and confess your name, Lord.

Thus preparing himself for the journey to heaven and thirsting to reach God, the living fountain, he said:

> “To you, Lord, my heart has said, ‘I have sought your face; your face, Lord, I shall seek. Do not turn your face away from me,’ before which the angels long to look.”

The festive day of the solemnity already drew near, on which our Head and Beginning went before into heaven so that the members of his faithful might follow there. [Note: The British Museum manuscript reads “Jesus” in place of the standard reading “there”; I collated the whole manuscript with Smith’s text.] The blessed man seemed to behold Jesus already ascending, and sighed with his whole being to follow him. With his spirit already panting in his hands, he stretched them out in praise of that same ascension of Jesus Christ and, himself soon to ascend, cried out:

> “O King of glory, Lord of hosts, who today have ascended triumphantly above all the heavens, do not leave us orphans, but send upon us the Father’s promise, the Spirit of truth. Alleluia.”

After he had added praise of the holy and indivisible Trinity—“Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit,” with the naming of the Holy Spirit—his spirit was released from the flesh, and immediately he was carried into heaven by the blessed company of the holy spirits. There, mingling hymnic harmonies with the heavenly Jerusalem, blessedly he praises forever the King of the ages, God Sabaoth, one in substance and three in persons.

When the pillar of the Church and doctor, Venerable Beda, had thus entered upon the way of the Fathers, the devoted compassion of the brothers, grieving in tears over the fate of human frailty and bearing witness in hope to the joy of resurrection, duly celebrated his funeral rites with psalms resounding on every side. Together they solemnly committed to burial the body of their foster-son and teacher.

His repose in eternal peace took place while Ceolwulf was reigning, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 735, in the fifty-ninth year of Beda’s life. This was the one hundred and first year since the most illustrious and holy king and bishop—Oswald and Aidan, I mean—had first founded and established the Church of Christ in the province of the Bernicians. That Church lives and rejoices in the Catholic faith to this day, under God, its author and governor, God the Son, the Lord Jesus Christ, whom every spirit praises and worships as living and reigning with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever.

## LIFE OF VENERABLE BEDA BY AN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR

*(From the edition of Gilles)*

Beda the presbyter, servant of Christ, an Englishman by nationality, flourished in the time of Justinian II at the church or monastery of the apostles Peter and Paul, which was built in the city of Canterbury in England. From the age of seven he was carefully instructed in divine eloquence, first under Benedict, the abbot of that monastery, and afterward under Ceolfrid. Devoting himself zealously to divine study and being more fully imbued with the sacred writings, he advanced in wisdom and in admirable holiness of life.

In the twenty-fourth year of his age he received the diaconate, and in the thirtieth the priesthood, from Bishop John. From then until the seventieth year of his life he devoted himself to Scripture and brief works of divine wisdom, entrusting many memorials of his mind to learned men. For he published thirty-six volumes, which he divided into seventy-eight books.

By divine revelation he foresaw the day of his death seven weeks in advance. On the day of the Lord’s Ascension, which occurred that year on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, while he was celebrating Vespers with the other clergy in the church, he was troubled by no illness, but was sound in body and mind. As he sang the antiphon “O King of glory,” when it had ended he gave up his spirit while leaning against his stall. Immediately a wonderful fragrance began to issue from his body. He was buried in his monastery.

Although he is regarded by the Church as most holy and is counted among the confessors, he alone among the saints is called not “Saint” but “Venerable,” for two reasons, or because of two miracles, that occurred in connection with him.

First, when his eyes had grown dim from extreme old age and he had arrived, led by a disciple, at a heap of stones, the disciple began to persuade him that a great crowd had gathered there and was awaiting his preaching with the greatest devotion and silence. When the saint, fervent in spirit, had delivered a most elegant sermon and concluded, “Through all ages of ages,” the stones answered, “Amen, Venerable Presbyter.”

Second, when another of his disciples, after his death, intended to compose an inscription for his tomb, he began a Leonine verse with the words:

> “Here are in this tomb…”

He wished to finish it with “the bones of holy Beda” or “of the presbyter,” but the meter could not be made to work, and no other suitable word occurred to him. At last, wearied, he went to sleep. And behold, in the morning he found the following words carved on the tomb by angelic hands:

> Here are in this tomb the bones of Venerable Beda.

He rested in Christ on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, around the year of the Lord 700. His body was transferred to Genoa [Note: Thus it is read in the Basel edition; “Genoa” should be written.] and is honored with fitting veneration.
