Among other works, this man of God wrote one book on Genesis; three books on the tabernacle of Moses; four books on Samuel; one book on the temple of Solomon; two books on Ezra and Nehemiah; one book on Tobit; two books on Solomon’s Proverbs; five books on the Song of Songs; seven books on the canonical Epistles; four books on Mark; four books on Luke; one book on the Acts of the Apostles; one book on the Apocalypse; one book on questions concerning the Books of Kings, addressed to Nothelm; one book on schisms; and an outstanding and excellent volume on the Deeds of the English, in which a chronicle of the times is also included.

## LIFE OF BEDA COLLECTED BY TURGOT

### Preliminary Commentary on Saint and Venerable Beda, Monk and Presbyter in England; or, on His Age, the Life Collected by Turgot, His Sacred Cult, and the Testimonies of the Ancients Concerning Him

*(From the Bollandists, Acts of the Saints, May, vol. VI)*

### 1

Saint Benedict Biscop, abbot, built two distinguished monasteries in the seventh century of Christ, both in the ancient region of Northumbria, in that part subject to the bishopric of Durham.

The first arose in honor of the holy apostle Peter near the mouth of the River Wear, called by the English Wear; hence also Wearmouth, which, according to Camden, is now called Monkswearmouth—that is, “the mouth of the Wear”—belonging to the monks.

The other was built in honor of Saint Paul at the mouth of the River Tyne, Ingyrvum or Gyrvi, now called Jarrow. Saint Beda was born in its vicinity in the year of Christ 677, and when he was seven years old he began to live in the same monastery.

This man, having become England’s singular glory, acquired through piety and learning the surname “Venerable,” chiefly because his homilies were recited in the Church when he was either still alive or, at any rate, not yet inscribed in the catalogue of the saints. If this ancient title is genuine—about which Baronius reasonably doubts because of the silence of earlier writers—we have even greater reason to reject the old wives’ tales that are imagined to have provided the occasion for that title, and they do not deserve to be reported here. Nevertheless, we gladly use here the appellation that is most customary in the Church and approved in the Roman Martyrology.

He died, summoned to the eternal rest of his labors, on the feast of Christ’s Ascension, the seventh day before the Kalends of June, or 26 May, as his disciple Cuthbert wrote, who stood beside him as he was dying.

The year, therefore, was 735, when, with the fourteenth year of the lunar cycle, the sixteenth of the solar cycle, and the Sunday letter b, Easter fell on 17 April and the feast of the Ascension on the aforesaid 26 May.

In the Saxon Chronicle, after the Venerable Beda’s Ecclesiastical History, printed at Cambridge in 1643, his death is assigned to the preceding year, 734. Florence of Worcester modestly rejects this in his Chronicle under the year 734, where he writes:

> “The venerable priest, the monk praiseworthy in every respect, the wonderful computist, the most holy Beda, according to the English chronicles, breathed out his final spirit from the body in the present year; but according to his disciple Cuthbert, who described his death and was present at his departure together with many others, he did so in the following year, before the Lord’s Ascension, on Wednesday, that is, the eighth day before the Kalends of June, around the tenth hour, in great devotion and tranquility of mind. Thus, rejoicing, he departed to the heavenly kingdoms.”

So far Florence. But because the feast of the Ascension was considered to begin with its first Vespers, Cuthbert counted that tenth hour as belonging to the feast itself and assigned the death to the seventh day before the Kalends of June. On that same day, as is clear above from his acts, Augustine, bishop of Canterbury and apostle of the English, also departed this life.

### 2

The older manuscript Martyrologies assign both men to this seventh day before the Kalends, or 26 May. We possess one of them, written on parchment in England at least six hundred years ago. It first records the eulogy of the aforesaid Saint Augustine, and immediately adds:

> “Likewise, on the same island of Britain, the burial of blessed Beda the presbyter, the most discerning doctor of the English, whose merits and streams of doctrine are attested by the honeyed examples of good works.”

Then the passages that were placed before this in Usuard are read. In the same way Saint Augustine and Beda are celebrated first in the manuscript of Saint Martin of Trier.

But in Usuard, Saint Augustine is placed last. In the manuscript of the collegiate church of Saint Mary at Utrecht, written around the year 1140, the following is added to him:

> “Likewise, on the same island of Britain, [the burial] of blessed Beda the presbyter.”

In the same way these two are joined in the manuscript Martyrology of the monastery of Saint Cyriacus, which Baronius used extensively, and in the manuscript of Saint Patrick, which we found at Naples in the parchment codex of Antonio Caracciolo, a cleric regular:

> “In Britain, Saint Augustine, the first bishop of the English, and Beda the presbyter, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures.”

Similar passages are read in the manuscript of Saint Richarius at Centula and in the appendix called Adorus in Mosander and Rosweyde; likewise in Bellini’s Martyrology, enlarged according to the custom of the Roman Curia and printed at Paris around 1521; and in the Auctarium of Usuard prepared by Greven and Molanus, as well as in others.

Only Beda’s memory is celebrated on the same 26 May in the calendar of a very ancient manuscript Breviary that was used in the regions of the Rhine.

### 3

Because the solemnity of Saint Augustine interfered with the veneration of Saint Beda, the latter was transferred to this day, 27 May, as is clear from the calendar of the Enchiridion of the Church of Salisbury, which we possess written on parchment. Several manuscript Martyrologies of Usuard, enlarged for the use of the churches of Belgium around 1400 or somewhat later, agree with this, as does the manuscript Florarium.

The printed Martyrologies of Lübeck in 1475 and of Cologne and Lübeck in 1490 follow the same practice, together with printed Ambrosian Missals and Breviaries of 1522, 1539, and 1560. The monastic Martyrologies of Wion, Dorganius, Menard, Bucelinus, and the English Martyrology of Wilson also follow it.

The Roman Church confirmed this change of day by its own calculation in the revision of the Martyrology carried out at the command of Gregory XIII. For this reason we too have postponed treating him until that date, lest, if the cult of the saints is ever restored in England—which may it happen soon!—we should differ in this work from popular practice.

The burial of Venerable Beda the presbyter is, astonishingly, assigned to 10 May in the manuscripts of Liège, one belonging to the church of Saint Lambert and the other to the monastery of Saint Lawrence. Molanus followed this in the Auctarium of Usuard, and Canisius followed Molanus in the German Martyrology.

In the English Martyrology, Wilson replaced the burial with the translation of the body to Durham; but nowhere have we read that this translation should be assigned to this day.

### 4

We give the Life from the manuscript of Longpont belonging to Lord Belfort, collated with the copy that stands before his Ecclesiastical History, published in Latin and Saxon at Cambridge in 1643 from a manuscript of the Benedictine college.

It is nothing more than a very brief account, divided by us into three chapters. The first was taken from the history of the Church of Durham by Turgot—who was the earlier prior of Durham and flourished around the year 1100—which was incorrectly printed under the name of Simeon of Durham among the ten writers of English history. The material narrated here is found there in book I, chapter 8, while all the rest is reported in chapters 14 and 15.

The second chapter is reported in Beda’s own words. The third, which narrates his death, comes from the letter of the aforementioned disciple Cuthbert, who stood beside him as he was dying and intended to write a longer Life of him; but, greatly to be lamented, he never brought his well-conceived plan to completion.

We add a fourth chapter from book III, chapter 7, of the same Turgot, where the translation of his body to Durham is indicated.

Some abridgments of this Life are contained in a letter of Simeon of Durham to Hugh, dean of York, and at greater length in John Stubbs’s Chronicle, or Acts of the Bishops of York, where it is said:

> “Beda was born in 677, died in 735, and was buried in his monastery at Jarrow; but afterward his bones were translated to the body of Saint Cuthbert.”

### 5

We possess another set of Acts of Saint Beda copied from the library of the monastery of Böddeken, belonging to regular canons in the diocese of Paderborn, but we have not wished to bring them to light because they are filled with fables.

Others were printed by John Cagravius in the Legend of England, but various features in those too are displeasing, and they may be read there. In place of these, we prefer to gather several testimonies of distinguished men concerning his life and teaching.

Let the first be Saint Boniface, martyr and archbishop of Mainz, who flourished at the same time. In letter 9 to Huetbert, the abbot under whose governance Saint Beda died, he writes among other things:

> “We ask that you kindly send us some writings from the little works of Beda the monk, that most discerning investigator of the Scriptures, whom we have recently heard shone among you in the house of God like a candle of ecclesiastical knowledge of the Scriptures.”

The same Saint Boniface asks Egbert, archbishop of York—who held that dignity while Saint Beda was still alive—in letter 8, in these words:

> “May you deign to write and send me some treatises from the works of Beda the reader, whom, as we have recently heard, divine grace enriched with spiritual understanding and permitted to shine in your province, so that we too may enjoy the candle that the Lord has bestowed upon you.”

Again, when Saint Boniface had received some treatises, he wrote to the same archbishop in letter 85:

> “We received with grateful hearts, rejoicing, the gifts and little books of your sweetest blessedness, sent by you. Raising our hands toward heaven, we entreated the supreme King to repay you in the eternal court of the angels with flourishing rewards of merit. … Now, desiring them eagerly, we earnestly ask you to arrange to send us, for the joy of our sorrow, as you have done before, some small portion or spark of the candle that the Holy Spirit has kindled in your regions—that is, some portion of the treatises which Beda, the spiritual presbyter and investigator of the sacred Scriptures, composed by unlocking them. Above all, if it can be done, we ask for something that appears suitable, practical, and most useful for us in our preaching: a work on the annual Lectionary and on Solomon’s Proverbs, since we have heard that he composed a commentary on them.”

### 6

So far Saint Boniface. His devoted affection for Saint Beda passed also to his successor, Saint Lull, who, like Boniface, went from England to Germany and became archbishop of the same see of Mainz. Among the letters of Saint Boniface, numbered 111, he wrote the following to Abbot Cuthbert, formerly Saint Beda’s disciple:

> “We have sent your affection a few small gifts, a single silk pall. We also ask that, for the consolation not only of our pilgrimage but also of our illness, you deign to send books expounded by Beda of blessed memory: either on the building of the temple, or on the Song of Songs, or, if possible, all the epigrams composed in heroic or elegiac meter. If not, then three books on the building of the temple. Perhaps the request is difficult, but I think nothing is difficult for true charity.”

Saint Lull wrote this, and Abbot Cuthbert replied to him in letter 89, as follows:

> “I gladly received the little gifts of your affection, and all the more gladly because I learned that you sent them from the innermost devotion of your heart. That is, you sent a silk pall for the relics of Beda, our master, of blessed memory, out of remembrance and veneration for him.
>
> “It seems right to me that the whole English nation, in all the provinces wherever they are found, should give thanks to God, who bestowed upon them in their own nation so remarkable a man, endowed with diverse gifts and so diligent in exercising those gifts, and likewise living in good morals. For, having been trained at his feet through experience, I learned what I am telling you. …  
>
> “But now, since you have asked for something from the works of the blessed Father, I have prepared for your affection, as far as I could and according to my strength, together with my boys. I have sent, according to your wish, little books composed in verse and prose about the man of God Cuthbert; and if I had been able to send more, I would gladly have wished to do so. For the recent winter oppressed the island of our people for a long time and over a wide area with cold and frost and with storms of wind and rain. Consequently the scribe’s hand was delayed, so that it did not reach the number of many books. …  
>
> “As for the works of Beda, of blessed memory, which you do not yet have copied, I promise that, if we live, I shall fulfill your wish.”

This was Cuthbert, Saint Beda’s disciple, to Saint Lull.

### 7

Third among them should come Alcuin, teacher of the emperor Charlemagne, himself also an Englishman. He was educated under the aforementioned Egbert, archbishop of York, after the death of Saint Beda. In letter 49 to the brothers of the churches of Wearmouth and Jarrow, he writes among other things:

> “Remember how noble were the fathers you had, and do not be degenerate sons of such ancestors. … Recall the most noble teacher of our time, Beda the presbyter: what zeal for learning he had in his youth, what praise he now has among human beings, and how much greater the glory of his reward with God. Therefore, by his example, awaken your sleeping minds; attend upon teachers; open books; examine the letters; understand their meanings, so that you may be able both to nourish yourselves and to provide others with the adornment of spiritual life.”

In the same way, in a letter to King David, discussing the course of the moon through the several signs, he adds:

> “What could be said more clearly about the harmony of the solar and lunar courses through the signs of the bright zodiac than what Beda the master, investigator of such questions, has left us in his writings?”

A little farther below he praises him in the same manner. In poem 178 he adorns his verses on the Life of Saint Cuthbert with these distichs:

> Great was that Father too, bishop, shepherd, and priest,  
> Cuthbert, now the glory of your Church.  
> How much he accomplished through holy prayers, by the Lord’s gift—  
> There is no need for our little verses to tell.  
>   
> For earlier the renowned master Beda,  
> In heroic verse, set forth the illustrious deeds of the Father.

### 8

We do not wish here to enumerate the exceedingly learned disciples whom Beda left behind, as they are listed in the Life printed before his works. Among them, Rabanus, Albinus Alcuin, Claudius, and John Scotus are said to have excelled especially; they were the first to teach at Paris and to fill Gaul with the liberal arts.

We gave the Life of blessed Rabanus on 4 February, and in section 6 of the preliminary commentary we showed that he was born in 785, exactly fifty years after the death of Saint Beda. We reject, in section 2, number 7, the fable reported even by Vincent of Beauvais in book XXIII, chapter 173, of the *Speculum Historiale*, from the Chronicles.

In the time of this Rabanus, while he was still abbot of Fulda, the Council of Aachen was held in 836 and divided into three books. Since in the third book it had to be shown, as the preface states, that the temple of the Lord, built and dedicated by Solomon, was a figure of the Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world, and that Solomon its founder represented Christ, let us see—without prejudice to the exposition of the other outstanding Fathers on this matter—what Venerable and in modern times remarkable Beda the presbyter thought about that temple in his exposition of the Gospel of John. The rest may be read there at length.

This writer, here called venerable and remarkable, is called “doctor of the English” by blessed Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, in letter 3 to Pope Alexander II, who was elected in 1061.

After these came Turgot, prior of Durham, and Florence, monk of Worcester. From the former we give the Life of Saint Beda; the eulogy of the latter has been quoted above.

These were followed by William of Malmesbury, Henry of Huntingdon, Roger Hoveden, Matthew of Westminster, and other English writers, who celebrate him with exceptional praise. Among them, however, Malmesbury and Westminster report a letter of Pope Sergius to Abbot Ceolfrid. Sergius urges him that, since certain matters of ecclesiastical concern had arisen which needed to be more fully made known only after examination, men trained in literary learning were needed for consultation; therefore he should send without delay the religious servant of God Beda, presbyter of his venerable monastery, to the threshold of the apostles and to the sight of his mediocrity. …

But since Pope Sergius died on 9 September 701—that is, five years before Beda was ordained a priest—and before Beda had made public any work of his labors, that entire letter, unknown to earlier writers, appears to us fictitious.

We omit the enumeration of Trithemius and other more recent writers.

## LIFE OF VENERABLE BEDA BY THE AUTHOR AND COLLECTOR TURGOT, PRIOR OF DURHAM

*(From the Bollandists, Acts of the Saints, May, vol. VI)*

## CHAPTER ONE  
### His Birth, Education in the Monastery, Writings, and Death

### 1

The venerable servant of the Lord, Beda, presbyter and monk, was born in the province of Northumbria, in the territory of the monastery of the apostles Peter and Paul, which is at Wearmouth and Jarrow, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 677. This was the second year [Note: We showed from Turgot, in chapter 6 of the Life of Saint Cuthbert, that Cuthbert entered the solitary life on the island of Farne in the year 676; Beda’s Life, edited under his name, is given on 20 March.] of the solitary life of the most blessed Father Cuthbert.

When he was seven years old, the care of his relatives placed him in that monastery to be educated under the most reverend abbot Benedict [Note: This is Saint Benedict, bishop, whose feast is celebrated on 12 January. There we published a Life from Beda’s homily; he also wrote another, recovered by James Ware and printed at Paris in 1666.], and afterward under Ceolfrid [Note: Ceolfrid died in Gaul, at Langres, on 25 September 716, while undertaking a journey toward Rome.], in the tenth year after the monastery of Saint Peter the apostle had been founded [Note: According to Beda, it was built in 674, therefore three years before Beda’s birth.], and in the third year after the monastery of Saint Paul had been begun.

These two monasteries had been joined in such peace and concord, familiarity and brotherly fellowship that—as Beda himself later describes them—they were regarded as one monastery situated in two places. Thus, in his History of the English, mentioning one of them, he says [Note: These words are read in the epilogue that is usually printed after the epitome]:

> “The monastery of Peter and Paul, which is at the mouth of the Wear and beside the River Tyne, in the place called Jarrow.”

### 2

While still a little child of good hope, he was carefully imbued with divine and secular learning. He was destined one day to become an instrument of the Holy Spirit, through whose illumination of his inmost heart he would compose, for the defense of the holy universal Church, many books of exposition on the New and Old Testament.

While he was being educated in the Latin language, he also acquired no ordinary knowledge of Greek. At that time he was studying in the aforementioned monastery, when Archbishop Theodore [Note: Saint Theodore, archbishop, died in 690, on 19 September.] and Abbot Adrian [Note: Saint Adrian, abbot, died in 709, on 9 January, the day on which we illustrated his Acts.], both abundantly instructed in sacred and secular learning, and most welcome throughout all Britain, gathered a company of disciples and daily poured forth streams of saving knowledge to water their hearts. Thus, along with the teaching of the sacred writings, they also handed on to their students the disciplines of metrics, ecclesiastical arithmetic, and astronomy, as Beda himself says about them [Note: Book IV of the Ecclesiastical History of the English, chapter 2].

Then he truly adds this:

> “To this day there remain some of their disciples who know the Latin and Greek languages equally as well as their own, in which they were born.”

When Father Cuthbert passed to the heavenly realms [Note: Saint Cuthbert died in 687, on Wednesday, 20 March], Beda—who would eventually become the distinguished author of his Life—was then eleven years old and had spent four years studying in the monastery.

### 3.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 734, in the seventh year of the reign of King Ceolwulf [Note: The Acts of Saint Ceolwulf, the king to whom Bede dedicated his History, were published under 15 January; further material may be added from Turgot.], and in the eleventh year of the episcopate of Ethelwold, that lamp of the Catholic Church reached the light which had illumined it; that spring of water leaping up into eternal life reached the living God, the fountain: namely, Bede, the Venerable priest and monk, compiler of the sacred books. He died in the fifty-ninth year of his age—101 years after King Oswald and Bishop Aidan had established the episcopal see and monastic dwelling on the island of Lindisfarne [Note: Oswald is celebrated on 5 August, and Aidan on the 31st of the same month.], and sixty-two years after the construction of the monastery of the Apostle Peter at Wearmouth, but forty-nine years after the passing of Father Cuthbert.

This Bede lived hidden in a remote corner of the world; but after his death, living on in his books, he became known to all in every part of the world. In them he frequently and minutely describes the locations, natural features, and qualities of the various lands and regions, as though he himself had travelled through them all, although from childhood he had been brought up in a monastery and had spent his entire life there, until the day of his summons. So that no one may suspect that we are saying anything about him other than the truth, it seems appropriate to append his own words about himself.

## CHAPTER II. The Manner of Life and Writings of Saint Bede, Reported in His Own Words

### 4.

“I, Bede,” he says, “servant of Christ and priest of the monastery of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, which is at Wearmouth and Jarrow, was born in the territory of that same monastery. When I was seven years old, I was entrusted by my relatives for education to the most reverend Abbot Benedict, and afterward to Ceolfrith [Col. 0061D]. From that time onward I spent my entire life in the dwelling of that monastery, devoting all my effort to the study of Scripture [Col. 0062A]. Between observing the regular discipline and undertaking the daily responsibility of singing in the church, I have always found it pleasant either to learn, to teach, or to write.”

[Note: Therefore, in the year 696.]

“In the nineteenth year of my life I received the diaconate [Note: In the year 707.], and in my thirtieth year the priesthood, both through the ministry of the most reverend Bishop John [Note: This was Saint John of Beverley, consecrated bishop of Hexham in 686 and afterward archbishop of York in 700. He eventually lived at Beverley and died there in 721, on 7 May, the day on which we published his Acts.], at the command of Abbot Ceolfrith. From the time when I received the priesthood until the fifty-ninth year of my life [Note: From this we conclude either that Saint Bede was born at the beginning of the year 677 and wrote this not long before his death, in 735, when he had begun his fifty-ninth year; or else that chronological years are being used, so that his first year, regardless of the month in which he was born, ended with the year 677.], I have taken care to make brief annotations on Holy Scripture, for my own needs and those of my brothers, from the works of the venerable Fathers, or also to add to them according to the form of their meaning and interpretation.”

### 5.

[Note: On these writings, see Trithemius, Sixtus of Siena, Possevinus, Bellarmine, Labbe, Miraeus, Vossius, and similar authors. We do not consider it part of our purpose to examine each item individually or to repeat what others have already done.]

Three books on the beginning of Genesis, up to the birth of Isaac and the expulsion of Ishmael.

Three books on the Tabernacle, its vessels, and the garments of the priests.

Four books on the first part of Samuel, that is, up to the death of Saul.

Two books on the allegorical exposition of the building of the Temple, as also of the other matters.

Likewise, a book of thirty Questions on the Books of Kings.

Three books on Solomon’s Proverbs.

Six books on the Song of Songs.

Three books on Ezra and Nehemiah.

One book on the Song of Habakkuk.

One book on the blessed Father Tobit: an allegorical exposition concerning Christ and the Church.

Likewise, chapters of readings on the Pentateuch of Moses, Joshua, and Judges; on the Books of Kings and Chronicles; on the book of the blessed Father Job; on Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs; and on the prophet Isaiah, as well as Ezra and Nehemiah.

Four books on the Gospel of Mark [Col. 0062B].

Six books on the Gospel of Luke [Col. 0062C].

Two books of Gospel homilies.

On the Apostle, whatever I found expounded in the works of Saint Augustine, I took care to transcribe in full and in order.

Two books on the Acts of the Apostles.

One book each on the seven canonical Epistles.

Three books on the Apocalypse of Saint John.

Likewise, chapters of readings on the whole New Testament, except the Gospel.

A book of Letters to various persons, including one on the six ages of the world; one on the encampments of the children of Israel; and one on Isaiah’s statement, ‘And they shall be shut up there in prison, and after many days they shall be visited.’

One book on the calculation of the leap year.

One book on the equinox, following Anatolius.

Likewise, from accounts of saints, I translated into prose the book of the Life and Passion of Saint Felix the Confessor from the metrical work of Paulinus [Note: We published this Life under 14 January.].

I corrected, as far as I could according to the sense, the book of the Life and Passion of Saint Anastasius, which had been badly translated from Greek [Col. 0063A] and even worse revised by some incompetent person [Note: We publish this on 20 March.].

I composed the Life of the holy Father Cuthbert, both monk and bishop, first in heroic meter and afterward in plain prose [Note: We mentioned above that this was published by Jacobus Waraeus.].

I wrote, in two small books, the History of the Abbots of this monastery—in which I rejoice to serve the heavenly goodness—Benedict, Ceolfrith, and Huetberht.

I wrote the Ecclesiastical History of our island and nation in five books [Note: We published this from eight manuscripts before volume II of the March Acts.].

I wrote a Martyrology of the feast days of the holy martyrs, in which I carefully strove to record all whom I could find, not only on what day, but also by what kind of contest, or under which judge, they conquered the world.

I wrote a Book of Hymns in various meters or rhythms.

I wrote a Book of Epigrams in theoretical or elegiac meter.

One larger book on the Nature of Things and on Times [Col. 0063B].

A book on Orthography, arranged in alphabetical order.

Likewise, a book on the Art of Meter, and another little book appended to it, On Figures or Tropes—that is, on the figures and modes of expression with which Holy Scripture is woven together.”

[Note: Up to this point the words are Bede’s; Turgot appended what follows to this chapter.]

### 6.

After he had produced these books with sleepless diligence, he died at Jarrow on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, and was buried there. But after many years his bones were transferred from there and placed together with the incorrupt body of the most holy Father Cuthbert.

In honor of this Bede, a portico on the northern side of the church of Saint Paul at Jarrow was consecrated and there preserves for the faithful a venerable memorial of his name. The place is also shown today where, possessing a little stone chamber, he used to sit, meditate, read, dictate, and write, free from every disturbance [Col. 0063C].

He passed away on the very solemn day of the Lord’s Ascension. We think it better to record his passing in the words of his disciple, Cuthbert, who was present and wrote as follows to a fellow disciple.

## CHAPTER III. The Illness and Death of Bede, Reported by His Disciple Cuthbert

### 1.

“To the most beloved Cuthwin, collector in Christ, Cuthbert, his fellow disciple in the Lord: eternal salvation.

I received with great pleasure the little gift which you sent, and I read with great gratitude the letter of your devoted learning. In it I found especially what I desired: that Masses and sacred prayers were being diligently celebrated by you for the sake of our beloved Father and teacher Bede [Col. 0063D]. Therefore, because of my affection for him, I am pleased to say in a few words, insofar as I possess the ability, how he departed from this world, since I understand that you also desired and requested this.

### 2.

He was weighed down by a very serious illness involving frequent breathlessness, though for nearly two weeks before the day of the Lord’s Resurrection he suffered almost no pain. Afterward, cheerful and joyful, giving thanks to almighty God every day and night—indeed, at every hour—until the day of the Lord’s Ascension, that is, the seventh day before the Kalends of June [Col. 0064A], he continued to live in this manner. Each day he gave lessons to us, his disciples, and for whatever part of the day remained he occupied himself, as far as he could, with the singing of psalms. He strove to spend the entire night awake in joy and thanksgiving, except insofar as a little sleep interrupted him. When he awoke, he immediately resumed his customary musical recitations of Scripture and never ceased giving thanks to God with outstretched hands.

I confess truly that I have never seen with my eyes or heard with my ears of anyone who gave thanks so diligently to the living God. O truly blessed man! He also sang the saying of the blessed Apostle Paul, ‘It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God,’ and many other passages from Holy Scripture, by which he urged us to rise from the sleep of the soul, anticipating the final hour [Col. 0064B]. He also recited several passages in our own language, that is, English, since he was learned in our songs.

For at that time, composing this saying in English verse, he would say with deep compunction: ‘Before the necessary departure, no one has ever been wiser than was needed to consider what good or evil he had done, and how he would be judged after his departure from this life.’

He also sang antiphons according to our custom and his own. One of them was:

> O King of glory, Lord of hosts,  
> who today ascended triumphantly above all the heavens,  
> do not leave us orphans,  
> but send upon us the Spirit of truth,  
> the Father’s promise, alleluia.

When he reached the words ‘do not leave us orphans,’ he burst into tears and wept bitterly. After an hour he began again to repeat what he had started, and he did this throughout the whole day. As we listened, we mourned with him. At one time we read, at another we wept; indeed, we always read with tears.

### 3.

In such joy we passed the fifty days up to the day mentioned above. He rejoiced greatly and gave thanks to God because he had been deemed worthy to fall ill in this way. He would say, and often repeated: ‘God chastises every son whom he receives,’ along with many other passages from Holy Scripture. He also quoted the saying of Saint Ambrose: ‘I have not lived in such a way that I am ashamed to live among you, nor am I afraid to die, because we have a good Lord.’

During those days he strove to complete two works worthy of much remembrance, apart from the lessons we received from him and the singing of psalms. First, he translated into our language, for the benefit of the Church, the Gospel of Saint John from its beginning up to the passage where it says, ‘But what are these among so many?’ [Col. 0064D] Second, he made extracts from the books of notes of Bishop Isidore, saying: ‘I do not want my disciples to read a falsehood and, after my death, labor over it in vain.’

### 4.

When Tuesday before the Lord’s Ascension arrived, he began to grow more seriously ill with breathlessness, and a slight swelling appeared in his feet. Yet throughout that entire day he taught and dictated cheerfully. From time to time he said among other things: ‘Learn with haste; I do not know how long I shall remain, or whether my Maker may soon take me away’ [Col. 0065A].

It seemed to us that he knew his departure well. Thus he spent the night awake in thanksgiving. When morning dawned—that is, on Wednesday—he ordered that what we had begun should be written down carefully, and we did this until the third hour.

From the third hour onward we processed with the relics of the saints, as the custom of that day required. One of us was with him and said: ‘There is still one chapter missing, most beloved teacher, from the book which you dictated. Does it seem difficult to you to be questioned any further?’

But he replied: ‘It is easy. Take your pen, sharpen it, and write quickly.’ And the man did so.

### 5.

At the ninth hour he said to me: ‘I have some valuable things in my little chest—pepper, *oraria* (liturgical cloths), and incense. Run quickly and bring the priests of our monastery to me, so that I too may distribute among them little gifts such as God has granted. The rich of this world take pains to give gold and silver and other precious things; but I, with great charity and joy, shall give my brothers what God has given.’

When they were present, he spoke to each of them, admonishing and beseeching them to celebrate Masses and offer prayers diligently for him. They willingly promised to do so. They all mourned and wept, especially because of what he had said, since they thought that they would not see his face much longer in this world.

They rejoiced, however, at what he said: ‘It is time—if it so seems right to my Maker—for me to return to him who made me, who created me, who, when I did not exist, formed me from nothing. I have lived a long time; the merciful Judge has wisely foreseen my life. The time of my release is near, because I desire to depart and be with Christ; for my soul desires to see my King Christ in his beauty.’

After speaking many other things for our edification, he passed the day joyfully until evening.

### 6.

Then the aforesaid boy, Wiberht, said again: ‘Beloved teacher, one sentence has still not been written out.’

He replied: ‘Write it quickly.’

After a short while the boy said: ‘The sentence has now been written.’

He answered: ‘Good. You have spoken the truth. It is finished. Take my head in your hands, for it gives me great pleasure to sit opposite the place of my sanctuary, where I used to pray, so that, sitting there, I too may invoke my Father.’

And thus, seated on the floor of his little cell, singing, ‘Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit,’ when he had named the Holy Spirit, he breathed forth his final breath [Col. 0065D]. And—as must doubtless be believed—because he had always labored here with the greatest devotion in the praises of God, he departed to the joys of his heavenly desires.

All who were able to hear or see the death of Bede, our father, said that they had never seen anyone else end his life with such great devotion and tranquility. For, as you have heard, as long as his soul remained in his body, he did not cease to offer ‘Glory to the Father’ and other spiritual words to the living and true God with outstretched hands, giving thanks [Col. 0066A].

I know, dearest brother, that I could tell many things about him; but now the brevity of my speech is caused by the unlearnedness of my tongue. Nevertheless, with God’s help, I am thinking of writing more fully about him, concerning what I saw with my eyes and heard with my ears.”

## CHAPTER IV. The Body of Saint Bede Transferred to Durham and Dispersed, from the History of Turgot and Wod. Whether His Relics Are in Rome

### 1.

Under Bishop Edmund [Note: Edmund was elected in 1020, but consecrated five years later; he died in 1048.], there flourished in the Church of Durham a priest named Elfred, son of Westou, who remained there until the time of Bishop Egelwin [Note: After Edmund had presided for ten months, Egilric was ordained. He resigned in 1058 and was succeeded by Egelwin.].

He was devoted in all things to Saint Cuthbert, a very temperate man, devoted to almsgiving, constant in the practice of prayer, terrifying to the wanton and immoral, but venerable to the honorable and God-fearing, and an exceedingly faithful guardian of the Church . . .

When the priest mentioned above was living an honorable and religious life, he was ordered in a vision to travel through the ancient sites of monasteries and churches in the province of Northumbria. He raised from the earth the bones of the saints whom he knew to be buried there and left them placed above ground, to be displayed to the people and venerated . . .

He also used to come every year, when the anniversary of Bede’s death arrived, to the monastery at Jarrow, where he knew that Bede the teacher had lived, died, and been buried, and there to devote himself to prayers and vigils.

On one occasion, going there according to his custom, he spent several days alone in the church praying and keeping vigil. Then, unknown to his companions, he returned alone to Durham at first light—something he had never done before—because he did not wish to have any witness to his secret. For although he lived many years afterward, he no longer cared to visit the aforesaid monastery, as though he had already obtained what he had desired.

Consequently, when his close associates repeatedly asked him informally where the bones of the Venerable Bede were resting, he was certain about the matter and would answer as follows:

“Of this,” he said, “no one knows more certainly than I do. Be firmly convinced, my beloved, and certain beyond all doubt, that the same coffin which preserves the most sacred body of Father Cuthbert also contains the bones of the venerable teacher and monk Bede. Let no one seek any portion of his relics outside the shelter of this tomb.”

Having said this, he ordered his associates to keep it secret, lest outsiders who were then staying in that very church should contrive some injury [Col. 0066D]. Their greatest concern was to carry off the relics of the saints, especially those of Bede, if they could.

Therefore, when he placed the bones of the saints with the body of Saint Cuthbert, as stated above, he strove to do it entirely in secret.

A poem composed in the English language also agrees with his judgment concerning Bede [Note: The language meant is Anglo-Saxon, which remained in use until the time of the Normans, when the English language of today was gradually introduced.] [Col. 0066D]. This poem survives in Anglo-Saxon script and language after Turgot’s history, in column 76; a somewhat similar one also survives on page 76 [Note: The poem is found there.]. In it, when the condition of this place and the relics of the saints contained there are discussed, Bede’s relics are also mentioned along with the others [Col. 0067A].

These are evidently the bones which many years later, together with the incorrupt body of Father Cuthbert, were separated from the other relics and found placed in a little linen sack [Note: Malmesbury, in Book III of the Deeds of the Bishops of the English, states that the bones of Saints Bede and Ceolwulf were packed in separate linen sacks. In our handwritten account of the translation of Saint Cuthbert’s body into a new tomb in 1054, published under 20 March, no. 6, we read: “The bones of the Venerable Bede, who had written the Life of Saint Cuthbert with clarity, had their resting place together with his body; a linen sack likewise contained them.”] [Col. 0067B].

### 2.

Antony Wod, Book II of his History and Antiquities of the University of Oxford, p. 61, says:

“Saint Bede rested in the monastery of Jarrow. His relics were afterward transferred to Durham, honorably enclosed in a shrine, and then, at the beginning of the reign of Queen Elizabeth, Whittingham, the unworthy dean of Durham, seized by fanatical zeal, removed them from the church and completely dispersed them.”

### 3.

In the Description of the Old Vatican Basilica, composed by Romanus, a canon of that Church, in the time of Pope Eugenius III, and published with notes by Paolo de Angelis, p. 117, Romanus himself speaks as follows:

“Also resting before the Silver Door, beneath the porphyry wheel, as we have received from our ancestors, is the Venerable Bede, the priest who composed the homilies. Out of reverence for him, our ancestors did not pass through it at all, nor did they allow us to pass through it.”

Paolo added the following note:

“Romanus the priest, our authority, rightly noted in this description of the basilica of Saint Peter the burial of the Venerable Bede in that basilica. Yet this tradition appeared so tenuous to later generations that, when listing the relics of this church, Onuphrius, On the Seven Churches of the City, pp. 54–55, Pompeius Ugonius, in his History of the Stations, p. 103 and following, and many others throughout did not wish to mention the Venerable Bede.

“Nor is he mentioned in the order of divine worship, in which the veneration of other saints is prescribed whose sacred bodies or notable relics are preserved there.

“Just as the city of Genoa had its own much later Bede, who was also a saint, and whom we discussed under 10 April, and wrongly confused him with the English teacher, so it also appears to have happened at Rome, perhaps because of some Bede who was buried there many centuries later.”

## An Investigation into the Commentaries on Paul by the Venerable Bede and Florus, Deacon of Lyons, Compiled from the Sayings of Saint Augustine

*(Mabillon, Old Analecta)*

I find three ancient authors who composed commentaries on the Epistles of the Apostle Paul from excerpts taken solely from Saint Augustine. The first is Peter, abbot of the province of Tripoli, who is said to have annotated the Epistles of Saint Paul from chapters of the works of the blessed Augustine, “so that through another’s mouth he might reveal the secret of his own heart,” as Cassiodorus says in On Divine Readings, chapter 8.

The second is the Venerable Bede, whose words occur at the end of the Epitome of his History: “On the Apostle, whatever I found said in the works of Saint Augustine, I took care to transcribe in order.”

The third is Florus the deacon—or, as Wandalbert, a monk of Prüm and his contemporary, thought, subdeacon—of the Church of Lyons, a man renowned in his time for learning and scholarship.

Of these three commentaries, we possess one printed among the works of the Venerable Bede and prefaced with his name. But whether it should truly be attributed to Bede has long been a matter of serious dispute among scholars.

This is attested by Robert of Torigni, abbot of Mont Saint-Michel, in the prologue which he prefixed to the Abbreviation of the Exposition of the Epistles of the Apostle according to Augustine. In that prologue, published by our Acherius in an appendix to Guibert, Robert judges that the lengthy Commentary—which I do not doubt is the same work that now appears among Bede’s writings—should rather be attributed to Peter, abbot of Tripoli, than to Bede. To Bede, he assigns another, shorter work, likewise excerpted from the books of Saint Augustine; “that book,” he says, “does not equal in size even half of the exposition of the Epistle to the Romans alone, which is found in the other commentary.”

A long time after Robert, the illustrious Cardinal Baronius, under the year of Christ 562, judged that the commentaries published in print were not Bede’s but those of Peter the abbot, agreeing with Robert on this point. He differed from him, however, by denying that Bede had composed any such commentary on Paul. He said that Bede’s words quoted above had entered his Epitome through an addition by someone else.

Bellarmine disagrees with Baronius in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers. He says that nothing prevents two authors, Peter the abbot and Bede the priest, from having labored at different times and in different places to explain Paul from the writings of Augustine. Indeed, nothing prevents us from adding a third to these two, Florus the deacon of Lyons, as I shall demonstrate later.

Although this is so, the judgments of scholars concerning the commonly circulated commentary remain divided. Some believe it should be attributed to Bede; others take it away from him. For my own part, when I once composed Bede’s eulogy in the third Benedictine century, it seemed to me to be Bede’s genuine offspring; but afterward, when I discovered a genuine commentary by Bede in manuscript libraries, I was forced to abandon that opinion.

### I.

Everyone ought to be convinced that Bede composed some commentary on Paul from the sayings of Augustine. This is so, first, because Bede explicitly testifies to it in his Epitome, as both printed books and manuscripts prove; and second, because Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, and Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, praise this collection of Bede.

Hincmar says in his later work against Gottschalk, chapter 1:

“Nevertheless, if anyone does not possess these same books, let him consult the collection of the Venerable Bede the priest, drawn from the works of Saint Augustine on the Apostle; there he will be able to learn what he previously did not know.”

Lupus, in Letter 76 to the same Hincmar, writes:

“I have hesitated to send Bede’s collection on the Apostle, drawn from Augustine’s works, because the book is so large that it could neither be hidden in one’s bosom nor conveniently contained in a traveling bag.”

Therefore, no one can now call into question whether Bede published a collection on the Apostle. Baronius too would not have doubted it if he had directed his attention to the arguments I have just presented. It remains to be seen, however, what sort of commentary Bede’s is.

### II.

I found two parchment codices containing such a collection under Bede’s name, one nearly eight hundred years old and the other seven hundred. The first codex bears this title:

> Bede’s Collection on the Apostle from the Works of the Blessed Augustine.

The commentary then begins with the words, “Paul, servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle,” and so forth, in this manner:

> From the book Against Five Heresies. The order to be followed is this: when speaking about the Gospel, I must not remain silent about the prophets, and so forth.

This codex ends in the Epistle to the Thessalonians, with other leaves torn away.

The second codex is entitled:

> Here begins the book of the collections of the Venerable Bede the priest, compiled from the writings of the blessed Augustine, bishop, and prepared on the Epistles of the blessed Apostle Paul.

It has the same beginning as the first and ends as follows:

> Here ends the collection of Bede the priest from the works of the blessed Augustine on the Epistles of the Apostle Paul.

We have not yet obtained a copy of this genuine commentary by Bede, which has not yet been published in print. God willing, we shall eventually bring it to light together with other monuments of this kind [Col. 0069D].

### III.

We must now determine to which author the collection circulated under Bede’s name should be attributed. It should be attributed to Florus, deacon of the Church of Lyons, as many manuscript codices demonstrate, several of which have come into my hands.

First of all, this is proved by two parchment volumes of the Corbie Library. At the very beginning of the first we read:

> This volume contains expositions of the Epistles of the blessed Apostle Paul from the books of Saint Augustine, the outstanding teacher, collected by a certain Florus.

Then, at the end of each Epistle, the name of Florus the author is repeated, and again at the beginning of the next.

At the end of the second volume, the following subscription is found:

> This book was composed—that is, written—by Richer, subprior, and by John, his scribe and one-eyed assistant, in the year when the church of Saint John at Corbie was restored, and Tours was the second seat of the Roman city, in the year 1164, under Louis, king of the Franks, Theodoric, bishop of Amiens, and John, abbot of Corbie.

The learned Stephen Baluzius already noticed and discussed this remarkable passage in his note on Lupus’s Letter 76. He observes that the scribe here refers to the synod held at that time in the city of Tours by Alexander III. Since Alexander was then residing there, the scribe calls that city “the second seat of the Roman city.”

Baluzius is quite appropriate in this interpretation. Nevertheless, I should not omit that I remember reading in Book XIV of Brower’s Annals of Trier [Col. 0070B], where the epitaph of Cardinal Ivo, who was buried at Trier, is reported. Its final couplet reads:

> When the sun turns the twelve Kalends of July,  
> Second Rome performs my venerable funeral rites.

Here the city of Trier is called a second Rome, perhaps because that city abounds in sacred relics, or because crowds of people frequently flock there for the sake of fulfilling vows.

For the same reason I read that our Corbie was also given this name by Gerard in Book IV of On the Miracles of Saint Adalhard. After recounting Adalhard’s miracles, he adds:

> The fame of such things began to spread so far and wide that Corbie rightly came to be considered and called another Rome.

But to return to the matter at hand: not only the Corbie codex but also several others attribute the aforesaid commentary to Florus the deacon. Among them is the codex used by Trithemius. Perhaps because he found it in the monastery of Saint Trudo, Trithemius supposed that the deacon Florus whose name the codex bore had been a monk of Saint Trudo.

To these codices I add the Aquicinctine manuscript, in which the first part of the exposition of the Epistles of the blessed Paul from the books of Saint Augustine is said to have been collected by a certain Florus—namely, the part read under Bede’s name.

Furthermore, this lengthy collection is attributed to Florus in the very old collection of canons which seems to have been written toward the end of the ninth century, that is, in Florus’s own century, and is preserved in the monastery of Saint Marianus at Auxerre.

In that collection the following passages are cited:

> COLLECTED FROM THE BOOK OF SAINT AUGUSTINE BY LORD FLORUS:  
> “Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh. What the prophets foresaw and foretold, this the apostles saw and proclaimed. He who was became—what was he? What did he become? The Word was; he became flesh,” and so forth.

These passages are found in the commonly circulated commentary attributed to Bede on the Epistle to the Romans.

Likewise, on page 17 of the aforesaid copy, a Saying of Lord Florus is cited in these words:

> “Anathema” is a curse, a condemnation; likewise, condemned, detestable, abominable, alienated, and so forth.

Another passage reads:

> “If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema: maranatha.” He uses a word from both Syriac and Greek. “If anyone does not love,” and so forth. In Greek speech he called *anathema* “condemned”; he defined *maranatha* as “until the Lord returns.”

These two passages are found in the commonly circulated collection attributed to Bede: the first at the beginning of the commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, and the second at the end of the First Epistle to the Corinthians.

Finally, Sigebert, in Book On Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 92, mentions a commentary compiled by Florus on the Epistles of Paul from the books of Saint Augustine.

From these facts, if I am not mistaken, it is manifestly established that this commentary is not Bede’s but that of Florus, deacon of Lyons.

I do not deny, however, that it is attributed to Bede in some manuscript codices, but almost always with the name of Florus added—as though Florus were not a proper name but a common noun meaning a collection of flowers, or florilegium.

Hear Robert of Torigni, speaking of this commentary in the prologue cited above:

> This work is called Florus by some because it has been excerpted from various little works of the blessed Augustine and, as it were, stripped of its flowers. But many people doubt by whom the work was collected and arranged. Some attribute it to Bede the priest, and they do so because, at the end of his History of the English, when listing his works, he placed among them, word for word: “On the Apostle, whatever I found said in the Works of Saint Augustine, I took care to transcribe in order.” Consequently, some people, taking these words and several others connected with them from the same History, place them as a sort of prologue before the aforesaid collection of sayings of Saint Augustine, wishing thereby to prove Bede the author of this work.

I have certainly found Robert’s statement to be true in the Clairmarais manuscript collection, contained in two volumes. In the first volume appears this inscription:

> In this volume is contained the exposition of the Epistles of the blessed Apostle Paul, collected by the Venerable Bede the priest—as the Deeds of the English testify—from the books of Saint Augustine, bishop, outstanding teacher, and most faithful author, as is indicated in the individual passages, and so forth.

At the end of the second volume the following is added:

> Here ends the Epistle to the Hebrews, and the third part of the Florus collected by the Venerable Bede the priest from the sayings of Saint Augustine.

Here one sees Bede’s name attached to this collection together with the name Florus, which is used in the sense of a florilegium. From this it is understood that the collection was attributed to Florus in antiquity.

One objection may be raised: Florus composed another collection on Paul from the Fathers, and it does not seem likely that he himself composed yet another from the writings of Saint Augustine.

On the contrary, this fact strongly supports our position. For Florus later extracted the latter collection from the works of twelve Fathers, omitting Augustine—whom he certainly would not have omitted unless he had already published a separate collection from Augustine.

Peter Francis Chiffletius, an learned priest of the Society of Jesus, copied this later collection from a manuscript of the Grande Chartreuse and sent it as a gift to our Acherius. He observes at once in the preface that this collection was excerpted not from ten Fathers only, as Sirmondus wrote in his notes on Avitus, but from twelve Fathers: Cyprian of Carthage; Hilary of Poitiers; Ambrose of Milan; Pacianus of Barcelona; Theophilus of Alexandria; and Gregory Nazianzen, all bishops; Ephrem the deacon; Pope Leo; Cyril of Alexandria; various canons and decrees of the Roman pontiffs and councils; Fulgentius of Ruspe; Paulinus of Nola; and finally Avitus, bishop of Vienne.

Florus divided his collection, contained in a single volume, into twelve books, corresponding to the twelve Fathers. He compiled a thirteenth book from Augustine and enclosed it separately in one volume because it was more substantial.

### IV.

These matters concerning Bede’s and Florus’s commentaries on Paul had to be discussed at greater length, so that no one in future might be uncertain which work belongs to whom. I shall refrain from speaking of the commentary of Peter, abbot of Tripoli, since I have been unable to make any observations about it. Perhaps, indeed, it has been lost, or did not reach our region.

[Col. 0071]

# DISSERTATION ON THE WRITINGS OF THE VENERABLE BEDE, PRIEST AND MONK

By Caspar Oudinus.

(From Oudin, *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I.)

[Col. 0071D] Bede, born in Britain of Anglo-Saxon stock, was born in the territory of Girwy, not far from the mouths of the River Tyne, in the year 673. Having embraced the monastic life from childhood, he persevered in it for many years under Benedict and Ceolfrith, abbots of the monastery of Saints Peter and Paul on the Tyne, in the diocese of Durham. He was commonly called an English priest and “the Venerable,” although he was devoted to the monastic institution.

According to Sixtus of Siena in the *Bibliotheca sancta*, he became a priest at the age of thirty, in the year of the Lord 703, through Bishop John, at the urging of Acca, archbishop of York, and many of the brethren. He then undertook to write various volumes of explanations on all of Scripture, divided into four classes: *rhapsodies*, questions, commentaries, and homilies. In the rhapsodies, or *stromata*, or collections, he gathered mystical rather than historical interpretations from the most approved opinions of the doctors of the Church, and so forth. In his commentaries, questions, and homilies, in which he more frequently employs both his own speech and his own meaning, he has a style that is neither altogether inelegant nor eager for affected eloquence, but balanced and moderate.

He died in the year 735, on 26 May, or the seventh day before the Kalends of June, on which the commemoration of the Lord’s Ascension was celebrated. The anonymous appendix to the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, which he brought down to the year 731, at the age of fifty-nine, and dedicated to Ceolwulf, king of the Northumbrians, speaks of him; so does his epitaph; Alcuin, in Letter 5, where he calls him the most distinguished teacher of his age; and Honorius of Autun, at the beginning of Book IV of his *Little Book on the Luminaries of the Church*, where he falsely asserts that Bede died at Rome and was buried there. Sigebert of Gembloux, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 68, assigns his death less accurately to the year 634, as may be inferred from the day of the Ascension coinciding with 26 May, which occurred in the following year. William of Malmesbury, Book I, chapter 3, claims that he was summoned to Rome by Pope Sergius, although it is absolutely certain that he never set foot outside England. Among more recent writers, Cardinal Baronius discusses him at length in his *Annals*, but is mistaken both in determining his age and in certain other matters. There are also Gerard John Vossius, Book II of *Latin Historians*, chapter 28, and John Mabillon, who treats him most fully in his learned eulogy, composed in Volume I, page 534 and following, of the third century of the *Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*. In many matters we follow Mabillon.

All the works of the Venerable Bede, which had previously been printed separately here and there in various imperfect editions, were first collected into one body and published at Paris in 1544, in three folio volumes, by Francis Jamet. Since the work was successful with booksellers, the same material, furnished with new corrections and additions, was reprinted there in 1554 in eight folio volumes. It was then published likewise in eight volumes at Basel in 1563, by John Herwagen, and finally at Cologne in the same number of volumes in 1612, by Antonius Hierat. These are the four editions of the works of the Venerable Bede, of which the last three follow the same arrangement. We shall follow the last, the Cologne edition of 1612, which was eventually reprinted there in 1688 in the same order, and shall examine each volume and the works contained in it individually, since few have carefully examined the works attributed to Bede in preparation for more accurate editions.

# CHAPTER ONE  
## On the First Volume of the Works of the Venerable Bede

[Col. 0073D]

This volume contains works relating to grammar, arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, music, and similar arts. It is arranged in a suitable order, provided that Bede’s doubtful works had all been placed at the end of each volume, or in a final volume of all the works. Let us now examine each item individually.

### *Beginnings of the Grammatical Art* of Donatus, p. 1.

### *A Book on the Eight Parts of Speech*, p. 14.

The Venerable Bede compiled a list of his principal works, by which the genuine can easily be distinguished from the spurious. We read that he composed it only four years before his death, namely in 731, at the age of fifty-nine, near the end of his *History of the English*. Thus, although he may have written some works afterward, his most important writings are contained in this little catalogue. Bede does not mention either of the two works under discussion in his catalogue; nevertheless, there is nothing in them that requires us to deny them to Bede.

### *A Book on Metrical Art*, p. 25.

### *On the Figures of Sacred Scripture*, p. 42.

### *On the Tropes of Sacred Scripture*, p. 47.

### *A Book on Orthography*, p. 53.

Bede mentions all these works at the end of his catalogue in the following words:

“A book on Orthography, arranged in alphabetical order; likewise a book on Metrical Art, and attached to it another little book on Figures, or Tropes—that is, on the figures and modes of expression with which Holy Scripture is composed.”

Bede the priest’s work *On Orthography*, edited from the manuscript of Bongarsius, was first published at Hanover in 1605, in quarto, by the learned young man Elias Putschius, among the ancient grammarians, pp. 2327–2350. It differs from the little work on the same subject commonly attributed to Bede, which has often appeared among his works and is presented below by Putschius together with his single book *On the Principle of Metrical Composition*, pp. 2350–2383.

### *On Arithmetical Numbers*, p. 72,

together with the dialogue *On Numerical Signs and the Reckoning of Time*. These belong to Bede, who mentions them in his catalogue of works.

### *On Arithmetical Propositions*, p. 100.

This appears to be by the same Bede.

### *On the Method of Calculation*, p. 111,

and *On the Division of Numbers, addressed to Constantine*, appear to be by the same author.

### *Little Work on Speech by the Gestures of the Fingers*, p. 127.

Likewise, the little book *On the Method of Reckoning Ounces*, p. 141. [Col. 0074C] These are certainly by Bede himself, since in the preface he speaks of his little works *On the Nature of Things* and *On the Reckoning of Time*, which he calls little books and says he once composed in a concise—that is, brief—style. These two little books are, as it were, preludes to the greater work *On the Reckoning of Time*, which he later judged it necessary to write at greater length.

The Venerable Bede the priest’s short treatise *On the Computus, or Speech by the Movement of the Fingers*, appears in the latest Cologne edition of Bede’s works, dated 1688, volume I, p. 127, with glosses by Bridefert, a monk of Ramsey, though extremely meager ones, and with scholia by John of Nijmegen. Barthius observes that this book departs in many respects from the practice of the ancients, *Adversaria*, Book II, chapter 12. Compare Rhabanus, abbot of Fulda, *On the Computus*, which Stephen Baluze published in Volume I of his *Miscellanies*, and Nicholas of Smyrna’s *Notation of Numbers by the Movement of the Fingers*, which Frederick Morellus published in Greek and Latin together with Bede’s *On Finger-Reckoning*, in octavo, at Paris. After Morellus, Peter Possinus published it at Rome in 1673, in folio, at the end of the *Catena of the Greek Fathers on Mark* and of his *Evangelical Spicilegium*. Possinus also added notes by I know not whom and had figures of χειρολογιστικοὶ σχηματισμοί—“gestural formations” or “manual signs”—engraved in copper, p. 449 and following.

### *Little Book on the Lunar Arguments*, p. 143,

which he does not mention specifically.

### *The Common Computus, Called the Ephemeris*, p. 169 and following,

together with the Calendar, is in no way by the Venerable Bede the priest. This is recognized beyond all doubt from the reading of the calendar, in which countless commemorations occur of saints who lived after Bede. I therefore marvel with what audacity, or rather shamelessness, men could attribute such a work to Bede, who died in 735.

To summarize much in a few words, this author mentions, on 5 June, Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, who died in 754, approximately twenty years after Bede. On 4 July he mentions Saint Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, who died in the tenth century. In the same month, on 11 July, he mentions the translation of the body of Saint Benedict to Gaul. On 15 August he mentions the feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary. On 8 September he mentions the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary; these feasts among the Latins do not extend beyond the ninth century. Finally, in the verses with which he gathers together the entire distribution of the year at the end of the work, he mentions Saint Elizabeth of Thuringia, of the Order of Saint Francis, who flourished only in the thirteenth century:

> Fertile Thuringia sings the praises of Elizabeth.

Some have thought that the author of this laborious work was Wandelbert, a monk of Prüm, who flourished in the ninth century. But, good God, how extravagantly they conjecture! How can someone who lived and died in the ninth century mention Saint Elizabeth the widow, who flourished and died in the thirteenth century? It is certain that the author of these *Ephemerides* was a German, judging from his affection for listing the saints, martyrs, and bishops of Germany, as will be clear to the reader. Whoever he may be, he does not seem, as far as the period in which he lived is concerned, to exceed the middle or end of the thirteenth century. The good Cavus did not notice this, since he never read Bede’s works.

### *Computus on the Method of the Embolisms*, p. 216.

It seems to me to be by the same author as the aforementioned *Ephemerides*. Certainly, the Venerable Bede would not have forgotten such a lengthy work in the catalogue of his writings, which he composed in 731, only four years before his death. Nor is it believable that the Venerable Doctor, with old age weakening him, occupied himself with such calculations before his death.

Finally, it is clear that this work does not belong to Bede but to an author of later times, as we said above concerning the *Ephemerides*, from his words on folio 231, where he writes:

“Having found the day you seek, and noted the letter which the Martyrologies have on the fifth line back.”

In Bede’s time there were not yet Martyrologies, since he himself was the first to compose one, leaving it blank on many days, as Usuard testifies. They became common only toward the end of the ninth century. Thus anyone who writes in this way reveals himself to be an author of later times. Finally, the entire expression of this work—clear and straightforward, and instructing the reader in what it investigates by many different methods—shows that its author is not earlier than the thirteenth century. Cavus did not notice this.

Certainly, the author of both works is an Englishman named Ralph of Linham, known to very few; we shall speak of him later under the year 1250.

### *The Nineteen-Year Cycles*, p. 257,

together with those written by Dionysius the Roman, surnamed Exiguus, and by Blessed Cyril, extending to the year 1595 of salvation and containing three great cycles. The preface placed before it, p. 256, asserts that this work is by the Venerable Bede. Although the preface is anonymous in the printed editions, I read that it is by Abbo, abbot of Fleury, who died in 1004. John Mabillon treats his printed and lost writings with great learning in Volume II of his *Analecta*, p. 240, where he introduces various matters.

### *On the Paschal Cycle*, p. 306.

For more information, consult Giles Bucherius, priest of the Society of Jesus, in his very learned commentaries on the paschal canon of Victor of Aquitaine, which he published in folio at Antwerp, from the Plantinian press, at the expense of Balthasar Moretus, in 1633.

### *A Book on the Constitution of the Celestial and Terrestrial World*, p. 323.

It is by no means unworthy of being attributed to Bede, although I have nothing by which I can affirm that it is his, and Bede himself does not mention it in his catalogue of works.

### *Two Little Books on Theoretical and Practical Music*, p. 344.

These are falsely attributed to Bede for several reasons.

First, in the second little book, *On Practical Music*, this author makes a show of adducing examples of chants taken from the offices of feasts of the Blessed Virgin Mary, such as:

> O Mary, blessed mother, etc.;  
> In praise of Mary, with devoted service, etc.

But these feasts of the Blessed Virgin by no means became established in the Latin Church before the ninth century, in the time of Louis the Pious or Charlemagne. They therefore cannot in any way belong to Bede.

Second, these examples are sequences, such as:

> O Mary, virgin of David, etc.,

as well as others that he adduces from sequences concerning the Holy Spirit:

> May the grace of the Holy Spirit be present with us, etc.;  
> Come, Holy Spirit, and send forth from heaven, etc.

But, according to the more learned writers on liturgical rites, the use of such sequences in ecclesiastical offices and Masses cannot be traced back before the twelfth century, and most of them were introduced especially in the thirteenth century. These little books therefore cannot in any way belong to Bede, who died in 735.

Finally, this author may be either French or English, since on p. 364 he gives the beginnings of certain songs in French and English. In French:

> *Demenant grande joye* (“bringing great joy”), etc.

In English:

> *Suant voile dont tans und*, etc. [meaning uncertain; the printed English incipit is unclear]

It seems to me scarcely possible that these existed before the fourteenth century.

### *On the Circles of the Sphere and the Pole*, p. 365;

### *On the Method of the Planets and Signs*, p. 369;

[Col. 0076D] ### *On the Signs of the Sky*, p. 373.

I can neither affirm nor deny anything about these works.

### *Little Book on Thunder*, addressed to Herenfrid, p. 387.

This was merely translated into Latin by Bede, and Bede himself acknowledges its simplicity. It therefore does not properly belong to Bede.

### *Little Books on the Prognostications of the Weather*, p. 390; *On the Measurement of a Clock*, p. 392; *On the Astrolabe*, p. 394; *On the Prognostic Birth of Infants*, p. 397; *On Bloodletting*, p. 398; *On the Seven Wonders of the World*, p. 400.

These really are little books, but it is in no way established that they are by Bede. Indeed, several of them are wholly unworthy of being attributed to the Venerable Bede, among them *On the Prognostications of the Weather*, *On the Birth of Infants*, and *On Bloodletting*.

### *Hymns Inscribed to Bede the Priest*, p. 401 and following.

These do not appear to belong to Bede. It is indeed certain that Bede wrote a book of hymns in different meters or rhythms, as he himself states in the catalogue of his works that he composed. But those hymns were varied, concerned sacred subjects, and were written in different meters or rhythms; none of this agrees with the meters or verses called hymns here.

For these are poems, not meters; most concern computational matters, not sacred subjects; natural or prognostic topics, not ecclesiastical offices. In both subject and style, they seem to me to agree with the poems of Manfred, which appear on p. 435 after Bede’s book *On the Computus*.

[Col. 0077B] ### *Little Book on the Method of the Computus*, p. 418.

This unquestionably belongs to Bede. Helpericus mentions it; according to Peter Francis Chiffletius, Helpericus was writing in 930 in the preface to his work *On the Computus*. Various very ancient manuscript codices of it exist under Bede’s name in many libraries of Gaul, especially in Paris, including one in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés at Paris, no. 546, as John Mabillon reports in his eulogy of the Venerable Bede. Indeed, Helpericus undertook his own work on the same subject in imitation of Bede’s little book *On the Computus*.

# CHAPTER TWO  
## On the Second Volume of the Works of the Venerable Bede

### *A Book on the Nature of Things*, p. 1.

### *A Book on the Reckoning of Time, or on Times*, p. 43.

### *Chronicle, or Little Book, on the Six Ages of the World*, p. 103.

### *A Book on Times*, p. 118.

I see no room for doubt that these four works belong to Bede. He mentions at least three of them in his catalogue of works: a book *On the Nature of Things*, a book *On Times*, and another, longer book *On Times*. These are Bede’s own words. The works would have been arranged more suitably as follows:

1. The book *On the Nature of Things*, p. 1.  
2. The shorter book *On Times*, p. 118.  
3. The longer book *On Times*, p. 43, which Bede seems to have written after the shorter one.  
4. The *Chronicle, or Little Book, on the Six Ages of the World*, p. 103.

Bede does not mention the last of these in his catalogue of works, but it certainly belongs to him. It is not surprising that he did not mention it, since it is virtually a part and abridgment of the larger work *On the Reckoning of Time*.

That work was written, according to Bede’s reckoning, in the year 4680, A.D. 726, in the ninth year of the emperor Leo. This was nine years after the death of his abbot Ceolfrith, which he describes under the year 4671, A.D. 716, in these words:

> In those times many noble and humble people of the English nation—men and women, leaders and private persons—were accustomed, through the prompting of divine love, to come from Britain to Rome. Among them was also my most reverend abbot Ceolfrith. He was seventy-four years old, had been a priest for forty-seven years and an abbot for thirty-five, when, having reached Langres, he died there and was buried in the church of the blessed twin martyrs. Among the other gifts he had planned to bring, he sent to the church of Saint Peter a *Pandect*, translated by blessed Jerome into Latin from a Hebrew or Greek source.

The *Chronicles of Herman the Contracted* agree with this number of years; Herman says that the same number of years of the world is contained in Bede’s larger book *On Times*, or *On the Reckoning of Time*. Thus, according to Herman, this chronicle belongs to Bede’s larger book *On the Reckoning of Time*.

What we said—that Bede’s shorter book *On Times* is much earlier than the larger book—is very easy to establish, since the shorter work ends in the fifth year of the emperor Tiberius III, which is the year of Christ 701 or 702. Bede therefore concludes that book as follows:

> From this point Tiberius completed his fifth year. What remains of the sixth age is known to God alone.

The other book *On Times*, as we said above, runs as far as the ninth year of Leo the Isaurian, and A.D. 726.

### *Sentences, or Philosophical Axioms*, p. 124.

### *Sentences Excerpted from the Works of Cicero*, p. 166.

### *An Alphabetical Book of Proverbs from Sacred Scripture*, p. 185.

These three little works do not belong to Bede at all, but to some more recent writer who, in my view, does not exceed the fourteenth century. A reading of the prefaces alone—both of the book of *Sentences from the Works of Cicero* and of the *Proverbs from Scripture*—is sufficient to prove this, since they display no antiquity but novelty and a recent age.

One and the same author appears to have composed these three collections; this is certain of the first two. In the introductory remarks to the collection of *Sentences from Cicero*, he alludes to sentences collected by himself from Aristotle in the following way:

> Now, since the length and magnitude of Aristotle’s authorities have increased, it is more convenient to explain, in the second treatise of the present little work, the remaining proverbs concerning the blessed life, so that fatigue may not impede the mind.

Whoever wishes to attribute works of this kind to Bede will plainly show himself a novice in ancient diction and styles.

### *Little Book on Substances*, p. 200.

This is incorrectly entitled. It should be entitled *A Collection of Various Instructions Useful to Clerics and Laypeople*. It is called *On Substances* because, near the beginning, it strongly argues that monasteries’ possessions, or goods, must not be alienated, donated, or squandered. Thus the little work received its title from its first chapter.

It cannot in any way belong to the Venerable Bede. Rather, it is by some Benedictine monk who is not earlier than the eleventh or twelfth century. The matters recounted in chapter 1—monasteries very frequently being seized and usurped by laypeople, and their possessions being squandered by the abbots and prelates themselves—cannot possibly fit the time of the Venerable Bede.

Let us hear this anonymous author:

> What, I ask, could be worse than that monasteries, built by ancient princes for the praise of God and the veneration of the memory of his saints, should now be destroyed because of the insatiable greed of certain people? For what religious person, observing how well known divine commands and miracles and the teaching of the holy Fathers now are to very many, would not immediately infer that the destruction of monasteries—carried out not only by laypeople eager to seize and plunder their estates, but also by clerics and the abbots themselves, who voluntarily offer up as if they were saleable certain goods entrusted to them, goods from which not only the monks but also the household entrusted to them, as well as the poor and visiting pilgrims, were to be supported—means the destruction of the holy Church? Who would not immediately grieve that the ancient enemy has been able to inflict such wickedness and persecution upon Christians through other Christians, and especially through those who have been appointed pastors of the Church?
>
> For if such destruction of holy places were carried out by barbarians, they would have to be restrained by war waged by Christians, if they could not otherwise be corrected.
