But, alas, such peace and harmony prevail in this wickedness that, with very few exceptions, there are none who care about the misery of so great a persecution, as though they were ignorant of the Christian religion and had forgotten that all monasteries were built for the honor of Christ and his saints.
>
> What I say is pitiable to relate, but far more pitiable in practice, since those who were specially chosen to live in monasteries under religious and spiritual discipline, to serve God, and continually to intercede for the salvation of those who are still unable to restrain themselves from worldly pomp, are deprived of the possessions necessary for their daily food and clothing, and so forth.

These matters certainly do not fit the time of Bede, but do fit the period when the Church was afflicted in the eleventh century on account of the investitures, in the time of Pope Gregory VII. During the disorders arising from them, laypeople plundered and destroyed monasteries.

Second, this anonymous author expressly indicates that he is writing after the year 1000 and consequently not before the eleventh century:

> But because our adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, continually prowls about, seeking someone to devour, and because, alas, among so many thousands of people more are now found fragile than strong against that same adversary, it is necessary for all the faithful, as they too go about seeking how they may resist so great an adversary, to instruct and admonish one another in various ways, lest the holy Church, well founded and supported in the times that have passed, be utterly destroyed in our times, in which, after a thousand years have been completed, Satan appears to have been released, according to the prophecy foretold in the Apocalypse.

For he does not deceive people only by hidden snares, as before, but also breaks forth openly, overthrowing even the most learned and inciting them to every kind of evil.

Finally, later, when he speaks of the administration of the divine office, he calls it “divine service,” an expression that seems to me not to have been used before the twelfth century. Thus whoever takes away from the monks the estates from which they are to be supported is shown to be a destroyer both of divine service and of the whole monastic religion. This little book, therefore, cannot in any way be by Bede.

### *Περὶ Διδάξεων* (“On Teachings”), or *On the Elements of Philosophy*, Four Books, fol. 206.

These belong to William of Conches, the great philosopher of the twelfth century, who flourished around 1140, and who was attacked by many for his unusual opinions, especially by Saint Bernard and his followers, William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, and others.

Anyone who doubts this should consult the Parisian libraries, where a manuscript is preserved entitled *The Lesser Philosophy* of this William of Conches, including, among others, the Colbert manuscript Cod. 6109 and the Victorine manuscript, shelfmark MM 17, fol. 172, where this same work is attributed to William of Conches. A third manuscript in the library of Leiden, among the Latin manuscripts no. 96, should also be consulted. Its existence is recorded in the catalogue of that library, p. 404, printed in quarto at Leiden in 1674.

William of Conches reveals himself and the speeches he had to endure from his rivals in the preface to Book II. These words cannot in any way apply to the Venerable Bede:

> We preferred to put forward the naked truth rather than a disguised falsehood. But who is there to whom the dryness of our speech would be displeasing, if he knew the occupations of our mind? We have not sought ornament in our speech; rather, he will marvel at what we are doing. For what room could there be for ornament when we must consider what and how we should read, then explain it through reading, declaim against falsehoods in disputations, judge the discoveries of others, and sharpen our tongue against the slanders of the envious? Thus what was said of the children of Israel has now been fulfilled in us: while rebuilding the Temple, they held a sword in one hand and a stone in the other.

William of Conches further betrays himself in the preface to Book III, where he writes:

> Although, being occupied with the work of teaching, we have little time for writing, nevertheless, since we know that many have cut away parts of philosophy and, having seized the scraps, have gone away believing that the whole of it had fallen to them, we have been roused by the voice of philosophy itself crying out, lest she remain naked. We sew the severed pieces together with the pen of our small ability, not unaware that we are exposed to the bites of envy, since today it is dangerous both to know and to possess.

By these words William of Conches, a Norman, alludes to many masters of philosophy who, having abandoned the schools—of which they had founded many philosophical ones at Paris—left both their profession and this city because of the scarcity of students.

These circumstances certainly cannot apply to Bede, who could never have complained that, being occupied with teaching, he had little time for writing, since he himself composed so many works. The preface to Book IV likewise identifies William of Conches as the author of the work. But this is enough.

[Col. 0080D] ### *Letter on the Vernal Equinox According to Anatolius*, p. 230.

This certainly belongs to Bede. Bede himself mentions it in his catalogue of works, which he composed at the end of his *History* in 731; therefore this letter was written before that year.

Accordingly, the example in the letter addressed to the most reverend priest Wichred, concerning the present year 776, is an interpolation by the scribe who copied the letter in that year and wished to explain Bede’s statement by means of a supplied example. John Mabillon says this in his eulogy of the Venerable Bede, no. 29, Volume I of the third century of the *Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*.

Peter Francis Chiffletius, however, published this letter in a pure form, free of every addition, before Bede’s *History*, p. 13, in quarto, at Paris in 1681, by Gabriel Martin, on the Rue Saint-Jacques, under the Golden Sun.

### *On the Divination of Life and Death*, p. 233; *The Likeness of Noah’s Ark*, p. 235; *Treatise on the Languages of the Nations*, ibid.; *Interpretation of the Sibylline Words*, p. 236.

These are trifling productions utterly unworthy of being attributed to this Venerable Priest, as will be clear to anyone who reads them, even at first glance.

# CHAPTER THREE  
## On the Third Volume of the Works of the Venerable Bede

As regards Volume III of the works of Bede the priest, there are far more spurious than genuine works. Concerning them John Mabillon writes as follows in his distinguished *Eulogy of Bede*, nos. 29–30:

> He composed a book on the six ages, which he completed in the ninth year of Leo the Isaurian, A.D. 724. After completing this, he published the *Ecclesiastical History of His Nation*, which he finished together with the accompanying Epitome in 731. For in the excellent manuscript that we possess, the aforesaid Epitome does not extend beyond that year, as we noted above. Below, the *Lives of the Saints* should likewise be placed among the doubtful works, except for the acts of Saints Felix, Cuthbert, and Anastasius, which Bede acknowledges as his own.

Thus all, or at least most, of the works in this volume are spurious. It will not be a waste of time to discuss them at length.

### *Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation*, presented to Ceolwulf, king of the English.

### *Epitome of the Same History*, to the year 731.

Bede mentions this work in the catalogue of his writings, which he himself appended to the end of the said Epitome, so that no one could ever doubt its authorship. Although in many printed editions and manuscript codices this Epitome extends to the year 766, in other printed and manuscript codices it does not exceed the year 731. Thus the additional material must have been added by some anonymous writer.

Bede’s English history has so far appeared in three forms.

First, by itself: at Strasbourg in 1514; at Antwerp in 1550, in small folio; at Cologne in duodecimo in 1601; and at Cambridge in an Anglo-Saxon folio edition in 1644, with an English translation by King Alfred.

Second, it appeared together with several older writers on British affairs, at Heidelberg, from the press of Commelinus, in folio, in 1587. Many copies of this same edition were falsely claimed by Renatus Potelerius, a printer of Lyon, as having been printed by him at Lyon in the same year, 1587, after changing the title page, and he offered them for sale under his own name. Thus one would search in vain for a Lyon edition of that year different from the Heidelberg edition.

Third and finally, Bede’s English history appeared with his other works, through Francis Jamet, in three volumes in 1544; there in eight volumes in 1554; likewise at Basel in eight volumes in 1563, through John Herwagen; and finally at Cologne in the same number of volumes in 1612, through Antonius Hierat.

This is what Chiffletius says in the notes at the end of this edition of the *History*, p. 319. He had it printed in a form corrected against manuscript codices, finally at Paris in quarto in 1681, by Gabriel Martin, on the Rue Saint-Jacques, under the Golden Sun.

### *Life of Saint Cuthbert, Bishop of Lindisfarne*, together with

### *Life of Saint Felix, Bishop of Nola in Campania*.

These certainly belong to Bede. He himself mentions them in the catalogue of his works at the end of his *Epitome of the English History*.

### *Life of Saint Vedast, Bishop of Arras*.

This does not belong to Bede but to an anonymous Gaul.

### *Lives of Saints Columbanus, Attala, and Eustasius, Abbots of Luxeuil*.

All of these belong to Jonas, a monk of Luxeuil, distinguished around the year 630. He wrote about the first abbots of Luxeuil. Labbeus discusses him in his *Dissertation on Ecclesiastical Writers*, volume I, under the entry “Jonas, monk of Luxeuil.” John Mabillon also treats him learnedly in his Benedictine centuries, where he discusses Saints Columbanus, Attala, and Eustasius. The reader should consult that work.

### *Life of Saint Patrick* in Two Books.

This belongs to a certain Probus, as is clear from the end of the work. The Bollandist associates, or Bollandus himself, speak of him at tiresome length in the legends and notes on the *Acts of Saint Patrick, Apostle of the Irish*.

### *Life of Saint Bertulf, Abbot of Bobbio*.

This was written by the same Jonas mentioned above.

### *Life of Saint Arnulf, Bishop of Metz*.

This is a work of Paul the Deacon, who is said to have written it on the basis of the accounts of elders who had once known Arnulf.

Finally, the *Life of Saint Burgundofara, Abbess*, is attributed to Bede by many. It certainly cannot belong to Bede, since its author, when discussing certain miracles, cites as witnesses Burgundofara herself, Saint Faro, bishop of Meaux, and Saint Waldebert, abbot of Luxeuil, thereby making himself their contemporary. But none of this can apply to Bede, who was flourishing in 730 and never left England, and therefore could not have been a witness to miracles heard from the bishop of Meaux or the abbot of Luxeuil.

### *Passion of Saint and Most Blessed Justin the Martyr*.

This has no connection with Bede whatsoever.

### *Martyrology as It Appears in the Works of the Venerable Bede*.

This does not belong to Bede. It is certainly true that Bede wrote such a work, as he himself testifies in 731 in the catalogue of his writings, in these words:

> A Martyrology of the birthdays of the holy martyrs, in which I have diligently endeavored to record all whom I was able to discover—not only the day on which they triumphed, but also the kind of contest by which they conquered the world, or under which judge.

Thus, after Eusebius and Jerome—though it is not sufficiently clear what was actually done by them in this field—the Venerable Bede was the first to compile a Martyrology through private study. Usuard praises Bede’s Martyrology in his own.

Bede himself also includes it in the catalogue of his works. Although the Basel edition of 1563 makes no mention of his Martyrology, it is explicitly included in the other editions, and also in the Saxon translation of King Alfred, which Abraham Whelocus brought to light in 1644.

Nevertheless, Bede left one hundred and eighty days without names in his Martyrology. Usuard speaks of this, and Florus of Lyon, the deacon, supplied many of them, though not all, as Ado, archbishop of Vienne, testifies in the preface to his Martyrology.

Learned men long awaited Bede’s genuine work, but at last the Bollandist associates published it after discovering it, comparing it with various manuscript codices, and purging it as far as possible of various interpolations. They published it in Volume II of their *March*, together with the additions of Florus of Lyon the deacon and others. The addition of Florus was printed in smaller type so that it would not again be confused with Bede’s text.

Even in this genuine Martyrology of the Venerable Bede, however, it is uncertain whether the feast of All Saints ought to have a place, since Bede lived only four years after the accession of Pope Gregory III, who instituted this solemnity.

This demonstrates how difficult it is to restore works interpolated by later writers to their original purity and integrity.

Apart from Bede’s prose Martyrology, another metrical work has been published under his name in volume X of the *Spicilegium*, pp. 126 ff., in heroic verse. John Mabillon retrieved it from a very ancient Codex of Saint Remigius at Reims [Col. 0083B]. Whether this metrical Martyrology is truly Bede’s, or belongs to some industrious scholar who rendered the prose work into verse, I cannot readily determine. Certainly the Remigian Codex, which is at least eight hundred years old, bears this title: “Here begins the Martyrology which Bede composed in heroic verse.” Yet in his *Epitome* Bede seems to have indicated not a metrical but a prose work; nor does the metrical text entirely agree with the prose Martyrology printed by the Bollandists. Perhaps Bede himself composed the metrical work after completing the *Epitome*, though I would not wish to assert this. In fact, the Remigian copy was written no more than a century after his death, through the diligence of Bertigarius the monk, during the pontificate of Ebo, archbishop of Reims [Col. 0083C].

This Martyrology does not begin on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, but on the very Kalends of January. Several saints who are found in Bede’s prose Martyrology in Henschenius are omitted from the metrical one: in January, Pope Auterus, Salvius in Africa, Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, Felix, presbyter of Nola, and Pope Marcellus; in February, Scholastica; and so on; Mellitus in April; Augustine in May; and so forth. Its author is inferred to have been an Englishman from the various English saints it contains. He is conjectured, indeed, to have been a monk of the monastery at Girwy, on the basis of the Feast of the Dedication, which is recorded on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, although the *Monasticon Anglicanum* states that the Dedication of the Girwy church took place on the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

No saints later than Bede are celebrated in this Martyrology [Col. 0083D]: neither Saint Boniface of Mainz nor any other illustrious saint; indeed, no one later than the younger Saint Wilfrid, who is mentioned in April. Wilfrid died in 732, one year after Bede completed his history. It is therefore unsurprising that Bede does not list the metrical Martyrology in his catalogue of works, since he survived the younger Wilfrid by only three years.

Thus Lucas Dacherius introduces that Martyrology. Anyone wanting more should read the said Dacherius in the prolegomena to volume X of the *Spicilegium*; the Bollandists in the prolegomena to volume II of the month of March; John Mabillon in the preface to volume II of the fourth century of the Benedictine order, chapter 6, fol. 85, no. 170; and in his *Eulogy of the Venerable Bede* in volume I of the third century of the Benedictine order, no. 34, p. 560.

[Col. 0084A] The little book *On the Holy Places* seems to me to be Bede’s, since at the end of the work he names himself, although it was omitted from Bede’s catalogue of works—perhaps because it was written after that catalogue itself.

*Interpretations of the Hebrew Names of Scripture*, arranged in alphabetical order, are found anonymously in manuscript in many libraries. But in the Victorine Library at Paris, under the shelfmarks QQ 22 and QQ 19, and elsewhere, they are attributed to Remigius of Auxerre, a monk who flourished at the beginning of the tenth century. After examining manuscripts of the finest quality, I have no doubt that this work belongs to him.

*Excerpts from the Fathers; Collections; Flowers from Various Sources; Questions and Parables.*

Bellarminus speaks of these works as follows in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year 720, third observation concerning the works of the Venerable Bede [Col. 0084B]:

“Likewise, among the *Collections* and *Flowers* contained in the third volume, there is almost nothing worthy of Bede’s intellect. A *Collection on the Lights of the Church* is also found in the fourth volume of Saint Jerome’s works, but it belongs neither to Jerome nor to Bede. The *Collection on the Four Kinds of Wood in the Lord’s Cross* contains nothing substantial. The little prayer in which the three Jameses are invoked, and the other in which the angels Uriel and Rumiel are invoked, are far removed from Bede’s gravity and learning.”

## CHAPTER FOUR. On the Fourth Volume of the Works of the Venerable Bede

*Hexameron*, or *A Little Book on the Creation of the Six Days.*

*Exposition on Genesis.*

[Col. 0084C] *Explanation of Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.*

*Allegorical Exposition of the Four Books of Kings*, in four books.

*Thirty Questions on the Books of Kings.*

*Allegorical Exposition of the Prophets Ezra and Nehemiah*, in three books.

*Allegorical Exposition of the Book of Tobit.*

*Commentary on the Book of Job*, in three books.

*Exposition of Solomon’s Proverbs*, in three books.

*Exposition of the Song of Songs*, in seven books.

*Exposition on the Tabernacle, Its Vessels, and the Priests’ Vestments*, in three books.

Of all these works contained in this fourth volume of Bede’s writings, there is no doubt that they belong to him, since he himself mentions each of them in his catalogue of works, which he compiled in 731 [Col. 0084D]. Only the commentary on the Book of Job, written in three books, is disputed. Indeed, there should be no doubt, since it does not belong to Bede in any way, but to a certain Philip, a presbyter and disciple of Saint Jerome, who presented this work to someone named Nectarius.

We have already spoken of him under the year 330, at the entry “Philip the presbyter,” but here it is useful to remove this work more fully from the Venerable Bede. First, Gennadius, who was writing in 494, mentions it in his work *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 62, and attributes it to Philip—more than two hundred years before Bede. Therefore no one should doubt that this work is Philip’s. We saw it in manuscript in a very ancient Codex of the library at Igny, in the Reims region, with Gennadius’s authority prefixed to the work [Col. 0085A].

Second, Bede himself, in his little book *On the Calculation of Unciae*, assigns these very commentaries to their proper author, saying:

“Many unlearned people are perplexed because Philip, in his exposition of blessed Job, while describing the heat of the Ocean sea, added that this three-quarter portion of the equinoctial hour comes later without interruption, whether by day or by night.”

This passage cited by Bede is found in the *Expositions on Job* that Hervagius recently printed under Philip’s name, book III, in the explanation of the statement: “Have you entered into the depths of the sea?” (Job 38). Thus writes Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca sancta*, book IV, fol. 289. Therefore, according to Bede himself, this commentary belongs to Philip, as we said above.

Third, Faustus, bishop of Riez in Gaul, in his little book *Against Those Who Say That There Is Something Incorporeal in Created Things*, no. 7, quotes words from this commentary on Job under the name of Saint Jerome, in order to prove that souls and angels are corporeal. In connection with Job 25:5, “The stars are not clean in his sight,” he cites the following from these commentaries: “They suppose that the globes of the stars are embodied spirits.” And again: “If the heavenly bodies of angels are said to be unclean in comparison with God, what do you think a human being should be considered?” Both statements are found in these commentaries.

Therefore these commentaries already existed in the time of Faustus, bishop of Riez, around the year 475 or 480. Consequently, since they are cited approximately two hundred years before Bede lived, they cannot in any way be a work composed by that Venerable presbyter. As for Faustus’s attribution of them to Saint [Col. 0085C] Jerome, this has no bearing on the question at hand. It was very easy for Faustus to attribute to the master what belonged to the disciple, and he may perhaps have done so deliberately in order to secure greater authority for his unusual opinion.

Fourth, this same work was printed under the name of Philip the presbyter in 1527 at Basel by Adam Petri, both in quarto and in folio in the same year—a very rare circumstance—and long before it was printed under the name of Bede the presbyter. The latter occurred only in the Paris edition of all Bede’s works, published in 1554 by Franciscus Jametius, who collected them in eight volumes. Although this work is included among Bede’s writings, it is nevertheless much more accurately edited both in the separate Basel edition of 1527 and among the complete works of Saint Jerome, where it is also found. Let this observation suffice for the forthcoming edition [Col. 0085D].

## CHAPTER FIVE. On the Fifth and Sixth Volumes of the Works of the Venerable Bede

The following short works are contained in the fifth volume of Bede’s works:

*Exposition on the Gospel of Matthew*, in four books, p. 1.

*Exposition on the Gospel of Mark*, in four books, p. 92.

*Exposition on the Gospel of Luke*, in six books, p. 217.

*Exposition on the Gospel of John*, p. 451.

*Exposition on the Acts of the Apostles*, p. 625.

*On the Names of the Places or Cities Mentioned in the Book of Acts*, p. 666.

*Exposition on the Seven Catholic Epistles*, p. 673.

[Col. 0086A] *Explanation of the Apocalypse of Blessed John the Apostle*, p. 761.

As for the expositions on the Gospel of Mark, the Gospel of Luke, the Acts of the Apostles, the seven Catholic Epistles, and the Apocalypse of John the Apostle, it is certain that all belong to Bede, since he himself mentions them in his catalogue of works, compiled in 731. Only three are disputed: the exposition on the Gospel of Matthew, the exposition on the Gospel of John, and the book on the names of the places or cities mentioned in Acts. I shall discuss each briefly.

Most people reject the exposition on the Gospel of Matthew, fol. 1, as spurious, although they offer no reason for this condemnation, contenting themselves with the fact that Bede’s catalogue is silent about the work. This is the judgment of John Mabillon in his *Eulogy of the Venerable Bede*, in the third century of the saints of the order of Saint Benedict, volume I, paragraph 10, no. 30 [Col. 0086B]:

“The expositions on Matthew’s Gospel, the commentary on the Psalms, and the Lives of the Saints, except for certain works, should be relegated to the class of doubtful writings.”

The same judgment is given by Natalis Alexander, who here abridged Mabillon, in the selected chapters of his *Ecclesiastical History*, eighth century, chapter 3, article 2, p. 255. I was not permitted to read the work, and therefore confess that I do not know whether there are grounds for suspecting it. Those who wish to devote themselves to publishing Bede’s works in a polished form will deal with this question.

The commentaries on the Gospel of John appear to have Bede as their author [Col. 0086C], and are therefore believed to have been published by him after 731. They appear to be a kind of abridgment of Augustine’s exposition, with statements from other Fathers inserted here and there. Thus, in chapter 4, when discussing Regulus, the text cites words of Saint Gregory the Great. Certainly Jonas, bishop of Orléans and a contemporary of Louis the Pious, cites several verses from Bede in his twentieth homily on the Gospel, which are found in the aforementioned commentaries, chapter 2. Accordingly, we suspect that Jonas should read “in the second homily on the Gospel.” Alcuin, moreover, in the preface to his commentary on John’s Gospel, admits that he took much from the homilies of blessed Bede the presbyter.

It therefore seems to me beyond doubt that this exposition belongs to Bede, as Mabillon likewise holds in the place cited [Col. 0086D]. Furthermore, when Bede lay ill with his final sickness, he rendered the Gospel of John into his native language, as his disciple Cuthbert testifies in the letter he wrote concerning Bede’s death.

The book on the names of the places and cities mentioned in Acts belongs to the same author, on the evidence of the manuscript Codices I have seen. The *Interpretations of the Hebrew Names of Sacred Scripture*, arranged alphabetically, belong to the same person whom we identified when examining the third volume of Bede’s works—namely, Remigius of Auxerre, the monk, as we said there.

The sixth volume of the works of the Venerable Bede properly contains only three works: *Retractations on the Acts of the Apostles*, p. 1, with a few questions; *Exposition on the Fourteen Epistles of Saint Paul the Apostle*, p. 31; and *Sermons of Saint John Chrysostom on the Praises of Saint Paul*, p. 824.

It is certain that these sermons on the praises of Saint Paul belong to Saint John, bishop of Constantinople. It is equally certain that the *Retractations on the Acts of the Apostles* belong to Bede. The question concerns the enormous commentaries on the fourteen Epistles of Saint Paul, compiled from the words of Saint Augustine: do they belong to Bede or to a certain Florus, a deacon of the Church of Lyons?

To settle this question, I shall use the words of John Mabillon himself, who in volume I of his *Analecta*, p. 12, gives a special investigation of the commentaries on Paul’s Epistles by the Venerable Bede and Florus, deacon of Lyons, based on the statements of Saint Augustine.

[Col. 0087B] “I find,” he says, “three ancient authors who composed commentaries on the Epistles of the Apostle Paul from nothing but excerpts stitched together from Saint Augustine. The first is Peter, abbot of the province of Tripoli, who is said to have annotated Saint Paul’s Epistles from chapters of the little works of blessed Augustine, ‘so that through another’s mouth he might reveal the secret of his own heart,’ as Cassiodorus says in book 8 of *On Divine Readings*.

“The second is the Venerable Bede, whose words occur at the end of his *Epitome of the History*: ‘Whatever I found said about the Apostle in the little works of Saint Augustine, I took care to transcribe in order.’

“The third is Florus the deacon—or, as it seemed to Wandalbert, a monk of Prüm and his contemporary, the subdeacon—of the Church of Lyons, a man distinguished in his time for learning and education [Col. 0087C].

“Of these three commentaries, we possess one among the works of the Venerable Bede, bearing his name; but whether it ought truly to be attributed to Bede has long been a matter of great dispute among scholars. Robert, abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael, testifies to this in the prologue he prefixed to his *Abbreviation of the Exposition of the Apostle’s Epistles According to Augustine*. In this prologue, published by Lucas Dacherius in an appendix to Guibert, Robert judges that the lengthy commentary—which I have no doubt is the same work that now exists among Bede’s works—should rather be attributed to Peter, abbot of Tripoli, than to Bede. To Bede he assigns another, shorter work, likewise excerpted from the books of Saint Augustine:

“‘That book,’ he says, ‘does not equal in size even half of the exposition of the Epistle to the Romans alone, which is found in the other lengthy commentary’ [Col. 0087D].

“Long after Robert the abbot, the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius, under the year of Christ 562, judged that those printed commentaries were not Bede’s but Peter the abbot’s, agreeing with Robert on this point. But he differs from him in denying that Bede composed any such commentary on Paul, asserting that the words of Bede which I cited above entered his *Epitome* through an addition by someone else.

“Bellarminus disagrees with Baronius in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year 720, second observation concerning Bede’s works. He says that nothing prevents two authors—Peter the abbot and Bede the presbyter—from having labored at different times and in different places to explain Paul from Augustine’s writings. Indeed, nothing prevents us from adding a third to these two, Florus of Lyons, the deacon, as I shall demonstrate later [Col. 0088A].

“Although matters stand thus, the votes of scholars remain divided concerning the published commentary: some judge it Bede’s, while others withdraw it from him. For my part, when I once composed Bede’s eulogy in the third century of the Benedictine order, it seemed to me to be Bede’s genuine offspring. But later, after discovering in manuscript libraries a genuine commentary by Bede, I was compelled to abandon that opinion.

“That Bede assembled some commentary on Paul from the statements of Saint Augustine ought to be the settled conviction of everyone. Bede explicitly testifies to this in his *Epitome*, and both printed and manuscript books support him. Moreover, Hincmar, archbishop of Reims [Col. 0088B], and Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, praise this commentary by Bede.

“Hincmar says in his later work *On Predestination Against Gottschalk*, chapter 1: ‘If anyone nevertheless does not possess those same books, let him consult the collection of the Venerable Bede the presbyter, drawn from the works of Saint Augustine on the Apostle. There he will be able to learn what he previously did not know.’

“Lupus, in Letter 76 to that same Hincmar, writes: ‘I hesitated to send Bede’s collection on the Apostle from Augustine’s works, because the book is so large that it could neither be hidden in one’s bosom nor conveniently carried in a satchel.’

“Therefore no one can now question whether Bede published a collection on the Apostle; nor would Baronius have doubted it had he considered the arguments I have just presented. But we must now examine what sort of commentary this Bede’s work is [Col. 0088C].

“I found two parchment Codices containing such a collection under Bede’s name, one nearly eight hundred years old and the other seven hundred. The first Codex bears this title: ‘Bede’s Collection on the Apostle from the Works of Blessed Augustine.’ The commentary then begins with the words, ‘Paul, servant of Jesus Christ, is called an Apostle,’ and proceeds as follows: ‘From the book Against the Five Heresies. This order must be followed: when speaking of the Gospel, I must not be silent about the prophets.’ This Codex ends in the Epistle to the Thessalonians, with other leaves torn away.

“The second Codex is entitled: ‘Here begins the book of the Collections of the Venerable Bede the presbyter, compiled from the writings of blessed Augustine the bishop and elaborated on the Epistles of blessed Paul the Apostle.’ It has the same beginning as the first. It ends as follows [Col. 0088D]: ‘Here ends the Collection of Bede the presbyter, from the little works of blessed Augustine, on the Epistles of blessed Paul the Apostle.’

“We possess a copy of this genuine commentary of Bede, not yet printed, which, God willing, we shall someday bring to light together with other monuments of this kind.”

Thus John Mabillon in the place cited, where he also offers further arguments proving that the commentary on the Epistles of Saint Paul, printed among Bede’s works from the words of Saint Augustine, unquestionably belongs to Florus, deacon of Lyons. We too shall establish this later, in the ninth century, under Florus the deacon.”

## CHAPTER SIX. On the Seventh Volume of the Works of the Venerable Bede

This volume contains:

*Thirty-three Summer Homilies on the Liturgical Season*, p. 1.

[Col. 0089A] *Thirty-two Summer Homilies on the Saints*, p. 91.

*Fifteen Winter Homilies on the Liturgical Season*, p. 183.

*Twenty-two Lenten Homilies*, p. 218.

*Sixteen Winter Homilies on the Saints*, p. 290.

*Twenty-two Various Sermons to the People*, p. 339.

Thus, according to the printed editions, the homilies or sermons of the Venerable Bede have grown to one hundred and forty. Yet in the ancient manuscript Codices there are only forty-nine. One is therefore compelled to marvel at the impudence of modern scholars over approximately the past two hundred years, who, without foundation or reason, and in order to attribute everything to their own conjectures, preferences, or fantasies, have not merely enlarged the writings of the ancient Fathers with innumerable extraneous works but corrupted them, to the great disgrace of the Church.

This shows how necessary and beneficial it is for the Christian commonwealth to return to the manuscript Codices now collected in considerable number in the principal libraries of Europe, so that, by comparing the editions with them, spurious works may be separated from genuine, false from true, and certain from uncertain [Col. 0089B].

A notable example of this matter is provided by the sufficiently rare manuscript Codices of the sermons of the Venerable Bede the presbyter, now held in the Colbert Library under numbers 102 and 1062, formerly in the Thuanean Library under numbers 144 and 38. In the first, no. 144, written eight hundred years ago, thirty-nine homilies are presented in continuous sequence. In the other, no. 38, which is six hundred years old, they are divided into two books, with tables of contents prefixed to each.

John Mabillon collated and reproduced both copies in his *Eulogy of Bede*, paragraph 31. We reproduce them after him because this accords with our purpose and provides a substantial demonstration of the modern audacity involved in interpolating the writings of the ancient doctors of the Church [Col. 0089C].

The later Codex proceeds as follows:

### HERE BEGINS THE TABLE OF CONTENTS OF BOOK I OF THE HOMILIES OF BEDE THE PRESBYTER, NUMBERING TWENTY-FIVE

1. Homily on the reading of the holy Gospel according to Luke, “THE ANGEL GABRIEL WAS SENT.” In the first Codex: “Homily of the lord Bede.” In both it begins after the Gospel words: “Today’s reading from the holy Gospel commends the beginning of our Redemption,” and so forth, as in the printed editions for the Feast of the Annunciation of blessed Mary.

2. Homily on the reading of the holy Gospel according to Luke, “MARY ARISING,” and so forth. In both it begins: “The reading from the holy Gospel that you have heard.” It is printed among the summer homilies on the saints.

3. Homily on the reading of the holy Gospel according to Mark, “JOHN WAS IN THE DESERT.” In the earlier Codex: “Homily of the lord Bede, ON THE ADVENT OF THE LORD.” In both it begins: “John, preceding the coming of the Lord’s preaching,” and so forth.

4. Homily on the reading of the holy Gospel according to John, “JOHN BEARS WITNESS.” It begins: “The precursor of our Redemption, bearing witness about him,” and so forth. It is absent from the earlier Codex.

5. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “WHEN SHE HAD BEEN BETROTHED.” In the earlier Codex: “Homily of the lord Bede, ON THE VIGIL OF THE LORD.” In both it begins: “The birth of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ, who is eternal before the ages,” and so forth.

6. Homily on the holy Gospel according to Luke, “THE SHEPHERDS WERE SPEAKING.” It begins: “When the Lord was born in Bethlehem,” and so forth, as in the printed editions. It is absent from the first Codex. Nevertheless, it is cited by Jonas, bishop of Orléans, book II of *On Lay Instruction*, chapter 16.

7. Homily on the holy Gospel according to John, “IN THE BEGINNING WAS THE WORD.” In the earlier Codex: “Homily of the lord Bede, ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD.” In both it begins: “Because the temporal coming of the Mediator of God and human beings,” and so forth, as in the printed editions.

8. Homily on the holy Gospel according to John, “JESUS SAID TO PETER, FOLLOW ME,” to be delivered ON THE NATIVITY OF SAINT JOHN THE EVANGELIST. In both it begins: “The reading of the holy Gospel that has just been read to us.”

9. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “THE ANGEL OF THE LORD APPEARED,” to be delivered ON THE NATIVITY OF THE INNOCENTS. In both it begins: “Concerning the precious death of the martyrs of Christ, the Innocents,” and so forth, as in the printed editions.

10. Homily on the Gospel according to Luke, “WHEN THE EIGHT DAYS WERE COMPLETED,” to be delivered ON THE OCTAVE OF THE LORD. It begins in both: “The holy and venerable remembrance of the present feast,” and so forth, as in the printed editions.

Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “THE ANGEL OF THE LORD APPEARED,” to be delivered ON THE VIGIL OF THE EPIPHANY. There is no homily in either copy.

11. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “THEN JESUS CAME FROM GALILEE TO THE JORDAN.” In the earlier Codex: “Homily of the lord Bede, ON THE HOLY DAY OF THE THEOPHANY.” In both it begins [Col. 0090C]: “The reading of the holy Gospel that we have just heard, brothers,” and so forth, as in the printed editions for the octave day.

12. Homily on the Gospel according to Luke, “JESUS’ PARENTS WENT EVERY YEAR.” In the first Codex: “Homily of the lord Bede, THE FIRST SUNDAY AFTER THE THEOPHANY.” In both it begins: “The reading of the holy Gospel has been opened to us, dearest brothers,” and so forth, as in the printed editions.

13. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “A WEDDING TOOK PLACE.” In the first Codex: “Homily of the lord Bede, THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER THE THEOPHANY.” In both it begins: “When our Lord and Savior was invited to a wedding,” and so forth, as in the printed editions.

14. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “JOHN SAW JESUS COMING TOWARD HIM.” In the earlier Codex: “Homily of the lord Bede, THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER THE THEOPHANY.” In both it begins: “John the Baptist and precursor of the Lord.” But it does not appear in the table of contents of the later Codex.

15. Homily on the Gospel according to Luke, “WHEN THE DAYS WERE FULFILLED,” to be delivered ON THE PURIFICATION OF HOLY MARY. In both Codices it begins: “The solemnity of today’s celebration,” and so forth, as in the printed editions.

16. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “IT WAS THE FEAST DAY OF THE JEWS.” It is absent from the first Codex. It begins: “Today’s reading from the holy Gospel conveys to us two miracles of human healing together.”

17. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “JESUS WANTED TO GO OUT INTO GALILEE.” In the first Codex: “Of the lord Bede, AFTER THE THEOPHANY.” It is absent from the later Codex. It begins: “We have heard from the reading of the Gospel, dearest brothers, the gracious mercy of our Redeemer.”

18. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “THE SON OF MAN WILL COME IN THE GLORY OF HIS FATHER.” In the first Codex: “Homily of the lord Bede, THE SECOND SUNDAY IN LENT.” In both it begins: “Because the Lord and our Redeemer,” and so forth.

19. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “JESUS WITHDRE INTO THE REGION OF TYRE,” and so forth. It is absent from the first Codex. It begins: “In the reading of the holy Gospel that has just been read to us,” and so forth. It appears in the printed editions for the Second Sunday of Lent.

20. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “JESUS WENT TO THE MOUNT OF OLIVES.” In the first Codex: “Homily of the lord Bede, THE THIRD SUNDAY OF LENT, ON THE SABBATH.” In both it begins [Col. 0091B]: “We should consider the reading of the present holy Gospel all the more attentively,” and so forth.

21. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “JESUS WENT ACROSS THE SEA OF GALILEE.” In the first Codex: “Homily of the lord Bede, IN LENT.” In both it begins: “When they rightly read the signs and miracles of our Lord and Savior,” and so forth, as in the printed editions for the Fourth Sunday of Lent.

22. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “JESUS WENT DOWN TO CAPERNAUM.” In the first Codex: “Homily of the lord Bede, MONDAY IN LENT.” In both it begins: “It is accustomed to trouble some people that at the beginning of this reading,” and so forth.

23. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “WHEN JESUS DREW NEAR TO JERUSALEM.” In the first Codex: “Homily of the lord Bede, ON PALM SUNDAY.” In both it begins [Col. 0091C]: “The mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who for the sake of the human race,” and so forth, as in the printed editions.

24. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “THE PASSOVER OF THE JEWS WAS NEAR.” It is absent from the first Codex. It begins: “It is customary for prudent people,” and so forth, as in the printed editions.

25. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “BEFORE THE FEAST OF THE PASSOVER.” In the first Codex: “Homily of the lord Bede, ON THE LORD’S SUPPER.” In both it begins: “When the evangelist John was about to write down that memorable mystery of the Lord,” and so forth, as in the printed editions.

After the first book of homilies, the later Codex reads: “Here ends the first book of the Homilies, numbering twenty-five.” Yet only twenty-three homilies are actually present in that Codex, the others being supplied from the first Codex.

The later Codex continues:

### HERE BEGINS THE TABLE OF CONTENTS OF THE READINGS OF THE HOLY GOSPEL, NUMBERING TWENTY-FOUR, IN BOOK II OF THE SAME AUTHOR

[Col. 0091D]

1. Homily on the holy Gospel according to Matthew, “IN THE EVENING OF THE SABBATH.” In the first Codex: “Homily of the lord Bede, ON THE VIGIL OF EASTER.” In both it begins: “The vigils of this most sacred night,” and so forth, as in the printed editions.

This homily was read at the vigil—that is, at the matins service—of Easter. Yet in the first Codex, a homily of Saint Gregory normally read on Holy Easter is inserted in this place. The same should be observed concerning the vigil of Pentecost below.

2. Homily on the Gospel according to Luke, “JESUS STOOD IN THE MIDST OF HIS DISCIPLES.” In the first Codex: “Homily of the lord Bede, TUESDAY IN EASTER.” In both it begins [Col. 0092A]: “The Lord and our Redeemer,” and so forth, as in the printed editions.

3. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “THE ELEVEN DISCIPLES.” In the first manuscript: “Homily of the lord Bede, FRIDAY IN EASTER.” In both it begins: “The Gospel reading, dearest brothers, which we have just heard,” and so forth, as in the printed editions.

4. Homily on the Gospel according to Luke, “ON THE FIRST DAY OF THE WEEK, VERY EARLY.” It is absent from the first Codex and from the printed editions. It begins: “A reading about the Resurrection of the Lord and our Redeemer has been recited to us, brothers.”

5. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “A LITTLE WHILE, AND YOU WILL NOT SEE ME.” In the first Codex: “Homily of the lord Bede, ON THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF EASTER.” In both it begins: “The joyful promises of the Lord and our Savior,” and so forth [Col. 0092B], as in the printed editions.

6. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “I AM GOING TO HIM WHO SENT ME.” In the first Codex: “Homily of the lord Bede, THE THIRD SUNDAY AFTER HOLY EASTER.” In both it begins: “As we have heard from the Gospel reading, dearest brothers,” and so forth, as in the printed editions.

7. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “IF YOU ASK THE FATHER FOR ANYTHING,” and so forth. It is absent from the first Codex. It begins: “It may trouble weak hearers,” and so forth, as in the printed editions.

8. Homily on the Gospel according to Luke, “ASK, AND IT WILL BE GIVEN TO YOU.” In the first Codex: “Homily of the lord Bede, ON THE GREATER LITANY.” In both it begins: “Our Lord and Savior, toward the joys of the heavenly kingdom,” and so forth. It is absent from the printed editions.

[Col. 0092C] 9. Homily on the Gospel according to Luke, “THESE ARE THE WORDS THAT I SPOKE,” to be delivered ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD. In both manuscript Codices it begins: “As the Lord was about to ascend into heaven,” and so forth; the printed editions have a different beginning.

10. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “WHEN THE PARACLETE COMES,” to be delivered ON THE SUNDAY AFTER THE LORD’S ASCENSION. In both manuscripts and in the printed editions it begins: “In many passages of the holy Gospel we find,” and so forth. This homily is cited by Amalarius, book I of *On the Offices*, chapter 37, and likewise book II, chapter 1.

11. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “IF YOU LOVE ME,” to be delivered ON THE VIGIL OF PENTECOST. In both manuscripts and in the printed editions it begins: “Because today, dearest brothers, we celebrate the coming of the Holy Spirit,” and so forth.

[Col. 0092D] 12. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “THERE WAS A MAN OF THE PHARISEES.” In the first Codex: “Homily of the lord Bede, ON THE OCTAVE OF PENTECOST.” In both it begins: “As you have heard from the reading of the holy Gospel, dearest brothers,” and so forth. It appears in the printed editions for the Feast of the Finding of the Holy Cross, and is cited in the letter that Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, wrote in the name of the Council of Tusey to Rodulfus, bishop of Bourges, and Frotarius, bishop of Bordeaux.

13. Homily on the Gospel according to Luke, “THERE WAS IN THE DAYS OF HEROD,” to be delivered ON THE VIGIL OF SAINT JOHN. In both the manuscript and printed editions it begins: “Our Lord and Redeemer, who was to come in the flesh,” and so forth.

14. Homily on the Gospel according to Luke, “ELIZABETH’S TIME TO GIVE BIRTH WAS FULFILLED,” to be delivered ON THE NATIVITY OF SAINT JOHN [Col. 0093A] THE BAPTIST. In both Codices and in the printed editions it begins: “The Nativity of the Lord’s precursor,” and so forth.

15. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “JESUS SAID TO SIMON PETER,” to be delivered ON THE VIGIL OF THE APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL. In both manuscript Codices and in the printed editions it begins: “The power of perfect love,” and so forth.

16. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “JESUS CAME INTO THE REGION OF CAESAREA,” to be delivered ON THE FEAST OF THE APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL. In both manuscript Codices and in the printed editions it begins: “The reading of the holy Gospel that we have just heard, brothers, should be considered all the more attentively,” and so forth.

17. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “SIMON PETER SAID TO JESUS, BEHOLD, WE HAVE LEFT EVERYTHING,” to be delivered ON THE FEAST OF SAINT BENEDICT, namely the bishop. It is absent from the first Codex, but present in the later one and in the printed editions. It begins [Col. 0093B]: “When Peter heard from the Lord,” and so forth.

18. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “THE MOTHER OF THE SONS OF ZEBEDEE APPROACHED JESUS,” to be delivered ON THE FEAST OF SAINT JAMES THE APOSTLE. The first Codex adds: “James, the brother of the Lord.” In both it begins, as in the printed editions: “The Lord, Creator and Redeemer, the wounds of our pride,” and so forth.

19. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “JESUS DEPARTED FROM THE REGION OF TYRE.” It is absent from the first Codex. It begins: “That deaf and mute man whom the Lord wondrously healed,” and so forth, as in the printed editions.

20. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “HEROD THE TETRARCH HEARD,” to be delivered ON THE BEHEADING OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST. It is absent from the first Codex. It begins: “As we celebrate, dearest brothers, the day of blessed John,” and so forth [Col. 0093C], as in the printed editions.

21. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “THE DEDICATION TOOK PLACE,” to be delivered ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH. In both it begins: “We have heard from the Gospel reading, dearest brothers, that the Dedication took place,” and so forth, as in the printed editions. In the later Codex this homily follows the next one; in the earlier Codex it precedes it.

22. Homily on the Gospel according to Matthew, “JESUS SAW A MAN SITTING AT THE TAX BOOTH,” to be delivered ON THE FEAST OF SAINT MATTHEW THE APOSTLE. In both it begins: “We read, as the Apostle says, that all have sinned,” and so forth, as in the printed editions.

23. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “JOHN WAS STANDING, AND TWO OF HIS DISCIPLES,” to be delivered ON THE FEAST OF SAINT ANDREW THE APOSTLE. In both Codices it begins: “So great and so lofty is the sublimity of divine Scripture,” and so forth, as in the printed editions, for the vigil of the feast.

24. Homily on the Gospel according to John, “JESUS WANTED TO GO OUT INTO GALILEE.” It is absent from the first Codex, since that copy is damaged; it is present in the other and begins: “We have heard from the Gospel reading, dearest brothers, the gracious mercy of our Redeemer.” It is absent from the printed editions.

The later Codex ends as follows: “Here ends the second book of the Homilies of Bede the presbyter, numbering twenty-four.”

From this we understand that all the homilies for every weekday of the Sundays of Lent, for the Sundays after Trinity, and for the feasts of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, Saint Scholastica, Saint Mary Magdalene, the Transfiguration of the Lord, the Assumption of blessed Mary, Saint Bartholomew, the Nativity and Conception of blessed Mary, Saint Michael, Saint Luke the Evangelist, the Presentation of blessed Mary, as well as others for the common of martyrs and so forth, are either spurious, doubtful, or at least extracted from Bede’s genuine commentaries on Mark and Luke [Col. 0094A].

I certainly have no doubt that in Bede’s time the Gospel was read in the churches in the manner found in these manuscript Codices. In those days there were not yet hired preachers of the Gospel who, because of Lazarus, would proclaim Christ to the people in the principal cities on each weekday of Lent; this practice arose only in the thirteenth century on the occasion of the mendicant orders. Consequently, the less familiar the Gospel was, the more eagerly it was received by the hearers and the more solemnly, with greater weight of words and greater sweetness, explained by those who proclaimed it.

Those who so disfigured these homilies of Bede by their interpolations that they turned forty-nine homilies into one hundred and forty arranged them according to the modern order of the distributed Gospel readings, which is scarcely four hundred years old, paying little attention to whether later critics might thereby accuse them of ignorance and negligence in their work.

We shall here briefly consider only the various homilies to the people, numbered XXII, most of which are altogether unworthy of the serious man whom we know the Venerable Bede to have been. The two homilies on Saint Wigbert cannot be by the Venerable Bede, who died twelve years before Wigbert, the abbot, died [Col. 0094C] in the year 747, on 13 August. Likewise, the homily on Saint Scholastica is attributed in a manuscript of Monte Cassino to Saint Bertharius, abbot of Cassino; it seems rather to belong to Paul the Lombard, the Cassinese deacon. The sermons on Saint Bartholomew the Apostle, John the Evangelist, the Finding of the Holy Cross, and the Chains of Saint Peter are so absurd and fabulous that they provoke laughter. The sermon customarily read on the feast of All Saints is attributed in some copies to Rabanus Maurus—I do not know whether correctly. This point is significant: the feast of All Saints was instituted by Pope Gregory III, as is proved by the oldest copies of Usuard and by Hugh Menard, in his commentary on Saint Gregory’s Sacramentary, p. 184; Gregory began to sit [as pope] in the year 731. Yet since this sermon has Bede’s style, [Col. 0094D] Bede may have composed it at the beginning of the institution of this festival.

*Scintillae*, or *Commonplaces from the Fathers*, p. 370, are attributed to Bede solely on conjecture, because he was accustomed to excerpt from others. For in all manuscripts—where they are extremely common in the ancient libraries of Gaul—they are invariably found anonymously. These *Scintillae* consist of eighty sermons on various subjects relating to virtues and vices. The Englishman Humphrey Wanley published in 1706, in folio, at Oxford, in the Sheldon Theatre, a book on ancient Northern literature in which, p. 180, he says that there exists in the library of Saint James at Westminster, among other works, a manuscript Book of *Scintillae*, or Sentences, which Bede collected both from Holy Scripture and from the writings of the Fathers and explained in an interlinear [Col. 0095A] Saxon version. Among the manuscript codices of the cathedral churches of England and of other celebrated libraries of that kingdom it exists as Codex 6622; in the manuscript codices of Charles Theyer, Codex 252, and manuscript codices 8135 and 8250; in the manuscript codices of the Jacobaean Library, Codices 413 and 528: the *Book of Scintillae* with an interlinear Saxon version.

The little book *On the Strong Woman*, p. 459, is not unworthy of the Venerable Bede. For it plays with highly appropriate allegories, which are not foreign to his genius, although I have nothing by which I can positively attribute it to him.

The little book *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, p. 467, excerpted from the sayings of certain Fathers, cannot belong to Bede. For when it speaks of seventy, sixty, fifty, and forty, it cites material taken from Anastasius, who wrote the *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, in the Life of Pope Melchiades. Yet no one is unaware how long before Anastasius Bede himself died. Thus no lengthy gloss is needed to remove this little work from Bede.

The fragments of allegorical interpretations of Solomon’s *Proverbs*, found in an ancient codex and printed on p. 476, are of uncertain authenticity and authorship.

## CHAPTER SEVEN  
### On the eighth and final volume of the works of the Venerable Bede

The little book *On Solomon’s Temple*, p. 1, is, in my judgment, not unworthy of being attributed to Bede; for it possesses a certain gravity and a reasonably Latin diction, not inconsistent with Bede’s style. I add that near the end of chapter 24 this author, in almost the final words, cites books on the Tabernacle and priestly vesture that he himself had written:

> We have spoken more fully of the table, the candlestick, both altars, and the foundation of the Lord’s house in the books that we wrote on the Structure of the Tabernacle and on Priestly Vesture.

Now this agrees with Bede, who, in the catalogue of his works composed by himself in the year 731, says that he wrote three books on the Tabernacle, its vessels, and the priests’ vestments. Finally, this work is written from earlier Fathers, as the preface testifies—a practice frequent and almost perpetual in Bede.

The little books *On the Creation of the Six Days*, p. 52, *Questions on Genesis*, p. 78, and [works] on Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, [Col. 0095D] Ruth, the four Books of Kings, together with the Book of Various Questions, are by one and the same author and do not belong to Bede. They rather belong to an author later than Bede, since this author, in his Questions on Genesis, cites once and again an alphabetical *Interpretation of Hebrew Names*, which manuscript codices attribute to Remigius of Auxerre, a monk famous for his learning around the year 900. Hence all these little works are by one author who did not precede the tenth century of the Church.

The *Commentary on the Book of Psalms*, p. 307, contains nothing by which it can be affirmed to be Bede’s; it should therefore be considered spurious.

The *Sermon on Psalm 52*, on the words “The Lord looked down from heaven,” etc., p. 902, is by one and the same author as the treatise entitled *On Substances*, which belongs to volume II of Bede’s works. For just as the first, so also this final work is addressed to clerics, and it makes, word for word, the same complaints against those who in his time were squandering the properties and monasteries necessary for the sustenance and clothing of monks, to the great detriment of the whole Church. Let us hear him, p. 909:

> I beg you, O rulers, attend to these things, and remembering what is written—“A VERY SEVERE JUDGMENT WILL BE UPON THOSE WHO RULE”—exhort one another to restore the destroyed monasteries: first, that the estates taken from them be returned to the monks; then, that those who fear the Lord and walk in his ways be placed before the others. For God has been especially offended by the fact that those places which had been assigned and consecrated to him and to his saints have been destroyed through the negligence of rulers. If those serving God in monasteries possessed what was necessary, they could certainly perform divine service more eagerly; they could pray more devotedly for the salvation of the king, bishops, and rulers, and also for the condition of the whole Church; they could likewise be corrected more freely by their pastors if any of them exceeded the rule of their profession. But, alas, all these matters are treated with such negligence by very many bishops, etc.

This same argument is pressed much more strongly here than in the book *On Substances*. Moreover, shortly before this the author reports testimony drawn from the *Life of Gregory the Great* by John the Deacon, written one hundred and fifty years after the death of Saint Bede. Finally, in the book *On Substances* he indicates that he is writing after the year 1000 of the Incarnation, as we have already noted there. This little work, therefore, by no means suits Bede.

The *Commentary on Boethius’s Book on the Trinity*, p. 925, reeks of the method of the recent scholastic school and is therefore far removed from Bede’s own times. It is rightly cast by all among the spurious works, into the babbling of the scholastic school.

The *Meditation on the Passion of Christ*, adapted to the seven canonical hours of the Office, p. 955, belongs not to Bede’s times, when such products of human invention did not yet exist, but to our own or to the preceding age, in which many such things were devised by devout people. Yet, when the very words or mysteries of the ecclesiastical Office are considered, it is far preferable to such novel inventions.

*On Remedies for Sins*, p. 961. Spelmann attributes this work to Egbert in volume I of the *Councils of England*, fol. 281, although Regino, abbot of Prüm, in his collection of canons, cites the *Penitential Book of Theodore, or Bede*, book I, chapter 297, and Ivo and Gratian quote from Bede’s *Penitential* the chapter on a priest vomiting up the Eucharist. These observations concern many works inscribed with the name of the Venerable Bede, but they could not necessarily be left unmentioned.

Let us now briefly set out, from John Mabillon’s eulogy of Bede, at the place cited, paragraph 34, certain genuine works of his that are lacking from the printed works of Bede, for the benefit of a fuller forthcoming edition.

The *Explanation of the Song of Habakkuk*, which Bede mentions in his catalogue and which exists in manuscript in Codex 275 of the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris. It begins as follows:

> The song of the prophet Habakkuk, which you asked to have explained to you, dearest sister in Christ, chiefly proclaims the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion. Hence, following the custom of the holy universal Church, on the sixth day of the week, on which that Passion was completed, it is solemnly repeated every week at the morning praises, etc.

It is also found in manuscript codices 1059 and 3587 of the Colbert Library.

The *Poem on Divine Judgment*, addressed to Bishop Acca, is lacking; it was published by Simeon of Durham in his *Book on the Deeds of the Kings of the English*, and is also attributed to Bede in a Colbert manuscript.

The *Letter on the Sixth Age of the World* to Plegwina, together with the *History of the Abbots of the Monasteries of Wearmouth and Jarrow* and the letter to Egbert, archbishop of York, was recently published in England by Waraeus. It was also published in sextodecimo at Paris in 1666 by Louis Billaine. Finally, there is a letter to a certain Englishman named Albinus, published by John Mabillon in volume I of the *Analecta*.

The *Acta eruditorum*, Leipzig, July 1693, p. 289, make the following notable mention of Bede’s works:

> Certain theological works of the Venerable Bede, now published for the first time, as well as historical works previously published once. Added are the dialogue of Egbert, archbishop of York, on Ecclesiastical Instruction, and the book of Aldhelm, bishop of Sherborne, on Virginity, corrected from a very ancient codex. London, Robert Clavell, 1693, quarto.

“Bede’s works were published at Paris in 1544, in three volumes by Jamet, and in 1554, at the same place, in eight volumes; likewise in eight volumes at Basel by Johann Herwagen in 1563, and at Cologne by Antonius Hierat in 1612. Since that time some monuments of Bede that are lacking in those volumes have seen the light. Mabillon inserted Bede’s letter to Albinus in volume I of the *Ancient Analecta*, p. 9; shortly afterward, p. 51, he also promised that Bede’s genuine commentary on the Pauline Epistles, different from the one published, would eventually be brought to light. From the Codex of Saint-Remi at Reims, the same Mabillon had transcribed Bede’s metrical Martyrology, which Dacherius published in volume X of his *Spicilegium*. Bede’s prose Martyrology, however, differing greatly from the one read among his works, was published by Henschenius and Papebrochius at the beginning of the March volume II of the *Acta Sanctorum*. Nor should James Waraeus be passed over in silence: in Dublin, in 1664, he published Bede’s history of the lives of the abbots of Wearmouth and Jarrow, together with two letters by the same author. One of these, addressed to Plegwina, defends his treatise on the Six Ages against those who had judged him too harshly. The other, addressed to Egbert, instructs him concerning the proper performance of the sacred office and censures certain defects of the ecclesiastical order. He published these works, together with Egbert’s dialogue on Ecclesiastical Instruction.

“Following their example, Henry Warthon also wished to serve Bede’s monuments. Three years earlier, in his *Appendix to Ussher’s Dogmatic History of the Controversy over Scripture and Sacred Vernacular Languages*, he had excerpted certain fragments from Bede’s exposition of Genesis and from his commentary on the Song of Habakkuk. Now he has brought those two little works of Bede out of the darkness in which they had hitherto lain, lest anyone, following Oudinus, Colomesius, and others, reproach the English nation because it leaves the writings of its countryman Bede wholly neglected in the recesses of its libraries. The *Exposition on Genesis*, p. 1, proceeds as far as chapter 22 and begins at verse 4 of chapter 2, since the preceding material on the Hexaemeron is read in volume IV of his works. He transcribed this *Exposition on Genesis* from a manuscript codex of the Lambeth Library, in [Col. 0098B] which he also found two copies of the *Exposition on the Song of Habakkuk*, p. 191. He transcribed one and noted the variant readings of the other. To these two never-before-published little works he appended those works by Waraeus mentioned above. Since only a few copies of that edition reached England, and still fewer other regions, and since many had long desired it, the distinguished Warthon thought he would perform a useful service if he arranged for this *History of the Abbots of Wearmouth and Jarrow*, p. 221, together with Egbert’s dialogue, p. 268, and Bede’s two letters, p. 241, to be sent to press again, and for Waraeus’s notes, which had been relegated to the end in the Dublin edition, to be restored to their proper places. He also added, p. 291, Aldhelm’s book *On Virginity*—not the one written in verse and printed in volume V of Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*, but the one composed in prose and found in the *Monuments of the Orthodox Writers* and in the *Library of the Fathers*. The celebrated Gronovius undertook to correct both, which had been badly edited, in chapter 4, sections 8, 15, and 20 of his *One-Book of Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*. Warthon judges that the correction of the metrical treatise succeeded quite happily with the aid of an Oxford manuscript, but not so the correction of the other, prose treatise, since that was based solely on conjectures of ingenuity. Warthon therefore decided to restore this elegant treatise of Aldhelm to its original polish from the ancient Lambeth Codex; another manuscript copy was supplied by the library of Salisbury Cathedral, from which he transcribed the table of contents. Guided by it, he chose to divide the treatise into several sections.”

These remarks were added by me after the dissertation had already long been composed and written.

## CHAPTER EIGHT  
### How Bede’s works should henceforth be arranged in future editions

In my judgment, it would be more convenient, and without prejudice to sounder opinions, if the works of the Venerable Bede were distributed in future editions as follows: all the doubtful works, whether philosophical or relating to other arts, should be thrown into the final volume; works belonging to identifiable authors should be excluded; the rest should be arranged in this manner:

## VOLUME ONE  
### Works relating to the liberal arts and philosophy

*Beginnings of Donatus’s Art of Grammar.*

*Book on the Eight Parts of Speech.*

*Book on the Art of Meter.*

*On the Figures of Sacred Scripture.*

*On the Tropes of Sacred Scripture.*

*Book on Orthography.*

*On Arithmetical Numbers*, together with the dialogue on numerical notation and the reckoning of time.

*On Arithmetical Propositions.*

*On the Method of Calculation and the Division of Numbers*, addressed to Constantine.

*On Speech through the Gestures of the Fingers.*

Also, the little book *On the Method of Twelfths (unciae)*.

*The Little Book on Lunar Arguments*, p. 143.

*The Nineteen-Year Cycles*, p. 257.

*On the Paschal Cycle*, p. 306.

*Book on the Structure of the Heavenly and Earthly World*, p. 323.

*On the Circles of the Sphere and the Pole*, p. 365.

*On the Method of the Planets and Signs*, p. 369.

*The Little Book on Thunder*, addressed to Herenfrid, p. 387.

*The Little Book on the Method of Computation*, p. 418.

*Book on the Nature of Things*, volume II, p. 1.

*On the Reckoning of Time*, or *On Times*, volume II, p. 43.

*Chronicle of the Six Ages of the World*, or little book, volume II, p. 103.

*Book on Times*, volume II, p. 118.

*Letter on the Vernal Equinox*, according to Anatolius, volume II, p. 230.

## VOLUME TWO  
### Commentaries on the Books of the Old Testament

*Hexaemeron*, or little book *On the Creation of the Six Days*.

*Exposition on Genesis*, with the following works, most of which are contained in volume IV:

*Explanation of Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy.*

*Allegorical Exposition of the Four Books of Kings*, in four books.

*Thirty Questions on the Books of Kings.*

*Three Books on the Tabernacle, its Vessels, and the Priests’ Vestments.*

*Little Book on Solomon’s Temple*, properly belonging to volume eight.

*Exposition of Solomon’s Parables*, in three books.

*Exposition of the Song of Songs*, in seven books.

*Allegorical Exposition of the Book of Tobit.*

*Allegorical Exposition of the Prophets Ezra and Nehemiah*, in three books.

*Exposition of the Song of Habakkuk*, widely preserved in manuscripts, about which we have spoken.

*Little Book on the Strong Woman*, volume VI, p. 459.

## VOLUME THREE  
### Commentaries on the Books of the New Testament and Sermons

All of these are contained in volumes V and VI of Bede’s editions, namely:

*Exposition of the Gospel of Mark*, in four books, p. 92.

*Exposition of the Gospel of Luke*, in six books, p. 217.

*Exposition of the Gospel of John*, p. 451.

*Exposition of the Acts of the Apostles*, p. 625.

*Retractations on the Acts of the Apostles*, volume VI, p. 1.

*Exposition, or Commentary, on the Fourteen Epistles of Saint Paul the Apostle*, taken from the actual opinions of Saint Augustine—not the one contained in volume VI, but the manuscript work, not yet printed, mentioned above.

*Exposition of the Seven Catholic Epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude*, p. 673.

*Explanation of the Apocalypse of Blessed John the Apostle*, p. 761.

*Sermons of the Venerable Bede*, or two books of Homilies, containing forty-nine homilies only, together with the homily on the feast of All Saints, which appears most closely to approach the genius of Saint Bede; the sermons are to be excluded in the form in which they were miserably interpolated in volume VII of all printed editions.

*Scintillae*, or *Excerpts from the Holy Fathers*, eighty sermons, volume VII, p. 370.

## VOLUME FOUR  
### Historical works, or works relating to ecclesiastical history

*The Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, which he presented to Ceolwulf, king of the English.

*The History of the Abbots of the Monasteries of Wearmouth and Jarrow*, in two books, together with the letter to Plegwina on the sixth age of the world and the letter to Egbert, archbishop of York.

*The Life of Saint Cuthbert, Bishop of Lindisfarne*, in two books.

*The Life of Saint Felix, Bishop of Nola*, with all other works excluded as belonging to other authors.

*Bede’s Martyrology*, not in the form in which it was printed in volume III of Bede’s works, but in the form in which the Bollandists published it—namely, with the interpolations of Florus printed in smaller type. As for the metrical work mentioned above, it does not appear to be Bede’s at all.

*Little Book on the Holy Places*, volume III, p. etc.

## VOLUME FIVE  
### Works attributed to Bede whose authors are uncertain

*Ephemerides*, or *Common Computus*, volume I, p. 169 [Col. 0100D] and following, by an uncertain author.

*On the Computation of Embolisms*, volume I, p. 215 and following.

Two little books on theoretical and practical music, volume I, p. 344 and following.

The little books *On Weather Prognostics*, p. 390; *On Measuring the Clock*, p. 392; *On the Astrolabe*, p. 394; *On Prognostics from the Birth of Infants*, p. 397; *On Bloodletting*, p. 398; *On the Seven Wonders of the World*, p. 400—truly little books unworthy of being attributed to the venerable Bede.

*Hymns Ascribed to Bede the Priest*, p. 401 and following.

*Sentences*, or *Philosophical Axioms*, volume II, p. 124.

*Sentences Excerpted from Cicero’s Works*, volume II, p. 166.

*Alphabetical Book of Proverbs*, volume II, p. 185.

*Little Book on Substances*, or *Moral Sentences*, volume II, p. 200.

*On Divination concerning Life and Death*, volume II, p. 233, together with the following works in the printed editions, which are mere trifles.

*Interpretations of the Hebrew Names of Sacred Scripture*, arranged alphabetically, volume III, at the end.

*Excerpts from the Fathers, Collections, Flowers from Various Sources, Questions, Parables*, etc., in the same volume.

*Exposition of the Gospel of Matthew*, in four books, volume IV, p. 1.

*On the Names of the Places or Cities Mentioned in the Book of the Acts of the Apostles*, volume IV, p. 666.

*Little Book on Ecclesiastical Offices*, volume VII, p. 467.

*Fragments of Allegorical Interpretations of Solomon’s Proverbs*, same volume, p. 476.

*Little Book on the Creation of the Six Days*, volume VII, p. 52.

*Questions on Genesis*, same volume, p. 78; on Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, and the four Books of Kings, together with the Book of Various Questions, in the same volume.

*Commentary on the Book of Psalms*, volume VII, p. 307.

*Long Sermon on Psalm 52*, same volume, p. 909.

*Commentary on Boethius’s Book on the Trinity*, same volume, p. 925.

*Meditation on the Passion of Christ*, adapted to the seven canonical hours of the Office, same volume, p. 955.

*On Remedies for Sins*, same volume, p. 961.

## WHAT SHOULD BE EXCLUDED, OR PLACED OUTSIDE BEDE’S WORKS?

*Four Books on the Elements of Philosophy*, volume II of Bede’s works, p. 206; these are the *Minor Philosophy* of William of Conches.

*Lives of Saints Columbanus, Attala, and Eustasius*, abbots of Luxeuil, volume III.

Likewise, the *Lives of Saints Patrick*, in two books; Bertulf, abbot of Bobbio; Arnulf, bishop of Metz; Vedast, bishop of Arras; Burgundofara, abbess; etc., about which we have spoken in the same place.

The Martyrology in the form in which it was falsely printed there.

*Commentary on the Book of Job*, in three books, volume IV, which is known to belong to Philip the priest.

The great *Commentary on the Fourteen Epistles of Saint Paul the Apostle*, which belongs to Florus, deacon of Lyon.

The homilies *On the Praises of Saint Paul*, which are by Saint John Chrysostom.

These are the observations we thought should be made concerning the writings of Saint Bede the priest. We do not doubt that others may also observe other matters, to which our observations in no way prejudice us; for no one of us knows everything. William Cave observes, in his *History of the Writers of the Church*, under the year 701, p. 476, that there are many manuscript codices in England bearing the name of Bede. I would judge that they should not be neglected in a future edition of Bede’s works, although I have very serious doubts about most of them, and not without reason.

[Col. 0101]

# FABRICIUS’S NOTICE ON THE VENERABLE BEDE

(*Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini*)

[Col. 0101C] Nothing more certain can be offered concerning Bede’s homeland, status, and age than what he himself says at the end of the *History of the English*, volume III, p. 151:

> I, Bede, servant of God and priest of the monastery of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, which is at Wearmouth [Note: [Col. 0101D] At the mouth of the River Wear. See volume VI, p. 31] and Jarrow, arranged these things with the Lord’s help. I was born in the territory of that same monastery [Note: [Col. 0101D] Bede was therefore not a Saxon German, although this is reported by Frederick Lange and Engelhus, whose testimony Meibomius rightly calls into question, volume I of the *Germanic Affairs*, p. 809. He may appear to have been born in 672, since he says, p. 147, that he completed the *History of the English* in the year 731 and here mentions the fifty-ninth year of his age. But Pagius noted, under the year 693, no. [Col. 0102D] 8, that Bede could not have added these words before the year 732 or 733], and when I was seven years old I was entrusted by the care of my relatives for education to the most reverend Abbot Benedict, and afterward to Ceolfrith. From that time I spent my entire life in the dwelling of that same monastery, devoting all my effort to the study of the Scriptures; and amid the observance of the regular discipline and the daily duty of singing in the church, I always found it sweet either to learn, teach, or write. In the nineteenth year of my life I received the diaconate, and in the thirtieth the priesthood [Note: Add Pagius under the year 701, no. 2; Nicholas Hieronymus Gundling, *Selected Observations*, 7, book I]. I received both ministries through the agency of the most reverend Bishop John—then of Hexham, afterward of York—at the command of Abbot Ceolfrith of the monastery of Wearmouth. From the time when I received the priesthood until the fifty-ninth year of my age, I took care to make brief notes for my own needs and those of my brothers on Sacred Scripture from the short works of the venerable Fathers, or even to add something according to the form of their meaning and interpretation.

This Bede the priest, whose useful writings made him venerable to the Church, died in the year 735 [Note: Blondel, p. 77, *On Bishops*. John Ciampini also rejects the fable that Bede was buried at Rome, in *On the Sacred Buildings Constructed by Constantine the Great*, chapter 4, section 10, no. 130. A similar fable concerns Bede’s homeland, Genoa, mentioned by the author of the *Boethius*]. Concerning him, see Mabillon, part I of the third Benedictine century, and the *Acta Sanctorum*, 27 May, volume VI, pp. 718 ff.; there, p. 720, is also a Life written by Turgot, prior of Durham, around the year 1100, from his *History of the Church of Durham*, improperly printed under the name of Simeon of Durham among the ten writers of English history. Oudinus discussed his works more diligently after Possevinus, volume I, p. 1672 and following. Nevertheless, I believe I am not repeating what has already been done if I too list the writings of so great a man distinctly: first, those extant in the eight volumes of his works, most recently published after the Paris editions of 1544 and 1554, the Basel edition of 1563, and the Cologne edition of 1612, at Cologne in 1688; then, those lacking from these volumes.

## VOLUME I

*The Restored Foundations of Donatus’s Art of Grammar*, p. 1.

*On the Eight Parts of Speech*, p. 14.

*On the Art of Meter*, addressed to Wigbert the Levite, p. 25 and following. It also appears in Putsch’s *Grammarians*, pp. 2350 and 2383. A portion is prefixed to the ecclesiastical hymns edited by George Cassander in 1556 and included among Cassander’s works, Paris 1616, folio; that edition also presents Bede’s hymns on pp. 195, 206, 239, 244, 254, 263, 266, 274, 280, 281, and 293.

*On the Figures of Sacred Scripture*, p. 42, and *On the Tropes*, p. 48. It was also published separately at Venice in 1522, and together with figurative expressions collected from Augustine and Chrysostom by Bartholomew Westheimer, Basel 1536, octavo; it also appears among the *Rhetoricians* of François Pithou, pp. 342 and 355.

*On Orthography*, p. 53, arranged alphabetically. Another book on this subject appears in Putsch’s *Grammarians*, [Col. 0103C] pp. 2327 and 2350.

*On Arithmetical Numbers*, p. 72.

*On the Various Kinds of Numbers and the Pythagorean Table*, p. 75.

*Dialogue on Computation*, p. 85.

*On the Divisions of Time*, p. 89. Mabillon recommends a fuller manuscript codex, volume I of the *Italian Museum*, p. 69.

*On Arithmetical Propositions*, or Problems, p. 100.

*Little Book on the As and Its Parts, and on the Method of Calculation*, p. 111.

*On the Division of Numbers*, addressed to Constantine, p. 123.
