*On Speech through Finger Gestures and on the Reckoning of Time*, p. 127, with glosses by Bridfert of Ramsey and scholia by J. Noviomagus. Petavius considers this little book to be falsely attributed to Bede, p. 159 of his *Letters*. John Aventine held a different view, as I noted above, p. 391.

*Little Book on the Method of Twelfths (unciae)*, p. 140.

*On Lunar Arguments*, from Victorius of Aquitaine, Dionysius the Greek, etc., p. 143.

*Common Computus*, or *Ephemeris*, p. 169. Oudinus proves that it is by a younger Bede, volume I, p. 1683.

*Martyrology in Hexameter Verse*, beginning:

> First, January is now called by the name of the month,

p. 191. It is by Wandelbert of Prüm, not Bede. Another brief Martyrology, likewise in hexameter verse and published under Bede’s name by Dacher, begins:

> The year revolves through the circuit of twelve months,

volume X of the *Spicilegium*, p. 126, and volume II of the new folio edition, p. 23.

*Computus on the Method of Embolisms*, p. 215, with four-line poems for each month. Oudinus also argues that this computus must be denied to Bede and attributed to the Englishman Ralph de Linham.

*The Nineteen-Year Cycles of Dionysius Exiguus, Blessed Cyril, and Bede*, extending to the year 1595, with a preface by Abbo of Fleury, p. 257.

*On the Paschal Cycle*, p. 306.

*Canons of the Nineteen-Year Cycles*, p. 321.

*On the Structure of the Heavenly and Earthly World*, p. 323.

*Theoretical Music*, p. 344, and practical [thus read, in place of “fourth”], or measured music, p. 351. Oudinus maintains that the author was a later writer; see him, volume I, p. 1685.

*On the Circles of the Sphere and the Pole*, p. 365.

*On the Method of the Planets and Signs*, p. 369, according to the thought of the Hebrews, Chaldeans, and Egyptians, p. 371.

*Signs of the Months*, p. 377.

*Little Book on Thunder*, addressed to Herenfrid, whom he calls “Venerable Father,” p. 387, translated from Greek, perhaps from John Laurentius Lydus of Philadelphia, concerning whom see the *Greek Library*, book III, chapter 20, p. 513.

*Weather Prognostics*, p. 390.

*Measurement of the Clock*, p. 392, where there is also discussion of the Egyptian days, p. 394.

*Little Book on the Astrolabe*, p. 394.

*On the Birth of Infants*, p. 397.

*On Bloodletting*, p. 398.

*On the Seven Wonders of the World*, p. 400.

*On the Year, the Reckoning of Time, the Celebration of Times, and Various Rules of Computation*, poems in hexameter verse, p. 401.

*Dionysius on Years*, in trochaic verse, p. 413.

*Little Book on the Method of Computation through Questions and Answers*, p. 418. Compare Rabanus’s book *On Computation*, written in the seventh year of Emperor Louis and published by Baluze at the beginning of volume I of the *Miscellany*, and Helpericus, who also praises Bede in the preface to his book *On Computation*, composed in the year 930.

*On the Twelve Signs, the Ages*, etc., poems; and Priscian’s *On Astronomy*, p. 434. Manfred’s poems, p. 435; the method of embolisms, in prose, p. 450. Verses on the city of Rome and on Trier, p. 449.

## VOLUME II

*Book on the Nature of Things*, with glosses by an uncertain author, Bridfert of Ramsey, and John Noviomagus, p. 1. Stephen Vitus denied that this and the following book were Bede’s, but Petavius rightly opposed him, p. 157 of his *Letters*.

*On the Reckoning of Time*, with scholia by the same Bridfert and Noviomagus, p. 43. See this book collated with the codex of the cathedral library of Würzburg in J. George Eckhart’s *Commentaries on the Affairs of Eastern Francia and the Bishopric of Würzburg*, volume I, p. 825.

*On the Six Ages of the World*, or *Chronicle*, from the origin of things to the ninth year of Leo the Isaurian, year 4680 of the world (A.D. 726), p. 103. The appendix from various authors, which is printed after it in the Basel edition, is absent from the Cologne edition. This *Chronicle* had been published at Paris by Jean Petit in 1507, quarto, and with scholia by John Bronchorst at Cologne in 1537. The brief *Chronicle of Bede*, continued to the year 810 and published from a manuscript codex by André du Chesne, volume III of the *Writers of the Franks*, pp. 125 and 129, should also be consulted.

*Book on Times*, for understanding the computation of the times of Sacred Scripture, p. 118, with scholia by J. Noviomagus. See a fragment from Sebastian Münster’s *Cosmography*, book II, in Colomesius’s *Paralipomena on Sacred Ecclesiastical History*, p. 220.

*Sentences*, or *Philosophical Axioms*, from Aristotle, p. 124, arranged alphabetically. They were often published separately, for example at London in 1592, octavo; Ingolstadt in 1593, octavo; and Paris in 1604, octavo.

*Sentences from Cicero’s three books On Duties*, p. 166; *On Friendship*, p. 173; *On Old Age*, p. 176; *Paradoxes*, p. 178; the five books of the *Tusculan Disputations*, p. 180; and Book Six of *On the Republic*—that is, *Scipio’s Dream*—p. 183. Three epitaphs of Cicero, p. 184.

*Book of Proverbs and Sentences*, arranged alphabetically, p. 185. Oudinus argues that this and the two preceding books of sentences are unworthy of Bede and by a much later author.

*Little Book on Substances*, p. 200, in which some Benedictine author of the eleventh or twelfth century, according to the same Oudinus, discourages the dissipation of the properties or goods of monasteries and gives various other useful instructions to clerics and laypeople.

*Διδάξεων*, or *Four Books of the Elements of Philosophy*, p. 206—not by Bede but by William of Conches, concerning whom see below.

*Book on the Celebration of Easter*, or *On the Vernal Equinox*, according to Anatolius the Egyptian, in Eusebius, a letter to the priest Wichred, whom he calls “most holy brother,” p. 230. In it he also praises Proterius and Cyril, Alexandrian bishops, on the same subject; Victor of Capua; the Paschal letters of Dionysius Exiguus; and the arrangement of the Paschal weekdays by Bishop Theophilus of Caesarea and the synod of the remaining bishops, p. 232. The example of the year 776, p. 232, was added by a later hand. It is absent from the edition of Pierre-François Chifflet, printed before Bede’s *English History*, Paris 1681, quarto; Mabillon noted that it is also absent from the very ancient codex of the library of Lobbes, in his *Eulogy of Bede*, no. 29, and volume I of the *Analecta*, p. 11 (new edition, p. 398). Petavius observes in his *Letters*, p. 157, that the book *On the Equinox* is attributed in manuscripts to Philip the priest. But it undoubtedly has Bede as its author, and Bede himself mentions it in the catalogue of his works at the end of his *History*.

*On Divination concerning Death and Life*, a letter of Petosiris to Necepsos, king of Egypt, p. 233. Oudinus classes this together with the two following writings among the trifles unworthy of Bede. To the same category belongs the *Wheel of Life and Death*, which Arnold Wion presents under Bede’s name in volume II of the *Tree of Life*, p. 827, and which Possevinus takes from him in volume I of the *Apparatus*, p. 204.

*Noah’s Ark, a Type of the Church*, p. 235, and *On the Languages of the Nations*, in the same place.

*Interpretation of the Sibylline Words*, p. 236. It also appears at the end of the *Sibylline Books* of John Opsopoeus, p. 515. According to Muratori, Bede’s *Book on Times* exists in an Ambrosian Codex written, in his judgment, a thousand years ago, in which chapters 16 and 17 through the end differ from the printed editions. They also report that at the end a chronological addition by someone else after Bede was appended; it reaches up to the present year—“thus it reads there”—which is the forty-second year of Charles’s reign and the ninth of his empire.

## VOLUME III
*Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, in five books, addressed to King Ceolwulf, p. 1, from the first arrival of Julius Caesar in Britain up to the year of Christ 731, and from the arrival of the English in Britain, p. 285. A splendid work, although Montagu accuses Bede, *Origins*, II, p. 210, of sometimes pursuing foolish stories while omitting matters more worthy of notice. After the older editions of Strasbourg, 1500 and 1514; Hagenau, [Col. 0106C] 1506; Antwerp, 1550; Louvain, 1566; and Cologne, 1601, in octavo; and after the collection of English historical writers printed by Commelin in 1587, with the continuation mentioned above, p. 267, and without it among Bede’s works, three more recent editions must be mentioned: the Cambridge edition, with the Saxon version—or rather paraphrase—of King Alfred and the notes of Abraham Wheloc, 1644, folio; the fuller Paris edition, with notes and dissertations by Pierre-François Chifflet [Note: [Col. 0105D] *Journal des Savans*, 1681, p. 316; *Acta Eruditorum*, 1682, p. 330.], S.J., 1671, quarto; and the London edition of 1722, folio [Note: [Col. 0106D] The same, 1724, p. 124. *Literary Memoirs of Great Britain*, vol. X, p. 520.], together with both Lives of Cuthbert, the *Chronicle*, the *History of the Abbots of Weremouth and Jarrow*, the book on the Holy Places, the *Life of Felix*, and the *Martyrology*, edited by John Smith.

*Epitome*, or *Brief Summary of the History of the English*, p. 147. This must have been continued by someone else after Bede down to the year 766, for in the very ancient manuscript examined by Mabillon it does not go beyond 731.

*Life of Cuthbert, Bishop of Lindisfarne*, addressed to Eadfrith, bishop, and the brothers of the island of Lindisfarne, p. 151. To this work, which is also found in Surius under 20 March, should be added the *Acts of Cuthbert*, written in hexameter verse and published by Canisius, vol. V, part II, *Ancient Readings*, p. 692, and at the beginning of vol. II of the new Basnagian edition. Both works are included in the *Acts of the Saints* and were again edited by J. Smith among certain writings of Bede, London, 1722, folio. Barthius illustrates several passages in that poem, *Adversaria*, III, 19.

[Col. 0107A] *Life of Blessed Felix the Confessor*, from the metrical work of blessed Bishop Paulinus, p. 186. It is also found in the *Acts of the Saints*, 14 January, vol. I, p. 943, and was edited by J. Smith, London, 1722, folio.

*Life of Saint Vedast, Bishop of Arras*, p. 191, together with a homily for his birthday, to be delivered to the people, p. 198. Oudinus maintains that the author was some Gaul, not Bede. Compare the *Acts of the Saints*, 6 February.

*Life of Saint Columbanus*, p. 199, and of Abbot Attala, p. 222. The author is Jonas of Luxeuil, about whom below; add Surius, 21 November, and Thomas Massingham’s *Florilegium of the Saints of Ireland*, p. 219; Mabillon’s *Acts of the Benedictine Order*, vol. II, pp. 1001, 1031.

*Life, Miracles,* [Col. 0107B] *and Passing of Blessed Patrick, Apostle of the Irish*, in two books, p. 225. Its author is Probus the Irishman. See Baronius, under the *Martyrology*, 17 March, and the place where the Life itself is found, *Acts of the Saints*, March, vol. III, pp. 97 ff.

*Life of Saint Eustasius*, who was a disciple of Saint Columbanus, p. 243. The author is Jonas of Luxeuil.

*Life of Bertholf*, abbot of Bobbio, p. 248. The same Jonas is the author.

*Life of Arnulf, Bishop of Metz*, p. 253. It has Paul the Deacon, not Bede, as its author.

*Life of Saint Burgundofara, Abbess*, p. 258. Likewise falsely attributed to Bede.

*Passion of Saint Justin*, a nine-year-old boy and martyr under Diocletian and Maximian, p. 266, in free iambic quaternary verse.

[Col. 0107C] *Martyrology*, p. 277. It is by no means Bede’s authentic work, but was interpolated in many ways, as it appeared at Antwerp in 1565, duodecimo. See Bollandus, preface to vol. I of the January *Acts of the Saints*, pp. 40 ff.; Albertinus, *On the Holy Eucharist*, p. 263; and Launoy, dissertation *On the Victorines*, p. 36. Henschenius and Papebrochius present Bede’s genuine work—who left 180 days blank, and for which even Florus, according to Ado, did not supply all the omissions—together with supplements by Florus and others, printed in a distinct typeface, in the prolegomena to the second volume of the March *Acts of the Saints*. In it one finds the passages cited from Bede by Amalarius, II, XXIV, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, and *On the Order of the Antiphonary*, chapter 28, as Colomesius had already noted. J. Georg Eckhart presents an addition to Bede’s *Martyrology* from a Würzburg manuscript of the ninth century, together with a necrology inserted into Bede’s *Martyrology*, vol. I of his *Commentaries on the Affairs of Eastern Francia and the Bishopric of Würzburg*, pp. 829–830. On the differences between the metrical *Martyrology* published by Dacherius (mentioned above, p. 498) and this Henschenian one, see, if you please, Oudinus, vol. I, p. 1683.

*Booklet on the Site of Jerusalem and the Holy Places*, abridged from the works of earlier authors, p. 363. Drawn from Arculf and Adamnan, mentioned above, p. 15.

*Interpretation of Hebrew Names*, in alphabetical order, p. 371. Oudinus reports that in manuscripts of excellent quality it is attributed to Remigius of Auxerre.

[Col. 0108A] *Excerpts from the Fathers, Collections, Flowers from Various Sources, Questions and Parables*, p. 480. These works likewise, and those that follow later in this volume, are judged by learned men to be little worthy of Bede’s abilities.

*On the Twelve Stones*, p. 491.

*On the Twelve Luminaries of the Church*, ibid. This is also transmitted under Jerome’s name as *On the Twelve Doctors*, addressed to Desiderius, and I have included it in the *Ecclesiastical Library* under Jerome’s catalogue, p. 226, although it has neither Jerome nor Bede as its author.

*On the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit*, p. 492.

*On the Seven Orders*, p. 493.

*On the Fifteen Signs before the Day of Judgment*, p. 494.

*On the Lord’s Cross; On the Four Orders*, p. 495.

[Col. 0108B] *On Receiving the Eucharist*, p. 469.

*Hymns for the Day of Judgment*, p. 496 ff.

*Six Forms of Prayers*, or supplications, pp. 498–500.

## Volume IV

*Hexaemeron*, or *On the Creation of the Six Days*, addressed to Abbot Acca, p. 1. Add vol. VIII, pp. 52, 79 ff.

The remaining chapters, XXI onward, of Genesis, addressed to the same Acca, are in manuscripts in the Lambeth Library; from that manuscript H. Warthon published them, as I shall say below.

*On Genesis*, p. 19; *Exodus*, p. 87; *Leviticus*, p. 121; *Numbers*, p. 139; and *Deuteronomy*, which in Latin is *The Second Law*, p. 156.

*Allegorical Exposition of the Prophet Samuel, or of His First Book*, in four books, pp. 167, 203, 246, 293.

*Questions on the Books of Kings*, that is, the books of Samuel and Kings, thirty questions in one book, p. 353.

*Allegorical Exposition of the Prophets Ezra and Nehemiah*—the latter also called the Second Book of Ezra—in three books, pp. 348, 375, 405; *on Tobit*, p. 347.

*On Job*, three books, addressed to Nectarius, bishop, whom he calls “most blessed Father,” pp. 447, 511, 575, published at Basel in 1527 under the genuine name of Philip the presbyter. That these commentaries on Job belong to Philip, although praised under Jerome’s name by Faustus of Riez, is demonstrated by Bede himself in his book *On the Calculation of Unciae*. See below, under Philip.

*On the Parables*, three books, pp. 634, 658, 698, wrongly published among Jerome’s works.

*On the Song of Songs*, seven books, the first of which is against Julian of Celano [Note: [Col. 0107] See Vossius, *History of Pelagianism*, book I, chapter 4, § 4, and chapter 6.], bishop, who had scattered Pelagian errors against the grace of God throughout his commentaries. The seventh book is entirely drawn from the sayings of Gregory the Great, just as Paterius had compiled a *Chain* on the whole of Scripture from Gregory’s writings, pp. 714, 728, 748, 763, 786, 807, 827.

*On the Tabernacle, Its Vessels, and the Priestly Vestments*, three books, pp. 838, 859, 889.

## Volume V

*On Matthew*, four books, pp. 1, 23, 45, 66. John Aventinus testified to Melanchthon that he had read in a Passau manuscript an exposition of the words of the Lord’s Supper that is lacking in the printed editions.

*Exposition of the Lord’s Prayer*, p. 91.

*On Mark*, four books, pp. 92, 122, 152, 183.

*On Luke*, addressed to the presbyter Acca, preceded by his exhortatory letter, p. 213; six books, pp. 217, 262, 301, 338, 375, 415.

*On John*, preceded by a brief summary divided into fourteen chapters, p. 451. Thomas sometimes cites in his *Catena* passages from Bede that are absent from the printed editions and agree with the commentaries of Eric.

*Learned Exposition of the Acts of the Apostles*, addressed to the presbyter Acca, p. 625.

*Exposition of the Names of the Places Mentioned in the Book of the Acts of the Apostles*, p. 665, in alphabetical order.

*On the Catholic Epistles*: that of the holy James, bishop of Jerusalem, p. 673; First Peter, p. 694, and Second Peter, p. 713; First John, chiefly from Augustine, p. 727; Second John, p. 752; Third John, p. 754; and Jude, p. 755. William Cave published the prologue in his *Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year 700.

*On the Apocalypse*, with a prologue to his brother Eusebius, concerning its seven divisions and the seven rules of Tyconius for understanding it, pp. 761, 816. Many scholars, including Nicolaus Zegerus in his notes on the New Testament and Richard Simon, vol. III of his *Critical History of the New Testament*, p. 345, highly esteem this commentary, in which Bede does not deny that he also followed Primasius.

## Volume VI

[Col. 0109C]

*Book of Revisions on the Acts of the Apostles*, p. 1. In this book, the same Simon noted, p. 340, Bede’s great learning and judgment. Add his dissertation *On the Manuscripts of the New Testament*, pp. 59 ff., and John Mill’s prolegomena to the New Testament, § 1022 ff.

*Five Questions on the Same Book of Acts*, p. 29.

*Exposition of the Pauline Epistles*, compiled from the writings of Saint Augustine [Note: [Col. 0109D] Bede himself testifies at the end of the *History of the English* that this work was composed under his supervision]: *on the Epistle to the Romans*, p. 31; *on First Corinthians*, p. 253; *on Second Corinthians*, p. 447; *on Galatians*, p. 511; *on Ephesians*, p. 562; *on Philippians*, p. 609; *on Colossians*, p. 647; *on First Thessalonians*, p. 673; *on Second Thessalonians*, p. 689; *on First Timothy*, p. 697; *on Second Timothy*, p. 738; *on Titus*, p. 759; *on Philemon*, p. 765; and *on Hebrews*, p. 766.

Seven homilies of Chrysostom, from the translation of Anianus [Note: [Col. 0109D] See above concerning him.], together with his letter to Evangelus, follow, p. 823, as does a letter of Geoffrey Foussard, of Le Mans, to Peter Securibilis, archdeacon of Rouen, concerning Bede’s work on Paul’s Epistles.

Although Bede himself testifies that he compiled such a commentary, and Lupus of Ferrières, letter 76, and Hincmar, *Against Gottschalk*, II, also praise it, Bede’s genuine commentary on Paul’s Epistles has not yet seen the light. It existed in manuscript at Mabillon’s [Note: [Col. 0110D] Vol. I of the *Analecta*, p. 51, and new edition, folio 788], under the title *Bede’s Collection on the Apostle, from the Works of Blessed Augustine*.

The work published by the aforementioned Boussard in 1499, folio, is neither Bede’s, nor the work of Peter, abbot of the province of Tripoli—although Cassiodorus, chapter 8 of *Divine Readings*, confirms that Peter composed a similar work—nor that of Bartholomew of Urbino, whose Augustinian *Milleloquium* was mentioned above, p. 485. Rather, it is by Florus, a master of Lyons and monk of Saint-Trond, who compiled a similar commentary not only from Augustine, who seems to be the very work published here under Bede’s name, but also from another collection drawn from other Fathers: Cyprian, Hilary, Ambrose, Pacianus, Jerome, Ephraem the deacon, Paulinus, Augustine, Pope Leo, [Col. 0110B] Fulgentius, and Avitus. Compare Sirmondus’s notes on Avitus, vol. II of his works, p. 147; Chifletius, in *Pauline Illustrated*, and the preface to Ferrandus’s Fulgentius, p. 322; Baluzius, on Lupus’s letter 76; and Richard Simon, III, XXIV, of the *Critical History of the New Testament*, pp. 344 ff.

In the vernacular dialogues of the distinguished W. E. Tentzel one may read that Mabillon promised to publish a twofold commentary by Bede on Paul’s Epistles; but everyone can see that “genuine” ought to be read.

## Volume VII

*Thirty-five Summer Homilies on the Liturgical Season*, p. 1.

*Thirty-three Summer Homilies on the Saints, the Dedication of Altars and Churches, and the Common of Saints*, p. 91.

[Col. 0110C] *Fifteen Winter Homilies on the Liturgical Season*, p. 183.

*Twenty-two Lenten Homilies*, p. 218.

*Sixteen Winter Homilies on the Saints*, p. 290.

*Twenty-one Various Sermons*, of which the first two are for the feast of Saint Wigbert, and the third for Saint Scholastica, in whose praise several poems are also read, p. 350 ff. Homilies and sermons under Bede’s name—or, as they are called in Saint Boniface’s ninth letter, the *Annual Lectionary*—were printed separately in Paris and Louvain, in two octavo volumes. Among them are some that are not complete sermons, but scraps torn from Bede’s sermons or commentaries, as Sixtus of Siena has already noted. For the individual pieces, see specifically what Mabillon and, following him, Oudinus advise, vol. I, pp. 1699 ff.

[Col. 0110D] *Sparks*, or *Commonplaces of Sentences Drawn from Sacred Scripture and the Fathers*, arranged by chapters or titles, eighty in number [Note: [Col. 0110D] In Speelmann, vol. I of the *Councils of England*, there are seventy-two titles.], p. 370. On the Anglo-Saxon translation of the *Sparks*, see Francis Junius, preface to his *Glossary of Ulfilas*, and Humphrey Wanley, in the catalogue of northern books in the libraries of England, vol. II of Hickes’s work, p. 86. See also below, under Defensor.

*Booklet on the Strong Woman*, p. 459, on Proverbs 31:10 to the end.

*Booklet on Duties*, excerpted from sayings of the Fathers, p. 467. It is scarcely worthy of Bede’s collections, in Quesnel’s judgment, [Col. 0111A] p. 551, in his notes on Leo the Great; and it must belong to a younger writer, since Anastasius is cited in the *Life of Pope Melchiades*.

*Fragments of Allegorical Interpretation* on certain chapters of Proverbs, p. 476; Wisdom, pp. 481, 485; Ecclesiasticus, p. 483; Psalm 90, p. 484; and *On King Solomon*, p. 486.

## Volume VIII

*Book on Solomon’s Temple*, p. 1. Bede mentions this work of his, on the structure of Solomon’s Temple and its allegorical interpretation, in his letter to Abbot Albinus.

*On the Creation of the Six Days*, p. 52. Add vol. IV, p. 1, and in this same volume VIII, pp. 79 ff. Some of these matters [Col. 0111B] were attributed, irrelevantly, to Junilius Africanus as author. See Dallaeus, *On the Use of the Fathers*, p. 16.

*Questions Drawn from the Sayings of the Fathers*—Augustine, Jerome, Isidore, Sedulius, and others—*on Genesis*, p. 78; *Exodus*, p. 196; *Leviticus*, p. 219; *Numbers*, p. 228; and *Deuteronomy*, p. 241, in the form of a dialogue between teacher and pupil; *on Joshua*, p. 248; *Judges*, p. 255; *Ruth*, p. 261; *the four books of Kings*, pp. 262, 273, 275, 278. Lupus of Ferrières requested that Bede’s questions on the Old and New Testaments be sent to him, letter 62.

*Book of Fifteen Miscellaneous Questions*, p. 286.

*Exegesis of the Book of Psalms*, p. 307 through p. 896, where Psalm 151 is also mentioned and seventy-nine *diapsalmata* are enumerated.

*Interpretation of Rare Words in the Psalms*, denoting musical instruments or other unusual things, p. 899.

*Interpretation of Hebrew Names*, p. 901.

*Sermon on Psalm 53:3, “God Looked Down from Heaven,”* p. 904. By the same author as the book *On Substances*, vol. II.

*On Boethius’s Book on the Most Holy Trinity*, p. 925. Learned men do not doubt that this work has been falsely attributed to Bede, whether its author was Edmund Albanus or someone else, as I have already noted in *Latin Library*, III, XV, 8. See W. E. Tentzel, *On the Athanasian Creed*, pp. 68 ff.

*Prayer on the Seven Words of Christ on the Cross*, p. 954.

*On Meditating on Christ’s Passion during the Seven Hours of the Day*, p. 965.

*On Remedies for Sins*, excerpted from the canons of the Fathers, or from penitentials, for the healing of souls, of Archbishop Agbert, pp. 961, 968. It exists together with the Roman Penitential, or penitential canons, published by Antonio Augustino, Venice, 1584, quarto, p. 102, and in Henry Speelmann’s *Councils of England*, p. 281, who testifies that in the manuscript it is attributed to Agbert himself, or to Archbishop Egbert, as its author.

We must not omit what Sixtus of Siena noted, in the fourth book of his *Sacred Library*, p. 265, concerning the four kinds of Bede’s commentaries on Holy Scripture: [Col. 0112A]

> In the thirtieth year of his age, having been ordained presbyter by Bishop John, and at the urging of Bishop Acca of York and many of the brethren, he undertook to write several volumes of explanations on the whole of Holy Scripture, divided into four classes, namely, RHAPSODIES, QUESTIONS, HOMILIES, and COMMENTARIES.
>
> In the Rhapsodies, or *Stromata*, or *Collections*, he gathered mystical rather than historical expositions from the most approved sayings and teachings of the doctors of the Church, collected here and there in interrupted and fragmentary fashion, inserting also some material of his own in imitation of their meaning wherever appropriate, so that the various discourses and periods of the Fathers might either be joined together more suitably or made shorter and clearer.
>
> And, lest he seem to be stealing the sayings of earlier writers and assembling them as though they were his own, he had decided to insert the names of the doctors throughout and to indicate by name what had been said by each author. But when this seemed too laborious, he placed only the first syllables of their names in the margins opposite each sentence; these later disappeared from all copies through the ignorance or negligence of scribes.
>
> In the Commentaries, Questions, and Homilies, in which he more frequently uses both his own language and his own thought, his style is neither entirely inelegant nor concerned with affected elegance, but moderate: it produces neither weariness through an excess of words nor obscurity through brevity, but proceeds with a brief and most agreeable ease.

The same Sixtus, drawing on chapter 242 of Trithemius, mentions Bede’s commentary on Ecclesiastes and eighteen books on the major and minor prophets. For other unpublished and lost works of this writer, Cave should be consulted. Bede’s catalogue of his works, which he himself composed at the end of the *History*, is also found in Sigebert, chapter 68, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

The following are missing from the volumes of Bede’s works:

A letter to Albinus, mentioned above, published by James Ware with notes; and an apologetic letter in defense of the book *On the Six Ages*, addressed to Plegwin the monk against the objections of another monk, David.

A letter to Egbert, archbishop of York, on the duties of a Christian bishop, written shortly before his death.

*The Lives of the Five Earlier Abbots of Weremouth and Jarrow*, in two books.

Henry Warthon gave these works, from the Dublin edition of 1664, octavo, for republication [Col. 0112D] in London, 1693, quarto [Note: [Col. 0111D] *Acta Eruditorum*, 1693, p. 286]. He also appended an *Exposition of the First Twelve Chapters of Genesis*, of which only the exposition of the first chapter and the beginning of the second had appeared in volume IV, and a commentary on the Song of Habakkuk. Warthon had published fragments from both works in the *Supplement to Ussher’s Dogmatic History of Scripture and Sacred Vernacular Writings*, London, 1689, quarto, pp. 356 ff. He also added Archbishop Egbert of York’s *Dialogue on Ecclesiastical Instruction*, and Bishop Aldhelm of Sherborne’s book *On Virginity*, written in prose and much more accurately corrected than in the earlier editions.

[Col. 0113A] Following Warthon’s example, John Smith, canon of Durham, and, after his death, his son George Smith, published at Cambridge in 1722, folio, from carefully collated manuscript copies and with historical notes, Bede’s historical writings. In addition to those already available in the volumes of his works—the *Chronicle of the Six Ages*, the *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, the *Life of Cuthbert*, the *Life of Felix*, and the booklet *On the Holy Places*—these included an Anglo-Saxon [Note: [Col. 0113B] Besides this Anglo-Saxon version of King Alfred, there is also an English version dedicated to Queen Elizabeth by Thomas Stapleton, S.J., Antwerp, 1565, quarto.] version of the *Ecclesiastical History*, based on Wheloc’s edition and corrected from three manuscripts; the *Life of Cuthbert* written in verse, which Canisius and Mabillon had published; and the *Lives of the Abbots of Weremouth and Jarrow*, published by Ware and Warthon, corrected from three manuscript codices. They also included the letter to Egbert and, finally, Bede’s genuine *Martyrology*, which I have said was published by Henschenius in the second volume of the March *Acts of the Saints*. Prefixed to all these were a Life of Bede written by his disciple Cuthbert, another by an Anonymous author now published for the first time, and an account of Bede recorded by Mabillon. Finally, the volume is adorned with a geographical map of Britain as it was in those times and an appendix of charters, letters, and dissertations by the editor, which cast considerable light on the writers and history of that age.

Most recently, Edmund Martene, in the fifth volume of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, brought to light, besides the commentaries on Genesis, p. 115, and on the Song of Habakkuk, p. 295, which I have already said were published by Warthon, eleven homilies of Bede, p. 317, and a booklet of Prayers, p. 483.

Peter Pithoeus published a composition on the sundial, in hexameter verse, under Bede’s name, at the end of his *Epigrams and Ancient Poems*, p. 488 of the Paris edition of 1590, duodecimo. I have a note of it in Isaac Casaubon’s hand: in the ninth verse he correctly reads *Junia* rather than *Janua*, and verse 77:

> The third closes the bright course with eleven,

and verse 79:

> The fifth holds seven, etc.

The same poem appears in the fuller Lyon edition of those poems, 1596, octavo, p. 609. But its author is [Col. 0114B] not Bede, but Wandalbert, a deacon of Prüm, as Mabillon has already noted. Oudinus published the eclogue *On the Conflict between Spring and Winter*, which Pithoeus had judged unworthy of publication, in vol. II of his *Commentaries on Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 326, under the name of Milo of Elnone. It had already appeared in Frankfurt in 1610, octavo, appended to Ovidian love poems under Bede’s name, together with another eclogue *On the Cuckoo*, which Mabillon published as though previously unpublished under the name of Alcuin, vol. I of the *Analecta*, p. 369 (new folio edition, p. 409).

[Col. 0113]

# TESTIMONIES OF ANCIENT WRITERS CONCERNING THE VENERABLE BEDE

## Pope Sergius I, Letter to Ceolfrith

[Col. 0113C]

In what words and forms of expression can we proclaim the mercy of our God and his unspeakable providence, and offer worthy thanksgiving for his immense benefits toward us—he who brings those placed in darkness and the shadow of death into the light of knowledge?

And below:

Know in the meantime that we have gladly and cheerfully received, just as it was sent by your devotion, the gift of blessing that your devout community sent to us through the present bearer. Therefore, with the closest devotion favoring the timely and worthy requests by which your solicitude is to be embraced, we exhort the goodness of your God-beloved religious devotion that, since certain matters of ecclesiastical affairs have arisen which must be examined and will become known more fully in due course, we need men trained in literary skill for consultation—as befits a God-devoted helper of the holy mother, the universal Church.

Do not cease to apply obedient devotion to this exhortation of ours. Without any delay, send the religious servant of God Bede, presbyter of your venerable monastery, to the thresholds of the apostles, my lords Peter and Paul, your beloved patrons and protectors, so that he may appear before our humble person. With God’s favor, do not doubt that, through your holy prayers, he will return safely to you after the desired solemn observance of the matters mentioned above has been completed with God’s help. For, as we trust, whatever benefit his excellence imparts to the universal Church will also profit all those entrusted to you.

## Boniface, Apostle of the Germans, Letter 85, to Egbert

The brevity of a letter prevents me from recounting all the evils that we suffer both outwardly and inwardly. At present, however, we eagerly beg you to take care to send us, for the joy of our sorrow, as you have done before, some portion or spark from the candle of the Church which the Holy Spirit has kindled in your regions—that is, some portion of the treatises which Bede, the spiritual presbyter and investigator of the Holy Scriptures, composed by opening them up. Above all, if it can be done, send what seems useful, portable, and very inexpensive [Al., “most useful”] for our preaching: material on the *Annual Lectionary* and the *Proverbs of Solomon*, since we hear that he composed commentaries on them.

In the meantime, necessity compels us to seek your counsel and judgment. Suppose I find a presbyter who fell into fornication long ago and was restored by the Franks to the office of his rank after doing penance, and who now lives alone in a very extensive district of faithful but erring peoples, without other priests, administering baptism and celebrating the solemn Mass. If I remove such a man according to the strictest canons, infants will die without the sacred font of regeneration because of the scarcity of priests, unless I have a better man with whom to remedy the former priest’s lapse. Judge, therefore, between me and the misguided people whether it is better, or at least the lesser evil: for such a man to perform the ministry of the holy altar, or for a multitude of pagans to die because he could not obtain a more chaste minister.

Or suppose that among a multitude of priests I find someone who has fallen into the same sin and has again been restored to his former rank after penance, and in whom the entire multitude of priests and peoples has placed confident trust in his good reputation. If he is now degraded, his secret sin will be revealed, the multitude of the common people will be scandalized, very many souls will perish through the scandal, and there will be the greatest detestation of priests and distrust of the Church’s ministers, so that all will regard them as faithless, untrustworthy, and contemptible [Perhaps: objects of contempt]. For this reason we have boldly presumed to allow him to persist in the divine ministry, judging that the doubtful danger and presumption of one man is lighter than the ruin and destruction of the souls of nearly the entire people.

Concerning all these matters, I earnestly desire to see and hear in writing, according to your counsel, what I ought to endure when necessity compels me to avoid scandals and what I ought to reject. Moreover, as a token of intimate charity, we have sent your Eminence two small cups of wine through this bearer of the letter, asking you to make a joyful day with your brothers through our prayers and charity. We therefore beseech you to act on these requests of ours, so that the rewards of your merit may shine at the summit of heaven.

## Boniface, Apostle of the Germans, Letter 150, to Cuthbert

With our inmost prayers we beseech the piety of your brotherhood to assist us, laboring among the wild and ignorant peoples of Germany and planting the grains of the Gospel, through your sacred prayers. May the fierce heat of the Babylonian flame be extinguished in us by the prayers of your holiness, and may what has been scattered in the furrows rise, multiplied, to bear fruit. For, according to the Apostle’s saying, “Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth,” so that the word may be granted to us in the opening of our mouth, and that the word of the Lord may run and be glorified (1 Corinthians 3).

In the meantime, we ask you to send us the remaining works of the most discerning investigator of the Scriptures, the monk Bede, whom we recently heard had shone among you in the house of God, like the candle of the Church, through his knowledge [Perhaps: ecclesiastical knowledge] of the Scriptures. And, if it is not burdensome for you, send one of them to us as a great consolation in our pilgrimage.

As a sign also of our intimate charity, we have sent you goatskin bedding—so it is called here—which we ask you to accept in remembrance, although it is not worthy of you. May the gracious Trinity and the one Godhead strengthen and preserve your brotherhood, which is advancing here in holy virtues, and may he glorify you by rewarding you in the future blessedness, rejoicing among the shining ranks of the angels.

## Saint Lull, Letter to Coena, among Boniface’s Letter 109

I humbly beseech the reverence of your holiness to remember perpetually the friendship once joined between us in Christ and begun at that time, lest it grow old and be handed over to oblivion—the friendship that we pledged before God in a faithful promise. For we ought to glory in insults and tribulations for the name of Christ and in the exaltation of his Church, which is daily beaten, oppressed, and wearied, because the rulers of our time establish new customs and new laws according to their desires.

For this reason, with supported prayer, we earnestly implore your excellence to be a constant intercessor for the salvation of our soul. I am compelled by continual bodily illnesses and mental anxiety to depart from this wretched life, full of dangers, and to render an account to the merciful yet strict Judge.

I have sent your affection a small gift, namely, a very fine silk cloak, through the bearer of this letter. I beg you to obtain and send us any one of the books that the presbyter Bede, of blessed memory, expounded for the consolation of our pilgrimage: namely, his four books on the first part of Samuel, up to the death of Saul; or his three books on Ezra and Nehemiah; or his four books on the Gospel of Mark. Perhaps I ask for much, but I impose nothing burdensome on true charity.

## Cuthbert, Letter to Lull, among the Letters of Bishop Boniface, 89

I received the little gifts of your charity with gratitude, and with even greater gratitude because I learned that you sent them with the deepest devotion: namely, the silk cloth that you sent for the relics of our master Bede, of blessed memory, in remembrance and veneration of him.

It seems right to me that the entire English people, in all the provinces wherever they are found, should give thanks to God because God granted them, in their own nation, so remarkable a man, endowed with various gifts, so diligent in exercising those gifts, and likewise living according to good morals. I learned this by experience, having been nurtured at his feet, and what I recount is what I learned.

You likewise sent me a patterned covering to clothe my body, on account of the cold. I gave it, with great joy, to almighty God and blessed Paul the apostle, to cover the altar consecrated to God in his church, because I too lived under his protection in this monastery for forty-three years.

Now, because you asked for something from the works of the blessed Father, I have prepared, with my boys and according to our abilities, what I could for your affection. I have sent you booklets about the man of God Cuthbert, composed in verse and prose, according to your wishes. If I had been able to do more, I would gladly have wished to do so, for the conditions of the past winter oppressed the island of our people for a long time and over a wide area with terrible cold, ice, storms of wind, and rain; therefore the scribe’s hand was delayed, lest he produce a larger number of books.

Six years ago, through my presbyter Hunwini, who came to your region and desired to see Rome, I also sent your brotherhood some small gifts: twenty knives, and a *gunna* [Perhaps: a *gurda*] made from otter skins. That presbyter Hunwini, however, reached the city called Beneventum and there departed this life. Therefore, neither through him nor through any of your people have I ever received a reply as to whether these things reached you.

We have taken care to send your fatherhood two cloaks of the finest workmanship, one white and the other dyed, together with the booklets and a cloak, such as I happened to have at hand. I beg you not to disregard my request and need.

If there is anyone in your parish who can make glass vessels well, when the time is favorable, please send him to me. Or if such a person happens to be under the authority of someone else beyond your borders, outside your parish, I ask your brotherhood to persuade him to come to us, because we are ignorant and poor in that craft. If it should happen that, through your diligence and God’s will, one of the glassmakers is permitted to come to us, I will receive him with kindly gentleness, with life as his companion.

I should also like to have a harpist who could play the harp—the instrument that we call the *rotta*—because I have a harp but no craftsman. If it is not burdensome, send this man also to me as I request. I beg you not to despise this request of mine or assign it to ridicule.

As for the works of Bede, of blessed memory, that you do not yet possess in transcription, I promise that, if we live, I will assist your wishes [Perhaps: obey your wishes].

## Cuthbert, Abbot, Letter to Bishop Lull, among Boniface’s Letters, 95:

I received the letters, or rather the gifts, with great gratitude: a shaggy garment and a linen cloth, which your Fraternity deigned to send me. I received them all the more gratefully because I do not doubt that they were sent from the depths of your affection. Therefore, repaying this kindness, I too do not cease to care for you in my daily prayers.

The names of the brothers whom you sent to us are also recorded together with the names of the brothers of this monastery who sleep in Christ, so that I have ordered ninety and more Masses to be celebrated for them. Moreover, I took care to send you, for the consolation of your pilgrimage, the book which the most illustrious teacher of the Church of God, Bede, composed on the building of the temple [Al., “I ordered to be sent”]. I humbly beseech your Fraternity to preserve firmly, to the end, the bonds of friendship once agreed between us, especially in this respect: that, together with all those whom divine providence has willed to be subject to you, you may diligently intercede for my infirmities before the heavenly Judge.

## B. Alcuin, Letter 70, to the Lord King

A traveler came flying, carrying in his hand a letter of inquiry from Your Authority, shorter in syllables than my eager mind would have wished, but higher in its questions than the humility of my little intellect could reach. It urged an old man of frail understanding to investigate heavenly things—one who has not yet learned the principles of earthly matters—to explain the wandering courses of the stars that move through the heavens—one who is scarcely able to recognize the natures of the herbs growing on earth. It is wonderful how anyone can bring their wandering paths back into a fixed order. They are called “wandering” because they are thought to have uncertain courses.

Or what could our smallness fail to discover concerning the moon’s daily labors, when we possess, investigated by the manifold reasoning of Catholic teachers and ancient philosophers, regular explanations of them? For what could be said more clearly about the agreement of the courses of the sun and moon through the signs of the zodiac than what the investigator of such questions, the teacher Bede, left to us in his writings? Or what could be investigated more acutely than what Pliny the Elder, that most devoted investigator of natural things, explained concerning the order of the heavenly bodies?

But as we travel, we lack the presence of the books in which these matters are discussed. We dare not rashly answer the very profound questions of Your Wisdom. We ask your clemency to order that the first books of the aforesaid teacher Pliny the Elder be sent to us—those in which he attempts to explain the many obscure arguments concerning the varying course of the stars—so that, if by God’s gift we can extract something from one place or another, it may perhaps appear worthy to be displayed before Your Most Holy Presence.

Nevertheless, lest your little letter find me so unprepared, or sluggish with the sleep of inactivity, as though nothing were stored for me in the secret chamber of memory that I could produce in answer to your question, I shall say what, in the confusion of my mind, was suddenly able to occur to me—more by inquiry than by explanation. If a fuller answer should be required, I shall reserve it for the aforesaid books of the learned.

Your first question concerned the agreement between the three hundred and sixty divisions and the lunar course through the twelve signs. It was expressed in these words:

“Just as, in the solar course, an agreement has been found between the division of days, hours, and points, and the three hundred and sixty-five and one-quarter days, so also, in the lunar course, make twenty-seven days and eight hours agree, through the division of days and hours, with the three hundred and sixty divisions of the zodiac.”

I will not evade saying what I think Your Sagacity perceived in this inquiry: namely, either that something must be added to the moon’s course in each sign, so that it may reach the lawful and defined divisions of the whole year marked out in the zodiac, or that the number of divisions must be reduced so that the lunar course may agree with the divisions of the zodiac.

The aforesaid teacher Bede appears to have explained this question in a certain chapter whose beginning, I believe, is: “But if anyone, ignorant of the signs yet desirous of knowing the lunar course, etc.” As the moon moves twelve divisions farther from the sun each day, Pliny the Elder says—if I remember correctly—that the moon traverses the zodiac thirteen times during its twelve months. He says “during its own months,” not during the months of the sun. He also added that the moon passes through each sign in two days, six hours, and one forty-eighth of an hour.

If this is true, the number of three hundred and sixty divisions appears to correspond very well to the lunar course. I thought it not unworthy that this should be shown by a single diagram rather than by an abundance of words, since a few things suffice for the wise. I therefore considered it better to place the formula of that diagram after the text of this letter than to divide the sequence of our discourse with it.

In that diagram, anyone who wishes to examine it more carefully will also be able to recognize the difference between the hours, since solar and lunar hours are reckoned differently. In some places even the points themselves are reckoned in different ways, so that in some calculations an hour is found to contain five points, and in others four. Calculators also arrange the divisions differently, while mathematicians customarily divide them in another way. We likewise find that minutes are presented differently in the most subtle arguments of mathematicians, to the extent that they even speak of “minutes of minutes.” . . .

## B. Lanfranc, Letter to Pope Alexander

Your blessedness, humble in excellence and excellent in humility, ought to remember that, when we were with you, the archbishop of York openly murmured against me, secretly slandered me, and raised an accusation in the presence of Your Highness. He said that I wished to act unjustly because I was attempting, by the authority of your Church, to exercise primacy over him and over his Church by right.

In the matter of the subjection of certain bishops whom he attempted to attach to his Church, he did not hesitate, in his complaint, to violate an ancient custom. Concerning these matters, you promulgated a judgment in writing, as was fitting and necessary for a holy and prudent shepherd: namely, that an assembly of the English realm, consisting of bishops, abbots, and other persons of religious order from both sides, should hear, examine, and determine the arguments of each party.

And so it was done. At the Paschal solemnity, bishops, abbots, and others from the sacred and lay orders assembled at the regular court in the city of Winchester—persons who, by their rank, conduct, and moral integrity, were properly suited to assemble. First, those summoned by us through your authority were united by holy obedience.

Then the royal power itself charged them, by the faith and oath through which they were bound to it, to hear this case with the utmost attention and, once heard, to bring it to a definite and just conclusion without favoring either party. All accepted both obligations unanimously and promised, under the aforesaid bond, to act accordingly.

The *Ecclesiastical History of the English People* [the printed text reads *dentis*, perhaps an OCR error for *gentis*], which Bede, a priest of the Church of York and teacher of the English, composed, was therefore brought forward. Passages were read which demonstrated, to the satisfaction of all, that from the time of blessed Augustine, the first bishop of Canterbury, until Bede’s final old age—a period extending for nearly one hundred and forty years—my predecessors had held primacy over the whole Church of York and over the entire island called Britain, as well as over Ireland; that they had provided pastoral care for all; and that, in York itself and frequently in neighboring places wherever they deemed it appropriate, they had celebrated episcopal ordinations and councils, and had summoned the bishops of York to those councils. . . .

## Honorius of Autun, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Bede, a monk and priest of the English province, wrote innumerable works, among which are these:

Four books on Genesis; four books on the Tabernacle, its vessels, and the garments of the priests; two books on the building of the temple; one book on the Book of Kings; thirty Questions; three books on Solomon’s Proverbs; seven books on the Song of Songs; three books on Isaiah, Daniel, the Twelve Prophets, part of Jeremiah, Ezra, and Nehemiah; two books on Tobit; one book on the Song of Habakkuk; likewise, many chapters on the Books of Kings and Chronicles, Job, the Pentateuch of Moses, Joshua, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, Isaiah, and Ezra; four books on the Gospel of Mark; six on Luke; two books of Gospel homilies; many chapters on the Apostle; two books on the Acts of the Apostles; seven books on the Canonical Epistles; three on the Apocalypse; chapters on the whole of the New Testament; one book of letters to various persons; one on the six ages; nine books on the stations of the children of Israel; one on Isaiah; one on the intercalary year; nine on the equinox; and works on the histories of the saints.

He transferred the *Book of the Life and Passion of Saint Felix the Confessor* from verse into prose. He corrected the *Life and Passion of Saint Anastasius* from Greek into Latin. He composed the *Life of Saint Cuthbert, Monk and Bishop*, in verse and prose. He published the *History of the English* in five books; a martyrology of the birthdays of the saints; a book of hymns in various meters or rhythms; a book of epigrams in elegiac meter; one book each *On the Nature of Things* and *On Times*; another, larger book *On Times*; a book *On Orthography*; a book *On the Art of Meter*; and a book *On Figures and Tropes*, that is, on the figures and modes of expression of Sacred Scripture.

He flourished under Leo and died and was buried at Rome.

## Trithemius, *On Writers*

Bede, a monk and priest of the monastery of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, which is in England, of the order of Saint Benedict, was a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures, highly learned, and extremely skilled in secular literature. He was a philosopher, astronomer, calculator, and distinguished poet; he was not ignorant of the Greek language; he excelled in intelligence, was not showy in eloquence, but was nevertheless pleasant and well composed.

He wrote many volumes, in which the sharpness of his intellect is demonstrated. When he was seven years old, his relatives entrusted him to Abbot Benedict for education; afterward to Ceolfrith of the aforesaid monastery of Monkwearmouth. From then on he spent the whole period of his life in that monastery, devoting all his effort to the study of Scripture. Between the observance of regular discipline and the daily responsibility of singing in church, he always found it pleasant either to learn, teach, or write.

In the nineteenth year of his age he received the diaconate, and in the thirtieth the priesthood, both through the ministry of John the bishop, at the command of Abbot Ceolfrith. From the time he received the priesthood until the end of his life, he composed the works listed below.

- Four books on Genesis as far as Isaac.
- One book on Exodus.
- One book on Numbers.
- One book on Leviticus.
- One book on Deuteronomy.
- Three books on the Tabernacle and its vessels.
- Three books on the beginning of Kings.
- One book on thirty Questions on Kings, “To the Most Beloved Brother.”
- Two books on the building of the temple, “The chosen vessel exhorts us.”
- One book on Joshua.
- One book on Judges.
- One book on Chronicles.
- Three books on Solomon’s Proverbs, “Parables in Greek, Lat. . . .”
- One book on Ecclesiastes.
- Six books on the Song of Songs, “With the grace of Scripture assisting . . .”
- Three books on Ezra and Nehemiah, “The outstanding interpreter of Sacred . . .”
- One book on Tobit, “The book of our holy father.”
- Two books on the prophet Isaiah.
- Two books on Jeremiah.
- One book on Ezekiel.
- One book on Daniel.
- Twelve books on the Twelve Minor Prophets.
- Four books on the Gospel of Mark, “An exposition of the Gospel.”
- Six books on the Gospel of Luke, “The blessed evangelist Luke.”
- Two books of homilies on the Gospels, “The beginning of our redemption.”
- Fourteen books on the Epistles of Paul.
- Seven books on the Canonical Epistles, “James, etc., said concerning . . .”
- Two books on the Acts of the Apostles, “But the Acts of the Apostles . . .”
- Three books on the Apocalypse, “The Apocalypse of Saint John.”
- One book on times and the nature of things, “On the nature of things and calculation.”
- Another, shorter work in two books.
- One book of sparks from the sayings of the Fathers, “The Lord says in the Gospel.”
- Five books of the *Deeds of the English*, “Britain, an island of the ocean . . .”
- Two books of blessed Gregory’s passages on the Song of Songs, “In the exposition of the Song.”
- One book of the deeds of various saints.
- One book on the passion of Saint Felix.
- Two books on the life of Saint Albert, bishop.
- Two books of the chronicle of his monastery.
- One book of the martyrology.
- One book of hymns in various meters, “First, God made the sphere of heaven . . .”
- One book of epigrams in heroic meter.
- One book on the holy places.
- One book of readings on the Old Testament.
- One book of readings on the New Testament.
- One book of distinctions on Jeremiah.
- One book of distinctions on Job.
- Two books on Christ and the Church.
- One book on the Song of Habakkuk.
- One book on the art of meter, “Whoever possesses knowledge of meter . . .”
- One book on figures, “Sometimes it is customary . . .”
- One book on orthography.
- One book of letters to various persons.

He also published many other works which have not come to our notice. His works were of such authority even while he was still alive and continually writing new ones that, by order of the bishops of England, they were publicly read in the churches.

When, as was customary, they wrote the name of the author, “the priest Bede the Venerable,” in the placement of his homilies, they were unable to call him by another name while he was alive. Thus the title first assigned to him has endured to the present day, so that he is called “Bede the Venerable” rather than “Bede the Saint.” For it was not permitted to give a living person another name, even if he should be a saint.

Some invent other explanations for this title “Venerable”: some derive it from the inscription of his epitaph; others, dreaming that Bede was blind, offer that as the reason. But they are mistaken, since Bede was not blind, nor do we know that such an epitaph was inscribed on his tomb. Indeed, if I were not concerned with brevity, I could very easily refute these ravings.

He died under the emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 732, in the fifteenth indiction, at the age of seventy-two, on the day before the Kalends of June.

## Inscription formerly displayed in the church of Saint Paul at Jarrow

**The dedication of the basilica of Saint Paul, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the fifteenth year of King Ecgfrith and the fourth year of Ceolfrith, abbot and founder of the same church, by God’s authority.**

## Epitaph which William of Malmesbury says was inscribed on the wall of the church at Jarrow

Here lies the priest Bede, buried in the flesh;

Grant, O Christ, that his soul may rejoice in heaven forever,

And grant him to be made drunk from the fountain of Wisdom,

For which he sighed in prayer with ever-focused love.

## Eulogy

Bede, servant of God, noble star among monks,

Benefited the Church throughout the farthest regions of the earth.

Skilled in searching everywhere into the meaning of the Fathers,

He flourished in eloquence and composed very many works.

He duly lived three times thirty years in this life,

A priest in office, useful in intellect.

On the seventh day before the Kalends of January, deprived of his flesh,

He earned, as an Englishman, the angelic homeland.

## Another, from Leland, *Collection* III

England celebrates you; the whole world resounds with your name.

## Another, from the same source, *Collection* II

These verses, deservedly, were written for you, Albinus, venerable abbot,

By Bede, servant of God, lover of the heavenly word.

He composed them, a teacher renowned in our world,

With wondrous poetic art;

Many monuments of his intellect shine forth,

Never to be erased by the passage of time.

## Another, from Necham, in his account of Saint Cuthbert

Bede, an outstanding man, is associated with him;

His intellect the world could not contain,

But a small coffin covers his honored body.

## Inscription placed by Hugh Pudsey, bishop of Durham, on the reliquary containing the bones of the Venerable Bede

This reliquary contains the bones of the Venerable Bede;

Christ gave understanding to the maker and bronze to the giver.

Peter made the work; Bishop Hugh gave this gift;

Thus, in both, he honored each of his patrons.

## Inscription in the sacred church of the Holy Virgin at Durham

Bede, servant of God and priest, a man no less venerable for holiness than for knowledge, lies here. He was born in the territory of the monastery at Jarrow, which is now called Jarrow.

When he was seven years old, he was given to Abbot Benedict, and afterward to Ceolfrith, to be educated there. From then on he spent the whole of his life in the habitation of that monastery, devoting all his effort to the study of Scripture. Between the observance of regular discipline and the daily responsibility of singing in church, he always made it his practice either to learn, teach, or write.

In the nineteenth year of his life he received the diaconate, and in the thirtieth the priesthood, both from John of Beverley, archbishop of York.

He was a man greater than any praise. The most learned men of his age pronounced this eulogy concerning him: that an Englishman born in the remotest corner of the world surpassed the whole world by his intellect, since he penetrated the secrets of nearly all the sciences and of the whole of theology. His many works and volumes, well known throughout the Christian world, abundantly testify to this. Even while he was alive, they possessed such fame and authority that many passages from his homilies were added to the sacred readings and were publicly and solemnly recited everywhere in the ecclesiastical office.

It is known that he once had very celebrated pupils, distinguished lights of the Church soon afterward: Alcuin, tutor of King Charlemagne, and Claudius and Clement, who were the first to teach at Paris and to illuminate Gaul with the liberal arts.

He died in the monastery at Jarrow in the year of the Lord 734, at the age of fifty-nine, on the day on which the memory of the Lord’s Ascension is celebrated, and was buried there. Later his bones were transferred here to Durham, first with the head of King Oswald and the body of Saint Cuthbert, and afterward to this Galilee and tomb constructed by Bishop Hugh.

This epitaph concerning him is widely circulated:

These are the bones of Bede the Venerable in this grave.

# The Didactic Works of Bede the Venerable, Anglo-Saxon Priest

## The First Part of All His Works

### First Section: Genuine Works

## Book on Orthography

### A

The letter **A** is also a mark of a personal name when it alone signifies Augustus.

**B** is close to the letter **P**, which often changes into it, as in *supponit*, “he places beneath,” and *opponit*, “he places against.”

**C** is a mark of a personal name when it signifies Caesar; it is also a numeral when it means one hundred. [Note: These readings are taken from the London manuscript of *De Orthographia*, designated E, or from the Basel edition, designated B. EDIT.] [Note: E reads *Gaium*, i.e. *Caium*.]

The letter **D** is close to these consonants: **c, g, l, p, r, m, t** [Note: E reads *quae* in place of *quia hae*.], because these take its place, as in *accipe* (“receive”), *aggregа* (“join”), *alliga* (“bind”), *appare* (“appear”), *arripe* (“seize”), and *ammitte* (“send away”). [Note: B has *committe*, “commit.”]

**D** is a mark of a personal name when it alone signifies Decius; it is also a numeral when it means five hundred.

**L** alone signifies Lucius.

**M** alone signifies Marcus. [Note: B has *Marius*, “Marius.”]

**N** alone signifies Numerius; prefixed by **G**, it signifies Gnaeus.

**P** alone signifies Publius; with **R**, the Roman people; with **R** placed after it, the republic; and with **C** placed before it, **P.C.**, “the enrolled senators,” or “after the consulship.”

The letter **Q** is also a mark of a personal name when it alone signifies Quintus; it is a mark of office when it signifies Quaestor; and a mark of the people when it signifies Quirites.

**T** is a mark of a personal name when it alone signifies Titus.

**V** joined to **C**, with a horizontal stroke placed above it, signifies *vir clarissimus*, “most illustrious man.” **V** doubled, with a horizontal stroke above it, signifies *verbi gratia*, “for example.” **V** doubled with **C** doubled, **VVCC**, signifies *viri clarissimi*, “most illustrious men.”

## A

**Ante**, the preposition, has many meanings. It signifies time when it is said: “Before me no God was formed, and after me there shall not be”; it signifies presence, as in: “Before the sight of the nations he revealed his righteousness,” that is, “in the presence of the nations.” It signifies rank, as in: “He placed Ephraim before Manasseh”; and: “He who came after me was made before me,” that is, “was preferred to me.”

**Aula** in Latin means a royal house; in Greek it is called an *atrium*, “court.” Hence it should be noted that in the psalm where we read, “Worship the Lord in his holy aula,” *aula* should not be understood as a palace, but according to the Greek term as a court.

**Ausculto** may take a person in the dative: “I listen to the adviser”; and it may take a thing in the accusative: “I listen to the teacher’s instructions.” *Ausculto* and *audio*, “I hear,” are translated from the same Greek verb, **ἀκούω** (*akouō*), “I hear.”

**Arrha** is the Latin word; **arrhabon** is Greek, “pledge” or “earnest.”

**Agon** is Greek; in Latin, *certamen*, “contest.”

**Ἄρουρα** (*aroura*) is Greek; in Latin, *arvum*, “plowed land.”

**Ἄσφαλτος** (*asphaltos*) is Greek; in Latin, *bitumen*, “pitch.”

**Acer**, “sharp,” forms the superlative *acerrimus*, not *acerissimus*.

**Agilis**, “active,” forms *agillimus*, not *agilissimus*; likewise in the adverbs *acerrime* and *agillime*.

**Adjuvo**, “I help,” has a perfective form; **adjuto**, “I assist repeatedly,” has a frequentative form.

**Audeo**, “I dare,” has the perfect *ausus sum*, “I dared.”

**Acervo**, **aggero**, and **accumulo**, “I heap up,” derive from the same Greek verb, **σωρεύω** (*sōreuō*), “I heap up.”

**Aeger**, “sick,” applies to the mind; **aegrotus**, “ill,” to the body. Both are written with the diphthong *ae*.

**Aboleo**, “I destroy,” has the perfect *abolevi*.

**Arceo**, “I restrain,” has the perfect *arcui*.

**Alibi** means “in another place.”

**Alias** means “at another time”; nevertheless, we sometimes find *alias* used for *aliter*, “otherwise,” or for “in another place.”

**Abstineo me cibo**, “I abstain from food.”

**Alienus sum crimine**, “I am free from guilt.”

**Anteibat sapientia Salomon cunctis mortalibus**, “Solomon’s wisdom surpassed all mortals.” Julian said this.

**Admoneo** takes *interfectorem*, “the murderer,” and *caedis*, “of murder,” as well as *caedem*, “the killing.”

**Aequalis** means “equal in stature to another.”

**Aequabile** means “something that can be made equal.”

**Appetens cibum** and **appetens cibi** are both used, “desiring food.” Ambrose wrote: “As the crab is desirous of food, so it is watchful of danger.”

**Accuso** takes *sacrilegum*, “I accuse a sacrilegious person”; **insimulo**, “I charge” or “impute guilt.” Both derive from the same Greek verb, **κατηγορῶ** (*katēgorō*), “I accuse.”

**Animadverto in te** and **vindico in te**, “I punish you,” derive from the same Greek verb, **κολάζω** (*kolazō*), “I punish.”

**Aer**, “air,” is used only in the singular. Although we say *aera*, we do not use it in every case.

**Autumnus** is masculine, and **autumnum** is neuter; both are used in the singular.

We say both **aurichalcum** and **orichalcum**, “brass” or “golden bronze,” and this word is used only in the singular, as are the other metals.

The prepositions **ab** and **ex**, when the following word begins with a vowel, are pronounced in full, as in *ex oppido*, “from the town,” and *ab illo*, “from him.” When consonants follow, they lose their final letter, as in *e foro*, “from the forum,” and *a sacerdote*, “from the priest.” These prepositions differ in this way: when someone says that he is coming *a theatro*, he means that he is coming not from the theater itself but from a place near the theater; but whoever says that he is coming *ex theatro* means that he is coming from the theater itself.

**Ad** and **in** correspond to the preceding prepositions with an opposite force. To go *in forum* is to enter the forum itself; to go *ad forum* is to go to a place near the forum. Thus to come *in tribunal* and to come *ad tribunal* are not the same: the litigant comes *ad tribunal*, “to the tribunal,” whereas the praetor or judge comes *in tribunal*, “into the tribunal.”

**Ancillor**, **blandior**, and **adulor** all mean the same thing, namely the Greek **κολακεύω** (*kolakeuō*), “I flatter,” and they take the dative case.

**Aufero**, **eximo**, **adimo**, **subtraho**, and **subduco**, “I take away,” are translated from the same Greek verb, **ἀφαιροῦμαι** (*aphairoumai*), “I remove.”

**Abdico** can take an accusative noun or pronoun with a dative. Ambrose wrote: “Those who renounce worldly pleasures.”

**Alius**, “another,” has two forms in the dative: *alii* and *alio*. In Sacred Scripture we read: “And I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes”; and to another, “Come,” and he comes. Again: “To one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one.”

When dividing **Aegyptum** in writing, join the *p* to the following syllable. In **aspectum**, join the *c* to the following syllable; do likewise in **affectum** and **afflictum**, and in other words of this kind.

**Assuere**, “to sew onto,” and **assumentum** of cloth must be written with *s*, not *a*; likewise **assumere**, “to take up,” is written with *s*. [Note: B omits this entirely.]

**Appropriat**, “he appropriates,” is written with *p*; **apponit**, “he places beside,” likewise.

**Accurrit**, “he runs toward,” is written with *c*; **amministrat**, “he administers,” with *m*; **applicat**, “he applies,” with *p*; **allिगat**, “he binds,” with *l*; **assequor**, “I attain,” with *s*; **allevat**, “he raises,” with *l*; **assidue**, “continually,” with *s*; **aggredior**, “I approach,” with *g*. [Note: B omits *assidue* under the discussion of *s*.]

**Assarius** was the ancient term; now **as** is used, not *assis*. Properly, *assis* is the genitive.

**Allium**, “garlic,” and **dolium**, “jar,” are written with *i*, not *e*, unlike *oleum*, “oil.” Virgil wrote *allia* and *serpillum* with *i*.

**Ambo** and **duo** are neuter; **ambos** and **duos** are masculine. Some, however, following the Greeks, say *hos duo* and *hos ambo*, because the Greeks say **τοὺς δύο** and **τοὺς ἄμφω**.

Virgil wrote:

> But when you have recalled both leaders to battle.

Although **anguis**, “snake,” is masculine, Ovid, Varro, and Acinius also used it as feminine.

**Acer** forms the plural *acri*; **acris** forms the plural *acres*.

**Absconditus**, “hidden,” not *absconsus*.

**Alter**, “the other,” is used of two; **unus**, “one,” of several. Although we read *unus ex duobus*, “one of two.”

**Audacter** is Latin, but **audaciter** is better, because nouns ending in the letter *x* take *-citer* in their adverbs: *atrox*, *atrociter*; *ferox*, *ferociter*.

**Accersit** refers to one who summons; **arcessit** to one who accuses.

**Acervus** is a heap or mass.

**Acerbus** means unripe or harsh.

**Adficimur honore**, “we are honored,” and **adficimur injuria**, “we are injured.”

**Apparet**, “he appears,” and **apparet**, “he obeys,” are understood in different senses, not according to regular grammatical usage but for the sake of distinguishing the meanings.

**Arbor** refers to every kind of wood or tree; **arbusta** only to fruit-bearing trees.

**Avenae**, “oats,” are sterile grain; **habenae**, “reins,” are restraints for beasts of burden. The latter is named from the power of holding; the former from eagerness to seize.

**Accidunt** are evils; **contingunt** are good things; **eveniunt** are both.

One is **advocatur** when he is summoned to provide legal assistance; **evocatur** when he is summoned to offer service; **invocatur** when he is called upon to provide help.

**Adportare** means to bring something; **comportare**, to bring together into one place; **deportare**, to set down; **exportare**, to carry off.

**Agnoscimus** refers to things that had slipped from us. [Note: B reads “things that had slipped from us.”] **Cognoscimus** refers to things previously unknown and unseen. [Note: B reads “all things that come together.”]

**Alium** signifies both upward and downward.

We correctly call a drink **aquata**, “watered,” when it receives water from elsewhere; but a place that pours forth water from itself is **aquosus**, “watery.”

**Album**, “white,” belongs only to natural color; **candidum**, “bright white,” often also implies diligence or refinement, and is sometimes applied both to body and mind. Thus we properly say *albos capillos*, “white hair,” and *candidam carnem*, “bright flesh.”

**Alvus** is properly used of men; **uterus**, “womb,” of women; **venter**, “belly,” of either sex.

**Acceptor** and **accipiter** are both used. Virgil uses *accipiter*; Lucilius uses *acceptoris et ungues*, “the claws of the hawk.”

**Apud** is written with *d*; **caput** with *t*, because its genitive is *capitis*.

**Armarium** is a place where the instruments of any arts are stored.

**Armamentarium** is a place where only weapons are kept.

**Accedit**, “he approaches,” is written with *e*, deriving from walking or approaching.

**Accidit**, “it happens,” is written with *i*, deriving from an event.

## B

**Beelzebub**, not *Belsebul* or *Belsebud*.

**Belial**, not *Beliar*.

**Byrsa**, Greek **Βύρσα** (*Byrsa*), is Latin *corium*, “hide” or “leather.”

**Bellus**, “beautiful,” has the superlative *bellissimus* but no comparative. Instead one should say *magis bellus*, “more beautiful,” and conversely *minus bellus*, “less beautiful,” that is, “less handsome.”

**Buccina** is the instrument with which a trumpeter gives a signal.

**Buccinus** is the sound produced by it.

The **buccina** is a pastoral instrument, made with a curved horn; hence it is also called in Greek **κερατίνια** (*keratinia*), “horn instruments.” The **tuba**, however, is made of bronze or silver and resounds at solemn occasions. [Note: E has “gold.”] [Note: E has “is struck” instead of “resounds.”]

**Baptismus**, *baptismi*, is masculine; **baptisma**, *baptismatis*, is neuter; and **baptismum**, *baptismi*, is likewise neuter.

We say **barbam** of a human being, “beard,” but **barbas** of animals.

**Buxus** is the tree; **buxum** is the wood itself.

The ancients said both **balneum** and **balineum**; there is no difference between them when referring to private baths. Public baths, however, are feminine and always plural: *balneae*. [Note: B omits *frequenter balneos*, “frequently *balneos*.”]

**Belluae**, that is, “wild animals,” begin with *b*.

**Barathrum** is used only in the singular. The pagans called the place among the dead by this name.

**Blanditiae**, “flatteries,” and **bigae**, “a pair of horses,” as also **trigae**, “a team of three,” and **quadrigae**, “a team of four,” are used only in the plural. Yet in the writings of our authors we find both *bigam* and *quadrigam* in the singular.

## C

**Cana** and **Simon Cananaeus** are written with a simple *c*.

**Chanaan** and the woman **Chananaea** are written with an added aspiration.

**Κυνόμυια** (*kynomuia*), written with *y*, signifies a dog-fly, for **κύων** (*kyōn*) means “dog” in Greek. **Κοινόμυια** (*koinomuia*), with the diphthong *oe*, signifies a common fly, for **κοινόν** (*koinon*) means “common” in Greek. Hence **coenobium**, “monastery,” received its name from communal life. We believe that in Exodus and in the Psalter it was especially translated so as to signify every kind of fly, but through carelessness arising from similarity of sound it happened that *cynomia* was written instead of *coenomia*. [Note: B has “from community.”]

**Coitus** generally means any coming together, whether of a journey, an agreement, or a marriage.

**Carduus**, “thistle,” has three syllables, like **arduus**, “steep,” **fatuus**, “foolish,” and **mortuus**, “dead.” It must therefore be declined in the same way: *hujus cardui*, *huic carduo*, *hunc carduum*; in the plural: *hi cardui*, *horum carduorum*, *his carduis*.

**Cubicularius** is the keeper of a bedchamber.

**Cubicularis** is a bed suited to a bedchamber, as *caligarius* is a craftsman who makes boots, and *caligaris* a boot nail.

Melissus used **clunes**, “buttocks,” as feminine; Verrius Flaccus proves that the word is used as masculine.

We **commodamus**, “lend temporarily,” a horse, garment, or slave to a friend, intending to receive back the very thing we gave. We **mutuo damus**, “lend,” money, grain, wine, and similar things, which necessarily must be returned in another equivalent form.

**Canities**, “gray hair,” not *canitia*.

According to Verrius Flaccus, **camara** is the correct form, not *camera* with *e*. But Lucretius, by writing *cameris ex teretibus*, “from rounded chambers,” shows that *camera* may also be used.

**Curriculus**, masculine, is a diminutive of *currus*, “chariot.”

**Curriculum**, neuter, is a space suitable for running, or the activity of running itself.

**Clypeus**, masculine, is used to signify a shield; in the neuter, it signifies an image. But usage varies between the two.

**Caseus**, “cheese,” is masculine, although Pomponius used the neuter *caseum molle*, “soft cheese.”

**Cuspis**, “point” or “spear,” has the genitive *cuspidis*, not *cuspes*.

Varro used **capparis**, “caper,” as feminine, and in Greek it too is feminine: **ἡ κάππαρις** (*hē kapparis*).

We say **cassidem**, “helmet,” from the nominative **haec cassis**; but many say **cassidam**, as Propertius does:

> After the golden helmet had uncovered her forehead.

And Virgil: “A golden helmet for the seer.” CAPO is the current form; but Varro, in *On the Latin Language*, says: “From a castrated barnyard cock comes *capus*.” CINGULA, when referring to human beings, is neuter; for animals, we also say *has cingulas* in the feminine. CAPAX means “one that easily contains”; CAPABILIS, “one that is easily contained.” COLLOCAT must be written with *l*, not *conlocat* with *n*.

[Col. 0128D] CALUMNIA is a false accusation: when an adversary either charges us with an evil we have not committed, or tries to interpret as its opposite some good that we are proved to have done. CONSULO TIBI (“I advise you”), PROSPICIO (“I look out for”), and PROVIDEO (“I provide for”) derive from the same Greek verb, Προνοέω (*pronoéō*). CONTEMNO HOSTEM (“I despise the enemy”), DESPICIO (“I look down on”), SPERNO (“I reject”), and ASPERNOR (“I disdain”) derive from the same Greek verb, Καταφρονέω (*kataphronéō*). COMMEIO LECTUM (“I urinate into a bed”) and PERMEIO (“I urinate through”): *comminxi* and *perminaei*. COMITOR AMICUM (“I accompany a friend”), and COMITOR AMICIS (“I accompany friends”).

[Note: [Col. 0129] B.: “It signified bloody and black.”]

[Col. 0129A] CORINTHIUM CIVEM (“a Corinthian citizen”), but CORINTHIACUM VAS (“a Corinthian vessel”). We fight COMINUS with swords, but EMINUS with javelins, because the former does not leave the hand, while the latter is thrown from the hands [Note: [Col. 0129] B.: “from the hands”]. CLYPEUS is the term for a weapon; CLYPEUM belongs to an image. CADIT (“falls”) may be used even of someone falling on level ground; DECIDIT (“falls down”) is used of a fall from above. CAERULUS is a natural color; CAERULEUS is represented or fashioned. Thus one is what it is, the other what it becomes. CLARITAS applies both to light and to clarity; CLARITUDO to lineage. The former therefore concerns splendor, the latter nobility. CRUCIATUS is bodily pain, or the condition in which one person is tortured by another. CRUCIAMENTUM is that which causes torture. CERNO (“I discern”) and CRESCO (“I grow”) have the same perfect tense, *crevi*.
