CAEDO (“I cut”), *cecidi*, is written with the *ae* diphthong: “And the linden is cut down, light before the yoke,” says Virgil. CEDO (“I yield”), *cessi*, is written with a simple *e*. CUPIO has the forms *cupivi* and *cupii*. Cicero, in *Against Cluentius*, wrote: “He desired both the son and this man to be killed, especially the son”; *cupiit* stands for *cupivit*.

CALUMNIOR INNOCENTI (“I bring a false accusation against an innocent person”), not *innocentem*; although some interpreters, following the Greek construction, have used the accusative, saying: “And pray for those who persecute and slander you.” CUR, the adverb “why,” more often takes an indicative verb. Gregory: “It must be investigated why something is said to have happened on a certain day before the Lord.” CLAVUS likewise, when it means a purple garment, is feminine in gender. CALLUM and COENUM are also singular-only nouns.

[Col. 0129C] CANI, CANCELLI, and CASSES have no singular number. CASSES means nets. CAULAE likewise; also CERIMONIAE, CUNAE, and COMPEDES; and in the neuter gender, CASTRA, CIBARIA, CREPUNDIA, and CUNABULA. CRUOR has no plural, although Virgil uses it in the plural: “He was drying the black bloodstains on his garment.” CONTAGIUM and CONTAGIA are to be treated as neuter; but CONTAGIA, in this meaning, is feminine. COMOEDIA means songs sung at banquets, because a banquet is called Κῶμος (*kômos*) in Greek. Κάρταλλος (*kártallos*) in Greek is FISCELLA in Latin. CALAMUS in Greek is ARUNDO in Latin.

[Col. 0129D] CANON in Greek is REGULA in Latin. CADOS in Greek is SITULA in Latin. CUNABULA are the swaddling cloths of infancy; but John, bishop of Constantinople, writes that Lazarus was wrapped in swaddling cloths in the tomb. CANTATOR and CANTATRIX derive from the verb *canto*. From the verb *cano*, the correct forms are CANTOR and CANTRIX. COMBURO must be written with *m*, not *n*. The same applies to COMPARO, COMPONO, and other forms of this kind. When CONSPECTUS is divided in writing, join the *c* to the following syllable.

[Col. 0130A] COMPLACEO, not *conplaceo*; COMMORATUS, not *conmoratus*. COMPREHENDO is written with *m*. CAMELUS is written with one *l*. COMM­ODAT and COMMENDAT are written with *m*. COMPUTRESCIT is written with *m*. COMPLURES is written with *m*. When COLUMNA is divided in writing, attach the *m* to the following syllable. The same applies to CALUMNIA. CELO, *celas*, meaning “I conceal,” is written with a simple *e*. CAELO, *caelas*, when it means “I engrave or paint,” is written with the *ae* diphthong. Hence *caelum* is better understood as deriving from the fact that it is depicted with the varied array of stars, like an engraved work, than from the idea that it conceals from mortals invisible and uncertain mysteries. CANTHARUS is an animal; CANTHARUM is a chamber or house.

[Col. 0130B] CLAMO is used of a simple cry; CONCLAMO, of crying out together with many others; ACCLAMO also means to murmur or shout in response. PROCLAMO expresses an exultant cry of praise or supplication. DECLAMO means to practice rhetoric. EXCLAMO is used when I raise my voice with all my strength. CURRO means only that, while on a journey, I do not postpone the matter until the day after tomorrow. CURSO means that, compelled by some necessity, I am forced to hurry somewhat faster; CURSITO, that I flee while an enemy pursues me. CIRCA refers to visible matter or a place. ERGA, however, concerns the mind, especially when one has a more favorable feeling toward someone. CIRCUM refers to time. CIRCITER refers to number.

[Col. 0130C] CARCER, the place where people are confined, is singular. CARCERES, the starting gates from which chariots pour forth, is plural; both forms are masculine. CEPIT, from *capio*, is written with a simple *e* [Note: [Col. 0129] B. omits “with a simple *e*”]. COEPIT, from *incipio*, is written with the *ae* diphthong [Note: [Col. 0129] B. omits “with the *ae* diphthong”]. COEPTA is written with the diphthong; INCEPTA with a simple *e*. COLUMBAE are pigeons that can be tamed and accustomed to houses. PALUMBES are wild birds inhabiting rocks and woods. CONSCRIBERE means to write many things together. EXSCRIBERE means to transfer something to others. TRANSCRIBERE is used when our right passes to another. INSCRIBERE belongs to an accusation. [Note: [Col. 0129] B. omits: “ASCRIBERE belongs to assignment.”] ASCRIBERE belongs to assignment. DESCRIBERE belongs to diction or arrangement.

[Col. 0130D] CONSUESCIMUS is used of good things; INSU­ESCIMUS of bad things; ADSUESCIMUS of both. CRASSARI refers to the body and fatness; GRASSARI to the mind and cruelty.

## D

DILIBUIT UNGUENTO (“he anointed with ointment”), not *delibuit*. DISERTUS means an orator; DESERTUS means abandoned. DELATOR is one who reports someone for prosecution. DILATOR is one who postpones something in order to bring it forward later. DELUIT means “cleanses”; DILUIT, “dilutes” or “moderates.”

[Col. 0131A] DEDUCO refers to bringing a friend out. DIDUCO means “I separate” or “draw apart.” I drank a DIMIDIATUM CALICEM (“half-filled cup”); we should not say *dimidium*, for one does not drink the vessel itself but what is inside it. DONAMUS applies both to the thing that we give and to the person to whom we give it [Note: [Col. 0131] B.: “to him”]. DELICTUM means a sin or offense. DELECTUM means the selection of soldiers or the choice made in some examination. DILIGI (“to be loved”) belongs to affection; DELEGI (“to have chosen”) to judgment. DAEMON must be marked with the diphthong; DEUS with *e* alone. DAMNATUS, ADDICTUS, and ABSOLUTUS. Virgil: “Whom toil condemns”—that is, may his own excellence acquit him or make him victorious.

[Col. 0131B] DOLIUM must be written with *i*, not DOLEUM with *e*. DILECTIO and DILIGO are written with *i*, as are the forms derived from them. DOMUNCULA is a house made up of small rooms; DOMICILIUM is a bird’s nest. You may say DESCENDO MONTES, meaning “I descend through the mountains” or “into the mountains.” DESCENDO SCALAS or PISCINAM means “I descend by way of the stairs” or “into the pool.” We correctly say DEGREDIOR MONTE, meaning “I descend from the mountain.” DISCRUCIOR and CRUCIOR may be constructed with *animi*, *animo*, or *animum*. DECUS belongs to honor; DECOR to appearance. DELICIAE and DIVITIAE have no singular number.

[Col. 0131C] DENARIUS is masculine in Latin; DENARION is neuter in Greek. DIALOGUS is Greek; DISPUTATIO is Latin. DRAMA is Greek and neuter; FABULA is the Latin equivalent. When DEFUNCTUS is divided in writing, the *c* must be joined to the following syllable. DIDYMUS means “twin” or “double”; its first syllable is written with *i*, the second with *y*. DELIRAMENTUM, not *deleramentum*, because it derives from the verb *liro*, “to plow a furrow.” Just as oxen are said to *delirare* when they turn aside from the proper course of furrowing, so people are said to *delirare* when they turn their hearts away from good things toward evil.

DILUCULUM, not *deluculum*, because it displays the slight light of day.

[Col. 0131D] DESIDERIUM concerns absent things that have not yet been attained; CONCUPISCENTIA concerns both kinds. Things that one possesses and things that one does not possess are coveted. Through coveting, a person enjoys the things he has; through longing, he covets things that are absent. DITO and DIVITO mean “I enrich”; in Greek, Πλουτίζω (*ploutízō*). DECORIO, *decoriavi*, and DECUMO, *decumavi*, mean the same thing; in Greek, δεκατῶ (*dekatô*). DIMITTERE means “to abandon”; DEMITTERE means “to send downward,” as in: “Who sent down its cornerstone.” DOMINOR may be constructed with *tui* or *tibi*.

[Col. 0132A] DOGMATA is Greek; DECRETA is Latin. DOGMATIZO means “I decide” or “I judge.” DUM, the conjunction “while,” sometimes takes an indicative verb. Gregory: “While it knows and does not love, ignorance puffs itself up.” Again: “While he considers that she once did not possess it, let him moderate his grief over what he has lost” [Note: [Col. 0131] B.: “although”]. DOLEO VICEM TUI, and *tuam*, and DOLEO TIBI. Pope Gregory, concerning Benedict’s father: “Although he loved his persecutor, he grieved more for him than for himself.”

DUM, the conjunction, sometimes takes the subjunctive and sometimes the indicative, as in: “While my heart was anxious”; and: “While it is said to me every day, ‘Where is your God?’” And blessed Pope Gregory: “Therefore, since Job’s friends did not know how to distinguish the kinds of blows, they believed that the stricken man had been struck because of his guilt.” At times DUM has the sense “until,” as in the poet:

“Tityrus, while I return—for the road is short—feed the little goats.”

[Col. 0132B] DESPERATUS is written with *e*; DISPERSUS with *i*. DISCEDO is written with *i*; DESCENDO with *e*. DIASTOLE is Greek; INTERDICTUM is Latin. It is a mark placed at the foot of a letter to separate letters that have been improperly joined, so that a boy reading does not make a mistake; for example:

“Free, he moved his footsteps across the glassy fields.”

DOMUS has two ablative forms, ending in *o* and in *u*. From *domo*, the plural genitive is *domorum*; from *domu*, *domuum*.

## E

EGEO may be constructed with *victus*, *victum*, or *victu*. ERIPIO FLAMMAE HOMINEM (“I rescue a person from the flames”). EGREDIOR DOMO ET CIVITATE (“I go out from the house and the city”). ERROR is a defect in a thing, as are AMOR and DOLOR; ERRATIO concerns a fixed path. ERRATRIX refers to a person, as in the textually uncertain example: “The wandering hunter, ivy of the vine.”

ELOQUENTIA and ELEGANTIA are always singular. EXUVIAE, EXSEQUIAE, and EXCUBIAE are plural-only nouns; EXCUBIAE are called νυκτοφυλάκια (*nyktophylákia*) in Greek. EXTA likewise occurs only in the plural. EMPORIA is feminine and Greek; in Latin, MERCATUS (“market”). EMOLUMENTUM must be written with a simple *e*. AEMULATIO with the *ae* diphthong. EQUO SEDEO (“I sit on a horse”) is said with the dative or ablative without a preposition; EQUUM SEDEO with the accusative; likewise *in equo* and *super equum*.

[Col. 0132D] EMANAT FONS (“a spring flows forth”), or EMANAT TERRA AQUAM (“the earth gives forth water”), means “produces and brings forth.” EMANAT AQUA DE FONTE or DE TERRA means “water flows out.” Gregory: “That place, situated about forty miles from the city of Rome, sends forth cold and clear waters.” And again, concerning the same tomb: “The fragrance of its sweetness flowed forth.” EXPROBRAT is used of one who recalls benefits he has conferred. OPPROBRAT is used of one who casts a reproach— that is, a fault—at someone. EXSPECTATUR means “he is awaited because he is going to come”; SPECTATUR, “he is looked at,” or “approved.”

EXERCITUS LABORIBUS (“trained by hardships”); EXERCITATUS STUDIIS (“trained in studies”). EXSTRUERE means to build upward. INSTRUERE ACiem [Note: [Col. 0133] B. omits “expressing”] means to draw up a battle line or arrange an action. ADSTRUERE means to affirm; CONSTRUERE, to join by building together; SUBSTRUERE, to build underneath after placing something above.

[Col. 0133A] EXCUBIAE must be written with *b*; EXUVIAE with *v*. EORUNDEM and EARUNDEM must be written with *n*, not *m*.

## F

FIMBRIA is feminine; FIMBRIUM is neuter. FIDES, *fidei*, concerns belief. FIDES, *fidis*, concerns a stringed instrument; both are long. FLEMINA are places where the legs abound in blood; FLEMINAS are furrows in calloused hands or feet. FASTUS, referring to pride, forms the plural genitive *fastuum*. FASTUS, referring to calendar books, forms *fastorum*.

[Col. 0133B] FUNGI means “to perform” or “carry out”; DEFUNGI, “to complete.” FREMOR is the murmur of human beings; FREMITUS, the roar of wild animals. FLAVUM means red or yellow-red, as in “yellow Ceres.” FURVUM means black. FULVUM means blackish-red; thus we speak of a tawny lion, a tawny eagle, tawny gold, and a tawny battle. The word may also describe a cloud that contains something fiery from heaven and something grimy from mourning [Note: [Col. 0133] B.: “but concerning a cloud”]. Gold is certainly called *fulvum* when something blackish has been added to the splendor of its beauty.

FORUM, neuter, means a place designated for conducting business, or is used when we mean commerce. FOROS, masculine, means the decks of ships where the rowers sit.

[Col. 0133C] FORNAX should be feminine, because its diminutive is *fornacula*, not *fornaculus*. PHALANX refers to soldiers; PHALANGA to a staff to which something is tied. FEDUS, meaning “ugly,” is written with a simple *e*. FOEDUS, meaning “a pact,” is written with the *oe* diphthong. FORMOSUS is written without *n*, like *speciosus*. When we say FRUCTUM [Note: [Col. 0133] B.: “when you say or write it”], if it is divided in writing, join the *c* to the second syllable. The same applies to FACTUM and FICTUM and other forms of this kind.

FALSO is a noun, a verb, and an adverb. As a noun it is the ablative of *falsum*: *ab hoc falso*. As a verb it belongs to the first conjugation: *falso, falsas*. As an adverb: “You speak falsely.” FLAGITIA are the sins we commit against the Lord; FACINORA are those committed against a human being. FLAGRO AMORE (“I burn with love”) and ARDEO AMORE (“I am on fire with love”) derive from the same Greek verb, καίομαι (*kaíomai*).

FIDENS SUM may be constructed with *animi* or *animo*. FIDUS means “he will be a friend”; call a servant FIDELEM. Likewise, let someone be *fidelis* as a servant is to his master; *fidus* concerns nature. Thus one is recognized at a particular time, while the other is found consistently. FIMUS and FUMUS have no plural number. FAMES likewise; also FENUM and FEL.

FUR, FURES, and FRENI are always masculine plural forms; nevertheless, we also find *frena* and *frenum*. FAR, FRUMENTUM, and the other names of grain are always singular, although we read *frumenta* and *hordea*. FAUCES has no singular, although *faux* is also found.

[Col. 0134A] FIDUS, FIDISSIMUS has no comparative; instead one should say *magis fidus*, and conversely *minus fidus*. FACILIS forms the superlative *facillimus*, not *facilissimus*; likewise *difficillimus*. In the adverbs: *facile, facillime*; *difficile, difficillime, difficilius*. We do not say *faciliter* or *difficiliter*, although the ancients did. FULGEO and FULCIO have the same perfect, *fulsi*.

[Col. 0134B] FRICO, *fricas*, has the perfect *fricui*. FRIGO, *frigis*, has *frixi*. FACINUS and FACINORA designate not only sins but sometimes good works as well; the noun is formed from *facere*, “to do.” FRATRES refers not only to males born of the same parents, but also to males and females—or to several persons of both sexes—born of the same father and mother; all are called *fratres* without distinction.

## G

[Note: [Col. 0133] B.: “Guba.”]

GULA should be said, not *gyla*, because no word of our language adopts the letter *y*. GOBIUS, the name of a fish, is sometimes read as *gobio*. GAUDIUM is joy of the mind; EXSULTATIO also includes words and bodily movements.

GREMIUM means the inner, girded recess of a garment; SINUS the outer receptacle formed by a folded garment. GLUTEN is neuter, with the forms *glutinis, glutini*; but Sallust also uses *glutinum, glutini, glutino*. GITH is a *monoptoton*—a word with one form for all cases—and has no plural. It is neuter and is declined through all cases. GRACILIS forms *gracillimus*, not *gracilissimus*. GAUDEO, *gaudes*, has the perfect *gavisus sum*.

## H

HILARUS forms the plural *hilari*. HILARIS forms the plural *hilares*. HOSPES means both the person who receives and the person who is received. HORRENDUM may describe something despised as well as something astonishing:

“Fixing his terrible eyes upon the maiden.”

HERBIDUM describes a place in which there is grass, even if it is usually dry. HERBOSUM describes something that readily produces grass, even if it is temporarily dry. HAURIO and HAUSTUS must be written with aspiration. The same applies to HARENAM, because it is said to derive either from *haerere*, “to cling,” or from *haurire aquam*, “to draw water.”

HEBESCIT describes one who grows dull from the ordinary use of his nature; HEBETESCIT one who loses his sharpness. HI, the plural pronoun, is written with one *i*. HIS likewise with one *i* [Note: [Col. 0135] B.: “with the *e* lengthened”].

[Col. 0135A] HOLOCAUSTOMA is singular; HOLOCAUSTOMATA is plural. HAMO, *hamas*, and the noun HAMUS must be written with aspiration [Note: [Col. 0135] B.: “So also *humo*, whose perfect is *humavi*”]; likewise INHAMO and its perfect *inh­amavi*. HERBESCIT AGER (“the field grows grassy”) is used when it produces grass, just as *adolescit* and *pubescit* are used when the ears of grain approach maturity. HUMILIS is opposed to *superbus* and is a virtue of the mind; it is also opposed to *sublimis*, which concerns social condition. A lower-lying place is likewise called *humilior* or *humiliatus*; someone afflicted by oppression is also called *humiliatus*.

## I

INTEMPESTA NOX is midnight, when one ought to rest. It is so called because it is unsuitable for the activity of those who are awake. The ancients called *tempestivum* “opportune” and *intempestivum* “inopportune”; the words are derived from *tempus*, “time,” not from the disturbance of the air that is ordinarily called *tempestas*. Historians, however, freely use this word when they say *ea tempestate*, meaning “at that time.”

IMMATURITAS is a nighttime period that is not *maturum*, that is, not suitable for carrying out an activity while awake; in ordinary speech it is called an inconvenient hour, in Greek ἀωρία (*aōría*). “I came beforehand in the untimely hour”: ἐν ἀωρίᾳ (*en aōría*). For the meaning it makes no difference whether one says *maturitate* or *in maturitate* [Note: [Col. 0135] B.: “whether it is said *maturitate* or *in immaturitate*”], just as it makes no difference whether someone says that he did something *galli cantu* or *in galli cantu*—“at cockcrow.”

INTERIOR and INTIMUS have no positive degree. INFERIOR and INFIMUS likewise.

[Col. 0135C] IPSUM must be neuter, not *ipsud*, just as *illud* and *istud*. In the same way, the ancients used not *ipse* but *ipsus* as the masculine nominative. IMPINGO has the perfects *impinxi* and *impegi*. IMMUNES PERICULI and IMMUNES A PERICULO are both possible. INDIGUS and PRODIGUS are written with one *u*; INDIGA and PRODIGA without *u*. Augustine: “Avarice gathers money; extravagance scatters it. The former is needy, the latter wasteful.” INCREDIBILE is something that cannot be believed. INCREDULUS is one who does not wish to believe.

IN, the preposition, sometimes means what the adverb *valde* means, and strengthens the force of the verb to which it is prefixed, as in *increpuit*, *insonuit*, *infregit*. Sometimes it means “not,” as in *invalidus* and *infirmus*. Sometimes it stands for “among,” as in: “Blessed are you among women.” Sometimes it means “against,” as in: “Two will be divided against three, and three against two.” Sometimes it refers to a span of time, meaning “until,” as when we say *a mane in noctem*, intending “until night.”

[Col. 0135D] INTEREST and REFERT, meaning “to differ” or “to matter,” have the same meaning, corresponding to the Greek διαφέρει (*diaphérei*). We say *interest mea* and *refert mea*; *interest ejus* and *refert illius*; *interest nostra* and *refert nostra*; *interest illorum* and *refert illorum*.

[Col. 0136A] IMPLEOR may be constructed with *vini* or *vino*. INTUEOR TE and INTUEOR IN TE (“I look at you” / “I look upon you”). INCURRO TE and INCURRO IN TE; its perfects are *incurri* and *incucurri*. INVIDEO DIVITEM (“I envy the rich man”); INVIDEO EI PULCHRITUDINEM (“I envy him his beauty”). IRATUS arises from an offense; IRACUNDUS is a matter of nature. Anger therefore arises through a sudden movement. IRACUNDIA is a persistent vice. IGNIS has an ablative ending in both *e* and *i*. INTESTINA and INCUNABULA are always plural.

INSTAR ILLIUS REI should be said, not *ad instar*. ILLUVIES is filth; INGLUVIES is the throat or belly. The former derives from not washing; the latter from swallowing. INSITA is a tree into which a foreign shoot is inserted after an incision has been made. ADSITA is one to which something else is attached while it remains intact. INVIDEO TIBI DIVITIIS, not *divitias*.

[Col. 0136B] INERMUS forms the plural *inermi*; INERMIS forms the plural *inermes*. ILLIUS SIMILIS refers to manners; ILLI SIMILIS to appearance. INVIDUS is one who envies; INVIDIOSUS is one who bears envy [Note: [Col. 0135] B. omits “bears envy”]. IDEM, with a short vowel, is neuter; IDEM, with a long vowel, is masculine in both numbers.

INTERPRETOR and the forms derived or inflected from it must be written with a simple *e*. IMBERBI is the correct form, not *imberbes*. Varro says: “Beardless young men.” Cicero likewise wrote: “He led him forth beardless,” not *imberbem*. Titus Livius, however, uses *imberbis* in the singular. IMPUTRIBILE must be written with *m*, not *n*. IMPONO and IMMITTO are treated similarly, as are related forms.

[Col. 0136C] IRRIGO, not *inrigo*. IMPLEO, not *inpleo*. IMMUNDUS, not *inmundus*. INQUILINI are people who have no home of their own and live in another’s house [Note: [Col. 0135] B. omits “they live in another’s house”]. INCOLAE and ADVENAE derive from the same Greek word, πάροικος (*pároikos*), which we find translated in the sacred writings. From these come INCOLATUS and INQUILINATUS. INQUILINUS, like PEREGRINUS, sometimes takes a dative construction, as Augustine says concerning the reprobate: “They too are strangers and sojourners in this earth, but they are not of the people of God.”

IMPONERE means to place something—whether corporeal or incorporeal—upon something else. But *imponere* is sometimes used for “to deceive”; hence *impostura* is named. This applies when silver or gold is adulterated with a cheaper metal; the person who does this is called an *impostor*. In common usage, therefore, someone who practices fraud or pretense is also called an *impostor*. Pope Gregory: “He began to call him a pretender and, in rustic language, an impostor.” Hence one also finds in sacred Scripture: “Why have you deceived me? Did I not serve you for Rachel?” And in the Books of Kings: “Why have you deceived me? For you are Saul”; that is: “Why did you wish to deceive me by pretense and commit fraud?” Augustine likewise says: “And therefore the wretched man deceives himself”; for he defrauds himself when, by loving worse things, he loses better ones.

## J

JOCUM is singular and neuter; in the plural, *hi joci* and *haec joca*. JUGA MONTIUM (“mountain ridges”) is always plural; JUGUM is the yoke of draft animals. But Virgil says: “You have overcome this ridge.” JUVENTUS, like SENECTUS, is not inflected in the plural. JUVENIS and JUVENIOR do not take a superlative, nor do SENEX and SENIOR. JUNIOR and SENIOR are commonly used of one another to mean “younger” and “older,” even if neither has reached or approached old age.

Ambrose: “The sun is younger than the grasses, younger than the hay.” JUVENTUS refers to a group of young people; JUVENTAS to one person’s age; JUVENTA to the goddess herself—as the Greeks or poets say—the daughter of Juno and wife of Hercules. We read in the books of the *Fasti* that the month of June was named after her.

## L

LARGE and LARGITER are both correctly used by Julius Modestus; but *large* expresses quality, whereas *largiter* expresses quantity. LIBIDINOSUS, from *libido*, is written with *b*. LIVIDUS, from *livor*, is pronounced with *u*. LARBA is written with *b*. LUDIFICOR STULTUM (“I mock a fool”) and DELUDOR (“I am deceived”) derive from the same Greek verb, ἀντιπαίζω (*antipaízō*); their perfect is *ludificatus sum*. The ancients, however, used *ludificavi*.

LABIUM refers to the upper lip; LABRUM to the lower lip. ROSTRUM is used only for something curved. [Col. 0137C] LATERE and ABSCONSUM ESSE mean “to be hidden,” while *late patere* means “to be widely evident.” Virgil: “And they hide the concealed shields.” LEPUS is the animal; LEPOS is pleasantness or delight. Hence we call something agreeable *lepidum*. LIMEN belongs to buildings; LIMES to regions. LARGITAS is associated with humanity or generosity; LARGITIO with ambition. LIGAT QUIS VINCULO (“someone binds with a bond”); LEGAT TESTAMENTO (“someone bequeaths by will”).

LOQUI belongs to a human being. OBLOQUI belongs to a detractor, as do OBJICIT and OPPONIT. ALLOQUI belongs to one who persuades, exhorts, or commands; ELOQUI to an orator.

LAURENTIUS, CAELIUS, and many similar names, whose nominative singular ends in *-ius*, form the singular genitive with a double *i* and the singular vocative with a single *i*: *hic Laurentius, Caelius; hujus Laurentii, Caelii; o Laurenti, Caeli*. Or the vocative may end in *-ie*: *hic impius, hujus impii, o impie*. It should be noted that in the Acts of the Apostles, when Cornelius saw an angel of God entering to him and saying, “Corneli,” the vocative is correctly pronounced with a simple *i*; in Greek, however, it is written with *-ie*, *Cornelie*.

LIMUS, LUX, LABES, and LAETUM have no plural. LIBERI, when it means “children,” and LATEBRAE have no singular. LAC, LIQUAMEN, LENTICULA, and LENS are always singular. [Col. 0138A] LOCUS is masculine in the singular; in the plural, *haec loca*. LUTER is Greek: λουτήρ (*loutḗr*), masculine; in Latin it is LABRUM. LUCEO and LUGEO have the same perfect, *luxi*. LIBERO TE PERICULO (“I free you from danger”); LIBEROR A MOLESTIA (“I am freed from trouble”). LINO and LINIO have the perfects *linui* and *linivi*.

## M

MARGARITA is feminine; MARGARITUM is neuter. In Proverbs: “Golden earrings and a shining pearl.” MALOGRANATUM and MALUM GRANATUM are both commonly used, and both are declined. Thus: *malogranatum, hujus malogranati*, and *haec malogranata, horum malogranatorum, his malogranatis*, and so forth. Likewise: *hoc malogranatum, hujus maligranati*, and *haec malagranata, horum malorum granatorum*, and so forth.

MISERET ME SENIS (“I pity the old man”); MISEREOR SENIS and MISEREOR SENEM; MISERTUS PAUPERIS uses the genitive; MISERATUS PAUPEREM uses the accusative. MISEROR means “I have compassion,” and in Greek is συμπάσχω (*sympáskho*).

MEREO HONOREM and MEREOR HONOREM are both used; a soldier MERET STIPENDIUM (“earns pay”). MEMINI HONORIS and MEMINI HONOREM (“I remember the honor”) are both possible. MARITIMA are places near the sea; MARINA refers to a ship or sea creature. METO has *metui*; METUO likewise. MATERIES concerns the products of craftsmanship; MATERIA concerns plans. Some instead distinguish them by referring *materies* to the mind and *materia* to a tree, or *materies* to the quality of one’s talent and *materia* to what is suitable for craftsmen.

MAS is the positive form; MASCULUS is the diminutive—not *mascellus*, as some say. MUSCUS, the plant that clings to walls or tree bark, is used only in the singular. MEMORIA, MALITIA, and MURMUR likewise [Note: [Col. 0137] E.: “murmur and similar words are singular”]. MINAE, MANUBIAE, MOENIA, and MAGALIA—the huts of Africans—are always plural. MARE has no plural except *maria*. MEL, MULSUM, and MURIA, that is, γάρος (*gáros*), together with other precious liquids, are singular-only, although we read *mella* and *vina*.

[Col. 0138D] MATURE, MATURIUS, and MATURISSIME are the forms to be used; nevertheless, authors also use *maturrime*. MUNIO, *munis*, has the perfects *munii* and *munivi*. MEMINI, *meministi, meminit, meminimus, meministis, meminerunt*, is inflected in the same way in the present and perfect tenses; for this reason it is called defective or irregular. MULCEO and MULGEO have the same perfect, *mulsi*.

When MAJESTAS is written and pronounced, the *s* must be joined to the following syllable [Note: [Col. 0137] B.: “to be joined”]; the same applies to similar words.

[Col. 0139A] MIRAMUR OPERA (“we admire works”); ADMIRAMUR VIRTUTES (“we admire virtues”). We say MINORES ESSE RES ALIQUAS AUT HOMINES (“that certain things or people are lesser”). MINORIS EMPTUM or AESTIMATUM (“bought or valued at a lower price”) is correctly written.

MEMINI ME FACERE should be said, not *memini me fecisse*, because *memini* is wholly a verb of past time that brings a completed action into the present. If you say *memini me fecisse*, you join two past tenses together. Virgil uses the latter only once:

“For I remember having seen, beneath the lofty towers of Aeolia, an old Corycian man,”

which the poet was permitted to use for the sake of the meter.

We call a drink MERACAM when it has received unmixed wine from elsewhere; but we call the wine itself MEROSUM. [Col. 0139B] MULIEBRE refers to something done by a woman; MULIEBRIARIUM to something organized by women but carried out by men. MERULA is correct, not *merulus*. MATTHAEUS and MATTHIAS must be written with two *t*’s, because the Greeks write them with τ and θ.

We say MOESTUM ANIMO (“sad in spirit”), but TRISTEM ASPECTU (“sad in appearance”). MALUS, “mast of a ship,” is masculine; MALUS, “fruit-bearing tree,” is feminine. MENDUM is neuter. Varro, in his *Admiranda*, used *magnum mendum*; but Ovid used the feminine:

“By night the flaws lie hidden.”

And again:

“The day itself will remove all blemishes from the body.”

[Col. 0139C] Therefore MENDUM is used in the sense of a falsehood; MENDA for a fault in a work or in the body. MUNIFICUS is analogous to BENEFICUS and MALEFICUS; MUNIFEX to OPIFEX and ARTIFEX. Thus *munificus* distributes gifts, whereas *munifex* performs a service. MORTICINA is used only of the dead; MORTALIA may also refer to living bodies.

## N

NIMIS is used of anything that exceeds what is proper. What is less than what is proper is *parum*; between the two lies the measure called *satis*, “enough.” Since it is useful in life and conduct that we do absolutely nothing beyond what is proper, we ought rather to acknowledge than deny the truth of the saying, “Nothing in excess.” Yet Latin sometimes abuses this word, using *nimis* in the sense of *valde*, “very,” and we find it so used in sacred writings and employ it in our own speech. In the Psalm: “You have commanded that your commandments be kept exceedingly,” we understand *nimis* as “very greatly,” if we understand the passage correctly. And when we say to someone especially dear, “I love you exceedingly,” we do not mean “more than is proper,” but wish it understood that we love him greatly.

Indeed, the Greek saying “Nothing in excess” does not contain the word found here. There it is ἄγαν (*ágan*), which means “excessively”; here it is σφόδρα (*sphódra*), which means “very greatly.” But sometimes, as we have said, we find and use *nimis* in the sense of “very greatly,” which is why some Latin manuscripts do not have: “You have commanded that your commandments be kept.”

[Col. 0140A] NOCEO, OBSUM, INCOMMODO, MALEFICIO, and OFFICIO are used with one meaning, corresponding to the Greek Βλάπτω (*bláptō*), and all take the dative. NULLUS applies both to a thing and to a person. NEMO applies to a person, as though it meant “not a human being.” NATALES means “nobilities” or “births.” NUPTIAE, NONAE, NARES, NUNDINAE, NUGAE, and NANIAE are plural-only. We also find *nar* in the singular. *Nenias* means epitaphs, that is, poems written on tombs in memory of the dead.

NEQUAM and NUGAS are of every gender and number and run through all the cases, always with the same form. Nevertheless, Augustine says *nugae, nugarum, nugis*. It is reported that *nugas* is a Hebrew word and means among them what it means among us: people who are frivolous and of corrupt mind.

[Col. 0140B] NOVI, *nosti, novit, novimus, nostis, noverunt*, are inflected in the same way in the present and perfect tenses; ODI and MEMINI are similar. NOCEOR, *noceris*, is correctly said, although some grammarians insist that one should not say *noceor* but *nocetur mihi*. Jerome certainly did not lack knowledge of grammatical rules when he did not hesitate to translate the prophet Habakkuk as follows: “And you will not save when I am harmed.”

NECTO has the perfect *nexi*. NOCTU is an adverb of time; NOCTE is a noun. Women NUBUNT; a man *ducit* a wife, a woman *nubit*, because she covers her head and cheeks with a veil. NONGENTOS, not *nungentos*, derives from *novem*. NEQUAM does not mean “evil” but “useless.” NUBO has the perfect *nupsi*. In NUPTIAE, when a vowel follows, *b* should be used; when a consonant follows, *p*.

[Col. 0140C] NASCITUR refers to what falls from the womb; ENASCITUR to what rises from earth or water. NIHIL is an adverb; NIHILI is a noun. A person of no importance is called *nihili*. NAVIS is the name of a single vessel; NAVIGIUM means an entire naval expedition. NAUCLERUS refers to the whole company; NAVALIS to a naval army; NAVIGATOR to the chief person in an expedition; NAUTA to anyone who performs the labor of sailing. NAVIS has an ablative ending in both *e* and *i*.

## O

ORGANUM properly denotes one musical instrument, but in general all musical instruments may be called *organa*. John, bishop of Constantinople: “Upon the willows in its midst we hung our instruments”—that is, the cithara, psaltery, lyre, and so forth. ORGANARIUS is one who uses an organ. OBRIZA, *obrizae*, is feminine; OBRIZUM, *obrizi*, is neuter. ORIGO, *originis*, means “beginning.” ORIGO, *origonis*, is neuter; it is a ship’s sail and has the plural *origona*. OBTINEO LAUDEM (“I obtain praise”) and IMPETRO (“I obtain”) derive from the same Greek verb, ἀντιτυγχάνω (*antitynkhánō*).

[Col. 0141A] OBJURGO, INCREPO, and CORRIPIO are translated from the same Greek verb, ἀντιπλήττω (*antiplḗttō*). HOMILIA is Greek; in Latin, SERMO or COLLOQUIUM. OTIUM and SILENTIUM derive from the same Greek word, ἡσυχία (*hēsychía*). ORDIBO and ORDIAR TELAM (“I will begin / I begin a web”) are both used. OSTREA is feminine, not the neuter *ostreum*. OCIMUM is commonly used as a neuter noun; but Macer more correctly says:

“Basil will be counted among the herbs of former times.”

ORDIOR HANC REM, INGREDIOR, and INCIPIO derive from the same Greek verb, ἄρχομαι (*árkhomai*). ONUS applies to beasts of burden; SARCINA to human beings. OPTIMATES, called πρωτοπολῖται (*prōtopolîtai*) in Greek, is used only in the plural.

[Col. 0141B] OBLITUS NOSTRI is correct, not *oblitus nos*; nevertheless, the ancients also used the latter form. OLIVA is the tree; OLEA the fruit; OLEUM the liquid. ODI, *odisti, odit, odimus, odistis, oderunt*, is inflected in the same way in the present and perfect past tenses; for this reason it is called defective.

## P

PETRA is both a Greek and a Latin word, with one and the same meaning in both languages. Hence the name of the apostle Peter, in both languages, contains the same reference to invincible faith derived from *petra*, “rock.” PLATEA likewise has the same meaning in both languages; but, as the logic of its etymology proves, the name is drawn from Greek and derives from breadth, since “broad” is πλάτυν (*platyn*) in Greek.

PRO, the preposition, means “before,” as in:

“Before the gates, Messapus and bold Atinas  
alone sustain the battle line.”

It is also used in place of the preposition *in*, as when we say *pro rostris* (“before the speaker’s platform”) and *pro tribunali* (“before the tribunal”). It also stands for the Greek ἀντί (*antí*), “in place of” or “for,” as in: “May he come for sweet Ascanius”; and for the Greek ὑπέρ (*hypér*), “on behalf of,” as in:

“This one thing for you, goddess-born, and this one thing for all,  
I shall proclaim.”

PUDET me amoris. I am ashamed of love. POENITET me muneris. I repent of the gift. PIGET me profectionis. I am weary of the journey. PATIENS SUM laboris. I endure labor. PERTAESUM EST me injuriae. I am utterly weary of insult. PLENUS SUM bonorum, et bonis. I am full of good things, and of good people. [Col. 0141D] PRAEEO illi. I go before him. PALPOR and PALPO equo. I stroke the horse. PRAECURRO praetori. I run ahead of the praetor. PROCURO pupillo, and CURO pupillum. I act on behalf of the ward, and I care for the ward. POTIOR fructus and fructum dicitur, apud antiquos POTIOR hanc rem. *Potior* is used with *fructus* and *fructum*; among the ancients, *potior hanc rem* was used. PRAEDA victos spoliat. Plunder strips the defeated. RAPINA subito venit. Robbery comes suddenly. PAX is expressed only in the singular. Sallustius: “He brought back peace[s]: judgments, wars, and peace[s].” PROSAPIA, that is, nobility, which in Greek is called εὐγενία (“noble birth”), is used only in the singular. PELAGUS likewise. PUGILLARES, PROCERES, PRIMORES, POSTERI are used only in the plural; but our authors used *pugillaris* in the singular. Likewise, in the feminine gender, PLAGAS, that is, nets, and PRIMITIAE; and in the neuter, PRAECORDIA, PALARIA, when soldiers are trained at stakes. PROCASTRIA are the things that are before the camp. PORRUM is singular neuter; in the plural, *hi porri*. PROVERBIUM is, in Latin, παραβολὴ (“parable”), feminine; hence the title of Solomon’s book among the Septuagint translators, παροιμίαι (“Proverbs”). PIUS and piissimus do not admit a comparative degree. POTIOR and potissimus have no positive degree. PROPRIUS has neither a comparative nor a superlative, but instead of these we use *magis proprius* and *maxime proprius*; [Col. 0142B] conversely, *minus* and *minime*. PAVEO and PASCO converge on the same perfect form, *pavi*. PENDEO, *pendes*, *pependi*; but if it has a preposition, it is not declined in this way: *suspendo, suspendis, suspendi*, not *suspependi*. PASSIM means “everywhere”; it is derived from a single Greek word, πανταχοῦ (“everywhere”). PERINDE, AEQUALITER, SIMILITER: from the one Greek word ὁμοίως (“likewise”). PELLO, *pelii* and *pepuli*; DEPELLO, *depuli*. PETO, *petivi* and *petii*. PROSPICIENS periculi: the participle is used in place of a noun; and PROSPICIENS periculum. PERENDIE is said in the same way as HODIE or CRAS. PERENDINUS [Col. 0142C] DIES, like HODIERNUS, HESTERNUS, CRASTINUS. POTAMUS is used of the person to whom we offer a drink, and *potamus vinum* of the wine that we drink. PRIMITIAE is used only in the plural. PROBO, the verb, has a double meaning. We *probamus* what we choose, and in that sense approve it. We also *probamus* what we have tested to determine what it is like, as in: “Test me, Lord, and know my heart.” PECTO caput, not *pectino*; PEXTUM, not *pectinatum*; *pexi memet*, “I combed myself,” and *pectam cras*, “I shall comb tomorrow.” PRAESAGIO, *praesagis, praesagiunt*. PAUPERIES is a loss; PAUPERTAS is the condition itself. We say PATRIUM from *patria*, “fatherland,” and PATERNUM from *pater*, “father.” We say PINNAS of walls, and PENNAS of birds. PECUS is the name for every animal except a human being. [Col. 0142D] POLENTA, not *pulenta*, must be said, because it is polished for human use. PROOEMIUM is written with a diphthong. PRETIUM, PREMO, PRECOR are written with a simple *e*. Likewise PREHENDO and INTERPRETATOR. PRECARI means “to ask”; DEPRECARI means “to excuse oneself” or “to clear oneself.” Virgil: “I have indeed deserved it, nor do I excuse myself,” he says. PLURIS is used of something assessed at a greater sum. PLURES refers to a multitude. *Plures* is a comparative degree, whose positive is *multi*. [Col. 0143A] POCULUM is a vessel; POTIO is what is drunk. PIGNERA refers to things; PIGNORA to children and affections. PROCUL means both “far away” and “near”: “The arrow shaken from the shield, and far from its noble author.” PERTINACIA is perseverance in an evil matter; CONSTANTIA, in a good one. We say PERCUSSUM of the body, PERCULSUM of the mind. PERICULUM pertains to danger; PERICULUM also to testing. Something is POSTULATUR honorably, POSCITUR improperly. Cicero, in the *Speech on the Grain Law*: “They begin to demand, to insist, and to threaten.” PUBES, when used with the meanings “youth,” “down,” and “the part in which puberty occurs,” has the genitive *hujus pubis*; but when it signifies age, *hujus puberis*. Nevertheless, when a preposition is added, we do not say *impuberis* but *impubis*: “And the companion of the underage Iulus,” Virgil said. Cicero, however, says: “And his underage son.” PULMENTARIUM and PULMENTUM are both used; for Cato, in the third book of the *Origines*, calls laserpitium *pulmentarium*; likewise: “They used much *pulmentum*.” PODAGROSUS is derived from *podagra*; but also PODAGRICUS, from an ailment of the feet. PUGILLARES should be used in the masculine gender and always in the plural, because a *pugillus* is something that contains several tablets. Laberius, however, in *The Fisherman*, used the singular *hoc pugillar*. PAVUS, *pavi*; and PAVO, *pavonis*. PANNICULAE, πρωτοτύπιον, is cloth. Lucilius: “A cloth is the outer covering.” [Col. 0143C] PAROPSIDES are said in the feminine gender, evidently from the dish which they call ὄψον. Virgil used PALUMBES in the feminine gender: “To which the airy doves withdrew”; but Lucilius used it in the masculine: “and lean doves.” Varro, however, in *Scaurus*, says *palumbi*, which ordinary usage has also adopted. We say POMETA of a place where fruit grows, like *oliveta*. POMARIA, however, is a place where fruit is stored. PENE, which is a conjunction, is written with *e*. POENA, meaning “punishment,” is written with *oe*; likewise Poenus, that is, “an African.” When dividing PRAEGNANTEM in writing, join the *g* to the second syllable; likewise PIGNUS and PUGNA, and other words of this kind. In dividing PROPTER, join the second *p* to the second syllable; in PROSPERE, join the *s* to the second syllable. PARTIO, PRAEDO, and POPULO are sometimes used in the active voice; these same words are also frequently found as deponent verbs of common gender: PARTIOR, POPULOR, PRAEDOR. PONO means simply to set something in place; DISPONO means to undertake some more substantial work or plan. *Disponere* also means to arrange a treaty. PROPONO is sometimes used to put a question. APPONO expresses addition; IMPONO, imposition; SUPERPONO, [Col. 0144A] assigning some assessment or labor to each individual. PRAEPONO means to prefer something; likewise ANTEPONO. POSTPONO indicates placing something lower. COMPONO belongs to adornment, eloquence, or craftsmanship. SEPONO means to separate. SUPPONO means to introduce something beneath. DEPONO means to weaken or to depart from life. PEREGRINUS, the noun, often takes another noun joined to it in the dative, as when saints are called “strangers to this world.” PRAESTOLARI, not *praestulari*, because it comes from the verb *praesto sum*. PUPPIS forms its accusative in *-em* and *-im*, and its ablative in *-e* and *-i*. [Note: [Col. 0143] B., *Palleo, pallui*.] PSALLO forms its perfect as *psallui*. [Col. 0144B] POTIOR, *potitus sum*, and PERFRUOR, *perfructus sum*, derive from the one Greek word ἀπολαύω (“to enjoy”). We say PASCUAS in the feminine gender, and PASCUA in the neuter, in the plural. PRIMITIAE is used only in the plural, but is sometimes to be understood in the singular, [Note: [Col. 0143] B., “as in the Apostle, omitting ‘in the psalm . . .’ Likewise.”] as in the psalm: “the first fruits of all labor.” For in Greek it has the singular ἀπαρχῆς (“first-fruit”). Likewise in the Apostle: “Christ the first fruits.”

## Q

QUOD, QUIA, QUUR, and QUARE, when joined to verbs, sometimes take an indicative verb and sometimes a subjunctive. Gregory: “He knew that they could scarcely be without fault.” And again: “He knew that they must be cleansed by sacrifices.” And again: “He withdrew from evil, not because he restrained himself from doing it, but because he condemned it by coming.” He also says: “That rest is signified by this number.” Likewise: “Some exalt themselves inwardly because through them the grace of purification is conveyed.” QUOTIES, TOTIES, SEPTIES are written without *n*. QUICQUID and QUICQUAM must be written with *c* in the first syllable, not *d*. QUANQUAM has *n* in the first syllable. QUORUNDAM, like EORUNDEM, must be written with *n*, not *m*. QUERELA and LOQUELA are written with one *l*. QUATENUS, an adverb of place or time, meaning “as far as” or “until,” is written with *e*; QUATINUS, a causal conjunction meaning “so that,” is written with *i*. QUAERITUR concerns inquiry; *queritur*, lamentation. [Col. 0144D] QUAESTUS means profit; QUESTUS, tears. QUERIMONIA likewise must be written with a simple *e*. QUEROR de te, “I complain about you”; QUEROR tibi de illo, “I complain to you about him”; likewise CONQUEROR. QUO vadis means “to what place are you going?” QUA vadis means “by which way are you going?” QUO is sometimes used for *ubi*. Augustine: “You find a smoky house where good people live,” that is, “in which they live.” QUOT pertains to number, as does TOT. QUANTI and TANTI pertain to measure; but our authors sometimes use *quantos* for number. [Col. 0145A] Gregory: “But when the net is said to be full of large fish, ‘and how many,’ namely 153, is added.” QUANTUS means “how great.” QUOTUS means “of what age”; hence we also say *quota luna*, “which day of the lunar month.” Augustine: “At what age can anyone appear and exist who is not proved to be a sinner?” That is, “at what age, at what number of days or years?”

## R

RADIUS is masculine, not neuter *radium*. RUBOR is a color; ROBUR is strength; *robur* is also a tree. RAPIO tibi pecunias: “I seize money from you.” REDOLEO unguentum: “I smell of perfume.” REGIUM is what belonged to a king; REGALE is what is worthy of a king. [Col. 0145B] RABIES is used only in the singular. RELIQUIAE and ROSTRA, the place where public speaking takes place, are used only in the plural. REMEDIUM removes impending dangers; MEDICAMENTUM heals those already inflicted. Thus a remedy is desired so that we may not face danger, whereas a medicine is desired for sudden dangers. ROSEUM is unmixed; ROSARIUM is mixed. RUDIS has neither comparative nor superlative; instead we use the adverbs *magis* and *maxime*, as *magis rudis* and *maxime rudis*. We say RECENS FECI, “I recently did,” not *recenter*, using the noun as an adverb. Ῥύθμος in Greek is MODULATIO in Latin. Ῥυθμίζω is MODULOR.

## S

[Col. 0145C] SUPER, the preposition, is sometimes used for *de*, “about,” as in:

“Making many inquiries about Priam, many about Hector.”

Sometimes it is used as the preposition *pro*, “for,” as in: “I am moved by nothing concerning authority.” It is also used for *insuper* and *amplius*, “in addition” and “more,” as in:

“For whom among the Danaans there is no place anywhere, and besides, the hostile Dardanians themselves demand punishment with blood.”

It is used for *desuper*, “from above,” as in: “And the Trojans look out from above the rampart.” It is also used for *superest*, “remains,” as in:

“But for them no escape from danger now remains.”

Sometimes it means “beyond,” as in: “He will extend his empire beyond the Garamantes and Indians.” SUB, the preposition, sometimes means “above,” as in: “They throw their bodies onto the horses in a leap,” that is, “they throw them above.” Sometimes it is used as the preposition *in*, as in:

“For while he surveys each thing beneath the great temple.”

That is, “in the temple.” It also means “near,” as in: “And the fleet near Antenor himself.” Sometimes it is used for *clam*, “secretly,” as in *subripuit*, that is, “he stole secretly.” SIMILIS SUM tui, moribus: “I resemble you in character”; SIMILIS tibi, facie: “I resemble you in appearance.” STUDIO tibi feci, that is, “I did it while taking an interest in you.” STUDIO tui feci, that is, “I did it with you taking an interest.” SARTRIX, or SERTRIX, is a woman who mends. SUBIGO hostem is a simple verb; [Col. 0146A] SUBAGITO is frequentative. SALUBRE refers to a place and to food. SALUTARE is advice. Thus SALUBRE does not harm; SALUTARE benefits. SUPELLEX, SANIES, SOCORDIA, SITIS, and, in the neuter, SULPHUR, SCRUPULUM, SINAPI, and SILER are used only in the singular; but Virgil said *sulphura viva*, and Terence used *scrupulum* in the masculine. SENTES, that is, thorns; SARCINAE, when it means vessels; SARCINAE, that is, auxiliary forces; and SCOPAE, SALINAE, SCALAE, and, in the neuter, SPONSALIA, are always plural; but our authors used *scalam* in the singular. SPONTE mea venio, “I come of my own accord,” has no other cases. SI amem, ames, amet is the conjugation of the subjunctive verb, as when we say *cum amem, ames, amet*. [Col. 0146B] SCYLLA has its name from stripping or harassing sailors. [Note: [Col. 0145] B., “For *spolio* is.”] SPOLIO, in Latin, is called in Greek SCYLLO, σκύλλω (“to flay, harass”), and VEXO (“to harass”). SANNO, *sannis, sannui*. This SANNIUM is a complaint. SORS, *sortis*, and SORS, *sordis*, are both used. Ambrose: “He cleanses the vessels, lest any dregs discolour the charm of the wine,” although some deny that *sors* has a nominative case. SI and ETSI sometimes take an indicative verb. Gregory: “In vain do we display a miracle outwardly if that which should work within is absent.” Likewise: “Although these things do not pertain to perfection, they nevertheless hold faith.” SENSUS is a noun of the fourth declension and the past participle of the passive verb *sentior*, whose perfect is also *sensus sum, es, est*, not *sentitus*. SECTURUS, not *secaturus*, from the verb *seco*. SCAMMA are the things placed beside higher beds. SCABELLA are the things placed beside small beds or seats for climbing up. SCABELLUM and SUPPEDANEUM are also names for something beneath the feet. Say STERCERATOS AGROS, not *stercoratos*, of fields into which manure is brought for fertilization. When you say or write SOLEMNEM, join the *m* to the following syllable. SOMNIUM likewise. SAEVUS, *saevio, saevi, saevisti*, is written with the diphthong *ae*. SERO, *sevi, sevisti*, “I sow,” is written with a simple *e*. SAGENA, when it means nets, is written with *e*. SAGINA, meaning fattening or fat, is written with *i*. [Col. 0146D] SOL is declined in both numbers; but in the singular *sol* signifies the heavenly body itself, whereas in the plural *soles* we name the days in which the sun illuminates the whole world. Some of the ancients, however, called poems themselves *Soles*, as Horace did at the beginning of a certain volume, which he began as follows: “I commend my suns to your whole Church.” And Maro:

“. . . Often I remember, as a boy,  
that I brought my long days to an end through song.”

SECUNDUM is a preposition of imitation. POST pertains to time or order. [Col. 0147A] SEGNITIES belongs to vice. SEGNITIA belongs to coldness or sluggishness. SUBSCRIBO epistolis: “I subscribe to letters.” SUPPLICO is used similarly, as in: “I appeal to divine mercy.” SIMPLEX has its ablative in both *-i* and *-e*, and its plural genitive in both *-um* and *-ium*, as *ab hoc simplice* or *simplici*, *horum simplicum* and *simplicium*. SUAVIS has its ablative in both *-e* and *-i*. STACHYS, σταχύς (“ear of grain”) in Greek, is SPICA (“ear of grain”) in Latin. SANDALIA is Greek and neuter; CALIGA is the Latin term. SERTUM and CORONA are translated from the one Greek word στέφανος (“crown, garland”). SOLIUM is properly a royal seat, which in Greek is called βασιλικός θρόνος (“royal throne”). SENEX and senior have no superlative degree. SOBRIUS admits neither a comparative nor a superlative; [Col. 0147B] instead we say *magis sobrius* and *maxime sobrius*. SENECTA and SENIUM are two nouns for old age, distinguished by the Greeks, among whom one term denotes the gravity that follows youth, and another the final age that comes after that very gravity. A presbyter is called *gravis*, “grave,” and γέρων, “old man.” Since, however, Latin lacks the separation between these two nouns, both *senecta* and *senium* are used of old age. Thus Augustine. Gregory, however, says: “The eleventh is the age called decrepit or veteran; hence the Greeks call the very old not γέροντας but presbyters,” [Note: [Col. 0147] B., “call presbyters; omits ‘they call them . . . more advanced.’”] indicating that those whom they call more advanced in age are more than merely old. SUSPIRO, the verb, takes a dative and an accusative, [Col. 0147C] as in: “We sigh for the heavenly fatherland,” [Note: [Col. 0147] B. omits “and: We sigh for the kingdom of God.”] and: “We sigh for the kingdom of God”; with a preposition added: “We sigh for immortal life.” SUBDUCIMUS means both “to withdraw what is behind” and “to bring forward what is at hand.” SUPREMUS means highest and last, and signifies both what is above and what is below. SUPEREST is what projects or rises above. SUPRA is what has something beneath it. SUBTER is what is pressed down by something above. SUBTUS is what, being lowered from something higher, is not touched by it. SERVITIUM is a multitude of slaves. SERVITUS is the condition of serving; but the ancients used *servitium* indiscriminately also for *servitus*. SINAPI (“mustard”), like GUMMI (“gum”), is Greek, and Plautus said: “The mustard is ground.” Its genitive is pronounced with *s*; the remaining cases are like the nominative. SIBILUS should be said. Virgil in the *Bucolics*:

“For neither does the whistle of the coming South Wind affect me so greatly.”

But some also used it in the neuter, as Cornelius Severus:

“And the savage whistles harmoniously sound together.”

And Macer:

“Whistles of the theriac resounding from the long neck.”

SERENUS is a gentle whistle. [Col. 0148A] SAL is used in both the masculine and neuter genders. SATURITAS is used only of food; in other matters, SATIETAS is used. But Virgil wrote: “She rested, sated with hatred.” Learned authors also used SIMIAM in the masculine. Say STRIGEM hanc, “this bird,” in that sense; STRIGA is a military term signifying the interval between ranks in which horses are drawn up. Hence people with lean bodies are also called *strigosi*. STIRPS, in the sense of offspring, is feminine; but when it signifies material, the ancients used the masculine, as in *stirpem recisum*, “cut-off stock.” Yet it is also masculine in the sense of offspring, as Pacuvius wrote: “who killed my stock.” SERO rumores, that is, “I spread rumors”; and SERO fruges, *sevi*, “I sow crops.” [Col. 0148B] SERO, meaning “I close” — whence *sera*, “a bolt,” is derived — has the perfect *seravi*. Terence: “Go away, and bolt the door from within.” SUFFRAGOR, not *suffrago*; and SUFFRAGATUS SUM, not *suffragavi*. SORBEO, *sorbui*, not *sorbsi*. SOMNIO, not *somnior*; SOMNIAVI, not *somniatus sum*. SANGUIS is the term while it remains within the body; once poured out, it is CRUOR. SUMIMUS ipsi, “we take for ourselves”; we receive from another. Thus, when we give, we should say *Accipe*, “Receive”; when we permit someone to take it himself, we should say *Sume*, “Take.” SCORPIO is a military object; SCORPIUS, an animal. SCRIBO, *scripsi, scriptum*: when a vowel follows, the *b* must remain; when a consonant follows, it becomes *p*. SACER means both venerable and accursed. Virgil: “The accursed hunger for gold.” SUFFRAGIA are the votes of the people; the term is used both of those that honor and of those that condemn.

## T

TESTOR aliquid, confirming a statement. CONTESTOR, affirming with a certain authority. PROTESTOR, openly warning by taking precautions. OBTESTOR, compelling someone to swear. ATTESTOR, calling to testify someone distinguished in rank or authority. DETESTOR, rejecting something as accursed. TRUX has its ablative in both *-i* and *-e*, and its plural genitive in both *-um* and *-ium*. THERION, θηρίον in Greek, is FERA in Latin; hence *theriaca*, because it kills in a beastly manner. [Col. 0148D] TACITURNITAS is the opposite of speech; SILENTIUM, of confused voices or disturbances. But it must be understood that SILEO, TACEO, CONTICEO, and RETICEO all derive from the one Greek word σιωπάω. TENAX beneficii means “mindful of a favor.” TORQUES is a noun of common gender; for Livy used it in the masculine in the story of Marius, while Cicero used *torquem* in the feminine. TRIUMPHAT nos Deus when God grants assistance to overcome enemies. “To God,” he says, “who always triumphs over us in Christ Jesus, be thanks”; and again: “Stripping principalities and powers, he triumphed over them in himself.” TRANSMIGRO is used when I travel from one place to another. It is also used with an accusative added when I transfer someone from one place to another, as in: “Nebuchadnezzar transported the Jews from Jerusalem,” and “he departed from the tabernacle.” An example of the preceding verb is: “Migrate to the mountain like a sparrow.” TRANSMIGRANS, the participle, is likewise understood in two ways: someone passing from one place to another, and someone transferring another from one place to another. TURTUR is used in both the masculine and feminine genders. TUNC is an adverb of time; TUM, of sequence or order. TERGA are the backs of human beings; the singular is *tergum*. [Col. 0149B] TERGUS refers to four-footed animals and forms the plural *tergora*, that is, hides. TINGUERE must be said, not *tingere*. TEMERITAS is action without deliberation; AUDACITAS follows deliberation. TEMPERANTIA refers to dispositions; TEMPERATIO, to things; TEMPERIES, to breezes. TAPETE has the forms *tapetis* and *tapeti*; in the plural, *tapetia, tapetium, tapetibus altis*. There are also *hoc tapetum, hujus tapeti, huic tapeto*; and in the plural *tapeta, tapetorum, tapetis*. Virgil:

“Winged horses spread with purple and embroidered carpets.”

But he also uses the masculine:

“and embroidered carpets.”

[Col. 0149C] TURBO, if it is a proper noun, forms *turbonis*; for whether it means a wind or the object with which boys play, it is called *turbo*. Virgil: “The top beneath the twisted lash.” TUMULUS means equally a mound, a swelling earth, a small mountain, and a tomb. TELONEUM is written with a simple *t*, not *thelonium* with an added aspiration. It is Greek τέλων [Possibly τελώνιον], Latin VECTIGAL, “customs duty” or “tax.” TABES is used only in the singular. TENDICULAE and TENEBRAE are used only in the plural.

## U

USQUEQUAQUE means “in every way”; in its place we read in the Greek psalm ἕως σφόδρα, which can be rendered more precisely in Latin as *usque valde*, “exceedingly.” [Col. 0149D] UT is sometimes an adverb of time and means “after”; sometimes an adverb of manner and means “how”; sometimes an optative particle and means “would that”; sometimes an exclamation of wonder and means “O how”; sometimes a causal conjunction, as in: “I want them also to be where I am.” UTOR takes both the ablative *divitiis* and the accusative *divitias*. ULTERIOR and ULTIMUS have no positive degree. [Col. 0150A] UTERQUE is used of two; UTRIQUE, of two or of several placed on both sides. *Uterque venit*, “each of the two came”; *utrique venerunt*, “both came.” ULTUS means both avenged and punished. ULCUS is what arises or develops. URGEO, not *urgo*. Virgil: “By which punishments they are pressed.” UNGO, *unxi*, like PINGO, *pinxi*: both are without *u*. Their derivatives, however, add *u*, as *pinguis*, “fat,” and *unguine ceras*, “with ointment, waxes”; thus one says *ungu entum*, not *ungentum*.

## V

VACAT mihi is the Greek σχολάζω, “I have leisure.” VACO militia, with the perfect *vacavi*, means “I am exempt from military service.” VULGUS is neuter and has no plural; but Virgil used *vulgum* in the masculine, as in: “Hence scattering ambiguous voices among the crowd.” [Col. 0150B] VAS, *vadis*, is masculine; VAS, *vasis*, is neuter and refers to a small vessel. VIS has a double meaning: power, called δύναμις (“power”) in Greek, and violence, called βία (“violence”). VECORDIA and VIRUS are used only in the singular. VEPRES, VERBERA, and VISCERA have no singular declension, except *verbere* and *viscere*. Virgil: “And the top flying beneath the twisted lash.” Ovid: “With the entrail divided.” VER is always singular. VERVEX, meaning “sheep,” must begin with *v*. VERUS pertains only to truth according to nature. VERAX is said of one who does not lie; hence one may say *verus daemon*, “a true demon,” but not *verax*. VALLESTRIA of fields, like CAMPESTRIA, is used. VETO culpam and VETO a culpa mean “I forbid wrongdoing” and “I forbid someone from wrongdoing.” Sedulius: “And he would forbid them from the bitter fruits,” that is, “from the fruits.” And Fortunatus:

“Not marriage indeed, but I prefer the womb of a virgin.”

VULTUS changes; FACIES remains. VAE must be followed by a dative or accusative, as in: “Woe to the people of the Moors!” and “Woe to the people of the Moors!” VENEUNT are those who are sold. VELOCITAS refers to feet and bodies; CELERITAS, to minds and actions. VULNUS is what is inflicted by another. Virgil used VULTUR in Book Six; Lucilius also used *vulturius* in Book One. [Col. 0150D] VERBUM is everything expressed by the tongue and voice. SERMO, whose name is composed from *serere* and *movere*, “to sow” and “to move,” is more polished and deliberate. SENTENTIA is what is conceived by the mind. LOQUELA, moreover, is an ordered expression of speech with a certain eloquence. ORATIO is speech that has advanced as far as the craft of describing it with the hands.

[Col. 0149]

# A BOOK ON THE ART OF METER ADDRESSED TO WIGBERT THE DEACON (C)

## 1. On the Letter

[Col. 0149D]

Whoever wishes to possess knowledge of the art of meter must first diligently learn the difference between letters and syllables. There are twenty-one Latin letters in all: of these, five are called vowels—*a, e, i, o, u*—and all the rest consonants. Of these consonants, seven are called semivowels—*f, l, m, n, r, s, x*—and the remaining nine are mutes—*b, c, d, g, h, k, p, q, t*. The Latins also adopted *y* as a sixth vowel and *z* as a seventeenth consonant because of the Greek words that we customarily use; for otherwise they would not have known how to write *typum*, *zelum*, or other words of this kind.

After receiving the Christian faith, they also retain the Greek letters η (eta), χ (chi), ρ (rho), α (alpha), and ω (omega), though they do not admit them into the order of the alphabet, because they occur in the sacred writings: η, which among the Greeks is written with a double form, just as the letter H among the Latins, was introduced on account of the authority of the name Jesus; χ and ρ on account of the name Christ; α and ω on account of the authority of the Lord’s saying, “I am α and ω.” α differs from our *a* only in name; in every other respect, both in form and in power, it corresponds to it. The Greek ρ differs from our *r* both in form and in name. η and ω differ from our letters in that they are always long, whereas all our vowels are dichronic—that is, capable of occurring in both short and long syllables—as are their α, ι, and υ; for ε and ο among them remain naturally always short.

Thus all the letters we use number twenty-seven: eight vowels and nineteen consonants. Yet among these vowels, *i* and *u* often pass into the function of consonants, either when they are doubled between themselves, as in *jumentum* and *vinum*, or when they are joined to other vowels, as in *janua, jecur, jocus, vanitas, veritas, volatus*. *V* also sometimes precedes another *v*, as in *vultus*; it also occupies the place of another consonant when we name *aurum* in Latin or the Gospel in Greek. It is strange why Donatus said that it is sometimes considered neither a vowel nor a consonant when it stands between the consonant *q* and another vowel, as in *quoniam* and *quidem*, unless perhaps because it is then pronounced so softly that it can scarcely be perceived. His reasoning, however, does not seem sound. Explaining his view, Pompeius and Sergius say that it cannot be a consonant because another consonant, namely *q*, precedes it; nor can it be a vowel because a vowel follows it, as in *quare* and *quomodo*. For this reason they write that it is then not a letter. But what of this? When we write *statim*, should we say that *t* cannot be a consonant because another consonant, namely *s*, precedes it, nor a vowel because a vowel follows it? Indeed, when we say *stratum*, we must acknowledge that *r* is a letter, although a vowel follows it and two consonants precede it; likewise *t* is still a consonant, although another consonant precedes it and a vowel follows it. *I* has this special property among vowels: whenever, functioning as a consonant, it has another vowel before it in the same part of speech, it always makes that vowel long by position, even if it was naturally short, as in *majus* and *perjurium*; hence it is also called double. The consonant *x*, being of the same power, is likewise called double, as in *axis*. There are also four liquid letters—*l, m, n, r*—which, in different ways but according to a definite rule, often tend in meter to lose the ordinary force of consonants, and sometimes make syllables that are naturally short appear long.

## 2. On the Syllable

A syllable is a combination of letters, or the utterance of a single vowel, capable of containing temporal units, because every syllable is either short and receives one time-unit, which metricians call an *atom*, as in *pater*, or long and receives two time-units, as in *mater*. For in *ma* when we say *mater*, the length of its circumflex occupies twice as much time as *pa* when it is pronounced with an acute accent in *pater*. There are therefore long, short, and common syllables. Long syllables arise in two ways: by nature and by position. By nature they arise in two ways: either through the lengthening of individual vowels, as in *navis, sedes, finis, omen, unus*, or through the joining of two vowels, which they call a diphthong, as in *aevum, poena, augustus, Eurus, hei*. Thus Arator:

“Alas for me! Now I see the temple’s famous building,  
long celebrated, about to collapse in sudden ruins.”

Or when we say *Tydeus, Tydei*, where we do not separate *e* and *i* but pronounce them together, lest it signify the fifth rather than the first declension: Greek names acquire this diphthong; it is not found in Latin [Col. 0152C] words.

Syllables become long by position in six ways: when a shortened vowel either ends in two consonants, as in *ast*; or in one double consonant, as in *dux*; or ends in one consonant and is followed by another, as in *arca*; or is followed by the double consonant *x*, as in *axis*; or by *i* placed in the position of a consonant, as in *Troia*, a position that is sometimes divided into three syllables in meter [Note: [Col. 0151] Paris., “into three”], as in:

“Arms, the man, and the tablets, and Troy’s treasure upon the waves”;

or ends in a consonant and is followed by *i* or *u* placed in the position of consonants, as in *advena* and *adjumentum*.

Short syllables are those that have none of these features. But certain people are mistaken when they do not count some syllables among the long ones, claiming that a shortened vowel followed by the double letter *z*, as in *Mezentius*, or by two consonants, as in *acre* or *acris*, is not long. For whenever *z* follows a short vowel in the same part of speech, it can lengthen it if the poet so wishes, as in *gaza*. But when a following word begins with the letter *z* after a word ending in a short vowel, it has no power to lengthen it. Hence:

“And wooded Zacynthus.”

The letter *r*, a liquid like *l*, when it follows a short vowel in the middle of a word and is preceded by any consonant, can by poetic license make that vowel long. But when either liquid follows a consonant at the beginning of a word, it cannot lengthen a vowel that was naturally short at the end of the preceding word. There are also syllables that are long in both ways, by nature and by position, as *dens, gens, mons, fons, frons*. [Note: [Col. 0153] Paris adds *gens, mens, mons*.]

## 3. On Common Syllables

Common syllables arise in nine ways. By these methods, syllables naturally long are transferred into short ones by poetic license, or naturally short syllables into long ones. A short syllable is transferred into a long one when a shortened vowel in the same word is followed by two consonants, the latter of which is a liquid. It is naturally short here:

“The mind, covered by its own darkness.”

It is long by position here:

“And the darknesses of death.”

In this matter Sergius uses an improper example: “Nor by the lash.” For *flagellum* begins with a liquid letter subject to a consonant; a preposition can never make the naturally short syllable of the preceding word long.

Likewise, a naturally short syllable may, at the poet’s discretion, be transferred into a long one when a shortened vowel ends in a consonant and is followed by the letter *h*. It is naturally short here:

“They kept the porcine flock; the black, shaggy one bristles.”

It is long by the poet’s choice here:

“A humble man, cast down from a sorrowful gaze upon the earth.”

And likewise:

“Savage death subjected the world to itself through miserable man.”

Here certain grammarians also give a doubtful example:

“We weary the backs with a spear.”

For even if *mus* were not followed by *h*, it could nevertheless be long by poetic license, because a complete metrical foot remained, just as in the following example, which they also give:

“Love conquers all, and let us yield to love.”

Here *mor* could be lengthened because, after complete feet had been scanned, it ends a part of speech, even though a vowel follows.

The third type of common syllable occurs when a word ending in a shortened vowel is followed by two consonants, the first of which is *s*. It is naturally short in this line of Fortunatus:

“White emerald is set among varied ranks.”

It is long by position in this line of Sedulius:

“Let that kingdom come, now, now indeed.”

But when *s* at the beginning of a word is attached to another consonant, it cannot at all lengthen the final syllable of the preceding word, which ended in a short vowel, as in Sedulius:

“To stand in the choir and sing heavenly things with gentle words.”

And Fortunatus:

“With alternating voices they sing divine poems.”

[Col. 0154A] Pompeius falsely defined *s* as unable to become liquid unless it itself precedes, as in: “Let each one set his hopes before himself.” Virgil, however, when he found it suitable, passed over *s* in the manner of a liquid even in the middle of a word when it stood before another consonant:

“Mnestheus exhorts: Now, now rise to the oars.”

Unless perhaps we think this verse should be scanned in such a way that *Horta* is a spondee, *tur Mne* a spondee, and *stheus nunc* a spondee, with the vowels joined together in what they call a diphthong. Hence Donatus rightly said, when speaking of liquid letters, specifically concerning the letters *h* and *s*: “It possesses a power of its own, by which in meter it often loses the force of a consonant.”

The fourth type of common syllable occurs when, after any foot, one short syllable remains from a word, and this syllable either ends in a vowel and is followed by a consonant belonging to the next word, or ends in a consonant and is followed by a vowel. It is naturally short here:

“Whose burden is light, whose yoke is pleasant to bear.”

It is long by poetic permission here:

“There was a leafy fig tree, in whose trunk there was nothing.”

This type of syllable should either be entirely avoided among long syllables or used very sparingly. Hence one does not readily find an example of it among more recent poets, although it is not uncommon in Virgil and not very frequent in Homer.

The fifth type occurs when a part of speech ends in a diphthong and is immediately followed by a vowel. It is naturally long here: “The Aonian Muses”; by license it is short here: “The islands in the great Ionian Sea.” Later poets preferred this to occur within a single part of speech; hence you will readily find examples of it in the poems of our own writers. But when a diphthong is followed by a vowel belonging to another word, they said that it must be passed over by synaloepha [Note: [Col. 0153] See below, col. 166, note *. EDIT.], as Prosper says in the preface to the *Epigrams*:

“Nor is this within our power; from him this dew is taken,”

[Preceding fragment: “He who commanded waters to pour forth from the dry rock.”]

## Sixth mode

[Col. 0154D]

The sixth mode, as Donatus says, is when a long vowel is followed by another vowel. It is long in:

> O that I had gone into the bridal chambers of the hated Caesar.

It is short in:

> You, Corydon, O Alexis; each is drawn by his own desire.

Modern versifiers have generally preferred this to occur within the same phrase, as in:

> The Magi of the East came, and the savage tyrant.

> The splendid East-star shines from the author’s head.

Again, it is long by nature in:

> The angel sang in haste to the untouched Mary.

It is short by poetic license in:

> Mary rejoices when she first perceived the words.

Or, when a long or even a short vowel [Paris manuscript: “which”] ends one phrase, and is followed by a vowel belonging to another word [Col. 0155A], the preceding vowel is removed by synaloepha, as in Prosper:

> For if, trusting in your own virtue, you believe that you can climb to the heavenly realms,  
> driven down from above, you fall to the depths.

Although Arator, imitating the ancients, also wrote:

> O that you, faithful youth, had wished first to obey  
> our counsels, lest you should leave the shores of Crete,  
> destined to suffer the mad rage of the deep.

## Seventh mode

The seventh mode is when a pronoun ending in the letter *c* is immediately followed by a vowel. It is long in:

> Not because he who is the supreme Father is, and the Son is this;

but short in:

> But because what the supreme Father is, the Son is this.

It is short in:

> This man, this is he whom you often hear promised to you.

An adverb ending in *c* likewise makes a common syllable. It is long in this line of Paulinus:

> Until God, breathing upon the feeble efforts,

but short in this passage of Prosper:

> The care of healing must be provided to those afflicted by disease,  
> so long as life remains in the sick body.

## Eighth mode

The eighth mode is when a shortened vowel in the same phrase is followed by *z*, the Greek double consonant. It is long in Juvencus:

> It is difficult for those fixed to the earth by abundant treasure.

It is short in the same author:

> And the gleaming possession of wealth stood apart from other things.

## Ninth mode

The ninth mode is that every final syllable of a verse, in whatever meter, is indifferent. In Greek this is called *adiáphoros* (ἀδιάφορος), “indifferent”: at the poet’s discretion, it may be shortened when long or lengthened when short. This occurs so frequently that examples are unnecessary.

It must nevertheless be understood that the letter *x*, although double, never makes a common syllable. When it follows a vowel within the same word, it always has that vowel long, either by nature, as in *pax* (“peace”), *lex* (“law”), *lux* (“light”), *rex* (“king”), *vox* (“voice”), or by position, as in *fax* (“torch”), *nex* (“violent death”), *nix* (“snow”), *nox* (“night”), *nux* (“nut”), and *exul* (“exile”), *exitus* (“departure”), and *exitium* (“destruction”).

But when it occurs at the beginning of a word, it cannot lengthen the final syllable of the preceding word if that syllable ended in a short vowel, as in:

> Xerxes brought the shores together with bridges laid across them.

The letter *n* likewise, unless I am mistaken, when preceded by another consonant in the middle of a word, always makes the preceding syllable long, whether by nature or by position, as in *regna* (“kingdoms”) and *calumnia* (“slander”) [Col. 0155C–D].

But when, at the beginning of a word, it is preceded by another consonant, as in *Cneus* and *gnarus* (“knowing”), it allows the final syllable of the preceding word—if that word ended in a short vowel—to remain short as it was, and has no power to lengthen it. Prosper bears witness to this:

> Yet the knowledgeable man does not thereby drive from his whole body  
> the capacity to distinguish the nature of those who err from their faults.

[Paris manuscript: instead of *pro hoc . . . corpore*, it reads *habet hos foedere* (“it has these by a covenant”).]

Thus *n* is also counted among the liquids, although not in the same way as *b* or *r*, which are accustomed to make syllables common.

## 4. On initial syllables

[Col. 0156A]

Let this suffice as a brief account of the difference among syllables. Anyone who has learned to scan heroic verse can distinguish them very largely by their own examples. But anyone who has not yet reached that point should meanwhile be urged to examine more diligently the syllables of all parts of speech at the beginnings of heroic verses.

Every hexameter verse, which consists of six feet, and every pentameter, which consists of five, has a long first syllable, because it begins either with a spondee or with a dactyl. The former [editorial note: delete *pars* (“part”) in the Latin] consists of two long syllables; the latter of one long and two short syllables. Thus, whenever you take into your hands a codex of hexameter or elegiac poetry, open whatever page you wish, seize and read whatever verse you wish: without any doubt you will find its first syllable long either by nature or by position, since it is evidently the beginning of either a spondee or a dactyl [Col. 0156B].

Often the first syllable can also be recognized from the structure of a word. If you do not know what quantity *pius* (“devout”) has, you can discover the quantity of *pius* from its compound *impius* (“undevout”), although this fails in some cases. For when we say *nubere* (“to marry”), *nu* is long; but when we say *innuba* (“unmarried woman”) or *pronuba* (“bridesmaid”), *nu* becomes short in composition. Likewise, in *lux, lucis* (“light”), *lu* is long, whereas in *lucerna* (“lamp”) it is short. Likewise, *homo* (“human being”) is short everywhere, whereas *humanus* (“human”) has long *hu*.

In:

> He goes into the ancient forest,

the *i* is long [Paris manuscript: *i* long]. In:

> He is going toward the light above,

it is short [Paris manuscript: *i* short]. This, however, is rarely encountered. But if any part of speech is compounded with prepositions, we recognize its initial syllables from them. For almost every compound syllable will retain the quantity of the preposition itself, as in *deceptus* (“deceived”) and *abundans* (“abounding”): *de* is long, while *a* is short [Paris manuscript: *ab*].

The prepositions *ad* and *ob*, *in* and *sub* are used differently in verbs. They are shortened when, by expansion, they produce disyllabic words, as in *adit* (“he approaches”), *obit* (“he dies”), *init* (“he enters”), *subit* (“he approaches”) [Paris manuscript: “when, by growing, they make from themselves disyllabic words; below, trisyllabic”]. They are indifferent when they make trisyllables, as in *adjicit* (“he adds”), *objicit* (“he throws before”), *injicit* (“he throws in”), and *subjicit* (“he subjects”) [Paris manuscript omits the *i* in the following verbs and gives *adicit*, etc.]. They are lengthened when they themselves produce tetrasyllables, as in *adjicio*, *objicio*, *injicio*, and *subjicio*.

Forms written with *prae* and *que* in their initial syllables are likewise lengthened [the transmitted wording is uncertain]. They are shortened, however, in *pretium* (“price”), *precor* (“I pray”), *premo* (“I press”), *prehendo* (“I seize”), *queror* (“I complain”), that is, “I lay down a complaint,” and in forms derived from these by derivation, declension, or composition; likewise in the conjunction *que*.
