Conversely, in compounds formed with the same prepositions, they are shortened, as in *dehinc* (“from here onward”), *profectus* (“having departed”), *professus* (“having professed”), *profusus* (“poured forth”), *profatus* (“having spoken”), *proavus* (“great-grandfather”), *pronepos* (“great-grandson”), and so forth [Col. 0156C–D].

There are also several verbs whose initial syllables change in quantity according to tense. The forms collected below lengthen them in every perfect past tense [Paris manuscript omits “and”], and either in every pluperfect or only in one future perfect subjunctive form; in the other moods and tenses they are shortened [Paris manuscript: “in the others”]:

- *lego, legi, cum legero* — “I read, I read [perfect], when I shall have read”;
- *faveo, favi, cum favero* — “I favor, I favored, when I shall have favored”;
- *venio, veni, cum venero* — “I come, I came, when I shall have come”;
- *fugio, fugi, cum fugero* — “I flee, I fled, when I shall have fled”;
- *facio, feci, cum fecero* — “I do, I did, when I shall have done”;
- *sedeo, sedi, cum sedero* — “I sit, I sat, when I shall have sat”;
- *fodio, fodi, cum fodero* — “I dig, I dug, when I shall have dug”;
- *video, vidi, cum videro* — “I see, I saw, when I shall have seen”;
- *voveo, vovi, cum vovero* — “I vow, I vowed, when I shall have vowed”;
- *juvo, juvi, cum juvero* — “I help, I helped, when I shall have helped”;
- *ago, egi, cum egero* — “I do, I did, when I shall have done”;
- *emo, emi, cum emero* — “I buy, I bought, when I shall have bought”;
- *lavo, lavi, cum lavero* — “I wash, I washed, when I shall have washed”;
- *odio, odi, cum odero* — “I hate, I hated, when I shall have hated”;
- *sero, sevi, cum severo* — “I sow, I sowed, when I shall have sown”;
- *sino, sivi, cum sivero* — “I allow, I allowed, when I shall have allowed”;
- *caveo, cavi, cum cavero* — “I beware, I guarded against, when I shall have guarded against.”

[A reader’s marginal note in the English edition followed here: *foveo, fovi, cum fovero*—“I cherish, I cherished, when I shall have cherished.”]

Conversely, some forms are long in the present tense and shortened in the perfect: *pono, posui* (“I place, I placed”); *cogo, coegi* (“I compel, I compelled”); *do, dedi* (“I give, I gave”); *sto, steti* (“I stand, I stood”).

Likewise, all verbs whose past forms gain an additional initial syllable shorten the initial syllable, as in *pendeo, pependi* (“I hang, I hung”); *tondeo, totondi* (“I shear, I sheared”); *posco, poposci* (“I demand, I demanded”); *curro, cucurri* (“I run, I ran”); *tendo, tetendi* (“I stretch, I stretched”); *pello, pepuli* (“I drive out, I drove out”).

In verbs written with the same letters, quantity must be noted. *Liber*, if it means “book” or “bark,” has short *li*; if it means “free,” it has long *li*. *Pila*, if it means “a vessel,” has long *pi*; if it means “a ball,” it is short. *Domus* has short *do*; *doma*, that is, “roof,” has long *do* [Paris manuscript adds: *securus* has long *se*, *securis* short *se*, *domus*, etc.]. *Plaga*, when it means “climate,” has short *pla*; when it means “punishment,” it has long *pla*. *Palus, paludis* (“marsh”) has short *pa*; *palus, pali* (“stake”) has long *pa*. *Populus*, when it means “people,” has short *po*; when it means “poplar tree,” it has long *po*. *Nitens*, from *nitor* (“brightness”), has short *ni*; *nitens*, from *nisus* (“effort”), has long *ni*.

Likewise, *educo, educis* (“I lead out, you lead out”) has long *du*; *educo, educas*, that is, “I nourish,” has short *du*. *Concido*, *decido*, *incido*, and *occido*, when they concern falling, have shortened *ci*; when they concern cutting, they have lengthened *ci*. *Colo, colis* (“I cultivate, you cultivate”) has short *co*; *colo, colas* has long *co*. *Placo, placas* (“I appease, you appease”) has long *pla*; *placeo, places* (“I please, you please”) has short *pla*. *Pareo, pares*, that is, “I appear” or “I obey,” has long *pa*; *paro, paras*, that is, “I prepare,” and *pario, paris*, “I give birth,” have short *pa*.

*Parentes*, when it means “those appearing,” has long *pa*; when it means “parents,” it has short *pa*, as does *parientes* (“those giving birth”). The same syllable, when the word is neuter, is shortened; when masculine, it is lengthened in both numbers.

*Levitas*, if it denotes instability of mind or lightness of weight, has short *le*; if it denotes smoothness of touch—from which wooden objects in a building are said to be *levigata*, “smoothed”—it has long *le* [Col. 0157C].

## 5. On medial syllables

We recognize medial syllables in three ways: by position, by diphthong, and by accent. We have already treated position and diphthongs above. Accent, however, is so called as though from *adcantus*, “additional singing,” because it enables us to recognize syllables through the melody of the voice. There are two vocal accents relevant to the matters under discussion: the shortened and the lengthened.

The shortened accent occurs whenever we pronounce medial syllables without any pause in the voice, as in *moenia* (“walls”) and *tabula* (“tablet”) [Col. 0157D]. The lengthened accent occurs whenever we utter medial syllables with some prolongation of the voice, as in *fortuna* (“fortune”) and *natura* (“nature”).

It must nevertheless be understood that those forms which are pronounced with a shortened *i* in their verbs, when they occur in the middle and change that *i* into *e*, are shortened everywhere, as in *legis, lege, legere* (“you read, read!, to read”), except when they are followed by the three consonants *b*, *m*, and *t*, as in *legebam* (“I was reading”), *legemus* (“we shall read”), and *legetur* (“it will be read”) [Col. 0158A].

The remaining cases are better determined by accents [Paris manuscript: “the matters we are treating”]. In trisyllabic and tetrasyllabic words, and beyond them, accent should be considered as follows. If one asks of how many syllables *amicissimorum* (“of the most friendly [people]”) consists, we learn that the first is short, as in:

> He loved his friend exceedingly.

We find the second long by accent, the third long by position, and the fourth short by accent, because in *amicissimus* (“most friendly”) we find the penultimate syllable with a short accent; the fifth is long by accent. As for the final syllable, its quantity will be shown according to the individual parts of speech in the following discussion [Paris manuscript: “according to the rule”].

## 6. On the final syllables of nouns, pronouns, and participles

The singular nominative has the following short endings:

- *a*, as in *citharista* (“harpist”), *vinea* (“vineyard”), *toreuma* (“relief work”);
- *e*, as in *sedile* (“seat”);
- *o*, as in *ordo* (“order”), *virgo* (“virgin”);
- *u*, as in *cornu* (“horn”);
- *el*, as in *mel* (“honey”);
- *il*, as in *vigil* (“watchful”);
- *ul*, as in *consul* (“consul”);
- *m*, as in *tectum* (“roof”);
- *n*, as in *carmen* (“song”);
- *us*, as in *justus* (“just”), *cursus* (“course”), *cedrus* (“cedar”), *nemus* (“grove”);
- *ir*, as in *vir* (“man”);
- *or*, as in *doctor* (“teacher”);
- *t*, as in *caput* (“head”).

The following are long:

- *i*, as in *frugi* (“useful”);
- *il*, as in *Tanaquil*;
- *ol*, as in *sol* (“sun”);
- *as*, as in *facultas* (“ability”);
- *c*, as in *halec* (“salt fish”).

The following are long in monosyllables but short in disyllables, trisyllables, and other polysyllables:

- *ar*, as in *far* (“spelt”), *nar* [reading and sense uncertain], *Caesar*;
- *er*, as in *ver* (“spring”), *pater* (“father”);
- *ur*, as in *fur* (“thief”), *murmur* (“murmur”);
- *is*, as in *vis* (“force”), *glis* (“dormouse”), *fortis* (“brave”);
- *al*, as in *sal* (“salt”), *Hannibal*.

*Torcular* and *pulvinar* are lengthened, because some preferred the forms *torculare* rather than *torcular*, and *pulvinare* rather than *pulvinar*.

A word ending in *s* is lengthened if it belongs to the fifth declension, as in *dies* (“day”). If it belongs to the third declension, it is long when the singular genitive does not add a syllable, as in *labes* (“stain”), *caedes* (“slaughter”), *tabes* (“wasting”), *pubes* (“puberty”), *clades* (“disaster”), *fames* (“hunger”), *vulpes* (“fox”), *claves* (“keys”), *aedes* (“temple”), *strages* (“massacre”), *Hercules*, *proles* (“offspring”), and *nubes* (“cloud”), although some preferred to pronounce the nominative *nubs* [Paris manuscript: “preferred”].

It is also long when, although the genitive adds a syllable, it has a lengthened *e* before the final syllable, as in *merces, quies, mercedis, quietis* (“wages, rest, of wages, of rest”). It is likewise long when the nouns are monosyllabic or derived from monosyllables, as in *pes* (“foot”), *bipes* (“two-footed”), and *sonipes* (“hoofed”). Here it must be noted that *pes*, like *sal* and *par*, is long when it is a monosyllable. But when it begins to be declined through other cases, it shortens its initial syllable.

Likewise, *Ceres* (“Ceres”), *aries* (“ram”), *paries* (“wall”), and *abies* (“fir tree”) lengthen *es* in the nominative and vocative, but shorten it in the other cases. *Es* is shortened when either its *e* changes into *i* in an expanded genitive, as in *miles, militis* (“soldier, of a soldier”), or when it is intrinsically short, as in *seges, segetis* (“crop, of a crop”).

The monosyllable *os* is lengthened when it means “mouth”; it is shortened when it means “bones.” When this syllable *os* occurs in disyllables or trisyllables, and the medial syllable of the genitive remains long by nature, it is long, as in *nepos, nepotis* (“grandson, of a grandson”); but if that syllable is shortened, it is short, as in *compos, compotis* (“master of oneself, of one who is master of himself”) [Col. 0158C–D].

*Us* is lengthened when it remains long in the expanded genitive, as in *virtus, virtutis* (“virtue, of virtue”) and *tellus, telluris* (“earth, of earth”), except for *palus*, whose genitive is distinguished as *palus, paludis* (“marsh, of a marsh”). Hence:

> The king’s work, and the barren marsh long sterile, suitable for oars.

But if *us* does not remain long in an expanded genitive, or if the genitive does not add a syllable, it is shortened, as in *pectus, pectoris* (“breast, of a breast”) and *vulgus, vulgi* (“common people, of the common people”) [Col. 0159A].

The genitive, dative, and ablative are lengthened. But the genitive, when it belongs to the third declension, is shortened together with its ablative when the latter ends only in the letter *e*, as in *a fonte, fontis* (“from a fountain, of a fountain”), except for one form which is lengthened: *ab hac fame* (“from this hunger”), because the ancients declined it as *hujus famei*, not *hujus famis*, and *huic famei*, not *huic fami*.

It must be noted that nouns of the fifth declension whose genitive and dative end in the letters *ei*, with the two vowels separated and each long, are such as *faciei* (“of the face”), *diei* (“of the day”), and *fidei* (“of faith”). The accusative is always short, and the vocative likewise, except when it ends in *i*, as in *Laurenti* (“O Laurence”).

It must also be noted that nouns ending in *-ius* have two *i*s in the genitive and one in the vocative; both are long, as in *filius, filii, o fili* (“son, of a son, O son”). Alternatively, they end their vocative in a shortened *e*, as in *impius, impie* (“ungodly, O ungodly one”). When that vocative is identical to the nominative, it follows the nominative rule, as in *haec paupertas, o paupertas* (“this poverty, O poverty”).

The plural nominative, accusative, and vocative are lengthened in the masculine and feminine genders, but shortened in the neuter. *Ambo* (“both”) and *duo* (“two”), when neuter, are shortened; when masculine, they are lengthened. The plural genitive is short in all cases [Paris manuscript: “the plural genitive”]. The dative or ablative, when ending in *-is*, is long, as in *doctis* (“for/to the learned”); when ending in *-bus*, it is shortened, as in *rebus* (“for/to things”).

This rule includes all nouns, pronouns, and participles. The declension of pronouns differs only in this respect: monosyllables consisting of vowels, such as *me*, *te*, *se*, and *qui*, are lengthened in every case [the transmitted wording is uncertain]. The genitive is shortened when it ends in *-us*, as in *illius* (“of that one”). The dative, as with nouns, is always long, except for *mihi*, *tibi*, and *sibi*, which may be pronounced indifferently. The remaining cases likewise take their rule from nouns [Col. 0159B–C].

In Greek words, the following singular nominatives are short:

- *a*, as in *ecclesia* (“church”), *baptisma* (“baptism”);
- *as*, when the genitive has *-dos*, as in *Arcas, Arcados* (“Arcadian, of an Arcadian”), *Pallas, Pallados* (“Pallas, of Pallas”);
- *os*, when the genitive has a diphthong, as in *Delos, Deli* (“Delos, of Delos”).

The following are long:

- *e*, as in *schole* (“school”) and *synagoge* (“synagogue”), which Latin usage ends in *a*;
- *o*, as in *Dido*;
- *an*, as in *Titan*;
- *en*, as in *lien* (“spleen”), *syren* (“siren”);
- *in*, as in *delphin* (“dolphin”);
- *on*, as in *Memnon*;
- *er*, as in *aer* (“air”), *aether* (“ether”);
- *as*, as in *Aeneas*;
- *es*, as in *Anchises*.

The genitive is shortened when it ends in *-dos* or *-tos*, as in *Arcados* (“of an Arcadian”) and *poematos* (“of a poem”). The dative is shortened when it ends in *i*, as in *Palladi* (“to Pallas”). The accusative is shortened when it ends in *a* or *on*, as in *Thesea* (“Theseus”) and *Delon* (“Delos”).

Otherwise the vocative is long when it ends in *a*. In masculine nouns alone it is long, as in *Aenea* (“O Aeneas”); in feminine nouns it is shortened, as in *haec cathedra* (“this chair”) [Paris manuscript: “it is long”].

An ending in *e* is lengthened, as in *schole*, *synagoge*, *pentecoste* (“Pentecost”), and *parasceve* (“preparation day”), except in nouns whose nominative ends in *os*, as in *Petros, Petre* (“Peter, O Peter”). An ending in *i* is shortened, as in *o Alexi* (“O Alexis”). An ending in *o* is lengthened, as in *Dido*.

The plural nominative and vocative are short when they end in *a* or *es*, as in *rhetores* (“rhetors”) and *charismata* (“gifts”); otherwise they are long, as in *ecclesia* (“churches”) [Paris manuscript: *ecclesia*].

The genitive is long if the word is declined in Greek, as in *laon* and *cedron*, that is, “of peoples” and “of cedars.” A dative ending in *s* is shortened, as in *Arcas*; otherwise it is long, as in *lais*, that is, “to peoples.” An accusative ending in *as*, derived from a singular genitive ending in *os*, is shortened, as in *Arcados, Arcadas* (“of an Arcadian, Arcadians”); otherwise it enjoys length, as in *ecclesias* (“churches”) [Col. 0160A].

## 7. On the final syllables of verbs and adverbs

In verbs of the first conjugation, *a* and *as* are lengthened, as in *ama, amas* (“love!, you love”). In the second conjugation, *e* and *es* are lengthened, as in *sede, sedes* (“sit!, you sit”). In the long-vowel third conjugation, *i* and *is* are lengthened, as in *nutri, nutris* (“nourish!, you nourish”). In the shortened third conjugation, *e* and *is* are shortened, as in *cerne, cernis* (“discern!, you discern”) [Paris manuscript supplies: “in the second …; in the third, lengthened …; in the third, shortened …”].

In all verbs, *o* is shortened, as in *amo* (“I love”), *sedeo* (“I sit”), *cerno* (“I discern”), and *nutrio* (“I nourish”), although authority varies.

In the infinitive mood, the penultimate syllables *a*, *e*, and *i* are likewise lengthened, as in *amare* (“to love”), *sedere* (“to sit”), and *nutrire* (“to nourish”). The *e* is shortened in *cernere* (“to discern”). Similarly, in other moods the same vowels are lengthened, as in *amarem, amares, amaret* (“I might love, you might love, he might love”), and so forth according to their form. The *e* is shortened in verbs of the shortened third conjugation, as in *cernerem, cerneres*, and so forth [Col. 0160B].

*Es* is shortened, as in *sum, es* (“I am, you are”), and in compounds made from these, as in *adsum* (“I am present”), *ades* (“you are present”), *possum* (“I can”), and *potes* (“you can”). But *faxis* (“you will do”), *velis* (“you may wish”), and *adsis* (“you may be present”) are long [Paris manuscript: “long”], because the plural number lengthens them, as in the lengthened medial syllables of *adsitis*, *velitis*, and *faxitis* (“you may be present,” “you may wish,” “you may do”).

All final syllables of verbs of the following kinds, *res* and *ses*, are long, because the plural number lengthens them, as in *amares, amaretis, amasses, amassetis* (“you might love, you might love [plural], you might have loved, you might have loved [plural]”).

Forms ending in *c* are to be lengthened, as in *fac* (“do!”), *dic* (“say!”), *duc* (“lead!”), and *induc* (“lead in!”); likewise those ending in *i*, as in *amavi* (“I loved”), *amari* (“to be loved”); and those ending in *u*, as in *amatu* (“by being loved”). Forms ending in *m* or *es* are shortened, as in *amem, ames* (“I may love, you may love”); those ending in *us*, as in *amamus* (“we love”); those ending in *t*, as in *amat* (“he loves”); those ending in *re*, as in *amare* (“to love”); and those ending in *tis*, as in *amatis* (“you love”) [Col. 0160C].

Adverbs ending in *a* are lengthened, as in *una* (“together”). Those ending in *e*, when derived from nouns and preserving degrees of comparison, are lengthened, as in *docte, doctius, doctissime* (“learnedly, more learnedly, most learnedly”). But if they arise independently, as *saepe* (“often”); or if they do not admit comparison, as *rite* (“properly”); or if they fail to form comparison, as *bene* (“well”) and *male* (“badly”), they are shortened.

Adverbs ending in *i* are lengthened, except *quasi* (“as if”), *ibi* (“there”), and *ubi* (“where”), and forms derived from them, such as *sicubi* (“if anywhere”); *heri* (“yesterday”) is lengthened. An ending in *o* is indifferent, as in *falso* (“falsely”). An ending in *u* is lengthened, as in *noctu* (“by night”). Endings in *l* and *r* are shortened, as in *semel* (“once”) and *pariter* (“equally”); *ul* is shortened in *simul* (“at the same time”); *m* in *tam* (“so”).

An ending in *n* is shortened everywhere except in *non* (“not”), *en* (“behold”), and *an* (“whether”) [Paris manuscript: *non* and *an*], as in *forsan* (“perhaps”). An ending in *s* is shortened, as in *magis* (“more”) and *funditus* (“utterly”), except when preceded by *a*, as in *alias* (“otherwise”). An ending in *c* is lengthened, as in *hic* (“here”), *illic* (“there”), and *adhuc* (“still”) [Col. 0160D].

Monosyllables are lengthened, as in *cur* (“why”) and *plus* (“more”), except *bis* (“twice”) and *ter* (“three times”).

But *ne* (“lest”) is pronounced in two ways. It is lengthened when used as a prohibition:

> Let not intrusive care labor to search out hidden things;

or when it stands for *ut non*, “so that not,” as the same Prosper says:

> And thus brief vengeance ends guilty crimes,  
> lest punishment should hold the guilty without end.

It is shortened when used in a question or rebuke, as in:

> Then, savage one, bloodstained, fierce, bold, insane, rebellious?

The *s* in numerals is shortened, as in *toties* (“so many times”), *quoties* (“how many times”), *septies* (“seven times”), and *decies* (“ten times”) [Col. 0161A].

## 8. On the final syllables of conjunctions, prepositions, and interjections

Almost all conjunctions are shortened. Those ending in *a* or *i*, however, are lengthened, except *qua* (“by which”), *ita* (“thus”), and *nisi* (“unless”), as in *propterea* (“therefore”), *interea* (“meanwhile”), *si* (“if”), and *ni* (“if not”) [Paris manuscript: “short, as *tamen*; *quamvis* is lengthened, except …”].

Conjunctions ending in *n* are lengthened if they have *a* or *i* before it, as in *an* (“whether”) and *sin* (“but if”); likewise *alioquin* (“otherwise”). The others are shortened, except those made long by position, such as *ast* (“but”) and *aut* (“or”) [Col. 0161A].

Only accusative prepositions ending in *a* are lengthened, as *intra* (“within”), together with the one monosyllable *cis* (“on this side”). Ablative prepositions are all shortened, as *ab* (“from”), except monosyllables consisting of vowels, such as *a* (“from”), or ending in vowels, such as *de* (“from, concerning”).

Common prepositions are evidently shortened, as *super* (“above”) [Paris manuscript: *in*, *super*].

Nor should verbal prepositions be passed over, although they are placed not at the end but always at the beginning of words. These are *am*, *co*, *con*, *di*, *dis*, *re*, and *se*. *Am* and *dis* seek position, as in *amplector* (“I embrace”) and *disjungo* (“I separate”), and therefore become long. *Co* is dichronous, as in *coerceo* (“I restrain”) and *connecto* (“I connect”). *Con* is long, as in *conjicio* (“I throw together”). *Di* is long, as in *dirigo* (“I direct”). *Se* is long, as in *secerno* (“I separate”). *Re* is shortened everywhere, as in *remitto* (“I send back”), except in *refert* when it means “it makes a difference,” as in:

> Besides, it now makes no difference whether the fodder is changed;

and in the single word *rejicio* (“I throw back”):

> Throw it back, lest it stain the fleeces with dark marks.

All interjections, if monosyllabic, are lengthened, as *heu* (“alas”). The others are to be judged by analogy with similar parts of speech. Likewise, all interjections borrowed from Greek, as Audacius says, take a rise in their final syllables, such as *papae* (“ah!”) and *atat* (“alas!”). In the same way, the others likewise take either an acute or circumflex accent on the final syllable [Col. 0161B–C].

## 9. On feet

A foot is a definite counting of syllables and times. It is so called because we use it, as though a foot-rule, to measure a verse.

There are four disyllabic feet, eight trisyllabic feet, and sixteen tetrasyllabic feet, each distinguished by name. Feet increased by doubling these are generally called *syzygia* (συζυγία), that is, “conjunctions.” Thus all feet from disyllabic through hexasyllabic amount to one hundred and twenty-four. Anyone who wishes can find a complete account of them in Donatus. For the present treatise, however, it is enough for us to remember only the disyllabic and trisyllabic feet.

The four disyllabic feet are these:

- The pyrrhic, consisting of two shorts and two times, as in *amor* (“love”).
- Its opposite is the spondee, consisting of two longs and four times, as in *aestas* (“summer”).
- The iamb consists of a short and a long, totaling three times, as in *parens* (“parent”).
- Its opposite is the trochee, consisting of a long and a short, also totaling three times, as in *versus* (“verse”).

The eight trisyllabic feet are these:

- The tribrach, consisting of three shorts and three times, as in *macula* (“spot”).
- Its opposite is the molossus, consisting of three longs and six times, as in *Aeneas*.
- The anapest consists of two shorts and a long, totaling four times, as in *pietas* (“piety”).
- Its opposite is the dactyl, consisting of a long and two shorts, totaling four times, as in *regula* (“rule”).
- The amphibrach consists of a short, a long, and a short, totaling four times, as in *arena* (“sand”).
- Its opposite is the amphimacrus, consisting of a long, a short, and a long, totaling five times, as in *impotens* (“powerless”).
- The bacchius consists of a short and two longs, totaling five times, as in *poetae* (“poets”).
- Its opposite is the antibacchius, consisting of two longs and a short, totaling five times, as in *natura* (“nature”).

These are followed, as I said, by sixteen tetrasyllabic feet, thirty-two pentasyllabic feet, and sixty-four hexasyllabic feet [editorial correction: “hexasyllabic”]. For the present, however, we think this sufficient for our work on the art of meter [Col. 0161D–0162A].

## 10. On dactylic meter, hexameter and pentameter

[Col. 0162B]

Dactylic hexameter, also called heroic meter because it was used especially to sing of the deeds of heroes, that is, brave men, is more beautiful and loftier than all other meters. It has therefore become suitable for works both lengthy and concise, both humble and elevated.

It consists of dactyls and spondees, or trochees, in such a way that it admits a spondee in every position except the fifth, a dactyl everywhere except the last, and a trochee only in the final position. Or, as some define it, the final position is always a spondee, and every position except the fifth may likewise be a spondee; a trochee occurs nowhere. For although the final syllable is short by nature, it makes a spondee according to the poets’ choice, because, as we said above, all verses treat their final syllable as indifferent. Otherwise the legitimate number of twenty-four times would not be present in the hexameter verse; for in its perfection it ought to contain as many times as a full pound contains half-ounces.

An example is:

> The sky fills many summits with radiant light.

[Col. 0162C]

After Homer, this meter received the name “heroic.” Previously it was called Pythian, because the oracles of Apollo were delivered in this meter.

Closely related to it, and almost familiarly attached to it—so that I have never seen it used without the support of the former—is dactylic pentameter. It admits a spondee in the first and second positions, and a dactyl in all positions. It is catalectic in the middle and at the end.

An example is:

> And the holy ranks rejoice in devout choruses.

Some maintain that the verses of this meter should be scanned as containing five complete feet: a spondee or dactyl in the first and second positions, always a spondee in the third, and anapests in the fourth and fifth, as if one were to say:

> Seek the kingdoms of heaven, seek the kingdoms of heaven.

They scan it:

> *Quaerite* — dactyl; *regna po* — dactyl; *li quae* — spondee; *rite re* — anapest; *gna poli* — anapest.

But this seems to me less consistent with the nature of the meter, since all who used it divided the whole verse in the middle and wished it to consist of two penthemimeres, the first of which freely admitted either a dactyl or a spondee in each of its two regions, while the second admitted only dactyls in both [Col. 0163A].

When this meter is joined to the one described above, the result is called elegiac poetry. Philosophers call the wretched *eleos*, and the melody of this poetry suits the lamentation of the wretched: the first verse is hexameter, the following one pentameter.

It is said that among the Hebrews the Song of Deuteronomy and Psalms 118 and 144 were written in this kind of meter. They also assert that the Book of blessed Job was written in simple hexameter.

In elegiac poetry one must observe that nothing from the sense of the pentameter verse should ever remain unexplained and be supplied in the following hexameter verse [Paris manuscript: “left unexplained”]. Rather, each verse should either complete its own meaning, as in Sedulius:

> Let us sing, companions, let us sing honor to the Lord;  
> let the sweet love of Christ resound from the devout mouth.

Or the preceding hexameter and following pentameter should be mutually joined, as the poet wishes, according to Prosper:

> The sinner alone serves badly; although he may enjoy  
> an ample kingdom, he is a wretched servant indeed.

For although the following little verses are attached to these, they are nevertheless joined to one another, and the second supplies what the first lacks:

> When the mind is ruled too greatly by the carnal tyrant,  
> he serves as many scepters as there are vices to which he is given.

## 11. What is the best form of poetry

[Col. 0163C]

In hexameter poetry, a chain of several verses is usually most pleasing. You will often find this in Arator and Sedulius: sometimes two, sometimes three, sometimes four or five verses connected with one another, occasionally six or seven, or even more. Such is the following:

> When Lot fled from Sodom’s ruin, while his wife looked back,  
> she remained in astonishment, changed into a pillar of salt,  
> transformed into her own punishment; for no one who looks behind  
> while avoiding the guilty dangers of the despised world  
> will be saved, nor should a plowman,  
> while practicing worthy work, look too much behind him.

And Arator:

> The laws of ministry suited to sacred altars  
> were established in seven men, whom, chosen from every side,  
> it pleases us to call Levites. How splendidly the hand  
> of the Church began to shine, mixing the cups of life  
> and offering its liquids with blood to the fire.

Such a connection, however, if it proceeds beyond measure, produces disgust and weariness. Hymns, on the other hand, which ought to be sung by alternating choirs, must be clearly separated into individual verses, as all the Ambrosian hymns are [Col. 0163D].

The best and most beautiful arrangement of a dactylic verse occurs when the penultimate elements correspond to the first, and the final elements to the medial ones. Sedulius frequently used this arrangement, as in:

> The divided sea opened passable blue paths;

and:

> The dry marble stones marveled at foreign feet;

and:

> The animal uttered human speech.

Likewise in the pentameter:

> He deigned to recline upon our couches;

and:

> The red vegetable which the placed dish supplies.

This should not, however, be done continuously, but only after several intervening verses. For if you always arrange the feet in one way, even if the verse is excellent, its form quickly becomes cheap. Sometimes it is pleasing to complete a verse with nouns alone, as Fortunatus does:

> Lilies, narcissus, violets, rose, nard, amomum  
> delight my minds; no grasses do so.

He did the same with proper names:

> Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel, Esther, Judith, Anna, Naomi,  
> although they especially raise the summit toward the stars.

He did it also with verbs:

> He flatters, restores, venerates, honors, overshadows,  
> and places his chaste limbs in the bridal chamber.

One should also attend to metrical elegance, insofar as the art of diction permits: mobile nouns should be placed before fixed ones, but harmonious nouns should not be placed next to one another. Some other part of speech should be inserted between them, as in:

> The gentle branch is animated against the fierce dragon.

He placed *gentle* before *branch*, and *fierce* before *dragon*, but did so with separation, inserting the verb *is animated* between them. This is not something that must always be observed, but when it is done, it contributes to elegance. Prosper also produced a very pleasing verse by changing this order:

> In holy conduct the harmony of peace is beautiful.

And again:

> God’s eternal law governs all things with a steadfast command,  
> nor does it alter its purpose with changing time.

The veteran poet Lucan, about to describe the battles of Caesar and Pompey, begins as follows:

> Wars more than civil across the Emathian fields,  
> and the right granted to crime, we sing, and the mighty people  
> turned its conquering hand against its own entrails.  
> When proud Babylon was destined to be despoiled of  
> Ausonian trophies, and Crassus’ unavenged shadow wandered,  
> it pleased them to wage wars that would have no triumphs.

## 12. On the scansions, or caesuras, of heroic verse

There are four kinds of scansion in verse: joined, separated, mixed, and divided.

Joined scansion, considered more praiseworthy than the others, occurs when a foot nowhere ends together with a word, as in:

> Nothing immortal is held within the structure of the world.

Separated scansion occurs when words end together with feet, as in:

> These are your good things, because you, being good, create all things.

This kind of versification is extremely rare. For if a syllable does not remain after two or three feet—what they call *penthemimeris* and *hepthemimeris*—the verse cannot be considered regular. Thus in the example just given, *sunt* remains after two feet, and *tu* remains after three [Col. 0164D].

Mixed scansion contains both forms: in some places the verse is joined, while in others it is separated, as in:

> For us there is certain faith, eternal through ages of praise;

and:

> God adopts peaceful offspring for himself in due number.

Divided scansion occurs when the first three feet are joined together and separated from the remaining feet, as in:

> From there the pious virgin Mary, Mother of God, shines forth.

And Prosper:

> The Word begotten from the Father’s heart creates and governs all things.

The form of the caesuras must be considered no less carefully. These too are four: *penthemimeris*, *hepthemimeris*, *catatriton trochaeon*, and *bucoliceptomen*.

*Penthemimeris* occurs when, after two feet, a half-foot is found that divides the verse and completes a phrase.

*Hepthemimeris* occurs when, after three feet, a syllable is found, as in:

> When your Gentiles strive.

They are called *penthemimeris* and *hepthemimeris* in Greek, as though “half-fivefold” and “half-sevenfold,” because when they are formed with spondees, the former consists of five syllables and the latter of seven: the former contains a half-foot in the fifth syllable, the latter in the seventh.

*Catatriton trochaeon* occurs when a trochee is found in the third position—not because it can exist in the middle of the verse, but because, with one syllable removed from a dactyl, a trochee remains, as in:

> To march in sonorous rhythms.

*Bucoliceptomen* occurs when nothing remains after four feet, as in:

> Always the beginning, the scepter, the yoke, glory, the partner;

and:

> Christ was bread, Christ a rock, Christ amid the waters.

This caesura gets its name because it often occurs in bucolic poetry.

When a syllable remains after two feet, it is called a *comma*; when nothing remains after two feet, it is called a *colon*. These names are also used indifferently by orators, who call a complete sentence a *period*. Its parts are called *cola* and *commata*, as, for example:

> For you endure it if someone brings you into slavery—

this is a colon;

> if someone takes—

this is a colon;

> if someone devours—

this is a colon;

> if someone is exalted—

and so forth until the complete sentence: these are cola and commata.

A complete sentence is a period. *Colon* is interpreted as “limb,” *comma* as “incision,” and *period* as “closure” or “circuit” [Col. 0165A–C].

## 13. On synaloepha

[Col. 0165; Editor’s note: it should be written *synaloephe*; the Greek is συναλοιφή (*synaloiphē*).]

The principle of synaloepha should also be mentioned, because sometimes the final syllable of a word, or part of a syllable, appears to be consumed. Hence it is called *synaloepha* in Greek, as though it were passing over by a kind of leap.

It occurs in two ways. First, when some part of speech ends either in a vowel or in the consonant *m*, and the following part of speech begins with a vowel, the following part of speech consumes with its own vowel either the preceding vowel or the syllable that ended in *m* [Col. 0165D].

What I mean is illustrated by:

> The way is narrow, truly, that leads to the halls of life.

It is scanned as follows:

> *Arcta vi* — dactyl; *est ve* — spondee, with the syllable *a* intercepted by synaloepha.

A part of a syllable is likewise removed, as the same Prosper says:

> Take the table that wisdom has set out, however great it may be.

[End of supplied source.]

Scansion is therefore as follows: *Sumite* is a dactyl, *quam ma* a spondee, *gnapposu* a dactyl, with part of the syllable removed by synaloepha. Likewise, a part of a syllable ending in *m* is intercepted by synaloepha when the following verses are spoken:

> *Nullus enim est insons sola formidine poenae,*  
> *Qui sanctum et justum non amat imperium.*

“For no one is innocent through fear of punishment alone, who does not love holy and just authority.”

The scansion is: *Nullus e*, a dactyl; *nest in*, a spondee, with the *m* absorbed by synaloepha; and again, *Qui sanc*, a spondee; *tet jus*, a spondee, with synaloepha removing the part of the syllable *um*. Likewise, an entire syllable ending in *m* disappears through synaloepha in:

> *Magnum praesidium est sacro libamine pasci,*  
> *Si cor participis crimina nulla premunt.*

“Great protection is to be nourished by sacred offering, if no crimes oppress the heart of the one who shares in it.”

The scansion is: *Magnum*, a spondee; *praesidi*, a dactyl; *est sa*, a spondee, with the syllable *um* intercepted by synaloepha. Accordingly, whenever words end in *m*, unless they are protected by the positional effect of a following consonant, synaloepha breaking in either destroys or diminishes the final syllable [Note: [Col. 0165] Paris. adds: “they always lose them.”], except when the following speech begins with the letter *h*. In that case it is left to the poets’ judgment whether *h*, like the stronger consonants, prevents synaloepha, or whether, according to the weakness proper to it, it has no force at all.

The poet’s intention prevailed in:

> *Nomine Johannem hunc tu vocitare memento.*

“Remember to call this man John by name.”

And:

> *Progenitum fulsisse ducem hoc coelitus astra.*

“The stars shone from heaven that this leader had been begotten.”

On the other hand, *h* did nothing to repel synaloepha in the line which the poet allowed to undergo it:

> *Qui pereuntem hominem vetiti dulcedine pomi.*

“Who [—] a perishing man by the sweetness of the forbidden fruit.”

It must be understood, however, that synaloepha can never occur in the middle of the same syntactic unit. If two vowels come together within a word, and the first is long, the following vowel may, if the poet so wishes, make the first short instead of long; but the poet has no power to remove it altogether.

The vowel is naturally long in this line of Paulinus:

> *Ut citharas modulans unius verbere plectri.*

“Like one playing harps with a single stroke of the plectrum.”

It is permissibly short in this line of Sedulius:

> *Unius ob meritum cuncti periere minores.*

“Because of the merit of one, all the lesser ones perished.”

Likewise, it is naturally long in this line of Paulinus:

> *Discutiebat ovans galea scutoque fidei.*

“Rejoicing, he was scattering them with the helmet and shield of faith.”

It is permissibly short in this line of Prosper:

> *Divitias jam nunc promissi concipe regni,*  
> *Virtute et fidei quod cupis esse tene.*

“Now conceive the riches of the promised kingdom, and by virtue and faith hold fast what you desire to be.”

This, as we have said above, is counted among the common syllables. But when in verse *prendo* is read for *prehendo*, or *secla* for *saecula*, or something similar occurs, this is not synaloepha but syncope, which is a species of metaplasm. For in such a case no letter or syllable is removed in scansion; rather, poetic freedom has ensured that it would never be written.

Thus, concerning the verse of Virgil:

> *Nec tota tamen ille prior praeeunte carina.*

“Nor, although preceding the keel, was he nevertheless wholly the first.”

Reason proves that it must be scanned in this way: first *Nec to*, a spondee; then *ta tamen*, a dactyl; *ille pri*, a dactyl; *or praee*, a dactyl, with the diphthong shortened because of the following vowel; and finally *unte carina*, a dactyl and a spondee, which complete the line.

For who would listen to Victorinus teaching us to scan *unte carina*, making synaloepha in the middle of a syntactic unit, something the earlier poets never did? Synaloepha occurs in every part of the verse, even at the end, as in Prosper:

> *Sed rerum auctori nullus non cognitus ordo est.*

“But no order of things is unknown to the author of things.”

Synaloepha also occurs after one verse and extends toward the beginning of the following verse, as in Paulinus:

> *Quae decus omne operum perimebant improba foedaque*  
> *Obice prospectum caecantia lumina complent.*

“Those wicked and foul things that destroyed every glory of works, filling the blinded eyes with an obstruction that blocked their sight.”

The feet of the final verse are a dactyl and a spondee, *improba foeda*; those of the first part of the following verse, through synaloepha, are *que obice*, a dactyl, and *prospectum*, a spondee.

## 14. On Episynaloepha, or Diaeresis

[Col. 0167B]

The joining and separation of syllables, which the Greeks call *episynaloepha* and *diaeresis*, must be recognized by the metrician as permissible wherever necessary: joining, namely, when two syllables are made from three; separation, when two are made from one syllable.

An example of joining is:

> *Aedificant sectaque intexunt abiete costas.*

“They build, and weave the ribs together with cut firwood.”

And:

> *Custodes sufferre valent, labat ariete crebro*  
> *Janua . . . . .*

“The guards are able to endure it; the gate wavers under the repeated battering-ram . . .”

And:

> *Tenuia nec lanae per coelum vellera ferri.*

“Nor are the thin fleeces of wool borne through the sky.”

In *abiete*, there are four short syllables. Compress the word, and it becomes long by position, because the vowel *a* is closed by *b* and is followed by *i* used as a consonant. The same applies to *ariete*: *a* is naturally short; join *r* to it, and join *i* and *e* to one another, and *ar* becomes a long syllable by position, because it is followed by *i*, which is placed as a consonant.

Likewise, in *tenuia*, compress *ten* and make *u* consonantal; thus, from a four-syllable proceleusmatic you will make a three-syllable dactyl.

The same applies to:

> *Fluviorum rex Eridanus.*

“Eridanus, king of the rivers.”

*Fluvio* is an anapest; but if, by compression, you make one syllable *fluv* and another *io*, you turn the anapest into a spondee.

This joining or separation most often occurs with the letters *i* or *a*, of which our native poets also provide many examples. Paulinus writes:

> *Sum profugus mundi, tanquam benedictus Jacob.*

“I am an exile from the world, like blessed Jacob.”

Fortunatus writes:

> *Dirigit: et Jacobos terra beata sacros.*

“It directs; and the blessed land [directs] the holy Jacobs.”

The former separates *i* and *a*; the latter joins them.

Paulinus likewise writes:

> *Parietibus novitas latet intus operta vetustas.*

“Within the walls, novelty lies hidden, covered by antiquity.”

He made *parieti* a dactyl from a proceleusmatic by unnaturally joining *a* and *r* into one syllable, and *i* and *e* into another.

Sedulius, by separating *u* and *a*, writes:

> *Cujus onus leve est, cujus juga ferre suave est.*

“Whose burden is light, whose yoke is pleasant to bear.”

Prosper, by joining them, writes:

> *Nec Christi [Note: [Col. 0167] Paris.: *e templo*.] exemplo suavior exit odor.*

“No sweeter fragrance issues forth than the example of Christ.”

Paulinus, by naturally separating *u* and *i*, writes:

> *Conscia servitii quid gesseris, et cui tandem.*

“Conscious of your servitude, what have you done, and for whom at last?”

Fortunatus, joining them according to poetic license, writes:

> *Cui tamen hoc opus est eum virginitatis honore,*  
> *Ut placeat sponso mens moderata suo.*

“Yet this work is necessary for him, with the honor of virginity, so that a disciplined mind may please its bridegroom.”

Again, Paulinus separates the same vowels in another pronoun:

> *Cum subito aut illis corda hostibus, aut huic ora.*

“When suddenly either the hearts of those enemies, or the face of this man . . .”

Prosper joins them:

> *Huic homo, si recte famulatur, proximus haeret.*

“To this man a person clings closely if he serves him rightly.”

Virgil joins *e* and *i*:

> *Tityre, pascentes a flumine reice capellas.*

“Tityrus, drive the grazing she-goats back from the river.”

Elsewhere he naturally separates them:

> *Reice ne maculis infuscet vellera pullis.*

“Drive them away, lest it stain the fleeces with dark spots.”

Unless I am mistaken, Paulinus also joins the same vowels when he says:

> *Ast alii pictis accendunt lumina cereis.*

“But others kindle lights with painted candles.”

[Col. 0168B] Unless perhaps he should be said to have placed a dactyl in the final part of the verse contrary to custom.

The letter *r* also admits separation, although in a different manner. In the examples just mentioned, when vowels are separated or joined, a syllable contrary to nature either increases or disappears. Here, however, a syllable customarily grows through a vowel assumed in vocal pronunciation even though it is not written, as in:

> *Illi continuo statuunt ter dena argenti.*

“They immediately set up thirty [things] of silver.”

And Paulinus:

> *Et spatii coepere et culminis incrementa.*

“And the increases of space and of the summit began.”

And again:

> *Sic prope, sic longe sita culmina respergebat.*

“Thus, near and thus far away, he was sprinkling the situated summits.”

Prudentius, in the *Psychomachia*, had written:

> *. . . . . Et laeta libidinis interfectae.*

“And the joys of slain lust . . .”

And the same poet, in the same work:

> *Palpitat atque aditu spiraminis intercepto.*

“And it throbs when the passage of breath has been obstructed.”

For it was not customary to place a spondee in the fifth foot of a heroic verse. Nevertheless, I think that in verses of this kind they wished to scan the words so that, with a vowel added in pronunciation although not written, there would be a dactyl rather than a spondee: *interecepto*, *increementa*, *interefectae*, *resperigebat*, and, through synaloepha, *denarigenti*.

This happens more readily with the letter *r* than with the other consonants [Note: [Col. 0167] Paris.: “because it . . .”], because *r*, naturally harsher in sound, becomes harsher when followed by other consonants; consequently, a vowel sound is added to it, whose moderation softens its harshness. Those who know how to perform the Church’s songs properly often do the same with the letter *r* in antiphons, responsories, and other such compositions sung with melody.

This too must be mentioned: nouns ending in *-ius* or *-ium* ought to have two *i*’s in the genitive, in a case equally composed of two syllables. Yet metricians sometimes pronounce one syllable in that genitive where there should be two, either by removing one of the two *i*’s or by joining both into a single syllable, although many, according to Donatus, deny that this can be done.

Paulinus says:

> *Oblectans inopem sensu fructuque peculii.*

“Delighting the poor man with the perception and fruit of his property.”

If someone were to say that here he placed a dactyl at the end of the little verse according to ancient custom, let him read what the same poet says elsewhere:

> *Excoluit bijugis laquearii et marmore fabri.*

“He adorned the ceiling with paired beams and marble craftsmanship.”

*Excolu* is a dactyl; *it biju*, a dactyl; *gis laque*, a dactyl. What, then, is the fourth foot? *arii et* has four syllables—one long, one short, and two long. An epitrite cannot occur in a heroic verse; perhaps, therefore, it is a spondee, with synaloepha consuming two vowels through the arrival of one.

You will not easily find this either permitted by grammarians or used by poets, although Fortunatus wrote:

> *Vincentii Hispania surgit ab arce decus.*

“The glory of Vincent rises from the citadel of Spain.”

The scansion of this verse is the same as that of the preceding one, unless perhaps they followed Lucilius’ rule. Lucilius considered that *Lucilius*, *Aemilius*, and other names which have *i* before *u* could be written with one *i*, not only in the vocative but also in the genitive.

## 15. How Authority and Necessity Often Violate the Decisions of Metricians

Nevertheless, we must observe that both authority at times and the necessity of metrical discipline legitimately disregard the rules. Necessity applies to words which cannot otherwise be placed in a verse, such as those with four short syllables—*Italiam*, *basilica*, *religio*—or three initial short syllables, as in *reliquiae*, or one short syllable in the middle, as in *veritas* and *trinitas*. Such words can make neither the customary dactyl nor a spondee, and this most often occurs with proper names.

An example is:

> *Italiam sequimur fugientem, et mergimur undis.*

“We follow Italy as she flees, and are submerged in the waves.”

He placed the letter *i* contrary to nature as long, because he could not name Italy, as he so often had to do, in any other way unless he either lengthened a naturally short syllable or placed a tribrach in the position of a dactyl.

Similarly, when he wished to name beehives while speaking of bees, he placed an antibacchius in a dactylic verse out of necessity:

> *Seu lento fuerint alvearia vimine texta.*

“Whether the beehives have been woven with pliant wicker.”

And Paulinus writes:

> *Qui simul ac sancta pro religione coistis.*

“You who gathered together at once on behalf of holy religion.”

He made *re* contrary to nature long, because the hexameter could not otherwise accommodate the word.

The same poet has:

> *Basilicis haec juncta tribus patet area cuncti.*

“This court, joined to three basilicas, lies open to all.”

But elsewhere the same syllable is used as short, as Fortunatus says:

> *Hic Paulina, Agnes, Basilissa, Eugenia [Note: [Col. 0169] Paris.: *regnant*.] regnat.*

“Here Paulina, Agnes, Basilissa, and Eugenia reign.”

I believe that it was because of these and similar necessities that Jerome, speaking of the book of blessed Job, after saying that it had been written among the Hebrews for the most part in hexameter verses, added: “Since they lack the dactyl and spondee, because of the idiom of the language they frequently admit other feet of the same temporal value, though not of the same number of syllables.”

Authority, however, disregards the rule of the grammarians. Thus Sedulius, in the closing section of the poem mentioned above, after saying:

> *Gloria magna Patri, semper tibi gloria, Nate,*

“Great glory to the Father; glory forever to you, Son,”

adds:

> *Cum sancto Spiritu gloria magna Patri.*

“With the Holy Spirit, great glory to the Father.”

The first syllable of *Spiritus* is long. Therefore the true scansion of this verse is: *cum san*, a spondee; *cto spiri*, an antibacchius, not a dactyl. But the poet, in order to celebrate aloud the glory of the holy and undivided Trinity, disregarded the rule of grammatical arrangement.

The same poet, in his Paschal poem, writes:

> *Sic ait ipse docens: Ego in Patre et Pater in me.*

“Thus he himself said while teaching: ‘I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.’”

It is scanned as follows: *Sic ait*, a dactyl; *ipse do*, a dactyl; *cens e*, a trochee; *gin pa*, a spondee, with the *o* removed by synaloepha. Or, if you wish to scan *cens ego* and make a dactyl, you act contrary to Sedulius’ own practice, which he maintained throughout, by leaving the second vowel free when another vowel follows.

In the same work he writes:

> *Clarifica, dixit, nomen tuum, magnaque coelo.*

“‘Glorify,’ he said, ‘your name,’ and [be] great in heaven.”

Here, in order to commend the truth of the Lord’s speech more clearly, he set aside the order prescribed by secular discipline.

Again:

> *Scribitur et titulus: Hic est rex Judaeorum.*

“And the inscription is written: ‘This is the king of the Jews.’”

Let whoever can judge how he wished this to be scanned: either with *Judaeorum* forming two spondees in the fifth and sixth feet, contrary to custom, or, with the syllables separated as we showed above, a dactyl and a spondee.

## 16. How the Ancient Poets Presented Certain Things Differently from Modern Poets

In the examples of the ancients one also finds, at times, two spondees at the end of a verse, just as occasionally two dactyls occur, as in these lines of Virgil:

> *At tuba terribilem sonitum procul excitat horrida.*

“But the dreadful trumpet raises its terrifying sound from afar.”

And:

> *Aut leves ocreas lento ducunt argento.*

“Or they draw the light greaves with pliant silver.”

Although this is found very rarely, it generally occurs only when the verse is arranged so that the final syllable of the dactyl at the end is joined by synaloepha to the following verse, and the spondee in the fifth foot contains the letter *r* either before or after another consonant. Its harshness is softened by the added vowel, so that it is perceived in pronunciation as a dactyl, although it appears in writing as a spondee. We showed above examples of both practices.

The ancient poets also used many other metrical rules with considerable freedom, whereas modern poets have preferred to observe them more distinctly according to a fixed standard. Thus they considered a short vowel followed by *q*, *u*, and any vowel to be common, as Lucretius writes:

> *Quae calidum faciunt aquae tactum atque vaporem.*

“Things which make the touch and vapor of hot water.”

They also counted as common syllables a short vowel at the end of a word when it was followed by a consonant and a liquid, as Virgil writes:

> *Aestusque pluviasque et agentes frigora ventos.*

“Both heat and rains and winds that drive the cold.”

And:

> *Si tibi lanitium cura est, primum aspera sylva*  
> *Lappaeque tribulique absint: fuge pabula laeta.*

“If wool is your concern, let the rough forest first, and burrs and thistles, be absent: avoid rich pastures.”

Modern poets now decide that this should occur more particularly within the same syntactic unit, as we explained above.

The same poet counted as common a shortened vowel at the end of a word when followed by the letter *z*, as in:

> *Eurique Zephyrique tonat domus.*

“The house of Eurus and Zephyrus thunders.”

He also employed synaloepha with the same freedom. At times he preserved a final *m* when he wished, despite the absorption of a following vowel:

> *Iterum iterumque movebo.*

“Again and again I shall move.”

He allowed a long vowel to remain long:

> *Sit pecori apibus quanta experientia parcis.*

“How great is your skill in sparing cattle and bees.”

When he wished, he shortened a long vowel:

> *Et multum formosa vale, vale, inquit, Iola.*

“And farewell, very beautiful Iola, farewell, he said.”

And:

> *Credimus an qui amant ipsi sibi somnia fingunt.*

“Do we believe it, or do lovers themselves fashion dreams for themselves?”

He preserved a diphthong:

> *Ulla moram fecere neque Aoniae Aganippae.*

“Nor did the Aonian Aganippe cause any delay.”

And he shortened the same diphthong:

> *Insulae Ionio in magno.*

“Islands in the great Ionian Sea.”

All these practices, as I have said, you will find observed more precisely by later poets.

## 17. On the Phalecian Metre

Since we have discussed what seemed relevant concerning heroic metre, it is also fitting to mention briefly the kinds of other metres, at least those which we have found more useful [Note: [Col. 0171] Paris.: “to be found.”].

The Phalecian is a five-foot dactylic metre consisting of a spondee, a dactyl, and three trochees. An example is:

> *Cantemus Domino Deoque nostro,*  
> *Cui [Note: [Col. 0171] “Should *cujus* be read?”] gloria cum honore pollens,*  
> *Sese magnificis decorat actis,*  
> *Dum currus celeres Aegyptiorum,*  
> *Junctis equitibus gravique turba,*  
> *Rubri marmoris enecat fluentis,*  
> *Adjutor [Note: [Col. 0171] Paris.: *validus*.] validae meae salutis,*  
> *Plebem de medio tulit profundo.*  
> *Custos et genitor salusque vera*  
> *Hic est, hic dominus meus et altor,*  
> *Ipsum conspicua sacrabo laude,*  
> *Est qui progenitor mei parentis.*  
> *Ipsum vocibus arduis fatebor,*  
> *Qui bellum tulit obruitque fortes,*  
> *Dignus nomine quo Deus vocatur.*

“Let us sing to the Lord and to our God,  
to whom glory, mighty with honor,  
adorns itself with magnificent deeds,  
while he destroys the swift chariots of the Egyptians,  
with their joined horsemen and heavy multitude,  
in the streams of red marble.  
The helper of my powerful salvation  
has lifted the people from the midst of the deep.  
He is guardian, begetter, and true salvation;  
he is here, here my lord and nourisher.  
Him I shall consecrate with conspicuous praise;  
he is the one who is the begetter of my parent.  
Him I shall confess with exalted voices,  
who waged war and overwhelmed the strong,  
worthy of the name by which God is called.”

## 18. On the Sapphic Metre

The five-foot dactylic Sapphic metre consists of a trochee, a spondee, a dactyl, and two trochees. After three verses in this metre, a heroic comma is added.

Saint Bishop Paulinus composed the sixth book of his work on blessed Felix in this metre. Its beginning is:

> *Jamne abis et nos properans relinquis,*  
> *Quos tamen sola regione linquis*  
> *Semper adnixa sine fine tecum*  
> *Mente futurus.*

“Are you already leaving and hastening to abandon us,  
whom nevertheless you leave behind in this single region,  
though you will always remain with us  
in mind, clinging to us without end?”

A little later he says:

> *Sicut Aegypto praeeunte quondam,*  
> *Noctis et densae tenebris operta,*  
> *Qua Dei [Note: [Col. 0171] Paris.: *vivi*.] jussu sacra gens agebat,*  
> *Lux erat orbi.*

“As once, when Egypt went before,  
covered by the darkness of dense night,  
where the holy people lived at God’s command,  
there was light for the world.”

> *Quae modo in toto species probatur,*  
> *Orbe, cum sanctae pia pars fidei*  
> *Fulgeat Christo, reliquos tenebris*  
> *Obruat error.*

“Such is now the appearance proved throughout  
the world, when the devout part of holy faith  
shines in Christ,  
while error overwhelms the rest in darkness.”

> *Sic [Note: [Col. 0171] Paris.: *meo . . . . Nicetae*.] mea qua se feret actus hora,*  
> *Cuncta Niceta Dominus secundet,*  
> *Donec optatam patriam vehatur*  
> *Laetus ad urbem.*

“Thus, at whatever hour my course shall carry me,  
may the Lord prosper all things for Nicetas,  
until he is borne joyfully  
to his desired fatherland and city.”

## 19. On Catalectic Tetrameter

Catalectic four-foot dactylic metre consists of a spondee, a dactyl, a catalectic foot, a dactyl, and a spondee. Saint Ambrose used it in his prayer for rain, whose beginning is:

> *Squalent arva soli pulvere multo;*  
> *Pallet siccus ager, terra faciscit;*  
> *Nullus ruris honos, nulla venustas,*  
> *Quando nulla viret gratia florum;*  
> *Tellus dura sitit nescia roris,*  
> *Fons jam nescit aquas, flumina cursus.*

“The fields lie barren beneath abundant dust;  
the dry land grows pale, the earth cracks;  
the countryside has no honor, no beauty,  
when no grace of flowers grows green;  
the hard earth thirsts, ignorant of dew;  
the spring now knows no waters, the rivers no course.”

Its conclusion is:

> *Jam coelos reseres arvaque laxes,*  
> *Fecundo, placidus, imbre rogamus;*  
> *Eliae meritis impia [Note: [Col. 0171] Paris.: *saecla . . . . pluvia*.] foeda*  
> *Donasti pluviam, nos quoque dones.*

“Now open the heavens and loosen the fields;  
we ask you, gentle one, with fruitful rain.  
Through Elijah’s merits you gave rain  
to impious and foul generations; may you give it also to us.”

He used the same metre in his prayer for fair weather, which begins:

> *Obduxere polum nubila coeli,*  
> *Absconduntque diem sole fugato,*  
> *Noctes continuas sidere nudas.*

“The clouds of heaven have covered the sky  
and conceal the day, driving away the sun;  
they make continuous nights bare of stars.”

Its conclusion is:

> *Jesu, parce tua morte redemptis:*  
> *Prior diluvium protulit aetas,*  
> *Ut mundaret aqua crimina terrae;*  
> *Sed mundata tuo sanguine terra est,*  
> *Jam nunc missa ferens ore columba,*  
> *Ramum pacificae munus olivae,*  
> *Exutas liquido flumine terras,*  
> *Laeto significet lapsa volatu.*

“Jesus, spare those redeemed by your death.  
The former age brought forth the flood  
to cleanse the crimes of the earth with water;  
but the earth has been cleansed by your blood.  
Now let the dove, sent forth and carrying in its mouth  
the branch, the gift of the peaceful olive,  
signify with joyful flight  
that the lands have been stripped of the flowing waters.”

## 20. On Iambic Hexameter

Iambic hexameter admits the iamb in every position; the tribrach in every position except the last; the spondee, dactyl, and anapest only in the odd-numbered positions; and the pyrrhic only in the final position.

The most distinguished Spanish scholar, Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, used this metre for the prologue to the *Psychomachia*, that is, the book composed in heroic verse concerning the struggle between virtues and vices. It begins:

> *Senex fidelis prima credendi via*  
> *Abram, beati seminis serus pater,*  
> *Adjecta cujus nomen auxit syllaba,*  
> *Abram parenti dictus, Abraham Deo.*

“Faithful old man, first path of belief,  
Abram, late father of blessed offspring,  
whose name an added syllable enlarged:  
called Abram by his parent, Abraham by God.”

## 21. On Iambic Tetrameter

Iambic tetrameter admits the iamb in every position and the spondee only in the odd-numbered positions.

Sedulius’ hymn was written in this metre:

> *A solis ortus cardine,*  
> *Ad usque terrae limitem,*  
> *Christum canamus principem.*

“From the rising of the sun  
to the farthest limit of the earth,  
let us sing of Christ the prince.”

The Ambrosian hymns also especially proceed in this metre:

> *Deus creator omnium*  
> *Jam surgit hora tertia,*  
> *Splendor paternae gloriae,*  
> *Aeterne rerum conditor.*

“God, creator of all things;  
now the third hour rises;  
splendor of the Father’s glory,  
eternal maker of things.”

There are many others. Among them the hymn of the blessed martyrs is composed with especially beautiful elegance. Its odd-numbered positions contain spondees, and its even-numbered positions iambs [Note: [Col. 0171] Paris.: “spondee, iamb.”]. Its beginning is:

> *Aeterna Christi munera,*  
> *Et martyrum victorias,*  
> *Laudes ferentes debitas*  
> *Laetis canamus mentibus.*

“Let us sing with joyful minds  
the eternal gifts of Christ  
and the victories of the martyrs,  
bringing forth their due praises.”

According to Mallius Theodorus, this metre sometimes also admits the tribrach in every position except the last, and the dactyl and anapest only in odd-numbered positions. Thus:

> *Geminae gigas substantiae*  
> *Alacris ut currat viam.*

“A giant of double substance,  
so that he may run the way with alacrity.”

We have few examples of the remaining forms.

## 22. On Anacreontic Metre

The iambic tetrameter *colophon*, which is called Anacreontic [Note: [Col. 0173] Paris.: *colophonium*], admits an anapest, two iambs, and a half-foot.

Prosper Tyro used it at the beginning of his exhortation to his wife, saying:

> *Age jam, precor, mearum*  
> *Comes irremota rerum*  
> *Trepidam brevemque vitam*  
> *Domino Deo dicamus.*

“Come now, I beg you, companion of my affairs,  
inseparable from me:  
let us dedicate our anxious and short life  
to the Lord God.”

> *Celeri vides rotatu*  
> *Rapidos dies meare,*  
> *Fragilisque membra mundi*  
> *Minui, perire, labi.*

“You see the swift days pass  
in rapid rotation,  
and the fragile members of the world  
diminish, perish, and slip away.”

> *Fugit omne quod tenemus,*  
> *Neque fluxa habent recursum,*  
> *[Note: [Col. 0173] *Cupidas vagasque*, in the edition of Cassander.] Cupidasque vana mentes*  
> *Specie trahunt inani.*

“Everything we possess flees,  
and fleeting things do not return;  
empty appearances draw  
our desirous and wandering minds.”

> *Ubi nunc imago rerum est,*  
> *Ubi sunt opes potentum,*  
> *Quibus occupare captas*  
> *Animas fuit voluptas?*

“Where now is the image of things?  
Where are the riches of the powerful,  
for whom it was a pleasure  
to seize captive souls?”

## 23. On Trochaic Metre

Trochaic tetrameter, which Greek and Latin poets use very frequently, admits a trochee in every position and a spondee in every position except the third.

It proceeds in alternating verses, so that the first has four feet and the second has three feet and a syllable. An example is the whole of that most beautiful hymn:

> *Hymnum dicat turba fratrum,*  
> *Hymnum cantus personet,*  
> *Christo regi concinentes,*  
> *Laudes demus debitas.*

“Let the congregation of brothers sing a hymn;  
let song resound as a hymn;  
singing together to Christ the king,  
let us offer due praises.”

In this metre you will sometimes also find a spondee in the third position of the first verse, as in:

> *Factor coeli, terrae factor,*  
> *Congregator tu maris.*

“Maker of heaven, maker of earth,  
gatherer of the sea.”

And:

> *Verbis purgas leprae morbos.*

“With words you cleanse the diseases of leprosy.”

## 24. On Rhythm

It is enough to have mentioned these more distinguished metres, whose fuller examples we find among writers. Besides these, there are very many other metres which anyone who wishes may find displayed through simple examples in the books of *Centimetra*.

Some are also found in that famous volume of the poet Porphyrius, by which he deserved to be freed from exile after it had been sent to the Emperor Constantine [Note: [Col. 0173] Paris.: “which . . . having been sent.”]. Since these poems were pagan, I did not wish to touch upon them.

Rhythm seems similar to metre. It is a measured composition of words examined by the judgment of the ears not according to metrical rules but by the number of syllables, as in the songs of popular poets.

Rhythm can exist without metre, but metre cannot exist without rhythm. This may be defined more clearly as follows: metre is measure with modulation; rhythm is modulation without measure. Nevertheless, by some accident you will often find even a measure preserved in rhythm—not through an artist’s regulation, but because sound and modulation themselves lead the way. Popular poets must do this rudely, while educated poets do it skillfully.

In this manner, very beautifully fashioned in the likeness of iambic metre, is that celebrated hymn:

> *Rex aeterne Domine,*  
> *Rerum creator omnium*  
> *Qui eras ante secula*  
> *Semper cum patre filius.*

“Eternal King, Lord,  
creator of all things,  
who existed before the ages,  
always the Son with the Father.”

There are also many other Ambrosian hymns of the same kind.

Likewise, they sing an alphabetic hymn about the day of judgment in the form of trochaic metre:

> *Apparebit repentina*  
> *Dies magna Domini,*  
> *Fur obscura velut nocte*  
> *Improvisos occupans.*

“The great day of the Lord  
will suddenly appear,  
like a thief in the darkness of night,  
overtaking those who are unprepared.”

## 25. That There Are Three Kinds of Poem

Since we have discussed many things concerning poems and metres, it should be mentioned at the end that there are three kinds of poem.

One is active or imitative, which the Greeks call *dramatikon* or *mimetikon* [Note: [Col. 0173] “*mimetikon* should be read, and below *exegetikon*.”]. Another is narrative, which the Greeks call *exegetikon* or *apangeltikon*. The third is common or mixed, which the Greeks call *koinon* or *miktón*.

The dramatic, or active, kind is that in which speaking characters are introduced without the poet’s intervention, as in tragedies and plays. For *drama* means “play” in Latin. The following eclogue was written in this kind:

> *Quo te, Moeri, pedes, an quo via ducit in urbem.*

“Where are your feet taking you, Moeris—or where does the road lead into the city?”

Among us, the *Song of Songs* was written in this kind, where the alternating voice of Christ and the Church is clearly found, although the writer does not intervene in the dialogue.

The *exegetikon*, or narrative kind, is that in which the poet himself speaks without the insertion of any character, as in the whole of the three books of the *Georgics* and the first part of the fourth, and in the poems of Lucretius and similar works.

Among us, the *Proverbs of Solomon* and *Ecclesiastes* were written in this kind. In their own language, like the Psalter, they are composed in metre.

The *koinon*, or *miktón*, is the mixed kind, in which the poet himself speaks and speaking characters are introduced, as in Homer’s *Iliad* and *Odyssey* and Virgil’s *Aeneid*. Among us, the history of blessed Job belongs to this kind, although in its own language it is not written entirely in poetic speech but partly in rhetorical, partly in metrical or rhythmic language.

These things, dearest son and fellow Levite Cuthbert, I have carefully endeavored to extract for you from the little works of ancient writers. What I had found scattered and gathered through prolonged labor, I have presented to you collected together, so that just as I have striven to instruct you in the divine Scriptures and ecclesiastical constitutions, I might also diligently train you in the art of metre, which is not unknown to the divine books [Note: [Col. 0173] Paris.: “and in . . .”].

I have also thought it appropriate to append a small book concerning the figures or modes of expression which the Greeks call *schemata* or *tropi*. I earnestly ask your affection to devote yourself to reading, especially of those writings in which we believe that we have eternal life.

[Col. 0175]

# BOOK ON THE FIGURES AND TROPES OF SACRED SCRIPTURE (C)

## PART ONE: ON FIGURES

[Col. 0175A]

Sometimes in Scripture the order of words is found arranged figuratively, for the sake of elegance, in a manner different from the ordinary course of speech. Grammarians call this in Greek *schema* [Note: [Col. 0175] Paris.: “Greek”]; we rightly call it habit, form, or figure, because through it speech is, so to speak, clothed and adorned.

Again, figurative speech is sometimes found, produced by transferring a word from its proper meaning to an improper likeness, for the sake either of necessity or of ornament. The Greeks indeed boast that they were the discoverers of such figures and tropes.

But so that you may understand, dearest son—and so that all who wish to read these things may understand—that holy Scripture surpasses all other writings not only in authority, because it is divine, and in usefulness, because it leads to eternal life, but also in antiquity and in the very arrangement of its speech, I have decided, after collecting examples from Scripture itself, to show that the teachers of eloquence in no age can claim any such figures or tropes which it did not anticipate [Note: [Col. 0175] Paris has *saecularis* in place of *ullis saeculis*.] [Note: [Col. 0175] The Paris manuscript ends abruptly here, and I have been unable to find elsewhere any manuscript of the *Figures*. GILES.].

[Col. 0175C]

There are many species of figures and tropes. Nevertheless, Scripture possesses several principal figures and more select tropes, as though excerpted from those familiar to grammarians. The first and most general trope is metaphor, for all the others seem to belong to this class:

*Metaphora*, metaphor; *catachresis*, catachresis; *metalepsis*, metalepsis; *metonymia*, metonymy; *antonomasia*, antonomasia; *characterismos*, characterization; *exoche*, distinction; *epitheton*, epithet; *synecdoche*, synecdoche; *onomatopoeia*, onomatopoeia; *periphrasis*, circumlocution; *hyperbaton*, transposition; *hysterologia*, after-ordering; *hysteron-proteron*, “the later before the earlier”; *anastrophe*, inversion; *parenthesis*, parenthesis; *synchesis*, confusion; *tmesis*, division; *diacope*, separation; *hyperbole*, hyperbole; *allegoria*, allegory; *ironia*, irony; *antiphrasis*, antiphrasis; *aenigma*, riddle; *charientismos*, graceful expression; *paroemia*, proverb; *sarcasmos*, sarcasm; *asteismos*, witty expression; *mycterismos*, mockery; *homoeosis*, comparison; *homoeologia*, similar speech; *soresmos*, accumulation; *icon*, image; *icasmos*, likeness; *catatyposis*, vivid representation; *hypotyposis*, vivid description; *metastasis*, transference; *enargia*, vividness—not *energia*; *parabola*, parable; *antapodosis*, corresponding return; *paradigma*, example.

Thus far you have the nomenclature of the grammatical tropes. Now follow the figures:

*Prolepsis*, anticipation; *zeugma*, conjunction; *protozeugma*, initial conjunction; *mesozeugma*, medial conjunction; *hypozeugma*, final conjunction; *hysterozeugma*, concluding conjunction; *synezeugmenon*, joined construction; *enexaerumenon*, separated construction; *hypozeuxis*, subjunction; *syllepsis*, conception; *asyntheton* or *asyndeton*, lack of conjunction; *dialyton*, dissolution; *polysyntheton*, abundant conjunction; *anadiplosis*, reduplication; *anaphora*, repetition at the beginning; *epanalepsis*, repetition; *epizeuxis*, immediate reduplication; *epimone*, insistence; *paronomasia*, word-play; *prosonomasia*, near-naming; *schesis onomatôn*, relation of names; *paromoeon*, similarity; *homoeoteleuton*, similar ending; *homoeoptoton*, similar case-ending; *polyptoton*, multiple case-forms; *metabole*, change; *hyrmos*, connection; *diasyrmos*, ridicule; *climax*, gradation.

Grammarians, however, arrange other kinds of figures in the following order. First come faults of speech, namely barbarism and solecism. Second come obscurity and disorder. Then comes metaplasm. Finally come figures and tropes.

The species of obscure speech are: *acyrologia*, improper diction; *pleonasmos*, pleonasm; *perissologia*, redundancy; *amphibologia*, ambiguity; *tautologia*, tautology; *battologia*, idle repetition; *macrologia*, prolixity; *eclipsis*, omission; *aposiopesis*, abrupt silence; *aenigma*, riddle.

The species of disordered speech are: *tapinosis*, abasement; *aeschrologia*, foul speech; *cacozelia*, bad imitation; *cacosyntheton*, bad arrangement; *cacophaton*, harsh sound.

The species of metaplasm are: *metaplasmus*, alteration of form; *prosthesis*, addition at the beginning; *epenthesis*, insertion; *anadiplosis*, reduplication; *epectasis*, extension; *paragoge*, addition at the end; *aphaeresis*, removal at the beginning; *syncope*, omission in the middle; *apocope*, removal at the end; *ectasis*, lengthening; *systole*, shortening; *diaeresis*, separation; *synaeresis*, contraction; *eclipsis*, omission; *synaloepha*, absorption; *antithesis*, opposition; *metathesis*, transposition; *parallage*, alteration.

Having enumerated these, receive the seventeen more distinguished figures of divine Scripture:

*Prolepsis*, anticipation; *zeugma*, conjunction; *hypozeuxis*, subjunction; *syllepsis*, conception; *anadiplosis*, reduplication; *anaphora*, repetition or reference; *epanaphora*, subordinate repetition; *epanalepsis*, repetition; *epizeuxis*, doubling; *paronomasia*, denomination; *schesis onomaton*, relation of names; *paromoeon*, similarity; *homoeoteleuton*, similar ending; *homoeoptoton*, from similar cases; *polyptoton*, from several cases; *hyrmos*, connection; *polysyndeton*, rich in conjunctions; *dialyton*, or *asyntheton* or *asyndeton*, dissolution.

*Prolepsis*, anticipation or presumption, is so called when things that ought to follow are placed first. Thus in Psalm 86:

> *Fundamenta ejus in montibus sanctis, diligit Dominus portas Sion.*

“Its foundations are on the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion.”

He placed *ejus* first and afterward *cujus*, that is, “of the Lord.”

Likewise in Psalm 21:

> *Diviserunt sibi vestimenta mea, et super vestem meam miserunt sortem.*

“They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast a lot.”

Here *diviserunt* and *miserunt* stand for “they will divide” and “they will cast.”

Likewise Ezekiel begins in chapter 1 without placing anything before the expression:

> *Factum est in tricesimo anno, etc.*

“It came to pass in the thirtieth year, etc.”

He placed the connective expression without first supplying anything to which it could be attached.

*Zeugma*, conjunction, is the figure in which many dependent expressions are concluded by one verb or one sentence. By one verb, as the Apostle says in Ephesians 4:

> *Omnis amaritudo et ira et indignatio et clamor et blasphemia tollatur a vobis.*

“Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be taken away from you.”

By one sentence, as the Psalmist does in Psalm 14, setting out:

> *Qui ingreditur sine macula, et operatur justitiam; qui loquitur veritatem in corde suo; qui non egit dolum in lingua sua, nec fecit, etc.*

“He who walks without blemish and practices righteousness; he who speaks truth in his heart; he who has not acted deceitfully with his tongue, nor done [anything else], etc.”

At the end he concludes:

> *Qui facit haec, non commovebitur in aeternum.*

“He who does these things will never be shaken.”

*Hypozeuxis* is the opposite of the preceding figure. Here individual words or sentences are attached to their own individual clauses.

Such is the passage in Psalm 144, in individual verbs:

> *Virtutem terribilium tuorum dicent, et magnitudinem tuam narrabunt; memoriam abundantiae suavitatis tuae eructabunt, et in justitia tua exsultabunt.*

“They will speak of the power of your terrible deeds, and proclaim your greatness; they will pour forth the memory of the abundance of your goodness, and rejoice in your righteousness.”

Likewise in 1 Corinthians 13:

> *Sive prophetiae evacuabuntur, sive linguae cessabunt, sive scientia destruetur.*

“Whether prophecies will be abolished, tongues will cease, or knowledge will be destroyed.”

In separate sentences, as in Psalm 26:

> *Si consistant adversum me castra, non timebit cor meum; si exsurgat adversum me praelium, in hoc ego sperabo.*

“Though armies encamp against me, my heart will not fear; though battle rise against me, in this I shall hope.”

*Syllepsis* occurs when differing cases are gathered into a single meaning, as in Psalm 77:

> *Attendite, populus meus, legem meam.*

“Attend, my people, to my law.”

Likewise in Psalm 149:

> *Ad faciendam vindictam in nationibus, increpationes in populis.*

“To execute vengeance among the nations, rebukes among the peoples.”

For *ad faciendam* is singular in number, while *increpationes* is plural.

Syllepsis also occurs in meaning, that is, when one is used for many or many for one.

One for many occurs in Psalm 77:

> *Immisit in eis muscam caninam, et comedit eos rana, et exterminavit eos.*

“He sent among them the dog-fly, and the frog devoured them, and destroyed them.”

This is so although he sent not merely one fly or one frog to destroy the Egyptians, but countless ones.

Many for one occurs in Psalm 2:

> *Astiterunt reges terrae, et principes convenerunt in unum.*

“The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together as one.”

The apostles understood “kings” to mean Herod and “rulers” to mean Pilate, as is contained in the fourth chapter of the Acts of the Apostles.

*Anadiplosis* is the reduplication of a word which is repeated at the end of the preceding verse and at the beginning of the following one, as in Psalm 121:

> *Stantes erant pedes nostri in atriis tuis, Jerusalem, Jerusalem quae aedificatur ut civitas.*

“Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem—Jerusalem, which is built as a city.”

Likewise in Jeremiah, chapter 2:

> *Me dereliquerunt fontem aquae vivae, et foderunt sibi cisternas, cisternas dissipatas, quae continere non valent aquas.*
