“They have abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and dug cisterns for themselves—cisterns, broken cisterns, which cannot hold water.”

*Anaphora* is repetition, when the same word is repeated twice or more at the beginnings of verses, as in Psalm 26:

> *Dominus illuminatio mea, et salus mea, quem timebo? Dominus defensor vitae meae, a quo trepidabo?*

“The Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life; from whom shall I tremble?”

And below:

> *Si consistant adversum me castra, non timebit cor meum. Si exsurgat adversum me praelium, in hoc ego sperabo.*

“Though armies encamp against me, my heart will not fear. Though battle rise against me, in this I shall hope.”

Anaphora also occurs within the same verse, at the beginnings of clauses, as in Psalm 18:

> *Vox Domini in virtute, vox Domini in magnificentia, vox Domini confringentis cedros.*

“The voice of the Lord is in power, the voice of the Lord is in majesty, the voice of the Lord breaks the cedars.”

This figure is extremely common in the Psalms.

Some call this *epanaphora*.

*Epanalepsis* is the repetition at the end of a verse of an expression placed at its beginning, as the Apostle says in Philippians, chapter 4:

> *Gaudete in Domino semper, iterum dico, gaudete.*

“Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice.”

Likewise in Psalm 82:

> *Deus, quis similis erit tibi? ne taceas, neque compescaris, Deus.*

“God, who will be like you? Do not be silent, and do not be still, O God.”

*Epizeuxis* is the doubling of the same word in the same verse without any intervening delay, as in Isaiah, chapter 40:

> *Consolamini, consolamini, populus meus, dicit Dominus vester.*

“Comfort, comfort my people, says your God.”

And again in the same prophet, chapter 51:

> *Elevare, elevare, consurge, Jerusalem.*

“Rise up, rise up, stand, Jerusalem.”

And again in the same prophet, chapter 38:

> *Vivens, vivens, ipse confitebitur tibi.*

“The living, the living—he himself will confess you.”

The Psalmist likewise has something similar in Psalm 18:

> *Dies diei eructat verbum, et nox nocti indicat scientiam.*

“Day pours forth the word to day, and night declares knowledge to night.”

Elsewhere, repetition of the same expression bears the name *pallilogia*.

[Col. 0178B] Paronomasia is called “word-play by derivation” whenever an almost similar expression is used with a different meaning, namely, with a letter or syllable changed, as in Psalm 21, according to the Hebrew truth: “In you they trusted, and they were not confounded.” And in Philippians 3: “Observe the evil workers; observe the mutilation; but we are the circumcision, who serve God in spirit.” The prophet Isaiah most elegantly fashioned this figure in his own language, where he says: “I expected him to execute judgment, and behold, iniquity; and righteousness, and behold, a cry.” For in Hebrew, “judgment” is called [word absent], “iniquity” [word absent], “righteousness” [word absent], and “a cry” [word absent]. Thus, by adding or changing a single letter, he beautifully modulated the similarity of the words, so that instead of [the word for] “judgment” he used [the word for] “iniquity,” and instead of [the word for] “righteousness” he put [the word for] “a cry” [the relevant source words are absent or corrupt in the supplied text].

[Col. 0178C] *Schêsis onomatōn*, that is, “a multitude of joined names,” signifying one thing with different sounds, as in Isaiah 1: “Woe to the sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, an evil seed, wicked children!” Likewise in Psalm 105: “We have sinned with our fathers, we have acted unjustly, we have committed iniquity.”

*Paromoion* occurs when different words are taken from the same letters. This figure, insofar as it concerns the arrangement of letters, is better sought in the language in which it was written and published. Nevertheless, we have examples in our own translation from which to draw an illustration. It is said in Psalm 117: “We have blessed you from the house of the Lord; God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us.” And in Psalm 17: “His wrath is according to the likeness of a serpent, like a deaf asp, which stops its ears.”

[Col. 0178D] *Homoeoteleuton* means “similar termination.” It is a figure in which the middle and final parts of a verse or sentence end in a similar syllable, as in Ecclesiasticus 6: “It is better to see what you desire than to desire what you do not know.” And again, chapter 7: “It is better to be reproved by a wise man than to be deceived by the flattery of fools.” Poets and orators often use this figure. Poets do so in this manner:

> The divided waters of the sea could be crossed.

Orators, however, use it thus: Blessed Job, known to God alone and to himself in his tranquillity, was to be brought to wider renown; he was therefore struck with a blow, so that he might spread the fragrance of his powers farther and wider, just as perfumes give off a stronger scent when they are burned. The blessed Pope Gregory, who said this, is frequently found to have used this kind of figure. I think that these are the sorts of compositions which Jerome calls polished rhetorical declamations.

[Col. 0179A] *Homoeoptoton* occurs when many expressions end in similar sounds, as in Psalm 97: “Sing, rejoice, and make music.” And in Ezekiel 18: “If he begets a son who is a robber, shedding blood,” and shortly afterward: “eating upon the mountains, defiling his neighbour’s wife, grieving the needy and the poor, committing robbery, not returning a pledge, lifting his eyes to idols, committing abomination, lending at interest, and taking more besides—shall he live?”

*Polyptoton* occurs when an expression is varied through different cases, as in Romans 11: “For from him, and through him, and [Col. 0179B] in him are all things; to him be honour and glory for ever and ever.” Likewise in Psalm 67: “They shall be whitened with snow in Selmon, the mountain of God. A mountain of curds, a rich mountain; why do you suspect mountains of curds? The mountain in which it pleased God to dwell.”

[Col. 0180A] *Hirmos* means “coherence,” when the sequence of speech preserves its course right to the end, with no other cause or person being changed, as in Psalm 53: “Save me, O God, by your name,” and so forth, until he says: “They have not set God before their eyes.” For the prophet is praying to be delivered from the pursuit of his enemies by the help of the Lord his Saviour.

*Polysyndeton* is a sentence bound together by many conjunctions, as in Psalm 40: “May the Lord preserve him, and give him life, and make him blessed, and cleanse his soul on earth, and not deliver him into the hands of his enemies.”

*Dialyton*, or *asyndeton*, is the opposite of the preceding figure, lacking conjunctions, as in Psalm 65: “Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; sing a psalm to his name. Give glory to his praise. Say to God: How terrible are your works, O Lord.”

Thus there are seventeen figures of divine Scripture.

## PART TWO—ON TROPES

[Col. 0179]

[Col. 0179B] A trope is an expression transferred from its proper meaning to an improper one, for the sake of ornament or necessity. There are thirteen *tropoi*, which may be rendered in Latin as “modes” or “manners,” namely:

1. metaphor;
2. catachresis;
3. metalepsis;
4. metonymy;
5. antonomasia;
6. epithet;
7. synecdoche;
8. onomatopoeia;
9. periphrasis;
10. hyperbaton, with five species: hysterology, anastrophe, parenthesis, tmesis, and synchysis;
11. hyperbole;
12. allegory, with seven species: irony, antiphrasis, enigma, *charientismos*, proverb, sarcasm, and *asteismos*;
13. homoeosis, with three species: eicon, parable, and paradigm.

### 1. On Metaphor

Metaphor is the transference of things and words. It occurs in four ways:

1. from an animate being to an animate being;
2. from an inanimate thing to an inanimate thing;
3. from an animate being to an inanimate thing;
4. from an inanimate thing to an animate being.

Accordingly:

[Col. 0179D] 1. From an animate being to an animate being: as in Psalm 2, “Why did the nations rage?” And: “The Lord who delivered me from the mouth of the lion and from the hand of the bear.” Likewise in Psalm 138: “If I take my wings before the light.” For human beings, beasts, and birds all possess a soul.

2. From an inanimate thing to an inanimate thing: as in Zechariah 11: “Open your doors, Lebanon.” Likewise in Psalm 8: “He who walks through the paths of the sea.” This is a transference from a city to a mountain and from land to sea, none of which possesses a soul.

3. From an animate being to an inanimate thing: as in Amos 1: “The summit of Carmel has been dried up.” Human beings, not mountains, have a crown or summit.

4. From an inanimate thing to an animate being: as in Ezekiel 11: “I will take away from you your heart of stone.” For it is not a stone but a people that possesses a soul.

This trope is also applied to God in many ways: from birds, as in “Protect me beneath the shadow of your wings”; from wild beasts, as in “The Lord will roar from Zion”; from human limbs, as in Psalm 16 [Note: [Col. 0179] Here and below Bede or the scribes have made an error: the words “Who has measured the waters in his fist,” and so forth, are from Isaiah 40; the following words, “I have found David,” and so forth, are found in Acts 13]: “Who has measured the waters in his fist, and weighed the heavens with his span?” From the inner person, as in Isaiah 40: “I have found David, son of Jesse, a man after my own heart.” From movements of the human mind, as in Psalm 2: “Then he will speak to them in his anger”; Genesis 6: “It repents me that I made man”; and Zechariah 8: “I have been jealous for Zion with great jealousy.” There are countless examples of this kind.

It also comes from insensible things, as in Amos 2: “Behold, I will creak over you as a cart creaks when loaded with hay.” This trope is exceedingly common in ordinary speech as well, when we say that crops “wave,” vines “put forth gems,” youth is “flowering,” and grey hair is “milky.”

### 2. On Catachresis

[Col. 0180D] Catachresis is the misuse of a noun or verb to signify a thing that lacks its proper designation. It differs from metaphor in this respect: metaphor bestows a word upon something that has a proper word of its own, whereas catachresis, because the thing has no proper term, uses a borrowed one. Thus we call someone who has killed his brother a *parricide*, and a body of water that contains no fish a *fish-pond*. Unless these things borrowed their names from elsewhere, they would have no names of their own.

A similar example is: “Place bars in the four corners of the table, one at each foot, and the sixth covering the front of the double roof, and there he breaks the horns of the bows.” And in 2 Chronicles 4: “Its rim was like the rim of a cup, and like a lily turned outward.” Feet, front, horns, and rim belong properly to human beings and animals, not to inanimate things. If Scripture had not imposed these names upon the things mentioned, it would have no proper terms by which to designate them.

This trope also includes what is written in John 5: “Now there is at Jerusalem a sheep-pool.” The water received its name from fish, although it was not collected for fish but, as they report, for washing victims; hence it acquired the name “Sheep-pool.”

### 3. On Metalepsis

[Col. 0181A] Metalepsis is an expression proceeding step by step toward what it indicates and suggesting, from what precedes, what follows, as in the Psalmist: “You shall eat the labours of your fruits.” For he put “labours” in place of the goods acquired through labour.

Likewise in Psalm 103: “This dragon whom you formed to mock him.” By “dragon” the devil is meant; through the devil, the good angel is to be understood, such as he was formed by God.

### 4. On Metonymy

[Col. 0181B] *Metonymia* is a kind of “renaming,” transferred from one meaning to a neighbouring one. It has many species. It indicates what is contained by means of what contains it; what contains by means of what is contained; the thing invented by means of the inventor; the inventor by means of the thing invented; the effect by means of the cause; and the cause by means of the effect.

It indicates what is contained by means of what contains it, as in Genesis 24: “Pouring the jar into the channels”; or conversely, “Receive your letters.” For it was not the jar that was poured out, but what it contained; nor were letters taken into the hands, but the paper containing the letters.

Again: “Release her, and let her go, and you shall see.” For it was not the ark but the cart in which the water was contained, or the oxen that drew the cart, that could go. This also designates the effect by means of the cause and, conversely, the cause by means of the effect.

### 5. On Antonomasia

[Col. 0181C] *Antonomasia* is a designation placed in the position of a name. Through accidental characteristics it signifies a particular person, and this occurs in three ways: from the mind, from the body, or from external circumstances.

From the mind, as in Isaiah 11: “Was it not you who struck the proud?” From the body, as in 1 Samuel 17: “A bastard of a man, six cubits and a span in height.” Here the devil is understood from the pride of his mind; Goliath the giant is signified by the size of his body.

External characteristics are divided into several species. They are taken from a class, as in: “Will the son of Jesse give all of you fields?” From a place, as in: “The author of the sedition of the sect of the Nazarenes.” From an action, as in Matthew 26: “But he who betrayed him gave them a sign, saying.” From an event, as in John 19: “That disciple whom Jesus loved.”

By this trope the Lord himself is sometimes indicated: from a class, as in Matthew 21: “Hosanna to the Son of David”; from a place, as in “He who sits above the cherubim appears”; from an action, as in Job 7: “I have sinned; what shall I do for you, O guardian of mankind?”

### 6. On the Epithet

[Col. 0181D] An epithet is an expression placed before a pronoun. Antonomasia takes the place of a name, whereas an epithet never exists without a name, as in Ecclesiasticus 45: “Moses, beloved of God and of men.” And: “The merciful and compassionate Lord.” [Col. 0182A] And: “Righteous Lot, oppressed.”

An epithet also occurs in three ways: from the mind, from the body, and from external circumstances. By these two tropes—antonomasia and epithet—we either blame someone, identify someone, or adorn someone.

### 7. On Synecdoche

*Synecdoche* is a signification capable of a complete understanding, when one says either more or less than is meant. It indicates the whole from a part, as in John 1: “The Word became flesh.” And in Acts 27: “We were in the ship, two hundred and seventy-six souls in all.”

Or conversely, it indicates the part from the whole, as in John 19: “Therefore, because it was the Preparation of the Jews, since the tomb was nearby, where they placed Jesus.”

### 8. On Onomatopoeia

[Col. 0182A] *Onomatopoeia* is a name formed from a sound, as in 1 Corinthians 13: “A clanging cymbal.” And in Isaiah 58: “Raise your voice like a trumpet.” And in Jeremiah 4: “Blow the trumpet.” And: “Will you surround the horse with a neighing?” And in Isaiah 56: “The roaring of a lion.” And in Job 4: “The voice of the lioness.” And in Isaiah 56: “Dumb dogs, unable to bark.”

Some consider the hissing of serpents, the squealing of pigs, and the confused cries of other animals to belong to this trope; these too are frequently represented in the sacred Scriptures.

### 9. On Periphrasis

[Col. 0182B] *Periphrasis* is circumlocution. It is used either to describe and expand brevity splendidly, or to avoid coarseness by means of a circuitous expression.

Truth extended splendidly appears in 2 Corinthians 5: “We know that if our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, we have an edifice from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.”

Circumlocution avoiding coarseness appears in Romans 1: “For their women exchanged the natural use for that which is against nature; likewise the men, abandoning the natural use,” and so forth.

### 10. On Hyperbaton

[Col. 0182C] *Hyperbaton* is a kind of transposition that disrupts the order of words. It has five species: hysterology, anastrophe, parenthesis, tmesis, and synchysis.

#### On Hysterology

Hysterology, *hysterologia* or *hysteron proteron*, is a sentence in which the order of the words is changed, as in Psalm 23: “He shall receive a blessing from the Lord and mercy from God his Saviour.” For the Lord first customarily justifies the impious by showing mercy, and afterward crowns the righteous by blessing him.

#### On Anastrophe

Anastrophe is merely an inverted order of words, as in Job 5: “For which reason I will entreat the Lord,” instead of “on account of which reason.”

#### On Parenthesis

Parenthesis is an inserted line of reasoning within a divided sentence. Such is the Apostle’s statement in Galatians 2: “For he who worked through Peter (in the apostleship of the circumcision) worked also through me among the Gentiles.” And: “When James, Cephas, and John had recognized the grace (which was given to me), they gave the right hand of fellowship to me and Barnabas.”

#### On Tmesis

Tmesis is the division of a simple verb or of a single compound verb by one or more inserted expressions. Although this species is not easily found in sacred Scripture [the supplied text reads *facile*, with the variant *non facile*], it occurs in a Christian poet, as follows:

> Hiero whom David’s offspring begot at Jerusalem.

That is, “Jerusalem.”

#### On Synchysis

Synchysis is hyperbaton confused in every respect. In Psalm 67: “If you sleep among the middle allotments, the wings of a silvered dove, and the hinder parts of its back in the appearance of gold.”

First, as Augustine says, the order of the words must be sought: how the sentence is to be completed, since it certainly hangs unfinished at the words “If you sleep.” Then it is uncertain whether the words mean “these wings,” or “O you wings,” as though he were addressing the wings themselves.

Thus it is uncertain whether the sentence is completed by the preceding words, giving this order: “The Lord will give the word to those who evangelize with great power, if you sleep among the middle allotments, O you silvered wings of a dove”; or by the words that follow, giving this order: “If you sleep among the middle allotments, the wings of the dove, silvered with snow, shall be whitened in Selmon.”

That is, the wings themselves shall be whitened if you sleep among the middle allotments. This may be understood as addressed to those who are divided like spoils for the adornment of the house, that is: “If you sleep among the middle allotments, O you who are divided for the adornment of the house through the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good”—for “to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith, to another kinds of tongues, in the same Spirit,” and so forth. If, therefore, you sleep among the middle allotments, then “the wings of the dove, silvered with snow, shall be whitened in Selmon.”

It may also be understood in this way: “If you, silvered wings of the dove, sleep among the middle allotments, they shall be whitened with snow in Selmon.” Human beings are to be understood here, those who receive remission of sins through grace. Hence the Church herself is also described in the Song of Songs 8: “Who is this that comes up whitened?”

For God’s promise is held out through the prophet Isaiah, chapter 1, who says: “If your sins are like scarlet, I will make them white as snow.”

It may also be understood in this way: in the words “the silvered wings of the dove,” the verb “you shall be” is understood, so that the meaning is: “You who are divided like spoils for the adornment of the house, if you sleep among the middle allotments, you shall be silvered wings of a dove”; that is, you shall be raised to higher things while nevertheless remaining joined to the structure of the Church.

For I think that no other dove can better be understood here as the silvered dove than the one of whom it is said in the Song of Songs 6: “My dove is one.” It is silvered because it has been instructed in the divine utterances. For the utterances of the Lord are called pure utterances elsewhere: “Silver tested by fire, purified in the earth sevenfold,” in Psalm 11.

It is therefore a great good to sleep among the middle allotments. Some have wished these to be understood as the two Testaments: to sleep among the two middle allotments means to rest in the authority of those Testaments, that is, to assent to the testimonies of both Testaments, so that whenever something is brought forth and proved from them, every dispute may be ended in peaceful repose.

### 11. On Hyperbole

[Col. 0183D] Hyperbole is an expression exceeding belief, for the purpose of magnifying or diminishing.

For magnifying, as in 2 Samuel 1: “Faster than the eagles of heaven, stronger than lions.”

For diminishing, as in: “The sound of the flying throne will terrify you.” And in Lamentations 4: “Their faces have become blacker than charcoal.”

### 12. On Allegory

[Col. 0184A] Allegory is a trope in which something other than what is said is signified, as in John 4: “Lift up your eyes and see the regions, for they are already white for the harvest.” That is: understand that the peoples are already prepared to believe.

It has many species, of which seven are especially prominent: irony, antiphrasis, enigma, *charientismos*, proverb, sarcasm, and *asteismos*.

#### On Irony

Irony is a trope that attempts to show something by means of its opposite, as in: “Cry out with a louder voice, for he is a god; perhaps he is speaking, or is staying in an inn, or is on a journey, or is asleep, so that he may be awakened.”

Unless the gravity of the delivery supports it, this would seem to confess what it is striving to deny.

#### On Antiphrasis

Antiphrasis is the irony of a single word, as in Matthew 26: “Friend, why have you come?” The difference between irony and antiphrasis is that irony indicates what it wishes to be understood by delivery alone, whereas antiphrasis signifies the opposite not through the speaker’s tone of voice but through its words alone, whose origin is contrary.

#### On Enigma

An enigma is an obscure statement expressed through a hidden comparison of things, as in Psalm 67: “The wings of a silvered dove, and the hinder parts of its back in the appearance of gold.”

This signifies the utterances of spiritual Scripture, full of divine light, while their inner meaning shines with the greater grace of heavenly wisdom; or certainly it signifies the present life of the holy Church, rejoicing in the wings of virtues, and its future life in heaven, destined to enjoy eternal glory with the Lord.

#### On *Charientismos*

*Charientismos* is a trope by which harsh things are expressed more pleasantly, as in Genesis 29: “Did I not serve you for Rachel? Why then have you imposed upon me?” By the very mild word “imposed upon,” he expressed more temperately the very grave injury that he had suffered.

#### On the Proverb

A proverb is a saying suited to circumstances and times, as in 2 Peter 2: “The dog has returned to his vomit,” and in 1 Samuel 10: “Is Saul also among the prophets?”

We use the first when we say that someone has returned to vices after having performed penance; we use the second when we see an unlearned person undertake the office of teaching, or arrogate to himself some other art that he has not learned.

This trope extends so widely that the book of Solomon which, following the Hebrews, we call “Proverbs,” received from it among the Greeks the name *Paroimiai*, that is, “Proverbs.”

#### On Sarcasm

Sarcasm is a hostile mockery filled with hatred, as in Matthew 27: “He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is the king of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him.”

#### On *Asteismos*

*Asteismos* is a varied trope of considerable and manifold force. For *asteismos* is thought to be anything expressed without rustic simplicity and polished with sufficiently witty urbanity, as in: “Would that those who disturb you would cut themselves off.”

It should certainly be noted that allegory is sometimes made through deeds and sometimes through words alone.

[Col. 0185A] Through deeds, as it is written: “Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman,” which, as the Apostle explains, are the two Testaments.

Through words alone, as in Isaiah 11: “A shoot shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root.” This signifies that the Lord and Saviour was to be born from David’s stock through the Virgin Mary.

Sometimes one and the same thing is signified allegorically through deeds and words together. Through deeds, for example, in Genesis 37: “They sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites for thirty pieces of silver”; through words, in Zechariah 11: “They weighed out my wages—thirty pieces of silver.”

Likewise through deeds, as in 1 Samuel 16: “David was ruddy and handsome in appearance, and Samuel anointed him in the midst of his brothers”; through words, in the Song of Songs 4: “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen among thousands.”

Both passages mystically signify the mediator between God and human beings: beautiful in wisdom and virtue, yet rose-red through the shedding of his own blood, and anointed by God the Father with the oil of gladness above his companions.

Again, allegory through word or deed sometimes announces figuratively a historical matter, sometimes a typological matter, sometimes a tropological—that is, moral—meaning, and sometimes an anagogical meaning, that is, a sense leading upward to higher things.

Through history, history is figured when the work of the first six or seven days is compared with the same number of ages of this world.

Through the word of history, when what the patriarch Jacob says in Genesis 49—“Judah is a lion’s cub; you have gone up to the prey, my son,” and so forth—is understood of the kingdom and victories of David.

[Col. 0185C] Through the word, a spiritual meaning concerning Christ or the Church, when the patriarch’s same speech is faithfully understood of the Lord’s Passion and resurrection.

Likewise, allegorical deeds designate tropological, that is, moral, perfection. Thus the long, many-coloured tunic which the patriarch Jacob made for his son Joseph in Genesis 37 signifies the grace of various virtues with which God the Father has commanded and granted that we should always be clothed until the end of our life.

Allegory through words signifies the same perfection of conduct, as in: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning,” and so forth.

Allegory through deeds expresses an anagogical, that is, upward-leading, meaning, as in: “Enoch, seventh from Adam, was translated from the world.” This figuratively foreshadows the Sabbath of future blessedness, which is reserved at the end for the elect after the good works of this world, carried out through its six ages.

Allegory through words likewise reveals the joys of heavenly life, as in Matthew 24: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered,” because where the mediator between God and human beings is in the body, there also souls now lifted up to heaven will be gathered, and, when the glory of the resurrection has been celebrated, the bodies of the righteous will likewise be assembled.

Sometimes, in one and the same thing or word, history together with the mystical meaning concerning Christ or the Church, tropology, and anagogy are all intimated figuratively. Thus the temple of the Lord is, according to history, the house built by Solomon; according to allegory, the Lord’s body, of which he says in John 2: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up,” or his Church, to which it is said: “The temple of God is holy, which you are.”

According to tropology, it is each of the faithful, to whom it is said in 1 Corinthians 3: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you?”

According to anagogy, it is the dwelling places of heavenly joy, toward which he aspired who said: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you.”

In the same way, what is said in Psalm 147—“Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion, for he has strengthened the bars of your gates; he has blessed your children within you”—can rightly be understood according to history, allegory, tropology, and anagogy: of the citizens of the earthly Jerusalem, of the Church of Christ, of the elect soul, and of the heavenly homeland, respectively.

We have spoken of the Church according to allegory, following the example of the most learned interpreter Gregory, who in his *Moral Works* habitually called “allegory” in the strict sense those things said or done figuratively concerning Christ or the Church.

### 13. On Homoeosis

[Col. 0186B] Homoeosis is the demonstration of a less familiar thing through a comparison with one that is more familiar. It has three species: eicon, parable, and paradigm.

#### On Eicon

An eicon is a comparison between persons, or between things that happen to persons, as in John 1: “We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father”; and in Luke 20: “They neither marry nor are given in marriage, for they can no longer die, because they are equal to the angels.”

#### On Parable

A parable is a comparison of things dissimilar in kind, as in Matthew 13: “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed”; and in John 3: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.”

#### On Paradigm

A paradigm is the presentation or narration of an example for exhortation or warning.

For exhortation, as in James 5: “Elijah was a man like us, subject to suffering, and he prayed that it might not rain upon the earth; and it did not rain for three years and six months.” And in Matthew 6: “Consider the birds of the air, for they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them.”

For warning, as in Matthew 24: “At that hour, whoever is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, let him not come down to take them; and whoever is in the field, likewise let him not return. Remember Lot’s wife.”

Thus there are thirteen general tropes of sacred Scripture.

[Col. 0187]

# THE BOOK ON THE NATURE OF THINGS

[Note: [Col. 0187] A, B, and C designate manuscript codices preserved in the National Library of Paris. They are numbered in the 1827 catalogue as Sorbonne 1827, Saint-Germain 989, and 5239.] (C)

[Note: [Col. 0187A] B omits this.] PREFACE

[Col. 0187A]

**The various natures of things, and of fleeting time**

[Note: [Col. 0187A] C reads: “He briefly summarized.”]

I have briefly summarized in headings the broad periods of fleeting time,

Bede, servant of God; I beg you, who read the stars,

with fixed mind contemplate the everlasting day above.

## CHAPTER ONE  
### On the Fourfold Work of God

[Note: [Col. 0188B] BRIDEFERTUS’S GLOSSES.—The divine operation by which he created and governs the ages. God is said to govern the ages in two ways: either by preserving what has been made or by restoring it through successive generations.]

[Note: [Col. 0188B] “Without an act of dispensation.” The dispensation, the counsel of God, and the art are themselves God, because nothing can exist in him apart from himself.]

[Note: [Col. 0188B] “They are eternal.” Therefore everything made by him through his ordering is eternal, just as he is eternal and is then God. For, as blessed Augustine says, things made beneath him exist in one way, whereas things that are in God exist in another way—God existing in the act of ordering; hence everything that exists is God.]

[Note: [Col. 0188B] “The Father is working until now.” Who could explain in words how God both works in repose and rests while working, in the statement that God rested on the seventh day? The Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ himself, who spoke these things and said, “My Father is working until now, and I am working,” signified a great mystery, because the Lord Jesus is certainly God.

For he is the Word of the Lord, since “in the beginning was the Word,” and not merely any word: “the Word was God,” and all things were made through him.

The Father made the light, but he said that light should come to be. If he spoke, he worked through the Word. His Word was I; I am he. Through me the world was made in those works; through me the world is governed in these works.

My Father was working then, when he made the world, and he is working until now, when he governs it. God therefore works not by creating new things but by governing what has been created.

They were indeed present to God before they had been created; but they are eternal, before all time, that is, before any creation. Before the creation of the world there was time, certainly, but not such as it is now, because at that time there was no alternation of day and night.]

[Note: [Col. 0187A] GLOSSES OF AN UNCERTAIN AUTHOR.—A gloss receives its name from the Greek interpretation of the word “language.” Philosophers call it an adverb, because it designates in one single word the expression whose precise meaning is being sought. It explains what that expression is by means of a single word, as in: “To be silent means to keep quiet”; likewise: “The side draws in the open wound”—“draws in” means “strikes.” Similarly, when we call a limit an “end,” or interpret “ravaged” as “laid waste”; and, in general, whenever we make the meaning of one word clear through a single word.]

**Verses of the presbyter Bede.**—A verse is named from the fact that it flows and turns back upon itself. Properly, a verse is so called from “turning,” because it can be reversed, so that what it has at the end may be placed in the middle, and conversely, as in:

> The horns of the veiled ships, we turn the antennae, the horns of the veiled ships.

Or it is called a verse because the writer’s hand turns from the end back to the beginning:

> I sing of arms and the man, who first from the shores of Troy—

“The various natures of fleeting time.”

Whatever is visible or invisible, perceptible or intelligible, creating or created, is called “nature.” Nature is therefore the general name for all things, both those that exist and those that do not exist.

Those things are said not to exist which can neither be perceived nor understood, but which are such as to transcend every knowledge of body and mind.

Nature is spoken of in two ways. God is called nature because he causes all things to come into being. Every creature is also called nature, because it comes into being.

“Of things,” that is, of the causes of created things, both visible and invisible. “Various,” that is, diverse, manifold, and unlike one another, as they are found in the world. “Fleeting,” that is, running onward and failing. “Time,” *aion* in Greek, *saeculum* in Latin; hence *aevum* is called an age.

“I have summarized,” that is, “I have written briefly.” To summarize properly means to abbreviate by recounting something concisely.

“In headings.” A heading is called such from *Titan*, that is, “sun,” because just as the sun illuminates the world by its presence, so a heading illuminates the page that follows. For if you erase the heading from the front, the page remains mute, as someone has said: “Erase the heading from the front, so that the page may be mute.”

“Broad periods,” that is, extensive ones. “Briefly,” that is, in short form. “In headings,” that is, in brief introductory statements beginning in this way: “On the fourfold work of God,” and so forth.

**Bede.** The pronoun “I” is understood. “Servant of God,” that is, “slave” or “servant.”

“Who read,” namely, my book. He addresses the reader by apostrophe. “I beg,” namely, you, O reader. “Contemplate,” that is, “look upon.” “The everlasting day,” that is, perpetual light—God, namely, who is the eternal day before every day and brighter than every sun. “With the mind,” that is, with the power and discernment of understanding. “Fixed,” namely, that mind fixed there. “Above the stars,” that is, above the heavens, where the stars are; concerning them we shall discuss in this little work, with God’s help.

[Note: [Col. 0188A] JOHN THE NEW’S SCHOLIA.—“The natures of things.” In a written and sufficiently old exemplar this distich had been extended into a tetrastich, with these two lines added:

> Bede, servant of God, I beg you, with fixed mind  
> Who read these things, contemplate the everlasting day above.

They appear to have been added by someone else. Bede was a tolerable versifier, as is clear from the work he composed in hexameters on the Life of Guthbert.]

[Col. 0187A]

> The various natures of things, and of fleeting time,  
> I have briefly summarized in headings, the broad periods in short form,  
> Bede, servant of God; I beg you, with fixed mind,  
> Who read the stars, contemplate the everlasting day above.

## CHAPTER ONE  
### On the Fourfold Work of God

[Note: [Col. 0188B] GLOSSES OF BRIDEFERTUS.—The divine operation by which he created and governs the ages. God is said to govern the ages in two ways: either by preserving what has been made or by restoring it through successive generations.]

[Note: [Col. 0188B] “Without an act of dispensation.” The dispensation, the counsel of God, and the art are themselves God, because nothing can exist in him apart from himself.]

[Note: [Col. 0188B] “They are eternal.” Therefore everything made by him through his ordering is eternal, just as he is eternal and is then God. For, as blessed Augustine says, things made beneath him exist in one way, whereas things that are in God exist in another way—God existing in the act of ordering; hence everything that exists is God.]

[Note: [Col. 0188B] “The Father is working until now.” Who could explain in words how God both works in repose and rests while working, in the statement that God rested on the seventh day? The Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ himself, who spoke these things and said, “My Father is working until now, and I am working,” signified a great mystery, because the Lord Jesus is certainly God.

For he is the Word of the Lord, since “in the beginning was the Word,” and not merely any word: “the Word was God,” and all things were made through him.

The Father made the light, but he said that light should come to be. If he spoke, he worked through the Word. His Word was I; I am he. Through me the world was made in those works; through me the world is governed in these works.

My Father was working then, when he made the world, and he is working until now, when he governs it. God therefore works not by creating new things but by governing what has been created.

They were indeed present to God before they had been created; but they are eternal, before all time, that is, before any creation. Before the creation of the world there was time, certainly, but not such as it is now, because at that time there was no alternation of day and night.]

[Note: [Col. 0189A] GLOSSES OF AN UNCERTAIN AUTHOR.—The divine operation by which he created and governs the ages. God is said to govern the ages in two ways: either by preserving what has been made or by restoring it through successive generations.

“By a fourfold method,” that is, by a four-part understanding. “In the dispensation of the Word,” that is, of the Son of God, in his ordering and providence. “Not made,” that is, they are not temporal.

“They were indeed present to God before they had been created, but they are eternal,” before all time, that is, before any creation. Before the creation of the world there was time, certainly, but not such as it is now, because there was no alternation of day and night.

“Before the ages of the world,” that is, before the establishment of the world. “Formless matter,” that is, confused matter, when heaven and earth did not yet possess their own forms and shapes. “The elements of the world,” that is, earth and water, fire and air.]

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—**Divine operation.** Bede begins with the generation of the world, since it is already universally acknowledged that the world was created by God, as it is written at the beginning of Genesis: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” In theological discussions, however, the duration of time is commonly questioned—namely, how much time God spent in producing it. For from the beginning of Genesis it is understood in one way as having been instantaneous, that is, as though everything came into being in a single moment of time; in another way, the duration of creation is said to have been *hexamerous* (ἑξάμετρος), extending over six days. Therefore, lest there seem to be a contradiction in sacred writings, Bede here enumerates four kinds of operation by which the world is said to have been made.

The first is that which God conceived from eternity, so to speak. For theologians say that it is heretical to posit in God some new plan for making something. If he had conceived what is best only later, it would follow either that he had previously been ignorant of it or that he had been unwilling to make it—neither of which can apply to God, since neither failure to recognize what is best nor unwillingness to do it can be attributed to him. Thus, from the beginning of the ages, that is, from eternity, the creation of the world existed in the divine mind. John speaks of this conception at the beginning of his Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word,” and so forth; and the Apostle says to the Ephesians: “He predestined us before the ages to the kingdom.”

The second creation is that by which God, when the world was just about to come into being, created in a single moment out of nothing an unformed matter—that is, a kind of material for all things, from which they were afterward to be formed through the application of forms. In this unformed matter there was as yet the form of no thing—not of a tree, nor of a human being. The pagan philosophers denied that this matter had been made and thought that it had existed eternally; they called such matter *Chaos*, a term signifying the confused material of all things. Of this creation it is written: “He who lives forever created all things together,” that is, the matter of all things.

The third creation is that by which God began to fashion and produce from that Chaos the forms and appearances of things—of the heavens, lands, seas, trees, and animals. This was a temporal operation and, according to Scripture, took place over six days.

The fourth operation is that by which God daily preserves, vivifies, and governs the world. For the opinion of certain philosophers is false: they suppose that the world is preserved and governed aimlessly and without any power of God. Through this operation animals are born from other animals, the earth produces trees from itself, and seeds buried in the fields return with increase. Thus God produces new things of the same kind every day. Concerning this it is written in Psalm CXLVI: “He covers the heavens with clouds and prepares rain for the earth; he produces grass on the mountains and herbs, and he gives their food to the beasts and to the young ravens that call upon him.”

The first creation, therefore, took place from eternity; the second, in a moment; the third, over the space of six days; the fourth is daily and continues until the consummation of the age. These questions are discussed everywhere by sacred commentators, by blessed Augustine in Book IX of *The City of God*, by Peter Lombard in Book II of the *Sentences*, distinction 11, by Saint Thomas, and by others.

**Before the secular ages.** Secular time is that which is observed from the revolutions of heaven and the stars. There is another time before secular time: an everlasting duration without any change. Philosophers call this everlasting duration αἰῶνα (*aiōna*). See Aristotle, *On the Heavens*, Book I, chapter 9.]

Divine operation, by which he created and governs the ages, is distinguished in four ways: first, because these things, in the dispensation of the Word of God, were not made but are eternal: “He predestined us,” as the Apostle testifies [Note: [Col. 0187A] A., bearing witness.] “before the secular ages to the kingdom”; second, because the elements of the world were likewise made in unformed matter, when “he who lives forever created all things together”; third, because that same matter, according to causes created together with it, is fashioned not all at once but through the distinction of the first six days into heavenly and earthly creation; fourth, because from the seeds and primordial causes of that same creation the whole course of time is completed according to the natural order, while the Father works until now, and the Son also—when God feeds the ravens and clothes the lilies.

## CHAPTER II. On the Formation of the World

[Note: [Col. 0190B]

**BRID. GLOSSES.**—**In the very beginning.** In the very beginning: on the twentieth day before the Kalends of April, in the first part of Aries, because Aries has thirty degrees. In its first six degrees the entire world was made. But the question is: what kind of light was there before the sun had been made? They say: it was without heat—that is, mild—and extended from east to west and from north to south. This light was afterward transformed into the light of the sun.

**Heaven, earth, and angels.** Here we must understand “heaven” as the spiritual heaven, which contains the angels and was certainly made in the beginning out of nothing, before any day. But that heaven which is the firmament was made from the waters on the second day. The higher heaven is called spiritual because it contains spiritual creatures; concerning it we read only that it was made, or that it exists.

**Light was made.** The light made on the first day was not as bright as this light is now, because everything was filled with water, though with water that was less dense and exceedingly fine. Light itself was made out of nothing, that is, from no matter—not according to its cause but according to its matter. For what comes from God does not come from nothing. God had no other matter except himself; therefore such things cannot be from nothing.

**Firmament.** The firmament is where we see the constellations. It supports the waters above and is of a cold nature. For as far as the sun is distant from the earth, so far is the firmament distant from the sun; therefore it is of an icy nature.

**In the midst of the waters.** He says “in the midst of the waters” because there were waters on every side of the firmament, above and below. Many say that these upper waters fell in order to produce the Flood. But Augustine asks what happened to this air. For as far as the air extends from the earth, so far the Flood extended upward to the moon—that is, 125,000 stadia. From this, according to Augustine, it is more easily understood that the light which was made in the beginning was not as bright as it became after the creation of the sun and moon, but had the appearance of dawn, as before sunrise. For he says that this air was changed into water, and again, after a year, the water was changed back into air. Air and water cannot exist together in the same way; nor did the air have a place where it could remain while the Flood lasted. No water or storm can occur above the moon, but they always occur below the moon.

**The soul.** According to some, when the angels were created, the soul too was created. But blessed Augustine [Col. 0191A] and Jerome did not rashly attempt to affirm anything about the soul; rather, they ingeniously declared that they did not know from where it came or when it entered the body—whether at the time of conception or at some other time. Philosophers, however, spoke of *palingenesis* (παλιγγενεσία), that is, repeated generation, intending to say either that the soul passed from one person into another or that the soul descended from a soul, as flesh descends from flesh. Some of them said that it had been prepared and was given at conception or at some other time.

We, however, ought truthfully to believe that it comes from nothing, although we do not know the time appointed for it, leaving this matter to God alone. It is asked whether one soul was created on the sixth day or many; but the question is open. For if one human being was created, why not one soul also? And just as all human bodies were derived from that one human being—as Scripture says, “in whom we all sinned”—why should souls not likewise be derived from that one soul? From this it is also understood that the seed, when it is emitted, possesses a soul.

Our soul was created in the image of God. In it there is not merely a small portion of us, but the substance of the whole universe. It is undoubtedly free, and, through its diffused thoughts and plans, wanders here and there and observes everything by contemplation. It is therefore in the image of God: it is not regarded as corporeal, but through the power of the mind it sees what is absent, crosses the seas, travels everywhere through desire, searches out hidden things, and in a single moment carries its senses here and there through all the regions of the earth and the secrets of the world. It is joined to God, clings to Christ, descends into hell, and ascends again. In this soul, indeed, you are wholly human; without it you are nothing but earth, and into earth you will be dissolved.

Jerome speaks differently in the passage where he says: “The dust returns to its earth from which it was taken, and the spirit returns to the Lord.” Those who think that souls are sown together with bodies and are generated not by God but by the parents of bodies deserve considerable ridicule. Since the flesh returns to the earth and the spirit returns to the Lord who gave it, it is clear that God the Father is the Father of souls, not human beings.

**By governance.** The power of the Creator, and the strength of the omnipotent and all-sustaining one, is the cause of existence for every creature. For the world could not stand even for the blink of an eye if God withdrew from it the governance of itself—just as a builder, after constructing a building, departs, yet the work remains when he ceases and withdraws.

**We are.** We are not in him as though we were his substance; rather, since we are something other than he is, we are in him because he contains and orders all things. Through that ordering “we live and move and have our being” in him. Hence it follows that if he withdraws, we shall neither live, nor move, nor exist.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—**In the very beginning.** The division of creation into six days was explained at great length in the *Hexameron* of Basil the Great. His brother Gregory of Nyssa wrote its supplement, entitled *On the Generation of Human Beings* (Περὶ τῆς τῶν ἀνθρώπων γενέσεως), translated by Dionysius the Roman, surnamed Exiguus. Several months ago we brought this work, previously unpublished in print, into the light.

**And man, bodily from the earth.** Man was created last, after all things had been produced, for whose sake—as both theologians and pagan philosophers have written—all things were established. It is entirely according to nature that things destined for a work should be prepared before the work itself. For, as the philosophers say, the end is first in intention but last in production.

[Col. 0192A] **He is placed in paradise, which the Lord had planted from the beginning.** Man was born in the region of Damascus and was transferred from there into paradise. Bede says that the Lord had created paradise before man; these were gardens of delight intended for human use. Where paradise is located is disputed by theologians according to various opinions. Most, however, adopt the view that the entire passage concerning paradise is to be understood enigmatically, and that paradise is nothing other than this world.

Just as the pagans call the world the dwelling and temple of the gods, a work worthy of the highest veneration because of its inexplicable beauty, so in sacred interpretation this world should be understood as the place of delight. Its complete elegance, than which nothing more ornamented can be imagined, is such that the mind of man, admiring the variety of nature in its adornment, cannot be filled with pleasure. For they interpret the fountain from which the four rivers flow as the Ocean, from which—as Homer too approved—the courses and sources of all rivers and springs arise.

For how could it be understood that the Nile, Euphrates, and Ganges come from the fountain of paradise unless by paradise we understand this world, and by the fountain the sea, which, spread far and wide through hidden subterranean channels, supplies moisture to all rivers? Since these thoughts have occurred to me in passing, I have set them down in this way—not to define anything as certain concerning matters outside my profession, but to leave material for learned men to debate this question further.

**On the seventh day the Lord rested, not from governing creation.** The action of the final day is described; the Jews call this day the Sabbath. Some derive the name from *sabe*, which in their language means “seven”; others interpret it as “rest”; some derive it from the Greek σέβειν, “to sacrifice.” Ridiculous are those who have referred this cessation to the dominion of the planets, claiming that people were commanded to rest on the Sabbath because Saturn, who is lord at that time, makes that day unsuitable for activities; for Saturn is an ill-omened star. This opinion is learnedly refuted by Pico della Mirandola in the books he wrote against astrologers.]

In the very beginning of creation, heaven, earth, angels, air, and water were made out of nothing. On the first day light was made, also out of nothing; on the second, the firmament in the midst of the waters; on the third, the forms of the sea and the earth, together with the things rooted in the earth; on the fourth, the lights of heaven from the light made on the first day; on the fifth, swimming and flying creatures from the waters; on the sixth, the remaining animals from the earth, and man [Note: [Col. 0189A] A, B, C, bodily.]—bodily [Col. 0191A] from the earth, but created in soul from nothing—who was placed in paradise, which the Lord had planted from the beginning. On the seventh day the Lord rested, not from governing creation—for “in him we live,” [Note: [Col. 0191A] A, B, C, “and move.”] “and move, and have our being”—but from creating a new substance.

## CHAPTER III. What the World Is

[Note: [Col. 0192C]

**BRID. RAMES. GLOSSES.**—**Heaven and earth.** He used “heaven” both for heaven itself and for all that is in it; similarly, he used “earth” both for the element itself and for the things contained in it.

**A complete globe.** That roundness is complete—that is, perfect—which has as much length as breadth and is everywhere equally distant from its center. A thing is called complete when it depends upon or is supported by nothing. Hence we are not complete, since we are supported by the earth.

**By the fire through which the stars shine.** This is an order of descent. For fire is above and occupies the highest place in all creation; after fire comes air, then water, and after water earth occupies the lowest place.

**By encircling and penetrating.** Water surrounds the earth on every side and penetrates it, so that the earth, which is dry, does not crumble into dust. There are veins in the earth through which waters secretly remain and rivers increase. For this reason the sea cannot overflow, since the veins of the earth which emit water absorb it again.

**Middle and lowest.** It is also asked whether what is middle can be lowest, or whether what is lowest can be middle, since this seems to be implied by these words. The meaning is therefore as follows: it is “middle” whenever the world revolves in such a way, and is so situated around the earth, that the distance from earth to heaven is always equal, whether below the earth or above it. It is therefore always necessary that half of the whole world be below and half above. It is “lowest,” however, because in the order of the four elements of which the world consists, it occupies the final place.

What is more excellent is better. Fire is better than air, air than water, and water than earth, because those things which are near the earth are more corporeal. Hence the earth, remaining motionless, always clings to one position and encompasses the middle place of the world.

**It is called κόσμος.** Κόσμος is a Greek word which we Latins have adopted for common use. From it heaven is called οὐρανός in Greek, and that is also the name used by the Greeks when the world is called by this term. It ought all the more to be derived from adornment, since the world is more beautiful than the elements which are called by the name “world.”]

**GLOSSES OF AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR.**—The world is the whole universe, consisting of heaven and earth, and rounded into the form of a complete sphere from the four elements. The four principal elements are fire, air, water, and earth, of which earth is the last and middle element. Around the earth is water, namely the Ocean; around the water is air, from which heaven is called aerial; around the air is ether, which is fire, from which heaven is called ethereal. This whole universe is rounded—that is, spherical—and joined together.

He used “heaven” both for heaven itself and for all that is in it; similarly, “earth” both for the element itself and for the things contained in it. “Into the form,” that is, into the shape of a sphere, that is, of a certain roundness. That roundness is perfect which has as much length as breadth and is everywhere equally distant from its center. A complete sphere—that is, a distinct and perfect sphere—has its own proper form. A thing is called complete when it depends upon or is supported by nothing. Hence we too are not complete, because we are supported by the earth.

Likewise, “rounded,” that is, the whole universe joined together by fire and air, or by the sun, since everything is illuminated by the sun. It is asked how what is middle can be lowest, or what is lowest can be middle, since this seems to be implied by these words. The meaning is therefore as follows: it is “middle” because the whole world revolves in such a way, and is so situated around the earth, that the distance from earth to heaven is always equal, whether below the earth or above it. It is therefore always necessary that half of the whole world be below and half above. It is “lowest,” however, because in the order of the four elements of which the world consists, it occupies the final place.

What is more excellent is better. Fire is better than air, air than water, and water than earth, because those things which are near the earth are more corporeal. Hence the earth, remaining motionless, always clings to one position and encompasses the middle place of the world. “Balanced,” that is, suspended or made equal, because the distance from earth to heaven is always equal in every direction. This refers either to the universe of the elements or to the firmament. Fire holds the highest and first place among the elements; air the second; water the third; earth the fourth and last. It hangs motionless because it is supported by no creature.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—**The world is the universe, and so forth.** This chapter contains a definition of the world, an enumeration of its parts, and finally an explanation of its name. The definition appears to have been taken from Aristotle’s book *On the World to Alexander*, which reads as follows: “The world is a structure composed of heaven and earth” (Κόσμος ἐστὶ σύστημα ἐξ οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς). He added what follows: “And of the natures contained within these—namely, fire, air, and moisture”; then: “And also of those things which are naturally composed from these.” For physicists teach that everything is formed from fire, or hot spirit, moisture, and earth. Thus those four are called elements. Just as all words and utterances are contained in the twenty-three letters, so these four are the simple parts and matter of all things; for this reason they are rightly called the elements of the world.

**Rounded into the form of a complete sphere.** Pliny treats the form of the world in the same way in chapter 2 of Book II. Moreover, arguments do not merely show that the shape of the world is spherical; the agreement of human beings does so as well, since they call it an orb because of its roundness. Aristotle proves this by many arguments in Book II of *On the Heavens*.

**By the fire through which the stars shine.** Many distinguished writers have believed that heaven is fiery and that the stars themselves are eternal fires, since they shine, impart heat to things, and are driven by perpetual motion—all of which are natural properties of fire. For this reason Anaxagoras of Clazomenae wished heaven to be called *aether* from burning: αἴθω means “I burn.”

Aristotle, however, vigorously maintained that this belief is false, asserting that there is nothing elemental in heaven. For what is elemental can be corrupted by nature, whereas heaven has an incorruptible and eternal essence, different from the fiery, airy, watery, and earthly essences. Cicero calls this the “fifth nature.” According to Aristotle, it is called *aether* from its eternal course. Nevertheless, this question has many great writers on both sides; it seemed sufficient for us to note it briefly.

[Col. 0194C] In the expression “world,” heaven is also called by reason of its perfect, complete elegance. According to Aristotle, “heaven” has several meanings. The entire world is called heaven, as among the Greeks are κόσμος and οὐρανός. Thus, in Pliny, chapter 1, “world”—and that which it has pleased him to call heaven by another name, under whose curvature all things are covered—at times signifies the whole aether, that is, the entire structure of heavenly things, from the moon to the circumference of the world. Most people call this the second heaven and the second world.

The first world, or heaven, is the combination of the four elements. It is corruptible and has been called by more recent philosophers the sphere of active and passive things. The third heaven contains immortal and divine things; because of the radiance of the divine light it is called *empyrean* (ἐμπύρεον). On the basis of this distinction some interpret the Apostle’s passage concerning being caught up into the third heaven.

“Heaven” also signifies the orbit of each planet; thus Cicero says that the moon occupies the lowest of the heavens. Finally, it specifically signifies the eighth heaven from the moon, which the Greeks call ἀπλανής, “unwandering,” and the Latins call the firmament, since it contains the fixed stars. Marcus Varro thinks that it is called heaven because it is adorned with starry signs.

Yet this passage of Bede is not without awkwardness. For “world” and *cosmos* take their name from complete elegance, beauty, and order. Heaven, as has already been said, is called οὐρανός by Plato because it is the boundary of the higher things—that is, ὅρος ἄνω; Cleomedes agrees with him in his *Meteora*. The name “world,” however, by broad agreement derives from adornment, which Aristotle thinks resides above all in order. “You would more appropriately call the universe,” he says, “κόσμος—that is, a structure of things composed and arranged in harmonious order—than ἀκοσμία, that is, a confused and disordered heap.”

Others also derive adornment from figure and color and from the flames of the shining stars, which Pliny calls the eyes of the world. The story of Argus, whom Juno killed, belongs here. For physicists understand Juno as the air; when it becomes condensed into clouds, it removes the sun and stars from our sight—that is, it plucks out Argus’s hundred eyes.]

[Col. 0192A]

The world is the whole universe [Note: [Col. 0191A] A, of every creature.], consisting of heaven and earth and rounded into the form of a complete sphere from the four elements: fire, through which the stars shine; air, through which all living things breathe; waters, which support the earth by encircling and penetrating it; and the earth itself, which, as the middle and lowest part of the world, hangs motionless, balanced within the universe that revolves around it.

But by the name “world” heaven is also called on account of its perfect and complete elegance; among the Greeks, too, it is called κόσμος, from adornment.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Elements

[Note: [Col. 0195A]

[Col. 0195B] **BRID. GLOSSES.**—**The elements differ from one another both according to nature.** The nature of the elements is their very quality: fire is hot and dry, while earth is cold and dry. We say *elementa*, *elimenta*, and *hylementa*. *Elementa* is as though from *elevamenta*, “elevations,” because everything consists of the elements. *Elimenta* derives from *elimo*, “I form,” because everything is formed from them. *Hylementa* derives from Greek ὕλη, *hyle*, “unformed matter,” from which all things were made into their respective forms.

There are four elements: heaven, fire, water, and earth, and they are mixed with one another in all things. Indeed, in earth you will find fire, which is frequently struck out of stones and iron; and in heaven, although it is fiery and sparkles with shining stars, the pole may be understood to be water.

**They are mixed together.** He says a little about the *syzygies*, that is, the conjunctions of the elements. Every corporeal thing consists of the four elements mentioned above, each of which has two qualities: one proper to itself and another belonging to a different element. Thus earth has coldness and dryness. Dryness is therefore a quality proper to earth; coldness is not proper to earth but belongs to water. The same applies to the others.

Coldness is the proper quality of water, while moisture comes to it from air. Similarly, moisture is proper to air, while heat descends to it from fire. Likewise, heat is proper to fire, but it receives dryness from earth.

Thus syzygies are formed from six qualities. Four of these are called immediate and connected, requiring no intermediary by which they may be joined. The heat of fire is joined with the coldness of earth in dryness. Again, the moisture of water is joined with the dryness of earth in coldness. The heat of air is joined with the coldness of water in moisture, while the moisture of air is joined with the dryness of fire in heat. These are the four called immediate and connected.

Two remain, called mediated and discordant, because they cannot be joined without an intermediary, owing to the difference of their qualities. Hot and dry fire cannot be joined with moist and cold water without an intermediary, namely earth. Again, moist and hot air cannot be joined with earth, which is cold and dry, without an intermediary, namely water, which occupies the middle position and joins the two.

**Cloudy and earthly.** Understand “cloudy” as thick clouds, which always contain water. The difference between *nubila* and *nubes* is that we call dense and very thick clouds *nubila*, while *nubes* may refer both to thick and to thin clouds.

**GLOSSES OF AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR.**—The elements differ from one another not only in nature but also in position. The nature of the elements is their very quality: fire is hot and dry, earth dry and cold. We say *elementa*, *elimenta*, and *hylementa*. *Elementa* is as though from *elevamenta*, “elevations,” because everything consists of the elements. *Elimenta* derives from *elimo*, “I form,” because everything is formed from them. *Hylementa* derives from *hyle*, “unformed matter,” from which all things were made into their forms.

“Position” means place, or the arrangement and order of places. “Differs” means “is distant.” According to Isidore, *elementum* is Greek and means “matter” in Latin; for Greek ὕλη means “unformed matter” in Latin. According to Ambrose, however, the word is Latin and derives from *elimo*, “I form”; what we call *elementum*, the Greeks call στοιχεῖον.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—**If it should happen to be placed beneath water in a vessel.** A clod or any portion of earth falls downward through water. This demonstrates that earth is heavier than water, for things that naturally fall downward are heavy.

**Fire kindled materially.** There are several kinds of fire, which I shall briefly enumerate here. The first is that bright heavenly fire which nurtures, preserves, and gives life to all things. The second is that immediately beneath the moon, extending to the regions of the clouds; it does not shine, but is like heated air, such as is found in bathhouses, embers, and extinguished flames. It shines only when it finds material upon which to exercise the force of its heat. From this arise beneath the heavens sudden fires, which some call falling fires and others flying fires. The third is the fire which the human race uses for various necessary purposes. The fourth is that which nature, with supreme artistry, has breathed into living and nonliving things alike; nothing is entirely without heat.

**Yet they are so mixed with one another by a certain kinship of nature.** The elements of the world, which are joined by place and position, are *symbola*, that is, agreeing in one quality: water and earth agree in coldness, while air agrees with water in mobility and moisture; elements separated by an interval are *asymbola*, as water and fire, with air intervening.]

[Col. 0195A]

The elements differ from one another both in nature and [Note: [Col. 0195] A, B, C, also] in position. Earth, being the heaviest and unable to be supported by another nature, occupies the lowest place among creatures. Water, however, is lighter than earth and heavier than air. If it should happen to be placed beneath water in some vessel, it immediately rises upward as the lighter substance.

Fire too, when materially kindled, immediately seeks its natural position above the air; but, lest it reach there, it vanishes into the soft air, by whose surrounding it is pressed down. Yet they are mixed with one another through a certain kinship of nature, so that dry and cold earth is associated with cold water; cold and moist water with moist air; moist and hot air with hot fire; and hot and dry fire with dry earth. Hence we see fire in the earth, and in the air cloudy and earthly bodies.

## CHAPTER V. On the Firmament

[Note: [Col. 0197B]

**BRID. GLOSSES.**—**Heaven is subtle.** Heaven is not round like a ball but is extended lengthwise from the regions of the poles.

**And of fiery nature.** He calls it fiery in nature because of the stars, which possess a fiery nature and are placed within it.

**From the center of the earth.** As much space extends from this place on earth to heaven, so much space extends from each side of the earth to heaven; this is measured equally in every direction from the center of the earth. For the earth occupies the position of a point in the middle, around which heaven turns like a compass. Consequently, no more than half of it can be seen—the half that is always above the earth.

**Is governed by the counter-motion of the planets.** The planets move against the world’s rotation; therefore the world is moderated and held in place.

**By the evidence of the stars.** An argument is that which gives credibility to a doubtful matter; it is called *argumentum* as though from “cleverly discovered.” By the evidence of the fixed stars in heaven, the rotation of heaven around the earth has been recognized by learned men.

[Col. 0197C] **Shorter among the northern constellations.** The northern constellations [Col. 0198A] have shorter circles because of the sharper pole situated there, and they never set. Where heaven spreads out and expands into a greater roundness, they trace larger circles.

**They call them poles.** The pole is the very short star at the summit of the northern circle; from it that entire region is called the pole. Just as the stars of the northern pole are always visible to us because they are above us, so the stars of the southern pole never appear to us because they are beneath the earth.

[Col. 0198B] **Boreas.** Boreas is always visible to us; it never sets for us or goes beneath the earth. It takes its name from the pole—that is, from the northern Boreas—from the wind called Boreas, which blows from the northern region and is also called Aquilon.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—**To be carried around every day with indescribable speed.** This means in the space of twenty-four hours. The explanation of the speed can be perceived from the parts of heaven. The entire sun rises in a brief moment of time, yet it is more than thirty times larger than the whole circumference of the earth. From this comparison it is understood that nothing beneath heaven—neither winds, nor the flight of birds, nor the cast of projectiles—can be carried along so swiftly that it could be compared with that incredible speed.

As for what writers, even very serious ones, say on Pliny’s authority—that heaven would fall, that is, would depart from the order of its motion, which is completed through a certain succession of its parts, unless it were moderated by the contrary course of the planets, which proceeds from the right-hand parts toward the left—this is a charming statement rather than a physical one.

[Col. 0199B] **The northern constellations tracing shorter circles as they move around the pole.** Through the rotation of the world, each visible sign in heaven describes a circle that is conceived only by the mind. For mathematicians say that each passage of a point produces a distinct line. Thus, when a sphere revolves around an immovable pole, the signs that are near the extreme end of either pole describe narrower circular paths; those in the middle of the sphere produce the largest circles. This is demonstrated by Euclid in his treatment of the rotation of the sphere.

Let the sphere in the accompanying diagram [preceding page] be A B C D, and let the axis around which it revolves be A D. When the sphere revolves on the line A D, the circles described by the parts of the signs become narrower the nearer they are to either endpoint, A or D; the largest of all is the circle described from B toward C.

**Whose two extreme vertices, around which the sphere of heaven revolves, they call poles.** The Greeks call the extremities of the axis πόλοι, “poles,” while the Latins call them vertices, as in Cicero and in Aratus: “The other vertex of the axis is said to be a pole.” Virgil likewise says in Book I of the *Georgics*:

> Here the one vertex is always high above us, but the other  
> Is seen beneath our feet by black Styx and the shades below.

They are called by the same term in Greek and Latin from the idea of turning, because heaven turns around these extremities while the point itself remains motionless. Thus the stars near the poles describe narrow circles. In our own region, for example, the Great Bear and the Little Bear revolve around the pole through the entire night without setting in a narrow circuit. The star itself near the pole, which they call the Pole Star, situated at the extremity of the Little Bear, is visible all night in the same part of heaven, without any inclination, through the shortest of revolutions.

**Melting away in icy cold.** The sun revolves through the middle of the sphere. Therefore the extremities, since the sun never approaches those regions, are always cold.]

[Col. 0197A]

Heaven is subtle and fiery in nature, round, and equally distant in every direction from the center of the earth. [Col. 0198A] Hence the learned have said that it is convex and concave, whichever way it is viewed, and revolves daily with indescribable speed, so that it would fall if it were not moderated by the counter-motion of the planets. Relying on the evidence of the stars, [Col. 0199A] which always move around in a fixed course, while the northern constellations perform shorter circles around the pole, they call the two extreme vertices around which the sphere of heaven revolves “poles.” These poles melt away in icy cold. One of them, rising toward the northern region, is called Boreas; the other, sloping toward the south and opposite the earth, is called the Southern Pole, which Holy Scripture calls “the inner regions of the south.”

## CHAPTER VI. On the Varying Altitude of Heaven
[Note: [Col. 0199C]]

**BRID. GLOSSAE.**—**Stars.** The stars wandering or revolving around the pole—namely the northern stars, that is, Arcturus and the others—[Col. 0199D] because the sky does not rise to an upright height but ascends only slightly, like a sloping spiral; hence the stars that appear elevated to us situated in the north appear low to those situated near the south, because of the intervening earth.

**The globe of the earth.** He says “the globe of the earth” because the earth is spheroidal, that is, round.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—**But the world is not thus.** The height of the poles does not remain the same in all regions. For if one travels sixty stadia from any place toward the north, the northern pole becomes higher by one degree (there being 360 such degrees in the great circle); but if one turns toward the south, that same pole becomes lower by one degree over the same distance. As one pole becomes higher, so the other, opposite it, becomes lower beneath the earth. It therefore happens that the stars which under this sky are visible to us throughout the whole night are not seen for part of the night by those who have crossed toward the south. Thus the Lyre of Orpheus does not set in Germany; but in most parts of Italy it is hidden beneath the horizon for two hours before it rises again.

**In certain regions of India they appear only for fifteen days of the year.** Similar are the things Pliny says about the moon’s risings and settings in Taprobane, and many other matters which Bede here accepts as established facts. Yet if these are brought into correspondence with a precise description of the sphere and compass, whose principles are certain, this point about the northern regions certainly cannot stand. We have not thought it opportune to discuss these matters here.]

But the world does not rise so high at this pole that these stars are visible everywhere. Rather, the same stars are believed to be higher for those who are nearest to them, and the same stars submerged for those who are farther away. Just as this pole now appears elevated to those situated in the lowlands, so, for those who have crossed into that slope of the earth, the other pole rises, while those stars which here were lofty sink; the globe of the earth intervenes against the middle of their sight, so that the northern stars, which hang above us from the pole, appear in certain regions of India for only fifteen days [Note: [Col. 0199] A, “nights.”] of the year.

## CHAPTER VII. On the higher heaven

[Note: [Col. 0200B]]

**BRID.
