GLOSSAE.**—**The heaven of the higher circle.** The first heaven extends from the waters to the moon and is the air; the second extends from the moon to the firmament and is the aetherial heaven; the third and fourth extend from the firmament to infinity and constitute the higher heaven. Within these, however, there are seven regions around the equinoctial circle, because those places are far from the pole and therefore the stars there do not appear continually, as they do here with us, but only at certain times.

**At equal distances.** Just as the firmament is everywhere equally distant from the earth, so that higher heaven, where the angels are, is equally distant from the lower heaven.

**Aetherial bodies.** Angelic power sent to us assumes an aetherial body, since its subtlety cannot be seen by bodily eyes; and not merely an aetherial body, but also an aerial one. Demons, however, assume a body from this air.

**This God.** He is speaking against Augustine. Augustine says that the four elements are contained within the firmament, and that water always occupies its place beside the earth, while fire possesses the higher place. Therefore, on what grounds are we compelled to learn that icy waters exist above the firmament, when there is no earth there and above it is the place where only fire exists? Thus what is said about the waters above the heavens is understood to signify the angels.

[Col. 0200D] **The lower elements.** For this reason they infer that the higher heaven is fiery, because fire occupies the highest place among all created things. If, therefore, that heaven is higher, it must be fiery.

**Of diverse form.** By saying “not uniform,” he means that its forms do not revolve in one part but in different parts. For the firmament continually turns toward the right, from east to west; against it, the sun continually turns toward the left, toward the east, as do the remaining planets. Yet they follow their courses in different ways, and by their manifold motion the firmament is made firm, lest, according to the philosophers, it fall because of its excessive speed. We should understand that the firmament was called so not on account of its standing still, but on account of its firmness, or because it is the impassable boundary between the upper and lower waters.]

The heaven of the higher circle, distinguished by its own proper boundary and placed at equal distances on every side, contains the angelic powers. When they come forth to us, they assume aetherial bodies so that they may even resemble human beings in eating, and when they return there they lay those bodies aside. God tempered this heaven with icy waters so that it would not set the lower elements on fire. Then he made the lower heaven firm by a varied, not uniform, motion, calling it the firmament because it supports the waters above.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the heavenly waters

[Note: [Col. 0201B]]

**BRID. GLOSSAE.**—**The firmament.** The firmament was made in the manner of crystal from frozen waters. Yet it has a fiery quality because the stars placed within it are fiery. Just as air and water yield to the weight of the earth so as to reach the earth, so the air itself yields to the weight of the waters so as to reach either the earth or the water. If someone could lower even a small portion of air into those lofty spaces of heaven, it would fall by its own weight until it reached the aerial spaces below. By such arguments the philosophers infer that waters cannot exist above the aetherial heaven. They are answered as follows: If water, as we see, can be reduced to such tiny drops that it is carried vapor-like above this air, which by nature is lighter than water, why can it not also be carried above that lighter heaven in smaller drops and lighter vapors? Whatever the nature and form of those waters may be, we do not doubt that they exist there. The authority of Holy Scripture is greater than the entire capacity of human understanding.

[Col. 0201C] **The fire of the stars.** The stars are of such fiery nature that they would be consumed unless they were tempered by waters. Just as this earth would be consumed by the sun’s fire if water were not present within and around it, so the firmament would be consumed by that same fire of the sun and by the fire of the constellations within it unless it had waters above it.

**INC. AUCT. GLOSSAE.**—**The waters placed above the firmament, lower indeed than the spiritual heavens.** Concerning the waters above the heavens, this is the opinion of blessed Ambrose: The learned of the world say that waters cannot exist above the heavens, declaring that the heaven is fiery and that the nature of waters cannot be reconciled with it. They add that the sphere of heaven is round, revolving, and burning, and that in such a revolving circuit waters cannot possibly remain. For they must flow and fall when that sphere bends from the higher regions toward the lower; consequently, they say, the waters cannot remain there, since the axis of heaven, twisting with rapid motion, would spill them as it revolved. But let such people finally cease their madness and, confounded, recognize that he who was able to create all things from nothing was also able to establish the nature of those waters in heaven with icy solidity. Since they themselves say that the sphere of heaven revolves, shining with burning stars, did divine Providence not arrange that water should overflow within and above the sphere of heaven, to temper the burning of that fervent axis?

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—Others more correctly say that the waters were suspended to temper the fire of the stars. See Isidore, bishop of Seville, in his book *On the Nature of Things*, where he mentions these waters. This discussion, I think, arose from the song of the three youths: “Bless the waters that are above the heavens.” From this, learned men were given the task of investigating the nature of these waters.]

Some affirm that the waters placed above the firmament [Note: [Col. 0201] A, B, C, “above the firmament”] are lower than the spiritual heavens but nevertheless higher than every corporeal creature; some say that they were reserved for the inundation of the Flood, while others, more correctly, maintain that they were suspended to temper the fire of the stars.

## CHAPTER IX. On the five circles of the world

[Note: [Col. 0201D]]

**BRID. GLOSSAE.**—**Circles.** The circles of which he speaks here contain both the earth and the heavens.

**The stars for us.** It is not surprising that the stars above us never set for us, because their circles are very short, being situated in the narrower part of the sky; we see them from every side, both rising and setting.

**The highest.** Cancer and Capricorn are called tropical, that is, turning signs; of these, Cancer is the highest part of the zodiac. They are called turning signs because the sun turns either upward or downward. The sun’s station is in Cancer on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, when, traversing the solstitial circle, it reaches the solstice on the twelfth day before the Kalends of that month. In Capricorn it remains on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, when, completing its wintry course, it makes another solstice on the twelfth day before the Kalends of that month, from which it returns to its higher courses. “Solstice” is understood as *solis statio*, “the sun’s station,” not because the sun stands there, but because there it ends its course.

**Equinoctial.** The equinoctial circle is so called because whenever the sun passes through it, an equinox occurs. In September, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, this happens in the sign of Libra; in March, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, [Col. 0202C] in the sign of Aries. It is also called equinoctial because there night and day are equal throughout the world. When the sun rises in the middle of the world, everyone sees it, and likewise when it sets; this is not so when it comes toward us or goes toward the southern regions, for then the days and nights vary.

**Uninhabitable.** Because the sun travels through that entire circle and through its middle, it is uninhabitable because of excessive heat. In the upper solstitial circle mentioned above, however, the sun travels neither through the middle nor through the whole circle, but touches it only on one side; therefore that region is temperate.

**Wintry.** The wintry circle is so called from the shortness of the days or from the sun’s return. As far as we are concerned, the interval from the rising of the winter day to its setting is short. *Bruma* is “devouring” in Greek, because in winter people consume most of whatever they have produced by labor.

**Southern.** The fifth circle is called southern from the wind that blows from that direction. Just as the most familiar sign in the north is the Great Bear, so in the south it is Canopus. Just as the pole never sets for us, so Canopus never sets for the Egyptians.

**Inequalities.** He speaks of unequal periods because one region is hot and another cold; one has long days and another short ones. Or it is because when the sun is in the solstitial circle, the days are long and the nights short, whereas when it is in the equinoctial circle, days and nights are almost equal, as on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April and the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, for the equinoxes occur then. When it is in the wintry circle, the nights are long and the days short because the sun is far from us. This occurs on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January, when the winter solstice takes place.

**Thule.** From Britain to Thule, the last of all the islands, is a journey of nine days; from there, after one day’s sailing, one reaches the frozen sea. Pliny says that the inhabitants of this island feed on milk in winter, but in summer they pluck grass with their mouths among their cattle.

[Col. 0203A] **JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—**The world is divided by five circles.** This chapter concerns the parallel circles, [Col. 0204A] by whose intervals the five zones in heaven and on earth are distinguished, of which writers frequently make mention. [Col. 0203C] These are parallel circles, described by the revolution of the world. There are also circles in heaven that are not parallel, such as the horizon, meridian, and colures, which are not produced by the motion of the heavens.

Of the parallel, or equidistant, circles there are three described by the sun. The equinoctial circle is described twice each year, in March [Col. 0203D] and September, in the first parts of Virgo and Libra. It is the greatest of all the equidistant circles, for it is drawn through the middle of the sphere. The other two are called tropics; the Greeks call them τροπαί (*tropaí*, “turnings”). One is described on the solstitial day, when the sun is in the first part of Cancer; the other on the wintry day, when the sun has entered the first part of Capricorn. These are the sun’s limits, beyond which it does not advance farther toward the ends of the world. The remaining two circles are such that one contains the stars that are always visible, while the other contains stars perpetually submerged beneath the horizon.

These last two differ from the upper ones in that their size is not the same in every region. As one travels northward, they continually become larger: in Greece, for example, the circle is drawn from the hind foot of the Great Bear, whereas in Germany it is drawn from the star that shines most brightly in the Lyre.

Let the sphere and its axis be represented in the diagram above by *a b c d* and *a b*. When the sphere is turned upon the axis *a b*, a parallel is described in the middle of the sphere from *c* toward *d*, namely the equinoctial circle; then from *m* toward *n*, the summer tropic; from *k* toward *l*, the other tropic, that of Capricorn; then from *e* toward *f*, the Antarctic circle containing the stars that never come into our sight; finally, from *g* toward *i*, the Arctic circle containing the stars that never set.

The space enclosed between the line *m k* and again between the line *n l*, across which the line *m l* is drawn, is the torrid zone. For this sky, to which the corresponding region on earth is subject, is scarcely habitable because of the intensity of the sun’s heat. Similarly, the extreme regions, namely *g a i* and *e b f*, are uninhabitable because of cold, for the sun’s rays do not penetrate to them. Apart from these, there are two habitable regions: one is ours, namely *g i m n*; the other belongs to the inhabitants of the opposite earth, namely *k l e f*.]

The world is divided by five circles. By their distinctions, some regions are inhabited because of their temperate climate, while others are uninhabitable because of the severity of their cold or heat. The first is the northern circle, uninhabitable because of cold; its stars never set for us. The second is the solstitial circle, situated at the highest part of the zodiac; toward the northern region it is temperate and habitable. The third is the equinoctial circle, passing through the middle course of the zodiacal sphere; it is torrid and uninhabitable. The fourth is the wintry circle, situated toward the southern pole at the lowest part of the zodiac; it is temperate and habitable. The fifth is the southern circle, around the southern pole, which is covered by the earth; it is uninhabitable because of cold.

The three middle circles [Note: [Col. 0203] A, “distinguish the inequalities of time . . . .” B.] distinguish the unequal periods, since the sun occupies one at the solstice, another at the equinox, and the third at the winter solstice. The extreme circles are always deprived of the sun. Hence, from the island of Thule, after one day’s sailing northward, one finds the frozen sea.

## CHAPTER X. On the regions of the world

[Note: [Col. 0204D]]

**BRIDEF. GLOSSAE.**—**Eastern.** They call the east the gate of heaven because in that region heaven opens, as it were, and becomes visible when the sun rises in the morning. Hence Virgil:

> Meanwhile the house of almighty Olympus opens.

They call the west so because in that region the world’s exit is, as it were, made, and there is reception into the hidden places of heaven. Or they are called the gates of heaven because all the signs rise there and travel toward the west. No sign rises or sets from either the southern or northern region; therefore those regions are called not the gates but the sides of heaven.

[Col. 0205A] **These are equal only in the middle of the earth.** In Jerusalem, a city situated in Judaea, or in those situated in Asia, the length of the day in summer is almost the same as in winter. Since they are near the navel, that is, the middle of the earth, the rising of the sun is not extended among them, nor is its setting.

**The rising and setting.** The summer day extends its rising from the winter rising to the summer rising. Similarly, it extends its setting from the winter setting to the summer setting. This occurs among us, who are in the north, around whom both the rising and setting of the sun are visible; but it narrows the other regions, namely the southern and northern ones.

For when the sun rises for us in midsummer, it is not immediately seen by those who are in the south, until it seeks the higher parts of its circle. Similarly, when it sets, it is not seen by them, because the place where it sets for us in the north is far from them. It likewise narrows the northern region, because it holds it with a very early rising and a very late setting; and in the north it nearly rises where it sets.

Indeed, on the northern island of Britain, there are eighteen consecutive days each year without night during the summer. Hence Horace calls it rich in light, and Juvenal says:

> The Britons content with the shortest night.

In winter, too, they have just as many nights without day. Thus the summer solstitial rising and setting appear to us to occur only in the northern region, and therefore we see there only a narrow interval between setting and rising. From the rising of the summer day to the winter rising, however, we see a great interval. Again, the rising of the winter day and the setting occur only in the southern region, and therefore that region is narrowed. For the interval there is small.

Likewise, from the winter setting to the summer setting, a great interval is seen; hence he says, “extending the rising and setting,” and what follows. Thus even the winter day extends the solstitial rising, because it rises late, and the night itself contains three regions. Similarly, it extends the setting because it sets early in the same region in which it rises.

[Col. 0205D] **Likewise among the southerners.** What is long for us is short for them, and what is short for us is long for them. Summer days are long for us, while winter days are short. Conversely, summer days are short for them, while winter days are long, though not in the same way. For our summer day is not shortened for them to the same extent as their winter day is shortened for us; hence he says, “more moderate.”

Although these things occur according to the arrangement of the circles, they are nevertheless believed to occur by divine disposition. The southerners could not endure the heat of the sun, which would be almost continually near them, if their days were as long as ours; the earth itself would also be scorched.

**The winter setting.** He does not say that the sun has a winter setting when it rises in the solstitial region, since this never happens. Rather, after the interval of the months has passed, it slips toward that setting to which the line drawn from the solstitial region reaches. Therefore, when he says: [Col. 0206A] “Although the winter setting corresponds everywhere to the solstitial rising along the same line,” the meaning is as if he said: “Although we have variation in the length of days and nights, we nevertheless do not have variation in the lines.” For the solstitial rising and the winter setting are always on the same line.

**Always after six months.** The sun rises for six months, then, retreating for the other six months along the same line, returns toward the setting. Therefore the sign that sets today will be rising after six months. For example, if Cancer is rising this morning, after six months it will be setting at the beginning of the night, while Capricorn will be rising in the morning.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—**Climates, that is, the regions of the world, are four.** He improperly uses “climates” for “regions.” For in the fields, *clima* signifies an area extending sixty feet in every direction; in the world, however, climates are stretches of land that distinguish two parallels separated by half-hour intervals. The globe of the earth is divided by such intervals from the equinoctial circle—beneath which the longest day is no more than twelve hours—to the place where the solstitial day contains sixteen equinoctial hours.

Since the climates are separated by half-hours, there are eight climates. A region, however, is one of the four parts of a boundary divided by four limits. This is how Pliny understands the term. Others call them the poles of heaven, astrologers call them centers, and in ordinary speech we call them angles. Of these, the south and north are fixed; the rising and setting vary, because the sun does not always rise from the same place on account of the bending of the zodiac.

Learned men therefore established three risings and the same number of settings. One is the place from which the sun rises when it enters the first part of Cancer, which occurs on the solstitial day and lies near the north. Another is the place from which the winter sun rises beneath the Nones of December, which lies near the south. Between these is the middle place from which it rises on the equinoctial days, when the sun is in the first parts of Aries and Libra. This is the true rising.

Similarly, on the western side of the sky there are the same number of settings. Their breadth increases for one traveling toward the north and decreases toward the south, as is clear from spherical geometry.

**From these they call the eastern and western regions…** Just as the world is opened by the rising, so it is closed by the setting; therefore each region is a gate. Such a gate is also mentioned in the sacred writings: in Psalm 77, it is said that he opened the gates of heaven.]

Climates, that is, the regions of the world, are four: the eastern region extends from the summer rising to the winter rising; the southern from there to the winter setting; the western from there [Col. 0205A] to the summer setting; and the northern extends from the summer setting until it meets the rising of that same region. The eastern and western regions are therefore called the gates of heaven.

These regions are equal only for those situated in the middle of the earth. For those dwelling beneath the north, the winter day is shorter and the summer day longer, extending the rising and setting and narrowing the other regions. Among the southerners, likewise, each of the aforementioned days is more moderate and alters the distinction described above, although everywhere [Col. 0206A] the winter setting corresponds to the solstitial rising along the same line. For every rising [Note: [Col. 0205A] A omits “of the sun.”] of the sun is likewise matched by a setting after six months.

## CHAPTER XI. On the stars

[Note: [Col. 0206D]]

**BRIDEF. RAM. GLOSSAE.**—**Borrowing their light from the sun.** All the stars and the moon receive their light from the sun. Although they are fiery in nature and were made from the same light as the sun, their fire is nevertheless thin and subtle and they do not possess enough power to shine fully without the sun. They are therefore illuminated by the rays of the sun, whose fire has greater power.

This is presented figuratively in Christ and his saints, who receive from him whatever virtue they possess. In the mystical sense, the stars also signify holy men, concerning whom it is said: “He numbers the multitude of the stars.” [Col. 0207B] Just as all the stars are illuminated by the sun, so the saints are made radiant by Christ with the glory of the heavenly kingdom. And just as they are dimmed by the sun’s brightness and the immense force of its light, so the splendor of the saints is, in a certain sense, obscured in comparison with the glory of Christ. And just as the stars differ from one another in brilliance, so there is diversity among the righteous according to the distinction of their merits.

**Of the full moon.** In Greek, the full moon is called πανσέληνος (*pansélēnos*), “full moon.” It occurs on the fifteenth day of the lunar month, and by its brightness the stars around it are obscured. By similar reasoning it is proved that the sun obscures the stars during the day. This is especially evident during a solar eclipse, when, even if it occurs at midday, the stars are visible in the sky. This pertains to the higher regions, where it is said that the fixed stars are in the firmament.

**Little fires falling from the aether.** Although we see little fires falling from the aether, which the common people, seeing them, believe to be stars falling from the firmament, that is not what happens. When the wind rushes through the air, it also touches the aether and carries away from it sparks shining like stars.

[Col. 0207C] **But other stars.** Stars and constellations differ from one another. A star is any single star, named from *stare*, “to stand,” because it always stands fixed in the sky. Constellations, however, are formed from many stars, such as the Hyades and Pleiades. *Astra* are large stars or stellar formations, such as Orion and Boötes. But writers confuse these names, using *astra* for stars and *stellae* for constellations.

**The Little Pigs in the forehead of Taurus.** The stars called the Little Pigs (*Succulae*) are so named as though they were “beneath the eyes.” They are in the forehead of Taurus, or they are named from *succus*, “sap,” because they provide moisture. Hence in Greek they are called Hyades, that is, “watery ones.” In Greek, ὕδωρ (*hydōr*) means “water.” Or they are called Hyades, ἀπὸ τοῦ ὕειν (*apo tou hyein*), that is, “from raining.” By another name they are called the Vergiliae, because they rise in spring.

**Because some rise of their own accord.** Up to this point he has spoken of the planets and of the signs of the zodiac through which the planets travel. Now he speaks of signs through which the planets do not travel; therefore he says “of their own accord,” or without being compelled by any planet.

[Col. 0207D] **The rising of the Kids.** The Kids are in the sign of the Charioteer when they rise. The Charioteer, or Auriga, is Erichthonius himself. It is a northern sign, on whose back is a star called the Goat, and before him he drives two Kids. He is speaking about the rising of these stars and of the others now under discussion.

Each sign has four risings: morning, midday, evening, and midnight. Of these, two are complete, namely the morning and evening risings. Here he is speaking of the morning rising. When the sun rises in the east in the morning, and these stars rise beside it, rain, hail, and other such phenomena occur.

**And of Arcturus.** He is not speaking of that Arcturus which is seen every day. Arcturus is a star in the breast of Boötes. The sign of Boötes is called in Greek Ἀρκτοφύλαξ (*Arktophýlax*), that is, “guardian of the Bear” [ [Col. 0207] **Editorial note:** The glossator or copyist was mistaken: ἀρκτοφύλαξ means “guardian of the Bear,” not “guardian of the planets.”] For in Greek *phylax* means “guardian” in Latin.

**Stormy Orion.** Up to this point he has spoken of the signs that [Col. 0208B] are on the northern side of the zodiac; now he speaks of those that are on the southern side.

**The Little Dog.** The Little Dog is the star in the mouth of the Dog. Rising in July, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, it provokes excessive heat, diseases, and storms. It is otherwise called the Tongue of Sirius, that is, “of the Dog.” Hence those days are called the dog days.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—**Borrowing their light from the sun.** Pliny the Younger, on the praises of the sun: “He had made his own light for the other stars as well, brilliant, exceptional, observing everything and even hearing everything, as I see that Homer, the foremost of writers, was pleased to say of the ruler in a single passage.”

**Except those called planets, that is, wanderers.** They are not called wanderers because, with the spheres in which they are situated at rest, they roam loose and uncontrolled, or because their courses are not stable and their paths are not defined by fixed intervals; rather, they are so called because they do not maintain equal intervals of place either among themselves or with those that enter among them, and also because, according to the inclination of the zodiac, they are sometimes low and at other times raised toward the summit of the world.

[Col. 0208C] **Although we see little fires falling from the aether.** Beneath the sky and above the clouds, certain sudden fires are produced by motion. Some are driven toward the earth, while others are carried in a straight course in another direction; some people call these “flying stars.”

**But other stars are fertile in moisture dissolved into liquid.** This concerns the meanings and effects attributed to the planets and fixed stars; on these matters see Pontanus, Book III of *On Heavenly Things*.

**As the Little Pigs in the forehead of Taurus.** The Romans ineptly called these stars *suculae*, as though the Greek were ὑάδες ἀπὸ τῶν ὑῶν (*hyádes apo tōn hyōn*), that is, “from pigs” by diminutive formation, rather than ἀπὸ τοῦ ὕειν (*apo tou hyein*), “from raining.” See Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*.

**As the rising of the Kids and of Arcturus.** Understand “rising” as heliacal rising, that is, when they withdraw from the sun. The Kids are on the shoulders of the Charioteer. Arcturus follows close after the Great Bear. For their meanings, see the first *Georgic*.

[Col. 0208D] **Stormy Orion and the Little Dog.** Orion is a storm-bringing constellation when it sets and rises; it is the largest in the magnitude and number of its stars. See Aristotle, Book II of the *Meteorologica*. The Little Dog is the largest of all the fixed stars, in the mouth of the Great Dog. The Greeks call it σείριον (*seírion*), from “dryness”; others think that the Little Dog is meant, which the Greeks call προκύων (*prokýōn*). Cicero translated it as *antecanem* in Aratus:

> *Antecanis*, προκύων (*prokýōn*), which is called by the Greek name.]

The stars, borrowing their light from the sun, are said to revolve with the world, since they are fixed in one place, and, while the world does not stand still, to be carried along as wanderers, except those called planets, that is, wanderers. The brightness of the full moon and the eclipse of the sun prove that they are concealed by the coming of day and never [Col. 0207A] fall from the sky [Note: [Col. 0207A] A, “depart.”].

Although we see little fires falling from the aether, borne along by winds and imitating the wandering light of a star as fierce winds swiftly arise. Other stars [Note: [Col. 0208A] A, “are said to be”] are fertile in moisture dissolved into liquid [Note: [Col. 0208A] A adds “to exist”]; others are condensed into frost [Note: [Col. 0207A] Instead of “either . . . or,” A has “some . . . others”], or compressed into snow, or frozen into hail. Some produce warm air, others vapor, others dew, and others cold.

It is not only the wandering stars, such as Saturn, whose passages become rainy, but also certain fixed stars near the pole, when they have been impelled by the approach or rays of the wandering stars [Col. 0208A], such as the Little Pigs in the forehead of Taurus. For this reason the Greeks call them by the rainy name Hyades. Some even rise of their own accord and at appointed times, such as the rising of the Kids and of Arcturus, which rises around the Ides of September with stormy hail; and stormy Orion; and the Little Dog, which, burning with excessive heat, rises on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August.

## CHAPTER XII. On the course of the planets

[Note: [Col. 0208D]]

**BRIDEF. RAM. GLOSSAE.**—**Between heaven and earth, etc.** Pythagoras, the most perceptive of the Greek philosophers, calculated by geometric measurement the distance by which heaven is separated from earth. He said that the distance from earth to the moon was 125 stadia, from the moon to the sun twice that, and from there to the firmament three times that distance.

He also designated these intervals with musical terms. From earth to the moon, he said, there is a tone; from there to Mercury, a semitone; from Jupiter to Saturn, [Col. 0209A] a semitone; and from Saturn to the firmament, three semitones. Together these make six tones, by which the octave harmony is completed.

A tone therefore contains 15,625 miles. A semitone contains 7,812½ miles. From the moon to the sun there are two tones, that is, 31,250 miles; from there to Saturn there are two tones, that is, the same number of miles; from there to the zodiac, two and a half tones, that is, 39,062½ miles. The total contained in these seven tones is 875 stadia, that is, 109,875 miles.

**Always plunging to the right.** The heaven bends to the right, from east to west; the planets, on the contrary, revolve toward the left from west to east. Yet the speed of the heavenly sphere is so great that it impedes the course of the planets and carries them along with its own motion. Therefore they appear to us to travel toward the west, although they are always carried toward the east. They never abandon their course, even though they appear to be borne along with the course of the heavenly sphere.

What he says about the planets being carried to the left and the world to the right is understood in various ways. First, as follows: When a person turns his face toward the setting sun, his left side will be toward the southern region, against which all the planets travel from setting toward rising. Or the earth, which is called the world, may be imagined like a man lying on his back, whose head is toward the east and whose feet are toward the west. All the planets travel against his left hand. Alternatively, anything contrary is called “left.” Because, therefore, they travel contrary to the world, they are said to travel to the left.

**By the rays of the sun.** The power of the sun is so great that when the other wandering stars are struck by its rays, they sometimes become irregular, sometimes retrograde, and sometimes stationary; that is, sometimes they travel unevenly, sometimes they are driven backward, and sometimes they remain in one place.

They are called irregular because they cannot then travel on account of the sun. For the sun’s ray does not allow them to travel in a straight course through the breadth of the zodiac. They are called retrograde when the sun’s ray draws them backward. For example, if you see a planet appearing before the sun, the sun’s ray compels it to be seen after the sun.

They are stationary when the sun’s ray throws them upward. For we who are on earth, when we see a planet going upward, it appears to us to stand in one place, although it does not stand still but rises upward. This happens especially with the three planets that are above the sun, namely Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars.

[Col. 0210B] **JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—**Following a course contrary to the world, that is, to the left.** Which parts of heaven are right and left is discussed at length by Aristotle in Book II of *On the Heavens*. Astrologers assign the right to the west and the left to the east. For they turn their breast toward the south, where the motion of the stars observed by that discipline is swiftest. In this arrangement, the planets proceed from right to left, and this is their natural motion.

It is easy to detect this motion with the eyes, first in the moon. Observe the moon in the sky on any night, together with some fixed star near it; on the following day it will be clear that, across a great interval of the sky, the moon has passed beyond that star. The order of the planets and the manner in which they circle the zodiac may be seen in the diagram below.

Let there be a zodiacal circle on which A, B, C, and so on are inscribed, up to M, placed in the twelfth position. Beneath this circle, seven lower stars revolve among themselves in perpetual motion, though unequal and dissimilar, those nearer the center moving in the more rapid orbit; the center will be discussed in the following chapter.

Interposed between heaven and earth, seven stars hang at fixed intervals. They are called “wandering stars,” because they pursue a course contrary to that of the universe, namely, toward the left, while the universe itself is always rushing toward the right. Although they are raised by the universe’s constant revolution at immeasurable speed and carried toward the setting, they are nevertheless observed to move in the opposite direction along their respective paths, wandering now lower, now higher, because of the obliquity of the zodiac. But when obstructed by the sun’s rays, they become anomalous, retrograde, or stationary.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Their Order

[Note: [Col. 0211B]]

**BRIDEF. RAM. GLOSSES.**—The highest of the planets is the star of Saturn. Saturn’s star occupies the uppermost position among all the planets. Saturn is said to have been named from *saturitas* (“abundance”), because during a time of famine he nourished Italy from his own resources. For, according to the myth, driven from his kingdom by his son, he came to Italy and was received by Janus, king of Italy, to whom he showed the use of grain. Or Saturn was so called because he is “filled with years.” He is imagined as having habitually eaten the children born from him, because age consumes the spans of time and is insatiably filled with years that have passed. His star, Saturn, completes its course in thirty years—not because it is slower than the other planets, but because it is nearer the firmament and therefore travels through a wider circle than all the others, spending more time completing it. By nature it is cold, that is, frigid, because it is near the waters above the heavens; hence it is also depicted as an old man. Alternatively, it is between the temperate region of the firmament and the heat of the ether, just as the moon derives coldness from the air and heat from the ether.

**Jupiter.** Jupiter’s star is tempered by the cold of Saturn, situated above it, and by the heat of Mars, positioned below it. *Jovis* is either a nominative or a genitive form. Its nominative, however, is *Jupiter*: it is called Jupiter as though meaning “the father who helps” (*juvans pater*), that is, the one who provides for all; or as though “the father of rays” (*jubarum pater*), which are the locks or rays of the sun; or Jupiter, as though “father of fire” (*Zetos pater*). For among the Greeks fire is called ζῆτος or πῦρ.

**Mars.** Mars is called as though from *mors* (“death”), the god of war, because he brings about deaths. Hence among the Greeks he is also called Ares, that is, “strength.”

**The middle sun.** The sun is said to be “middle” because it is in the middle of the planets, having three planets above it and three below it. It is called the Sun because, once risen, it alone shines while all the other stars are obscured. And because it is in the middle among the planets, it is called *Mese*, from the name of the string that is likewise the middle string on a lyre.

**By a quarter.** A quarter is the fourth part of anything. A day together with its night consists of twenty-four hours; its quarter, that is, its fourth part, is six hours. What remains after the quarter has been subtracted is called *dodrans*, and the word is a compound: *dodrans* is as if from “with a quarter removed” (*dempto quadrante*).

**Venus.** Venus is called Venus at midnight, from the beauty of its light; in the morning it is called the Morning Star (*Lucifer*) because it brings light before sunrise, and it is called the Evening Star (*Vesper*) because it appears in the evening after sunset. Venus has this distinctive feature: it alone among the stars casts a shadow.

**“Farther from the sun by six and forty.”** When he says that Venus never stands more than forty-six degrees away, it must be understood that here a “degree” means the distance through which the sun advances in one day in any sign. Thus, in forty-six days the sun can reach the place of the sign in which Venus is now; but Venus can never advance so far ahead of the sun that, after forty-six days, the sun will not reach the place from which Venus has now departed. For Venus precedes the sun because it occupies the narrower circle below it. For example, if the sun is now in Aries and Venus in Taurus, that is, in the following sign, then after forty-six days—or, if not earlier, at least after that interval—the sun will arrive in Taurus, where Venus is now.

**Mercury.** The star of Mercury sometimes precedes and sometimes follows the sun. Since, because of the smallness of its circle, it has no room in which to range, it is always near the sun and is therefore depicted as scorched. Hence it is also said to be the messenger of the gods.

**“In the conjunction of the sun.”** In conjunction, that is, in passage—as though he were saying: when the moon is at the ninth or thirtieth [day], it does not appear because it is positioned opposite the sun and is obscured by the sun’s brightness. Astronomers call this a conjunction.

**“They are hidden,” etc.** We understand these occultations in two ways. First, when each planet travels through the region of another, as Mars does through Saturn’s region. They cannot be distinguished, because they appear as though they were a single star. In the second way, they are hidden during the day: for throughout so many days they rise during the day and hold their circles beneath the earth at night, and therefore are not seen by human beings. It was said above that the planets are hidden when they hold their circles beneath the earth during the night; now they are again said to be hidden when, accompanying the sun, they lie concealed by its brightness. This occultation occurs as long as they are within eleven degrees of the sun. After they have passed eleven degrees, they begin to be seen.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—They are hidden while traveling with the sun. Astronomers call this hiding the heliacal setting, that is, the solar setting. For, just as rising is of two kinds, true and apparent, so is setting. The true setting is produced by the revolution of the universe; by it, within twenty-four hours, every star among those not always visible rises and sets. The apparent setting is this concealment of the stars, which is called setting. For the sun, because of the majesty of its light, obscures all the fixed stars that are not separated from it in every direction by fifteen degrees. It covers the larger planets when they are within eight degrees and the smaller when they are within ten degrees. As long as these stars are entangled in the sun’s rays and cannot be seen, astronomers call them *hypauga* [Greek ὑπάυγα, “under the rays”]. Such risings and settings of the fixed stars occur at fixed times; hence poets and writers on agriculture derive from them the division of the seasons. The wandering stars, because of their varying motions, do not produce heliacal risings and settings on fixed days.

There are certain passages in this book and the next that have been explained in old commentaries by an unknown author. Since they had been assigned to these chapters in an ancient copy, I transferred them here word for word as they were written there—both because of the copy’s antiquity, which possesses a certain venerability in itself, and because of their learning—adding the title “Old Commentary” so that our material would be distinguished from theirs. What follows, therefore, refers to the figure just mentioned.

**OLD COMMENTARY.** According to the order in which they are arranged here in the figure, the twelve signs of the zodiac rise in alphabetical order. The sun and moon follow the order backward from Aries; for this reason they are called ὑστεροληπτικά (“moving afterward” or “following behind”). The remaining planets can move both forward and backward.

**[Col. 0213D] Square formula.**

The rising of these twelve signs at any hour of day or night can be clearly determined if, beginning from the Kalends of October, the hours of the days and nights are added up to the hour that one has selected. Let their sum be measured by twenty-four, and divide whatever exceeds that number, as the square formula below instructs.

Since, from whatever sign is rising in the east, the seventh sign always sets, and from the west the seventh always rises, each of the two middle signs—that is, the fourth—is said to be the center.

**Which signs set when these signs rise**

The highest of the planets is the star of Saturn, cold by nature, completing the zodiacal course in thirty years. Next is Jupiter, temperate, in twelve years. Third is Mars, hot, in two years. The middle [Note: [Col. 0211] A adds *est*, “is.”] sun completes its course in 365 days and a quarter. [Col. 0212A] Beneath the sun is Venus, also called Lucifer and Vesper, [Note: [Col. 0211] A reads “348.”] completing its course in 347 days and never [Note: [Col. 0211] A reads “not remaining away.”] standing more than forty-six degrees from the sun. Next to it is the star of Mercury, completing its swifter orbit in nine days, shining now before sunrise and now after sunset, never more than twenty-two degrees distant from the sun. Last is the moon, completing the zodiacal course in twenty-seven days and one third of a day; then, remaining in conjunction with the sun, it is not visible in the sky for two days. The star of Saturn and that of Mars are hidden for as many as 170 days; Jupiter for thirty-six days, or at least ten days fewer; Venus for sixty-eight days, or at least fifty-two; Mercury for thirteen days, or at most eighteen. They are hidden while traveling with the sun, [Col. 0214A] never more than eleven degrees away [Note: [Col. 0213A] A, B read “in degrees”]; sometimes, however, they emerge even at seven degrees.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Their Apsides

[Note: [Col. 0215A]]

**BRIDEF. RAM. GLOSSES.**—**The circles of the planets.** The planets have their own proper circles, in addition to those possessed by the universe. They are different circles because they differ not merely in name from the circles of the universe—such as the parallels, the colures, the zodiac, the Milky Way, and the horizon. For those circles remain equal even in their position. The circles of the universe, that is, of the sphere of heaven—the zodiac and the others—always revolve through equal distances, and therefore the earth is always their center, that is, their middle. The planets, however, do not always maintain a straight order, nor do they always revolve in the same way, but wander. Sometimes they approach the earth, sometimes they withdraw from it, as will appear below; therefore they have circles different from those of the universe.

**“By the principle of the compass.”** He says that the circles of the universe are constituted according to the principle of the compass because each has its own center and its own circle, equal as though formed with a compass; or “by the principle of the compass” because, although they differ in their position, they are alike in this respect. From this it follows that the circles of the universe and the circles of the planets have both similarity and difference. They are similar because all are constituted according to the principle of the compass; they differ because the circles of the planets do not approach the earth at equal distances, as the circles of the universe do.

**Apsides.** The circles of the planets are called *apsides*, a Greek term, because *apsis* in Greek means “circle” in Latin. Hence the term remained in use for the semicircular structures—*apsides*—found in certain churches, where the altar is located; and from this, by an improper extension, some also call the entire area beside the altar the *apsis* of the church. Here *apsidas* is the Greek accusative. Some, however, say that *apsis* means “side,” and therefore derive *parapsis* from “equal sides of an apsis.” Others oppose them, saying that *apsis* is a Greek noun of the third declension and therefore cannot have *absidis* as its ablative. These latter say that *parapsis* means a cheap vessel, as though from *paropsis*, from *obsonium* (“food”), because all kinds of food are served in it.

**“Toward the center of the earth.”** When Saturn is in Scorpio and Jupiter in Virgo, they are higher above the earth; likewise, when the other planets are in these signs, they are higher above the center of the earth. The higher they are lifted toward heaven, the lower they are depressed toward the earth. This is what is meant by “lowest and nearest to the center of the earth.”

**“And thus it happens,” etc.** It does not happen quite in this way; rather, by one and the same unchanging motion, they traverse a shorter arc more quickly and a longer one more slowly.

**“Individually.”** Individually, that is, undivided. For there can be no variation within a single thing.

**“Drawn down.”** “Drawn down,” that is, proceeding from the highest or most elevated part of the circles. Properly speaking, an *apsis* is the broader shell of a building.

**“Especially in the moon’s elevations.”** He says that what was stated above is especially demonstrated by the moon’s elevations because, although this can also be recognized in other signs, it is not so evident. Apart from the fact that the moon appears in the higher signs, it also rises to greater heights within its own circle. For just as it wanders widely here and there through the breadth of the zodiac, so it also wanders upward by ascending; and for that reason its motion is somewhat diminished when it ascends while wandering in this way. This is demonstrated as follows: when we calculate that the moon is sometimes new, we still cannot see it. What holds it back then except the ascent that occurs as it wanders within its own circle? At times it is visible even before we calculate the new moon; this is caused by its passage through the lower parts of its circle.

**INC. AUCT. GLOSSES.**—Each planet has its own circles, which the Greeks call *apsides* in the stars. The circles of the planets are called *apsides*, a Greek term. But because the moon’s circle—now near heaven, now adjoining the mountains—sometimes enters the region of the shadow and causes an eclipse, and sometimes climbs into the ether and passes beyond the shadow, it does not suffer a defect, because it is illuminated by the sun. The comparison is with the spokes of wheels and their common motion. A likeness may be drawn from ants if channels are cut into the spokes of a wheel and the ants run along them: although they move with the same motion and at the same speed, when one has completed its course—or has not completed it—the others do not necessarily do likewise.

Their motion increases as long as they are near the earth, because they complete their course more rapidly when they are close to the earth. “Of the moon”—that is, the moon, which appears slower, as though it had rather begun to ascend. “Elevations,” that is, ascents. “Especially”—that is, although this can also be recognized in the other signs. Apart from the fact that the moon ascends in the higher signs, it also ascends to greater heights within its own circle. Just as it wanders widely here and there through the breadth of the zodiac, so it also wanders upward by ascending; and for that reason its motion is somewhat diminished when it ascends while wandering in this way. This is demonstrated as follows: when we calculate that the moon is sometimes new, we still cannot see it. What holds it back then except the ascent that occurs as it wanders within its own circle? At times it is visible even before we calculate the new moon; this is caused by its passage through the lower parts of its circle, which appears slower, as though it had rather begun to ascend. “We have excerpted,” that is, “we have drawn out.”

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.** Each planet has its own circles, which the Greeks call *apsides* in the stars. We have already established that each planet possesses its own orbit, into which it is fixed and in which, through the motion of the universe and through the motion of its own orbit—that is, its proper motion—it determines its courses. Thus the moon has its own orbit, whose beginning lies at the boundary between the elemental world and the end of the ether, where the sphere of Mercury begins.

It must be observed, especially for understanding Pliny’s second book, that the sphere of each planet is divided into circles, at least three in number. The highest has, in its outer circumference, the same center as the universe, namely A B C D, but in its inner circumference it is eccentric, with a center removed from the earth, namely F. The lowest, on the contrary, has its inner circle concentric with the universe, with E as its center, while its outer circle is eccentric, with F as its center. These circles have in common an inequality of parts, so that they gradually taper from broad to narrow. Between them is a middle orbit which, in relation to the outer and inner circles, does not have the same center as the universe. It is entirely eccentric, though its motion is uniform.

In the sphere of every planet, this orbit has a star fixed in its middle. As the orbit itself is carried around by its own motion, the planet is sometimes higher above the earth and at other times nearer. For example, the moon is once each month in the lowest part of its heaven, then in the middle, and finally in the highest; this is also evident to the eye, since it appears at one time larger and at another smaller even when full, according as it is in the higher or lower part of its orbit.

The curved part of the highest circle is called its *apsis*, where thickness gives way to thinness; it is the highest apsis, for this curvature is always highest above the earth. The narrower part of the lowest circle is called the lowest apsis, for this part is always closest to the earth. *Apsis* signifies the curvature of such a circle. More recent writers, using a foreign term, call the highest apsis the *auge*, and its opposite the lowest *auge*. To make this clear to those inexperienced in astronomy, I have inserted here the following geometrical demonstration.

Let the sphere of any planet, such as the sun, A B C D E, be divided into three parts. The uppermost part, G H, has, in its outer circumference—namely A B C D—the same center as the universe, E; but its inner circumference, G H, has another center, removed from the earth, namely F. The lowest part, I, has E, the center of the universe, as its inner center, but F as its outer center. The middle circle, G, although equal in circumference to the orbit, has F as its center in relation to both the outer and inner circles.

Of these three, the middle one carries a star fixed in it according to the order of the signs, beginning at Aries and proceeding through the following signs. As this circle advances from A toward B, the star fixed in this orbit, namely G, must be higher above the earth when it is near the sign A; but it is nearer when, after traversing the space A B, it reaches H.

**“And others different from the universe.”** We have restored this passage from the reading of Pliny, from whose work this chapter was taken almost word for word, although it was corrupted in many places through the carelessness of copyists. The meaning of the sentence is this: the planets have particular circles whose uppermost and lowest parts are not equally distant from the earth and from the poles of the universe. The earth is indeed the center of the universe, but not of these eccentric circles.

These words therefore contain a definition of the circles that astronomers call deferents. To understand this more clearly, look again at the diagram described above. The poles are what Pliny calls the vertices: one is A and the other B. The center E is the earth, which is the center of heaven and of the zodiac—that is, of the eighth sphere and of all the lower spheres. The eccentric circle G has another center, namely F, and other poles. These poles will be the extremities of the line which, drawn through the center F, divides the eccentric into four equal parts together with line A D, just as line C B divides the outer circumference into four parts together with line A D, as the diagram above makes clear.

All these matters are established by the principle of the compass, which is always certain. I have omitted the more extended discussion in favor of linear demonstrations. For these things cannot be adequately explained in words; they are submitted to the eyes through compass drawings, whose rationale is certain and evident. It is like the principles called lemmas in geometry: before a diagram is supplied, they are often ambiguous to those inexperienced in the discipline, but once the lines have been drawn, every doubt disappears.

Thus the apsides of each planet arise from its own center. The apsides of the planets are not all situated beneath the same degrees of the signs, nor do they remain perpetually beneath the same ones. Thus, in Pliny’s time, the sun’s apsis was in the middle degrees of Gemini; in our time it is in the second degree of Cancer. For, by their motion according to the order of the signs, they move out of those eccentric circles of unequal thickness from A toward B and onward to C D. Consequently, the highest apsis, which lies beneath the thin portion of the highest orbit, is not perpetually beneath the same degrees of the zodiac. This will become evident from the demonstrations.

We found at this point an old commentary with many diagrams. It plainly appears to be by some ancient writer, and I do not even know whether the author may have been Greek, since the matter is handled with Greek letters. To avoid doing violence to the copy and its antiquity, I have appended it word for word as I found it.

**OLD COMMENTARY.** The seven spheres in which the seven planets travel are subordinate to the sphere called *aplanes*, that is, the heaven. They are also enclosed by an outer sphere that contains them internally; and each is far removed both from heaven and from the others. Each of these wandering bodies, although it may appear to be carried along mixed with the stars of the signs of the zodiac, is never actually mingled with any of them by adhering to them; rather, it is said to be in that sign which lies above the vertex of the wandering sphere.

Some maintain that the planets are carried in eccentric spheres—that is, spheres which contain the earth within themselves, though not as their center. Others prefer epicycles, that is, globes separated from the earth and not suspended over it.

Let the solstitial eccentric circle be Θ Ξ Η Κ, and let it have a point beneath E Z, immediately circumscribing it, namely where M is. Let this circle be divided into 365 parts and one quarter of a part. In order to equalize these parts, the circumference H K will contain ninety-four parts; Z H, ninety-two; H K, eighty-four and three hours; and K E, ninety parts and three hours. It is therefore necessary that, when the sun approaches E, it should appear to us looking from Θ—that is, from the earth—as though it were above A, although that region is not the summit of the solstitial circle but of the zodiac, which is much higher and which our sight cannot reach.

Proceeding uniformly along the circumference E Z, which is larger than the other three circles by several portions, as is required by the number of days, it will appear, when it reaches Z, to have reached B, since it has completed the larger circumference. Again, after traversing the circumference Z H, it is believed to have reached Γ after traversing A B. Likewise, while it passes from H to K, it appears to pass from Γ to A. Similarly, while it traverses the circumference K E, it passes from Δ to A, that is, to another summit of the zodiacal circle.

If the two points of the solstitial eccentric and the zodiacal circle are joined—that is, M Θ—and if the line N Ξ is drawn through them, then, since E Z H K has M as its midpoint, the lines N M and M Ξ will be equal. Therefore N M is larger than H Θ, and consequently N Θ is much larger than Θ Ξ. When the sun is carried through N, A Θ—that is, the earth—appears to us from a distance smaller and slower; but when it is carried through Ξ, being nearer the earth, it is thought larger and faster, since in the former position it is believed to be at the fifth and a half degree of Gemini, and in the latter at the fifth and a half degree of Sagittarius.

**[Col. 0219A] (That the solar circle is eccentric to the earth.)**

If, as some think, the sun is carried through epicyclic globes, we shall nevertheless demonstrate from the form of the epicycles that it completes its annual courses with measured and regulated steps. For an epicycle is a globe that is carried around another circle.

Let there be a zodiacal circle delimited by A B Γ Δ; let the solstitial [circle], excluding the zodiacal circle’s point E Ξ H K [the lettering is uncertain], be understood as an epicycle having its own point M; and, with Θ as its center and M as its interval, let the circle M O N Ξ be described.

The epicycle is therefore carried with the universe from east to west by the daily rotation. Yet it is naturally carried contrary to the course of the universe, and the sun, positioned in that same epicycle, moves according to the revolution of the whole universe. Thus the sun, proceeding in its epicycle with a motion contrary to that of the universe through the circle M O N Ξ, completes its course in the space of a year.

For when the epicycle has proceeded from M to the letter O, it will have traversed a quarter of the universe, and at that time the sun will move from E to Ξ. The sun will therefore be where the letter O is; yet, to us observing from the earth, that is, from Θ, with our line of sight directed straight ahead, it appears to be at the marked point B. Thus, when the epicycle again proceeds from O to N, the sun proceeds from K to H, although it appears to be where Γ is. Again, the same epicycle passes from N to Ξ, and the sun from H to Z, while it appears to us to be at Δ. Finally, the same epicycle traverses the remaining quarter from Ξ to M, and the sun, represented as moving from Z to E, will after a year appear to be in its proper place, where A is; and it will be thought to have traversed the path of the zodiacal circle.

From this it is also clear that, according to the motion of the epicycle, things appear to us differently from the way they actually occur. The sun appears slower and smaller when it is, as it were, in Gemini, but largest and fastest when it is, as it were, in Sagittarius. In the sun’s circuit the greatest distance is from Θ to E, that is, from the earth to the highest boundary of the solstitial epicycle; the smallest is to its lowest boundary.

It remains to investigate why the planets sometimes stand still, sometimes advance, and sometimes move backward through particular signs of the zodiac.

**[Col. 0220A] (On the sun’s epicycle.)**

Let there be a zodiacal circle A B Γ Δ whose point is Θ. Let the epicycle of any wandering star be E Z H, whose point is the letter M, through which, as through its own axis, the same epicycle is carried from east to west together with the star placed within it.

From Θ let two oblique lines also be drawn, touching the extreme circumferences of the epicycle on either side: Θ Z B and Θ H Δ. Through the point M of the epicycle let the line Θ M A be drawn upward.

Therefore, when the star is at Z, it will be thought to be at B; and when it is at H, it will be judged to be at Δ. When it advances from Z to E, it is thought to have advanced from B to A, that is, toward the preceding signs. For when it withdraws a considerable distance from A Z, it appears to remain for a long time in the same place, as though it were at B.

Mathematicians, however, think that the universe and all the stars are carried around uniformly according to their nature. Therefore, when the star is at H, it will appear to be near Δ; and when it has traversed the circumference H E, it will be believed to have traversed the circumference Δ A of the zodiacal sphere according to the order of the following signs. Thus the apparent stations, advances, and retrogressions become clear. Having explained these, let us proceed to the conjunctions, that is, the encounters of the wandering stars.

**[Col. 0220C] (On the epicycle of the planets.)**

The sphere called *aplanes* has beneath it the seven spheres of the planets. When one of the planets nearer to us is placed before our sight—which naturally extends in a straight line—so that the higher planet cannot be seen, a sudden obscuration of that higher planet occurs, followed afterward by a sudden reappearance.

Finally, the moon, and no other lower star placed opposite a higher one, makes the higher star accessible to our sight. Nor is this surprising, since some planets obscure others not only by opposition but also by nearness. For the moon, which is lowest of all, is obscured—not by a star, but by the terrestrial shadow—when it is diametrically distant from the sun. Thus, if you establish two plane or level orbits opposite one another, one belonging to the sun and one to the moon, and arrange them in such a direct position that a line—called a diameter—passes through the center of each, the moon sometimes takes the sun away from our eyes, although it is smaller; at other times the moon’s light is extinguished by the earth’s obstruction. If it deviates even by half a moment, however, it escapes the eclipse; it never suffers an eclipse if it shifts northward or southward away from the diameter.

The reason why a solar eclipse does not occur over the entire earth at one moment of a single day is as follows: since the moon is smaller and placed before the sun, if it deprives one region of its light, it cannot deprive another, as the illustration demonstrates.

**[Col. 0221B] (On the useful figure of a solar eclipse.)**

The moon, according to some, is smaller than the earth; according to others, larger; according to still others, equal to it. But if the illuminating fire is equal in size to the body from which the shadows proceed, the shadows themselves will be produced in the form of a cylinder. Let the body bringing light be A B, and let the body illuminated be Γ Δ; let both likewise be equal and spherical. It is clear that one ray, A Γ, and the other, B Δ, are straight, raised alongside one another, and placed at an equal distance, rightly so because the diameter A B is equal to the diameter seen.

Let these rays extend upward. Then A Γ E will be a ray at an equal distance from the ray B Δ Z, maintaining equal firmness—that is, without inclination. However far they may extend, their summits, namely E and Z, will never meet.

**[Col. 0222B] (On a lunar eclipse.)**

But if the illuminating body is smaller, such as H Θ, and the illuminated body is larger, such as K A, with the diameters Γ Δ, it is clear that the shadow of the sphere K A—namely K M and A N—will be formed in the shape of a basket, whose form will increase without limit. For since the diameter K A is larger than the diameter H Θ, both the ray H K M and the ray Θ A N, extended without limit, will produce an increasingly broader shadow the farther they extend.

**(On the eclipse of all the planets.)**

The illuminating sphere must always be larger than the bodies that are illuminated. If, therefore, the body bringing the light is greater in size, such as Ξ Ο, and the body illuminated is smaller, such as Π Ρ, with both spherical, the shadow is produced in the form of a cone, narrowing to a point. The rays Ξ Π and Ο Ρ extend upward and meet one another at the point marked C. This happens because the diameter Π Ρ is smaller than the diameter Ξ Ο; therefore the form of the shadow will be cone-shaped.

Since Hipparchus teaches that the sun is greater in size than the earth by 880 parts, and that the earth is in turn twenty-seven times greater than the moon, and that the sun is much higher than the moon, it is evident that the earth’s shadow is formed in the likeness of a cone. For the sun’s rays Ξ Π and Ο Ρ narrow toward the diameter of the earth, Π Ρ, while illuminating everything to the right and left. The earth, placed before the sun’s light, surrounded by the light flowing around it, produces a shadow that advances from the width of its diameter into narrowness and becomes thinner all the way to the farthest end of its tapering.

When the nocturnal moon, diametrically distant from the sun, enters this shadow, it is plunged into darkness. But when the diametrical line does not pass through the centers of the sun and moon, the moon suffers no obscuration, escaping the earth’s shadow.

The center is the middle point of a circle, equally distant in every direction from the intervals of the line drawn around it. Since several transverse lines can be drawn in the same circle from one side to the other, no line is ever called a diameter except that single line which, dividing the circle equally, passes straight through its central midpoint.

**(On the moon, sun, and earth.)**

There are two parts of the essence which Plato calls a series. For, he says, God divided neither matter nor body, but—as when someone divides the straight line A B lengthwise and makes a chi [Greek χ] from the two segments, Γ Δ Ε Ζ—.

[Col. 0225A] It finally bends back upon itself and forms two interlinked circles, Η Θ Κ Α and Η Μ Κ Ν. These it binds within yet another outer circle, whose motion is always reversed and uniform, as is that of the outermost sphere (*aplanos*), which, rising from the right-hand side of the world, is likewise carried along.

*(On the interlinking of two circles from one essence.)*

For the demonstration of the Sun and Venus there will be one straight line from the middle of the earth, indicating the Sun by the letter Χ; and two other straight lines, likewise to the right and left: on the one hand, lines separated from the Sun by 50 minutes, and from one another by 100 minutes—the right-hand line extending toward the east through Χ and Α, the left-hand one toward the west through Χ and Γ. Let the zodiacal circle also be Α Β Γ, whose several points are separated from one another by 50 minutes. When the Sun is at Β and, on the line Χ Β, the Sun’s position is at the letter Κ, this line, namely Χ Γ, sets earlier and rises earlier than the Sun; the other, Χ Α, sets later and rises later. It is therefore necessary that the letter Α indicate Hesperus after sunset, and Γ Lucifer before sunrise.

*(On the Sun and Venus.)*

[Col. 0226A] Plato and others, however, assert that the globe of Lucifer is somewhat higher than the Sun’s, bounded by Α Ε Ζ Η, with Α touching the line through the letter Ε and Κ Γ touching the line through Η. Thus, when Lucifer is at Ε, he will appear to be at Α; and when he is at Η, he will be thought to be at Ε. But when he is beside Δ, there is no doubt that he appears higher than the Sun when near it; and when he is at Ζ, lower, nearer the earth.

Now one must observe that, whether Lucifer withdraws toward the east or toward the west, he returns after approximately 584 days to the point from which he had previously departed; and that he traverses Η Δ Ε in 445 days, as the larger circuit, while he completes the smaller and lower circuit in the remaining 133 days.

*(Likewise on the Sun and Venus.)*

When, with the fixed pivot of a compass pressed down or loosened, whether accidentally or by our intention, circles are drawn such that the end of the line being traced not only reaches its starting point but, deviating from the proper straight course, repeatedly forms circles narrower or wider than the line already traced, we call this kind of circle a spiral, an *acanthus*, or a volute. Since, then, the outermost sphere carries the planets in this way by its daily revolution, so that it does not permit them to be represented in the same place or, as it were, in the seat from which they had advanced, [Col. 0227A] they are rightly said to revolve in a spiral and, as it were, in a winding counter-volute, because of their irregular and unequal revolution—as when any wandering star is in the sign Aries and is carried toward the preceding signs, Pisces and Aquarius. Conversely, if the carrying motion is weaker, it will withdraw from Aries toward the succeeding signs, Taurus, [Col. 0228A] Gemini, and Cancer, in curving circuits that deviate from their origin and proper course.

*(On heliacal circuits.)*

This is the zodiac which the planets never traverse except in the manner prescribed above. Its length is 365 paces and its width 12, as you can also see on the lower wheel.

*(A rule for discovering in which sign the planets are.)*

[Col. 0227A] The Greeks call these circuits *heliacal*, from the Sun, whose power the planets yield to. Two wheels remain, [Col. 0228A] one of which displays the planets’ irregular circuits beyond the apsides; [Col. 0229A] the other, how many degrees the wandering planets occupy in the zodiac.

*(On the apsides of the planets.)*

*(On the planets’ movement through the zodiac.)*

][Col. 0215A]

Each planet has its own circles, which [Col. 0216A] the Greeks call *apsides* in the stars, and which are different from the circle of the world, since the earth, from the two points which they called the poles, is the center of the heavens and also of the zodiac, which is situated obliquely between them. [Col. 0217A] All these things are established by the unfailing principles of the compass. Thus the apsides of each planet arise from a different center, and therefore they have different spheres [Col. 0218A] and dissimilar motions. Since the inner apsides must necessarily be shorter, the highest apsides from the center of the earth are: for Saturn, in Scorpio; for Jupiter, in Virgo; for Mars, in Leo; for the Sun, in Gemini; for Venus, in Sagittarius; for Mercury, in Capricorn; [Col. 0219A] and for the Moon, in Taurus—in each case at the middle point of the sign. Conversely, they are lowest and nearest to the center of the earth; [Col. 0221A] [Note: [Col. 0221A] A reads “thus … is made.”] and so it happens that they appear to move more slowly when they are carried along the highest circuit—not because their natural motions, which are fixed and individual for each of them, are accelerated or retarded, [Col. 0224A] but because the lines drawn from the highest apsis must be narrowed toward the center, just as the spokes in wheels are; [Col. 0225A] and the same motion is perceived as greater or smaller according to its proximity to the center. [Note: [Col. 0227A] A reads “Motion.”] Their motion is increased as long as they are near the earth, and when they withdraw into the heights it is diminished; this is demonstrated especially by the Moon’s elevations. If you wish to know more fully about these matters, read Pliny the Second, from whom we have also excerpted this material.

CHAPTER XV. Why they change colors.

[Note: [Col. 0229A]

BRIDEP. RAM. GLOSSES.—“Radiant Mercury.” The star Mercury is fire-emitting, as he says, because few people have seen it.

[Col. 0231C] “Into whose atmosphere,” etc. For example, if the star of Jupiter should enter Saturn’s atmosphere, it is uncertain whether it belongs to Jupiter or to Saturn; and the same happens with the other planets. When they ascend to higher circles, they change colors, because when they seek the higher regions of their own circle, they enter the lower parts of the superior sign. The same must be understood of their descent.

“Black into darkness.” He says that the Sun produces black darkness because by its brightness the other planets are deprived of their light. He also means the junctions of the apsides, at which the planets meet, where their circles converge: one of them is darkened there, and they appear, as it were, to be a single star. He also means the outermost orbits, that is, the higher and farthest parts of the circles, because the higher they are, the more they are darkened. Thus these three things produce black darkness.

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—“Rejoicing Lucifer.” Pliny reads *candens* (“glowing”), and I think that should be read here as well.

[Col. 0231D] “Shining Vesper.” In Pliny it is *vesper refulgens* (“the gleaming evening star”).

“Afterward shining.” This can indeed be read with some sense; but in Pliny it is *postea radians* (“afterward radiant”).

“Into whose atmosphere, Venus.” In place of *aerea* I suspect that *aera* should be read, for the atmosphere of any planet is meant, such as Jupiter’s atmosphere and Saturn’s atmosphere.

“The Sun and the junctions of the apsides.” The junctions are the circles called καταβιβάζων καὶ ἀναβιβάζων, that is, the head and tail of the dragon, where eclipses of the Moon and Sun occur.]

[Col. 0230A]

Each has its own color: Saturn is white, [Col. 0231A] Jupiter bright, Mars fiery, Lucifer joyful, Vesper shining, Mercury radiant, the Moon gentle, and the Sun fiery when it rises; afterward [Note: [Col. 0231] A reads “day comes.”] daylight. But the proportion of the heights modifies the colors, since they assume the appearance of those atmospheres [Note: [Col. 0231] C reads “that.”] into which they descend; and the passage of a foreign circle, approaching from either side, tints them: a colder circle produces pallor, a hotter one redness, a windy one a chill, while the Sun, the junctions of the apsides, and the outermost orbits produce black darkness.

CHAPTER XVI. On the zodiacal circle.

[Note: [Col. 0231D]

BRIDEF. RAM. GLOSSES.—“Zodiac or sign-bearer.” *Zodiacus* is Greek, *signifer* Latin. For *zoa* means animals, because they possess a living soul, which in Greek is called ζωή. Or it is called *zodiac* from the signs, because the figures of animals appear to be in it; these are called *zodia*. It is so named, according to Macrobius.

“Nor is anything else inhabited,” etc. Only the region beneath the zodiac is inhabited by human beings, since nothing in the world is inhabited except what lies beneath it. Hence Lucan says that Aethionia is uninhabitable unless it were touched by the outstretched foot of Taurus. The zodiac touches three zones: the solstitial, the equinoctial, and the winter zone. Two of these—the solstitial and the winter zones—are inhabited because of the moderation of the Sun, which runs through the zodiac.

“The rest are barren beneath the poles.” Two zones, extending from the northern pole to the zodiac and from the southern pole to the zodiac, are uninhabitable because of the cold, and therefore are barren.

“Only the star of Venus.” Venus is said to exceed the zodiac by two divisions toward the northern region and by two toward the southern, or by one toward the north and one toward the south.

“From these the star of Mercury.” Apart from Venus and the Moon, no other planet occupies as much space in the zodiac as Mercury. He alone wanders through eight divisions of it, while the others wander through fewer than eight. It should be noted that he calls the upper region the one from which the Moon, beginning its course, traverses the breadth of the zodiac in its wandering; and the lower region the one where Venus, beginning her course, exceeds it by two divisions both above and below.]

The zodiac, or sign-bearer, is an oblique circle consisting of twelve signs, through which the wandering stars are carried. Nothing on earth is inhabited except what lies beneath it; [Col. 0231B] the rest [Note: [Col. 0231] A, B, and C read *apolis* (“without cities”).] beneath the poles is barren. Only the star of Venus exceeds it by two divisions. The Moon also wanders through its entire breadth, but does not exceed it at all. Among these, the star of Mercury ranges most widely, though of the twelve divisions—for that is the total breadth—it traverses no more than eight; nor does it traverse these equally, but two in the middle, four above, and two below. The Sun then moves midway between two divisions, following an unequal, winding course like that of a dragon. The star of Mars occupies four middle divisions, Jupiter the middle one and two above it, and Saturn two, like the Sun.

CHAPTER XVII. On the twelve signs.

[Note: [Col. 0232D]

BRIDEF. RAM. GLOSSES.—“The twelve signs, whether from annual causes.” The signs are named either from annual events which naturally occur each year, or from the myths which the pagans handed down in written monuments, or from both. Aries, Taurus, and Gemini derive from myth alone; Cancer and Virgo from both; Pisces and Scorpio from nature; and the others from both.

They assign Aries to the month of March because of Ammonian Jupiter. The story is as follows. When Liber Pater was returning from the Indian war, the people began to be endangered by thirst.
