When he invoked Jupiter, a ram immediately appeared to them, standing in the sand. As they pursued it, it suddenly disappeared, and at the very place where it had appeared they found a spring. From this they understood that it had been Jupiter, and they called Jupiter Ammon, as though “of the sand,” because he had appeared in the sand. For *ammonia* in Greek means “sand” in Latin. For this reason too his image is depicted with ram’s horns—or else because his responses are uncertain and exceedingly obscure. Others assign to the month of March the ram by which Phrixus crossed the sea.

Taurus to April. Taurus is assigned to April because Jupiter was once transformed into a bull, supposedly on account of a girl named Europa. Out of love for her he changed into a bull, swam across the sea, and carried her away on his back; or because of the bull of Agenor, to kill which Hercules was sent by King Aristaeus.

Castor and Pollux to May. Castor and Pollux are called *Dioscuri* in Greek. They were, as the story goes, brothers devoted to one another, so much so that they neither contended for supremacy nor did anything without common deliberation. They were born from Leda, daughter of Theseus, and were brothers of Helen, whom Paris—also called Alexander—carried off. Because of their courage they are assigned to May, when the strengthened seeds burst forth into leaves; or because wars occur at that time, since one of them redeemed his brother’s death with his own life.

Cancer to June. The crab is a six-footed animal which, when touched, moves sideways in either direction. It suits June because, after completing its upper course, it seeks the lower. Pliny says in the *Natural History* that around the summer solstice—that is, when the Sun passes through that part of the sign-bearer—the crab changes into a scorpion, leaves the waters, and seeks the land. Hence it seems probable that the sign in which the Sun remains when the crab changes into a scorpion is appropriately called Cancer. For just as a crab, driven by some cause, moves backward, so the Sun, when it has climbed the upper regions of the sign-bearer—that is, the eighth division, or, according to others, the fourth division—soon seems, as though repelled in some way, to return toward the south.

Leo … to July. Leo is a fiery animal, and in July the summer is hot; at that time the earth is known to dry out more intensely.

Libra to September. For just as the scales balance weights, so during this month the nights and days are equal.

They assign Scorpio and Sagittarius to October and November. Scorpio strikes from behind. Sagittarius is also depicted with a dart, and lightning falls in Spain and Italy during these months. Sagittarius is Chiron himself, the son of Saturn and Philyra; he is the Centaur. For when Saturn joined with Philyra, at the approach of his wife Ops, he changed himself into a horse; [Col. 0234A] and from this was born the Centaur, half man and half horse.

Capricorn to December. The first part of Capricorn is depicted in the likeness of a goat, in memory of Olenia, Jupiter’s nurse; the final part is depicted in the likeness [Col. 0234B] of a fish, because of the rainy character of that month. Its beginning is also hardened like a horn into ice.

Each sign has thirty divisions. There are thirty degrees in each of the twelve signs. Multiply thirty by twelve, and the result is 360 days; likewise multiply ten hours by twelve, and the result is 120 hours. Divide these by 24, and five days result. Again multiply half-hours by twelve, and the result is six hours, which complete one-quarter of a day; hence the leap day in the fourth year.

“Degrees.” A degree is the daily progress through twenty-four hours. One degree in the heavens amounts to forty stadia at the lesser measure, and seven hundred at the greater.

“Because the Sun traverses it in thirty days and ten and a half hours.” What he says about thirty is not strictly true, but plausible, since the Sun remains in the individual signs for varying and different intervals. In Gemini it travels for thirty days; conversely, it passes through Sagittarius in thirty-one days. [Col. 0234C] It likewise completes its course variously in the other signs. Hence it remains in no sign for exactly that interval—thirty days and ten and a half hours. Nevertheless, this is plausible because, if someone divides the entire cycle or sum of the year—that is, 365 days and six hours—into twelve equal parts according to the number of signs, he will find one-twelfth to consist of thirty days, ten hours, and half an hour.

“From the middle of the month.” But in January it begins to move and enter through their signs on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February. Each sign occupies half of one month and likewise half of the next, always beginning from the middle of the month.]

[Col. 0232A]

The twelve signs took their names either from annual causes or from the myths of the pagans. Thus they assign Aries to the month of March because of Ammonian Jupiter; hence they fashion ram’s horns on his image. Taurus is assigned to April because of the same Jupiter, who is fabled to have been transformed into a bull. Castor and Pollux are assigned to May because of their outstanding virtue. Cancer is assigned to June, when the Sun returns toward the lower regions, because a crab usually moves backward when provoked. Leo, which Hercules killed, is assigned to July because of the force of the heat. Virgo is assigned to August because the earth, scorched by the heat, produces nothing then. Libra is assigned to September because the day and night are equal. They assign Scorpio and Sagittarius, the latter deformed with horse’s legs, to October and November because of the lightning of those months. Capricorn is assigned to December because of Jupiter’s nurse, the goat, whose extremities are painted like those of a fish because the end of that month is rainy. Aquarius is assigned to January, and Pisces to February, because these are rainy months. Each sign has thirty degrees, divided into three decades, because the Sun traverses it in thirty days and ten and a half hours, beginning from the middle of the month, that is, always on the fifteenth day before the Kalends.

CHAPTER XVIII. On the Milky Circle.

[Note: [Col. 0234C]

BRIDEF. RAM. GLOSSES.—“The Milky Circle.” In Greek, the Milky Circle is *galactites*. They say that it is as broad as the zodiac. When Hercules had been placed beside the sleeping Juno to drink the divine milk, she awoke and realized that he was not her son, [Col. 0234D] and withdrew herself. On that occasion drops of milk scattered through the sky and created the Milky Circle. Macrobius says: “The Milky Circle surrounds the zodiac by an oblique curve, encircling it in such a way that it intersects it where the two tropical signs, Capricorn and Cancer, are carried.” It must nevertheless be understood that it does not intersect the zodiac in Cancer and Capricorn, but merely touches it in Gemini and Sagittarius. Again, Macrobius Theodosius says in his books *On the Dream of Scipio* that the Milky Circle shines more brightly than the other celestial regions because the solar rays, first coming almost to their natural seat, the sign-bearer, are reflected from it; when the reflected rays reach the Milky Circle, they make it shine and cause it to gleam more brightly than the rest. For example, just as a ray of the Sun falling upon the surface of water placed in a vessel, when reflected, shines more fully and brightly in some other place than in the water itself upon which it first fell, so in general the solar rays illuminate the Milky Circle, to which they arrive after being reflected from the sign-bearer, more than they illuminate the sign-bearer itself, toward which they first strive after issuing from the body of the Sun. Hence philosophers call the same Milky Circle the reflection of the sign-bearer.

“Except in the region of Sagittarius.” Here too the falsity of certain people is exposed: they say that the Milky Circle intersects the zodiac in Capricorn and Cancer, as was shown shortly above.

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—“The Milky Circle is a figure.” A description of the circle which the Greeks call *Galaxias*, from its milky whiteness. Aristotle, in his original wording, calls it γάλα (“milk”). The circle is also commonly known, since of all the things in the sphere it alone is perceived by the senses. Among poets it is the road by which the gods ascend and descend through heaven. Aristotle reports many opinions concerning the nature of this circle; to decide anything about them is not the concern of this place. I shall merely indicate through which stars it is drawn, since this is worth knowing and not unpleasant. It is drawn in the sphere from north toward south through the middle of the sign-bearer. Beginning in the north, it returns through the signs and the parts of the signs that follow: through the middle of Cassiopeia, along the right side of Perseus, along the left side of Erichthonius, and through both of his feet; then through the horns of Taurus, through all the feet of Gemini, along the right side of Orion, and through the back of the Dog; then [Col. 0235C] through the middle of the ship Argo, through the lowest feet of the Centaur, through the Altar, through the tail of Scorpio and the bow of Sagittarius, through the Eagle and the Arrow; from there through Cygnus and the head of Cepheus, back to Cassiopeia, from which we began.]

[Col. 0233A]

The Milky Circle is a brighter figure through the middle of the vault of heaven. People commonly say that it shines in this way because of the brightness of the Sun moving through it [Note: [Col. 0233A] A reads “to shine.”]; but this is vain, since it is never touched by the Sun except in the region of Sagittarius and Gemini, where the sign-bearer surrounds the white circle.

CHAPTER XIX. On the course and size of the Sun.

[Note: [Col. 0235C]

BRIDEF. RAM. GLOSSES.—“They say that the Sun’s fire is nourished by water.” The poets say that the Sun, wearied by its daytime course, sinks into the Ocean and remains there throughout the night, until in the morning it appears brighter, as though restored and refreshed. After rains it also seems to emit a more brilliant light. For this reason the boundless Ocean is naturally placed beneath the equinoctial circle, so that it may always nourish and feed the Sun, running on the equinoctial circle or close to it on either side, with an abundance of water, and restrain its excessive heat with the coldness of the waters.

“And much larger than the Moon.” They say that the body of the Sun exceeds the Moon threefold in size, while the Moon is larger than the earth. Hence some ask why the earth is said to obscure the Moon, if the Moon is three times larger, when the Moon falls into the earth’s shadow or even descends toward its lower regions. This happens because the shadow is affirmed to be three times larger than its body.

“With varying course.” They also say that the Sun moves by itself and does not turn with the universe. For if the Sun remained fixed in the heavens like the stars, all days and nights would be equal.

“The tempering of the atmosphere.” When the Sun rises from the equinoctial region toward Cancer, it gives summer to the people who live between the solstitial and northern regions. When it descends from Cancer to the equinoctial Libra, it produces autumn. When it withdraws to the winter line, winter is established, because once the heat has been removed, torpor invades. Again, when it rises from the winter Capricorn to the equinoctial Aries, spring returns; from there summer’s burning heat appears once more in Cancer.

[Col. 0236A] “Another region would be heat,” etc. For example, if the Sun were always in the south, the earth would be scorched by its heat and Scythia would perish from cold. Therefore God established different courses for the Sun, as well as different places and seasons, lest, if it always remained in the same places, it should quickly be consumed by its daily vapor.]

[Col. 0234A]

They say that the Sun’s fire is nourished by water and that it is much larger than the Moon; but the Moon is larger than the earth, and therefore it appears to all [Note: [Col. 0234A] A reads “of the same.”] to be of a single magnitude. What appears to us to be about a cubit in size is made so by the immense height and distance; otherwise it appears larger when rising to the Indians and larger when setting to the Britons. Although it is fiery by nature, it also increases its heat through its great motion. With varying course it divides days and months, seasons and years, and by approaching or withdrawing it distributes the tempering of the atmosphere according to the seasons, lest, if it always remained in the same places, heat should consume one region and cold another.

CHAPTER XX. On the nature and position of the Moon.

[Note: [Col. 0236B]

BRIDEF. RAM. GLOSSES.—“Illuminated by the Sun.” According to Martianus, the Moon is not illuminated by itself but by the Sun. Just as a mirror has neither brightness nor an image from itself, yet receives light and an image from things placed outside it, so the Moon, when it withdraws from the Sun, is gradually illuminated by it; then it is said to grow. But when it approaches the Sun after the fifteenth day, it is gradually darkened until it is wholly obscured by its nearness to the Sun; then it is said to diminish, although its body never actually diminishes or grows.

“Seen lying on its back.” It is asked why, when the day is growing, the new Moon appears supine, but when the day is declining, not prone but upright, when it ought to appear prone in the decline just as it appears supine in the increase of light. The explanation is as follows. As the day grows, the Moon is naturally higher than the Sun, and therefore the Sun illuminates the upper surface of the Moon situated above it and makes it supine. But when the day declines, the Sun and the new Moon are found to be at the same altitude according to their natural position; consequently the Sun does not light the Moon from below, but from the side, and therefore makes it upright.

“High when the Sun is low.” When the Sun travels through the southern circles, which are lower, in winter, the Moon traverses the northern circles, which are higher; then it is higher than the Sun and therefore lies supine, with its horns turned upward like a ship, because it is lit from its lower side, the side facing the Sun. Again, when the Sun moves through the northern circles, the Moon seeks the southern ones. Since it is then lower than the Sun, it is illuminated from its upper side, the side facing the Sun, and has its horns turned toward the earth and toward the northern circles. For example, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, the days are still growing. If the Moon is illuminated in Aries, it will quickly pass into Taurus, as though it were higher than the Sun with respect to the sign-bearer.

A *dodrans* is what remains of anything after a quarter, or fourth part, has been removed. An hour consists of twelve unciae and contains forty moments. Of those forty moments take thirty, since that is a dodrans, and leave ten, since that is a quarter. Again divide those forty moments by twelve, so that from them you may find the semunciae mentioned above. In the first division you understood a dodrans as four parts: forty moments divided by twelve three times yield thirty-six, with four remaining. From those thirty-six take three moments, since that is their twelfth part; and from the four that remain take a third of one moment. For if you reduce one to twelve, three moments become a portion of those forty moments. Hence a third of one moment is one uncia, since it is the twelfth part of that group of forty. Again divide that uncia in half; the result is one moment and a half and a sixth, that is, one-sixth of a moment. This is the semuncia of which he said that the Moon increases or decreases daily by dodrantes and semunciae. This interval, which is accurately and precisely expressed from the full Moon according to the Moon’s natural course, Bede, for ease of calculation, chose to call by the name and measure of four points in his computation. If anyone wishes to know the difference between dodrantes and semunciae and the interval of four points, let him know that the difference is like that between thirty-two moments and thirty-one and a half, that is, two parts of one moment. This difference is found in one-third of a moment. Thus four points exceed a dodrans and a semuncia by one-third of a moment. In our computation we use four points for ease of calculation, but this other reckoning is exact and precise.

“Within thirteen,” etc. The Moon traverses thirteen degrees daily in the zodiac, but before it moves beyond thirteen degrees it is not seen, because it is in conjunction with the Sun. The Moon is not seen when it is near the Sun, within thirteen degrees—that is, within the space which the Sun traverses in thirteen days—but as soon as it has emerged into the fifteenth degree, it begins to be visible. There are two possible meanings here. When he says that it is always hidden within thirteen degrees of the Sun, this may always be understood to mean that the new Moon can never appear before it has either withdrawn thirteen degrees from the Sun or, arising on the other side, approached the Sun. Thus, while the new Moon remains within thirteen degrees of the Sun, it will not appear in any sign except Aries; as soon as it withdraws farther from the Sun, it will become visible to the earth. Or it may be understood as follows: it is hidden within thirteen degrees of the Sun, that is, the Moon traverses thirteen degrees each day. In twenty-four hours the Moon traverses thirteen degrees of the sign-bearer. Thus he says that it is hidden, that is, daily separated from the Sun by thirteen degrees until the full Moon, whether it withdraws from the Sun or approaches it from the side; it will have the same number.

“On the same day or night.” It sometimes happens that, on its thirtieth or twenty-ninth day, the Moon appears in the east at the beginning of the day, completes its course, and, approaching the more slowly moving Sun, is illuminated by it at some intermediate hour of the day; then on that very evening it appears in the west.]

[Col. 0236A]

They say that the Moon neither diminishes nor grows, but that, illuminated by the Sun, it gradually turns toward us either its bright side or its dark side, according as it withdraws from or approaches the Sun. As the day grows, the new Moon is seen supine, since it is higher than the Sun and rising toward the north; as the day declines, it is upright and cast down toward the south, while when full it is always opposite the Sun. It is high when the Sun is low and low when the Sun is high. It is said to shine by dodrantes and semunciae of hours, adding them from the second [day] until the full orb and subtracting them in its waning. It is always hidden within thirteen degrees of the Sun. The last and first Moon is seen on the same day or night in no sign other than Aries [Note: [Col. 0237] C reads “he sees.”]. [Note: [Col. 0237] A and B omit this entire passage through chapter 21.] If it is upright in its rising, it will appear supine at its morning rising. Likewise, if it is seen supine, in the manner of a ship, at its rising, it will be seen upright at its morning rising. It therefore has three states: supine, upright, and prone; at some times it is seen in each of them.

CHAPTER XXI. A computation of the Moon’s course through the signs.

[Note: [Col. 0237D]

BRIDEF. RAM. GLOSSES.—“The Moon [traverses] the zodiac,” etc. In each of its months the Moon circles the twelve signs in twenty-seven days and one-third of a day, and in addition one further sign. By this unusual computation it is discovered that the Moon circles the zodiac thirteen times, more accurately than by the customary computation. This can be proved if you examine the Moon for thirty days according to this computation. For this computation is more accurate, because the calculation is here worked out precisely. The other computation reckons a sign as thirty days, which reason clearly shows not to be so, since the Moon’s age is completed in twenty-nine days and twelve hours. Nevertheless, we assign thirty days to it in that computation for ease of calculation. This computation, being more exact, is therefore more accurate; and this is proved as follows: according to this computation you will find that the thirtieth Moon has completed thirteen signs, whereas according to the other it has completed no more than twelve.

“Thirteen times.” How thirteen times? After the Moon has been illuminated in the first degree of a sign, it traverses twelve signs in twenty-seven days and eight hours, until it reaches that degree of the first sign in which it was illuminated; then it traverses again through the sign from which it began for two days and four hours. For only this much remains of its age before it is complete and before it begins another course of the signs from the beginning. In this way it completes what are virtually thirteen signs in each of its courses.

[Col. 0238C] “Namely, two days,” etc. Multiply those two days by twelve, and they yield twenty-four days. Likewise multiply the aforementioned six hours by twelve, and the result is seventy-two hours. Divide by twenty-four: three times twenty-four yield three days. In each sign there still remain two-thirds of an hour. Thus twelve two-thirds make eight hours. Add them together, and the result is twenty-seven days and eight hours. In these twenty-seven days and eight hours the Moon completes the entire sign in which it began and in which it ends, before beginning its second course. In this way it traverses thirteen signs in each of its courses, and thus it can be understood that thirteen times in its year, that is, in 354 days, it traverses the twelve signs.

“Divide,” etc. Five times nine quarters—*quinquis* (sic)—make forty-five, and of the forty-eight quarters there remain three still undivided after the forty-five; these make eighteen hours, since each of these quarters contains six hours. If you carefully multiply each number—that is, each quarter—by six hours according to this computation, you will find that in each group of nine quarters there are fifty-four hours, which yield two days and six hours. Therefore the Moon traverses one sign in that many days and hours, together with two-thirds of an hour, because what the Sun accomplishes in five days the Moon accomplishes in fifty-four hours. This is proved as follows: six times five is thirty, and one-sixth of thirty is five. This pertains to the Sun, which traverses each sign in thirty days. Conversely, the Moon completes each sign in two days and six hours, which amount to fifty-four hours. Three quarters remained after the forty-five, and each is multiplied by six hours, as stated above.

[Col. 0239A] “Always through three signs.” He correctly says “through three signs,” because the two-thirds of an hour remaining in the Moon do not amount to two hours except in three signs: if you place eight unciae four times, they make two hours, since each hour has twelve unciae.

Subtract two. Therefore he commands that two hours be taken away for every three signs, because when he included the signs in groups of nine quarters, he did not count the two-thirds (*besses*) of those signs, which make two hours in three signs; and although we did not count them, the *besses* have made up the total. Accordingly, by our computation the moon has traversed so many signs—that is, in which numbered sign the moon is found at its distance from the sun—from the time when it was kindled. For example, if the moon was kindled in the third or fourth part of Aries, and if, on the zodiacal line through which the sun always travels, the body of the moon was placed between the sun and the earth, then [Col. 0240A] it is three signs distant from the sun. From the fourth sign you will take three or four parts and complete the whole [Col. 0240B] of Aries. Hence he says: “Whatever parts you remove, remember to add the same number.” But if it was kindled in the twentieth part, or in any other part after the middle of the sign, you will not count the sign in which it was kindled, but the one after it. And when you have reached the sign in which the moon is, withdraw from that sign as many parts as the moon retained from the sign in which it was kindled, provided that it was kindled after the middle; and for this reason you will not count as whole the sign in which the moon is.

[Col. 0238A]

The moon [Note: [Col. 0237] A indeed adds this here.] completes the zodiac thirteen times in its twelve months, traversing each sign in two days, six hours, and a two-thirds part (*bes*)—that is, eight twelfths of an hour. If, therefore, you wish to know in which sign the moon is, take whatever moon you wish to calculate—for example, the twelfth; multiply it by four, making forty-eight. Divide by nine: nine times five, forty-five [Note: [Col. 0237] A, B, C: *quadrais* (uncertain reading)]. Thus, after five signs have elapsed from the sign in which the moon was born—for it is undoubtedly always kindled in the same constellation in which the sun is—in the sixth sign the twelfth moon dwells. If one remains, know that six hours of the following sign have been completed; if two, twelve hours; if three, eighteen; if four, a complete day; if eight, eight times six [Col. 0239A] hours—that is, two additional days. Of these hours, however, remember always to subtract two for every three signs. For it is laborious to divide the hours minutely into twelfths in each sign. Thus, in the present case, although three remained in the ninth divisions, the twelfth moon completed not eighteen hours [Note: [Col. 0239A] A, B, and C nevertheless add this.] but sixteen of the sixth sign. This is a ready calculation when the moon is born in the first or middle part of any sign; but if it was born elsewhere, remember to subtract from or add to the following signs as many parts as the moon, when kindled in the first sign, either removed or retained [Col. 0240A], with nine hours reckoned for the moon against five days for the sun.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Eclipse of the Sun and Moon

[Note: [Col. 0240B]]

**BRIDEF. RAM. GLOSSARY.**—Conjunction. When, in the middle, the light of the sun is taken away from the earth. For it cannot pass through the body of the moon to those who are then beneath the moon: [Col. 0241A] this is a solar eclipse. But if it has passed across that line diametrically, either on one side or the other, receiving its light from the sun, it does not produce an eclipse of the sun. For it is clearly not then positioned between [Col. 0241B] the sun and the earth, but at the sides of the sun. The sun is improperly said to fail, because it suffers no loss; but the moon fails with good reason, because its light is entirely taken away, though only when it is full.

[Col. 0239] *(A useful diagram of the solar eclipse.)*

If the earth were larger than the moon. But the moon is larger than the earth, and therefore it can conceal the light of the sun so that it is not seen from the earth. Martianus proves with the most certain arguments that the moon is larger than the earth. For when the moon is eclipsed in the southern regions of the world—that is, in Egypt and Ethiopia—its shadow obscures no more than four climates: the first, the Demaric [*Dema Diameroes*]; the second, Diasennes; the third, Dialexandrias; the fourth, Diarrhodu. But the geometers of King Ptolemy affirm that one eighteenth of the entire circumference of the earth is contained within these four climates. Yet because that shadow is less than the lunar body by a factor of three—for the moon exceeds its shadow threefold, just as nine follows three—since the lunar shadow occupied one eighteenth of the whole earth, the moon itself, whose shadow it is, must occupy one sixth of that same earth. The earth, therefore, is six times larger than the moon itself. It is also clear that the moon’s shadow exceeds the earth eighteenfold. Hence the moon’s shadow is one eighteenth of the whole earth, while the moon itself is one sixth of the earth.

“From the preceding.” From the preceding—that is, from March—or from that month in which the earlier eclipse occurred.

“The same twice in thirty days.” This is not surprising. For the sun was eclipsed at the new moon, that is, at the first moon, and the moon at the full moon. Thus an eclipse of both can occur within fifteen days.

“But so that an eclipse would not occur every month.” The breadth of the zodiacal circle has twelve divisions, that is, twelve paths, which the moon traverses each month. For as much space as the sun travels in longitude through twelve days, so much space does the breadth of that same zodiac possess. The moon cannot suffer an eclipse unless it is on the line above on which the sun is below. Thus the different lines of the breadth of the zodiacal circle, through which the moon passes, come to its aid so that it does not suffer an eclipse; the varying height of the apses also assists it in this. For sometimes it is far from the earth and sometimes near. When it is near, if they are on one line, it then suffers an eclipse; and when it is in those signs that are higher above the earth for us—that is, higher above our zenith—it does not suffer an eclipse. But when it is in those that are nearer the earth to us—that is, those that are southern for us—it does suffer one.

“The breadth of the zodiac.” For if the moon occupied the middle line of the zodiac just as the sun does, it would necessarily suffer an eclipse at every full moon. For it can move above or below the sun in its course, and through this breadth of the zodiac it is freed from suffering an eclipse.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—“The sun through the intervention of the moon.” Matters contributing to a more exact explanation of this chapter have been set out above in the older Commentary.

They report that the sun is concealed from us through the intervention of the moon, and the moon through the interposition of the earth; but that an eclipse of the sun occurs only at the last or first moon, which they call conjunction, while an eclipse of the moon occurs only at the full moon. They also say that it would not be possible for the whole sun to be taken away from the earth by the intervening moon if the earth were larger than the moon. Every year, however, eclipses of both heavenly bodies occur on appointed days and at appointed hours [Col. 0241A] beneath the earth [Note: [Col. 0241A] A, B, and C: “eclipses.”], though, when they occur above, they are not visible everywhere—sometimes because of clouds, but more often because the globe of the earth obstructs them through the curvature of the heavens. An eclipse of the moon sometimes occurs in the fifth month after the preceding one, while an eclipse of the sun occurs in the seventh. The same body is concealed above the earth twice in thirty days, though this is seen by different peoples. Once, it is said, both heavenly bodies failed within fifteen days; and once, by a marvelous arrangement, the moon was eclipsed at its setting while both bodies were visible above the earth. But so that an eclipse would not occur every month, the breadth of the zodiac sends the moon above or below.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Where It Does Not Occur, and Why

[Note: [Col. 0242A]]

**INC. AUCT. GLOSSARY.**—The inhabitants of the East do not experience evening eclipses of the sun and moon. An eclipse of the sun [Col. 0242B] that occurs for us in the evening is not experienced by the inhabitants of the East—that is, by eastern peoples—because, on account of the globe of the earth, it is already night for them. Nor do those living toward the setting experience morning eclipses, namely, eclipses in the east, as we do, because night still remains for us at that time. “Obstructing,” that is, hindering. “Although the same,” that is, although it is one and the same day or night. “At the same time,” that is, it does not occur equally. “By opposition,” that is, by the opposition of the globe, namely, the earth. “The whole world into night,” namely, for them. “Or by its circuit,” namely, that of the sun, that is, by its course. “Day,” namely, bringing it to us. The same moon was eclipsed in Sicily. “Rising,” that is, while it was rising at the beginning of the night; for when the second hour of the night comes for them, it is the first for these. They have night before these others because they are nearer the eastern region. “Which,” namely, the eclipse, “was during the consulships,” that is, while they were governing. “Campania,” namely, experienced it—that is, Italy. “Armenia,” namely, experienced it in the East, because when evening falls in the regions of India, it is midday in Campania.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—“The globe of the earth obstructing.” Let the circumference of the heavens be the greatest circle A B C D; let the horizon of those inhabiting the eastern region be A B D, their visible heaven, while A C D is invisible; and let D be the east, B the south, and A the west. Let another horizon belong to those who live toward the western regions, ninety degrees—that is, a quarter of the world—removed from the upper horizon: let it be B C, with visible heaven B A C, while the lower or invisible heaven is B D C; and let B be the east, A the south, and C the west. Therefore, if an eclipse of the moon or sun occurs for those inhabiting the East at its rising—that is, at D—it is clear that it cannot be seen by those whose horizon is B C and whose visible heaven is B A C [Col. 0243B]. When the eclipse occurs near B—that is, at midday—it is seen by those who live toward the East, and the same eclipse is seen by those who have the other horizon at rising, since B was the rising point on that horizon. When the eclipse is seen at point A, those who have the horizon A D see it at setting; but for those whose horizon is B C, it is midday. Thus an eclipse that occurs for eastern peoples at midday and the sixth hour occurs for western peoples at setting and the twelfth hour. These horizons are a quarter of the world apart, that is, six hours, since the whole world contains a span of twenty-four hours. Their meaning will be readily understood if one reads what we shall say more fully in the final book concerning meridians and the longitude of the heavens.

“Nor is night or day, although the same.” Night, which is the shadow of the earth, is always opposite the sun. Therefore, just as the sun encircles the world from rising toward setting, so night, gradually moving away from setting, follows an underground course toward rising, as will be taught more fully concerning the position and shape of the earth.

“And the eclipse of the sun which occurred during the consulship of Ipsanius and Fonteius.” In Pliny it is read not *Ipsanius* but *Vipsanius*. I suspect that Bede’s reading has been corrupted. It occurred on the day before the Kalends of May, not on the third day, as Bede reads.

The inhabitants of the East do not experience evening eclipses of the sun and moon, nor do those living toward the setting experience morning eclipses, because the globe of the earth obstructs them [Col. 0243A]. For night and day, although the same, are not simultaneous throughout the whole world: the globe brings night by its opposition and day by the sun’s circuit. In the time of Alexander the Great, the moon was eclipsed in Arabia at the second hour of the night, while the same moon was rising in Sicily. And the eclipse of the sun that occurred during the consulship of Ipsanius and Fonteius [Note: [Col. 0243A] A, B: *II Kal.* (“the second day before the Kalends”).] on the day before the Kalends of May was experienced in Campania [Note: [Col. 0243A] A: *horam* (“at the hour”).] between the seventh and eighth hour of the day, and in Armenia between the tenth and eleventh.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Comets

[Note: [Col. 0243C]]

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—Comets are stars crowned with flames like hair. *Κομητής ἀπὸ τῆς κόμης* is said from *kome*, that is, “comet” is derived from *coma*, for *coma* in Latin means hair or a head of hair. Some students of nature think that they are produced accidentally by fire and by the sudden ignition of the air above the clouds, at the boundary of the ether. For that region is hot from the motion of the upper heaven, by which it is also swept toward the setting. Others think that they are permanent stars in the heavens, but are visible only when, at the proper distance, they have moved away from the sun, as also happens with Mercury and Venus.

“Foretelling a change of kingdom, pestilence, wars, or [Col. 0243D] winds.” Affections of the body often produce movements of the mind. Thus, when the qualities of bodies have been disturbed by influences from heavenly things and from the air, human will and judgment are driven toward different decisions. For example, when bile is aroused—which they attribute to Mars and to comets, since they belong to this school—people are agitated by anger and fury. It is therefore natural that, under different influences, people should feel, desire, and do different things. Comets, however, which are carried nearest to the earth, exert the strongest influence upon bodies. For since they produce droughts by drawing off moisture, they may naturally also be regarded as signs of the things of which they are prognostic. Droughts are followed by sterility, earthquakes, pestilential disease, floods, atmospheric disturbances, and other things of this kind.

“Some of which move like the wandering stars, while others remain fixed.” Tails are sometimes spread among the stars, whether fixed or wandering, as Aristotle recorded happened in his own time with the star in the thigh of the Greater Dog. Others are free fires in the wandering air; their motion is slower than that of the world because of the air above the clouds, which gently follows the motion of the heavens. All such things are below the heavens, though in a higher region than the winds, showers, or rains.

“Beneath the very north.” The explanation is derived from the nature of that place. For there the sun, from which this region is remote, dissolves and disperses the material of these fires.

“But a comet never occurs in the setting part of the heavens.” I think the setting region can be understood as the equinoctial setting; for this is midway beneath the sun’s path, where comets are rarely seen. See Aristotle, Book One of *On Meteorological Phenomena* (*τῶν μετεώρων*). It is worthwhile to note here that there are many kinds of comets, whose differences are determined by their shapes and sizes. “Comet” is generally used as a universal term, but sometimes specifically, as in Aristotle, for one whose hair is spread in every direction in a rounded form. Others are called *pogoniae*, in which a mane projects from the lower part in the form of a beard: *πώγων* means “beard.” Others are *acon­tiae*, directed in a thinner but longer form, resembling a javelin, from the Greek *ἀκόντιον*, which means a javelin, a smaller missile than a spear. Others are shorter and resemble a sword, with a pointed tip; the Greeks call these *ξιφίαι*, for *ξίφος* means “sword.” These are the palest of all, with something of the gleam of a sword and without any rays. There is also one which the Greeks call *disceas* (*δισκέας*), silver-colored, from *diskos*, which is familiar. Others are called *pithet­es*, shaped like jars, for *πίθος* means “jar.” In these a certain hollow appears, because the outer white rim gradually fades into a smoky light. There is also one in which the hair is bent into the shape of a horn; the Greeks call these *keratias* (*κερατίας*), from *κέρας*, which means “horn.” There are also those that receive their shape and names from animals, such as the *Hippeus*, from the horse, which is called *hippos*: it has horse-like manes bent around above it. Some are also called *Tragi*, or goats, surrounded by the appearance of shaggy hair and a kind of mane. According to Pliny, there is also a bright silver-haired comet, shining so intensely that it can scarcely be looked at, and displaying in itself an image of the divine in human form.

Comets are stars crowned with flames like hair, suddenly appearing, and foretelling a change of kingdom, pestilence, wars, winds, or heat. Some move like the wandering stars, while others remain fixed. Almost all occur beneath the very north, though not in one definite part of it, and especially in the bright region that has received the name of the Milky Circle. The shortest period during which they have been observed is recorded as seven days [Note: [Col. 0244A] A: “eight.”], and the longest as eighty. Sometimes their hair is scattered among the wandering stars and the other stars, but a comet is never in the setting part of the heavens.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Air

[Note: [Col. 0244D]]

**BRIDEF. RAM. GLOSSARY.**—“Powers of the air.” Therefore, when the heavens are also called the air itself—the place where winds, clouds, storms, and whirlwinds arise—no one should suppose that evil demons are there, where God established the sun, moon, and stars. For we ought not to think that the devil and his angels inhabit the established heavens of the stars, from which we believe that they fell.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—Air is everything that, resembling emptiness, pours forth this vital breath. Students of nature teach that immediately beneath the heavens there is not air but fire; for the region of the air ends above the clouds. This is shown by the nocturnal fires, some of which are hurled from heaven to earth, while others move straight onward with extreme speed, like the flight of birds. The whole uppermost part of this lower world, reaching to the moon, is aflame: first, because all hot things seek the highest regions; and then because all that extends from the clouds to the boundary of the ether is swept toward the setting with the greatest speed together with the world. For motion, dissolving matter, produces fire. Thus they wish the region beneath the moon to be air heated beyond its natural condition by the motion of the ether. Yet this air is neither flame nor any material capable of providing light, such as a live coal or anything of that sort. Flame arises when fire has found material upon which to exert the force of its heat. But this is a heated emptiness, like that in hypocausts, furnaces, and other bath chambers in which fire is placed beneath: in these there is no flame, but such heat that, if tow or a similar powder should happen to fall into the place, it would immediately ignite. Therefore [Col. 0245C] God did not fill this interval extending to the moon with a single body or element, so that there might be a proper order and harmonious proportion among the elements.

For above the moon all things are pure and full of daylight. It has been shown above that the earth’s shadow, which is called night, does not reach higher than the moon; for the form of that shadow resembles a pyramid whose cone or vertex ends within the heavens. Thus the sun illuminates everything with the most abundant light, and there is no night or darkness anywhere in the heavens, but only among mortals, so that it may remind us of our mortality.

“Whose vicinity Olympus is said to touch.” What is related about Olympus resembles the tales of mythology. The mountain mentioned here is in Macedonia near Larissa; another, less famous, is in Phrygia. It is called *Ὄλυμπος*, as the Greeks say, as though from *ὅλος λαμπρός*, that is, “entirely luminous.” This is the point in the passage where Greek poets add to it the word *ἀνύχιος*, “without night”: although the sun has long since sunk below the horizon, it is still day on the summit until the second watch of the night, and in the morning it shines before the neighboring plains for an equal number of hours.

“But by us throughout the night.” Just as, on a clear day, stars can be seen from deep darkness—from wells and caves of similar depth—when the surrounding darkness has been dimmed by the light, so in the night we look at the stars in the region of light, though surrounded by darkness. If we were standing above the globe of the moon, however, because of the sun’s light no star in the heavens, either below or above, would be visible.

Air is everything that, resembling emptiness, pours forth this vital breath beneath the moon, and is capable of bearing the flight of birds, clouds, [Col. 0245A] and storms. There also the aerial powers, cast down from their heavenly seat with torment, await the day of judgment, when they will then be condemned more severely. From there, appearing to human beings, they assume aerial bodies corresponding to their merits. For above the moon, which moves at the boundary between air and ether, all things are pure and full of daylight, and Olympus is said to touch its vicinity. But by us the stars are seen during the night, like the other lights [Note: [Col. 0245A] A: *in* for *e*.] from darkness. The upper and clear air is assigned to the heavens; the lower air, which becomes dense through moist exhalations [Note: [Col. 0246A] A, B, and C: “becomes thick in swollen bodies.”], is assigned to the earth [Col. 0246A]. There are fire, hail, snow, ice, and the forces of storms, which are commanded to praise the Lord from the earth. Yet the air itself is sometimes called heaven; hence Peter says that the heavens perished in the Flood, when the turbulent air was turned into waves. The “heavens of heavens” are also called the starry heavens of these aerial heavens, as the higher are above the lower.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the Winds

[Note: [Col. 0245D]]

**BRID. RAM. GLOSSARY.**—“Wind is air, etc.” Just as a wave is nothing other than the movement of the sea, so wind is nothing other than moving air.

**INC. AUCT. GLOSSARY.**—Wind is air moved and stirred, as can be demonstrated with a small fan. Some say that winds arise because air comes from water, and winds from air. Clement, however, says that because lofty mountains are situated in certain places, the air, as though compressed and constricted by them, is compelled and squeezed out by God’s ordering into winds. By their breathing, the seed of crops conceives and summer heat is moderated when the Pleiades have grown hot with the sun’s fiery heat. Winds are sometimes understood as the spirits of angels, who are sent throughout the world from God’s hidden places for the salvation of the human race. Sometimes winds are also understood as spirits that incite, because, by the breath of evil suggestion, they kindle the hearts of the wicked toward earthly desires, in accordance with what is written: “The burning wind will carry him away.”

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—Wind is air moved and stirred, as can be demonstrated with a small fan. He presents the generation of winds according to the opinion of the Stoics. For the Stoics think that air, clouds, winds, and rains are the same in matter and underlying substance, differing only according to the various conditions of nature. They hold that winds are air in motion, as though struck or shaken, while air remaining still thickens and produces rain [Col. 0246C]. Aristotle, however, criticizes this as a cold conjecture. An explanation was needed of what natural force drives the air in this manner from every direction. Do the parts themselves—such as the east or north—push the air in this way? And if this is so, why do gusts arise at intervals rather than being perpetual? Others think that these forces are something like the earth’s breath, since caves and hollows in the earth are not without a current of air. The poet’s description of the winds in the first book of the *Aeneid* can be brought forward in support of the same view. It runs as follows:

> With turned spearpoint he struck the mountain on its side;  
> They, as though in battle formation,  
> Rush out wherever a gate is given,  
> And blow across the lands with a roar.

According to the different parts of the heavens, the winds receive different names. The order and names of the winds are derived from the different parts of the horizon. There are especially four, and twelve in all, which writers have accepted by common agreement. Those who make more than twelve follow nautical practice more than natural philosophy; among the ancients, we know that not even more than four were established. But so that the entire matter may be clearly understood, we shall proceed by diagrams. Let the horizon be a circle dividing the visible part of the world from the invisible, which we see beneath the open sky in a rounded circuit above the earth. Let the point from which the sun rises on the equinoctial day be marked A. From there let a line be drawn to the opposite side, whose endpoint is B, the equinoctial setting. Through this let a line be drawn from right to left, with the right-hand part H indicating the south, and the left-hand part G the north. From these two boundaries, intersecting each other at right angles in the center, four principal points immediately arise on the horizon. Then let another line be drawn leftward from F toward C, of which F indicates the summer rising—for after the eastern point, the sun rises in summer toward the north—and C the winter setting. Let another boundary cross this from D toward E [Col. 0247B], of which D indicates the winter east and E, opposite it, the summer west. Thus these four boundaries produce eight points. Let there also be another point midway between the north and the rising point, namely K, at the contact with the arctic circle. From this point let a line be drawn through the center of the circle to the opposite point, M. At the same interval, M will be as far from the south toward the rising point as K is from the equinoctial east toward the north. Then let another line be drawn midway between the north and the summer setting, from point I to the opposite point N. It is therefore clear that three rising points and the same number of setting points produce six points, marked by three bisecting lines or diameters; then the seventh comes from the south and the eighth from the north, shown by the fourth diameter. The remaining four are added by the two contacts of the narrower line near G and of the other near H, so that in all there are twelve points on the horizon, determined partly by the sun and partly by the contact of the arctic and [Col. 0247C] antarctic circles with the horizon, as the accompanying diagram shows. There are five parallel, that is, equidistant, lines in this circle. I K represents the arctic circle; the next line represents the winter and summer risings; the third represents the spring rising and setting, that is, the equinoctial points; the fourth represents the winter and summer settings; the fifth represents the antarctic circle; the sixth is parallel to none, for it cuts the lines mentioned above. Thus how, in the delineation of the horizon, diameters arise from the endpoints of the parallels, from which mutually opposed winds blow, is evident from the preceding description.

]

Wind is air moved and stirred, as can be demonstrated with a small fan [Col. 0247A]. It is understood as nothing other than a wave of air which, as Clement says, is forced and squeezed out by God’s ordering from certain lofty mountains, as though compressed and constricted, to raise waves and moderate heat. According to the different parts of the heavens, it receives different names.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The Order of the Winds

[Note: [Col. 0248B]]

**BRIDEF. RAM. GLOSSARY.**—“Because they blow from low ground.” For they blow from below, that is, from the lowest part of the world, unlike the northern winds, which breathe from above.

“Some are peculiar to particular peoples.” These winds are said to emerge from the chasms of mountains.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—There are four cardinal winds. They are called cardinal because they arise from the four principal regions of the world, which are marked by two boundaries intersecting the horizon into four quarters. Together with these four, all the others function as though they were their subdivisions. Those on the right and left of the north are called northern, and the same arrangement applies to the others. In our vernacular language, too, we use only four simple names for the winds; we express the intermediate winds by combining the names of the extremes. The ancients likewise made no more than four. See Strabo, Book One of the *Geography*. How they are placed around the horizon, from which regions they arise, and which winds are their neighbors and opposites is clear from the preceding diagram. It should be arranged so that its rising corresponds to the rising point in the world; once this is done, it will easily be possible to determine which wind is present at any moment.

“From here, on the right, Euroauster.” Euroauster and Euronotus are synonyms, for *νότος* means “south.” Bede therefore uses Euronotus improperly for Phoenicius. This is what the Greeks call the wind that blows from the region on the left [Col. 0249A]—the south wind. For it blows toward Greece from the part of the world in which Phoenicia lies, that is, Judaea. “Right” and “left” should be understood when one is standing with one’s back turned toward the wind of which another wind is said to be right or left.

“On the left, Corus, also called Argestes, brings clouds in the east.” I suspect that this passage has been corrupted. India lies in the east. Consider, therefore, whether “west” should be read in place of “east.” Aristotle states that this wind is snowy and rainy; this must undoubtedly be understood of the western winds if we consider the position of India.

“Circius for the people of Narbonne.” In addition to Pliny, see Gellius, Book Two, chapter 12. Marcus Cato does not call this wind Circius in the books of his *Origins*, but Certius.

“Altanus on the sea.” Vitruvius, in Book One of *On Architecture*, calls Altanus the wind that inclines slightly from the south toward the west—that is, midway between Auster and Libanotus—for he makes twenty-four winds, apparently following the sailors.

There are four cardinal winds. The first is Septentrio, also called Aparctias, blowing straight from the pole and producing cold and clouds. On its right is Circius, also called Thrascias, producing snow and hail; on its left is Aquilo, also called Boreas, compressing the clouds. The second cardinal wind is Subsolanus, also called Apeliotes, thundering from the rising of the sun and temperate. On its right is Vulturnus, also called Caecias, drying everything; on its left is Eurus, generating clouds. The third cardinal wind is Auster, also called Notus, humid, warm, and lightning-bearing. On its right is Euroauster, warm; on its left is Euronotus, temperate and warm. Because the southern winds blow from below, they produce greater storms at sea than the northern winds. Therefore, after southern winds, especially destructive earthquakes occur. The fourth cardinal wind is Zephyrus, also called Favonius, dissolving winter and producing flowers. On its right is Africus, also called Libs, stormy and producing thunder and lightning; on its left is Corus, also called Argestes, producing clouds in the East and clear weather in India.

There are also certain winds peculiar to particular peoples, which do not extend beyond a fixed limit: among the Athenians, Sciron, bending slightly away from Argestes; among the people of Narbonne, Circius, [Col. 0248B] which does not even reach Vienna, a city in the same province [Col. 0249A]. There are two others beyond these [Note: [Col. 0249A] A: “everywhere.”], which are rather breaths than winds: aura and altanus. *Aura* is a gentle movement of air on land; *altanus* is such a movement at sea.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Thunder

[Note: [Col. 0249C]]

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—They say that thunder is generated from the crashing of clouds. Students of nature hold various opinions about thunder. Some say that fire falling from heaven into the clouds produces a hissing sound, like red-hot iron when it is plunged into water. Aristotle thinks it is produced by the movement of forces that burst out of the clouds with a stronger effort. At this point Bede appears to be reviewing the opinion of Lucretius, whose verses I shall quote:

> First the blue spaces of heaven are shaken by thunder,  
> Because clouds, flying high in the ether,  
> Come together, with opposing winds fighting.  
> For no sound of heaven arises from a clear region.  
> But wherever the clouds are gathered in denser ranks,  
> There the great rumbling more often rises with a mighty roar.  
> Moreover, clouds cannot have bodies so dense  
> As stones and beams, nor yet so thin  
> As flying mists and smoke.  
> For, pressed by their weight, they would fall headlong  
> Like stones; or, like smoke, they could not hold together,  
> Nor contain cold snow and showers of hail.  
>   
> They also give sound when spread across the open spaces of the world.  
> In this way, too, all things seem to be shaken by thunder,  
> Often trembling with a heavy crash and suddenly torn apart,  
> And the greatest walls of the capacious world to split open.

Or it is like a bladder, which, although small, nevertheless emits a great sound when burst. This, too, is apparently taken from Lucretius’ physical account of thunder, where he writes:

> When suddenly a storm of mighty winds, gathered together,  
> Has twisted itself within the clouds, and, enclosed there,  
> Rolls the cloud more and more in a whirling motion,  
> It forces it to become hollow within a dense body all around.  
> Then, when its force and fierce impetus have stirred it,  
> It sends forth a crash with an earth-shaking sound.  
> Nor is it surprising, since a small bladder full of air  
> Often emits a similar sound when suddenly burst.

]

They say that thunder is generated from the crashing of clouds, when the forces of the winds, conceived within their hollow, roam about turning there, and, through the mobility of their power, burst violently in every direction [Col. 0250A], resounding with a great roar [Note: [Col. 0250A] A: “in the manner of”] like chariots leaping from their stalls, or like a bladder which, although small, nevertheless emits a great sound when burst.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Lightning

[Note: [Col. 0249D]]

**BRIDEF. RAM. GLOSSARY.**—“Than the flash penetrates to the eyes.” Sight is sharper and more subtle than the other senses [Col. 0250A]. Therefore, although the fire of lightning and the sound of thunder are produced simultaneously, the fire is seen before the thunder is heard.

[Col. 0250B] “Vaporously.” Vapor is an emanation or exhalation of the earth, namely, when water rises upward from the depths of the earth by exhaling, as in the thinnest mists.

“Caumatically.” *Cauma* is Greek; in Latin, “heat.” *Zetos* is likewise Greek; in Latin, “heat.” Hence *zetae* are called hot baths, and a *zetarius* is the person in charge of the *zetae*, that is, the baths.

“Through subtler elements.” It is clear from this that heavenly fire is more penetrating than earthly fire, whose effect is invisible but is perceived through heat and colors.

**INC. AUCT. GLOSSARY.**—Lightning arises from the friction of clouds, like flints struck together. When clouds have been dashed against one another, lightning is immediately emitted, and thunder follows. Although the sound is slower than the preceding flash, both are nevertheless emitted together with the brightness of the shaken light. But the sound reaches the ears more slowly than the brilliance of the flash reaches the eyes, like the sound of an axe cutting a tree at a distance: one sees the blow before its sound reaches the ears. Lightning is produced by cloud, rain, and wind. For when the wind is violently stirred in the clouds, it becomes so hot that it catches fire. Then, as has been said, flashes and thunder are emitted together. But the bright thing is seen more quickly; the other reaches the ears more slowly. After the stroke of lightning, the violence of the winds bursts out, and thus they release upon the earth the fury of the storm that they had been exercising while confined within the clouds. Horace:

> And lightning strikes the highest mountains.

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—But sound penetrates the ears more slowly than lightning-flash penetrates the eyes. It is certain that sound is produced together with fire: for when the collision has occurred, flame immediately bursts forth. But the reason why the flash is seen sooner than the thunder is heard is simply that light is swifter than impact. Light suddenly and without succession illuminates the air, just as when a lamp is brought into a dark place, everything at once becomes full of light wherever the ray of fire can reach; but sound, which is produced by the movement of the air, travels like a stone thrown into still water, from whose center innumerable circles proceed in every direction and gradually reach the earth. See Aristotle, Book II, *On the Soul*.

And let it draw fire by heat from the upper regions. *Caumaliter* is an adverb derived from the Greek καῦμα (*kauma*), which signifies heat and burning.

Therefore the fire of lightning has greater power to penetrate. There are several kinds of lightning: the first is moist, which does not burn but blackens; Aristotle calls it *psolōen* [Greek: ψολόεν]. Others are dry and likewise do not burn, but disperse. The third is what the poets, as Aristotle says, call ἀργές (*arges*). Pliny seems to interpret this as “bright”: it is of marvelous nature, for it empties jars while leaving their coverings untouched and without leaving any other mark. Gold, bronze, and silver are melted inside, while the purses themselves are in no way scorched; and a pregnant mare, struck by lightning, survived with no other injury after the foal had been killed by the blow.

Lightning is born from the friction of clouds, like flints struck together, with thunder occurring at the same time; but sound penetrates the ears more slowly [Note: [Col. 0251] A: “to the ears.”] than the flash [Note: [Col. 0251] C: “lightning-flash.”] penetrates the eyes. For every collision of things creates fire. [Note: [Col. 0251] In A the following phrase is found here: “Therefore,” etc.] Some say that, while the air draws water vaporously from below and fire by heat from above, thunderous crashes are produced when these elements clash; and if fire prevails, it harms the crops, but if water prevails, it benefits them. The fire of lightning therefore has greater power to penetrate because it is made of subtler elements than the fire we use.

## CHAPTER XXX. Where Lightning Does Not Occur, and Why

[Note: [Col. 0251B]

BRIDEF. RAM. GLOSSES.—“What is the reason for Scythia?” Scythia is an extremely cold region; therefore lightning does not occur there because of the cold, just as it does not occur in Egypt because of the heat.

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—They say that lightning is rare in winter and summer. Almost all of this is taken word for word from Pliny. [Col. 0251C]]

Lightning is rare in winter and summer, because in winter the cold air [Note: [Col. 0251] A: “higher regions.”] extinguishes whatever fiery vapor it receives. In summer, hot vapors are rarely and thinly condensed into clouds [Note: [Col. 0251] A: “in winter.”], without which there is no lightning. This is why Scythia and Egypt are protected from lightning; Italy lies between them, where, with milder winter and rainy summer, it is always in some fashion spring or autumn.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the Rainbow

[Note: [Col. 0251C]

BRIDEF. RAM. GLOSSES.—“From the sun opposite.” When the clouds are opposite the sun, the rainbow is formed; it should also be understood that it is formed from the moon when she is full.

“Like wax returning the image of a ring.” For the image of a ring is an arc: just as the image of any object is impressed in wax, so the image of the sun is figured in the clouds.

INC. AUCT. GLOSSES.—The four-colored arc in the air is formed from the sun opposite the clouds. *Arc*, that is, rainbow. For the rainbow is an impression of the solar body. “Four-colored,” that is, of four colors. “And is formed from the clouds.” A cloud appears small to us, yet it is so large that it often conceals the sun from us and refracts its rays into itself. “Repelled,” that is, its ray’s edge is reflected. “A hollow cloud,” that is, a dense cloud. When the clouds are opposite the sun, the rainbow is formed. It should also be understood that it is formed from the moon when she is full. “Into the sun,” that is, opposite the sun. “Is refracted,” that is, is reflected. “Like,” that is, after the manner or likeness of wax. “Returning the image of a ring.” For the image of a ring is an arc: just as the image of any object is impressed in wax, so the image of the sun is figured in the clouds. “Which”—namely, the arc—“draws a fiery,” that is, red, color from the sky. “From the waters,” that is, from the sea, purple, that is, rose-colored. From the air it draws hyacinthine color, that is, the color of the hyacinth stone. From the earth it draws grassy color, that is, green. It is rarer in summer than in winter—that is, the arc is formed in the air—because larger clouds occur in winter than in summer. And it is formed rarely at night, because it is produced from the full orb of the sun. Nor is it seen at night except at full moon, since it shines back from the moon. Again: without sun and clouds the rainbow never appears, because its appearance is formed from the warmth of the sun’s ray. It is four-colored and draws into itself appearances from all the elements. From the sky it draws its fiery color, from the waters its purple, from the air its white, and from the earth it gathers black. This arc, because it shines from the sun in the clouds, signifies the glory of Christ shining forth in prophets and teachers. Others have said that its two colors—that is, the watery and fiery colors—signify two judgments: one through water, when the wicked perished in the Flood; the other through which sinners will afterward be burned in hell. Again, *iris* in Greek is called *arcus* in Latin. The arc appears on the day of rain and is a sign of mercy, as the Lord said to Noah at the time of the Flood: “I will set my bow in the clouds, and I will remember my covenant,” etc. There are two principal colors in the arc, namely green, the watery color, and red; and in these are plainly signified the water of baptism and the blood of redemption, or the grace of the Holy Spirit. Through these two we are cleansed from all sins. The whole Church is girded by these two mysteries, and through them is renewed into the newness of God’s grace. Or by the two colors we may understand two judgments: one accomplished through water and the other to be accomplished through fire.

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—“The four-colored arc in the air.” Aristotle, in *Meteorology*, Book III, mentions only three colors and gives their explanation.

“And rarely at night.” A nocturnal rainbow is also seen, but rarely. In Aristotle’s lifetime it was seen at night once in sixty years, and then only on the fifteenth day, when the moon is full.]

The four-colored arc in the air is formed from the sun opposite the clouds, when the sun’s ray is cast upon a hollow cloud and, its edge being reflected, is refracted back toward the sun, like wax returning the image of a ring. It draws from the sky a fiery color, from the waters a purple color, from the air a hyacinthine color, and from the earth a grassy color. It is rarer in summer than in winter, and is rarely seen at night [Note: [Col. 0251] A, B: “the rare vapors … are condensed.”], and only at full moon, since it shines back from the moon.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On Clouds

[Note: [Col. 0252C]

INC. AUCT. GLOSSES.—Clouds are gathered into a mass from air condensed drop by drop. Thus the waters of the sea are seized by the clouds and are again returned by them to the earth. But so that they may be sweet, they are cooked in the rains by the fire of the sun. Others say that clouds do not condense only from the waters of the sea, but that mists also grow from vapors exhaled by the earth; when these are condensed and gathered together, clouds rise higher, and as they sink they pour down rains. Clouds signify the apostles and teachers. The rains of the clouds are therefore the words of the apostles, which come, as it were, drop by drop—that is, sentence by sentence—but pour forth the fruitfulness of teaching more abundantly.

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—Clouds are gathered from air condensed drop by drop, which possesses the lightness of smoke. Physicists report that the places through which suspended rains are carried are cold by *antiperistasis*, whereby the property of nature causes wells and underground places to be warm in winter but cold in summer. Thus, when the seas, lakes, and ponds are touched by the sun’s warmth, vapors are drawn out and lifted by the force of heat into the heights of the clouds. Because of the cold they are condensed into clouds, which, before their moisture has gathered into a mass, support themselves there by their own force and by a kind of emptiness. At first, therefore, because of the smallness of their moisture, they do not fall; but when moisture has gathered from the cloud, they can no longer support themselves because of its weight, and it is carried down again to the earth. [Col. 0253B]]

[Col. 0252B] Clouds are gathered from air condensed drop by drop, which [Note: [Col. 0251] A, B, C: “smoke-like.”], with natural lightness, lifts the vapors of waters from land and sea and, as long as they remain in the form of the tiniest drops, suspends them on high by its own force. There they become sweet either by being boiled by the fire of the sun or changed during their passage through the air, just as we customarily alter the flavor by pouring sea water over earth, or fresh water over sea plants.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On Rains

[Note: [Col. 0253C]

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—We call rains slow and continuous. *Rain* is the general name for all heavenly waters; dew is not formed on high and is not called rain. Sudden showers are abrupt and violent; Aristotle calls them λαβρότερα (*labrotera*). Another kind falls in very small but dense drops, like dew; the same author calls it ψεκάς (*psekas*). A rain shower is moderate, neither dew-like nor violent.]

Rain showers arise from the drops condensed from clouds, when they come together into larger drops and the nature of the air can no longer bear them; now the wind drives them, now the sun dissolves them, and they fall in mass upon the earth. But we call rains slow and continuous, and showers sudden and violent.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On Hail

[Note: [Col. 0253C]

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—Hailstones are made from raindrops. Hail differs from snow in manner, place, and time: snow is moderately compacted, like flakes or roasted salt, whereas hail is solid ice. Snow forms in the clouds, hail lower down; for rain freezes while falling because of the sudden change between hot and cold, through *antiperistasis*. Hence there are snowy mountains without hail, since hail forms lower down. Snow is formed in cold places and seasons, but hail in temperate ones.

[Col. 0253D] “But they melt more quickly than snow.” Whatever is produced by *antiperistasis* immediately returns to its natural state; this is why hail melts at once.

“And they fall more often by day than by night.” Nights are cold because of the absence of the sun, but hail forms when cold moisture is received by warm air.]

[Col. 0253B] Hailstones are formed from raindrops, congealed in the air by the force of cold and wind [Note: [Col. 0253B] A, B, C: “severity.”]; but they melt more quickly than snow and fall more often by day than by night.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On Snow

[Note: [Col. 0253D]

INC. AUCT. GLOSSES.—Snow is formed from the vapor of waters, not yet condensed into drops, but seized by frost; it is said not to fall on the high seas. Blessed Ambrose says that often waters stiffened by the icy blasts of winds are solidified into snow, and, when the air is broken, the snow is poured down. Hail is coagulated in a similar way. The waters of clouds are compressed into ice by the force of cold and winds and become hard. Then the ice itself, partly shattered into fragments by the crashing of the winds, partly melted by the vapor of the sun, falls to the earth in pieces. The fact that it appears round is caused by the heat of the sun and by the delay imposed by the resisting air as it travels over a long distance toward the earth. Figuratively, hail is the hardness of unbelief, cold with the numbness of wickedness. Snow signifies unbelieving people, extremely cold and sluggish, depressed toward lowly things by the numbness of their mind. Again, in another interpretation: snow signifies people cold in love, who, although white with the purity of baptism, do not burn with the spirit of charity.]

[Col. 0254A]

Snow is formed from the vapor of waters, not yet condensed into drops, but seized by frost; it is said not to fall on the high seas.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Signs of Storms or Fair Weather

[Note: [Col. 0254C]

BRIDEF. RAM. GLOSSES.—“The sun spotted at its rising.” He speaks prognostically. Things that signify future events are called prognostics.

“He foretells.” *Sagare* means to perceive keenly; from it dogs are called *sagaces*, “keen-scented.”

“When dolphins leap from the waves more often.” Dolphins move against the winds, lest the winds, gathering them in the waves, dash them against the shores and destroy them.]

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—“The sun spotted at its rising.” Consideration of storms through prognostics also belongs to the nature of things and is useful to those engaged in agricultural work. These signs are drawn not only from the sun, moon, and heavenly bodies—although chiefly from them—but also from animals and even from lifeless things. A clear sunrise without heat, as Pliny records, announces a fair day. If the sun is pale, it indicates winter hail; if it sets clearly and rises clear again on the following day, it is an unmistakable sign of fair weather.

“Or hidden beneath a cloud.” Especially if something like a beam from a higher place hangs over the sun’s orb and is soon concealed again.

“If it is red, [the weather is] clear.” If clouds redden before sunrise, there will be winds; if black clouds are joined with them, winds will be mixed with rain. If the setting sun is red and rises red again in the morning, it foretells rain; but if clouds redden around the west, the following day will be fair.

“If pale, into black clouds, [it signifies] a north wind.” If, from the rising of the sun, clouds are dispersed to the right and left, it is a sign of winds with rain; but there will be a severe storm if the sun sets with rain.

“If the fourth moon is red.” The fourth moon is especially observed in prognostications: if it shines brightly with clear radiance, it signifies fair weather; if reddish, winds; if black, rain. In the same way the phases called διχότομος (*dichotomos*), ἀμφίκυρτος (*amphikyrtos*), Πανσέληνος (*Panselēnos*), again διχότομος, then ἀμφίκυρτος, [Col. 0255A] then μηνοειδής (*mēnoeidēs*), and finally the silent phase are observed—that is, the first, fourth, seventh, tenth, fifteenth, nineteenth, [Col. 0256A] twenty-third, twenty-seventh, and the interlunium.]

The sun, spotted at its rising or hidden beneath a cloud, foretells a rainy day. If it is red, clear weather; if pale, stormy weather; if it appears hollow, so that, shining in the middle, it sends rays toward the south and north, wet and windy weather; if it sets pale into black clouds, a north wind. If the sky is red in the evening, it signifies a clear day; if in the morning, stormy weather. Lightning from the north and thunder from the east portend a storm, while wind from the south portends heat. If the fourth moon is red like gold, it indicates winds; if it grows black with spots at the tip of its horn, [Col. 0255A] [Note: [Col. 0255A] A: “rainy.”] the beginning of a rainy month; if in the middle, a clear full moon. Likewise, when water sparkles against the oars during night navigation, there will be a storm. And when dolphins leap from the waves more frequently, the wind will arise from the direction in which they are moving; and from the direction in which the clouds are scattered and open the sky, [the wind will come].

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On Pestilence

[Note: [Col. 0255A]

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—Pestilence arises from air through excess of dryness, heat, or rain. The origin of pestilence, like that of other natural events, is also investigated by physicists, although many think that the entire inquiry should be left to physicians. They suppose that a poisonous breath rises from the earth; while the sun causes the poison to seethe, it brings it into the air, which, infected far and wide by this poison—for one person is infected more readily and more completely than all others—then infects through this breath not only human bodies but also those of quadrupeds and birds. Thus they refer the cause of this plague to the sun, whom the poets otherwise make a healer, and call him Apollo, from the Greek ἀπολεῖν (*apolein*), which means “to destroy.” The poet Lucretius, one of the earliest, has some verses on this subject that are neither inelegant nor unpleasant; I shall cite them, since they agree with Bede’s opinion:

“Now I shall explain what the cause of diseases is, or from where suddenly

A diseased force can arise and bring a deadly destruction

Upon the human race and the herds of cattle.

First I have shown above that there are many seeds of things

That are vital to us;

And, conversely, that many are flying about

Which are necessary for disease and death.

When these have arisen by chance

And disturbed the sky, the air becomes diseased.

And all that force of diseases and pestilence

Either comes from outside, like clouds and mist from above

[Col. 0257B] through the sky, or often arises itself

And rises from the earth, when it has encountered decay,

Struck by untimely rains and sunlight.

Do you not also see that those who arrive far from their homeland

And home are attacked by the strangeness of sky and waters,

Because conditions differ greatly?

For how much do we think the sky differs in Britain,

And what is it like in Egypt, where the axis of the world limps,

And how much does what is in Pontus differ from what is at Gades,

And from what extends as far as the black peoples,

Scorched by heat?

When we see these four regions differing from one another,

Being divided among the four winds and parts of the sky,

Then the color and appearance of human beings also seem to differ,

And diseases in their various kinds widely possess the races.”

][Col. 0256A]

Pestilence arises from air corrupted, according to the merits of human beings, by dryness, heat, or excessive rains; taken in through breathing or eating, it generates plague and death. Hence we often see the whole season of summer turned into winter storms and whirlwinds. But when these occur in their proper season, they are called storms; when they occur at other times, they are called prodigies or signs.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the Twofold Nature of Waters

[Note: [Col. 0257B]
