JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—By the twofold nature of waters all things that are generated on earth are formed and reformed. He follows the very ancient opinion of Thales of Miletus, who is counted among the Seven Sages. As Aristotle says, Thales wrote that moisture is *pansperma* (πάνσπερμα), “the seed of all things,” both those that exist and those that arise in heaven and on earth. The fable of Homer about Oceanus as father agrees with this [*Iliad* X]. This water is therefore spread beneath all the other seas; as Pliny says, Oceanus washes against three seas. It supplies the material for all other kinds of waters. But it nourishes living things after its thickness and harshness have been removed while it is filtered through sands—that is, sifted, so to speak—and thus makes all waters sweet. Rivers are sweet, for they nourish not only fields and plants but also serve as drink for animals. For this reason they are called ποταμοί (*potamoi*) in Greek, from drinking, and among poets “cups,” since the same idea is involved.

“By the waves of the sea.” Larger regions are separated by seas, smaller ones by rivers. Thus one who penetrates to foreign regions crosses the seas; hence “transmarine letters and studies” in Jerome means the school of the Athenians and philosophers among them. The prophet likewise praises the seas through the Spirit of God for their use in navigation and commerce among peoples. Whether the sea exists and whether it is naturally salty, and also concerning the origin of rivers, see Aristotle, Book I of the *Meteorologica*. [Col. 0257D]]

By the twofold nature of waters all things that are seen on earth are formed and reformed [Note: [Col. 0257] A omits: “which … on earth.”]. For salty waters, meeting mortal needs, nourish fruits on land and in the air, while fresh waters are more suitable for nourishing fruits and quenching thirst. But which of these is natural is disputed. Both qualities, however, are found: one can be poured into the other, the salty through the ashes of sea plants, and the fresh through earth; the sea’s straits, moreover, separate the expanses of the earth [Col. 0258A] with repeated divisions, both enclosing the boundaries of peoples and enriching all provinces through commerce with mutual resources.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the Tides of the Ocean

[Note: [Col. 0257D]

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—The preceding commentary—we placed the commentary after the Joan. Nov. Scholia for the sake of the diagram—is by some later writer than the explanations that precede it, as can easily be inferred both from its manner of expression and from its treatment of the foreign words *laedon* or *laedona* and *malina*. Nevertheless, we have given the diagram and commentary for printing exactly as we found them in the manuscript copy. As for the tides—for this must be noted both because of Ptolemy’s *Cosmography* and for physical reasons—they do not occur everywhere, nor do tides always occur in the same places. There is a certain fiery and hidden cause by which the waves are driven, especially in the mouths of shores; these forces gradually disappear through the usage of a longer time, just as the vital growth in trees and animals gradually dies away. Hence some observations of the ancients are regarded as false and unconfirmed: for example, Ptolemy lists more tides on the British shore than are found on those shores today; and the facts concerning that famous tide between Attica and Euboea—which the Greeks call the Euripus are now found to be quite different from what the ancients recorded. In Ptolemy’s maps, because the translator did not translate the Greek term—which could conveniently have been done—the person ignorant of Greek supposes that a town of that name is located there. Aristotle states—although some write that, overcome by impatience at the problem, he threw himself into the sea because he could not discover the cause of the alternation at the Euripus, adding this saying as the cause of his death, “Aristotle could not grasp the Euripus, but it will grasp Aristotle”—that this alternation arises from hidden winds, which are expelled when the air compressed in the hollows of these places is released. He thinks this occurs especially in narrow places and where opposing shores, meeting face to face, form a strait. For movement is first and most clearly detected in a confined place; in the open sea, because of its breadth, it is dispersed without limit and thus disappears. See Aristotle, Book II of the *Meteorology*.

“And becoming unusually powerful and turbulent at the equinoxes or solstices.” This too is natural, since Aristotle also left it written that these changes of seasons disturb the air because of the violent stars located in Aries and Orion. See Aristotle again, Book II of the *Meteorology*.

VETUS COMMENTARIUS.—This wheel (see the following page) concerns the concord of the sea and the moon; when they agree, the tide is greatest, as Bede teaches in Book II of *The Reckoning of Time*. For the tide of the Ocean is said to come and return twice each day, namely at the rising and setting of the moon. Its ascents are divided into *laedones* and *malinae*, that is, into lesser and greater tides. *Malina* is so called from the greater moon, while *laedona* is derived from “injured” [*laesa*], hence its name. The times at which these ascents begin and how long they last are marked in the diagram. The inner wheel bears the names of the three parts of the world. The space outside it, representing the air that surrounds the earth on every side, bears the names of the winds blowing through the air. The outer wheel [Col. 0259A] has the ages of the moon, from the first to the thirtieth. Beneath this, the narrower circular line enclosing the water signifies the Ocean, which circles the whole world. Below this, a line contains the number of days during which the aforesaid tides advance or retreat [Col. 0260A]. Thus, opposite the first number, it is always marked outside on which day of the moon each of these advances begins, at the rising of the *malina* or *laedona*.

(On the concord of the sea and the moon.)]

The tide of the Ocean follows the moon, as though it were drawn backward by her breathing and, when her impulse is withdrawn, poured forth again. It appears to flow and ebb twice each day, with an interval of one hour, three quarters, and half an ounce always passing between them; and its entire course is divided into *laedones* and *malinae*, that is, lesser and greater tides. The *laedon* advances for six hours and retreats for the same number; the *malina* advances for five hours but retreats for seven. The *laedon*, beginning on the fifth and twentieth day of the moon [Note: [Col. 0257] A omits “and on the twentieth.”], advances for as many hours as it retreats. The *malina*, beginning on the thirteenth and twenty-eighth days [Note: [Col. 0259] B: “on XXI or XXVIII.”], is swifter in its advance but slower in its retreat; it lasts seven days and twelve hours [Note: [Col. 0259] B: “fifteen.”], always displaying in its middle the first and fifteenth day of the moon, and becoming unusually more turbulent at the equinoxes and solstices. After eight years [Note: [Col. 0259] A: “also,” instead of “but”], at the beginnings of its movement and with equal increases, it is recalled to the same point by the moon’s most certain circuit; she always keeps the northern tides milder than when, having moved toward the south, she exerts her power with a nearer and stronger effort. [Note: [Col. 0259] A: “the northern … the southern.”]

## CHAPTER XL. Why the Sea Does Not Increase

[Note: [Col. 0259A]

INC. AUCT. GLOSSES.—They say that the sea is not increased by the flow of rivers because fresh water is naturally consumed in salty channels [Col. 0260A]. Whether waters are raised by the breath of winds, increase through the course of the moon, or decrease because the sun draws them up, this is known to God alone, whose work is the world and to whom alone the whole order of the world is known. The incomparable size and unnavigable breadth of the Ocean prevent this from being determined. Philosophers of the world say that there is no land beyond the Ocean, but that the sea is enclosed by dense, cloudy air alone, just as the earth is enclosed beneath. Solomon says: “To the place from which the rivers flow, they return.” Hence it is understood that the sea does not increase, because through certain hidden passages the waters may flow back to their springs and return by their usual course above their streams. The sea was made so that it might receive the courses of all rivers. Although its depth is varied, the equality of its surface is nevertheless uniform. Hence it is believed to have been called *aequor*, because its surface is level. Physicists, however, say that the sea is deeper than the lands.

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—“Fresh water is consumed in salty channels.” Namely, because of heat, which also produces ashes.

“Consumed by the vapor of the sun.” Aristotle expresses this opinion in Book II of the *Meteorology*.

“Lakes and pools.” That is, *lacus* and *lacunae*; both forms are used. This can be seen in marshes which, standing in winter rain, are dried by the sun in summer.

“Or even flow back by a hidden passage into their springs.” As it is written in Ecclesiastes: “All the rivers enter the sea, and the sea is not filled. To the place from which the rivers flow, they return, so that they may flow again.” [Col. 0261D]]

The sea is not increased by the flow of rivers [Note: [Col. 0259] A, B, C: “by the meeting of rivers”], they say, because fresh water is naturally consumed in salty channels [Col. 0261A], or is carried away by winds or by the vapor of the sun—as we observe in lakes and pools, which are dried in a short time—or it may even flow back by a hidden passage into its springs and return by its customary course through its streams. Fresh waters, being lighter, are poured over the marine waters; the marine waters themselves, being of heavier nature, support the waters poured over them more effectively.

## CHAPTER XLI. Why the Sea Is Bitter

[Note: [Col. 0261D]

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—“But in fresh waters there is nourishment for the moon, as in the sea there is nourishment for the sun.” He speaks according to the opinion of those who regard the heavenly bodies and stars as fires, nourished by vapors drawn upward from the earth and seas. Most think that this idea originated from Homer’s fable: in the *Iliad* he relates that Zeus went with the other gods to the Ethiopians for a banquet. Physically, the idea is understood as referring to the place of night, when the stars and especially the sun seem to fall into the Ocean. On this opinion see Strabo, Book I.]

They say that the sea remains salty, although watered by so many rivers and rains, because the sweet and thin liquid is drawn off by the sun—the fiery force easily attracts it—and everything harsher and thicker is left behind. Therefore the uppermost water of the seas is sweeter than the deep water [Note: [Col. 0261] A: “of the waters”; C: “of the sea”; A: “in the deep.”]. [Col. 0261B] But in fresh waters there is nourishment for the moon, as in the sea there is nourishment for the sun.

## CHAPTER XLII. On the Red Sea

[Note: [Col. 0261D]

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—The Red Sea received its name from its rosy color [Col. 0262B], although it does not naturally possess that color. The Red Sea, that is, the Arabian Gulf, is called by the Greeks Ἐρυθρὰ θάλασσα (*Erythra thalassa*), either because a king named Erythras ruled in those regions or because it has red waters; for the Greeks call red ἐρυθρόν (*erythron*). Other writers disagree about the origin of the name: some, like Pomponius Mela in Book III, think it was named after a king; Herodotus in *Melpomene* holds this view. Pliny agrees with Pomponius. The more common report—and it is confirmed by travelers who penetrated by way of the Holy Land as far as those regions—is that it appears red, but that the color comes from the redness of the sand and seabed, which shines through the otherwise clear and uncolored waves. See much about this sea in Strabo, Book XVI. It is more productive of large animals and sea monsters than any other sea; Aristotle gives the reason for this both in the *Problems* and in his short work *On Length and Shortness of Life*. This is the sea most frequently named in Holy Scripture in connection with the Israelites’ return from Egypt to Judea.]

The Red Sea takes its name from a rosy color, which it does not naturally possess but acquires from the neighboring shores, which are red like blood. For this reason red ocher and other pigments, as well as red gems, are collected there. It is divided into two gulfs: the Persian Gulf extends toward the north, and the Arabian toward the west; the latter lies 115 paces from the Egyptian sea.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the Nile

[Note: [Col. 0262C]

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—“By the river Nile.” This is the largest of all the rivers known to the earth. Aristotle writes in the first book of the *Meteorology*, concerning the origin of rivers, that it rises from the Silver Mountain—which Ptolemy, in Book IV of his *Cosmographical Works*, calls the Mountain of the Moon—beyond Ethiopia, toward the promontory of Prassum. It is an exceptionally great river and one of the most marvelous works of nature. Servius writes that it was formerly called the Melon, and afterward the Nile, as though from νέαν ἕλιδα [Greek; the precise phrase is uncertain]. Since the ancients possessed no certain knowledge of its origin, they made it uncertain. Hence Lucan says in the tenth book of the *Pharsalia*:

“Nature has revealed her secret source to no one,

Nor has she permitted peoples to see you, Nile, small.”

]

By the river Nile [Note: [Col. 0261] A: “by what river”], which rises between the sunrise and the south, Egypt uses it in place of rains, since it rejects rains and clouds because of the heat of the sun. In May, when its mouths—through which it flows into the sea—are blocked by heaps of sand driven in by the west wind, it gradually swells and is forced backward [Col. 0262B], watering the flat lands of Egypt; but when the wind ceases and the heaps of sand are broken through, it is restored to its own channel.

## CHAPTER XLIV. That the Earth Is Joined by Waters

[Note: [Col. 0262D]

VETUS COMMENTARIUS.—The return-flow of the Ocean around the world, occupying a fourth part of the whole earth.

The torrid zone of the earth, around which the Ocean flows on every side, above and below; from its two extremities, east and west, the Ocean flows back toward the north [Col. 0263B] and south. By this returning flow of the current—that is, by the boiling movements of the sea—the tides appear to be produced.

All the earth inhabited by us is a small island, because each of the four inhabited regions also forms a kind of small island, with the Ocean surrounding them twice, as you see. From it all the seas have taken their names from the neighboring regions. For if you consider the surface of our island, you can understand another island opposite it below; and again, beyond the Torrid Zone, you should understand an upper and lower habitable island.

]

The Creator girded the globe with water around its middle [Col. 0263A], so that it would tend from every side toward the center of the earth but, pressing inward, could not fall into the interior. Thus, since dry and arid earth could not stand by itself without moisture, and water could not stand unless supported by earth, they were joined in mutual embrace: the one opening its hollows, the other penetrating throughout, within, without, above, and below, running through veins as through bonds and even bursting forth upon the highest ridges.

## CHAPTER XLV. The Position of the Earth

[Note: [Col. 0263C]

INC. AUCT. GLOSSES.—“The earth is founded upon its own stability; the abyss is clothed around it like a garment.” Concerning how the earth is believed to be founded upon the air and to stand balanced by its weight, blessed Ambrose says: “As for the nature or position of the earth, let what is written according to Scripture in Job suffice: ‘Know that he suspended the earth upon nothing.’” Philosophers likewise think that the earth is supported by dense air, that it is sponge-like, and that it hangs immobile in the midst of the air by the mass of its own weight. Thus, as though supported by oars like wings and balanced on every side, it leans with equal movement this way and that, because it is written: “He founded the earth upon the waters.” Yet how can soft and thin air support an earthly mass, or how can so immense a weight stand upon the waters? Why does it not sink, or how does it maintain the balance of equality so that, leaning to one side, it does not fall? No mortal is permitted to know this, nor may anyone among us examine or investigate so great an excellence of divine workmanship, since it is clear that, by the law of God’s majesty, it remains stable both upon the waters and above the clouds. For who, Solomon says, is sufficient to recount his works, or who has searched out his wonders? Therefore what is a secret to the nature of mortals must be left to divine power.

The old commentary that follows shows that the surface of the water is spherical and that the earth itself is a globe.

[Col. 0265B] OLD COMMENTARY.—The form of the sea and of all water, when it is calm and still, appears globular. Therefore, if we suppose the surface of the water to be flat and arranged in a straight line, as A B Γ, and if a line K B is drawn from the point on the earth, namely K, while the lines K A and K Γ are joined, each of which is as much longer than the middle one, K B, as A B is in relation to H, then the calm water is curved everywhere along A H Γ.

[Col. 0266B] The letters A B C D have been assigned to the sphere of the earth. Around it lies the sphere of the air, to which the letters E F G L M have been assigned. Let a line drawn from E to L divide both spheres—that is, the sphere of the earth and that of the air. That one will be upper, since we possess the other beneath our feet. Unless, therefore, all the weight fell upon the earth, the earth would receive a very small portion of the rains, from A to C. The sides of the air, however, would carry their moisture into the heavens. It follows that the moisture of the air must flow upon the lands from every side.

[Col. 0267A] JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—Troglodytice and neighboring Egypt do not see the Bears. The Troglodytes are called so in Greek because they inhabit caves instead of houses, as the extreme intensity of the heat requires. Some of them are in Asia; others—those mentioned here—are in the interior of Africa beyond Egypt, in the torrid zone and beyond the equinoctial circle. See Ptolemy’s description.

Nor does Italy see Canopus. Canopus was the helmsman of Menelaus, who, while the Greeks were sailing to Egypt to recover Helen, was drowned at the mouth of the Nile, which is therefore called Canopic. He was placed among the stars and set in the ship Argo, but the northern regions do not see this part of it. Aristotle and Pliny say the same about this star. But there are also other arguments by which it is demonstrated that the earth is a globe: namely, the eclipse of the moon, which occurs through crescent-shaped and ἀμφικύρτους [convex on both sides] figures; from this it is evident that its shadow is pyramidal, and that such a shadow arises from no other material than something globular. The old commentary presented this point in the following diagram [Col. 0268A].

Where night comes from.

The commentary was followed by the figure that we have immediately inserted here as well. It demonstrates that the earth is divided by the same circles as the heavens; it has been taken from Macrobius’ commentary on the Dream of Scipio.

[Col. 0267] How the five zones of the heavens lie above the five zones of the earth.

[Col. 0267C] OLD COMMENTARY.—There is the globe of the earth, to which the letters A B C D have been assigned here. You can see how the lines between the letters placed around its circumference are to be drawn. Two regions opposite one another—namely, from C to I, the northern region, and from D to F, the southern region—are understood to be overwhelmed by perpetual frost. This is shown by the line from I to G and from F to E. Between these two outer belts and the middle one are two regions granted to mortals: one from I to N and the other from F to L. From these, too, lines are drawn showing the zones from N to M and from L to K. For between I and N lies the summer zone, and between L and F the winter zone; both enjoy, on either side, a balance of cold and heat, since from N to L the sun is always burning.

Above the inner circle, which precedes these five zones of the earth, lie the five zones of the heavens. They are all distinguished by letters, just as the aforementioned globe of the earth is. For there is the sphere of the heavens A B C D, and within it is enclosed the sphere of the earth S X T V. Once these have been drawn, it is clear that each part of the earth receives its character from the corresponding part of the heavens situated above its own vertex.

JOAN. NOV. SCHOL. After this chapter we found a certain piece of writing added in the place of an exposition, namely, a fragment from Book II of Ptolemy’s Περὶ Μεγάλης Πραγματείας [On the Great Treatise]. We thought it worthwhile to assign the whole [Col. 0269A] of that commentary to this chapter, since it contains in full this entire division concerning climates and parallels. Once it is properly understood, students will work with profit in cosmography, especially in Pliny.

### Explanation of the properties of the individual parallels

(From chapter 6 of Book II of Ptolemy, On the Great Work, which is entitled the Almagest.)

In the same way, after taking the general and stated properties of the other parallels as well, increasing the declination by increments of a quarter of an equinoctial hour, we shall have done enough if we set out their general exposition before descending to particulars.

Let us therefore begin with the parallel that lies beneath the equinoctial itself. It separates most nearly from the whole fourth part of our world that portion which lies toward the south, and it alone has all days and nights equal to one another. For only there are all the parallels in the sphere divided by the equinoctial circle into two equal parts, so that the portions above the earth are individually similar and equal to the corresponding subterranean portions. This occurs under no other declination at all. The equinoctial alone, being again divided equally everywhere by the horizon, makes the days that occur under it perceptibly equal to the nights. For it too is the greatest of the circles, whereas the others, being divided unequally according to the declination of our world, make the southern portions above the earth smaller than the subterranean portions and therefore make the days shorter than the nights; the northern portions, on the contrary, make the portions above the earth larger and the days longer.

The shadows of this parallel are also double: the sun passes twice over the vertex of those living beneath it, according to the paths of the equinoctial and oblique circles. Consequently, only then can gnomons at noon cast no shadow. When the sun travels through the northern semicircle, shadows from the gnomons are cast toward the south; when it travels through the southern semicircle, they are cast toward the north. In these regions, when the gnomon is 60 parts, each of the summer and winter shadows is approximately 26 30 parts. We shall speak generally, however, except concerning those shadows that occur at noon. For we cannot determine the exact noon either at the equinoctial points or at the solstitial points. Nevertheless, when we take the shadow at these times at the hour of noon, it will be close to the truth, and no perceptible error will result from the cause.

Above the vertex of those who dwell beneath the equinoctial come the stars that revolve upon the equinoctial itself, and all appear both to rise and to set. For since the poles of the sphere are themselves upon the horizon, they make no circle parallel to the equator—whether a circle that is always visible or one that is never visible—that intersects the meridian circle.

Many maintain that habitations can exist beneath the equinoctial, as in a region of exceptionally moderate climate [ [Col. 0269] Beneath the equator there is habitation, according to most people of our time, 1522]. For they say that the sun does not remain over the vertex at the equinoctial points, because its withdrawal in latitude rapidly decreases from the equinoctial points, making the summer temperate; nor is it far from the vertex at the solstices, so that the winters are very mild. We cannot say with any probability what these habitations are. For to this day the people of our world have scarcely penetrated there. Thus anyone will consider what is told about them to be conjecture rather than true history.

But enough has been said briefly about the properties of the parallel beneath the equinoctial. As for the others, by which some estimate that habitations are encompassed, the same points should be repeated for each individually. We shall add that, above the vertex in each case, those stars appear that are separated from it by an equal arc of the circle passing through the poles of the equinoctial—an arc equal, that is, to the arc by which the corresponding parallel is likewise distant beneath it. We shall also add that the circle which is described by the northern pole of the equinoctial and by the elevation of the pole always appears; all the stars contained within it are always visible. Conversely, the circle described by the southern pole through the same distance never appears; the stars contained within it are never visible.

The second parallel is one at which the longest day is 12 15 equinoctial hours. It is 4 degrees 15 minutes distant from the equinoctial and passes through the island of Taprobane. Here too the shadows are double. The sun passes twice over the vertex of those who dwell beneath it, and deprives their gnomons of shadow at noon when it is 79 degrees 30 minutes from the summer solstice on either side. Thus, while it travels through these 159 degrees toward the south, the shadows of the gnomons extend toward the south; while it travels through the remaining 201 degrees, they extend toward the north. Here, when the gnomon is 60 parts, the equinoctial shadow is 4 25 parts, the summer shadow 21 20, and the winter shadow 32.

The third parallel is where the longest day is 12 30 equinoctial hours. It is 8 degrees 25 minutes from the equator and passes through the Avalitic Gulf. Here too the shadows are double, for the sun passes twice over the vertex of those who dwell beneath it; and it also deprives the gnomons of shadow at noon when it is 69 degrees from the summer solstice on either side. Thus, while it travels through these 138 degrees, the shadows of the gnomons extend toward the south; while it travels through the remaining 222 degrees, toward the north. Here, when the gnomon is 60 parts, the equinoctial shadow is 8 50, the summer shadow 16 50, and the winter shadow 37 54.

The fourth parallel is one where the longest day is 12 45 equinoctial hours. It is 12 degrees 30 minutes from the equinoctial and passes through the Adulitic Gulf. Here too the shadows are double: the sun passes twice over the vertex and deprives the gnomons of shadow at noon when it is 57 degrees 50 minutes from the summer solstice on either side. Thus, while it travels through these 115 degrees 40 minutes, the shadows of the gnomons extend toward the south; while it travels through the remaining 244 degrees 20 minutes, toward the north. Here, when the gnomon is 60 parts, the equinoctial shadow is 13 20, the summer shadow 12, and the winter shadow 44 10.

The fifth parallel is beneath which the longest day is 13 equinoctial hours. It is 16 degrees 27 minutes from the equinoctial and passes through the island of Meroe. Here too the shadows are double, and the sun passes twice over the vertex. It deprives the gnomons of shadow at noon when it is 45 degrees from the summer solstice on either side. Thus, while it travels through these 90 degrees, the shadows of the gnomons extend toward the south; while it travels through the remaining 270 degrees, toward the north [Col. 0271A]. Here, when the gnomon is 60 parts, the equinoctial shadow is 17 45, the summer shadow 7 45, and the winter shadow 51.

The sixth is the parallel beneath which the longest day is 13 15 equinoctial hours. It is 20 degrees 14 minutes from the equinoctial and passes through Napata. It too has double shadows: the sun passes twice over the vertices, and deprives the gnomons of shadow at noon when it is 31 degrees from the summer solstice on either side. Thus, while it travels through these 62 degrees, the shadows of the gnomons extend toward the south; while it travels through the remaining 298 degrees, toward the north. Here, when the gnomon is 60 parts, the equinoctial shadow is 22 10, the summer shadow 3 45, and the winter shadow 58 10.

The seventh parallel is where the longest day is 13 30 equinoctial hours. It is 23 degrees 51 minutes from the equinoctial and passes through Syene. This is the first of those called parallels of single shadow. For beneath it the shadows of the gnomons at noon never extend toward the south; only at the summer solstice does the sun pass over the vertex of those who dwell beneath it, and the gnomons are then seen to be without shadow. It is as far from the equinoctial as the summer tropic point; throughout the rest of the year it casts its shadow toward the north. Here, when the gnomon is 60 parts, the equinoctial shadow is 26 30, the winter shadow 65 50, while at summer the gnomons have no shadow.

All the parallels farther north than this, up to the one that divides our world and marks the limit of habitable regions, have single shadows. Beneath them, at noon, the gnomons are seen to be completely without shadow; they always cast their shadows not toward the south but toward the north. Yet the sun never passes over their vertices.

The eighth parallel is one beneath which the longest day is 13 45 equinoctial hours. It is 27 degrees 40 minutes from the equinoctial and passes through Ptolemais in the Thebaid, which is also called Mercury. Here, when the gnomon is 60 parts, the summer shadow is 3 30, the equinoctial shadow 3 50, and the winter shadow 70 10.

The ninth parallel is where the longest day is 14 equinoctial hours. It is 30 degrees 22 minutes from the equinoctial and passes through Lower Egypt. Here, when the gnomon is 60 parts, the summer shadow is 6 50, the equinoctial shadow 35 12, and the winter shadow 83 15.

The tenth parallel is one at which the longest day is 14 15 equinoctial hours. It is 33 degrees 18 minutes from the equinoctial and passes through central Phoenicia. Here, when the gnomon is 60 parts, the summer shadow is 10, the equinoctial shadow 39 30, and the winter shadow 93 5.

The eleventh parallel is one beneath which the longest day is 14 30 equinoctial hours. It is 36 degrees from the equinoctial and passes through Rhodes. Here, when the gnomon is 60 parts, the summer shadow is 12 55, the equinoctial shadow 43 50, and the winter shadow 103 20.

The twelfth parallel is one at which the longest day is 14 45 equinoctial hours. It is 38 degrees 35 minutes from the equinoctial and passes through Smyrna. Here, when the gnomon is 60 parts, the summer shadow is 15 20, the equinoctial shadow 47 50, and the winter shadow 114 55.

The thirteenth parallel is one at which the longest day is 15 equinoctial hours. It is 40 degrees 56 minutes from the equinoctial and passes through the Hellespont. Here, when the gnomon is 68 parts, the summer shadow is 18 30, the equinoctial shadow 52 10, and the winter shadow 127 50.

The fourteenth parallel is where the longest day is 15 15 equinoctial hours [Col. 0272A]. It is 43 degrees 5 minutes from the equinoctial and passes through Massilia. Here, when the gnomon is 60 parts, the summer shadow is 20 50, the equinoctial shadow 55 55, and the winter shadow 140 15.

The fifteenth parallel is where the longest day is 15 30 equinoctial hours. It is 45 degrees 1 minute from the equinoctial and passes through central Pontus. Here, when the gnomon is 60 parts, the summer shadow is 23 15, the equinoctial shadow is 60, and the winter shadow 155 15.

The sixteenth parallel is one beneath which the longest day is 15 45 equinoctial hours. It is 46 degrees 51 minutes from the equinoctial and passes through the sources of the Danube. Here, when the gnomon is 60 parts, the summer shadow is 25 30, the equinoctial shadow 63 55, and the winter shadow 171 33.

The seventeenth parallel is wherever the longest day is 16 equinoctial hours. It is 48 degrees 23 minutes from the equinoctial and passes through the mouths of the Borysthenes. Here, when the gnomon is 60 parts, the summer shadow is 27 30, the equinoctial shadow 67 50, and the winter shadow 188 35.

The eighteenth is wherever the longest day is 16 15 equinoctial hours. It is 50 degrees from the equinoctial and passes through the middle of Lake Maeotis. Here, when the gnomon is 60 parts, the summer shadow is 29 55, the equinoctial shadow 71 20, and the winter shadow 208 20.

The nineteenth parallel is one at which the longest day is 16 30 equinoctial hours. It is 51 degrees 35 minutes from the equinoctial and passes through the southernmost parts of Britain. Here, when the gnomon is 60 parts, the summer shadow is 31 25, the equinoctial shadow 75 25, and the winter shadow 229 20.

The twentieth is the parallel beneath which the longest day is 16 45 equinoctial hours. It is 52 degrees 50 minutes from the equinoctial and passes through the mouths of the Rhine. Here, when the gnomon is 60 parts, the summer shadow is 33 20, the equinoctial shadow 69 5, and the winter shadow 253 10.

The twenty-first is the parallel where the longest day is 17 equinoctial hours. It is 54 degrees 1 minute from the equinoctial and passes through the mouths of the Tanais. Here, when the gnomon is 60 parts, the summer shadow is 34 55, the equinoctial shadow 82 35, and the winter shadow 278 45.

The twenty-second parallel is one at which the longest day is 17 15 equinoctial hours. It is 55 degrees from the equinoctial and passes through Brigantium in Great Britain. Here, when the gnomon is 50 parts [Col. 0272D], the summer shadow is 36 15, the equinoctial shadow 85 20, and the winter shadow 304 30.

The twenty-third is the parallel where the longest day is 17 30 equinoctial hours. It is 56 degrees from the equinoctial and passes through central Great Britain. Here, when the gnomon is 60 parts, the summer shadow is 37 20, the equinoctial shadow 88 58, and the winter shadow 335 15.

The twenty-fourth parallel is one beneath which the longest day is 17 45 equinoctial hours. It is 57 degrees from the equinoctial and passes through the cataracts of Britain. Here, when the gnomon is 60 parts, the summer shadow is 39 20, the equinoctial shadow 92 25, and the winter shadow 372 40.

The twenty-fifth parallel is where the longest day is 18 equinoctial hours. It is 58 degrees from the equinoctial and passes through southern Little Britain. Here, when the gnomon is 60 parts, the summer shadow is 40 44, the equinoctial shadow 96, and the winter shadow 419 5.

[Col. 0273A] The twenty-sixth parallel is where the longest day is 18 30 equinoctial hours. It is 59 degrees 30 minutes from the equinoctial and passes through central Little Britain. Here we have not used the increment of a quarter of an hour, both because the parallels become more numerous here and because the difference in their elevations does not add up even to a whole degree [Col. 0273B]. Moreover, since not everything needs to be investigated in the same way in the more northerly regions, we have thought it superfluous to set out the proportions of the shadows to the gnomons in separate and remote places.

Wherever the longest day is 19 equinoctial hours, that parallel is 61 degrees from the equinoctial and passes through the northern parts of Little Britain.

Wherever the longest day is 19 30 equinoctial hours, that parallel is 62 degrees from the equinoctial and passes through the islands called the Hebrides.

Wherever the longest day is 20 equinoctial hours, that parallel is 63 degrees from the equinoctial and passes through the island of Thule.

Wherever the longest day is 21 equinoctial hours, that parallel is 64 degrees from the equinoctial and passes through unknown Scythian peoples.

[Col. 0273C] Wherever the longest day is 22 equinoctial hours, that parallel is 65 degrees 30 minutes from the equinoctial.

Wherever the longest day is 23 equinoctial hours, that parallel is 66 degrees from the equinoctial.

Wherever the longest day is 24 equinoctial hours, that parallel is 68 degrees 40 minutes from the equinoctial. This is the first of those called *periscii*, that is, in Latin, “circumumbrous”: only at the summer solstice, when the sun does not set, do the shadows of the gnomons turn toward every part of the horizon. Here the summer-tropic parallel is always visible, while the winter parallel is never visible; for both alternately touch the horizon.

The oblique circle that passes through the middle of the signs, when the true equinoctial point rises, coincides with the horizon. If anyone seeks, for purposes of observation, the more general phenomena that occur at the northern declinations, he will find that where the elevation of the pole is approximately 67 degrees 15 minutes, no degrees of the zodiac—that is, no parts of the circle passing through the middle of the signs—set on either side of the summer solstice. Thus the longest day and the turning of the shadows toward every part of the horizon [Col. 0274A] become nearly monthly. These matters too are easily understood from the table of obliquity already set out. For whatever parallel we find to be distant from the equinoctial by such a number of degrees that, for example, it intercepts 15 degrees on either side of the tropic and then is either always or never visible, the elevation of the northern pole will fall short of 90 degrees—the fourth part of the whole—by exactly as many degrees as are contained in the intercepted part of the circle that passes through the middle of the signs [Col. 0274B].

Where the elevation of the pole is 69 degrees 30 minutes, no one will find the sun to set for 30 degrees on either side of the summer solstice; consequently the longest day and the circumumbrous gnomons occur for approximately two months.

Where the elevation of the pole is 73 degrees 20 minutes, no one will find the sun to set for 45 degrees on either side of the summer solstice; consequently the longest day and the periscian gnomons extend for approximately three months.

Where the elevation is 78 degrees 20 minutes, no one will find the sun to set for 60 degrees on either side of the summer solstice; consequently the longest day and the turning of the shadows extend over four months.

Where the elevation of the pole is 84 degrees, no one will find the sun to set for 75 degrees on either side of the summer solstice; consequently the longest day lasts nearly five months, and the shadows of the gnomons turn around during the same period.

[Col. 0274C] But where the northern pole is elevated 90 degrees above the horizon—the full fourth part—there, the semicircle of the zodiac north of the equinoctial—that is, half of the circle passing through the middle of the signs—is never beneath the earth, while the southern semicircle is never above the earth. Thus one day and one night each last approximately six months of the year, while the gnomons are always periscian. The distinctive features of this declination are that the northern pole lies above the vertex, the oblique circle assumes the position of a circle that is always visible and never visible, and the northern hemisphere, situated above the earth, always makes the southern hemisphere lie beneath the earth, while the equinoctial assumes the position of the horizon.]

The earth is founded upon its own stability; the abyss is wrapped around it like a garment. For just as the seat of fire exists only in fire, of water only in water, and of spirit [Col. 0264A] only in spirit, so the earth has no place except in itself, with all things adhering to it, nature restraining it and denying it anywhere to fall. Situated at the center, or pivot, of the world, it occupies the lowest and middle place among created things, as the heaviest, while water, air, and fire, by the lightness of their nature and likewise by their position, rise above it.

## CHAPTER XLVI. That the earth resembles a globe

We speak of the globe of the earth, not because it has the form of a perfectly regular sphere, given the great inequality of mountains and plains, but because, if all its features are enclosed within the circumference of lines, its overall embrace produces the figure of a perfect sphere. Hence it happens that the stars of the northern region always appear to us, while those of the southern region never do [Col. 0265A] [Note: [Col. 0265] A, “are seen”], and again these are not seen by those people, because the globe of the earth intervenes. Troglodytice and neighboring Egypt do not see the Bears, nor does Italy see Canopus, although nearly twice as much of the same globe is inhabited from east to west as from south to north, access being prevented on one side by heat and on the other by cold.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On the circles of the earth

The earth is divided into eight circles according to the variation of the days.

The first extends from the southern part of India, along the residents (*accolas*) of the Red Sea [Note: [Col. 0265] A, B, *incolas* (“inhabitants”)] and the maritime regions of Africa, to the Pillars of Hercules. On the day of the equinox, at noon, an eight-foot gnomon casts a shadow four feet long [Col. 0265B] [Note: [Col. 0265] A, B, C, “VII”]. The longest day has fourteen equinoctial hours.

The second runs from the western part of India through the Medes and [Note: [Col. 0265] A, “through the Persians”] Persians, Arabia, Syria, Cyprus, Crete, Lilybaeum, and the northern parts of Africa. At the equinox a gnomon of thirty-five feet casts a shadow twenty-three feet long [Col. 0266A] [Note: [Col. 0265] A, “twenty-six”]. The longest day has fourteen hours plus one-fifth of an hour.

The third begins among the Indians nearest to Imaus [Note: [Col. 0265] A, “and extends”], and runs through the Caspian Gates, Taurus, Pamphylia, Rhodes, the Cyclades, Syracuse, Catina, and Gades. All its gnomons cast a shadow of thirty-eight inches [Note: [Col. 0265] A, “to the gnomon”]. The longest day is fourteen and a half hours, with one thirtieth of an hour added [Note: [Col. 0265] A, “part of an hour”].

The fourth extends from the other side of Imaus through Ephesus, the sea of the Cyclades, northern Sicily, the eastern parts of Narbonese Gaul, and the maritime regions of Africa toward the west. A gnomon of twenty-one feet corresponds to a shadow of sixteen feet. The longest day has fourteen hours and two-thirds of an hour.

The fifth circle contains, from the entrance to the Caspian Sea, Bactria, Armenia [Col. 0266B], Macedonia, Tarentum, the Tuscan Sea, the Balearic Islands, Spain, and Media. A gnomon of seven feet has a shadow of six feet [Note: [Col. 0265] A, “Seven feet correspond to the gnomon”; A and B omit “feet”]. The longest day is fifteen hours.

The sixth encompasses the Caspian peoples, the Caucasus, Samothrace, the Illyrians, Campania, Etruria, Massilia, Spain [Col. 0267A], central Tarraconensis, and thence Lusitania. A gnomon of nine feet has a shadow of eight feet. The longest day is fifteen hours plus one-ninth of an hour.

The seventh begins at the opposite shore of the Caspian Sea and proceeds through the remote parts of Thrace, Venetia, Cremona, Ravenna, Transalpine Gaul, the Pyrenees, and Celtiberia [Col. 0269A]. A gnomon of thirty-five [Note: [Col. 0269A] A and B omit “feet” and have “a shadow”] feet has a shadow of thirty-six feet. The longest day is fifteen hours and three-fifths of an hour.

The eighth enters Gaul from the Tanais through Lake Maeotis, the Sarmatians, the Dacians, and part of Germany [Col. 0270A]. The longest day is sixteen hours.

To these circles the ancients add two: one passing through the island of Meroe and Ptolemais, a city on the Red Sea, where the longest day is twelve hours and a half [Col. 0272A]; the other passing through Syene in Egypt, where it is thirteen hours.

They add two beneath them: the first passes through the Hyperboreans and Britain [Col. 0273A], where the longest day is seventeen hours [Note: [Col. 0273] “Where the longest day is [etc.] is omitted by A, B, C]; the other passes through the Scythian region, from the Rhipaean Mountains to Thule, where day and night continue alternately.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. The gnomonic account of the same matters

[Note: [Col. 0274C]

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—The upright post, which they call the gnomon. Gnomonics are determined from the rays of the sun. A staff erected perpendicular to a plane at a right angle necessarily casts a shadow when it is in the light. This principle is essential for the construction of sundials, for the inclination of the world, and for cosmography.

Let the gnomon, that is, the upright staff A B, be represented in the diagram under discussion. When the sun is shining it casts a shadow—long when the sun is low, short when it is high. Let the sun therefore be at D; a ray from the point where it touches the gnomon, namely A, descends to G and produces the shadow B G, half as long as the gnomon. Let the staff be sixty feet and the shadow thirty. This is the situation on the equinoctial day—always understanding the sun to be at noon—in Egypt; the same occurs on the solstitial day at Cologne Agrippina. On the same day, in the town of Syene, there is no shadow: at noon the sun will be at A, while the ray descends straight to B. The proportion of the shadows continually changes as they incline toward the south and north. Thus, in most parts of Germany, the winter shadow will be B C, for the sun will be at F. But when the sun is at E, the shadow H B is produced, one-twelfth longer than the gnomon; this occurs at Cologne on the equinoctial day.

The twelfth part of Taurus and the fourteenth of Leo. As is clear from the corresponding parts of the signs, this cannot happen. For the twelfth part of Taurus has as its corresponding part the eighteenth of Leo, not the fourteenth, as we shall explain more fully below concerning the corresponding parts of the signs. It is also read differently in Pliny, but that reading too does not fit the more recent division of the parts. See below, under “On the equinox.”]

The shadow of the upright post, which they call the gnomon, in Egypt at midday on the day of the equinox amounts to a little more than half the measure of the gnomon [Col. 0275A] [Note: [Col. 0275] A, “half”]. In the city of Rome, one-ninth of the gnomon is lacking from the shadow. At the town of Ancona, one thirty-fifth remains beyond it. In that part of Italy called Venetia, during the same hours the shadow is equal to the gnomon. In a similar way, above Alexandria, five thousand stades away, at midday on the day of the solstice, no shadow is cast [Note: [Col. 0275] A wrote “to cast,” followed by “Onesicritus, Alexander’s general. Thus also …”]. The same is said to occur in India above the river Hyphasis. Among the Troglodytes, they say, this occurs forty-five days before and after the solstice, with the shadow lying toward the south during the intervening ninety days. Moreover, on the island of Meroe in the Nile, five thousand stades from Syene, the shadows disappear twice a year, when the sun occupies the eighteenth part of Taurus and [Note: [Col. 0275] A, “the twelfth”] the fourteenth of Leo.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On earthquakes

[Note: [Col. 0275D]

GLOSSES OF AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR.—They say that an earthquake is caused by wind enclosed in the earth’s cavernous entrails, like those of a sponge. An earthquake usually occurs where the earth is hollow, places into which winds enter and cause an earthquake; where it is sandy or solid, however, no earthquake occurs. This movement of the earth pertains to judgment, when sinners and earthly people, shaken by the spirit of God’s mouth, will be moved. Likewise: the movement of the earth is the conversion of earthly people to faith. Hence it is written: “The feet stood, and the earth was moved,” certainly in order to believe.]

[Col. 0275B]

They say that an earthquake is caused by wind [Note: [Col. 0275] A, “and its”] enclosed in the cavernous entrails of the earth, like a sponge. Passing through it with a terrible [Note: [Col. 0275] A and C, “roaring”] tremor and striving to escape, the wind shakes it with varied rumbling and forces itself to pour out, either by trembling or by splitting the earth open [Note: [Col. 0275] A, “while trembling”]. Hence hollow regions of the earth are subject to these movements, since they can contain wind; sandy and solid regions lack them. Earthquakes occur only when the sky and sea are calm and the wind has been enclosed in the veins of the earth. What trembling is in the earth, thunder is in the cloud; what a rift is there, lightning is here. Floods of the sea also occur together with an earthquake, when the same breath is poured in or received back into the hollow of the sea.

## CHAPTER L. The eruption of Etna

The soil of Sicily, being cavernous and covered with sulphur and bitumen, is almost entirely exposed to winds and fires. As the breath within struggles with the fire, it often belches forth smoke, vapors, or flames in many places; or, when the wind presses more violently, it throws up masses of sand or stones [Note: [Col. 0275] A, “raises them”]. Hence, after the example of Mount Etna, there persists an exceptionally long-lasting eruption of fire resembling Gehenna. They say that the fire of Etna is nourished by the waters of the Aeolian Islands: the waters, rushing together and carrying the breath with them into the deepest depths, suffocate it for so long until, spread through the veins of the earth, it ignites the fuel of the fire. Hence the dogs of Scylla are imagined to bark, when sailors far away are terrified by the roaring of the waters [Col. 0276B], which the surge dashes together as it swallows them in the whirlpool.

## CHAPTER LI. The division of the earth

[Note: [Col. 0275D]

GLOSSES OF AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR. — The whole globe of the lands, surrounded by Ocean [Col. 0276C], is divided into three parts: Europe, Asia, and Africa. The earth, as Hyginus testifies, is placed in the middle region of the world and, ending at an equal distance on every side, occupies the center. Ocean, poured out along the circumference of the sphere, washes almost all the boundaries of the globe. Thus the setting constellations too are thought to fall into it.

The region of the earth is divided into three parts: one is called Europe, another Asia, and the third Africa. The sea divides Europe from Africa, from the outermost boundaries of Ocean and the Pillars of Hercules. The mouth of the Nile, called the Canopic mouth, separates Asia from Libya together with Egypt. Asia, as Blessed Augustine says, extends from the south through the east to the north; Europe from the north to the west; and from there Africa extends from the west to the south.

Thus Europe and Africa appear to occupy one half of the globe, while Asia alone occupies the other half. But those two are made into two parts because, between them, whatever waters flow between the lands enters from Ocean and makes for us the Great Sea.

Geometers estimated the measure of the whole earth [Col. 0276D] at 180,000 stades. Ambrose, in the Book of the Hexameron, says: “We read ‘heaven’; let us understand heaven. We read ‘earth’; let us understand fruitful earth. Why should I ask what the measure of its circumference is, which geometers have estimated at 180,000 stades? I willingly confess that I do not know what I do not know—or rather, that it would be of no benefit to know what it would not help me to know. How can we comprehend what Scripture demonstrates to be impossible for human beings, when the Lord says: ‘Who measured the waters in his hand and heaven with a span, and enclosed all the earth in his hand?’”

This whole earth is girded by three margins,

And a slanting line bends its side through every region,

[Col. 0277A] The lands of the Indians on this side, and on that side the Thetian waters enclose,

Which the rising Titan sees with his first light:

[Col. 0278A] The Indus, immense, marks the western boundaries,

Reaching toward Thule, where it shines by night and by day.

]

The entire world of the lands, surrounded by Ocean, is divided into three parts: Europe, Asia, and Africa. It begins at the setting of the sun and at the Strait of Cádiz, where the Atlantic Ocean, breaking through, pours into the inner seas. [Note: [Col. 0275] A: “of the sea . . . is spread abroad.”] As one enters from there, Africa is on the right and Europe on the left; between them lies Asia, comparable in size to the other two. Their boundaries are the rivers Tanais and Nile. The jaws of the Ocean which we mentioned are open for fifteen miles in length and five in breadth. Europe therefore extends from the west to the north; Asia, from the north through the east to the south; and from there Africa extends from the south to the west.
