# THE BOOK ON TIMES

(C, S)

## Argument of the Book of the Venerable Bede on Times

In the preceding book, the reader was instructed in the world and its principal parts by brief and clear rudiments in the *Cosmography*, since that discipline is a preparation for knowledge of the times and histories to which this work is devoted. This volume, entitled *On Times*, merely sets forth in passing the divisions, kinds, and distinctions of time; for in the preceding work the same subject is treated more fully. It was proper—and indeed natural—that after explaining the cause from which time proceeds, namely the world, the discussion should now be directed to its effects and consequences. Since these are presented at greater length in the preceding book, we have reserved for that work the explanation of difficult passages.

## Chapter I. The Division of Time

[Note: [Col. 0279B]

**Beginning of the Author’s Glosses.**—Times are so called from *temperamentum* (“balance”), because they balance one another through heat and cold. They are divided into moments, hours, days, months, years, centuries, and ages. “Centuries,” that is, the lifetime of one person. According to some, a century consists of two hundred and twenty years; but Servius says that the age or lifetime of each individual can be called a century. Blessed Jerome says thus in the book of the *Hebrew Questions*: “Human life, therefore, is not confined—as many mistakenly think—to one hundred and twenty years, since we find that after the Flood Abraham lived one hundred and seventy-five years, and others more than two hundred and three hundred years.”

**The sun yields.**—By following its course, the sun both yields and succeeds to itself. It yields when it passes from one place of its circle to another; but it succeeds to itself when, as though continually following itself, it returns through the same regions. Or it yields when it is in its first part and comes to its last; alternatively, it yields while ascending as far as midday and succeeds to itself while descending as far as sunset.

**At brief intervals.**—A brief interval is the span from one moment to another.

**When something.**—That is, some heavenly body, when it yields its place to the sun in the eyes of human beings; that is, when some heavenly body gives place and succeeds for human observers—not so as to pass away, but merely to move itself.

**John the New’s Scholion.**—“Hour” is a Greek word. *Ὥρα* is aspirated, whereas in Latin *ora* does not signify time but the extremity of any space or magnitude, such as that of places, regions, or even garments; it has a light [or slight] sense. The two words are therefore not identical, since the Greek and Latin are distinguished by their aspiration. The Greeks also call the four known quarterly divisions of the year “hours”—what are commonly called spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Eustathius says that Homer understands these as the four goddesses called Hours in the *Iliad*, two of whom open the sky and the others close it. The sky is opened, as the physicists teach—and Aristotle proves in Book II of *On Generation and Corruption*—from the winter solstice to the summer solstice, which is the season of generation; conversely, it is closed from the summer solstice to the winter solstice, which they call the season of corruption. Throughout this period the sun is declining. In the more common sense, however, “hour” signifies a particular moment of time, the twenty-fourth part of the civil day. Writers call these equinoctial hours, and they are equal throughout the year. As they occur, one twenty-fourth of the natural day—the day distinguished from the night—comes into being. In another sense, the word signifies one-twelfth; these hours are unequal, for in summer hours of this kind are much longer. Since the winter night is therefore extended, it has longer night-hours.]

Time is divided into moments, hours, days, months, years, centuries, and ages. A moment is the smallest and narrowest measure of time, so called from the movement of the heavenly bodies. It is the extremity of an hour at brief intervals, when one thing yields to and succeeds itself. An hour is a Greek word, though it sounds Latin: for an hour is the end of time, just as there are ends of the sea, rivers, and garments. [Note: [Col. 0279] A: “An hour is an end.” See what we said at the beginning of the variants of the preceding book concerning the collated manuscripts.]

An hour consists of four points, ten minutes, fifteen parts, and forty moments. [Note: [Col. 0279] A, B, and C omit “fifteen parts.”] It should be noted, to avoid error, [Note: [Col. 0279] A adds “is.”] that computation rests partly on nature and partly on authority or custom: on nature, for example, in saying that a common year has twelve lunar months; [Note: [Col. 0279] A: “as it is said.”] on custom, in counting months as thirty days; and on authority, in holding that a week consists of seven weekdays.

## Chapter II. On the Day

[Note: [Col. 0279D]

**John the New’s Scholion.**—The ordinary day belongs to the sun. Common usage improperly calls this an “artificial” day; others, as we have already frequently stated, call it “natural.” It certainly takes its name from Jupiter, whom the Greeks call *Δῖα*; physicists understand “Jupiter” to mean the sun, as is clear from the well-known verse of Orpheus and Ennius. The sun, therefore, is the author of the day.

The Chaldaeans and Persians reckon this day from one sunrise to the next. For the varying beginnings of days, see Gellius and the readings of Caelius.]

The ordinary day is the presence of the sun above the earth, and properly consists of twenty-four hours. [Note: [Col. 0279] A, B, and C: “is completed.”] The Hebrews, Chaldaeans, and Persians count it from one sunrise to the next; the Egyptians from one sunset to the next; the Romans from midnight to midnight. [Note: [Col. 0279] A: “from midday to midday.”] The Umbrians and Athenians reckon from midday to midday. Moses, however, calls the period from morning to morning one day. But when the Lord rose, the evening of the Sabbath was dawning into the first day of the week, so that humanity, having fallen from light into darkness, might thereafter return from darkness to light.

## Chapter III. On the Night

[Note: [Col. 0280B]

**John the New’s Scholion.**—Night is the absence of the sun. The word “night” comes from a Greek term with the alteration of one letter: in Greek, *νὺξ* signifies night. Aristotle defines it in the first book of the *Meteorologica* as *σκίαν τῆς γῆς*, that is, “the shadow of the earth.” For, as physics and optics demonstrate, whenever a body is placed in light, a shadow necessarily forms on the side opposite the light. Thus, while the sun travels below the boundary which the Greeks call the horizon, the shadow of the earth must be spread widely through the air toward the sky, but it does not penetrate as far as the outermost heavens, as astrologers and physicists teach. As regards its shape, this shadow resembles a truncated cone or pyramid. On this subject, see certain diagrams described above, where the matter itself is treated more fully.

**Made for mortals’ rest.**—Night is unsuitable for carrying out activities. For this reason some writers say that its name derives from harming; poets make it the offspring of Earth, the reason for which is evident from what we have just said. She immediately bore *Ὕπνον καὶ Θάνατον*, that is, Sleep and Death, twin brothers—both because night brings sleep, which takes half of life away from human beings, making them, as it were, half-dead, and because it is cleverly conceived that death is the brother of sleep, as in Seneca’s tragedy:

> The dread brother of languid death.

**Where it is more severe.**—Sleep is prolonged in cold conditions but induced by warmth. See Aristotle in the short work *On Sleep and Waking*. Nature has therefore provided that winter nights should be longer than summer nights, and increasingly so the nearer a region lies toward the north, beyond the sun’s path. Thus Britain has a winter night of seventeen hours, Germany sixteen, and Italy fifteen; Ireland, however, has twenty-four. Moreover, in Thule, which is the farthest of the lands, a single night lasts for several months. Conversely, during the solstitial period the days last for the same number of hours; thus the proportion of light and darkness is equal in all regions when equal and unequal quantities are compared.

**When the star of this name appears.**—This is the star of Venus. When it follows the sun and is seen toward the part of the sky where the sun is about to set, it is called Vesper, Hesperus, and Vesperugo. But if the same heavenly body precedes the sun in the morning, it is called Lucifer, or in Greek *Phosphoros* (*Φωσφόρος*), and is the largest and brightest of all the stars in the sky. It casts a shadow that is as much smaller than the moon’s as the moon’s own shadow is surpassed by that of the sun.]

Night is the absence of the sun, formed by the earth’s shadow, and made for the rest of mortals, lest humanity, worn out by prolonged labor, should fail. Where it is more severe, it is also longer, both for reducing work and for warming the limbs. Its parts are seven:

- Twilight, that is, uncertain light between light and darkness; for we call something doubtful *creperum*.
- Evening, when the star of that name appears.
- The time of silence, when everything is quiet. [Note: [Col. 0279] A: “the untimely hour.”]
- The dead of night, which is the middle and inactive period of the night.
- Cockcrow, when the rooster cries.
- Morning, between the withdrawal [Note: [Col. 0281] A: “of the darkness of night”] of the darkness and the coming of dawn.
- Daybreak, as though it were the small light of day already beginning. [Note: [Col. 0281] A: “a certain small light”; C: “the beginning of day.”] This is also the dawn that precedes the sun.

## Chapter IV. On the Week

[Note: [Col. 0281C]

**John the New’s Scholion.**—*Ἕβδομα* or *ἑβδομάς*, and *hebdomada*—for it is called by all these names—is a period of seven days, from which it also receives its name in Latin; for we call it a *septimana*. The Jews first arranged these days, not from the revolutions of the stars, from which nearly everything else is derived, but by the authority of God, who, as stated earlier, completed the creation of the world in six days and rested on the seventh. They assigned six days to ordinary secular activities and the seventh to religion and rest; hence it was called the Sabbath. The Gentiles and Christians later imitated this practice, though for different reasons. First they called the first day from the Sabbath the first day of the Sabbath, then the next the second day of the Sabbath, and so on; the Church uses the order of weekdays instead. Religion forbade naming these days after pagan gods, such as Friday and Tuesday. The reason for this practice has been discussed more fully elsewhere.

The Gentiles gave these days their names from the planets. If you wish to know precisely about the bodily influences which poets attribute to those born under them, read Book IV of Pontanus, *On Celestial Matters*.]

A week consists of seven days, but the eighth day is the same as the first: one returns to it, and the week begins again from it. The Gentiles gave these days names from the planets, believing that from the sun they received spirit, from the moon the body, from Mars blood, from Mercury intelligence and speech, from Jupiter self-control, from Venus pleasure, and from Saturn sluggishness. But Saint Sylvester decreed that they should be called weekdays, naming the first the Lord’s Day. [Note: [Col. 0281] A, B, and C: “should be called.”] He imitated the Hebrews, who name the first day of the Sabbath, the second day of the Sabbath, and the remaining days likewise by number. Among them a week also extends over the same number of years; they likewise had a week of weeks both in days and in years, calling the fiftieth day Pentecost and the fiftieth year the Jubilee, that is, liberation.

## Chapter V. On the Month

[Note: [Col. 0281D]

**John the New’s Scholion.**—While it traverses a little more than the zodiac in twenty-nine and a half days. “A little more” is correctly said, for in this number of days it traverses the entire zodiac and nearly one-twelfth of it. A month is the time before the moon returns to the same part of the zodiac from which it departed in the preceding month; it is the interval between two conjunctions of the moon with the sun, which the Latins call *coetus*. In the preceding book we discussed our own and foreign months at greater length.]

The lunar month is completed by the waxing and waning of the moon, as it traverses a little more than the zodiac in twenty-nine and a half days. But ease of computation alternates lunar months of thirty and twenty-nine days. The solar month is longer by twenty-two hours; eleven of these become epact days, by which the sun exceeds the moon’s course each year. Twelve times twenty-two makes 264, just as eleven times twenty-four completes the same number. The Hebrews begin their months with the new moon; the Romans with the Kalends; the Egyptians on the fourth day before the September Kalends and continue to the ninth day before those same Kalends, counting their months as thirty days. [Note: [Col. 0281] A, B, and C: “they call the remaining five days intercalary.”] They call the remaining days intercalary. They were the first to begin ending months according to the sun’s course, lest the moon’s swifter and uncertain course impede their calculations.

## Chapter VI. On the Months of the Romans

[Note: [Col. 0282D]

**John the New’s Scholion.**—The Romans, under Romulus. Because the first establishment of his people demanded it, Romulus was more devoted to military discipline than to celestial matters, as Ovid attacks him in his well-known verse:

> Surely, Romulus, you knew arms better than the stars.

Macrobius treated this subject at length in the *Saturnalia*. Moreover, Quintilis, Sextilis, September, and October are named merely from numbers; for the syllables *-tilis* and *-ber* were added because of the form of the words and signify no more than they do in *MEDITULLIO Tullius*.

They call April after the opening of crops. Others prefer to derive the name from Venus, who is called Aphrodite in Greek, since this month belongs to Venus, as astrologers also teach. Taurus, through which the sun passes in April, is the domicile of Venus.

For *iduare* means “to divide” in the Etruscan language. Festus and Macrobius both teach this; hence *viduus* and *vidua* have survived, as though meaning “separated from their spouses.”]

The Romans, under Romulus, followed a year arranged in ten months, consisting of 304 days. [Note: [Col. 0281] A and C: “they arranged the year, but conducted it in 304 days.”] He dedicated the first month to his father Mars; he named the second April after the opening of crops; he consecrated the third to Maia, the mother of Mercury, and the fourth to Juno. Quintilis and Sextilis—now named after the birth of Julius Caesar and the triumph of Augustus—and the remaining months he named numerically. He called their beginnings the Kalends, because at that time the people were summoned, that is, called into the Capitol, and the number of days remaining until the Nones was announced after the word *calo*, meaning “I call,” had been spoken five or seven times. [Note: [Col. 0281] A: “they were announced.”] He called them the Nones because on the ninth day before the Ides the people gathered in the city [Note: [Col. 0281] A: “to inquire”; B and C omit this] to ask what had to be done in that month. The Ides, moreover, are the day that divides the month in the middle; for *iduare* means “to divide” in Etruscan. Numa added two months to these, naming January after Janus and February after Februus, the god of purification, and arranged the year according to the moon’s course in 354 days. Julius Caesar added eleven days and established the calendar as it is observed today.

## Chapter VII. On the Solstice and Equinox

[Note: [Col. 0283C]

**John the New’s Scholion.**—On the eighth day before the Kalends of January and July. In Cicero’s time the arrangement of the solstices and equinoxes was different; now, because of the movement of the firmament or of the new sphere, they occur later. What is written—that the moments of the seasons occur in the eighth degrees of the signs, whereas all astrologers unanimously hold that they occur in the first degrees of the signs—must be referred to the ancient method of dividing the degrees. For the ancients divided the signs differently; Ziegler discussed this learnedly in his commentaries on the second book of Pliny.

But the equinoctial day is equal throughout the world. A demonstration of this appears in Euclid’s *Phenomena*, concerning the revolutions of the spheres. All great circles on a sphere intersect one another in two equal parts, as the horizon and the equator do. The remaining circles, which the sun describes around the world, are divided unequally by the horizon except beneath the equinoctial circle. The varying increase of days and nights was treated in the preceding book with several demonstrations, and again in the book *On the Nature of Things*, concerning sundials and the proportions of shadows.]

[Col. 0283A]

There are thought to be two solstices and two equinoxes: the eighth day before the January and July Kalends, and the eighth day before the April and October Kalends—that is, in the eighth degrees of Capricorn, Cancer, Aries, and Libra. [Note: [Col. 0283] A omits “in.”] But the equinoctial day is equal throughout the world. Because the increase of daylight varies, the longest day at Meroë amounts to twelve equinoctial hours and eight parts of an hour; at Alexandria, fourteen hours; in Italy, fifteen; and in Britain, seventeen. There, the bright nights in summer clearly testify to what reason compels us to believe: during the days of the solstice, as the sun approaches nearer to the pole of the world, the earth lying beneath its narrow circuit of light has continuous days for six months, while the nights, conversely, are displaced toward the winter solstice. Pytheas of Massilia writes that this occurs on the island of Thule, six days’ sailing north of Britain.

## Chapter VIII. On the Seasons

The seasons are the alternations of changes by which the sun, approaching or receding, regulates the circuit of the year. Winter is cold and wet because the sun lingers farther away; spring, as it returns, is wet and warm; summer, as it burns intensely overhead, is hot and dry; autumn, as it withdraws, is dry and cold. The ancients began these seasons on the seventh day before the Ides of February, May, August, and November, so that the solstices and equinoxes would fall in the middle of the seasons. Spring is compared with the east, because at that time everything rises from the earth; summer with the south, because that region is more inflamed by heat; [Note: [Col. 0283] A, B, and C: “more burning.”] autumn with the west, because, owing to the boundary between heat and cold, it brings serious diseases; winter with the north, because it is numb with cold.

## Chapter IX. On the Years

[Note: [Col. 0283D]

**Ancient Commentary.**—Let the zodiacal circle be Α Β Γ Δ, with Θ, representing the earth, at its center, through which two lines are drawn. Let each be understood as a diameter: one from Α to Γ, and the other from Β to Δ. Thus, when the sun approaches Α, it produces one equinox; at Γ, the autumnal equinox; at Β, the summer solstice; and at Δ, the winter solstice.

**John the New’s Scholion.**—The solar or civil year. “Civil” is usually added to days, not years. Some days are civil, consisting of a period of twenty-four hours, day and night together; others are natural, consisting of the interval between sunrise and sunset. These years are otherwise called revolving years, as in Cicero, Book VI of *On the Republic*, because they are produced by the sun’s revolution through the zodiacal circle. The Greeks, led by the same analogy, call a year *ἐνιαυτός*, because it turns back upon itself, which is the nature of circular motion. Concerning the great year, also called the Platonic year, there are various opinions among writers.]

The solar or civil year is the time in which the sun traverses the zodiac in 365 days and a quarter. The Romans begin it at the winter solstice, the Hebrews at the spring equinox, the Greeks at the summer solstice, and the Egyptians in autumn. A common lunar year consists of twelve lunar months, that is, 354 days. [Note: [Col. 0283] B: “intercalary.”] An intercalary year consists of thirteen lunar months and 384 days, beginning with the paschal moon. [Note: [Col. 0283] Thus in the manuscripts.] The great year is the period in which, after completing their appointed courses, all the heavenly bodies return to their proper places. Josephus says that it is completed in six hundred solar years.

## Chapter X. On the Leap Year

[Col. 0284B]

The leap year is produced from the quarter-day over a four-year period, when the sun returns to the sign from which it departed not in 365 days but with an additional quarter of a day. For example, if the rising sun now enters the equinoctial place of the sky, in the following year it will return to that place at midday; in the third year, in the evening; in the fourth, at midnight; and in the fifth, again at sunrise. It consequently announces that a day must be added, lest, if one were not added, after 365 years the spring equinox should occur on the winter-solstice day. The Egyptians insert it at the completion of their year, that is, on the fourth day before the September Kalends; the Romans on the sixth day before the March Kalends, from which it also received its name. [Note: [Col. 0283] A: “after the year had been completed.”]

In the shorter and more common explanation, the leap year is generated by the sun’s delay, since it does not fully return to the same line in 365 days. If, for example, you carefully observe the sun rising at the spring equinox—which, according to the Egyptians, occurs on the twelfth day before the April Kalends—you will find that in the following year it rises somewhat lower on the same day. In the third, fourth, and fifth years you will find the same decline increasing to such an extent that, unless a day is added beforehand, the sun will rise from the middle of the east on the eleventh day before the April Kalends, producing the equinox; and it will preserve the same delay in the remaining risings. [Note: [Col. 0285] A and B: “in the others.”]

## Chapter XI. On the Nineteen-Year Cycle

The nineteen-year cycle was established by the Council of Nicaea on account of the fourteen paschal moons, because, after completing 235 revolutions over nineteen years, each moon returns by an unerring course to the same day of the solar year. The cycle is divided into an eight-year period and an eleven-year period, that is, into eight and eleven years. Eight lunar years exceed the same number of solar years by only two days: one of these is supplied to complete the eleven-year period, while the other is consumed by the leap; otherwise the solar eleven-year periods would exceed the lunar ones by one day. Some, however, vigorously attempt to supply these days from the leap days of the eight years. [Note: [Col. 0285] Basil edition: “from leap years.”] But the leap day, customarily added to the sun and moon in February, does not prejudice the future period, and they themselves add no leap day to the eleven-year period. To state the matter more clearly: the two lunar days left over in the eight-year period make up the two days lacking in the eleven-year period.

## Chapter XII. On the Lunar Leap

The lunar leap is produced over nineteen years by the earlier place and hour of the moon’s illumination. Although some, counting each lunar month as twenty-nine and a half days, alternate the illuminations between midday and midnight, they are not seeking the truth of nature in this but ease or brevity of calculation. For if you inquire into the natural course of the moon of the first month, which is now illuminated at midday, and of the second, which is now illuminated at midnight, in the following year the illumination will occur one hour, one point, ten moments, and half a moment—a nineteenth part of one point—earlier than midday or midnight. [Note: [Col. 0285] A and the Basil edition omit “half a moment”; B and C place “half a moment” after the preceding words.]

This distinction, however, tends not toward a fixed endpoint of the intercalary or common year but toward an equal division of the nineteen years. Thus, over nineteen years, the lunar illumination gradually anticipates itself and loses the space of one day, causing the final year of the nineteen-year cycle to be counted as 383 days. If you neglect to do this, then after fifteen nineteen-year cycles the moon will meet you fifteen days away from where it is thought to begin.

## Chapter XIII. The Contents of the Same Cycle

[Note: [Col. 0286D] **John the New’s Scholion.**—Here the rationale is given for those indicators which were added at the end of the final book. They consist of 532 years, after which everything returns to its original state, as it was at the beginning, as has been explained more fully elsewhere. We have restored these cycles to their original dignity, for in the copies that have until now been in use they were excessively corrupted.]

The same paschal cycle is marked out in eight lines.

The first order contains the years from the Incarnation of the Lord, increasing by one each year. [Note: [Col. 0285] Basil edition: “increasing.”]

The second contains the Roman indictions, which revolve within themselves over a course of fifteen years. [Note: [Col. 0285] A, B, and C, and the Basil edition always have “within themselves.”]

The third contains the eleven lunar epacts, which increase each solar year in accordance with the moon’s course and are always added in order to find the moon of the Kalends, being set on the eleventh day before the April Kalends.

The fourth contains the recurring days of the week. Since they are set on the ninth day before the April Kalends, they are necessarily completed in twenty-eight years because of the loss caused by the leap year. Their arrangement requires twenty-eight nineteen-year cycles to be written, so that each recurring day may begin one cycle, and the entire sum of the paschal calculation may be unfolded in 532 years.

The fifth contains the lunar cycle, which the nineteen-year cycle precedes by three years and which is itself also contained within nineteen years.

The sixth contains the fourteen moons with which the ancients celebrated Easter. [Note: [Col. 0285] A: “which.”] These wander in varying courses from the twelfth day before the April Kalends to the fourteenth day before the May Kalends, and their time of illumination is taken from the eighth day before the Ides of March to the Nones of April. From the fourteenth moon to the fourteenth moon of the following year there are 354 days if it is a common year, or 384 if it is an intercalary year.

In the seventh, the Sunday of Easter is found between the eleventh day before the April Kalends and the seventh day before the May Kalends; because of the reckoning of intercalary years, it may be extended freely.

In the final order, the moon of the paschal feast varies from the fifteenth to the twenty-first because of the Sunday. [Note: [Col. 0285] A: “the final moon.”] For the leap removes a night and adds an age, which has grown throughout the entire cycle. [Note: [Col. 0285] B adds “it adds.”] Night is removed in the sense that the moon is thought to decline beforehand. [Note: [Col. 0285] B: “has declined.”] In reality, however, the night itself remains—the night which is the beginning of the coming year and the starting-point of the cycle that is beginning. For this reason, the same final year, retaining eighteen epacts, supplies twelve days to the first year rather than eleven, as normally happens in the other years. Since the cycles revolve at the end of thirty days, no epact is placed at the beginning of the cycle.

## Chapter XIV. The Rules of the Paschal Tables

[Col. 0286D]

If you wish to know how many years have passed since the Incarnation of the Lord, ascertain how many orders of indictions there have been. For example, in the fifth year of the emperor Tiberius there were forty-six; multiply these by fifteen, and the result is 690. Always add the regular number twelve, because, according to Dionysius, the Lord was born in the fourth indiction, and add the indiction of whichever year you wish—for example, in the present case, one. The result is 703. These are the years from the Lord’s birth.

If you wish to know which indiction it is, take the years of the Lord, add three, divide by fifteen, and the remainder is the indiction of the present year.

If you wish to know the number of the lunar epacts, divide the years of the Lord by nineteen, multiply the remainder by eleven, then divide by thirty; the remainder is the epact.

If you wish to know the recurring days of the week, take the years of the Lord and add their fourth part. To these also add four regular numbers, because there were five recurring days in the year of the Lord’s birth. [Note: [Col. 0287] A adds “regular numbers.”] [Note: [Col. 0287] A, B, and C: “because.”] Divide these by seven, and the remainder gives the solar epacts.

If you wish to know which year of the nineteen-year cycle it is, take the years of the Lord and add one—because the Lord was born in the second year of that cycle—then divide by nineteen; the remainder is the year of the nineteen-year cycle.

If you wish to know which lunar cycle it is, take the years of the Lord, subtract two, and divide by nineteen; the remainder is the year of the lunar cycle.

If you wish to know the leap year, divide the years of the Lord by four; the remainder gives the number of years since the leap year.

Once these matters have been determined precisely, you will easily find the day of Easter and the moon. If you wish to know Easter a number of years after the present year—for example, after one hundred years—it is sufficient to find the epacts and the recurring solar days. Divide one hundred by nineteen, and the remainder is five. Know, therefore, that these will be the epacts in the hundredth year. [Note: [Col. 0287] B: “which will be in the hundred and fifth year.”] In the same way, dividing one hundred by twenty-eight, you will find the recurring solar days in the hundredth year, which will be sixteen.

## Chapter XV. The Mystery of the Paschal Season

Easter does not return to the same day of the year, as the season of the Lord’s birth does, for in the case of the Nativity only the memory of the birth itself is solemnly celebrated. Here, however, the mysteries of the life to come are celebrated and gifts are received. Hence the name “Pascha,” signifying passage from death to life, seeks a season fitting to its mysteries.

First, it is celebrated after the equinox has been passed, so that the darkness of death may be overcome by the true light. Second, it is celebrated in the first month of the year, called the Month of New Things, so that the joys of new life may be observed. Third, because the resurrection occurred on the third day and in the third age of the world—that is, under grace [Note: [Col. 0287] C: “made manifest”]—when it had previously lain hidden in a prophetic enigma before the Law and under the Law, it is honored in the third week of the moon. At that time, the moon’s own turning also teaches that the glory of the mind is changed from earthly to heavenly contemplation.

Finally, the Lord’s Day, distinguished by the origin of light and worthy of reverence because of Christ’s triumph, is recalled to our memory as something desirable for us through our own resurrection.

## Chapter XVI. The Ages of the World

[Col. 0288A]

The times of the world are distinguished into six ages.

The first age extends from Adam to Noah. It contains ten generations and 1,656 years. It perished entirely in the Flood, just as forgetfulness commonly drowns infancy.

The second extends from Noah to Abraham and likewise encompasses ten generations, but 292 years. In this age language was discovered—that is, the Hebrew language. For after infancy, when a person cannot speak, human beings begin in childhood to learn how to speak.

The third extends from Abraham to David and contains fourteen generations and 942 years. Since a person begins to be capable of procreation in adolescence, Matthew began his genealogy with Abraham, who was also established as the father of the nations. [Note: [Col. 0287] A: “because.”]

The fourth extends from David to the migration to Babylon, comprising, according to Matthew, an equal number of fourteen generations and extending over 473 years. [Note: [Col. 0287] London manuscript, B, and C: 483.] From this age the times of the kings began, for youthful dignity is suited to kingship.

The fifth then extends to the coming of the Savior in the flesh, likewise comprising fourteen generations and extending over 559 years. [Note: [Col. 0287] C: 588.] In this age the Hebrew people are shaken, exhausted as though by grievous old age, by increasingly frequent calamities.

The sixth is the age now in progress. It has no fixed sequence of generations or times but, like an age grown decrepit, will end with the death of the entire world.

## Chapter XVII. The Course and Order of the Times

The first age therefore contains, according to the Hebrews, 1,656 years; according to the Septuagint translators, 2,242.

Adam, aged 130, fathered Seth, who was born in place of Abel. Seth, aged 105, fathered Enos. He began to call upon the name of the Lord. Enos, aged 90, fathered Cainan. Cainan, aged 70, fathered Malaleel, whose name means “plantation of the Lord.” Malaleel, aged 65, fathered Jared. Jared, aged 162, fathered Enoch, who was taken up by God. Enoch, aged 65, fathered Methuselah. The sons of God desired the daughters of men. Methuselah, aged 187, fathered Lamech. Giants were born. Lamech, aged 182, fathered Noah, who built the ark. In Noah’s six-hundredth year the Flood came. [Note: [Col. 0287] C: “in his six-hundredth year.”]

Shelah, aged 30, fathered Eber, from whom came the Hebrews. Eber, aged 34, fathered Peleg. The tower was built. Peleg, aged 30, fathered Reu. The gods were first worshiped. ## Notice of the Patrology Editor

“The following work, sometimes designated under the title *The Greater Book on Times*, was published under this title together with the book *On the Nature of Things*, at Basel in 1529. It is found separately in volume II of the Cologne edition. Both recensions place it before the book *On Times*, although it was written after that work and as a kind of supplement to it. In both, chapters 66 and 67 were also printed separately under the single heading *Chronicle, or On the Six Ages of the World* [Note: [Col. 0291] See what Smith says about this *Chronicle* in his preface, which we give before Bede’s *Ecclesiastical History*, and Oudin, *Commentaries*, vol. I (above, col. 71).] The *Chronicle* is extended up to the reign of Leo the Isaurian, that is, to the year 4680 of the world and 726 of Christ. It was printed at Venice in 1505, with P. Victor’s *Description of the Regions of the City of Rome* appended at the end and a brief Life of Bede at the beginning; at Paris in 1507; at Basel in 1529, together with the book *On the Nature of Things*; and in 1537 at Cologne, with Bronchorst’s continuation and notes. Smith published separately a work collated with four manuscripts—Bodley Library F. 3. 5, Magdalen College, Oxford, N.E., the Royal Library E, 904, and St. John’s College, Cambridge. Duchesne appended to the *Chronicle* in his *French Writers* (vol. III) a continuation extended to the year 820. Finally, in the edition of Bede’s *Minor Ecclesiastical Works* published by the English Historical Society, only the *Sixth Age of the World* is included, revised after Smith and the manuscripts of the Royal Library, 13. A. XI and 12. D. IV, both from the twelfth century.”

[Col. 0293] “In our edition the Basel text of the book *On the Reckoning of Time* is reproduced, but collated with the oldest and most distinguished manuscripts of the British Museum. On the authority of these, we have also restored to their proper places, namely chapters 1 and 4, two short treatises on Finger-Reckoning and on the Reckoning of Ounces, which had been given as separate works in earlier editions. The editor had long before been led to suspect that these treatises were genuine fragments, both from their style and from the fact that they were inscribed by the printer on the pages of Bridefert’s *Commentaries* and of the heading *On the Reckoning of Time*—a fact which might at first have appeared to be an error. At the same time the same opinion occurred to Dr. Wright; and, in fact, the treatises seem to have found their proper place in the Basel edition.”

Thus speaks Dr. Giles, whose English we have translated. Since we have followed the order observed by him, we shall add nothing to his words except that we have appended to the text, which alone he supplied, the glosses of Bridefert, the scholia of John of Nijmegen, and Smith’s notes.

[Col. 0293]

## Argument to the Book of the Venerable Bede on the Reckoning of Time

It is customary for writers, at the beginning of their books, to set down three things: the person, the place, and the time; therefore these three must be sought. “Person” is so called because it sounds through itself—that is, by sounding through itself it displays itself. “Place” is so called from *locare*, “to locate,” because something is situated there. A place is position or location, because whatever is corporeal is contained in a place and cannot exist except in a place. That is, whatever has a right and a left, a front and a back, an above and a below, is local and corporeal; whatever lacks these is incorporeal and without place, that is, spiritual. What time is you will find in chapter one.

The place is the monastery of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, which is at the mouth of the River Wear and beside the River Tyne, in the place called Jarrow. The blessed father Bisi, surnamed Benedict, built it, together with his collaborator and partner in that work, Ceolfrith, who, after Benedict, was abbot of that monastery for thirty years.

The time is that of the great Charles, son of Pippin, son of Ansigisus, who begot Pippin, the father of Charles.

The person is Bede, who, as he himself demonstrates below, was a native of the English people. There is, then, an island of the Ocean that once had the name Albion and is now called Britain. It lies between the North and the West, opposite Germany, Gaul, Spain, and the greatest parts of Europe, at a considerable distance.

At the present time, in accordance with the number of books in which the divine law is written, it investigates and professes, in the languages of five peoples, one and the same knowledge of supreme truth and true sublimity: namely, the languages of the English, Britons, Scots, Picts, and Latins; through meditation on the Scriptures this knowledge has been made common to all the others.

According to the blessed Gregory, the English are interpreted as though they were “angels,” because of the beauty of their bodies. From the lineage, then, of these English the venerable Bede was descended. Born in the territory of the monastery mentioned above, when he was seven years old he was entrusted, for upbringing, to the care of the most reverend abbot Benedict by his relatives, and afterward to Ceolfrith. Spending all the remaining time of his life in the residence of that same monastery, he devoted all his effort to the study of the Scriptures. Amid observance of the regular discipline and his daily responsibility for singing in the church, he always found it a delight either to learn, to teach, or to write.

In the nineteenth year of his life he received the diaconate, and in the thirtieth the priesthood, both through the ministry of the most reverend Bishop John, at the command of Abbot Ceolfrith. From the time he received the priesthood until the sixty-first year of his life, he took care briefly to annotate Holy Scripture from the works of the venerable Fathers, or also to add material according to the form of their interpretation and meaning.

On the beginning of Genesis, up to the birth of Isaac and the expulsion of Ishmael, four books; on the Tabernacle, its vessels, and the garments of the priests, four books; on the allegorical construction of the Temple, two books; also, thirty Questions on the Book of Kings; three books on Solomon’s Proverbs; seven books on the Song of Songs; three books on Ezra and Nehemiah; one book of allegorical exposition on Christ and the Church in the book of the blessed father Tobit; also, chapters of readings on the Pentateuch of Moses, Joshua, and Judges; on the Books of Kings and Chronicles; on the book of the blessed father Job; on the Parables and Ecclesiastes; four books on Matthew’s Gospel; four books on Mark’s Gospel; six books on Luke’s Gospel; on the Gospel of Saint John; on the Apostle, he took care to transcribe in order everything he found expounded in the short works of Saint Augustine; two books on the Acts of the Apostles; one book each on the six canonical Epistles; three books on the Apocalypse of Saint John; also a book of letters to various persons, including one on the Six Ages of the World, one on the Reckoning of the Leap Year, and one on the Equinox according to Anatolius.

He described the Life of the holy father Cuthbert, monk and bishop, first in heroic meter and afterward in plain prose; the Ecclesiastical History of his island and people in five books; a Martyrology of the birthdays of the saints, in which he diligently endeavored to record, for all whom he could find, not only on what day but also by what kind of contest, or under which judge, they conquered the world; a book of Hymns in various meters or rhythms; a book on Orthography arranged in alphabetical order; also a book on the Art of Meter, with another little book appended to it on Figures or Tropes—that is, on the figures and modes of expression with which Holy Scripture is composed; and individual books on the Nature of Things and on Times.

Among all these works he composed this most beautiful book in the year 725 from the Incarnation of the Lord, according to Dionysius. He entitled it *On Times*, or *On the Reckoning of Time*, and afterward lived happily for nine years, then departed to Christ, for whose love he despised the present world. (COLONIA EDITION.)

[Col. 0293]

## On the Reckoning of Time (C, S)

### Preface

[Col. 0293A] Once I composed, in concise language, two little books, which I thought necessary for students, on the nature of things and the reckoning of time. When I began to give and explain them to certain brothers, they said that they had been arranged much more briefly than they wished, especially [Col. 0294A] [Note: [Col. 0293A] To the manuscripts cited up to this point must be added another Paris manuscript, 1362, which we shall designate D.] [Note: [Col. 0293A] Smith reads *illum*, which is the correct reading, but all the manuscript books have *ille*.] the book *On Times*. Its use seemed to be especially needed because of the reckoning of Easter; and they urged me to discuss more fully the state, course, and end of times.

Yielding readily to them, after examining the writings of the venerable Fathers, I published a longer book on times [Col. 0295A], as far as I was able through the generosity of him who, while remaining eternal, established times whenever he willed, and who knows the ends of times; indeed, through the courses of times as they pass away, he himself will impose an end whenever he wills.

In this work, lest anyone perhaps be offended that in the sequence of the preceding age I have followed the Hebrew truth more than the edition of the Seventy Translators, I have also inserted that edition in every case where it seemed to differ, so that every reader may see both together and choose whichever he thinks ought to be followed more fully.

But this conviction is firmly established in me, and I believe that no prudent person should reproach it: just as the most reverend interpreter of that same Hebrew truth said to the detractors of his work, “I do not condemn or criticize the Seventy, but I prefer the Apostles to all these” [Col. 0295B], so I too confidently profess that I do not criticize the ancient chroniclers who are shown sometimes to have followed the translation of the Seventy Interpreters and sometimes, as they pleased, to have held it in contempt, as will also be shown in the course of this little work. But I prefer to all of these the complete purity of the Hebrew truth, which the most eminent of teachers—Jerome in his books of Hebrew Questions, Augustine in his book *On the City of God*, and Eusebius the chronicler himself in the third book of his *Ecclesiastical History*, drawing on the words of the historian Josephus in his writing against the grammarian Appion—demonstrate to contain “a shorter sequence of times than is commonly said to be contained in the edition of the Seventy” [Col. 0295C] [Note: [Col. 0295] C reads “edition.”] [Note: [Col. 0295] C reads “to be contained.”] [Col. 0296A].

Nor do even those who exalt the Seventy to the heavens with great and divine praises hesitate to say that this shorter sequence ought to be followed. Whoever examines their statements, I believe, will soon cease to slander our labor, unless, heaven forbid, he views it with envious eyes.

However they may receive it, then, you who read these writings, I offer to you, my dearest abbot Huetbert, the little book first published according to my ability, to be read through and examined. I earnestly beg that, if you detect anything blameworthy in it, you immediately point it out to me for correction. But when you see that it has been done in an orderly and reasonable manner, give devout thanks with me to God, who granted it and without whom we can do nothing.

If anyone is offended even by this [Note: [Col. 0295] C reads “by what.”] [Note: [Col. 0295] C reads “offends.”]—why I presumed to attempt a work of this kind, and why [Col. 0296B] I myself undertook to compose a new work from matters that could be found scattered through ancient writings [Note: [Col. 0295] B and C read “could be found.”]—let him listen to Saint Augustine, who says: “For this reason it is necessary that many books be produced by many people, in different styles but not with different faith, even on the same questions, so that the matter itself may reach many people: to some in one way, and to others in another.”

Let him also hear me, answering simply on my own behalf: Whoever dislikes or considers it superfluous that, at the brothers’ request, I have gathered these materials from every source and brought them together in a single little book may leave them unread, if he wishes, and draw instead from the common fountains of the Fathers whatever he considers sufficient for himself and his own people; nevertheless, let him preserve with me the inviolate obligations properly owed by brotherhood [Col. 0296C].

## Here Begins the Book

[Col. 0295]

## CHAPTER I. On Reckoning, or the Language of the Fingers

Since, with the Lord’s help, we are going to speak about the reckoning of time, we have judged it necessary first to demonstrate briefly the very useful and very easy skill of bending the fingers, so that, after providing the greatest facility in counting, we may approach the investigation and clarification of the sequence of times with the readers’ minds better prepared for calculation.

For the rule by which almost all interpreters of Holy Scripture are shown to have embraced the matter, no less than the forms of letters, is not to be despised or considered of little account [Col. 0295D] [Note: [Col. 0295] B and C read “embraced.”] Indeed, many others in various ways, and Jerome himself, the interpreter of divine history, did not hesitate to take up this discipline as an aid in his exposition of the Gospel passage:

“The hundredfold, the sixtyfold, and the thirtyfold fruit,” he says, “although produced from one soil and from one seed, nevertheless differ greatly in number. Thirty refers to marriage; for the joining of the fingers itself, embracing and binding them together as though with a gentle kiss, depicts husband and wife. Sixty refers to widows, because they are placed in distress and tribulation; therefore they are pressed down on the upper finger. And the greater the difficulty of abstaining from the enticements of pleasure once experienced, the greater also is the reward” [Col. 0296C].

Moreover, the number one hundred is transferred from the left hand to the right, using the same fingers but not the same hand. With the fingers by which married women and widows are signified on the left hand, a circle is formed to express the crown of virginity.

First, finger-reckoning is performed on the left hand, in the following manner.

When you say “One,” bend the little finger of the left hand and press it into the hollow at the center of the palm. When you say “Two,” bend the next finger from the little finger and place it in the same spot. When you say “Three,” bend the third in the same way. When you say “Four,” likewise raise the little finger [Note: [Col. 0295] D omits “likewise.”] When you say “Five,” raise the next finger from the little finger in the same way. When you say “Six,” raise the third as well, leaving only the middle finger—called the medical finger—fixed in the center of the palm.

When you say “Seven,” place only the little finger, with the others raised for the moment, upon the base of the palm. When you say “Eight,” place the medical finger beside it. When you say “Nine,” place the impudent finger opposite it [Note: [Col. 0295] Instead of “opposite,” D reads “beside.”] When you say “Ten,” place the nail of the index finger in the middle joint of the thumb. When you say “Twenty,” insert the tip of the thumb between the middle joints of the index and impudent fingers. When you say “Thirty,” join the nails of the index finger and thumb in a gentle embrace [Col. 0297A].

When you say “Forty,” pass the inner side of the thumb over the side or back of the index finger, with both fingers raised. When you say “Fifty,” bend the thumb at its outer joint in the form of the Greek letter gamma, Γ, and incline it toward the palm. When you say “Sixty,” carefully encircle the bent thumb, as above, with the bent index finger from the front. When you say “Seventy,” fill the bent index finger, as above, by inserting the thumb, with only the nail of the thumb raised across the middle joint of the index finger [Note: [Col. 0297] B, C, and D read “with its nail raised.”] When you say “Eighty,” fill the bent index finger, as above, by extending the thumb lengthwise, with its nail inserted into the middle joint of the index finger [Note: [Col. 0297] C omits “its.”] When you say “Ninety,” press the nail of the bent index finger into the base of the thumb [Note: [Col. 0298] B, C, and D read “of the raised thumb.”]

Thus far on the left hand. But “One hundred” is made on the right hand in the same way as “Ten” on the left. “Two hundred” on the right, as “Twenty” on the left. “Three hundred” on the right, as “Thirty” on the left. And so on in the same manner up to nine hundred.

Likewise, “One thousand” is made on the right as “One” on the left; “Two thousand” on the right as “Two” on the left; “Three thousand” on the right as “Three” on the left, and so on up to nine thousand.

When you say “Ten thousand,” place the left hand face upward in the middle of the chest, with only the fingers raised toward the neck [Note: [Col. 0298] B, C, and D omit “in.”] When you say “Twenty thousand,” place the same hand, extended, broadly over the chest. When you say “Thirty thousand,” place the same hand face downward but raised, and insert the thumb into the cartilage at the center of the chest [Note: [Col. 0297] C reads “the same hand face downward, but with the thumb raised.”] When you say “Forty thousand,” turn the same hand face upward at the navel. When you say “Fifty thousand,” place the thumb of the same hand, face downward but raised [Col. 0297C], upon the navel. When you say “Sixty thousand,” grasp the left thigh from above with the same hand face downward. When you say “Seventy thousand,” place the same hand face upward upon the thigh. When you say “Eighty thousand,” place the same hand face downward upon the thigh. When you say “Ninety thousand,” grasp the loins with the same hand, turning the thumb toward the groin.

But “One hundred thousand,” “Two hundred thousand,” and so on up to nine hundred thousand, you complete in the same order on the right side of the body as has been described. When you say “Ten times one hundred thousand,” clasp both hands together, interlacing the fingers of one with those of the other.

There is also another method of reckoning, proceeding joint by joint. Since it pertains especially to the reckoning of Easter, it will be explained more appropriately when we reach that subject in due order.

From the reckoning I have described, a certain manual language can also be devised, both for exercising the mind and for playing a game [Note: [Col. 0298] C reads “how those who”; B omits “who.”] By displaying the letters one by one through the fingers, a person may entrust words made up of those same letters to another who also knows this skill, even at a distance, to be read and understood; or, by hinting at necessary matters more secretly through it, he may deceive the uninitiated as though by divination [Col. 0298A].

The order of this game or language is as follows: when you wish to indicate the first letter of the alphabet, hold up one finger; for the second, two; for the third, three; and so in order for the remaining letters.

For example, if you wish to warn a friend placed among ambushers to act cautiously, display with your fingers III, I, XX, XIX, V, I, VII, V [Note: [Col. 0297] B and C read “cautiously.”] The letters of this sequence signify *Cautè age*, “Act cautiously.” It can also be written this way if the secret nature of the matter requires it.

But these matters can be learned and practiced together more easily through Greek reckoning and letters. Unlike the Latins, who customarily express their numbers with a few letters repeated, the Greeks deploy the whole character-set of their alphabet as numerical signs and represent the three higher sets of numbers by individual signs, following almost the same order in representing numbers as in writing the alphabet, as follows:

For this reason, as soon as they have learned to indicate numbers with their fingers, they also know, without any intervening delay, how to assign the same letters to them.

But enough of this. Now let us proceed to explain the times, insofar as the Lord, the creator and arranger of times, will deign to assist us.

## CHAPTER II. On the Threefold Reckoning of Time

[Col. 0297D]

### Glosses of Bridefert on the Reckoning

“Times” receive their name from *temperamentum*, “regulation” or “balance,” either because each of their intervals has been separately regulated, and so forth. Each time is regulated by another, as he says below, where he speaks about times; and all fruits in their seasons receive their proper balance from cold, heat, and rain, and from that balance the times are named.

“Their interval has been regulated,” namely by another; separated from one another, as spring. For spring has a different regulation from summer, and likewise, and so forth. The same may be understood of the months.

“World-ages” (*saecula*) are said to derive from the god Secus, whom the pagan philosophers thought to be the god of the ages. *Secus*, however, is a Greek name and is interpreted as “form.” Ages consist of generations; hence they are called *saecula* from following, from the verb *sequor*, “I follow,” because they follow one another. For when some depart, others succeed them.

They say that an age ends after fifty years. Hence that Hebrew man with the pierced ear is ordered to serve “for ever,” that is, for up to fifty years.

An age is a period constructed from many things. For *aetas* is used for one year, for seven years, for one hundred years, and for any period of time. “Let them be regulated,” that is, arranged.

“Distinguished by a threefold reckoning,” that is, separated.

The span of each time is ninety-one days.

“It runs its course,” namely, the reckoning of time.

“In two ways,” that is, by two methods.

“Human,” namely by human authority—that is, something established by human beings. Time proceeds not only by divine authority but also by human authority; human, for example, as in the Olympiads.

Mount Olympus is in Greece, near which there is a city called Olympias, built in honor of the Sun. There, at the end of four years, contests and sacred rites were celebrated in honor of the Sun; these were called Olympiads.

Among the Greeks, an Olympiad is a period of four years, during which the rites of the Sun and Olympian Jupiter were performed. For it always completes its course in a four-year leap-year period, in which the intercalary year also occurs among the Romans. Hence a period of five years is also called a lustrum. For a contest was always held at the beginning of the fifth year, when the rising sun, from the equinoctial point, begins the first year after the intercalary year.

An Olympiad is said to be named as though from *O olampias*, that is, “complete illumination”; and Olympus as though from *hololampus*, that is, “entirely bright and burning,” because of its proximity to the sun. And because its height rises beyond the clouds, authors frequently use it as a term for heaven.

In the same way we call garments *holoserica*, that is, “entirely silk,” because *holos* in Greek means “whole” in Latin.

Nundinas, that is, market dealings, from the Nones to the Ides. Nundinae are gatherings of pagans and likewise of country people, who assemble either to attend to their own business or to procure merchandise. Nundinae are public meetings and commercial markets, so called as though “nine days,” that is, the Nones and Ides. Nundina is also the Roman goddess, named from the ninth day of those being born, which is called the lustral day. The lustral day is the day on which infants are purified and receive their names; but for males it is the ninth day, and for females the eighth.

Indictions are so called from a fixed indication of years. In the first lustrum bronze money was paid, then silver, then gold. A lustrum is *penteresin*, that is, a five-year period, which the Romans are said to establish in the fifth year. It is therefore a five-year span; it is called this because, after the census had been completed over five years in the republic, the city of Rome was purified.

Of fifteen years: because this number is easy to multiply. Also of the day, namely the leap day.

A quadrant is a fourth part of a day. For the sun traverses the zodiacal circle in 365 and a quarter [days]; hence, in four years, it completes the entire day that naturally ought to have been inserted on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, because it was placed there at the creation of the world and began its course. Now, however, among the Romans the leap day is placed on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, and among the Egyptians on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, because time proceeds according to human authority [Col. 0300A].

The Lord commanded in the Law that the fiftieth year be called the jubilee. The jubilee year is named from rejoicing, because in that year trumpets sounded. *Jubilaeam*, that is, remissible.

The jubilee is also called the year of remission, because in that year all debts and every labor of agriculture were remitted; purchased slaves too were released. For the fiftieth year in the Law was ordered to be called the jubilee, that is, the year of remission, or one filled with rejoicing, in which the people would rest from every work, all debts would be canceled [Col. 0300B], purchased slaves would return free, and that year itself would stand out above the others through greater solemnities and divine praises.

By this number, deservedly, that perfect tranquility of supreme peace is signified, when, as the Apostle says, at the most famous voice of the archangel and the sounding of the trumpet, with all rising again, the ancient possession of the flesh will return to everyone. Then the flesh will return to its ancient land, in which Abel lived and from which he was expelled by Cain. Then Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and likewise all the souls of mortals, will receive their bodies again, from which they had departed, so that they may possess them forever. When the labors and hardships of this age have ceased and the debts of all faults have been dismissed, the entire people of the elect will rejoice forever in the contemplation of the divine vision alone, once that desirable command of our Lord and Savior has been fulfilled: “Be still and see that I am God.”

Barbarian peoples are said to be so called from *barba* (“beard”) and *rus* (“countryside”).

By human custom it has been established that a month should be reckoned as thirty days [Col. 0300C], although this agrees neither with the course of the sun nor with that of the moon. Indeed, those who have investigated the matter more carefully testify that the moon has twelve hours less, without compromising the calculation of the *saltus*, while the sun has ten and a half hours more. When, therefore, you reach the eleventh chapter below, you will find sufficiently what these hours amount to. And when you reach the forty-second chapter, you will see more clearly what the *saltus* is.

Indeed, the moon has twelve hours less, without compromising the calculation of the *saltus*. The calculation of the lunar *saltus*—that is, the material from which the *saltus* is formed—is preserved if we subtract nothing from those twelve hours in which the moon remains after twenty-nine days, until we arrive at the appropriate place for discussion.

Moreover, guided by nature, it has been discovered that the solar year, etc.

Here he speaks of the nature of time.

By a quarter, that is, six hours.

If it is common, that is, composed of twelve months, it is completed in 354 days. If it is an embolismic year, that is, one that exceeds the ordinary measure, it has thirteen months. In each lunar month the *saltus* increases by four moments, and by one ounce of a moment, and by an atom. For one lunar month is always of thirty days, and the next of twenty-nine.

Multiply, therefore, six times thirty and six times twenty-nine, and you will find 354.

And the entire course of the moon. The entire course of the moon is completed in nineteen years. For it will not return to the same places of the signs in which it is now, for example, illuminated, nor to the same day of the month, the same moment of rising, the same latitudes and altitudes of the zodiac, or the same conjunction with the sun, before it completes 235 conjunctions, that is, months, in the nineteen-year cycle.

For this moon, which is now in its present designation, will not bear that same designation again until nineteen years have passed. This can be demonstrated very easily by an example. January has nine regular days for determining the moon’s age; but if we join to them the twenty-two epacts, there are thirty-one altogether. When thirty is removed, one remains. The moon was first on the Kalends of January this year; it will by no means again be first on those Kalends until nineteen years have been completed.

This nature was not, in accordance with the madness of the pagans [Col. 0301A], a creative goddess, one among many, but was created by the one true God.

Nature is so called because it causes something to be born. The pagans say that it is the creator of all things, although it is itself not a creator but rather created.

The pagans, that is, the Gentiles.

“One among many”: for there were many goddesses, such as Juno, Minerva, and Venus.

[Col. 0301B] “Was created,” namely, nature itself as it relates to times.

“Inserted,” that is, placed within.

“That they may be signs,” that is, things that signify. For weather and clear skies are often recognized from the stars.

He does not mean those signs whose observation is a matter of superstition, but useful signs, necessary for the uses of this life: those which sailors observe in steering, or which other people observe in order to anticipate the qualities of the air during summer and winter and the temperate conditions of autumn and spring.

And surely he calls these things “times”—those produced through the stars—not intervals of duration, but changes in the conditions of this sky.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—Times therefore receive their name from *temperare*, “to regulate” or “to temper.” M. Varro, in Book V *On the Origin of Words*, accepts the same etymology. “Time,” he says, “is said to be the interval of the world and of motion.” This, divided into several parts, is chiefly determined by the course of the sun and moon; and so time was named from their measured regularity. It may also be noted in passing that in these works of Varro there is a definition of time which M. Cicero, in the books *On Invention*, says can more easily be understood than expressed. Macrobius, in Book I of the *Saturnalia*, and Rodolphus Agricola, in Book I, set out that definition in more explanatory language, so that time is “the result of the revolution of the heavens,” etc.; the passage is well known in both authors.

The day, too, which is composed of quadrants. “Composed of quadrants,” that is, of six-hour divisions, for the sun’s course through the zodiac is completed in 365 days and a fourth part of a day. Therefore the year cannot complete its course with the sun unless an additional day is drawn from four times six hours; every fourth year one civil day is intercalated. The Romans do this by the institution of Numa Pompilius in the month of February, which for this reason Cicero calls intercalary; that day is also called the intercalary day.

It was intercalated in February because that month is the shortest of all. It was not placed at the end, lest it be uncertain whether it belonged to February or to the following month. It occupied the sixth day before the Kalends rather than another day, so that by the designation “sixth” it might indicate its origin in six-hour divisions [Col. 0301D].

It is called *bissextus* either because the sixth day before the Kalends of March is named twice before proceeding to the seventh, or because the day was established as a day of measure, as Festus Pompeius says, with the letter *e* changed into *i*. Others think that the remainder is merely an empty supplement of the word, as in *postliminium* and *meditullium*, where *liminium* and *tullium* have no independent meaning; so in *bissextus*, *bis* is likewise only an appendage.

“It was established by human custom.” The calculation of months and years will be discussed elsewhere.

“But also the wandering stars.” The time in which each planet completes its course through the zodiac is a year, for *annus* signifies a circuit, whence *annulus*, “ring.” Thus Saturn’s year consists of thirty ordinary, that is, solar years; Jupiter’s of twelve; Mars’s of two. These are called revolving years, in distinction from that great year which Plato is reported to have been the first to note, concerning which Cicero speaks in Book VI of *On the Republic*.

“What nature was not, in accordance with the madness of the pagans.” [Col. 0302A] Bede incidentally rebukes the opinion of those who make nature a goddess, as Plato, Pliny the Elder, and others do. For nature is not itself a goddess, but a certain power implanted by God in the stars, so that they may be signs and times for us, as it is written in Genesis, chapter one. The stars themselves, however, lack a soul and therefore also a will [Col. 0302B]; hence they are not gods but instruments of God, through which he governs the world.]

Times therefore receive their name from [Note: [Col. 0297] B, C, *temperamento*, “regulation” or “tempering”], either because each of their spans has been separately regulated, or because all the courses of mortal life are regulated by moments, hours, days, months, years, centuries, and ages.

Concerning each of these, as the Lord grants, we shall expound. First, however, we advise the reader that the reckoning of time is distinguished in a threefold manner. For time proceeds either by nature, by custom, or by authority.

And authority itself is divided in two ways [Note: [Col. 0297] C, “in two ways”]: human authority, namely, as Olympiads are celebrated in four-year cycles, nundinae in nine-day cycles, and indictions in cycles of fifteen years [Col. 0299A]. The day, too, which is composed of quadrants, the Greeks, Egyptians, and Romans ordered to be intercalated in February or August, each according to his own understanding.

Divine authority, on the other hand, established that the Sabbath be observed on the seventh day, that in the seventh year one abstain from rural labor [Col. 0300A], and that the fiftieth year be called the jubilee, as the Lord commanded in the Law. For although barbarian peoples are also shown to have weeks, it is clear that they borrowed them from the people of God [Note: [Col. 0299] B, C, “borrowed”].

By human custom it has been established that a month be reckoned as thirty days [Col. 0301A], although this agrees neither with the course of the sun nor with that of the moon. Indeed, those who have investigated the matter more carefully testify that the moon has twelve hours less, without compromising the calculation of the *saltus*, while the sun has ten and a half hours more.

Moreover, guided by nature, it has been discovered that the solar year is completed in 365 days and a quarter; the lunar year, if common, in 354 days; and if embolismic, in 384 days, and that the entire course of the moon is contained within a nineteen-year cycle. The wandering stars, too, are carried around the zodiac in their several periods. Nature was not, in accordance with the madness of the pagans, a creative goddess, one among many, but was created by the one true God, when he commanded that the stars, set in the heavens, should be signs, seasons, days, and years.

## CHAPTER III. On the Smallest Divisions of Time

[Note: [Col. 0302B]

**BRID. RAM. GLOSSES.**—An hour is the twelfth part of a day, since twelve hours complete a day, and so forth. An hour contains four points, ten minutes, fifteen parts, forty moments, and in certain lunar calculations five points.

An hour consists of four points—that is, an hour according to the sun. One point is a fourth part of an hour. There are four points in an hour; two minutes in one point; four moments in one minute; 564 atoms make one moment. Nevertheless, mathematicians, when investigating human nativities, strive to reach even the atom.

*Mathesis* means “learning.” Hence *mathematicus*, “learned” or “instructional.” Mathematicians are vain philosophers, that is, astrologers, who dispute about natures and stars.

*Mathesis* without aspiration signifies vanity, that is, empty teaching; with aspiration, it signifies true doctrine and perfect knowledge [Col. 0302C].

“Nativities” means births, that is, what people will be like—whether good or evil.

“They strive”: they contend concerning the twelve signs. For mathematicians say that whoever is born under the sign of Pisces will be a fisherman. And so forth—matters which blessed Gregory wisely destroys in his homily on the Epiphany of the Lord.

Into twelve points. These are larger than the other points mentioned above, and mathematicians use them. For one of these points contains one hour within it.

Into sixty omens. An omen is the manifestation of some sign. Fate is a fortunate outcome. Virgil writes: “Fate is whatever the gods speak,” whether good or evil. This refers to the mathematicians’ observation of the stars.

“We shall all indeed rise again.” Jerome: “Or, according to certain manuscripts, ‘We shall not all sleep.’ ‘We shall all be changed,’ namely, into glory.”

“Into an atom.” Augustine: “With utmost speed.” In Greek, *atomos* means “indivisible.”

“In the twinkling of an eye.” The movement of the eye is the swiftest emission of rays from the pupils toward the object at which they are directed.

“Trumpet,” that is, by proclamation or sign. Supply: therefore, without that observation of the mathematicians, we ought to use this expression just as the Apostle does.

“For although calculators necessarily distinguish.” Calculators take their name from calculation. *Calculus* is named from the stone used in counting. *Calci* are very small, round, smooth pebbles; they are so called because they can be trodden upon without discomfort. The ancients used them to count everything.

Before the invention of numerals, the ancients, not knowing how to count, reckoned their periods and days by pebbles: white ones in prosperity, black ones in adversity. Hence Persius:

> “Count this day, Macrinus, with the better pebble,”

that is, with a white one.

“They distinguish,” namely, the atom from the other intervals of time.

A moment in the eye extends from the movement of the eyelid to its next movement, that is, as long as the eyelid remains at rest.

There are four points in an hour, and they make ten minutes, that is, forty moments; those forty moments make fifteen parts. From the beginning of the rising of each sign to its end, two hours pass. There are twenty-four hours between day and night, and twelve signs in the heavens; therefore two hours belong to each sign as it rises.

The calculation is as follows. The natural order is that the sun should circle the whole earth in twenty-four hours, and that there should be thirty parts—that is, thirty lines—in each sign. During each of those twenty-four hours, fifteen of those lines appear in the rising of each sign, when it begins to rise above the earth, coming upward from below.

Alternatively: an hour, namely a solar hour, contains four points; but insofar as it concerns the moon, a lunar hour contains five points, and this results from the moon’s speed.

A lunar point has two minutes, that is, one fifth of an hour. A solar point has two and a half minutes, three and a half parts, and a quarter of a part, ten moments. A minute has one and a half parts and four moments. A part has two and two-thirds moments.

Fifteen parts occur in the rising of a sign. The motion of the heavens through fifteen parts produces an hour: fifteen parts of the zodiac rise, set, or move from place to place in one hour. Each part moves in two moments and half a moment, that is, in two-thirds of a moment. Fifteen times that interval of two and a half moments makes a complete hour. For this reason an hour is said to contain fifteen parts.

The 365th portion of the zodiac is called a part. The twenty-four hours—that is, the entire day—in which the sun illuminates that portion of the zodiac, and the interval in which that portion moves from one place to another, are called parts. But just as the measure of hours varies according to the length of days, so too does the measure of moments.

Sometimes an hour is equinoctial, that is, natural; sometimes longer or shorter. Hence, whatever the length or brevity of an hour may be, its fortieth part is called a moment.

As has already been said, an hour contains forty moments and sixty omens, or, according to the mathematicians, 2,400 omens and 22,560 atoms [printed: *IICCCC, atomos XXIIDLX*]. In certain lunar calculations, namely, for a night-hour, it contains five points.

These divisions—hour, point, minute, part, moment, omen, and atom—are not natural divisions of time. Rather, they appear to be conventional, that is, artificial and nominal, invented and named by authorities.

Calculators, that is, reckoners, are so called from *calculi*, pebbles, by which they counted. They counted in twelve hours, or in four points, or in ten minutes, or in fifteen parts, or in forty moments, or, when necessary, in still smaller divisions, such as omens and atoms, or in larger ones, such as thirds, quarters, and three-quarters. They also counted years in days and months, and in weeks or days of the week.

“What it means to distribute the small divisions.” *Quid*, “what,” that is, something—namely, by which terms. *Alterutrum*, used adverbially, means what one part was and what the other was.

“Hour,” that is, a limit and boundary. *Hora*, “hour,” is derived from *ora*, “boundary,” with aspiration; the other things are written without aspiration.

“Calling them points.” A point is a fourth part of an hour, namely, in solar reckoning: the passage of one point. *Punctus* is named from *pungere*, “to prick,” because it is marked on clocks by certain prick-like indications.

A clock, *horologium*, is a sequence of hours from one point to the next.

Minutes are so called from the smaller interval, namely, that of a point. For a minute is a smaller span than a point, specifically a tenth part of an hour.

“Calling them parts”: a fifteenth part of an hour, named from the division of the zodiacal circle. In each day the sun traverses one part of the zodiac, that is, of the zodiacal circle, over twenty-four hours, insofar as this concerns the course it makes against the firmament. But insofar as it concerns the course it makes with the firmament, the same part that it traverses during twenty-four hours is a fifteenth part of half a sign, for half a sign contains fifteen parts.

It moves from place to place through a fifteenth part of an hour, that is, through two moments and two-thirds of a moment. Therefore Bede correctly said that the parts of hours are named from the parts of the zodiacal circle, since the same thing is both a part of an hour and a part of a sign, although the two courses are to be understood.

Because different meanings are frequently encountered, they must be distinguished individually. Sometimes the twelve signs of the zodiac are called parts or small divisions. The interval that the sun completes in twenty-four hours is also called a part, namely, the part that is a fifteenth of half a sign; and the hour itself is said to contain fifteen parts. “Parts” derives from the division of the zodiacal circle.

**RECAPITULATION OF THE GLOSS.**—The sun makes two courses in the heavens [Col. 0304D]: one with the firmament and another against the firmament. For each day it advances one part in the heavens over twenty-four hours. Yet the heavens themselves revolve around the earth in twenty-four hours—that is, through the twelve signs.

Half the heavens, namely six signs, revolves in twelve hours. If six signs revolve in twelve hours, one sign revolves in only two hours. If one sign revolves in two hours, half a sign revolves in one hour, and half a sign contains fifteen parts. For a complete sign contains thirty parts, whereas half a sign contains fifteen.

Thus a fifteenth part of half a sign—that is, one part—moves from place to place through a fifteenth part of an hour.
