Therefore Lord Bede correctly said that the sun’s course is completed through one part, that is, through [Col. 0305A] twenty-four hours. Yet the movement of that one part from place to place with the heavens occurs in a fifteenth part of an hour [Col. 0305B].

Here again it must be asked whether the heavens themselves revolve around the earth in an equal interval of time, both independently and together with the sun. The answer is that they revolve unequally. For from sunrise until the next sunrise there are twenty-four hours; but in the revolution of the heavens a fifteenth part of an hour is lacking.

For example: today the sun rises in the first part of Aries, early in the morning. Tomorrow, however, the sun will rise in the second part of Aries, and before the sun the entire first part of Aries will rise during a fifteenth part of an hour. Thus, after fifteen days, half a sign rises before the sun; after a whole year, the entire heavens revolve before the sun.

Hence, while the sun circles the earth 365 times, the heavens circle it independently 366 times. For in one revolution the heavens exceed the sun’s revolution.

The calculators divide this zodiac into thirty-day portions, that is, into thirty days [Col. 0305C].

Now, concerning moments. A moment occurs at the beginning of motion. The beginning of motion by which some heavenly body moves is called a moment—not the entire movement of the heavenly body or of anything else, but the instant when something is perceived to give way from its place and then enter and succeed in another place. This is demonstrated through an opening when a star is seen.

One sign moves in two hours; a single star moves with the greatest speed, that is, through one moment. This is perceived by calculators.

The atom is the smallest of all things, namely, of all periods of time. Time is constituted in the following way: when, dividing larger intervals of time, such as a day or an hour, by points or other smaller divisions, you reach a particle which, because of its minuteness, has no duration that can in any way be divided—such as the twinkling of an eye—you should know that this is an atom.

“Which, because of its minuteness, is more visible to grammarians than to calculators.” Namely, because calculators possess only things that they can divide [Col. 0305D].

Grammar is the science of speaking correctly, and the origin and foundation of the liberal arts. It was devised within the disciplines through common letters, so that those who had learned letters might thereby know the method of speaking correctly.

Grammar takes its name from letters. For the Greeks call letters *grammata*. An art is so called because it consists in precise rules and precepts.

Nevertheless, the discussion of mathematicians investigating human nativities, and the other matters that follow, was already explained above; it ought nevertheless to have been placed here in its proper order.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—An hour is the twelfth part of a day. He defines the temporal hour, which is now called unequal; others also call it planetary. It is one-twelfth of each natural day, or, as it is commonly called, the artificial day.

It is easy to understand that these hours are longer on summer days and shorter in winter, because the interval between sunrise and sunset is not always equal. Hence, in good authors, we understand the solstitial hours to be the longest and the wintry hours [Col. 0306B] the shortest. Thus in Plautus *aestiva hora*, “a summer hour,” means a long hour.

The Romans and Jews alike used hours of this kind in dividing time. The first began at the rising of the sun; the sixth always fell at midday. Hence Persius, speaking of sluggish young men:

> “We snore until the fifth line is touched by the shadow,”

that is, according to our present reckoning, until the eleventh hour.

The hymns that the Church sings at the canonical hours of prayer are likewise distributed in this way. For the first hour has: “Now the star of light has risen”; the sixth has: “And with the fires, midday.”

These are the hours that must be understood wherever the sacred Scriptures mention hours—for example, in the Gospel, where those who came at the eleventh hour came one hour before sunset; and in Cicero, where “at the ninth hour of the day” is used proverbially.

There are other hours, equinoctial hours, which are called equal. The ancients did not use them except with the water clock; we use them now when a signal is given by mechanisms of iron wheels, which cannot be adapted to temporal hours.

In place of these mechanisms, the ancients used sundials, which consisted of no more than twenty-two lines. They are called equinoctial hours because they are reckoned from the portions of the equinoctial circle that have passed. Thus, when one half-ounce of the equinoctial circle has risen, one hour has also passed; when twelve hours have passed, the entire circle has likewise passed.

These hours must be fewer on winter days and more numerous on summer days. I have discussed this at greater length so that we do not suppose that the sacred use of hours refers to equinoctial hours. The passage cited by Bede is John 11.

“An hour contains four points.” Large sundials have intervals between the lines divided by three points, by which the quarters of hours are detected. The individual hours are likewise marked as divided into four parts on astrolabes, and certain iron mechanisms give a signal at each quarter of an hour.

“Ten minutes.” Understand ordinary minutes, not physical minutes. Ordinary minutes are any portions of a whole divided into any number of parts. Thus, if you divide an *as* into twelve parts, each twelfth is a minute. These are used less frequently in the disciplines.

Physical minutes are portions produced by dividing something by sixty. Thus the thirtieth part of a sign—or, as more recent writers say, one degree—is divided into sixty first minutes; each of these is again divided into sixty others, called second minutes; those are divided into third minutes, and so on down to tenths.

The Greeks, from whom we borrowed this terminology, express them as follows: *πρῶτα λεπτά*, “first minutes”; *λεπτὰ δεύτερα*, “second minutes”; *λεπτὰ τρίτα*, “third minutes”; *τέτρατα*, “fourths.” I have noted this because these terms are used only in mathematics.

“Calling it an hour.” *Hora* is a Greek word. The Greeks also call by this name the four parts into which we divide the year: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Homer celebrates four goddesses of this name who close and open heaven. The scholiast understands the already mentioned divisions of the year through this poetic fiction.

“Parts, from the division of the circle.” An unequal hour has fifteen parts [Col. 0307D], because while an hour passes, fifteen parts of the equinoctial circle—or fifteen degrees, that is, half a sign—rise.

“Also dividing each of the individual parts into twelve points.” I have found no observation of these points, nor of the omens, as he calls them, in other writers.]

An hour is the twelfth part of a day, since twelve hours complete a day, as the Lord himself testifies when he says: “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble.”

Although, allegorically, he called himself the day and the disciples who were to be illuminated by him the hours, he nevertheless defined the number of hours according to the customary human reckoning.

It must be noted, however, that if all the days of the year are reckoned as having twelve hours, summer days must necessarily contain longer hours and winter days shorter hours. But if we wish to make all hours equal—that is, equinoctial—then we must necessarily assign fewer of them to a winter day and more to a summer day.

An hour contains four points, ten minutes, fifteen parts, forty moments, and in certain lunar calculations five points. These divisions of time are not natural but appear to be conventional [Note: [Col. 0303A] C, “conventional”].

For whenever calculators needed to distribute the day into twelve parts, or the hour into four, ten, fifteen, or forty parts, or into any other smaller or larger divisions [Col. 0304A], they sought terms by which they could name what they intended and distinguish one division from another.

They called it an hour because it is the boundary of a definite period, just as we call the limits of garments, rivers, and the sea *orae*, “boundaries.” They called them points from the small crossing of a point that occurs on a clock, and minutes from the smaller interval.

They called them parts from the division of the zodiacal circle, which they divide into thirty-day sections through the individual months. They called moments after the swift movement of the stars, when something is perceived to yield and succeed itself within the briefest intervals.

They named the smallest of all periods of time—which cannot be divided in any way—an atom, in Greek, that is, “indivisible” or “uncuttable.” Because of its minuteness, it is more visible to grammarians than to calculators [Col. 0305A]. For when grammarians divide a verse into words, words into feet, feet into syllables, and syllables into temporal quantities, assigning two times to a long syllable and one to a short one, they have nothing further into which to divide it [Note: [Col. 0305] B, C, “anything”]; therefore they chose to call this an atom [Note: [Col. 0305] B, C, “this”].

Nevertheless, mathematicians, when investigating human nativities, strive to reach the atom. They divide the zodiacal circle into twelve signs, each sign into thirty parts, each part into twelve points, each point into forty moments, and each moment into sixty omens, so that, by considering [Col. 0306A] the position of the stars more carefully, they may ascertain the fate of the person who is born as though without error.

Since this observation is vain and alien to our faith, let us disregard it and see instead why the Apostle uses this term for time to indicate the swiftness of the resurrection. He says: “We shall all indeed rise again, but we shall not all be changed, in an atom, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet” [Note: [Col. 0305] B, C, “for the rapidity”].

Nor should it be passed over that, although calculators necessarily distinguish the terms, many writers use indifferently for the briefest interval of time in which the eyelid of our eye can move—that which passes in the stroke of a blink and cannot be cut up or divided—now “moment,” now “point,” and now “atom” [Col. 0307A].

## CHAPTER IV. On the Calculation of Ounces

To know also the division of ounces—which is no less useful for reckoning periods of time and other things than for reckoning coins—is no insignificant discovery. Because both scattered histories and sacred Scripture itself use these divisions, we have taken care to append their names and symbols in brief [Note: [Col. 0307] B, C, “of them”].

A *libra*, or *as* or *assis*: twelve ounces.

A *deunx*, or [Note: [Col. 0307] Jabus, B, C] *labus*: eleven ounces.

A *decunx*, or *dextans*: ten ounces.

A *dodrans*, or *dodras*: nine ounces.

A *bes*, or *bisse*: eight ounces.

A *septunx*, or *septuns*: seven ounces [Col. 0307B].

A *semis*: six ounces.

A *quincunx*, or *quinquus*: five ounces.

A *triens*, or *treas*: four ounces.

A *quadrans*, or *quadras*: three ounces.

A *sextans*, or *sextas*: two ounces.

A *sexcunx*, or *sescuncia*: one and a half ounces.

An ounce: twenty-four scruples.

A half-ounce: twelve scruples, that is, a third of an ounce.

Two *sextulae*, or *sesc-lae*: eight scruples.

A *sicilicus*: six scruples.

A *sextula*, or *sescla*: four scruples.

Half a *sextula*, or *sescla*: two scruples.

A scruple: six siliquae.

These terms—or symbols—of weights apply not only to measuring money but also to measuring any bodies or periods of time. Hence the practice or custom has arisen that, in the notation of calculations, children substitute “one” and “two” more often with *as* and *dipondius*. Likewise *tressis*, *quartussis*, *quincussis*, *sextussis*, *septussis*, and similar terms signify three asses, four asses, and so forth; and in the same way many subsequent numerical terms are formed.

Thus, whether you wish to divide one hour, an entire day, a month, a year, or some other larger or smaller period of time into twelve parts [Note: [Col. 0307] B, “to divide”], the twelfth part itself is an ounce; the remaining eleven are called a *deunx*.

If you divide it into six, the sixth part is called a *sextans*; the five remaining parts are called a *dextans*, or, as others say, a [Note: [Col. 0307] C, *dextas*] *distas*.

If into four, the fourth part receives the name *quadrans* [Col. 0308A]; the remaining three receive the name *dodrans*.

This rule of the discipline resolves a matter that confuses many inexperienced people. When Philip, in his exposition of blessed Job, describes the tide of the Ocean as coming twice each day, he adds that it comes after [Note: [Col. 0307] B, C, “one”] three-quarters of an equinoctial hour have passed, later without interruption, whether by day or by night.

If you wish to divide something by three, you will call the third part a *triens*, and the two remaining parts a *bes*. If by two, the half is called a *semis*. The same applies to the rest; these things can be learned and taught more effectively through the spoken word of a teacher than through the style of a writer.

Likewise, if you need to divide bodies—whether a mile, a *stadium*, an acre, a *pertica*, or even a cubit, foot, or [Note: [Col. 0307] C, “palm”] palm—you will proceed according to the method stated above.

Finally, in Exodus also, half a cubit is called a *semis*. Moses relates that the Ark of the Covenant had two and a half cubits in length and one and a half cubits in height.

In the Gospel, the fourth part of the entire worldly body, namely the earth, is mystically designated by the name *quadrans*, when the sinner is told, as he is sent into punishment: “You will not leave there until you have paid the last quadrans”—that is, until you have expiated earthly sins—as blessed Augustine explains:

> “For this,” he says, “the sinner heard: ‘You are earth, and to earth you will go’” [Note: [Col. 0307] B, C, “and the sinner”].

The fourth part of the distinct members of this world is found to be the last, the earth [Note: [Col. 0307] B, C, “and it is earthly”], if you begin with heaven, count the air second, water third, and earth fourth.

Augustine also remembers this discipline in his exposition of the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0307] Add. “of the Gospel,” B, C], where it is written: “It was the day of Preparation for the Passover, about the sixth hour.” He says:

> “For it was not yet fully the sixth hour, but approximately the sixth,”

that is, the fifth had been completed and something of the sixth had begun [Note: [Col. 0307] B, K, “also”]. Yet one would never say “the fifth and a quarter,” or “the fifth and a third,” or “the fifth and a half,” or anything of that kind [Col. 0308C].

# CHAPTER V. On the Day

[Note: [Col. 0307D]]

**BRID. RAM. GLOSSES.**—The day is air illuminated by the sun, taking its name from the fact that it separates and divides the darkness—namely, from light. “Day” (*dies*) is so called from separating, because it divides light from darkness. Naturally, a day is a period of twenty-four hours, from sunrise to sunrise. The day is commonly understood in two ways: properly, from sunrise until it rises again; improperly, from sunrise until it comes to sunset.

Mystically, too, the day bears the image of the Law. For just as the brightness of day illuminates the obscurity of darkness, so the Law, showing the way of life, drives away the darkness of errors, declares the light of virtues, and, reproving the sins of the wicked, leads the good toward better things.

God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. If one asks in what places light was made at God’s command, since the abyss still covered the whole expanse of the earth, it is plainly evident that the original light shone in those upper regions of the earth which even now the daily light of the sun customarily illuminates. The infused light therefore did not dispel all the darkness of the world, but, illuminating one part of it, left the other dark.

And if someone again asks what the daylight could have been like before the creation of the stars, it is not unreasonable to believe that it was like what we see every morning as sunrise approaches and before the sun appears over the earth, when day does indeed shine by the dim rays of the stars, but the sun has not yet risen and shone forth. Hence there could then be no distinction of times except that of day and night.

Again, God said, “Let there be light.” And there was light, [Col. 0309C] and God called the light “day.”

Remigius: God said—not with a bodily voice or with movement of the lips, but he “said,” that is, he willed. His willing is his saying. Hence it is written, “He spoke, and they were made.” Or again, he “said,” that is, he begot the Son, through whom all things were made.

“Let there be light.” Light is so called from *luere*, that is, from cleansing the darkness. That light, however, was not of the kind that now exists when the sun is placed above the earth, but like that which occurs either before sunrise or after sunset.

“And God saw that the light was good”—not because he then saw it for the first time, since this had always been evident in his presence, but he “saw,” that is, he wished the light to be seen by us as good.

For there are certain Fathers who, concerning what is written, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth; but the earth was empty and void,” [say the following].

Bede, in *Genesis*: God did not create heaven and earth “in the beginning of time.” God made time, and therefore, before he made time, there was no time. We cannot say “when” God had not yet made anything. Therefore God did not make heaven and earth at the beginning of time; rather, the Beginning must be understood as the Son.

What is said—“In the beginning God created heaven and earth”—shows the matter of the whole creation, rational and bodily, angelic and of other kinds. God therefore made both matter and form; voice and word come into being together, although voice is prior in origin. Hence it is written, “You who made the world from unformed matter.”

Accordingly, before every day and before all time God created two things: the angelic creation and unformed matter, although, as Solomon says, all things were made together: “He who lives forever created all things together.” Yet, as we have said, the origin of unformed matter precedes its formed appearance, just as voice precedes word.

Thus God did not make everything from nothing, but some things from nothing and some from something. He made the world, the angels, and the soul from nothing; man from something.

Finally, Saint Clement, a disciple of the Apostles and the third bishop of the Roman Church after Peter, writes as follows in the sixth book of his *Histories*:

“In the beginning God made heaven and earth; but the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss, and the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters.”

[Col. 0310C]

Remigius: Plato said that there were three principles: God, the exemplar, and matter. He did not say that God created everything as its author from nothing, but rather that matter provided assistance to God, as to a craftsman, in creating things.

Aristotle, however, said that there were two principles: matter and form. Someone else, wishing—I do not know what—to assert a third, called it the operative principle.

Moses, therefore, opposing their errors, as one chosen by the Lord, demonstrated the truth of the matter. He showed that God formed everything from nothing—not indeed “in time,” but at the beginning of time—when he said, “In the beginning.” Since “in the beginning” implies “of time,” it is beyond doubt that time then began, whereas previously it did not exist.

“God created heaven and earth.” By “heaven” we must not understand this visible firmament, but the empyrean—that is, fiery—or intellectual heaven. It is called fiery not because of heat but because of brightness, and it was immediately filled with angelic spirits, concerning whom it is said in Job: “When the morning stars praised me together and all the sons of God shouted for joy.”

“But the earth was empty and void”—that is, useless, unfruitful, and unformed. For all the elements were mixed and confused, and the whole expanse of air extending from earth to heaven was full of waters. These waters, however, were not of the quality they now possess, but were thin, like mist; this is the quality retained by the waters above heaven.

“And darkness was over the abyss.” Darkness is so called from *tenere*, “to hold,” because it holds the eyes so that they cannot see.

God made both things, light and darkness: light so that people might work in it, and night so that they might rest. Thus darkness also is God’s work. Hence, in the hymn of the three young men, in which every creature is invited to bless God, darkness is placed together with light.

“And the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters.” Just as the mind or wisdom of a craftsman is borne over the work he is about to make, so that he may make it as he wishes, so the Holy Spirit was borne over the waters, foreordaining and, as it were, arranging beforehand what he wished to make and how he wished to make it.

Allegorically, in what is said, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” we may appropriately understand by “the Beginning” the Son of God, just as he himself says of himself to the Jews: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you.” God the Father is indeed the Beginning, but not from a beginning, because he is from no one. The Son, however, is the Beginning from the Beginning, because he was not made or created by the Father, but begotten.

Through that Beginning God the Father created heaven and earth, that is, heavenly and earthly beings. Heaven signifies those who lead a heavenly life; earth signifies those who are intent upon earthly occupations. Both were created through the Beginning, because, when Christ Jesus became man, it was revealed who were heavenly and who were earthly.

“But the earth was empty and void.” This means that the human body was empty of heavenly meditation and void of the fruit of good works.

“And darkness was over the face of the abyss,” because the darkness of unbelief and ignorance covered the abyss of the human heart.

“And the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters,” because divine foreknowledge was borne over the fluid and unfruitful hearts of human beings, foreseeing and arranging in whose hearts it could worthily dwell.

“Let there be light.” By the word “light,” faith is understood. It was therefore fitting that light should be made on the first day, because faith is commended in the first commandment of the Law, when it says: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one.”

Augustine, speaking of true innocence: The order of times exists without time in God’s eternal wisdom, and there is nothing new with him, who made the things that were to be. Therefore the will of God is the first and highest cause of all bodily and spiritual movements. Nothing visible occurs that is not either commanded or permitted, according to his ineffable justice, from the invisible and intelligible court of the supreme ruler.

Again, Augustine, in the eleventh book of *The City of God*: We must consider what we should answer those who agree that God is the creator of the world and yet ask about the world’s time; and we must also consider what they themselves should answer about the world’s place.

For one may ask why the world was made then rather than earlier, just as one may ask why it was made here, where it is, rather than elsewhere. If they imagine infinite stretches of time before the world, in which God, as they think, could not have remained inactive, let them similarly imagine infinite expanses of place outside the world. If someone says that the Almighty could not have remained inactive there, will they not consequently be forced, like Epicurus, to dream of innumerable worlds? The only difference would be that Epicurus asserts that they are generated and dissolved by the chance movements of atoms, whereas these people would say that they were made by God’s work. Yet, because they are unwilling to leave empty the immeasurable expanses of place extending in every direction outside the world, they would also say that these worlds, like this one, cannot be dissolved by any cause.

If it seems incredible to anyone that channels of water can receive light, let him observe the work of sailors, who make the depths of the sea transparent to themselves by sprinkling oil upon them. Nor is it astonishing that, through divine action, light can shine in waters, since it is also established that through human action they are often illuminated—namely, by sailors who, immersed in the depths of the sea, release oil from their mouths and thereby make the water clear and bright for themselves. If a human being can do such things through the oil of his mouth, how much light should we believe that God can create through the breath of his mouth?

Moses describes the matter in this way: “And evening came to be,” he says, “and morning came to be: one day.”

It must be understood that, just as the day has an evening, so also does the night. The difference between them is that the evening of day customarily darkens into night, while the evening of night brightens into day.

Ambrose: Some ask whether, since Scripture mentions evening first and then morning, it might seem to signify night before day. They fail to observe that it first mentioned day, saying, “God called the light day and the darkness night”; then, that evening is the end of day and morning the end of night.

Therefore, in order to grant priority and precedence to the birth of day, Scripture first signified the end of day, after which night was to follow, and then added the end of night.

Bede: “Evening came to be” when the light gradually set, after the span of the day’s length had been completed and it passed beneath the lower regions of the world, as now occurs through the customary circuit of the sun.

“Morning also came to be” when that same light gradually returned above the earth and began another day. Up to this point, one day had been completed—namely, twenty-four hours.

By commending this expression, Scripture carefully admonishes us to learn that the light which was made illuminates the lower parts of the world by its setting. For if this did not happen, but the whole of it gradually perished when evening came and was again gradually restored and rose at morning, Scripture would not say that one complete day was made at the morning of the following day, but rather at the evening of the first day.

Hence it preferred to say that evening and morning were made, rather than that night and day were made, in order to indicate that the activity of the primordial light followed a circuit, as now occurs through the circuit of the sun by day and night. The only difference is that, after the stars were created, night too is filled with its own light, though less than the light of day; whereas during those first three days it remained wholly dark and obscure.

It was entirely fitting that the day, beginning with light, should be extended to the morning of the following day, so that it might be signified that the work of him who is the true light, and in whom there is no darkness at all, begins with light and is brought to completion in light.

Again, blessed Augustine, in the eleventh book of *The City of God*: We see that these familiar days have no evening except from the setting of the sun, nor morning except from its rising. But those first three days passed without the sun, which is said to have been made on the fourth day. At first, light was made by the word of God, and God is said to have separated it from the darkness; he called that light day and the darkness night.

But what sort of light it was, and by what alternating movement it produced evening and morning, is beyond our senses. Nor can we understand it as it actually was; nevertheless, it must be believed without any hesitation.

The Hebrews, Chaldeans, and Persians, following the course of the day according to the order of the first creation, reckon it from morning to morning, and so on.

The Hebrews were named from Heber, who was a great-grandson of Shem.

The Chaldeans—who are now called Chaldeans—were named from Casech, son of Nahor, Abraham’s brother.

The Persians were named from King Perseus, who, crossing from Greece into Asia, subdued the barbarian peoples there in a long and severe war; finally, as victor, he gave his name to the people he had subjected.

The Egyptians were named from a certain king of theirs, Egypt. In the Hebrew language they are interpreted as “the afflicters,” because they afflicted the people of God before that people was delivered by divine aid.

[Col. 0314C]

The Romans were named from Romulus, who founded the city of Rome and gave his name to the people and the state. Previously they had been called Saturnians from Saturn and Latins from Latinus.

The Umbrians are a people of Italy.

Granus succeeded Cecrops, king of the Athenians. Granus’s daughter, Athis, gave her name both to the region and to the people. From her the Attic people, that is, the Athenians, received their name.

This change in the reckoning of time also signifies that we, once transferred from the light of paradise into the valley of tears, are now to be transferred from the darkness of sins to heavenly joy.

Here he is speaking specifically of the evening hour, to show the very change of time by which we now reckon all days from evening to evening.

In the Gospel, where it says, “On the evening of the Sabbath, as it dawns toward the first day of the Sabbath, Mary Magdalene came,” and so forth, the morning hour is to be understood, when the women came to the tomb on the Lord’s Day. The feminine form is used there when it says “as it dawns,” because both *vesper* and *vespera* are used: masculine and feminine forms of “evening.”

One may say either *vespere Sabbati* or *vespera Sabbati*, because *vesper vesperis* and *vespera vespere* mean the same thing—that is, the time when night declines and day follows.

*Vesperum* is the time when the sun descends from the ninth hour, from the center of the sky toward night.

Previously night followed day—that is, time was reckoned from morning to morning—because the first day was made before night. Now, however, day follows night, that is, it is reckoned from evening to evening. Formerly, after the joy of paradise, death and darkness followed; now, after the darkness of death and sin, Christ having come, heavenly joy follows, like light after darkness.

Therefore the day always begins at sunset, although some think otherwise. They say that it begins at midnight, at sunrise, or at the sixth hour of the day. This must by no means be believed or followed.

Haimo: At the Lord’s resurrection the order of time itself was also changed. From the beginning of the world until the Lord’s resurrection, day preceded and night followed. From the Lord’s resurrection onward, the preceding night belongs to the day that follows, because he who rose from the dead during the last part of that night made the night itself bright and radiant, and in a certain way changed it into day. Of that night it is written: “And night shall be illumination in my delights.”

It was once fitting that day should precede night, because the first man, departing from the true light, fell into the darkness of error. It is also fitting that now day should follow night, because through the Lord’s resurrection we have been freed from the darkness of error and turned toward the true light, as the Apostle says: “The night has gone before, but the day will draw near.”

For it cannot otherwise be explained, except by placing night before the day, how the Lord was in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights, after the likeness of Jonah.

The story of Jonah is well known: when he fled from the presence of the Lord toward Tarshish, he was swallowed by a sea-monster and remained there for three days and three nights. By this event he signified the Lord’s death, who lay hidden in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights.

But how is the Lord said to have lain in the tomb for three days and three nights, when it is clear that he did not remain there for those complete days and nights? He was crucified on Friday at the sixth hour, and at the ninth hour he gave up his spirit. In the evening, after sunset, he was taken down from the cross and placed in the tomb; he lay there for no more than thirty-six hours.

Here, however, the rule of Scripture must be observed: frequently the whole is shown by a part. If we take Friday together with the preceding night, the Sabbath together with its preceding night, and the Lord’s night together with the following day, then according to this reckoning the Lord is found to have remained in the tomb for three days and nights.

Augustine therefore says in the fourth book of *On the Holy Trinity*: Scripture itself testifies that the three-day period was not complete and entire. The first day was counted as a whole from its final part, and the third day as a whole from its first part. The middle day, that is, the second day, was wholly complete with its twenty-four hours—twelve in the night and twelve in the day.

From the evening of the burial until dawn at the resurrection there were thirty-six hours, which is the square of six.

Jonah means “dove” or “sorrowful.” “Dove” because of his lamentation, when he was in the sea-monster’s belly for three days; “sorrowful” either because of the sadness he felt over the salvation of the Ninevites or because of the ivy that suddenly withered, whose shade had protected him from the heat of the sun.

He is also the son of Amathi, the widow of Sarepta, as the Jews assert—the son whom Elijah raised from the dead, after which his mother said to him: “Now I know that you are a man of God, and that the word of God in your mouth is true.”

If you wish to know how many atoms, moments, minutes, points, and hours there are in a day, a week, and also in a natural month, consider the following calculation, and you will find them.

Let us begin first with the hour: 564 atoms make one moment; four moments make one minute; two and a half minutes make one solar point; four points make one solar hour.

A lunar hour contains five points, ten minutes, fifteen parts, forty moments, and sixty *estenta*.

A lunar point contains two minutes, three parts, eight moments, and twelve *ostenta*.

One minute contains one and a half parts, four moments, and six *ostenta*.

One part contains two moments, two-thirds of a moment, and three *ostenta*.

One moment contains one and a half *ostentum*.

One hour contains 60 *ostenta*, forty moments, fifteen parts, ten minutes, and four points according to the sun; according to the moon, five points.

A day has twenty-four hours, ninety-six points according to the sun, 120 according to the moon, 240 minutes, 360 parts, 5,460 moments, 1,400 *ostenta*, and 541,240 atoms.

A week has 168 hours, 662 points, 1,680 minutes, 2,420 parts, 7,220 moments, 10,030 *ostenta*, and 3,290,800 atoms.

A month of thirty days has 720 hours, 2,880 points, 7,200 minutes, 43,200 *ostenta*, and 16,243,200 atoms.

If you wish to know how many hours there are in a year, multiply 300 by thirty-four: the result is 7,200. Then multiply sixty by twenty-four: the result is 1,440. Then multiply five—the five which exceed the number 335—by twenty-four: the result is 120. When these are added together—7,200, 1,440, and 120—they produce 8,760.

That, therefore, is the number of hours in a common year of 365 days. It must be multiplied by twenty-four because there are twenty-four hours in each day.

If you wish to know how many points there are in a year, multiply 8,760 by four: the result is 35,040. Then multiply 700 by four: the result is 2,800. Then multiply sixty by four: the result is 240. Add this entire number together, and you will find 35,040.

It is appropriate to multiply the hours of the whole year by four because four points make one solar hour.

If you wish to know how many minutes there are in a year, multiply the number stated above; the result is 70,080. Also add half of the points stated above, that is, 18,520. Add the whole number together, and you will have 87,600.

We said that the number of points should be multiplied by two and that half of them should additionally be added because two and a half minutes make one point.

If you wish to know how many moments there are in a year, multiply the number stated above by four, that is, 87,600; the result is 350,400. We said that the number of minutes should be multiplied by four because four moments make one minute.

There are also in a year 511,360 *ostenta* and 197,760,560 atoms. If you do not believe that all these figures are correct, investigate carefully.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—The day is air illuminated by the sun.

Philosophers define the day in this way: “The day is the sun’s passage above the horizon,” as Aristotle says. Others define it as the interval between sunrise and sunset. This is the definition of the natural day, which the common run of educated people calls the artificial day. Bede calls it the common day.

There is another day, the civil day, which is now called the natural day: the period during which the sun travels around the earth above and below it, a circuit completed in twenty-four equinoctial hours.

“Taking its name from the fact that it separates and divides darkness from light.”

Festus derives *dies* from *deus*, “god.” Others derive it from *dius*, which signifies the daylight beneath the sky; hence we say *sub dio*, “under the open sky,” meaning outside buildings.

I therefore think that *dies* is derived from Jupiter, whom the Greeks call *dia*, for we also understand the sun through Jupiter, as is attested by the well-known verse of Orpheus:

> One is Zeus, one is Hades, one is the sun, one is Dionysus.

And Jupiter is called *Diespiter*, because he is the father of day and light.

Unless, perhaps, this belongs to poetic fictions. There have also been philosophers who seriously argued that, when the sun sets, it sinks into and is extinguished by moisture, and that it is rekindled when it rises. The Epicureans held this opinion, and Lucretius follows them. See Strabo’s first book of the *Geography*.

In truth, it is now generally known that the sun travels beneath the earth in as swift a course as it does above it.

“Umbrians and Athenians.” I think that Bede suffered a lapse of memory, since it is commonly established that the Athenians begin the day at sunset. On this subject, read more in Gellius and Macrobius.]

The day is air illuminated by the sun, taking its name from the fact that it separates and divides darkness from light. For when, at the beginning of creation, darkness was over the face of the abyss, God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light, and God called the light “day.”

This definition is divided in two ways [Note: [Col. 0309] C: “in two ways”], namely, commonly and properly.

The common people call the entire period during which the sun is present above the earth “day.” Properly, however, the day is completed in twenty-four hours, that is, by the sun’s circuit as it illumines the whole globe. Since it always and everywhere carries the daylight with it, it is believed to be elevated through no smaller extent of air at night beneath the earth than above the earth by day. The authority of many writings—both our own and secular—attests this.

For us, it is enough to cite the testimony of one Father, Augustine, who says in the second book of *Questions on the Gospel*, explaining figuratively the number of the seventy-two disciples:

> Just as the whole world is completed and illumined in twenty-four hours, so the mystery of illuminating the world through the Gospel of the Trinity is disclosed in the seventy-two disciples.

[Note: [Col. 0309] B, C: “For twenty-four taken three times is seventy-two (*dipondius*).”]

He says the same in the first book of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*:

> Should we say that, when this work of God had quickly been completed, the light remained for as long as it took to complete the span of day, with no night following it, and that night remained for as long as it took the span of nighttime to pass, until morning came for the following day, with the first day having elapsed? But if I say this, I fear that I shall be mocked both by those who have learned with certainty and by those who can very easily observe that, when it is night for us, those parts of the world are illuminated by the presence of light through which the sun returns from setting to rising. Consequently, throughout all twenty-four hours, by the circuit of the entire circle, day is nowhere absent, though it is day in one place and night in another.

A little later, after recalling the statement of Ecclesiastes concerning the sun, he says:

> When the southern part has the sun, it is day for us; but when the sun travels around and passes through the northern part, it is night for us. Yet in another region it is day only where the sun is present—unless perhaps we should incline our minds toward poetic fictions and believe that the sun plunges into the sea, is washed there, and then rises in the morning from the other side. Even if this were so, the abyss itself would be illuminated by the sun’s presence, and there would be day there. For the sun could illuminate the waters, since it could not be extinguished by them. But it is monstrous to suppose this.

Before the creation of the sun, what is now done through the sun was done through the circuit of the primordial light: on the first and second days, through the waters of the abyss, which had covered the whole earth; and on the third day, through the air, which was empty and was illuminated by its circuit.

For there are certain Fathers who, concerning what is written, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth; but the earth was empty and void, and darkness was over the face of the abyss,” think that the unformed condition of heaven, earth, and water, and the confusion of all the elements, is signified. They think also that neither water, nor earth, nor heaven is indicated, but rather, so to speak, one seed-bearing [*seminaria*] matter common to them all.

Therefore, since they found no place in the world capable of containing the primordial light, they necessarily dogmatized—by searching more deeply—that everything they read concerning the first seven days must be understood otherwise than the custom of our age maintains.

But the interpretation is much easier if, in accordance with the traditions of the Fathers and of Catholics, the name “heaven” is understood to indicate the circle of the higher heaven.

By “earth,” the earth itself is meant, enclosed within its various boundaries, as it is now, except that it had produced neither the green shoots of plants nor any living creatures.

By “abyss,” an infinite expanse of waters is meant, washing over the whole earth, in the midst of which the firmament of heaven is later said to have been made.

Finally, Saint Clement, a disciple of the Apostles and the third bishop of the Roman Church after Peter, writes as follows in the sixth book of his *Histories*:

> In the beginning God made heaven and earth; but the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss, and the Spirit of God was borne over the water.

That Spirit of God, at God’s command, separated light from darkness, as though it were the very hand of the Creator. After that invisible heaven, he brought forth this visible heaven, so that he might make the upper dwellings for angels and the lower ones for human beings.

> For your sake, therefore, at God’s command, the water that was over the face of the earth withdrew, so that the earth might produce fruits for you.

Ambrose, bishop of Milan, agrees with this in the second book of his *Hexameron*.

Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, also agrees. In the fourth book of the same work he says:

> “Let the waters be gathered together, so that the dry land may appear.” The covering is withdrawn so that what had not previously been visible might become manifest.

Jerome, likewise, the most learned interpreter of sacred history, remembers the higher heaven in his exposition of the prophetic statement: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne.’” He writes:

> Did he say this before he fell from heaven, or after he fell from heaven? If he was still in heaven, how does he say, “I will ascend into heaven”? But since we read, “The heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord,” while he was in heaven—that is, in the firmament—he desired to ascend into the heaven where the Lord’s throne is situated, not through humility but through pride. But if he speaks these words of arrogance after he fell from heaven, we must understand that, even though he has been cast down, he does not rest; he still promises himself great things—not that he may be among God’s stars, but above them.

As far as we who follow the footsteps of the Fathers are able to conjecture, when God said, “Let there be light,” the darkness that had covered the abyss immediately departed. Light emerged from the east between the waters and covered the entire surface of the earth with the breadth of its radiance, reaching the northern and southern regions as well as the western shores.

Then, as the span of one day was completed, it gradually withdrew and, circling beneath the earth, entered its lower regions. When dawn came, it proceeded in the same order and completed the second and third days. It differed from sunlight only in lacking the nourishing warmth of heat. Since the stars did not yet exist, it left those nights obscure with their ancient darkness. [Note: [Col. 0313] B, C: “it left them.”]

If it seems incredible to anyone that the channels of the waters could receive light, let him observe the work of sailors, who make the depths of the sea transparent to themselves by sprinkling oil upon them. Let him understand from this that God, the creator of all things, could illuminate any depth of water much more fully by the breath of his mouth—especially since the waters are believed to have been thinner then, before the Creator gathered them into one body so that the dry land might appear.

The Lord defined the common day by the statement that I cited above, saying: “Are there not twelve hours in the day?”

Moses, however, described the proper day in this way: “And evening came to be,” he says, “and morning came to be: one day.”

The Hebrews, Chaldeans, and Persians, following the order of the first creation, reckon the day from morning to morning, placing the time of shadows beneath the light. The Egyptians, by contrast, reckon from sunset to sunset. The Romans reckon from midnight to midnight. The Umbrians and Athenians preferred to reckon their days from noon to noon.

Divine authority, however, which decreed in Genesis that days should be reckoned from morning to morning, likewise established in the Gospel that the time of the whole day begins at evening and ends at evening. For he who at the beginning of the world first called the light “day” and then the darkness “night” himself, at the end of the ages, first illuminated the night by the glory of his resurrection and thus consecrated the day by showing himself to his disciples.

As evening advanced, he confirmed them more fully in faith in his resurrection by eating with them, offering himself to be touched, and granting them the grace of the Holy Spirit.

And because at that time, after the light had been created, “evening came to be and morning came to be: one day,” whereas now “the evening of the Sabbath dawns toward the first day of the Sabbath,” this change of time signifies that we too, once transferred from the former light of paradise into the valley of tears, are now to be transferred from the darkness of sins to heavenly joy. [Note: [Col. 0313] C: “which.”]

For it cannot otherwise be explained, except by placing night before day, how the Lord was in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights after the likeness of Jonah. Here, by synecdoche, if you take the portion of the day of Preparation on which he was buried together with the preceding night as a night and a day, then the whole night and complete day of the Sabbath, and the Lord’s night together with the day dawning with it—thus taking a part for the whole—you certainly have three days and three nights.

It is rightly asked why the people of Israel, who always observed the order of the day according to Moses’ tradition from morning to morning, nevertheless began and completed all their festivals in the evening, just as we do today, since the lawgiver says: “From evening to evening you shall celebrate your Sabbaths.”

# CHAPTER VI. Where the First Day of the World Was

[Note: [Col. 0316D]]

BRID. RAM. GLOSSES.—For there he established the beginning of time who, after creating the heavenly bodies, said that they should be for signs, seasons, days, and years. For the preceding three days, as everyone has understood, without any measurement of hours—for the stars had not yet been made—held light and darkness in equal balance. Before the stars were made, there was nothing by which the order of times could be marked by indications; there was no means of distinguishing the midday hour before the sun, fiery, had climbed to the middle of the sky; there was no means of marking the remaining hours of day and night, until the stars divided the firmament between day and night in equal measure. For that entire preceding three-day period had passed in the course of its progression through the wilderness, having no measurement of hours at all, since the primordial light still generally filled everything and had no particular source: nowhere had more intense rays shone, nor did any shade grow cool beneath a rock or tree as though in a more remote place.

“For signs, and seasons, and days, and years”: this is said either with reference to the determination of Easter, since the moon is the sign of the paschal term, which is celebrated only on the fourteenth day of the moon; or because the stars are signs for sailors traveling across the sea and for travelers journeying through Libya, where the path of travel is scattered by the movement of the wind. Finally, on the fourth morning, the sun, proceeding from the middle of the East, with the hours running along their lines by means of shadows, began the equinox that is observed annually. For when first created, the sun possessed in every respect the power that it is now believed to possess. Before the creation of the sun there was neither time nor hour, because there was nothing to cast a shadow by which the determination of time or an hour could be made.

“Equinox.” The sun was created equinoctial; the equitable God made nothing unequal. Through its increase by a quarter-day, it comes about that the point of the vernal equinox itself occurs now in the morning, now at midday. The sun’s first position in Aries occurs in the morning in the first year, at midday in the second year, in the evening in the third year, and at midnight in the fourth year, with the morning understood again thereafter. Thus now also, to signify the joy of our redemption, at first the day equals the night in length. First the day—that is, Christ—goes before; then the Church follows.

Although now, because of the honor paid to the Lord’s resurrection, the day follows the night, nevertheless at the equinox, according to the order of the first creation, the night follows the day; and, because of the grace of the sacrament, the completion of the equinox takes place in that following night. The reason for this sacramental observance is sufficiently demonstrated here by the lord Bede: namely, the following night, which is assigned to the equinox. Then the fullest moon floods it with light, for the sake of a sure mystery. For the perfection of the sun, which is present in the equinox, must precede, and the perfection of the moon must then follow.

The hour was awaited which would signify the illumination that was once to come in Christ. Thus, just as in the mystery of the heavenly sacrifice it is not permissible to offer wine alone or water alone, so it is not fitting that the first day, second, third, or fourth should be offered, when the sun was created for the Church before the moon was created in the evening; likewise, neither wine alone nor water alone ought to be offered before the blood of the grape is mixed with water, and the grain of wheat, crushed by grinding, is mixed with water. And just as it is not proper to offer wine without water or water without wine, so Easter ought not to be celebrated, on account of the sun’s equinoctial course, before the fifteenth day of the moon has arrived.

The evening hour was awaited, by which the Church illuminated by Christ is understood. By the morning hour Christ, the illuminator of the Church, is understood; by the evening hour the Church illuminated by Christ is understood.

The same is to be observed in keeping the time of this sacrifice. At the paschal festival both things must be observed: the vernal equinox, and the fourteenth moon after the equinox. If only the equinox is observed, it is as though merely a demonstration of our belief in God were made, while his governance is entirely removed from us. If, however, only the fourteenth moon is observed, it is as though the human race both possesses and has possessed no salvation from Christ, but from itself.

This is why, as an indication of its primacy, I think the ancients wished to place the beginning of the zodiacal circle there. “Its primacy,” that is, its origin and dignity; “there,” that is, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April; “the beginning,” that is, of the seasons. For on that day no month or year of the Romans, Greeks, or Egyptians begins, for which this would be the reason. On that day neither a Greek nor an Egyptian year or month begins, and no other reason is found except that, because it was the day of the beginning, the beginning of the zodiac was placed on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April.

From those people the patriarch Abraham was instructed, as Josephus testifies. Josephus reports that two of Noah’s sons, Shem and Japheth, were the inventors of all the liberal arts; the third, Ham, however, was the inventor of the magical arts, such as astronomy, in which mathematics and related disciplines are included. When they heard from their father that a flood was coming, by which everything might perish either by fire or by water, they wrote these arts on two columns, one of brick and one of stone, so that what they had wisely discovered would not be erased from memory, but would survive after the flood had passed and come to human knowledge. The stone column is said to have survived the flood and to remain in Syria to this day.

In the book of blessed Job, who lived not long after Abraham, we read of *mazaroth*, that is, the signs of the horoscope. It does not signify the nature of one sign alone, but is used figuratively of the whole zodiac. “Horoscope,” *horarum speculator*, “observer of the hours,” from *hora* and Greek σκοπεῖν (*skopein*), “to see.” Figuratively, however, it signifies the entire zodiac. *Mazaroth*, that is, the twelve signs, or a sign of many stars, or the names of the twelve signs. “Of the horoscope,” that is, of the zodiacal circle.

Job, son of Terah of Bosra, was the fourth king of the Idumeans after Esau, successor to Bela son of Beor. He was a Gentile, firm in faith, outstanding in humility, distinguished in hospitality, gentle in discipline, generous in almsgiving, and wealthy in possessions. Immediately he became poor though rich; suddenly he was deprived of his children and handed over to temptation. But he was armed against temptation by the faith of his religion and became glorious in the contest. Even-minded in grief, he endured the loss of his possessions, mourned the deaths of his children, and patiently received the wounds of his body; amid his sufferings he always glorified God. He also patiently endured a wife who urged evil and overcame the words of his friends.

For such great virtue of patience he was raised up at the end by a twofold recompense, receiving, after the loss of his possessions, a manifold splendor of gifts. After the night of sorrow he brought forth a day; after the stench of ulcers he produced the fragrance of cassia; after rejection he obtained a horn for the anointing of kingship and took up the pipe in the accent of praise. He lived for 170 years after his affliction, and all the days of his life were 248. He died and was buried in his own region.

The Hebrews assert that he was not of Esau’s lineage, but descended from the stock of Nahor, Abraham’s brother, and that he lived in the age of the patriarchs. For Nahor fathered Hus (Uz), from whose stock Job is believed to have been born, according to what is noted at the beginning of his book: “There was a man in the land of Hus (Uz), whose name was Job.”

Saint Jerome says the following in his *Book of Hebrew Questions*: “Hus (Uz), the firstborn of Nahor, Abraham’s brother, was born to him by his wife Milcah, the daughter of Haran; from his stock Job descended, as it is written at the beginning of his book: ‘There was a man in the land of Hus (Uz); Job was his name.’” Some therefore wrongly thought that Job was of Esau’s lineage. For what is found at the end of Job’s book—that it was translated from the Syriac language, that he was fourth after Esau, and the other statements contained there—is not found in the Hebrew books.

This first portion of the twelve is the vernal equinox. For all these things naturally occur in Aries, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. He calls the twelve signs “portions”; the first is Aries and the last Pisces. “The beginning of the months,” that is, of the years, or “the head of the circle,” that is, of the zodiac or of the year. Naturally, in the first sign, where the sun and moon were created—that is, in Aries—is the beginning and end of the months and years; there the course of all the planets is bound together, that is, brought into a single harmony, and there all the circles naturally come to an end.

“Completion”: God is the end and limit of labor, that is, of work.

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—At what point, precisely, the first day of the world occurred. Theologians debate when the world was created: in spring or in autumn? Those who say that the world was created in autumn are moved by this reasoning: if it had been made in spring, the first human beings would have perished from hunger, since no fruits would yet have ripened. The more probable opinion is that the first day occurred while the sun held the sign of Aries. Astrologers also debate this question. See Jovianus Pontanus, book 1 of *On Heavenly Matters*.

We read, “*Mazaroth*, that is, the signs of the horoscope.” The horoscope is that portion of a sign which rises when someone is born. For example, when Lucius was born, the eighth degree of Taurus was rising; he therefore has his horoscope in Taurus, as astrologers express it: “Lucius has his horoscope in Taurus.” Homer, as has been observed, had his in Sagittarius; Plato in Aquarius; the city of Rome in the fifteenth degree of Libra—for cities also have a horoscope. Hence the verb ὀροσκοπεῖν (*horoskopein*), for which we use *horoscopare*: when Paris was born, Capricorn was his horoscope.

[Col. 0317A]

At what point, precisely, the first day of the world occurred: some, seeking to determine this, thought that it should be marked on the eighth day before the Kalends of April; others, on the twelfth day before the same Kalends. Both relied on the same argument, namely the equinox, as though it accorded with reason that, since God at the beginning divided light and darkness into equal portions, the head of the world should be especially located there where the equinox is now believed to occur [Note: [Col. 0317] C, “and.”] [Note: [Col. 0317] C, “then.”]. They investigated the matter well, but did not fully perceive what they were saying [Note: [Col. 0317] B, C, “seeing through.”]. They would have proceeded much more skillfully if they had assigned the time of the equinox not to the first day, when light was made, but rather to the fourth, when the luminaries were made.

For there he established the beginning of time who, after creating the luminaries, said: “Let them be for signs, and seasons, and days, and years.” For the preceding three days, as everyone has understood, without any measurement of hours—for the stars had not yet been made—held light and darkness in equal balance. Finally, on the fourth morning, the sun, proceeding from the middle of the East, with the hours running along their lines by means of shadows, began the equinox that was to be observed annually. When it first rose over the earth, it was positioned in that region of the sky which philosophers call the first quarter of Aries; after completing its annual circuit, it would return to the same place after 365 days and six hours. Through the addition of a quarter-day it comes about that the point of the vernal equinox itself occurs now in the morning, now at midday, now in the evening, and now at midnight.

The moon, by contrast, is fullest in the evening. For the perfectly equitable Creator instituted nothing imperfect. While all the stars shone together, the moon, appearing in the middle of the East, occupied the first quarter of Libra, which they assert to be the autumnal equinox, and consecrated the beginning of Easter by its rising.

For there is no other rule for observing Easter than that the vernal equinox should be completed by the following full moon. But if the fullness of the moon precedes the equinox by even one day, the moon is already reckoned not as belonging to the first month but to the last.

For just as then the sun first received authority over the day, and then the moon with the stars received authority over the night, so now, to signify the joy of our redemption, first the day should equal the night in length, and then the fullest moon should flood it with light, for the sake of a sure mystery. For that created sun, illuminator of all the stars, signifies the eternal and true light which enlightens every human being coming into this world. The moon and stars, which shine not, as they say, by their own light but by borrowed light received from the sun, signify the body of the Church and the individual saints. They know how to be illuminated, not to illuminate; they know how to receive the gift of heavenly grace, but not to give it.

And so, in the celebration of the greatest solemnity, Christ had to be placed before the Church, which shines only through him. For if anyone should contend that the paschal full moon can occur before the equinox, let him show either that the holy Church existed in perfection before the Savior came in the flesh, or that any one of the faithful could possess some heavenly light before the arrival of his grace.

Nor was the observance of the paschal season—by which the salvation of the world was fittingly both prefigured and brought about—arranged by divine providence without reason. It was not to begin on the first day, when light was made; nor on the second, when the firmament was made; nor on the third, when the dry land appeared; nor immediately at the beginning of the fourth, when the equinoctial sun came forth like a bridegroom from his chamber; rather, it was to receive its beginning only when the moon finally rose in the evening.

The hour was awaited which would signify the illumination of the Church once to come in Christ. Thus, just as in the mystery of the heavenly sacrifice it is not permissible to offer wine alone or water alone—for the offering must not pertain exclusively to God or exclusively to humanity, but we temper with the water of our frailty the blood pressed out in the winepress of the cross [Note: [Col. 0317] B, C, “we temper the blood of the grape expressed in the press,” etc.]; and we also mix with water the grain of wheat crushed by the millstone of the Passion [Col. 0319A]—so that, as the Apostle says, by clinging to the Lord we may become one spirit with him.

The same is likewise to be observed in keeping the time of this sacrifice. We must not consider only the course of the sun, as though we believed in God but thought that he had been exalted beyond concern for us, following those who say: “He has made the clouds his hiding place; he does not consider us, and he walks around the hinges of heaven.” Nor should we seek only the full rising of the moon, as though, following the Pelagians, we could not be blessed without heavenly grace [Note: [Col. 0319] B, C, omit “not”]. Rather, in accordance with him who said, “My God, his mercy will go before me,” in our celebration of Easter let us consecrate the equinoctial rising of the sun, which conquers every obstacle of darkness, with the full moon of our devotion following immediately after it.

He completed the meaning of the Mosaic Passover on the day of his own resurrection, who came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it. Concerning each of these matters we shall explain more appropriately in its proper place, as the Lord grants. For now it is enough to point out that the occurrence of the equinox on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, and three days earlier—that is, on the fifteenth day before those same Kalends—should be marked as the first day of the world. As an indication of this, I think the ancients first wished to establish there the beginning of the zodiacal circle.

For on that day no month or year of the Romans, Greeks, or Egyptians begins, for which this would be the reason [Note: [Col. 0319] C, “This”]. Nor did astronomy begin with these peoples, although the Greeks boast of it; rather, it began with the more ancient Chaldeans. Abraham the patriarch was instructed by them, as Josephus testifies, and, having come to know God through the revolutions of the heavens and the stars, he soon brought this discipline, understood more truly, to the Egyptian people while he was living among them as an exile.

In the book of blessed Job, who lived not long after Abraham, we likewise read of *mazaroth*, that is, the signs of the horoscope. Therefore, according to the division of the zodiac, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, when light was made, the sun enters the sign of Aries. But according to the order of its first creation, on the twelfth day before the Kalends mentioned above it raises the beginning of its circuit and the head of all time together. Anatolius, bishop of Laodicea, clearly asserts this when writing about the equinox:

“On that day,” he says, “the sun is found not only to have ascended the first portion of the zodiac, but also already to possess a quadrant in it—that is, in the first of the twelve portions. This first portion of the twelve is the vernal equinox; it is itself the beginning of the months, the head of the circle, and the completion of the course of the stars called planets, that is, wanderers; it is also the end of the twelfth portion and the limit of the entire circle.”

Here he both understood the matter most truthfully and expressed it most elegantly: in relation to nature, the head of the zodiac is found only at the vernal equinox. There the twelve signs—which are now called “portions” after that bishop [Note: [Col. 0321] C, “after that”—or “from that”—bishop]—have their beginning and their end; there is the quadrant which we call the leap-year quarter; there the moon’s leap begins and ends; and there the great year, that is, the course of the planets, receives its beginning and its end.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Night

[Note: [Col. 0321C]]

Night is so called because it harms sight or human activities. Night is the darkness of the world, the hiding-place of evils, and the rest of living beings. It is the absence of the sun, the earth’s shadow, made for created mortals to rest, lest humanity, eager for work, fail through continuous labor; and where it is harsher, there it is longer, for shortening work and refreshing the limbs. Just as day sometimes signifies prosperity and knowledge of the divine law, so in Scripture night sometimes signifies the tribulation of persecution and sometimes ignorance and blindness of character, according to the prophet’s saying: “I have likened your mother to night; my people have become as though they had no knowledge”—as if he had said, “Having no light.”

“He who feeds among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows bend.” Christ, of course, feeds among the lilies—that is, amid the purity of faith and the brightness of virtues. “Breathes,” that is, illuminates. Alternatively: those who feed among lilies are those who delight in the purest and clearest senses of the Scriptures. “Until the day breathes,” that is, until that eternal day comes, which the Psalmist desired when he said: “One day in your courts is better than thousands.” “And the shadows bend,” that is, the sorrows and disturbances of this age pass away. “Until the day breathes,” that is, rises. For the day will appear—that is, rise—when that true sun of righteousness, Christ, appears. Then the shadows will bend: all the clouds of sorrow and the darkness of the present age will pass away.

If, however, we wish to consider the literal sense itself, it finely expresses the rising of day and the setting of night. For night is nothing other than the earth’s shadow, which rises when the sun descends beneath the earth. When the sun rises again, the shadows bend—that is, night falls. Thus they feed among lilies until the day breathes and the shadows bend, because the preaching and teaching of holy doctors are necessary only in the present life. In the other life, after the eternal day has appeared and the night of the present age has ended, no one will need to be taught, because all will behold the Lord’s glory with unveiled face. Hence the Lord also says through the prophet: “No man shall teach his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord’; for all shall know me, from the least to the greatest.”

Blessed Ambrose, in the *Hexameron*, asks how great an expanse of air the earth’s shadow occupies in producing night for us. When the sun withdraws and takes the day away from us, it illuminates the lower regions of the northern axis. Every body makes a shadow, and a shadow naturally adheres to a body, so much so that painters strive to render the shadows of bodies before they paint them, and maintain that art does not interrupt the force of nature. Therefore, just as in daytime, when a human body or a tree stands in the sun’s path, a shadow remains on the side from which the light is reflected, so, when day withdraws and the sun reaches the place where it is said to set, it is separated from us by the height of mountains. Thus the air is shadowed on the northern side by the interposition of the earth, so that this very shadow of the earth makes night for us.

Philosophers say that this shadow of night rises to the boundary of air and ether and that the moon, which moves lowest among the planets, is sometimes reached by darkness pointed like pyramids. “Pointed darkness,” that is, very sharp and peaked, from the word *acumen*. “Like pyramids,” that is, like tombs, which spread broadly below and taper above. Thus the darkness and shadow of night are broad and wide below, above the earth, but narrow and sharp above; the moon is said sometimes to be touched and darkened by them if the sun is beneath the earth at the center—that is, in the same lower part of the sky in which the moon is above. A pyramid is a tomb broad and wide below but narrow and constricted above, resembling *pyr*, “fire.” For the ancients made such tombs. Every structure or building pointed above is called a pyramid from fire, because fire spreads below and tapers above. As Isidore says, a pyramid is a figure rising from a broad base to a point in the manner of fire; for fire is called *pyr* among the Greeks.

No other heavenly body suffers eclipse—that is, a loss of its own light—in this manner. That is, the other wandering bodies do not fail as the moon fails. The sun suffers an eclipse in such a way that its splendor does not fail, but the moon does not appear because the earth is interposed. The wandering stars likewise do not lose their own light; but when some are hidden by others, they are said to fail—failures which philosophers call occultations of the heavenly bodies. The moon, however, suffers eclipse so as to be wholly deprived of light, as the philosophers say. “On every side,” that is, the sun’s splendor is diffused from every direction. For the sun is much larger than the earth and therefore, whether by night or by day, sends its splendor around the earth on every side. At night it cannot irradiate the places near the earth because of the earth’s shadow, but it does irradiate the higher spaces of ether beyond the moon and far from the earth.

But, lest the moon suffer this at every full moon, the breadth of the zodiac, which is of twelve portions, and the varying height of the apsides come to its aid. You will find the full gloss on this little verse in the preceding twenty-seventh chapter. This breadth of twelve portions is that of the twelve signs and of the differing apsides. In the height of the apsides the moon does not suffer this—that is, eclipse—but does so when it is near the earth, as the philosophers say. *Apsides*, a Greek term, are the circles of the planets. But because the moon’s circle varies—for it is now close to heaven and now contiguous with the mountains—when it comes into the region of shadow it produces an eclipse; when it climbs into the ether, it escapes beyond the shadow and therefore does not suffer loss, because it is illuminated by the sun.

For in making a shadow, three things must necessarily concur: light, a body, and an obscured place. Just as there are three elements in making a shadow—light, body, and place—so there are three kinds of shadows: pyramids, *chilindrides*, and *turbonides*. For the light must be greater than the body, smaller than the body, or equal to it. If the light is greater than the body, the shadow is called pyramidal, as is the earth’s shadow, that is, night; for, as Macrobius and many others teach, the sun is eight times larger than the earth. If the light is smaller than the body, it is called *turbonides*; if light and body are equal, it is called *chilindres*. A *chilindres* is a square figure having a semicircle above it. Thus light is necessary, since by its absence shadow comes to be; otherwise a body cannot make a shadow except in light.

“The sun knew its setting; ... the beasts of the forest.” Remigius: “The sun knew its setting,” that is, Christ died, and at his death darkness was placed over the whole world.

“You established darkness, and night came to be.” Spiritually, when darkness was established, night came to be because, in Christ’s Passion, unbelief arose in the hearts of the apostles. “In that night all the beasts of the forest pass through,” that is, demons, inciting either the Jews to crucify Christ or the apostles to deny him.

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—“Night is so called because it harms.” Varro likewise, in the fifth book of *On the Origin of Words*, writes that night is called so because it harms. In Greek it is called νὺξ (*nyx*), which natural philosophers define as σκία τῆς γῆς (*skia tēs gēs*), “the shadow of the earth.” It is not, however, just any shadow of the earth, but one that arises from the sun’s subterranean course. For since the earth is a globe, as was shown earlier, and likewise the sun is a globe, indeed larger than the earth, it necessarily follows—as is evident from optics—that a shadow issues from the side of the earth which the sun does not behold, resembling a goal-post or pyramid. For when a round luminous substance has another, dense or opaque substance placed in its rays, the side of the opaque substance facing the light must necessarily be illuminated, while the other side is dark, with the shadow extending farther into a pyramidal shape. From this it is readily understood that this shadow is always situated directly opposite the sun and, as the sun begins to sink, plunges toward the west; on the eastern side the shadow raises itself only as high as the sun goes beneath the earth. But when half the night has passed and the sun is in the *hypogeion*—for this is the Greek name for the subterranean place occupied by the sun at midnight—the earth’s shadow, high above the earth, slopes toward the south. Hence poets speak, on physical grounds, of deep and lofty night. If you wish to understand this more clearly, look at the figures of shadows which we placed in the first book.

“The moon, which travels lowest among the planets, is sometimes reached.” How an eclipse of the moon occurs, I think will be sufficiently understood from what we said in the scholia to the first book. The reason why the other heavenly bodies are not deprived of light by the earth’s shadow is that they are higher than the earth’s shadow can reach. Thus above the moon the shadow ends in the cone of a pyramid, that is, in its vertex or pointed extremity. The sun’s orb is far and much larger than the earth’s sphere; therefore, as the nature of light requires, a body’s shadow cannot reach an immeasurable height, and the sun gathers its rays again not far from the earth. Hence the sun is said to see all things, as Homer celebrates in his well-known verse:

> Ἥελιοσθ` ὃς πάντ` ἐφοᾷ καῖ πάντ` ἐπακούει — “Helios, who sees all things and hears all things.”

He also calls heaven ἀνύχιον (*anychion*), that is, “without night”; for the earth’s shadow, called night, cannot reach heaven.

“When it has sought the lowest apsides of its circle at full phase.” What apsides are in the planetary orbits is readily understood from the scholia and figures appended to the first book. But here Bede took *apsides* to mean the junctions of the circles, which more recent writers call the head and tail of the dragon, ἀναβιβάζοντα καὶ καταβιβάζοντα, “the ascending and descending [nodes].”

“The Creator’s marvelous providence tempered it thus.” Sleep is brought on by cold; therefore it was for the benefit of mortals that people should be given longer rest in cold seasons and places.

Night is so called because it harms sight or human activities, or because thieves and robbers find in it an opportunity to harm others. Night is the absence of the sun, the shadow of the earth, created for mortals to rest until the sun returns from setting to rising; nature and the poet describe it accordingly:

> Night rushes from the ocean,  
> Enveloping earth and pole in a great shadow.

Solomon likewise expressed this in the sacred writings: “He who feeds among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows bend”—calling the departure of night, with elegant meaning, the bending of the shadows.
