For according to the conditions of the regions through which the sun’s course extends, and because the mass of earth interposed between us and the sun excludes its brightness, that shadow—which is the nature of night—is raised so high that it appears to extend as far as the stars. With the opposite change, therefore, namely the rising of the light, he indicated that the shadows bend, that is, that night is pressed down and driven away.

Philosophers say that this shadow of night is raised as far as the boundary between the air and the ether, and that its pointed darkness, like pyramids, sometimes reaches and darkens the moon, which travels lowest among the planets. No other heavenly body suffers an eclipse of its light in this way, because the splendor of the sun, diffused on every side around the limits of the earth, freely sees what lies far from the earth; therefore the regions of the ether beyond the moon are always filled with the light of day, whether illuminated by the sun itself or by the radiance of the stars.

And just as, on a blind night, when you look at torches burning in the distance, you do not doubt that all the surrounding places are bathed in the same light, although, because the darkness of night stands in the way, you are able to see no more than the flames of the torches themselves, so, they say, that pure and heaven-adjacent void, with the fires of the stars spread everywhere, is always bright. But because our sight is obstructed by denser air, the stars themselves appear radiant with light, while the illumination reflected from them is not visible.

They say that the moon, when it has reached the lowest apsides of its circle at full phase, is sometimes darkened by the shadow described above, until, after gradually passing beyond the center of the earth [Note: [Col. 0323] B, C, “having passed beyond”], it is again seen by the sun. But to prevent this from happening at every full moon, the breadth of the zodiac—which consists of twelve portions—and the varying height of the apsides come to its aid.

For since three things must come together in the making of a shadow—light, a body, and an obscured place—where the light is equal to the body, an equal shadow is cast; where the light is weaker than the body, the shadow increases without limit; where the light is greater than the body, the shadow gradually becomes thinner and disappears. They argue that the sun is larger than the earth, although because of its immense distance it appears small [Note: [Col. 0323] C, “to be small”], and that therefore the shadow of night, because it gradually diminishes, disappears before it reaches the ether.

Blessed Ambrose also mentions this shadow and night in the sixth book of the *Hexameron*, saying:

“Did he not”—that is, Moses—“think it necessary to say how much of the expanse of air the shadow of the earth occupies when the sun withdraws from us and covers the day [Note: [Col. 0323] B, ‘leads away’; C, ‘covers’], illuminating the lower regions of the axis, and how the orb of the moon, falling into the region of this shadow, produces an eclipse?”

The shadow of night was given to mortals for bodily rest, so that humanity, eager for work, would not weaken and perish through uninterrupted labor. It also gives certain living creatures that cannot endure the sun’s light, and even wild animals that fear human presence, the opportunity to roam everywhere and seek their food. Accordingly, the Psalmist sings in praise of God:

> The sun knows its setting;  
> You establish darkness, and it becomes night;  
> In it all the beasts of the forest pass through, and so forth.

The Creator tempered this arrangement with marvelous foresight: where night is more severe because of the sun’s distance, there it is longer, so that work may be shortened and the limbs cherished. For winter is longer than summer throughout the world, and in winter it is much longer among the Scythians than among the Africans. Likewise, in summer the day burns much longer in Scythia than in Africa. If the day in Libya were not shorter in proportion to its greater heat, it would long ago have consumed the whole region [Note: [Col. 0325] C, “devoured”].

The parts of night are seven: twilight, evening, the time of silence, the dead of night, cockcrow, morning, and dawn.

Twilight is uncertain light, for we call *creperum* “uncertain”; that is, it lies between light and darkness.

Evening is marked by the appearance of the star of that name, concerning which the poet says:

> Before daybreak, Vesper will set the heavens behind their closed gates.

The time of silence is when everything becomes silent, that is, ceases to speak.

The dead of night is midnight, when, because everyone is resting in sleep, there is no time for any activity.

Cockcrow is when the roosters raise their song.

Morning lies between the departure of darkness and the arrival of dawn.

Dawn is as if a small light of day were already beginning; it is also the aurora, extending up to the rising of the sun.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Week

[Note: [Col. 0326B]]

## Brid. Ram. Glosses

“Week” (*hebdomada*) takes its name in Greek from the number seven. In Greek, *hebdomada*, in Latin *septimana*, means that it has seven mornings—that is, that it runs through seven days. The difference between *hebdomada* with **b** and *hepdomada* with **p** is this: *hebdo* means “I conceive,” whence weeks are called “conceptions”; *hepda*, with **p**, means “seven.” Hence *hepdomada* means “a week.”

Marcus Varro, in his books entitled *On Hebdomads*, describes the various properties of the number seven. Marcus Varro, the sharpest-minded of all men and, without any doubt, the most learned, wrote forty-one books of antiquities, among which he composed six on times. Terentianus briefly says of him in a most elegant verse:

> “Varro, learned in every field, who read so much that we wonder he found time to write anything; he wrote so much that we can scarcely believe anyone could have read so much.”

If you wish to hear what blessed Augustine says about him, read the sixth book of *The City of God*.

This number—the number seven—forms the greater and lesser Bears in the heavens, as well as the Vergiliae, which the Greeks call the Pleiades, and the wandering stars. The zodiac itself is not without the number seven. For in the seventh sign the solstice occurs from the winter solstice; in the seventh, the winter solstice from the summer solstice; and in the seventh, the equinox from the equinox. The moon, too, completes nearly its full course in four times seven days.

The first, singular week, therefore—the one from which the others take their form—had only seven days. Here it must be noted that the number six is not perfect because the Lord completed the works of the world in it, but, as Augustine says, namely in Book XI of *The City of God*, because that number—the number six—is perfect. An even number is one that can be divided into equal parts, such as two, four, and eight. An odd number, however, is one that cannot be divided into equal parts, with one either remaining in the middle, or lacking, or exceeding, such as three, five, seven, and nine.

A perfect number is one that is completed by its own parts, as is six, which requires no addition of another number for its perfection; when divided, it has neither more nor less than the perfect number itself. Thus twenty-eight is contained within one hundred; likewise 496 within 1,000; and 8,128 within 10,000. This is also true through the number six, which is the first to be completed by its own parts. It is first because there are also other perfect numbers that are similarly completed by their parts: by the sixth part, namely one; by the third part, namely two; and by the half, namely three.

After the example of this divine week, a second week was commanded to be observed by human beings. The second week, which received its form from the first, likewise had seven successive days. But when the Gentiles learned the observance of the week from the people of Israel, they immediately diverted it into praise of their own gods.

The pagans are called *pagani* from the villages (*pagi*) of the Athenians, where they arose. For there, in rural places and villages, the Gentiles established sacred groves and idols, and from this beginning they acquired the name “pagans.” Gentiles are those who are without the Law and have not yet believed. They are called Gentiles because they are as they were born—that is, as they descended in the flesh, serving idols under sin and not yet regenerated. For this reason they were first called Gentiles. In Greek they are called *ethnici*. *Ethnici* is translated from Greek into Latin as *gentiles*, for *ethnos* in Greek means “nation.”

They consecrated their days to the same monsters to which they consecrated the wandering stars:

> Between heaven and earth hang seven stars, distinguished by fixed intervals. They are called wandering stars because they pursue a course contrary to the world—that is, toward the left—while the world itself always rushes toward the right. Although by its constant revolution and immense speed the world raises them with it and carries them toward the setting, each is nevertheless seen, by a movement contrary to that of the sphere, moving along its own course—that is, its own advance and progress—wandering now lower, now higher, because of the obliquity of the zodiac. When impeded by the rays of the sun, they become irregular, retrograde, or stationary.

“Between heaven”—that is, the firmament—“and earth,” that is, in the ether, are the seven stars. He says of the planets that they “hang,” namely because they are not attached. He says that they hang because they are not fixed in the firmament like the other stars. The sun and moon and the five planets are not placed in the firmament, but hang in the ether; because they are near the firmament, however, they are said to be placed in the firmament.

“Distinguished” means “separated.” They are distant from and divided from one another by fixed intervals. “Pursuing a contrary course”—that is, a leftward, or left-hand, course—means that they proceed contrary to the world. The heaven bends toward the right from east to west; the planets, in the opposite direction, roll leftward from west to east.

Although the agility of the heavenly sphere is so great that it obstructs the course of the planets and carries them along by its own force, they therefore appear to us to run toward the west, although they are always borne toward the east. They never lose their own course, even though they seem to be carried along with the course of the heavenly sphere.

This passage is understood in various ways. First, in this manner: when a person turns his face toward the setting sun, his left side will be toward the south, in the direction opposite to which all the planets run from setting to rising. Or again, the earth is called the world—namely, a human being lying on his back, whose head is toward the east and whose feet are toward the west—and all the planets run contrary to his left hand. Or again, everything that is contrary is called “left”; because they run contrary to the world, therefore they are said to run toward the left. The “world” is the one that always turns toward the right. “Rushing” means “rolling” or “revolving.”

“Constant” means “continuous,” because the world revolves around the earth each day, together with its night, in twenty-four hours.

Again: the sun and moon and the other planetary stars are not fixed in the heaven like the other stars, but are carried through the air. In Greek they are called *planetae*, while in Latin they are called “wandering stars”—not because they themselves wander, for they complete their courses according to the administration of divine command, but because they make us err in investigating their movement, when they are carried sometimes toward the south, sometimes toward the north, often, as some say, contrary to the world, and sometimes with the world.

Again: the wandering stars, which are seven, do not always rise or set in the same place where they did the day before. Sometimes they descend to the lowest regions of the winter zone; sometimes they ascend to the heights of the summer zone; sometimes they return to the middle line of the equinoctial zone. So, indeed, so are heretics: while promising the light of truth, they never persist in the same condition of teaching. Shaping their doctrine now one way, now another, they themselves show how contemptible is the display of light that they promise.

I believe that the sun, placed in the middle of the planets, appears to warm and, as it were, give life to the whole world in the likeness of a spirit. Its course is placed in the fourth circle. Because it is brighter than all the others, it has therefore been placed in the middle, so that it may provide light both to those above and to those below. The moon, however, has been placed nearest to the earth so that it might more easily provide us with light at night.

Ecclesiastes bears witness to this. He is called *Ecclesiastes* because he gathers an assembly—that is, the Church. *Qohelet* is Hebrew, *Ecclesiastes* Greek, and *concionator* Latin. He is called *concionator* because he addresses the people—that is, speaks—and his speech is directed not particularly to one person but generally to everyone, saying that all the things we see in the world are fleeting and brief and therefore should by no means be desired.

> “The spirit goes, going in circles, and returns to its circuits.”

You will find a full gloss on this verse above, in Chapter 26.

The star of Mars, being close to the sun, is hot both in warmth and in nature. Mars is called *Ares* in Greek; *Ares* is interpreted as “power.” Mars is therefore called as if it were “great power.”

Mercury is as if *kyrios* (κύριος) of merchants—that is, “lord of merchants.” Speech abounds among merchants; therefore he is said to be intermediate between gods and human beings, for speech takes place between gods and human beings. They believed that he was sometimes in heaven and sometimes on earth.

Venus, by the beauty of its appearance, attracts human beings to look upon it. It alone among the planets, apart from the sun and moon, is said to cast a shadow. Venus is called both Vesper and Lucifer.

Saturn is said to derive its name from “satisfying,” or “filling.” There was, they say, a certain man in Italy who, when he satisfied people dying of hunger with his wealth, was called Saturn and was raised to divine honor.

Jupiter is therefore called as if *zetos pater*, that is, “father of thunderbolts.” This star receives water from Saturn’s circle and draws fire from the star of Mars, which is below it. When pregnant with fire and water, it becomes like moist wood cooked by flame and scatters thunderbolts that appear like a wandering star.

The seven planets are arranged in this order: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon.

The first pope, Sylvester, taught the clergy to observe holy days. Thus it is read in Leviticus, chapter 23, where the Lord speaks to Moses:

> “These are the holy festivals of the Lord, which you shall celebrate at their appointed times. In the seventh month, on the fourteenth day of the month, toward evening, is the Passover of the Lord; and on the fifteenth day of this month is the solemnity of the unleavened bread of the Lord. For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. The first day shall be most celebrated and holy for you, and so forth.”

He retained the Sabbath from the Old Scripture, without fearing the rods of grammarians, who decree that, like *Kalends*, *Nones*, and *Ides*, the word *feriae* must likewise be used only in the plural. A *ferula* was a grammarians’ staff, so that by means of that very instrument they might remind students that they ought to be ardent and burning in the pursuit of learning, since the *ferula* is of a fiery nature: one struck with it feels heat rather than pain.

The third kind of week is observed in the celebration of Pentecost. Here seven days are reckoned as one day, because seven times seven make forty-nine, and with one added they make fifty.

> “When the days of Pentecost were being completed.”

Some manuscripts incorrectly have *Pentecoste*. For *Pentecoste* in the nominative means “the fiftieth”; *Pentecostes* in the genitive means “of the fiftieth”; and *Pentecosten* in the accusative means “the fiftieth.” No grammatical rule allows us to say, “When the days were completed, the fiftieth” (*dies quinquagesimam*); rather, we must say, “When the days of the fiftieth were completed” (*dies quinquagesimae*), or certainly, as it is read in Greek, in the singular number: “And when the day of the fiftieth was completed.”

In the prayers for that same day, however, one should say: “And celebrating the most sacred day, Pentecost”—that is, “the fiftieth.” From the customary use of this word, some who do not know Greek suppose that the solemnity of this day should also be called *Pentecosten* in the nominative case.

It must be noted, however, according to the historical account, that among the ancients Pentecost—the fiftieth day on which the Law had been given—was counted from the slaughter of the lamb. Here, however, the fiftieth day on which the Holy Spirit was sent is counted not from the Lord’s Passion but, as blessed Augustine explains, from his resurrection. By restoring the example of the ancient sign, the Holy Spirit most clearly consecrated this day for himself through his advent: the Lord’s Day, on which the true Passover was also shown to be celebrated.

For here, as there, God appeared in a vision of fire. Exodus says:

> “The whole mountain of Sinai was smoking, because the Lord had descended upon it in fire.”

There, too, there were both fire and sound; here, tongues divided like fire are read, along with sound. In the very giving of the Law and grace, the clearest distinction between the Old and New Testaments appears. There the people stood far away in terror; here the faithful rejoiced after receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit. There was fear; here, love. There the mountain caused terror; here, he entered the house. There he wrote the Law with his finger on stone; here he inscribed his grace by the Holy Spirit upon the heart.

Read above, in the earlier gloss beginning, “The beginning and cause of the festival,” which also ends in this way: “They handed it down in reverence for the Lord’s resurrection.”

The fourth week of the seventh month. The fourth week was that of the seventh month, namely September, which is seventh from March. Here a month is placed for one day. The seventh month, by the number of its position in the sequence, is called a week. Or certainly those same seven months are called a week because of the property of the number seven, which through seven days made the first week.

It must be known, according to Augustine, that the high priest entered the Holy of Holies every day throughout the year, but did not offer the sacrifice of blood except on this one designated day. For this reason, too, he is said to have entered once a year—namely, by offering the sacrifice of blood. On that one day of the year the high priest entered the Holy of Holies, leaving the people outside.

There was in fact only one solemnity each year during which, while the high priest entered the Holy of Holies, no human being at all was permitted to remain within the temple doors; everyone was ordered to pray during the time of the offering. This was the solemnity of Passover, appointed in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month. That day was called the Day of Propitiation or Atonement, because after victims had been offered on the altar of burnt offerings, blood was carried into the Holy of Holies for expiation.

The fifth week was that of the seventh year, during which, by command of the Law, the whole people abstained from agricultural labor. Here a year is placed for one day, because these seven years are counted under the name of “week” only on account of the number seven.

The sixth is the week of the jubilee year, that is, of remission. It is formed by seven weeks of years, namely forty-nine years. Here seven years are placed for one day.

The jubilee years are the fiftieth years, that is, the years of remission. The jubilee is formed—that is, completed—by seven weeks of years, for seven years multiplied by seven yield forty-nine.

This sixth week is produced by counting the week of the fifth kind seven times; therefore it is said to derive from seven weeks of years. The fifth week contains seven years; this one contains seven times seven, namely forty-nine.

Above, in the fifth kind, a year is placed for one day; here seven years are placed for one day. Insofar as it pertains to seven weeks, a year is placed for one day; insofar as it pertains to one week, seven years are placed for one day.

When this sixth kind of week had been completed, trumpets sounded more loudly than at the other solemnities. At that time everyone came to the city, the trumpets sounded, hired male and female servants were set free, and fields and vineyards returned freely to their former owner.

Read in Leviticus, chapter 25, where it is written:

> “For six years you shall sow your field,”

and where you will find written concerning the fifth and sixth weeks and the trumpets:

> “You shall number seven weeks of years for yourself, that is, seven times seven, which together make forty-nine. And you shall sound the trumpet in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, at the time of propitiation, throughout all your land. You shall sanctify the fiftieth year and proclaim remission to all the inhabitants of your land; for it is the jubilee.”

At the Lord’s command, priests sounded these trumpets when, before Joshua, the walls of Jericho collapsed completely. This is mystically fulfilled in the Church, in which, for seven days—that is, throughout the whole period of this life—while preachers sound the trumpet of doctrine, all the strength of unbelievers falls.

## John the New: Scholia

Thus far Bede has treated the divisions of time produced by the revolution of the world—that is, natural divisions. From this point onward he discusses times derived from the mystical example of divine activity, which he previously said were established by God’s authority.

A week, or *hebdomada*, is a Greek word meaning a period of seven days. We understand it as a span of seven days, which is discerned neither by the measure of time drawn from the circuit of the world nor from the course of the stars; it was introduced by divine command so that human beings might work at secular tasks for six days and devote the seventh to God by abstaining from external affairs. This is like the fact that God himself created the world in six days and rested on the seventh.

The first day of this week is the Sabbath; the remaining six are named in order from the preceding Sabbath: the first of the Sabbath, the second of the Sabbath, and so forth. We use “Monday,” “Tuesday,” “Wednesday,” and so on, but that is a pagan custom. The Church calls the remaining days *feriae*; Pope Sylvester of Rome first introduced this usage.

But, as Augustine says, “The Lord, who created everything at once,” and so forth. Mathematicians discuss the perfection of the numbers six and seven at length, for example Boethius in Book I of his *Arithmetic*, and Georgius Valla in Book II, chapters 16 and 17. See Macrobius, *On the Dream of Scipio*, Book I, chapters 5 and 6.

Much has also been written by Christians and pagans in praise of the number seven. Pythagoras calls it at once a virgin, Minerva, and *Ametor*, meaning “motherless,” because of the numbers within ten it neither generates nor is generated by any. Four is generated from two, and with two produces eight; six is likewise generated from the dyad and generates three; three in turn generates six and nine; five likewise generates ten. Seven alone is generated by unity and gives birth to no other number, since twice seven produces more than the numbers contained within ten. On the strength of many arguments, they give the number seven precedence on account of this subtle property. See also Aulus Gellius, Book III, chapter 10.

The first day was assigned to the sun. The Gentiles gave the days of the week the names of the planets, a trace of which is preserved also in the German language. They call the Lord’s Day after the sun, *Sontag*; the next after the moon, *Montag*. I have not yet discovered what the German names of the third and fourth days signify. The fourth, *Donnerstag*, meaning “Thursday,” is understood to belong to Jupiter, the god of thunder. The name of the following day has been corrupted from Venus, though its origin remains. The last is *Saturstag*.

It is commonly believed that the first hour of the day, which begins at sunrise, is under the dominion of the planet from which the day receives its name; the second is under the planet that follows in order toward the earth from heaven, and so on in the order in which they are arranged in the heavens. When this sequence is completed, it returns to Saturn—[the passage is corrupt, according to the editor]. Thus the first hour of the Lord’s Day belongs to the sun, the second to Venus, the third to Mercury, the fourth to the moon, the fifth to Saturn, and the sixth, which is at midday, to Jupiter.

But this reasoning has no basis, and I do not find it handed down by the ancient astrologers. As for why the order of the planets was not preserved in assigning names to the days, Bede gives an excellent physical explanation drawn from the qualities and powers of the stars. On this subject see more in Pontanus, in his commentaries on the one hundred propositions of Ptolemy, and in Book IV of *On Heavenly Matters*.

### “Which are Lucifer and Vesper”

When it precedes the sun at its morning rising, it is called Lucifer, because of its shining color. When it follows the sun, it is called Hesperus, with its radiant color. Hence the Greeks call places situated toward the west *Hespera*: for Hesperus always appears at the beginning of night after sunset, the part which the Latins call *vespera*, “evening.” Bede took this from Book II, chapter 8, of Pliny.

### “Never more than twenty-two degrees distant from it”

Pliny reads “twenty-three,” and the more recent authorities agree with him. I therefore think that the error was committed through carelessness in copying, or that Bede suffered a lapse of memory.

“Week” (*hebdomada*) takes its name in Greek from the number seven. It is conducted, according to human custom, through seven days alone, but by the authority of sacred Scripture it is distinguished in many forms. Yet all these forms, unless I am mistaken, look toward one end: namely, to admonish us that after the perfection of good works we should hope for perpetual rest in the grace of the Holy Spirit.

The first, singular week, therefore, from which the others derive their form, is exalted by divine activity, because the Lord completed the adornment of the world in six days and rested from his works on the seventh. Here it must be noted that the number six is not perfect because the Lord completed the works of the world in it, but, as Augustine says:

> “The Lord, who was able to create everything at once, chose to work in that number because it is perfect, so that through it he might also show his works to be perfect. It is first completed by its own parts: the sixth, third, and half, which are one, two, and three, and together make six.”

[Note: [Col. 0327] B, C reads: “sixth, third, and.”]

After the example of this divine week, a second observance was commanded to human beings, as the Lord says:

> “For six days you shall labor and do all your work; but the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God. On it you shall do no work of service. For in six days God made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day.”

In ancient times the week was reckoned by the people of God in this manner: the first of the Sabbath, or one of the Sabbath, or of the Sabbaths; the second of the Sabbath; the third; the fourth; the fifth; the sixth; and the seventh of the Sabbath, or the Sabbath itself. This does not mean that all the days could be days of Sabbaths—that is, of rests—but that each was counted in order from the day of rest, which stood out above the others by its name and worship, as the first, second, third, and so forth.

But when the Gentiles learned the observance of the week from the people of Israel, they immediately diverted it into praise of their own gods. [Note: [Col. 0327] B, C reads *ediscerent* (“learned”) for *addiscerent* (“learned”).] They named the first day for the Sun, the second for the Moon, the third for Mars, the fourth for Mercury, the fifth for Jupiter, the sixth for Venus, and the seventh for Saturn, consecrating their days to the same monsters as the wandering stars, although they arranged them in a different order. [Note: [Col. 0327] B, C has *dicantes* (“consecrating”) for *dicentes* (“naming/saying”).]

They believed that they received spirit from the Sun, body from the Moon, heat from Mars, wisdom and speech from Mercury, moderation from Jupiter, pleasure from Venus, and sluggishness from Saturn. I believe this was because the sun, placed in the middle of the planets, appears to warm and, as it were, give life to the whole world in the likeness of a spirit, as Ecclesiastes bears witness when he says of it:

> “The spirit goes, going in circles, and returns to its circuits.”

Through the ministry of moisture, the moon supplies growth to all bodies. The star of Mars, being close to the sun, is hot both in warmth and in nature. Mercury, continually moving around the sun, was thought to radiate as if with the inexhaustible light of wisdom. Jupiter is tempered on either side by the cold of Saturn and the heat of Mars. Venus attracts those who behold it by the beauty of its light, which it receives from its proximity to the sun. Saturn moves more slowly than the other planets because it is also higher than they are.

For Saturn completes the zodiac in thirty years; Jupiter in twelve years; Mars, the third, in two years; the sun, the fourth, in 365 days and a quarter. Below the sun is Venus, which is both Lucifer and Vesper: it completes its course in 348 days and never moves more than forty-six degrees away from the sun. Next to it is Mercury, which completes its circuit in nine days, shining sometimes before sunrise and sometimes after sunset, and never more than twenty-two degrees distant from the sun. Last is the moon, which completes the zodiac in twenty-seven days and eight hours.

Such, then, was the folly of the Gentiles, supported by false reasoning. As if by right, they thought they should consecrate the first day to the sun because it is the greatest luminary, and the second to the moon because it is the second luminary. Then, in an ordered alternation, they placed before the third day the first star from the sun, before the fourth the first from the moon, before the fifth the second from the sun, before the sixth the second from the moon, and before the seventh the third from the sun.

The first pope, Sylvester, taught the clergy to observe holy days. Those who devote themselves to God alone should never be permitted to engage in worldly military service or business, as the Psalmist says:

> “Be still and know that I am God.”

Likewise the Apostle says:

> “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs.”

He called the first day—the day on which light was made in the beginning and Christ’s resurrection was celebrated—the Lord’s Day. John testifies that this name had already been given to it in the earliest times of the Church, saying in the Apocalypse:

> “I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s Day.”

Then, adding the second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth *feria* according to his own system, he retained the Sabbath from the ancient Scripture, without fearing the rules of grammarians, who decree that, like *Kalends*, *Nones*, and *Ides*, *feriae* must likewise be expressed only in the plural.

The third kind of week is observed in the celebration of Pentecost: namely, completed by seven weeks of days and one additional day, that is, by fifty days. On that day Moses, ascending the burning mountain, received the Law from heaven, and Christ sent the grace of the Holy Spirit from heaven in fiery tongues.

The fourth was the week of the seventh month, which was almost entirely occupied by splendid solemnities. Among them [Note: [Col. 0331B] C adds “solemnities.”] the Day of Propitiation stood out above all. On that day alone during the year the high priest, leaving the people outside, entered the Holy of Holies, after the annual fruits—grain, wine, and oil—had first been gathered in their proper order. He signified that Jesus, the great High Priest, after completing the dispensation of the flesh, would enter the gates of the heavenly kingdom through his own blood, so that he might now appear before the face of God for us, while we, still placed outside, await and love his coming.

Here it must be noted that just as certain unclean persons were commanded by the Law to be purified on the first, third, and seventh days, so the first, third, and seventh months were each made solemn by their own ceremonies.

The fifth was the week of the seventh year, during which the whole people abstained from agricultural labor by command of the Law, as the Lord says:

> “For six years you shall sow your field; in the seventh you shall cease.”

The sixth is the week of the jubilee year, that is, of remission. It is formed by seven weeks of years, namely forty-nine years. When it had been completed—that is, when the fiftieth year had finally begun—the trumpets sounded more loudly, and, according to the Law, the ancient possession returned to everyone.

## Chapter IX. On the Prophetic Seventy Weeks

### Brid. Ram. Glosses

The seventh kind of week is the one used by the prophet Daniel. There is a variety of interpretation among the Fathers concerning the seventy abbreviated weeks imposed upon the people of God, so that the transgression of the whole world might be completed in Christ’s Passion, when he removed the sin of the world and brought in the righteousness of the Gospel.

The prophet Daniel wrote such weeks. He uses this kind of week in the manner of the Law because each week here likewise comprises seven years, just as it does in the sixth kind. “According to the Law,” that is, according to the Law, he comprises seven years in each of the seventy weeks, gathering them together. He brings these kinds to an end, but by a new method—that is, because this had not previously been done by anyone except Daniel.

He abbreviates the seventy years of weeks by removing intercalations. He abbreviates the years themselves.

It must be noted in this reckoning of the weeks that, although they are counted by Daniel, illuminated by the spirit of prophecy, as though they were common—that is, lunar—years from the issuing of the word of King Artaxerxes until Christ’s Passion, they were not nevertheless reckoned by human beings in this manner. Rather, according to the sequence of time, they were counted in the customary way using common and intercalary years. In one manner they were numbered by the prophet; in another, they were completed according to the sequence of time.

The prophet Daniel therefore placed no intercalary year there, but treated all the years as common, even though the Hebrews count according to our custom by inserting intercalations, as we do. He did not abbreviate those years for the purpose of removing intercalary months. For when the intercalary months had reached the number twelve, he says that the course of the sun and moon coincided there. He inserted those intercalary months together as a complete year.

Rather, he abbreviated them in this respect: he assigned only twelve months to all those years. He therefore introduced years shorter than ours—which have thirteen months in every second or third year—and consequently more of them. Thus, after thirty-three years, when the intercalary months had reached the number twelve, he designated those twelve intercalations as one complete year; and from that point onward, to the end of the seventy weeks—that is, to the end of the 490 years—he reckoned in the same way.

Because years of thirteen months are not counted in this reckoning, but only twelve-month years, it follows that more years are understood than in our reckoning, and that they are shorter. If someone were to count the years according to this calculation, no age could have been understood to be so great, and the number counted would not have been smaller.

Daniel did this in the manner of prophecy, which is accustomed to speak obscurely. He exercised the ingenuity of anyone who sought to understand it, secretly admonishing the reader to recognize that years shorter than usual had been indicated.

For, as we have already said above, the prophet Daniel did not insert intercalary years into this reckoning, but used common years. If he had counted the years in the customary manner, inserting intercalary years among the common years, fifteen years fewer than 490 would be found.

Therefore know and understand: from the issuing of the word that Jerusalem should be rebuilt until Christ the prince, there shall be seven weeks, and sixty-two weeks; and the street and the walls shall be rebuilt again, though in a time of distress.

Know therefore and understand—namely, what I am telling you: from the issuing of the decree of King Artaxerxes, when he gave permission for the walls of Jerusalem to be rebuilt. Or, “from the issuing of the word,” that is, from the time when the king’s reply went forth that Jerusalem should be rebuilt. This occurred in the twentieth year of his reign, at the request of Nehemiah, who was his cupbearer.

“Until Christ the prince”—that is, the Son of God—there shall be seven weeks, that is, seven years, which contain forty-nine years. “And the street shall be rebuilt again.” That is, and so it happened: the rebuilding took place within those seventy weeks. “In a time of distress,” that is, within a period of fifty-two days.

From the first year of Cyrus until the sixth year of Darius there are forty-nine years, that is, seven weeks, during which the entire work of the Temple was completed. Yet he is not speaking here of those weeks. Indeed, the Jews in the Gospel, following this opinion, say to the Lord: “This Temple has been built for forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?” By saying that the Temple was built for forty-six years, they refer not to its first construction but to its second rebuilding, when the children of the captivity, under the leaders Zerubbabel and Jeshua son of Nun, were unable to complete the work they had begun for forty-six years because of the opposition of the neighboring nations. For that many years elapsed from the first year of King Cyrus, who granted freedom to the Jews wishing to return to their homeland, until the sixth year of King Darius, under whom all the work of the Temple was completed.

In the second year of their arrival, in the second month, they laid the foundations of the Temple—in the seventy-second year of his *incensio* [reading uncertain], according to Africanus—but because they were obstructed by the Samaritans and the other nations in the surrounding region, the work was suspended until the second year of Darius. Josephus, moreover, adds three further years, during which the enclosure of the Temple and certain other remaining works were completed. Added to the forty-six years, these make forty-nine years.

Finally, Africanus the Chronicler includes these weeks not from Cyrus’s first grant of permission—for there are more than seventy weeks from that point, and considerably more—but from the day on which the angel spoke to Daniel. In this he should not be followed. We ought rather to believe that the seventy weeks are counted from the issuing of the decree of King Artaxerxes than from the time when the angel spoke to Daniel.

Eusebius, however, counts sixty-nine weeks—from the sixth year of Darius, who reigned over Persia after Cyrus and his son Cambyses, when the work of the Temple was completed, until Herod and Caesar Augustus, that is, until the first year of Herod’s reign and the tenth year of Caesar Augustus. These weeks amount to 483 years. At that time Christ—that is, Hyrcanus, the last high priest of the family of the Maccabees—was slain by Herod, and, in accordance with the law of God, the succession of high priests came to an end.

The completed years, therefore, are not believed to refer to this Christ, although Eusebius says so; rather, the seven weeks and sixty-two weeks refer to Christ, the Redeemer of the world. Seven weeks are forty-nine years; sixty-two weeks are 433 years. Add the forty-nine and the 433 to the final week, which, like the others, contains seven years, and the total is 490 lunar years, as Eusebius Pamphilus says.

Nor should we be troubled by the fact that seven weeks are counted first, then sixty-two, and that the final week is again divided into two parts. This is an idiom—that is, a characteristic—of the Hebrew language and of the language of the ancient Latins: they count the smaller number first and the larger afterward. For example, in accordance with the usage of our language we now say, “Abraham lived 175 years.” They, by contrast, say: “Abraham lived five and seventy and one hundred years.” It is therefore not fulfilled exactly as it is read, but it reaches its end when the whole number is counted together.

Read the exposition of the tenth vision, and hear what blessed Jerome says there about this number. Add also the seven surplus months and the portion of the eighteenth year of the reign of Tiberius, in which the Lord suffered.

It should be noted here that, if the endpoint of this prophetic week is reckoned from the month of Nisan—that is, from the paschal moon—in which the king’s decree went forth that Jerusalem should be rebuilt, until that Nisan on whose fifteenth day Christ suffered, and if no more than 489 years and seven months are found between these two endpoints, then five months are lacking to complete the final year. Accordingly, these five months are added.

If they are taken from part of the seventeenth year, they are not contained within the number of the weeks, since they fall after Christ’s passion—unless perhaps the years of this week are to be reckoned as beginning with the Kalends of January preceding the Nisan in which the decree was issued and ending with the Kalends of January before the Nisan of the Lord’s passion. In that case, the portion which he commands to be added from the seventeenth year of Tiberius would extend from those Kalends of January, on which the number of years was completed, up to the Lord’s passion itself.

But if this is so, we are brought back to the difficulty of the same question. For it makes no difference whether five months are added after the year following the weeks, since they are not found within the weeks themselves.

There are some, however, who wish to solve the question in this way: the five months are supplied from the quarterly portions of the leap-days of all the years and from the intercalary months. For if you gather the intercalary months of all the years and divide them all into equal portions, so that one portion contains months of thirty days and the other months of twenty-nine, much will remain for you.

The intercalary months of all the years amount to 175. Half of these is 87½; from them you collect an equal number of days, namely, one day from each month, making eighty-eight days. Next consider the 475 years and how many leap-days they contain. Four hundred years contain one hundred leap-days; seventy-five years contain eighteen days. Together these make 118.

Add to these the eighty-seven intercalary days mentioned above, and the total is 205. Divide these by months, that is, by thirty-day months. Six times thirty makes 180, leaving twenty-five—or even twenty-eight, if you wish to subtract three days from the six thirty-day months. Thus six months and twenty-eight days are obtained.

You can therefore complete not only five months; fifty-eight days also remain for you, and within the weeks themselves you have found the entire number of years. Yet I am also simply pleased with the view that the number of the prophetic week ends not in complete years but in seven months. Divine Providence preferred this arrangement so that the perfection of the entire period might be indicated by the number seven in the months, at whose end the sevenfold grace of the Spirit shone upon the world.

But he will confirm the covenant with the many for one week, and so forth.

“He will confirm the covenant,” that is, the ordinance and law of God. “One week,” that is, the final week itself, during which John the Baptist, or the Lord and the apostles, converted many to the faith by preaching.

“With the many for weeks”—he speaks of those sixty-nine weeks, from which the final one remained, as I have said. “And in the middle of the week the offering will fail,” that is, the sacrifices of the Jews. It is as though he had said: before the seventieth week is completed, the Jewish sacrifice will fail, because when Christ began to preach and to baptize, the sacrifices of the Jews began to be held in less esteem.

Thus, for three years and six months, according to the evangelist John, Christ preached the Gospel and confirmed the worship of the true God to many—clearly to the apostles and believers—when, after the Lord’s passion, in the middle of the week, the offering and sacrifice again ceased.

For this reason, setting forth the prophet’s entire testimony, we have expounded it as far as our ability permitted. The prophet’s testimony—that is, what he heard the angel demand—required us to explain those years in such a manner, namely, as years abbreviated in this way. Otherwise, if the Hebrews had possessed years of that kind, the entire sequence of the Old Testament would totter. No human lifespan could have been understood to be as long as the one recorded in the Old Testament, since every lifespan was reckoned according to longer and shorter years.

[Col. 0338C]

It should certainly be understood that Africanus was an author of chronological cycles of weeks. The same Africanus also wrote to a certain Aristides concerning the apparent disagreement among the Gospels and why Matthew and Luke are said to give different genealogical accounts of Christ. There he demonstrates the most evident agreement between the two, as blessed Jerome teaches in the sixth chapter of the first book of his Ecclesiastical History.

“Chronicle” is called in Greek what in Latin is termed a sequence of times, such as the work published among the Greeks by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, and translated into Latin by the presbyter Jerome. For Greek *chronos* is interpreted in Latin as “time.”

## JOHN NOV. SCHOLIA

**Seven times seven weeks.** The prophet Daniel foretold the time of the Lord’s passion by weeks of years, which Bede explains lucidly and learnedly in this chapter. In our own age, certain men have also labored over an exposition of the same little work. Moreover, there is a disputed passage in Daniel.

[Col. 0333A]

The seventh kind of week is the one used by the prophet Daniel. Following the usage of the Law, he comprises each week in seven years, but by a new method abbreviates those years themselves, determining each by twelve lunar months. As for the intercalary months, which ordinarily grow out of the eleven epact days of the year, he does not add one in the third or second year according to the national practice; instead, when they have increased to the number twelve, he inserts them all together as a complete year.

He did this not out of jealousy toward those seeking knowledge of the truth, but, in accordance with the manner of prophecy, to exercise the intelligence of those who sought it. He preferred that his pearls, concealed from his children, should be sought through fruitful toil rather than scattered before swine and trampled in contemptuous disdain.

But so that these matters may shine forth more clearly, let us now consider the angel’s very words to the prophet:

“Seventy weeks,” he says, “are abbreviated over your people and over your holy city, so that transgression may be completed, sin may reach its end, iniquity may be blotted out, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed.”

No one doubts that these words designate the incarnation of Christ, who took away the sins of the world, fulfilled the Law and the Prophets, and was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions. They also indicate that the seventy weeks, divided into seven-year periods, signify 490 years.

It should be noted, however, that he asserts that these weeks were not simply marked down or counted, but abbreviated, secretly warning the reader to understand that years shorter than usual are indicated.

“Know therefore,” he says, “and understand: from the issuing of the word that Jerusalem should be rebuilt until Christ the prince, there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks; and the street and the walls shall be rebuilt again in a time of distress.”

From Ezra’s account we learn that Nehemiah, being the cupbearer of King Artaxerxes, obtained from him in the twentieth year of his reign, in the month of Nisan, permission to restore the walls of Jerusalem, while the Temple had been constructed long before with Cyrus’s permission. The work itself, as has been said, was completed in a time of distress: it was so fiercely attacked by the neighboring peoples that the builders are said to have fought with one hand, their loins girded with swords, while restoring the wall with the other.

From that time, therefore, until Christ the prince, count seventy weeks—that is, 490 years of twelve lunar months—which are 475 solar years. For the Persians ruled from the aforementioned twentieth year of King Artaxerxes until the death of Darius for 116 years. From that point the Macedonians ruled until the death of Cleopatra for 300 years. Afterward the Romans held the monarchy until the seventeenth year of Tiberius Caesar for 59 years. Together, as we have said, these make 475 years.

They are contained in twenty-five nineteen-year cycles: for twenty-five times nineteen makes 475. Since seven intercalary months are added in each cycle, multiply twenty-five by seven, and the result is 175. These are the intercalary months of the 475 years.

If you wish to know how many lunar years they can make, divide 175 by twelve. Twelve times fourteen is 168; therefore they make fourteen years, with seven months remaining. Add these to the 475 years written above, and together they make 489 years. Add also the seven surplus months and the portion of the eighteenth year of Tiberius’s reign in which the Lord suffered, and you will find, from the appointed time until his passion, seventy abbreviated weeks—that is, 490 lunar years.

At his baptism, however, when the Holy of Holies was anointed, with the Holy Spirit descending upon him like a dove, not only had the seven and sixty-two weeks been completed, but part of the seventieth week had already begun.

“And after the sixty-two weeks,” he says, “Christ will be slain, and his people will not be”—that is, the people who would deny him.

Christ was not slain immediately after the sixty-two weeks, but at the end of the seventieth week. He separated this week from the others, as far as we can conjecture, because he had more to say about it. For Christ was crucified in that week, and he was denied by the faithless people not only at the time of his passion but continually from the moment when John began to preach about him.

What follows—“And the people with the coming prince will destroy the city and the sanctuary, and its end will be devastation, and after the end of the war desolation has been decreed”—does not belong to the seventy weeks. It had been foretold that those weeks themselves would extend to the rule of Christ. But Scripture, having foretold his coming and passion, also shows what would happen afterward to the people who would refuse to receive him.

By “the coming prince” he means Titus, who, in the fortieth year of the Lord’s passion, so destroyed both the city and the sanctuary with the Roman people that not one stone remained upon another.

Having briefly anticipated these matters, he immediately returned to expounding the event of the week that he had passed over:

“But he will confirm the covenant with the many for one week.” That is, in the final week itself, during which either John the Baptist or the Lord and the apostles converted many to the faith by preaching.

“And in half a week the offering and sacrifice will fail.” The middle of this week was the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, when, with Christ’s baptism having begun, the purification associated with sacrifices gradually began to lose its value among the faithful.

Likewise, what follows—“And in the Temple there will be the abomination of desolation, and desolation will continue until the consummation and the end”—refers to subsequent times. The truth of this prophecy is attested both by the history of ancient events and by the outcome of our own times today.

For this reason, setting forth the prophet’s entire testimony, we have expounded it as far as our ability permitted, because we have learned both that it is unknown to many readers and that it requires a special kind of week. Those who think that the Hebrews used years of this kind are mistaken. Otherwise, the entire sequence of the Old Testament would totter, and no lifespan as great as the one written there ought to be understood literally; rather, it must be constrained by the course of the moon.

We read that the ancient Greeks counted a year according to the course of the moon as 354 days. Every eighth year they intercalated ninety days, which arose when the quarter-day was combined eight times with the eleven epact days; these ninety days were distributed into three months of thirty days each.

The Jews, however, did not follow this practice, but ordinarily inserted, in the second or third year, a thirteenth lunar month, which we call an intercalary month, as the well-known calculation of the paschal fourteenth moon clearly proves.

It should certainly be understood that Africanus, whose reckoning of the weeks we have carried to the seventeenth or eighteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, in which we believe the Lord suffered, according to the Chronicle of Eusebius, begins from the same starting point as we do. But he considers the weeks completed in the fifteenth year of that emperor, in which he believes Christ suffered. He assigns 115 years to the reign of the Persians, 300 to the Macedonians, and 60 to the Romans.

Let the diligent reader choose whichever view he judges should more properly be followed.

## CHAPTER X  
### On the week of the ages of the world

[Note: [Col. 0338D]

**BRID. RAM. GLOSSES.**—The eighth kind of week is uniform and exists alone, without the cycle of revolution. It is uniform, not varied, because time is not varied within it. It is alone because all time is contained within it. It is without a cycle because times do not revolve within it. It is called uniform because it has only one form of time. Time is not repeated within it; rather, it contains all time in itself. It corresponds to the pattern—that is, the example—of the first week, in which the world and everything in it were created.

Not long after the giants were born, the whole earth was corrupted, until the Creator, repenting that he had made humanity, decided to destroy the world by the Flood. God is said to repent, as it is written: “It repents me that I made humankind upon the earth.” And again: “It repents me that I established Saul as king over Israel.” How can he be one who repents, when he does not grieve that he did what he had once done? One is said to repent when what he has done displeases him and, by changing it, he does something else in its place. Because God himself is immutable, yet changes what he wills, he is said to repent, although he changes the thing and not his purpose.

Read the twentieth book of Saint Gregory’s *Morals*, in which these sacred words are contained: “Those who gathered together to build the tower of pride were changed by the division of languages and were scattered from one another.”

Haimo: Babylon was a city and the metropolis of the Chaldeans, extremely powerful and of such vast size, as Herodotus and many other Greek historians report, that it extended from corner to corner in a square for sixteen thousand paces—that is, sixty-four thousand paces in all—which make forty-two leagues and two parts of another. It was built by a queen called Semiramis. At its center was a citadel, or capitolium: the tower which the sons of Adam built after the Flood, before they were dispersed throughout the whole world. That tower is said to have reached a height of three thousand paces, that is, two leagues, narrowing gradually from a broad base to a narrower summit so that the overhanging weight might more easily be supported by the sides.

Because there the language of the whole earth was confused, it is called *Babel* in Hebrew and *Babylon* in Greek.

Isidore: The diversity of languages arose during the building of the tower after the Flood. Before the pride of that tower divided human society into the different sounds of signs, there was one language among all nations, which is called Hebrew. The patriarchs and prophets used it not only in their speech but also in the sacred writings.

In the beginning, there were as many peoples as languages. Later there were more peoples than languages, because many peoples arose from one language. In this passage, “languages” means the words produced by the tongue, according to that figure of speech by which the agent is named through the thing produced, just as “mouth” is sometimes used for words and “hand” for writing.

When God had completed his works on the seventh day, he rested and, sanctifying it, commanded that it be called the Sabbath.

Augustine, in Book XI of *The City of God*: When God rests on the seventh day from all his works and sanctifies it, this must not be understood in a childish way, as though God had grown weary through working—he who spoke and they came to be—by an intelligible and eternal word, not by a sounding and temporal one. Rather, God’s rest signifies the rest of those who rest in God, just as the joy of a house signifies the joy of those who rejoice in the house, even though it is not the house itself but some other thing that makes them joyful. Likewise, when a letter is called joyful, it signifies the joy of those whom it makes joyful when they read it.

Accordingly, when prophetic authority most appropriately tells us that God rested, it signifies those who rest in him and whom he himself causes to rest. The prophecy also promises this to the human beings to whom it speaks and for whose sake it was written: after the good works which God performs in them and through them, if they first approach him in this life in some manner through faith, they will have eternal rest in him.

Concerning the perfection of the number seven, we have already written above.]

When the holy receive their bodies in their own land, they will possess double blessings, and everlasting joy will be theirs. “In their own land,” that is, in the land of the living and the meek. “They will possess double blessings,” that is, in body and soul, when they receive immortality and incorruption in the body, and unchangeableness in the soul; and everlasting joy will be theirs.

## ALSO, FROM ABOVE

In the very beginning of creation, heaven and earth, the angels, the air, and the water were made from nothing. On the first day light itself was made, also from nothing. On the second, the firmament was placed in the midst of the waters. On the third, the appearance of the sea and the earth was made, together with the things rooted in the earth. On the fourth, the heavenly lights were made from the light created on the first day. On the fifth, the swimming creatures and the birds were made from the waters. On the sixth, the remaining animals were made from the earth, and the human being was created: flesh from the earth, but the soul from nothing. He was placed in the paradise which the Lord had planted from the beginning. On the seventh day the Lord rested—not from governing creation, since in him we live, move, and exist, but from creating a new substance.

### The beginnings of the world in seven days

The first day took its beginning from the origins of light in the world.

The second, in hours of flowing brightness, established the heavens.

The third gave the sea, wandering over the waters, together with the earth’s growth.

The fourth possesses Phoebus, the moon, and the stars of heaven.

The fifth brought forth feathered birds and swimming fish.

The sixth has creeping four-footed creatures and intelligent human beings.

The seventh is the Lord’s rest, when these things had duly been completed.

## JOHN NOV. SCHOLIA

**The eighth kind.** The final kind of week is the consummation of all the ages of the world from the beginning of time; its seventh day is everlasting rest, enduring through infinite ages. The parts of this week are called the ages of the world. The course of their times was typologically expressed by the first seven days of creation, a subject which Bede treats lucidly through the comparison and application of histories.]

The eighth kind of week, uniform and existing alone without the cycle of revolution, is completed according to the pattern of the first week as the ages of this world pass away.

On the first day light was made; in the first age, humanity was placed in the pleasantness of paradise. Light was divided from darkness, evening came, and, when the sons of God had been separated from the wicked offspring, the whole earth was corrupted not long after the giants were born, until the Creator, repenting that he had made humanity, decided to destroy the world by the Flood.

On the second day the firmament was balanced in the midst of the waters; in the second age the ark was carried in the midst of the waters, supported on one side by the fountains of the abyss and drenched on the other by the cataracts of heaven. Its evening came when the sons of Adam, moving their feet from the East, who had gathered to build the tower of pride, were punished by the division of languages and scattered from one another.

On the third day, when the waters had been gathered into one collection, dry land appeared, adorned with forests and grasses. In the third age, when the nations had been established in the worship of demons, the patriarch Abraham, abandoning his kinship and homeland, became fruitful through the seed of the saints.

Evening also came when the Hebrew people, compelled by the pressure of evils, contrary to God’s will asked for a king. Once appointed, he first slaughtered the Lord’s priests and prophets; afterward he himself, together with the whole people, perished by the sword of the Philistines.

On the fourth day heaven was adorned with lights. In the fourth age that people, renowned for heavenly faith and glorious through the kingdoms of David and Solomon, was also ennobled throughout the world by the height of its most holy Temple.

But it too received an evening, when, as sins multiplied, that kingdom was destroyed by the Chaldeans, the Temple was demolished, and the whole people was transferred to Babylon.

On the fifth day fish and birds were brought forth from the waters: the former remained in their native waters, while the latter flew through air and over earth. In the fifth age, the people of Israel multiplied in Chaldea. Some, supported by the wings of heavenly desires, sought Jerusalem; others, deprived of the flight of virtues, remained amid the streams of Babylon.

Evening followed, when, with the Savior’s advent already near, the Jewish people, because of the enormity of their crimes, became tributary to the Romans and was further oppressed by foreign kings.

On the sixth day the earth was filled with its living creatures, and the first human being was created in the image of God. Soon afterward, a woman was fashioned from the rib taken from his side while he slept. In the sixth age, while the prophets proclaimed, the Son of God appeared in the flesh to recreate humanity in the image of God. When he fell asleep on the cross, blood and water flowed from his side, from which he consecrated the Church for himself.

The evening of this age, darker than the others, will come in the persecution of Antichrist.

On the seventh day, when he had completed his works, God rested and, signifying this, commanded that it be called the Sabbath; it is not recorded as having an evening. In the seventh age, the souls of the righteous, after the finest labors of this life, rest perpetually in the life to come. It will never be stained by any sadness but will instead be enriched by the greater glory of the resurrection.

This age began for human beings when the first martyr Abel entered, in body, the tomb, but in spirit the Sabbath of perpetual rest.

It will be completed when the holy receive their bodies and possess double blessings in their own land, and everlasting joy will be theirs. This is also the eighth age, for which Psalm 6 is entitled. I believe that, during the six ages of this world, supplication is to be made for the seventh or eighth age of the world to come. Since the righteous will receive joys in it but the reprobate punishments, this Psalm begins, proceeds, and ends in great fear:

“Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER XI  
### On the months

[Note: [Col. 0341D]

**BRID. RAM. GLOSSES.**—The months are so called from the measure by which each of them is measured; but it is better to derive the word from the moon, which in Greek is called *mene* (μήνη). Nor is this novel: the moon is called *mene* in Greek, from which the word *neomenia* is formed, meaning “the beginning of the new moon.” From *mene*, which means “moon,” the word “month” is used among those who begin and end the first day of the Kalends not according to the course of the sun and the varying lengths of the months but according to the circuit of the moon, as the Hebrews do.

Jerome: A *neomenia* is the beginning of a month, which, according to the usage of the Latin language, we can call the Kalends. But because among the Hebrews the month is reckoned according to the course of the moon, and among the Greeks *mene* means “moon,” *neomenia* means, as it were, “new moon.”

Thus Jesus son of Sirach, who certainly wrote in Hebrew, says concerning the moon: “The month is named according to it.” In the book of Ecclesiasticus it is written:

“The moon is the indication of the time and the sign of the age. The month is named according to it.”

The moon’s first name is *mene*. The moon’s second name is “month,” that is, *Jaret*, which is also called May. The twelfth month, Adar, corresponds in the same way to March.

He says “in the same way” because the moon which corresponds to May sometimes begins in April and ends in May; sometimes it begins in May and ends in June; sometimes it begins and ends within May itself and is wholly contained in that month. The same is to be understood of the remaining months.]

I am therefore troubled by no small scruple.

“Therefore”—that is, because lunar months alternate in this way, one having thirty days and the other twenty-nine. “By no small”—that is, by a very great and serious matter. “I am troubled”—that is, I, Bede. “By a scruple”—that is, by uncertainty.

Our predecessors—that is, the Hebrews, who reckon according to the moon—the day on which the Law was given as the third day of the third month. The Jews sacrificed the lamb in Egypt on the fourteenth moon of the first month, at the spring equinox; this was the first Passover. Christ was sacrificed on the fifteenth moon of the first month; this was the second Passover.

He awaited the fifteenth moon so that he might celebrate the first Passover—that is, the fourteenth moon—with his disciples. The Jews received the Law on the third moon of the third month, that is, on the forty-ninth day from the fourteenth moon of the first month. The apostles received the Holy Spirit on the forty-ninth day after the Lord’s resurrection.

It is therefore apparent that we and the Jews do not celebrate Passover and Pentecost on the same day or under the same moon, although we celebrate them close to one another.

“What is the third”—that is, the third month, namely June—from that month in which the full moon occurs after the equinox, which is always the paschal month. “The fiftieth”—that is, counting from the slaughter of the lamb, from the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May. “They count”—that is, the Hebrews. “Of the first month”—that is, the paschal month, April. “The remaining days”—that is, from the slaughter of the lamb, or Passover.

Above, in the eighth chapter, we wrote that the second month ought to be completed not as a thirty-day month but as a twenty-nine-day month.

Priscian, in his book *On the Forms of Numbers*: We say *undeviginti* for nineteen, that is, “one short of twenty.”

Horace, in the second book of the *Satires*:

“Seventy-nine years old, for whom a blanket garment…”

He says *unde-octoginta*, meaning one who is seventy-nine years old—that is, eighty less one.

*Duodeviginti* is used for eighteen; *undetriginta* for twenty-nine; and similarly in such cases.

Unless perhaps it should be thought that, by synecdoche—which is a very common rule of Holy Scripture—the whole is counted from a part.

“Synecdochically,” used adverbially. This is the kind of rule in which the whole is understood from a part—for example, so that “forty-nine” is understood as fifty. In synecdoche, forty-nine is said to be fifty. Scripture has this custom: it sets down the whole by a part, especially in matters of time.]

Nor should it be understood otherwise in Genesis. “Nor otherwise,” namely, although the Hebrews reckon their months by the moon. “Where Noah was with his own,” namely, with his sons and wives. Thus it is read in Genesis, chapter 7:

> “In the six-hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, all the fountains of the great deep were broken open, and on that day Noah entered the ark with his own.”

And afterward:

> “In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth was dried, and Noah came out of the ark.” [Col. 0343D]

But Saint Jerome says in the *Book of Hebrew Questions*: “Ararat: Armenia. For it is reported that the ark came to rest after the Flood in the mountains of Ararat, and that traces of it remain there even to this day.”

For the moon which in the present year, for example, was seventeen on the Nones of May, will in the following year occur on the twenty-seventh day, on the day before the Nones of May. He says “the day before the Nones,” and not “the Nones,” because he is seeking the weekday, not the calendar designation. For on the very weekday on which this year it is called the Nones of May, in the following year it will be called the day before the Nones of May, on that same weekday. The weekday remains, whereas the calendar designation shifts from one day to the next each year. Hence this designation, which is on the first weekday in the present year, will be on the second in the following year; but if it is a leap year, it will also fall on the third.

Thus festivals and anniversaries likewise shift from day to day in the year along with their calendar designations. This is the reason that causes the designation to change. A solar year has 365 days. Divide these by seven: one remains; in a leap year, two remain. These one or two days in the leap year, exceeding the number seven, produce that change. And although the change of the designation from one day to the next occurs in the year, there are nevertheless no more designations than weekdays. For even if the designation shifts from one weekday to another, it does not thereby increase the number of weekdays.

Indeed, as more careful investigation of natural phenomena has taught, the moon completes the Zodiac in twenty-seven days and eight hours, but completes the full course of its own cycle in twenty-nine days and twelve hours, without reckoning its leap.

See above, chapter 16, since I have been unable to find a better gloss on this verse. But in reckoning both months, custom, authority, or at any rate the convenience of calculation has prevailed over nature. Nature dictates that a solar month should have thirty days, ten hours, and a half; custom, authority, or convenience of calculation nevertheless makes it have thirty days. Nature likewise dictates that a lunar month should have twenty-nine and a half days; custom, authority, or convenience of calculation nevertheless makes it have twenty-nine days, or even thirty.

And, what is more serious, calculators differ so greatly among themselves—that is, disagree—that sometimes, on one and the same day, one of them, namely Anatolius, insists that the moon should be reckoned as being on the fourteenth day; another, namely Dionysius, on the fifteenth; and another, namely Victorius, on the sixteenth. This is because of the insertion of the embolismic month: where one inserts an embolism, the other does not. Hence it happens that their first years begin from the leap day on the third day before the Kalends of September. For some place both the leap day and the lunar leap differently. Some place them earlier, as Anatolius, Victorius, and others do; others place them later, as we do.

Those who place the leap day on the fourth day before the Kalends of September have, on the fourth day before the Ides of December, the fourteenth lunar day; those who place the leap have the seventeenth; and those who place neither have the fifteenth.

For example: We are now, among ourselves, in the final year of the nineteen-year cycle, which has eighteen epacts. If you join these to the regular calculation on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, you will find the second lunar day on the Kalends of August. You will advance this to the thirtieth day on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, because the leap day is placed there; on the third day before the Kalends, it becomes the first; on the second day before the Kalends, the second; on the Kalends of September, the third. Continuing this calculation, you must arrive at the fourth day before the Ides of December, and there you will find, on that same day, the fourteenth lunar day according to the person who inserted the leap day; according to the person who inserted the lunar leap, the sixteenth; and according to the person who inserted neither, the fifteenth. [Col. 0344B–0345B]

For the leap day diminishes one age, while the lunar leap increases one age in advance. The leap day increases the moon and decreases the age; the lunar leap decreases the moon and increases the age. In the following months that age appears to increase or decrease.

Moreover, the discrepancy which we say arises in leap years from the time when they intercalate the quarter-day is caused by the intercalation among the Greeks on the fourth day before the Kalends of September. For, except in leap years, the fourth day before the Kalends of September is always the first day of their year; in leap years, however, that day is the last, namely the fourth day before the Kalends of September, because the quarter-day is intercalated there.

Therefore the festival which we celebrate on the fourth day before the Kalends of September is celebrated by them, that is, by the Egyptians, on the third day before the Kalends. And from the time when they intercalate that quarter-day, the same difference continues until the time of our intercalation.

For example: One and the same festival which is celebrated among us today will occur among them tomorrow. Likewise, one and the same lunar age—for example, the seventh—which among us falls on the first day of the week, will among them fall on the second day of the week, though remaining the seventh lunar age.

It should be noted, however, that the difference in festivals and the difference in lunar ages do not begin at the same time. The difference in festivals always begins on the fourth day before the Kalends; the difference in lunar ages, however, arises from the moon of August. For in every leap year their month has thirty days, whereas ours has twenty-nine. Hence a difference exists between us and them until the sixth day before the Kalends of March; the difference in lunar ages, however, ends with the close of the moon of February, which among us has thirty days in a leap year, but among them twenty-nine.

## Likewise from the Above

A lunar month is completed through the moon’s increase and waning, while it traverses slightly more than the Zodiac in twenty-nine and a half days. But the convenience of calculation alternates lunar months between thirty and twenty-nine days. A solar month is longer by twenty-two hours, from which eleven epact days accrue, by which the sun each year surpasses the moon’s course. For twelve times twenty-two makes 264, and eleven times twenty-four completes the same number.

The Hebrews begin their months with the rising moon; the Romans with the Kalends; the Egyptians, reckoning their months from the fourth day before the Kalends of September to the ninth day before those same Kalends, count thirty days in their months and call the remaining five days intercalary. They were the first to begin ending months according to the sun’s course, so that the moon’s swifter and uncertain course would not impede their calculations.

Most authorities, however, maintain that Cingius, king of the Sabines, first divided the year into months and established the Ides, Kalends, and intercalary days.

The books of the Holy Scriptures show that there were twelve months, even in the year before the Flood. For thus we read there:

> “The waters were diminishing until the eleventh month. In the eleventh month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains appeared.”

Thus months were then counted as they are now—not those bounded by the Kalends, but those bounded by the beginning and end of the moon. We say that “Kalends” derives from *colere*, “to worship,” because among the ancients the beginnings of months were always observed with religious rites. The Ides likewise are said to derive from *dies*, “days,” and the Nones from the *nundinae*, the market days.

Among the Latins, months begin with the Kalends; among the Hebrews, with the return of the rising moon; among the Egyptians, the beginnings of months are announced four, six, seven, or eight days before the Kalends. “Months” derives from measurement, as stated above.

## John the New: Notes

“Months” derives from measurement. Up to this point he has explained the variations of weeks; now he explains the reckoning of months, which are, as it were, the larger divisions.

Monthly periods are partly established by nature and partly by human discretion.
