The months of the Greeks are derived from the interval between two lunar conjunctions, a natural interval gathered solely from motion. A natural month is likewise the span in which the sun completes one sign, namely thirty days, ten hours, and a half. But this month is difficult to observe, because just as in the moon’s revolution, human beings cannot perceive by any manifest sign that the sun has passed from one sign into another. For that reason, nations rarely use such months.

The Macedonians do use them, naming them from the celestial signs. Thus *κριός*—“ram”—is the month, or period, during which the sun is in the sign of Aries. Its first day is the fifth day before the Ides of March, and its last the third day before the Ides of April. Likewise *ταῦρος* and *δίδυμοι*—“Taurus” and “Gemini”—are solar months.

The natural months of the Latins, however, are not natural. They consist of an arbitrary number of days: January has thirty-one, February twenty-eight, and April thirty days. Although the epacts, the embolismic leap-months, and other intercalations arise from the natural motion of the stars, they are nevertheless inserted or added in different months according to human judgment.

But better, from the moon. Months are called as though from *mensa*, “a table,” that is, measured periods; or from the Greek *μήνη* (*mēnē*), which means “moon” in the language of the Arcadians, and *μήν, μηνός* (*mēn, mēnos*), “month.” The Athenians call the lunar orb itself *σελήνη* (*selēnē*), “moon,” because it receives brightness.

Varro agrees with the former derivation, namely, that “month” is named from the moon, from which it naturally proceeds. In German likewise we call a month *ein Monath*, a word which sometimes means the four weeks by which the moon’s course through the Zodiac is defined, and sometimes the Roman month, as in August, *der Augstmonath*.

“Which, because of its wandering course.” Lunar years, which consist of twelve lunar months, are shorter than solar years by twenty-two and a half hours. Hence among the Greeks the beginnings of months do not always correspond to ours, although their year ends together with the solar year, just as ours does through the intercalation of the epacts.

It should certainly be noted that Bede refutes the crude error concerning the lunar month, lest anyone suppose that it is the period in which the moon traverses the Zodiac—a course completed in twenty-seven days and seven hours. Rather, it is the time between two lunar conjunctions, which is longer than a complete Zodiac. For while the moon traverses the entire Zodiac, the sun meanwhile advances through almost one-twelfth of the Zodiac. Before the moon reaches that point, two days and four hours have elapsed. Added to twenty-seven days and eight hours, these make twenty-nine and a half days, which is the length of the lunar month.

It seemed appropriate at this point to describe the months of the Latins, and to set them alongside, in corresponding order, those of the Greeks, Hebrews, and other nations, whose months must be learned from reliable authorities.

First, it should be noted that no months are fixed except those of the Romans and Egyptians. That is, the first day of each month—for example, January—always comes on the twentieth day after the winter solstice, and the first of March on the tenth day before the spring equinox. The months of the other peoples, namely the Greeks, Hebrews, and Arabs, do not follow the same pattern.

Furthermore, the Romans begin the year at the winter solstice; hence January is the first of the Roman months. The Hebrews begin at the spring equinox. Their first month, therefore, is the one whose middle—the fourteenth lunar day—is nearest after the equinox. Others make that fourteenth lunar day which shines nearest after the summer solstice the first month; others begin with the one occurring in autumn, as do the Egyptians.

You will easily discern all this from the table appended below, which we have carefully compiled from reliable authorities. Entries placed opposite one another occur at the same time.

It should nevertheless be observed that the reckoning of the Greek months is not very consistent among writers. Anthesterion corresponds to November in Gaza, to April in Macrobius, and is assigned by others to March. The same variation occurs with Gamelion and certain other months.

The months of the Alexandrians have the same order and number of days as the Egyptian months. Each consists of thirty days, except the last, which has thirty-five, and every fourth year thirty-six. The first is Thoth, whose first day falls on the fourth day before the Kalends of September.

## [Col. 0341A]

Months are called from the measure by which each of them is measured. But better, from the moon, which in Greek is called *μήνη* (*mēnē*); for among them months are also called *μηνές* (*mēnes*). Among the Hebrews as well, according to Jerome, the moon—which they call *yare*—gave its name to the months. Hence Jesus son of Sirach, who certainly wrote in Hebrew, says, speaking of the moon: “The month is according to its name.”

For the ancients customarily reckoned their months not from the course of the sun but from that of the moon. Therefore, whenever Sacred Scripture—whether in the Law or before the Law—indicates on what day of the month something happened or was said, nothing other than the moon’s age is signified. The Hebrews, to whom the utterances of God were entrusted, have never ceased observing months by that ancient custom of their fathers. [Col. 0341B]

They call the first month of the new year, which is consecrated to the ceremonies of Passover, Nisan. Because of the moon’s wandering course, it now falls in March, now in April, and now occupies several days of May. But it is more correctly assigned to April, because it always either begins in that month, ends in it, or is wholly contained within it. The rule mentioned above is observed: the moon that appears on the fifteenth day after the equinox makes the first month of the following year; the moon appearing before that makes the last month of the preceding year, and so in order.

Their second month, Iyar, corresponds to May; the third, Sivan, to June; the fourth, Tammuz, to July; the fifth, Ab, to August; the sixth, Elul, to September; the seventh, Tishri, to October. Because of the gathering of the crops and the very famous festivals celebrated in it, they call Tishri the new year. The eighth, Marcheshvan, corresponds to November [Note: [Col. 0341] C, November]; the ninth, Kislev, to December [Note: [Col. 0341] C, December]; the tenth, Tebeth, to January; the eleventh, Shebat, to February; and the twelfth, Adar, to March.

Because the lunar cycle consists of twenty-nine and a half days, they alternate months of thirty and twenty-nine days. At the end of the second or third year, they intercalate an extra month, which is ordinarily formed from the eleven epact days.

I am therefore moved by some perplexity as to how our predecessors reckon the day on which the Law was given—which is the third day of the third month—as the fiftieth day from the slaughter of the lamb. They assign ten and seven remaining days to the first month, because thirteen earlier days had elapsed before Passover; thirty days to the second; and three to the third. These together make fifty days.

Yet it is clear that two lunar months end not in sixty but in fifty-nine days. Therefore, if the paschal month is reckoned as thirty days and retains seventeen days of its course after Passover, the second month ought to end not in thirty but in twenty-nine days. Consequently, in the total of the period mentioned, no more than forty-nine days are found. [Col. 0342A]

Unless, perhaps, we should suppose that the rule of *synecdoche*—the most frequent rule in Sacred Scripture—has been applied, so that the whole is counted from a part. “Synecdochically” (*synecdōchikōs*), that is, according to the figure by which the whole is understood from a part.

However these matters may have been performed or calculated, it is nevertheless clear that the Hebrews were accustomed to observe their months according to the course of the moon.

The same must rightly be understood in Genesis, where Noah is said to have entered the ark with his companions on the seventeenth day of the second month and to have come out after the Flood on the twenty-seventh day of that same month. This describes a complete solar year, namely 365 days, because the moon which in the present year, for example, is seventeen on the Nones of May will in the following year occur on the twenty-seventh day, the day before the Nones of May.

It should certainly be noted that those who think that a month is, or was defined by the ancients as, the time in which the moon traverses the circle of the Zodiac are greatly mistaken. For, as more careful investigation of natural phenomena has taught, the moon completes the Zodiac in twenty-seven days and eight hours, but completes the course of its own cycle in twenty-nine days and twelve hours, without reckoning its leap.

It is therefore more correctly defined as follows: a lunar month is the circuit and renewal of lunar light, from new moon to new moon. A solar month is the sun’s passage through one-twelfth of the Zodiac, that is, the circle of the signs. This is completed in thirty days and ten and a half hours, being twenty-two and a half hours longer than a lunar month. Of this excess, eleven epact days and a quarter ordinarily accrue each year.

For twelve times twenty-two makes 264, and it is readily evident that these are the hours of eleven days, since eleven times twenty-four produces the same total. Moreover, twelve times a half makes six, which are the annual hours of a quarter-day. For, as stated, the moon completes its twelve months eleven days and a quarter earlier than the corresponding twelve solar months; in completing them, it traverses the circuit of the Zodiac thirteen times.

But in calculating both kinds of month, custom, authority, or at any rate the convenience of calculation has prevailed over nature. For not only do they arrange lunar months, as calculation requires, into alternations of thirty and twenty-nine days; many also intercalate the extra lunar month wherever they please, although according to nature it should have been intercalated at the end of the year.

And, what is more serious, calculators disagree so greatly among themselves that sometimes, on one and the same day, one declares that the moon should be reckoned as the fourteenth day, another as the fifteenth, and another as the sixteenth. Nor does each nation measure the solar months by anything like the same rule or order.

Finally, the Egyptians, who were the first to begin reckoning their months according to the sun’s course because the moon’s course was swifter and they wished to prevent its speed from producing computational error, took the beginning from autumn. They are said to enclose these months within thirty days each.

The first month, Thoth, begins on the fourth day before the Kalends of September; the second, Phaophi, on the fourth day before the Kalends of October; the third, Athyr, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November; the fourth, Choiak, on the fifth day before the Kalends of December; the fifth, Tybi, on the sixth day before the Kalends of January; the sixth, Mechir, on the seventh day before the Kalends of February; the seventh, Phamenoth, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March; the eighth, Pharmuthi, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April; the ninth, Pachon, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May; the tenth, Payni, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June; the eleventh, Epiphi, on the seventh day before the Kalends of July; and the twelfth, Mesori, begins on the eighth day before the Kalends of August. [Col. 0345B]

They end Mesori on the tenth day before the Kalends of September and call the remaining five days *epagomenae*—that is, intercalary or added days. In addition, every fourth year they attach the sixth day, which is formed from the quarter-days.

Hence in their years the first year begins on the third day before the Kalends of September, because of the leap day, while the other years begin on the fourth day before those same Kalends. Leap years themselves end on the fourth day before the Kalends; the others end on the fifth day before the aforementioned Kalends.

The discrepancy which we say arises in leap years from the time when they intercalate the quarter-day cannot enter into agreement with the course of our year in lunar reckoning or in the celebration of those festivals before the time of our intercalation, which occurs on the sixth day before the Kalends of March. The same festival, and the same lunar age—for example, the seventh—which among us falls on the second day of the week, is counted among them on the third day of the week [Note: [Col. 0345B] C, “is counted”], and so with the rest in this manner.

## Chapter 12. On the Months of the Romans

[Note: [Col. 0347B]]

## Bridferth’s Ramified Glosses

According to the authority of Romulus, the Romans arranged the year in ten months, comprising 304 days. He dedicated the first month to his father Mars; he named the second April from the opening of the crops; he dedicated the third to Maia, the mother of Mercury; and he consecrated the fourth to Juno. He named Quintilis and Sextilis—which are now called after the birth of Julius Caesar and the triumph of Augustus—and the remaining months after their numerical order.

He called their beginnings the Kalends because at that time the people were called to the Capitol—*kalata*, that is, “called”—and, after the word *kalo*, “I call,” had been spoken five or seven times, the number of days remaining until the Nones was announced.

The Nones were so called because on the ninth day before the Ides people gathered in the city to learn what had to be done in that month. The Ides divide the month in the middle. For *iduare* means “to divide” in the Etruscan language.

Adding two months, Numa named January from Janus and February from Februus, the god of purification, and arranged the year according to the course of the moon, with 354 days.

Julius Caesar, adding eleven days, established the arrangement preserved to this day.

But afterward, in honor of the dictator Julius Caesar, when Marcus Antonius, the consul, brought forward the law, the month was renamed. All Roman emperors were called Caesars after the first Gaius Caesar, who was called Caesar for two possible reasons: either because he emerged from his mother’s womb after her belly had been cut open, or because he was born with a head of hair—*caesaries*, that is, “hair.”

Dictators exercised authority for a five-year period. They held greater honor than consuls, who possessed annual powers. They were called dictators as though they were leaders and instructors; hence they were also called masters of the people, and hence the word “edicts” is derived.

A little later, Numa added one day in honor of the odd number and gave it to January, so that both in the year and in the individual months, except for February, an odd number would be preserved.

He withdrew one day from each of the six months which had thirty days. All six—April, June, August, September, November, and December—and in addition January, have twenty-nine days, because of the odd number. Four months—March, May, Quintilis, and October—had thirty-one days under Romulus. Thus the number was odd in all months except February.

Alternatively, the explanation is this: when he placed thirty-one days in four months and twenty-nine in seven, he gathered a total of 355 days. They overlooked one day, as we noted above, which they themselves had added to the Greek number in honor of the odd number. “They overlooked” means that the Romans forgot one day. Or “one day” is used for “one [additional] day.”

The Greeks, however, reckoned the year according to the lunar course and had only 354 days in their year. To these they added eleven epact days and a quarter, so that they could align themselves with the solar course. They established that in every eighth year ninety days should be intercalated, from which they made three months.

The Romans wished to imitate them and were able to do so. For when, according to Pompilius’s distribution, they placed thirty-one days in four months, twenty-nine in seven, and twenty-eight in one—February—they gathered 355 days in all. If they added eleven days in the Greek manner, they would be short—or rather, one day would remain in excess of the Greek correspondence.

Therefore they devised a way of reckoning the year according to the solar course, in the Egyptian manner, adding only ten days and a quarter to the aforementioned number, not eleven. The Greeks now also reckon the year according to the sun’s course in our manner.

But anyone who wishes to know what error arose from this and how a remedy was found for it will discover it in the discussion of Hori and Praetextatus mentioned above, from which we have also extracted this material.

This discussion has already been written above. It begins: “The Romans, under the authority of Romulus, are shown to have had a year of ten months.” As Macrobius demonstrates, that year began with the month of March and consisted of 304 days.

## John the New: Notes

“From which the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth.” These months derive their names in sequence from their number: September, October, November, and December. The element *-ber* belongs to the form and completion of the word, not to its meaning, as *-trius* in *quinquatrius* and *-ullium* in *meditullium*. Thus the fifth and sixth months were still called Quintilis and Sextilis in Cicero’s time. The syllable *-ber* is not conveniently added to them because of their different endings; for this reason the numerical names are inflected differently there.

“Second they name April, as though *aperilem*.” In this month the year opens, with Favonius blowing and dispersing winter’s harshness while the sun is in Taurus, the house of Venus. Learned men devised—or rather discovered—this explanation, lest I offend the astrologers, because in this month all things first emerge more abundantly from the earth: not only kinds of plants but also the swarms of worms and other creatures that had nearly died beneath the winter. Almost all animals, moreover, are then more strongly tempted by the desire to reproduce.

This force of nature—which Aristotle says is especially according to nature, that is, directed toward the preservation of nature—was called Venus by ancient natural philosophers, because, as Cicero says, it comes to all things. Hence some also called this month April as though *aph ril*; for *ἀφρός* (*aphros*) gave Venus her name among the Greeks.

The most learned of poets gathered all these matters together with remarkable brevity in a single verse:

> “The Bull, with gilded horns, opens the bright year.”

This contains both etymologies.

“Let it be opened for the horoscope-observers.” I confess that I do not know what Bede means here by *horoscopi*. For *ὡροσκόπος* (*hōroskopos*) and *horoscopium* signify the part of the circle of the signs which rises above the horizon at someone’s birth, and also an observer of celestial matters and times. If you wish to understand the word in that sense here, I do not see why April should open the year for such observers. Winter nights are just as suitable for this—and indeed more suitable—than spring or summer nights.

## [Col. 0347A]

The reason why the Romans have months of such differing lengths is, as we read in the discussion of Horus and Praetextatus, the following.

When Romulus, with a keen but rustic intelligence, was organizing the established order of his own rule, he took the beginning of the month from the day on which the new moon happened to be seen. Since it does not always appear on that day, but according to certain causes sometimes later and sometimes earlier, it happened that when it appeared later, more days were assigned to the preceding month, or when it appeared earlier, fewer. The first occurrence thus established a permanent numerical rule for each month, and it came about that some months received thirty days and others thirty-one.

He dedicated the first month to Mars, whose son he wished to be thought, because it is established that Juno bore Mars in Phrygia during this month. That this month was formerly the first of the year is proved above all by the fact that the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth months still preserve to this day the names anciently assigned to them according to their number.

He named the second month April, as though *aperilem*, because in it, once the clouds, frosts, and storms of winter have been removed, the sky, earth, and sea are opened to sailors, farmers, and astrologers; trees and herbs also begin to open into bud, and all living creatures into offspring.

He established May as the third month and June as the fourth, in honor respectively of the elders and the younger people, into whom he divided the people, so that one part might protect the state by arms and the other by counsel.

Others maintain that Maia, the mother of Mercury, gave her name to May. They prove this chiefly from the fact that in this month all merchants sacrificed jointly to Maia and Mercury.

June is named either from that division of the people, as we have said, or, as Cincius thought, was formerly called *Junius* among the Latins. This designation remained for a long time among the ancestors, but later, after certain letters had worn away, *Junius* became *Junius* in its shorter form. The temple of Juno Moneta was also dedicated on the Kalends of June.

The month of July retained the name Quintilis, which it had received from its number, even after two months had been placed before March. Later, however, when Marcus Antonius, son of Marcus, brought forward the law in honor of the dictator Julius Caesar, it was called July, because Julius Caesar was born in that month, on the third day before the Ides of Quintilis.

August was formerly called Sextilis, until honor was granted to Augustus by decree of the Senate, because on the first day of that month he had defeated Antony and Cleopatra and consolidated the power of the Roman people.

September, October, November, and December retain their original names, indicating by their names how many they are counted from the spring month, March; or perhaps because rains threaten during them.

This was Romulus’s annual arrangement. He established a year of ten months and 304 days. He arranged the months so that four of them—March, May, Quintilis, and October—each had thirty days, while the other six had thirty days as well, and so that the former had the fifth-day Nones and the latter the seventh-day Nones. In those having the seventh-day Nones, the Kalends returned from the Ides on the seventeenth day; in those having the fifth-day Nones, the beginning of the Kalends returned on the eighteenth day.

But because this number agreed neither with the course of the sun nor with the calculations of the moon, it sometimes happened that the cold of the year occurred in the summer months and, conversely, heat in the winter months. When this happened, they allowed as many days without any month’s name to pass as were necessary to bring the year to the point at which the condition of the heavens would be suitable for the month then beginning.

Numa then followed and added fifty days, extending the year to 354 days, the number in which he believed the course of the twelve moons was completed. To the fifty days he had added, he added another six taken from the six months that had thirty days—one from each—making fifty-six days. He divided these into two new months according to the same principle.

Of the two, he named the first January and wanted it to be the first month of the year, as the month of the two-headed god, looking backward toward the end of the completed year and forward toward the beginning of the coming year. Some think that January was named because it is the boundary and doorway of the year.

The second he dedicated to Februus, that is, Pluto, who was believed to preside over purifications. The city had to be purified in that month, and he decreed that obligations should be discharged to the spirits of the dead.

Christian religion has rightly changed this custom of purification. In the same month, on the feast of holy Mary, the entire people, together with priests and ministers, proceeds through the churches and suitable places of the city with hymns sung in harmonious voices. All carry in their hands the candles given by the bishop, burning; and as this good custom has grown, they have learned to do the same at the other festivals of that blessed and perpetual virgin mother—not as a purification for an earthly empire lasting five years, but in perpetual remembrance of the heavenly kingdom.

Then, according to the parable of the wise virgins, all the elect, coming to meet their bridegroom and king with the lamps of good works shining, will immediately enter with him into the marriage feast of the heavenly city. [Col. 0351D–0352A]

A little later, Numa added one day in honor of the odd number and gave it to January, so that both in the year and in each month, except February, an odd number would be preserved, as though both diminution and an even number belonged to the underworld.

When, therefore, following Pompilius’s distribution, the Romans reckoned their own year according to the lunar course, as did the Greeks, they necessarily instituted an intercalary month in the Greek manner.

The Greeks had observed that they had recklessly arranged the year at 354 days, since it was apparent from the sun’s course—which completes the Zodiac in 365 days and a quarter—that eleven days and a quarter were lacking from their year. They therefore devised intercalations according to a fixed system, intercalating ninety days every eighth year, which they reckoned as three months of thirty days each.

The Romans likewise decided to imitate this arrangement, but without success, since they overlooked one day, as we noted above, which they themselves had added to the Greek number in honor of the odd number. For that reason, the number and order could not correspond over an eight-year period. Anyone who wishes to know what error arose from this and how it was remedied will find the answer in the aforementioned discussion of Horus and Praetextatus, from which we have also taken this material.

At last Gaius Julius Caesar, imitating the Egyptians, established the year according to the solar number, as it is preserved today. He added ten days to the former reckoning, so that the year would consist of 365 days, in which the sun itself traverses the Zodiac.

To prevent the quarter-day from being lost, he decreed that every fourth year the priests responsible for the months and days should intercalate one day, in the month and at the place where the month had also been intercalated among the ancients: namely, before the final five days of February. He ordered that this should be called the leap day.

February was assigned to every intercalation because it was the last month of the year. This too they did in imitation of the Greeks, for the Greeks inserted their extra days into the final month of their year.

They differed from the Greeks in one respect. The Greeks intercalated after completing the final month; the Romans, without completing February, intercalated after its twenty-third day, when the Terminalia had already been celebrated. Then they added the remaining five days of February after the intercalation, presumably according to the ancient custom of their religion, so that March would follow February without fail.

## Chapter 13. On the Kalends, Nones, and Ides

[Note: [Col. 0352D]

### BRID. RAM. GLOSSES

In ancient times this responsibility was entrusted to the lesser pontiff. That is, it was extended, committed, or entrusted. “And the appearance”—namely, the star of that moon—or “appearance,” that is, sight and manifestation. “To the sacrificial king,” that is, to the greater pontiff, who was so called by the king—namely, by the older and greater pontiff—for the sake of flattery. “The same pontiff,” that is, the lesser one. “The Calabrian [place],” that is, the summoning place, which is nearest to Romulus’s hut: he announced how many days in number remained from the Kalends to the Nones—namely, whether five days or seven. “The Curia Calabra”: the name of the place. “Quintanas,” namely, the Nones. “And hence,” that is, from this circumstance. “To the curia itself and to the assembly,” namely, the Calabrian one, because *classis* is Greek, “summoning” in Latin. “Would be called,” that is, “would be summoned” (*kalaretur*). “Of festivals,” that is, solemn celebrations. “Those who would know,” that is, those who would inquire. “As though the beginning of a new observance,” that is, from a new observance; “from that day,” that is, from the Nones. “Would be reckoned,” namely, [uncertain: *com.*]. “Divides,” that is, separates. “Very much divided,” namely, from a man. *Idea* in Greek means “appearance” or “form” in Latin. “On that day,” that is, on the Ides. “When we read ‘Kalends’”: although the Hebrews do not have Kalends, the Romans nevertheless designate the beginnings of their months by their own term. “Of Numbers”: the books of Moses, the book called Numbers.

### JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA

It should be noted that when we read “Kalends” in Holy Scripture, Greece has no Kalends; among the Greeks the beginnings of the months are called *noumēnia* (νουμήνια). Hence, as a proverb, when we wish to signify something that will never happen, we say: “at the Greek Kalends.”

In ancient times, therefore, this responsibility was entrusted to the lesser pontiff, so that he might observe first the appearance of the new moon and announce it to the sacrificial king. Accordingly, after the king and the lesser pontiff had celebrated the sacrifice, that same pontiff, having summoned the people to the Capitol—near the Curia Calabra, which was closest to Romulus’s hut—announced how many days remained from the Kalends to the Nones. When five remained, he proclaimed them by saying the word *καλῶ* five times; when seven remained, he repeated it seven times. The word *καλῶ* is Greek, meaning “I call” or “I summon.” It was decided that the day which was first among those days that were summoned should be called the Kalends. Hence the curia itself, to which they were summoned, received the name Calabrian, and so did the assembly, because the entire people was summoned into it.

The lesser pontiff therefore announced by summons the number of days remaining until the Nones because, on the day of the Nones after the new moon, the country people were required to gather in the city to receive from the king of sacred rites the reasons for the festivals and to learn what had to be done during that month. Hence some think that the Nones were so called as though they were the beginning of a new observance, or because from that day nine days were always reckoned to the Ides.

It was decided, moreover, that the day which divides the month should be called the Ides. For *iduare* means “to divide” in the Etruscan language. Hence *vidua*, as though *valde idua*, “very much divided,” or *vidua*, “separated from a husband.” Some hold that the Ides were named by a Greek word derived from appearance, which among the Greeks is called *εἰδέα*, because on that day the moon displays its full appearance.

It should also be noted that when we read “Kalends” in Holy Scripture, we must understand nothing other than the rising of the new moon, according to the passage in Numbers: “On the Kalends—that is, at the beginnings of the months—you shall offer burnt offerings to the Lord.” For, as stated above, the Hebrews know no beginnings of months other than the *neomeniae*, that is, the new moons.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Months of the Greeks

### JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA

But also the Greeks and Egyptians. Theodore Gaza wrote about the months of the Greeks; consult him if you wish to learn more about them. Learn from the table below what system is used for noting the days both among the Greeks and among the Latins. There it is shown that, just as the Latins divide the days of the months into Kalends, Nones, and Ides, so the Greeks—according to Pollux, in the first book of the *Onomasticon* (*ὀνομαστικόν*)—divide them into thirty days and three groups of ten. The first is called *standing* (*ἱσταμένον*), the second follows the natural order, and the third is called *waning* (*λήγον* or *φθῖνον*). We have taken January and the month corresponding to it among the Greeks, Gamelion; for this opinion is more correct than that of those who say that the corresponding month is October. Aristotle states, in Book I of the *Meteorology* (*Μετεώρων*), that in Gamelion the sun is at the winter turn, which falls partly in December and partly in January.

The relation of the days, Kalends, Nones, and Ides is not the same in all months. The variation is expressed in these verses, which we used to learn as boys:

> July, April, and the seventh and ninth [months] have thirty days each.  
> May, October, July, and March have six days before the Nones.  
> The remaining February holds eight times twenty days, with one more.  
> Each of the other four has the Ides on the eighth [day].

### BRID. RAM. GLOSSES

The Greeks and Egyptians, of whom we spoke above, observe no distinction of Kalends, Nones, and Ides in their months—obviously because they have neither Kalends, Nones, nor Ides. “Without error,” that is, without mistake. “They proceed by order,” counting. For they say: “The first day of March, the second day of March,” and so forth.

The book of the holy father Anatolius, which he composed concerning Easter, also supports this. It says: “Therefore, in the first year…” That same book also affirms that the Greeks mark off their months by the same number and order of days as we do. The Egyptians begin March on the fifth day before the Kalends of March; we and the Greeks begin it on the Kalends.

“Supports”: from *stipulor*, “I inquire.” *Stipulari* means “to inquire.” Isidore says: “A stipulation is a promise; hence those who make promises are called stipulators.” The stipulation was named from *stipula*, “straw.” For in ancient times, whenever people promised something to one another, they broke a straw; then, joining the pieces again, they recognized their promises—or because, in accordance with a playful custom, they called it a binding oath.

> Therefore, in the first year there is the beginning of the first month, which is the beginning of the nineteen-year cycle. The beginning of the nineteen-year cycle falls on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, because when the moon is thirty days old on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, the first year of the nineteen-year cycle occurs, beginning with the first moon of the first month. In that year it occurs there, though on the following day, namely, the tenth day before the Kalends of April. Its twenty-sixth day is not the eighth day before the Kalends of April but the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. The twenty-sixth day of that month—that is, the day which is the beginning of the nineteen-year cycle—is accordingly the same as the twenty-second day among the Greeks and the twenty-sixth day among the Latins. It is therefore better to say “the eleventh day before the Kalends of April,” because the eighth day before the Kalends is not found on the twenty-sixth day, but the eleventh day before the Kalends is. The twenty-sixth day of Phamenoth, the twenty-second of Distrus, and the eleventh day before the Kalends of April are one and the same day, and there is always the beginning of the nineteen-year cycle. He said all these things in order to show that Greeks and Romans mark their year and their months according to one order, but not the Egyptians, who have that beginning on the twenty-sixth day. In describing their calendar—namely, that of the Egyptians—we marked it accordingly. For Phamenoth begins among them on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, as we said above, and therefore its twenty-sixth day falls on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. We marked this in the foregoing chapter when describing their calendar. The difference between history and calendars is that history concerns the times we have seen, whereas calendars concern those times and years which our age has not seen.

The Greeks and Egyptians, of whom we spoke above, observe no distinction of Kalends, Nones, and Ides in their months. Instead, from the beginning of each month until its end, they arrive at the reckoning by counting the sequence of the days as it simply and continually increases. The Greeks—for we discussed the Egyptian year and months above—after altering and correcting all the complications of the aforementioned intercalations, arranged a fixed cycle in the twelve months of the revolving year. Most of them begin their year with the Kalends of December, and they mark off the months with the same number of days as the Romans. As we have already said, they pay no attention to the Roman Kalends, Nones, or Ides, but count each month from the first day to the last by a gradually increasing number.

Among them, December itself is called *Elaphebolion* (ἐλαφηβολιών), January *Nychion* (νυχίων), February *Thargelion* (θαργηλίων), March *Dystros* (δίστρος), April *Xanthikos* (ξαντικός), May *Artemisios* (ἀρτεμίσιος), June *Daisios* (διέσιος), July *Panemos* (πάνεμος), August *Loos* (λῶος), September *Gorpiaios* (γορδιαῖος), October *Hyperberetaios* (ὑπερβερεταῖος), and November *Dios* (διός).

That they observe the year and the months in this order is shown both by the calendar of theirs recently sent to us from Rome and by the canons called those of the Apostles, which taught the same thing in older writings. There it is stated that the twelfth day of the month Hyperberetaios is the fourth day before the Ides of October. From this it is clearly inferred that the two months begin alike, since each is shown to have the same twelfth day.

The book of the holy father Anatolius, which he composed concerning Easter, also supports this. It says:

> “Therefore, in the first year there is the beginning of the first month, which is the beginning of the nineteen-year cycle: according to the Egyptians, on the twenty-sixth day of the month Phamenoth; according to the Macedonians, on the twenty-second day of the month Distrus; but according to the Romans, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April.”

By affirming here that the twenty-second day of the month Distrus is likewise the twenty-second of March, he clearly indicates that both months begin at the same time. And lest anyone say that Anatolius wrote in this passage not “the eleventh day before the Kalends” but “the eighth day before the Kalends of April,” the Egyptian month Phamenoth proves that this is not so. Its twenty-sixth day is not the eighth day before the Kalends but the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. Those who read either “the eighth day before the Kalends of April” or “the eleventh day before the Kalends of April” in Anatolius nevertheless agree in marking the twenty-sixth day of the Egyptian month in the same passage; and without any doubt it is shown to fall on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, as we marked above when describing their calendar.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Months of the English

### BRID. RAM. GLOSSES

The ancient peoples of the English. “English” (*Angli*) is the name of the region in which the English peoples first began to exist. Read the *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*; there, in Book I, chapter 15, you will find in order how the aforesaid people first came to Britain in the year 449 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

### JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA

“The ancient peoples of the English.” The Britons from the neighboring shores—that is, from the Gallic and German shores—occupied the island which had previously been called Albion by the Romans, from its white mountains, which first come into view for those sailing toward it. Hence, from both languages, a tongue arose very similar to the German or Batavian language; it is clear that this people had previously been there. From Bede it is sufficiently evident that they still use nearly this language.

The ancient peoples of the English—for it does not seem fitting to me to describe the calendrical observance of other nations while keeping silent about my own—reckoned their months according to the course of the moon. Hence, following the custom of the Hebrews and Greeks, they also take their names from the moon. Among them, the moon is called *mona*, and the month *monath*.

Their first month, which the Latins call January, is called *Giuli*. Then come February, *Sol-monath*; March, *Rhed-monath*; April, *Eostur-monath*; May, *Thrimylchi*; June, *Lida*; July, likewise *Lida*; August, *Vueod-monath*; September, *Haleg-monath*; October, *Vuinter-fylleth*; November, *Blod-monath*; and December, *Giuli*, called by the same name as January.

They began the year on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, where we now celebrate the Lord’s Nativity. They called the very night that is now sacred to us by the pagan name *Modranicht*, that is, “the night of mothers,” because, as we suspect, they kept vigil during it for the sake of certain ceremonies.

Whenever the year was ordinary, they assigned three lunar months to each season of the year. When an embolismic year occurred—that is, a year of thirteen lunar months—they added the extra month to summer, so that at that time three months in succession were called *Lida*. For this reason that year was called *Thri-lidi*, having four summer months and, as always, three in each of the other seasons.

They divided the entire year principally into two seasons, winter and summer, assigning to summer the six months in which the days are longer than the nights, and to winter the remaining six. Hence they called the month in which the winter season began *Vuinterfylleth*, a compound name formed from “winter” and “full moon,” because winter took its beginning from the full moon of that month.

Nor is it out of place to interpret what the names of their other months signify. The months *Giuli* receive their names from the sun’s turning toward the increase of daylight, since one of them precedes and the other follows that turning. *Sol-monath* may be called “the month of cakes,” because during it they offered cakes to their gods. *Rhed-monath* is named from their goddess Rheda, to whom they sacrificed during it. *Eostur-monath*, now understood as the paschal month, once took its name from their goddess Eostre, for whom they celebrated festivals in that month. From her name they now name the paschal season, calling the joys of the new solemnity by the customary term of the ancient observance.

*Tri-milchi* was so called because during it the cattle were milked three times each day. Such was formerly the fertility of Britain—or of Germany, from which the nation of the English entered Britain. *Lida* means “gentle” or “navigable,” because in both months the calmness of the breezes is gentle and the seas are customarily navigated. *Vueod-monath* is “the month of tares,” because they abound especially at that season. *Haleg-monath* is “the month of sacred things.” *Vuinterfylleth* may be rendered by the newly compounded expression “winter-full-moon.” *Blod-monath* is “the month of sacrifices,” because during it they vowed to their gods the animals they intended to slaughter.

Thanks be to you, good Jesus, who, turning us away from these vanities, granted us to offer you sacrifices of praise.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Signs of the Twelve Months

### BRID. RAM. GLOSSES

Each month has its own signs, in which it receives the sun. April, for example, has the sign of Aries, and so forth. This is because each sign reaches its completion in the middle of its respective month and takes its beginning from the middle of the preceding month.

### On the days on which the Sun enters each sign

| 15th day before the Kalends of July | Cancer |
| 15th day before the Kalends of August | Leo |
| 15th day before the Kalends of September | Virgo |
| 15th day before the Kalends of October | Libra |
| 15th day before the Kalends of November | Scorpio |
| 15th day before the Kalends of December | Sagittarius |
| 15th day before the Kalends of January | Capricorn |
| 16th day before the Kalends of February | Aquarius |
| 14th day before the Kalends of March | Pisces |

You may accept these points of completion according to custom and authority. But according to nature, you must understand the beginnings of the signs in the following way, as well as how the leap day increases.

### On the Preparation for the Leap Year

In the first year of the preparation for the leap year, at the first hour of the night preceding the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, the sun enters Aries. It leaves Aries at the second point of the eleventh hour of the night preceding the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

It enters Taurus at the third point of the eleventh hour of the night preceding the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, and leaves Taurus at the ninth full hour of the day, which is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June.

It enters Gemini at the tenth hour as the day begins, which is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June, and leaves Gemini at the second point of the eighth hour of the night preceding the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July.

It enters Cancer at the third point of the eighth hour of the night preceding the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, and leaves Cancer at the sixth full hour of the day, which is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August.

It enters Leo as the seventh hour of the day begins, which is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, and leaves Leo at the second point of the fifth hour of the night preceding the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September.

It enters Virgo at the third point of the fifth hour of the night preceding the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September, and leaves Virgo at the third full hour of the day, which is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October.

It enters Libra as the fourth hour of the day begins, which is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, and leaves Libra at the second point of the second hour preceding the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November.

It enters Scorpio at the third point of the second hour of the night preceding the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, and leaves Scorpio at the twelfth full hour of the night preceding the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December.

It enters Sagittarius as the first hour of the day begins, which is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, and leaves Sagittarius at the second point of the eleventh hour of the day, which is the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January.

It enters Capricorn at the third point of the eleventh hour of the day, which is the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, and leaves Capricorn at the ninth full hour of the night preceding the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February.

It enters Aquarius as the tenth hour of the night begins, preceding the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, and leaves Aquarius at the second point of the eighth hour of the day, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March.

It enters Pisces at the third point of the eighth hour of the day, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, and leaves Pisces at the sixth full hour of the night preceding the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April.

### On the Second Year of the Preparation for the Leap Year

In the second year of the preparation for the leap year, the sun enters Aries as the seventh hour of the night begins, preceding the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, and leaves Aries at the second point of the fifth hour of the day, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

It enters Taurus at the third point of the fifth hour, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, and leaves Taurus at the third full hour of the night preceding the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June.

It enters Gemini as the fourth hour of the aforementioned night begins, and leaves Gemini at the second point of the second hour of the day, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July.

It enters Cancer at the third point of the second hour of the day, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, and leaves Cancer at the twelfth full hour of the day, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August.

It enters Leo as the first hour of the night begins, preceding the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, and leaves Leo at the second point of the eleventh hour of the night preceding the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September.

It enters Virgo at the third point of the eleventh hour of the night preceding the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, and leaves Virgo at the ninth full hour of the day, which is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October.

It enters Libra as the tenth hour of the day begins, which is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, and leaves Libra at the second point of the eighth hour of the night preceding the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November.

It enters Scorpio at the third point of the aforementioned eighth hour of the night, and leaves Scorpio at the completion of the sixth hour of the day, which is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December.

It enters Sagittarius as the seventh hour of the day begins, which is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, and leaves Sagittarius at the second point of the fifth hour of the night preceding the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January.

It enters Capricorn at the third point of the aforementioned fifth hour of the night, and leaves Capricorn at the third full hour of the day, which is the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February.

It enters Aquarius as the fourth hour of the day begins, which is the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, and leaves Aquarius at the second point of the second hour of the night preceding the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February.

It enters Pisces at the third point of the aforementioned second hour of the night, and leaves Pisces at the twelfth full hour of the night preceding the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April.

### On the Third Year of the Preparation for the Leap Year

In the third year of the preparation for the leap year, at the beginning of the first hour of the day, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, the sun enters Aries, and leaves Aries at the second point of the eleventh hour of the day, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

It enters Taurus at the third point of the eleventh hour of the day, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, and leaves Taurus at the ninth full hour preceding the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June.

It enters Gemini as the tenth hour of the aforementioned night begins, and leaves Gemini at the second point of the eighth hour of the day, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July.

It enters Cancer at the third point of the eighth hour, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, and leaves Cancer at the sixth hour of the night preceding the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August.

It enters Leo as the seventh hour of the aforementioned night begins, and leaves Leo at the second point of the fifth hour of the day, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September.

It enters Virgo at the third point of the fifth hour of the day, which is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September, and leaves Virgo at the third full hour of the night preceding the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October.

It enters Libra as the fourth hour of the aforementioned night begins, and leaves Libra at the second point of the second hour of the day, which is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November.

It enters Scorpio at the third point of the second hour of the day, which is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, and leaves Scorpio at the twelfth full hour of the day, which is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December.

It enters Sagittarius as the first hour of the night begins, preceding the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December, and leaves Sagittarius at the second point of the aforementioned eleventh hour of the night, preceding the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January.

It enters Capricorn at the third point of the aforementioned eleventh hour of the night, and leaves Capricorn at the ninth full hour of the day, which is the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February.

It enters Aquarius as the tenth hour of the day begins, which is the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, and leaves Aquarius at the second point of the eighth hour of the night preceding the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March.

It enters Pisces at the third point of the aforementioned eighth hour of the night, and leaves Pisces at the sixth full hour of the day, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April.

### On the Fourth Year of the Preparation for the Leap Year

In the fourth year of the preparation for the leap year, the sun enters Aries as the seventh hour of the day begins, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, and leaves Aries at the second point of the fifth hour of the night preceding the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May.

It enters Taurus at the third point of the aforementioned fifth hour of the night, and leaves Taurus at the third full hour of the day, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June.

It enters Gemini as the fourth hour of the day begins, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, and leaves Gemini at the second point of the second hour of the night preceding the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July.

It enters Cancer at the third point of the aforementioned second hour of the night, and leaves Cancer at the twelfth full hour of the night preceding the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August.

It enters Leo at the full hour of the day, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, and leaves Leo at the second point of the eleventh hour of the day, which is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September.

It enters Virgo at the third point of the eleventh hour of the day, which is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September, and leaves Virgo at the ninth full hour of the night preceding the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October.

It enters Libra as the tenth hour of the night begins, preceding the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, and leaves Libra at the second point of the eighth hour of the day, which is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November.

It enters Scorpio at the third point of the eighth hour of the day, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, and leaves Scorpio at the sixth full hour of the night preceding the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December.

It enters Sagittarius as the seventh hour of the aforementioned night begins, and leaves Sagittarius at the second point of the fifth hour of the day, which is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January.

It enters Capricorn at the third point of the fifth hour of the day, which is the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, and leaves Capricorn at the third full hour of the night preceding the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February.

It enters Aquarius as the fourth hour of the aforementioned night begins, and leaves Aquarius at the second point of the second hour of the day, which is the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March.

It enters Pisces at the third point of the second hour of the day, which is the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March, and leaves Pisces at the twelfth full hour of the day, which is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April.

And so, in the first year after the leap day, the sun leaves Pisces at the sixth hour of the night at which it had entered Aries; in the second year, at the twelfth hour of that same night; in the third year, at the sixth hour of the following day; but in the fourth year, at the twelfth hour of that day, namely, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April. These twenty-four hours—that is, the night together with the day—are ordered to be intercalated on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, so that, once the leap year has again been completed, the sun may enter Aries at the first hour of the night preceding the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April.

The twelve signs received their names either from annual causes or from the fables of the pagans. For they assign Aries to the month of March because of Hammon-Jupiter; hence, in his image, they fashion the horns of a ram. Taurus belongs to April because of the same Jupiter, since he is said in fable to have been transformed into a bull. Castor and Pollux belong to May because of their outstanding valor. Cancer belongs to June, when the sun returns toward the lower regions, because the Crab is accustomed, when driven back, to direct its course in reverse. They assign the Lion, which Hercules killed, to July because of the force of the heat. Virgo belongs to August, because then the earth, exhausted by heat, produces nothing. Libra belongs to September because of the equality of day and night. They assign Scorpio to October and Sagittarius, deformed with horse’s legs, to November because of the thunderstorms of those months. Capricorn belongs to December because of Jupiter’s nurse, the she-goat, whose hind parts are painted like those of a fish, since the end of this month is rainy. They assign Aquarius to January and Pisces to February because these are rainy months.

Each sign is reckoned as having thirty parts, and each three parts as a decade, because the sun traverses it in thirty days and ten and a half hours, always beginning from the middle of the month—that is, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends.

The twelve signs, namely, those of the zodiac, received their names either from annual causes—that is, from historical events occurring in each year—or from the fables of the pagans, that is, their inventions, from which the signs are called what they are; or their names were imposed from annual occurrences, that is, from things that naturally happen each year; or from the fables which the pagans handed down in their writings; or even from both sources.

Aries: Abraham, because he offered a ram to the Lord in place of his son Isaac.  
Taurus: Jacob, who wrestled with the angel like a bull on Mount Bethel.  
Gemini: Adam and Eve, because they were made as one body in paradise.  
Cancer: the prophet Job, because he was afflicted with cancer.  
Leo: Daniel, who was in the lions’ den.  
Virgo: Mary, because she bore a son and remained a virgin.  
Libra: Judas Iscariot, who weighed out the price of the Savior on a balance.  
Scorpio: Pharaoh, because he was submerged in the sea through his desire.  
Sagittarius: David, who was a warrior against Goliath.  
Capricorn: Esau, who through his passion for hunting, and through a goat, lost the blessing.  
Aquarius: John the Baptist, because he baptized the Savior in the basin of the Jordan.  
Pisces: the prophet Jonah, because he remained in the whale’s belly for three days and three nights.

Each sign has thirty parts, and each three parts a decade. But when he says thirty, this is not exact but probable, for the sun remains in the individual signs for varying and different periods. In Gemini, for example, it travels for thirty-two days, whereas it passes through Sagittarius in twenty-nine days [Col. 0361D]. Likewise, in the other signs it completes its course variously. Hence it remains in no sign for precisely such a period, namely, thirty days and ten and a half hours.

It is probable for this reason: if someone divides the entire circuit or total of the year—that is, 365 days and six hours—into twelve equal parts according to the number of the signs, he will find one-twelfth to consist of thirty days, ten hours, and half an hour.

They are of such magnitude that they can neither rise nor set nor move from their position in less than the space of two hours. Each is assigned thirty parts because of the thirty days during which it is traversed by the sun. For no sign can move except over two hours. Therefore, since one sign moves in two hours, twelve signs move in twenty-four hours—that is, the entire firmament. From the beginning of the rising of each sign to its end, two hours elapse; there are twenty-four hours between day and night. [Col. 0362A] Therefore, two hours belong to each of the twelve signs, whether in rising or in setting.

The zodiac, or sign-bearing circle, is an oblique circle consisting of twelve signs, through which the wandering stars are carried. Nothing else on earth is inhabited except what lies beneath it; the rest is barren around the poles. The star Venus alone exceeds it by two parts; the moon also wanders through its entire breadth, but does not exceed it at all. From these, the star Mercury travels most widely, though of the twelve parts—for that is the full breadth—it traverses no more than eight. Nor does it traverse these equally: two parts through its middle, four above it, and two below. The sun moves through the middle, between two parts, unevenly in the winding course of the dragons. The star Mars occupies the four middle parts; Jupiter the middle part and two above it; Saturn two, like the sun.

[Col. 0362B] “Zodiac” in Greek, “sign-bearer” in Latin. *Zōdia* are called animals because they possess a living soul, which in Greek is called ζωὴ (*zōē*); or the zodiac is so called from the signs, because signs of animals appear to be in it, and these are called *zōdia*.

According to Macrobius, it is called an oblique circle, that is, a winding one. Its breadth consists of twelve parts, through which the stars travel in different ways. Through it—that is, through the zodiac—through whose parts the wandering stars are carried; they travel in many different ways, for some pass through three parts, others through four, others through five, others through eight, and some through twelve.

Nor is any other space inhabited on earth—that is, the place where we live. Human habitation exists only beneath the zodiac, because nothing in the world is inhabited except what lies beneath it.

Macrobius records the following: The moon almost never rises twice consecutively in the same sign, except in Gemini; yet this never occurs there, because, owing to the height of the sign, the sun spends more than thirty-two days in it. It happens very rarely in the other signs, if it proceeds from the sun near the first part of a sign. This may to some extent be understood according to nature, but it must by no means be accepted according to the correct and customary method of calculation.

Much could be said on this subject, but for my part I shall say only this about the sign-bearing circle and the twelve signs of the planets, that is, of the sun and moon, and so forth. *Meatus* means a passage, namely, against the motion of the world. Let us say for now only that the sun traverses the zodiac in 365 days and six hours, that is, a quarter-day, while the moon does so in twenty-seven days and eight hours. They traverse, that is, go around, the circumference of the zodiac.

The sun passes through each sign in thirty days and ten and a half hours—that is, half an hour—namely, it traverses it. Take thirty days twelve times, and there are 360 days; take ten hours twelve times, and there are 120 hours. Twelve half-hours therefore make six hours: this is the quarter-day. Thus, in the sun’s circuit through the zodiac, there are altogether 365 days and six hours.

The moon takes two days, that is, two days, and six hours, together with a *bisse* (two-thirds of an hour). Take two days twelve times, and there are twenty-four days. Take six hours twelve times, and there are seventy-two hours, that is, three days. Take the *bisse* twelve times, and there are eight hours. Thus, in the moon’s circuit through the zodiac, there are altogether twenty-seven days and eight hours.

The eight hours formed from twelve *bisses* are obtained as follows. Take four *bisses* away from twelve, and make from them eight thirds; give each of the eight remaining *bisses* one third, and there will be eight complete hours. For two thirds make one *bisse*. A *bisse* is two parts of one hour. If you divide something into three parts, the third part is called a *triens*, while two parts are called a *bisse*. The third part itself—that is, the part that remains—is called a *triens*.

Such is the extent of the heavenly space. For the moon traverses a greater distance in thirty days than the sun does in 365 days. As much as 360, and so forth. And in one-third of a day, that is, eight hours, it traverses as much as the sun does in 365 days—that is, twelve months—and in one-quarter of a day, that is, six hours, which is a quarter-day. And this is demonstrated by manifest truth.

As much space as the moon traverses in twenty-nine days and twelve hours, it traverses in thirteen of its own months. The course which the moon makes in its circuit, that is, in twenty-seven days and eight hours, the sun makes in its twelve months. The course which the moon makes in its own month, that is, in twenty-nine days and twelve hours, the sun makes in thirteen months.

For in two days and four hours the lunar month is longer than its circuit, during which it traverses twenty-eight parts and a sixth of a part in the sign-bearing circle. For the moon traverses thirteen parts in the zodiac each day. Therefore, in those two days it goes around twenty-six parts, and in the four hours—which are one-sixth of a day—it traverses two parts and a sixth of a part. Altogether this makes twenty-eight parts and a sixth of a part.

Hence the thirteenth month is called a month synecdochically (*synecdochicōs*). For it contains only twenty-eight parts and a sixth of a part. One day and ten hours are lacking from the thirty days of the sun, that is, five parts of a day.

[Col. 0363]

[Col. 0363B] It should indeed be noted that never can more than six of the twelve signs be seen at once, so that when one of them rises another sets. Thus, nine are seen throughout the whole night in succession, while the remaining three are not visible: the one in which the sun is, and the one that follows or precedes the sun.

Macrobius: The Milky Circle surrounds and encloses the zodiac in such a way, by the meeting of its oblique curvature, that it intersects the circle in which the two tropic signs, Capricorn and Cancer, are carried. Physicists called these the gates of the sun, because at each of them, when the solstice is encountered, the sun’s advance is restrained and it turns back toward the path of the zone, whose boundaries it never leaves.

Again, Macrobius, in the first part of his book: To say that the sun, the moon, and the five stars called wandering because of their deviation, besides the daily rotation of the heavens that carries them from rising to setting, themselves move eastward from westward, was judged not only by the unlearned but also by many initiated into learning to be contrary to faith and like a monstrosity. But to those who examine the matter more closely, it will become clear that this is true in such a way that it can be grasped not only by the mind [Col. 0363C] but also demonstrated by the eyes themselves.

Yet, since our discussion is with one who stubbornly denies this, come: pretend that all this is clear to you, and let us simultaneously divide into sections whatever contentiousness invents in disparagement of faith, and whatever truth itself suggests. Shall we say that these wandering stars, together with the two luminaries, are either fixed in the heavens or that the other stars do not indicate any motion of their own to our eyes, but are carried by the impulse of the world’s rotation? Or shall we say that they are moved by their own advance? Again, if they are moved, do they follow the path of the heavens from rising to setting, traveling both by the common motion and by their own, or do they move in the opposite direction, turning eastward from the western region? Apart from these possibilities, as I think, nothing can either exist or be imagined.

Let us now see what can be proved to be true by the force of the evidence. If they were fixed in place, they would never depart from the same station, but would always appear in the same places like the other stars. For look: among the fixed stars, the Pleiades never disperse from their own grouping, nor do they leave the nearby Hyades or abandon the region close to Orion; the constellation of the Bears is not broken apart. The Serpent, which glides among them, does not alter the embrace with which it once encircled them. But these stars are seen now in one region of the heavens, now in another, and often, when two or more have come together in one place, they are nevertheless afterward separated both from the place in which they were seen together and from one another. From this it is clear, with the eyes themselves confirming it, that they are not fixed in the heavens.

Therefore, they move, and no one can deny what sight confirms. It must therefore be asked whether they revolve by their own motion from east to west or in the opposite direction. But when we inquire into this as well, not only the clearest reasoning but sight itself will show us the answer.

Let us consider the order of the signs into which we see the zodiac divided or distinguished, and let us take our starting point from any one sign in that order. When Aries rises, Taurus emerges after it; Gemini follows Taurus, then Cancer, and the rest in order. If, therefore, these signs proceeded westward from the east, they would not revolve from Aries to Taurus, which is placed behind it, nor from Taurus to Gemini, the later sign; rather, they would proceed from Gemini to Taurus and from Taurus to Aries, in a straight advance consonant with the rotation of the world.

But since they revolve from the first sign to the second, from the second to the third, and thence to the others that are later, while the signs fixed in the heavens are carried along, there is no doubt that these stars move not with the heavens but against the heavens.

To make this fully clear, [Col. 0364C] let us establish the point from the course of the moon, which is more conspicuous both for its brightness and for its speed. After the moon departs from the sun and occupies the edge of the heavens, setting after it, it sets later on the third day than on the second, and so each day recedes farther from the west that on the seventh day it is seen near sunset in the middle of the sky.

After another seven days, when the sun is sinking, the moon rises; thus, at the middle of the month, by receding from west to east, it traverses half the sky, that is, one hemisphere. Again, after another seven days, it occupies the summit of the hidden hemisphere near sunset; the indication of this is that it rises in the middle of the night. Finally, after the same number of days has passed, it again catches up with the sun, and the rising of both appears close together for as long as it follows the sun. Then it moves again and again, gradually receding and always returning eastward, leaving the west behind.

The sun itself likewise moves from west to east; and although it completes its recession more slowly than the moon—since it traverses one sign in as much time as the moon traverses the entire zodiac—it nevertheless provides clear evidence of its motion, visible to the eyes.

Let us suppose that it is in Aries. Since this is an equinoctial sign, it makes the hours of sleep and of day equal. When it sets in this sign, we see Libra, that is, the claws of Scorpio, rise immediately, and Taurus appears near setting. For not long after the sun has sunk, we see the Pleiades and the Hyades, the brighter parts of Taurus. In the following month, the sun recedes into the later sign, that is, into Taurus; and so neither the Pleiades nor any other part of Taurus is visible during that month. For the sign that rises with the sun and sets with the sun is always hidden, so that even neighboring stars are concealed as the sun approaches.

Again, Macrobius: It must be asked, since there is one zodiac and it consists of stars fixed in the heavens, how the stars of the lower spheres are said to move through the signs of the zodiac. It is not difficult to find the explanation, which stands at the very threshold of the question.

It is true that neither the sun nor the moon, nor any of the wandering stars, is so situated in the zodiac as to mingle with its stars; rather, each is said to be in that sign which it has above its head while traveling through the corresponding region of its own circle, which lies beneath it. For reason has divided the circles of the individual spheres into twelve equal parts, just as it divided the zodiac; and whatever star has come into that part of its circle which lies beneath the part of the zodiac assigned to Aries is acknowledged to have come into Aries. The same observation is maintained for the stars as they migrate through the individual parts.

And because the way through the eyes is easier for understanding, let sight assign what speech has described. Let the zodiac be a circle marked A, and let seven other spheres be placed within it; and let the zodiac, beginning from A and proceeding in order through fixed marks to which the following letters are assigned, be divided into twelve parts. Let the space enclosed between A and B be assigned to Aries, that between B and C to Taurus, that between C and D to Gemini, the next to Cancer, and the remaining spaces to the remaining signs in order.

Once this has been established, let individual lines be drawn downward from each of the zodiac’s marks and letters through all the circles, down to the last. Without doubt, the passage of the lines will divide each sphere into twelve parts. Therefore, in whatever circle the sun, the moon, or any of the wandering stars may be traveling, when it reaches the space enclosed between the lines descending from A and B, it will be said to be in Aries, because it will have above its head the space assigned to Aries in the zodiac, as we have described. Similarly, in whatever part it has moved, it will be said to be in the sign beneath which it is.

This same diagram will also teach us, by the same concise method, why some stars traverse the same zodiac and the same signs over a longer period, and others over a shorter one. Whenever several spheres are placed within one another, just as the first is the largest and the last the smallest, so among the intermediate spheres the one nearer the upper sphere is larger than those below it, while the one nearer the last is shorter than those above it. Thus, among these seven spheres, the order of their positions assigns to each its degree of speed.

Therefore, the stars that travel through longer spaces complete their circuit in a longer time; those that travel through narrower spaces do so in a shorter time. For it is established that none of them proceeds more quickly or more slowly than the others; rather, since they all have the same manner of movement, the sole difference in their times is produced by the difference in the lengths of their spaces. To pass over the intermediate spheres for now, so that the same things may not often be repeated: the fact that Saturn circles and traverses the same signs in thirty years, and the moon in twenty-eight days, is due solely to the difference in the sizes of their circles, one of which is the largest and the other the smallest. Thus, in the case of the others as well, each one’s time of movement is extended or contracted according to the size of its space.

At this point the careful investigator of things will find something to ask. For, looking at the marks of the zodiac displayed by the diagram summoned in defense of the faith, he will say: Who, then, discovered or made the twelve divisions of the heavenly circle, especially since the beginnings of the individual divisions are not presented to the eyes?

Let history itself answer this necessary question, [Col. 0367A] relating how this difficult division was attempted and accomplished by the ancients. For the ancient Egyptians, whom we know to have been the first of all people to dare to investigate and measure the heavens, after they had discovered—through the benefit of their perpetually clear skies, as they continually gazed at the heavens with unobstructed sight—that, among all the stars and constellations fixed in the heavens, only five stars, together with the sun and moon, wandered; and that even these did not travel randomly through every part of the heavens without a definite law of their wandering—for they never deviated toward the northern summit, nor did they plunge to the depths of the southern pole, but all their movements remained within the boundary of one oblique circle; and that they did not all proceed and return together, but some reached the same place at different times; that some of them advanced, others moved backward, and they sometimes appeared to stand still—

after they had observed, I say, that these things occurred among them, they decided to establish definite parts within the circle itself and to mark them by divisions, so that there might be fixed names for the places in which the stars remained, from which they had departed, or to which they were again going to return; and so that the stars might announce these things to one another and transmit them to later generations to be known.

They therefore prepared two bronze vessels, one of which had a perforated bottom in the manner of a water-clock. They placed the intact vessel, empty, beneath the one full of water, setting the latter above it but having first closed its outlet. They then observed one of the fixed stars, the brightest and most conspicuous, rising. As soon as it began to emerge, they immediately removed the closure and allowed the water of the upper vessel to flow into the vessel beneath it.

The water flowed until the end of that night and of the following day, and into the second night, for as long as the same star returned again to its rising. When it had scarcely begun to appear, they immediately removed the vessel into which the water had been flowing. Since the observed star’s going and returning indicated the complete revolution of the heavens, they established the measure of the heavens according to the quantity of water received from it.

They then divided this quantity into twelve equal parts with reliable measurement and procured two other vessels of the same capacity, so that each would hold only one of those twelve parts.
