The entire quantity of water was poured back into its original vessel after its opening had first been closed, and of the two smaller vessels they placed one beneath it while setting the other beside it, ready for use.

Having prepared these things, on another night they watched for a star that was about to rise in that part of the heavens through which, after prolonged observation, they had learned that the sun, the moon, and the five wandering stars moved, and which they later called the zodiac. To this star they subsequently gave the name Aries.

At the beginning of its rising they immediately allowed the water above to flow into the vessel beneath. When that vessel was full, they quickly removed it after pouring out its contents and placed beneath it the other similar vessel. They carefully observed the signs and memorized and recorded the stars in that place which were rising when the first vessel was filled, understanding that at the time when one-twelfth of the entire quantity of water had flowed out, one-twelfth of the heavens had ascended.

From the place where, at the beginning of the star’s rising, the water began to flow into the first vessel, up to the place that was rising when the first vessel was filled, they declared there to be one-twelfth of the heavens, that is, one sign. When the second vessel had been filled and immediately removed, they placed beneath it the similar vessel that they had previously prepared after emptying it. They likewise marked the place that emerged when the second vessel was full, and from the end of the first sign to the place that rose at the end of the second quantity of water, they marked the second sign.

And so, changing the vessels in turn and marking, with each separate portion of the flowing water, the boundaries of the successive parts of the heavens that were rising, when the entire quantity of water had been completed through the twelve parts and they had reached the beginning of the first sign, they unquestionably possessed twelve divisions of the heavens, already divided and marked for themselves by definite observations and indications through so great an achievement.

This was accomplished not in one night but in two, because the whole heaven does not revolve in one night: its middle part passes through during the day, and the remaining half during the night. Yet the observation of two successive nights did not divide the whole heaven; rather, nocturnal measurement at different times marked both hemispheres in equal turns.

They preferred to call these twelve divisions “signs,” and assigned definite names to each for the sake of identification. And because the signs are called *zōdia* in Greek, they called the circle surrounding the signs themselves the zodiac, as though it were the sign-bearer.

Thus far Macrobius.

I have omitted the poets’ fables about the twelve signs because I thought there was no benefit to be found in them. For a reading that will harm the foolish more than it benefits the wise must be rejected. The poets named fables from *fari*, “to speak”; they are not things that happened, but merely inventions made through speech.

## Description of the Pole

There are two extreme vertices of the world, which they call the poles of the North and the South. One of them is always visible to us, the other never. In the one that we see, three signs are situated: namely, the two Bears and the Serpent, which moves around and between them like a river. The Great Bear is called *Helice*, and the Lesser Bear *Cynosura*; they face in opposite directions. Their backs are turned away from one another, with their feet turned this way and that.

The Serpent therefore encircles Helice with its tail and Cynosura with the rest of its winding course, yet in such a way that, gliding between them, it separates them. Its head appears extended toward the right foot of the figure who stands on his knees. That figure, whom they call Hercules, presses the serpent’s head with his right foot; his head is turned toward the South, and with his shoulders he touches the boundaries of the Crown. The Crown itself, situated behind Hercules, approaches the head of the serpent held by the Serpent-Bearer.

The Serpent-Bearer, whom the Greeks call *Ophiuchus*, is placed beneath Hercules toward the South. With his feet turned, he tramples Scorpio; he is girded with a serpent, which he holds in both hands. The serpent, stretched out to a great length, extends as far as the Crown.

Beside the winding coils of this serpent, with no other sign intervening, Boötes appears to be driven behind the Great Bear, with his feet turned toward Virgo; for Virgo is placed beneath the feet of Boötes.

Opposite the throat and forefeet of the Great Bear, at the intersection of the zodiacal and Milky circles, Gemini is located. On its left side it has the Charioteer with two Kids, who, facing toward the head of Helice, appears with his right foot to touch the left horn of Taurus.

Beside Gemini, where the zodiac rises most high, opposite the belly of the Great Bear, Cancer is situated. It has two Asses on its back, with a whitish cloud between them called the Manger.

Opposite the hind feet of the same Bear, between Cancer and Virgo, Leo is said to be placed, with Boötes beside it. Beneath the feet of the Charioteer lies Taurus, with one foot extended toward Orion, who is placed beneath it.

Cepheus stands between the Lyre and Cassiopeia, with arms outstretched and feet extended toward the back of the Lesser Bear. Cassiopeia stands opposite the great coil of the northern Serpent, between the Charioteer, Perseus, Andromeda, and Cepheus.

In the Milky Circle, between Pisces, Cassiopeia, and Aries, Andromeda is placed, together with the Triangle which she is said to have behind her. Her head is turned toward the belly of the Horse, which is placed above her.

Aries is situated at the intersection of the zodiacal and equinoctial circles, beneath the Triangle, with the Whale beneath it toward the South. Near this sign are two fish, one raised toward the North and the other sloping toward the South, joined together by a kind of bond at their tails. The northern fish extends toward Andromeda, the southern toward Aquarius.

Beside the feet of Andromeda, on the side of Cassiopeia, Perseus appears, holding the Gorgon’s head in his left hand. Beneath his left thigh, near the tail of Taurus, the Pleiades are seen placed.

The Lyre is placed between Hercules’ left leg and the Swan. The Swan, however, with wings outspread and resembling a bird in flight, extends its right wing toward the right hand of Cepheus and its left toward the feet of the Horse.

Between Pisces and the Horse, and the tail of Capricorn, Aquarius is placed, pouring water from an urn; the outflow runs as far as the Great Fish.

In the lowest part of the zodiac, near Sagittarius and the Eagle, Capricorn is situated at the intersection of the winter circle and the sign-bearing circle. Behind it is Sagittarius, placed at the intersection of the zodiacal and Milky circles beneath the Dolphin.

There is also a certain arrow lying alone beneath the Swan, near the Eagle.

[Col. 0369B] Above the head of Capricorn is the Dolphin, behind the tail of the serpent held by the Serpent-Bearer. Beneath the Serpent-Bearer they say that Scorpio is located, so that it is touched by the Serpent-Bearer’s feet. Beneath it, toward the South, is the beast Centaur, holding in his hand something as though carrying it to an altar.

This altar is called by some the shrine, and is placed toward the South opposite the tip of Scorpio’s tail.

The arms of Scorpio occupy the place called Libra, because in it the sun makes the autumnal equinox.

Hydra also lies in the equinoctial circle, stretched out to an immense length: its head lies beneath Cancer, its middle beneath Leo, and its tail beneath Virgo. It carries the Crow and the Urn on its back.

Under the breast of Taurus, Orion is seen, girded with a sword, with the Hare placed beneath his feet. Behind his tracks he has a dog, which they call Sirius and also the Little Dog, placed beneath the sign of Cancer; before it, beneath Gemini, you can recognize the Lesser Dog.

Behind the tail of Sirius, toward the South, the ship called Argo appears shining. Beneath Orion’s left foot, the river called Eridanus flows in a winding course as far as the Whale.

The Whale lies beneath Aries, extending in a very long course from the Fish. Behind its tail, at a considerable distance, extended southward beneath Aquarius and Capricorn, the Great Fish is seen, the last of the visible signs, receiving the outflow of Aquarius’ urn, which runs as far as it.

## Likewise concerning the same subject

Toward the northern regions the Bears revolve, and the Serpent.

After them comes Arctophylax, and likewise the Crown and the Knee.

The Fallen One, the Lyre, the Bird, Cepheus, and Cassiopeia.

The Charioteer and Perseus, the Delta, and the constellation of Andromeda.

Pegasus and the Dolphin, the Arrow, the Eagle, and the Serpent-Bearer;

Then beneath is the sign-bearer; here twice six stars complete the number.

Here are Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo:

Libra, Scorpio, the Archer, and Capricorn as far as the Water-bearer,

who holds [the urn] toward Pisces; afterward they are in the southern regions.

[Col. 0369D] Orion, Procyon, the blazing Sirius, Argo,

Hydra, Chiron, and also the censer, the Fish, and the Great Fish.

Here the Sea-Monster follows, together with the waters of Eridanus.

These twelve twice over mark the regions of the heavens,

which the learned pipe of master Priscian fashioned.

## On the Mansions of the Planets

The order of the planets is not arranged according to the order of the weekdays:

Cynthia, Mercury, Venus and the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Thez [reading uncertain].

Pisces and Chiron belong to Jupiter; Nepa (Scorpio) and Hammon belong to Mars.

Taurus likewise, and the Claws, will belong to the region of Ericina.

Cancer will be the moon’s region, Leo the sun’s;

The mansions of Mercury are sometimes Gemini, sometimes Virgo;

Saturn’s seat is in the urn or in Capricorn.

## On the Rising and Setting of the Twelve Signs

As Aries rises, it sinks the claws into the depths.

The gilded horns of Taurus submerge Scorpio.

Then the Archer rises above the sea as Gemini rises:

When Cancer rises, Capricorn is submerged in the waters.

The bearer of the little urn fears the signs of Leo.

Virgo drives away Pisces, and victory returns to the vanquished.

[Col. 0370A] Likewise:

Libra, which is Hammon, sinks; Scorpio rises with Taurus.

But the Archer flees the Twins, and Capricorn the Crab:

Then Leo drives away the water-pourer, and Virgo drives away Pisces.

Likewise:

Libra, which is Hammon; Scorpio, the Bull; flee the Twins, Chiron:

You drive the Goat, Cancer; the urn, Leo; and Virgo, Pisces.

The moon traverses the zodiac thirteen times in its twelve months, moving through each sign in two days, six hours, and a *bisse*—that is, eight twelfths of an hour. If, therefore, you wish to know in which sign the moon is situated, take the moon whose position you wish to calculate—for example, multiply twelve by four: the result is forty-eight. Divide by nine: nine times five is forty-five, and three remain.

Thus, after five signs have been completed from the point at which the moon was born, it is undoubtedly always kindled in the same constellation in which the sun is. In the sixth sign the moon on its twelfth day is situated. If one remains, know that six hours of the following sign have been completed; if two, twelve hours; if three, eighteen; if four, a whole day; if eight, eight times six hours—that is, two additional days. Of these hours, however, remember always to subtract two for every three signs. For it is laborious to divide the hours minutely among the individual signs by twelfths. Hence, although in the present calculation three remain after the ninth divisions, the moon will complete the twelfth [part] of the sixth sign not in eighteen hours but in sixteen.

This, then, is the ready calculation when the moon is born in the first or middle part of any sign. But if, in the first sign, the moon has either lost or retained some other number of parts, remember likewise to subtract or add that number in the following signs, with nine hours in the moon being reckoned as five days in the sun.

The moon [Col. 0370C] traverses the zodiac, that is, the circle. In each of its months—that is, in twenty-nine days and twelve hours—the moon circles the twelve signs and almost one more. By this unusual method it is discovered that the moon circles the zodiac thirteen times, more accurately than by that other, customary method; this can be proved if you consider the thirtieth moon according to this calculation. For this calculation is more accurate, because its reasoning is completely clear. The other calculation counts one sign as thirty days; manifest reasoning shows that this is not so, since the moon’s age is completed in twenty-nine days and twelve hours. Nevertheless, we assign thirty days to the moon by that calculation for ease of computation.

Therefore this calculation is more precise and consequently more accurate. It is proved in this way: according to this calculation, you will find that the thirtieth moon has traversed thirteen signs; according to the other, however, no more than twelve.

It traverses the twelve signs thirteen times in its months. How thirteen times? After the moon has been kindled in the first part of a sign, it runs through the twelve signs in twenty-seven days and eight hours, until it comes to that first part of the sign in which it was kindled; and through that sign from which it began it runs again for two days and four hours—namely, moving through each sign in two days, six hours, and a *bisse*, that is, eight twelfths of an hour.

Multiply those two days by twelve, and you will find twenty-four days. Likewise multiply the six aforesaid hours by twelve, and the result is seventy-two hours. Divide by twenty-four: the result is three days. There still remain, in each sign, two-thirds of an hour. Twelve two-thirds make eight hours. Collect these together, and the result is twenty-seven days and eight hours, in which the moon completes the entire zodiac.

Nevertheless, two days and four hours of its course are still lacking before the circuit is complete. During those two days and four hours it runs again through the sign from which it began and in which it ends, before it begins its second course. In this way it surveys, as it were, thirteen signs in each of its courses. Thus it can be understood that, thirteen times in its year—that is, in 354 days—it completes the twelve signs.

There are forty-eight [parts], namely quadrants, since four quadrants make a day. Divide by nine. Five times nine is forty-five, and three of the forty-eight quadrants remain undivided after the forty-five. These make eighteen hours, since each of these quadrants contains six hours. If you carefully multiply six hours by each number—that is, by each quadrant—in this calculation, you will find that in each group of nine, that is, in nine quadrants, there are fifty-four hours, which amount to two days and six hours.

Therefore the moon traverses one sign in this many days and hours, together with two-thirds of an hour. Thus, after five signs have been completed—that is, while the moon has traversed five signs—three remain after the forty-five, according to the same series of nine; six hours are multiplied by each of them, as stated above.

“Of the following sign,” that is, of the sixth. “Know,” namely, you who calculate. “In the same constellation,” that is, sign.

### If one remains

That is, one quadrant or one point. There is a certain kind of points in which each point contains six hours, that is, one quarter of a day. Or it is called a quadrant because it contains a fourth part of a day. Unless, in the passage where it says “Divide by nine,” you calculate each quadrant as six hours, you will not be able to understand how the moon traverses five signs through the same, that is, ninefold, number, in groups of three signs.

It rightly says “in groups of three signs,” because the two-thirds remaining in the moon do not complete two hours except in three signs. For if you place eight twelfths three times, they make two hours, since each hour has twelve twelfths.

### “Remember to subtract”

For this reason he orders that two hours be taken away for every three signs: when he comprehends the signs by nine quadrants, he has not counted the two-thirds belonging to those signs, which make two hours in three signs. Although we have not counted the two-thirds, the moon itself has nevertheless completed its own two-thirds.

Therefore, according to our calculation, it has traversed that many signs. “Calculation,” that is, the determination of the sign in which the moon is situated, having moved away from the sun from the time when it was kindled. But if it was born in another place, namely in the second, third, or any other part of a sign—

### “How many in the first sign”

For example, if the moon was kindled in the third or fourth part of Aries and is three signs distant from the sun, from the fourth sign you will take three or four parts and complete the whole of Aries. Hence the saying: “As many parts as you remove, remember to add.”

But if it was kindled in the twentieth part, or in any other part after the middle of the sign, you will not count the sign in which it was kindled, but the sign after it. When you reach the sign in which the moon is, remove from that sign as many parts as the moon retained from the sign in which it was kindled, provided that it was kindled after the middle.

For this reason you will not count as whole the sign in which the moon is, because the same moon retained ten parts for itself in the sign in which it was kindled. This is what he means by “as many as it retained”—namely, from the first sign—“remember to subtract so many,” namely, from the following signs.

To remove means that the lines have withdrawn from the sign before the moon was kindled, provided that it was kindled before the middle of the sign. But if it was kindled after the middle of the sign, this is understood as retaining.

Again: as many parts as the moon, when kindled in the first sign, has removed, remember to add from the following sign. This applies when the moon was kindled in the earlier part of the sign, that is, before the middle. But if it was kindled after the middle, remember to remove from the following sign as many parts as it retained from the final part of the sign in which it was kindled.

For example, if it retained twelve lines from the sign in which it was kindled, remove the same number from the extremity of the following sign.

## Recapitulation

“The moon traverses the zodiac thirteen times.” For thirteen lunar months, each having only twenty-seven days and eight hours, are unquestionably found in the zodiac, when one always reckons twenty-nine days in one moon and thirty in another. From the two days and four hours that remain for you after the twenty-seven days and eight hours of each month, you will complete the thirteenth month, even though one day is lacking.

### “Divide by nine”

For in these nine quadrants the moon traverses each sign. If you find only nine in the moon, you will have a completed sign; if twice nine, two signs; if three times nine, three, and so forth, always subtracting the two-thirds. For nine times six makes fifty-four. The moon traverses each sign in that many hours and two-thirds.

He himself demonstrates this in what follows, where he says: “If one remains, six hours,” and so on. Each part of four multiplied by six hours contains the same amount.

### “After five signs have been completed from the point at which the moon was born”

Take care here: in another passage in the calculation he said that the moon moves four points away from the sun; here, however, he is not measuring between the sun and the moon, but from the place where the moon was kindled up to the point of whatever sign through which it is running. That is, from the sign in which it was kindled up to the sign in which it is, always subtract two hours from the remaining hours left after the nine quadrants, namely, after every three signs.

### “How many parts the moon has removed or retained in the first sign”

For example, the present moon was born in the fifth part of Aries and afterward retained twenty-five parts, through which it ran. It removed five, which it did not touch.

If you then wish to determine in which sign the ninth-day moon is today, multiply nine by four: the result is thirty-six quadrants. Multiply seven of these quadrants by six, because there are six hours in each quadrant, and take three hours from the twenty-ninth quadrant; you will have forty-five hours. Assign them to Aries, because it traversed that many hours through it, always reckoning nine hours in the moon’s course for five parts, that is, for the sun’s days.

This also agrees well here: five times nine is forty-five, and five times five is twenty-five. For the moon always traverses as many parts in its hours as the sun does in its days.

Take twenty-seven quadrants from the five, and assign nine to Taurus, nine again to Gemini, and likewise nine to Cancer. You still have one and a half quadrants, which make nine hours. Of these, two hours will be assigned after three signs have been completed, and thus seven hours remain. Therefore the ninth-day moon will be seven hours into Leo.

“Which the moon has removed or retained,” namely, from the first sign at its beginning. Remember to remove as many from the end of the following sign and to add them to the first sign. Or “retained,” namely, from the end of the first sign: remember likewise to remove that many from the end of the following sign and to add them to the first sign.

“With nine hours in the moon reckoned for five days in the sun,” because what the sun accomplishes in five days the moon accomplishes in nine hours. This is proved as follows: six times five is thirty, and its sixth part is five. This pertains to the sun: it traverses each sign in thirty days. Conversely, the moon completes each sign in two days and six hours, which amount to fifty-four hours.

## Recapitulation

“The moon traverses the zodiac thirteen times,” and so forth. The zodiac is the sign-bearing [circle]. *Zoa* is Greek for “animals” (*animal* in Latin). Hence *zodiac* is derived from *zoa*, that is, “animals,” whose images are depicted there.

### “In two days and six hours, and two-thirds,” and so forth

If you inquire carefully, you will find that the moon remains in each sign for two days, six hours, and two-thirds of an hour, together with one-twelfth of an hour. If you wonder why he omitted that small fraction, I say that he knew it could not escape an experienced calculator, and therefore he spared the tedium of expression.

This reasoning can be proved in the following way. Just as nine hours in the moon correspond to five days in the sun, and nine quadrants in the moon correspond to a day in the sun, so twenty-seven days in the moon correspond exactly to 360 days in the sun. There still remain from the sun’s course five days, and from the moon’s course eight hours and twelve small fractions, from which a ninth hour is formed. Thus the courses of the sun and moon through the zodiac are shown to correspond. In this passage, nine quadrants and two days and six hours have the same numerical value.

### “For it is laborious in each sign,” and so forth

For it is laborious to assign eight twelfths immediately to each sign after every nine quadrants. Therefore, for the sake of brevity, they are omitted until three signs have been completed and two hours—that is, three two-thirds—are restored.

This calculation is readily made when the moon is born in the first or middle part of any sign, because the less that must be restored, the easier the calculation.

### “But if in another place, in the first sign,” and so forth

That is, if it was kindled in a place other than the first or middle part of the sign. “Removed,” namely, at the beginning of the sign; or “retained,” namely, from the end of the sign. Remember to subtract or add that amount in the following signs, that is, to the sign in which the moon was first situated.

You must carry out this restoration as follows. If you wish to restore one day, assign it nine points; for two days, eighteen; for three, twenty-seven; for four, thirty-six; for five, forty-five, which make nine hours. This is what is meant by “nine hours in the moon reckoned for five days in the sun.”

The same can also be done in this way: if you wish to restore one day, assign it two hours, from which you must always cut off a tenth part. If five days, assign them ten hours; after the tenth part has been removed, nine hours likewise remain.

## JOAN. NOV. Scholium

### “Each month has its own signs”

The distribution of the signs among the individual months is as follows, although it cannot conveniently be made in this way. For the beginnings of the Roman months—for these are the months under discussion—do not correspond to the beginnings of the signs. Rather, in the middle of the months the sun generally enters some new sign, as, for example, Aquarius on 11 January; yet this arrangement is not fixed.

For formerly, as it appears, the transition into another sign took place on the very Kalends of the months. Nor are there lacking those who think that Christ was born on the winter night, which is the longest night of the entire year: at that time it was the eighth day before the Kalends of January. In our own age, however, the winter solstice occurs on the day before the Ides of December, that is, thirteen days earlier. This happens because the solar year is somewhat shorter than it is reckoned.

For it consists of 365¼ days, though not a complete quarter. Since, for the convenience of intercalation, it is taken as a whole number, the year must end later than the sun has traversed the sign-bearing circle. This excess of time has not yet found a remedy through intercalation—or rather, through subtraction.

It could be removed in the following way, if the Church or the Roman pontiff, to whom the power of intercalation was first granted, should wish it. First, the days from 12 December, on which the winter solstice occurs, up to the Kalends of January would be subtracted from December—namely, nineteen days—so that in that year December would consist of only twelve days. In addition, no intercalation would be made in every 110th year, for intercalation adds more time than the sun’s circuit requires, and this cannot be removed except by subtraction.

In this way it would happen that throughout the ages the sun would consistently enter the constellation of Capricorn on the Kalends of January. This was the case five hundred years before Christ was born, if intercalation had continued for so long.

I have added this here not because I wish the seasons to be rearranged, but so that the reader may understand why the winter solstice now occurs nearer the Kalends of December than it did when our Savior was born, and why, after a long succession of centuries, December will eventually occur at the time which we now call November.

### “As one of the ancients also explained in verse”

I do not remember having read who among the ancient poets composed these verses. They appear to belong to someone more recent than Manilius, in whose work similar verses are found, though not these same ones.

Formerly, however, these little verses were customarily distributed among the individual months in calendars, as they are now marked out in rather undisciplined and wholly unlearned verses. I have seen an exceedingly old manuscript of sacred hymns and readings, written here and there in golden letters, with these same verses in the headings of the months. Cologne showed it to us in the church of Saint Gereon, through D. Andreas Barduiccensis, a canon of that place.

### “Aries of Phrixus for the Kalends”

*Phrixaeus* is an epithet of the heavenly Ram derived from the event in which it carried Phrixus and Helle across the sea—afterward called the Hellespont from her name. See Julius Hyginus, *Astronomical Poetics*.

### “May, of Agenor”

He calls the Bull “Agenorean” from Venus, whose house is in this sign. For the ancients understood *Agenorean* as referring to the goddess who rouses beings to action. This is none other than Venus, who stimulates all living things to procreate.

### “June sees the equal Laconians moving through the sky”

By the “equal Laconians,” understand the Twins, namely Castor and Pollux, whom Jupiter placed among the noble stars because of the moderation of rule which they jointly exercised over the Lacedaemonians.

### “Of the burning solstice”

The sun produces the solstice in the first part of Cancer. At that time shadows are nearly consumed and, because of the star’s elevation, the heat increases beyond measure. For this reason he called it “burning.”

### “Fiery Leo”

When the sun is in this sign, it makes the dog days intolerably hot for human bodies.

### “And October makes equal”

He refers to the autumnal equinox, which occurs in the first part of Libra.

### “Scorpio, headlong into winter”

We understand “headlong Scorpio” as referring to the sudden shortening of the days, which is most rapid under this constellation.

### “Tropical Capricorn establishes the beginning of January”

Capricorn is a tropical sign, as is Cancer. For just as the solstice occurs in Cancer, so the winter solstice occurs in Capricorn; these are the final points in the increase of light and darkness.

That it is said to possess the beginning of January does not correspond to our own age, but it was so two thousand years ago, as we showed above.

### “The constellation of Aquarius stands firm”

Why “firm,” when Lucan calls it “light,” and others call it “swift” or “headlong”? He refers here to the slow increase of the day, which at that time is scarcely yet perceptible.

Astrologers call the signs that immediately follow the tropical signs “fixed,” such as Aquarius. Those who use the other terms are referring to the length of time in which the whole sign rises. This occurs within an hour, whereas some other signs take more than two hours to rise completely, because of the curvature of the sign-bearing circle.

By Numa’s month, understand February, for Numa added it to the year established earlier by Romulus, along with January.

### “In the space of two hours”

Understand unequal or temporal hours, not equinoctial hours. Otherwise, it is easily evident from what is handed down about the unequal rising and setting of the constellations that the statement would be false.

### “Ten and a half hours”

Understand the hours by which the sun remains longer in each sign than the thirty days assigned to it.

### “Therefore, the first sign of Aries”

Bede indicates somewhat obscurely in which parts of the heavens, or in which signs, the sun is situated in each month—or, what amounts to the same thing, which sign rises with the sun in each month.

So that in our own age this may be known exactly for every month and every day of each month, I have appended at the end a table of the days and parts of the signs, calculated precisely for the year of salvation 1540.

### “And therefore, according to some, in its eighth part”

Pliny makes the following statement in Book II, chapter 19, of the *Natural History*: “The sun itself has four distinctions: twice, when day and night are equal, in spring and autumn, falling upon the center of the earth, in the eighth parts of Aries and Libra; twice, with the intervals changed to the increase of day, the winter solstice in the eighth part of Capricorn and the solstice of night in the same number of parts of Cancer.”

But someone may ask: since the relation of the oblique circle is unchanging, and the equinoxes cannot occur anywhere except where the sign-bearing circle and the equator intersect—and since one of these intersections is the first part of Aries and the other the first part, or first degree, of Libra, without any alteration—how, then, are we to understand the equinoxes as occurring in the eighth parts, when the intersection of the sign-bearing circle and the equator produces the first parts of Libra and Aries?

I answer as follows. The Egyptians—or, as Pliny has it, Anaximander of Miletus—when they first discovered the obliquity of the sign-bearing circle and the equinoxes or solstices of the sun within it, looked to the stars near those locations, to which the names Aries and Taurus were then being assigned. They marked the courses and lengths of these asterisms in the sky, so that they could identify each location by a clear sign.

Then, dividing the whole asterism into thirty parts, they marked the location of the equinox or solstice at a fixed part of the figure. For example, where the equinox then occurred, the eighth part of that asterism which is called Aries in the sky was found.

But when the fixed stars gradually moved eastward against the sky through the motion of the ninth sphere, this method could not remain stable. Consequently, following the entire circle of the sun, they divided it into twelve equal spaces, called in Greek *dodecamoria*. Each of these was divided into thirty parts, now called degrees, while the earlier calculation by the parts of the asterism was abandoned. For the size of the asterisms is not equal in every case.

In this way, I think, we should understand Pliny’s statement, and any other statement in which the equinoxes are said to occur somewhere other than in the first parts of Aries and Libra.

If anyone wishes to understand this more clearly, let him take the astrolabe which we published in earlier years and mark on it the first part of Cancer—not of the constellation itself, but of that *dodecamorion* which is fourth from the equinoctial intersection.

When the sun reaches that part, it is said to be in the first part of the *dodecamorion*, but not in the first part of Cancer, that is, of the constellation itself. Rather, it is near the second part of Gemini, which lies among the stars that form the front foot of Gemini. Hence the figure of Cancer is separated from it by an interval of several parts.

Therefore, to conclude: when we say that the sun is in Leo or in any other sign, we must understand not the constellation but the fourth *dodecamorion* from Aries. The sun traverses each of these in thirty days and ten hours and a half. The poet’s passage cited here by Bede from the First Book of the *Georgics* must be understood in this sense.

### “As Egypt, the mother of the arts, teaches”

Aristotle likewise states that the first invention of hidden arts belonged to the Egyptian priests, who were forbidden to engage in profane occupations. See the beginning of the *Metaphysics* in Aristotle.

The table encompasses a complete annual cycle. In it the months and the days of each month are set out in order; opposite them is the number of parts or degrees in the sign-bearing circle corresponding to each day. The third number is that of the minutes, which we explained elsewhere as *λέτρα πρῶτα* (“first minutes”).

[Col. 0358A]

Each month, moreover, has its own signs into which it receives the sun: April, Aries; May, Taurus; June, Gemini; July, Cancer; August, Leo; September, Virgo; October, Libra; November, Scorpio; December, Sagittarius; January, Capricorn; February, Aquarius; March, Pisces, as one of the ancients also explained in heroic verse:

> In April you behold the Ram of Phrixus at the Kalends.  
>   
> May marvels at the horns of Agenor’s Bull.  
>   
> June sees the equal Laconians move through the sky.  
>   
> In the solstice, July bears the star of burning Cancer.  
>   
> Fiery Leo scorches August with its flame.  
>   
> Virgo, under your constellation, September fattens Bacchus.  
>   
> October also makes Libra equal at seed-sowing time.  
>   
> Headlong Scorpio orders November to enter winter.  
>   
> [Col. 0358B] The Archer completes his signs in the middle of December.  
>   
> Tropical Capricorn establishes the beginning of January.  
>   
> In the middle of Numa’s month stands the solid constellation of Aquarius.  
>   
> The double Pisces advance into the season of March.

Because he spoke specifically of one December, he indicated that the same should generally be understood of the others: each of the signs ends in the middle of its own month and begins to rise from the middle of the preceding month.

Since we are about to instruct those who are ignorant of their position, I ask that this not be burdensome to those who already know.

Around the entire, perfectly rounded circuit of the heavens, along the line of the zodiacal circle—as though around a kind of zone encircling the immense sphere—distinct rows of twelve pairs, touching one another, occupy their positions. They are so large that they can neither rise, set, nor move from their place in less than the space of two hours.

Thirty parts are assigned to each, because they are traversed by the sun in thirty days. The ten and a half hours [Col. 0359A] that exceed this are disregarded in the calculation, since they do not amount to a complete portion of twenty-four hours.

Nevertheless, when the sun itself has made twelve circuits and completed five days and a quarter, it will become clear how much it has added to the thirty parts; and the complete solar year will be finished not merely in 360 days, but with five additional [Col. 0361A] days and a quarter.

The first sign, Aries, begins to rise in that part of the heavens which the sun occupies in the middle of [Col. 0362A] March. It is completed in the part through which the sun moves in the middle of April. Therefore, according to some, it displays the place of the vernal equinox [Col. 0363A] in its eighth part, but more accurately, according to the Egyptians, who are more knowledgeable than all others in calculations, in its fourth part [Col. 0364A].

The second sign, Taurus, begins its rising from that part of the celestial circle through which the sun moves in the middle of April and is completed in the part which it occupies in the middle of May. [Col. 0366A]

The third, Gemini, begins from the part of the sign-bearing circle which the sun occupies in the middle of May. The fourth, Cancer, begins its rising from the part which the sun traverses in the middle of June. Therefore, according to some, it receives the solstice in its eighth part [Col. 0368A]; but according to more careful investigation, the solstice occurs several parts earlier, since the position of the zodiac—that is, of the sign-bearing circle—has first been deflected downward [Col. 0369A].

The fifth sign, Leo, begins from the part through which the sun moves in the middle of July; the sixth, Virgo, from that through which it moves in the middle of August; the seventh, Libra, from that through which it revolves in the middle of September. Therefore, according to the common opinion, it offers the place of the autumnal equinox [Col. 0372A] in its eighth part, but according to the more precise view, somewhat earlier.

From this point, as the sign-bearing circle inclines toward the winter zone, the eighth sign, Scorpio, raises its head from the part which the sun occupies in the middle of October; the ninth, Sagittarius, from the part which it occupies in the middle of November; and the tenth, Capricorn, from the part which the sun inhabits in the middle of December. Therefore, as is commonly believed, it dedicates its dwelling to the winter solstice in its eighth part [Col. 0375A], but, as Egypt, the mother of the arts, teaches, several parts earlier.

Then, as the course of the sign-bearing circle turns back toward the higher regions, the eleventh constellation, Aquarius, begins from the solar part of the middle of January; the twelfth, Pisces, raises its head from the same part in February and ends in the middle of March, where the following Aries opens the beginning of its rising.

For all the signs are connected—not by the shape of their figures, but by the conjunction of their regions and by the logic of their mutual computation. Concerning them the poet says:

> Therefore the golden sun rules the measured sphere,  
>   
> divided into fixed parts, through the twelve stars of the world.

The sign-bearing circle receives the Milky Way in Sagittarius and Gemini. Much more could be said here, but such matters are better handled in conversation than in writing.

Since we have already discussed above the order and timing of the planets, whose passage lies along the sign-bearing circle, let us say only this for now: the sun traverses the circumference of the zodiac in 365 days and six hours; the moon, in twenty-seven days and eight hours. The sun passes through each sign in thirty days, ten hours, and a half; the moon passes through each in two days, six hours, and two-thirds of an hour.

If you ask what two-thirds signifies, we explained it at the beginning of this little work, in the discussion of calculations, and we repeat it briefly here. Two-thirds is as far short of a whole hour as eight is short of twelve, twenty is short of thirty, and ten is short of fifteen. For when a third part has been subtracted and only two parts remain, those two parts are called a *bisse*, while the third part itself is called a *triens*.

Therefore those who say that the moon traverses only as much celestial space in thirty days as the sun traverses in 365 are mistaken. Manifest truth shows, as we also briefly indicated above, that the moon completes in twenty-seven days and a third of a day as much of its course as the sun completes in 365 days and a quarter of a day; and as much space as the moon traverses in one of its months, the sun traverses in thirteen of its months.

[Note: [Col. 0379A] Add: “months.”]

## Chapter XVII. On the Moon’s Course through the Signs

[Note: [Col. 0381A]

### BRIDEF. RAMES. GLOSSES

The moon moves four points farther from the sun each day when waxing, or, when waning, is restored nearer to the sun than it had been the day before. Each sign has ten points, that is, two hours, as we also noted above.]

[Col. 0381B] The Moon moves away from the Sun each day by four points [Col. 0382A] until it becomes a full orb; and then, returning daily toward the Sun through the same interval, it approaches it again. Pliny the Elder usually calls these four points a dodrans and a semuncia in his *Natural History*. But since it is not readily clear how great and what kind of measure this interval of time is in which the Moon is said to wax or wane, we must make it clear [Col. 0382B] by explicit numerical examples [Col. 0381C].

No calculator should doubt that the fourth hour has very familiar subdivisions. It is sometimes divided into four points, sometimes into five, sometimes into ten minutes, and most frequently into forty moments; when divided most minutely, into sixty ostenta. All these divisions, however, were devised by the authorities for determining the passage of shadows on a sundial. They divided the sundial into twenty-four spaces, according to the number of the twenty-four hours in which the Sun traverses the whole world, and added subdivisions of each hour, so that they could most easily determine the passage of the hours by the movement of the shadow through the spaces of the sundial.

When, therefore, the shadow passed through a fourth part of one space, which signifies an hour on the sundial, they called it a “point”; that point itself contains ten moments. They also added another point when the shadow traverses a fifth part [Col. 0382C] of an hour, on account of the Moon’s course; this point contains eight moments. The Moon completes four such points each day, with the fifth remaining within it. For eight moments multiplied by five complete one hour.

A moment is the fortieth part of an hour. Thus the astrologers wished to apprehend the movement of the heavenly bodies in its smallest divisions through shadows, so that they might perceive the fortieth part of an hour when the shadow passed through the fortieth part, on the sundial, of the space signifying one hour. Nor was this enough for them: they added still smaller spaces, which are called *ostenta*. One *ostentum* contains half a moment.

The largest spaces in the divisions of an hour are therefore called points; the smallest are called ostenta or atoms. But, as we said above, there are two measures of points: one contains a fourth part of an hour, that is, ten moments; the other contains a fifth, having within it eight moments. A minute, however, is the largest part of an hour; an ostentum is the sixtieth part of an hour and contains 376 atoms. One hour contains 22,560 atoms.

Of the divisions mentioned above, only two unquestionably pertain to the present question, namely, to the Moon’s course: the division into five and that into forty. The division into five pertains to the course of the Moon alone; the other divisions are assigned to both the courses of the Sun and the Moon.

What Pliny the Elder reports—that the Moon rises or sets each day a dodrans and a semuncia of an hour later than it had risen or set on the previous day—contains this interval of time: thirty-one moments and two-thirds of a moment. For a dodrans in every measure contains three quarters. If, therefore, one hour has forty moments, it follows that a dodrans of an hour contains thirty moments.

When one hour is divided into twelve ounces, after the manner of an *as*, its twelfth part, which may be called an ounce, is found to contain three moments and one-third of a moment. Half of this ounce is one moment and one-half of a moment, together with one-sixth of a moment. Thus the aforesaid interval, namely a dodrans and a semuncia, comprises thirty-one moments and two-thirds—that is, a *bess* or *bisse*.

For *bes*, as Priscian teaches, is used in place of *des*. *Des* is a compound name, from *dempto*, “with the triens removed,” the word *triens* having been altered by the assumption of one letter. Hence *des* is formed from “with a third removed,” and for this name we use *bes*.

But the aforesaid interval, which Pliny the Elder expressed according to the natural course of the Moon, Bede chose, for ease of calculation, to call by the name and measure of four points. If anyone wishes to know what difference there is between the interval of a dodrans and a semuncia and that of four points, let him understand that the difference is the same as that between thirty-two moments and thirty-one moments and two-thirds of a moment. This difference is found in one-third of a moment. Four points therefore exceed a dodrans and a semuncia by one-third of a moment.

The calculation and measure of a dodrans and a semuncia can easily be grasped from the number twelve. Let the number twelve serve, for example, as one ounce. Divide that ounce into three parts: the third part is four. For four taken three times grows to twelve. Half of this third part, that is, of four, is two; and two is one-sixth of twelve. Hence it is shown that in every measure half of a third is found to be one-sixth of the whole.

Again, the dodrans of the same number twelve is nine. For what the dodrans contains in one hour, nine contains in the number twelve.

Alternatively: an hour has forty moments, and each moment has four thirds. The twelfth part of these forty moments is called an ounce. Take three moments from thirty-six moments, since that is their twelfth part; and from four moments take one third, that is, their twelfth part. Join that third to the three moments mentioned above, and you will have an ounce. Half of one ounce—that is, one moment and one-half, together with half of a third, which is called a sextans, or the sixth part of a moment—is called a semuncia.

Thus, as we said, an hour has forty moments, and each moment has three thirds. [Col. 0384A] Forty times three, or three times forty, is 120. Therefore one third of a moment is one 120th part of an hour.

The first Moon, shining after sunset, remains above the earth for the interval of a dodrans and a semuncia of an hour. The second Moon remains above the earth, shining, for one and a half hours and one ounce. The third, shining after sunset, remains for two hours, one third [Col. 0384B] of an hour, and a semuncia. The fourth, for three hours and two ounces. The fifth, for four hours less a semuncia. The sixth, for four hours and a dodrans. The seventh, for five and a half hours and a semuncia. The eighth, for six hours and one third of an hour. The ninth shines for seven hours and one and a half ounces. The tenth shines for eight hours less one ounce. The eleventh shines for eight hours, two-thirds of an hour, and a semuncia. The twelfth shines for nine and a half hours. The thirteenth shines for ten hours, a quarter, and a semuncia. The fourteenth shines for eleven hours and one ounce. The fifteenth shines for eleven hours, a *decunx*, and a semuncia—that is, twelve hours less one ounce and a semuncia.

If this calculation is increased each day by four points, according to Bede, the fifteenth Moon is found to shine above the earth for twelve hours. From this it becomes clear how much difference there is between Pliny the Elder’s calculation, which is accumulated by dodrantes and semunciae, and Bede’s, which is reckoned by four points. A difference of one and a half ounces is found. We should nevertheless not doubt that Pliny followed the natural course, while Bede chose ease of calculation.

If, therefore, you wish to know how long each Moon, according to Pliny the Elder’s calculation, shines at night from the first through the fifteenth, multiply its age by four. When you have determined how many points the resulting number gives, subtract from those points as many thirds of a moment as the Moon’s age has days.

For example, if the number is five, subtract five thirds of a moment—that is, one moment and two-thirds of a moment. If it is ten, subtract ten thirds of a moment—that is, three moments and one-third of a moment. If it is fifteen, subtract fifteen thirds of a moment—that is, five moments.

Those five moments yield one and a half ounces in the following way: three moments and one-third of a moment make an ounce. One moment and a half, together with one-sixth of a moment, complete half an ounce.

It is therefore clear that the calculation we gave above concerning the Moon’s course agrees in every respect with the advances and retreats of the sea. For the ebb and flow of the sea, and also the *malina* and *laedon*, naturally follow the Moon’s course. Thus, just as the Moon completes its course through the signs and revolves around the earth in its daily circuit, so the daily rising and falling of the sea, with the same intervals of delay, either approaches the land or recedes from it.

And just as the Moon, as we said above, rises today—or remains above the earth after sunset—a dodrans and a semuncia, or four points, later than it did yesterday, so the advance or retreat of the sea is likewise observed today at the same interval later than it was yesterday.

For just as an animal draws breath into itself, so does the Moon draw in the sea. That is, the Ocean’s tide flows in twice each day and, correspondingly, recedes twice—that is, advances twice. Between day and night, one hour’s dodrans is always transferred, together with a semuncia: that is, thirty moments, one moment and a half, and one-sixth of a moment. “Transferred,” that is, elapsed, appears by analogy with the Moon. And “its”—namely, the Ocean’s—“whole courses,” that is, its contractions.

Concerning the *laedones*. The Latin expression means “a hurt wave” (*laesa unda*). For the wave is restrained and driven back, because it is not allowed to travel over the land as far as the *malina*. *Malina* is so called as if from “greater Moon,” because in it both the Moon itself and the sea’s tide boil more strongly than in the *laedon*. *Laedon* is so called as if from “hurt wave,” because in it both the Moon and the Ocean’s tide boil less strongly.

The *malina* and the *laedon* divide the lunar month between them into four equal parts. The first *malina*, in which the first Moon is found, lasts seven days and nine hours. It begins with the twenty-eighth Moon and extends through the fifth. The *laedon* follows, lasting from the fifth through the twelfth and likewise enduring for seven days and nine hours.

Then, beginning with the thirteenth Moon, the second *malina* starts; in it the full Moon appears, and it ends with the nineteenth Moon. It is said to last for the same number of days and hours, namely seven days and nine hours.

Again, the *laedon*, beginning with the twentieth Moon and ending with the twenty-seventh, completes its course in the aforesaid number of seven days and nine hours. You have, I think, the lunar month divided equally between the *malinae* and the *laedones*.

“Tides,” that is, encounters or advances. But the *laedon*, that is, the lesser tide, begins—that is, it begins with the fifth and the twenty-fifth Moon, for there are two *laedones*. For as many hours as it advances—namely, seven—it also retreats, backward. The *laedon* begins with the fifth Moon and lasts through the eleventh and twelfth hours of the twelfth Moon, because each *laedon* and *malina* contains seven days and twelve hours.

[Col. 0385] **On the Agreement of the Sea and the Moon**

[Col. 0387A] The Moon moves away from the Sun each day by four points, whether, while waxing, it goes farther from the Sun, or, while waning, it is restored nearer to the Sun than it had been the day before, and so forth. Since the Moon moves away from the Sun by only four points each day—that is, twelve degrees—and since each sign has ten points, that is, thirty degrees, it is necessary that it traverse each sign in no less than two and a half days.

For it advances only four points each day in its separation from the Sun, that is, twelve degrees. Therefore, insofar as its separation from the Sun is concerned, it traverses ten points, that is, one sign, in two and a half days. But insofar as its own proper course is concerned, in which it completes thirteen degrees each day in the zodiac, it traverses each sign in two days, six hours, and two-thirds of an hour.

Therefore the route it completes in its entire journey in twenty-seven days and eight hours cannot be completed in its separation from the Sun in less than thirty days. Each sign has ten points, that is, two hours.

He now speaks of equinoctial hours. For one sign moves in two hours, since the entire zodiac moves in twenty-four, as we stated above, in chapter 14, where he said: “They cannot rise, set, or move from place to place except in the space of two hours.” They make an hour—that is, according to the Moon’s calculation.

Finally, whenever you see the Moon’s orb completely full, opposite the Sun, you see it low when the Sun is high, and high when the Sun is low.

Finally, “the Moon’s orb,” that is, the full Moon. If there is a full Moon at the summer solstice, when the Sun is in the fourth degree of Cancer, that same night the full Moon will be in the fourth degree of Capricorn, where the winter solstice occurs. As long as the Sun occupies the summer circle, where the days are longer, the Sun will be high and the Moon low. But when the Sun turns toward the winter region, the full Moon becomes high and the Sun low, for then the nights become longer.

And if there is a full Moon at the spring equinox, when the Sun is in the fourth degree of Aries, that same night the full Moon will be in the fourth degree of Libra, where the autumnal equinox occurs.

And by as many degrees as the Sun has passed beyond the equinox or solstice that it had most recently traversed, by that many degrees the full Moon passes that night beyond the corresponding equinox or solstice. For example, if the Sun is in the tenth degree of Aries—that is, in the sixth degree after the spring equinox—when the Sun is high, the Moon is low; and when the Moon is high, the Sun is low. By as much as the Sun has moved away from the summer solstice, by that much the fifteenth Moon approaches the other circle.

[Col. 0388B] Take the thirtieth Moon, which then falls on the third day before the Kalends of February, and multiply it by four: the result is 120. Divide by ten. Twelve times ten: “centum-vies,” that is, 120. The Moon occupies that part of the heavens—namely, the part where the Sun and Moon are in conjunction.

For the thirtieth Moon always occupies that part of the conjunction. The Sun cannot occupy that same part—that point of the heavens where it is now together with the thirtieth Moon—until twelve months have elapsed, that is, after the whole circle of the year.

The thirtieth Moon, whether of January or of any month, runs its course. After twelve months have been completed, that is, after the whole circle of the year has passed—after 360 days have been completed—the Sun returns to it.

The five days and a quarter are not included when he says that each sign has only ten points, that is, thirty degrees. Although they are not counted here, the Sun nevertheless completes its year through them as well; each sign has thirty degrees, and in addition there are ten and a half hours.

It is the same part in which the Sun was now moving and had received the Moon into conjunction. It is the same part, namely, the thirtieth. For when he says “it is the same part,” this refers to the thirtieth part of those thirty degrees which the Moon traverses from the first through the thirtieth in order to catch up with the Sun in the zodiac.

The Moon reaches conjunction in twenty-nine and a half days, and therefore we customarily say that it reaches conjunction in thirty days. But naturally it reaches conjunction in twenty-nine and a half days. In that same part in which the Sun was now moving, it had received the Moon into conjunction. For at the end of the thirtieth Moon and the beginning of the first, the Sun and Moon are always in one conjunction.

**SCHOLIA OF JOHN OF NOVIOMAGUS.**—“Divide by ten: three tens, ‘tries.’” In these multiplication formulas, the final word expressing the number, which explains what results from the multiplication, is often corrupt. Whether this happened through the British language, through the carelessness of copyists, or—as he said above—because children commonly pronounce it in this way, I do not know. But because we consistently find this practice, I have placed in the margin opposite each expression what those little words mean.

It should also be noted that in these calculations he uses the manner of speaking employed by arithmeticians in division. For they multiply the quotient—which they call the denominator—by the divisor. Thus, if I divide fifty by V, the V, I say, contains fifty ten times; then five times X makes fifty, and therefore nothing remains. By this method they test whether anything remains after the distribution has been made.]
