The Moon moves away from the Sun each day by four points, whether, while waxing, it goes farther from the Sun, or, while waning, is restored nearer to the Sun than it had been the day before. Each sign has ten points, that is, two hours, as we stated above [Col. 0382A]; five points make an hour.

Therefore, if you wish to know in which sign the Moon is, take whichever Moon you wish—for example, the fifth—and multiply by four: the result is twenty. Divide by ten: twice ten, “vies.” Therefore the fifth Moon is always two signs distant from the Sun.

Again, take the eighth Moon and multiply by four: the result is thirty-two. Divide by ten: three times ten, “tries,” [Col. 0383A] with two remaining. Therefore the eighth Moon is always separated from the Sun by three signs and two points.

Understand the two points as six degrees, that is, as much as the Sun traverses in the zodiac in six days. For a point has three degrees, since a sign also has ten points but thirty degrees.

Again, take the nineteenth Moon and multiply by four: the result is seventy-six [Col. 0384A]. Divide by ten: seven times ten, “septais,” with six remaining. Therefore the nineteenth Moon has always moved away from the Sun, along the route on which it began, by seven signs and one hour—which is half a sign—and one point, that is, three degrees.

And lest the suspicion of a deceptive calculation occur to you, examine the diameter of the heavens, which no one doubts is occupied by the fifteenth Moon [Col. 0385A]. Multiply fifteen by four: the result is sixty. Divide by ten: six times ten, “sexais.” For the fifteenth Moon is always separated from the Sun by six signs—that is, by half the celestial sphere—whether you look forward or backward.

Finally, whenever the Moon’s orb is completely full, you see it opposite the Sun: low when the Sun is high, and high when the Sun is low. For [Col. 0386A], when the Sun occupies the summer circle and the Moon is full, the Moon occupies the winter circle; when the Sun has declined toward winter and the Moon is full, the longest night shows that the Moon has climbed into the solstitial circle. But when the Sun is at the equinox at the full Moon, the Moon occupies the other equinox; and by as many degrees as the Sun has passed beyond the equinox or solstice that it had most recently traversed, by just so many degrees the full Moon appears to have passed beyond the opposite equinox or solstice.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Moon’s Course for Those Who Do Not Know the Signs

[Note: [Col. 0388D]

**BRID. RAMES. GLOSSES.**—So that the foregoing matters may be made clearer even to anyone of slower understanding. “Which,” namely, the matters stated above, “or clearer to anyone,” that is, to anyone whatever. “How much,” namely, the desire. “It,” namely, the Moon. “More distinctly,” that is, more plainly.]

[Col. 0389C] When the first Moon has completed its age, divide the first Moon into four points, and the four points into three parts; the result is twelve. For the first Moon is twelve degrees distant from the Sun.

“It is separated from the Sun by an interval”—that is, by four points—“of twelve days”: that is, it is separated from the Sun in its course by as much distance as the Sun traverses in twelve days. What is sought here is the route of its separation from the Sun, not its whole course. In its separation from the Sun it makes twelve degrees each day, and thirteen in its entire course.

Therefore the journey it makes in its entire course in twenty-seven days and eight hours cannot be made in its separation from the Sun in less than thirty days, for a shorter journey is sought in its separation than in its forward motion.

“Second,” namely, the Moon: by an interval of twenty-four days, that is, eight points. “Third”: by the interval of one month, that is, ten points, and six days, that is, two points. “Thirtieth”: by the interval of twelve months, that is, 120 points.

For the Moon makes in thirty days the journey that the Sun makes in one year, that is, in 360 days. The five days and a quarter, which are produced from the ten and a half hours remaining in each month, the authorities do not count, because it would have been tedious for them to calculate them. Yet, even if they are not counted, the Sun completes its course in them, that is, its year, while the Moon completes its month.

And as we said, the journey which the Sun makes in 365 days and six hours is, according to this calculation, traversed in thirty days, though naturally it is traversed in twenty-nine and a half days. These months are counted as only thirty days because each sign in them has thirty degrees and ten points. Thirty degrees, that is, ten points, make only thirty days.

Therefore, according to this calculation, twelve months contain only 360 days. Naturally, however, each month has thirty days and ten and a half hours; therefore twelve months naturally have 365 days and six hours.

In twenty-four hours the Moon traverses thirteen degrees, eight hours, four moments, and one atom. Each day, if I am not mistaken, the Moon passes through thirteen degrees, eight hours, two-thirds of an hour, and in addition one-third of a minute; and one minute still remains from the 365 days and a quarter.

Twenty-seven times thirteen yields 351 degrees. Twenty-seven times eight hours yields nine days. Those eight hours in which the Moon remains after twenty-seven days comprise three days and eight hours. From 365 days, twenty-two hours remain, that is, 220 minutes. Give each of the twenty-seven days eight minutes, and only four minutes remain.

Read the gloss written above concerning the two arguments mentioned earlier, namely 18 and 17, beginning: “If you wish to know how many degrees the Moon is distant from the Sun, multiply its age, whatever it may be, by four,” and continuing to “the Moon remains that day in the fifteenth degree of Gemini.” Also read chapter 21, beginning: “In which sign the Moon remains each day, or by how many degrees it is separated from the Sun on each successive day,” and continuing to “between the waning and the reborn Moon,” because these two arguments are discussed there with the greatest precision.]

If anyone, however, does not know the signs but desires to understand the Moon’s courses, let him know that the Sun completes one degree of its zodiac each day. For we ought to understand the degrees of the zodiac as nothing other than the Sun’s daily progress in the heavens. The Moon, however, completes thirteen degrees of that same zodiac each day, that is, four points and one degree. Since it completes thirteen degrees while the Sun completes one, it follows—as we taught above—that it is separated from the Sun in its daily progress by no more than four points, that is, twelve degrees.

Let him place the Moon wherever he wishes to begin the calculation—for example, as the first Moon on the Kalends of January. When it has completed that night and day as the first Moon, it occupies that place in the heavens which the Sun occupies after completing thirteen days of the same month.

When it is the second Moon, multiply two by four: the result is eight. Again, to pass from points to degrees, multiply eight by three: the result is twenty-four. Therefore Moon II occupies that part of the heavens which the Sun reaches after completing twenty-four days from that point, on the fourth day before the Nones of January.

When it is the third Moon, multiply three by four: the result is twelve. Divide by ten: ten times one, “decus,” with two remaining [Col. 0389B] points, that is, six degrees. Therefore Moon III occupies that part of the heavens which the Sun reaches after a whole month and six days have elapsed after the third day before the Nones of January—that is, after six days following the third day before the Nones of February.

When it is the fourth Moon, multiply it by four: the result is sixteen. Divide by ten: ten times one, “decus,” with six points remaining, that is, eighteen degrees. Therefore the fourth Moon occupies that part of the heavens which the Sun reaches after a month has been completed and eighteen days have elapsed after the day before the Nones of January.

When it is the fifth Moon, multiply five by four: the result is twenty. Divide by ten: twice ten, “vies.” Therefore, after two months have been completed, the Sun will reach the part of the heavens occupied by the fifth Moon, that is, on the day of the Nones of March.

When it is the eighth Moon, on the sixth day before the Ides of January, multiply eight by four: the result is thirty-two. Divide by ten: three times ten, “tries,” with two [Col. 0389C] points remaining, that is, six degrees. Therefore the eighth Moon occupies that part of the heavens on the sixth day before the Ides of January which the Sun will reach after three months and six days from that point—that is, six days after the sixth day before the Ides of April.

When it is the nineteenth Moon, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, multiply it by four: the result is [Col. 0390A] seventy-six. Divide by ten: seven times ten, “septais,” with six remaining. Multiply these by three: the result is eighteen. The nineteenth Moon revolves around that part of the heavens on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February which the Sun will reach after seven months and eighteen days from that point—that is, on the eighteenth day after the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September, which is the eighth day before the Ides of September.

And lest any doubt about a deceptive calculation arise in you, test it at the diameter of the year, which few are unaware is occupied by the fifteenth Moon. Multiply fifteen by four: the result is sixty. Divide by ten: six times ten, “sexais.” After six months have been completed—that is, after half the course of the year has been traversed—the Sun will enter the part of the heavens through which the fifteenth Moon revolves.

And because that is the fifteenth day of January, the Sun will of course reach that same part on the fifteenth day of July.

To reach the conclusion, take the thirtieth Moon, which then falls on the third day before the Kalends of February, and multiply it by four: the result is 120. Divide by ten: twelve times ten, “centum-vies.” The thirtieth Moon runs through that part of the heavens which the Sun will occupy after twelve months have been completed, that is, after the whole circle of the year has elapsed.

For it is the same part in which the Sun was now moving and had received the Moon into conjunction.

So that these matters may be made clearer even to anyone of slower understanding, we have taken care to record more distinctly, for each age of the Moon, how far it is distant from the Sun.

The first Moon, when it has completed its age, is separated from the Sun by an interval of twelve days; the second by an interval of twenty-four days; the third by an interval of one month and six days; the fourth by an interval of one month and eighteen days; the fifth by an interval of two months; the sixth by an interval of two months and twelve days; the seventh by an interval of two months and twenty-three days; the eighth by an interval of three months and six days; the ninth by an interval of three months and eighteen days; the tenth by an interval of four months; the eleventh by an interval of four months and twelve days; the twelfth by an interval of four months and twenty-four days [Col. 0391A]; the thirteenth by an interval of five months and six days; the fourteenth by an interval of five months and eighteen days; the fifteenth by an interval of six months; the sixteenth by an interval of six months and twelve days; the seventeenth by an interval of six months and twenty-four days; the eighteenth by an interval of seven months and six days; the nineteenth by an interval of seven months and eighteen days; the twentieth by an interval of eight months; the twenty-first by an interval of eight months and twelve days; the twenty-second by an interval of eight months and twenty-four days; the twenty-third by an interval of nine months and six days; the twenty-fourth by an interval of nine months and eighteen days; the twenty-fifth by an interval of ten months; the twenty-sixth by an interval of ten months and twelve days; the twenty-seventh [Col. 0391B] by an interval of ten months and twenty-four days; the twenty-eighth by an interval of eleven months and six days; the twenty-ninth by an interval of eleven months and eighteen days; the thirtieth by an interval of twelve months.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Same Subject for Those Who Have Not Learned to Calculate

[Note: [Col. 0391B]

**BRID. RAMES. GLOSSES.**—For it increases the entire sequence of the annual cycle. The Moon remains in each sign for two days, six hours, and two-thirds of an hour. Thus two-thirds repeated twelve times produce eight hours in the year; from these eight hours, one day grows after three years.

Nevertheless, that day is not found on the regular page, although in the annual series a vacant place is found between *o* and *a* in the third position. From the six hours, however, a day grows in the fourth sign, and for that reason the fourth sign is always multiplied three times.

“These”—namely, the letters—“we placed alternately,” that is, we made intervals there, leaving one vacant in it. For there are more days in the Moon’s cycle than letters in the alphabets, because we did not assign one letter to this work for every single day, that is, to the annual booklet. For as many letters as it contains, so many years does it also comprise.

**On the Regular Page.**]

Why is a vacant place not found between *o* and *a* for the third time in the regular table, as it is found in the annual sequence? It is not found because the moon traverses the zodiac in twenty-seven days and eight hours, and in the regular table there is a letter for each day, or a vacant place; the same alphabet is counted thirteen times in one year. If there had been a vacant place, twenty-eight days would have been found in every circuit, and from this the error would have become very great if a vacant place had been inserted between *o* and *a*.

It is likewise asked how, in the regular table, that constellation is found which is represented in the annual sequence by the vacant place between *o* and *a* in the third circuit, when no vacant place is found in that table. We can answer briefly that that constellation is recognized between *o* and *a* by the likeness of the leap-year sign, for which there is no vacant place in the annual sequence, but which is inserted between two solar days—that is, between the seventh and sixth day before the Kalends of March, in the place of the sixth day before the Kalends of March.

It is likewise asked why the fourth constellation is always written three times in the alphabet in the regular table. We can answer that one constellation is written three times because of the complete day that arises for each constellation from the six hours repeated four times. That day is therefore assigned to the constellation in which the moon is then located—that is, always to the fourth constellation.

It is likewise asked whether three days are counted in any sign that is not written three times in the regular table. They are indeed counted in the third lunar circuit, where there is a vacant place between *o* and *a* in the annual sequence.

It is likewise asked whether four days are counted in a constellation. They are indeed counted whenever one constellation is written three times because of the six hours mentioned above. The day that arises from the *bisse*—that is, from the eight hours repeated for the third time—is assigned to that constellation. Examine the seventh and eighth years, and the sixteenth, seventeenth, and eighteenth.

It is likewise asked why one alphabet is written thirteen times in the annual sequence in one year, but one alphabet is not repeated thirteen times. This too is resolved as follows: because of the number of solar days in which the sun traverses the zodiac—one alphabetic sequence is repeated thirteen times in the annual sequence, that is, in 365¼ days. But, as we said above, the moon traverses the zodiac in twenty-seven days and eight hours. It is therefore not necessary for the same alphabet to be repeated in order to designate the same days, so that the same signs may be displayed.

It is likewise asked why the alphabet of each year does not begin with *a* in the regular table. The answer is this: if it always began with *a*, the constellation of Aries would always be indicated. In the constellation in which the moon remains in the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, when the moon is nine days old on the Kalends of January, *a* is placed under that same constellation, namely, Aries. In the constellation in which the moon remains in the second year of the aforesaid cycle, when the moon is twenty days old on the Kalends of January—that is, in the sign of Virgo—*a* is written beneath it; and so with the others.

It is likewise asked why Aries is written at the end of the year and at its beginning. This is done because, in the extreme part of Aries, the moon is passing through when it is nine days old on the Kalends of January.

This is also connected with the repeated eight hours, because the moon remains in each constellation for two days and six hours and a *bisse*, that is, two-thirds of an hour. Twelve repetitions of the *bisse* therefore produce eight hours in a year. From these eight hours one day increases over three years. Nevertheless, that day is not found in the regular table, although in the annual sequence a vacant place is found between *o* and *a* in the third place. From the six hours, however, a day increases in the fourth constellation, and for that reason the fourth constellation is always multiplied three times.

Likewise, if you wish to find in which place the signs ought to be tripled, say that the moon traverses the zodiacal circle in twenty-seven days and eight hours. The number three is one quarter of twelve. Since the eight hours are omitted—those which, by increasing over three years, produce a complete day—the signs ought therefore to be tripled in the fourth place.

### JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA

At this point Bede begins to explain the use of the tables that were placed at the beginning of the work with the greatest care. First he explains the sixth table, which we marked with the letter *F*. We took pains to imitate word for word the most ancient exemplar, most accurately drawn in these tables, except where it was necessary to repair passages worn away by age, or where Greek characters had been poorly written for that period. If from Bede’s explanation you cannot discern the use of the tables, consult what we briefly added there under each index.

[Col. 0392A]

But if someone is less capable of calculation and yet is curious about the lunar circuit, we provide him with an aid suited to the capacity of his little intellect, by which he may find what he seeks. We have divided the entire sequence of the annual circuit, which is contained in twelve months, by means of alphabets, arranging it so that the first and second rows contain twenty-seven days each, while the third contains one more—the day that increases from the eight surplus hours repeated for the third time. And so that the letters would suffice for the days we wished to mark, we placed them not on each individual day but on alternate days; for that reason it was not necessary for the alphabet to extend beyond the letter *o*.

[Col. 0392B] We placed before this same work a regular table containing nineteen such alphabets, beginning with different letters, corresponding to the same number of years in the nineteen-year cycle. It also contained the names of the twelve months and signs, [Col. 0393A] arranged in this order according to the number of days in which the moon traverses the zodiac. It has twenty-seven lines in length, marked on one side with the names of the signs and on the other with the names of the months, so that someone unfamiliar with the signs may nevertheless find what he seeks from his knowledge of the months. It has nineteen lines in breadth, which display above them the order of the nineteen-year cycle, indicated by the number of the years.

When, therefore, in any year you wish to know on what day the moon is in a particular sign, or in what part of a particular month, open the book and note the letter assigned to that day. Then return to the regular table, in which the letters are arranged in an ordered mass; immediately find the same year from the heading at the top, and in that year’s alphabet you will find the letter belonging to the day you seek. Looking to the front and back, you will note which sign and which month stand opposite it.

Let us give an example that may strengthen you, reader, for the other cases. You ask where the moon is, for example, on the Kalends of April in the sixth year of the nineteen-year cycle. Open the book and look for the day of the aforesaid Kalends; you will find the letter *e* written above it. Return to the regular table. You will see year six; having examined its alphabet, you will find the letter *e*. Look to either side: on one side you will discover the end of Gemini, and on the other the beginning of the month of June. Whether you are an educated or a simple reader, you will rejoice openly that you have investigated what you desired.

Moreover, throughout that entire year, on whatever days you see the letter *e* written—whether the moon is waxing or waning—you will know that the moon is situated in those same regions of the sky. In this calculation you are not asking whether the moon is placed in the increase or decrease of its light, or opposite the sun or in conjunction with it; but if you also wish to know this, an aid handed down by the ancient observation of the Egyptians will be available.

## CHAPTER XX. What the Moon’s Age Is on Each Kalends

### BRID. RAMES. GLOSSAE

What the moon’s age is on each Kalends. It is as though he were saying: “What is the age of the moon beginning each Kalends?” In that year, namely, there are no epacts, because they are not added: at that time, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, where the seat of the epacts is, the moon is thirty days old. You therefore use that year to determine the moon’s age on the Kalends of each month; in the other years you will have the epacts and these regular numbers, always for finding the moon on the Kalends.

According to the Egyptians, these regular numbers are placed on the Kalends of January, that is, when the moon is thirty days old on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, from which the epacts are taken. In that year itself there are no epacts, because the moon’s age does not rise above thirty; rather, as many regular numbers as each month has, so old will the moon be in that year.

The epacts are taken from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April because it follows the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, when the sun was created, when the spring equinox occurs, and where the Paschal limit lies. Therefore the authorities decided that the epacts should be taken from that point in order to find the moon. Whatever the moon’s age is on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, that many epacts will there be in that year until the Kalends of September; and whatever epact there is on the Kalends of September, after it has changed, such will be the moon’s age on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April at the following time.

In the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, in which there are no epacts, the moon is nine days old on the Kalends of January; according to the Romans, the year begins then. Take these numbers for yourself—that is, the lunar numbers—which are the regular numbers. Subtract thirty; four remain. Why thirty? Because the moon’s age does not rise above thirty.

If, however, you prefer to take the beginning of the calculation from January, as we taught above, the moon falls on the Kalends of December at seven days old, although according to the calculation it was thought that it ought to be six days old. December has, according to the Romans, eighteen regular numbers. Add to these the Roman epacts, eighteen; together they make thirty-six. Subtract thirty; six remain. But if on the Kalends of December you count the moon as six days old, the ninth moon will not occur on the Kalends of January, but the eighth. It is therefore necessary to count it as seven days old on the Kalends of December rather than six.

Likewise, in year eleven, because the embolismic moon begins on the day before the Nones of December, it makes the moon twenty-eight days old on the Kalends of March, although the calculation indicates that it then exists as twenty-nine days old. In this year also the moon ought, according to the sequence of the epacts, to be twenty-nine days old on the Kalends of March; but because of the embolism, it appears as twenty-eight, except in a leap year. If this year is a leap year, then on the Kalends of March it will be twenty-nine days old, both according to the reading and according to the calculation of that year. This is also the February moon, and because of the leap year it ends on the sixth day before the Nones of March as a thirty-day moon; for the leap year always compels the February moon to be counted as thirty days old.

It should not be mentioned only in passing that some begin this calculation from September. Although the Egyptians and Romans place the regular numbers differently and begin the year differently, the same moon is found among both Egyptians and Romans on the Kalends of September and on the Kalends of all the months—that is, on the first month of the Egyptians and the penultimate month of the Romans—except only in the nineteenth year, when the lunar leap occurs. The epacts that the Egyptians have on the Kalends of September are those that the Romans have on the Kalends of January. The Egyptians begin the year from September and change the epacts there; the Romans likewise begin the year from January and change the epacts there, and the epacts produce this correspondence.

### JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA

This is the preceding calculation that we mentioned. We found a fragment of these annual tables among Bede’s nineteen-year cycles, extending from the elapsed year 532 to 1025; as is clear from this chronological reckoning, he himself began it from an earlier point and extended it farther. But in the written exemplar, which was defective both at the beginning and at the end, we extended it to 1600 from astronomical calculations, so that this calculation might also be useful to posterity. We placed it at the end of the book; there you may see several matters that are more useful for understanding this chapter.

In the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, in which there are no epacts, the moon is nine days old on the Kalends of January; on the Kalends of February, ten; on the Kalends of March, nine; on the Kalends of April, ten; on the Kalends of May, eleven; on the Kalends of June, twelve; on the Kalends of July, thirteen; on the Kalends of August, fourteen; on the Kalends of September, fifteen; on the Kalends of October, sixteen; on the Kalends of November, seventeen; and on the Kalends of December, eighteen.

Take these numbers as the regular numbers for the individual months. By adding the annual epacts to them, you will find without error the moon’s age on each Kalends. If you wish to know the moon’s age on the Kalends of January in the second year of the nineteen-year cycle, take the regular number nine and add the epacts, eleven; together they make twenty, so the moon is twenty days old.

If you wish to know the moon’s age on the Kalends of June in the third year, take the regular number twelve and add the epacts of that year, twenty-two; together they make thirty-four. Subtract thirty; four remain. The moon is four days old on the aforesaid Kalends.

If anyone should object that the order of this calculation or of the preceding one falters somewhere, let him himself offer a more truthful and more concise method for investigating such questions, and we shall gladly and gratefully accept it. We have already given the preceding calculation to some people for copying, and we judge that it should be placed at the beginning of this little work of ours. As for the present calculation, which we have set out for finding the moon on the Kalends, it is sufficient to have mentioned and taught it in this one place. For once the moon’s age on the Kalends is known, its age on the other days of each month will easily become clear by reciting that month and applying the concurrent days.

There are three years in the nineteen-year cycle in which this calculation cannot preserve the stability of its sequence: the eighth, the eleventh, and the nineteenth. The reason is the varied and dispersed insertion of embolisms throughout the year.

In the eighth year, for example, the moon on the Kalends of May is counted as twenty-eight days old according to the calculation, but because of the embolism inserted in the month of March it is shown to be twenty-seven days old. Likewise, on the Kalends of July the calculation could make the moon thirty days old, but because of the addition of the day brought by the excess of the embolism, it becomes twenty-nine.

Likewise, in year eleven, because the embolismic moon begins on the day before the Nones of December, it makes the moon twenty-eight days old on the Kalends of March, although the calculation says that it then exists as twenty-nine days old.

Likewise, in year nineteen, because the embolismic moon begins on the third day of the Nones of March, it compels the moon to be counted as twenty-eight days old on the Kalends of May, although according to the calculation it is recited as twenty-nine days old. In that year also, the calculation is challenged by the lunar leap, about which we shall speak below.

For if you begin the calculation according to the Egyptians from the month of September, where their year begins, it is necessary that in that year the moon of July have twenty-nine days, as it never has at any other time, having lost one day because of the lunar leap. For this reason the moon on the Kalends of August is made three days old, although according to the rule of the calculation it was counted as two.

But if, according to what we taught above, you prefer to take the beginning of the calculation from January, the moon falls on the Kalends of December at seven days old, although according to the calculation it was thought that it ought to be six. This is because the moon of November loses one day and is compelled to be content with only twenty-nine days instead of the customary thirty.

All these matters are taught better by discussion than by writing.

It should not be mentioned only in passing that some begin this calculation from September, assigning to September the regular number five, to October five, to November seven, to December seven, and so on, as we set out above. They do this quite reasonably on the authority of the Egyptians, imitating in the computation the beginning of the year of those from whom the origin of the calculation was taken.

Nevertheless, it seems much more suitable and convenient to others that the entire calculation should begin, insofar as the requirements of the calculation do not prevent it, from the beginning of the year even among the Romans, and should proceed from there to the end of the year in its proper and unbroken order.

## CHAPTER XXI. What Day of the Week Falls on the Kalends

### BRID. RAMES. GLOSSAE

In the other years you will add the concurrent days, however many are marked for the present year, to the regular numbers of the individual months. “However many” means the number of the weekday. On what weekday is the ninth day before the Kalends of April? Saturday—because it does not always happen, but only rarely, that the ninth day before the Kalends of April falls on a Saturday.

The concurrent day, which the Egyptians begin on the Kalends of March, the Romans begin two months earlier, namely, from the Kalends of January and February, joining that concurrent day to the regular numbers of January, which according to the Romans are two, and to the regular numbers of February, which likewise are five according to the Romans. Nevertheless, remember to subtract one from that number in every leap year, that is, from the regular numbers of January and February; [Col. 0396D] then the Kalends among them will correspond to those among the Egyptians, at the beginning of January and February. In the other months there is no need to do this.

A similar calculation is handed down for finding the weekday of the Kalends very readily, provided that, using different regular numbers, you do by means of the concurrent days what in the previous calculation you do by means of the epacts.

The regular numbers are as follows: January II, February VI, March V, April I, May III, June VI, July I, August IV, September VII, October II, November V, December VII.

These regular numbers specifically indicate the weekday of the Kalends in the year in which seven concurrent days have been assigned. In the other years you will add to the regular numbers of the individual months however many concurrent days have been marked for the present year, and in this way you will always find the weekday of the Kalends without error.

Remember only this: when a leap year is approaching, one of the concurrent days must be omitted. Nevertheless, use that number which you are going to omit in January and February, and on the first Kalends of March begin to calculate by the number contained in the solar cycle.

When, for example, you wish to find the weekday of the Kalends of January, you say: January II. Add the concurrent days of the week that belonged to the year for which you are calculating—for example, III; together they make five. The Kalends of January fall on the fifth weekday.

Likewise, in a year that has six concurrent days, take the regular number of the month of March, V, and add six concurrent days; together they make eleven. Subtract seven; four remain. The Kalends of March fall on the fourth weekday.

## CHAPTER XXII. A Calculation Concerning Any Moon or Weekday

### BRID. RAMES. GLOSSAE

This calculation proceeds without difficulty if you become accustomed to reciting from memory the number of each month counted by the Kalends, Nones, and Ides. January has one on the Kalends, five on the Nones, and thirteen on the Ides.

If you happen to ask where these days come from—that is, January one on the Kalends, February thirty-two on the Kalends, and so forth—say this: January has one day on the Kalends, and it also has four days before the Nones. Add one and four; together they make five, which is the number on the Nones. For it has eight days before the Ides. Five and eight together make thirteen, which is the number on the Ides. It also has nineteen days after the Ides before the next Kalends. Thirteen and nineteen together make thirty-two. Thus you can very easily find the whole number in this lesson from beginning to end.

### JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA

There is also an old calculation. The tables that he placed at the beginning of the work are to be referred to for this chapter, then for what follows, and also for what precedes—especially those that we marked with capital letters A, B, G, I, V, and X, as we also noted there.

There is also an old calculation, discovered not only for determining the moon or weekday on the Kalends but also for discerning them on any days between the Kalends. It is somewhat more difficult to learn, but it was handed down to us on the authority of our elders and therefore ought, by our equal diligence, to be handed down to those younger than ourselves.

If, therefore, you wish to know the moon’s age on a particular day, count the days from the beginning of the month of January up to the day in question. When you know that number, add the moon’s age on the Kalends of January. Divide the whole by fifty-nine; if more than thirty remain, subtract thirty, and what remains is the moon’s age on the day you seek.

Likewise, if you wish to know the weekday of a particular day, count the days from the Kalends of January up to the day in question. When you know that number, add the weekday on which the Kalends of January fell. If it is a leap year, remember also to increase the number after the leap day has passed. Divide the whole by seven, and what remains will show you the weekday wherever you are making the inquiry.

This calculation proceeds without difficulty if you become accustomed to reciting from memory the number of each month counted by the Kalends, Nones, and Ides.

January: on the Kalends I, on the Nones V, on the Ides XIII.

February: on the Kalends XXXII, on the Nones XXXVI, on the Ides XLIIII.

March: on the Kalends XL, on the Nones LXVI, on the Ides LXXIIII.

April: on the Kalends XCI, on the Nones XCV, on the Ides CIII.

May: on the Kalends CXXI, on the Nones CXXVII, on the Ides CXXXV.

June: on the Kalends CLII, on the Nones CLVI, on the Ides CLXIIII.

July: on the Kalends CLXXXII, on the Nones CLXXXVIII, on the Ides CXCVI.

August: on the Kalends CCXIII, on the Nones CCXVII, on the Ides CCXXV.

September: on the Kalends CCXLIIII, on the Nones CCXLVIII, on the Ides CCLVI.

October: on the Kalends CCLXXIIII, on the Nones CCLXXX, on the Ides CCLXXXVIII.

November: on the Kalends CCCV, on the Nones CCCIX, on the Ides CCCXVII.

December: on the Kalends CCCXXXV, on the Nones CCCXXXIX, on the Ides CCCXLVII.

If, for example, you wish to know the moon’s age on the Kalends of May in a year in which it is nine days old on the Kalends of January, say: May on the Kalends CXXI. Subtract the Kalends; CXX remain. Add IX; together they make CXXIX. Divide by LIX—fifty-nine times two, one hundred eighteen; subtract CXVIII; XI remain. The moon is eleven days old on the Kalends of May.

If you wish to know the moon’s age on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, say: June on the Kalends CLII. Subtract fifteen days before the Kalends of June; CXXXVII remain. Add IX; together they make CXLVI. Divide by LIX—fifty-nine times two, one hundred eighteen; subtract CXVIII; XXVIII remain. The moon is twenty-eight days old on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June.

If you wish to know the moon’s age on the seventh day before the Ides of December, say: December on the Ides CCCXLVII. Subtract seven; CCCXL remain. Add IX; together they make CCCXLIX. Divide by LIX—fifty-nine times five, CCXCV. Subtract CCXCV; LIIII remain. Subtract XXX; XXIIII remain. The moon is twenty-four days old on the day mentioned.

The usefulness of this calculation is increased if the calculator commits more carefully to memory the final products of the fifty-nine divisions:

- fifty-nine times six: CCCLIIII;
- fifty-nine times five: CCXCV;
- fifty-nine times four: CCXXXVI;
- fifty-nine times three: CLXXVII;
- fifty-nine times two: CXVIII;
- [printed text uncertain: “quinquies novies assis”] IX.

By the same procedure, adding the weekday of the Kalends of January, you may find the weekday at whatever time you wish.

If, for example, you wish to know on what weekday the eighth day before the Kalends of October falls in a year in which the Kalends of January fall on the fifth weekday, say: October on the Kalends CCLXXIIII. Subtract the eighth day before the Kalends of October; CCLXVI remain. Add the fifth weekday on which the Kalends of January fell; together they make CCLXXI. Divide by VII—seven times thirty, CCX; seven times eight, LVI; the remainder is V. The eighth day before the Kalends of October is therefore the fifth weekday.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The Moon’s Age, for Those Unable to Calculate

If someone is so lazy or dull that he wishes to know the course of the moon without any labor of calculation, let him rely on the alphabets that he sees arranged in the annual book according to the lunar course. There, three alphabets contain two lunar circuits—that is, fifty-nine days—and whichever letter the moon bears once at a particular age, it does not cease to have that same letter marked in the same way and at the same age throughout the entire year, unless perhaps—and this happens rarely—the arrangement of the embolisms alters it.

For example, in the third year of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon that will have thirty days always begins with an unmarked *a*; on the second day it is at *b*, on the third at *c*, likewise unmarked—that is, with no point marked—and so, in sequence, each letter preserves its lunar age.

Likewise, the moon that will have twenty-nine days begins with a *subnotated* *l*; on the second day it is always at *m*, on the third at *n*, marked with the same figure, and so the moon returning in sequence restores its age to each letter.

For the sake of distinction, antiquity provided that the first of the three alphabets should be marked by letters unmarked on either side, the second by letters marked below, and the third by letters marked above.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How Many Hours the Moon Shines

### BRID. RAMES. GLOSSAE

Likewise, when you reach the tenth moon, multiply by four; the result is forty. Divide by a fifth part. Five times eight makes forty; the tenth moon shines for eight hours. He did not mean equinoctial hours but artificial hours. A gloss on this calculation has already been written above; it begins: “If you wish to know by how many points or hours the moon shines, first consider whether it is waxing or waning,” and ends: “That period is called the interlunium.”

### AN OLD COMMENTARY

There are four figures on this page. The first, which is round, indicates by how many points the moon shines. Since the moon receives its light from the sun, and the first moon always rises when the sun sets—

#### By how many points the moon shines

[Col. 0399B] In the second figure, which is likewise round, the twelve signs are arranged externally, as if in the zodiac. Since it holds the beginnings of the individual signs in the individual months, let us suppose that I began with one of them, namely Aries; I marked beneath it, with Greek names, how many forms it has from the first through the fifteenth. It repeats these forms while waning, since it wanes at the same moments at which it waxes; this is indicated by the ages of the moon written beneath the signs.

Thus it comes about that the crescent (*menoides*) always appears toward the West, the upper half-moon (*dichotomos*) toward the North, the full moon (*panselenos*) toward the East, and the lower half-moon (*dichotomos*) toward the South.

Finally, it is separated from the sun by 180 parts, that is, by 180 days. The third figure below demonstrates this, being longer on one side than the other; for, advancing gradually by twelve degrees from the first, it marks the fifteenth moon at 180 parts opposite the moon. In this way the fourteenth, thirteenth, and the remaining phases correspond with the remaining ones opposite them, so that at last the twenty-ninth moon is twelve parts distant from the sun, like the first.

The total of the lunar circuit is found to be 360, as another sequence there indicates, although the thirtieth moon is missing.

Total calculation of the entire course.

In the fourth figure, where the preparation for the leap year is gathered, the years are written above: the first from the leap year, the second, the third, and the fourth. Opposite each of these, twelve hours are placed below, by which is marked at which of those hours the sun enters the sign placed above, namely, on the calendar date assigned beneath each sign.

Finally, the hours of the night are marked by the arithmetic numbering—1, 2, 3—and the hours of the day by the scholastic numbering, as they call it—I, V, X. Where there are three points above, the sun’s entry into the sign is marked at the third point of that hour; where there is nothing, the sign entered at the beginning of the hour. I placed beneath each hour the number thirty, represented by the letter X in this form, and at the end “XS,” because from the hour at which it enters, the sun remains in each sign for XXX days and XS hours.

The ancients also handed down a calculation by which one may determine for how many hours the moon shines at each age. Since, they say, the first moon shines for four points, this number is added each day from the second moon up to the full moon, and thereafter it is subtracted at equal intervals during the waning.

Therefore, if you wish to know how many hours the second moon shines, multiply two by four; the result is eight. Divide by five, because five points make an hour: five times one, with three remaining. The second moon therefore shines for one hour and three points.

Likewise, multiply three by four; the result is twelve. Divide by five: five times two is ten, with two remaining. The third moon shines for two hours and two points.

Likewise, when you reach the tenth moon, multiply by four; the result is forty. Divide by a fifth part: five times eight is forty. The tenth moon shines for eight hours.

And so that you may not think the calculation doubtful, take fifteen, they say, and inquire when the moon shines throughout the night. Multiply by four; the result is sixty. Divide by five: five times twelve is sixty. The fifteenth moon passes through twelve hours—that is, the whole night.

Likewise, if you wish to know how many hours the sixteenth, seventeenth, and the subsequent moons shine, recall how far each is from thirty, and construct the basis of the calculation from that. For example, if you wish to know how long the twenty-fifth moon shines, say: the amount by which it is less than thirty is five. Multiply by four: four times five is twenty. Divide by five: five times four is twenty. The twenty-fifth moon therefore shines for four hours, just as the fifth moon does.

This calculation proceeds in a properly fixed manner at the time of the equinox. But in the longest nights of winter, or likewise in the shortest nights of summer, when the duration of night is known sometimes to exceed twelve hours by a great amount and sometimes not to reach twelve hours at all, how are we to believe that the moon shines for twelve hours? Perhaps we must understand not equinoctial hours, but each night divided according to its own length or brevity into twelve equal portions, which we call hours, so that the division is made equally.

## CHAPTER XXV. When and Why the Moon Is Seen as Inclined, Supine, or Upright

[Note: [Col. 0403C]

BRID. RAMES. GLOSSES.—They say that the moon neither wanes nor grows, but that, illuminated by the sun on the side turned toward it, as it gradually withdraws from or approaches the sun, it turns toward us either its bright or its dark side. As the day increases, the new moon is seen lying on its back—namely, above the sun and rising toward the north; but as the day decreases, it is seen upright and lowered toward the south. When full, it is always opposite the sun. The higher the sun, the moon is low; when the sun is low, the moon is high. They say that it adds three-quarters of a half-ounce of an hour each day from the second moon until the full orb, and removes the same amount during its waning. They say that it always remains hidden within thirteen degrees of the sun; but that the last moon and the new moon can be seen on the same day or night in no sign other than Aries. If it is upright at its illumination, it will appear lying on its back at its morning rising. Likewise, if at its illumination it is seen lying on its back in the form of a ship, it will be seen upright at its morning rising. Thus it has three states in which it is sometimes seen: lying on its back, upright, and lying face-down.

They say, that is, the learned, that the moon neither wanes nor grows, but is always full on one side. According to Martianus, the moon is illuminated not by itself but by the sun, just as a mirror possesses neither brightness nor an image from itself, yet receives light and an image from things placed outside it. When the moon withdraws from the sun, it is gradually illuminated by the sun, and then is said to grow; but when, after the fifteenth moon, it approaches the sun, it is gradually darkened until it is completely obscured by its proximity to the sun. Then it is said to wane, although its body itself never diminishes or grows.

“Illuminated,” that is, they say that it is lit up. “Toward it” (the sun), that is, turned opposite it; or “withdrawing from it” (the sun), they say that it turns toward us its bright side; or “approaching it,” its dark side, that is, its black side [Col. 0404C]. For the nearer it comes to the sun, the more its light is taken away from us. And “as the day increases,” that is, while the day is growing.

It is asked why, as the day increases, the new moon appears lying on its back, but as the day decreases it appears not face-down but upright, although it ought to appear face-down in the decrease just as it appears lying on its back in the increase of light. The explanation is as follows. As the day increases, the moon is naturally higher than the sun; therefore the sun illuminates the upper side of the moon placed above it and makes it lie on its back. But when the day decreases, the sun and the new moon are found, by their natural position, to be at the same altitude. Consequently, the sun does not illuminate the moon placed beneath it but the moon placed beside it, and therefore makes it upright.

“To be seen” (by us), “the new moon,” that is, the first moon, “as being above the sun.” This is established not by reference to the zones but by reference to the zodiac. When the sun circles the southern circles, which are lower, during winter, the moon traverses the northern circles, which are higher, and is then higher than the sun; therefore it lies on its back, with its horns turned upward in the form of a ship, because it is illuminated from its lower side, by which it faces the sun. Again, when the sun moves through the northern circles, the moon seeks the southern ones; and because it is then lower than the sun, it is illuminated from its upper side, by which it faces the sun, with its horns turned downward toward the earth and toward the northern circles.

For example: On the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, the days are still increasing. If the moon has been illuminated in Aries, then, quickly passing into Taurus, it will be, in relation to the zodiac, as though it were higher than the sun. “Rising toward it,” that is, ascending—namely, the moon. “As the day decreases,” they say that it is upright, that is, at the side. “And lowered,” that is, low, “toward the south,” that is, toward midday. “Full,” they say, namely, the moon. “Opposite the sun,” that is, situated directly across from it, that is, facing the sun.

“High,” namely, the moon in the north; “with the sun low,” namely, toward the south. “And low,” namely, the moon; “with the sun high,” namely, the sun. They say that the moon adds three-quarters of a half-ounce. What a three-quarter and a half-ounce are has already been explained most accurately above. “Adding,” namely, those three-quarters and half-ounces from the second moon. He says “from the second moon” because the first moon occurs at the conjunction with the sun. “Until the full orb,” that is, until the fifteenth moon.

They say that it remains hidden within thirteen degrees, that is, thirteen days. It traverses thirteen degrees each day in the zodiac, but before it reaches beyond thirteen degrees it is not seen. Each hour contains forty moments. Of those forty moments, take thirty, because that is three-quarters, and leave ten, because that is one-quarter. Again divide those forty moments by twelve, in order to find from them the half-ounces mentioned above. For by the first division you understood the three-quarters: forty moments divided by twelve three times make thirty-six, with four remaining [Col. 0405C]. From the twelve take three moments three times, because that is one-twelfth of them; and from the four that remain take one-third of a moment. If you reduce one-twelfth of those forty moments to one unit, three moments result, together with one-third of a moment; that is one ounce, because one-twelfth of the number forty is three and one-third. Again divide that ounce in half: this yields one and a half moments, together with a sixth, that is, one-sixth of a moment. This is the half-ounce of which he said that the moon increases or decreases by three-quarters of a half-ounce each day.

“Always hidden,” that is, the moon does not appear when it is near the sun within thirteen degrees—that is, within the space which the sun traverses in thirteen days.

But as soon as it has emerged into the fifteenth degree, it begins to be seen. At this point a twofold interpretation is possible. For what he said—“it always remains hidden within thirteen degrees of the sun”—can be understood as meaning that the new moon can never appear before it has either withdrawn thirteen degrees from the sun or, by nature, approached the sun from another side. Therefore, while the new moon remains within thirteen degrees of the sun, it will appear in no sign except Aries [Col. 0405D]. But as soon as it has withdrawn farther from the sun, it will appear to the earth. “In no other sign,” that is, in no sign except Aries.

The old moon can appear in the morning before the sun, and on that same day the new moon can appear after sunset. “To be seen”—although it is in other signs, it is nevertheless not seen, because it sometimes happens that the thirtieth or twenty-ninth moon, appearing in the east at the very beginning of the day and completing its course while approaching the slower-moving sun, is illuminated by it at midday or at some other hour of the day and appears that same evening in the west.

What then? Is it credible that the position of the moon, which remains fixed in the ether, can, because of changes in the winds or clouds lying beneath it, be turned in another direction from that in which it had been? Why call it fixed, since it is one of the seven planets? But it is called fixed because its nature is immovable; consequently it cannot be disturbed by the force of the winds, since it is not in the air but in the ether. For in the ether there is no storm.

Hyginus says that the moon must move through different risings and settings, not remain still; and this is easier to understand than it is in the case of the sun. Since it receives its light from the sun and thus appears to us to shine, there is no doubt that it moves rather than remains stationary. The moon, being near the earth, revolves in a shorter orbit, and completes the path which the sun traverses in 365 days and six hours in twenty-seven days and eight hours.

When it begins to withdraw from the sun, it is illuminated also on the side turned toward the earth, and necessarily begins at the horns, until it becomes full, opposite the sun; for then it rises when the sun sets. The first moon appears only in the evening in the west, as the sun descends toward the lower regions. Although the first moon often comes to be in every part of the sky—in the east, at midday, and in other places—it is nevertheless not seen or reckoned as the first except in the west, because of the sun’s brightness and because of its initial condition: in the other places it is simultaneously above the earth.

The full moon, however, necessarily appears in the evening in the east and in the morning in the west, because the full moon is always six signs distant from the sun; and the full moon is above the earth by night and beneath the earth by day. The first moon, on the other hand, is above the earth by day when the sun is above the earth, and beneath the earth by night when the sun is beneath the earth.

Philosophers say that the body of the sun exceeds the moon threefold in size, and that the moon is three times larger than the earth. The fact that the moon appears to us to be of the same size as the sun results from the sun’s being much farther and higher from the earth than the moon; therefore we who live on earth cannot at all discern how great its size is. For everything placed farther away habitually appears smaller.

Thus, when the new moon is seen after sunset, and is going to set north of the sun’s setting-place, it is clearly situated not beside but above the sun. There are three kinds of the moon’s illumination [Col. 0406D]: under-illumination, middle illumination, and over-illumination. Under-illumination occurs when the moon is illuminated from below by the sun for sixty days and twenty hours, around the eleventh day before the Kalends of January, because then the moon is higher than the sun. Middle illumination occurs when the moon is illuminated by the sun equally for thirty days and ten hours, around the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, because then the sun and moon are equal in altitude. Over-illumination occurs when the moon is illuminated from above for sixty days and twenty hours, around the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, because then the sun is higher than the moon.

It is certainly clear, and easy for anyone paying attention to understand, that the moon appears to our eyes to grow only by withdrawing from the sun, and to wane only by approaching the sun from the opposite side. From the sun, therefore, it receives its light; and when it is beneath the sun, it is always small. But when it has withdrawn farther from the sun, it becomes large and full in its circumference. For if it used its own light, it would necessarily always be equal in size and would not become small on the thirtieth day. And if it used its own light, it would never undergo an eclipse [Col. 0407A].

As far as the mystical interpretation is concerned, the moon represents the appearance of this world. Just as the moon suffers decline through its monthly completions, so the world, advancing toward the completion of time, falls through daily declines. In sacred language the moon signifies the decline of human frailty: as it grows through monthly hours, it expresses the mutability of our misery. We grow by being born, decrease by dying, increase in prosperity, and diminish in adversity.

Sometimes the same moon is also understood as the Church, because just as the moon is illuminated by the sun, so the Church is illuminated by Christ. For just as the moon wanes and grows, so the Church has its declines and risings. Often it has grown through its declines and deserved to be enlarged by them: it is diminished by persecutions and crowned by the martyrdom of confessors. Likewise, just as the moon is rich in dew and guides moist substances, so the Church is watered by the rains of baptism and preaching [Col. 0407B].

And just as all fruits grow when the moon grows and diminish when it diminishes, so we understand the Church: in its increase we advance along with it; when it suffers persecution and is diminished, we too suffer and are diminished with it [Col. 0408A]. Likewise, just as the moon has seven forms, so the Church has as many graces of merits. The distribution of the charisms bestowed through the Holy Spirit upon the faithful of the whole Church is likewise established by this number.

The seventh and a half, and the twenty-second and a half, are in the middle of their orbit; the others are proportional.

Ambrose, in the book *Hexameron*: “For the moon undergoes a diminution of light, not of body, when through its monthly changes it seems to lay aside its own light in order to borrow it from the sun. This can easily be inferred from pure and transparent air, when no overhanging cloud makes it dark. For the entire orb of the moon remains, even though its whole does not shine equally as its parts do. And although it appears deprived of a certain portion of its light, it is always of the same magnitude as it customarily appears when full of light; its horns therefore shine forth, because it is a body diffused into a circular form, and, as the light of one part fails, it seems to insinuate itself.”

[Col. 0407]

[Col. 0407B] Finally, many philosophers have stated that the sun is nineteen parts distant from the moon, reckoning the same number of parts as the moon is from the earth. Pythagoras, the most discerning of the Greek philosophers, calculated by geometrical measurement the distance separating heaven from earth, saying: from the earth to the moon there are 126,000 stadia; from the moon to the sun, twice that; and from there to the firmament, three times that. He also called these distances by musical names: from the earth to the moon, he said, there is a tone; from there to Mercury, a semitone; from Jupiter to Saturn, a semitone; and from Saturn to the firmament, three semitones. Altogether there are seven tones, by which the harmony of the octave is completed. A tone contains 7,812½ miles.

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—There are those who have attempted to investigate the winds. In this chapter Bede gives the reason why the horns of the waxing moon sometimes face upward toward the sky and at other times are lowered face-down toward the earth; he also explains why this phenomenon is not an indication of weather except accidentally. For it occurs according to a fixed principle arising from the difference of place from which the moon draws its light [Col. 0409D].

First, it is established that the moon does not shine with its own light but with another’s, namely, the sun’s, which lends light to all the stars. Next, since the sphere that is always luminous on one half— or, as Cleomedes proves, somewhat more than half, because of the sun’s size, whose rays illuminate somewhat more than a hemisphere, as optical writers also teach—must shine on the side that faces the sun, and since that side is often positioned so that it is slightly distant from the sun, the side opposite the sun cannot be facing the earth. Hence, according to the varying intervals between the sun and moon, different configurations appear to us.

But the reason why the horns sometimes face the sky—which occurs when the days are decreasing—is partly the sun and partly the moon’s position. For when, after the turning-point of the days, the sun descends toward the lower regions of the zodiac, the moon likewise draws its light from the sun below it. While this occurs, the circumference of the light is face-down, whereas its extremities, which are called horns, are turned upward. But when the days increase again, the moon has the sun positioned above it from a lower place. Hence the opposite occurs, as will easily be evident to anyone who can test the matter on a sphere or an astrolabe.]

[Col. 0403A]

There are those who, having attempted to investigate the winds, say that whenever the new moon is seen with both horns turned upward, it portends a stormy month; whenever one horn is upright, it portends fair weather. Natural reasoning reveals that the matter is quite otherwise. What then? Is it credible that the position of the moon, which remains fixed in the ether, can, because of changes in the winds or clouds lying beneath it [Col. 0404A], be turned in another direction from that in which it had been, and that, as if fearing future storms, it should raise one horn somewhat higher than the order of nature required? This is especially impossible since the same fluctuating wind cannot exist over all lands, whereas the moon’s position and its turning, according to the sun’s changing course, remain the same.

For they say, as blessed Augustine also teaches in his exposition of the tenth Psalm, that the moon does not possess its own light but is illuminated by the sun [Col. 0405A]. But when it is with the sun, it presents to us the side that is not illuminated, and therefore no light is seen on it. When it begins to withdraw from the sun, it is illuminated also on the side turned toward the earth, and necessarily begins at the horns, until it becomes full opposite the sun. Then it rises as the sun sets, so that anyone who has watched the setting sun, when he begins no longer to see it, may turn toward the east and see the moon rising.

From that point onward, as it begins to approach the sun from the opposite side, it turns toward us the side that is not illuminated, until it returns to the horns and then disappears altogether, because at that time the side that is illuminated is turned upward toward the sky, while the side which the sun cannot illuminate is turned toward the earth.

Therefore, as the day increases and the sun gradually rises from the southern regions toward the northern regions [Col. 0406A], the moon, which was born at that time, must outstrip the sun on its quicker passage toward the northern signs. Thus, when the new moon is seen after sunset and is going to set north of the sun’s setting-place, it is clearly situated not beside but above the sun. Since its lower side is illuminated, it appears to extend nearly equal horns and to move upward like a ship.

But when, after the summer solstice, the sun’s course turns back downward and southward, the moon born in those months must likewise direct its course toward the lower regions. Consequently, the moon that is going to set south of the sun that has set is, without any doubt, seen immediately after sunset not above the sun but beside it, situated toward the south. Therefore its northern sides are seen upright as it moves, with the sun looking upon them.

For the moon, with its horns turned away from the sun, always presents its rounded part toward it. According to this ordering, the longer the day, the higher the new moon; and the shorter and more southward-sloping the day, the lower the new moon appears [Col. 0407A].

From this arose the popular belief that when the moon moves high and lying on its back, it signifies storms; but when it is upright and lowered toward the south, it signifies calm weather [Col. 0408A]. This is because the condition of the revolving year is such that during the six months in which the days decrease, the movement of the air is much milder than during the other six months.

The same reasoning applies to the waning moon: it explains why at its morning rising it sometimes appears upright and sometimes lying on its back. It also explains why during the day it often proceeds face-down, namely because the sun’s rays strike it from a higher position [Col. 0409A].

Therefore the moon’s turning, which is natural and fixed, cannot portend the condition of the coming month. But those who are curious about such matters often investigate the future condition of the air from changes in the color of the moon, the sun, the sky itself, the stars, or the clouds, or from any other signs. Finally, they consider a fourth moon, if it is clear and has neither blunt horns nor horns dulled, to give an indication of fair weather for the remaining days until the month is complete, and they hold similar opinions about other such signs.

**CHAPTER XXVI. How, although the moon is lower in position, it is sometimes seen to be higher than the sun.**

[Note: [Col. 0410C]

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—There is no need for wonder. In this chapter Bede teaches from optical reasoning how the moon—which is much nearer to the earth than the sun—is sometimes seen from the earth to be higher than the sun. Although it is not truly so, the character of the place and the manner of seeing make it necessary for it to appear so, as we shall shortly demonstrate from the inner principles of the discipline itself.

“Finally, many philosophers.” This is taken word for word from the second book of Pliny’s *Natural History*, chapter 21, in full. It should be observed that, of these two opinions concerning the distances between the heavenly bodies, the Pythagorean is the more accurate. Although more of recent astronomy agrees with it, the latter nevertheless differs considerably from the Pythagorean opinion.

Alfraganus, whom people now follow very extensively, writes that the moon is C. IX MXXXVII.M. thousand paces from the earth. The distance from there to the sun comprises III.M.DXXXM.IXC.LXIII thousand paces—that is, “ten times three hundred, eight hundred thousand, nine hundred and sixty-three thousand paces” (the transmitted numerical expression is uncertain)—which agrees neither with Pythagoras nor with any other opinion; for the distance between the moon and the sun is more than thirty times the distance from the earth to the moon.

“For the zodiac is itself 365¼ parts long around the circuit of heaven.” Here you should understand “parts” not as people now commonly understand degrees, but as the amount of space which the sun traverses each day in the zodiac. Otherwise, we always understand “parts” as the thirtieth portion of one sign of the twelve-part zodiac.

[Col. 0411A] “Of these the sun traverses only two in the middle.” This too is taken from Pliny, from the *Catholic* [i.e. general] account of the stars; but there it reads: “The star of Mars traverses four middle parts, Jupiter one middle part and two above it, Saturn two, as does the sun.” Yet it is already sufficiently established that the sun moves through the middle part of the zodiac, which they call the ecliptic, without any inclination toward the north or south. Accordingly, the text should perhaps be read differently, somewhat as follows: “But the sun traverses none,” or else some other wandering of the sun is intended, which occurs through the apses upward and downward. Whatever the truth of the matter, Bede does not correctly adapt this passage to his subject.

“Each suspended in its own pharos.” By *pharos* he calls those crowns in which the arrangement of lamps from the bottom to the summit is such that the successive upper tiers are narrower than the lower ones, displaying the shape of a pyramid or tower. Such objects are suspended from the ceilings of sacred buildings, or such as are kindled at sacred funeral rites.

He proves from the manner of seeing that, among objects equally high, those nearer the summit appear higher. For example, in the floors of buildings, the part farther from the observer appears lower, while the nearer part appears higher, as Euclid also teaches in the *Optics*. Let the eye, for example, be B in the diagram below, situated beneath the plane FD. From it rays proceed: one to D, another to C, and a third to F. Of all the lines extending from point B to the elevated plane DF, the lowest is line BF; and line BC is also lower than line BD. For line DC is viewed through the two rays BD and BC, while CF is viewed through the rays BC and BF. Therefore DC must necessarily be seen as lower than CF.

[Col. 0411D] ]

There is no need for wonder when we see the moon, moving through the southern signs, revolve much lower and nearer to the earth than the sun when it remains in the same regions [Col. 0409B]. For the moon moves much lower not only than the sun but also than Venus and Mercury, which are the lowest of the stars; it runs along the boundary between this turbulent air and the pure ether.

Finally, many philosophers have stated that the sun is nineteen parts distant from the moon, reckoning the same number of parts as the moon is from the earth. Pythagoras, a man of discerning mind, calculated that there are 126,000 stadia from the earth to the moon, twice that distance from the moon to the sun, and three times that distance from there to the twelve signs.

But anyone who is concerned may rightly ask and wonder why, when the moon travels in the solstitial circle, it runs so much higher than the summer sun as to appear to make shadows shorter. The point must be briefly explained: the zodiac’s breadth produces this passage of the moon beyond the sun in both regions of the sky, namely the southern and the northern, and in the southern region the moon’s own descent also contributes to it.

For the zodiac itself is 365¼ parts long around the circuit of heaven [Col. 0410A], but twelve parts wide. Of these, the sun habitually traverses only the two middle ones, whereas the moon wanders through all of them.

When the moon reaches the southern regions, it appears somewhat lower than the winter sun, not only because it is nearer to the earth but also because it has sometimes passed approximately five or even six parts beyond the limits of the sun’s course toward the south. The farther it penetrates into the inner regions of the south, the lower it appears to our eyes, which observe it from the north.

But when it travels in the solstitial circle, it often appears somewhat higher than the summer sun. Since it is nearer to the earth than the sun, it sometimes also exceeds the limits of the sun’s course by five or six parts toward the north. Therefore, to our eyes—which are positioned on earth and look at both heavenly bodies from below—it appears to seek the heights of the sky the more elevated the farther it withdraws toward the north [Col. 0410B].

This can be demonstrated by the following example. At night you enter some very large house—certainly a church—remarkable in length, breadth, and height, and filled with an immense number of burning lamps in honor of the martyr whose birthday is being celebrated. Among these are two especially large and wonderfully constructed *pharos*, each suspended from the ceiling by chains. The one nearer to you as you enter is also nearer to the floor beneath it. But the house is so vast, and the height of the distant *pharos* so great, that in the darkness you can distinguish the light and locks of flame more easily than the actual vessels containing the fires.

When you begin to approach the *pharos* and raise your eyes directly toward it, and through it toward the opposite parts of the ceiling or walls [Col. 0410C], the *pharos* nearer to you appears higher. The closer you come, the more elevated the one that had seemed lower appears to you, until, having perceived the truth more accurately, you recognize that everything is positioned as it actually is [Col. 0411A].

So it is with us. Situated beneath the two great lights of heaven, and having both of them toward the south, the lower of the two rises northward and comes increasingly nearer to us. As we direct our eyes toward them and through them toward the sky, that body appears higher which, as clear reasoning shows, is actually moving lower.

**CHAPTER XXVII. On the magnitude and eclipse of the sun and moon.**

[Note: [Col. 0411D]

BRID. RAMES. GLOSSES.—They report that the sun is hidden from us by the intervention of the moon, and the moon by the interposition of the earth; but that an eclipse of the sun occurs only at the last or first moon, which they call conjunction, whereas an eclipse of the moon occurs only when it is full. They say that the whole sun cannot be taken away from the earth when the moon intervenes, if the earth is larger than the moon. They also say that eclipses of both heavenly bodies occur every year, on appointed days and at appointed hours beneath the earth. Yet although they occur above, they cannot always be seen everywhere, sometimes because of clouds [Col. 0412A], and more often because the globe of the earth obstructs them through the convexities of the world. They say also that an eclipse of the moon sometimes occurs in the fifth month after the preceding one, and an eclipse of the sun in the seventh month. They report that the same eclipse is hidden above the earth twice in thirty days, though this is seen by different people; and that once both heavenly bodies have been eclipsed within fifteen days [Col. 0412B]. They also report, as a remarkable phenomenon, that the moon has been eclipsed at its setting while both heavenly bodies were visible above the earth. But so that an eclipse would not occur every month, the breadth of the zodiac carries the moon above or below the sun.

“By the intervention of the moon.” When the body of the moon is placed between the sun and the earth on the middle line of the zodiac, through which the sun always travels, the sun’s light is taken away from the earth. For the sun’s light cannot pass through the body of the moon to those who are then beneath the moon; this is a solar eclipse.

But if the moon passes either here or there around that middle line, receiving light from the sun, it does not cause an eclipse of the sun. For it is then clearly situated not between the sun and the earth but at the side of the sun.

“By the intervention of the moon,” that is, by its interposition—not, however, as though the sun lost its own light, as the moon does. “And the moon,” that is, with the moon placed opposite between the sun and the earth. “By the objecting of the earth,” that is, by the earth’s interposition between the sun and the moon. For the sun is then beneath the earth, while the moon is above it. Or “by the objecting of the earth,” that is, by the earth’s shadow, when the moon, after sunset, rises into the higher regions. For the sun casts the earth’s shadow along its own line.

“To us,” that is, they report that it is hidden from human beings. The sun is said to fail improperly, because it suffers no diminution; but the moon truly fails in a plausible sense, because its light is entirely taken away, though only when it is full.

They report, namely, an eclipse of the sun. “At the last,” that is, on the thirtieth or twenty-ninth day, or on the first. And this does not occur every month, but only when the whole of its [text as supplied: *sui*] … The moon’s “conjunction,” that is, they say that its eclipse occurs only when it is full, that is, at the full moon.

They report that the sun cannot be taken away, that is, withdrawn or hidden, from the earth by the intervening moon—that is, by the moon’s coming between them. But the moon is larger than the earth, and therefore it can hide the sun’s light so that it is not seen on earth.

Martianus proves by uncertain arguments that the moon is larger than the earth. For when the moon is eclipsed in the southern parts of the world—that is, in Egypt and Ethiopia [Col. 0412D]—its shadow obscures no more than four climates: the first climate, Diameroes; the second, Diasenes; the third, Dialexandrias; and the fourth, Diarrhodu.

But geometers affirm that the eighteenth part of the entire circumference of the earth is contained within these four climates. Since that shadow is less than the lunar body by a factor of three—just as the moon exceeds its shadow threefold, as nine exceeds three—it follows that, since the lunar shadow covered an eighteenth part of the whole earth, the moon itself, whose shadow it is, must occupy a sixth of that same earth.

Therefore the earth is six times larger than the moon, while it is clear that the earth’s shadow exceeds the moon eighteenfold. Hence the moon’s shadow is an eighteenth part of the whole earth, whereas the moon itself is a sixth part of the earth.

They report that eclipses occur of both heavenly bodies, namely, the sun and the moon. “At appointed times,” that is, on the days and at the hours mentioned above; “beneath the earth,” not above but underneath.

Nevertheless, they cannot be seen everywhere—that is, from all parts of the earth—when they occur above the earth. “Above” is used adverbially, that is, upward or above the earth, because they sometimes occur beneath the earth.

“Because of clouds,” namely, they cannot be seen because when the sky is covered by clouds, even if the eclipse itself occurs, it is not visible to us. He says this of the moon, but not of the sun.
