“More often because the globe of the earth obstructs them,” they report that they cannot be seen everywhere. “Through the convexities,” that is, through the obliquities; and the word is in the dative case, because we say, “I obstruct you.”

“And an eclipse of the moon,” they report that it sometimes occurs “in the fifth month after the preceding one,” that is, after March or after the month in which the eclipse occurred. “But of the sun,” namely, an eclipse, “in the seventh,” namely, month, “after the preceding one,” that is, after September.

They report that the same eclipse of the sun and moon is hidden above the earth twice in thirty days, that is, that both have been eclipsed. This is not surprising. For the sun fails at the new moon, that is, at the first moon, and the moon at the full moon. Therefore the eclipses of both can occur within fifteen days.

“Once,” they report, “the moon was eclipsed at its setting,” while both heavenly bodies were above the earth: the sun already positioned in the west but still visible, and the moon situated in the eastern region.

The circle of the zodiac has twelve parts, that is, twelve paths, which the moon traverses each month. For the amount of space the sun travels longitudinally through the zodiac in twelve days is the same amount of space contained in the breadth of the zodiac.

The moon cannot undergo an eclipse unless it is on the line on which the sun is beneath it. Hence the different lines of the breadth of the zodiac through which the moon passes come to its aid so that it does not undergo an eclipse; the differing height of the apses also assists it in this. For at one time it is far from the earth, at another near.

When it is near, if the moon and sun are on the same line, the moon then undergoes an eclipse. When it is in those signs that are higher above the earth for us—that is, higher above our zenith—it does not undergo an eclipse. But when it is in those signs that are near the earth for us—that is, toward the south—it does undergo one.

“The breadth of the zodiac carries the moon above or below,” that is, transfers it. For if the moon always remained on the middle line of the zodiac, as the sun does, it would necessarily undergo an eclipse at every full moon. But because the sun always follows the middle line while the moon wanders through the whole breadth of the zodiac, it is not necessary for it to undergo an eclipse at every full moon. It can pursue its course above or below the sun, and is thereby freed by the breadth of the zodiac from undergoing an eclipse.

When, therefore, the sun above and the moon below meet on one line, the upper part of the moon is bright, while the lower part, which it presents toward the earth, meanwhile becomes dark.

Finally, it should be known that a solar eclipse is natural when the moon is first or thirtieth, because then the lunar body is placed opposite the solar body and makes the sun dark. If a solar eclipse occurs at another time, it is not natural but is a sign of something, as in the Passion of the Lord, when the moon was neither first nor thirtieth but fifteenth.

And so that this darkness of the sun should not be called sudden and abrupt, it was prolonged not for one hour only but also for three hours—that is, from the sixth hour until the ninth hour.

It should be believed that just as the sun then suffered darkness above the earth, so the moon beneath the earth withdrew the rays of its light, fulfilling the prophecy of Joel: “The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood.” The sun withdrew its rays so that it might not see its Lord dying on the cross; or else so that the Jews, the ministers of iniquity, might not enjoy its light.

An eclipse of the moon naturally occurs when it is fourteenth or fifteenth, because then it is accustomed to fall into the earth’s shadow and to be darkened. But if its eclipse occurs when it is ninth, eighth, or any other day, it foreshadows some sign.

[Col. 0414A] They say that the sun’s fire is nourished by water, that the sun is much larger than the moon, and that the moon is larger than the earth; hence all three appear to be of one size. The fact that the sun appears to us to be about a cubit in size is caused by the immense distance of its height. Otherwise, when it rises it would appear larger to the Indians, and when it sets larger to the Britons. Since it is fiery by nature, it also increases heat through its exceedingly rapid motion.

By its varying course it divides days, months, seasons, and years; and, by approaching or withdrawing according to the order of the seasons, it regulates the temperature of the air, lest, if it always remained in the same places, heat should consume some regions and cold others.

Poets call the sun fire, etc. They say that the sun’s body exceeds the moon threefold in size, while the moon is three times larger than the earth. Hence some ask why the earth is said to obscure the moon, if it is three times larger, when the moon falls into its shadow or even descends toward its more distant regions. This happens for the reason that a shadow is asserted to be three times larger than its body.

“Larger,” that is, greater. For the solar circuit is twelve times larger than the lunar, since the moon completes its course in one month, whereas the sun completes his in twelve. “Of one size.” The sun is indeed of such magnitude that he illuminates and fills everything with his light. Otherwise—that is, if he were not at such a height—the sun would appear larger when rising for the Indians, because the Indians are near him at his rising, and larger when setting for the Britons. “Setting,” that is, larger.

“By excessive motion,” that is, by rapid revolution and very swift course. He increases the heat, because every motion produces heat. “He”—that is, the sun—“by his varying course divides days, months, and seasons”: in summer his course is longer, in winter shorter. We also say that the sun moves by himself, not by turning with the world [perhaps *verti*, “to be turned,” rather than the transmitted *vergi*]. For if the sun remained fixed in the sky like the stars, all days and nights would be equal.

“And the tempering of the air,” that is, of heat and cold. “By approaching,” namely, toward the north in summer, or “by withdrawing,” namely, from us toward the south in winter. For when the sun rises toward Cancer from the equinoctial region, he produces summer for those who are between the solstitial and northern regions. When the sun descends from that same Cancer toward the equinoctial balance, he produces autumn; when he withdraws toward the winter solstice, winter is established, because when the heat has been removed, torpor invades. Again, when he rises from winter Capricorn toward the equinoctial Aries, the spring season smiles upon us; and when he proceeds from there once more toward Cancer, torrid summer returns.

“He distributes”: he arranges and orders. “Would remain in these places.” For example, if the sun were always in the south, the earth there would be scorched by his heat and Scythia would crack from the cold. For this reason God appointed different courses for the sun, as well as different seasons and places, so that, if he always remained in those regions, the world would not be consumed by daily heat. “The other”—namely, places—“cold would consume,” that is, destroy.

On the size of the sun and moon, blessed Ambrose, in the *Hexameron*, bears witness as follows:

**[Col. 0414D]** “The sun’s ray is no nearer to one person or farther from another; similarly, the orb of the moon is equal for everyone. The sun appears alike to Indians and Britons: at the same moment he is seen by both when he rises. Nor, when he inclines toward setting, does he appear smaller to those in the East; nor is he considered lower by those in the West than by those in the East. As far as the East is distant from the West,” he says, “so far are these regions distant from one another; but the sun is distant from no one: he is present to no one more, and remote from no one more. Nor should anyone be disturbed because, as though of cubit-size, he appears in his sphere when he rises. One ought instead to consider how great the space is between the sun and the earth—a distance which the weakness, and a certain infirmity, of our sight can scarcely traverse. The learned describe him as larger by several degrees than the earth.

“The ancients say that the moon is smaller than the sun. For everything that is nearer to us appears larger, whereas sight grows weak through the distance of places. We therefore see the moon as near to us, yet our sight does not see her as larger than the sun. And so, since the sun is higher than the moon and nevertheless appears larger to us, if he were to approach us, he would clearly appear much larger.”

Ambrose likewise says:

“What is the sun? The eye of the world, the delight of day, the beauty of heaven, the grace of nature, the excellence of creation. But when you see him, consider his author; when you marvel at him, praise his creator. If the sun, a fellow and participant of creation, is so pleasing, how good is that **SUN** of righteousness? If this sun is so swift that in his rapid courses he traverses everything by day and night, how great is he who is everywhere always and fills all things with his majesty? If he is admirable who is commanded to go forth, how far above admiration is he who says to the sun—and, as we read, it does not rise?”

**[Col. 0415B]** The sun is so called because he appears *alone* (*solus*), his radiance obscuring all the stars. The moon is called as though *lucina* (“the light-bringer”), with the middle syllable removed; concerning her Virgil says: “Chaste Lucina, favor us.” She received her name derivatively from the sun’s light, because she receives light from him and gives back what she has received.

And what is the sun? The splendor of heaven, the honor of day, and the distributor of hours. And what is the moon? The brightness of night.

Ambrose likewise says:

“For the sun is fiery. Fire both illuminates and scorches. Some say that the sun’s fire is nourished by water and receives the power of its light and vapor from the contrary element. Hence we frequently see the powerful sun dripping with water; in this there is clear evidence that he has taken up the element of water for his own tempering. From him come the hours; from him comes day when he has risen; from him also comes night when he has set; from him months and years are counted; from him the changes of the seasons arise. Although he is a good and gracious minister for regulating the changes of the seasons, yet whenever, according to the will of our God, correction is imposed upon mortals, he burns more fiercely, scorches the world with more violent flames, disturbs the air, imposes upon the earth a plague and corruption of human beings, and inflicts pestilence upon living creatures and a plague-filled year upon mortals everywhere.”

This concerns his nature. But according to spiritual understanding, the sun is Christ, as is also written in Malachi: “But for you who believe, the Sun of righteousness shall rise, and healing is in his wings.” Christ is rightly understood as having been called the sun, because according to the flesh he set at his death, while according to the spirit he rose again from his setting.

The sun likewise illuminates and scorches; in the dark season he warms healthy people, but burns those suffering from fever with the blaze of doubled heat. So Christ illuminates believers by the Spirit that gives life to their faith, while those who deny him he will scorch with the heat of eternal fire.

Haimo says:

“For Christ is not compared to the sun without reason. The sun has a rising and a setting; hence Solomon says: ‘The sun rises, and the sun sets, and returns to its place; and, rising there again, it circles toward the south and turns toward the north.’

**[Col. 0415D]** “The sun rose when Christ was born. He came to his setting when he died for us. Thus he returned to his rising, because his humanity is shown to have returned from the passion of death to the glory of resurrection. And, rising there again, he circles toward the south, because, rising from the dead, he enlightened the hearts of the disciples with the warmth of faith and the Holy Spirit. Those in whom the Sun of righteousness poured forth the greater warmth of the Spirit are rightly called the south.

“By circling toward the south, he turns toward the north, because he is brought, through the preaching of the apostles, to gather the Gentiles, among whom that cold wind held sway which, lifted up in pride, is reported first to have said: ‘I shall set my throne in the north.’ And what follows—‘The Spirit, traversing all things, proceeds’—pertains to this: the whole world is shown to be filled with preaching. Hence the words: ‘The voice of your thunder is in the wheel; your lightning flashes have shone forth,’ etc. And he returns to his circles, because after the gathering of the nations the multitude of the Jews will also be illuminated; and when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved.”

The learned say that the sun runs higher, while the moon is nearer to the earth. When, therefore, the moon descends to the same sign or line used by the sun, she places herself before the sun and produces darkness throughout the whole world. This, however, occurs at the monthly conjunction. For then the moon is in the same part of the sign as the sun and consequently becomes near to him; because of her opposition, his light appears to be obscured from our eyes. It is as if someone held an outstretched hand before another’s eyes: the more closely he did so, the less the other would be able to see; the farther away he withdrew, the more fully everything would appear to him.

**[Col. 0416B]** By a similar reasoning, when the moon reaches the sun’s place or line, she appears to be near him, and her disk so obstructs his rays before our eyes that his light cannot be cast forth. When the moon has withdrawn from that place, the sun casts his light and transmits it to our eyes. Thus the moon is placed before the sun, just as the earth is set against the moon. When the lights of either of these bodies do not reach the earth, they are said to have suffered an eclipse.

Nevertheless, our teachers have said mystically that the mystery of this eclipse was fulfilled in Christ. For then, when the course of the eternal covenant was interrupted, the elements, disturbed in their order, contrary to custom, lost their proper condition. The true sun, horrified by the sacrilegious deed of the conspiracy, inserted their darkness among the Jewish people, and for a little while hid himself through death; placed upon the cross, he concealed himself in the tomb and darkened himself, until on the third day he displayed to the world, and to the nations, the power of his glory, more august than usual. Like the sun shining in his strength, he illuminated the darkness of the ruined age.

The cause of this eclipse long remained obscure, but was explained by a certain Milesian philosopher. Miletus is a city or island, from which the Milesian came.

The moon does not fail, but is overshadowed; she suffers no diminution of body, but through the interposition of the earth that overshadows her, she undergoes a loss of light. This happens around the full moon—that is, on the fourteenth, fifteenth, or sixteenth day of the moon. It is therefore established that the moon receives her light from the sun’s rays, and that, when she cannot see the sun because of the earth’s interposition, she loses her light.

Figuratively, however, the Church’s sufferings are understood through the moon’s eclipse. When, through the slaughter of martyrs and the shedding of blood, the moon seems, as in that eclipse and darkness, to display a bloodstained face, this is so that we weak people may not be terrified by the Christian name. But just as the moon becomes bright after the eclipse through a clear illumination, so that she appears to have suffered no harm, so the Church, after shedding her blood for Christ through the confession of the martyrs, shines with a greater brightness of faith, and, adorned with more distinguished light, spreads herself more widely throughout the whole world.

**[Col. 0416D]** Concerning the size and eclipse of the sun and moon, Pliny the Elder, in his splendid work *Natural History*, described the matter as follows:

“It is clear that the sun is hidden by the intervention of the moon, and the moon by the interposition of the earth, and that the alternation is reciprocal: the moon, by placing herself between, removes the same rays of the sun from the earth, and the earth does the same to the moon. When the moon passes beneath the sun, sudden darkness covers the earth; and again, by the moon’s shadow, the star is dimmed. Night is nothing other than the shadow of the earth.

“Both eclipses are fixed rather than monthly, because of the obliquity of the zodiac and the moon’s many wandering deviations, as has been said, since the movement of the heavenly bodies does not always correspond at the same divisions.”

“‘At the divisions,’ that is, at the moments of the regions—that is, of the days. ‘At the divisions,’ that is, at the positions themselves or the lines. ‘Of the regions,’ that is, of the places. ‘The movement of the stars does not correspond’ along the same lines, at the same hours, on the same days, or under the same designation of year, month, and week.”

“He casts shadows for however many thousands of paces at equal intervals, as though he were midway through the entire space.”

“‘At equal intervals,’ that is, because when trees of the same size, separated from one another by however many thousands of stadia, have shadows of the same size, it is clear that the sun is midway between them all. Their shadows would not be equal unless the sun were midway between both. For the whole sun could not be taken away from the earth by the moon’s interposition if the earth were larger than the moon.”

Hipparchus, in the work entitled *On the Separations and Distances of the Sun and Moon*, teaches that the sun is 1,880 times greater than the earth, and that the earth in turn is twenty-seven times greater than the moon.

Martianus says that the moon is smaller than the earth, as has already been written above in the present chapter; another, on the contrary, says that the moon is larger than the earth. If anyone wishes to examine this disagreement carefully, let him place a compass at the center of the earth and draw it around in every direction to the limit; then let him do the same with the moon. Immediately, once he has done this, he will recognize from the compass’s measurement which of the two speaks more truly.

“It is certain,” he says, “that an eclipse of the sun occurs only at the last or first moon, which they call conjunction; an eclipse of the moon, however, occurs only when she is full and always only when she is as near as possible.” Every year there are eclipses of both heavenly bodies, on appointed days and hours beneath the earth; yet when they occur above, they are not visible everywhere, sometimes because of clouds, more often because the globe of the earth obstructs them. Through the curvatures of the world, this was discovered within two hundred years by the ingenuity of Hipparchus.”

“The eclipse of both bodies”—that is, of the sun and moon—“was first made widely known among the Roman people by Sulpicius Gallus, who was consul with Marcellus. Among the Greeks, Hipparchus was the first of all to investigate it. Nor is it surprising that in other nations others discovered this eclipse; so did the aforementioned Milesian.”

Blessed Jerome, interpreting the Gospel passage in which it is said that darkness occurred during the Lord’s passion, says the following as he explains this verse:

**[Col. 0417C]** “‘From the sixth hour darkness came over the whole earth until the ninth hour’: those who wrote against the Gospels suppose that there was an eclipse of the sun, which normally occurs at definite and fixed times, and that the disciples of Christ, through ignorance, interpreted it in relation to the Lord’s resurrection, although an eclipse of the sun can occur only at the rising of the moon. No one doubts, however, that at the time of Passover the moon was completely full. And lest it perhaps appear that the earth’s shadow, or the lunar orb opposed to the sun, had produced a brief and rusty darkness, a period of three hours is specified, so that every opportunity for such explanations might be removed. I think it happened so that the prophecy might be fulfilled which says: ‘The sun shall set at midday, and the light shall be darkened over the earth in the daytime.’ And elsewhere: ‘The sun set while it was still midday.’ It seems to me that the world’s clearest light—that is, the greater luminary—drew back his rays, either so that he would not see the hanging Lord, or so that he would not protect the impious blasphemers with his light.’”

Macrobius, in the first part of his book, recalls the following:

**[Col. 0417D]** Physicists chiefly wished to determine, in every investigation concerning the sun’s size, how much larger it could be than the earth. Eratosthenes, in his books of *Measurements*, says: “Multiplying the measure of the earth twenty-seven times produces the measure of the sun.” Posidonius says “many times more,” and each of them invokes the eclipse of the moon as evidence on his behalf. When they wish to prove that the sun is larger than the earth, they use the testimony of the eclipsed moon; when they attempt to establish the moon’s eclipse, they borrow their proof from the sun’s magnitude. Thus it happens that, while each point is constructed from the other, neither is established with probability, since their mutual testimony continually wavers between them. For what can be proved by means of something that itself still requires proof?

But the Egyptians, speaking not in conjectures, wished to prove, by an independent and unobstructed argument—not calling the moon’s eclipse to their aid—by how much the sun is larger than the earth, so that they might finally show, through his magnitude, why the moon is eclipsed.

They understood that this could in no way be discovered otherwise than by finding the measurements of both earth and sun, so that the distinction might be established by comparison. The measurement of the earth was readily determined by the aid of reason and the eyes. But they saw that the sun’s measurement could not be found except through the measurement of the heaven through which he travels. Therefore they first had to measure the heaven, which they established as the sun’s path, so that through it they might learn the sun’s size.

But, I ask, if anyone has ever been so idle, so released from every serious occupation—[*series*, genitive *seriei*, means the order of times or of any matter; *seriae*, however, are jars in which the ancients preserved must for many seasons. Hence Terence: “I filled all the casks, all the *seriae*.” This *serium* and this *seria* mean respectability, household property, or something prudent and useful. Hence Prudentius: “Serious things, playful things; words, jokes.”—] as to take up even such matters, would he not either recoil from or ridicule such an ancient undertaking as nearly insane?

Indeed, ingenuity made a way toward a matter that seemed naturally incomprehensible, and they discovered through the earth what the measure of heaven is. To make the reasoning of their invention clear, a few preliminary points must first be stated in an orderly fashion, so that access to what follows may be better prepared.

In every orb or sphere, the middle is called the center. The center is nothing other than the point by which the middle of a sphere or orb is distinguished through the most exact observation.

**[Col. 0418C]** Again, a line drawn from any point of a circle that marks its circumference to any summit of that same circle must divide some part of the orb; but the division does not necessarily separate half the orb. Only that line divides the middle of the orb into equal parts which is drawn from one summit to another in such a way that it must pass through the center. This line, which divides the orb equally, is called the diameter.

Again, every diameter of any orb, tripled and with one-seventh of itself added, gives the measurement of the circle enclosing the orb. Thus, if it contains seven inches, you triple seven, producing twenty-one. Add one-seventh, namely one, and you will declare that the measure of this circle is twenty-two inches, whose diameter extends seven inches.

We could prove all this by the clearest geometrical reasoning, but we suppose that no one doubts it and wish to avoid extending the volume beyond reasonable length.

It should also be known that the earth’s shadow—which the sun, traveling after sunset in the lower hemisphere, forces upward to be emitted, producing darkness over the earth called night—is multiplied sixty times in height from the measure of the earth’s diameter.

**[Col. 0418D]** Raised to this length toward the very circle through which the sun travels, it pours darkness back upon the earth by excluding the light. We must therefore determine the length of the earth’s diameter, so that it may be clear what can be obtained by multiplying it sixtyfold. With these preliminary matters stated, let us return to the discussion promised by the argument.

By the clearest and most certain measurements it has been established that the circumference of the whole earth—including every region where it lies inhabited or uninhabitable—is 252,000 stadia. Since its circumference is so great, its diameter is without doubt 80,000 stadia, or little more, according to the tripling with the addition of one-seventh that we explained above in the regular account of the diameter and circle.

Since, in producing the length of the earth’s shadow, it is not the earth’s circumference but its diameter that must be multiplied—for it is the diameter that must again be extended sixtyfold—you must multiply the earth’s 80,000-stadium diameter. This yields 4,800,000 stadia from the earth to the sun’s path, which, as we have said, is where the earth’s shadow reaches.

The earth is placed at the center of the heavenly circle through which the sun travels, like a center. Therefore the measure of the earth’s shadow constitutes half the diameter of the heavenly circle. If an equal measure is extended from the other side of the earth to that same circle, the complete diameter of the circle through which the sun travels is found.

**[Col. 0419B]** Doubling the 4,800,000 stadia therefore gives the complete diameter of the heavenly circle: 9,600,000 stadia. Once the diameter has been found, it easily reveals the measure of the circumference itself. You must multiply the sum that gave the diameter three times and add one-seventh, as has often already been said. You will thus find that the circumference of the entire circle through which the sun travels contains 30,000,170 stadia.

Having stated these points, by which the earth’s measure—whether circumference or diameter—and also the dimensions of the circle through which the sun travels, or its diameter, have been shown, we shall now indicate the sun’s measure and how those exceptionally intelligent investigators discovered it. For just as the size of the circle through which the sun moves could be discovered from the earth’s shadow, so the sun’s measure was found through that circle, by the following course of investigative ingenuity.

On the day of the equinox, before sunrise, a stone vessel was placed level. It was carefully curved in the shape of a hemisphere, and below, lines were marked in accordance with the twelve-hour number of the daytime; the shadow of an upright projecting rod would distinguish them as the sun passed by.

The function of such a vessel, as we know, is this: the shadow of the rod travels from one end of it to the other during the same length of time in which the sun measures half the heaven from rising to setting—that is, in the revolution of one hemisphere. For the complete revolution of the whole heaven comprises day and night. It is therefore established that the shadow moves through this vessel for as long as the sun moves through his circle.

**[Col. 0419D]** Once the vessel had been placed level, the attentive gaze of the careful observer remained fixed upon it around the time when sunrise was approaching. When, at the first ray emitted by the sun, the first summit of his emerging orb, whose shadow fell from the tip of the rod, touched the first projection of the vessel’s curved rim, the very spot that received the beginning of the shadow was marked by an impressed sign. The observer watched until, above the earth, the sun’s entire orb appeared in such a way that its lower edge still seemed to rest upon the horizon. Then the place to which the shadow had migrated in the vessel was marked.

By measuring the distance between the two marks of the shadows—which measured the complete solar orb, that is, the diameter marked by its two summits—one-ninth of the space contained between the upper rim of the vessel and the line of the first hour was found. From this it was established that, in the sun’s course, the repeated passage of his orb makes one equinoctial hour of time nine times over.

Since the revolution of the celestial hemisphere completes the day after twelve hours, and nine times twelve produces 108, there is no doubt that the sun’s diameter is one hundred and eighth of the equinoctial hemisphere. Therefore it is one two-hundred-and-sixteenth of the entire equinoctial circle.

It was proved earlier that this circle contains 30,000,170 stadia. If, therefore, you consider one two-hundred-and-sixteenth part of that sum, you will find the measurement of the sun’s diameter. That part is approximately 140,000 stadia. The sun’s diameter must therefore be said to be approximately 140,000 stadia.

Hence it is found to be almost twice the earth’s diameter. Geometrical reasoning establishes that, when the diameter of one of two spheres is twice that of the other, the sphere whose diameter is doubled is eight times larger than the other. Therefore, on these grounds, the sun must be said to be eight times larger than the earth. We have briefly excerpted these remarks on the sun’s magnitude from many others.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—On the size or eclipse of the sun. Since almost everything in this chapter is taken from Book Two, chapters 10 and 11, of Pliny’s *Natural History*, I think that explaining it belongs no more to Bede than to Pliny. Therefore, if the Lord grants me life, we shall discuss these matters more exactly on another, more convenient occasion.

“**For the whole sun could not be taken away.**” If this is the genuine reading in Pliny, as the manuscripts commonly have it, he is in serious error—although others defend him against that error—for he believed that the earth was smaller than the moon. But if, in place of the conditional particle *si* (“if”), you read *nisi* (“unless”), the statement will be true and suitable to the argument. Therefore, if we were permitted to alter something, consider whether it might be read as follows: “For the whole orb of the moon could not be taken away from the earth by the interposed shadow, if the moon were larger than the earth.” But I determine nothing here; perhaps he follows others without exercising his own judgment, so that the authority of the author whom he venerates may be regarded as greater.

“**At the rising of the moon.**” Understand “the moon’s rising” as the moon’s silence, or conjunction; otherwise the sense is not coherent.

Concerning the size or eclipse of the sun or moon, Pliny the Elder, in his splendid work *Natural History*, describes the matter as follows:

**[Col. 0412A]** “It is clear that the sun is hidden by the intervention of the moon, and the moon by the interposition of the earth, and that the alternation is reciprocal: the moon, by placing herself between, removes the same rays of the sun from the earth, and the earth removes them from the moon. When the moon passes beneath the sun, sudden darkness covers the earth; and again, by the moon’s shadow, the heavenly body is dimmed. For night is nothing other than the earth’s shadow.

“Both eclipses are fixed rather than monthly, because of the obliquity of the zodiac and the moon’s many wandering deviations, as has been said, since the movement of the heavenly bodies does not always correspond at the same divisions. This explanation lifts mortal minds into heaven and, as though for those contemplating from there, reveals the magnitude of the three greatest portions of nature. For the whole sun could not be taken away from the earth by the moon’s interposition if the earth were larger than the moon. From both phenomena the sun’s immense size is more certainly revealed, so that it is unnecessary to investigate by the evidence of the eyes and by conjecture of the mind the magnitude of that body which, standing midway through the entire space, casts the shadows of trees extended along boundaries at equal intervals over however many thousands of paces.”

And shortly afterward:

**[Col. 0417A]** “‘It is certain,’ he says, ‘that an eclipse of the sun occurs only at the last or first moon, which they call conjunction; an eclipse of the moon, however, occurs only when she is full and always only when she is as near as possible.’ Every year there are eclipses of both heavenly bodies, on appointed days and hours beneath the earth. Yet when they occur above, they are not visible everywhere: sometimes because of clouds, more often because the globe of the earth obstructs them through the convexities of the world. This was discovered within two hundred years by the ingenuity of Hipparchus.’”

But lest we seem to complete the chapter solely with the words of a Gentile, let us also ask what the teachers of the Church thought about this. Blessed Jerome, interpreting the Gospel passage in which it is said that darkness came over the earth during the Lord’s passion, says:

**[Col. 0420A]** “‘Those who wrote against the Gospels,’ he says, ‘suppose that there was an eclipse of the sun, which is wont to occur in spring and summer, and that the disciples of Christ, through ignorance, interpreted it in relation to the Lord’s resurrection, although an eclipse of the sun can occur only at the rising of the moon. No one doubts, however, that at the time of Passover the moon was completely full.’”

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Moon’s Effective Power

[Note: [Col. 0420C]]

**BRID. RAMES. GLOSSAE.**—On the moon’s effective power, blessed Bishop Ambrose, in Book Four of the *Hexameron*, records the following:

“Similar considerations concerning the moon are applicable to those which we mentioned concerning her companion and brother. ‘Blessed’ (*beatus*) is so called as though ‘well increased’ (*bene auctus*), namely, from possessing what he wishes and suffering nothing he does not wish. But the truly blessed person is one who possesses all the good things he wishes and wishes for nothing evil. From these two conditions the blessed person is made.

“‘Bishop’ (*antistes*) is as though ‘standing before’ (*ante stans*), that is, before the altar; hence some prefer to derive it from *antestis*. It is better, however, to derive it from the verb *antisto*, *antistas*, which means ‘I stand above’ and ‘I surpass,’ because he surpasses the whole people in dignity and honor.

“The sun is called the moon’s companion because they share the whole world equally.”

“Because my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the nights.” The head of Christ is God the Father; the curls, however, are the innermost thoughts of the saints, which do not flow loosely and disordered but are bound by the bond of fear and love of God. Dew and drops of the nights here signify minds made dark and cold by unbelief. The bridegroom’s head is therefore full of dew when worldly people grow numb toward the love of God, in accordance with what the Lord says: “Because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold.” And when such people persecute and hate the saints of God as they meditate on heavenly things, the bridegroom’s curls are, as it were, full of the drops of the nights.

For the elements also sympathize with the moon’s decline, and as she advances, those things that had been emptied are filled again, just as the brains of marine animals become moist.

It is indeed reported that oysters and many other things are found fuller when the lunar orb grows.

**[Col. 0421D]** The returning flow of the channels of the *euripi* also indicates this, as does the ebb and flow of the Syrtes, which are regarded as near the Ocean and which, according to the moon’s configurations, local inhabitants have reported to be stirred.

The Syrtes are sandy places in the open sea, exceedingly frightening and dangerous, because they customarily draw and tear everything toward themselves and, as the shallow sea approaches, hold fast whatever comes near. They lie near the Egyptian sea and are joined to it in the same way.

*Euripus* is interpreted as “the course of springs.” The *euripi* are channels of water that boil and surge more strongly when the moon is born.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—“Who also observe this.” Architects prescribe that timber should be cut from the beginning of autumn until the time before the west winds (*favonii*) begin to blow. See Vitruvius, *On Architecture*, Book II, chapter 9.

“But also the stone selenite.” This stone takes its name from the moon, which the Attic Greeks call σελήνη (*selēnē*, “moon”). According to Pliny, it is born in Arabia. I shall quote his words from the end of his last book:

**[Col. 0422C]** “Selenite shines through with a white color and honey-colored radiance; it contains the image of the moon and reproduces it day by day in the manner of her waxing and waning. It is thought to originate in Arabia.”

Marsilio Ficino also wrote much about this gemstone in his little book *On Obtaining Life from Heaven*. Dioscorides likewise mentions it, chapter 995. Albert the Great does so as well, in Book II of *On Minerals*.

“**The channels of the euripi.**” He uses *euripus* for any sea tide. *Euripus* is properly the name of that most famous tide between Attica and Euboea, into which some write that Aristotle threw himself headlong. Its tide is of an especially remarkable nature, as is evident throughout the writings of historians and natural philosophers.

On the moon’s effective power, blessed Bishop Ambrose, in Book Four of the *Hexameron*, records the following:

**[Col. 0421A]** “Similar considerations concerning the moon are applicable to those which we mentioned concerning her companion and brother, since she has undertaken the same ministry as her brother: to illuminate the darkness, warm the seeds, and increase the fruits. She also has many features distinct from her brother. For when the sun’s heat has dried the moisture of the earth throughout the day, the dew restores that moisture during the brief period of night. The moon herself is also said to be rich in dew. Finally, when the night is clearer and the moon remains awake throughout it, the dew is said to pour more abundantly over the fields, and many who rest beneath the open sky have noticed that the more they remained under the moon’s light, the more moisture they had gathered on their heads.

“Thus Christ also says in the *Canticles* to the Church: ‘Because my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the night.’ Then she diminishes and grows, so that she is smaller when she rises new, and, when she has waned, is filled again; in this there is a great mystery. For the elements also sympathize with her decline, and as she advances, those things that had been emptied are filled again, just as the moist brains of marine animals. Indeed, oysters and many other things are reported to be found fuller when the lunar orb grows. Those who have discovered this through habitual observation make the same claim concerning the inner parts of trees.”

The craft and daily practice of all architects also confirm these words of blessed Ambrose. They teach that particular care should be taken to cut trees from the fifteenth moon through the twenty-second, when the timber is intended either for constructing light boats (*liburnae*) or for any public works. Only during these eight days does the cut timber remain free from decay; on the other days, timber cut even in the same year is consumed by the internal gnawing of worms and reduced to powder.

They also observe that timber should be cut after the summer solstice—that is, after the month of July—and in August, through the Kalends of January. For during these months, as the moisture dries out, the wood is drier and therefore stronger.

The stone selenite in Persia likewise wonderfully demonstrates the effect of lunar power. Containing the image of the moon, it shines through with a white, snowy brilliance and is said to increase or diminish each day in accordance with the course of that heavenly body.

Basil, the most reverend Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, writes things consistent with this in Book Six of the *Hexameron*, saying:

**[Col. 0422A]** “I think that the moon’s changes also contribute no little formation to the creation of animals and to all the other things that the earth produces. At one time their bodies appear looser and emptied, when the moon wanes; at another they appear whole and filled, when she waxes, because she secretly infuses into them a certain moisture mingled with heat. Those who sleep beneath the open sky in the moonlight demonstrate that this is so: after rising, they find their heads wet with abundant dew. Fresh meats, too, if they lie beneath the moon, quickly become corrupted by fluid putrefaction. The same is indicated by the brain of sheep, and also by the viscera of marine animals, which are more moist, as well as by the marrow of trees.”

And shortly afterward:

**[Col. 0422B]** “The movement of the air is also governed by these same changes, as the moon’s new phase attests. After a long period of calm weather, it suddenly raises clusters of clouds and disturbances. The returning flow of the channels of the *euripi* also indicates this, as does the ebb and flow of the Syrtes, which are regarded as near the Ocean and which, according to the moon’s configurations, local inhabitants have reported to be stirred.

“The *euripi* also customarily turn their gentle currents in both directions during all the rest of the time. But when the moon is born, they cannot remain still in any way; they surge continually with violent agitation until the moon appears again and brings calm to the stirred whirlpools.”

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Concord of the Sea and the Moon

[Note: [Col. 0422D]]

No sooner does the moon pass by than [the tide], itself receding, leaves this measure to its native sweetness, as though it were unwillingly drawn onward by certain breaths of the moon; and, when her force again ceases, it pours back into its proper measure. The tide of the Ocean follows the moon, as though drawn backward by her breathing and, when her impulse has withdrawn, poured back again. It appears to flow in and ebb twice each day, after a delay of three quarters of an hour and a half-uncia (47½ minutes); and its entire course is divided into *laedones* and *malinae*, that is, lesser and greater tides. The *laedon*, beginning on the twenty-fifth day of the moon, advances for as many hours as it retreats; but the *malina*, beginning on the thirteenth and twenty-eighth days, is swifter in its advance but slower in its retreat. It persists for seven days and twelve hours, always displaying the first and fifteenth moons at its midpoint, and swelling more powerfully than usual at the equinoctial solstices. Every eight years, according to the beginnings of its motion and equal increases, it is brought back to the same starting points by the moon’s most certain cycle.

The moon always remaining in the north produces milder tides than when, having moved toward the south, she exerts her force with a nearer impulse. For the advance and retreat of the sea, and likewise the *malina* and *laedon*, follow naturally, and so forth. This gloss has therefore already been written above, in chapter 15, because what is said here and there agrees sufficiently.

Again, on the concord of the sea and the moon.

[Col. 0423A] Just as the moon, through the natural slowness of her course, returns from west to east in the evening over twelve days, so also the tide of the Ocean, now an evening tide, becomes a morning tide over fifteen days; or, with the daily delay removed from the morning tide, the evening tide rises. And just as the moon customarily rises and sets each day four points later than she rose or set the previous day, so also the tide of the sea—whether it is a daytime and evening tide, or a morning and evening tide—does not cease each day to arrive later and return later, at nearly the same interval.

The question why, in fifty-nine days, the moon does not make fifty-nine circuits around the earth is answered as follows. The moon makes two courses: one with the firmament, which revolves around the earth in twenty-four hours, and another against the firmament. For the firmament circles the earth fifty-nine times in fifty-nine days; but because the moon does not cease making one course against the firmament, the course [text uncertain]. Thus, in her two months, that is, in fifty-nine days, she circles the earth no more than fifty-seven times.

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—The nature of the Ocean is by far the most astonishing of all. Most of this material is also taken from Pliny, book II, chapter 97. Bede distinguishes the tide of the sea into two kinds, one of which he calls *malina*, from the greater moon—through corrupted forms of the word, for that is when it occurs—and the other *laedon* or *laedona* (for I find both forms in Bede), as though meaning a “wounded wave.” I have not, however, found these terms elsewhere.

[Col. 0422C]

Most astonishing above all is so great a partnership of the Ocean with the moon’s course. At every rising and every setting of the moon, the Ocean likewise sends forth the force of its swelling, which the Greeks call *ῥεῦμα* (*rheuma*, “current” or “flow”), and spreads it widely over the shores; when that force is recalled, it uncovers them again. It also abundantly mingles and gathers the sweet currents of rivers together with the salty waves. No sooner does the moon pass by than the tide, itself receding, leaves these things to their native sweetness and measure, as though unwillingly drawn onward by certain breaths of the moon; and, when her force again ceases, it pours back into its proper measure. For just as the moon, as we have also taught above, customarily rises and sets each day four points later than she rose or set the previous day, so also each of the sea’s tides—whether it is a day tide and a night tide, or a morning and evening tide—does not cease to come later and return later each day, at nearly the same interval. A point is one-fifth of an hour, for five points make an hour. Hence, because in her two months, that is, in fifty-nine days, the moon circles the earth fifty-seven times, the Ocean tide in the same period rises toward the upper shore twice that number of times, namely 114 times, and withdraws back into its channel an equal number of times. For in twenty-nine days the moon makes twenty-eight circuits around the earth, and in the twelve hours remaining to complete the natural month she makes half a circuit of the earth. Thus, for example, the moon which in the previous month followed the sun above the earth at midday now follows it beneath the earth at midnight, when the sun is to be kindled; over the same period, therefore, the tides are doubled in their occurrences, fifty-seven times.

[Col. 0425B] The deep seas swell,

the barriers broken, and then settle back into themselves. For in half a month, that is, in fifteen nights and days, the moon circles the earth fourteen times, and in addition once circles half the earth. Thus, when full, she occupies the east in the evening, whereas previously, when new, she had occupied the west in the evening. During that time the sea flows and ebbs twenty-nine times. And just as, over fifteen days, as we said, the moon, through the natural slowness of her course, returns in the evening from west to east, so that what today was a morning moon occupying the east will, fifteen days later, be seen as a morning moon in the west, so also the tide of the Ocean, now an evening tide, becomes a morning tide after fifteen days; conversely, the morning tide, with its daily delay removed, rises as an evening tide.

And because over a year—that is, over its twelve months, which comprise 354 days—the moon circles the earth 342 times, twelve times fewer, the Ocean tide in the same period washes over and withdraws from the shores 684 times. The sea imitates the moon’s course not only in its common advance and retreat, but also in a perpetual increase and decrease of its condition, so that each day the tide returns not merely later than on the preceding day, but also greater or smaller. The rising tides they have chosen to call *malinae*, and the declining tides *ledones*. By alternating successively over seven or eight days, they divide each month among themselves through the fourfold variety of their changes.

Often each completes its course in an equal allotment of seven and a half days; often, whether because winds drive them forward or backward, or because some other natural force intervenes and compels them, they arrive earlier or later and swell more or less violently than usual. Thus sometimes, when their order has been disturbed, the *malina* claims more tides for itself in one month and fewer in another. For this reason either movement is accustomed sometimes to arise with the evening tide and sometimes with the morning tide.

If it happens that a *malina* begins with an evening tide, either at the new moon or at the full moon, then during the following seven days of the *malina* that same tide becomes greater and more violent than the morning tide. Likewise, if a *malina* has arisen with the morning tide, the morning tide, now the greater, covers the land with a larger expanse of sea for several days. The evening tide, however, confines itself to the boundaries at which the morning tide had begun and declines to extend its course farther, although in some months each tide advances with an entirely unequal increase.

The more extensively the greater tide has covered the shores and lands and filled the rivers and straits, the more widely, when it recedes, it customarily drains and bares those same shores. Hence let anyone who can judge whether the report is true consider what some people, with Philip as their witness, assert and affirm: that the immense outpouring of the Ocean sea through the rivers of all regions and countries occurs at a single point in time.

For we who inhabit the different shore of the British sea know that when this sea begins to swell, another begins at that very hour to subside from its tide. From this some people infer that, as a wave recedes from one place, it runs back toward another, and that, after abandoning the shores it had reached, it hastens to return to those it had previously left. For this reason, they say, when the greater *malina* departs from these shores, it withdraws farther for a time, so that, arriving elsewhere, it may be able to overflow more abundantly. This can readily be understood from the moon’s course.

For example, when this sea lies near the winter rising of the sun or the summer setting of the sun, the moon, whatever her age, whether she is above the earth or beneath it, usually raises the tide; but when she lies near the winter setting of the sun or the summer rising of the sun, she turns it back. In other regions, the moon’s recession from that part of the sky indicates the sea’s advance here. Moreover, even on one and the same shore, those who live farther north customarily receive and return the entire tide of the sea much earlier than I do, while those who live farther south receive and return it much later. In every region the moon maintains the rule of association with the sea that she has once established.

Thus we have found that the *malina* usually begins about five days before the new or full moon, and the *ledon* about the same number of days before the half moon. Around the two equinoxes the tides rise greater than usual; they are empty at midwinter and still more so at midsummer. Natural reason compels us to observe that the tides always flow more mildly when the moon is in the north and farther removed from the earth than when, having moved into the south, she exerts her force with a nearer impulse. Over nineteen-year periods, according to the order of the lunar cycle, the course of the sea likewise returns to the beginnings of its motion and to equal increases.

CAPUT XXX. On the equinoxes and solstices.

[Note: [Col. 0425D]

BRID. RAMES. GLOSSAE.—There are thought to be two solstices and two equinoxes: on the eighth day before the Kalends of January and July, and on the eighth day before the Kalends of April and October—that is, in the portions of Capricorn and Cancer, and of Aries and Libra. But the equinoctial day is equal throughout the whole world. Because the increase of daylight varies, the longest day at Meroe contains twelve equinoctial hours and eight parts of an hour; at Alexandria, fourteen hours; in Italy, twelve; and in Britain, seventeen. There the bright summer nights plainly testify to what reason compels us to believe: when the sun approaches more closely to the world’s summit at the solstice, the earth beneath it has continuous days for six months within the narrow circuit of light, and conversely nights for six months when the sun withdraws toward winter. Pythias of Massilia writes that this occurs on the island of Thule, six days’ sailing north of Britain.

That the equinoxes must be observed on the eighth day before the Kalends of April and the eighth day before the Kalends of October, and that the solstices must be observed on the eighth day before the Kalends of July and the eighth day before the Kalends of January, is clearly the opinion of many wise men of the age and of Christians. Since the sun completes his course without interruption and never fixes himself in a stationary condition, why is it called a solstice? “Solstice” means the sun’s station—not because he ever stood without motion, but because he establishes the limits of his height or depth: the limit of his ascent toward the north in Cancer and of his descent toward the south in Capricorn, which he never surpasses. Isidore, in the sixth book of the *Etymologies*: “*Canon* in Greek is called *regula* in Latin. A rule is so called because it leads straight,” and so forth.

For it is not only the institution of our own time, but also the legal and Mosaic ordinance, that the Paschal feast must not be celebrated before the day of this equinox has been passed, as Philo and Josephus clearly teach, as Anatolius testifies. In book VII, chapter 28, of Eusebius of Caesarea’s *Ecclesiastical History*, which blessed Jerome translated from Greek into Latin, we find the following written:

“Many small works also, magnificently composed by Anatolius, have come down to us. From among them I think it worthwhile to present in his own words what he thought concerning Easter. He says: ‘In the first year, the beginning of the first month is on the twenty-sixth day of Phaminoth; according to the Macedonians, on the twenty-second day of the month Dystros; but according to the Romans, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. On that day the sun will be found not only to have ascended through the first part, but already to possess a quarter of it—that is, the first of the twelve parts. This portion, the first of the twelve, is the vernal equinox; it is itself the beginning of the months, the head of the circle, and the completion of the course of the stars, which are called planets, that is, wanderers. It is also the end of the twelfth portion and the boundary of the entire age. Therefore we say that those who think Easter should be celebrated before the beginning of this new year are committing no small offense.

“‘Nor does this calculation take its beginning from us. It is demonstrated to have been established among the Jews from the most ancient times and observed before the coming of Christ, as Philo and Josephus plainly teach. Even earlier than these were Agathobulus, and Aristobulus of Paneas, who was instructed by him. Aristobulus was one of the seventy elders who had been sent by the priests to Ptolemy, king of the Hebrews, to translate the Hebrew books into Greek. They answered many questions put to them by the king concerning the traditions of Moses.

“‘When they were expounding the questions raised by Exodus, they said that Passover must not be sacrificed before the vernal equinox had passed. Aristobulus adds this also: on the day of Passover it must be observed not only that the sun has passed the vernal equinox, but also the moon. For since there are two equinoxes, of spring and autumn, separated by equal intervals, and since the fourteenth day of the first month is appointed as a solemnity after evening, when the moon is found opposite the sun and directly facing it—as may also be confirmed by the eyes—it follows that the sun occupies the portion of the vernal equinox, while the moon, conversely, occupies that of the autumnal equinox.’

“I have read many other matters set forth in their books concerning these most forceful arguments, which clearly show that the solemnity of Easter must in every respect be celebrated after the equinox.”

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—Concerning the equinox, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. Thus far he has spoken of the months, the effects of the moon, and their other circumstances; next Bede proceeds to discuss the times derived from the sun’s course. These are first the four divisions of the seasons—spring, summer, autumn, and winter—which existed among several peoples as divisions of the year. For just as the moon produces the month, so the sun, by his course, determines the revolving year and its principal parts.

It may be worth noting in passing that these seasons—spring, summer, and the others—are divided in various ways. The common people and physicians define spring differently and assign it a different number of days from mathematicians or natural philosophers. The common people divide the year into three-month periods, making March, April, and May spring; the next three months summer; and so on with the rest. According to the sun’s course, however, these seasons begin later than the months. The natural and true beginning of spring is the sun’s entry into the first part of Aries; summer extends from the beginning of Cancer to the beginning of Libra; from there to the first part of Capricorn is autumn; finally, winter occupies the remainder of the zodiac. Each of these portions contains 91 days and 7 hours. You will learn the beginnings and ends of these seasons above, from the table concerning the true motion of the sun.

Others divide these portions unequally, taking account of the sun’s motion through the eccentric circle, which is swifter through the quadrants of the lower apsis, as we explained in the scholia on the first book. This division was also used by certain ancients, by Marcus Cato in *On Agriculture*, and by Varro. Thus, from winter to the equinox there are 94 days; from there to the solstice, the same number and a half; from the solstice to the autumnal equinox, 92 and a half; and from there to winter, no more than 88, since the sun travels through the narrower quadrant of his eccentric, as the figure we placed in book I shows. I see that ancient physicians also used this same division.

Hippocrates, the *ἀρχίατρος* (*archiatros*, “chief physician”), writing to King Antigonus, also says the following. Bede’s memory has failed him in attributing this letter to Hippocrates, since no work by Hippocrates is thought to survive addressed to Antigonus. They attribute the letter instead to Paul of Aegina; it appears in his *Medicine*, book I, chapter 100. I have therefore thought it appropriate to insert here the words that Bede cites rather carelessly. They are as follows, in the translation of Johannes Andernacus. The solstices of the year, during which these conditions usually arise, must not be passed over in silence; but we shall briefly explain what foods are appropriate to each, beginning with winter.

Winter solstice.

From the winter solstice to the vernal equinox, catarrhs and moistures increase in human beings. Therefore one should use warmer foods, drink more abundantly and stronger wine, drink from the organ, and also indulge in sexual intercourse. The days up to the equinox number ninety.

[Col. 0430C] Vernal equinox.

At this time phlegm increases in human beings, and the sweet serum of the blood continues until the rising of the Pleiades. At that time especially, juicy and sharp foods should be taken; the body should be exercised; sexual intercourse is safest. There are forty-six days up to the rising of the Pleiades.

The rising of the Pleiades.

This season of the year advances black bile up to the autumnal equinox. Therefore cold water and everything fragrant should be used. Sexual intercourse is harmful; or, at least, use it more harmlessly according to the prescriptions we have given. There are ninety-three days up to the autumnal equinox.

Autumnal equinox.

This part of the year generates an abundance of phlegm and thin discharges until the Pleiades set. At that time it is appropriate to draw the humors from the head and to take the sharpest and most nutritious foods; one should not provoke vomiting, but should exercise and avoid sexual intercourse. The days up to the setting of the Pleiades number forty-six.

The setting of the Pleiades.

At this time phlegm overflows in human beings until winter. Therefore one should take the most bitter foods, the sweetest wine, use fatty foods, and exercise. There are forty-five days up to the winter solstice.

On the setting of the Pleiades. The Pleiades are seven stars above the neck of Taurus, although only six are seen. Aratus gives the reason for this in the *Phenomena*. In Greek they are called *Pleiades*, from their plurality; in Latin, *Vergiliae*, from spring, because they rise at the time when the sun is with them—that is, as astronomers and poets say, when they set. This occurs when the sun approaches Taurus. For further material that contributes to a clearer understanding of this chapter, consult the scholia and diagrams in the book *On the Nature of Things.

Concerning the equinoxes, which must be observed on the eighth day before the Kalends of April and the eighth day before the Kalends of October, and concerning the solstices, which must be observed on the eighth day before the Kalends of July and the eighth day before the Kalends of January, the opinion of many wise men of the age and of Christians is widely evident. Finally, Pliny Secundus, at once orator and philosopher, says in book II of the *Natural History*:

“The sun himself has four distinctions: twice he makes day equal to night, when, in spring and autumn, he falls upon the center of the earth, in the eighth degrees of Aries and Libra; twice he changes the intervals, increasing the day at winter in the eighth degree of Capricorn and, at the summer solstice, increasing the night by the same amount in the eighth degree of Cancer. The cause of equality is the obliquity of the zodiac, since an equal portion of the world is made above and below the earth at every moment. But the signs that rise straight at their rising retain the light for a longer course, whereas those that rise obliquely pass through it in a shorter interval.”

Hippocrates, the *ἀρχίατρος* (“chief physician”), writing to King Antigonus concerning how he should regulate himself throughout the year in order to prevent weakness, says:

“Let us therefore begin from the solstice, that is, the eighth day before the Kalends of January. From that day moisture increases in the bodies until the vernal equinox, a period of ninety days. This time increases human phlegm, from which catarrh, discharge from the uvula, pain in the sides, dimness of vision, and ringing in the ears frequently arise, and people become unable to smell anything. At such a time, therefore, use hot and laser-flavored foods, and excellent foods containing pepper and mustard; rarely use wool; cleanse the head without interruption; indulge in wine; do not spare Venus, for forty-five days.

“Next come ninety days from the aforesaid day up to the vernal equinox. From the aforesaid day, the eighth before the Kalends of April, to the eighth before the Ides of May, there are forty-five days. During these days sweet humors, that is, blood, increase in human beings. Use foods that smell good and are very sharp.

“Likewise, from the eighth day before the Ides of May to the eighth day before the Kalends of July there are forty-five days. During these days bitter bile, that is, red choler, increases. Use sweet foods, indulge in wine, spare Venus, and do not undertake fasting.

“Then the summer season begins on the eighth day before the Kalends of July. At that very moment the increase of red bile ceases and black choler increases; this continues until the autumnal equinox, that is, until the season of cold. Use all sweet and fragrant foods, and foods that are cooler and soften the bowels, for ninety days.

“From the autumnal equinox, which begins on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, until the eighth day before the Kalends of January, the bitterness of black bile ceases and the thickness of the humor increases. Use all hot and sharp foods, abstain from Venus, and wash your hands.

“From the day written above until the setting of the Pleiades—that is, until the sixth day before the Ides of February—there are forty-six days, up to the setting of the Pleiades. During this period blood increases in human beings. It is therefore appropriate to eat the most splendid [or, perhaps, ‘most luxurious’] foods, and to indulge in wine and Venus. These winter days number forty-seven.”

These are the teachings of pagans. Many teachers of the Church have handed down similar teachings concerning the seasons, saying that on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, at the vernal equinox, the Lord was conceived and suffered; that he was born at the winter solstice, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January; that the blessed forerunner and baptizer of the Lord was conceived at the autumnal equinox, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October; and that he was born at the summer solstice, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July. They add the explanation that it was fitting for the author of eternal light to be conceived and born together with the increase of temporal light, while the herald of repentance, whom it was necessary to diminish, was likewise generated and conceived with the beginning of the decrease of light.

But since, as we learned in the calculation of Easter, the vernal equinox is specifically marked by the opinion of all Easterners, and especially of the Egyptians, who are known to be highly skilled in calculation, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, we think that the other three divisions of the seasons should likewise be marked somewhat earlier than common writings indicate.

To speak briefly of the vernal equinox, which the origin of the world teaches to be the head of the four mentioned annual changes, ecclesiastical observance, confirmed by the Council of Nicaea, maintains that the day of Easter must be sought between the eleventh day before the Kalends of April and the seventh day before the Kalends of May. Likewise, the rule of Catholic institution commands that Easter not be celebrated before the passage of the vernal equinox.

Therefore, anyone who thinks that the equinox falls on the eighth day before the Kalends of April must necessarily either say that it is lawful to celebrate Easter before the equinox, or deny that it is lawful to celebrate Easter before the eighth day before the Kalends of April. He must also affirm either that the Easter which the Lord celebrated with his disciples on the day before he suffered did not occur on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, or that it occurred before the equinox. For it is not only the institution of our own time, but also the legal and Mosaic ordinance, that the Paschal feast must not be celebrated before the day of this equinox has been passed, as Philo and Josephus clearly teach, with Anatolius as witness; so also their predecessors Agathobulus and Aristobulus of Paneas, instructed by him, teach this. Aristobulus was one of the seventy elders who had been sent by the priests to Ptolemy, king of the Hebrews, to translate the books into Greek, and who answered many questions put to them by the king concerning the traditions of Moses.

When they were expounding the questions raised by Exodus, they said that Passover must not be sacrificed before the vernal equinox had passed. Therefore, to preserve the rule of truth, we must state openly that Passover must not be sacrificed before the equinox and the darkness have been overcome, and that this equinox must truly be assigned to the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, as we are taught not only by the authority of the fathers but also by consideration of the horological calculation. The other three boundaries of the seasons must likewise, by similar reasoning, be marked several days before the eighth day before the following Kalends.

CAPUT XXXI. On the unequal length of days and the varying condition of shadows.

[Note: [Col. 0431C]

BRID. RAMES. GLOSSAE.—In the part of Italy called Venetia, the shadow of the gnomon is equal to the height of the gnomon at the same hours. The farther one withdraws from the sun, the nearer the sun appears to the earth itself, and the longer the shadows grow. Thus in Italy, as the ancients also wrote, around the day of the Lord’s birth, nine feet are measured in the shadow of a human figure at the sixth hour. I, however, established in Gaul, in a place called Teotonis Villa, measured the shadow of my height and found it to be nineteen and a half feet.

Likewise, in the opposite direction, the nearer one approaches the sun toward midday, the shorter the shadows always appear, to such an extent that at the summer solstice, when the sun is at mid-heaven, no shadows are seen in Egypt, Jerusalem, or places situated in their region. In Arabia, however, at that very time the sun is seen above at mid-heaven toward the north, while the shadows, conversely, appear toward the south. Again, on the island of Meroe, the city of Asine, the capital of the Ethiopian people, is situated on the river Nile.

The shadow of the navel, which they call the gnomon, in Egypt at midday on the day of the equinox is a little more than half the length of the gnomon. In the city of Rome, one-ninth of the gnomon is lacking from the shadow. In the town of Ancona, one thirty-fifth remains. Likewise, five thousand stades beyond Alexandria, at midday on the day of the solstice, no shadow is cast, as also in India above the river Hypasis. They say that the same thing occurs among the Troglyodites forty-five days before and after the solstice, while during the intervening ninety days this shadow falls toward the south. On the island of Meroe, five thousand stades from the Nile city of Asine, shadows are also consumed twice a year, when the sun occupies the twelfth part of Taurus and the fourteenth of Leo.

Meroe is the greatest of all islands. In it is the city of Syene, which has a well that philosophers once dug, wishing to test whether the sun penetrated to its bottom. Descending into it, they saw the sun’s rays illuminating its bottom at midday; from this they discovered that at that time the sun stood directly above the place—namely, on the forty-fifth day.

BRIEF SUMMARY.—“The equinoctial day is equal and one throughout the whole world,” and shortly afterward: “The horoscopes’ vessels are not equally useful at three hundred stades, or, at the greatest distance, at five hundred, where the shadows of the sun change.”

The vessels of the horoscope—that is, certain instruments made in vessels of water and in a bowl, by which they could determine the exact hour—are not alike in every region. *Scopon* in Greek means “intention” in Latin. *Horoscopus* is a compound name from *horologium* and *scopon*. A horoscope is a horological intention. “They are not equally useful” means that they are not equal.

Eratosthenes, the most precise of geometers, placed horoscope vessels at intervals throughout different locations and, on one day, caused the shadows at midday to be observed and recorded everywhere, noting their length. Thus he discovered that beyond five hundred stades the shadow did not correspond to a gnomon of the same length. The stade is a Greek measure. It is said to derive from *stare*, “to stand,” because Hercules, running there in a single breath, stood after 125 paces. By this measure the Greeks measured the places where they held games; there, while playing, walking about, and practicing athletic exercises, they paced out the distance.

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—“The equinoctial day.” The equinoctial day is produced by the sun when he travels beneath the equinoctial circle. This circle receives its name from the fact that it makes nights equal to days, just as *aequidialis* is so called because it makes days equal to nights. Among the Greeks it is likewise called *ἰσημέρινος* (*isēmerinos*) and *ἰσονύκτιος* (*isonuktios*). It is also called the equator because this circle is arranged in the sphere so that, being equidistant from the poles, it divides the whole sphere into two equal parts.

Since it lies midway between the north and south, it is necessary that all peoples receive an equal amount of light when the sun is beneath this circle, as is clear from the revolutions of the sphere described by Euclid. But when the sun is in the parts of the zodiac that incline toward the south, our daylight is shorter and our night longer. The opposite occurs when the same star is in those regions of the sky that lie on this side of the equinoctial circle, near our zenith.

From this varying height of the sun follows the variation of shadows. For when the sun is low, as happens when he is nearer the earth, the shadows of bodies are long; when he is high, they are short, as at midday. This requires no proof. It should be understood, however, that when writers discuss the measurement of shadows, they always mean midday shadows. Other shadows are disregarded unless the increase of shadows is being described for each hour of the day, as happens in writers on agriculture.

We too shall add here a diagram of this sort, which we found in a written copy. The measurement of shadows, called gnomonics, in cosmography means midday shadows. Thus Germany always has shadows on the right, that is, lying toward the north. For among poets the north is the right-hand part of the world, since they turn their faces toward the west.

Even at midday, when the sun is present, he does not always have the same height. In winter he is low even at midday; in summer he is high, and on each day he has a different height at midday. Hence the variation of shadows arises. Learned men, however, observe only three shadows throughout the entire year: the winter, equinoctial, and summer shadows, and they do this in different regions. Since on any given day the midday sun is higher at Rome than on that same day at Cologne or in Britain, it follows that, at the same time, the shadows of a gnomon—that is, a perpendicular object ten feet high, for example—are shorter at Rome than at Cologne, and shorter at Cologne than in Britain.

Cosmographers teach this gnomonic method so that from it we may determine the position of regions in relation to the parts of the sky. There is another method of measuring shadows according to individual days and hours, by which people in the fields determine times and moments; this is taught by those who have written on agriculture. I have appended a diagram from which you can easily determine the measurement of shadows. It is adapted to the location of Cologne Agrippina.

Shadows of gnomons, such as they are at Cologne Agrippina

[Col. 0433]

[Col. 0433D] The gnomon is A B, divided into sixty feet. The summer sun is II; the summer shadow, from the point where the gnomon touches the ground, is B C, thirty-one and one-third feet. The equinoctial sun is G; the shadow of the gnomon, B D, is seventy-five and a half feet. The winter sun is F; the shadow of the gnomon, B E, is 229 feet and two-thirds. The proportion is different in other places. For if they incline nearer toward the south, because the midday sun is higher there, the shadows are shorter; if they turn toward the north, leaving the sun, they immediately grow longer.

Hence they are also called *ἄσκιοι* (*askioi*) in Greek. The variation of shadows produces four distinctions of places. *Ἄσκια* (*askia*) are places where the sun is sometimes at the zenith—that is, where the sun hangs directly above the heads of those walking, by the perpendicular. When this occurs, it is obvious that the shadows are consumed and that upright objects are illuminated all around by the sun.

There are no such places in Europe; in Asia there is only coastal India; in Africa, all the interior regions. The beginning of such places is where the solstitial circle is at the zenith, and the end is where the winter circle is at the zenith. Between these boundaries lie the intermediate places, which have the sun at the zenith every year—namely, in the parts called *antisis* (sic), for thus the Greeks call places that have the same elevation above the tops of their regions. At the extreme boundaries this happens only once: at one boundary on the solstice, as at Syene, and at the other on the winter day, as in the farthest parts of Africa.

The second kind are *amphiscia*, which have shadows to the right and left, such as Arabia, called Felix, and all the regions that we have already said lie beneath the torrid zone. These same places are both *ascia* and *amphiseia*, but in different respects.

The third kind are *heteroscia*, which have shadows only to the right or only to the left, as do all places where the sun does not pass above the zenith. Such is everything that is comfortably inhabited between the heat and the cold.

The fourth are *periscia*, which have the sun for several days or even months without intervening nights, above the entire surrounding region of the sky’s horizon. Such are the places situated at the extreme north, which are scarcely inhabited because of the severity of the cold.

[Col. 0435] The horoscope vessel.

The vessels of the horoscope. In Pliny one reads not *horoscopi*, but, appositionally, *vasa horoscopa*.
