These are horoscope vessels hollowed out in the shape of a hemisphere; along their inner circumference they contain an image of the sphere, adapted to the observation of times and celestial courses. Vitruvius reports that their invention was received from Aristarchus of Samos, calling the instrument a *scaphe* and a hemisphere.

I remember that several years ago I restored such an instrument for the magnificent and thoroughly honorable man D. Reinhard, Count of Westenburch, dean of the greater church of Cologne, when he first requested this work from me. He possesses both an exceptional understanding of such matters and a great fondness for them. I drew its form on a flat surface as best I could.

Understand A B to be the upper, flat rim or opening of the excavated material; F G the upright pointer, whose extremity G indicates the Arctic Pole and F the Antarctic Pole; C the center of the inner hollow, corresponding to the subterranean point called the nadir; D E the zodiac, traced on the inside of the hollow along the zodiacal parallels, using a quadrant for this purpose in place of an index.

[Col. 0435D] At Syene. For it is situated beneath the Tropic of Cancer, at the entrance to the torrid zone. See Pliny, Mela, Strabo, and Solinus.

Again, on the island of Meroë, which is the capital, etc. All these statements are taken from Pliny, Book Two, chapters seventy-one, seventy-two, and seventy-three. We have explained above what it means for shadows to be consumed, in what places this occurs, and why. But when he says that shadows are consumed when the sun is in the eighteenth part of Taurus, and then again in the fourteenth part of Leo, these must now be understood not as the parts of the zodiacal images, as above, but as corresponding parts—for the eighteenth part of Taurus is the antisian part of the fourteenth of Leo. I shall not hesitate to explain what this means.

It must therefore be understood from astrology that there are signs and degrees corresponding to one another. The months too are antisian in the same way, with respect to the proportion of shadows and days: Gemini and Cancer, for example, are antisian, or equal, signs; for as much as the days diminish after the first degree of Cancer, they increase by the same amount after the nineteenth. Thus, as I began to say, the antisian pairs are Gemini and Cancer, Taurus and Leo, Aries and Virgo, Pisces and Libra, Aquarius and Scorpio, and finally Capricorn and Sagittarius.

These signs have the same proportion of light and shadows, but in such a way that the end of the earlier sign must be compared with the beginning of the following sign, and the middle degrees of the signs correspond to one another. For example, Taurus and Leo, as we have said, are antisian in such a way that the final degree of Taurus and the second degree [Col. 0436D] of Leo are equal. Therefore, when the Sun once consumes the shadows in the eighteenth degree, it does so a second time in the corresponding degree; and that degree will be, as is clear from what we have just said, the fourteenth degree of Leo, since these degrees are equally elevated in the sphere. So that this matter may be understood more clearly, I have appended a figure in which it will be seen which degrees correspond as antisian pairs.

[Col. 0437]

[Col. 0437C] Among the people of India there is a mountain of the Orites, etc. These statements are still cited from Pliny, but with considerable confusion. It will therefore be necessary to consult them in the original source. As for what follows immediately—that the Bears are visible there for fifteen days—this too is one of the passages that must be referred to Pliny’s opinion, though he follows the authority rather than the reliability of his sources. For I cannot be persuaded that Pliny was so delirious as not to see that this was false from the revolution of the sphere.

I therefore think it more correct to read the passage with the negative *non* inserted and the particle *tantum* deleted. For among the other nations the Bears remain perpetually above the horizon, and there is no day on which they are not visible during some part of the night—except in the torrid zone, where they rise with the Sun in August and cannot be seen during those days. Yet scholars discover many passages of this kind; if one were allowed to alter them at will for the convenience of readers, there would never be an end to correcting this author.

[Col. 0437D] “The Bear was observed there, while Alexander was staying there, to be visible only during the first part of the night.” See Ziegler’s commentaries on this passage, on the second book of Pliny, chapter seventy-three. The material that follows to the end of the chapter is taken from the same passage of Pliny.

“Pythias of Massilia writes that this occurs on the island of Thule.” [Col. 0438C] Strabo’s view, and Pliny’s elsewhere—namely, in Book Seven, concerning Thule—is more accurate. For Thule does not have the pole at its zenith, which would be necessary if either night or day lasted six months. There is a passage in Strabo, chapter 35.]

[Col. 0431A]

Indeed, the equinoctial day is equal and one for the entire world; but the solstitial day, and all the others, differ in length according to the varying climates and shadows. This is shown more clearly than daylight by the books produced through the industry of Christians and pagans alike, and by reliable witnesses who have come from both regions, that is, from the northern and southern lands.

Finally, blessed Ambrose, discussing the times and course of the Sun in the fourth book of the *Hexameron*, says among other things:

> “At midday the shadow is also shorter than it is either at the beginning or at the end of the day—and this is so among us, in the western region. But there are people situated in the southern regions who for two days of the entire year become shadowless, because, having the Sun directly above their heads, they are illuminated all around; hence they are called *ἄσκιοι* [askioi, shadowless] in Greek. Many also report that the Sun travels so directly overhead that, through the narrow opening of wells, they have seen the water deep below reflecting its light. Those who are in the south are said to be *ἀμφίσκιοι* [amphiskioi], because they cast their shadows on both sides.”

A little later he writes:

> “For there are people in this inhabited world of ours who are situated around the south and appear to cast their shadow toward the southern region. This is said to happen at the height of summer, when the Sun is directed toward the north.”

Basil writes similarly, also in his exposition of Genesis. Pliny too, in secular but not contemptible writings, explains these same matters at greater length as follows:

> “Sundials are not equally useful over three hundred stadia, or, at the greatest distance, over five hundred, because the shadows of the Sun change. Thus the shadow of the central pointer, which they call the gnomon, at midday in Egypt on the day of the equinox amounts to a little more than half the length of the gnomon. In the city of Rome one-ninth of the gnomon is lacking from the shadow. In the town of Ancona the shadow exceeds it by one thirty-fifth. In that part of Italy called Venetia, at the same hours, the shadow of the gnomon is equal to the gnomon itself.
>
> “In a similar way, they report that at Syene, a town situated five thousand stadia above Alexandria, no shadow is cast at midday on the day of the solstice, and that a well made for this experiment is entirely illuminated; from this it appears that at that time the Sun is directly above that place. Onesicritus wrote that the same thing occurs in India above the river Hypasis at the same season. It is established that in the city of Berenice of the Troglodytes, from which the town of Ptolemais—founded on the shore of the Red Sea at the beginning of the elephant-hunting country—is four thousand eight hundred and twenty stadia distant, the same thing occurs for forty-five days before the solstice and for an equal number afterward; and after those ninety days shadows are cast toward the south.
>
> “Again, on the island of Meroë, the capital of the Ethiopian people, inhabited in the Nile River five thousand stadia from Syene, shadows are consumed twice a year, when the Sun occupies [Note: [Col. 0431] B, *duodevicesimam* (eighteenth).] the eighteenth degree of Taurus and the fourteenth degree of Leo. In the land of the Orites in India there is a mountain called Maleus, near which shadows are cast southward in summer and northward in winter; the Bear appears there for only fifteen nights. In India, at the famous harbor of Patala, the Sun rises on the right and shadows fall toward the south. The Bear was observed there, while Alexander was staying there, to be visible only during the first part of the night.
>
> “Onesicritus, his commander, wrote that in those parts of India where there are no shadows, the Bear is not visible; that these places are therefore called *Ascia* [shadowless], and that hours are not counted there. Eratosthenes reported, contrariwise, that throughout the whole of the Troglodyte country shadows fall in the opposite direction for twice forty-five days of the year.
>
> “Thus, through the varying increase of daylight, the longest day at Meroë comprises twelve equinoctial hours and eight parts of an hour; at Alexandria, fourteen hours; in Italy, fifteen; and in Britain, seventeen. There, in summer, the bright nights undoubtedly confirm what reason compels us to believe: as the Sun approaches more closely to the summit of the world during the days of the solstice, the earth beneath the narrow circuit of light has continuous days for six months, while, conversely, it has nights when the Sun has withdrawn toward the winter solstice.
>
> “Pythias of Massilia writes that this occurs on the island of Thule, six days’ sailing north of Britain.”

In weaving these statements about the unequal length of the solstitial days into his account, Pliny left it to be understood what the length of the winter days is in the various regions. He also made equally clear the measure of the night at both seasons, since, whatever the length of the days, day and night together must complete a period of twenty-four hours.

But it should be noted [Note: [Col. 0435] Add *hoc* C.] that Solinus wrote differently about Thule:

> “Thule,” he says, “is the farthest land. There, at the summer solstice, when the Sun passes through the constellation of Cancer alone, there is no night; at the winter solstice, correspondingly, there is no day.”

Pliny too did not omit this in Book Seven:

> “Thule is the farthest of all the lands mentioned. We have stated that at the solstice it has no nights, when the Sun passes through the sign of Cancer, and, conversely, no days during the winter solstice. Some believe that this lasts for six months.”

**CHAPTER XXXII. The cause of the inequality of these same days.**

[Note: [Col. 0438C]

**BRID. RAMES. GLOSSES.**—The heaven of the upper circle, separated by its own boundary and situated at equal distances in every direction, contains the angelic powers. When these go forth to us, they assume ethereal bodies so that they may resemble human beings even in eating, and when they return there they lay them aside. God tempered this heaven with icy waters, so that the lower elements would not be consumed. Then he solidified the lower heaven, not uniformly but in multiple form, calling it the firmament because it supports the waters above.

The heaven is of a subtle and fiery nature, round, and gathered at equal distances in every direction from the center of the earth. Hence the wise men of the world said that its convex middle, wherever it is observed, revolves daily with indescribable speed, so that it would fall if the planets’ opposition did not restrain it. They rely as evidence on the stars, which always wheel around in a fixed course, while those in the north complete shorter circuits around the pole. The two extreme vertices around which the sphere of heaven revolves are called the poles, numbed by icy cold. One of these rises toward the northern region and is called Boreas; the other slopes toward the south and, opposite the earth, is called the Southern Pole, which Holy Scripture calls the innermost south.

Heaven—that is, the firmament—is of a subtle nature, being composed of water and fiery nature, that is, quality, because the stars placed in it have a fiery nature. It is also round. Round, not in the manner of a ball, but extended lengthwise from the region of the poles, and from the center—that is, from the middle point or midpoint—of the earth. Gathered from every direction, that is, sloping: such is that heaven. As great as the distance from this place on earth to heaven is, so great is the space extending from either side of the earth to heaven. For the globe of earth is situated in the middle of the whole world, that is, of heaven—not merely round in the circuit of its breadth, like a round shield, but rather resembling a ball, curved in every direction, with an equal roundness.

For in such a mass and magnitude, however enormous—that is, vast—I would not believe that the distance between mountains and valleys differs by so much as one finger, any more than it does in a toy ball. All the elements are above the earth and are, as it were, supported by it; but the earth is supported by no element, because it occupies the lowest place. The Psalmist says: “Stretching out heaven like a skin.” Literally: God stretched out heaven like a skin, because just as the skin of animals covers the entire body, so heaven surrounds the whole earth above and below.

Hence—namely, because it is round [Col. 0439C] and convex, on account of the more sloping region of the southern pole. Convex, that is, curved in the manner of a vaulted roof. And it is middle, namely. It is itself the middle of heaven, wherever it is observed, just as a compass is central wherever one considers any part of it. Heaven itself also appears central to everyone, because half of it is always above the earth. It also appears joined, that is, inclined. For wherever one stands on earth, that place is considered to be in the middle of heaven. Wherever, that is, toward whichever region. And wherever heaven itself is seen, half of it always appears.

To revolve, namely heaven itself, that is, to be carried around. The wise, that is, philosophers. It would fall, that is, it would collapse. Of the planets. For the planets move against the world; therefore the world is moderated and held in place by them. It would be moderated, that is, slowed or tempered. As evidence, or demonstration, that is, investigation. What “evidence” is and why it is so called has already been written above.

Indeed, the same globe is truly situated in the middle of the entire world, not merely round in the circuit of its breadth, like a round shield, but rather resembling a ball, with an equal roundness in every direction. Macrobius recalls the matter in the first part of his book as follows:

> Heaven is equally distant from every part of the earth. And just as it is seen from our habitation, so too from the sides and from the region regarded as lower than us it is viewed at an equal immeasurable height. Therefore, unless all weights were carried toward the earth, the rains that fall beyond the sides of the earth would fall not upon the earth but upon heaven. This exceeds even the absurdity of a vulgar jester’s joke.
>
> Let the sphere of earth be marked A, B, C, D. Around it let the sphere of air be marked E, F, G, L, M, and let a line drawn from E to L divide both spheres—that is, the spheres of earth and air. The upper part is the one we inhabit, and the other lies beneath our feet. Unless, therefore, every weight fell upon the earth, the earth would receive far too small a portion of the rains, from A to C. But the sides of the air—that is, from F to E and from G to L—would pour their moisture into the air and heaven. From the lower hemisphere, rain would flow outward and would therefore be unknown to nature, as the diagram appended below shows.

[Col. 0439]

[Col. 0439D] Concerning the name of heaven, Saint Ambrose says this in the books he wrote on the creation of the world:

> Heaven is called *οὐρανὸς* [*ouranos*] in Greek. Among the Latins it is called *caelum* because, having the lights of the stars impressed upon it like signs, it is said to be *caelatum*, “engraved,” just as silver that shines with raised figures is called *caelatum*.

That it has a subtle nature is also demonstrated by Scripture, which says that he established heaven like smoke. Its parts are the east, the axis, the climate, the pivots or cardinal points, the convex regions, the poles, and the hemispheres.

The east is the region in which heaven is contained. Hence Ennius too says:

> “Scarcely had they filled the eastern land, amid the terrors of heaven.”

The axis is the straight northern line that extends through the middle of the sphere like a ball. It is called the axis because the sphere revolves upon it like a wheel, or because the wagon is situated there.

The climate is a pole or region of heaven. The climates of heaven—that is, its regions or parts—are four. The first is the eastern region, from which certain stars rise. The second is the western region, where certain stars set for us. The third is the northern region, where the Sun reaches during the longer days. The fourth is the southern region, where the Sun reaches during the longer nights.

The east is named from the rising of the Sun; the west because it causes the day to set and perish. For it hides the light from the world and brings on darkness. The north is called *Septentrio* from the seven stars of the axis, which revolve and turn upon it. This is properly also called the vertex, because it turns.

The south is called *meridies* either because the Sun makes midday there, as though *medidies*, or because the ether then shines more purely. For *merum* means “pure.” The pivots or cardinal points (*cardines*) of heaven are the extreme parts of the axis, and are so called because heaven turns through them, or because they revolve like a heart.

Pope Gregory says:

> “Tell me, I ask, if you know the circuits of heaven, the poles of the earth, and the abysses of the waters—where they end and where they hang suspended. We know that what was made from nothing hangs upon nothing. But if there is something called nothing, then it is no longer nothing. If, however, nothing is nothing, nowhere does the mass of the world hang, nor is there a place where that which was created to exist can be. How, then, is that nowhere which we know exists?”

The convex regions of heaven are its extremities, named from their curvature, as in the verse:

> “Whenever the damp night encloses the vaulted heaven.”

For *convexum* means curved, as though turned or inclined, and thoroughly arched.

The poles are circles that run through the axis. One is the northern pole, which never sets and is called Boreas; the other is the southern pole, which is never seen and is called Austronotus. They are called poles because they are the circles of the axis, a term taken from the use of wagons, being named from *polire*, “to polish.” But the northern pole is always visible and Austronotus never, because the right-hand regions of heaven are higher, while those of the south are depressed.

A sphere is an equal roundness in every direction, as follows.

The sphere of heaven is a kind of form fashioned into a round shape, whose center is the earth and which is enclosed on every side. They say that this sphere has neither beginning nor end, because, by reason of its roundness, it is not easily grasped where it begins or where it ends, like a circle. For it is said to be gathered equally from every side, looking similarly toward all things and separated from the center of the earth by equal spaces. Through this equality of itself it is so stable that the equality gathered in every direction does not allow it to incline toward any side, and it is supported without being carried by any support.

A hemisphere is half of a sphere. The hemisphere above the earth is that part of heaven which is entirely visible to us; the hemisphere beneath the earth is the part that cannot be seen so long as it remains beneath the earth.

The motion of the sphere turns upon two axes, one of which is northern, never setting and called Boreas; the other is southern, never seen and called Austronotus. They say that the sphere of heaven moves upon these two poles, and that, with its motion, the fixed stars circle within it from east to west, while those in the north complete shorter circuits near the pole.

[Col. 0442A] The sphere of heaven turns once in a day and night from east to west, over a period of twenty-four hours, completing by its revolution its course above and beneath the earth. It is therefore said to be placed above the waters so that it may revolve in them and so that they may temper its burning.

If anyone asks how heaven can make so great a revolution in twenty-four hours, let him consider how Habakkuk could cross such vast expanses of earth twice within a moment of an hour. We therefore remain uncertain of the size and material of heaven; we know, nevertheless, that it revolves with incredible speed. The sphere of heaven is said to run with such speed that, unless the stars moved against its headlong course and slowed it, it would bring about the ruin of the world.

Hence Lucan too wrote:

> “Those whose flight alone governs Olympus among the stars,
>
> and whose differing power meets the pole in contrary course.”

For there is such a sound and such sweetness there that, as blessed Isidore says, if human ears were capable of hearing it, they would pass from east to west, following the motion of the celestial sphere.

Plato, treating the perfection of the sphere or circle through many arguments, indicates the rational work of the world’s Maker: first, because the zodiac, drawn from the five angles of lines, consists of a single line; second, because it is without beginning and without end; third, because it is produced from a point; further, because it possesses motion from itself; then because it lacks the judgment of angles; because it contains within itself all the figures of the stars; and because it has an indescribable motion [perhaps “an inerrant motion”], since six other motions are errant—forward, backward, to the right, to the left, upward, and downward. Finally, it is produced by necessity, so that this line cannot be extended beyond the circle.

Spiritually, heaven is the Church, which in the night of this life shines with the virtues of the saints, like the brightness of the stars. In the plural, however, the name “heavens” is understood to mean all the saints or the angels. We should also understand the heavens to be the prophets and apostles, who rain down words, flash with miracles, and of whom it is said: “The heavens declare the glory of God”—because they themselves announced to the world, as glory, Christ’s coming and death, and also his resurrection.

Blessed Ambrose speaks thus in the book of the *Hexameron*:

> “We read in David: ‘Praise him, heavens of heavens.’ Whether there is one heaven or several is disputed: some assert that there are many, while others deny that there is more than one. The philosophers of the world introduced seven heavens, that is, the planetary spheres, whose harmonious motion they describe as encompassing all things. They believe that these spheres, interwoven with one another and inserted into one another, revolve backward and are carried in opposition to the other motions.
>
> “Indeed, in ecclesiastical books both ‘heaven’ and ‘heavens of heavens’ are read, and the apostle Paul understands himself to have been caught up to the third heaven. But human presumption must not venture anything about their number.
>
> “God made them—not shapeless or confused, but distinguished in their proper order by a certain rational arrangement. For he extended the heaven of the upper circle, separated by a boundary and situated at equal distances in every direction, and established in it the powers of spiritual creatures. The Maker of the world tempered the nature of this heaven with waters, lest the conflagration of the upper fire ignite the lower elements. Then he solidified the heaven of the lower heaven, not with uniform but with multiple motion, calling it the firmament because it supports the solidified waters above.”

Julianus [Col. 0443A] Pomerius, a man of sound judgment, says that the first heaven is the aerial heaven, from which birds are also called “birds of heaven.” He understands the second to be the starry heaven, in which the twelve signs and the other stars, apart from the seven planets, are contained; this is also called the firmament. He understands the third to be spiritual or mental, [Col. 0444A] where the angels and the souls of the saints are placed in contemplation of God, contemplating above themselves God almighty, who presides over every creature, so that by presiding he supports all things, by supporting he surrounds them, and by surrounding he fills them.

[Col. 0444B] Macrobius recalls the matter as follows in the second part of his book:

[Col. 0443C] Because a conception grasped by the mind enters it more easily than a description expressed in words, let the globe of earth be marked A, B, C, D; around A let N and L be marked; around B, M and K; around C, G and L; and around D, E and F. Let straight lines be drawn from sign to sign: from G to I, from M to N, from K to L, and from E to F.

Let the two spaces opposite one another—that is, one from C to the line drawn to L, and the other from D to the line drawn to F—be understood to have been stiffened by perpetual frost. The upper extremity is northern, the lower is southern; and let the middle region from N to L be the torrid zone.

It remains that the belts from I to N be tempered by the heat below and the cold above. Likewise, let the zone between L and F receive a tempering from the heat above and the cold beneath. Although these two zones are temperate, they have not both been granted to human beings of our kind. Only the upper one, from I to N, is inhabited by every kind of people we can know, whether they are Romans, Greeks, or barbarians of any nation. The region from L to F is understood only by reasoning to be similarly inhabited because of its similar temperateness; but by whom, we have never been permitted, nor shall we ever be permitted, to know.

For the torrid zone lying between them denies both human races communication and passage to one another. The reason is therefore evident why this zone is always subject to flames: the Sun, both the source and administrator of the entire ethereal fire, never leaves it. Thus both outermost regions—that is, the northern and southern regions, to which the Sun’s heat never comes—are necessarily oppressed by perpetual frost.

As we said, the Sun tempers two regions, one on either side, through their nearness to heat and cold. Finally, in this same zone that we inhabit, which is entirely called temperate, the regions nearest the scorched belt are nevertheless hotter than the others, such as Ethiopia, Arabia, Egypt, and Libya. There the heat so thins the body of the surrounding air that it is either never or only rarely forced into clouds; consequently they have almost no use of rain. In the opposite direction, the regions nearer the cold boundaries are more closely pressed by frost, so severely that it is not easy to explain the extent of the injury caused there by excessive cold. The regions temperate in the middle, because they are far removed from both extremes, possess a true and healthful temperateness.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—The cause of the inequality. With a sphere at hand, this is easy to understand. It is demonstrated that the inequality results from the roundness of the earth—for it is now established that the earth is a globe—and from the fact that the Sun rises earlier for peoples situated in the east and later for those in the west. Thus day begins earlier for the Jews than for us, and earlier for us than for the Spaniards. It also follows from the diversity of climates that winter and summer days are shorter in some places and longer in others. The first of these facts is commonly known; the second is taught by the inclination of the world.

For as people travel southward, certain stars are continually seen rising toward the south. Canopus, for example, a conspicuous star in the shaft of the Argo, is nowhere visible in Italy; at Rhodes it merely flashes above the horizon from the lower region of the world; at Alexandria it remains above the horizon at the proper time. Hence the southern people have winter days longer than ours. For certain stars remain above the earth for ten hours for them, while for us they remain scarcely eight.

They have shorter summer days, however, because what is north of the equator remains longer above the horizon; this is taught by Euclid in the *Revolutions of the Sphere*, or in the *Phenomena* attributed to him. To indicate this matter, cosmographers devised two kinds of circles: some drawn through the poles, called meridians, running from north toward south, whose function is to distinguish the differences of the hours and the eastern regions from the western; others are circles on the sphere, *παράλληλοι* [parallels], which divide the aforementioned meridians and distinguish climates and the inequality of days and seasons. These will be discussed in the following chapter.

But not even Italy, indeed. On Canopus, see chapter seventy of Pliny’s second book, from which these statements are taken; that passage, however, is not free from error.]

The cause of the inequality of these same days is the roundness of the earth. For it is not without reason that the earth is called a globe both in the pages of divine Scripture and in those of secular literature. The same globe is truly situated in the middle of the entire world, not merely round in the circuit of its breadth, like a round shield, but rather resembling a ball, with an equal roundness in every direction. Nor, in such a great mass and magnitude, however enormous, would I believe that the distance between mountains and valleys differs by so much as one finger, any more than it does in a toy ball.

The earth, therefore, having such a form and given to mortals for habitation, the circuit of the Sun shining in this world, by God’s fixed ordinance, gives day in one place while leaving night in another. And since, as Ecclesiastes says, “The Sun rises and sets, and returns to its place, and, rising there again, circles toward the south and bends toward the north,” it must be the case that, as it circles, it brings morning, midday, and evening first to those in the east and later to those in the west who lie beneath the same line. Nevertheless, it makes the days of equal length for both throughout the entire year, and likewise the nights. It must also be the case that for all those situated opposite one another under the northern and southern regions and beneath the same line, during the circuit that turns throughout the year, at one and the same moment of time,

> “The fiery Sun climbs to the middle of heaven’s vault.”

Yet it does not rise or set for both at the same moment or hour. When, in winter, it travels around the southern region, it reaches those inhabiting the southern side of the earth at an earlier rising, but leaves them later at sunset than it leaves us, who are situated toward the north. Because the globe of the earth obstructs it, we receive its rising later but its setting earlier.

Conversely, when it is traveling in its summer circuit, it appears to us, who inhabit the same region, to rise much earlier and to set much later than it does for those living in the southern hollow of the earth. They are prevented by the covering of the same earth from seeing it earlier and are compelled to lose sight of it sooner. Therefore they have shorter days than we do in summer and longer days in winter.

This can be recognized not only from the Sun’s circuit but also from the position of all the stars that travel beneath different regions of the poles. For the roundness of the earth produces the same effect: some of the brightest southern stars never appear to our climate, while our northern stars are likewise hidden from them to a considerable extent. Finally, the Bears themselves, which rise above our vertex and never set, are not seen in the Troglodyte country or neighboring Egypt.

Moreover, neither we Britons nor even Italy can see Canopus, that very great star, once worshiped under the name of a god—not because the light of the stars gradually grows weaker and disappears with greater distance, but because the mass of the earth lying in the way blocks the space required for viewing it. All these facts can very easily be proved from any very high mountain inhabited all around.

**CHAPTER XXXIII. In which places shadows or days are equal.**

[Note: [Col. 0445D]

**BRID. RAMES. GLOSSES.**—The earth is divided into eight circles according to the variation of the days.

The first extends from the southern part of India, through the inhabitants of the Red Sea and maritime Africa, to the Pillars of Hercules. At midday on the day of the equinox, a seven-foot gnomon produces a shadow four feet long. The longest day has fourteen equinoctial hours.

The second runs from the western part of India through the Medes and Persians, Arabia, Syria, Cyprus, Crete, Lilybaeum, and the northern parts of Africa. At the equinox, a thirty-five-foot gnomon produces a shadow twenty-three feet long. The longest day has fourteen hours, with an additional two-fifths of an hour.

The third begins near the Indians adjoining Imaus and extends through the Caspian regions, Taurus, Pamphylia, Rhodes, the Cyclades, Syracuse, Canetum, and Gades. The shadows of the gnomons are thirty-eight inches long. The longest day has fourteen and a half hours, with an additional thirtieth of an hour.

[Col. 0446B] The fourth extends from the other side of Imaus through Ephesus, the sea of the Cyclades, northern Sicily, Narbonese Gaul, and coastal Africa, toward the west. A twenty-one-foot gnomon corresponds to a shadow of six feet. The longest day has fourteen hours and two-thirds of an hour.

The fifth circle includes, from the entrance to the Caspian Sea, Bactria, Armenia, Macedonia, Tarentum, the Tyrrhenian Sea, the Balearic Islands, and central Spain. A seven-foot gnomon has a six-foot shadow. The longest day has fifteen hours.

The sixth encompasses the Caspian peoples, the Caucasus, Samothrace, the Illyrians, Campania and Ruria, Massilia, central Tarraconese Spain, and from there the region of Pelusium. A nine-foot gnomon has an eight-foot shadow. The longest day has fifteen hours, with an additional ninth of an hour.

The seventh begins at the other shore of the Caspian Sea and runs through the far side of Thrace, Venetia, Cremona, Transalpine Gaul, the Pyrenees, and Celtiberia. A gnomon of thirty-five units has a shadow of thirty-six. The longest day has fifteen hours and three-fifths of an hour.

The eighth begins at the Tanais and passes through Lake Maeotis and the Sarmatians, Dacians, and part of Germany, entering Gaul. The longest day has sixteen hours.

The ancients place two circles before these: one through the island of Meroë and the city of Ptolemais on the Red Sea, where the longest day is twelve and a half hours; the other through Syene in Egypt, to which they assign thirteen hours and two additional parts. They add two after them: the first through the Hyperborean regions and Britain, with seventeen hours; the second is the Scythian circle, extending from the Riphaean mountains to Thule, where days and nights continue in alternation.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—Since we have discussed above the difference in the length of days, etc., this chapter concerns the breadth of regions, which is distinguished by parallel lines, which we call equidistant lines. The breadth of a region is its distance toward the south and north. Its starting point is taken from the middle of the torrid zone, or, which is the same thing, from the equator. Thus a city situated under the equator, such as the town of Julia Africana, has no breadth; but as soon as it inclines from this point toward the north, it begins to have some degrees of breadth.

This breadth is marked by circles drawn at the poles, surrounding the pole from which they are drawn with a compass, generally separated by an interval of ten degrees. On maps—for that is what people commonly call tables on which the globe is depicted—the intervals are measured by quarters of hours. When the longest day in one region has increased by a quarter-hour over the nearest region, there is another parallel there. But beyond Britain, because of the excessively steep inclination of the sphere, the intervals are no longer calculated by quarters of hours. I have therefore thought it useful to append here the entire *μάθησις* [mathematical doctrine], taken from Ptolemy’s second book, *περὶ μεγάλης πραγματείας* [On the Great Treatise]. Before that, however, we shall set down what we find in Bede concerning shadows.

[Col. 0447] The correspondence of the twelve months through the shadow, whose gnomon will be the length of a human body.

And since above we demonstrated from the statements of Pliny the Elder the distances between the solstitial days among those who are separated from one another toward the south and north, it seems appropriate now to explain these matters more fully, and also, in the words of the same author, the correspondence of the days among those who dwell in any part of the world beneath the same line drawn from east to west.

Thus, writing about these matters in the sixth book of the *Natural History*, he says:

> “There are several divisions of the world, which our people have called circles, but the Greeks *paralleloi* (παράλληλοι). An equinoctial gnomon [Col. 0448A] [Note: [Col. 0447] B, twenty.] of thirty-five feet casts a shadow thirty-three feet long. > “The fifth division contains, from the entrance of the Caspian Sea, Bactria, Iberia, Armenia, Mysia, Phrygia, the Hellespont, the Troad, Tenedos, Abydos, Scepsis, Ilium, Mount Ida, Cyzicus, Lampsacus, Sinope, Amisus, Heraclea in Pontus, Paphlagonia, Lemnos, Imbros, Thasos, Cassandria, Thessaly, Macedonia, Larissa, Amphipolis, Thessalonica, Pella, Edessa, Beroea, Pharsalus, Carystus, Euboea, Boeotia, Chalcis, Delphi, Acarnania, Aetolia, Apollonia, Brundisium, Tarentum, Thurii, Locri, Rhegium, Lucania, Naples, Puteoli, the Tuscan Sea, Corsica, the Balearic Islands, and central Spain. A gnomon of nine feet casts a shadow of eight feet. The longest day lasts fifteen equinoctial hours plus one-ninth of an hour, or, as Nigidius preferred, one-fifth.

These excerpts from the writings of Pliny the Elder may appropriately occupy this place in our little works.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the five circles of the world and the subterranean course of the stars

[Note: [Col. 0449C]

**BRID. ROME. GLOSSES.**—The world is divided by five circles. In some of the regions distinguished by them people dwell because of their temperate climate; others are uninhabitable because of the severity of their cold or heat. The first is the northern circle, uninhabitable because of the cold; its stars never set for us. The second is the solstitial circle, temperate and habitable, extending from the highest part of the zodiac toward the north. The third is the equinoctial circle, running through the middle circuit of the zodiacal sphere; it is torrid and uninhabitable. The fourth is the winter circle, temperate and habitable, extending from the lowest part of the zodiac toward the southern pole. The fifth is the southern circle, around the southern summit; it is covered by the earth and uninhabitable because of the cold.

The three middle circles distinguish the unequal lengths of the seasons, since the sun occupies one at the solstice, another at the equinox, and the third in winter. The outermost circles are always deprived of the sun. Hence, one day’s voyage northward from the island of Thule brings one to a frozen sea.

Isidore, in the shorter work which he wrote to King Sisebutus, says:

> Philosophers customarily distinguish the inequalities of the seasons, or of the sun’s annual courses, by these names. The formation of the world is demonstrated in this way: just as the world rises toward the northern region, so it declines toward the south. Its head, as it were, is the eastern region; its farthest part is the north. [Col. 0450D] For its parts are four. The first part of the world is the east, the second the south, the third the west, and the final and outermost part the north. Of this Virgil says:
>
> “Around which, at the farthest limits, right and left are drawn,
>
> “Blue and congealed with ice.”
>
> And Lucan says:
>
> “The lowest part of the world lies there, which the snowy zone
>
> “And perpetual winters oppress.”

Likewise, concerning the five circles of the world: in defining the world, philosophers say that there are five circles, which the Greeks call *paralleloi*, that is, zones, in which the terrestrial globe lies. Virgil displays these in the *Georgics*, saying: “Five zones hold the heavens.” They are called zones or circles because they exist in the revolution of the sphere.

But let us imagine them in the shape of our right hand, so that the thumb is the arctic circle, uninhabitable because of the cold. The second circle is the *therinos* (“summer” or “tropical”) circle, temperate and habitable. The middle circle is the *hisemerinos* (“equinoctial”) circle, torrid and uninhabitable. The fourth circle is the *exemerinos* (“winter” or “tropical”) circle, temperate and habitable. The smallest circle is the *antarcticos* (“antarctic”) circle, cold and uninhabitable. Of these, the first is northern, the second solstitial, the third equinoctial, the fourth winter, and the fifth southern. Varro speaks of them as follows:

> “Five zones gird the ethereal globe,
>
> “And vast winters ravage its depths, while heats ravage its middle;
>
> “Thus the earth’s outer regions and middle are inhabited,
>
> “Which the sun’s powerful fire never wholly removes.” [sic]

The divisions of these circles are therefore called zones or circles because they exist in the revolution of the sphere.

The equinoctial circle is uninhabitable because the sun, traveling through the middle of the heavens, produces excessive heat in these regions, so that crops cannot grow there because the earth is scorched, nor are human beings permitted to dwell there because of the excessive heat. Conversely, the northern and southern circles are uninhabited because they lie far from the sun’s course and waste away under the excessive cold of the heavens [Col. 0451C] and the icy blasts of the winds.

The solstitial circle, which in the east is situated between the northern and summer circles, or the one which in the west lies between the summer and southern circles, is temperate because it receives cold from one circle and heat from the other. [Col. 0452A] Of these Virgil says:

> “Between these and the middle, two zones, granted to suffering mortals
>
> “By the gift of the gods.”

Those who are nearest the summer circle are the Ethiopians, scorched by excessive heat.

Isidore, in the third book of the *Etymologies*, chapter twenty-two:

> It is called *arctic* because within it the signs of the Bear are seen enclosed; these, being fashioned more particularly in the shape of bears, are called the Septentrions. The *therine tropical* circle is so called because the sun, moving around within it, makes summer at the boundaries of the north and does not pass beyond that circle, but immediately turns back; hence it is called tropical. The *himerine*, or *hisemerine*, is called equinoctial in Latin because, when the sun reaches that sphere, it produces the equinox. *Himerinos* in Latin means “day and night,” since in that circle half of the sphere is seen to be established. The *cimerine tropical*, or *exemerine*, is called winter or brumal by the Latins because, when the sun reaches that circle, it makes winter for those who are toward the north, [Col. 0452C] but summer for those who dwell in the southern regions. It is called *antarctic* because it is opposite the circle which we call arctic. The divisions of these circles are shown by the following figure.

[Col. 0451]

Northern, arctic: uninhabitable because of the cold.

Solstitial or summer: *terinos*, tropical, temperate, habitable.

*Himerinos*, or *hisemerinos*: equinoctial, torrid, uninhabitable.

Solstitial, or winter or brumal: *cimerinos*, or *exemerinos*, tropical, temperate, habitable.

Antarctic, southern: uninhabitable because of the cold.

[Col. 0451C] He who makes Arcturus, Orion, the Hyades, and the inner regions of the south. In Greek speech, *hyetos* (ὑετός) means “rain.” The Hyades received their name from rains because, when they rise, they undoubtedly bring showers. Orion also [sic], [Col. 0452C] rises at the very height of the winter season; at its rising it arouses storms and disturbs the seas.

When we read these names of stars in Scripture, let us not give assent to the empty ravings of poets, [Col. 0453B] who, on the basis of false opinions, assigned these names to the stars from the names of human beings or of other creatures. For the wise men of the nations gave names to certain stars, just as they did to the days. But when sacred Scripture also uses the same names, it does not thereby approve their empty fables. Rather, by making visible things figures of invisible realities, it uses names widely known among human beings, so that whatever is signified by something unknown may more easily become known to human understanding through what is known.

“He stretches out the north over the void.” Gregory: In sacred language the devil is customarily called by the name “north.” To constrict the hearts of the nations with the cold of sluggishness, he said: “I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north.” He is stretched out over the void because he possesses those hearts which are not filled by the grace of divine love.

Arcturus is the star which the Latins call the Septentrion. Shining with the rays of seven stars, it revolves and turns upon itself; it is called the Wagon because it rolls like a vehicle, sometimes raising three stars to the highest point and sometimes lowering four. Established on the axis of the heavens, it is always turning and never sinks; but as it revolves upon itself, the night comes to an end.

By this Arcturus, that is, the Septentrion, we understand the Church shining with sevenfold virtue. For just as Arcturus on the axis of heaven is continually lowered and raised again, so the Church is humbled by various adversities but soon rises again and is often exalted by virtues. And just as the number seven is completed from three and four, so the Church is perfected from faith in the Trinity and the works of the four principal virtues; for a person is justified by faith and works.

Nor should assent in any way be granted to the fables about the Antipodes. No historian has reported having seen, heard, or read that anyone crossed the winter sun toward the southern regions, leaving it behind his back, passed beyond the heat of the Ethiopians, and found beyond them habitable abodes of mortals temperate on one side through heat and on the other through cold.

In the sixteenth book of *The City of God*, chapter nine, Augustine says the following:

> As for what people fabulously assert about the Antipodes—that is, human beings on the opposite side of the earth, where the sun rises when it sets for us, walking with their footprints opposite ours—this must not be believed in any way. Nor do they claim to have learned it through historical knowledge, but rather conjecture it as if by reasoning: because the earth hangs within the vault of heaven, and the world has the same lowest and central point, they suppose that the other side of the earth, which is below, cannot be without human habitation.
>
> They do not consider that, even if the world is believed to be globular and round in shape, or demonstrated to be so by some reasoning, it does not follow that on that side also the land is free from the mass of waters. And even if it is free from them, it does not immediately follow that it contains human beings. How, then, can this Scripture be false, which gives credence to events it narrates as having occurred in the past, since its predictions are fulfilled? It is exceedingly absurd to say that some people could have sailed across the immense expanse of Ocean from this side to the other and arrived there, so that even for those people the human race would have been established from that one first human being.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—Since we have been speaking about the seasons: there are five circles in the sphere, *krikōtē* (κρικώτῃ), or, as more recent writers call it, the material sphere, namely, *paralleloi*. Although these are commonly encountered in other authors, he nevertheless wished to explain them here, so that Bede—or anyone else—might understand them.

Let five be drawn, not because there are not more, but because it is superfluous to posit more: three of these are traced by the sun, and the remaining two by the stars. For it must be understood that, when the sphere is revolved, every marked point describes a circle.

Those described by the sun are the equator, the winter circle, and the solstitial circle. The sun makes four distinctions in three parts of the heavens, which careful students must note. When it is farthest from us toward the south—which occurs around the Nones of December, for it is not difficult to observe how far the sun then is, at midday, from our zenith—it describes, on that day, through the revolution of the world, the circle from which on the following day it again begins to ascend and turn toward us. Therefore that circle is called tropical, because from that point the sun always turns back.

In Greek it is called *tropē cheimerinos* (τροπὴ χειμερινός), that is, “winter turning.” The Latins call that day the *bruma*, as Nonius noted, as though from *brachý hēmar* (βραχὺ ἦμαρ), “short day.” For this reason our people call it the winter circle. It occurs when the sun is in the first part of Capricorn, and therefore it is also called the circle of Capricorn.

Then, after ninety days, the sun occupies the middle of the world, where it describes the equinoctial circle. On that day, in every region, the days and nights are equal. After this turning point, the sun becomes closer each day to the north, until the solstice, on which day the third parallel is described, called the solstitial circle. In Greek it is more significantly called *tropē therinos* (τροπὴ θέρινος), that is, “summer turning”; in German likewise, by the same reasoning, *des sommersche son vuendte* (“the summer sun-turning”).

It occurs in the first part of Cancer, and therefore it is also called the tropical circle of Cancer, or the circle of Cancer. The whole region contained by the outermost circles and the middle one is called the torrid zone by writers; for the regions lying beneath these parts of the heavens are continually afflicted by heat.

Two other parallel circles remain, drawn around the poles of the world. Within them the stars contained there never set. They are not described in the same way everywhere: in Greece the circle is drawn from the hind foot of the Great Bear, while at Cologne it is drawn from the lyre or small harp. Others draw these circles not from the stars but from the poles of the zodiac, which are equal in every region. But those described by the stars that never set vary according to the climates: as one goes southward they become narrower, and toward the north broader. Aristotle calls these circles “always visible.”

One of them, around the northern pole, is called northern or arctic; the other, which corresponds to it beneath the earth toward the south, is called antarctic. The regions between these circles and the torrid zone are called the temperate zones, one of which is ours and the other that of the Antichthones. Those lying beneath the polar circles are excessively cold and untempered. The following figure teaches this.

The world is divided into zones, to which the letters A, B, C, and D have been assigned here. How the lines run between the letters can be seen: the two areas opposite one another—that is, from C to I toward the north and from D to E toward the south—are understood to have frozen under perpetual [perhaps “winter”], since this is shown by the lines from I to G and from F to E.

Between these outermost circles and the middle circle are the two zones granted to mortals: from I to N and from F to L. From these, lines are also drawn showing the zones from N to M and from L to K. For between I and N lies the summer zone, and between L and F the winter zone; both enjoy, on opposite sides, a tempering of cold and heat, because from N to L the sun always glows, and likewise in the other smaller zone; the concluding wording concerning its containment within the larger five zones is textually unclear.

Within the five zones of the earth there lie five zones of heaven above the earth. These are distinguished by the letters O, P, Q, and R, by which they are divided, together with the large letters A, B, C, and D of the world. From this it is evident that each part of the earth receives its quality from the corresponding part of heaven placed above its own zenith.

[Col. 0455D] Hence it happens that within the solar year Arcturus, Orion, and so forth. Each of the planetary spheres moves against the heavens from west to east; hence, while they complete the whole circle of heaven, they make one fewer revolution around the earth than the firmament itself. Thus, when Saturn has lost one circuit after thirty years, the sun moves once each year—for every day it advances one part against the heavens—and the moon once every twenty-seven days and a third, each completing one revolution around the world fewer than the firmament itself.

If this were not so in the case of the sun, the same stars would rise for us at the same hours throughout the whole year. But we observe something different: Orion rises sometimes at midnight, sometimes in the evening, and sometimes at dawn.

Arcturus. Arcturus is a star of the first brightness [Col. 0457C] within the feet of Boötes. Orion, says Aristotle, is the largest constellation in the magnitude and number of its stars, and is commonly known because of the brightness of its asterism. The Dog is situated between the Milky Way and the feet of Orion. The star placed in its mouth is called the Dog-star (*canicula*); Sirius is so called by the Greeks because of the dryness that occurs when this star rises with the sun.

“Nor, indeed, the Antipodes.” The Antipodes, or *Antipodae*—for Latins may inflect the word in either way, as Priscian attests—are denied by Lactantius and Augustine. More recent writers, however, have sufficiently answered them. If they thought the Antipodes impossible because the world on the opposite side of the heavens did not have the same shape as ours, they deny that the world is round; yet this has already been adequately demonstrated by many. If they thought it impossible because they believed that part of the globe contained not human beings but seas or uncultivated places, this has now been discovered through voyages.]

Since, then, in speaking about the seasons we have repeatedly had to mention the equinoctial, solstitial, or winter circle or zone, we have thought it appropriate to discuss them somewhat more fully.

Philosophers customarily distinguish the inequalities of the seasons, or [Note: [Col. 0451] the annual course of the sun.] of the sun’s annual courses, by these terms. They call the equinoctial zone, or circle, that region of heaven through which the sun travels around the equinoxes; the solstitial zone, that through which it travels around the solstice; and the winter zone, that through which it customarily circles the world in winter.

The circles or zones are called such [Col. 0452A] because they are produced by the sun’s circuit. Of these, the equinoctial zone, which is the middle one, curves around the earth above and below it at equal distances. The solstitial zone, however, travels over as little space beneath the earth as the winter zone does above it.

Likewise, the winter zone, which is narrow above the earth, has as broad a circuit beneath the earth as the solstitial zone has above the earth. For at the equinox the sun travels by night beneath the earth through as much space as it traverses by day above the earth, being hidden beneath the northern regions by as great a distance as it turns aside visibly on its course toward the south.

In winter it circles far and wide beneath the lower regions of the earth through as much space as it sweeps above the earth at the solstice in a long and broad curve. Similarly, when moving in its summer—that is, solstitial—circle, it makes by night as brief a departure beneath the northern regions of the earth as it makes by day in winter a brief ascent above its southern regions.

For just as each night of the revolving year has the length which the day had six months earlier and will have six months later, so each night the sun travels beneath the earth as far as it traveled six months earlier and will travel above the earth six months later; and by night it now travels toward the north as far as it then travels by day toward the south.

Moreover, after completing a six-month course, all the stars traverse by day the region of heaven which they had previously traversed by night, and, after repeating an equal period of months, they return to the same region and carry out their customary watches by night. Each makes a course beneath the earth proportionately broader than its course above it, and likewise a course beneath the earth proportionately shorter than its extended course above it.

Hence, in the solar year, Arcturus, Orion, the Dog, the Milky Way, and the rest of the army of heaven circle the globe of the earth once more than the sun itself.

Besides these three solar circles, they place two circles, one on each side: the northern and the southern. The northern circle, always visible to our eyes, is formed not by the sun but by the circuit of Arcturus and the stars around it; because it is distant from the sun, it remains cold. The southern circle is similar: because of its distance from the sun it is icy, and because the earth lies in the way, it is always hidden from us.

Concerning both of them it is said in praise of God:

> “Who makes Arcturus, Orion, and the Hyades,
>
> “And the innermost regions of the south.”

And elsewhere:

> “Who stretches out the north over the void.”

The Poet also mentions them:

> “Five zones hold the heavens, one of which, glowing with the shining sun,
>
> “Is always red and always torrid with fire.”

This is the equinoctial zone. Since the sun always illuminates it, whether directly present or near it on one side or the other, the earth beneath it is inevitably scorched and burned by flames, and is roasted by the heat at close range.

> “Around it, at the farthest limits, right and left are drawn
>
> “Blue, congealed with ice and black rains.”

He means the northern and southern zones. Everything beneath them, because of the absence of the sun and of the gentler stars, is oppressed by perpetual harshness and frost, as is demonstrated by the frozen sea which lies one day’s voyage north of the island of Thule.

> “Between these and the middle, two zones, granted to suffering mortals
>
> “By the gift of the gods.”

He signifies the solstitial and winter zones, which, lying close to the hot and icy zones on either side, are tempered by their power. Therefore both are called habitable—that is, suitable for habitation—and they do not repel mortals from themselves either through the enormity of cold or through heat, although only one of them can be proved to be inhabited.

Nor should assent in any way be granted to the fables about the Antipodes, nor has any historian reported that he saw, heard, or read of people who crossed the winter sun toward the southern regions, leaving it behind their backs, passed beyond the heat of the Ethiopians, and found beyond them dwellings of mortals that were temperate on one side through heat and on the other through cold.

Finally, the most diligent investigator of natural matters, Pliny the Elder, who does not deny that the earth, although shaped like a pine nut, is nevertheless inhabited everywhere, see what he says about the zones:

> “Only the two zones between the scorched zone and the frozen ones are temperate, and even these are inaccessible to one another because of the blazing heat of the stars. A very easy example of these zones is offered by people who, in the most bitter cold of winter, warm themselves beside a fire made in an elongated arrangement: the fire itself is like the middle zone, and the areas nearest it are altogether untouchable because of the heat; [Col. 0457B] but those farther from the flames on either side are numb with common cold. The regions temperate between these on either side and suitable for warming are those in which people may stand, whether on one side of the fire or the other, having prepared this source of heat and light for themselves in the darkness of a cold night beneath the open sky. If the fire could move around like the sun, it would certainly produce five circles; but because it remains stationary, it makes five lines: one hot line in the middle, two cold lines around it, and two temperate lines between these.”

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the four seasons, the elements, and the humors

[Note: [Col. 0457D]

**BRID. RAMES. GLOSSES.**—The seasons are successive changes by which the sun, approaching or withdrawing, regulates the circuit of the year. Winter, when the sun remains farther away, is cold and damp; spring, when it returns, is damp and warm; summer, when it burns overhead, is hot and dry; autumn, when it declines, is dry and cold.

The ancients began these seasons on the sixth day before the Ides of February, May, August, and November, so that the solstices and equinoxes would fall in the middle of the seasons. Spring is compared with the east because at that time everything rises from the earth; summer with midday because its part of the day burns more intensely with heat; autumn with the west because, owing to the boundary between heat and cold, it has serious illnesses; winter with the north because it grows torpid through cold.

The seasons are four divisions of the year, in which the sun, traversing different regions of the heavens, regulates the world beneath it. Among the Hebrews, “time” means a complete year, according to the passage in Daniel: “A time, times, and half a time.” By “time” he signifies one year, by “times” two years, and by “half” six months.

Among the Latins, four seasons are assigned to a single year: winter, spring, summer, and autumn. Allegorically, winter is understood as temporal tribulation, when the storms and whirlwinds of the world bear down upon us. Summer is the persecution of faith, when the teaching of unbelief is dried up by aridity. Spring is the renewal of faith or peace, when, after the tribulation of winter, tranquillity is restored to the Church; when the month of new things, that is, Easter of the Lamb, is celebrated; and when the earth, that is, the Church, is adorned with the flowers of the assemblies of the saints.

Likewise, in spring and autumn, when the Pleiades rise or set around the middle of the day or night, they mark the beginning of the season. The Pleiades are many fixed stars, which we also call a cluster because of the multitude of stars. They are said to be seven, but no one can see more than six. They rise from the east, and as the brightness of day approaches, their arrangement is spread out.

The Pleiades are so called from their multitude, because the Greeks call plurality *apo tou pleistou* (ἀπὸ τοῦ πλείστου), “from the greatest number.” The Latins called them the Vergiliae because they rise after spring. They are praised above the other signs especially because their rising signifies summer, while their setting indicates winter—something that has not been handed down concerning the others.

By these stars, because they are seven and shine brilliantly, all the saints shining through the sevenfold virtue of the Spirit are signified. Because they draw near to one another but do not touch, they show God’s preachers close to one another in charity but separated in time.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—The beginnings of these seasons. We have already mentioned above that authors vary in their calculation of the seasons. Most attend to their qualities, which arise from heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. When nature first sets these in motion and arouses them, the distinctions among the seasons are established from the visible operations that follow. But because this does not occur in the same way every year, the seasons are distinguished by the risings of the fixed stars.

Each season has elemental qualities: spring, being moist and warm, has taken on the nature of air; summer is dry and warm, like fire; autumn is cold and dry; winter is cold and damp, like the nature of moisture. For winter is also called winter from *hyein* (ὕειν), which means “to rain.”

[Col. 0459D] Midway through winter, with the blowing of the Etesian winds. The Etesian winds are those which they call annual winds. They blow from the north for forty days after the rising of the Dog, and their blasts are stronger in the southern than in the northern regions. See Book Two of the *Meteorologica*.

The figures which I have placed here I found drawn in this way in a written exemplar. Since they contributed something to this chapter, they seemed not to be omitted. The following had been written beside the first figure:

[Col. 0459]

“On the seasons, their parts, and the qualities of the year: a diagram.”

[Col. 0461C] S, the sign for a half, signifies a half. For every word denoting a measure, or every portion of an *as*, had its own character [sic], concerning which there is discussion in Bede, too, in his treatment of the parts of the *as*, and in several other ancient grammarians. But through the ignorance or negligence of copyists these signs have been corrupted. [Col. 0462C] For the signs placed by Bede do not correspond to those engraved or painted in ancient sources.

I have appended here another figure, which I found letter for letter in a very ancient codex. The following had been written beside it:

“On the correspondence of the cosmos, the microcosm, and the year.”

[Col. 0461]

[Col. 0457C] There are four seasons of the year, during which the sun, traversing different regions of the sky, regulates the world beneath it—divine wisdom, certainly, providing that it should not remain perpetually in the same places and lay waste to the adornment of the world through the dryness of its heat, but should gradually move through different regions and preserve the appropriate conditions for earthly fruits to be born and ripened. The seasons seem to have received their name from this regulation, or certainly because, tempered together by a certain likeness of their qualities, they revolve in mutual harmony; hence they are rightly called *tempora*, “seasons.” Winter, since the sun is farther removed, is cold and damp. Spring, when it returns above the earth, is damp and warm. Summer, when it burns intensely overhead, is warm and dry. Autumn, when it descends toward the lower regions, is dry and cold. Thus, as each season embraces and moderates what surrounds it, all things are enclosed together in mutual relation like a sphere. The elements of the world likewise are distinguished by these qualities, different in themselves but joined to one another by mutual association. Earth is dry and cold, water cold and damp, air damp and warm, and fire warm and dry; therefore earth is compared with autumn, water with winter, air with spring, and fire with summer.

The human being himself, whom the wise call *microcosmos*, that is, “the smaller world,” has a body tempered throughout by these same qualities. Each of the humors of which he consists imitates the character of the season in which it is strongest. Blood, which increases in spring, is damp and warm. Red bile, which prevails in summer, is warm and dry. Black bile, which prevails in autumn, [Col. 0459A] is dry and cold. Phlegm, which prevails in winter, is cold and damp. Blood is especially vigorous in infants; red bile in adolescents; melancholy in mature adults—that is, bile mixed with the dregs of black blood; and phlegm dominates in the elderly.

Blood makes those in whom it is strongest cheerful, happy, compassionate, prone to much laughter and talk. Red bile makes people lean, though great eaters, quick, bold, irritable, and active. Black bile makes them steady, serious, composed in character, and deceitful. Phlegm produces slowness, sleepiness, and forgetfulness.

Different authorities assign different beginnings to the seasons. Isidore, bishop of Hispania, said that winter begins on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, spring on the eighth before the Kalends of March, summer on the ninth before the Kalends of June, and autumn on the tenth before the Kalends of September. The Greeks and Romans, whose authority in this discipline has generally been followed rather than that of the Spaniards, determine that winter begins on the seventh day before the Ides of November, spring on the seventh before the Ides of February, summer on the seventh before the Ides of May, and autumn on the seventh before the Ides of August. They mark the beginnings of winter and summer by the evening or morning rising and setting of the Pleiades, and place the beginning of spring and autumn when the Pleiades rise and set approximately at midday or midnight.

Finally, in the most authoritative and distinguished books of cosmography, we find these same seasons marked out exactly, with the rising of the Pleiades noted on the seventh day before the Ides of May and their setting on the seventh before the Ides of November. Pliny the Elder, in Book Two of his *Natural History*, likewise judged that the seasons should be distinguished in this manner.

The holy man Anatolius of the Church, in his Paschal work, after discussing with great precision the equinoxes and solstices and the increase of hours and moments, ended both his discussion and the little book itself as follows:

> “Do not fail to observe this: although the four boundaries of the seasons that we have mentioned approach the Kalends of the following months, each nevertheless occupies the middle of its season—that is, of spring, summer, autumn, or winter. The beginnings of the seasons therefore do not commence from the point at which the Kalends of the months begin. Rather, each season is to begin in such a way that the equinox divides the season from the first day of spring; likewise, summer is divided on the ninth day before the Kalends of July, autumn on the eighth before the Kalends of October, and winter on the eighth before the Kalends of January.”

Where the people of God made the beginnings of the seasons according to the law, Scripture bears witness. It commands:

> “Observe the month of new crops and the first of springtime, and you shall celebrate the Passover to the Lord your God.”

The Egyptians appear to have followed this rule, since their most learned bishop, Protereus, says:

> “One must also observe that those who establish the beginning of the first month’s lunar course absolutely on the twenty-fifth day of the month Phamenoth, which is the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, are greatly mistaken, because at that time the beginning of spring seems to have been fixed with the utmost care by those who sought to determine it.”

Spring is called *ver* because in it all things become green—that is, they grow vigorous. Summer is named from the heat (*aestus*) that it supplies for ripening fruits. Autumn takes its name from the ripening of the fruits gathered in it. Winter is interpreted by the teachers as cold and sterility. These names for the seasons correspond to those used in our regions.

But the Indians, where the appearance of the sky and the risings of the stars are different, are said to have two summers and two harvests in the year, with winter between them and the blowing of the Etesian winds [Note: [Col. 0461] C, “between the two summers” (*illas*)]. During our winter they are said to have gentle breezes and a navigable sea there [Note: [Col. 0461] C, “where” (*ubi*)]. Egypt too, in the middle of our winter, is said to have fields especially rich in flowering plants and woods laden with fruit.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On Natural Years

[Note: [Col. 0461D]]

**BRID. RAMES. GLOSSES.**—The year received its name either from renewing all things that had passed according to the natural order, or from the circuit of time, because the ancients used *am* for *circum*, “around,” [Col. 0462D] and so forth. A solar or civil year occurs when the sun traverses the zodiac in 365¼ days. The Romans begin it at the winter solstice, the Hebrews at the spring equinox, the Greeks at the summer solstice, and the Egyptians in autumn. A common lunar year consists of twelve moons, that is, 354 days; an embolismic year consists of thirteen moons and [Col. 0463C] 384 days, taking its beginning from the Paschal moon. A great year occurs when all the stars, having completed their appointed courses, return to their proper places; Josephus says that it is completed in 600 solar years.

Then, because of the virtues and glorious benefits that they continually sought—namely, astrology and geometry—God granted them longer spans of life. Geometry is the discipline of magnitude and shapes. It takes its name from earth and measurement: earth is called γῆ (*gē*) in Greek, and *metra* means “measurement.” The Egyptians were the first to discover astronomy; the Chaldaeans were the first to teach astrology and the observation of births.

There is some difference between astronomy and astrology. Astronomy consists of many branches of inquiry. It defines what the world is, what the heavens are, the position and courses of the spheres, the axis and poles of heaven, the climatic zones of the sky, and the courses of the sun, moon, and stars. Astrology, however, is partly natural and partly superstitious. It is natural when it describes the courses of the sun and moon or the fixed stations of the stars at particular times. [Col. 0463D] It is superstitious in the form followed by the mathematicians, who take omens from the stars and distribute the twelve signs of heaven among the individual members of the soul or body, attempting through the movement of the stars to predict human births and characters.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—“The year from renewing.” Up to this point Bede, by way of preparation for describing the seasons of the year, has explained certain effects of the sun and other related circumstances. From this chapter to the beginning of the annals, however, he has collected material concerning the variety of years. The year was the final division of time among those that we proposed at the beginning of the book. It was therefore appropriate that, before explaining the annals, he should give an account of years.

A year, if we define it generally, is a determinate interval of time produced when some wandering star completes the sign-bearing sphere in its motion through the sequence of the signs. Hence the epithet applied by the ancients to the year, taken from astrology, *vertens annus*, “the turning year”: it is produced by the revolution of any planet through the zodiac. Some writers use this epithet to express the nature of the year, and sometimes to distinguish years that are not calculated by the movements of the stars but by human convention. Thus the true solar turning year consists of 365¼ days; the common year is shorter by a quarter; and the leap year is longer by half a day and a quarter. Lunar years likewise are either turning years or common years—that is, years from which, for the sake of easier calculation, we have either subtracted or added something.

Because the ancients used *am* for *circum*, “around.” So also Fabius Pompeius. “*Am*,” he says, “as a preposition in ordinary speech, means ‘around’; hence *servus ambactus*, that is, ‘a servant led around.’” The Greeks too, looking to the same idea, call the year ἐνίαυτος (*eniautos*), because it returns into itself; such is the nature of a circuit and a circle.

“Which they specifically call the great year.” They call it the great year when all the movements of the stars, even the slowest, have once completed their courses. Cicero calls this a true turning year in the sixth book of *On the Republic*, in his discussion of the brevity of human life, where many thousands of turning years are contained. But the number is not yet sufficiently established. More recent authorities set it at 69,000 solar years. If you wish to learn more about this, see Macrobius’ *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*. Solar years are also called great in comparison with lunar years, as in the Poet:

> “Meanwhile the sun revolves through the great year.”

The nature of the turning year is also established by this verse.

“Embolismic”—that is, “inserted” or “added.” See Macrobius; but he calls the inserted months ἐμβολισμοί (*embolismoi*), not the year.

“A great year.” Plato also calls this the Platonic year, for his views concerning this year were remarkable.]

A year received its name either from renewing all things that had passed according to the natural order, or from the circuit of time, because the ancients used *am* for *circum*, “around.” Thus Cato says in his *Origines*, *oratorum amterminum*, that is, *circumterminum*, “the boundary around”; and *ambire* is used for *circumire*, “to go around.”

[Col. 0462B] There is a lunar year, a solar year, a year belonging to the individual wandering stars, and one belonging to all the planets together, which they specifically call the great year.

The lunar year is understood in four ways. The first is when the moon, traversing the zodiac in 27 days and 8 hours, returns to the sign from which it departed. The second is longer by two days and four hours; this is ordinarily called a month, when, after 29 days and 12 hours have elapsed, the moon, already waning, returns to the sun from which it had newly departed. The third is completed in twelve such months, that is, in 354 days, and is called common because two such years very often run concurrently. The fourth, called in Greek ἐμβολισμός (*embolismos*), “superaddition,” has thirteen months, that is, 384 days. Among the Hebrews, both years begin with the beginning of the Paschal month and end there as well. Among the Romans, the year begins with the emerging moon of the month of January and ends there.

The solar year occurs when the sun returns to the same places among the stars, after completing 365 days and 6 hours, that is, a quarter [Col. 0463B] of a whole day.
