This quarter, taken four times, requires one day to be inserted, which the Romans call the leap day, so that the sun may return to the same circuit. Every fourth year of the solar cycle is a leap year, one day longer than the other three. When it has been completed, the sun returns to all the places of the signs at the same hours of day and night as it did four years earlier.

The year of the wandering stars is the period in which each of them traverses the circuit of the zodiac, as we have explained above. The great year occurs when all the wandering stars together return to their respective places, which they had occupied together.

Josephus, in Book One, chapter 4, of the *Antiquities*, mentioned this while describing the longevity of the first human beings:

> “Let no one, comparing the life of the ancients with modern life and the brevity of the years in which we now live, suppose that what has been said about them is false; nor, because human life is no longer extended over so long a period, let him believe that they too failed to reach that length of life. For since they were devout and had been created by God himself, and since suitable provisions had been prepared for them for a longer time, they rightly lived through spans of so many years. Then, because of the virtues and glorious benefits that they continually sought—namely, astrology and geometry—God granted them longer spans of life. They could not now have learned these things unless they lived for six hundred years, for the great year is completed in that many years. The civil year, that is, the solar year, the Hebrews begin at the spring equinox, the Greeks at the solstice, the Egyptians in autumn, and the Romans at the winter solstice.”

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the Unequal Years of the Ancients

[Note: [Col. 0464D]]

**BRID. RAMES. GLOSSES.**—Some even thought that Holy Scripture had reckoned years differently in the earliest ages of the world, making them so short that one of our years was believed to contain ten of theirs. They thought this because they did not believe that human beings in the earliest ages lived for nine hundred years, or even for longer than people live now. They therefore supposed that Holy Scripture had calculated the span of years differently from the present system, which must in no way be believed.

“Thus,” he says, “among them individuals are reported to have lived for thousands of years.” After these words, following a short interval, blessed Augustine adds:

> “What shall I say of Cainan, who among us is found to have been 170 years old, whereas among the Hebrews he is read as having been 70 years old when he begot Malaleel? He would have begotten a son at the age of seven if what were then called seventy years were the seven years that they were. But when I say this, the reply immediately comes that this is a falsehood of the Jews.”

Again, shortly afterward:

> “Let us now see how it can clearly be shown that the years were not so short that ten of theirs made one of ours, but were of the same length as those we now have—years reckoned by the circuits of the sun, through which those people lived their very long lives. It is written that the flood occurred in the six-hundredth year of Noah’s life. When we read there, ‘And the waters of the flood came upon the earth in the six-hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month,’ if that year were the smallest kind, of which ten made one of ours, and had thirty-six days, such a year, if it received that name according to the ancient custom, would either have no months, or its month would be three days long, so that it might have twelve months. How, then, could it be said here ‘in the six-hundredth year, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month,’ unless the months were then of the same kind as they are now? For how else could it be said that the flood began on the seventeenth day of the second month?

> “Then, at the end of the flood, we read: ‘And the ark rested in the seventh month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, upon the mountains of Ararat. The waters diminished until the tenth month; and in the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains appeared.’ If the months were of this kind, then surely the years too were of the kind we now have. Those three-day months could not have had twenty-seven days. Or if one-thirtieth of a three-day period was then called a day, so that everything was reduced proportionally, then that great flood, which is said to have occurred over forty days and nights, did not even last four of our days. Who could endure such absurdity and vanity?

> “Therefore this error must be removed—an error that seeks, through a false conjecture, to support the credibility of our Scriptures in one place while destroying it in another. The day was just as long then as it is now, determined by twenty-four hours in the course of day and night. The month was just as long as it is now, bounded by the moon’s beginning and completion. The year was just as long as it is now, completed by twelve lunar months, with five days and a quarter added for the solar course. Such were the years in the six-hundredth year of Noah’s life; such was the second month and its seventeenth day when the flood began, during which forty successive days of torrential rain are recorded.

> “Those days did not consist of two hours or a little more—namely, four minutes—but of twenty-four hours, day and night, having fully elapsed. Consequently, those ancient people lived years just as long as ours, even for more than nine hundred years: as Abraham later lived 175, his son Isaac 180, and his son Jacob nearly 150; as Moses, after an intervening span of some years, lived 120; and as people now live 70 or 80 years, or not much more, of whom it is said: ‘And more than this is labor and sorrow.’”

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—When Pliny the Elder had mentioned, and so forth, the passage occurs in Pliny concerning the longest spans of life, Book Seven, chapter forty-eight.

“Arcadians,” he says, “whose years consist of three months.” The Arcadians are thought to have been the first of mortals and the first to observe time by the course of the moon; hence the story became widespread that they were older than the moon. There is also a representation of the crescent moon—called μηνοειδής (*mēnoeidēs*)—which is still an emblem both of Arcadia and of Greece, and which the nation of the Turks claims for itself.]

Let this suffice concerning natural years. Blessed Augustine also teaches that the ancient peoples of different nations deviated in various ways from the truth in their observation of the year. In Book Twelve of *The City of God*, he argued against those who thought that Holy Scripture had reckoned years differently in the earliest ages of the world—that is, as being so short that one of our years was believed to contain ten of theirs. They said:

> “When anyone hears or reads that a person lived for nine hundred years, he ought to understand ninety: ten of their years were one of ours, and ten of ours were one hundred of theirs.”

Among other things, Augustine says:

> “To make it less incredible that the year was then reckoned differently, they add what is found in the histories of many writers: that the Egyptians had a year of four months, the Acarnanians one of six months, and the Lavinians one of thirteen months.”

When Pliny the Elder had reported that it had been recorded that one person lived 152 years, another ten years more, others 200 years, others 300, others 400, some as many as 500, others 600, and some even reaching 800, he judged that all these cases resulted from ignorance concerning time.

> “Some,” he says, “defined a year by summer and another by winter; others by four divisions of the seasons, as did the Arcadians, whose years consisted of three months.”

He also added that the Egyptians—whose short years, as we said above, consisted of four months—sometimes bounded the year by the course of the moon.

> “Thus,” he says, “among them individuals are reported to have lived for thousands of years.”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the Calculation of the Leap Day

[Note: [Col. 0466C]]

**BRID. RAMES. GLOSSES.**—Because it is recognized that the sun completes the annual circuit of the heavens—that is, the twelve well-known signs of the zodiacal circle—not in 365 days but with six additional hours: if you wish to know where the leap day comes from, understand that the sun remains in each sign for thirty days and ten and a half hours. Therefore multiply twelve by thirty: the result is 360. Again, because it remains for ten hours, multiply twelve by ten: the result is 120 hours. Divide these by twenty-four. Twenty-four hours make one day; forty-eight make two; ninety-six make four; 120 make five. Thus there are 365 days. Again, because it remains for ten and a half hours, multiply twelve by the half-hour: the result is six hours. From these six hours the leap day customarily increases each year. Therefore, in the first year of preparation for the leap day, at the first hour of the day that precedes the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, the sun enters Aries. This gloss has already been written out in full above.

The leap day is produced from the quarter-day calculation over four years: the sun returns to the sign from which it departed not in 365 days, but with a quarter of a day added. For example, if the rising sun now enters the equinoctial point of the heavens, it returns to that point in the following year at midday, in the third year in the evening, in the fourth at midnight, and in the fifth again at sunrise. It therefore necessarily warns that a day must be added, lest, if it were not added every 365 years, the spring equinox should eventually occur on the day of the summer solstice.

The Egyptians insert this day when their year is completed, that is, on the fourth day before the Kalends of September; the Romans insert it on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, from which it also received its name.

According to the shorter and commoner method of reckoning, the leap day is produced by the sun’s delay, since it does not fully return to the same line after 365 days. If, for example, you carefully observe the sun rising from the middle of the east at the spring equinox—which, according to the Egyptians, occurs on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April—you will find that in the following year it rises somewhat lower on the same day. In the third, fourth, and fifth years you will find the same diminution increasing to such an extent that, unless you add a day beforehand, the sun will rise from the middle of the east on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April to produce the equinox, while maintaining the same delay in its other risings as well.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—“For there are some who, by the ease of calculation…” This method of calculation is not difficult. It is accomplished by dividing the parts of the zodiacal twelfth, and also by distributing among the individual days the minutes that make up the solar year—namely, the number of minutes by which the sun advances each day less than a complete thirtieth part of the zodiacal twelfth, which we mentioned above. But here it seemed useful to append a table of the movements of the sun and moon, indicating how much of the zodiacal space they traverse at each moment of time.

[Col. 0467D] In this diagram, the first row shows how many signs the heavenly body traverses during that period; the second, the thirtieth-parts of the zodiacal twelfth; the third, how many first minutes; the fourth, second minutes; and the fifth, third minutes. The first minutes are the sixtieth parts of each thirtieth-part, or degree. Mathematicians proceed in this division indefinitely, by dividing each preceding minute into sixty parts.

It is clear from this table that, by the calculation of addition, somewhat more is intercalated than the sun’s true movement requires. For this reason the solstice, winter solstice, and equinoxes occur earlier in our age, as far as the calculation of the months is concerned, than in the time of Cicero or Pliny. More has been said about this above.

“Which the Egyptians insert when their year has solemnly been completed.” Although the Egyptians intercalate differently from the Romans, the principle is the same in both cases. Both add the intercalary day to the final month, because the outermost portions of magnitudes ought to increase by addition. For the Romans, March was originally the first month, before they began intercalating. The Egyptians likewise add the day around autumn, at the end of the year.

“At least by the lines of a sundial on the ground.” The sundial is to be understood as the kind I described above—namely, the *horoscopum*, a vessel which Vitruvius calls a *scaphe*. I do not know how this could be detected in any other way.]

I do not now wish to devise anything new concerning the calculation of the leap day, but have decided to insert into this little work what I once said in a letter to a friend who had asked about it. After a suitable preface, I added the following:

> “Just as the so-called leap of the moon is produced over nineteen years by the place and time of its earlier illumination, so conversely the leap day is generated by no other cause than the delay of the sun’s course. There are some who can easily calculate, without difficulty, how much of the increasing leap-day fraction is completed in each year, month, week, and successive day. Yet they do not know how this fraction increases, what causes it, what its rationale is, or what destructive error would arise if the leap day itself were not intercalated in its proper order according to custom.

> “The leap day is therefore produced from the quarter-day calculation over four years. A quarter is ordinarily called the fourth part of anything—of money, time, or place, for example. Thus the fourth part of a day, which is completed in twenty-four hours together with its night, namely six hours, is commonly called a quarter-day.

> “The method by which this quarter is gathered over four years into a complete day and intercalated in its proper place is as follows: the sun is known to complete the annual circuit of the heavens—that is, the twelve most famous signs of the zodiacal circle—not in 365 days but with six additional hours. Hence, if, for example, the rising sun now enters the equinoctial point of the heavens in the morning, it returns to that point in the following year at midday, in the third year in the evening, in the fourth at midnight, and on the fifth day once more at sunrise, after the entire circuit of the day has been completed. It therefore necessarily indicates that an extra day must be inserted somewhere and joined to the fullness of the fourth year.

> “The Egyptians customarily intercalate it when their year has been solemnly completed, that is, on the fourth day before the Kalends of September; the Romans do so on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, and therefore call it the leap day. If any calculator, neglecting to do this, should suppose that all years must consist only of 365 days, he will soon find that a great loss has arisen in the annual circuit. After several cycles of turning years, the careless calculator will be horrified to find spring occurring in the summer months, winter in the spring months, autumn in the winter months, and summer in the autumn months.

> “If what we have said briefly about the zodiacal circle and the circuit of the heavens is unknown to anyone, we have taken care to satisfy him by a commoner, perhaps shorter and clearer, method, so that one who did not learn to attend to the signs of heaven in childhood at school may at least grasp what is necessary from the lines of a sundial drawn on the ground. Let him therefore know that, through its pauses and daily delay, the sun serves the Creator’s ordering of this annual quarter. More careful investigation shows that it cannot be fully brought back to the same line of the sundial in 365 days. If, for example, in the present year it has risen from the middle of the east at the spring equinox—which, according to the Egyptians, who hold the palm among calculators, customarily occurs on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April—it will rise somewhat lower on the same day one year later. In the third, fourth, and fifth years, the moderation of its natural course increases the same diminution to such an extent that, unless the leap day has already been intercalated according to custom, it will rise from the middle of the east on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April to produce the equinox. Nevertheless, it will preserve the same consistency of delay in all its other risings and settings throughout the entire year.”

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the Measurement of the Increase and of the Leap Day

[Note: [Col. 0469D]]

**BRID. RAMES. GLOSSES.**—“It is powerful by the number six,” and so forth, because there are six divisions. The first order of numbers runs from one to ten; the second from ten to one hundred; the third from one hundred to one thousand; the fourth from one thousand to ten thousand; the fifth from ten thousand to one hundred thousand; [Col. 0470D] and the sixth from one hundred thousand to nine hundred thousand. In the second order, sixty has the same value. Just as the number six is contained in six in the first order of numbers, so the number six is contained in sixty in the second order. Six times one is six; six times ten is sixty.]

[Col. 0469A]

So that my view concerning the measurement of the leap-day increase may not be hidden from you, I say that its quarter-day—that is, six hours—increases each year; one hour every two months; half an hour every month, speaking of the sun’s natural course; and a quarter of an hour, that is, a point, every half-month. For we know that the sun traverses the zodiacal circle—that is, the twelve signs of the horoscope—in 365 days and 6 hours; that it naturally completes each sign of the same zodiac in 30 days and 10½ hours; and that it traverses half of each sign in 15 days, 5 hours, and a quarter of an hour.

Nor do we think that the opinion of those should be accepted who, as though attributing nothing to the night, affirm that only three hours are added annually to the leap day. If this were so, the complete day that had accumulated would not be completed before the circuit of eight years. Even the common and uneducated populace knows that a whole day, together with its night, consists of twenty-four hours. If they do not deny that the whole is completed over four years, by what reasoning do they deny that a quarter of it is completed in each of the four years?

But if anyone thinks our assertion on this point should be rejected, let him read the fourth book of blessed Aurelius Augustine on the Holy Trinity. There, while discussing the perfection of the number six, in which the world was made, he did not fail to mention this quarter—or rather, to teach that it was provided and made by the almighty wisdom of the Creator for a definite mystery:

> “One and two and three make six; this number is therefore called perfect because it is completed by its parts. It has three such parts: a sixth, a third, and a half, and no other part that can be expressed as a fraction is found in it. Its sixth is therefore one, its third two, and its half three. One, two, and three together complete the same number six, whose perfection Holy Scripture commends especially in this: that God made his works in six days; that on the sixth day the human being was made in the image of God; and that, in the sixth age of the human race, the Son of God came and became the son of man, so that he might restore us to the image of God.

> “A single year also, if its twelve complete months are considered—months completed by thirty days each, for the ancients observed such a month, as the lunar circuit demonstrates—is powerful by the number six. What six are worth in the first order of numbers, which consists of units and reaches ten, sixty are worth in the second order, which consists of tens and reaches one hundred. The number sixty is therefore the sixth part of the year.”

A little later he says:

> “Accordingly, the six of the first order is multiplied as though it were the six of the second order, and six times sixty produce 360 days, which are the twelve complete months. But because, just as the lunar circuit demonstrates the month to human beings, the solar circuit reveals the year, five days and a quarter of a day remain for the sun to complete its course and bring the year to an end. Four quarters make one day, which must be intercalated after the circuit of four years—a practice they call the leap day—so that the order of the seasons may not be disturbed.

> “If we consider those five days and the quarter, the number six has great force in them as well. First, because, as often happens when the whole is reckoned from a part, there are no longer five days but rather six, since the quarter is taken as a day. Next, because within those five days there is one-sixth of a month. The quarter itself has six hours, since a whole day—that is, day together with night—contains twenty-four hours, and its fourth part, the quarter-day, is found to contain six hours. Thus, in the course of the year, the number six has great force.”

I have wished to excerpt these words from so great an author so that, when rereading my modest account of the nature of the leap day, you may understand from the mouth of so learned a teacher not only that it increases by six hours each year, but also the multiple perfection of that same number six, by which the year itself is constituted.

## CHAPTER XL. Why the Leap Day Is Intercalated on the Sixth Day before the Kalends of March

For this reason the Romans decided to intercalate the leap day in the month of February: it was shorter than the other months and was the final month of the year. They did not, however, wait until it had been completed, as the Egyptians and Greeks wished to do after the entire course of their year had elapsed, lest, by completely severing their ancient rule, they separate the beginning of March from the end of February.

They therefore did not place it before the sixth day before the Kalends of March because, honoring the god Terminus, they absolutely refused to move the sacred Terminalia, which they had instituted to be celebrated once on the twenty-third day of that month, to another day. After celebrating those rites in due order, they eventually inserted, for a time, several necessary days, and, as knowledge increased through the ages, one quarter-day.

Alas, miserable fools! They did not know that the one whose kingdom will have no end, who said, “I am the beginning, and this is what I speak to you” [Note: [Col. 0469] C, “who”], was the Terminus to be honored with divine worship, and that sacred rites and sacrifices were to be offered to him. More miserable still are the mad who, possessing the promise of the heavenly kingdom, seek to cling instead to things subject to an end, rather than hasten toward eternal things, where they will live without end.

## CHAPTER XLI. That the Moon Also Has a Quarter-Day

[Note: [Col. 0471B]

**BRID. RAMES. GLOSSAE.**—Therefore, just as, when the rule of the quarter dictates it, in the fourth year—which we call leap year—we usually place, on one and the same line of the sixth day before the Kalends of March, for example, the third and the fourth weekday, so also then we must remember to count the third and the fourth lunar age together in that same place, for example. We must always be extremely attentive to this procedure, so that when we have caused the Moon of February to have one day more than it was accustomed to have, nevertheless, on the days of the Kalends of March—except only in the eleventh year of the nineteen-year cycle—the Moon may retain the same age that it had previously.

Whoever reads this argument and perhaps encounters that deceptive gloss which teaches that one lunar age is to be counted twice within one Moon, namely on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, today, and likewise on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, tomorrow—that is, the first today and the first tomorrow—by counting in a confused order, must take care not to believe it at all. Rather, one should state it in the proper and orderly sequence: today the first, tomorrow the second; or, if today is the second, tomorrow the third; or, if today is the third, tomorrow morning the fourth. The same is to be understood of all the remaining lunar ages, from the first through the thirtieth, because otherwise February cannot have a thirtieth Moon in a leap year, and otherwise the fourteenth Moon at the Paschal term will not be the fourteenth but rather—something impious to say—the fifteenth.

[Col. 0471A]

Meanwhile, the calculator must remember to reckon the Moon of February as having twenty-nine days in ordinary years, but thirty in a leap year, whether it happens to end before or after the intercalated quarter-day. By the addition of this day, the lunar year is completed—if it is an ordinary year—in 355 days, and, if it is an embolismic year, in 385 days.

For it is plainly evident that the quarter-day under discussion pertains not only to the course of the Sun but equally to that of the Moon. For if you refuse to accommodate a quarter-day to the Moon as well, and in a leap year assign February a lunar month of the same length as you had previously assigned it, it will certainly follow that the Paschal fourteenth Moon of that year arrives one day earlier than it ought. Consequently the Paschal reckoning will waver, and soon the course of the entire year will totter, while the ever-inviolable structure of the nineteen-year cycle, increasingly disturbed, will be overthrown.

Therefore, just as, when the rule of the quarter-day dictates it, in the fourth year—which we call leap year—we usually place, on one and the same line of the sixth day before the Kalends of March, for example, the third and the fourth weekday, so also then we must remember to count the third and the fourth lunar age together in that same place, for example. We must always be extremely attentive to this procedure, so that when we have caused the Moon of February to have one day more than it was accustomed to have, nevertheless, on the days of the Kalends of March—except only in the eleventh year of the nineteen-year cycle—the Moon may retain the same age that it had previously.

For this is especially why we advise that a quarter-day be assigned to the Moon: lest, being older than usual at the Kalends of March, it deflect the established course of the Paschal observance from its straight path. But how and by what divisions of time this same lunar quarter-day increases requires more extensive investigation. For, together with the quarter-day itself, the frequent interruption caused by embolisms and the reckoning of the leap also prevent the entire extent of the lunar course from being clearly discerned.

## CHAPTER XLII. On the leap of the Moon

[Note: [Col. 0471D]]

**BRID. RAMES. GLOSSAE.**—The leap of the Moon, by making the place and time of its lighting earlier, occurs over nineteen years. Although some people, reckoning each individual Moon as twenty-nine and a half days, make their lightings alternate perpetually between midday and midnight, they are not seeking in this the truth of nature but ease of calculation. For if you inquire into nature, the Moon of the first month, which now lights at midday, and that of the second month, which lights in the middle of the night, will in the following year be illuminated one hour, ten moments, half a moment, and one nineteenth of half a moment before midday or midnight.

This distinction, however, does not relate to the fixed end of an embolismic or ordinary year but to an equal division of nineteen years. For in this way, over nineteen years, the Moon’s lighting gradually anticipates itself, losing the span of one day, and causes the final year of the nineteen-year cycle to be reckoned as having 383 days. If you neglect to do this, then, over fifteen nineteen-year cycles, the fifteenth lunar age that is reckoned as the first will meet you.

**The leap of the Moon.** Just as one day is inserted because of the Sun’s delay, so one day is omitted because of the Moon’s speed; calculators call this the leap of the Moon. “Of its lighting,” that is, of the Moon’s. “Twenty-nine and a half each,” that is, twelve hours. The calculators say that each Moon is always lit either at midday or at midnight, without observing in this the truth of nature. For although this sometimes happens, the Moon is not always lit at midnight or at midday.

“If you inquire into nature,” that is, into the Moon’s lighting: in the lunar circuit, the Moon of the first month after the leap—that is, August—which now lights at midday, and the Moon of the second month after the leap—that is, September—which now lights in the middle of the night, will in the following year, that is, in the second or subsequent year, be illuminated one hour and ten moments—which is one point—and one nineteenth of a point before midday or midnight; that is, each year earlier and earlier.

“Distinction,” that is, division. “The end of the ordinary year,” that is, it pertains to nineteen solar years, not ordinary or embolismic years.

**Again, from above.**—First, it must be understood that in the entire nineteen-year cycle one day of the lunar leap is added. Next, one must ask how it gradually increases through the individual lunar months until it reaches a complete day. For in nineteen years there are 235 lunar months, including the embolisms. It is therefore necessary to divide the aforesaid day into as many parts as there are lunar months in the nineteen-year cycle.

This can be done in no more economical way than by dividing the twenty-four hours of the day into minutes. One hour contains ten minutes. Multiply ten minutes by twenty-four, and you will have 240 minutes. Of these 240 minutes, assign to the aforementioned 235 lunar months the same number of minutes—that is, one minute to each lunar month—and five minutes will remain.

These five minutes make half an hour, that is, twenty moments. Divide each moment into twelve ounces, and you will find 240 ounces. For twelve ounces multiplied twenty times complete the aforesaid number, and five still remain from the aforementioned 240 ounces. Divide these five again among 235 atoms. There are that many lunar months in the nineteen-year cycle, as we noted above, and you will find that in each lunar month of the said cycle the lunar leap increases by one minute, one ounce of a moment, and one atom.

“Anticipating, preceding, and going before.” “Losing, forfeiting.” It causes the final year of the nineteen-year cycle to be reckoned as having 383 days; that is, the fourth day is consumed by the reckoning of the leap. If you neglect to do this—that is, if you do not make the leap—then over fifteen nineteen-year cycles, that is, 285 years, the fifteenth lunar age will meet you when you ought to be reckoning the first.

**Again, from above.**—If some calculator wishes to investigate the lunar leap more precisely, he must know that the Moon traverses the zodiacal circle in twenty-seven days and eight hours. But in order to reach its lighting, two days and four hours must be added, so that it has twenty-nine days and twelve hours. Before it completes the twelfth hour, however, it loses from it four moments, one ounce, and one 564th part of a moment. For a moment consists of 564 atoms.

Therefore, if you wish to know this, collect for each lunar month—that is, from one lighting to the next—four moments, a twelfth of a moment, and one atom, which anticipate the Moon’s lighting. You will find that in nineteen years there are twenty-four hours, that is, one complete day, in which the lunar leap is completed.

Collect the aforesaid months over nineteen years. Twelve of these are ordinary years, each of which has twelve months and 354 days, and seven are embolismic years, which have thirteen months but 384 days. Therefore multiply the four complete moments twelve times—that is, by the twelve months of an ordinary year—and there are forty-eight moments. Again, multiplying forty-eight by twelve, according to the number of ordinary years, gives 576.

Likewise, multiplying the four moments by the thirteen lunar months of an embolismic year gives fifty-two; multiplied by seven, that is, by the seven embolismic years, they give 364 moments. When these are added to the aforementioned 576, the total is 740 moments. Dividing these by forty, because an hour consists of forty moments, gives twenty-three forties, that is, twenty-three hours, and in addition one twenty, which is half of forty—that is, twenty moments.

Thus, from complete moments alone, over nineteen years, twenty-three and a half hours are completed toward the twenty-fourth. It remains for the half-hour of the twenty-fourth hour that is left over to be supplied from parts of moments and atoms.

It must therefore be understood that in nineteen years there are 235 lunar months, both ordinary and embolismic. As many months as there are, so many twelfth-parts of a moment and, finally, so many atoms must be taken. When these parts are divided by twelve, they yield nineteen groups of twelve, that is, 228, which are nineteen moments, because in the annual cycle, which consists of 354 days, a complete moment is formed from these parts. Seven parts still remain from the 235 months, arising from the seven embolismic years.

Thus you have nineteen complete moments toward the twenty-fourth hour, collected from the parts of moments over nineteen years. Add these to the twenty mentioned above, and you will have thirty-nine moments; one moment is still lacking. Take, therefore, the seven twelfth-parts that we said remained, and make half a moment from six parts; seven remain.

Now take the atoms of the nineteen years by individual months, that is, 235, and divide them by forty-seven, which is a twelfth of a moment. You will find five times forty-seven. Add these to the seventh part mentioned above that remained, and make half a moment. Add to it the other half-moment found above, and you have one complete moment, which contains 564 atoms.

Joining this moment to the thirty-nine moments mentioned above, you will have forty moments, which make one complete hour of the day. Add this hour to the twenty-three hours mentioned above, and you will have one complete day of twenty-four hours.

**Again, from above.**—If you wish to know how the lunar day called the leap is prepared and increases over nineteen years, and how much of this increase grows in each lunar month—that is, in each lunar month among the 235 months (for that many lunar months are in the nineteen-year cycle)—multiply 235 by four, or four times 235, because four moments increase in each month. Therefore all 235 months are multiplied by four, producing 940 moments.

If this entire number is divided by forty, it yields twenty-three forties and twenty moments, that is, twenty-three and a half hours. But if you wish to know how the other half-hour, which appears to be lacking, is gathered and increases, it is undoubtedly understood as follows.

For not only do four moments of this lunar increase grow in each month; in addition, a twelfth of a moment and an atom—that is, a 564th part of a moment—also increases in every lunar month. Thus, in twelve months one moment is gathered. For the present, set aside those atoms, about which we shall speak later. In this way, over nineteen years, as though all the years had been ordinary and the seven embolisms had meanwhile been omitted, nineteen moments increase.

The one moment that appears to be lacking is gathered from the seven embolismic months and the atom of each month. From six [lacuna] embolismic months half a moment is gathered, containing 282 atoms; another half-moment is gathered from one embolismic month, namely a twelfth of a moment, in which part there are forty-seven atoms.

Therefore collect the atom of each month, which total 235, and add them together with the forty-seven; they make 282, that is, another half-moment. Add 200 and 200 together: they make 400. Then add eighty and eighty: 160. Add two and two: four. Thus, altogether, there are 564 atoms, that is, one moment. Added to the nineteen moments, this produces twenty moments, that is, the other half-hour.

Add this to the twenty-three and a half hours, and the result is twenty-four hours, that is, one natural day, which is called the lunar leap.

**Recapitulation of this argument.**—For how could it happen that over nineteen years one day necessarily had to be removed from the customary number of lunar days, unless some speed of the lunar revolution gradually brought this about throughout the entire period of the nineteen-year cycle? One day is removed from the Moon over nineteen years because at the end of the nineteen-year cycle, on the third day before the Kalends of August, where the thirtieth should have been, the first occurs.

This, then, is according to the Egyptians, whose opinion we follow in this calculation. Similarly, according to some authorities, on the seventh day before the Kalends of December, where the thirtieth ought to have been, the first occurs; where the first was, the second occurs; where the second was, the third occurs; and so on to the end of the year.

Finally, Anatolius, who most correctly establishes the beginning of the months, the head of the entire cycle, and its end at the spring equinox. Anatolius does not arrange his cycle in the same order as we do. For where we have the eighth year, the ogdoad, he has the fourteenth year of his cycle. Therefore the Moon that was last year, that is, in the thirteenth year, the eighth, he does not add eleven but twelve, so that it becomes the leap; and in the following year, that is, the fourteenth, at the equinox it becomes the twentieth. For with him the equinox is on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

There is therefore always one Moon between us and him, since he reckons the Moon from midday to midday. Thus, in the seventh year of our cycle, the Moon on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April is the sixth; on the tenth day before the Kalends it is the seventh; on the ninth day before the Kalends it is the eighth; and on the eighth day before the Kalends it is the ninth, which he makes the eighth. Adding twelve to it in the following year—that is, in the year of the ogdoad—he makes it the twentieth.

Therefore he said, “From the eighth to the twentieth,” whereas for us it is “from the ninth to the twentieth,” since we have not yet made the leap.

Victorius, by contrast, judged that this Moon should be inserted in the third year before the end of the ogdoad, at the Kalends of January, converting the fourth into the sixteenth—contrary, that is, to Anatolius’s opinion. In the other year, at the Kalends of January, he converts the fourth into the sixteenth; that is, while we convert the fourth into the fifth Moon at the Kalends of January, when at the end of the nineteen-year cycle we shall make the leap and therefore have the younger lunar age.

For he converts the fourth into the sixteenth, so that what had been the fourth, in the fifth year at the following Kalends of January—that is, in the seventh year, at the same Kalends, where it ought to have been reckoned the fifteenth because of the leap—is reckoned the sixteenth. Therefore he said, “From the fourth to the sixteenth,” whereas for us it is “from the fourth to the fifteenth,” since we have not yet made the leap.

The Egyptians, moreover, whose opinion the Catholic Church now follows, place the same change in the first year of the nineteen-year cycle. They make the annual lunar epacts, whose place is on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, make the leap from the eighteenth to the null—“null” meaning the thirtieth.

“Church” is a Greek word translated into Latin as *convocatio* (“assembly”), because it calls everyone to itself. “Catholic” is interpreted as “universal” or “general.” For it is not confined, like the gatherings of heretics, to certain parts of the regions; rather, spread throughout the whole world, it extends and diffuses itself.

Because of the present pilgrimage, the Church is called Zion, since, placed at a distance from the length of this pilgrimage, it watches for the promise of heavenly things; therefore it receives the name Zion, that is, “watchtower” or “place of contemplation.” Because of the future peace of the homeland, however, it is called Jerusalem, since Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace.”

**Again.**—“To make the leap from the eighteenth to the null.” “Null” means the thirtieth. For at the end of the nineteen-year cycle the Moon occurs at the Kalends of March. Calculate it by the argument of twenty-seven, and you will find that in that same year, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, the Moon is the eighteenth. Add to eighteen not eleven, as in the other years, but twelve because of the leap, and you will find, in the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, the thirtieth Moon. This is what he means: “From eighteen to null,” that is, to thirty.

The lunar year is shorter than the solar year by eleven days. Therefore, in order for the lunar year to correspond to the solar year, the epacts of the following year exceed those of the preceding year by twelve days. For this reason, in that year they rise from eighteen to null, that is, to thirty, twelve having been added. Whenever there is a leap, twelve lunar ages are always added; in other years, eleven.

The leap is naturally placed in the final year of the nineteen-year cycle. Therefore Anatolius and Victorius place the leap in an unsuitable location when they put it in other years, and consequently complete that same year—if it is not a leap year—in 353 days.

It is understood that if that year is a leap year, it then receives the lunar age that it had lost because of the leap, for in a leap year one lunar age increases, namely in the month of February, and that year has 355 days. In the year in which the leap occurs, one lunar age decreases, and that year has 383 days; the fourth day is consumed because of the leap.

This leap, indeed, appears to be more appropriately restored to the year on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, that is, according to the nature of the matter. Nevertheless, it is not placed there because of the terminal day. We take care to count it from the fourteenth Moon of the last Easter—that is, of the nineteenth year—to the fourteenth Moon of the first year of the same cycle.

For this reason Dionysius begins the aforesaid year with the fourteenth Moon and not the fifteenth, so that because of the lunar leap one day might not appear to be missing from that year. Yet such an arrangement—that one day should be counted as two—does no good, because the year in fact consists not of 354 but of 353 days.

No one should be troubled by the fact that the lord Bede says that the lunar leap is suited to the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. For he immediately adds: “Whether you make it here”—that is, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April—“or there”—that is, in the Moon of November—“or elsewhere”—that is, on the third day before the Kalends of August, as the Egyptians do—“and so forth,” clearly following the example of the Egyptians, who are said to make it in the penultimate month of their year, which is our July.

For the Egyptians, in their penultimate month—that is, July, since they begin the year in September—place the leap, just as some place it in our penultimate month, November. Therefore, in the nineteenth year, when they make the leap, the Moon of July does not rise to the thirtieth, one Moon having been lost because of the leap, but to the twenty-ninth. For this reason the third Moon is restored at the Kalends of August, although according to the calculation it is counted as the second.

Among the Egyptians the leap is placed on the third day before the Kalends of August, that is, the first Moon in place of the thirtieth; from this the third Moon comes to the Kalends of August in that year. Those who place the leap on the seventh day before the Kalends of December—that is, the first Moon in place of the thirtieth—count the seventh Moon at the Kalends of December in that year.

From August through December they disagree with the Egyptians, who hold the preeminence among calculators, because they do not make the leap simultaneously on the third day before the Kalends of August. After this, however, they come into agreement.

Nevertheless, the Egyptians terminate the leap more correctly than the others, because the others disagree with the epacts at the Kalends of September, October, and November, whereas the Egyptians disagree only at one point, namely the Kalends of August, as was said above.

**JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.**—The rationale of the lunar leap is that more time is intercalated through the embolisms in the lunar periods than the Moon itself requires; for it is somewhat faster than it is reckoned. The small excess by which it returns to the Sun earlier, owing to the minute division, cannot easily be noticed. This excess of time is removed in the nineteenth year, beginning with the first subtraction.

Similarly, as we explained above, more is intercalated in leap years than the Sun requires altogether. Hence it happens that in our age the winter solstice occurs before the Ides of December, whereas in Cicero’s time it occurred near the Kalends of January. But this excess of time is not removed by a leap because of the delay.

Concerning this leap, however, it appears probable that it is produced by the place and time of the Moon’s lighting, which occur earlier than is commonly thought. For how could it happen that over nineteen years one day necessarily had to be removed from the customary number of lunar days, unless some speed of the lunar revolution gradually brought this about throughout the entire period of the nineteen-year cycle?

Conversely, it has been demonstrated that, because of the slowness of the Sun’s course, one day is added to its course every four years. Although the order of this lunar speed and, so to speak, anticipation is not easily apparent, its measure is by no means hidden. For it is established that the diminution and removal of one day—which, however it occurs, is completed over nineteen years—increases by one hour, one point, and one nineteenth of a point in each year.

A day has twenty-four hours. When you distribute these among the nineteen years of the nineteen-year cycle, five remain. Multiply these by four, since an hour consists of four points; the result is twenty. Assign one to each year, and one remains. Divide this by nineteen, and you will see that, in order to complete the lunar leap, one hour, one point, and one nineteenth of one point increase annually, as we have said.

The Moon’s lighting therefore does not occur at one and the same temporal interval or under one and the same region of the sky. Rather, it always occurs somewhat earlier than it did in the preceding month, so that there may be a basis for leaping over one day in the nineteenth year.

At different points of the nineteen-year cycle, various calculators thought that this same lunar leap should be inserted—that is, that the lunar month which in other years was accustomed to have twenty-nine days should be made to contain thirty days. The natural rationale, however, is readily available: all such increases or decreases of the Sun and Moon should begin and end at the divisions of the equinoxes, where they were first created—those of the Sun at the spring equinox, and those of the Moon at the autumnal equinox.

Finally, Anatolius, who most correctly establishes the beginning of the months, the head of the entire cycle, and its end at the spring equinox, did not place this lunar change at the beginning or end of his nineteen-year cycle, but in its fourteenth year, which is the final year of the ogdoad. He made the Moon rise at the equinox from the eighth to the twentieth.

Victorius, by contrast, judged that this Moon should be inserted in the third year before the end of the ogdoad, at the Kalends of January, converting the fourth into the sixteenth. The Egyptians, moreover, whose opinion the Catholic Church now follows, assign the same change to the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, making the annual lunar epacts—whose place is on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April—make the leap from the eighteenth to the null.

Therefore they complete that same year, if it is not a leap year, in 353 days. Dionysius also seems to touch upon this in his letter when he says:

> “From the fifteenth Paschal Moon of the preceding year, for example, to the fourteenth of the following year, if it is an ordinary year, there will be 354 days; if it is an embolismic year, 384. But if one day more or less should occur, it is an evident error—except, of course, in the first year of the aforesaid nineteen-year cycle, which we take care to count from the fourteenth Paschal Moon of the last, that is, nineteenth, year to the fourteenth Moon of that same first year.”

For this reason, in that final year, while retaining eighteen lunar epacts—that is, additions—it assigns twelve days in the first year rather than eleven, as is customary in the other years. And because the cycles turn at the end of thirty days, no epact is placed at the beginning of the cycle itself.

The second year, however, receives eleven epacts. Therefore, as we said, from the fifteenth Paschal Moon of the first cycle to its end, there is no doubt that in ordinary and embolismic years we find the prescribed number of days.

This difference, then, compels us to consider the Moon to have the same age as Victorius only in the first six years of the nineteen-year cycle. Thereafter, once the leap has been inserted, it never ceases to have one day more than ours until we too insert it at the completion of the entire cycle.

This leap appears to be more appropriately restored to the year on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, because of the origin of the condition of the heavenly bodies mentioned above: the Moon of March, which on that day becomes the twenty-ninth, should then be changed into the ninth.

There are some, however, who think that this should rather be done in the Moon of November, so that, once such impediments have been settled with the end of the preceding year, they may thereafter enter the new year with an unencumbered reckoning, following the example of the Egyptians, who are said to do this in the penultimate month of their year, which is our July.

But whether you do it here, there, or elsewhere, it is necessary, if I am not mistaken, to count three months of twenty-nine days each in that place.

## CHAPTER XLIII. Why the Moon sometimes appears larger than it is reckoned

**BRID. RAMES. GLOSSAE.**—What reason is there for reckoning the Moon’s change from the hours of midday, when it is then neither placed in the sky nor risen above the earth, and when none of the solemn observances of the law begin or end at midday or after midday, but all begin and are completed during the evening hours? Unless perhaps it is because Adam, after sinning, was rebuked by the Lord at the afternoon breeze and was driven from the joys of paradise, from which we began to be exiled. The hour therefore ought to be marked, so that, when we say that the beginning of the Moon is at midday, although it has a defective nature, we may recall that at the same hour we too were expelled from paradise and began our state of defect.

Gregory says:

> “For after his fault Adam could not see the Lord in the substance of divinity, but heard the words of rebuke through an angel. Concerning this it is written: ‘When he heard the voice of the Lord walking in paradise at the afternoon breeze, he hid himself among the trees of paradise.’ What does it mean that after the human being’s sin the Lord no longer stands in paradise but walks, except that the more fervent light had departed and the coldness of his sin constricted the sinful soul? Therefore, while walking, he rebuked Adam, so that he might reveal his wickedness to blind minds not only through words but also through events: so that sinful humanity might hear through words what it had done; through the walking, might perceive the instability of its mutability after losing the state of eternity; through the breeze, from which the heat of charity had been driven out, might recognize its own torpor; and through the sun’s decline might understand that it was drawing near to darkness.”

Read the twenty-ninth book of the *Moralia*, in which I found these sacred words.

[Col. 0478D]

Remigius: “The Lord God had planted the garden of delight from the beginning,” that is, at the beginning, after removing the waters from the surface of the earth and gathering them into one place. Where we have *paradisum a principio* (“paradise from the beginning”), some manuscripts have *Eden ad ortum* (“Eden toward the rising [sun]”). From this we can conjecture that paradise was situated in the east.

Whatever part of the world it may occupy, we know that it is earthly and that, separated from our world by the intervening Ocean and opposing mountains, it is very far removed from us. For it is situated in a very high place, extending as far as the lunar sphere; hence it is also said that the waters of the Flood did not reach it at all.

In which he placed man. From the statement that man was placed in paradise, it is understood that he was not created there, but on this mortal earth of ours, because divine foreknowledge foresaw that he would sin there and therefore be driven from that holy land into this valley of misery.

Allegorically, paradise signifies the present Church, which is rightly called a garden of delights, since spiritual delights are provided for us in it. The tree of life in the midst of paradise is Christ in the midst of the Church. Concerning him a certain wise man says: “The tree of life is for those who grasp him.” He is also the fountain that, descending from the substance of the Father, came to irrigate his holy Church. Concerning it Zechariah says: “There shall be an open fountain for the house of David, for the washing of the sinner and of the menstruating woman.”

The house of David is the holy Church, for which—that is, for whose salvation—the fountain is open: namely, Christ, for the washing of the sinner. A sinner is one who carries out in deeds the evil that he conceives in his mind. A menstruating woman is one who does not touch another’s flesh but is defiled by her own; she signifies the sinful soul, which does not bring to completion in action the evil it conceives. Hence it is not disfigured externally, as by another’s flesh, but is polluted inwardly, as by its own flesh, through its thoughts.

Let us therefore sigh more ardently for that life blessed with eternal peace, when the light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun sevenfold, like the light of seven days.

Isaiah: “And the light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun sevenfold, like the light of seven days.” When will this be? When there shall be a new heaven and a new earth.

Everything that almighty God wrought over the span of six days was made for man, and at his fall all the elements suffered loss. For previously the earth did not produce thorns and thistles. This air was not of such density, but was pure. Likewise, the sun, moon, and stars suffered a diminution of their light.

On the day of judgment, however, when that appointed examination has taken place and all the rejected, together with the devil, have been shut up in hell, the Lord Jesus will rise up together with his body—which consists of all the elect—into heaven. Then the moon will borrow the sun’s splendor, and the sun will shine seven times more brightly than now, like the light of seven days; that is, it will shine manifoldly, and it will recover the sun’s light and splendor, which it lost when the first man sinned.

The blessed Isidore also says in the Book of Creatures that thereafter neither the sun nor the moon will set, but will remain forever in the place in which they were created, in accordance with Habakkuk: “The sun and moon stood in their dwelling”—for “they shall stand.” And why is this? So that those who will be in the underworld may not enjoy the brightness of the sun or moon.

Isaiah also speaks of this state: “Your sun shall no longer set, and your moon shall not diminish.” Isaiah likewise: “The moon shall be ashamed, and the sun shall be confounded, when the Lord has reigned in Zion and in Jerusalem.”

“The moon shall be ashamed,” that is, it shall waste away on the day of judgment, and the sun shall be confounded. Will they be so confounded that they fall from heaven? No. The Lord himself says: “The sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give its light, and the powers of heaven shall be shaken.”

For the blessed Augustine says that neither the sun, nor the moon, nor the stars will lose their light; rather, in comparison with the true light, which is Christ, all the stars and luminaries appear to be darkened. What brightness does the light of a candle provide if it is placed in the midst of the sun’s rays, or what increase of light does it give to those who look at it? None.

Joel: “The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood.” This is believed to have been partly fulfilled in the Lord’s Passion and partly to be destined to occur before the great day of the Lord, that is, the day of judgment. At that time the sun was indeed darkened, but the moon, having been turned to blood, could not openly appear to human beings, since it was then, as it were, at the fifteenth day of the paschal moon and was at times hidden from mortal sight by the interposition of the earth.

Alternatively: “The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and dreadful day of the Lord comes.” That is, the splendor of certain of the faithful, failing under the final tribulation, will be darkened, and the Church will be stained with the blood of martyrs.

But if the moon is kindled after the setting of the sun, one must not reckon it as the first moon until it has first seen evening; rather, it should be considered the thirtieth. For if the moon is kindled before evening, it is not for that reason counted as the first before evening, but in the evening. Similarly, if it is kindled after evening, that is, after sunset, it will not on that account be counted as the first until another evening has come and it is seen there—that is, in the evening—namely, because of its first condition.

But if someone, pressing this question more seriously, should say that in the year in which the saltus is to be inserted—that is, in the last year of the nineteen-year cycle—he saw the new moon two days before it was called the first, with many witnesses, namely on the fourth day before the Nones of April, this proves that the saltus is naturally placed in the last year of the nineteen-year cycle, because nearly all the moons of that year appear two days before they are called first; this happens in no other year. This is customarily the case as the saltus approaches; when it recedes, however, the moon is reckoned as it appears.

We are supported by the aid of paternal authority while we follow the decrees of the Council of Nicaea, which fixed the fourteenth moons of the paschal feast with such firm stability that their nineteen-year cycle can nowhere waver or deceive.

Nicaea is the metropolitan city of Bithynia, in which the emperor Constantine, as the tenth book of Ecclesiastical History relates, convened a council of 318 bishops; Arius was anathematized there. Hence it is called the Nicene Council, because it was held at Nicaea.

The Greek word *synodos* (σύνοδος) may be translated into Latin as “company” or “assembly.” An assembly is a meeting or gathering, from *coeundo*, that is, “coming together in one place.” Hence it is also called a *conventus*, just as a *conventus*, assembly, or council derives from the association of many people into one.

“Decrees” are what the common people establish; they are called *scita* because the people know them, or because the people inquire and ask that they be made.

What then? Is it to be believed that no one among those 318 bishops who sat in the Nicene Council saw the new moon that we saw on the fourth day before the Nones of April? They therefore saw the moon become visible on the fourth day before the Nones of April, yet they did not count it as the first, lest from this a contradiction of the rule governing common and embolismic years be fostered.

Then, under Pope Zosimus of holy memory, because water did not come until daylight, those who were to be baptized withdrew without being consecrated. Then likewise, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, when they themselves thought holy Easter ought to be celebrated.

*Baptismus*, “baptism,” is translated from Greek into Latin as *tinctio*, “dipping” or “immersion.” It is called immersion because there a person is changed for the better by the spirit of grace and becomes altogether different from what he was. For just as water cleanses the body externally, so, invisibly, its mystery through the Holy Spirit purifies the soul as well; its sanctification is as follows: when God has been invoked, the Holy Spirit descends from heaven and, having medicinally purified the waters, sanctifies them from himself. They receive the power of cleansing, so that in them both flesh and soul, defiled by impurities, may be cleansed.

He rejoiced laudably at being defeated. For he rejoiced at being overcome by the Easterners, who acted according to the definition of the Nicene Council, although he seemed inclined to favor his Westerners.

## JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA

**It should certainly be noted.** This is readily clear from the preceding chapter: one month is subtracted, which ought to have been subtracted from each month, if that were possible. The sudden subtraction therefore causes the moon’s shining to display a greater age than is reckoned, once a subtraction of one day has been made.

**The distinguished monk Pachomius.** Recently I obtained a little book of this Pachomius—or, as others write, Pachubius—from a certain scholar. When he gave me access to it, I indicated that, on account of its antiquity and piety, it deserved publication.

It should certainly be noted that the principle of this lunar saltus, through the long overflow of its increase, sometimes makes the moon appear larger than it is thought to be, so much so that even when the thirtieth day is drawing toward evening it can happen that it appears in the sky not slender. The nearer the end of the nineteen-year cycle approaches, the more frequently this occurs, for the evident reason that the saltus of which we speak is by then already completed for the most part.

But in asserting the natural truth, which is also confirmed as having been approved by the Council of Nicaea, this special rule must be observed: we must understand that the moon’s age changes not, as some maintain, from midday or half past midday, but rather from the evening hour. For since the moon first arose into the world in the evening, it is necessary that from then onward it take one age after another at evening hours, completing each successive age in twenty-four hours. By contrast, the sun, which first rose in the morning, completed one day from morning to morning, as the testimony of the book of Genesis shows.

What rational basis is there for calculating the moon’s change from midday hours, when it is neither then set in the sky nor has returned above the earth, and when none of the solemn observances of the law begins at midday or afternoon, but all begin and end together in the evening hours?

Unless perhaps it is because Adam, after sinning, was reproved by the Lord at the afternoon breeze and was driven from the joys of paradise. In repayment for the heavenly life that we exchanged for the misery of this age, the lunar change—which imitates our labors through its perpetual increase and decrease—ought to have been marked especially at the hour at which we began to be exiles. Thus, from that very hour of the moon’s change, we would daily be reminded of the verse: “The fool is changed like the moon, but the wise man will remain with the sun.” We would also sigh more ardently for that life blessed with eternal peace, when the light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun sevenfold, like the light of seven days.

But since, as it is written, “the moon is a sign of the festival day,” and just as the first light of the moon illuminated the world from evening, so every festival day in the law is commanded to begin at evening and to be completed at evening, the moon’s age will more appropriately be reckoned as new from the evening hour than from any other point, and it will retain the same age that it begins in the evening through the following evening.

And indeed, if it should happen that the moon is kindled by the sun shortly before evening, it must immediately be counted as the first moon and be so considered when the sun sets, because it has reached the hour of the day at which it first began to shine upon the earth. But if it is kindled after sunset, it must not be reckoned the first before it has seen evening; rather, it should be reckoned the thirtieth.

Even if, after sunset, it completes twenty-three hours from the time it was kindled, it must nevertheless retain until the following sunset the age that it had when the sun set, so that the order of its first condition is not disturbed.

Nor is it surprising that the moon, after spending so many hours as a new moon, should be shown openly in the sky, since it sometimes appears even at the sixth or seventh hour after its kindling. For it often happens, especially when it is positioned in Aries, that on one and the same day it is seen both in the morning and in the evening, owing evidently to a movement of its rising that occurs around midday.

But if someone, pressing this question more seriously, should say that in the year in which the saltus is to be inserted—that is, in the last year of the nineteen-year cycle—he saw the new moon two days before it was called the first, with many witnesses, namely on the fourth day before the Nones of April, while the fourteenth paschal moon of that same year is recorded in the aforesaid cycle on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, and therefore cannot be the first moon except on the day before the Nones of April, and should demand from us an explanation of this matter, then our humble weakness, lest it fail through its own frailty, must hasten to the aid of paternal, indeed divine, authority.

We are supported by the aid of paternal authority while we follow the decrees of the Council of Nicaea, which fixed the fourteenth moons of the paschal feast with such firm stability that their nineteen-year cycle can nowhere waver or deceive.

In that cycle, no calculator doubts that the paschal moon of the year in question becomes the first moon on the second day before the Nones of April. Therefore no one of the faithful is permitted to define it otherwise.

What then? Is it to be believed that no one among those 308 bishops who sat in the Nicene Council, and no one among the lower-ranking members of the assembly who assisted them in their deliberations and decrees, saw the new moon that we saw on the fourth day before the Nones of April? Is it not rather to be understood that, when they marked the paschal moon of that year as beginning on the day before the Nones of April, they thereby avoided a greater danger—namely, that if they decided otherwise, the indissoluble arrangement of common and embolismic years would be broken—which they had learned from the Hebrews to be inviolably observed by the authority of divine law?

We also defend the lunar observance that we maintain by particular indications of divine authority. We read, as the blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, writes, that Pachomius, a distinguished monk renowned for the works of apostolic grace and founder of the Egyptian monasteries, issued letters to the monasteries he governed, which he had received through the dictation of an angel, so that they would not fall into error in calculating the paschal solemnity and would know the moon of the first month in a common year and in an embolismic year.

We read, as Cyril likewise reports, that if the Nicene Council had not written down the lunar cycle of the first month, the cycle of the selenite stone in Persia would have sufficed as an example for the paschal calculation, since its inner whiteness waxes and wanes with the moon of the first month.

We also read, as the holy Paschasius, bishop of Lilybaeum, writes to the most blessed Pope Leo, that in the time of Pope Zosimus, when it was the last year of the nineteen-year cycle, certain people were inclined to keep Easter on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, celebrating it on the eighth day before the Kalends of April—that is, treating a common year as an embolismic year—and that the truth of the paschal observance became clear through a manifold miracle of heavenly power:

> “There is a certain very poor estate called Melthinas, situated among steep mountains and very dense forests. There is there a very small church built with poor workmanship. In its baptistery, on the holy paschal night, at the hour for baptizing, although there is no channel or pipe and no water at all nearby, a fountain fills itself. After a few people have been consecrated, since it has no conduit, the water departs of its own accord, just as it came. At that time, under Pope Zosimus of holy memory, because water did not come until daylight, those who were to be baptized withdrew without being consecrated. But on that night which was dawning into the Lord’s Day, the tenth day before the Kalends of May, the sacred fountain was filled at the appointed hour. Thus it became clear through an evident miracle that the error had belonged to the western regions.”

It is therefore clear that this is an ancient question concerning the moon’s age, one once carefully investigated through the diligence of the blessed Pope Leo himself. It is the same question that produced a long and serious controversy between the Churches of East and West. It persuaded Pope Hilary, after so many years had passed since the Nicene Council, to seek a new cycle, and Victor to construct a new paschal cycle.

In the contest over this matter, the aforesaid Pope Leo, assisted by Prosper, a most learned and eloquent man, diligently strove to win; yet at last, because those who adhered invincibly to the decrees of the Nicene Council were unanimous, he laudably rejoiced to be defeated.

Therefore, concerning this question, I find nothing better for myself and my readers to do or say than what I discover him to have done—he who surpasses us so greatly in knowledge, merit, and authority: namely, to follow the most revered judgment of the Fathers in matters that are doubtful and uncertain to us. For we must not suppose that we can detect the diversity of the moon’s course more acutely than the ancients, or discern more safely which path ought especially to be followed amid that diversity.

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the Nineteen-Year Cycle

### [Note: [Col. 0483C]]

**BRID. RAMES. GLOSSAE.**—The Council of Nicaea established the nineteen-year cycle on account of the fourteenth paschal moons, because each moon, after completing 235 revolutions over nineteen years, returns by an errorless course to the same day of the solar year. The cycle is divided into octads and hendecads, that is, into periods of eight and eleven years.

Eight lunar years exceed the same number of solar years by only two days. One of these days is used to complete the hendecad, while the other is consumed by the saltus. Otherwise the solar hendecad would exceed the moon by one day, although some forcibly attempt to make up these days from the leap days of the eight years, even though the leap day is customarily added to the sun in the month of February and does not prejudice the moon’s future reckoning; nor do they add any leap day to the hendecad itself. To put it more clearly: the two lunar days left over in the octad will make up the two days lacking in the hendecad.

**The nineteen-year cycle.** The lunar cycle and the nineteen-year cycle are almost the same, for both are completed in eighteen years. But they differ in this respect: by the lunar cycle one discovers what the moon is on the Kalends of January, where the year begins and where the cycle itself begins; by the nineteen-year cycle one determines how Easter ought to be announced. Its beginning is marked by the fourteenth paschal moon.

It is called the nineteen-year cycle because it is completed in nineteen years. It is a compound name formed from “ten,” “nine,” and “year.” This is because, by that nineteen-year arrangement, the same paschal term is reached—the term at which the paschal moon is always fourteen—which term always falls between the twelfth day before the Kalends of April and the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May.

The bishop Eusebius of Caesarea in Palestine composed the order of the nineteen-year cycle on account of the fourteenth moons of the paschal feast and in order to discover the very day of Easter. But when Lord Bede says above that the nineteen-year cycle was instituted by the Council of Nicaea on account of the fourteenth paschal moons, he speaks truly, and it should be understood in this way.

Many people had previously labored over this matter in many ways, including the aforementioned Eusebius, Bishop Hippolytus, Theophilus of Alexandria, Prosper, an Aquitanian by nationality, Victor, and Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria. They issued multiple cycles after multiplying the methods for determining the same feast. Later, the council sought to confirm whatever it had found more firmly established concerning this matter, as the tenth book of Ecclesiastical History reports in these words:

> “Accordingly, when they had issued decrees concerning these matters as reverence for the divine laws required, and had also handed down to the Churches the ancient canon concerning the observance of Easter, by which no further variation would arise, once everything had been properly arranged, peace and faith were preserved throughout the Churches in both the eastern and western regions as one and the same.”

The cycle is so called because it has been arranged in a circle and, as though disposed within a ring, embraces the order of the years without any variation and without any artificial device.

### JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA

**Eusebius and the nineteen-year cycle.** The nineteen-year cycle was made for calculating the moon. It consists of nine rows of numbers: the first contains the years of the Lord, the second the indictions, the third the epacts, the fourth the concurrent days, the fifth the lunar cycles, the sixth the fourteenth moons, the seventh the Sundays of Easter, the eighth the moon’s age on that same day, and the ninth the octads and hendecads. Bede will subsequently explain their reckoning.

The first to compose the order of the nineteen-year cycle was Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, on account of the fourteenth moons of the paschal feast and in order to discover the very day of Easter. He did so because the moon, whatever its age, returns after so long a period to the same day of the solar year—not because Egypt, or the other Church of Christ throughout the East, did not know how to find the moon’s course or the paschal day correctly, but because the things that they had investigated each year with labor and repeatedly disseminated throughout the world were often liable to become matters of dispute. Once a circular rule had been fixed, however, they could be observed always and learned without the anxiety of uncertainty.

It is said, moreover, that in ancient times the duty was assigned to the bishop of the Church of Alexandria to devote official attention and care to investigating the paschal computation, so that, by announcing it to the bishop of the apostolic see, he might cause the other leaders of the Churches to recognize the solemn day of Easter through him.

Accordingly, when the most blessed Pope Leo was petitioning the emperor Marcian to assign the matter to the bishop of Alexandria, so that he might examine carefully the paschal computation of the holy Theophilus, in which Easter appeared to have been fixed on the eighth day before the Kalends of May—Leo believing that the day had been recorded incorrectly—he says, among other things:

> “The holy Fathers indeed took care to remove the occasion for this, assigning all this responsibility to the bishop of Alexandria, since among the Egyptians expertise in this computation seemed to have been handed down from ancient times. Through him the day of the aforesaid solemnity was announced each year to the apostolic see, and the indication of that written notice traveled onward to the more distant Churches. But so that this kind of labor might eventually cease, the aforementioned man composed the cycle now widely known, by which, embracing in order the fourteenth moons of the first month, he left the day of Easter—which was to occur on the following Sunday—very easy for anyone to discover.

> “Proterius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, gave a brilliant account of this cycle in response to the inquiry of the holy Pope Leo, and deserved to have the following words of his reply proclaimed concerning it: ‘The letter of your affection, which our brother and fellow bishop Nectarius delivered in pious service, has made me glad. For it was fitting that such writings should be sent from the bishop of the Church of Alexandria to the apostolic see—writings showing that, through the teaching of the most blessed apostle Peter, the Egyptians had learned from the beginning through his disciple, the blessed Mark, what the Romans are known to have believed.’”

## CHAPTER XLV. On Embolismic and Common Years

### [Note: [Col. 0485B]]

**BRID. RAMES. GLOSSAE.**—The same cycle is divided into embolismic and common years, which are known to have been observed also on the authority of the ancient Hebrews. *Emblema* means a variation in pavement or an abundance. Hence an embolismic year is called “abundant.”

Embolismic and common years are found as follows. If there are 384 days from the fourteenth paschal moon of the preceding year to the fourteenth of the following year, it is an embolismic year; if there are 354, it is a common year.

Finally, in common years the moon is seen to lack eleven days in relation to the solar year; in embolismic years it appears to exceed the same solar year by nineteen days. The lunar year is shorter than the solar year by eleven days. These accumulate over three years and become thirty-three days; hence in the third year an embolismic year occurs, that is, the lunar year is then increased by thirty days, since three times eleven makes thirty-three.
