The three days that remain, together with the three remaining from the following three years, make thirty-six. Add these six to the two years that contain twenty-two days—the eleven days of the solar year taken twice—and they become twenty-eight days. Therefore a common year does not follow the seventh year, since twenty-eight days are immediately added, from which one month is formed, although two days are lacking; these, however, are supplied from the solar hendecad.

It should also be known that those who think that the solar year and the common or embolismic year begin simultaneously are mistaken. At the beginning of the nineteen-year cycle, the end of the embolismic year occurs at the appearance of the moon of April. For example, in the present year, which is the seventh of the nineteen-year cycle, the embolismic year will end at the appearance of the moon of April, since the preceding year—that is, the sixth year of the nineteen-year cycle—began at the appearance of the moon of April.

It should also be remembered that the moon of an embolismic year belongs to no month.

The Romans, who have unequal months, did not wish to insert embolismic months in one fixed place, but preferred to find, wherever possible, a vacant and suitable place among the middle periods of the year between the Kalends. They therefore said that the first embolismic moon was born on the fourth day before the Nones of December, the third on the day before the Nones of March, the fourth on the day before the Nones of December, the fifth on the fourth day before the Nones of November, the sixth on the fourth day before the Nones of August, and the seventh on the third day before the Nones of March.

### Computation of the Seven Embolismic Moons

In the first embolismic year, that is, the third year in the octad, there are twenty-two epacts. Therefore the moon is twenty-seven on the Kalends of September and October, and twenty-nine on the Kalends of November and December.

The moon that is twenty-nine on the Kalends of December and disappears there belongs to its own month. But the moon that begins on the fourth day before the Nones of December and ends on the thirtieth day, on the second day before the Kalends of January, belongs to the embolismic year. The moon that is first on the Kalends of January belongs to that month, and you must count it as ending on the thirtieth. Behold: you have found the embolismic moon in the first embolismic year, the thirtieth moon on the second day before the Kalends of January.

### On the Second Embolismic Year, That Is, the Sixth Year in the Octad

In the second embolismic year, that is, the sixth year in the octad, there are twenty-five epacts. The moon is thirtieth on the Kalends of September and disappears there, because it belongs to that month.

The moon that begins as the first on the fourth day before the Nones of September and ends on the thirtieth day, on the Kalends of October, belongs to the embolismic year. The moon that begins as the first on the sixth day before the Nones of October and ends on the third day before the Kalends of November is the twenty-ninth moon of October. On the Kalends of November and December it becomes the second moon; on the Kalends of January, the fourth, as the order requires.

### On the Third Embolismic Year, That Is, the Eighth Year in the Octad

In the third embolismic year, that is, the final year of the octad, there are seventeen epacts. The moon is twenty-two on the Kalends of September and October; twenty-four on the Kalends of November and December; twenty-six on the Kalends of January; twenty-seven on the Kalends of February; twenty-six on the Kalends of March; twenty-seven on the Kalends of April and May; twenty-nine on the Kalends of June and July; first on the Kalends of August; and third on the Kalends of September.

Why do you make one lunar age on the Kalends of April and on the Kalends of May, when this is found nowhere in the computation? Precisely because the moon that begins on the second day before the Nones of March and is twenty-seven on the Kalends of April is twenty-eight on the fourth day before the Nones of April, twenty-nine on the third day before the Nones of April, and thirty on the second day before the Nones of April. It belongs to the embolismic year and disappears there.

The moon that begins as the first on the Nones of April is the paschal moon. It is fourteen on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May and ends as the twenty-ninth on the fifth day before the Nones of May.

The moon that is first on the fourth day before the Nones of May and ends on the thirtieth, on the fourth day before the Nones of June, belongs to May. The moon that begins as the first on the third day before the Nones of June and ends as the twenty-ninth on the Kalends of July belongs to June. The moon that begins on the sixth day before the Nones of July and ends on the thirtieth, on the second day before the Kalends of August, belongs to July. Thereafter the moon is first on the Kalends of August and third on the Kalends of September, as the order requires.

For if you had not made one lunar age on the Kalends of April and on the Kalends of May, the paschal term, which is the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, would have fallen in that year not on the fourteenth but on the fifteenth moon, and there would have been an error both in Easter and in the lunar ages.

### On the Fourth Embolismic Year, in the First Hendecad

In the first embolismic year of the hendecad there are twenty epacts. Therefore the moon is twenty-five on the Kalends of September and October, and seventeen on the Kalends of November and December.

The moon that begins as the first on the day before the Nones of December and disappears as the thirtieth on the third day before the Nones of January belongs to the embolismic year. The moon that begins on the third day before the Nones of January and disappears as the thirtieth on the Kalends of February belongs to January. The moon that begins as the first on the fourth day before the Nones of February and ends as the twenty-ninth on the sixth day before the Nones of March belongs to February.

If it is a leap year, that moon of February is counted as thirtieth, as in the other leap years. The moon of March begins on the fifth day before the Nones of that month and ends as the thirtieth on the Kalends of April. The moon that begins on the fourth day before the Nones of April and ends as the twenty-ninth on the second day before the Kalends of May belongs to April. The moon that occurs as the first on the Kalends of May belongs to that month. The remaining moons follow their proper order.

I mention this embolismic moon as occurring on the second day before the Nones of December so that anyone who reads both accounts may know that both are valid.

### On the Fifth Embolismic Year, in the Sixth Hendecad

In this year there are twenty-three epacts. The moon is twenty-eight on the Kalends of September and October, and thirtieth on the Kalends of November and December.

The moon that ends as the thirtieth on the Kalends of November belongs to November. The moon that begins on the fourth day before the Nones of November and ends as the thirtieth on the Kalends of December belongs to the embolismic year.

The moon that begins as the first on the fourth day before the Nones of December and ends as the twenty-ninth on the third day before the Kalends of January belongs to December. On the Kalends of January it is the second moon; on the Kalends of February, the third. The remaining moons follow their proper order.

### On the Sixth Embolismic Year, in the Ninth Hendecad

In this year there are twenty-six epacts. Nevertheless, you will not find the embolismic moon through those epacts unless you return to the epact of the preceding common year. For in the preceding common year there were fifteen epacts.

The moon is therefore twenty-nine on the Kalends of August and ends there, because it belongs to that month. The moon that begins as the first on the fourth day before the Nones of August and ends as the thirtieth on the second day before the Kalends of September belongs to the embolismic year. Thus, on the Kalends of September and October, through the twenty-six epacts, it becomes the first moon. The remaining moons follow their proper order.

### On the Seventh Embolismic Year, Which Is the Last of the Nineteen-Year Cycle

In the final embolismic year of the hendecad there are eighteen epacts. The moon is twenty-three on the Kalends of September and October; twenty-five on the Kalends of November and December; twenty-seven on the Kalends of January; twenty-eight on the Kalends of February; twenty-seven on the Kalends of March; twenty-eight on the Kalends of April; thirtieth on the Kalends of May; first on the Kalends of July; third on the Kalends of August, because of the saltus; and fifth on the Kalends of September.

We therefore make one lunar age on the Kalends of April and May because the moon that begins on the third day before the Nones of March is twenty-nine on the Kalends of April, twenty-nine on the fourth day before the Nones of April, and thirty on the third day before the Nones of April. It belongs to the embolismic year.

The moon that begins as the first on the second day before the Nones of April and extends to the sixth day before the Nones of May is the twenty-ninth moon of April. It is the paschal moon and occurs as the fourteenth on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May.

The moon that begins on the fifth day before the Nones of May and ends as the thirtieth on the Kalends of June belongs to May. The moon of June begins on the fourth day before the Nones of that month and ends as the twenty-ninth on the Kalends of July.

Therefore the moon that is first on the Kalends of July and ends as the twenty-ninth on the fourth day before the Kalends of August belongs to July. Although it ought to end as the thirtieth on the third day before the Kalends of August, it loses one day—that is, the thirtieth—because of the computation of the saltus. The moon is therefore counted as third on the Kalends of August, although the calculation of the computation shows that it should be second. It also ends as the twenty-ninth on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, and the remaining moons follow their proper order.

But this same cycle is divided into embolismic and common years, which are known to have been observed also on the authority of the ancient Hebrews: twelve months in common years, that is, years of 354 days; but an embolismic year, that is, of 384 days, containing thirteen months. The first and second are common years, the third embolismic; the fourth and fifth common, the sixth embolismic; the seventh common, the eighth embolismic; the ninth and tenth common, the eleventh embolismic; the twelfth and thirteenth common, the fourteenth embolismic; the fifteenth and sixteenth common, the seventeenth embolismic; the eighteenth common, and the nineteenth embolismic.

Both kinds of year, as was said above, begin from the start of the first month, which the Hebrews call Nisan—that is, from the lighting of the paschal moon. The beginning of that month must be observed according to this rule: the fourteenth moon of Easter must never precede the spring equinox, but must occur either on the equinox itself—that is, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April—or after it has passed. Hence the beginnings of lunar years must be sought from the eighth day before the Ides of March up to the day of the Nones of April.

That same fourteenth moon, occurring first on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April and last on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, causes the day of the paschal feast to be sought from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April up to the seventh day before the Kalends of May.

As Dionysius says, the following rationale for embolismic years is shown to exist: they make up the deficiencies of common years, so that the lunar course may be brought into equality with solar time. For although the moon passes around the sun’s annual cycle through the individual months, it cannot complete its own cycle within twelve months. Consequently, in common years the moon is observed to fall eleven days short of the solar year; but in embolismic years the moon appears to exceed that same solar year by nineteen days.

The Hebrews, who knew and observed in the Law only lunar months, explained the twelve months of common years according to the moon’s natural course as months of thirty and twenty-nine days. In the third year, or in the second when appropriate, they added at the end of the year a thirteenth month of thirty days as an embolismic month.

The Romans, however, who have unequal months, did not wish to insert embolismic months by counting them at one fixed point, but rather wherever they might find an empty and suitable place between the Kalends in the middle periods of the year.

Accordingly, they said that the first embolismic moon is born on the fourth day before the Nones of December, the second on the fourth day before the Nones of September, the third on the day before the Nones of March, the fourth on the day before the Nones of December, the fifth on the fourth day before the Nones of November, the sixth on the fourth day before the Nones of August, and the seventh on the third day before the Nones of March. They took the greatest possible care that, whenever a moon of any age occurred on the Kalends, it should be considered and called the moon of that same month.

Nevertheless, they could not accomplish this in every case because of the predetermined course of the paschal moon. Since its end sometimes falls on the Kalends of May and occupies also the second or even the third day after the Kalends, it must be called not merely the moon of May, but rather the moon of April, as it must always be called.

## CHAPTER XLVI. On the Ogdoad and the Hendecad

[Note: [Col. 0488C]

BRID. RAMES. GLOSSES.—There is also another division of the aforementioned cycle, by which it is divided into an ogdoad and a hendecad—that is, into eight and eleven years—because in the eighth and eleventh years the paschal moon reaches the furthest limits of its birth.

“Furthest limits,” that is, lower limits—that is, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May. “Limits,” that is, the end. “Reaches,” that is, enters. The paschal moon does not rise beyond that limit, which occurs in the eighth and eleventh years; the eleventh year is the last of the nineteen-year cycle, and there it holds the final limit of its birth.

In the eighth year, the first paschal moon occurs on the Nones of April, and on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May it becomes the fourteenth moon. In the eleventh year, the first moon occurs on the second day before the Nones of April, and the fourteenth moon on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

Eight times 365 make 2,920. The solar ogdoad has 2,920 days. The lunar ogdoad has 2,922 days. The solar hendecad has 4,015 days. The lunar hendecad has 4,014 days. Subtract one intercalary day, and 4,013 remain. For the solar hendecad has two days more than the lunar hendecad.

Those two days by which the solar hendecad exceeds the lunar hendecad are assigned to the solar ogdoad, which is two days shorter than the lunar ogdoad. Thus at last the courses of the moon and the sun come into agreement at the end of the hendecad.

Add the 120 days of the embolismic months: the total is 4,014. Subtract one intercalary day; 4,013 remain. One hundred twenty-one days increase in the hendecad from the eleven annual days, and in addition one day—that is, 122 days—because in the nineteenth year not eleven days increase, as in the other years, but twelve, on account of the intercalation.

This can be proved as follows. The solar hendecad has 4,015 days. Divide these by 354, that is, by lunar years. Eleven times 354 make 3,894. Subtract one, because the final lunar year in the nineteen-year cycle is known to have 353 days; 3,893 remain. There are still 122 days left from the solar hendecad, of which four are embolismic months, and in addition two days, with whose help the solar ogdoad needs to be completed.

There is no doubt, and it is plainly evident, that in reconciling these periods the leap years do not prejudice anything. Rather, however many occur in the nineteen-year cycle, they are all equally beneficial to both heavenly bodies, according to what we have explained.

In eight years, that is, in an ogdoad, there are two leap years; in eleven years, that is, in a hendecad, there are two leap years and eighteen hours of a fifth leap year. In the solar cycle, that is, in twenty-eight years, there are seven leap years.

In the first year of the nineteen-year cycle there are no epacts, because the moon’s course ended on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. The moon is then the thirtieth moon, and its course therefore ended, because whenever the thirtieth moon is found on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, the moon’s course always ends there.

Likewise, in the ninth year of the same cycle—that is, after 2,922 days—on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, the moon is the thirtieth moon. The order of the epacts, which are then twenty-eight, clearly confirms this.

If the solar and lunar courses were equal in the number of days at the end of the ogdoad, as they are at the end of the hendecad, the thirtieth moon would then be on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, as it is at the end of the hendecad. But because the lunar ogdoad exceeds the solar ogdoad by two days, the thirtieth moon is on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, not on the eleventh.

It is therefore necessary to add to the solar ogdoad the tenth and ninth days before the Kalends of April, which come after the eleventh day before the Kalends, so that the solar course may agree with the lunar course. The tenth and ninth days before the Kalends of April are added to the moons that increase beyond the solar ogdoad.]

[Col. 0488B]

There is also another division of the aforementioned cycle, by which it is divided into an ogdoad and a hendecad—that is, into eight and eleven years—because in the eighth and eleventh years the paschal moon reaches the furthest limits of its birth, and one common year precedes each of them in the usual manner of the embolismic years.

[Note: [Col. 0489C] C: “in an unusual manner.”]

Or perhaps because it seemed to the ancients that eight solar years were equal in number of days to the same number of lunar years—a view that later, more learned teachers discovered could not be true unless eleven years were added—the entire revolution of the moon has been arranged into ogdoads and hendecads as an indication of both observances.

For formerly the Greeks, whom even the most ancient Romans are said to have imitated, when they still reckoned years according to the lunar course, intercalated three embolismic months together after eight common years had been completed in the same manner. For if you calculate eight times eleven and a quarter, you will make ninety days, that is, three months.

Even now there are some who think that eight solar years can be matched with an equal number of lunar years, and likewise eleven solar years with an equal number of lunar years, in the number of days.

First, however, it must be said that the following is beyond all contradiction: if eight years of the two heavenly bodies ever agree in length, they will always do so in the same way, and there will be no place for an equality of eleven-year periods. But if the eleven years of both begin and end together even once, they will always do so, and there will never be a return of the agreement of eight years.

Next, the number itself must be tested, and it must be seen that eight solar years contain, excluding leap years, 2,920 days; for eight times 365 make 2,920. But see how many days the same number of lunar years contains: eight times 354 make 2,832. Add the ninety days of three embolismic months, and the total is 2,922. The two days by which the lunar ogdoad exceeds the solar ogdoad must be supplied by adding two leap days.

Let us examine the hendecad of each heavenly body, to see whether the sun perhaps requires the assistance of a leap year; for both periods must necessarily be included under one rule. Eleven times 365 make 4,015. Likewise, eleven times 354 make 3,894. Add the 120 days of the embolismic months, and the total is 4,014. Subtract one intercalary day, and 4,013 remain.

See, then, whether the solar hendecad requires the aid of a leap year, so that, by adding two or three days, it might be sufficient to compensate for the lunar hendecad. It certainly does not need the quarter-year assistance in order to equal the lunar hendecad; rather, it is shown to exceed it by two further days, and by its own excess it fills out what is lacking in the solar ogdoad.

It is plainly evident that in reconciling these periods the leap years prejudice nothing. Rather, however many occur in the nineteen-year cycle, they are all equally beneficial to both heavenly bodies, according to what we explained above.

Finally, to examine the inner details of the matter: in the first year of the nineteen-year cycle there are no epacts, because the moon’s course ended on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. Likewise, in the ninth year of the same cycle—that is, after 2,922 days—on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, the moon is the thirtieth moon. The order of the epacts, which are then twenty-eight, clearly confirms this.

What need, then, would there be to add two days of the solar course to complete the lunar ogdoad—that is, the tenth and ninth days before the Kalends of April—if two leap intercalations could accomplish this? Therefore, the two days by which the solar ogdoad is shorter than the lunar ogdoad are supplied not by the intercalation of two leap days, but rather by adding the two days by which the solar hendecad exceeds the lunar hendecad.

Nor does it matter that we said the lunar intercalary day, which some place at the beginning of the ogdoad, should be placed in the hendecad. Wherever you insert it, the question proposed will be resolved with the same result.

The nineteen-year cycle contains 228 solar months and 235 lunar months, and, excluding leap years, 6,935 days. For nineteen times twelve make 228; add seven, and the total is 235. Likewise, nineteen times 365 make 6,935; nineteen times 354 make 6,726; add the 210 days of seven embolismic months, and the total is 6,936. Subtract one lunar intercalary day, and you will prove that the nineteen-year cycle contains the courses of the sun and moon in one and the same number of days.

Likewise, the solar ogdoad has ninety-six months, whereas the lunar ogdoad has ninety-nine; the solar hendecad has 132 months, whereas the lunar hendecad has 136. The number of days has been discussed above.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On the Years of the Lord’s Incarnation

[Note: [Col. 0491B]

BRID. RAMES. GLOSSES.—In the first line of the nineteen-year cycle, the order of the times is set out, which the Greek calculators observed from the years of the emperor Diocletian.

And shortly afterward: Since the lunar cycle consists of nineteen years, whereas the solar cycle is completed in twenty-eight years, when the two are multiplied by one another, the sum of 532 years is obtained. For this moon, which in the present reckoning bears a certain designation, will not bear the same designation for nineteen years; therefore it is a nineteenth-moon cycle. The solar year, however, is completed in twenty-eight years, because it cannot be completed before the leap year has touched all the days of the week.

With these matters established, investigate carefully the year of the Lord’s Passion. The way of seeking it is not unknown, if the computation has not erred somewhere. The way of seeking it is not unknown—namely, the way of seeking the years from the Lord’s Passion—if the computation has not erred somewhere.

Yet it does err, and therefore the way of seeking the years from the Lord’s Passion is unknown. For if you begin counting from the very year in which Dionysius thought the Lord’s Incarnation occurred, you will not find in the thirty-fourth year a fourteenth moon on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, a Thursday, the Lord’s paschal day, and a seventeenth moon on the sixth day before the Kalends of April.

For, unless I am mistaken, the faith of the Church holds that the Lord lived in the flesh somewhat more than thirty-three years until the time of his Passion, since he was baptized when he was thirty years old, as the evangelist Luke testifies, and preached for three and a half years after his baptism, as John demonstrates in his Gospel—not only through his mention of the returning Passover—but also in his Apocalypse. Daniel likewise indicates this prophetically in his visions.

He was baptized when he was thirty years old, as the evangelist Luke testifies, namely in chapter 3, where he says: “And Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years of age, being—as was supposed—the son of Joseph.”

Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ was thirty years old when he came to John to be baptized; then he established the beginning of his evangelical preaching.

Divine Scripture reports that he spent the entire period of his teaching under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas. Thus, he began to teach during the high priesthood of Annas, and his teaching extended to the beginning of Caiaphas’s term; yet within these intervals not even four full years are contained.

He preached for three and a half years after his baptism, as John demonstrates in his Gospel through his mention of the returning Passover, namely in chapter 18, where he says: “The cohort, the tribune, and the servants of the Jews seized Jesus, bound him, and brought him first to Annas; for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.”

The same is also shown in his Apocalypse, namely chapter 12, where he says: “And the woman fled into the wilderness, where she had a place prepared by God, so that there they might nourish her for 1,260 days.” And shortly afterward: “And two wings of a great eagle were given to the woman, so that she might fly into the wilderness, where she is nourished for a time, and times, and half a time, from the face of the serpent.”

If you wish to hear the exposition of this verse, turn to the treatise of Haimo, who says among other things: “For just as the Antichrist will reign for 1,260 days, so Christ preached for 1,260 days, that is, for three and a half years.” Therefore, we can understand the whole present period through this number, beginning from the time when divine preaching began and ending with the last preachers.

Daniel likewise indicates this prophetically in his visions, namely in chapter 9, where he says: “And they will be delivered into his hand for a time, and times, and half a time.” “Time” in this passage signifies one year. “Times,” according to the peculiarity of the Hebrew language, which also has a dual number, foreshadows two years. “Half a time” signifies six months, during which the saints will be handed over to the power of the Antichrist, so that the Jews may be condemned—those who, not believing the truth, accepted falsehood.

The Savior also speaks of this period in the Gospel: “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would have been saved.”

This is also testified by the little notices that the Church customarily writes annually on its candles, namely because there are always thirty-three years less from the Passion, annually on the vigil of Easter.

The number of years of the Lord is always thirty-three years less—that is, from the Lord’s Passion.

In the seven-hundredth year, in the fourteenth indiction. This occurred in Bede’s time. They reported that he had seen this written on the candles of Saint Mary and had copied it from there: “From the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, there are 668 years.” Since in the seven-hundred-and-first year they were there and saw 668 years from the Lord’s Passion written on the candles of Saint Mary, it is apparent that there are thirty-three years less from the Passion. Thirty-three years extend from the Nativity to the Lord’s Passion.

Therefore, the year of the Lord’s Passion and resurrection from the dead is 566, because just as 533 agrees with the first year, so 566, the thirty-fourth year from the Lord’s Nativity, in which he suffered and rose again, agrees throughout the courses of the sun and moon.

Just as there was a conjunction of the heavenly bodies in the thirty-third or thirty-fourth year after the revolution—that is, after the completion of Dionysius’s first cycle—so the conjunction of the heavenly bodies will be completed: just as 533 agrees with the first year, namely the year of the Lord’s Nativity, so the five-hundred-and-sixty-sixth year, namely the year of the Lord, agrees with the thirty-fourth year from Dionysius’s beginning, after the completion of the first cycle.

The Lord’s paschal day was on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, with the seventeenth moon, namely the moon of that day. Everything occurred in that year when the Lord suffered.

“Let us give thanks to God, because what you were seeking, as he himself promised, he has granted you to find.” This is said ironically, since it is found in no way. Irony is a statement whose meaning, through its manner of utterance, is contrary to its words. Irony is a form that mocks someone by praising him, as Elijah said: “Cry out with a louder voice. For he is a god; perhaps he is speaking, or is staying in an inn, or is asleep, so that he may be awakened.”

Unless the seriousness of the delivery assists it, this statement would appear to affirm what it strives to deny. For no Catholic is permitted to doubt that the Lord ascended the cross on the fifteenth moon, on Friday, and rose from the dead on the first day of the week, that is, Sunday.

“On the first day of the week” must be understood as the first day after the Sabbath, which, out of honor and reverence for the Lord’s resurrection, we call Sunday. For just as we say first day, second day, third day, and the rest in order, so the Jews called them first of the Sabbath, second of the Sabbath, third of the Sabbath.]

Although Theophilus of Caesarea—an ancient teacher, clearly close to apostolic times—in his synodical letter, and so forth.

“Synodical,” namely, the letter he composed in the synod against those who celebrated Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth moon.

I did not wish to place that letter here, because it offers more mockery to the foolish than edification to the wise, since it declares that our Lord Jesus Christ suffered on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April and rose on the eighth day before the Kalends. This is exceedingly absurd.

“And is it not impious that the Lord’s Passion, the mystery of so great a sacrament, should be excluded beyond the boundary?” That is, it is extremely impious. It should be read interrogatively.

Theophilus says that the Lord suffered on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April and rose on the eighth day before the Kalends; but this is not true, because he did not lie in the tomb for four days. I wonder why anyone would have recalled such an absurd matter.

Blessed Augustine, in book 4 of On the Holy Trinity, says that he was conceived on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, and that he also suffered on that day. Blessed Jerome likewise testifies in the Martyrology, saying: “On the eighth day before the Kalends of April, the Lord was crucified at Jerusalem, and on the sixth day before the Kalends of April the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ was celebrated at Jerusalem.”

How will three days be excluded beyond the boundary? It appears that Theophilus’s three days of the Lord’s Passion are excluded by the Westerners who say that Christ suffered on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

If the Passion is celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, how will the three days—that is, the eleventh, tenth, and ninth—be excluded beyond the boundary? He says this against us, who celebrate the Lord’s Passion on the Kalends of April.

It was established in that synod that Easter should be observed from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April up to the eighth day before the Kalends of May, whereas among us it is observed from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April up to the seventh day before the Kalends of May.

[Col. 0494D]

For the Gauls, on whichever day the eighth day before the Kalends of April occurred when Christ’s resurrection was reported, always celebrated Easter. They did not pay attention either to Sunday or to the rule of the fourteenth moon; rather, on whichever day the eighth day before the Kalends of April fell, they celebrated Easter.

The holy fathers prohibited this practice at the Council of Nicaea, establishing that it was necessary to seek not only the paschal moon and the month, but also to observe the day of the Lord’s resurrection.

But if you will not be able to find the year you were seeking—namely, the year from the Passion, 566—in the place where you thought it would be found, attribute the blame either to the negligence of the chronographers—that is, writers of times—or rather to your own slowness, if you say that the Lord and Savior underwent the sacred mystery of the cross either in the fifteenth or sixteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, or in the twenty-ninth or thirtieth year of his own age.

For he was not crucified in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar or in the thirtieth year of his own age, but was baptized.]

In the first line of the nineteen-year cycle, the order of the times is set out, which the Greek calculators observed from the years of the emperor Diocletian.

But Dionysius, the venerable abbot of the city of Rome, endowed with no ordinary knowledge of both languages, Greek and Latin, when writing the paschal cycles, did not wish—as he himself testifies—to link them with the memory of an impious persecutor. Rather, he chose to mark out the periods of the years from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that the beginning of our hope might be more clearly known to us and the cause of human restoration—that is, the Passion of our Redeemer—might shine forth more plainly.

By placing in the first cycle he composed the five-hundred-and-thirty-second year of the Lord’s Incarnation at its head, he clearly taught that the second year of his cycle was the year in which the mystery of that holy Incarnation began.

Since the lunar cycle consists of nineteen years, whereas the solar cycle is completed in twenty-eight years, when both are multiplied by one another, the sum of 532 years is obtained. When this has been repeated, the entire order of the solar and lunar revolutions turns back upon itself along its own tracks, restoring the same year of the nineteen-year lunar cycle, the same lunar epacts, the same concurrent days of the sun, the same fourteenth moon, and the same day and moon of the Lord’s Easter in due order.

Victorius also clearly proved this, although he established a different system, when he composed the paschal cycle after setting out such a number of years.

Since, therefore, the five-hundred-and-thirty-third year from the Lord’s Incarnation was completed in the second year of the cycle that Dionysius first wrote, this is evidently, according to the conjunction of the heavenly bodies, the year in which he deigned to become incarnate. For this second year of the nineteen-year cycle is the eighteenth year of the lunar cycle; it has eleven epacts, five concurrent days of the week, and the fourteenth paschal moon on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. Everything at that time was very similar; and if there had been someone who then celebrated Easter on Sunday according to the custom now followed by the churches, that day would certainly have fallen, as it is recorded here, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April and would have had the sixteenth moon.

Finally, Dionysius himself silently demonstrates what we are saying in the calculations he wrote for the paschal tables. To discover which year of the nineteen-year cycle it is, he instructs us to take the years of the Lord and, before dividing them by nineteen, first add one, signifying that when the Lord became incarnate one year of the nineteen-year cycle had already been completed.

Likewise, to determine which year of the lunar cycle it is, he advises us to take the years of the Lord, always subtract two, and then divide by nineteen. In this way, after subtracting the two years that then remained, he divided the others by the nineteenth part, retaining whatever remained.

To determine the number of lunar epacts, he instructs us properly to take, divide, and multiply the years of the Lord.

Likewise, he orders division without subtracting or adding anything, because in the second year of the nineteen-year cycle the epacts began, and in order to find their position they did not require anything to be added to or subtracted from the years of the Lord that began together with them.

If we wish to know the solar additions—that is, the concurrent days of the week—he instructs us to take the years of the Lord, add a quarter of them, and always add four regular units; then finally divide by seven. For there were five concurrent days in the year in which the Lord was born, and so, in order that the fixed series of computation might proceed, the calculator necessarily had to add the four that preceded it.

With these matters established, investigate carefully the year of the Lord’s Passion. The way of seeking it is not unknown, if the computation has not erred somewhere.

For, unless I am mistaken, the faith of the Church holds that the Lord lived in the flesh somewhat more than thirty-three years until the time of his Passion, since he was baptized when he was thirty years old, as the evangelist Luke testifies, and preached for three and a half years after his baptism, as John demonstrates in his Gospel—not only through his mention of the returning Passover, but also in his Apocalypse. Daniel likewise indicates this prophetically in his visions.

The holy Roman and apostolic Church itself also testifies that it holds this faith through the little notices that it customarily writes annually on its candles. There, recalling the time of the Lord’s Passion to the people, it records a number of years always thirty-three years fewer than the number Dionysius assigns from his Incarnation.

Finally, in the year 701 from his Incarnation according to Dionysius, in the fourteenth indiction, our brothers who were then in Rome reported that they had seen the following written on the candles of Saint Mary on the Nativity of the Lord and had copied it from there: “From the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, there are 669 years.”

Since, as we mentioned above, the paschal cycle revolves through 532 years, add thirty-three, or rather thirty-four, so that you may reach the very year in which the Lord suffered; the total is 566.

Therefore, this is the year of the Lord’s Passion and resurrection from the dead. For just as the five-hundred-and-thirty-third agrees with the first, so the five-hundred-and-sixty-sixth agrees with the thirty-fourth throughout the courses of the sun and moon.

And therefore, when the cycles of blessed Dionysius are opened, if in the year 566 from the Lord’s Incarnation you find the fourteenth moon on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, a Thursday, and the Lord’s Easter day on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, with the seventeenth moon, give thanks to God, because what you were seeking, as he himself promised, he has granted you to find.

For no Catholic is permitted to doubt that the Lord ascended the cross on the fifteenth moon, on Friday, and rose from the dead on the first day of the week, that is, Sunday. Otherwise he might appear equally unbelieving toward the Law, which commands that the paschal lamb be sacrificed on the fourteenth day of the first month at evening, and toward the Gospel, which says that the Lord, seized by the Jews that same evening, was crucified and buried on Friday morning and rose on the first day of the week.

That he was crucified on the eighth day before the Kalends of April and rose on the sixth day before those same Kalends is widely established and reported as the opinion of many ecclesiastical teachers.

Although Theophilus of Caesarea—an ancient teacher, clearly close to apostolic times—in the synodical letter that he wrote together with the other bishops of Palestine against those who celebrated Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth moon says the following:

“And is it not impious that the Lord’s Passion, the mystery of so great a sacrament, should be excluded beyond the boundary? For the Lord suffered from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, on the night when he was handed over by the Jews, and rose from the eighth day before the Kalends of April. How will three days be excluded beyond the boundary?”

It was established in that synod that Easter should be observed from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April up to the eighth day before the Kalends of May, as was written above in the same book.

For the Gauls, on whichever day the eighth day before the Kalends of April occurred when Christ’s resurrection was reported to have taken place, always celebrated Easter.

But if you will not be able to find the year you were seeking in the place where you thought it would be found, attribute the blame either to the negligence of the chronographers or rather to your own slowness, taking the greatest care that, by defending the writings of the chronicles, you do not appear to attack the inviolable testimony of the Law or the Gospel. Do not say that the Lord and Savior underwent the sacred mystery of the cross either in the fifteenth or sixteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, or in the twenty-ninth or thirtieth year of his own age, since the Gospels clearly indicate that in the fifteenth year of Tiberius the Lord’s forerunner began to preach and soon afterward baptized Jesus among others, when he was already beginning to be about thirty years old.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On the Indictions

[Note: [Col. 0495D]

BRID. RAMES. GLOSSES.—The second order of the nineteen-year cycle comprises indictions, which return always to their own tracks in a circuit of fifteen years. That is, they return after a circuit of fifteen years. “Industry,” that is, diligence and prudence.

Some think that, because formerly in the republic—

“Republic,” as though “of the people,” because it pertains to the whole people.

“To proclaim” means to command. Hence comes “indiction,” or edict, an imperial command. To proclaim is a general command concerning taxpayers, which was imposed generally on everyone throughout the entire world. An indiction was carried out over fifteen years: in the first five-year period a gold coin was imposed, in the second a silver coin, and in the third five-year period a bronze coin was paid.]

The second order of the nineteen-year cycle comprises indictions, which return always to their own tracks in a circuit of fifteen years. We know that the ancient Roman diligence instituted them to guard against the error that might perhaps arise concerning dates. [Note: C reads *aboriri*.]

For, if for example an emperor died or left the throne in the middle of a year, it could happen that one historian assigned that year to the reign of the same ruler because he had reigned during part of it, while another historian thought that the same year should rather be attributed to his successor because the successor likewise possessed part of it in his reign.

But so that error might not grow in the chronology through such disagreement, they established indictions, by which both writers—and indeed the entire populace—could easily preserve the sequence of times. For ease of calculation they decided that there should be fifteen of them, so that, by means of a very simple number, convenient for multiplication, the state of elapsed time could more briefly be recalled to memory.

Some think—perhaps, “since”—that the indictions were established because formerly, in the republic, after the census had been completed in the fifth year, the city of Rome was purified, and that the indictions were created as an indication of the threefold purification and census.

The indictions begin on the eighth day before the Kalends of October and end there as well.

## CHAPTER XLIX. The Method for Finding Which Indiction It Is

By this method you will discover which indiction it is in whatever year you wish to calculate. Take however many years from the Lord’s Incarnation have elapsed in the present reckoning—for example, 725. Always add three, because according to Dionysius the Lord was born in the fourth indiction; the total is 728. [Note: C reads *hos*.]

Divide this by fifteen: fifteen times forty is six hundred, fifteen times eight is one hundred twenty; eight remains. It is the eighth indiction.

But if nothing remains, it is the fifteenth indiction.

## CHAPTER L. On Lunar Epacts

[Note: [Col. 0497B]

BRID. RAMES. GLOSSAE. For example, today, as I write, if the moon is in its fifth day, on this same day after one year it will be in its sixteenth day, after two years in its twenty-seventh, and after three years in its eighth. The gloss on this verse has therefore already been written above; its beginning is: “If you wish to know what the moon was like in the past year on each of the dates.” *Today* means “on this day.” *Daily*—not *cotodie*—is as if one said “on whatever days.” *Tomorrow* means “what comes afterward.” Finally comes *pridie* (“the preceding day”), called “final” because that day itself is already outside us and, as it passes, becomes foreign to us. *Pridie* means, as it were, “on the previous day.” *Perendie* means “the day after tomorrow,” that is, “through the preceding day,” or “in advance,” that is, “earlier.”

Always observing this rule fixed for its course, so that whenever the epacts have a number smaller than fifteen, they indicate the paschal moon. For if the epacts have a number greater than fifteen on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, those epacts do not indicate the paschal moon. By “epacts,” therefore, understand here the age of the moon. The principle is as follows: if the moon is fifteen days old on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, the fourteenth moon of Easter ought not to precede the equinox but to follow it, or at times to become fourteen days old precisely at the equinox. Hence it is clear that those who determine that the beginning of the paschal moon must be sought on the third day before the Nones of March are greatly mistaken, because the moon born there displays its full moon before the time of the equinox. Thus the moon’s first age, which existed at the beginning of the world, was as follows: it was born on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, approximately the eighth day before the Ides of March; [Col. 0497D] therefore those who seek the beginning of the paschal moon on the third day before the Nones of March are mistaken.

For just as the moon and the stars, as they say, do not have their light from themselves but from the sun, so the Church and all the saints possess the good by which they live not through the merit of their own virtue but through the grace of the giver. The stars, borrowing their light from the sun, are said to turn with the world, as though fixed in one place, and to be carried in motion with the revolving world, except for those called planets—that is, wanderers. The coming of day conceals them, and the brightness of the full moon and the eclipse of the sun prove that they never fall from heaven, although we see little sparks falling from the ether, borne by the winds, and imitating the wandering light of a star when fierce winds arise. Some heavenly bodies are fertile with moisture dissolved into liquid; others consist of moisture congealed into frost, compacted into snow, or frozen into hail; others are made of warm air, others of vapor, others of dew, and others of cold. It is not only wandering stars, such as Saturn, whose passages produce rain, but also certain fixed stars which, when the wandering stars approach them or when they are struck by their rays, produce effects—such as the little stars on the forehead of Taurus, which the Greeks, for this reason, call the Hyades, using a name associated with rain. Indeed, certain stars rise of their own accord at appointed times, such as the rising of the Kids and of Arcturus, which rises around the Ides of September with storm-bearing hail; Orion, heavy with rain; and the Dog Star, which rises exceedingly hot on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August.

The stars’ light comes from the sun—that is, just as the saints borrow from Christ, receiving from him. All the stars and the moon receive their light from the sun. For although they are of a fiery nature, and although they were made from the same light as the sun, [Col. 0498C] they nevertheless do not possess such power that they can shine by themselves without the sun. Everything is illuminated by the sun’s rays; this is presented to us as a figure of Christ and his saints, who receive from him whatever virtue they possess.

The stars are said not to have their own light but to be illuminated by the sun; nor are they ever said to depart from heaven, but rather to be concealed when the sun comes. All the heavenly bodies are obscured when the sun rises, and they do not fall. For when the sun has sent ahead the signs of its rising, all the stars’ fire vanishes beneath the brilliance of its light, so that no heavenly body’s radiance is seen apart from the sun’s fire. Hence the sun is also called *sol* because it alone appears when all the heavenly bodies have been obscured. Nor is this surprising in the case of the sun, since even when the full moon shines throughout the night, most of the stars do not shine. That stars exist in heaven during the day is proved by a solar eclipse: when the sun has been obscured by the moon’s intervening disk, the brighter stars appear in heaven.

The stars are called *stellae* from *stare*, “to stand,” because they always stand fixed in heaven. The stars are motionless and are carried with the heavens in perpetual motion. Those fixed in heaven are carried along and revolve with the heavens; others move, such as the planets—that is, the wandering stars—which complete their wandering courses according to a fixed order.

“Stars,” “constellations,” and “heavenly bodies” differ from one another. A star is any single one; constellations are formed from many stars, such as the Hyades and the Pleiades; heavenly bodies are large stars, such as Orion and Boötes. Writers, however, confuse these names, using *heavenly bodies* for stars and *stars* for constellations.

According to the mystical interpretation, the stars signify holy men, concerning whom it is said: “He numbers the multitude of the stars.” For just as all the stars are illuminated by the sun, so the saints are glorified by Christ with the glory of the heavenly kingdom. And just as the heavenly bodies are dimmed by the sun’s brilliance and the immense power of its light, so every splendor of the saints is, in comparison with Christ’s glory, obscured in a certain manner. And just as the stars differ from one another in brightness, so there is a diversity among the righteous according to the discernment of their merits.]

[Col. 0497A]

The third line of the aforementioned cycle contains the lunar epacts, which customarily increase annually by eleven days in relation to the course of the sun. Hence they are called *epacts*, a Greek term meaning “additions,” because, as we have said, they accumulate an increase of eleven days each year. Or, certainly, because nine are added throughout the entire year in order to discover how old the moons are on the Kalends, as we explained above, they are rightly called *epacts*, that is, “additions”; and indeed, throughout the entire revolving course of the year, each day has its own lunar addition of eleven days. [Note: [Col. 0497B] C reads *suas* (“its own,” feminine) for *suos*.] For example, if today, as I write, the moon is in its fifth day, on this same day after one year it will be in its sixteenth day, after two years in its twenty-seventh, and after three years in its eighth; nor will the same moon return here, as it is now, before the completion of the twenty-nine-year cycle.

Properly speaking, however, the epacts marked in the nineteen-year cycle indicate what day of its age the moon has reached on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, where the feast of Easter begins, always observing the rule fixed for its course: whenever they have a number smaller than fifteen, they indicate the paschal moon; whenever they have a larger number, they show that Easter must be sought in the following moon. For the fullness of the paschal moon ought not to precede the equinox but, as was ordained at the beginning of creation, rather to follow it. First the sun rose at the beginning of the day, holding the spring equinox; then the moon rose at the beginning of the night, holding within itself a portion of the autumnal equinox.

Hence it is clear that those who determine that the beginning of the paschal moon must be sought on the third day before the Nones of March are greatly mistaken, because the moon born there displays its full moon before the time of the equinox. It is therefore unsuitable for the paschal solemnity, in which, as we have said, the sun must first ascend to the state of the primal creation and then the moon, so that the former by passing beyond the equinox surpasses the length of the night, while the latter by its fullness illumines its entire, however small, length.

There is scarcely anyone who doubts that this refers to the mystery of Christ and the Church. We touched on it briefly at the beginning of this little work, and now let us repeat it in a few words. For just as the moon and the stars, as they say, do not shine from themselves but possess their light from the sun, so the Church and all the saints possess the good by which they live not through the merit of their own virtue but through the grace of the giver. And just as we preserve our strength not by the power of our own will but because he receives us and his mercy goes before us, and we are not sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God, so likewise, at the time when we celebrate the tokens of our redemption, the perfection of the sun’s radiance, which illuminates the moon that is illuminated, must precede it.

## CHAPTER LI. How Some Err concerning the Beginning of the First Month

[Note: [Col. 0499B] C reads “IV.”]

BRID. RAMES. GLOSSAE. That Sunday of the Lord’s Passion—that is, the Friday before the fourteenth moon. [Col. 0499C] “That Sunday,” namely, the day; “before the fourteenth moon,” that is, on the fourteenth moon.

The beginning of the first month extends, evidently, from the eighth day before the Ides of March through the day of the Nones of April; the fourteenth moons of Easter, however, extend from the twelfth day before the Kalends of April through the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May. It is therefore established that in the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, when no epact is placed at the beginning, the moon is nine days old on the Kalends of March and sixteen days old on the eighth day before the Ides of March. Subtract thirty from this and begin again with the first; the fourteenth moon occurs on the Nones of April, which is the limit of the nineteen-year cycle.

Again, add eleven to the same sixteen that you had in the preceding year on the eighth day before the Ides of March; the moon on that same day will be twenty-seven days old. When you subtract thirty from this, the following fourteenth moon occurs on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, which is the second limit. And so, for each lunar month up to the nineteenth year, always adding eleven on the same day—namely, the eighth day before the Ides of March—to the moon’s age on that day in the preceding year, whatever its age within thirty may be, subtract thirty from it, and subtract again until you reach the fourteenth moon; wherever the fourteenth moon occurs, there, without any ambiguity, will be the paschal limit.

If, however, the thirtieth moon falls on that same day—which happens only once in nineteen years—subtract the following moon in the customary manner; wherever the fourteenth moon occurs, there will also be the limit. But when the first moon occurs on the eighth day before the Ides, it will unquestionably be paschal. Take the greatest care over this: do not count as paschal a moon born before the eighth day before the Ides of March. Whatever moon occurs on that day, either retain the thirtieth moon on that day or subtract thirty and do not hesitate to regard as paschal the following moon wherever its fourteenth day occurs.

This order and method could never have been, nor can it ever be, disturbed by anyone from the day on which it was established; rather, the one who appears to wish to disturb it will himself be shaken. When the nineteenth year has been completed and the final limit of that year has been fixed, if you wish to test again whether this method is grounded in reason and whether this authority rests upon authoritative foundations, add to the age of the moon on the same often-mentioned day, the eighth day before the Ides of March, not eleven as before but twelve, on account of the lunar leap; the moon will again appear for you on that day as it did at the beginning, sixteen days old, and everything that follows will occur in the same order as previously.

But lest the lovers of Victorius tear us apart for having rashly attacked him, let them read the book of that most learned and holy man Victorius, namely, the bishop of Capua, concerning Easter, which was thought ought to be celebrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth indiction, nine times after the consulship of Basil. Gregory.

Among the ancients, it is reported that this custom existed: whoever became consul held, according to the order of the times, the place appropriate to his honor; thus, if someone later attained the consulship and became consul not once but perhaps twice or three times, he would surpass even in praise and honor those who had been consuls no more than once. Consuls were called from *consulere*, “to deliberate,” just as kings are called from *regere*, “to rule,” and laws from *legere*, “to read,” because they deliberated—that is, provided—for the commonwealth. For when the Romans could not endure the arrogant domination of kings, they established annual commands and made two consuls for themselves. The royal office was based not on the goodwill of one who deliberated but on the arrogance of one who dominated. Hence they were called consuls either because they deliberated for the citizens or because they governed all things by counsel. Nevertheless, they chose to change them each year so that no insolent man might remain too long and a more moderate one might quickly succeed him. Thus there were two equals, one administering civil affairs and the other military affairs. They ruled for four hundred and sixty-seven years.

Proconsuls were subject to the consuls and were called *proconsuls* because they acted in the place of a consul, just as a procurator acts in the place of a curator, that is, an administrator. *Ex-consuls* were those who had already left or withdrawn from the consulship after completing the year of their office. If, therefore, one of the consuls had administered the commonwealth well during his term, although he was removed from the consulship itself, he was nevertheless restored by decree of the senate to administer an office of the same dignity. Hence the phrase read above: “nine times after the consulship of Basil.”]

[Col. 0499B]

But consider whether the error of those who think otherwise appears, even to those who enact such unjust laws and, by writing, write injustice, to be supported by sound judgment and truth. Victorius, who wrote their cycles, says among other things in the prologue to the same work:

> “For the Latins judged it especially necessary to observe the period from the third day before the Nones of March to the fourth day before the Nones of April—that is, twenty-nine days—so that whichever of those days the moon was born would constitute the beginning of the first month. If its fourteenth moon fell on a Friday, the following Sunday—that is, the sixteenth moon—was without doubt to be assigned to the paschal feast. But if the full moon happened to occur on a Saturday and the following Sunday was found to have the fifteenth moon, they declared that Easter ought to be transferred, after that week had been passed over, to another Sunday—that is, to the twenty-second moon—so that they would assign to the celebration of the mystery of the Lord’s day neither less than the sixteenth nor more than the twenty-second moon, preferring that the day of the paschal feast be extended to the twenty-second moon rather than that the Lord’s passion begin in any way before the fourteenth moon. They further assert that the fourteenth moons of that month are to be observed from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April through the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May.”

Again, at the end of the same prologue:

> “But when it happens,” he says, “that the twenty-seventh moon falls on a Saturday, or especially on the day of the Kalends of January, without a leap day, let Your Holiness know that Easter is never to be celebrated according to the Latins on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, even if the moon agrees; nor, according to the Egyptians, can it be found possible to observe it on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, although that is sometimes to be observed.”

Let us therefore see how Victorius commends his Latins. He says that they judged especially that a moon born on the third day before the Nones of March constituted the beginning of the first month, and that Easter should be celebrated on the sixteenth moon on a Sunday. He says again that, according to the Latins, Easter was never to be celebrated on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, even if the moon agreed, but rather, according to the Egyptians, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

It is established, however, that a moon born on the third day before the Nones of March is sixteen days old on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April. I ask you, holy brother Victorius: if a moon born on the third day before the Nones of March constitutes the beginning of the first month, what reason is there for us not to celebrate Easter at that time but instead to defer it to another month, when the Law so often commands that all who are able should celebrate Easter in the first month, while only those who are on a journey or unclean should celebrate it in the second month?

What do you mean, I ask, by adding “without a leap day”? Is it perhaps because, when the Kalends of January fall on a Saturday, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April falls on a Sunday if the year is not a leap year, whereas if a leap day has intervened, that same day falls on a Monday? Do you wish to teach that when the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April falls on a Monday and the moon is sixteen days old, Easter is rightly celebrated on the following Sunday, the seventh day before the Kalends of April, when the moon is twenty-two days old; but when that same thirteenth day before the Kalends of April has the sixteenth moon on a Sunday, Easter cannot be celebrated then because the equinox has not yet passed—and not on the following Sunday either, because the overage of the moon, that is, the twenty-third moon, falls on that day—and that, compelled by this necessity, the solemnities of Easter must be deferred to the time of the second month?

What a remarkable teacher of calculation you are, teaching first that a moon born on the third day before the Nones of March constitutes the beginning of the first month, and then, overcome by the very same reasoning, being compelled to admit that, unless a leap day intervenes, the moon born on that day is in no way suitable for the paschal feasts, but rather the moon kindled twenty-nine days later. If a leap day is present, then that moon becomes the first moon of the following year, whereas without the leap day it could have been the last moon of the preceding year.

And what do you mean when you say that Easter is never to be celebrated on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, “even if the moon agrees”? How can the moon agree with the paschal solemnities where paschal solemnities are never to be celebrated? And if Easter is never to be celebrated on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, even when the sixteenth moon occurs, then the Latins are certainly mistaken in deciding that the paschal moon begins on the third day before the Nones of March, since on its sixteenth and seventeenth days, because the equinox has not yet passed, Easter may not be celebrated.

Rightly disregarding their observance, you advise that in that year Easter should instead be deferred with the Egyptians to the eighth day before the Kalends of May. But if you think that what the Egyptians teach ought rather to be observed, why do you not follow their knowledge in every respect? Yet because you do not wish to do this, but walk midway between the two, you prescribe for your readers a calculation based more on the Latins whom you criticize than on the Egyptians whom you prefer.

We have therefore determined that everyone should follow the Egyptian discipline of calculation, which appears more correct both in your judgment and by the agreement of the universal Church: namely, that the beginning of the first month extends from the eighth day before the Ides of March through the day of the Nones of April; that the fourteenth moons of Easter extend from the twelfth day before the Kalends of April through the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May; and that the Sunday of Easter is to be sought from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April through the seventh day before the Kalends of May, on a moon from the fifteenth through the twenty-first.

But lest the lovers of Victorius tear us apart for having rashly attacked him, let them read the book of that most learned and holy man, namely Victorius, bishop of Capua, concerning Easter, which was thought ought to be celebrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth indiction, nine times while Basil was proconsul. There they will discover how highly his teacher was esteemed by prudent and catholic doctors of the Church. The beginning of the book is:

> “When we were carefully seeking on what day the venerable solemnity of Easter would most appropriately occur during the present year’s thirteenth indiction, and, in accordance with the decrees of the venerable Fathers, were saying that the Lord’s resurrection must unquestionably be celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, our answer seemed to some hardly reasonable, because a certain Victorius, in the paschal cycle that he published, had assigned another day for the Lord’s resurrection, although he had also designated the very day that we likewise profess ought to be celebrated.”

And later in the work:

> “But now,” I say, “the order of the discussion requires that I clearly expose the errors of the cycles published by Victorius, since he does not know how to determine the lawful day of Easter. Once it has been shown that he has erred in this way in the past, he will lack authority for the present and future, and will lose the opportunity for false persuasion.”

## CHAPTER LII. The Method for Determining the Number of Lunar Epacts

If you wish to know how many epacts there are in each year, take however many years of the Lord have elapsed—for example, in the present eighth indiction, 725—and divide them by nineteen: nineteen times thirty is 570; nineteen times eight is 152, making 722; three remain. Multiply these by eleven; they make thirty-three. Subtract thirty; three remain. There are three epacts, that is, three lunar additions.

## CHAPTER LIII. On the Solar Epacts

[Note: [Col. 0501D] C reads *inquit* (“he says”) for *inquam* (“I say”).]

BRID. RAMES. GLOSSAE.—On the fourth path of the nineteen-year cycle are marked the solar epacts, that is, the concurrent days of the week. “Concurrent” means the new day of the Kalends of April. For if you divide the year by seven, one day remains, which causes the Kalends and the other days not always to fall on the same weekdays. For example, if the Kalends of January fall on the first day of the week, in the following year they will fall not on the first but on the second; in the third year they will fall on the third day of the week. In the fourth year, therefore, they fall not on the fourth but on the fifth, because of the leap day. The solar cycle therefore extends to twenty-eight years, so that the leap day may occur on each day of the week.]

On the fourth path of the nineteen-year cycle are marked the solar epacts, that is, the concurrent days of the week, which increase by the addition of one day each year, and of two days in the leap year, until they reach the number seven. Their cycle contains four times seven years, that is, twenty-eight, because it cannot be completed before the leap day—which customarily returns every fourth year—has touched all the days of the week: Sunday, Friday, Wednesday, Monday, Saturday, Thursday, and Tuesday, for it runs through them in this order.

Since each year has its own concurrent days, those concurrent days specifically fixed in the cycle designate which weekday falls on the ninth day before the Kalends of April. Because they lie close to the beginning of the paschal feast, they readily reveal the weekday on which the day of the epacts, or the fourteenth moon, falls, and thereby make a clear path toward finding the Sunday of Easter.

The same annual day of the concurrents also occurs, a fact useful for the calculator to remember, on the second day before the Kalends of April, the seventh day before the Ides of April, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, and the eleventh day before those same Kalends.

The course of this cycle is such that whatever concurrents occur in a leap year also occurred five years earlier and will occur again six years later. Those that occur in the first year after a leap year also occurred eleven years earlier and return six years later. Those that occur in the second year after a leap year also occurred six years earlier and return eleven years later. Those that occur in the third year after a leap year also occurred six years earlier and return five years later. This pattern of distinctions encompasses all the days of the revolving years.

It should certainly be noted that the reason why twenty-eight nineteen-year cycles must be completed before the same course of paschal observance returns in every respect to itself is this twenty-eight-year solar cycle: every year of this cycle must establish the beginning of a nineteen-year cycle, and each year of the nineteen-year cycle must in turn attain this beginning. Consequently, the entire series of paschal observance is completed only after 532 years.

## CHAPTER LIV. The Method for Determining the Number of Solar Epacts and When the Year Is a Leap Year

Since the course of the epacts—that is, the solar additions—is shared and undivided with the leap year, learn by the following method what the condition of both is. If you wish to know when the leap day occurs, take the years of the Lord, 725, and divide them by four. If nothing remains, it is a leap year; if one, two, or three remain, it is respectively the first, second, or third year after a leap year. For example: four times one hundred is 400; four times eighty is 320; four times one is four; one remains, because it is the first year after a leap year.

If you wish to know the solar additions, that is, the concurrent days of the week, take the years from the incarnation of the Lord that have elapsed—for example, 725, in the eighth indiction—and always add the fourth part of the years that have elapsed, namely 181 in this case; together they make 906. Add four to these, making 910. Divide them by seven: seven times one hundred is 700, seven times thirty is 210, and nothing remains, because there are seven solar epacts, that is, seven concurrent days of the week.

## CHAPTER LV. On the Return and Articulated Computation of Both Kinds of Epacts

[Note: [Col. 0503D]]

BRID. RAMES. GLOSSAE.—For example, three hundred has ten thirties. Therefore the same concurrents that occur in the three-hundredth year will occur in the twentieth year in the future. For example, ten is the thirtieth part of three hundred years; twice ten makes twenty. Therefore the concurrents that will occur in the twentieth future year occurred in the three-hundredth year in the past.

If anything remains after the groups of thirty—that is, after the thirties—this is to be added. Such is the meaning: if anything remains beyond thirty. For example, divide one hundred by thirty; ten remain. Double the three—why? Because you had three thirties, making six—and add these to the remaining number, which remained after the division into thirties, namely ten; they make sixteen. It is thereby apparent that the concurrents that will occur in the sixteenth year likewise occurred in the hundredth year in the past.

The same should equally be understood of the fourteenth moon of Easter and of the other matters included in the nineteen-year cycle. If you wish to know, counting from the present, what will occur after some number of years—for example, after one hundred Easters—it is sufficient to find only the epacts and the concurrent days of the sun. Divide one hundred by nineteen; five remain. Know, therefore, that the epacts in the hundredth year are the ones that will occur in the fifth year. In the same way, dividing one hundred by twenty-eight, you will find the solar concurrents in the hundredth year to be those belonging to the sixteenth year.

[The following is supplied as an alternate form of the preceding gloss.] Whether someone wishes to arrange this for himself in this way or in another, the following may be used. If you wish to perform the same calculation in another manner, place the first concurrent with the leap day on the first day of the week, the second on the second, the third on the third, the fourth on the fourth, and the sixth with the leap day on the sixth, proceeding in this way to the end. Take care only to omit one in the fourth position every time, so that the leap day may touch all the days of the week.]

The one who keeps the cycles of the sun and moon in memory most readily understands the day of Easter and the other returns of the seasons, provided that he knows how to multiply and divide those same cycles by nineteen and by twenty-eight. Every calculator should remember that the solar concurrents thirty years ago are the same as those that will occur next year; those sixty years ago are the same as those that will occur in the fourth year; those ninety years ago the same as those that will occur in the sixth; those one hundred twenty years ago the same as those that will occur in the eighth; those one hundred fifty years ago the same as those that will occur in the tenth; and so the others will return in this manner.

For whatever number of years has elapsed, if you wish to know the concurrents, see how many times that number contains thirty; by doubling the thirtieth part, you will discover the correspondence of the revolving years. For example, three hundred contains ten thirties, and therefore the concurrents in the three-hundredth year are the same as those that will occur in the twentieth year; if anything remains, add that as well. The order of the concurrents likewise applies to past times.

Again, because the lunar cycle is nineteen years, the epacts of the present year return in the twentieth year, those of the following year after forty years, those of the third after sixty, those of the fourth after eighty, [Col. 0505A] those of the fifth after one hundred, those of the sixth after one hundred twenty, those of the seventh after one hundred forty, those of the eighth after one hundred sixty, those of the ninth after one hundred eighty, those of the tenth after two hundred, and the others similarly. The same should equally be understood of the fourteenth moon of Easter and of the other matters included in the nineteen-year cycle.

A diligent calculator can also record for himself in this manner longer returns of the periods that follow, always remembering that the condition of the past age corresponds as well. It seems worth mentioning that some people, for the sake of shortening the calculation, transfer the order of both cycles—the solar and the lunar—onto the joints of the fingers. Since the human hand has joints, with the nails added, ten and nine, they assign one year to each of these and begin the lunar course on the inner side of the left hand at the base of the thumb, completing it on the inner side of the little finger’s nail.

Again, since the two hands have twenty-eight joints, excluding the nails, they assign one year to each joint, beginning with the little finger of the left hand and completing the count at the thumb of the right. They do not, as in the lunar cycle, proceed through the fingers one by one in numerical order; rather, because of the quarter-cycle, they mark each four-year period transversely across four fingers. Thus the three pairs of joints of the little fingers contain the same number of leap years; likewise, the three pairs of joints of the fingers next to the little fingers indicate the same number of years following those two groups of leap years; and the second fingers similarly contain the second set of years, while the third fingers contain the third set according to the same reckoning. Finally, the seventh leap year, together with the three years following it, claims for itself two pairs of joints of the thumbs.

[Note: [Col. 0505] This, or in another manner.]

Whether a calculator wishes to arrange this for himself in this way or another, the hands will nonetheless readily grasp the cycle of either heavenly body. But countless matters in this discipline, as in the other arts, are better transmitted through the address of the living voice than through the work of the writing hand.

## CHAPTER LVI. On the Lunar Cycle

[Note: [Col. 0505C]]

BRID. RAMES. GLOSSAE.—The lunar cycle is included in the fifth division of the nineteen-year cycle. It begins from its fourth year and is completed in its third year. The third is reckoned according to the sun, while the fourth is reckoned according to the moon. For the first year according to the sun is the second according to the moon; nevertheless, two months of the lunar year still remain. The first year is the first year of the lunar cycle, with the first moon on the Kalends of January.
