The third year is the nineteenth-cycle year up to the fourteenth moon of Easter; the fourth year of the nineteen-year cycle begins with the fifteenth moon of Easter, while that same first lunar year continues up to the Kalends of January.

What Dionysius takes care to do in the paschal month, we shall do in January. Dionysius therefore continues this order as follows.

In the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, the seventeenth lunar year, from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May to the Nones of April, because it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In the second year of the nineteen-year cycle, the eighteenth lunar year, from the eighth day before the Ides of April to the eighth day before the Kalends of April, because it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In the third year of the nineteen-year cycle, the nineteenth lunar year, from the seventh day before the Kalends of April to the Ides of April, because it is an embolismic year, there are 384 days.

In the fourth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the first lunar year, from the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May to the fourth day before the Nones of April, because it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In the fifth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the second lunar year, from the third day before the Nones of April to the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, because it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In the sixth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the third lunar year, from the tenth day before the Kalends of April to the fourth day before the Ides of April, because it is an embolismic year, there are 384 days.

In the seventh year of the nineteen-year cycle, the fourth lunar year, from the third day before the Ides of April to the third day before the Kalends of April, because it is a common year, there are 354 days.

[Col. 0506C] In the eighth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the fifth lunar year, from the second day before the Kalends of April to the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, because it is an embolismic year, there are 384 days.

In the ninth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the sixth lunar year, from the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May to the seventh day before the Ides of April, because it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In the tenth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the seventh lunar year, from the seventh day before the Ides of April to the sixth day before the Kalends of April, because it is a common year, there are 354 days of embolism. [The source’s wording is internally inconsistent here.]

In the eleventh year of the nineteen-year cycle, the eighth lunar year, from the fifth day before the Kalends of April to the [possibly: seventeenth] day before the Kalends of May, because it is an embolismic year, there are 384 days.

In the twelfth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the ninth lunar year, from the sixth day before the Kalends of May to the second day before the Nones of April, because it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In the thirteenth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the tenth lunar year, from the Nones of April to the ninth day before the Kalends of April, because it is a common year, there are [Col. 0506D] 354 days.

In the fourteenth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the eleventh lunar year, from the eighth day before the Kalends of April to the second day before the Ides of April, because it is an embolismic year, there are 384 days.

In the fifteenth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the twelfth lunar year, from the Ides of April to the Kalends of April, because it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In the sixteenth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the thirteenth lunar year, from the fourth day before the Nones of April to the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, because it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In the seventeenth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the fourteenth lunar year, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April to the fifth day before the Ides of April, because it is an embolismic year, there are 384 days.

In the eighteenth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the fifteenth lunar year, from the fourth day before the Ides of April to the fourth day before the Kalends of April, because it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In the nineteenth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the sixteenth lunar year, from the third day before the Kalends of April to the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, because it is an embolismic year, there are 384 days.]

The lunar cycle is included in the fifth division of the nineteen-year cycle, beginning with its fourth year [Note: [Col. 0505] C: “of it”] and being completed in its third year. This cycle properly belongs to the Romans and pertains to the month of January. For just as each year of the nineteen-year cycle, because of the legal observance of the Hebrews, begins with the paschal month and ends there, so this cycle, according to Roman institution, begins with the moon of the month of January and ends there.

Like the other cycle, this one has first and second common years, a third embolismic year, fourth and fifth common years, a sixth embolismic year, a seventh common year, and an eighth embolismic year. The eleven-year lunar cycle, like the nineteen-year cycle, has seven common years and four embolismic years. Common years have twelve lunar months, that is, 353 days. Embolismic years have thirteen months, namely 384 days, except for the seventeenth year of this cycle, which is the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, in which one day is omitted because of the lunar leap.

To make this clearer, let us examine the course of the individual years in order, and what Dionysius takes care to do in the paschal month, we shall do in January.

In the first lunar year, the fourth year of the nineteen-year cycle, from the Kalends of January to the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, because it is a common year, there are 353 days.

In the second lunar year, the fifth year of the nineteen-year cycle, from the twelfth day before the Kalends of January to the fifth day before the Ides of December, because it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In lunar year III, nineteenth-year cycle VI, from the fourth day before the Ides of December through the fifth day before the Kalends of January, since it is an embolismic year, there are 184 days.

[Col. 0507B] In lunar year IV, nineteenth-year cycle VII, from the fourth day before the Kalends of January through the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, since it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In lunar year V, nineteenth-year cycle VIII, from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January through the eighth day before the Ides of December, since it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In lunar year VI, nineteenth-year cycle IX, from the seventh day before the Ides of December through the eighth day before the Kalends of January, since it is an embolismic year, there are 384 days.

In lunar year VII, nineteenth-year cycle X, from the seventh day before the Kalends of January through the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January, since it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In lunar year VIII, nineteenth-year cycle XI, from the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January through the fourth day before the Nones of January, since it is an embolismic year, there are 384 days.

[Col. 0507C] In lunar year IX, nineteenth-year cycle XII, from the third day before the Nones of January through the eleventh day before the Kalends of January, since it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In lunar year X, nineteenth-year cycle XIII, from the tenth day before the Kalends of January through the third day before the Ides of December, since it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In lunar year XI, nineteenth-year cycle XIV, from the second day before the Ides of December through the third day before the Kalends of January, since it is an embolismic year, there are 384 days.

In lunar year XII, nineteenth-year cycle XV, from the second day before the Kalends of January through the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January, since it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In lunar year XIII, nineteenth-year cycle XVI, from the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January through the sixth day before the Ides of December, since it is a common year, there are 354 days.

[Col. 0507D] In lunar year XIV, nineteenth-year cycle XVII, from the fifth day before the Ides of December through the sixth day before the Kalends of January, since it is an embolismic year, there are 384 days.

In lunar year XV, nineteenth-year cycle XVIII, from the fifth day before the Kalends of January through the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, since it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In lunar year XVI, nineteenth-year cycle XIX, from the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January through the Nones of December, since it is a common year, there are 354 days.

In lunar year XVII, nineteenth-year cycle I, from the Nones of December through the tenth day before the Kalends of January, since it is an embolismic year, there are 384 days.

In lunar year XVIII, nineteenth-year cycle II, from the ninth day before the Kalends of January through the second day before the Ides of December, since it is a common year, there are 354 days.

[Col. 0508A] In lunar year XIX, nineteenth-year cycle III, from the Ides of December through the second day before the Kalends of January, since it is an embolismic year, there are 384 days.

The reckoning of the seventeenth lunar year therefore begins on the very day on which the preceding year has ended, and not on the following day as in the case of the others, so that, because of the lunar leap—so called—this same year might not appear to lack one day. Dionysius himself demonstrated this, running through the nineteenth-year cycle in this order: he began the first year on the same day on which he brought the last year to its close.

## CHAPTER LVII. A method for determining what the moon’s age is on the Kalends of January

Anyone who wishes may derive a calculation from the lunar cycle for determining the moon’s age on the Kalends of January. Take any lunar cycle—for example, the fifth—and multiply it by eleven: the result is 55. Always add one regular number: the result is 56. Divide by 30; 26 remains. The moon is therefore 26 days old on the Kalends of January in the fifth year of the lunar cycle. Again, take eight and multiply it by eleven: the result is 88. Add one regular number and divide by 30; 29 remains. The moon is therefore 29 days old on the aforementioned Kalends in the eighth year of the lunar cycle. Remember only that in the seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth years of the cycle mentioned, you must add not one regular number, as in the remaining years, but two; then you will find the moon on the Kalends of January without error.

## CHAPTER LVIII. A method for determining which year of the lunar or nineteenth-year cycle it is

[Col. 0508C]

If you wish to know which year the lunar cycle is running, take the years of the Lord—for example, 725—and always subtract two; 723 remains. Divide this by nineteen; one remains, so it is the first year of the lunar cycle. Whenever nothing remains, it is the nineteenth year. And because the nineteenth-year cycle follows the same course as the lunar cycle, although it runs more quickly, if you wish to know which year of it is running, take the years of the Lord—for example, 725—and always add one; the result is 726. Divide this by 10 and 9; 4 remains, so it is the fourth year of the nineteenth-year cycle. If nothing remains, it is the final year.

## CHAPTER LIX. On the fourteenth moon of Easter

[Col. 0508D]

The sixth division of the often-mentioned cycle embraces the fourteen moons of the first month, which unambiguously indicate each year the day of the Lord’s Paschal observance. For the Sunday that occurs after the fourteenth moon is the day of the Lord’s Paschal resurrection. This fourteenth moon first displays its course to the earth at evening at the equinox—that is, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April—and finally on the twenty-ninth day thereafter, that is, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May. Within these limits the course of the legal observance of Easter is understood to be contained through the nineteen-year period. If it could happen that the fourteenth moon fell for everyone on the same day of the week each year, the time of our Paschal observance would differ in nothing from the legal observance.

[Col. 0509A] For then we too, in accordance with the commands of the law, would always sacrifice and eat the flesh of the spotless lamb on the evening of the fourteenth moon of the first month, sprinkling its blood on our doorposts to repel the destroyer—that is, [Note: [Col. 0509] Omitted in C: “water.”] the water of baptism—and, celebrating the solemn rites of Paschal Masses, would overcome the spiritual Egypt, and at daybreak on the fifteenth moon of the same month would enter the first day of Unleavened Bread. With due reverence we would complete the seven lawful days of that celebration, from the morning of the fifteenth day through the evening of the twenty-first day of the month—that is, from the Lord’s Pascha through the Sunday of Paschal Octave.

But because the same lunar day falls on different days of the week, it follows that, although we are taught to reserve the beginning of Easter for the Sunday because of the resurrection of our Redeemer, our feast sometimes begins on the seventh day after the beginning of the legal Unleavened Bread. Nevertheless, it never happens that our Paschal solemnity does not include within itself at least one of the legal days of Easter, and often all of them.

By contrast, those who think that the Lord’s Paschal day must be celebrated from the sixteenth through the twenty-second moon suffer a double misery: they never have the lawful beginning of Easter, and it frequently happens that they encounter none of the days prescribed in the law within their Paschal observance. They entirely reject both the evening of the fourteenth day, on which Easter was ordained to begin, and the morning of the fifteenth, on which the seven-day solemnity of Unleavened Bread [Col. 0509C] was commanded to begin. Moreover, as a punishment for this sin, they frequently decree the twenty-second day as the beginning of their Easter, although that day is not found mentioned even once in the entire Paschal institution given through Moses.

There are others who slip to the other side of the road, away from the way of truth, though into no lesser an error, since Scripture commands us to walk along the royal road and not to turn aside from it either to the right or to the left. By decreeing that the Lord’s Pascha is to be observed from the thirteenth through the twentieth moon, they too frequently anticipate the beginning of the legal Easter: what the law ordained to take place on the fourteenth moon, they transfer to the thirteenth; and what it ordained concerning the twentieth, consecrating it as a holy and most solemn day, they utterly disregard, as though it had no connection with Easter.

Among the other defenders of Catholic faith and practice, the blessed Theophilus, bishop of the Church of Alexandria, also defeats them by clear reasoning. He wrote to the emperor Theodosius the Elder:

“Since it sometimes happens that, because of the fourteenth moon of the first month, certain people fall into error—if the fourteenth moon itself falls on a Sunday, in which case it is necessary that the fast already be broken on the Sabbath, when the thirteenth moon is shown to occur, and we begin to do what is contrary to the law—it is therefore appropriate to observe carefully that whenever the fourteenth moon falls on a Sunday, we should postpone the Paschal day to the following week, for two reasons. First, so that we do not break the fast when the thirteenth moon is found on the Sabbath, which is not proper and which the law itself does not command, especially since the light of that moon still appears imperfect in its own orb. Second, so that we are not compelled to fast on Sunday when the fourteenth moon is present, doing something improper and unlawful; for this practice has been adopted by the sect of the Manichaeans.”

Since, therefore, we ought neither to fast when the fourteenth moon falls on a Sunday, nor consequently to break the fast when the thirteenth falls on the Sabbath, we necessarily assert that this must be postponed to the following week, as I explained above. Yet this postponement does not constitute any transgression concerning the Paschal calculation. For just as the number ten includes nine, so whenever the fourteenth moon falls on a Sunday, because it is not permissible to fast on that day, it is necessary to postpone the day of Easter to the following week. No diminution of Easter seems to result from this, because the days that follow include the remaining days as well.

## CHAPTER LX. A method for finding it

[Note: [Col. 0509D]

BRID. RAMES. GLOSSES.—Every skilled calculator ought to retain in memory the fourteenth moons of the first month, just as he does the annual lunar epacts. But if anyone wishes to find these by calculation as well, let him examine how many lunar epacts there are in whatever year he wishes to calculate. If you wish to find the Paschal term, look at the epact corresponding to that term. If you find it to be less than fifteen, complete it to the same number, fifteen, counting from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April; and on whatever calendar day that number is completed, there beyond doubt will be the term. When you find an epact of fifteen on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, you will have the Paschal term. But if the epact is greater than fifteen, complete the same number to forty-four, counting likewise from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April; and on whatever calendar day that number is completed, there will be the term. When there is no epact, one must always count from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April until the fifteenth number is completed—that is, through the Nones of April.]

Every skilled calculator ought to retain in memory the fourteenth moons of the first month, just as he does the annual lunar epacts. But [Note: [Col. 0509] “And” omitted in C.] if anyone wishes to find these by calculation as well, let him see how many lunar epacts there are in whatever year he wishes to calculate. If there are fourteen or fifteen, [Note: [Col. 0509] Added in C.] let him recognize that the fourteenth moon falls on the eleventh or twelfth day before the Kalends of April, respectively, since, as has often been said, the eleventh day before the aforementioned Kalends is the proper place of all epacts.

[Col. 0511A] But if there are fewer epacts, let him allow them to increase by days until they complete the number fourteen, and there let him be confident that he has the fourteenth moon of Easter. If, on the other hand, he has more than fifteen epacts, let him allow these to increase by days up to the number thirty—that is, the term of the month itself—and thus, beginning from the new moon and proceeding in order through the fourteenth, he will duly find the day suited to the Paschal observance.

This too must be noted: if the fourteenth moon is in a common year, it customarily returns eleven days earlier than it passed in the preceding year; but if it is an embolismic year, it returns nineteen [Note: [Col. 0511] C adds: “days.”] days later, with the sole exception of the first year of the nineteenth-year cycle, in which, because of the lunar leap, it usually precedes the interannual course by twelve days.

## CHAPTER LXI. On the Sunday of Easter

[Note: [Col. 0511C]

BRID. RAMES. GLOSSES.—The Sunday of Easter is contained under the seventh division of the nineteenth-year cycle, which took its beginning from the resurrection of our Savior from the dead. For, as our Savior was handed over on the fourteenth moon—that is, on the fifth day after the Sabbath—was crucified on the fifteenth, and rose on the third day, that is, on the seventeenth moon, which was then found on a Sunday, so too, as we learn from the observance of the Gospels, the blessed Theophilus, venerable bishop of Alexandria, whom I mentioned above, writes.

Matthew says: “Now on the first day of Unleavened Bread, the disciples came to Jesus, saying: ‘Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?’ But Jesus said: ‘Go into the city to a certain man,’ etc.”

Mark says: “And on the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover, his disciples said to him: ‘Where do you wish us to go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?’ And he sends two of his disciples, etc.”

Jerome: “The first day of Unleavened Bread is the fourteenth day of the first month, when the lamb is sacrificed, the moon is completely full, and leaven is cast away.”

Bede calls the first day of Unleavened Bread the fourteenth day of the first month, when, after leaven had been cast away, they were accustomed to sacrifice—that is, to kill—the lamb in the evening. Explaining this, the Apostle says: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed.” Although he was crucified on the following day, that is, on the fifteenth moon, nevertheless on this night, when the lamb was sacrificed and he handed over to his disciples the mysteries of his flesh and blood to be celebrated, and was seized and bound by the Jews, he consecrated the beginning of his own sacrifice—that is, of his Passion.

Again Mark says: “And when evening had come—for it was the Preparation, which is before the Sabbath—Joseph of Arimathea, a noble councillor, who himself was also awaiting the kingdom of God, came and boldly went in to Pilate, and asked for the body of Jesus.”

And Luke says: “And behold, a man named Joseph, who was a councillor, a good and just man. He had not consented to their counsel and deeds. He was from Arimathea, a city of Judea, and he too was awaiting the kingdom of God. He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus; and when it had been taken down, he wrapped it in a linen cloth and placed him in a tomb cut out of rock, in which no one had yet been laid. It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was dawning.”

From these statements it is therefore evident that our Lord Jesus Christ was handed over on the fourteenth moon, crucified on the fifteenth, lay in the tomb on the sixteenth, and rose from the dead on the seventeenth moon. Whatever remains to be explained concerning this chapter—namely, concerning the equinox, the first month, and also the third week of the fourteenth moon—you will find sufficiently set out above.

“In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, you shall eat unleavened bread. In Greek, leaven is called zýma (ζύμα); hence in Latin it is called azymus panis, ‘unleavened bread,’ without zýma, that is, without leaven: a means ‘without’; zýma, ‘leaven.’]

The Sunday of Easter is contained under the seventh division of the nineteenth-year cycle, which took its beginning from the Sunday of our Savior’s resurrection from the dead. For, since in the Old Testament the time of Easter is commanded to be observed by three indications, namely, after the equinox, in the first month, and in its third week—that is, from the evening of the fourteenth moon, which is the beginning of the fifteenth, through the evening, that is, the end of the twenty-first day—the observance has a fourth rule imposed upon us from the time of the Lord’s resurrection:

[Col. 0511C] When, after the equinox has been passed, we see the fourteenth moon of the first month rise in the evening, we must not immediately rush to celebrate Easter, but must await the Sunday on which he deigned, by rising, to accomplish Easter itself—that is, the passage from death to life, from corruption to incorruption, and from punishment to glory—and finally celebrate the appropriate Paschal rites on that day.

If someone objects that the lawgiver mentioned not the equinox but only the first month and its third week, let him know that, although the equinox is not expressly named [Note: [Col. 0511] Added in B and C.], nevertheless, by commanding that Easter be made after the full moon of the first month, he fully indicates that the equinox must already have passed. For it is beyond doubt that the moon which, after the equinox has passed, first displays its full orb is the moon of the first month.

Whenever, therefore, we have the Sunday immediately following the arrival of the fifteenth moon, our Paschal time differs in nothing from the legal observance, although we celebrate the solemn rites of that same Easter through other kinds of sacramental observances.

But whenever that Sunday occurs on the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh day thereafter, even so we do not abolish the law or the prophets; rather, we fulfill them through the sacraments of evangelical grace. For, as our Savior was handed over on the fourteenth moon—that is, on the fifth day after the Sabbath—was crucified on the fifteenth, and rose on the third day, that is, on the seventeenth moon, which was then found on a Sunday, so too the blessed Theophilus, venerable bishop of Alexandria, whom I mentioned above, writes, as we learn also from the observance of the Gospels.

We therefore have grounds on which to celebrate Easter correctly even when postponement has followed because of an intervening necessity: if the fourteenth moon of the first month falls on the Sabbath, or if it occurs on another day of the week before the Sabbath of the following week, we may celebrate Easter without hesitation. But if it falls on Sunday, we must in every way postpone it to the following week, for the reasons stated above.

After these matters have been demonstrated and made clear, this too must be considered: the law itself frequently commands that those who, because of some constraint of time, were unable to celebrate Easter in the first month should do so in the second. For in necessity it is better for those placed in such circumstances to follow what is higher rather than what is lower, since the lower is contained by the higher, whereas the higher cannot be included by the lower number. This makes clear once again what we have already stated: the number ten contains nine within itself, but nine cannot contain ten.

If, then, the law commands us to pass over into the second month when we cannot celebrate holy Easter in the first month because of certain necessities, I do not understand why, if the fourteenth moon falls on a Sunday, we should not reasonably postpone Easter to the following week, with both the first month and the fifteenth moon—the moon on which the Savior was crucified—remaining in place, and also the seventeenth, when he rose after three days.

As for the day on which the first Sunday of Christ’s resurrection occurred, it is reported in various ways. As we mentioned above, some assert that it was on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, others on the sixth, and still others on the fifth day before those Kalends.

Here it must be noted that if, as the earlier writers recorded, the Lord’s resurrection took place on the eighth day before the aforementioned Kalends, the fifth year of the nineteen-year cycle was then in progress, with seven concurrent days and the fourteenth moon, as always, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April.

But if the Lord rose on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, it was the thirteenth year of the aforesaid cycle, with five concurrent days and the fourteenth moon, as always, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April.

If, moreover, Christ’s resurrection was celebrated on the fifth day before the aforementioned Kalends [Note: [Col. 0513] C: “according to the second.”], the second year of the nineteen-year cycle was in progress, with four concurrent days and the fourteenth moon, as always, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. These dates all disclose, by an indisputable course, the seventeenth moon on which the first Sunday mysteries of the most holy resurrection were accomplished. One must be especially careful not to confirm, as some do, that this occurred on the sixteenth moon, lest we incur not only the unavoidable loss of our calculation but also the gravest danger to the Catholic faith.

## CHAPTER LXII. On the moon of that day

The final limit of the often-mentioned cycle unfolds the lunar dates of the Lord’s Pascha, enclosed within a range of seven days because the Sunday in question falls variously—that is, from the fifteenth through the twenty-first. These days are certainly prescribed by the law’s frequent testimony, the Lord saying:

“In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, you shall eat unleavened bread, until the twenty-first day of the same month at evening; for seven days no leaven shall be found in your houses.”

The rule concerning this first month and its seven days of Unleavened Bread is now as follows: whichever fifteenth moon occurs after the equinox is to be understood as belonging to the first month; and whichever Sunday it receives within the seven days up to the twenty-first, that Sunday it presents as suited to the joys of the Paschal feast.

I repeat this so often because there were some who, marking the Sunday of Easter—for example, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April—with the twentieth moon, would say: “Why do you show that we are sinning in fixing the time of Easter, when no calculator has ever forbidden Easter to be celebrated on the seventh day before the Kalends of April? Since everyone equally admits that the equinox has then passed, no one will deny that the twentieth moon is suitable for the Sunday of Easter.”

They should be answered that Easter may properly be celebrated both on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, when the moon is appropriate, and on the twentieth moon, when the suitable day occurs. But because the moon that is twentieth on the seventh day before the Kalends of April had its full moon before the equinox, it is not permissible to celebrate the Sunday of Easter on the seventh day before the Kalends of April when the moon is twentieth. The moon that is full at the equinox or after the equinox, however, will give the lawful Easter as soon as the Sunday arrives.

The same error receives the same response when the calculators mentioned decree that Easter should be celebrated on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April with the sixteenth moon; on the tenth day before the Kalends of April with the seventeenth moon; on the ninth day before the Kalends of April with the eighteenth moon; on the eighth day before the Kalends of April with the nineteenth moon; on the seventh day before the Kalends of April with the twentieth moon; on the sixth day before the Kalends of April with the twenty-first moon; and on the fifth day before the Kalends of April with the twenty-second moon. [Note: [Col. 0513] C omits the text from “on the ninth” through “the eighteenth.”]

They do this especially often in a year in which they have the twenty-fifth moon on the Kalends of January. But when they have the twenty-seventh moon there, they depart still farther from the truth, because they count as belonging to the first month a moon that was born on the third day before the Nones of March and is shown to have become full nearly three days before the equinox.

And because the fifteenth, sixteenth, and seventeenth moons cannot produce the Sunday of Easter—the reason being that these ages occurred on the fourteenth, thirteenth, and twelfth days before the Kalends of April—it follows that the remaining ages, even though they follow the equinox, cannot have their solemnities suitable for that same Sunday resurrection.

## CHAPTER LXIII. The difference between Easter and Unleavened Bread

Since we have touched briefly on the observance of Easter, it has also seemed appropriate to make clear that, according to the wording of the law, Easter is one solemnity and Unleavened Bread another.

There is one day of Easter, that is, of the Passover—the fourteenth day of the first month—on which, as evening came, the lamb was commanded to be sacrificed. Immediately during the following night the Lord passed through, striking the firstborn of the Egyptians and delivering the houses of the children of Israel marked with the lamb’s blood. The seven following days, namely, from the fifteenth through the twenty-first day of the same month, are properly called the days of Unleavened Bread.

For it is written in Exodus, where the lamb is commanded to be sacrificed on the fourteenth day of the first month at evening: “You shall eat in haste, for it is the Passover, that is, the Lord’s passage.” And: “I shall pass through the land of Egypt on that night, and I shall strike every firstborn in the land of Egypt.” A little later: “And when your children say to you, ‘What does this observance mean to you?’ you shall say: ‘It is the sacrifice of the Lord’s Passover, when he passed over the houses of the children of Israel in Egypt, striking the Egyptians and delivering our houses.’”

Likewise in Leviticus: “In the first month,” he says, “on the fourteenth day of the month at evening, it is the Lord’s Passover; and on the fifteenth day of this month is the solemnity of the Lord’s Unleavened Bread. For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. The first day shall be especially solemn and holy for you. You shall do no servile work on it, but you shall offer a sacrifice by fire to the Lord for seven days.”

And so that no one may suppose that we have understood the words of the law otherwise than truth requires, let the most learned authority on the legal writings, the priest Josephus, be consulted concerning his view of these matters. He writes in his *Antiquities* as follows:

“On the fourteenth moon of the first month the lamb is sacrificed; on the fifteenth the feast of Unleavened Bread follows, and it is celebrated for seven days. On the second day of Unleavened Bread, which is the sixteenth, they offer the firstfruits of the crops that they reap.” [Note: [Col. 0515] C omits “which is the sixteenth.”]

The custom of these legal sacred rites is also imitated, not without distinction, by the practice of the Church even now. She chiefly observes one night of the Lord’s passage—that is, of his resurrection from the dead—which he deigned to preserve for the faithful by his triumphant victory. At its rising, the blood of the spotless lamb himself cleanses from every sin his people, washed in the font of regeneration; thereafter she adds seven other days in fitting celebration in memory of that same Sunday resurrection.

Yet because that very day of Easter is also commanded to be cleansed of leaven, the Gospel sometimes calls it the first day of Unleavened Bread. “And on the first day of Unleavened Bread,” it says, “when they sacrificed the Passover, his disciples said to him: ‘Where do you wish us to go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?’”

Likewise, it calls the fifteenth day of the first month, from which the seven days of Unleavened Bread begin, by the name of Passover because of its proximity to it, when it says: “And they themselves did not enter the praetorium, so that they would not be defiled, but might eat the Passover.” [Col. 0516A] This is not because the Gospel writing is contrary to the law, but because it wished to impress more vividly upon us the sacrament it was fitting to convey through this association of names. [Note: [Col. 0515] B and C: “he was saying.”]

Without a more subtle examination, we may understand that each of us has celebrated the mystical solemnities of Easter on the day of baptism: by escaping the spiritual destroyer through the sign of the precious blood and passing spiritually through the darkness. Throughout the whole course of our advancing life that we thereafter spend in this pilgrimage, we celebrate the seven days of Unleavened Bread. During these, as the Apostle teaches, we must feast not on the leaven of malice and wickedness but on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

And because in baptism, if we are to pass from Satan’s power into the portion of the lot of the saints, we must hold to sincerity and truth, and because throughout the entire period of our pilgrimage—which revolves according to the number seven—we are commanded by daily progress to pass over to better things, we are understood to eat spiritually both the Unleavened Bread of Easter and to celebrate Easter spiritually during the days of Unleavened Bread.”

## CHAPTER LXIV. A typical interpretation of Easter

[Note: [Col. 0515C]

BRID. RAMES. GLOSSES.—For just as the entire observance of the ceremonies of Easter, so also the time at which it was commanded to be performed, is wholly redolent of sacred mysteries. And shortly afterward: “Then we attend to the first month of the year, which is also called the month of new things, in which we celebrate Easter,” etc.

In the book of Deuteronomy, chapter 16, the blessed Moses says this to the Israelite people:

“Observe the month of new crops and the first of the spring season, so that you may make the Passover to the Lord your God, because in this month the Lord your God brought you out of Egypt by night. And you shall sacrifice the Passover to the Lord your God, from sheep and cattle, in the place which the Lord your God will choose, so that his name may dwell there.”

He calls the month of new crops the first month of the Hebrews. Among them it is called Nisan, among the Greeks Ξαντικός (*Xanthikos*), and among the Latins April.

It is called the month of new crops because in it sheaves of grain—that is, the firstfruits of the harvest—were offered to the Lord by the reaper through the priest, as we read in Leviticus that the Lord commanded the children of Israel:

“When you have entered,” he says, “the land that I shall give you, and you have reaped its harvest, you shall bring sheaves of grain, the firstfruits of your harvest, to the priest. He shall lift up the sheaf before the Lord, so that it may be acceptable on your behalf.”

[Col. 0516C] For this reason too they are commanded by the Lord to make the Passover, that is, Easter, so that they may celebrate their deliverance from Egypt with an appropriate feast.

Thus we too are instructed by this example: since by the grace of God we have been liberated from spiritual Egypt and have put on the new human being, we should thereafter walk in newness of life, consecrating to God the firstfruits of good works and always presenting to him the acceptable offering of a devout life. We should also always remember the origin of the name of the solemnity itself: Passover, which we may call a passage, namely, so that, proceeding from worse things to better, we may leave behind dark Egypt and strive to reach the promised land happily.

For this reason Easter does not return to the same day of the year, as does the season of the Lord’s nativity. In the latter case, only the memory of his birth is solemnly observed; here, however, the mysteries of the life to come are celebrated and gifts are received. Hence the very name Easter, signifying passage from death to life, seeks a time appropriate to its mysteries.

First, so that, after the equinox has passed, the darkness of death may be overcome by the true light; second, so that in the first month of the year, which is called the month of new things, the joys of new life may be celebrated; third, so that the resurrection, which took place on the third day and was manifested in the third age of the world—that is, under grace, when it had previously lain hidden in prophetic enigma both before the law and under the law—may be honored in the third week of the moon; since at that time the moon’s own change also teaches that the glory of the mind must be changed from an earthly to a heavenly gaze; and finally, so that Sunday, marked by the creation of light and worthy of veneration because of Christ’s triumph, may be recalled to our memory as something also desired by us because of our own resurrection.]

For just as the entire observance of the paschal ceremonies, so also the time in which they are commanded to be performed is wholly fragrant with sacred mystery. First, in celebrating the Lord’s Pasch, we take care to pass beyond the equinox, in accordance with the decrees of the Law, so that the solemnity in which the Mediator between God and human beings, having destroyed the power of darkness, opened for the world a path of light may also show outwardly, through the order of time, what it contains inwardly. And what promises us the light of eternal blessedness is celebrated especially then, when the sun’s light, advancing through its yearly increase, first wins a victory over the shadow of night.

Next, we observe the first month of the year, which is also called the Month of New Things, in which we celebrate Pasch. This is the month in which this world was formed and the first human being was placed in the seat of paradise. For through the mysteries of this solemnity we hope to receive again our first robe and to reclaim the first kingdom of heavenly blessedness from which we departed into a distant region. Concerning the glory of that kingdom the blessed apostle Peter says: “But we await new heavens and a new earth according to his promises, in which righteousness dwells.” John likewise says in his Apocalypse: “And he who sat upon the throne said: ‘Behold, I make all things new.’”

We also observe the third week of that same month at Pasch, because it most fittingly corresponds to the joys of the Lord’s resurrection. For that most holy resurrection itself took place on the third day, and it appeared to the world in the third age of the world—that is, with the coming of heavenly grace—when his entire dispensation in the flesh, completed in the glory of the resurrection, was manifested. For he deigned to illumine the first periods of the world through the natural law given through the patriarchs, the middle periods through the written law given through the prophets, and the final periods through spiritual grace, coming in his own person.

The moon’s change at that time also offers us a most beautiful spectacle of heavenly mystery. The moon, made in the shape of a sphere, receives its light from the sun, as we have said above; and therefore it is always bright in the half of its orb that faces the sun, but always dark in the other half. From the first day until the fifteenth, its light increases toward the earth, while its waning side is turned toward the heavens. From the fifteenth day until the last, as its same light increases, turned away from earthly things, it gradually returns toward heavenly things.

For this change rightly signifies the mysteries of paschal joy, through which we are taught by contemplation to turn all the glory of our mind away from visible pleasures and fleeting favors, and to suspend it upon the light of heavenly grace alone. Or, if one wishes to interpret both of its changes in a favorable sense [Note: [Col. 0517D] C reads *conversationem* (“course” or “turning”) for *conversionem* (“change” or “turning”).], we may understand that the moon’s increasing light before human eyes signifies the grace of virtues through which the Lord, appearing in the flesh, illumined the world. Of these it is said: “And Jesus advanced in wisdom and age, and in grace with God and human beings.” Its increasing return toward the heavens signifies the glory of his resurrection and ascension, which came forth perfect at once in him himself, but does not cease to grow in the minds of the faithful through certain advances of its light until the end of the age.

For when the Lord rose from the dead, he appeared first to individuals and pairs, and then to larger numbers—sometimes to seven, sometimes to eleven, sometimes to twelve, and sometimes to more than five hundred brothers at once—and finally to all the disciples. In their sight, when he was about to ascend into heaven, he commanded them to be witnesses of his dispensation in Jerusalem, throughout all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.

And appropriately, when the moon increases before our eyes, it gradually moves away from the sun; but when it returns toward the heavens, it comes back to it at equal intervals. For this is what he himself said: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father.” And the Psalm says of him: “His going forth is from the summit of heaven, and his course reaches to its summit.”

Therefore, since the moon’s increase of light, as it comes forth from the sun and turns toward our gaze, signifies the teaching and virtues of the Lord our Savior in the flesh up to the time of his Passion, while its return to the sun, as it gradually gathers itself toward the heavenly face invisible to us, displays the miracles of his resurrection and subsequent glory, it is rightly declared that from the fifteenth day onward it is suited to the joys of the paschal vow.

Having taken these indications of paschal time from the observance of the Law, we heirs of the New Testament also add the Lord’s Day, which Scripture calls “one” or “the first” of the Sabbath. Nor is this without reason: it is eminent by the creation of the primordial light, is distinguished by the triumph of the Lord’s resurrection, and remains ever desirable to us because of our own resurrection.

The seven days of the moon, that is, from the fifteenth through the twenty-first, during which the Lord’s Day likewise proceeds according to the natural order, plainly signify the universality of the Church, which throughout the whole world has been redeemed by the paschal mysteries. Scripture, too, is accustomed very often to signify universality by the number seven. Thus, when the Prophet says, “Seven times a day I have praised you,” nothing better is understood than what he says elsewhere: “His praise shall always be in my mouth.”

John also testifies that the perfection of the whole Catholic Church is represented in particular by this number. Writing to the seven churches of Asia, he disclosed the mysteries of the universal Church throughout the world. Therefore, in all the exhortations he writes to the individual seven churches, he took care to weave in this verse: “Whoever has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches”—plainly showing that what he had said to each one he had said to all the churches.

The paschal seasons also commend to us no less a moral meaning. In the name of Pasch, they teach us to make a spiritual passage daily from vices to virtues. In the Month of New Things, in which the arrival of mature fruits announces by its coming the cessation of old things, they teach us to put off the old person with his deeds, to be renewed in the spirit of our mind, and to put on the new person, and so forth.

They teach us also that, invigorated by the variety of different virtues and shaded, as it were, by their leaves like a pleasant tree, we should sprout like joyful and fruitful crops at the full moon, bearing the perfect brightness of faith and understanding and being separated from the darkness of sin.

In the same lunar light returning toward the heavens, which begins from the fifteenth moon onward, we are taught that the greater we become, the more we should humble ourselves in all things, each of us saying with the Apostle: “By the grace of God I am what I am.”

Since this grace, the gift from above, was poured out more manifestly in the third age of the world, by a most beautiful correspondence of figures we are commanded to observe the third week of the moon at Pasch: its light, which until then had increased toward the earth, now begins to increase toward heavenly things. Thus we are beautifully instructed never to forget the grace we receive, but to remember, at every step of our spiritual passage, to repay its giver by obeying him.

Or certainly, as the moon increases toward human beings, a type of the active life is shown to us; as it returns toward the heavens, a type of the contemplative life. In this direction our love of neighbor is signified; in that direction, our love of the Creator. Here, the progress of its light admonishes us to perform good works outwardly; there, to perform those same good works with regard solely to the heavenly reward. Here: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works”; there: “so that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

On the One of the Sabbath, which is the proper solemnity of the New Testament, we are instructed that, in hope of our future resurrection in Christ, we should patiently endure in the present every adversity for Christ’s sake, even the injury of death, hearing the Apostle say: “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in us, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will give life also to our mortal bodies, through his Spirit dwelling in us.”

Since this Spirit has a sevenfold grace, it may appropriately be understood through the number of the seven lunar days by which the aforementioned One of the Sabbath—that is, the Lord’s Day—is carried around and signified.

But if anyone wishes to know more fully about the mystery of the time of Pasch, let him read the letter of the blessed Aurelius Augustine to Januarius concerning the reckoning of Pasch.

## CHAPTER 65. On the Great Paschal Cycle

[Note: [Col. 0519D] JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—“It seemed good.” We have appended to this book, at the end, all the cycles remaining from Bede and Dionysius that we have found. We have arranged them so that they extend from the beginning of the Lord’s Incarnation up to the year 600; after that year has passed, other diligent scholars will not be lacking who will extend the same cycle to their own age and further.][Col. 0519D]

The great paschal cycle is formed by multiplying the solar and lunar cycles together, and is completed in 532 years. For whether nineteen is multiplied by twenty-eight, or twenty-eight by nineteen, they produce the number 532.

Thus the same great nineteen-year cycle has twenty-eight lunar cycles and nineteen solar cycles, the latter ordinarily being completed in twenty-eight years; nineteen sets of seven leap days, that is, 133; 195 intercalary months; 228 solar months for each of the twenty-eight cycles, that is, 6,384; and 235 lunar months for each of the twenty-eight cycles, that is, 6,580 days, excluding leap days. Twenty-eight times 6,935 gives 194,180; with the leap days added, 194,313.

When it has completed the aforesaid total of months and days in order, it immediately turns back upon itself and always restores everything pertaining to the course of the sun or moon in the same sequence in which it had passed. Only the years of the Lord’s Incarnation advance by their fixed course into a greater number; and the indictions, however they proceed in their order, alter nothing in the course of the stars and therefore nothing in the order of the paschal calculation.

To make this clearer, it seemed good to place the same cycle in its complete order before the present work, beginning with the 532nd year of the Lord’s Incarnation, where Dionysius first began the cycle, and carrying the work through to the 1,063rd year of that same most holy Incarnation [Note: [Col. 0519] C: “the fourth.”], so that readers might be able not only to look ahead to the present and the future, but also to look back with incomparable insight upon the entire past state of paschal time; and so that, for clarification of ancient reading, all the years that had at some time come into question, when they existed and what kind they were, might be recognized more clearly [Note: [Col. 0519] B, C: “recognize.”]:

## CHAPTER 66. Chronicle, or On the Six Ages of This World

[Note: [Col. 0519] As stated above in the prefatory notice, we have taken the chronicle text, variant readings, and notes from Smith’s edition. EDIT.][Col. 0519]

[Note: [Col. 0520D]

JOAN. NOV. SCHOLIA.—“Above”: that is, chapter 10 of the larger book On the Reckoning of Time. This treatise is chapter 66 of that most excellent work, containing the part that alone belongs to our purpose, namely, the historical part; and because of both its size and its subject matter, it was formerly considered by the editors of Bede’s works worthy of being printed separately.]

We have already touched briefly above on the six ages of this world and on the seventh or eighth age of rest and heavenly life, in comparison with the first week in which the world was adorned. Now we shall explain the same matters somewhat more fully in comparison with the lifespan of a single human being, who is customarily called by philosophers in Greek μικρόκοσμος (mikrókosmos), that is, “a smaller world.”

The first age of this world, therefore, is from Adam to Noah. According to the Hebrew truth, it contains 1,656 years; according to the interpreters of the Seventy, 2,242 years [Note: [Col. 0521D] On the number of years in the first age according to the Greek interpreters, see the note below at their year 1,454, concerning Methuselah.]. In both editions it contains ten generations. This age was wiped out by the universal Flood, just as forgetfulness commonly submerges the first age of every human being; for who is there who remembers his infancy?

The second age extends from Noah to Abraham. According to the Hebrew authority, it comprises ten generations and 292 years; according to the interpreters of the Seventy, 1,072 years and eleven generations. This was, as it were, the childhood of the people of God, and therefore the Hebrew language was discovered in it. For after infancy—which is so called because it cannot speak—human beings begin in childhood to learn to speak.

The third age extends from Abraham to David. According to both authorities, it comprises fourteen generations and 942 years [Note: [Col. 0521D] On the number of years in the third age, see the note below at year 2,790, concerning Ajalon, and at year 4,194 according to the Seventy, concerning Eli, where, according to Bede, thirty years are lacking from the calculation of the interpreters of the Seventy for the completion of this number.]. This was, as it were, the adolescence of the people of God. Since human beings begin at that age to be capable of begetting, the evangelist Matthew accordingly took the beginning of his genealogies from Abraham, who was also appointed father of the nations when he received a changed name.

The fourth age extends from David to the Babylonian captivity. According to the Hebrew truth, it contains 473 years; according to the translation of the Seventy, twelve more; and according to both books, seventeen generations. Yet the evangelist Matthew, for the sake of a certain mystery [Note: [Col. 0522D] “Mystery”: namely, Azariah, Joash, and Amaziah were excluded from the genealogy of the Savior because of the enormity of their crimes. See below, at year 3,065.], gives fourteen.

From this age, as from the youthful age, the period of kings began among the people of God; for this is ordinarily the age among human beings suited to governing a kingdom.

The fifth age, as it were the senile age, extends from the Babylonian captivity to the coming of the Lord and Savior in the flesh. It too comprises fourteen generations and extends over 589 years. In it, as though exhausted by oppressive old age, the Hebrew people are shaken by increasingly frequent evils.

The sixth age, which is now taking place, has no fixed series of generations or times, but, like an age of decrepitude, will be completed by the death of the entire world. Those who have overcome these sorrowful and labor-filled ages of the world through a blessed death, having already been received into the seventh age of perpetual Sabbath, await the eighth age of blessed resurrection, in which they will reign forever with the Lord.

## THE FIRST AGE

In the first age of the world’s beginning, on its first day, God made the light, which he called day. On the second day he suspended the firmament of heaven in the midst of the waters; the waters themselves and the earth, together with the higher heaven and the powers created within it to praise the Creator, had been created before the beginning of these six days.

On the third day, having gathered into their proper place the waters that had covered everything, he commanded the dry land to appear. On the fourth day he placed the stars in the firmament of heaven; this day is now called, according to what we infer from the calculation of the equinox, the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.

On the fifth day he created aquatic and flying animals. On the sixth day he formed the terrestrial animals and the human being himself, Adam. From Adam’s side, while he slept, he brought forth Eve, the mother of all living beings. This day, as far as I consider credible, is now called the tenth day before the Kalends of April.

Accordingly, it is rightly believed—if the more truthful opinion does not prevail—that the blessed Theophilus [Note: [Col. 0522D] Theophilus of Caesarea, concerning whose opinion see Bede above, chapter 47, and Baluzius, in the Council of Caesarea.], disputing about Pasch with the other bishops not only of Palestine but also of very many other regions, wrote that the Lord was crucified on that same tenth day before the Kalends of April [Col. 0522B].

For it was fitting that he, put to sleep in a life-giving death for the salvation of the human race in accordance with Adam, should on one and the same day not only of the week but also of the month sanctify the Church as his bride through the heavenly sacraments brought forth from his side—the day on which he himself had first created Adam, the father, that is, of the human race, and, taking a rib from his side, built the woman, by whose help the human race would be propagated.

**[A. M. Hebr. 130. Sept. 230.]** Adam, at the age of 130, begot Seth; he lived 800 years after Seth’s birth. The interpreters of the Seventy, however, place 230 years before the birth of Seth and 700 afterward. Seth is interpreted as “resurrection,” signifying the resurrection of Christ from the dead; Abel, whose name is said to mean “mourning,” signifies his death inflicted by the Jews when he was killed by his brother Cain.

**[A. M. Hebr. 235. Sept. 435.]** Seth, at the age of 105, begot Enosh; he lived 807 years after him. The Seventy, however, place 205 years before the birth of Enosh and 707 afterward. Enosh is interpreted as “human being,” concerning whom it is rightly said: “This one began to call upon the name of the Lord,” because it is characteristic of human beings to remember their frailty and invoke the help of the Creator—at least of those who, living in the faith of Christ, rejoice to be sons of the resurrection.

**[A. M. Hebr. 325. Sept. 625.]** Enosh, at the age of 90, begot Cainan; he lived 815 years after him. The Seventy, however, place 190 years before Cainan’s birth and 715 afterward.

**[A. M. Hebr. 395. Sept. 795.]** Cainan, at the age of 70, begot Mahalalel; after his birth he lived 840 years [Col. 0523A]. The Seventy say 170 years before Mahalalel’s birth and 740 afterward.

**[A. M. Hebr. 460. Sept. 960.]** Mahalalel, at the age of 65, begot Jared; he lived 830 years after him. The Seventy place 165 years before Jared’s birth and 730 afterward.

**[A. M. Hebr. 622. Sept. 1122.]** Jared, at the age of 162, begot Enoch; he lived 800 years after him. In this generation the two books nowhere disagree.

We learn, on the testimony of the apostle Jude, that this Enoch wrote some things divinely [Note: [Col. 0523C] Manuscript Bold: “divine”; manuscript Magd.: “divine pages.”]. But, as the blessed Augustine says: “[Note: [Col. 0523C] ‘Not without reason.’ Augustine, City of God XV.23.] ‘It is not without reason that they are not in the canon of the Scriptures that was preserved in the temple through the careful succession of the priests of the Hebrew people, except because, on account of their antiquity, they were judged to be of doubtful reliability, and it could not be discovered whether these were the writings that he had written.’”

Therefore, the works circulated under his name, which contain those fables about giants—that they did not have human fathers—are rightly judged by prudent people not to be believed as his.

**[A. M. Hebr. 687. Sept. 1287.]** Enoch, at the age of 65, begot Methuselah; after his birth he lived 300 years, and walked with God. The Seventy place 165 years before Methuselah’s birth and 200 afterward.

And appropriately, in the seventh generation, God took from mortals Enoch, whose name is interpreted as “dedication,” because the city of the elect, laboring for God throughout the six ages of this world, awaits the glory of dedication in the seventh, future Sabbath. But because the reprobate are content with present happiness alone, Cain consecrates the city he founded not in the seventh generation but in his firstborn son, Enoch.

**[A. M. Hebr. 874. Sept. 1454.]** Methuselah, at the age of 187, begot Lamech; he lived 782 years after him, that is, until the Flood. The Seventy place 167 years before Lamech’s birth and 802 afterward.

As the reader will easily see, according to the Hebrew truth this number extends 20 years beyond the time of the Flood, but according to their authority it extends 14 years beyond it [Note: [Col. 0523C] “This number”: Scaliger unjustly accuses Bede here of error, Notes on the Greek Eusebius, p. 403. Nothing is clearer than what Bede says here: the number 802 carries the time of the Flood beyond it by twenty years.].

Concerning this most famous question [Note: [Col. 0523D] “Question”: The variation of readings in the editions of the Seventy has produced a variation in the number of years of this first age. The reading that Eusebius, Jerome, and Augustine say was found in nearly all the Greek books of their time assigns Methuselah only 167 years before Lamech’s birth and 802 afterward. But the reading followed by Africanus, found in the copies remembered by Augustine, Eusebius, and Syncellus, and confirmed by some modern editions of the Seventy, one of them Alexandrian, assigns Methuselah 187 years before Lamech’s birth and 782 afterward. If this is genuine, there is no room for doubt that, according to the Seventy, Methuselah died six years before the Flood; and thus the years of this age would be not 2,242 but 2,262, which is the total given by Epiphanius, the Alexandrian Chronicle, and others. But since, according to the Hebrews, Methuselah died in the very year of the Flood, a difference of six years remains between them and the Seventy, which can easily be reconciled as follows. The editions of the Seventy give Lamech 188 years before Noah’s birth; subtract six years and the result is 182, as in the Hebrew. Then the year of the Flood will not fall in year 2,262 but in year 2,256, which is the very year of Methuselah’s death. In this way Methuselah would have died in the same year—that is, in the actual year—of the Flood, both among the Hebrews and according to the Seventy.], the most learned Fathers—Jerome in the Book of Hebrew Questions and Augustine in the fifteenth book of The City of God—argue at greatest length.

**[A. M. Hebr. 1056. Sept. 1642.]** Lamech, at the age of 182, begot Noah; he lived 595 years after him. The Seventy place 188 years before Noah’s birth and 565 afterward. In this one generation the total differs throughout, because Lamech is found to have lived 24 years longer in the Hebrew books than in the books of the translators of the Seventy.

**[A. M. Hebr. 1656. Sept. 2242.]** In Noah’s six-hundredth year the Flood came, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month.

To be sure, concerning the difference in years between the Hebrew authority and that of the interpreters of the Seventy, lest anyone accuse us of raising new questions, let him read the aforementioned works of the Fathers and understand that this discrepancy was already well known in ancient times. When the blessed Augustine had most carefully investigated the origin of the discrepancy, he said in the book mentioned above, chapter 13, among other things:

“More credibly, therefore, someone might say that, when these things first began to be copied from the library of Ptolemy, something of this sort could have happened in one book, the first copied from that source, and from there could have spread more widely, where indeed a copyist’s error could also have occurred. And in that question concerning the life of Methuselah, it is not absurd to suspect this.”

And a little later:

“I would have no hesitation in saying that it is rightly done that, when something different is found in the two books—for both cannot be true with respect to the reliability of the events narrated—the language from which the translation into the other language was made through interpreters should rather be believed.”

## THE SECOND AGE

In the second age of the world, on its first day, which is the twenty-seventh day of the second month, Noah came out of the ark. In it, a few persons—that is, eight souls—were saved through water.

In recalling this, the blessed apostle Peter (1 Peter 3:21) immediately took care to explain it wonderfully when he added that “baptism, in a corresponding form, now saves us also—not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience toward God, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who is at the right hand of God.”

He teaches that the baptism was prefigured in the water of the Flood, the Church and its faithful in the ark and in the things it contained, and the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection—in whose faith we are baptized—in the number eight of the souls.

**[A. M. Hebr. 1658. Sept. 2244.]** Shem, at the age of 100, begot Arphaxad, two years after the Flood. Jerome writes that the Chaldeans originated from Arphaxad. After Arphaxad’s birth, Shem lived 500 years, that is, until the fiftieth year of Jacob’s birth.

**[A. M. Hebr. 1693. Sept. 2379.]** Arphaxad, at the age of 35, begot Shelah. Here the interpreters of the Seventy inserted one generation more than the Hebrew truth, saying that Arphaxad, when he was 135 years old, begot Cainan; and that Cainan, when he was 130, begot Shelah. The evangelist Luke appears to have followed their translation at this point.

But when the Greek chronographers [Note: [Col. 0525D] “Of the Greeks”: Bede rightly refers here both to Africanus and Eusebius, as well as to the other chronographers. This passage of Bede was therefore highly necessary, and we leave it for scholars to observe. (Scaliger, at the place cited above, p. 10.)] had corrected the sequence of generations according to the Hebrew authority, they removed Cainan, one generation, but did not correct the number of years in the generations that they held in common with them according to that authority. Following their own authority, they assigned this age a total of 942 years—130 fewer than the edition of the translators of the Seventy, but 650 more than the Hebrew truth.

After Shelah’s birth Arphaxad lived 303 years; yet the Seventy write that after Cainan’s birth he lived 430 years [Note: [Col. 0525D] The Basel and Cologne editions have 330, but incorrectly; hence the number is corrected in their margins.], while Cainan, after Shelah’s birth, lived 338 years [Note: [Col. 0525D] The same editions have 438; the Septuagint has 330. [Col. 0526D] The Westminst. and Vilk. manuscripts have 338, correctly.].

**[A. M. Hebr. 1723. Sept. 2639.]** Shelah, at the age of 30, begot Eber; he lived 403 years after him. The Seventy place 130 years before Eber’s birth and 330 afterward. From this Eber the name and people of the Hebrews arose.

**[A. M. Hebr. 1757. Sept. 2773.]** Eber, at the age of 34, begot Peleg; he lived 430 years after him. The Seventy place 134 years before Peleg’s birth and 270 afterward [Note: [Col. 0526D] The same editions have 260, incorrectly.].

Peleg is interpreted as “division.” His parents therefore gave him this name because at the time of his birth the earth was divided through the confusion of languages.

The rhetorician Arnobius recalls this division in his exposition of Psalm 104:

“To Shem, Noah’s firstborn, a portion was made from Persia and Bactria as far as India, and as far as Rhinocoruras [Note: [Col. 0525D] “Rhinocoruras”: a city of Egypt, so called because people who had once been sent there as colonists had mutilated noses, as Stephen of Byzantium says, On Cities.]. These stretches of land have twenty-seven languages in a barbarian speech. Within them are 406 peoples of distinct homelands—not of different languages, but, as I have said, of different homelands. For example, although there is one Latin language, under that one language there are different homelands: those of the Bruttians, Lucanians, Apulians, Calabrians, Picentines, Tuscans, and others of this kind, if we may speak in such terms.

“But Ham, Noah’s second son, possessed the territory from Rhinocoruras to Gadeira. He had languages in Punic speech on the side of the Garamantes, in Latin speech toward the north, in barbarian speech toward the south among the Ethiopians and Egyptians, and among the more remote barbarians twenty-two languages in varied speech, in 394 homelands.

“Japheth, the third son, possessed the territory from Media to Gadeira toward the north. Japheth has the river Tigris, which divides Media and Babylonia, in 200 homelands, with varied speech, in twenty-three languages.

“Thus altogether there are seventy-two languages. There are 500 homelands of peoples, situated in this order in the tripartite world. As we have said, Japheth has the river Tigris, which divides Media and Babylonia; Shem has the Euphrates; and Ham has the Gihon, which is called the Nile.”

**[A. M. Hebr. 1787. Sept. 2903.]** Peleg, at the age of 30, begot Reu; he lived 209 years after him. The Seventy place 130 years before Reu’s birth and 209 afterward.

In these times temples were first constructed, and certain leaders of the nations were worshiped as gods.

**[A. M. Hebr. 1819. Sept. 3035.]** Reu, at the age of 32, begot Serug; he lived 207 years after him. The Seventy place 132 years before Serug’s birth and 207 afterward.

The kingdom of the Scythians is said to have arisen; its first king was Tanaus.

**[A. M. Hebr. 1849. Sept. 3165.]** Serug, at the age of 30, begot Nahor; he lived 200 years after him. The Seventy place 130 years before Nahor’s birth and 200 afterward.

The empire of the Egyptians is said to have begun, with Zoves as their first king [Note: [Col. 0525D] “Zoves”: called Men by Herodotus, book II; Manes by Josephus (Antiquities VIII.2 §6). The name Zoves was assigned to him, and in the margin Vizoves, since he was counted among the gods, as it was customary for nations to honor their kings both with the title and the name of Jupiter. Thus Eratosthenes (in the Greek Eusebius, p. 18), interpreting the names of the Egyptian kings, calls Menes Dionysus, that is, “Jovian” or “Jove.” The same name is also found among Menes’ successors. Thus, in the third Memphite dynasty, the fifth king is called Zoyphis; in the fourth dynasty, the third king is Suphes, according to Manetho.].

**[A. M. Hebr. 1878. Sept. 3244.]** Nahor, at the age of 29, begot Terah; he lived 119 years after him. The Seventy place 79 years before Terah’s birth and 129 afterward.

The kingdoms of the Assyrians and Sicyonians arose: among the former Belus ruled first, and among the latter Aegialeus.

**[A. M. Hebr. 1948. Sept. 3314.]** Terah, at the age of 70 [Note: [Col. 0526D] So explicitly in Genesis 11:26, and the ancient interpreters unanimously agree on this. What recent writers object from Genesis 12:4 and Acts 7:4, on the basis of which they place Abraham’s birth in Terah’s 130th year, is not sufficiently difficult to undermine so clear an assertion historically handed down by Moses himself.], begot Abraham; he lived 135 years after him.

Here the second age of the world comes to an end. After reviewing its entire sequence, the blessed Augustine concluded in this way in The City of God XVI.10:

“Thus, according to the common edition—that is, that of the interpreters of the Seventy—the years from the Flood to Abraham amount to 1,072. But in the Hebrew books far fewer years are reported to be found, concerning which they give either no explanation or one of the greatest difficulty.”

## THE THIRD AGE

**[A. M. Hebr. 2023. Sept. 3389.]** The third age of the world began with the birth of the patriarch Abraham. When he was 75 years old, he left his native people and, in obedience to God’s command, came into the land of Canaan. There he received the promise of the Savior who was to be born from his seed, in whom all nations would be blessed, together with the promise that he himself would become a great nation. One of these promises is spiritual, the other carnal.

In these times Ninus and Semiramis ruled the Assyrians.

**[A. M. Hebr. 2034. Sept. 3400.]** Abraham, at the age of 86, begot Ishmael, from whom came the Ishmaelites. Ishmael begot twelve chieftains and lived 137 years.

**[A. M. Hebr. 2048. Sept. 3414.]** The same Abraham, at the age of 100, begot Isaac. He is recorded as the first and only person in the entire sequence of the Old Testament to have been circumcised on the eighth day; this privilege was granted to the son of promise not without great mystery.

**[A. M. Hebr. 2108. Sept. 3474.]** Isaac, at the age of 60, begot Esau and Jacob, the patriarchs of the Idumean and Israelite peoples. After their birth he lived 120 years.

In these times Inachus first ruled at Argos for 50 years. His daughter Io, whom the Egyptians worship under a changed name as Isis, was his daughter.

**[A. M. Hebr. 2238. Sept. 3604.]** Jacob, at the age of 130, went down into Egypt with 70 persons.

In his time Memphis in Egypt was founded by Apis, king of the Argives. Sparta too was founded by Spartan, son of the Argive king Phoroneus.

**[A. M. Hebr. 2453. Sept. 3819.]** The dwelling of the children of Israel, during which they remained in Egypt, lasted 430 years. When these had been completed, the entire army of the Lord went out from the land of Egypt on that same day, as Scripture testifies in Exodus.

Nevertheless, chronographers calculate the total of these years from Abraham’s seventy-fifth year, when he entered the promised land, following the edition of the interpreters of the Seventy, which says: “The dwelling of the children of Israel, which they dwelt in Egypt and in the land of Canaan, they and their fathers, was 430 years” [Note: [Col. 0527D] “Which”: so the manuscripts, following the Latin Vulgate; only Wilk. has “that,” following the Seventy, among whom one reads, ἣν κατῴκησαν (“which they inhabited”) (Exodus 12:40).].

The Hebrew truth itself necessarily shows that this reading must be followed. It relates that Kohath, the son of Levi, who is known to have been born in the land of Canaan, lived 133 years; that his son Amram, the father of Moses, lived 137 years; and that Moses himself was 80 years old at the time of the departure from Egypt. For it is clear that the total of these years cannot amount to 430.

The Apostle also confirms their translation when he says: “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed; he does not say, ‘And to seeds,’ as of many, but as of one, ‘And to your seed,’ who is Christ. Now this I say: the law, which was made 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously confirmed by God, so as to abolish the promises made to the fathers” [Note: [Col. 0527D] “To Abraham”: Galatians 3:16–17.].

[A. M. Hebr. 2493. Sept. 3859.] Moses governs the people of Israel in the wilderness for forty years after their departure from Egypt. In their first year he constructs the tabernacle for the Lord; completing the work in seven months, he erects it on the first day of the first month of the second year. Up to this point, as Eusebius records, the five books of Moses contain an account of 3,730 years, according to the translation of the Seventy Elders. But how many years this period contains according to the Hebrew truth, Josephus states as follows in the first book of his *Against Apion the Grammarian*:

> “Accordingly, we do not possess innumerable books that disagree with one another, but only twenty-two books, which contain the record of all time and are rightly believed to be divinely inspired. Of these, five belong to Moses, containing the laws of life and the genealogy of human succession, extending down to the end of Moses himself. They comprise a period of nearly three thousand years.”

[A. M. Hebr. 2519. Sept. 3885.] Joshua governs the people of Israel for twenty-six years, as Josephus teaches; for Holy Scripture does not state how many years his leadership lasted.

[Note: XXVI. Josephus attributes only twenty-five years to Joshua the leader (*Antiquities* V, 1, near the end).]

Why, then, Eusebius placed twenty-seven years in his *Chronicles*, we shall explain below. In the first year of his leadership, Joshua, in the first month, on the tenth day of the month, led the people into the promised land after the bed of the Jordan had been laid bare. In that year, as we find in the *Chronicles* of the aforementioned Eusebius, began the fifty-first jubilee according to the Hebrews: that is, 2,500 years had been completed from the beginning of the world, with each jubilee period reckoned as fifty years.

But our investigation has in no way been able to establish that this is the total for this period. For it is established that there were 1,656 years up to the Flood; from then to Abraham, 292 years, and he was seventy-five years old when he received God’s promise; the years of the promise were 430, and Moses’ leadership lasted forty years. This total certainly completes not 2,500 years but seven fewer—namely, 2,493 years—as we noted above.

[Col. 0528D] [A. M. Hebr. 2559. Sept. 3925.] Othniel, of the tribe of Judah, is appointed the first judge of Israel by the Lord’s command and serves for forty years. At the beginning of his time, the Israelites served Chushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, for eight years.

[A. M. Hebr. 2639. Sept. 4005.] Ehud, son of Gera, son of Benjamin, serves for eighty years. He used both hands as though they were his right hand. At the beginning of his leadership Israel served Eglon, king of Moab, for eighteen years, until Ehud himself struck down Eglon and liberated Israel. At this time the city of Cyrene was founded in Libya.

[A. M. Hebr. 2679. Sept. 4045.] Deborah, a prophetess from the tribe of Ephraim, serves for forty years together with Barak from the tribe of Naphtali. At the beginning of her leadership, Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned at Hazor, oppressed the Israelites for twenty years. But after Sisera, his commander, was killed by the Israelites, he was finally humbled and destroyed. At this time Miletus was founded.

[A. M. Hebr. 2719. Sept. 4085.] Gideon, of the tribe of Manasseh, serves for forty years. Under him Israel served the Midianites and Amalekites for seven years, but was liberated when Gideon fought. Tyre was founded 240 years before the Temple of Jerusalem, as Josephus writes.

[Note: Josephus, *Antiquities* VIII, 2, § 3.]

[A. M. Hebr. 2722. Sept. 4088.] Abimelech, son of Gideon, who ruled at Shechem, serves for three years. Hercules destroys Ilium.
