[A. M. Hebr. 2745. Sept. 4111.] Tola, son of Puah, the uncle of Abimelech, a man of Issachar, who lived at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim, serves for twenty-three years. The war of the Lapiths and Centaurs took place; Palaephatus writes in the first book of his *On Incredible Things* that they were famous horsemen of the Thessalians. In Troy, Priam reigned after Laomedon.

[A. M. Hebr. 2767. Sept. 4133.] Jair, of the tribe of Manasseh, serves for twenty-two years. Hercules established the Olympic contest; from that event until the first Olympiad 430 years are reckoned.

[Note: Olympiad. Two eras are transmitted for determining the first Olympiad. One is the contest of Hercules, which is placed here in Jair’s time, specifically in his fourteenth year; from that point 430 years are reckoned. The other is the capture of Troy, discussed below under the year 2798, where it is placed in Labdon’s time, in his third year; from that point, according to Eusebius, 406 years are reckoned. Eusebius places the beginning of the first Olympiad, according to both eras, in the fiftieth year of Azariah. Nevertheless, Bede places the beginning of the first Olympiad in the sixth year of Jotham, which is, from the contest of Hercules, according to Eusebius, 438 years, and according to Bede, 439; from the capture of Troy, according to Eusebius, 414 years, and according to Bede, 405. For the reason for the difference, see below under the year 3,208.]

[A. M. Hebr. 2773. Sept. 4139.] Jephthah the Gileadite serves for six years. The Philistines and Ammonites oppress Israel; the Ammonites are defeated by Jephthah, who says in the Book of Judges that from the time of Moses until his own time 300 years are to be reckoned.

[A. M. Hebr. 2780. Sept. 4146.] Ibzan of Bethlehem serves for seven years. Agamemnon rules at Mycenae for thirty-five years, and in his fifteenth year Troy is captured.

[Note: XXXV. Eusebius gives fifteen years; others, sixteen or seventeen. This appears to be an error in Bede’s manuscripts, although all the manuscripts agree on it; therefore I do not alter it.]

[A. M. Hebr. 2790.] Elon the Zebulunite serves for ten years. He is not found in the Septuagint interpreters with his ten years; to compensate for this loss, Eusebius assigned additional years to Joshua son of Nun, Samuel, and Saul, whose years Scripture does not state, adding more years than he read in Josephus, so that he might arrive at the total of 480 years from Israel’s departure from Egypt to the building of the Temple, a total proclaimed by Scripture.

[Note: He is not found. Thus Eusebius, and Bede after him, but contrary to the testimony of all the Septuagint copies. In them Elon is expressly found with his ten years (Judges 12:11). Since, however, this is Bede’s *Chronicle*, I present his calculations, omitting Elon’s years from the Septuagint computation in the margin.]

[Note: More. Eusebius is unjustly blamed for this concerning Samuel and Saul. He was so far from adding more years to Samuel and Saul than he read in Josephus that he actually assigned twelve years fewer. Eusebius, not arbitrarily but in agreement with Holy Scripture (Acts 13:20), assigns only thirty-two years to Samuel and Saul, whereas Josephus assigns fifty-two, as is clear to anyone comparing Josephus (*Antiquities* VI, 14–15). Bede therefore misunderstood Josephus, reckoning only thirty-two years instead of fifty-two: twelve years for Samuel instead of thirty, and twenty for Saul instead of twenty-two, as is evident below under Samuel and Saul.]

[A. M. Hebr. 2798. Sept. 4154.] Labdon, of the tribe of Ephraim, serves for eight years. In his third year Troy was captured, 375 years having elapsed from the first year of Cecrops, who was the first king of Attica, and 835 years from the forty-third year of the reign of Ninus, king of the Assyrians. After Labdon’s death Israel served the Philistines for forty years.

[A. M. Hebr. 2818. Sept. 4174.] Samson, of the tribe of Dan, serves for twenty years. Thus far the Book of Judges marks the period, comprising 299 years and twelve judges.

After the third year of the capture of Troy—or, as some wish, after the eighth—Aeneas reigned for three years among the Latins, who were later called Romans. After him Ascanius reigned for thirty-eight years. Before Aeneas, Janus, Saturn, Picus, Faunus, and Latinus ruled in Italy for approximately 150 years. Ascanius, son of Aeneas, founded the city of Alba.

[Note: Some. Among them Virgil:

> “[lacuna] For now the seventh carries you …”]

[A. M. Hebr. 2858. Sept. 4194.] Eli the priest serves for forty years. In the Hebrew book forty years are found, but in the Septuagint translation twenty.

[Note: XX. In the Septuagint calculation twenty years are in fact cut away here, and are nowhere restored to this period. Hence in the total of the years of this period there are not 942 years, as was noted at the beginning of this *Chronicle*, but thirty fewer: ten in Elon and twenty in Eli.]

The sons of Hector recovered Ilium after expelling the descendants of Antenor, with Helenus providing them assistance. The third of the Latins, Silvius, son of Aeneas, reigned for twenty-nine years. Because he was born after his father’s death and raised in the countryside, he received the names both Silvius and Posthumus; from him all the Alban kings were called Silvii. The kings of the Sicyonians, who had reigned from Aegialeus to Zeuxippus, came to an end after 962 years. After them priests of Carneus were appointed.

[Note: Of the Sicyonians. The kings of the Sicyonians are said to have lasted from the year 1,874 to the year 2,836—that is, from Aegialeus to Zeuxippus. But concerning this kingdom see Pausanias, in the *Corinthiaca*, who after Zeuxippus counts Hippolytus, during whose reign Agamemnon invaded the Sicyonians. He also adds Lacestades, under whom the Sicyonians were subjugated by the Dorians.]

[Note: Of Carneus. Eusebius has *of Carnean Apollo*, whose priests are said to have presided over the Sicyonians for thirty-three years (see Castor in Eusebius, p. 96).]

[A. M. Hebr. 2870. Sept. 4206.] Samuel serves for twelve years, as Josephus teaches. For in Holy Scripture it is by no means clear how long he presided. From this point the period of the prophets begins. The fourth of the Latins, Aeneas Silvius, reigned for thirty-one years.

[A. M. Hebr. 2890. Sept. 4226.] Saul, the first king of the Hebrews, serves for twenty years. Since his period is not given in canonical Scripture, we have recorded the length of his reign from Josephus’ Book of Antiquities. In Lacedaemon, Eurystheus, the first king, reigned for forty-two years; at Corinth, Alethes, the first king, reigned for thirty-five years.

## THE FOURTH AGE

The fourth age of the world begins not only with the establishment of the rule of the Jewish people, but also with the renewal of the promise once given to the fathers, and thus with the beginning of the Christian dominion, since the Lord swore in truth to David that one from the fruit of his womb would sit upon his throne.

[Col. 0531B] [A. M. Hebr. 2930. Sept. 4266.] David, the first king from the tribe of Judah, reigns for forty years. The fifth of the Latins, Latinus Silvius, reigns for fifty years. Ephesus was founded by Andronicus. Carthage was founded, according to some, by Charcedon the Tyrian; according to others, by his daughter Dido, 143 years after the destruction of Troy.

[A. M. Hebr. 2970. Sept. 4306.] Solomon, son of David, reigns for forty years. In the fourth year of his reign, in the second month, he began to build the Temple for the Lord in Jerusalem, 480 years after Israel’s departure from Egypt, as the Book of Kings also testifies. As a figure of the whole period during which Christ’s Church is built in this world and perfected in the future, he completed it in seven years and dedicated it in the seventh month of the eighth year. The sixth of the Latins, Alba Silvius, son of Silvius Aeneas, reigned for thirty-nine years. The queen of Sheba came to hear Solomon’s wisdom.

[A. M. Hebr. 2987. Sept. 4323.] Rehoboam, son of Solomon, reigns for seventeen years. Jeroboam, of the tribe of Ephraim, separated ten tribes from the house of David and from the Lord, as a figure of heretics who separate their followers from Christ and the Church. In his fifth year Shishak, king of Egypt, came to Jerusalem and plundered the Temple. The seventh of the Latins, Aegyptus Silvius, son of the preceding king of Alba, reigned for twenty-four years. Samos was founded, and Smyrna was enlarged to the status of a city.

[Note: Egypt. Eusebius has *Aegytus*; Livy has *Capetus*.]

[A. M. Hebr. 2990. Sept. 4326.] Abijah, son of Rehoboam, reigns for three years. He defeated Jeroboam when Jeroboam fought against him, killing 1,500 of his army because he had trusted in the Lord.

[Col. 0531D] [A. M. Hebr. 3031. Sept. 4367.] Asa, son of Abijah, reigns for forty-one years. Ben-hadad, king of Syria at Damascus, was hired by Asa against Israel and struck the whole land of Naphtali. The eighth of the Latins, Capys Silvius, son of the preceding king of Alba, reigns for twenty-eight years. Asa destroys the idols, cleanses the Temple, and with his army defeats Zerah the Ethiopian when he advances against him. Omri, king of Israel, bought the hills of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver and built the city. Hiel of Bethel restored Jericho.

[A. M. Hebr. 3056. Sept. 4392.] Jehoshaphat, son of Asa, reigns for twenty-five years. Elijah the Tishbite withheld rain for three and a half years because of the sins of Ahab and the people of Israel; among his other great deeds, he anointed Elisha son of Shaphat, who was from Abel-meholah, as prophet in his place. The ninth of the Latins, Carpentus Silvius, son of Capys, the preceding king, reigned for thirteen years. After him his son Tiberinus Silvius reigned for eight years; from him the river Tiber was named, having previously been called the Albula. After him Agrippa Silvius, his son, reigned for forty years. Jehoshaphat did what was right before the Lord.

[Note: Carpentus. Thus all Bede’s manuscripts and the first part of the Latin Eusebius; elsewhere *Calpetus* and *Carmentus*. Livy and Ovid have *Capetus*.]

[A. M. Hebr. 3064. Sept. 4400.] Jehoram, son of Jehoshaphat, reigns for eight years. Elijah is carried away in a fiery chariot as if into heaven, and Elisha, left as heir to the prophetic office, heals the waters of Jericho in his first miracle. In the days of Jehoram, Edom revolted so as not to remain under Judah and appointed a king for itself. Jehoram walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, for his wife was Ahab’s daughter.

[A. M. Hebr. 3065. Sept. 4401.] Azariah, son of Jehoram, reigns for one year. Jehonadab son of Rechab is renowned. Because of the enormity of their crimes, and because none of them was regarded as good by anyone—not father or son—Matthew the Evangelist excludes Azariah, together with his son Joash and grandson Amaziah, from the genealogy of the Lord and Savior.

[A. M. Hebr. 3071. Sept. 4408.] Athaliah, mother of Azariah, reigns for six years. When she saw that her son Azariah had been killed by Jehu, king of Israel, she killed the entire royal stock of the house of Jehoram, except Joash, son of Azariah. Jehosheba, Azariah’s sister and wife of Jehoiada the high priest, secretly rescued him from among the king’s sons while they were being killed. In the Septuagint interpreters Athaliah is said to have reigned for seven years.

[Note: VII. Thus Eusebius, but contrary to the Septuagint manuscripts, a fact Bede did not notice.]

[A. M. Hebr. 3111. Sept. 4448.] Joash, son of Azariah, reigns for forty years. Though he had a good beginning, he ended most wickedly. At the beginning of his reign he renewed the Temple; near its end, among his other crimes, he ordered Zechariah, son of Jehoiada, his former guardian and the one who had established him as king, to be stoned between the Temple and the altar. On account of his merits, the Lord in the Gospel calls him the son of Barachiah, that is, “blessed of the Lord.”

The twelfth of the Latins, Aremulus Silvius, son of Agrippa, the preceding king, reigned for nineteen years. He established a fortress for the Albans among the hills where Rome now stands. His son was Julius, the great-grandfather of Julius Proculus, who, migrating to Rome with Romulus, founded the Julian clan.

[A. M. Hebr. 3140. Sept. 4477.] Amaziah, son of Joash, reigns for twenty-nine years. The prophet Elisha dies and is buried in Samaria. Hazael, king of Syria, afflicts Israel. The thirteenth of the Latins, Aventinus Silvius, elder son of Aremulus, the preceding king, reigned for thirty-seven years. He died and was buried on the hill that is now part of the city, giving the place its enduring name.

[A. M. Hebr. 3192. Sept. 4529.] Azariah, also called Uzziah, son of Amaziah, reigns for fifty-two years. The thirty-sixth of the Assyrians, Thonos Concoleros, who in Greek is called *Sardanapalus*, founded Tarsus and Anchiale. Defeated in battle by Arbaces the Mede, he burned himself to death. History records that there had been Assyrian kings up to that time, and together their reigns amounted to 1,197 years.

[Note: In Greek. This is said not because the name *Sardanapalus* derives from the Greek language, but because its general usage became established among the Greeks. This is so true that the name *Thonos Concoleros* is scarcely found in ancient authors. It occurs in the *Suda* as Κονοσκοκόλορος.]

All the years of the Assyrians, however, are reckoned from the first year of Ninus: 1,240 years.

[Note: 1,197. That is, from Abraham’s birth, which is Eusebius’ era in the later book of the *Chronicle*.]

[Note: 1,240. That is, from the year of the world 1,905 to the year 3,145.]

The fourteenth of the Latins, Procas Silvius, son of Aventinus, the preceding king, reigned for twenty-three years. After him the fifteenth, Amulius Silvius, reigned for forty-four years. Arbaces the Mede, having destroyed the Assyrian empire, transferred the kingdom to the Medes, where he himself was the first to reign, for twenty-eight years. The Macedonian kingdom began, with Caranus as its first king, reigning for twenty-eight years. The kings of the Lacedaemonians came to an end, and those of the Lydians began.

[Col. 0533B] [A. M. Hebr. 3208. Sept. 4545.] Jotham, son of Uzziah, reigns for sixteen years. The first Olympiad was established by the Eleans 405 years after the capture of Troy.

[Note: Olympiad. It was noted above, under the year 2,767, that at the beginning of the first Olympiad there is a difference of eight years between the numbers of Eusebius and Bede—that is, from the fiftieth year of Azariah to the sixth year of Jotham. The reason is that Eusebius inserts between the capture of Troy and Jotham’s sixth year nine years that Bede omits: eight assigned to Samuel and Saul, and one to Athaliah. Since Eusebius assigns forty years to Samuel and Saul while Bede assigns only thirty-two, and Eusebius assigns seven years to Athaliah while Bede assigns only six, a difference of nine years remains. But because Eusebius further reckons 406 years from the capture of Troy, whereas Bede reckons only 405, one year is withdrawn, leaving only eight.

It should also be observed in passing that the Latin *Chronicle* of Eusebius itself wavers here in establishing the beginning of the first Olympiad, placing it between the second and third year of Aeschylus and between the forty-ninth and fiftieth year of Athaliah. This should be attributed not to Eusebius himself but to Jerome’s translation. For in the Greek text it is plainly placed after the completion of Aeschylus’ second year and during his third, and in Athaliah’s fiftieth year; consequently, the *Chronicle*, both Greek and Latin, begins the Olympiads from that year. Therefore Bede correctly says that it occurred after 405 years—that is, in the 406th year then current. H. Stephanus, in his edition of the Latin *Chronicle* of Eusebius (Paris, 1512), likewise has: “From the capture of Troy to the first Olympiad, 406 years; elsewhere, 405.” I leave to others the disputes in which critics argue at this point for or against Eusebius concerning other matters.]

Remus and Romulus are begotten by Mars and Ilia. Jotham, among his other works of good virtue, built the exceedingly lofty gate of the house of the Lord, which in the Acts of the Apostles is called the Beautiful Gate. All the Temple gates were on the ground except the Beautiful Gate, which was suspended; among the Hebrews it was called Jotham’s Gate.

[A. M. Hebr. 3224. Sept. 4561.] Ahaz, son of Jotham, reigns for sixteen years. During his reign, Tiglath-pileser, king of the Assyrians, hired by him, kills Rezin, king of Syria, and transfers the inhabitants of Damascus to Cyrene. Rome was founded on the Palatine Hill, on 21 April, by the twins Remus and Romulus, sons of Rhea Silvia, who was the daughter of Numitor, brother of King Amulius, a Vestal Virgin who had nevertheless been violated. In the third year from the founding of the city, the Sabine women were carried off during the Consualia games. Remus was killed with a shepherd’s mattock by Fabius, the commander of Romulus.

[A. M. Hebr. 3253. Sept. 4590.] Hezekiah, son of Ahaz, reigns for twenty-nine years. In his sixth year, Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, captured Samaria and deported Israel to Assyria. Its kingdom had stood for 260 years from the first year of Jeroboam. After the death of Romulus, who had reigned for thirty-eight years, the senators governed the republic for five days at a time, and thus one year was completed. After them Numa Pompilius reigned for forty years; he built the Capitol from its foundations.

[A. M. Hebr. 3308. Sept. 4645.] Manasseh, son of Hezekiah, reigns for fifty-five years. Because of his crimes he was chained and fettered and led away to Babylon, but on account of his repentance and prayers he was restored to the kingdom. The third of the Romans, Tullus Hostilius, reigned for thirty-two years. He was the first of the Roman kings to use the purple and the fasces, and he enlarged the city by adding the Caelian Hill.

[A. M. Hebr. 3310. Sept. 4657.] Amon, son of Manasseh, reigns for two years. In the Hebrew truth he is said to have reigned for two years, while in the Septuagint he is said to have reigned for twelve.

[Note: XII. Thus Eusebius, but not the Septuagint. See 2 Kings 21.]

The city of Histrus was founded in Pontus. Amon was killed by his servants.

[A. M. Hebr. 3341. Sept. 4689.] Josiah, son of Amon, reigns for thirty-one years. After cleansing Judah and Jerusalem and renewing the Temple, he celebrated a most solemn Passover to the Lord in the eighteenth year of his reign, after casting away the filth of idolatry. He was killed in battle with Necho, king of the Egyptians, in the plain of Megiddo, which is now called Maximianopolis.

The fourth of the Romans, Ancus Martius, grandson through his daughter of Numa, reigned for twenty-three years. He added the Aventine and Janiculum Hills to the city and founded Ostia by the sea, sixteen miles from Rome. After him Tarquinius Priscus reigned for thirty-seven years. He built the Circus at Rome, increased the number of senators, established the Roman games, built the walls and sewers, and constructed the Capitol.

In the Hebrew text Josiah is said to have reigned for thirty-one years; in the Septuagint interpreters, thirty-two.

[Note: XXXII. Thus Eusebius, but not the Septuagint. See 2 Kings 22.]

Eusebius also adds an extra year between his reign and that of Jehoiakim because of the two periods of three months during which Jehoahaz, or Jehoiakim, had reigned.

[Note: Of him and Jehoiakim. Eusebius did not add a year between Josiah and Jehoiakim, but between Jehoiakim and Zedekiah, on account of the three months each of Jehoahaz and Jeconiah. See Eusebius, p. 124.]

But Jeremiah reveals what the truth is: he says that he prophesied from the thirteenth year of Josiah until the fourth year of Jehoiakim, a period of twenty-three years; that Nebuchadnezzar began to reign in the fourth year of Jehoiakim; and that Jerusalem was destroyed in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign.

[A. M. Hebr. 3352. Sept. 4700.] Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, reigns for eleven years. After Josiah, his son Jehoahaz reigned for three months. Necho took him away in chains to Egypt and appointed Jehoiakim king. In his third year Nebuchadnezzar captured Jerusalem and, after taking many captives, among them Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael, transferred part of the Temple vessels to Babylon. Scripture reckons Nebuchadnezzar’s reign from Jehoiakim’s fourth year, because from that time he began to rule not only the Chaldeans and Jews but also the Assyrians, Egyptians, Moabites, and countless other peoples.

Jehoiakim, also called Jeconiah, son of Jehoiakim, reigns for three months and ten days. When Jerusalem was surrounded by the Chaldeans, he went out to the king of Babylon, together with his mother, and was led to Babylon with his people in the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign.

[A. M. Hebr. 3363. Sept. 4711.] Zedekiah, also called Matthias, son of Josiah, reigns for eleven years. In his eleventh year, which was the nineteenth year of the king of Babylon, Judah was taken captive to Babylon and the Temple of the Lord was burned, 430 years after its foundation was begun.

[Note: 430. Counting inclusively from Solomon’s fourth year. Eusebius here gives 442 years, excluding Solomon’s fourth year and admitting the first year of Athaliah, the tenth of Amon, the first of Josiah, and an additional year between Jehoiakim and Zedekiah. Josephus, however, says that the Temple was burned in the 470th year of its construction, in the sixth month and tenth day.]

The Jews who remained fled to Egypt; after Egypt was struck by the Chaldeans five years later, they too were transported to Babylon.

## THE FIFTH AGE

The fifth age of the world began with the destruction of the Jewish kingdom, which, according to Jeremiah’s prophecy, lasted seventy years.

[Col. 0535C] [A. M. Hebr. 3377. Sept. 4725.] In the fourteenth year after the city was struck down—which is the twenty-fifth year of the transmigration of King Jehoiakim, with whom Ezekiel was also taken captive—Ezekiel himself, brought in divine visions to the land of Israel, saw the renewal of the city, the Temple, and its rites. The sixth of the Romans, Servius, reigned for thirty-four years. He added three hills to the city—the Quirinal, Esquiline, and Viminal—dug ditches around the walls, and first instituted the census of Roman citizens.

[A. M. Hebr. 3389. Sept. 4737.] In the twenty-sixth year after the destruction of Jerusalem, which is the thirty-seventh year of the transmigration of King Jehoiakim, Evil-merodach, king of Babylon, in the year in which he had begun to reign, raised the head of Jehoiachin, king of Judah, from prison and set his throne above the thrones of the kings who were with him in Babylon.

The prophet Jeremiah refers to this time, still future, writing as follows:

> “Behold, I will send for and take all the tribes of the north, says the Lord, and Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, my servant, and I will bring them against this land, against its inhabitants, and against all the nations that surround it. I will kill them and make them an object of astonishment, a hissing, and everlasting desolations, and all these nations will serve the king of Babylon for seventy years. When the seventy years have been completed, I will visit the iniquity of the king of Babylon and of that nation, says the Lord, and of the land of the Chaldeans, and I will make it everlasting desolation.”

[Note: Jeremiah, chapter 25:9 and following.]

And elsewhere, writing to the deportation that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon with King Jeconiah, he says:

> “When seventy years begin to be completed in Babylon, I will visit you, and I will raise up for you my good word, and I will bring you back to this place, says the Lord.”

[Note: Elsewhere, chapter 29:10.]

Again, concerning that same period, now past, the *Words of the Days*—that is, the Book of Chronicles—recall:

> “If anyone had escaped the sword, he was led to Babylon and served the king and his sons, until the king of the Persians began to rule and the word of the Lord from the mouth of Jeremiah was fulfilled, and the land kept its Sabbaths. For throughout all the days of its desolation it kept Sabbath, until the seventy years were completed. In the first year of Cyrus, king of the Persians, to fulfill the word of the Lord spoken through the mouth of Jeremiah, the Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus, king of the Persians, etc.”

[Note: Again, 2 Chronicles 36:20.]

These words show that when the Chaldeans devastated Judaea, they did not, like the Assyrians in Samaria, send other colonists there; rather, they left the land deserted until the Jews themselves returned to it after seventy years. Josephus agrees with this, writing in the tenth book of his *Antiquities* that the Temple, Jerusalem, and all Judaea remained desolate for seventy years.

[Note: Josephus, *Antiquities* X, 12.]

When he again enumerates the kings of Babylon—if indeed he himself wrote it this way, and the fault does not lie in a corrupt manuscript—he makes nearly 100 years be reckoned from the destruction of Jerusalem to the overthrow of the Chaldean kingdom. For he writes that after Nebuchadnezzar, who, according to Holy Scripture, lived for twenty-five years after the destruction of Jerusalem, his son Evil-merodach reigned for eighteen years; after him his son Egesar for forty; and that his son Labosordoch succeeded him for nine months. After Labosordoch’s death, authority passed to Belshazzar, who is called Naboan. After he had already reigned for seventeen years, Josephus relates that Babylon was captured by Cyrus, king of the Persians, and Darius, king of the Medes.

[Note: XVIII. The editions have eighteen, contrary to the Paris edition of 1501 and to Josephus, indeed contrary even to Bede’s own manuscripts.]

Darius, son of Astyages, who destroyed the Babylonian empire, was then in his sixty-second year with his kinsman Cyrus when Babylon was invaded. He was known by another name among the Greeks; he took the prophet Daniel with him to Media and honored him greatly.

Daniel himself refers to this Darius as follows:

> “In the first year of Darius, son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, who ruled over the kingdom of the Chaldeans, I, Daniel, understood from the books the number of years concerning which the word of the Lord had come to Jeremiah the prophet, that the seventy years of Jerusalem’s desolations would be completed.”

[Note: Daniel, chapter 9:1.]

Eusebius, in his *Book of Times*, reckons thirty years from the destruction of Jerusalem to the beginning of the reign of Cyrus, king of the Persians; Julius Africanus reckons seventy.

[Note: Africanus, seventy. In Eusebius (*Preparation for the Gospel*, book X, p. 488).]

Moreover, Jerome, in his exposition of the prophet Daniel, says:

> “The Hebrews relate a story of this kind: when the seventieth year arrived, in which Jeremiah had said that the captivity of the Jewish people would be released—and about which Zechariah also speaks at the beginning of his book—Belshazzar, thinking that God’s promise had been annulled and the pledge false, turned to joy and held a great banquet, mocking, as it were, the hope of the Jews and the vessels of God’s Temple; but punishment immediately followed.”

[A. M. Hebr. 3423. Sept. 4771.] Cyrus, the first of the Persians, reigned for thirty years. To fulfill the word of the Lord spoken through Jeremiah, in the first year of his reign he released the Hebrews from captivity and caused nearly 50,000 people to return to Judaea, restoring to them 5,400 golden and silver vessels of the Lord’s Temple. They assembled in Jerusalem in the seventh month, built the altar, and from the first day of that month began to offer burnt offerings to the Lord.

In the second year after their arrival, in the second month, they laid the foundations of the Temple: in the year of its burning, according to Africanus, the seventy-second year; according to the *Chronicles* of Eusebius, the thirty-second. But because of the opposition of the Samaritans, the work was suspended until the second year of Darius; they had also written an accusation against the Jews during the reigns of Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes, and Artaxerxes replied that Jerusalem was not to be built.

The seventh of the Romans, Tarquinius, reigned for thirty-five years. He was expelled from the kingdom because of his son Tarquinius the Younger, who had violated Lucretia.

[A. M. Hebr. 3431. Sept. 4779.] Cambyses, son of Cyrus, reigns for eight years. After conquering Egypt, he detested its entire religion and abolished its rites and temples. He built Babylon in Egypt. The Hebrews are said to call him the Second Nebuchadnezzar, under whom the history of Judith was written.

[A. M. Hebr. 3432. Sept. 4780.] The Magian brothers reign for seven months. Jesus is high priest, and Zerubbabel is leader of the people. The prophets Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi become renowned. Pythagoras, the natural philosopher, is held in high esteem.

[A. M. Hebr. 3468. Sept. 4816.] Darius reigns for thirty-six years. We find in the books of Eusebius’ *Chronicles* that two Magian brothers reigned between Darius and Cambyses. Jerome, however, in his exposition of Daniel, writes that after Cambyses the Magian Smerdis reigned.

[Note: All editions and Bede’s manuscripts have *Magnum*, through a gross error.]

[Note: The Magian. Jerome, in Daniel, chapter 11:2.]

He writes that Smerdis married Pantapthes, Cambyses’ daughter; after Smerdis had been killed by the seven Magi and Darius had taken power in his place, that same Pantapthes married Darius and bore him a son, Xerxes.

In the second year of Darius, according to Eusebius, the seventieth year of Jerusalem’s captivity was completed. He cites the prophet Zechariah as witness, for in the second year of Darius an angel says:

> “Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which you have been angry? This is the seventieth year.”

[Note: “Lord of hosts,” Zechariah 1:12.]

Again, in the fourth year of King Darius the same prophet says:

> “When you fasted and mourned during these seventy years, did you truly fast for me?”

[Note: “When you fasted,” Zechariah 7:5.]

In the sixth year of Darius the construction of the Temple was completed, on the third day of the month Adar. This was the forty-sixth year since its foundations had been laid under Cyrus. Hence the Jews say in the Gospel:

> “This Temple has been under construction for forty-six years.”

[Note: In the Gospel, John 2:20.]

They began to build in the second year of Darius, in the sixth month, on the twenty-fourth day; and in the sixth year, as stated, in the twelfth month, on the third day, they completed it. From this it is apparent that a considerable part of the Temple had already been completed earlier, but that seventy years are to be reckoned from its destruction until permission for its complete restoration.

After the kings who had ruled for 243 years were expelled from the city, Rome scarcely retained dominion as far as the fifteenth milestone.

[Note: 243. Eusebius says that the Roman kings ruled for 240 years, or, as some prefer, 243. The number 243 is found in all Bede’s manuscripts, but appears to be a scribal error. In fact, according to Bede himself, the years of the Roman kings amount to only 241; Eusebius’ calculation is therefore one year shorter because he assigns Numa only forty years, whereas Bede assigns him forty-one. This deserves particular notice because the application of the years from the founding of the City to the Christian era depends upon it. See below, under 3952.]

After the expulsion of the kings, consuls first began to govern Rome, with Brutus as their founder; then came the tribunes of the plebs and dictators; and once again consuls held the republic for approximately 464 years, until Julius Caesar, who first seized sole power, in the 183rd Olympiad.

[Note: In the margin of the editions, IV; in the manuscripts and Eusebius, CLXXXIII.]

[Note: 183. Here too Bede follows Eusebius, reckoning 183 Olympiads from the first Olympiad to Julius Caesar, unaware of the inconsistency with his own calculation, according to which the total there falls short by twenty years of that many Olympiads. He begins the Olympiads in the year of the world 3,198, whereas Julius Caesar’s first year was the year 3,906, a difference of 709 years. But 103 Olympiads amount to 729 years, so twenty years are missing. Here the same explanation of the difference recurs as before: Eusebius counts the eight years discussed under the year 3,208 and the twelve years discussed under the year 3,363, years that Bede omits.]

[A.M. Hebrew 3488; Septuagint 4836.] Xerxes, son of Darius, for 20 years. He captured Egypt, which had revolted from Darius, and, intending to fight against Greece, is said to have had 710,000 armed men from his kingdom and 300,000 auxiliaries, as well as 1,200 beaked warships and 3,000 transports. Nevertheless, after being defeated, he fled back to his homeland. [Col. 0539A] Herodotus is recognized as a writer of histories; Zeuxis as a painter.

[A.M. Hebrew 3489; Septuagint 4837.] [Note: In the editions Artabanus is placed at A.M. 3488.] Artabanus, for seven months. Socrates is born.

[A.M. Hebrew 3529; Septuagint 4877.] [Note: In the editions Artaxerxes is placed at A.M. 3489.] Artaxerxes, also called Longimanus—that is, μακρόχειρ (“long-handed”)—for 40 years. In his seventh year, on the first day of the first month, Ezra the priest and scribe of the law of God went up from Babylon with letters from the king, and on the first day of the fifth month arrived in Jerusalem with 1,700 men. Among his other vigorous accomplishments, he rebuked the children of the captivity for their foreign wives. In his twentieth year, Nehemiah the cupbearer, arriving from the fortress of Susa, rebuilt the wall of Jerusalem in 52 days and provided leadership to the people for 12 years.

[Note: Up to this point. Since the chronology of the Old Testament ends here, I too would end here the reckoning of the Septuagint translators; but because from this point only a few marginal numbers remain before Christ, I am not changing the heading until that era is reached.]

Up to this point Holy Scripture contains the sequence of the ages. What was done among the Jews after this is presented from the book of Maccabees and from the writings of Josephus and Africanus, who thereafter carried the whole history forward to Roman times. Africanus, indeed, in the fifth book of his *Chronology*, mentions this period as follows:

“Thus the work remained incomplete until Nehemiah and the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes. At that time 115 years of the Persian kingdom had elapsed, while it was the 185th year of the captivity of Jerusalem. Then for the first time Artaxerxes ordered the walls of Jerusalem to be rebuilt; Nehemiah supervised the work, the street was built, and the walls were enclosed. From that time, if you wish to count, you will be able to find 70 weeks of years until Christ.”

[Note: Africanus. Cited by Jerome in his commentary on Daniel, chapter 9.]

[Note: The 70 weeks. In counting the 70 weeks, Bede proceeds by the hypothesis of lunar years, reckoning from the twentieth year of Artaxerxes to Christ the Leader 70 weeks—that is, 490 years of twelve lunar months, which amount to 475 solar years. From the aforesaid twentieth year of King Artaxerxes until the death of Darius, the Persians ruled for 116 years; thereafter the Macedonians ruled until the death of Cleopatra for 300 years; then the Romans held power until the seventeenth year of the monarchy of Tiberius Caesar for 59 years. Added together, these make 475 years. Bede discusses this extensively in the seventh—actually the ninth—chapter of *On the Reckoning of Time*, where he gives a careful exposition of this hypothesis.]

Xerxes, two months; after him Sogdianus, seven months. Plato is born. Hippocrates is regarded as an outstanding physician.

[A.M. Hebrew 3548; Septuagint 4896.] Darius, surnamed Nothus, for 19 years. Egypt revolted from the Persians. After the Jews returned from captivity, they were ruled not by kings but by high priests, up to Aristobulus, who began to assume the title of king along with the dignity of high priest.

[A.M. Hebrew 3588; Septuagint 4936.] Artaxerxes, surnamed Mnemon, son of Darius and Parysatis, for 40 years. Under this king the history of Esther appears to have been completed. He is the one whom the Hebrews call Ahasuerus and the translators of the Septuagint call Artaxerxes. The Athenians began to use 24 letters, whereas previously they had only 16. The famous war of the Carthaginians occurred. The Senonian Gauls under Brennus invaded Rome, sparing only the Capitol, and ravaged the burned city for six months. Military tribunes began to serve in place of consuls. Aristotle, at the age of 18, was a student of Plato.

[A.M. Hebrew 3614; Septuagint 4962.] Artaxerxes, also called Ochus, for 26 years. He added Egypt to his empire. King Nectanebo was driven into Ethiopia, and with him the Egyptian kingdom was destroyed. Demosthenes was celebrated by universal acclaim as an orator. The Romans defeated the Gauls. Plato died. After him Speusippus held the Academy.

[Col. 0540B] [A.M. Hebrew 3618; Septuagint 4966.] Arses, son of Ochus, for four years. Jaddus, the high priest of the Jews, was held in renown; his brother Manasseh built a temple on Mount Garizim. Speusippus died, and Xenocrates succeeded him.

[Note: “Of Ochus.” All the manuscripts read this, but it is plainly an error. Alexander began to reign over the Macedonians not in the time of Ochus but of Arses; his fourth year is the first of the seven years during which Alexander reigned before the death of Darius.]

In the fourth year of Ochus, Alexander, son of Philip and Olympias, at the age of 20, began to reign over the Macedonians.

[A.M. Hebrew 3624; Septuagint 4972.] Darius, son of Arsames, for six years. Alexander fought successfully against the Illyrians and Thracians; after overthrowing Thebes, he took up arms against the Persians. At the river Granicus, after defeating the king’s commanders, he captured the city of Sardis. After capturing Tyre, he likewise invaded Judaea, where he was favorably received, offered sacrifices to God, and treated Jaddus, the temple’s high priest, with the highest honors, leaving Andromachus as governor of the region. In the seventh year of his reign he founded Alexandria in Egypt. Soon afterward he took Babylon; Darius was killed, and with him the Persian kingdom was destroyed—the kingdom that had stood for 231 years. At this time the Latins too were subdued by the Romans.

[A.M. Hebrew 3629; Septuagint 4977.] After the death of Darius, Alexander reigned for five years, since he had reigned seven years previously. Alexander captured the Hyrcanians and Mardians, and, returning, founded Paraetonium in Hammon.

[Note: “And, returning, founded Paraetonium in Hammon.” That is, in the part of Egypt called Hammon, from which Paraetonium is called Hammonia by Strabo, book 17. It should be noted, however, that this clause is absent from the Greek text of Eusebius. The reason for its omission or addition is uncertain, as is also the basis for the accusations that Scaliger, in his customary manner, pours out here against the alleged culprit. For it was not impossible for Alexander to capture the Hyrcanians and Mardians, then return from there to Egypt and found Paraetonium.]

By victories rather than battles he reached as far as the Indian Ocean. Returning to Babylon, he died from drinking poison in the thirty-second year of his life and the twelfth year of his reign. After him, power was divided among many: Ptolemy, son of Lagus, held Egypt; Philip, also called Aridaeus, Alexander’s brother, held Macedonia; Seleucus Nicanor ruled Syria, Babylon, and all the kingdoms of the East; and Antigonus ruled Asia. In Daniel he is represented by the four horns of the goat that shattered the ram.

[Note: Daniel. Chapter 8, verse 8.]

[A.M. Hebrew 3669; Septuagint 5017.] Ptolemy son of Lagus was the first to reign in Egypt, for 40 years. Appius Claudius Caecus was renowned at Rome; he brought in the Aqua Claudia and paved the Via Appia. Ptolemy, having deceitfully brought Jerusalem and Judaea under his authority, transported many captives to Egypt. Onias, son of Jaddus, was renowned as the Jews’ high priest. In the thirteenth year of Ptolemy, Seleucus Nicator began to reign over Syria, Babylon, and the upper regions. From that time the Hebrew history of the Maccabees reckons the kingdom of the Greeks, and from it the people of Edessa also calculate their eras.

[Note: “Of the Greeks.” The Alexandrian, Seleucid, and Greek eras are the same. Beginning in the thirteenth year after Alexander’s death, the first year of Seleucus Nicator, this era continued under his successors, the Demetrii and the Antiochi, in Syria. At that time the Jews, living under the rule of the Greeks, were compelled to adopt it. Accordingly, in the books of the Maccabees the years among the Jews are designated by this name. The Edessene era is also the same; see below, at A.M. 4236. It must be carefully observed that in the First Book of Maccabees the Greek years begin with the month Nisan, while in the Second they begin with the following Tisri, so that an interval of six months lies between them.]

Seleucus founded the cities of Seleucia, Laodicea, Antioch, Apamea, Edessa, Beroea, and Pella. Simon, son of Onias, was renowned as the Jews’ most religious and devout high priest. After him his brother Eleazar undertook the temple service, leaving his son Onias still very young. Seleucus transferred Jews to the cities he had built, granting them the rights of citizenship and a municipal order alongside the Greeks, with equal honor.

[A.M. Hebrew 3707; Septuagint 5055.] Ptolemy Philadelphus, for 38 years. Sostratus of Cnidus built the Pharos at Alexandria. Ptolemy allowed the Jews who were in Egypt to be free, and, sending many gifts to Eleazar the high priest and vessels for the temple offerings at Jerusalem, requested the 70 translators who would render Holy Scripture into the Greek language. Aratus was recognized. After Eleazar, his uncle Manasseh assumed the high priesthood. This Ptolemy Philadelphus is said to have been so powerful that he conquered his father Ptolemy. Histories report that he had 200,000 infantry, 20,000 cavalry, 2,000 chariots, and 400 elephants—the first elephants he brought from Ethiopia—along with other forces of the same kind.

[A.M. Hebrew 3733; Septuagint 5081.] Ptolemy Evergetes, brother of the preceding king, for 26 years. He was called Evergetes by the Egyptians because, after capturing Syria, Cilicia, and nearly all Asia, he brought back, among the countless quantities of silver and precious vessels he seized, even the gods whom Cambyses had carried away to Persia after conquering Egypt. Onias, son of Simon the Just, was renowned as the Jews’ high priest. His son Simon likewise shone with no lesser glory. Under him Jesus son of Sirach composed the Book of Wisdom, which they call *Panaretos*, and also mentioned Simon in it.

[A.M. Hebrew 3750; Septuagint 5098.] Ptolemy Philopator, son of Evergetes, for 17 years. Antiochus, king of Syria, after defeating Philopator, brought Judaea under his control. Onias, son of Simon, was distinguished as the Jews’ high priest; to him Arius, king of the Lacedaemonians, sent ambassadors.

[A.M. Hebrew 3774; Septuagint 5122.] Ptolemy Epiphanes, son of Philopator, for 24 years. The Second Book of Maccabees contains among the Jews the events of this period. Onias the priest, taking many Jews with him, fled to Egypt. Received honorably by Ptolemy, he obtained the region called Heliopolis and, with the king’s permission, built in Egypt a temple like the temple of the Jews. It remained until the reign of Vespasian, for 250 years. Thus, under the pretext of the high priest Onias, countless multitudes of Jews fled into Egypt; at that time Cyrene too became filled with a multitude of them. The reason for Onias and the others seeking Egypt was that, while the great Antiochus and Ptolemy’s commanders were fighting one another, Judaea, lying between them, was divided into opposing factions, some favoring Antiochus and others Ptolemy.

[A.M. Hebrew 3809; Septuagint 5157.] Ptolemy Philometor, for 35 years. Aristobulus, a Jew by nation and a Peripatetic philosopher, was recognized; he wrote for Ptolemy Philometor commentaries explaining Moses. Antiochus Epiphanes, who after Seleucus surnamed Philopator reigned in Syria for 11 years, attacked the law of the Jews, filled everything with the pollution of idols, and placed in the temple an image of Jupiter Olympius. He also built in Samaria, on the summit of Mount Garizim, a shrine of Jupiter the Stranger, at the request of the Samaritans themselves that he do so.

But the priest Mathathias defended the ancestral laws, taking up arms against the commanders of Antiochus. After his death, his son Judas, called Maccabaeus, assumed leadership of the Jews in the 146th year of the kingdom of the Greeks and, in the twentieth year of Ptolemy, the 155th Olympiad.

[Note: “146.” Here Bede correctly follows the First Book of Maccabees, chapter 3, and Josephus, book 12, chapter 9, in placing the death of Mathathias and Judas’s succession to the leadership in the 146th year of the Greek kingdom. He is also correct in placing Philometor’s twentieth year in the 155th Olympiad according to Eusebius. But his placing of this year of Philometor and that Olympiad in the 146th year of the Greek kingdom derives from his own error. The 146th year of the Greek kingdom does not fall in Philometor’s twentieth year but in his thirteenth, nor in the 155th Olympiad but in the 153rd, specifically its second year. Nevertheless, if one notes that Judas assumed leadership immediately after his father’s death, which fell in Philometor’s thirteenth year, while the high priesthood was not conferred before Philometor’s twentieth year, in the 155th Olympiad, Bede will be found not to have treated the historical truth badly, although not without some trace of error. In a single chronological point, and in a place so confused among the earliest authorities, this can readily be forgiven.]

He immediately expelled Antiochus’s commanders from Judaea, cleansed the temple of the idols’ images, and after three years restored the ancestral laws to his fellow citizens. Thus, after the priest Onias’s withdrawal to Egypt, mentioned above, and the death of Alcimus, who, after driving out Onias, was attempting unworthily to seize the high priesthood, the priesthood was awarded to Judas Maccabaeus with the approval of all the Jews. After his death his brother Jonathan received it and administered it with the greatest diligence for 19 years.

[A.M. Hebrew 3838; Septuagint 5186.] Ptolemy Evergetes, for 29 years. Jonathan, leader and high priest of the Jews, made treaties of friendship with the Romans and Spartans. After Tryphon killed him, his brother Simon was appointed to the priesthood in the seventh year of Evergetes’ reign. After exercising it most vigorously for eight years, he handed it on to his son John. John, waging war against the Hyrcanians, received the name Hyrcanus. Seeking from the Romans the right of friendship, he was enrolled among their friends by decree of the Senate. He captured Samaria—which in our time is called Sebaste—and leveled it to the ground. Later Herod rebuilt it and wished it to be called Sebaste in honor of Augustus.

[A.M. Hebrew 3855; Septuagint 5203.] Ptolemy Physcon, also called Soter, for 17 years.

[Note: “Soter.” This surname was also given to Ptolemy son of Lagus, as Josephus and others attest.]

Cicero was born at Arpinum, to his mother Helvia and his father, a member of the equestrian order from the royal family of the Volscians. Aristobulus succeeded Hyrcanus in the high priesthood, which Hyrcanus himself had held for 26 years; he held it for one year. He was the first among the Jews to assume the insignia of the diadem as both king and high priest, after 484 years of Babylonian captivity.

[Note: “484.” Josephus has 481 (*Antiquities* 13.19). But from the capture of Zedekiah, from which these years are reckoned, to Aristobulus’s year, there are in fact 486 years.]

After him Jannaeus, surnamed Alexander, reigned for 27 years; he also administered the high priesthood and ruled his citizens with extreme cruelty.

[A.M. Hebrew 3865; Septuagint 5213.] Ptolemy, also called Alexander, for 10 years. In his seventh year Syria passed under Roman authority, after Philip was captured by Gabinius. Ptolemy Physcon, expelled from the kingdom by his mother Cleopatra, withdrew to Cyprus.

[A.M. Hebrew 3873; Septuagint 5221.] Ptolemy, who had been expelled by his mother, reigned for eight years. Returning from exile, he recovered the kingdom, because the citizens had driven out Alexander, who had preceded him, on account of his killing his mother. Sulla ravaged the Athenians.

[A.M. Hebrew 3903; Septuagint 5251.] Ptolemy Dionysius, for 30 years. From the fifth year of his reign, Alexandra, wife of Alexander the high priest, ruled the Jews for nine years after his death. From that time confusion and various disasters oppressed the Jews. After her death, her sons Aristobulus and Hyrcanus fought one another for power and gave the Romans an opportunity to invade Judaea.

Pompey accordingly came to Jerusalem, captured the city, opened the temple, and approached as far as the Holy of Holies. He led Aristobulus away in chains, confirmed Hyrcanus in the high priesthood, and then made Antipater, son of Herod the Ascalonite, procurator of Palestine. Hyrcanus remained in the high priesthood for 34 years.

Virgil Maro was born in the village called Andes, not far from Mantua, during the consulship of Pompey and Crassus. Pompey, after capturing Jerusalem, made the Jews tributaries. Virgil was educated at Cremona. Caesar conquered the Germans and Gauls, and also the Britons, who before him had not even known the name of the Romans; after defeating them and receiving hostages, he made them tributaries.

[Note: “The Britons as well.” See Bede, *Ecclesiastical History* 1.2.]

[A.M. Hebrew 3925; Septuagint 5273.] Cleopatra, sister of Ptolemy, for 22 years. When civil war arose between Caesar and Pompey, Pompey, after being defeated, went to Alexandria. There he was killed by the very Ptolemy from whom he had hoped for aid.

[Note: The editions read “Caesar himself,” incorrectly.]

As soon as Caesar arrived at Alexandria, Ptolemy too attempted to lay an ambush for him. Caesar therefore made war on him, and Ptolemy was defeated and died in it. Having gained control of Alexandria, Caesar gave the kingdom to Cleopatra, with whom he had maintained an adulterous relationship. In the third year of her reign, he was the first of the Romans to obtain sole power; from him the Roman emperors were called Caesars. Cleopatra entered the city with royal attendants.

[A.M. Hebrew 3910; Septuagint 5258.] Caesar, because of his arrogance, was stabbed to death in the Senate-house by 60 or more senators and Roman knights, after he had begun to reign four years and six months earlier.

[Note: The editions have five years in the text, contrary to the manuscripts; consequently the printed editions also placed four years in the margin.]

Cassius, after conquering Judaea, plundered the temple.

[A.M. Hebrew 3966; Septuagint 5314.] Octavian Caesar Augustus, the second Roman, reigned for 56 years and six months. From him the Roman kings were called Augusti. Of these years, 15 were lived while Cleopatra was still alive and 41 afterward.

In the eleventh year of Augustus, when the rule of the high priests in Judaea came to an end, Herod—who had no connection with that family, being the son of Antipater the Ascalonite and his Arabian mother Cypros—received from the Romans the rule over the Jews. He held it for 36 years.

[Note: “Herod.” Under him and the other rulers under the Romans, high priests were imposed upon the Jews at will. Josephus transmitted their history from Hyrcanus, mentioned above at A.M. 3903, to Phanasus, the last of them (*Antiquities*, books 15–20).]

Lest he perhaps be judged ignoble and an outsider to the Jewish seed, he burned all the books in which the nobility of the Jewish people had been recorded and preserved in the temple, so that, with the evidence destroyed, he too might be thought to belong to it. Moreover, in order to mingle his offspring with their royal stock, he set aside Dosis, a Jerusalem woman whom he had married as a private citizen and by whom he had had a son, Antipater, and joined himself to Mariamne, daughter of Alexander and granddaughter of Aristobulus, Hyrcanus’s brother, who had been king of the Jews before him.

She bore him five sons. Of them he himself killed two, Alexander and Aristobulus, at Samaria; and soon afterward he also murdered their mother, whom he had loved more than anything.

Of these Aristobulus had a son by Berenice, whom we read in the Acts of the Apostles was struck by an angel.

[Note: Acts. Chapter 12, verse 23.]

When a third war arose between Augustus and Antony—because Antony, who held Asia and the East, had divorced Augustus’s sister and married Cleopatra—Antony and Cleopatra were defeated and killed themselves. Some reckon the first year of Augustus’s monarchy from this time. Up to this point those called the Ptolemies, or Lagids, ruled in Egypt for 295 years.

SIXTH AGE.

[Col. 0545B] [A.M. 3952; A.D. 1.] In the 42nd year of Caesar Augustus—

[Note: “42.” Bede reckons these years from Caesar’s death; consequently Christ’s Nativity falls in the 4712th year of the Julian period, two years before the common Dionysian era. The other eras mentioned here by Bede agree in this year. The only question is whether this year should be included in the reckoning. Scaliger’s edition of Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, excluding this year, begins the era of Christ from Augustus’s forty-third year; but the edition of Henri Estienne includes year 42, as do nearly all the chronologists of the Middle Ages. So uncertain is the beginning of the Christian era among recent scholars that each person is free to choose which of these years he wishes, whether the current year or the completed year. I follow the reckoning of the current year, not only because it agrees better with Bede’s numbers in this *Chronicle*, but also because it coincides with the year of the Julian period in which the evangelical and true era is placed.]

—and in the 27th year from the death of Cleopatra and Antony, when Egypt was also made a province; in the third year of the 194th Olympiad; and in the 752nd year from the founding of the City—

[Note: “752.” What was noted above concerning the years of the Roman kings, at A.M. 3468, shows its usefulness here. For if the years of the Roman kings were 243, the year of Christ’s birth would not have been the 752nd year from the founding of the City but the 754th. It is therefore probable that the number 243 is an error in Bede’s manuscripts.]

—that is, in the year when, by God’s ordinance, Caesar brought about the firmest and truest peace, having subdued the disturbances of all the nations throughout the world, Jesus Christ, the Son of God, consecrated the sixth age of the world by his coming.

In the 47th year of Augustus’s reign, Herod died miserably and deservedly from dropsy and from worms swarming throughout his body. His son Archelaus, appointed in his place by Augustus, reigned for nine years, that is, until Augustus himself died. Then, because the Jews could no longer endure Herod’s ferocity and accused him before Augustus, he was banished to Vienna, a city of Gaul. To diminish the power of the Jewish kingdom and tame its arrogance, four of his brothers were made tetrarchs in his place: Herod, Antipater, Lysias, and Philip. Philip and Herod, who had previously been called Antipas, had already been appointed tetrarchs while Archelaus was still alive.

[A.M. 3989; A.D. 38.] Tiberius, Augustus’s stepson—that is, the son of his wife Livia by her former husband—reigned for 23 years. In his twelfth year, Pilate was sent by him as procurator of Judaea. Herod the tetrarch, who held the rule over the Jews for 24 years, founded Tiberias and Livia in honor of Tiberius and his mother Livia.

[Col. 0546A] [A.M. 3981; A.D. 30.] In the fifteenth year of Tiberius’s reign, after the baptism preached by John, the Lord announced the kingdom of heaven to the world. From the beginning of the world, according to the Hebrews, 4,000 years had elapsed, as Eusebius marks in his *Chronicles*, noting that the sixteenth year of Tiberius was the beginning of the eighty-first jubilee according to the Hebrews.

Why our reckoning judged that 19 fewer years should be set down can easily be discovered by anyone who has read the earlier parts of this little book.

[Note: “The earlier parts.” Namely, seven years at number 2519, one at 3071, ten at 3310, and two at 3341. These total 20 years; but because in the third age Eusebius had reckoned one year fewer than Bede, adding only nine years—one under Joshua and eight under Samuel and Saul, where he had subtracted ten, namely from Achialon—the difference is reduced to 19 years.]

According to the same *Chronicles* that Eusebius himself, as it seemed to him, composed from both editions, the number of years is 5,228.

[Note: The editions of Cologne and Basel read “true,” contrary to Sichardus and the manuscripts.]

[A.M. 3984; A.D. 33.] In the eighteenth year of Tiberius’s reign, the Lord redeemed the world by his passion. As the apostles were preaching throughout the regions of Judaea, they appointed James, the Lord’s brother, bishop at Jerusalem, and also appointed seven deacons. After Stephen was stoned, the Church was dispersed throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria.

Agrippa, surnamed Herod, son of Aristobulus, son of King Herod, and accuser of Herod the tetrarch, went to Rome and was thrown into chains by Tiberius. There he won many people to his friendship, especially Gaius, the son of Germanicus.

[A.M. 3993; A.D. 42.] Gaius, surnamed Caligula, reigned for three years, ten months, and eight days.

[Note: The editions of Cologne, Basel, and Sichardus have four years; the other editions and the manuscripts have three.]

He made his friend Herod Agrippa, after releasing him from prison, king of Judaea. Agrippa remained in the kingdom for seven years, that is, until the fourth year of Claudius. When Agrippa was struck by an angel, his son Agrippa succeeded him in the kingdom and continued until the destruction of the Jews, for 26 years.

Herod the tetrarch also sought the friendship of Gaius. At the urging of Herodias he came to Rome, but after being accused by Agrippa he lost even his tetrarchy. Fleeing with Herodias to Spain, he died of grief.

Pilate, who had pronounced the sentence condemning Christ, was so tormented by the anguish inflicted by Gaius that he killed himself. Gaius, claiming a place among the gods, profaned the holy places of the Jews with the pollution of idols. Matthew wrote the Gospel while preaching in Judaea.

[A.M. 4007; A.D. 56.] Claudius, for 13 years, seven months, and 28 days. After the Apostle Peter had first founded the Church at Antioch, he went to Rome, where he held the episcopal chair for 25 years, that is, until the last year of Nero.

Mark preached in Egypt the Gospel that he had written at Rome, sent there by Peter.

[Note: “At Rome.” This reckoning confirms the beginning of the years of Christ that we established above from the current year of the Nativity, namely Augustus’s forty-second year. For in the fourth year of Claudius Bede, in *Ecclesiastical History* 1.3, places the forty-sixth year of Christ. If we begin this from the completed year of the Nativity, namely Augustus’s forty-third year, it will not be Christ’s forty-sixth year but his forty-fifth.]

In the fourth year of Claudius there was a very severe famine, of which Luke makes mention.

[Note: Luke. Acts 11:28.]

In that same year Claudius himself went to Britain, which no one had dared approach either before Julius Caesar or after him. Without any battle or bloodshed, within a very few days he brought a large part of the island under his power. He also added the Orkney Islands to the Roman Empire and returned to Rome in the sixth month after his departure.

[Note: “Famine … Britain … Orkneys.” See *Ecclesiastical History* 1.3, at A.D. 46.]

In the ninth year of his reign he expelled the Jews who were rioting in Rome, as Luke also reports.

[Note: Luke. Acts 18:2.]

In the following year a very great famine seized Rome.

[A.M. 4021; A.D. 70.] Nero, for 13 years, seven months, and 28 days. In his second year, Festus succeeded Felix as procurator of Judaea. From Festus Paul was sent to Rome in chains; after remaining there for two years in open custody, he was released to preach, while Nero had not yet burst into the enormities that histories recount concerning him.

James, the Lord’s brother, after governing the Church at Jerusalem for 30 years, was stoned by the Jews in Nero’s seventh year, who took vengeance on him for their inability to kill Paul.

Festus was succeeded in the administration of Judaea by Albinus, and Albinus by Florus. The Jews, unable to endure Florus’s luxury, greed, and other crimes, rebelled against the Romans. Against them Vespasian was sent as military commander and captured many cities of Judaea.

Nero, the first to persecute Christians in addition to all his other crimes, also persecuted them. At Rome he killed their outstanding leaders, Peter by crucifixion and Paul by the sword.

[Note: “Nero … almost lost Britain … two towns.” See *Ecclesiastical History* 1.3.]

In military affairs he attempted nothing at all and almost lost Britain, for under him two of its most distinguished towns were captured and destroyed.

[A.M. 4031; A.D. 80.] [Note: Vespasian. Although Galba, Otho, and Vitellius ruled before Vespasian for one year and nine months, and Eusebius names them, they are omitted in Bede’s exemplar, following Orosius. Plutarch, in his *Life of Galba*, gives a witty but no less just explanation: they were emperors not so much of the Roman Empire as of some kind of comedy.]

Vespasian, for nine years, 11 months, and 22 days. Having been proclaimed emperor by the army in Judaea, and entrusting the war to his son Titus, he went to Rome by way of Alexandria.

Titus, in his second year, overthrew the kingdom of Judaea and leveled the temple to the ground, 1,139 years after its first construction.

[Note: “Its first construction,” namely, in Solomon’s fourth year.]

This war was completed in four years: two while Nero was alive and two afterward.

[Note: Vespasian … sent to Britain … captured the Isle of Wight. See *Ecclesiastical History* 1.3.]

While still a private citizen, Vespasian had been sent by Claudius to Germany and then to Britain, where he clashed with the enemy 32 times. He added two very powerful peoples, 20 towns, and the Isle of Wight, lying near Britain, to the Roman Empire. A colossal statue was erected, 107 feet high.

[A.M. 4033; A.D. 82.] Titus, for two years and two months. He was a man remarkable for every kind of virtue, so much so that he was called the love and delight of the human race. He built the Amphitheatre at Rome and, at its dedication, killed 5,000 wild beasts.

[A.M. 4049; A.D. 98.] Domitian, Titus’s younger brother, for 15 years and five months. He was the second after Nero to persecute the Christians. Under him the apostle John was exiled to the island of Patmos. Flavia Domitilla, niece through her aunt of the consul Flavius Clemens, was also exiled to the island of Pontia for bearing witness to the faith.

[Note: “Pontia.” Eusebius has Pontia. Pliny, 6.3, places Pontia opposite Formiae. There are several islands of this name, but the one to which Flavia Domitilla was exiled lies 32 miles from Tarracina, where she completed her martyrdom.]

Domitian is also said to have sent John himself into a vessel of boiling oil; but John emerged from the punishments as unharmed as he always remained free from corruption of the flesh.

[A.M. 4050; A.D. 99.] Nerva, for one year, four months, and eight days. In his first edict he recalled all exiles. Thus the apostle John too, freed by this general pardon, returned to Ephesus. Because, in his absence, he saw that the faith of the Church had been shaken by heretics, he immediately established it by setting down in his Gospel the eternity of the Word of God.

[A.M. 4069; A.D. 118.] Trajan, for 19 years, six months, and 15 days. The apostle John rested in peaceful death at Ephesus in the sixty-eighth year after the Lord’s passion and the ninety-eighth year of his own life.

While Trajan was stirring up persecution against the Christians, Simeon, also called Simon, son of Clopas and bishop of Jerusalem, was crucified. Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, was brought to Rome and handed over to wild beasts. Alexander, bishop of the city of Rome, was also crowned with martyrdom and buried at the seventh milestone from the city, on the Nomentan Way, where he had been beheaded.

Pliny Secundus of Novum Comum was regarded as a distinguished orator and historian; many works of his talent survive. The Pantheon at Rome, which Domitian had built, was burned by lightning. It received its name because the building itself is the dwelling place of all the gods.

The Jews, causing rebellions in various parts of the world, were struck down in a slaughter they deserved. Trajan greatly extended the boundaries of the Roman Empire, which after Augustus had been defended more than nobly enlarged.

[Col. 0548D] [A.M. 4090; A.D. 139.] Hadrian, son of Trajan’s cousin, for 21 years. Instructed by Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles, by Aristides of Athens, a man full of faith and wisdom, and by the envoy Serenus Granianus, through books composed on the Christian religion, he ordered by letter that Christians not be condemned without charges of crimes being brought against them.

He likewise subdued the Jews, who had rebelled for the second time, in a final massacre. He even took away their permission to enter Jerusalem, which he himself restored to an excellent condition by rebuilding its walls and ordered to be called Aelia after his own name.

He also built at Athens, as a highly learned man in both languages, a library of extraordinary workmanship. At Jerusalem, Marcus was the first Gentile to be appointed bishop, after those who had been Jewish ceased to hold office. There had been 15 of these, and they had presided from the Lord’s Passion for approximately 107 years.

[A.M. 4112; A.D. 161.] Antoninus, surnamed Pius, with his sons Aurelius and Lucius, for 22 years and three months. Justin the philosopher presented Antoninus with a book composed in defense of the Christian religion and made him well disposed toward Christians.

Not long afterward, when Crescens the Cynic stirred up persecution, Justin shed his blood for Christ at Rome under Pius, who was bishop. Hermes wrote the book called *The Shepherd*, which contains an angel’s command that Easter be celebrated on the Lord’s Day.

Polycarp came to Rome and corrected many who had recently been corrupted by the heretical teaching of Valentinus and Cerdo.

### [A. M. 4131. A.D. 180.]

Marcus Antoninus Verus, with his brother Lucius Aurelius Commodus, for nineteen years and one month. [Note: The numbers in the margin—4131, 4144, and 4145—are given according to Sichard, although the other printed editions and manuscripts have 4132, 4145, and 4146; but these numbers differ from the dates of the emperors by exactly one year.] These men were the first to administer the empire on equal terms, since until that time there had always been individual Augusti. They then waged war against the Parthians with remarkable courage and success. When persecution arose in Asia, Polycarp and Pionius suffered martyrdom; in Gaul also very many gloriously shed their blood for Christ. Not long afterward, too, a plague, the avenger of crimes, devastated many provinces far and wide, especially Italy and Rome. After the death of his brother Commodus, Antoninus made his own son Commodus his colleague in the kingdom. To the emperor Antoninus, Melito of Asia, bishop of Sardis, presented an *Apology for the Christians*. [Note: Lucius. Although Bede mentions Lucius here in the *Chronicle* after the death of Commodus, in the *Ecclesiastical History* he places him in the time of the brothers Verus and Commodus (Book I, chapter 4). In the *Chronicle* Bede follows Eusebius, according to whom Verus and Commodus the brothers began to reign in A.D. 162; Commodus died in A.D. 170; Eleutherus became pope in A.D. 177; Commodus the son became colleague in the kingdom in A.D. 178 and reigned alone in 181; Eleutherus died about A.D. 191. In the *Ecclesiastical History*, however, he follows Orosius. There Verus and Commodus begin to reign together in A.D. 156, and an entirely different chronological reckoning is established. I fear that any attempt to reconcile these calculations will have been fruitless. The order of the account concerning Lucius in this period of the *Chronicle* seems to favor the opinion that places Commodus the son in the position of Commodus the brother. If this is granted, then according to the calculation of this passage nothing prevents Lucius from having sent a letter to Eleutherus at the beginning of his pontificate; [Col. 0550D] but the wording of the account in the *Ecclesiastical History* requires the brother Commodus, just as its chronology allows Lucius to write to Eleutherus during the time of his brother. On this matter see more in *Ecclesiastical History* I, 4. Meanwhile, note that Bede is thought to have taken this history of Lucius from the *Liber pontificalis*. Concerning that book, besides Labbe, *Councils*, vol. I, and *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, see Lambecius, *Commentary on the Vienna Library*, Book II, p. 924, etc. Whatever its source, everyone agrees that Bede was the first to insert it into his *Chronicle*; after him Ado, Hermannus Contractus, and others published it in their own works.] Lucius, king of Britain, sent a letter to Eleutherus, bishop of Rome, and obtained his request to become a Christian. Apollinaris of Asia, at Hierapolis, and Dionysius of Corinth were regarded as distinguished bishops.

### [A. M. 4144. A.D. 193.]

Lucius Antoninus Commodus reigned thirteen years after the death of his father. He successfully waged war against the Germans; but in all other respects he was enslaved to luxury and obscenity, and displayed nothing resembling his father’s virtue or piety. Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, was regarded as eminent. The emperor Commodus ordered the head of the Colossus to be removed and the head of his own image to be placed upon it.

### [A. M. 4145. A.D. 194.]

Aelius Pertinax, six months. He was killed in the palace through the crime of Julianus the jurist; Severus defeated and killed Julianus at the Milvian Bridge in the seventh month after Julianus had begun to reign. Victor, the thirteenth bishop of Rome, issued widely circulated writings and decreed that Easter should be celebrated on the Lord’s Day, as his predecessor Eleutherus had also decreed, from the fifteenth day of the first month up to the twenty-first. Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, supporting his decrees, wrote against those who celebrated Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon, together with the other bishops who were present at the same council, a synodical and highly useful letter.

### [A. M. 4163. A.D. 212.]

[Note: Severus. Before Severus, Didius Salvius Julianus should have been placed. As Dio records, he reigned sixty-six days, or, according to Eutropius and Orosius, seven months; but in Bede’s judgment he was not important enough to be counted among the emperors.]

Severus Pertinax, eighteen years. [Note: So Sichard and the Basel and Cologne editions; but the manuscripts and the Paris edition have seventeen, and they are joined by the manuscripts of the *Ecclesiastical History*, except for only two manuscripts of lesser authority. Since Eusebius and other authors of the highest quality have eighteen, and the chronological sequence from Antoninus Pius to Severus seems to favor that number, I make no alteration.] Clement, presbyter of the Alexandrian Church, and Pantaenus, a Stoic philosopher, were regarded as highly eloquent in disputing the doctrine of our faith. Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem, and Theophilus of Caesarea, as well as Polycarp and Bachylus, bishops of the province of Asia, were regarded as distinguished. During a persecution against the Christians, very many throughout the various provinces, including Leonides, the father of Origen, were crowned with martyrdom. After Clodius Albinus, who had made himself Caesar in Gaul, was killed at Lyons, Severus transferred the war to Britain. There, to make the recovered provinces safer from barbarian incursions, he constructed a great ditch and a very strong wall, further fortified with frequent towers, for 132,000 paces from sea to sea, and died at York. Perpetua and Felicitas, at Carthage in Africa, were given to the beasts for Christ in the camp on the Nones of March.

[Note: The wall was 132 Roman miles long. It is necessary that there be an error here in the measurement of the wall, since the width of the island where the walls were placed does not admit so many thousands of paces in either direction. Bede, who lived near the inner wall, could not have been ignorant of this; but here he copied the Hieronymian Eusebius, in which the measurement of the wall was given as 132,000 paces, since the Greek has *σταδίοις χιλίοις*—“a thousand stadia”—which could not have been rendered by other numbers, namely eighty-two or thirty-two. The error, therefore, belongs to the authors, not to the manuscripts, as is commonly conjectured. The numerical letters C or L were neither omitted nor altered; rather, the Greek or Roman writers themselves wrote about a matter unknown to them, and Bede followed them too implicitly.]

### [A. M. 4170. A.D. 219.]

Antoninus, surnamed Caracalla, son of Severus, seven years. Alexander, bishop of Cappadocia, had come to Jerusalem out of a desire to visit the holy places while Narcissus, bishop of that city, was still alive, a man of extremely advanced age; and Alexander himself was there ordained bishop, the Lord revealing that this ought to be done. Tertullian the African, son of a proconsular centurion, was celebrated in the speech of all the Churches.

### [A. M. 4171. A.D. 220.]

Macrinus, one year. Abgarus, a holy man, reigned at Edessa, according to Africanus. Macrinus, together with his son Diadumenian, with whom he had seized the empire, was killed in a military revolt at Archelais.

### [A. M. 4175. A.D. 224.]

Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, four years. In Palestine the city of Nicopolis was founded; it had previously been called Emmaus, and Julius Africanus, the writer of chronological history, undertook its embassy with energetic advocacy. This is the Emmaus which the Lord, after his resurrection, graciously sanctified by entering it, as Luke relates. Hippolytus, bishop and author of many little works, brought the canon of times that he had written down to this point. He also discovered a sixteen-year cycle of Easter, thereby giving Eusebius the occasion to compose a nineteen-year cycle concerning the same feast.

### [A. M. 4858. A.D. 237.]

Aurelius Alexander, thirteen years. He was exceptionally devoted to his mother Mammea and for that reason beloved by everyone. Urban, bishop of Rome, led many noblemen to faith in Christ and to martyrdom. Origen was regarded as famous at Alexandria, indeed throughout the whole world. Finally, Mammea, Alexander’s mother, arranged to hear him and received him at Antioch with the highest honor.

### [A. M. 4191. A.D. 240.]

Maximinus, three years. He persecuted the priests and clerics of the Churches—that is, their teachers—especially on account of the Christian household of Alexander, whom he had succeeded, and of his mother Mammea, or above all because of the presbyter Origen. Pontianus and Antherus, bishops of the city of Rome, were crowned with martyrdom and buried in the cemetery of Callistus.

### [A. M. 4197. A.D. 246.]

Gordian, six years. Julius Africanus was regarded as eminent among ecclesiastical writers. In the *Chronicles* that he composed, he reports that he hastened to Alexandria, summoned by the celebrated reputation of Heraclas, whom rumor declared to be highly learned in both sacred and philosophical studies and in every branch of Greek learning. [Note: *In the Chronicles.* See the principal fragments of these *Chronicles* in Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, edited confusedly by Scaliger, but somewhat more distinctly by Goar in George the Syncellus’s *Chronography*.] [Note: So Jerome (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*), not “Heraclia,” as some have it.] Origen instructed in divine philosophy Theodore, surnamed Gregory, and Athenodorus, young brothers who later became highly distinguished bishops of Pontus.

### [A. M. 4204. A.D. 253.]

Philip, with his son Philip, seven years. He was the first of all the emperors to be a Christian. In the third year of his reign, the thousandth year from the founding of Rome was completed; thus this anniversary year, the most splendid of all those that had gone before, was celebrated by a Christian emperor with magnificent games. Origen replied in eight books to a certain Epicurean philosopher, Celsus, who had written books against us. To put it briefly, Origen was so industrious in writing that Jerome remembers, in one place, having read six thousand of his books. [Note: “In one place.” Jerome, *Apology against Rufinus*, Book II, has these words: “I do not want you to say what I have read, stated in a Catholic manner, about these same books in other passages of the same author, lest you send me to the six thousand books of his, which you accuse blessed Pope Epiphanius of having read.”] [Note: Most manuscripts have five thousand, but the Westminster manuscript and Jerome himself, in the passage cited below, have six thousand.]

### [A. M. 4205. A.D. 254.]

Decius, one year and three months. After he had killed Philip the father and Philip the son, he began a persecution against the Christians out of hatred for them. In it Fabian was crowned with martyrdom in the city of Rome and left the episcopal see to Cornelius, who himself was also crowned with martyrdom. Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem, was killed at Caesarea in Palestine, and Babylas at Antioch. This persecution, however, as Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, reports, did not begin by order of the emperor but, he says, a full year before the imperial edicts, through the agency of a minister of demons named Divinus in our city, who stirred up the superstitious crowd against us. [Note: “He says.” See these words in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI, 41.]

### [A. M. 4207. A.D. 256.]

Gallus, with his son Volusianus, two years and four months. Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, speaks of this reign as follows:
