> “But Gallus was unable either to see or to avoid the evil of Decius; rather, he stumbled against the same stone of offense. When his kingdom was flourishing at the beginning and everything was turning out according to his wishes, he persecuted the holy men who were praying to the supreme God for the peace of his kingdom. With them he drove away both his prosperity and his peace.”

Origen died before completing his seventieth year and was buried in the city of Tyre. Cornelius, bishop of Rome, at the request of a certain matron named Lucina, secretly removed the bodies of the apostles from the catacombs. He placed Paul’s body on the Ostian Way, where Paul had been beheaded, and Peter’s near the place where Peter had been crucified, among the bodies of holy bishops, in the temple of Apollo on the Golden Mount, in the Vatican, at Nero’s palace, on the third day before the Kalends of July. [Note: The printed editions have *Aurelio*, incorrectly, and therefore also placed *aureo* in the margin.]

### [A. M. 4222. A.D. 271.]

Valerian, with his son Gallienus, fifteen years. When he had begun a persecution against the Christians, he was immediately captured by Sapor, king of the Persians, and there, deprived of his eyes, grew old in miserable slavery. Consequently Gallienus, terrified by so clear a judgment of God, restored peace to our people; yet, whether because of his own guilt or his father’s war against God, he suffered countless losses to the Roman kingdom from the barbarians who rose against it. During this persecution Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, whose most learned little works survive, was crowned with martyrdom. His deacon Pontius, who endured exile with him until the day of his martyrdom, left an excellent volume about his life and passion. Theodorus, whom we mentioned above, surnamed Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, shone with great glory for his miracles. One of these was that, so that there might be sufficient space for building a church, he moved a mountain by his prayers. Stephen and Xistus, bishops of Rome, suffered martyrdom.

### [A. M. 4224. A.D. 273.]

Claudius, one year and nine months. He defeated the Goths, who for fifteen years had been laying waste to Illyricum and Macedonia. For this reason a golden shield was placed for him in the senate-house and a golden statue on the Capitol. [Note: This is the true name in Bede’s source, Jerome (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*), not Marcion, as Bede’s manuscripts corruptly have it; therefore Ado restored Malchion.] Malchion, a highly eloquent presbyter of the Church of Antioch, since he had taught rhetoric in that same city, disputed against Paul of Samosata, who, while bishop of Antioch, maintained as doctrine that Christ had been merely a man of common nature. Notaries recorded the debate, which survives to this day. [Note: “Survives to this day.” So Jerome (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*) wrote in his own time. Today that dialogue no longer survives, although the Byzantine Leontius quotes certain passages from it in Book III *Against Nestorius*. *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. IX.]

### [A. M. 4229. A.D. 278.]

Aurelian, five years and six months. After he had begun a persecution against us, lightning fell before him, greatly terrifying those who stood around; not long afterward he was killed by soldiers halfway along the road between Constantinople and Heraclea, at an old paved place called Caenophrurium. [Note: Most manuscripts have “at the place of Caenophrurium,” but with the sense mutilated; Sichard supplied *loco*, disregarding the relative clause.] Eutychianus, bishop of Rome, was crowned with martyrdom and buried in the cemetery of Callistus. He himself also buried 313 martyrs with his own hand.

### [A. M. 4230. A.D. 279.]

Tacitus, six months. After he was killed in Pontus, Florianus obtained the empire and held it for eighty-eight days; he was then killed at Tarsus. Anatolius, an Alexandrian by birth and bishop of Laodicea in Syria, learned in the disciplines of the philosophers, was celebrated for his extensive writings. The greatness of his intellect can be recognized most clearly from the book he composed on Easter and from his ten books on the foundations of arithmetic. [Note: “On Easter.” See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VII, 23, and Aegidius Bucherius, *On the Doctrine of Time*.] [Note: Bede’s manuscripts add here: “The insane heresy of the Manichaeans arose in these times,” which we have explained below.]

### [A. M. 4236. A.D. 285.]

Probus, six years and four months. He completely liberated Gaul, which had long been occupied by barbarians, through many severe battles, finally destroying the enemies. [Note: “Secondly.” In this year the epochs of many peoples have been heaped together without any event corresponding to them. “It was the year …” he says. But what year was this, marked by so many chronological notices more than others? Nothing is said here, and therefore Baronius lightly passes over the passage, since, he says, it contributes nothing to the ecclesiastical chronology calculated from the years of Christ (*Annals*, year 280). Indeed, it does contribute something, and something of no small importance. In the preceding period we had: “The insane heresy of the Manichaeans arose in these times. All the cities everywhere judged that its destruction should be entrusted to perpetual memory, and each city inscribed it in its public books according to its own era.” Eusebius, whom Bede explicitly cites here, left an account of this event in the following order: “In the second year of Probus, which according to the Antiochene reckoning was year 325, according to the Tyrians 402, according to the Laodiceans 324, according to the Edessenes 588, and according to the Ascalonites 380, the insane heresy of the Manichaeans arose as a common evil of the human race.” The copyists of Eusebius first published this clause about the Manichaeans as a separate entry; afterward Bede’s copyists transferred it to the preceding period under Tacitus. Scaliger perceived this and corrected the punctuation, but not the wording completely. I have restored both, as above in the text. It should further be noted that Bede added to Eusebius’s epochs, on his own authority, the Hebrew jubilee. As for the epochs placed here: the Antiochenes reckoned their years from the first year of Julius Caesar; the Tyrians from an uncertain epoch around A.M. 3829; the Laodiceans from the second year of Julius Caesar; the Edessenes from the first year of the Seleucids, A.M. 3[.....]42 [see Bede at year 3669]; and the Ascalonites from A.M. 3851, from an equally uncertain epoch.]

In the second year of this reign—which, as we read in the *Chronicles* of Eusebius, was year 325 according to the Antiochenes, 402 according to the Tyrians, 324 according to the Laodiceans, 588 according to the Edessenes, and 380 according to the Ascalonites, while according to the Hebrews it was the beginning of the eighty-sixth jubilee, signifying the year 4,250—the insane heresy of the Manichaeans arose as a common evil of the human race. Archelaus, bishop of Mesopotamia, composed in the Syriac language a book of the disputation that he held against Manichaeus, who had come out of Persia. Many people possess it in a Greek translation. [Note: “It has been translated.” Fragments of it may be seen in Cyril of Jerusalem (*Catechetical Lectures*), Socrates (*Ecclesiastical History* I, 22), Henri Valois, at the end of his annotations (p. 197), and Epiphanius (*Against Heresies* 66).]

### [A. M. 4238. A.D. 287.]

Carus, with his sons Carinus and Numerianus, two years. Gaius shone as bishop of the Roman Church; he suffered martyrdom under Diocletian. Pierius, a presbyter of Alexandria, taught the people with great distinction under Bishop Theonas and displayed such elegance in his discourse and in his various treatises, which survive to this day, that he was called “the younger Origen.” He was a man of remarkable frugality and a lover of voluntary poverty; after the persecution he spent the remainder of his life at Rome. [Note: “Treatises.” The treatises of Pierius do not survive.]

### [A. M. 4258. A.D. 307.]

[Note: Diocletian … Carausius, Allectus, Asclepiodotus … Alban, Aaron, and Julius, martyrs. *Ecclesiastical History* I, 6–7.]

Diocletian, with Herculius Maximian, twenty years. Carausius assumed the purple and occupied Britain. Narseus, king of the Persians, made war upon the East. The Quinquegentiani laid waste Africa. [Note: The Quinquegentiani were named from five cities of Libya: Cyrene, Ptolemais, Arsinoe, also called Teuchira, Darnis, and Berenice. Scaliger, in Eusebius, p. 243.] Achilleus seized Egypt. Because of this, Constantius and Galerius Maximian were taken into the government as Caesars. Constantius married Theodora, the stepdaughter of Herculius, by whom he later had six children, the brothers of Constantine; Galerius married Valeria, the daughter of Diocletian. After ten years, Britain was recovered by the prefect of the praetorium, Asclepiodotus. In the nineteenth year of Diocletian, he himself in the East and Maximian Herculius in the West ordered the churches to be devastated and the Christians to be harassed and killed.

In the second year of the persecution, Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan laid down the purple. Nevertheless, the persecution once begun did not cease raging until the seventh year of Constantine. Constantius, a man of the greatest gentleness and courtesy, died at York in the sixteenth year of his reign. This persecution burned so cruelly and continuously that within one month 17,000 martyrs are found to have suffered for Christ. Having crossed even the shores of the Ocean, it condemned Alban, Aaron, and Julius of Britain, together with many other men and women, to a blessed death. During it Pamphilus the presbyter also suffered, a close associate of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, who himself set out Pamphilus’s life in three books.

### [A. M. 4259. A.D. 308.]

In the third year of the persecution, in which Constantius also died, Maximinus and Severus were made Caesars by Galerius Maximian. Maximinus added his sorceries and debaucheries to the persecutions of the Christians. At that time Peter, bishop of Alexandria, suffered together with many Egyptian bishops; so too did Lucian, a presbyter of Antioch distinguished in character, self-control, and learning. Timothy also suffered at Rome on the tenth day before the Kalends of July.

### [A. M. 4290. A.D. 339.]

[Note: The printed editions have 4288, incorrectly.]

[Note: Constantine, son of Constantius by his concubine Helena … in Britain. Emperor. The Council of Nicaea. See *Ecclesiastical History* I, 8.]

Constantine, son of Constantius by his concubine Helena, was created emperor in Britain and reigned thirty years and ten months. From the fourth year of the persecution, Maxentius, son of Herculius Maximian, was called Augustus at Rome. Licinius, husband of Constantine’s sister Constantia, was created emperor at Carnuntum. Constantine was transformed from a persecutor into a Christian.

At the Council of Nicaea the Catholic faith was set forth, in the 636th year after Alexander, [Note: “After Alexander.” That is, after the first year of the Seleucids, which was A.M. 4277, 126 years before Christ, according to Bede.] on the nineteenth day of the month Desius according to the Greeks, which is the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Paulinus and Julianus, illustrious men. [Note: Bede’s manuscripts have ten, but the authoritative records of the Council of Nicaea, both at the council itself and at the Council of Chalcedon, act 2, have thirteen; the fact that the nineteenth day of the month Desius coincides with it also demonstrates that thirteen is correct.] [Note: The Westminster and Wilkins manuscripts have four hundred, as though the letters were numerical signs, whereas they are actually only abbreviations of the title “most illustrious men,” appended to the names of the consuls.]

Constantine built at Rome, where he was baptized, the basilica of blessed John the Baptist, which was called the Constantinian. He likewise built a basilica for blessed Peter in the temple of Apollo, and another for blessed Paul, surrounding the bodies of both with Cyprian bronze five feet thick. He also built the basilica in the Sessorian palace, called Jerusalem, where he placed a piece of the wood of the Lord’s cross. He built as well the basilica of the holy martyr Agnes at the request of his daughter, together with a baptistery in the same place, where his sister Constantia was also baptized with her daughter Augusta. He built a basilica for blessed Lawrence the martyr on the Tiburtine Way, in the Veranian estate. He built another on the Lavican Way, between the two laurel trees, for the blessed martyrs Peter and Marcellinus, as well as a mausoleum where he placed his mother in a purple sarcophagus. He built another basilica at the city of Ostia, near the harbor of the city of Rome, for the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and John the Baptist. He also built a basilica in the Albanian city for Saint John the Baptist, and another in the city of Naples.

Constantine restored Drepanum, a city of Bithynia, in honor of the martyr Lucian, who was buried there, and renamed it Helenopolis after his mother. He also established a city bearing his own name in Thrace and intended it to be the seat of the Roman Empire and the capital of the entire East. He further decreed that the temples of the pagans should be closed without any slaughter of human beings.

### [A. M. 4314. A.D. 363.]

[Note: From this year up to A.M. 4180, the first Paris edition and the better manuscripts precede the Basel and Cologne editions in their chronological calculation by one year, correctly.]

Constantius, with his brothers Constantine and Constans, twenty-four years, five months, and thirteen days. James of Nisibis was recognized as a bishop; through his prayers the city was often delivered from danger. The Arian impiety, supported by the protection of King Constantius, first persecuted Athanasius and then all bishops who did not belong to its party through exile, imprisonment, and various forms of affliction. Maximinus, bishop of Trier, was regarded as distinguished. When Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, was being sought by Constantius for punishment, Maximinus received him with honor. Antony the monk died in the desert at the age of 105. The relics of the apostle Timothy were brought to Constantinople.

When Constantius entered Rome, the bones of the apostle Andrew and of the evangelist Luke were received by the people of Constantinople with extraordinary enthusiasm. [Note: “Rome.” It is unusual to call Constantinople “Rome” without an added epithet. Nevertheless, I do not say that “New” is missing here, but that it must be supplied from the sense alone. Jerome (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Luke) says that the bones of Andrew were transferred from Patras to Constantinople in the twentieth year of Constantius; yet in the *Chronicle*, which for these times is not Eusebius’s but Jerome’s, he places it in the twenty-first year.] Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, who had been driven into exile in Phrygia by the Arians, returned to Gaul after presenting a book on his behalf to Constantius at Constantinople.

### [A. M. 4316. A.D. 365.]

Julian, two years and eight months. Julian, having turned to the worship of idols, persecuted the Christians. At Sebaste, a city of Palestine, pagans broke into the tomb of John the Baptist, scattered his bones, and then, after collecting them again and burning them, scattered them farther afield. But by God’s providence certain monks from Jerusalem arrived. Mingling with those who were gathering the remains, they carried away whatever they could and brought it to their father Philip. He immediately sent these things through his deacon Julian to the chief pontiff, Athanasius, for he considered it beneath himself to preserve so great a treasure by his own vigilance. Athanasius, having received them in the presence of a few witnesses, enclosed them beneath a hollowed-out wall of the sacristy and preserved them, through the prophetic Spirit, for the benefit of a future generation. His prediction was fulfilled under the emperor Theodosius by Theophilus, bishop of that same city, who, after destroying the shrine of Serapis, consecrated a church of Saint John there.

### [A. M. 4317. A.D. 366.]

Jovian, eight months. A synod was held at Antioch by Meletius and his followers, in which, after rejecting the *homoousion* (“of the same substance”) and the *anomoion* (“unlike”), they defended the Macedonian doctrine of the *homoiousion* (“of similar substance”) as a position midway between them. [Note: This is literally how Bede’s manuscripts read, and Scaliger supports them, affirming that all Jerome’s manuscripts agree in the same reading. Bede’s printed editions, however, have *ὀμοουσίω καὶ ὁμουσίω … ὁμοιούσιον*—“of the same substance and of the same substance … of similar substance”—incorrectly.] [Note: “And the unlike.” On this see Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History* III, 25, and Sozomen, VI, 4; also Socrates III, 10.]

Jovian, warned by the downfall of his predecessor Constantius, requested Athanasius in honorable and most dutiful letters, and from him received the formulation of the faith and the method of arranging the Churches. But death, arriving too soon, spoiled his pious and joyful beginnings.

### [A. M. 4328. A.D. 377.]

Valentinian, with his brother Valens, eleven years. Apollinaris of Laodicea, a bishop, composed writings on many aspects of our religion; afterward, having deviated from the faith, he established the heresy named after him. Damasus, bishop of Rome, built a basilica beside the theater for Saint Lawrence, and another in the catacombs, where the holy bodies of the apostles Peter and Paul had lain. At that place he adorned the very *platonium* where the holy bodies had lain with verses. [Note: The first Paris edition has *platoniam*, correctly; the other editions and manuscripts have *platomam*.]

Valens, baptized by Eudoxius, the Arian bishop, persecuted our people. Gratian, the son of Valentinian, was made emperor at Amiens in the third year of his father’s reign. At Constantinople the shrine of the Apostles was dedicated. After the late death of Auxentius, when Ambrose had been made bishop at Milan, all Italy was converted to the right faith. Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, died.

### [A. M. 4332. A.D. 381.]

Valens, with Gratian and Valentinian, the sons of his brother Valentinian, four years. Valens issued a law requiring monks to serve in the army and ordered those who refused to be killed with clubs. The race of the Huns, long shut away among inaccessible mountains, burst forth in sudden fury against the Goths and expelled them, scattered and thrown into confusion, from their ancient homes. The Goths crossed the Danube and, fleeing, were received by Valens without laying down their arms. Soon, through the greed of the commander Maximus, they were compelled by hunger to rebel; after defeating the army of Valens, they spread throughout Thrace and filled everything alike with slaughter, fires, and plunder.

### [A. M. 4338. A.D. 387.]

Gratian, with his brother Valentinian, six years. Theodosius, created emperor by Gratian, defeated those great Scythian peoples—the Alans, Huns, and Goths—in many great battles. The Arians, unable to tolerate his concord, abandoned the Churches that they had held by force for forty years. A synod of 150 Fathers was assembled in the imperial city against Macedonius, under Damasus, bishop of Rome. Theodosius made his son Arcadius his colleague in the empire.

Beginning in the second year of Gratian, when he himself was consul for the fifth time together with Theodosius, Theophilus wrote a calculation of Easter. [Note: All Bede’s manuscripts have this six times, but incorrectly, since Gratian was consul only five times.] [Note: Theophilus of Alexandria. See fragments in Theodoret, *Dialogue* 3.]

Maximus was indeed a vigorous and upright man, worthy of the rank of Augustus, had he not risen through tyranny against his sworn oath. Almost unwillingly, he was made emperor by the army in Britain, crossed into Gaul, and there, having ensnared Gratian Augustus by deceit, killed him at Lyons and expelled his brother Valentinian from Italy. Valentinian nevertheless paid a most just penalty of exile together with his mother Justina, because he had both polluted himself with the Arian heresy and harassed Ambrose, the foremost stronghold of the Catholic faith, with a treacherous siege. He did not abandon his wicked undertaking until the incorrupt relics of the blessed martyrs Gervasius and Protasius were brought forth, God revealing them.

[Note: Maximus in Britain, unwillingly … Gratian. See *Ecclesiastical History* I, 9.]

### [A. M. 4349. A.D. 398.]

Theodosius, who, while Gratian was alive, had already ruled the East for six years, reigned eleven years after Gratian’s death. He and Valentinian, whom he had graciously received after Valentinian’s expulsion from Italy, killed the tyrant Maximus at the third milestone from Aquileia. [Note: Maximus had stripped Britain … the tribes of the Scots and Picts overwhelm the island. See *Ecclesiastical History* I, 12.]

Because Maximus had stripped Britain of almost all its armed young men and military resources—those who followed the traces of his tyranny into Gaul never returned home—the most savage peoples from across the sea, seeing the island abandoned by soldiers and defenders, the Scots from the northwest and the Picts from the north, came and oppressed it for many years after laying it waste and plundering it. Jerome, interpreter of sacred history, brought the book that he wrote on the illustrious men of the Church up to the fourteenth year of the entire reign of Theodosius.

### [A. M. 4362. A.D. 411.]

Arcadius, son of Theodosius, with his brother Honorius, thirteen years. The bodies of the prophets Habakkuk and Micah were revealed through divine revelation. The Goths attacked Italy; the Vandals and Alans attacked Gaul. Innocent, bishop of Rome, dedicated a basilica to the most blessed martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, through the devotion expressed in the will of a certain distinguished woman named Vestina. [Note: Pelagius the Briton. See *Ecclesiastical History* I, 10.] Pelagius the Briton attacked the grace of God.

[A.M. 4377; A.D. 426.] Honorius, together with Theodosius the Younger, his brother’s son, for fifteen years. [Note: [Col. 0559D] Alaric invaded Rome. See Ecclesiastical History, I, 11.] Alaric, king of the Goths, invaded Rome and burned part of it in a conflagration on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, in the 1164th year of its foundation; and on the sixth day after he had entered it, having plundered the city, he departed. [Note: [Col. 0559C] The Cologne edition, in the margin, reads “on the third”; Ado and Paulus Aemilius, book I, agree with it, but it is contrary to all Bede manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0559D] The seventh of Honorius. Baronius places this revelation in the twenty-first year of Honorius and says that an error has crept into this passage of Bede because it places it in Honorius’s seventh year; but do not suppose that the difference is of so many years. For in this period Bede does not count Honorius’s years from the beginning of his reign, but only from the time when he reigned with Theodosius: “Honorius,” he says, “with Theodosius the Younger,” etc. Thus Baronius himself joins the eighth year of Theodosius here to the twenty-first of Honorius; that is, Bede places under Honorius’s name the years during which Honorius and Theodosius held the empire together, while Baronius places them under Theodosius’s. What remains of the difference is only one year, arising not from any error but from a variation in reckoning. This is all the more worthy of notice because, in the imperial years of these times, not Baronius alone but other learned men also have met with human error.] Lucian, a presbyter, to whom God revealed, in the seventh year of the reign of the emperor Honorius, the place of the tomb and relics of the blessed protomartyr Stephen, and of Gamaliel and Nicodemus, who are mentioned in the Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles, committed that revelation to writing in the Greek language for the benefit of all the Churches. [Note: [Col. 0560C] In the Greek language. See the Greek fragments of this revelation in Eustratius of Constantinople (*On the Life of the Dead*, translated by Leo Allatius), and in Photius (171). You have it complete in Latin in Baronius (A.D. 415).] Avitus the presbyter, a Spaniard by birth, translated this revelation into Latin, and, with a letter of his own added, gave it to the Westerners through the presbyter Orosius. Orosius himself, reaching the holy places—where Augustine had sent him to Jerome to learn about the nature of the soul—received the relics of the blessed Stephen and, returning to his homeland, was the first to bring them into the West.

[Note: [Col. 0560D] The Britons appeal for assistance . . . . . construct a stone wall. Bede relates this at greater length in *Ecclesiastical History*, I, 12, but antiquarians have labored greatly there over assigning the date. Here the place in the *Chronicle* sets the matter more clearly before our eyes. For here we have definite chronological indications that confine these events within a very narrow span. It is therefore evident that both embassies of the Britons to the Romans mentioned in the twelfth chapter of the *History* occurred not only within that fifteen-year period of the *Chronicle* during which Honorius and Theodosius reigned together, but also within the seventh year of Honorius, when the relics of Stephen were discovered, and the twelfth year of Honorius, when Jerome died. These years, marked off at either end and distinguished by a special sign, leave only a complete four-year interval—namely, below the year 414 and above the year 419 of the common era, although the years are arranged somewhat differently in Bede’s *Chronicle*, namely from A.D. 418 to A.D. 423.]

The Britons, unable to endure the attacks of the Scots and Picts, sent to Rome and, promising their submission, demanded aid against the enemy. A legion was immediately sent, which cut down a great multitude of the barbarians and drove the rest from the borders of Britain. As it was about to return home, it ordered its allies to construct, for keeping off the enemy, a wall across the island between the two seas. Built without an expert master craftsman, more of turf than of stone, it did no good to those who made it. For as soon as the Romans had departed, the former enemy, transported in ships, like a ripe harvest before them, cut down, trampled, and devoured everything in their path.

Again the Romans were asked for aid, and they hastened over, drove the slaughtered enemy beyond the seas, and, joining with the Britons, placed between the cities that had been built there out of fear of the enemy a wall solidly constructed of stone, not—as before—of earth and dust, extending from sea to sea. They also established towers at intervals on the southern shore of the sea, because an enemy was feared from that direction as well; and thus they bade farewell to their allies as though they would never return.

Boniface, bishop of Rome, built an oratory in the cemetery of Saint Felicitas and adorned her tomb and that of Saint Silvanus.

The presbyter Jerome died in the twelfth year of Honorius, on the day before the Kalends of October, in the ninety-first year of his age.

[A.M. 4103; A.D. 452.] Theodosius the Younger, son of Arcadius, for twenty-six years. Valentinian the Younger, son of Constantius, was made emperor at Ravenna. His mother Placidia was given the title Augusta.

The savage nation of the Vandals, Alans, and Goths crossed from Spain into Africa and defiled everything with sword, fire, and plunder, as well as with Arian impiety. But the blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo and the outstanding teacher of all the Churches, so as not to see the ruin of his own city, departed to the Lord in the third month of its siege, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, having lived seventy-six years and having completed nearly forty years in the clerical and episcopal office. At that time, after capturing Carthage, the Vandals also devastated Sicily. Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum, mentions this captivity in a letter that he wrote to Pope Leo concerning the calculation of Easter. [Note: [Col. 0561D] Lilybaean. A bishop in Sicily. See his letter in Bucherius (p. 75).]

Palladius, ordained by Pope Celestine, was sent in the eighth year of Theodosius as the first bishop to the Scots who believed in Christ. [Note: [Col. 0561D] Palladius . . . . . a letter to Aetius. *Ecclesiastical History*, I, 13.] When the Roman army withdrew from Britain, the Scots and Picts, learning that it would not return, came back themselves and seized the whole northern part of the island as far as the wall, in place of the native inhabitants. Without delay, after killing, capturing, and putting to flight the guards of the wall, and even breaking through the wall itself, the savage plunderer roamed within it.

A letter filled with tears and distress was sent to Aetius, a man of Roman power and three-times consul, in the twenty-third year of the reign of the emperor Theodosius, asking for assistance, but none was obtained. Meanwhile a dreadful and notorious famine afflicted the refugees. Compelled by it, some surrendered to the enemy, while others bravely resisted from the mountains, caves, and wooded places, inflicting slaughter upon the enemy.

The Scots returned home, though they were to return again after not much time. The Picts occupied the farthest part of the island, where they were to remain both then and thereafter. The famine mentioned above was followed by great abundance of crops; abundance by luxury and negligence; negligence by a most virulent plague; and then, more fiercely still, by the blow of new enemies, namely the English. The Britons, acting with unanimous counsel with their king Vortigern, chose to invite them as defenders of the homeland, but, once received, soon found them to be attackers and conquerors. [Note: [Col. 0561D] Vortigern . . . . . the Saxons. *Ecclesiastical History*, I, 14–15.]

Xistus, bishop of Rome, built the basilica of Saint Mary, the Mother of the Lord, which in ancient times was called by the surname of Liber.

Eudoxia, wife of the emperor Theodosius, returned from Jerusalem, bringing with her the relics of the most blessed Stephen, the first martyr, which are venerated after being placed in the basilica of Saint Lawrence.

The brothers Blaedla and Attila, kings of many peoples, ravaged Illyricum and Thrace.

[A.M. 4410; A.D. 459.] Martian and Valentinian, for seven years. The nation of the Angles, or of the Saxons, arrived in Britain in three longships. When news was carried home that their voyage had prospered, a stronger army was sent, which, joining the first arrivals, initially drove back the enemies against whom it had been summoned. It then turned its weapons against its allies and brought almost the entire island, from its eastern region to its western, under its control by fire or sword, inventing as a pretext that the Britons were not providing sufficient pay to those fighting on their behalf. [Note: [Col. 0561D] Most manuscripts read *quos petebat* (“those whom he was seeking”), and the reading is not inappropriate; nevertheless the other reading is preferable, and is also confirmed by Paris. 1. West and Wilk., with the words altered as far as could be done through the copyists’ ignorance.]

John the Baptist revealed his head to two Eastern monks who had come to Jerusalem for prayer, near the former dwelling of King Herod. It was afterward brought to Emesa, a city of Phoenicia, and honored with worthy veneration. [Note: [Col. 0561D] Emesa. In Adonis, Emessa, an archiepiscopal city under the patriarch of Antioch, on the river Orontes, between Laodicea to the south and Arethusa to the north.]

The Pelagian heresy disturbed the faith of the Britons. [Note: [Col. 0562D] Pelagius . . . Saints Germanus and Lupus. *Ecclesiastical History*, I, 17.] Seeking assistance from the Gallican bishops, they received Germanus, bishop of the Church of Auxerre, and Lupus, bishop of Troyes, both bishops of apostolic grace, as defenders of the faith. The bishops confirmed the faith by the word of truth and by signs of miracles. They also, by divine power, repelled the war undertaken at that time by the Saxons and Picts against the Britons, who had joined their forces. [Note: [Col. 0562D] The war of the Saxons and Picts in the time of Saints Germanus and Lupus. *Ecclesiastical History*, I, 20.] When Germanus himself had become commander in the war, he turned the savage enemies to flight—not with the blast of a trumpet, but with the cry of “Alleluia,” raised to heaven by the voice of the entire army. [Note: [Col. 0562D] The manuscripts of Basel and Cologne mutilate the sense by omitting “with a cry.”]

Afterward, when he reached Ravenna and was received with the highest reverence by Valentinian and Placidia, he departed to Christ. His body was carried to Auxerre in an honorable procession, accompanied by works of miraculous power.

Aetius the patrician, the great salvation of the Western state and once the terror of King Attila, was killed by Valentinian. With him the Western empire fell, and to this day it has not been able to recover.

[A.M. 4427; A.D. 476.] Leo, for seventeen years. On behalf of the Tome of Chalcedon, he sent throughout the world individual letters to the orthodox bishops, asking each of them to write back what he thought about that Tome. Their replies concerning the true incarnation of Christ were so harmonious that all seemed to have been written at one time and dictated by one person.

Theodoret, bishop of the city which, having been founded by Cyrus, king of the Persians, bore the name Cyrus, wrote against Eutyches and Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, who denied that Christ had human flesh, concerning the true incarnation of the Lord and Savior. He also wrote an Ecclesiastical History from the end of Eusebius’s books down to his own time—that is, to the reign of this Leo, under whom he also died. [Note: [Col. 0562D] Victorius. In Bucherius (*On the Doctrine of Time*).]

At the command of Pope Hilary, Victorius wrote a Paschal cycle of 532 years.

[A.M. 4444; A.D. 493.] Zeno, for seventeen years. The body of the apostle Barnabas, and the Gospel of Matthew written in his own hand, were discovered through a revelation made by Barnabas himself.

King Odoacer of the Goths took possession of Rome, which from that time onward their kings held for a long period. After Theodoric, son of Triarius, died, another Theodoric, surnamed Valamer, assumed the kingdom of the Goths. He ravaged both Macedonias and Thessaly, and, setting fire to many places of the royal city, also seized Italy as an enemy.

Honoric, the Arian king of the Vandals in Africa, exiled and scattered more than 334 Catholic bishops, closed their churches, and subjected the people to various punishments—indeed, countless ones—cutting off their hands and tongues. Yet he could not take away the power of speech from the Catholic confession.

The Britons, under the leadership of Ambrosius Aurelianus, a modest man who alone, perhaps, of the Roman people had survived the slaughter of the Saxons, his parents—clothed in purple—having been killed in the same massacre, challenged their victorious nation to battle and defeated it. From that time, now one side and now the other held the victory, until a more powerful newcomer took possession of the entire island over a long period. [Note: [Col. 0563D] Ambrosius Aurelianus. *Ecclesiastical History*, I, 16.]

[A.M. 4472; A.D. 521.] Anastasius, for twenty-eight years. Thrasamund, king of the Vandals, closed the Catholic churches and sent 220 bishops into exile in Sardinia.

Among the many works for the Churches that Pope Symmachus either built from their foundations or restored from antiquity, he constructed dwellings for the poor at Saint Peter’s, Saint Paul’s, and Saint Lawrence’s. Every year he also supplied money and clothing throughout Africa or Sardinia to the bishops who were in exile.

Anastasius, because he favored the heresy of Eutyches and persecuted the Catholics, perished by a thunderbolt from God.

[A.M. 4480; A.D. 329.] Justin the Elder, for eight years. [Note: [Col. 0563D] The Basel and Cologne editions have “nine,” but this is against the other manuscripts.] When John, pontiff of the Roman Church, came to Constantinople, crowds of people met him at the gate called the Golden Gate. In the sight of everyone, at the request of a blind man, he restored his sight.

When John later returned and reached Ravenna, Theodoric, moved by envy because Justin, the defender of Catholic devotion, had received him honorably, killed him and his companions by the sufferings of imprisonment. In that same year—that is, in the consulship of Probus the Younger—he had also killed the patrician Symmachus at Ravenna, and he himself died a sudden death there in the following year. His nephew Athalaric succeeded him in the kingdom.

Hilderic, king of the Vandals, ordered the bishops to return from exile and the churches to be restored, after seventy-four years of heretical profanation.

The abbot Benedict became renowned for the glory of his miracles, which the blessed Pope Gregory recorded in the book of the *Dialogues*. [Note: [Col. 0563D] The Westminster manuscript has “in the second book,” but it stands alone; it therefore seems to have been inserted by some reader.]

[A.M. 4518; A.D. 567.] Justinian, nephew of Justin through his sister, for thirty-eight years. The patrician Belisarius, sent by Justinian to Africa, destroyed the nation of the Vandals. Carthage was also recovered in the ninety-sixth year of its accession, after the Vandals had been defeated and expelled, and their king Gelismer had been captured and sent to Constantinople. [Note: [Col. 0564D] The Basel and Cologne editions have “97,” incorrectly and without manuscript authority. The marginal reading in those editions is “Geismer.”] [Note: [Col. 0563D] Gelismer. Hermannus Contractus, under the year 534, calls him Geilamer, adding that after several years he was made a count by Justinian and stationed on the frontiers of the Parthians to keep them in check.]

The body of Saint Antony the monk, discovered through divine revelation, was carried to Alexandria and buried in the church of the blessed John the Baptist.

Dionysius Exiguus wrote Paschal cycles, beginning with the year 532 from the Lord’s incarnation, which is the 248th year of Diocletian, after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, in which year the Justinian Code was promulgated to the world. [Note: [Col. 0563D] Dionysius Exiguus. See his two Paschal letters at the end of Petavius and Bucherius’s *On the Doctrine of Time*. For the remains of the Paschal cycles, see the *Chronicle* of Marianus Scotus; concerning his calculations, see Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 45—really chapter 47—and elsewhere.]

Victor, bishop of Capua, also wrote a book on Easter, in which he exposed the errors of Victorius. [Note: [Col. 0564D] Victor of Capua. See his fragments in Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 49—really chapter 51—and in the section on the spring equinox.]

[A.M. 4529; A.D. 578.] Justin the Younger, for eleven years. The patrician Narses defeated and killed Totila, king of the Goths, in Italy. Then, because of the Romans’ envy, he was accused before Justin and his wife Sophia of oppressing Italy, despite having labored much on behalf of the Romans against the Goths. He withdrew to Naples in Campania and wrote to the nation of the Lombards to come and take possession of Italy.

John, pontiff of the Roman Church, built and dedicated the church of the Apostles Philip and James, which his predecessor Pelagius had begun.

[A.M. 4536; A.D. 585.] Tiberius Constantine, for seven years. [Note: [Col. 0564D] Gregory the Apocrisiarius . . . . . *Exposition on Job* . . . . . the conviction of Eutychius. See *Ecclesiastical History*, II, 1.] Gregory, then an apocrisiarius in Constantinople and afterward bishop of Rome, composed books of exposition on Job. In the presence of Tiberius he convicted Eutychius, bishop of that city, of error concerning our resurrection. Indeed, the emperor himself, destroying Eutychius’s book on the resurrection with his own Catholic arguments, decided that it ought to be burned in the flames.

For Eutychius taught that our body, in the glory of that resurrection, would be intangible and subtler than winds and air, contrary to the Lord’s words: “Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have.”

The nation of the Lombards, accompanied by famine and pestilence, invaded all Italy and, as a destroyer, besieged Rome itself. At that time its king was Albuin.

[A.M. 4557; A.D. 606.] Maurice, for twenty-one years. Hermenegild, son of Leovigild, king of the Goths, was deprived by his Arian father of the insignia of kingship because of his unshakable confession of the Catholic faith. Cast into prison and fetters, he was finally struck on the head with an axe on the holy night of the Lord’s resurrection and entered the heavenly kingdom as king and martyr in place of an earthly kingdom.

As soon as his brother Reccared received the kingdom after their father, he converted the entire Gothic people over whom he ruled to the Catholic faith, at the urging of Leander, bishop of Seville, who had also instructed Hermenegild.

[Note: [Col. 0564D] Gregory converts the English. See *Ecclesiastical History*, I, 23; II, 1.] Gregory, pontiff of the Roman Church and an outstanding teacher, in the thirteenth year of Maurice’s reign and the thirteenth indiction, convened a synod of twenty-four bishops at the body of the blessed apostle Peter and issued decrees concerning the needs of the Church.

He also sent Augustine, Mellitus, and John, together with many other God-fearing monks, to Britain and converted the English to Christ. Aethelberht, promptly converted to the grace of Christ, together with the people of Kent whom he ruled and the neighboring provinces, endowed Augustine—his bishop and teacher—as well as the other holy bishops with episcopal sees.

The English peoples situated north of the River Humber, under the kings Aelle and Aethelfrith, had not yet heard the word of life. In the nineteenth year of Maurice, in the fourth indiction, Gregory wrote to Augustine and decreed that bishops of London and York, having received the pallium from the apostolic see, should also be metropolitans. [Note: [Col. 0565D] He decrees that they are to be metropolitans. See *Ecclesiastical History*, I, 29.] [Note: [Col. 0565D] “In the nineteenth.” The manuscripts in Bede’s *Chronicle* read “in the eighteenth”; but in *Ecclesiastical History*, I, 29, the letter of Pope Gregory concerning the establishment of metropolitans is dated to the nineteenth year of Maurice, the fourth indiction, and this is necessarily correct. Thus the thirteenth year of Maurice is also correctly called above the thirteenth indiction.]

[A.M. 4565; A.D. 614.] Phocas, for eight years. [Note: [Col. 0565D] Gregory departed. See *Ecclesiastical History*, II, 1.] In the second year of his reign, the eighth indiction, Pope Gregory departed to the Lord. At the request of Pope Boniface, he decreed that the see of the Roman and apostolic Church should be the head of all the Churches, because the Church of Constantinople was styling itself the first of all the Churches.

At the request of another Pope Boniface, he ordered that the ancient temple called the Pantheon, after its idolatrous pollution had been removed, should be made the church of the blessed ever-virgin Mary and of all the martyrs, so that where once the worship of all—not gods, but demons—had been conducted, there might thereafter be the commemoration of all the saints. [Note: [Col. 0565D] The Pantheon. See *Ecclesiastical History*, II, 4.]

The Persians, waging extremely serious wars against the Roman state, seized many Roman provinces and Jerusalem itself. Destroying the churches and profaning all sacred things, they carried away, among the ornaments of the places—whether belonging to saints or to public use—that they had taken, even the standard of the Lord’s cross.

[A.M. 4591; A.D. 610.] Heraclius, for twenty-six years. Anastasius the Persian, a monk, suffered a noble martyrdom for Christ. Born in Persia, he learned magical arts from his father as a boy; but when he learned the name of Christ from Christian captives, he immediately turned to him with his whole heart. Abandoning Persia, he sought Christ in Chalcedon and Hierapolis, and then went to Jerusalem. There, having received the grace of baptism, he entered, four miles from that city, the monastery of Abbot Anastasius. After living there according to the rule for seven years, he came to Caesarea in Palestine for the sake of prayer. He was captured by the Persians and endured many beatings for a long time amid prisons and chains under the judge Marzaban. At last he was sent to Persia, to their king Chosroes. The king had him beaten three times at intervals, and finally he was hanged by one hand for three hours of the day; then he was beheaded and completed his martyrdom with seventy other martyrs.

Soon afterward, a demoniac who put on his tunic was healed. Meanwhile the emperor Heraclius arrived with an army, defeated the Persians, and brought back the Christians who had been taken captive, rejoicing. The relics of the blessed martyr Anastasius were first brought to his own monastery and then to Rome, where they are venerated in the monastery of the blessed apostle Paul called *ad Aquas Salvias*.

In the sixteenth year of Heraclius’s reign, the fifteenth indiction, Aedwin, the most excellent king of the English, in Britain north of the Humber, received the word of salvation with his people through the preaching of Bishop Paulinus, whom the venerable archbishop Justus had sent from Kent. This occurred in the eleventh year of his reign, about 180 years, more or less, after the arrival of the English in Britain. He gave Paulinus the episcopal see at York. [Note: [Col. 0565D] Aedwin . . . . . Paulinus . . . . . York. *Ecclesiastical History*, II, 9.]

Indeed, as an omen of the faith and heavenly kingdom that were to come, the power of an earthly kingdom had also increased for that king, so that he brought under his rule all the regions of Britain inhabited by either English or Britons—something no English king before him had done.

At that time Pope Honorius rebuked by letter the error of the Quartodecimans that had arisen among the Scots concerning the observance of Easter. John also, who succeeded his successor Severinus, while he was still elected to the pontificate, wrote to them about the same Easter and about the Pelagian heresy that was reviving among them. [Note: [Col. 0566D] The letters of Popes Honorius and John to the Scots concerning Easter and Pelagius. *Ecclesiastical History*, II, 19.]

[A.M. 4593; A.D. 642.] [Note: [Col. 0566D] Heraclonas. In other authors, Heraclius Constantius or Constantine, his son by his former wife, follows. He is said to have been removed by poison by his stepmother Martina in the fourth month. After him came Heraclonas or Heracleonas with his mother Martina, for no more than six months; after him came Constans, whom Bede below calls Constantine, the son of Constantius or Constantine. Ado and Hermannus, however, follow Bede’s order and chronology.]

Heraclonas, with his mother Martina, for two years. Cyrus of Alexandria, Sergius, and Pyrrhus, bishops of the imperial city, reviving the heresy of the Acephali, taught as doctrine that in Christ there was one operation of divinity and humanity and one will.

Of these men, Pyrrhus came from Africa to Rome at that time, under Pope Theodore. With a repentance that later proved fictitious, he offered the same pope, in the presence of all the clergy and people, a document bearing his signature, in which everything that he himself or his predecessors had written or done against the Catholic faith was condemned. He was therefore kindly received by the pope as though he were the pontiff of the imperial city. But when he returned home, he resumed his domestic error. Pope Theodore, therefore, summoned all the priests and clergy to the church of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and condemned him under the bond of anathema.

(A.M. 4594; A.D. 643.) Constantine, son of Heraclius, for six months. Paul, the successor of Pyrrhus, afflicted the Catholics not only with the insane doctrine of his predecessors but also by open persecution. He punished the apocrisiarii of the holy Roman Church, who had been sent to correct him, some with imprisonment, some with exile, and some with beatings. He also overturned and plundered their altar, which had been consecrated in the house of Placidia, in the venerable oratory, and forbade them to celebrate Mass there. Therefore he too, like his predecessors, was condemned by the apostolic see to the just punishment of deposition.

(A.M. 4622; A.D. 671.) Constantine, son of Constantine, for twenty-eight years. Deceived by Paul, just as his grandfather Heraclius had been deceived by Sergius, bishop of the same imperial city, he issued the *Typos* against the Catholic faith, declaring that neither one nor two wills or operations in Christ should be confessed—as though Christ were to be believed to will or operate nothing.

Therefore Pope Martin, having convened at Rome a synod of 105 bishops, condemned under anathema the aforementioned heretics Cyrus, Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul. After this, Theodorus, sent by the emperor, seized Pope Martin from the Constantinian church and brought him to Constantinople. He was afterward exiled to Cherson, where he ended his life and continues to shine there, even to this day, through many signs of miraculous power. [Note: [Col. 0567D] Cherson. A city on the Cimmerian Bosporus, famous in those times as a place of exile for important men.]

The aforesaid synod took place in the ninth year of Constantine’s reign, in October, the eighth indiction.

The emperor Constantine, shortly after Vitalianus had been ordained pope, sent to the blessed apostle Peter golden Gospels adorned around the edges with white gems of extraordinary size. Several years later—that is, in the sixth indiction—he himself came to Rome and offered upon the apostle’s altar a pallium woven with gold, while his entire army entered the church with candles.

In the following year there was a solar eclipse remembered by our age, occurring as though at the tenth hour of the day, on the fifth day before the Nones of May.

The archbishop Theodorus and the abbot Hadrian, an equally learned man, sent by Vitalianus to Britain, enriched many of the Churches of the English with the fruit of ecclesiastical learning. Constantine, after inflicting many unheard-of depredations upon the provinces, perished, having been killed in a bath, in the twelfth indiction. Not long afterward Vitalianus also, the pope, departed to the heavenly kingdoms.

[A.M. 4639; A.D. 688.] Constantine, son of the preceding Constantine, for seventeen years. The Saracens invaded Sicily and, carrying off immense booty, soon returned to Alexandria.

At the request of Constantine and of the most devout emperors Heraclius and Tiberius, Pope Agatho sent his legates to the imperial city to bring about the union of the holy Churches of God. Among them was John, then a deacon of the Roman Church and not long afterward its bishop.

Received with the greatest kindness by Constantine, the most reverent defender of the Catholic faith, the legates were ordered to set aside philosophical disputations and to investigate the true faith through peaceful discussion. They were given from the Constantinopolitan library all the books of the ancient Fathers that they requested.

There were also present 150 bishops, with George, patriarch of the imperial city, presiding, and Macarius of Antioch. Those who asserted one will and one operation in Christ were convicted of having falsified very many statements of the Catholic Fathers.

When the conflict had ended, George was corrected, while Macarius, together with his followers and with his predecessors Cyrus, Sergius, Honorius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter, was anathematized. The abbot Theophanius of Sicily was made bishop of Antioch in his place.

Such grace accompanied the legates of Catholic peace that John, bishop of Porto, who was one of them, celebrated the public Mass in Latin on the Sunday of the octave of Easter in the church of Saint Sophia, before the emperor and patriarch.

This is the Sixth Ecumenical Synod, held at Constantinople and written in the Greek language in the time of Pope Agatho, with the most devout emperor Constantine conducting and presiding within his palace, while the legates of the apostolic see and 150 bishops likewise sat in session. [Note: [Col. 0567D] Held at Constantinople, in the Secretariat of the Great Palace called the Trullo. To this Sixth Synod, held in the time of Constantine Pogonatus, the Acts of the Synod of Hatfield should be referred; see *Ecclesiastical History*, V, 17. Note also that incorporated into this synod is the profession of faith of the Western Church, which Pope Agatho sent from the Roman synod and to which our Wilfrid subscribed; see *Ecclesiastical History*, V, 20.]

For the First Ecumenical Synod was assembled at Nicaea against Arius, consisting of 318 Fathers, in the time of Pope Julius and the emperor Constantine.

The Second was held at Constantinople, with 150 Fathers, against Macedonius and Eudoxius, in the time of Pope Damasus and the emperor Gratian, when Nectarius was ordained bishop of that city.

The Third was held at Ephesus, with 200 Fathers, against Nestorius, bishop of the imperial city, under the great emperor Theodosius and Pope Celestine.

The Fourth was held at Chalcedon, with 630 Fathers, under Pope Leo and in the time of the emperor Marcian, against Eutyches, leader of the most impious monks.

The Fifth likewise was held at Constantinople, in the time of Pope Vigilius and under the emperor Justinian, against Theodore and all the heretics.

This is the Sixth, of which we have just spoken.

The holy and perpetual virgin of Christ Aethelthryth, daughter of Anna, king of the English, was first given in marriage to another very noble man and afterward to King Ecgfrith. After preserving her marriage bed undefiled for twelve years, she became a consecrated religious virgin when, after being queen, she assumed the sacred veil. Without delay she also became a pious mother and nurse of holy virgins, having received for the construction of a monastery a place called Ely. The enduring merit of the saint is attested even by her dead flesh, which, after sixteen years of burial, was found incorrupt together with the garment in which she had been wrapped. [Note: [Col. 0568D] Aethelthryth. See *Ecclesiastical History*, IV, 3 and 10.]

[A.M. 4649; A.D. 698.] Justinian the Younger, son of Constantine, for ten years. He established peace with the Saracens for ten years, on land and sea. The province of Africa was also brought under the Roman Empire. It had been held by the Saracens, who had also captured and destroyed Carthage itself.

Because Sergius, the pontiff of the Roman Church and of blessed memory, refused to favor and subscribe to the emperor’s errant synod, which he had held at Constantinople, the emperor ordered him to be brought to Constantinople, sending his protospatharius Zacharias as well. [Note: [Col. 0568D] “Errant.” This was the synod held by Justinian Rhinotmetus as a supplement to the Fifth and Sixth Synods; hence it earned the name Quinisext. Bede calls it “errant” because, although it sought authority by every means and at times even obtained it, it could not retain authority that was fixed and stable, especially in the Latin Church.]

But the army of Ravenna and the neighboring regions forestalled the emperor’s wicked orders and drove the same Zacharias from the city of Rome with insults and injuries.

Pope Sergius also ordained the venerable man Willibrord, surnamed Clement, bishop for the people of the Frisians. To this day he remains among them as a pilgrim for the eternal homeland—for he is from Britain, of the nation of the English—and every day he inflicts countless losses upon the devil and brings increase to the Christian faith. [Note: [Col. 0569D] Willibrord. See *Ecclesiastical History*, V, 11–12.]

Justinian, deprived of the glory of the kingdom on account of his treachery, withdrew into exile in Pontus.

[A.M. 4652; A.D. 701.] Leo, for three years. Pope Sergius found, by the Lord’s revelation, in the sanctuary of the blessed apostle Peter, a silver chest that had lain for a very long time in a most obscure corner. In it was a cross adorned with various precious stones. Removing the four petals in which the gems were set, he saw within a piece of the life-giving wood of the Lord’s cross, of extraordinary size. From that time onward, every year on the day of its Exaltation, all the people kiss and adore it in the basilica of the Savior called the Constantinian.

The most reverend Cuthbert, bishop of the Church of Lindisfarne in Britain, formerly an anchorite, led a life renowned for signs of miracles from infancy to old age. After his body had remained buried for eleven years, it was afterward found incorrupt, as though he had died at that very hour, together with the garment that covered it. We ourselves, several years ago, recorded this in the book written about his Life and miracles, recently composed both in prose and in hexameter verse. [Note: [Col. 0569D] Cuthbert. See *Ecclesiastical History*, IV, 26–32, and the book on his Life, which we publish below in its proper place.]

[A. M. 4659. Chr. 708.] [Note: Tiberius. His imperial name was Tiberius; his family name was Apsimarus.] Tiberius, seven years. A synod was held at Aquileia. [Note: Because of ignorance of the faith. At that time the cause of the Three Chapters was not sufficiently understood.] Because of his ignorance of the faith, he hesitated to accept the Fifth Ecumenical Council, until, instructed by the salutary admonitions of the blessed Pope Sergius, he himself consented to approve it along with the other Churches of Christ.

Gisulphus, duke of the Lombard people, devastated Benevento and Campania with fire, sword, and captivity. Since there was no one able to resist his attack, the apostolic Pope John, who had succeeded Sergius, sent priests and very numerous gifts to him, ransomed all the captives, and made the enemies return home.

Another John succeeded him. Among many distinguished works, he constructed an oratory for the holy Mother of God, of most beautiful workmanship, within the church of the blessed Apostle Peter.

Hereberctus, king of the Lombards, restored to the jurisdiction of the Apostolic See many estates and patrimonies in the Cottian Alps, which had once belonged by right to that See but had long been taken away by the Lombards. He sent this donation, written in golden letters, to Rome. [Col. 0570A]

[A. M. 4665. Chr. 714.] Justinian, for the second time, with his son Tiberius, ruled six years. [Note: Six years. Baronius assigns eight years to Justinian after his restoration, but this is contrary to the testimony of the better authors who wrote about those times.] Having recovered the kingdom with the aid of Terbelis, king of the Bulgars, he killed the patricians who had driven him out, as well as Leo, who had usurped his place, and Leo’s successor Tiberius, who had kept him, expelled from the kingdom, under guard in that same city throughout the entire period of his own reign.

He sent Callinicus, the patriarch, to Rome after having his eyes torn out, and gave the episcopate to Cyrus, who had been an abbot in Pontus and had supported him in exile.

When he ordered Pope Constantine to come to him, he received and dismissed him honorably. Indeed, he ordered him to celebrate Mass for him on Sunday and received Communion from his hand. Then, prostrating himself on the ground, he asked him to intercede for his sins and renewed all the privileges of the Church.

When he sent an army to Pontus to seize Philippicus, whom he had exiled there, despite the apostolic pope’s strong opposition, the entire army went over to Philippicus’s side, made him emperor there, and returned with him to Constantinople. There they fought Justinian twelve miles from the city; after Justinian was defeated and killed, Philippicus assumed the kingdom.

[A. M. 4667. Chr. 716.] [Note: Philippicus Bardanes, so called from the name he assumed with the empire. Sichardus assigns him two years and six months, but the remaining manuscripts of Bede give one year, with which the sequence of the history also agrees.] Philippicus ruled one year and six months.

He expelled Cyrus from the patriarchate and ordered him to return to Pontus to govern his monastery according to the rights of an abbot.

He also sent Pope Constantine letters containing an erroneous doctrine, which Constantine rejected together with the council of the Apostolic See. For this reason he had paintings made in the portico of Saint Peter containing the Acts of the six universal holy synods. Since similar paintings were displayed in the imperial city, Philippicus had ordered them removed. The Roman people therefore decreed that the name of the heretical emperor should not be received in documents or on the image of the solidus; consequently, neither was his portrait brought into a church, nor was his name pronounced during the solemnities of Mass.

[A. M. 4670. Chr. 719.] [Note: Anastasius. His true name was Artemius. The year that Sichardus added to Philippicus, he subtracts from Anastasius, as does Baronius. But the chronology of the remaining manuscripts of Bede is correct.] Anastasius ruled three years.

He deprived Philippicus, after capturing him, of his sight, but did not kill him.

He sent letters to Pope Constantine at Rome through Scholasticus, patrician and exarch of Italy, in which he declared himself a supporter of the Catholic faith and a proclaimer of the holy Sixth Council.

Liuthbrandus, king of the Lombards, confirmed, at the admonition of the venerable Pope Gregory, the donation of the patrimony of the Cottian Alps that King Hereberctus had made and that Liuthbrandus had reclaimed. [Col. 0570D]

Ecberctus, a holy man of the English people, adorning both the priesthood and the monastic life, and a pilgrim for the sake of his heavenly homeland, converted by devout preaching many provinces of the Scottish people to the canonical observance of Easter, from which they had long strayed, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 716. [Col. 0571A]

[A. M. 4671. Chr. 720.] [Note: Theodosius. From Adramyttium.] Theodosius ruled one year.

Having been chosen emperor, he defeated Anastasius in a severe battle near the city of Nicaea. After Anastasius had sworn an oath of submission, Theodosius made him a cleric and had him ordained priest.

As soon as he received the kingdom, being himself a Catholic, he restored in the imperial city to its former place the venerable image depicting the six holy synods, which Philippicus had removed.

The river Tiber overflowed its bed and caused great destruction to the city of Rome, rising in the broad street to a height of one and a half men, so that the waters descending from the gate of Saint Peter as far as the Milvian Bridge joined together. [Col. 0571B] It remained so for seven days, until, when the citizens had performed frequent litanies, it finally withdrew on the eighth day.

At this time many people of the English nation—nobles and commoners, men and women, leaders and private persons—used to come from Britain to Rome, prompted by divine love. Among them was my most reverend abbot Ceolfrid. He was seventy-four years old, had been a priest for forty-seven years, and an abbot for thirty-five. When he reached Langres, he died there and was buried in the church of the blessed martyr-twins.

Among the other gifts he had intended to bring, he sent the church of Saint Peter a Pandect translated by the blessed Jerome into Latin from a Hebrew or Greek source.

[A. M. 4680. Chr. 729.] [Note: Leo. His name Isauricus came from his homeland; his baptismal name was Conon. Bede says that he reigned nine years, evidently because he was writing this while Leo was in his ninth year. In fact, Leo reigned twenty-four years, but, closing his Chronicle in Leo’s ninth year, Bede does not count farther. It is scarcely credible that this observation escaped learned men—even Ado himself and Hermannus. Yet such was the confidence of those times in following the words of authors that what Bede deliberately placed at the end of his Chronicle, they placed without reflection in the middle of their own accounts, and continued their calculations as though Leo had reigned only nine years. Leo’s ninth year is, according to the common reckoning, 724 from Christ’s birth; but according to Bede’s own Chronicle and the sequence of years that he arranged under the emperors, it reaches the year 729. Palmerius and others are not far from this, although they have written variously about the dates of these emperors, as indeed about the dates of almost all the others.] Leo ruled nine years.

The Saracens came to Constantinople with an immense army and besieged the city for three years, until, while the citizens cried out insistently to God, many of the Saracens perished from hunger, cold, and disease, and so, weary of the siege, withdrew.

After returning from there, they attacked in war the people of the Bulgars, who dwell beyond the Danube. Defeated by them also, they fled and returned to their ships. When they were making for the open sea, a sudden storm arose; many were drowned, while others were killed when their ships were wrecked along the shores.

Liuthbrandus, hearing that the Saracens, after ravaging Sardinia, had also desecrated the places where the bones of Saint Augustine the bishop had once been transferred and honorably buried because of the devastation of the barbarians, sent agents, obtained the relics by paying a great price, and transferred them to Pavia. There he reburied them with the honor so great a Father deserved. [Col. 0571D]

## CHAPTER LXVII  
### The Remnants of the Sixth Age

We have endeavored, as best we could, to work out from the Hebrew truth these matters concerning the course of the past age, judging it fitting that, just as the Greeks, using the edition of the Seventy translators, composed books of chronology for themselves and their descendants from it, so we too—who through the diligence of the blessed interpreter Jerome drink from the pure fountain of Hebrew truth—might be able to know the reckoning of times according to it.

If anyone should criticize this labor of ours as superfluous, let all such people receive, without prejudice to charity, the just reply that the aforementioned Jerome gives to the detractors of ancient cosmography: “If it displeases you, do not read it.”

For the rest, we advise everyone alike that whether someone marks the course of time from the Hebrew truth—which, through the aforesaid interpreter, is acknowledged even by our Jewish opponents to have come down to us in pure form—or from the translation of the Seventy translators, which, as many maintain, was first published with insufficient care, or, as blessed Augustine thinks, was later corrupted by pagans, or certainly from manuscripts in which the two have been combined according to his judgment; and whether he records longer or shorter periods of the past age, or finds them recorded as such, he should nevertheless never suppose from this that the remaining periods of the age will be longer or shorter. He should always remember the Lord’s saying: “For no one knows the day or the hour, not even the angels of heaven, but the Father alone.”

Nor should we in any way listen to those who suppose that the duration of this age was fixed at six thousand years from the beginning and, so as not to appear to contradict the Lord’s saying, add that it is uncertain to mortals in which year of the sixth millennial period the day of judgment will come, though its coming should nevertheless especially be expected near the end of the sixth millennium.

If you ask them where they have read or learned that these things should be thought or believed, they immediately become angry, since they have no other answer: “Have you not read,” they say, “in Genesis that God made the world in six days?” From this, they claim, it ought reasonably to be believed that the world will last approximately six thousand years.

More seriously still, there have been people who, because of the seventh day on which God rested from his works, hoped that after six thousand years of the saints’ labor in this mortal life, they would reign with Christ after the resurrection—immortal, in delights and great blessedness—for a seventh thousand-year period in this same life.

But since these ideas are heretical and frivolous, let us set them aside completely and understand sincerely and catholically that those six days in which God completed the adornment of this world, and the seventh in which he rested from all his work and therefore sanctified it with the blessing of perpetual rest, signify not six thousand years of the world’s labor and a seventh millennium of the blessed reigning on earth with Christ, but rather the six ages of the passing world, in which the saints labor for Christ in this life, and the seventh age of perpetual rest in the next life, which holy souls, released from their bodies, receive with Christ.

This Sabbath of souls is rightly believed to have begun when the first martyr of Christ, killed in the flesh by his brother, was immediately transferred in soul to eternal rest. It will be completed when, on the day of the resurrection, souls also receive their incorruptible bodies.

And since no one of the five past ages is found to have lasted a thousand years—some had more years, others fewer, and no one had the same total as another—it follows that this present age likewise has a duration whose course is unknown to mortals and known only to him who commanded his servants, with their loins girded and lamps burning, to keep watch, like people waiting for their master to return from the wedding feast.

## CHAPTER LXVIII  
### The Three Opinions of the Faithful concerning the Time of the Lord’s Coming

All the saints rightly love the hour of his coming and desire that it be near. But those who presume to think or proclaim that it is near or far act with considerable danger.

Accordingly, blessed Augustine most beautifully sets aside that wicked servant who says in his heart, “My master is delaying his coming”—for such a servant undoubtedly hates his master’s arrival—and gives the example of three excellent servants who thirstingly desire, watchfully await, and faithfully love the coming of their master.

One says: “Let us watch and pray, because the master will come soon.”

Another says: “Let us watch and pray, because this life is brief and uncertain, even though the master may come later.”

The third says: “Let us watch and pray, because this life is both brief and uncertain, and we do not know the time when the master will come.”

Therefore, if what the first predicted comes to pass, the second and third will rejoice with him. But if it does not happen, one must fear that those who believed him will be disturbed and begin to think that the master’s coming is not merely delayed but will not occur at all.

Those who believe what the second says—that the master will come later—will not, if this proves false and the master comes sooner, be disturbed in their faith; rather, they will enjoy unexpected joy.

Therefore, the one who says that the master will come sooner speaks more desirably, but is dangerously mistaken. The one who says that the master will come later, while nevertheless believing in, hoping for, and loving his coming, is, even if mistaken about the delay, happily mistaken. For he will have greater patience if the delay occurs and greater joy if it does not. Thus, among those who love the manifestation of the master, the former is heard more sweetly, while the latter is believed more safely.

But the one who confesses that he does not know which of these is true hopes for the one and endures the other. He errs in neither, because he neither weakens nor denies either possibility.

## CHAPTER LXIX  
### The Times of Antichrist

We have two completely certain signs that the day of judgment is not yet at hand: the faith of the Israelite people, and the kingdom and persecution of Antichrist. The faith of the Church holds that this persecution will last three and a half years.

But lest its unforeseen arrival overwhelm everyone it finds unprepared, Enoch and Elijah, the greatest prophets and teachers, will come into the world before his appearance. They will convert the Israelite people to the grace of faith and make them, among the elect, unconquerable in preparation for the pressure of so great a storm.

After they themselves have preached for three and a half years and, as Malachi the prophet foretold concerning one of them, Elijah, have turned the hearts of the fathers to the children—that is, after planting the faith and love of the saints of ancient times in the minds of those who will then be living—that dreadful persecution, blazing forth, will first crown them with the glory of martyrdom. Then, seizing the other faithful, it will make them either glorious martyrs of Christ or condemned apostates.

The Apostle John appears to signify this when he writes in the Apocalypse: “But cast out the court that is outside the temple, and do not measure it, because it has been given to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months”—that is, show that those who are faithful in name only and love merely outward things have been separated from the lot of the elect, because in that final persecution, lasting three and a half years, they too will turn to persecute the Church.

“And I will give,” he says, “to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth”—that is, girded for the strictest labors of self-restraint and affliction, they will preach.

A little later he says: “And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the abyss will make war against them, overcome them, kill them, and so forth.”

In another passage he likewise records that the servants of the same beast—that is, of Antichrist—will rejoice at the killing of these two witnesses, that is, martyrs, and will insult them even after their death: “And I saw,” he says, “a beast rising from the sea, and the dragon gave it his power and great authority.”

That is, I saw a man of most savage character, sprung from the turbulent stock of the impious. As soon as he was born, and had been instructed through magical arts by the worst teachers, the devil joined himself to him and brought him, as his inseparable companion, the whole power of his strength, through which he would perform deeds greater than all others by magic.

“And authority was given to him,” he says, “to act for forty-two months”—that is, three and a half years.

After that son of perdition has been struck down, whether by the Lord himself or by the archangel Michael, as some teach, and condemned to eternal punishment, we must not believe that the day of judgment will immediately follow. Otherwise, the people of that age could know the time of judgment, if it followed at once after the three and a half years from the beginning of Antichrist’s persecution.

Now, however, since everyone may know that the day of judgment will not come before the time of that persecution has been completed, it is granted to no one whatsoever to know after how long a period following the completion of that persecution it will come.

Finally, the prophet Daniel, who describes the kingdom of Antichrist as lasting 1,290 days, concludes as follows: “Blessed is he who waits and reaches the 1,335 days.”

Jerome explains this in the following manner: “Blessed,” he says, “is the one who, after Antichrist has been killed, waits beyond the 1,290 days—that is, three and a half years—for forty-five days, during which the Lord and Savior will come in his majesty. Why there should be a silence of forty-five days after the killing of Antichrist belongs to divine knowledge, unless perhaps we should say: The delay of the kingdom of the saints is a test of patience.”

## CHAPTER LXX  
### The Day of Judgment

The day of the Lord will come like a thief, because, as he himself testifies, we do not know when the Lord will come—whether in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow, or in the morning—when, he says, the heavens will pass away with a great rushing sound and the elements will be dissolved by heat.

The Apostle Peter explains shortly beforehand which heavens will pass away, saying: “The heavens existed formerly, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God; through these the world that then existed perished, being flooded with water. But the heavens and earth that now exist have been stored up by the same word, reserved for fire on the day of judgment.”

Therefore, it will not be the firmament of heaven, in which the fixed stars revolve; nor the ethereal heaven—that is, the immense empty space extending from the starry heaven to the turbulent air, in which the seven wandering stars are believed to move through the pure, calm air, always filled with daylight—but this airy heaven, which is near the earth and from which the birds that fly in it are called “birds of heaven.” This is the heaven that the water of the Flood once destroyed by rising above it while wiping out earthly things. The fire of the final judgment, growing until it reaches the same extent, will occupy and destroy it.

Not only does the statement of blessed Peter testify that those heavens will perish in the fire of judgment—those heavens that had perished through the water of the Flood—that the starry heaven will not be touched by that fire, however great it may be; the Lord’s saying testifies the same: “Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven.”

For the sun could not be darkened, the moon deprived of its light, or the stars fall from heaven if heaven itself, their dwelling place, were consumed and passed away in fire.

Now, however, the airy heaven will wither in the fire, while the starry heaven will remain unharmed. The stars will be darkened not because they are emptied of their own light, but because they will be covered by the power of a greater light at the coming of the heavenly Judge and will therefore not be seen. In this present life everyone can readily observe that the moon and all the stars suffer this from the stronger light of the sun during the day.
