When, after the judgment has been completed, the new heaven and the new earth have shone forth—that is, not other things in place of these, but these same things renewed through fire and glorified by a certain power of resurrection—then, as Isaiah foretold, “the light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, like the light of seven days.”

When John, in the Apocalypse, had said, “I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away,” he added: “And the sea was no more.”

Whether the sea will be dried up by that tremendous heat, or whether it too will be transformed for the better, is not easily clear. For we read nowhere that there will be a new sea, as we do of a new heaven and a new earth.

The statement “and the sea was no more” may also be understood figuratively, because at that time this age—the turbulent life of mortals, which is very often symbolized in Scripture by the name “sea”—will no longer exist.

The question of where precisely the assize of the final and universal judgment is to be held is often debated among many people.

It is established that when the Lord descends for judgment, the resurrection of all the dead will take place in the twinkling of an eye, and the saints will immediately be snatched up to meet him in the air.

The Apostle appears to indicate this when he says: “For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air.”

Whether the reprobate will then also be lifted above the earth to meet the Judge as he comes, or whether the weight of their sins will so burden them that, although they possess immortal bodies, they will be unable to rise to higher places, and whether, while the Lord presides in judgment, the saints will stand above at his right hand while they stand below at his left, will then become apparent.

But if that greatest and highest fire then covers the surface of the whole earth, and the unjust, raised from the dead, cannot be snatched upward, it is clear that, being placed upon the earth and surrounded by fire, they will await the Judge’s sentence.

Yet who would dare prejudge whether those who are not to be chastised through that fire but are instead to be condemned to eternal fire will themselves burn in it?

For blessed Augustine, in the twentieth book of *The City of God*, understands from the sayings of the prophets that some of the elect will be purified by that fire from certain lesser offenses. Saint Pope Gregory likewise, in his *Homilies on the Gospel*, explaining the Psalmist’s words, “Fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm around him,” says: “The storm and fire accompany the severity of so great a justice, because the storm tests whom the fire is to consume.”

It is sufficiently clear that when his perfected servants are snatched up by the sound of the trumpet to meet the Lord in the air, the conflagration of the world will not harm them, just as the surrounding furnace could not touch the still-mortal bodies of the three young men.

In all these matters, however, it is more useful for each person to present himself pure before the sight of the strict Judge than to debate the manner or location of that judgment.

When the Apostle had said, “We will be caught up with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air,” he added, “And so we will always be with the Lord.” This should not be understood as though he said that we would always remain with the Lord in the air, since he himself certainly will not remain there, because, having come, he will pass on.

We will go to meet him as he comes, not as he remains. Rather, “we will always be with the Lord” means that we will be in possession of eternal bodies wherever we are with him.

## CHAPTER LXXI  
### The Seventh Age and the Eighth Age of the Future World

This is that eighth age, which the faithful should always love, hope for, and long for: the time when Christ will lead their souls, endowed with the gift of incorruptible bodies, into the enjoyment of the heavenly kingdom and the contemplation of his divine majesty.

He will not take away the glory that, once released from their bodies, they had received in blessed rest from the very moment of their departure; rather, he will increase that glory by restoring their bodies to them.

As a type of this uninterrupted and continuous blessedness, Moses, after saying that the first six days in which the world was made began with light and morning and ended with evening, mentioned only the morning and not the evening of the seventh day, on which God rested from his works.

He concluded everything that he considered worth recalling about that day with the light of eternal rest and blessing.

For, as we recalled above, all six ages of this world, in which the just, with the Lord’s cooperation, devote themselves to good works, have been arranged by heavenly ordinance in such a way that, although each begins with some joyful things, it is consumed by no small darknesses of suffering and affliction.

The rest of souls, which they receive in the future age for their good works, will never fail, disturbed by anxiety over any concern. But when the time of judgment and resurrection arrives, it will be completed in the more glorious perfection of everlasting blessedness.

The time of the Lord’s passion, burial, and resurrection is compared with these ages.

For we read, as the Evangelist John writes, that Christ came to Bethany six days before Passover, where Judas, offended by the devotion of a woman’s service, betrayed him to the chief priests.

On the following day, he himself came to Jerusalem on a donkey amid a crowd singing praises to God. For five successive days he was assailed by their deceitful questions, and finally, on the sixth day, he was crucified. On the seventh he rested in the tomb, but on the eighth—that is, on the first day of the week—he rose from the dead.

For throughout the five past ages of this world, the saints never ceased to suffer the plots and hatred of the reprobate.

But in the sixth age, which the Lord graciously confirmed in faith by his incarnation, redeemed from the underworld by his passion, and kindled toward hope and love of the heavenly kingdom through his resurrection and ascension, the outstanding courage of the blessed martyrs endured more savage battles of persecution from unbelievers.

They conquered these battles all the more bravely because they knew with greater certainty that they were suffering for him who promised the thief who suffered beside him, but then became a confessor: “Today you will be with me in paradise.”

Because that most blessed rest of paradise has no end other than the beginning of the glorious resurrection, the Evangelist Matthew wished to signify this. After writing that the Lord suffered on Friday and was buried on the Sabbath, he begins his account of the resurrection as follows: “Now, in the evening of the Sabbath, as it dawns toward the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb.”

He says that the evening of the Sabbath, on which the Lord rested in the tomb, did not grow dark into night but dawned toward the first day of the week, because that same tomb was not destined to be touched by the corruption of the body it had received. Rather, as Isaiah says, “His tomb will be glorious,” and it was soon to be exalted by the power of the resurrection.

So too the rest of our souls after they have left their bodies will not be darkened by the shadows of any anguish, but will at the end be received and enriched by the gifts of the sun of true and perpetual light.

This is that great and unique eighth day for which Psalms 6 and 11 are written, and the Books of Chronicles record it thus: “Moreover, Mattathias, Heliphalu, and other Levites” sang on lyres “for the eighth,” an *epinicion*—that is, they sang praises to the victorious Lord for the Ogdoad that is to come forever and for the judgment.

For *epinicion* means triumph and the palm of victory.

Or they were prophesying the mystery of Christ’s resurrection, which is rightly called the unique and great eighth day, because every day of the passing age is an eighth day after the seventh Sabbath, while it is also the first day of the following week.

Just as the first day of the entire age was so truly first that it had no preceding seven days of which it could be the eighth, and is therefore uniquely first, so uniquely the day of the future resurrection is not only great but also the eighth. For it will come after the seventh Sabbath in such a way that it will have no succeeding days by which it could become the first; it alone will remain everlasting in heavenly light.

Hence the prophet, longing to see this day, rightly calls it “one,” saying: “For one day in your courts is better than thousands.”

Therefore, when we read of “the eighth” in Scripture, we should understand that mystically it can refer both to a day and to an age. The Lord rose from the dead on the eighth day, that is, after the seventh Sabbath; and we too will rise in the eighth age and day, not only after the seven days of this revolving world but also after the seven ages mentioned so often.

That day of life has remained, remains, and will remain eternal in itself. But for us it will begin when we have been found worthy to enter and behold it. There the Psalmist testifies what activity occupies the saints, renewed in the perfect immortality of spirit and flesh, singing to God in loving praise: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; they will praise you forever and ever.”

He next explains what vision delights them: “For he who gave the law will grant blessing; they will go from strength to strength; the God of gods will be seen in Zion.”

The Lord himself, who is the way, the truth, and the life, testifies what sort of people can come to this vision: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.”

Therefore, let our little book, written about the revolving and wave-tossed course of time, have an appropriate end in eternal stability and stable eternity.

If anyone should think it worthy of reading, I ask that he commend me to the Lord in his prayers and, as far as he is able, act with devout diligence before God and his neighbors, so that, after the temporal toils of heavenly pursuits, we may all be found worthy to receive the eternal palm of heavenly rewards.

[Col. 0579]

# BOOK ON THE RECKONING OF TIME

## CHAPTER I  
### On Time

[Col. 0579A]

**Question.** From what is “time” derived?

**Answer.** “Time” (*tempora*) is so called from *temperamentum*, because the duration of each of its parts has been separately proportioned. Or because all the courses of mortal life are measured out by moments, hours, days, months, years, ages, and periods of life.

**Question.** In how many ways is the method of reckoning time distinguished? [Col. 0579B]

**Answer.** In three: it proceeds according to nature, custom, or authority.

**Question.** How according to authority?

**Answer.** Authority is divided in two ways: namely, into human and divine.

**Question.** How according to human authority?

**Answer.** Such things as Olympiads of four years, market cycles of eight days, and indictions of fifteen years.

**Question.** How according to divine authority?

**Answer.** Likewise, that the Sabbath is observed on the seventh day and that one is forbidden to engage in rural labor on the seventh day; and that the fiftieth year is called a jubilee.

**Question.** How according to custom?

**Answer.** Human custom established that a month should be reckoned as thirty days, although this agrees with neither the course of the sun nor that of the moon. Indeed, those who have investigated the matter more carefully testify that the moon, with due allowance for the intercalation, falls twelve hours short, whereas the sun exceeds it by ten and a half hours.

**Question.** How according to nature?

**Answer.** Guided by nature, it was discovered that the solar year is completed in 365¼ days. The lunar year, when common, ends after 354 days; when embolismic, after 384 days. The entire course of the moon is contained within a nineteen-year cycle. The wandering stars, each in its own interval, are carried around the zodiacal circle.

## CHAPTER II  
### On the Hour

**Question.** What is an hour?

**Answer.** An hour is one-twelfth of a day. For twelve hours complete a day, as the Lord testifies when he says: “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks during the day, he does not stumble.” Although here he had called himself allegorically the day and the disciples hours, because they were destined to reflect his light, he nevertheless defined the number of hours according to the ordinary order of human reckoning.

It should be noted, however, that if all the days of the year are reckoned as consisting of twelve hours, the summer days must necessarily be comprised of longer hours and the winter days of shorter ones. But if we wish to equalize the hours—that is, to have equinoctial hours—then it is necessary to assign fewer hours to the winter day and more to the summer day.

**Question.** Into how many points is an hour divided?

**Answer.** Into four; but in some lunar reckonings, into five, ten minutes, fifteen parts, and forty moments.

[Col. 0580A]

**Question.** Are these divisions of time natural or not?

**Answer.** No, but conventional. For when calculators found it necessary to divide either the day into twelve hours, or the hour into fourteen, ten, fifteen, or forty parts, or into any other smaller or larger units, they sought names by which to designate what they were calling, so that they could distinguish one unit from another.

[Col. 0580B]

**Question.** From what is the hour named?

**Answer.** The hour is so called because it is the boundary of a definite period of time. We also customarily call the edges of garments, rivers, and the sea *orae*, “boundaries” or “edges.”

A point (*punctus*) is so called from the small mark made when a point is passed on a sundial.

We call them “minutes,” parts derived from a larger interval, from the division of the zodiacal circle, which they divide by thirty days in each month.

We call the smallest intervals “moments,” from the very rapid movement of the stars, since something is perceived to yield or advance for a very brief span.

The smallest of all periods of time, which cannot be divided by any means, they call in Greek an *atom*—that is, “indivisible.”

## CHAPTER III  
### On the Day

[Col. 0580C]

**Question.** What is a day?

**Answer.** Air illuminated by the sun.

**Question.** From where did it receive its name?

**Answer.** “Day” (*dies*) is so called because it separates and divides darkness from light.

**Question.** You said that a day is air illuminated by the sun, although at the beginning of creation we read that there were three days before the sun was made.

**Answer.** That is true. In the beginning of creation, darkness was over the face of the abyss. And God said: “Let there be light,” and there was light, and God called the light “day.”

Thus, light emerged from the east; after driving away the darkness, the breadth of its radiance illuminated the whole earth equally. For the first three days it completed its course, rising and setting, like the sun; and the luminaries are believed to have been formed from that light.

[Col. 0580D]

**Question.** What distinguished it from solar light?

**Answer.** This: it lacked the generative power of heat.

**Question.** In how many ways is the definition of a day divided?

**Answer.** In two ways: commonly and properly.

Interrogator: How is it understood in ordinary usage?

Respondent: For ordinary usage calls every presence of the sun above the earth, abusively, “day.”

Interrogator: How is it understood properly?

Respondent: Properly and naturally, a day is completed in twenty-four hours—that is, by the circuit of the sun as it illumines the whole globe. It is believed that the sun, always and everywhere carrying the light of day with it, is borne through the airy region both beneath the earth by night and above the earth by day.

Interrogator: Give the authority for both usages.

Respondent: The Lord defined the ordinary day in the Gospel when he said: “Are there not twelve hours in the day?” Moses, however, described the proper day in this way: “And there was evening and there was morning, one day.” Following the order of the first creation, the Hebrews and Chaldeans extend the course of the day from morning to morning, placing the time of darkness beneath the light. The Egyptians, by contrast, reckon from sunset to sunset; the Romans, from midnight to midnight; and the Athenians preferred to calculate their days from noon to noon.

Divine authority in Genesis calls the interval from morning to morning one day. But after the Lord’s resurrection, the same authority in the Gospel established the entire day from evening to evening, signifying that the human being, having fallen from light into darkness, should thereafter return from darkness to light.

I ask where the first day of the world was.

The beginning of the world and of the creation, according to the Egyptians—among whom Abraham, instructed by the Chaldeans, introduced the science of astrology—is said to have occurred on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, because the beginning of the zodiac was then established and, in accordance with the division of the zodiac, light was made on the day when the sun, returning to its beginning, entered the sign of Aries.

The sun was created on the fourth day of creation, namely at the beginning of the twelfth day before the Kalends mentioned above. By equally dividing light and darkness through its presence and absence, it made the vernal equinox on the day when, at the beginning of that day, the rising sun began to occupy the region of the heavens that astrologers call the fourth part of Aries.

Returning after 365 days and six hours, and therefore reaching noon in the following year because of those hours, it entered the vernal equinox on the third day at evening, on the fourth at midnight, and on the fifth again in the morning, just as it had first appeared. On that day the sun is found not only to have ascended into the first part of the sign, but also already to possess a quarter of it. By nature, this is the head of the zodiac: the twelve signs, which are called its portions, have there both their beginning and their end.

Anatolius reports that the quadrant is so called there, that the leap begins and ends there, and that there the great year—that is, the course of the planets—receives its beginning and its end.

On the evening of that same day, the full moon appeared from mid-heaven in the east and occupied the fourth part of Libra, which is the autumnal equinox; by its setting it consecrated the beginning of the Paschal season. There is no other rule for observing Easter: the vernal equinox must be completed, with the full moon following it. But if the fullness of the moon has advanced even by one day, the equinox is no longer considered to fall in the first lunar month but in the last.

Thus it is not without reason that the sun then has power over neither the first, nor the second, nor the third day, but the fourth. The moon, illuminated by the sun, finally assumes power over the night together with the stars at evening.

But the true sun, which is Christ, arose for us after the passage of time before the Law, under the Law, and through prophetic grace, beginning by himself. By the light of his grace he illumined the body of the Church, preceding [the following words are textually uncertain: *quosque virium*].

For the Paschal full moon cannot occur before the equinox. Therefore, after the equinoctial rising of the sun—which conquers every obstacle of darkness—we celebrate our Easter when the full moon of your devotion follows.

## CHAPTER IV — On the Night

[Col. 0582A]

Interrogator: From what was night named?

Respondent: Night (*nox*) was so called because it harms (*noceat*) the eyes or human activities, or because thieves and robbers find in it an opportunity to harm others.

Interrogator: What is night?

Respondent: Night is the absence of the sun, the shadow cast by the earth, until the sun returns from setting to rising. The poet, describing it according to its nature, says:

> Night rushes from Ocean,  
> enveloping the earth and the pole in a great shadow.

Solomon likewise expressed this in the sacred writings: “He who feeds among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows incline.” With elegant meaning he calls the withdrawal of night the inclination of the shadows.

This shadow, too, which appears to extend as far as the stars, belongs to the nature of night; at times it obscures the moon more than the other stars, so that it shares in the failure of its light. [The wording is difficult.] For the moon travels through the lower regions of the planets, while the higher regions nevertheless always shine with their own light or that of the stars.

When the moon, full, reaches the lowest apses of its course, it too is sometimes darkened by the shadow just mentioned, until, having passed beyond the center, it is again seen in the sun’s light. But, so that this may not happen at every full moon, the latitude, which consists of twelve different divisions, is said to have the height of the apses.

Interrogator: How many things produce a shadow?

Respondent: Three: light, a body, and an obscured place.

[Col. 0582C]

Interrogator: How?

Respondent: If the light is equal to the body, the shadow is equal to it. If the body is larger, the shadow also increases; if it is smaller, the shadow likewise diminishes.

The sun is said to be larger than the earth, although it appears small because of its great distance. Therefore philosophers say that the shadow of the night, gradually diminishing, fails before it reaches the ether, and that the earth’s shadow is raised toward the boundary between air and ether, with the darkness sharpened like pyramids.

Interrogator: Into how many parts is night divided?

Respondent: Into seven.

Interrogator: What are they?

Respondent: Twilight, evening, the time of silence, the dead of night, cockcrow, morning, and dawn.

Twilight (*crepusculum*) is uncertain light. We call it *crepusculum*, “uncertain,” because it lies between light and darkness.

Evening (*vesperum*) occurs when the star of that name appears. The poet says:

> Before day, evening closes Olympus beneath its seal.

The time of silence (*conticinium*) is when everything becomes silent—that is, ceases speaking.

The dead of night (*intempestum*) is midnight, when, because all are resting in sleep, there is no time for any activity.

Cockcrow (*gallicinium*) is when the roosters raise their song.

Morning (*matutinum*) lies between the departure of darkness and the coming of dawn.

Dawn (*diluculum*) is, as it were, the small light of day that is already beginning. It is the dawn that extends up to sunrise.

## CHAPTER V — On the Week and the Seven Planets

Interrogator: From what was the week named?

Respondent: The week (*hebdomada*) received its name from the number seven. The Romans likewise call it a *septimana*, “a period of seven days.” [Col. 0583A] For among the ancients, *manus* is said to mean “days” from purity. [The text is uncertain.]

Interrogator: How was it reckoned by the people of God?

Respondent: In ancient times the people of God reckoned it as follows: the first of the Sabbath, or one of the Sabbath, or of the Sabbaths; the second of the Sabbath; the third of the Sabbath; the fourth of the Sabbath; the fifth of the Sabbath; and the sixth of the Sabbath, or Sabbath itself.

This was not because all the days could not be days of Sabbaths—that is, days of rest—but because, in relation to the day of rest that excelled by its distinctive name and worship, the first, second, third, and remaining days were each designated in their proper order.

Interrogator: How did the gentiles reckon the week?

Respondent: When the gentiles learned the observance of the week from the people of Israel, they dedicated the first day to the Sun, the second to the Moon, the third to Mars, the fourth to Mercury, the fifth to Jupiter, the sixth to Venus, and the seventh to Saturn. They consecrated their days to the same monstrous beings to whom they consecrated the wandering stars, although they reckoned them in a different order.

Interrogator: What did they think they received from these?

Respondent: They thought that they received spirit from the sun, body from the moon, ardor from Mars, wisdom and speech from Mercury, moderation from Jupiter, pleasure from Venus, and slowness from Saturn.

Interrogator: I ask you to explain to me the effect of these according to your own judgment.

Respondent: I think that the sun, placed in the midst of the planets, appears to warm and, as it were, enliven the entire world like a spirit, as Ecclesiastes testifies when he says: “The spirit goes around, going in circles, and returns to its circuits.”

The moon, through the service of moisture, supplies increase to all bodies.

The star of Mars, being, as it were, close to the sun, is hot both in color and in nature.

Mercury, continually running around the sun, was thought to shine as though irradiated by the exhausted light of wisdom.

Jupiter is tempered on either side by the cold of Saturn and the heat of Mars.

Venus attracts those who see it by the beauty of its light, which it receives from its nearness to the sun.

Saturn is slower than the other planets because it also moves higher above them.

Interrogator: In how many years or days does the course of each appear to be completed?

Respondent: Saturn completes the zodiac in thirty years; Jupiter, in twelve years; Mars, third in order, in two years.

The sun, fourth, completes its course in 365 days and a quarter beneath the sun. Venus, Lucifer, and Vesper complete theirs in 387 days, never withdrawing more than forty-six degrees from the sun.

The star of Mercury, nearest to it, completes its course more rapidly in nine days. It shines sometimes before sunrise and sometimes after sunset, and is never more than twenty-two degrees distant from the sun.

The moon, last, completes the zodiac in twenty-seven days and four hours.

Interrogator: Why did you say earlier “and reckoning them in a different order”?

Respondent: Because this was the folly of the gentiles, supported by false calculation. They thought, as though by right, that the first day should belong to the sun because it is the greatest luminary, and the second to the moon because it follows as the second luminary.

In their disordered alternation, they placed before the third day the first star from the sun, before the fourth the first from the moon, before the fifth the second from the sun, before the sixth the second from the moon, and before the seventh the third from the sun.

Interrogator: How does the week proceed among the Greeks and Romans?

Respondent: In a course of seven days.

Interrogator: How among the Hebrews?

Respondent: It proceeds in a course of seven years. Daniel makes this clear in speaking of the seventy weeks.

Interrogator: Of how many weekdays does the week consist?

Respondent: Of seven, naturally.

Interrogator: From what was *feria* named?

Respondent: *Feria* derives from *fari*, “to speak,” as though it were *faria*, because in the creation of the world God said “Let there be” on each day.

Interrogator: Who first taught the observance of weekdays?

Respondent: Pope Sylvester established the clergy’s observance of weekdays, so that those devoted solely to God might never engage in worldly military service or commerce. The Psalmist says: “Be vacant and see that I am.”

He called the first day Sunday, because light was made in the beginning and because Christ’s resurrection was celebrated on that day. John testifies that this name had been given to it in the earliest times of the Church when he says in the Apocalypse: “I was in the spirit on the Lord’s day.”

He then designated the second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth days according to their order. He retained the name Sabbath from the ancient Scripture, without fearing the grammarians’ rods, even though they maintain that, like *Kalends*, *Nones*, and *Ides*, *feriae* too must be used only in the plural.

## CHAPTER VI — On the Months

[Col. 0584C]

Interrogator: From what were the months named?

Respondent: The months were named from measurement, because each is measured. But it is better to derive the name from the moon, which in Greek is called *mēnē*. Hence the Greeks call months *mēnes*. The Hebrew language also appears to preserve this etymology. Jesus son of Sirach, who wrote in Hebrew, says: “The month is according to its name.”

Interrogator: How did the ancients reckon their months?

Respondent: The ancients customarily reckoned their months not by the course of the sun but by that of the moon. Therefore, whenever sacred Scripture—or the Law that preserves the Law—indicates on what day of the month something happened or was said, nothing other than the moon’s age is signified.

The Hebrews, to whom the utterances of God were entrusted, have never ceased, according to the ancient custom of the fathers, to observe the months by the moon. They call the first month of the new year, which is consecrated by the rites of Passover, Nisan. Because of the moon’s wandering course, it now falls in March, now in April, and sometimes occupies several days of May.

It is more properly assigned to April, however, because it always either begins in that month, ends in it, or is wholly contained within it. The rule observed is that the moon which is on the fifteenth day after the equinox constitutes the first month of the following year, while the moon that occurs before it belongs to the last month of the preceding year.

Thus they reckon in order twelve lunar months. Because the lunar cycle consists of twenty-nine and a half days, the months alternate between twenty-nine and thirty days. After the second or third year has been completed, they intercalate an additional month, which is customarily formed from the eleven epagomenal days of the year. Chorus and Praetextatus said that this was the reason.

## CHAPTER VII — On the Months of the Romans

Interrogator: Why are they of such differing lengths?

Respondent: When Romulus, with a sharp but rustic intelligence, was organizing the constitution of the empire, he took the beginning of the month from the day on which the new moon happened to be seen.

Because it does not always appear on that day, but sometimes later and sometimes earlier according to definite causes, it happened that, when it appeared later, more days were assigned to the preceding month, and when it appeared earlier, fewer. Since the first observation thus established a permanent numerical rule for each month, the result was that some months received thirty days and others thirty-one.

Interrogator: How did he name his months?

Respondent: Romulus dedicated the first month to Mars, whose son he wished himself to be, because it is said that Juno gave birth to Mars in Phrygia in that month.

That this month was once the beginning of the year is especially demonstrated by the fact that the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth months still retain names derived from their number: September, October, November, and December.

He called the second month April, as though it were *aperilis*, “opening,” because in it, when the clouds, frosts, and winter storms have withdrawn, the sky, earth, and sea are opened to sailors, farmers, and astrologers. Trees and grasses also begin to open into bud, and living creatures likewise begin to open toward offspring.

He made May the third month and June the fourth, naming them from the *maiores* and *iuniores*, into whom he divided the people, so that one part might defend the commonwealth by arms and the other by counsel.

Others contend that May was named by Maia, the mother of Mercury. They offer as their chief proof the fact that in this month all merchants sacrificed equally to Maia and Mercury.

The month of June was named either from the division of the people, as we have said, or—as Cingius thinks—was formerly called *Iunonius* among the Latins. This name remained for a long time among the ancestors, but after some letters had been worn away it was called *Junius*, June. The temple of Juno Moneta was also dedicated on the Kalends of June.

The month of July, formerly Quintilis because it derived its name from the number five, retained that name even after the two months had been placed before March. Later it was called July in honor of Julius Caesar, because he was born on the fourth day before the Ides of Quintilis.

August was formerly called Sextilis, until the honor of Augustus was bestowed upon it by decree of the Senate, because on the first day of that month he had defeated Antony and Cleopatra and secured the power of the Roman people.

September, October, November, and December retain their principal names, indicating by their names their position relative to the spring month, that is, March, or perhaps because rains threaten during them.

This was Romulus’s annual arrangement. He established that the year should consist of ten months and 304 days, and he arranged the months so that four of them—March, May, Quintilis, and October—had thirty-one days, while the remaining six had thirty days.

In months having seventh-day Nones, the Kalends returned from the Ides to the seventeenth day; in those having fifth-day Nones, the beginning of the Kalends returned to the eighteenth day.

But since this number agreed neither with the course of the sun nor with the calculations of the moon, it sometimes happened that the cold of the year occurred in the summer months and its heat in the winter months.

When this happened, they allowed as many days as necessary to pass without assigning them to any month, until the point in the year was reached at which the prevailing condition of the sky was suitable for the month then in progress.

Interrogator: Who later added to the length of the year?

Respondent: Numa subsequently added fifty days, so that the year might extend to 354 days, which he believed completed the twelve lunar months.

Of the fifty days he added, he withdrew six days from the six months that had thirty days—that is, one from each—and thus, having made fifty-six days, divided them equally into two new months.

Of the two, he called the earlier January and wished it to be the first month of the year, as though it were a two-faced month looking toward the end of the past and the beginnings of the future. Some think January was so called because it is the boundary and doorway of the year.

Numa dedicated the second month to Februus, that is, Pluto, who was thought to be the father of purifications. It was necessary to purify the city in that month.

Christian religion now preserves this custom, though turned in a better direction, on the same day of the month. The whole people offer measured sacred services to blessed Mary, while priests and ministers carry burning candles in their hands.

Shortly afterward Numa, in honor of the odd number, added one day, which he gave to January, so that both the year and each month, except February alone, would retain an odd number, as though an odd number were appropriate to the lower world and to diminution.

Interrogator: Who first established the year according to the number of the sun among the Latins?

Respondent: Gaius Julius Caesar, imitating the Egyptians, established the year according to the sun, as it is observed today. He added ten days to the former reckoning, so that the year would consist of 365 days, the time in which the sun itself traverses the zodiac.

Interrogator: Who first imposed the quarter-day upon the year, or who gave the leap its name?

Respondent: The aforementioned Caesar himself, so that the quarter-day would not be lost, decreed that every fourth year the priests responsible for the months and days should intercalate one day.

They did this in the month and at the place in which the month had formerly been intercalated—that is, before the last five days of February—and he decided that this should be called the *bissextus*, “the twice-sixth.”

Every intercalation was assigned to February, as though it had been the last month of the year. The Romans did this in imitation of the Greeks, who inserted their additional days into the last month of their year.

The Romans differed from the Greeks in one respect. The Greeks intercalated after completing their last month; the Romans did so after completing February, but on its twenty-third day, after the Terminalia had already been celebrated. They then appended the remaining days of February, which were the fifth after the intercalation.

I believe that this was done according to the custom of the ancient religion, so that March would follow February without interruption.

[Col. 0587A]

Interrogator: Why is the intercalation made on the sixth day before the Kalends of March?

Respondent: The Romans chose to intercalate the leap day in February because it was shorter than the other months and was the last month of the year.

They did so before it was completed, lest, by wholly cutting off their ancient arrangement, they separate the beginning of March from the end of February, as the Egyptians and Greeks wished to do in reckoning the whole cycle.

Accordingly, they inserted the day after the Terminalia had been duly celebrated on the twenty-third of February. Because they worshipped the god Terminus, they did not dare to transfer those rites, which had been established once for all on that day; they then inserted one day of the quarter.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0587B]

Interrogator: I ask you to explain the Kalends, Nones, and Ides to us.

Respondent: In ancient times this responsibility was assigned to the lesser pontiff: he was to watch for the first appearance of the new moon and report what he saw to the sacrificial king.

After the king and the lesser pontiff had performed the sacrifice, the same pontiff summoned the people to the Capitol beside the Curia Calabra, which was near the house of Romulus. He announced how many days remained from the Kalends to the Nones. For months with fifth-day Nones he proclaimed the number by saying *calo*, “I call,” five times; for months with seventh-day Nones he repeated it seven times.

Interrogator: How is the word *calo* interpreted?

Respondent: The word *calo* means “I call” in Latin. It was decided that the first of the days on which the people were called should be called the Kalends.

From this the curia to which they were summoned received the name Curia Calabra, and the assembly received the name *classis*, because the whole people were called into it.

The pontiff announced by calling how many days remained until the Nones because, after the ninth moon, the country people were required to gather in the city on the day of the Nones, to receive from the king of sacred rites the reasons for the festivals and to learn what had to be done during that month.

Hence some think that the Nones were so called as though they marked the beginning of a new observation, or because from that day nine days were always counted to the Ides.

Interrogator: From what were the Ides named?

Respondent: It was decided that the day which divided the month should be called the Ides. For *iduare* means “to divide” in rustic speech; hence *vidua*, “widow,” as though “thoroughly divided.”

Some prefer to derive *Ides* from a Greek word connected with appearance, because among the Greeks *idea* is the form or appearance that is displayed in full on that day.

Interrogator: When we read of the Kalends in sacred Scripture, how should it be understood?

Respondent: Whenever we read of the Kalends in sacred Scripture, nothing other than the rising of the new moon should be understood. Thus Scripture says: “At the Kalends, that is, at the beginnings of the months, you shall offer burnt offerings to the Lord.”

For the Hebrews know no beginnings of months other than new moons. The Greeks and Egyptians likewise observe no distinction among Kalends, Nones, and Ides in their months. Instead, beginning from the start of each month and proceeding to its end, they count the succession of days in a simple and uninterrupted order.

The Egyptians begin their year on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, while the Greeks begin theirs at the Kalends of December.

*Kalends* is interpreted as “callings,” *Nones* as “new observance,” and *Ides* as “division.”

## CHAPTER IX — On the Four Seasons of the Year

Interrogator: How many seasons are there in the year?

Respondent: Four. Through them the sun, traveling through the regions of heaven during the seasons of the year, regulates the world beneath it.

Interrogator: How does it regulate the world?

Respondent: Winter, because the sun is farther away, is cold and moist. Spring, when the sun returns above the earth, is moist and warm. Summer, when it burns overhead, is hot and dry. Autumn, when it descends toward the lower regions, is dry and cold.

When these seasons thus embrace one another, all the regions of the world that they govern around themselves are brought into being.

Interrogator: How many principal elements are there?

Respondent: Four.

Interrogator: How are they distinguished?

Respondent: First, earth, which is dry and cold. Second, water, which is cold and moist. Third, air, which is moist and warm. Fourth, fire, which is warm and dry.

Therefore earth is compared with autumn, water with winter, air with spring, and fire with summer.

Interrogator: How do these seasons begin?

Respondent: They do not begin at the beginnings of the months but at their middles. Different authorities, however, assign them differently.

Isidore, bishop of Seville, said that winter begins on the ninth day before the Kalends of December; spring on the eighth day before the Kalends of March; summer on the eighth day before the Kalends of June; and autumn on the tenth day before the Kalends of September.

The Greeks and Romans, whose authority in such matters is usually followed more readily than that of the Spaniards, determine that winter begins on the eighth day before the Ides of November; spring on the seventh day before the Ides of February; summer on the seventh day before the Ides of May; and autumn on the seventh day before the Ides of August.

They mark the beginnings of winter and summer by the rising and setting of the Pleiades in the evening or morning. Likewise, they mark the entry of spring and autumn when the Pleiades rise and set approximately at midday or midnight.

Finally, in the authoritative and distinguished books of cosmography, we find the same seasons distinguished according to a fixed line, with the rising of the Pleiades noted on the seventh day before the Ides of May and their setting on the seventh day before the Ides of November. Pliny Secundus likewise judged in his book of *Natural History* that the seasons should be distinguished in the same way.

Interrogator: Why are these four seasons called by these names?

Respondent: Spring (*ver*) is so called because everything in it becomes green—that is, *vernet*, “grows green.”

Summer (*aestas*) is named from heat, because it is the season in which fruits ripen.

Autumn (*autumnus*) derives its name from the ripening and gathering of fruits, which are collected in it.

Winter (*hiems*) is called by learned authorities the season of cold or sterility.

## CHAPTER X — On the Vernal Equinox

Interrogator: I ask you to explain briefly the vernal equinox, which the origin of the world teaches to be the head of the four annual changes.

Respondent: Ecclesiastical observance, confirmed by the Council of Nicaea, establishes that the day of Easter is to be sought from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April to the seventh day before the Kalends of May.

The rule of Catholic institution likewise commands that Easter not be celebrated before the passage of the vernal equinox.

Therefore, whoever assigns the equinox to the eighth day before the Kalends of April must necessarily deny that it is lawful to celebrate Easter before the equinox. The Lord himself also celebrated the first Easter with his disciples on the day before he suffered.

Such a person must either affirm that the event did not occur on the eighth day before the Kalends of April or confirm that it occurred before the equinox.

This is not merely the decision of our own time; the legal and Mosaic institution likewise decrees that the feast of Passover must not be celebrated before the passage of this equinox.

Anatolius clearly attests this, as does Josephus, together with their predecessors Agathobulus and Panaeas. One of these was among the seventy elders who had been sent by the priests to King Ptolemy to translate the books of the Hebrews into Greek. They answered many questions that the king posed concerning the traditions of Moses.

When they explained the questions of Exodus, they said that the Passover was not to be sacrificed before this vernal equinox had passed.

Therefore we must openly declare that the rule of truth is to be observed: Passover must not be sacrificed before the equinox and the defeat of darkness, and this equinox must be assigned to the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.

We are taught this not only by the authority of the fathers but also by consideration of the clock and the hours. The remaining three seasons likewise must, by a similar reckoning, be marked in the corresponding regions several days before the eighth day before the Kalends of the following months.

## CHAPTER XI — On the Years

Interrogator: From what was the year named?

Respondent: The year received its name either from renewing all things that have passed away according to the natural order or from the circuit of time.

For the ancients used *annus* in the sense of “around,” as Cato says in the *Origines* concerning orators: “the term of a year,” that is, “around the term.” *Ambire* is likewise used for *circumire*, “to go around.”

Interrogator: In how many ways are years spoken of?

Respondent: There is a lunar year, a solar year, a year determined by the wandering stars, and one year belonging to all the planets, which they specifically call the great year.

Interrogator: In how many ways is the lunar year understood?

Respondent: In four ways.

The first is when the moon, traversing the zodiac in twenty-seven days and eight hours, returns to the sign from which it departed.

The second is longer by two days and four hours. This is customarily called a month: after twenty-nine days and twelve hours have elapsed, the moon, now diminished, returns to the sun from which it departed as new.

The third is completed by twelve such months—that is, in 354 days—and is called common because two such years very often run together.

The fourth is called in Greek *embolismus*, “an insertion” or “superaddition,” and contains thirteen months, that is, 384 days.

Among the Hebrews both kinds begin with the beginning of the month of Passover and end there. Among the Romans, however, the year begins with the new moon of January and ends there.

Interrogator: What do you say about the solar year?

Respondent: The solar year is completed when the sun returns to the same regions of the stars after 365 days and six hours—that is, one quarter of a whole day.

When this fraction has been accumulated four times, it produces one additional day, which the Romans call the leap day, so that the sun may return to the same circuit.

The fourth year of the solar cycle is leap-year and is one day longer than the other three. Once it has been completed, the sun returns to all the regions of the signs at the same hours of the days and nights as before the four-year period.

The year of the wandering stars is the period in which they too traverse the circuit of the zodiac.

The great year is completed when all the wandering stars together return to their respective places. It is completed in 532 years.

Interrogator: Where do the Hebrews, Greeks, Egyptians, and Romans begin the civil year—that is, the solar year?

Respondent: The Hebrews begin it at the vernal equinox, the Greeks at the solstice, the Egyptians in autumn, and the Romans at midwinter.

## CHAPTER XII — On the Zodiacal Circle and the Course of the Sun and Moon

[Col. 0590B]

The zodiacal circle consists of twelve signs, through which the seven wandering stars travel: the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn.

Together these signs contain 360 degrees, and individually thirty. By the degrees of the zodiac we ought to understand the sun’s daily progress through the heavens.

The signs are so large that no less than the space of two hours is required for them to rise, set, or move from their position.

Thirty degrees are assigned to each sign because the sun traverses it in thirty days, with ten and a half hours besides. These hours are more than a full twenty-fourth part of a day, but do not together make a whole day and are therefore disregarded in calculation.

Nevertheless, when these fractions have revolved twelve times, they complete five days and a quarter. How much they have added to the thirty degrees will then become clear, and the completed solar year consists not merely of 360 days but, with the addition of five days and a quarter, of 365 days and a quarter.

Therefore the zodiacal circle is 365 degrees in extent. The sun and moon customarily traverse two of its middle degrees—or, more probably, its middle regions.

The sun traverses the zodiac in 365 days and six hours; the moon in twenty-seven days and eight hours.

The sun passes through each sign in thirty days and ten and a half hours. The moon passes through each sign in two days and five-sixths of an hour.

If you ask what *bessis* means, it is the amount by which something falls short of a whole, just as eight falls short of twelve, ten of fifteen, and twenty of thirty. After a third has been subtracted, whenever only two parts remain, those two parts are called a *bessis*; the third part is called a *triens*.

They are therefore mistaken who say that the moon traverses as much celestial space in thirty days as the sun traverses in 360.

For the truth clearly reveals what we have stated above: the moon completes its course in twenty-seven days and one-third of a day, while the sun completes its course in a year. The amount of space that the moon traverses in one of its months is exceeded by the sun in thirteen of its circuits.

## CHAPTER XIII — On the Leap Year
## Question

There are some who, by an easy method of calculation and without labor, understand how much of the increment of the leap year is continually completed in individual years, months, weeks, and even days, yet do not know how that same increment grows, what causes and rationale govern its increase, or what harmful error would arise if the necessary leap day were not intercalated in its proper order according to custom. Explain all this by calculation.

### Answer

The leap year (*bissextus*) is completed over four years by the reckoning of the quarter. A quarter is customarily called the fourth part of anything whatsoever—for example, of money, time, or space. Thus the fourth part of a day, which is completed in twenty-four hours together with its night—that is, six hours—is commonly called a quarter.

The manner in which this quarter is gathered over four years into a complete day and intercalated in its proper place is as follows. The sun is known to complete its annual circuit of the heavens—that is, the twelve well-known signs of the zodiac—not in three hundred and sixty-five days, but with six hours added. Hence, for example, if it enters the equinoctial point of the heavens at sunrise this year, in the following year it will enter it at midday, in the third at evening, in the fourth at midnight, and in the fifth once again at the beginning of the day, as though it had completed the whole circuit of a day. Thus it necessarily indicates that an extra day must be inserted somewhere. The Egyptians, after solemnly completing their year, customarily intercalate it on the fourth day before the Kalends of September; the Romans, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, and for this reason they call it a leap day (*bissextus*).

But if some calculators should suppose that every year ought to consist only of three hundred and sixty-five days, they would soon find a great loss arising in the annual circuit, so that after the passage of several years the misguided calculator would be horrified to find spring in the summer months, winter in the spring months, autumn in the winter months, and summer in the autumn months.

If anyone is unfamiliar with what we have briefly said about the zodiac and the circuit of the heavens, we have taken care to satisfy him by a common—and perhaps more concise and evident—method, so that one who did not learn the signs of the heavens as a boy at school may at least grasp what is necessary from the lines of a sundial drawn on the ground.

Let him therefore also know that, through its pauses and daily slowness, the sun is the instrument of this quarter of the year, by the working of the Creator. More careful investigation shows that it cannot be brought back to the same line of a sundial in three hundred and sixty-five days. For example, if in the present year it rises from the middle of the east at the spring equinox—which, according to the Egyptians, who are pre-eminent among calculators, regularly occurs on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April—then on the same day one year later it will rise somewhat lower; and in the third, fourth, and fifth years this diminution in the reckoning of its course will increase to such an extent that, unless the leap day were intercalated in the customary manner before three hundred years had passed, it would rise from the middle of the east on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, making the equinox, while nevertheless maintaining the same constancy of its slowness in all the other risings and settings throughout the year.

## Chapter XIV — On the Measure of the Increase

### Question

I wish to learn about the leap-year increment.

### Answer

We say that the quarter of a day—that is, six hours—increases by one hour per year, by half an hour in two natural solar months, that is, thirty days and ten hours, and by a quarter of one hour, that is, one point, in half a month.

### Question

Where should the increases or decreases of the sun and moon, according to the order of nature, be inserted into the year?

### Answer

The order of nature requires that the increases or decreases of the sun and moon begin or end at the equinoctial points, where they were first created: those of the sun at the spring equinox, and those of the moon at the autumnal equinox. Yet different authorities sought to place the leap at different points.

Thus Anatolius placed it at the equinox and in the fourteenth year of his nineteen-year cycle, moving it from the eighth year to the twentieth. Victorius, on the other hand, judged that it should be inserted in the third year before the end of the eight-year period, on the Kalends of January, and added it from the fourth year to the sixteenth. The Egyptians, whose opinion the Catholic Church now follows, assign it to the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, at the point on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, counting from the eighteenth year as nothing.

It should be understood that wherever the addition is made, three months of twenty-nine days each are counted there together.

## Chapter XV

### Question

I wish to learn more fully about the leap of the moon.

### Answer

It appears probable that the lunar leap anticipates the place and hour of the moon’s renewal more quickly than is commonly supposed. For how could it happen that over nineteen years one day necessarily had to be added to the customary number of days, unless some speed in the moon’s revolution gradually produced this result throughout the whole period of the nineteen-year cycle? Just as it has been demonstrated that, through the sun’s slowness, one day is added to its course every four years, so the same principle applies here.

Although the order of this speed—or, as I may call it, anticipation—is not easily apparent, its measure is by no means hidden. It is established that the diminution and removal of one day, by which the entire nineteen-year period is completed, increases by one hour and one point in each year, together with one nineteenth part of a point.

A day has twenty-four hours. When nineteen of these are distributed among the nineteen years of the nineteen-year cycle, five remain. Multiply these by four, since an hour consists of four points, and they make twenty. Assign one to each year, and one remains. Divide this by nineteen, and you will see that, to complete the lunar leap, one hour, one point, and a nineteenth part of one point are added annually, as we have said.

The moon’s increase therefore is not observed at exactly the same divisions of time or regions of the heavens, but always occurs somewhat earlier than in the preceding month, so that there is a basis for one day being skipped in the nineteenth year.

## Chapter XVI — On the Nineteen-Year Cycle

The Council of Nicaea established the nineteen-year cycle because of the fourteen paschal moons. For, after two hundred and thirty-five lunar revolutions over nineteen years, each moon returns, in an unerring course, to the same day of the solar year.

The order of this cycle was first composed by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine. It is divided into eight-year and eleven-year periods—that is, into eight and eleven years. For eight lunar years exceed the same number of solar years by only two days. One of these is used to complete the eleven-year period, while the other is consumed by the reckoning of the lunar leap. Otherwise the eleven solar years would exceed the lunar period by one day, although some people forcefully attempt to make up these days from the leap days of eight years.

Since the leap day is customarily added to the sun in February and prejudices nothing concerning the moon’s future course, they do not themselves add a leap day to the eleven-year period. To put it more clearly: the two lunar days left over in the eight-year period will complete the two that are lacking in the eleven-year period.

Eight solar years, excluding leap days, contain two thousand nine hundred and twenty days.

The lunar period contains two thousand nine hundred and twenty-two days.

The eleven-year solar period contains four thousand fifteen days.

The lunar period contains four thousand thirteen days.

Eight solar years contain ninety-six months.

The lunar period contains ninety-nine months.

The eleven-year solar period contains one hundred and thirty-two months.

The lunar period contains one hundred and thirty-six months.

The nineteen-year cycle contains two hundred and twenty-eight solar months and two hundred and thirty-five lunar months.

Excluding the leap days of both heavenly bodies, they contain six thousand nine hundred and thirty-five days.

## Chapter XVII — On the Structure of the Nineteen-Year Cycle

The nineteen-year cycle is arranged in eight lines. Its first line contains the sequence of the years. The Greeks decided to reckon it from the years of Diocletian the persecutor. But Dionysius, the second Roman abbot, skilled in both languages, who wrote the paschal cycles in Greek and Latin, refused to reckon them from the years of that impious ruler. Instead, he preferred to record the sequence of years from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, advancing by one each year, for the sake of knowledge of the beginning of our hope and the cause of humanity’s restoration—that is, so that the Lord’s passion or resurrection might be found more easily.

But since the lunar cycle is nineteen years, while the solar cycle is completed in twenty-eight years, multiplying the two together produces a total of five hundred and thirty-two years. When this period has been repeated, the entire order of the solar and lunar courses revolves back upon its own tracks, restoring the same year of the nineteen-year lunar cycle, the same lunar epacts, the corresponding solar days, the same fourteenth moon, the same Sunday of Easter, and its moon in due order.

Thus, in the second year of the cycle, which Dionysius wrote as the first, the five hundred and thirty-third year from the Lord’s incarnation was completed. This is evidently, according to the concurrence of the heavenly bodies, the year in which he deigned to be incarnate. For this second year of the nineteen-year cycle had eleven epacts in the eighteenth lunar cycle, five concurrent days of the week, and the fourteenth paschal moon on the eighth day before the Kalends of April; everything then was similar.

And if someone had celebrated Easter at that time according to the custom now observed in the churches, on Sunday—that very day—which, as must be noted here, would have fallen on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, it would have had the sixteenth moon.

Since these matters stand as they do, there is a clear path for those seeking the year of the Lord’s passion. The faith of the Church, unless I am mistaken, holds that he lived in the flesh for a little more than thirty-three years until the time of his passion. For when he was about thirty years old, he was baptized, as the evangelist Luke testifies; and he preached for three and a half years after his baptism, as John in his Gospel makes clear not only by his repeated references to the successive Passovers, but also, prophetically, in his Apocalypse, as Daniel likewise indicates in his visions. This is indeed the teaching held by the holy Roman and apostolic Church.

How, then, as we mentioned above, does the paschal cycle revolve through five hundred and thirty-two years? Add thirty-three, or rather thirty-four, so that you may reach the very year in which the Lord suffered: the result is five hundred and sixty-six.

That, therefore, is the year of the Lord’s passion and resurrection from the dead. For just as the five hundred and thirty-third year corresponds in the first year [of the cycle], so the five hundred and sixty-sixth corresponds in the thirty-fourth, throughout the courses of the sun and moon.

Accordingly, when you open the cycles of blessed Dionysius, if you find that in the five hundred and sixty-sixth year from the Lord’s incarnation the fourteenth moon occurs on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, and that Easter Sunday occurs on the sixth day before the Kalends of April with the seventeenth moon, then you will have found the year in question.

No Catholic may doubt that the Lord ascended the cross on the fifteenth moon, on the sixth day of the week, and rose from the dead on the first day of the week, that is, Sunday. Nor may anyone disregard the command that the paschal lamb be sacrificed toward evening on the fourteenth day of the first month, together with the Gospel testimony, which appears to state that the Lord was crucified and buried by the Jews on that same evening and on the morning of the sixth day, and rose on the first day of the week.

The second order of the nineteen-year cycle comprises the indictions, which return in a circuit of fifteen years to their starting point. We have learned that these were instituted by the ancient Roman diligence to prevent an error that might arise concerning the dates.

For example, if an emperor should die in the middle of a year, either in life or in his reign, it could happen that one historian would assign that year to the period of the same king because he had ruled part of it, while another historian would consider it more appropriate to assign the same year to his successor because he too possessed an equal portion of the reign. To prevent chronological error from growing through such disagreement, they established indictions, by which both writers—and indeed the common people—could easily preserve the sequence at all times.

For ease of calculation they also wished there to be fifteen, so that, by a very simple number readily used for multiplication, the condition of elapsed time could be recalled more briefly. Indictions begin on the eighth day before the Kalends of October and end there.

The third line of the cycle mentioned above contains the lunar epacts, which annually increase in relation to the solar course by eleven days. Hence they are called *epacts*, from a Greek word meaning additions: additions which, as we have said, accumulate by eleven days each year. Or, more precisely, they are called additions because they are added on the twelfth day before the Kalends and throughout the entire year in order to discover which number the moons have.

Indeed, throughout the revolving course of the year, the lunar additions also have their own eleven days. For example, if today, as I write, the moon is five days old, one year later it will be in its sixteenth day; and so it continually increases by eleven additions each year until the thirtieth day. Whatever remains is the lunar age. Nor will this same lunar age recur until the nineteen-year cycle has been completed.

The epacts are recorded after the completion of the nineteen-year cycle to indicate the age of the moon on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, where the paschal festival begins. They establish this fixed rule of their course, always observing that whenever they have a number less than sixteen, the paschal moon is to be preferred. Whenever they have a number greater than sixteen, they show that Easter must be sought in the following moon. Their annual place is the eleventh day before the Kalends of April.

In the fourth line of the nineteen-year cycle are marked the solar epacts, that is, the concurrent days. These increase by three each year, and by two in a leap year, through addition, up to the number seven. Their cycle consists of four times seven years, that is, twenty-eight years, and cannot be completed before the leap year returns for the fourth time and all seven concurrent days have appeared:

Sunday, Wednesday, Monday, Saturday, Thursday, Tuesday.

This is the order in which the cycle runs. Although each year has its own concurrent days, the concurrent days fixed in the cycle particularly indicate which day falls on the ninth day before the Kalends of April. Since they are placed close to the beginning of the paschal festival, they readily reveal the day of the epacts or the weekday on which the fourteenth moon occurs, and thus make the path to finding Easter Sunday clear.

The annual concurrent days occur, as the calculator should remember, on the second day before the Kalends of April, the seventh day before the Ides of April, and the eighteenth day before the Kalends of March, reckoned from the eleventh day before those same Kalends.

The course of this cycle is such that the concurrent days belonging to any leap year were also in force five years earlier. After six years, the days that were concurrent in the first leap year recur; eleven years earlier they have passed, and after another six years those that were concurrent in the second year after the leap year return. Six years earlier they had passed, and eleven years later those belonging to the third year after the leap year remain; six years earlier they had passed, and after five years they return. This order of distinctions embraces all the days of the successive years.

Every calculator should remember that the same concurrent days that occur thirty years from now are those that will occur in the next year; the same as in sixty years are also those in four years; the same as in ninety years are those in six years; the same as in one hundred and twenty years are those in eight years; the same as in one hundred and fifty years are those in ten years; and so on in the same manner.

If you wish to know the concurrent day after any number of years has elapsed, observe how many times that number contains thirty, and, after doubling the thirtieth part, you will recognize the correspondence of the successive years. For example, three hundred contains thirty ten times. Therefore the concurrent day in the three-hundredth year will be twenty; if anything remains, add that also. The same order of the concurrent days applies to years already past.

Likewise, since the epacts of the present year in the nineteen-year lunar cycle return in the twentieth year, they return again in the forty-third, sixty-fourth, eighty-fifth, one hundred and sixth, one hundred and twenty-seventh, one hundred and forty-eighth, one hundred and sixty-ninth, one hundred and ninetieth, and so on in the same way. The same must be understood of the fourteenth paschal moon and of the other matters contained in the nineteen-year cycle. A diligent calculator will therefore also be able to record for himself the more distant recurrences of future times, always remembering that the condition of past ages corresponds to them as well.

The fifth region of the nineteen-year cycle contains the lunar cycle. It begins with its fourth year and extends through the third year of the cycle that properly belongs to the Romans and pertains to the month of January.

Just as each year of the nineteen-year cycle begins with the paschal month, on account of the legal observance of the Hebrews, and ends there, so this Roman cycle begins with the moon of January, according to the institution of the Romans, and ends there.

Like the other cycle, this one has a first and second common year, a third embolismic year, a fourth and fifth common year, a sixth embolismic year, a seventh common year, and an eighth embolismic year.

The eleven-year period, like the nineteen-year lunar cycle, has seven common years and four embolismic years. A common year has twelve lunar months and three hundred and fifty-four days. An embolismic year has thirteen months and three hundred and eighty-four days.

There is only one exception: the eighteenth year of this cycle, which is the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, in which one day is intercepted because of the lunar leap.

If you wish to know the age of the moon on the Kalends of January throughout the nineteen years, take any lunar cycle—for example, five. Multiply it by eleven; the result is fifty-five. Add the regular one, giving fifty-six. Divide by thirty; twenty-six remain. Therefore the moon on the Kalends of January in the fifth year of the nineteen-year cycle is twenty-six days old.

Again, take eight. Multiply by eleven; the result is eighty-eight. Add the regular one and divide by thirty; twenty-nine remain. The moon on the stated Kalends is therefore twenty-nine days old in the eighth year of the lunar cycle.

Only remember that in the sixteenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth cycles mentioned above you must add not one regular number, as in the others, but two; then you will find the moon on the Kalends of January without error.

The sixth place in the cycle embraces the fourteenth-day moons of the first month, which demonstrate without any ambiguity the Sunday of Easter in each year. For after the fourteenth moon comes Sunday, which is the day of the Sunday resurrection of Easter.

The fourteenth moon first appears at the equinox, that is, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. Its final appearance occurs twenty-nine days later, that is, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May. Within these limits, the course of the paschal observance is contained over the nineteen-year period according to the legal reckoning.

If you wish to find the fourteenth moon by calculation, take the lunar epacts of whatever year you wish. If they are fourteen or fifteen, recognize that the fourteenth moon occurs on the eleventh or twelfth day before the Kalends of April. For the stated Kalends are the proper place of all the epacts.

But if the epacts are fewer, allow them to increase day by day until they complete the number fourteen, and do not doubt that the paschal moon is found there. If the epacts are greater than fifteen, allow them to increase by days until thirty, the limit of that month. Beginning in this way with the new moon and proceeding in order up to the fourteenth day, you will properly find the day suitable for the paschal observance.

It must be noted, however, that the fourteenth moon habitually returns eleven days earlier than in the preceding year if the year is common, but nineteen days later if it is embolismic, except in the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, when, because of the lunar leap, it usually anticipates the annual course by twelve days.

The seventh title of the nineteen-year cycle contains the Sunday of Easter, which began from the Sunday of our Savior’s resurrection from the dead.

In the Old Testament, the time of Passover is commanded to be observed by three indications: first, after the equinox; second, in the first month; third, in the third week of that month—that is, from the evening of the fourteenth moon, which is the beginning of the fifteenth day, until the evening, which is the end of the twenty-first day.

A fourth rule has been imposed upon us in this observance from the time of the Lord’s resurrection: once the equinox has passed and we see the fourteenth moon of the first month rising in the evening, we do not immediately celebrate Easter—that is, the passage from death to life, from corruption to incorruption, from punishment to glory—but wait until, by rising, he deigned to accomplish it, and then celebrate the fitting solemnities of Easter.

If anyone objects that Moses established not the observance of the equinox but only that of the first month and its third week, let him know that although he does not expressly name the equinox, by commanding that Passover be celebrated at the full moon of the first month he plainly indicates that the equinox has been passed.

The eighth division of the cycle discloses the lunar dates of the Sunday of Easter, enclosed within the seven-day range of its varying occurrence—that is, from the fifteenth through the twenty-first day. These are certainly the days solemnly fixed by the notation of the law, when the Lord says:

> In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, you shall eat unleavened bread, until the twenty-first day of the month at evening. For seven days no leaven shall be found in your houses.

The rule concerning these seven days of unleavened bread is now as follows: when the fifteenth moon of the first month occurs after the equinox, whichever day of the seven it may be, through the twenty-first day, is understood to be suitable for the joys of the paschal festival.

You must know with certainty, however, that if the fourteenth moon of the first month falls on a Sunday, it must in every case be postponed to the following week.

## Chapter XVIII — On the Great Cycle of the Heavenly Bodies

The great paschal cycle is completed in five hundred and thirty-two years by multiplying the solar and lunar cycles together. Whether nineteen is multiplied by twenty-eight, or twenty-eight by nineteen, the result is five hundred and thirty-two.

Thus this same great cycle contains twenty-eight nineteen-year lunar cycles and nineteen solar cycles, each completed in twenty-eight years. It further has a corrupt numerical expression, literally “twice-six, ten-times-nine sevens,” glossed as one hundred and thirty-three, and twenty-eight times two hundred and twenty-eight solar months, stated as eight thousand two hundred and eighty-four. [The transmitted wording and arithmetic are inconsistent.]

The lunar months number twenty-eight times two hundred and thirty-five, that is, six thousand five hundred and eighty. Excluding the leap days of both bodies, the cycle contains one hundred and ninety-four thousand one hundred and eighty days; with the leap days added, one hundred and ninety-four thousand three hundred and thirteen days.

When this cycle has completed the stated sum of months and days in due order, it immediately turns back upon itself and restores all matters pertaining to the courses of the sun and moon exactly as they had been before.

If you wish to know which year it is from Adam according to the Greeks alone, multiply fifteen by four hundred and eighteen; the result is six thousand two hundred and seventy. Add the indiction of whatever year you wish—which is established to be nine in the present year—and the result is six thousand two hundred and seventy-nine [the transmitted text omits “six thousand”].

If you wish to know which year it is from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, calculate fifteen times fifty; the result is seven hundred and fifty years. Add the twelve regular numbers; the result is seven hundred and sixty-two. Add also the indiction of whatever year you wish, which is established to be nine in the present year; together they make seven hundred and seventy-one years from the incarnation of Christ.

Be careful to remember only this: when the fifteenth indiction has arrived, you should know that the first follows it.

Because the number of this calculation cannot be completed within a single indiction, in that year you will not multiply fifteen by five, as above, but fifteen times five and one unit. Proceed in this way in the following years, up to the fifteenth indiction. Calculate fifty-one by fifteen; when the seven regular numbers stated above are always added to these, you will complete the number of the years of the Lord, and nothing remains that can be added by twelve, just as something remains in the other indictions.

Thus in the first indiction one remains, in the second two, in the third three, and so on up to the fourteenth; as many remain from the calculation given above as the number of the indiction. By this method you will find the year of the Lord.

If you wish to know which indiction it is, take the years from Adam that you have and divide them by fifteen. Whatever remains is the whole indiction; if nothing remains, it is the fifteenth.

Likewise, if you wish to know which indiction it is, take the years from the incarnation of the Lord—that is, seven hundred and seventy-one—and always add three to them, making seven hundred and seventy-four. Divide this by fifteen; nine remain. Therefore it is the ninth indiction. If nothing remains, it is the fifteenth.

If you wish to know the epact, take the year of the nineteen-year cycle and always subtract one from it. Multiply the remainder by eleven, then divide by thirty. Whatever remains is the complete epact.

Again, calculate from the first year of the nineteen-year cycle up to whichever year you wish—for example, the fifth year. Set aside one; four remain. Multiply the four by the eleven annual epacts, and you will have four times eleven, making forty-four. Divide these by thirty; fourteen remain. The epact is therefore fourteen.

In the second nineteen-year cycle, calculate all nineteen years in the same brief manner.
