Likewise, divide the years of the Lord by eighteen, and multiply the remainder by eleven. Then divide by thirty; the remainder is the epact.

If you wish to know the solar epacts, that is, the concurrent days, take the years of the Lord and add their fourth part. Add four to these as well, because there were five concurrent days in the year of the Lord’s birth. Divide this total; the remainder is the number of concurrent days.

If you wish to know which concurrent day it is, take the solar cycle, which is now established to be twenty-eight, add its fourth part to that number, and divide by seven. Whatever remains is the concurrent day on the ninth day before the Kalends of April.

If you wish to know which lunar cycle it is, take the years from Adam and divide them by nineteen. Whatever remains is the cycle; if nothing remains, it is the eighteenth.

Likewise, take the number of years from the incarnation of the Lord, always subtract two, and divide the remainder by nineteen. Whatever remains is the nineteen-year lunar cycle; if there is a remainder, it is the nineteenth [the transmitted wording is uncertain].

If you wish to know which year of the nineteen-year cycle it is, take the years of the Lord and add one, because Christ was born in the second year of that cycle. Divide by nineteen; the remainder is the year of the nineteen-year cycle. If nothing remains, it is the eighteenth.

If you wish to know the leap year, divide the years of the Lord by four. Whatever remains is the number of years since the leap year.

If you wish to know how many points each moon shines by day according to the Romans, count the days from January. For example, on the Nones of March, the total is seventy-six.

See which lunar cycle it is—for example, six. Multiply that lunar cycle by five; the transmitted result, seventy-five, is arithmetically inconsistent. Add it to the days from January; the reported total, one hundred and forty-one, is likewise inconsistent with the preceding figures. Subtract sixty twice; the text then gives “one hundred and twenty,” with six remaining. These are the points of the moon that shine on that day: namely, the first hour and one point of the second hour.

If you wish to find the moon itself, remember the total you had before dividing by sixty, and however many times you subtracted sixty, add that many units to the same total. Then add the lunar cycle multiplied by six, divide by thirty, and you will find the moon of that day.

If you wish to know which solar cycle it is, take the years from Adam and divide them by twenty-eight. Whatever remains is the solar cycle.

---

## On the Celebration of Easter, or a Letter Concerning the Spring Equinox According to Anatolius

To the most reverend and most holy brother Wicrheda the presbyter, Bede wishes desirable peace in the Lord.

[Col. 0599D] I gladly received the letter of your kindness, most beloved brother in Christ, and I hastened, ready to copy and send to you, the chapters you requested, remembering the intimacy and affection with which, when I arrived there, you welcomed me. I have also endeavored now to explain at greater length that deservedly famous question [Col. 0600D] concerning ecclesiastical history, about which you questioned me when I was present and to which I then replied briefly as best I could: namely, concerning the spring equinox, which the most reverend bishop Anatolius is said to have recorded in the aforementioned book as occurring on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, whereas the other Egyptian teachers decree that it should rather be recorded on the twelfth day before those same Kalends.

For Saint Proterius, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, writing to the most blessed Pope Leo about Easter, says that, plainly and according to the course of the sun, the twenty-fifth day of the month Phamenoth—also known, according to the Roman reckoning, as the twelfth day before the Kalends of April—is the equinox. But the beginning of the first month ought not to be fixed entirely from this equinox according to the course of the moon; otherwise the moon’s movement ought in every respect to agree with the solar cycle. Saint Cyril, likewise, bishop of that same Church, says: “For the sun itself is enclosed each day over land and sea at the end of the day and opened at the beginning of the day, and the sun completes the course of the whole year on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.”

Hence you are rightly troubled, as are other learned men, by the question of how Anatolius, although he too was Egyptian by learning and birth, should write, as if contrary to the Egyptian teachers, that the same equinox usually occurs on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. “Therefore,” he says, “in the first year, the beginning of the first month, which is the beginning of the nineteen-year cycle, is, according to the Egyptians, on the twenty-sixth day of the month Phamenoth; according to the Romans, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April.” On that day the sun is found not only to have entered the first part, but also already to possess a quarter of it on that same day, that is, in the first of the twelve divisions. This division is the spring equinox, and it is itself the beginning of the months, the head of the cycle, and the completion of the course of the stars called πλάναι, that is, ‘wandering’; it is also the end of the twelfth division and the boundary of the entire cycle.”

[Col. 0601C] I believe, however, that it can very easily be shown by calculation that in this he is not contrary to the other teachers of Egypt and the East. For the calculation of the quarter-day—which they call the leap-day—causes the sun to occupy the equinoctial point of its course in the zodiacal circle sometimes at its first rising, sometimes at midday, sometimes at sunset, and sometimes at midnight. Whenever the equinox occurs in the morning or at midday, it belongs to the twelfth day before the Kalends of April; whenever it occurs in the evening or at midnight, it belongs to the eleventh day before those same Kalends. For without contradiction, every night, from the time when the Lord rose from the dead, is assigned to the times of the following day, not added to those of the preceding day.

Therefore Anatolius wisely does not forbid Easter to be celebrated on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, but does forbid it before that day, since in the same book he carefully affirms, from the writings of ancient as well as recent Fathers, that Easter cannot be celebrated before the passage of the equinox. He himself bore witness that, in writing this, he marked not the first moments of the equinoctial period but the last—namely, those from which he knew that the celebration of Easter could begin. For when, in the second or third year after the leap-day, Easter Sunday occurs on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, it is plainly evident that the time of Easter begins together with the equinox. The rites of this observance are celebrated during that first night, although no one doubts that the equinox is completed during it or even begins then, since that is precisely the hour at which the Lord’s resurrection is rightly celebrated, which took place at dawn.

[Col. 0601D] And so that you may clearly perceive that Anatolius specifically writes of the evening equinox as the point from which Easter may begin, and that this regularly pertains to the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, attend to what he records below from the opinion of the ancient Fathers:

“Since there are two equinoxes, of spring and autumn, separated by equal intervals, and since the solemnity of the fourteenth day of the first month is fixed after evening, when the moon is found set opposite the sun, as may also be verified with the eyes, the sun is found to occupy the region of the spring equinox, while the moon occupies that of the autumn equinox. What wonder, then, if he says that the equinox occurs on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, since he declares that he is speaking of that hour when, as the sun sets in the evening, the moon, in opposition, raises its own rising?”

Here we must likewise observe that he said the spring and autumn equinoxes are separated by equal intervals. From this we should conclude that we must count half a year from one equinox to the other, and record the autumn equinox on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, separated from the spring equinox by 182 days. An examination of the sundial also shows this to be entirely true, especially since he supports this most equal division of the year between the equinoxes with the words of the very ancient and learned teacher Aristaeus, who was one of the seventy illustrious translators of Holy Scripture.

As for Anatolius’s further statement that on that day the sun is found not only to have entered the first division but also already to possess a quarter of it—that is, in the first of the twelve divisions—he calls the twelve divisions the twelve signs of the horoscope, each of which holds the sun for thirty days and, in addition, a few hours. Hence Maro says of these same divisions:

> Therefore, the golden sun rules the sphere,  
> measured out in fixed divisions,  
> through the twelve stars of the world.

The first of these divisions, according to nature, begins at the place of the spring equinox. Since this first of the twelve is the spring equinox—because the beginning of that division, namely the point at which the sun is first positioned, contains the equinox—he rightly says beforehand that on that day the sun has not only entered the first division but also already possesses a quarter of it. For whenever, according to the calculation given above, the equinoctial moment falls on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, that quarter of a day which annually tends to increase is then recognized as naturally complete.

[Col. 0602D] For when the equinox occurs on the twelfth day before those same Kalends, that same quarter is completed on that very day and at that very equinoctial hour. We add “naturally” because human custom has assigned it to various times of the year, according to what seemed suitable to each people. By natural reckoning, however, it is added at the completion of the solar cycles, as Cyril indicated in the passage cited above, saying: “And the sun completes the course of the whole year on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.”

And lest anyone perhaps contend that we have failed to understand what Anatolius himself meant in this statement, I wish to append a few passages which the very learned Victor, bishop of the city of Capua, wrote concerning these same divisions and the equinox.

[Col. 0603A] “The celestial circle,” he says, “through which the sun, moon, and stars called planets are carried by their own motion against the movement of the entire heavens, has been distributed, by the judgment of wisdom, into twelve divisions. When these have been completed in 365 days—the whole period in which the year is fulfilled—and the sun has returned to the beginning of the first division of the aforementioned circle, the beginning of the year arises. This occurs from the twelfth day before the Kalends of April up to the eleventh. For it is often found to occur in the evening, sometimes at night, and occasionally on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April itself.

“Therefore, on the twenty-sixth day of the month March according to the Alexandrians—that is, according to the Latins, on the twelfth or eleventh day before the Kalends of April—the beginning of the first month is established according to the course of the sun. But lest anyone wish to accuse us of inconsistency because, wavering as though amid uncertainty, we do not precisely define the day of the first month, let such a critic—or rather investigator—know that the most careful teaching establishes that the first hour of the following day begins with the seventh hour of the day. Thus, although it is the twenty-fifth day of the month March, the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, if in the evening of that day the sun illuminates the extent of the first division, it is already reckoned as the twenty-sixth, according to the subtle and undoubtedly probable Egyptian tradition.”

[Note: [Col. 0603D] In our copy the reader erased “of March” and placed “Phamenoth” in the margin. EDIT.]

And shortly afterward:

“Therefore,” he says, “if the moon is found to be fourteen days old while the sun is positioned in the first division of its circle, it is rightly assigned to the first month. But if the moon has previously shone with this full light of its orb as a fourteen-day moon before the sun has reached the aforesaid first division of its circle, it is found—or will be reckoned—to belong to the twelfth month. And whenever this happens, the solemnity is deferred to the next full moon, which must occur while the sun is still positioned in the first of the twelve divisions of its circle.”

[Col. 0603C] I have thought it useful to draw these words from the blessed Victor so that the opinion of Saint Father Anatolius—which is obscure to many both in his own paschal work and in ecclesiastical history—might become clearer to you through Victor’s statements.

Nor should this be passed over: there are those who maintain that Anatolius in this statement placed not the eleventh but the eighth day before the Kalends of April. They say that, when he inserted this statement into ecclesiastical history, he changed one day for another, wishing to correct with a single word what he saw had been less perfectly expressed by Eusebius, while observing that everything else had been set down properly and philosophically. They claim that he did this so as not to expose publicly as blameworthy the man whom he had intended to praise, by incorporating into his histories Eusebius’s exact words as he himself had written them.

But it would be astonishing if Eusebius, a writer so circumspect in language and thought, could have been so eager for the praise of others that, burning with admiration for their writings, he fabricated that they had said what they had not said, without fearing to be accused once his readers had examined their complete works and discovered that the passages he had taken from them were set down differently in his sources.

It would also be astonishing if such an imposture escaped Victor, whose statements we have quoted and who was a man of equally outstanding learning. In another work, writing about Easter, he inserted this same statement of Anatolius from ecclesiastical history, adopting it as rightly worthy of praise and remembrance where it was appropriate to cite it; and he himself wrote “the eleventh,” not “the eighth,” day before the Kalends of April.

Dionysius, surnamed Exiguus, a man distinguished for his learning, likewise makes it astonishing that he himself should have sought, in his paschal letters, the support of Anatolius’s statement from ecclesiastical history, if he knew that the words there had been falsified. Since he was also highly skilled in the Greek language, he could not have been unaware of how these matters had originally been published.

But because it is not clearly established from the writings of Moses where this month takes its beginning or where it ends, “the aforementioned venerable 318 bishops, carefully investigating the observance of ancient custom and what had been handed down from Saint Moses—as is reported in the seventh book of Ecclesiastical History—declared that the new moon occurring from the eighth day before the Ides of March up to the day of the Nones of April constituted the beginning of the first month, and that from the twelfth day before the Kalends of April up to the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May the fourteen-day moon was to be carefully sought” (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book VII, chapter 28).

It therefore seems probable that Eusebius faithfully inserted into his histories what he had found in the Greek authority, but that Anatolius’s own little book was subsequently corrupted in certain Latin copies—by the fraud, no doubt, of those who, ignorant of the true date of Easter, desired to defend their error by the authority of so great a Father.

Those who believe that Eusebius corrected only one statement, rather than that others falsified Anatolius’s entire little book, ask how the book itself can contain the following:

“Therefore, in the first year, the beginning of the first month—which is the beginning of the nineteen-year cycle—is, according to the Egyptians, on the twenty-seventh day of Phamenoth; according to the Macedonians, on the twenty-second day of the month Distrus; but according to the Romans, on the twenty-fifth day of the month March, that is, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.”

The twenty-sixth day of the Egyptian month Phamenoth and the twenty-second day of the Macedonian month Distrus do not correspond to the eighth day before the Kalends of April, but to the ninth day before those Kalends. Does it not appear highly probable that the statement has been falsified, when the person who changed the ninth day before the Kalends of April to the eighth forgot also to alter the dates of the Egyptian or Greek months? He left unchanged what was less familiar, while altering only what was visible and familiar to him.

As to which of these alternatives is more truthful, let those who read Anatolius in Greek decide. Yet whether Eusebius altered one statement or someone else changed the entire little book from its original state, it is certain, beyond any doubt, that although many things have been altered, the equinox cannot occur on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. This will be demonstrated by clear calculation in an examination of the sundial.

[Col. 0605A] For the rule of ecclesiastical observance, approved both by the decrees of the earlier Fathers and, more clearly, by the Council of Nicaea, requires that Easter Sunday be sought from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April up to the seventh day before the Kalends of May. Likewise, the rule of Catholic institution commands that Easter not be celebrated before the passage of the spring equinox.

Therefore, whoever supposes that the equinox occurs on the eighth day before the Kalends of April must either say that it is lawful to celebrate Easter before the equinox, or deny that it is lawful to celebrate Easter before the seventh day before the Kalends. He must also affirm either that the Easter which the Lord celebrated with his disciples on the day before he suffered did not occur on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, or that it occurred before the equinox.

In the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is thirty days old on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, and in that same year the fourteenth moon falls on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, that is, on the Nones of April. Add thirty to it and take the regular number for the month of April; in that year the moon falls in April when its fourteenth day is reached. In the year when the fourteenth moon falls in the month of March, the March regular number is thirty-six. From the epacts you can easily recognize whether the fourteenth moon will occur in March or in April. If you have more than fifteen or fewer than five epacts, the fourteenth moon is reckoned in April.

Therefore, take thirty-five as the regular number for April, and always subtract that year’s epacts from it; what remains is the day on which the fourteenth moon occurs. For example, in the third year of the nineteen-year cycle there are twenty-two epacts. Subtract twenty-two from thirty-five, leaving thirteen: the fourteenth moon occurs on the thirteenth day of April, that is, on the Ides of April.

[Col. 0605C] If you seek the weekday of the fourteenth moon, add the concurrent number of that year to the number left over. For example, add it to the thirteen just mentioned, and in April also add the regular number seven. Add all these together, then divide by seven; what remains is the weekday of the fourteenth moon, and in this way you will reach Easter Sunday very easily.

For the month of March, take the regular number thirty-six and subtract that year’s epacts. For example, in the second year of the nineteen-year cycle, they amount to eleven; the fourteenth moon will then occur on the twenty-fifth day of that month, that is, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. If you seek the weekday of that same day, add to the prescribed number the concurrent number of that year and the regular number four for March. Add these together and divide by seven; what remains [Col. 0605D] is the weekday of the fourteenth moon. If nothing remains, it is the seventh weekday.

Thus, if thirty remains after the epacts have been subtracted, whatever remains after that is the day of the month on which you will find the fourteenth moon. In the year when there are four epacts, subtract four from thirty-five, leaving thirty-one. Subtract thirty, leaving one. The fourteenth moon occurs on the first day of the month, that is, on the Kalends of April.

If, after the epacts have been subtracted, thirty still remains, the fourteenth moon occurs on the fourteenth day of the month. This happens once in the nineteen years, when six epacts are assigned, and the fourteenth moon falls on the third day before the Kalends of April.

To instruct you by examples in finding the weekday on which the fourteenth moon occurs, take the present year of the Lord’s incarnation, 776. Take this year’s epacts, twenty-six, and subtract them from the regular number thirty-five; nine remain. Behold, then: the fourteenth moon is on the ninth day of the month, that is, on the fifth day before the Ides of April.

[Col. 0606B] Add also the concurrent number of the present year, namely one, to nine, making ten. Add seven to this, making seventeen. Divide this by seven: twice seven is fourteen, leaving three. It will therefore be the third weekday.

The following calendrical entries are transmitted in a corrupt and compressed form: “Fourteenth moon, IV; fourteenth, V; sixteenth, VI; seventeenth, VII; eighteenth, I; nineteenth—which is the day of Easter—V Ides of April. Fourteenth moon, IV Ides; fifteenth, III Ides; sixteenth, II Ides; seventeenth, Ides; fifteenth, IV; eighteenth, Kalends of May; nineteenth.” [The sequence as printed is materially uncertain.]

In the second year after this one, the number is seven. Since it is more than five and less than fifteen, the fourteenth moon belongs to March, and you will seek it as follows. Take the regular number for the month of March, thirty-six, and subtract seven; twenty-nine remain. The fourteenth moon occurs on the twenty-ninth day of March, that is, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April.

[Col. 0606C] To find the weekday, take the same twenty-nine and add the concurrent number of that year, namely two, making thirty-one. Add the regular number four for March, making the total thirty-five. Divide by seven. Since seven times five is thirty-five and nothing remains, it is the seventh weekday: the fourteenth moon falls on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, and the fifteenth moon on the third day before the Kalends of April; that is Easter Sunday, and this pattern applies throughout the individual years of the nineteen-year cycles.

Whenever you subtract the annual epacts from these regular numbers in this manner, you will find the fourteenth moon without error; and when you add the prescribed concurrent number to those regular numbers, you will also find the weekday of the fourteenth moon. Then, by counting the remaining weekdays of that week and assigning the waxing moon’s age to each successive day, you will determine with complete certainty both the moon’s position and its age.

These calculations, beloved companion, I have written out for you through my own labor. Now tell me with what gift you would vie with me today, while I, weary, give you such things.

An explanation of the dodrans and the semiuncia in divisions of the hours, [Col. 0606D] by which the calculation of lunar light is made among writers.

[Col. 0605]

FRAGMENT. (C)*

[Col. 0605D] After one dodrans and one semiuncia of each hour have elapsed—that is, after one hour has been divided into twenty-four semiunciae, since that many semiunciae make up a full libra—divide the twenty-four again by four, that is, into four groups of six. Three times six is called a dodrans, while once six is called a quadrans. This is what he means by “one dodrans of an hour,” namely, three parts of ten and eight semiunciae.

As for the additional semiuncia, he wished one of the six remaining semiunciae belonging to the quadrans to be added to the dodrans, so that there would be nineteen semiunciae, by which the tide of Ocean would come later each day and likewise recede later.

[Col. 0607]

ON THE ARRANGEMENT OF THE PASCHAL WEEKDAYS, BY THE BISHOP THEOPHILUS OF CAESAREA AND THE SYNOD OF THE OTHER BISHOPS. (C)*

[Col. 0607A] After the resurrection or ascension of the Lord and Savior, the apostles were unable to establish any arrangement concerning how Easter should be observed, because they were dispersed throughout the whole world and occupied with preaching. But on whatever day the fourteenth moon fell in the month of March, they celebrated Easter.

After all the apostles had passed from this world, the individual provinces maintained different fasts. For the Gauls celebrated Easter on whatever day fell on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, when Christ’s resurrection was traditionally commemorated. In Italy some fasted for twenty days, others for seven. The easterners, following the apostles as they had seen them do, as stated above, observed Easter on the fourteenth moon in the month of March.

When such observances were maintained in the individual provinces, this caused sorrow among the priests, because those whose faith was rightly one differed in their fasts. Then Pope Victor, bishop of the city of Rome, sent an authoritative letter to Theophilus, bishop and bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, so that an arrangement might be made there—where the Lord and Savior of the world had lived in the flesh—for the manner in which Easter should rightly be celebrated by all Catholic Churches.

Having received this authority, the aforesaid bishop summoned not only all the bishops of his own province but also those from various regions. [Col. 0607C] When that multitude of priests had assembled, Bishop Theophilus produced the authority sent to him by Pope Victor and showed what task had been entrusted to him.

Then all the bishops said together: “Unless we first investigate how the world was made in the beginning, nothing sound can be ordained concerning the observance of Easter.”

The bishops therefore said: “What do we believe was made first in the world, if not the Lord’s Day?”

Bishop Theophilus said: “Prove what you are saying.”

The bishops replied: “According to the authority of Scripture, there was evening and morning, the first day; then the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh. On that seventh day God rested from all his works, and he called that day the Sabbath. Since the Sabbath marks the last day, what can be the first except the Lord’s Day?”

[Col. 0607D] Bishop Theophilus said: “Behold, you have proved concerning the Lord’s Day that it is the first. What do you say concerning the season? For four seasons of the world are recognized: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Which season, then, was first made in the world?”

The bishops answered: “Spring.”

Bishop Theophilus said: “Prove what you are saying.”

They replied: “It is written: ‘Let the earth bring forth grass, plants according to their kinds, and fruit-bearing trees producing their fruit.’ This is understood to occur in the spring.”

Bishop Theophilus said: “At what point do you believe the beginning of the world occurred: at the beginning of time, in the middle of time, or at the end?”

The bishops answered: “At the equinox, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.”

Bishop Theophilus said: “Prove what you are saying.”

[Col. 0608A] They replied: “It is written that God made the light, and God called the light ‘day’; he made darkness, and called the darkness ‘night’; and he divided equal portions between light and darkness.”

Theophilus said: “Behold, you have proved your case concerning the day and the season. What is your opinion concerning the moon? Was it consecrated by God as waxing and already full, or as waning?”

The bishops answered: “Full.”

He said: “Prove what you are saying.”

They replied: “He made two great lights and placed them in the firmament of heaven, to shine upon the earth: the greater light for the beginning of the day, and the lesser light for the beginning of the night. This could not have been otherwise unless it had been full.”

“Now, then, we have investigated how the world was made in the beginning: on the Lord’s Day, in springtime, at the equinox, which is on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. At that very time the full moon and the elements rise again.”

Theophilus said: “Now, then, we must deal with the arrangement: how ought we to observe Easter?”

The bishops said: “Can the Lord’s Day be passed over, so that Easter is not celebrated on it, since it has been sanctified by so many and such great blessings?”

Theophilus said: “Tell me, then, by what and by how many blessings you assert that it was sanctified, so that we may write them down.”

The bishops said: “Its first blessing is that on it the darkness was removed and the light appeared. Its second blessing is that on it the people were liberated from the land of Egypt, as from the darkness of sins, through the Red Sea, as through the font of baptism. Its third blessing is that on the same day heavenly food, manna, was given to human beings.

[Col. 0608C] “Its fourth blessing is that Moses commands the people: ‘Let the first and the last day be observed for you.’ Its fifth blessing is expressed in Psalm 117: ‘They surrounded me like bees, and they burned like fire among thorns.’ Concerning the Lord’s resurrection he says: ‘This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it,’ up to the horn of the altar.

“Its sixth blessing is that on it the Lord rose again. You see, therefore, that the Lord’s Day of the resurrection may uniquely be observed at Easter.”

Theophilus said: “Concerning the season, God commanded Moses: ‘This month shall be for you the beginning of months; celebrate Easter in it.’ Therefore all thirty days have been consecrated by the Lord.”

The bishops said: “We have already given our answer above: the beginning of the world is the equinox on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. From the eighth day before the Kalends of April up to the eighth day before the Kalends of May, we read that the days were consecrated.”

[Col. 0608D] Theophilus said: “Behold, is it not impious that the Lord’s Passion, a mystery containing so great a sacrament, should be excluded beyond the limit? For the Lord suffered from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, the night on which he was handed over by the Jews, and he rose again on the seventh day before the Kalends. How, then, are three days excluded from the appointed boundary?”

All the bishops said: [Col. 0609A] “By no means should it happen that so great a sacrament be excluded beyond the boundary. Rather, these three days should be brought within the boundary, and the established limit should be drawn back below. Therefore, at that synod they decreed that Easter should be observed from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April up to the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, and that no one should be permitted to cross the appointed limit, either before or afterward.

“Likewise, the divine command concerning the moon must be maintained. Moses was commanded: ‘Let it be observed for you from the fourteenth moon up to the twenty-first.’ Since these seven moons are likewise to be observed at Easter, it is clear that they were consecrated.

“Therefore, when the Lord’s Day occurs within its proper boundary—from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April to the eleventh day before the Kalends of May—and the moon is the eighth of those sanctified moons, it has seemed right to us to celebrate Easter.”

Whatever the age of the paschal moon may be, if you subtract seven from it, the lunar age at the beginning of Lent will result. For example, if the paschal moon is fifteen days old, subtract twelve from fifteen, and three remain. The moon is therefore three days old at the beginning of Lent in the year when the fifteenth moon falls on Easter Sunday, and so likewise in the other cases.

Remember that in a leap year the moon of February has thirty days, and yet the moon of March also has thirty days, as it always does, so that the calculation of the paschal moon does not waver.

[Col. 0609]

A LITTLE BOOK ON THUNDER, TO HEREFRID.

[Note: [Col. 0609C] “The Little Book on Thunder, to Herefrid, whom he calls his venerable Father, translated from the Greek, perhaps from John Laurentius Lydus of Philadelphia, concerning whom see Greek Library, book III, chapter 20.” Thus Fabricius in his *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae aetatis*. Concerning John Laurentius in the cited passage he says: “Laurentius Lydus of Philadelphia, whether he was a Christian is uncertain; he lived under the emperors Anastasius, Justin, and Justinian, as testified by Theophylact Simocatta VII.16, p. 186, and Photius, codex 170. He had written three books to Gabriel, prefect of the city of Constantinople—about whom an epigram by Leontius Scholasticus is read at the beginning of the fourth book of the *Anthology*—one on the months, another περὶ διοσημειῶν καὶ ἄλλων τινῶν ὑποθέσεων μαθηματικῶν, ‘concerning weather-signs and certain other mathematical subjects,’ and a third of historical and civic content, περὶ πολιτικῶν ἀρχῶν, ‘concerning political institutions’; from the latter Lambecius quotes a passage in Greek in his notes on Codinus, p. 208.

“Besides Photius, Suidas mentions the first two books. Rutgersius, p. 289 of the *Variæ Lectiones*, and Meursius, in his notes on Leo’s *Tactica*, p. 447, suspect that the book on the months is the very one which Meursius transcribed from the Palatine Codex and which Rutgersius published in Greek on pp. 247–260 under the title: Ἐφήμερος βροντοσκοπία τοπικὴ πρὸς τὴν σελήνην κατὰ τὸν Ῥωμαῖον ΦΙΓΟΥΛΟΝ, ‘A daily local divination from thunder in relation to the moon, according to the Roman Figulus.’ [Perhaps this is the same *Brontologia* mentioned by Labbe in the *Bibliotheca nova manuscriptorum*, p. 121; but in the catalogue of manuscripts of the Palatine Library, p. 94, one reads: “Brontoscopia of Photius the Roman, translated by John Laurentius Lydus of Philadelphia, with the preface of the same Laurentius; likewise Figulus’ interpretation of thunders and lightnings from the Etruscan Tagetes.” Rutgersius published only the latter.] That is, Nigidius Figulus, outstanding among the Romans for astrological learning, whose fragments Rutgersius collected there. He prefaced them with this little book, translated from the Latin of Nigidius into Greek: ἐκ τῶν ΤΑΓΗΤΟΣ καθ᾽ ἑρμηνείαν πρὸς λέξιν, ‘from Tagetes, word for word by interpretation.’

“But it is rather a portion of the work on weather-signs, as is clear from its opening words: Εἰ ἐπὶ πάσης τῆς διοσημείας, ‘If throughout the whole system of weather-signs…’ Other parts of the same book are noted by the most learned Neocorus as existing in Codex 2432 of the Royal Library of Paris, including a work indicating throughout the year the risings and settings of the constellations, translated word for word into Greek from the books of Claudius Thuscus, and so forth.

“Joannes Scheferus, a distinguished man, thought that Lydus’s book περὶ διοσημείων, ‘concerning weather-signs,’ was of the same subject as Obsequens’s book *On Prodigies*. But from Aratus and others it is clear that διοσημεῖα or διοσημείαι are prognostications concerning weather, derived from winds, thunder, and other phenomena of this kind.

“Emperor Leo also seems to have referred to this book at the end of the *Tactica*, in words read by John Checo the translator but absent from the Greek manuscript of Meursius: ‘Those who carefully study Ptolemy and certain Chaldaean observations, the *Phenomena* of Aratus, and the daily and monthly observations of John Lydus…’

“Photius placed little faith in these observations or predictions: Ἀλλ᾽ ἡ μὲν περὶ διοσημείων ὅσαγε κατ᾽ ἐμὴν κρίσιν καὶ πεῖραν οὐδὲν ἢ ἐπ᾽ ὀλίγον διενήνοχε μύθων, ‘But as for the material concerning weather-signs, at least insofar as judgment and experience have taught me, it differs not at all, or only slightly, from myths.’

“The book *On the Months* is entirely different and adds various material concerning the gods, their images, and their worship; Codinus and Suidas drew material from it. Lambecius used a Greek manuscript from the Royal Library of Paris and quotes passages from that book in Greek in his notes on Codinus, pp. 152, 153, 154, 155, and 172. Photius says: Ἡ δὲ περὶ μηνῶν πραγματεία εἰ καὶ πολὺ τὸ ἄχρηστον ἔχει, ἀλλ᾽ οὖν πρὸς τὴν τῆς ἀρχαιότητος μάθησιν ἐπίχαρί τε καὶ λίαν χρειῶδες, ‘The treatise on the months, although it contains much that is useless, is nevertheless pleasant and highly useful for learning about antiquity.’ Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca*.]

[Col. 0609B] I received the long-desired letter of your affection, venerable Father Herefrid, in which you compelled me to undertake a very laborious and dangerous little work—one certainly exposed to the barking and blasphemies of detractors and the envious. They may perhaps assert that I did and devised these things under the influence of a diabolical spirit—which God forbid—or inspired by some wicked invention of magical art, and not enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, or imbued with a rhetorical spirit; that I have presumed to proclaim new predictions of events, as though with a prophetic mouth.

You entreated me, and repeatedly and firmly commanded me, to translate into Latin, according to the small spark of my talent, what the thunderclaps prophetically signify, since it is clear that something is missing from the wording in both places.

[Col. 0610B] Obeying your commands, I therefore made every effort to complete this little work, lest your venerable request appear to have been treated by me as worthless. Nevertheless, I earnestly beg you to oppose, with the shields of your prayers, those envious people who will attempt either to gnaw at or mock this little work with a dog’s tooth, or, like barking dogs, rage against me with rabid mouths—people who think themselves learned if they disparage others.

By the anchor of your holy discourse and of your faithful people, make this little work, translated from the discourse of your faithful servant into Latin, remain altogether secure and unharmed against the slanders of the envious and hostile.

I also ask you, dearest Father, since you have made me undertake so great a work, to intercede faithfully for me, a wretched sinner, in your holy sacrifices before the presence of the Most High.

I. ON THUNDER IN THE FOUR PARTS OF THE WORLD

From the East.—If thunder should arise from the eastern quarter, then, according to the traditions of subtle philosophers, that thunder portends a copious shedding of human blood during the course of that year.

From the West.—When thunder likewise rises from the western region, the wise, investigating with extraordinary subtlety and actively examining the omens of events, have said that it signifies that mortality among the offspring of Adam and a most grievous pestilence are impending in that year.

From the South.—Thunder from the south, as philosophers of keen intellect who have marked the omens of events through intellectual reflection and investigative prudence say, foreshadows that the inhabitants of the sea will die in a great disaster during the course of that year.

From the North.—When thunder roars from the north, according to the subtle judgment of those who have attempted to investigate the causes of events, it signifies the mortality of the worst sinners—namely, pagans and wicked Christians.

II. OMENS BY MONTHS

Concerning January.—If thunder resounds in the month of January, as the acumen of philosophers has discovered, it foreshadows that many people and animals—particularly sheep—will die during the course of that year, and it portends sterility or unproductiveness for the forests and woodlands.

Concerning February.—If thunder arises in the month of February, it is said to harm greatly the ears of those who hear it, and to pertain to the ear, which it disturbs.

[Col. 0611C] Concerning March.—Thunder in the month of March, according to the investigation of noble philosophers of keen intellect, signifies dangerous omens; for, as they say, it foreshadows mortality or the day of the fearful judgment.

### Of April

The thunder of the month of April, they say, signifies that danger threatens the seeds and crops during the course of that same year, and gives advance warning that it is exceedingly dangerous to sail amid the waves of the vast sea.

### Of May

But if thunder should sound in the month of May in any year, those who have carefully recorded the omens of things have said that the thunder signifies abundant rain and excessive fertility of crops and hay coming in that very year.

### Of June

If thunder likewise should arise in the month of June during the course of that year, the thunder declares that fish of various kinds, in manifold and diverse abundance, will come that year amid the blue-gray waves of the rivers.

### Of July

The philosophers who, through intellectual reflection and active study, have attempted to investigate the omens of things also said that the thunder of the month of July, in whatever year it occurs, foretells that a great danger of death threatens human beings during the course of that year, and excessive unfruitfulness threatens the trees.

### Of August

The discoverers and authors of great subtleties, endowed with outstanding philosophical prudence in examining matters and enriched in the hidden recesses of contemplation, likewise said that if the thunder of the month of August should sound during the course of any year, it foretells that the fish of the sea, in their groups and generations, and the harmful host of the serpent-kind will die violently in that same year.

### Of September

If thunder should arise in the month of September in any year—as philosophers of keen intellect have subtly investigated—the thunder mystically indicates that, during the course of that year, a great multitude of laypeople will depart from this world in companies.

### Of October

The authors who, through wondrous contemplation, investigated what the thunder of the seasons signifies assert that the thunder of the month of October signifies that, within the circuit of that year, very violent storms of the air and enormous winds will come.

[Col. 0612B]

### Of November

The thunder of November, whenever it sounds, indicates, according to the physical speculation of subtle philosophers, that excessive infertility and sterility of all things threaten during the course of that year.

### Of December

The doctors of the noblest intellect, with fortunate and skillful reflection, have attempted to discern matters in the spiritual mirror. They say that the thunder of the month of December foretells nothing harmful or bad for human beings, the other animals, or any crops; rather, it appears to them to be favorable and most healthful.

## III. OF THE SEVEN WEEKDAYS

### Of Sunday

If thunder should sound on a Sunday in any year, the thunder itself indicates, as the philosophers who have investigated the omens of things through active reflection assert, that a great mortality threatens among clerics and religious women.

### Of Monday

The authors of distinguished intellect, who through vigilant contemplation, according to the capacity of human understanding, have written down all things and the foretellings of things for those who desire to recognize them, say that if thunder should arise on a Monday in any year, the thunder foretells that companies of married couples will die and that the crops will suffer an eclipse.

### Of Tuesday

According also to the flourishing knowledge of philosophers of excessive acumen and the subtlety of philosophical contemplation, philosophers who, through physical reflection and as if with a prophetic mouth, declare what the omens of things signify mystically, say among other things as follows: if thunder should arise on Tuesday within the circuit of any year, no one should doubt that the thunder mystically signifies a magnificent and most abundant abundance of the crops of the earth.

### Of Wednesday

The lovers of wisdom, drawn onward by diligent care in acquiring knowledge of things, testify that among the various and diverse subtleties of things they have discovered the following concerning the foretellings of thunder on Wednesday. For, as they say, if it should happen that thunder rises on Wednesday, no one should doubt that the thunder foretells that prostitutes, harlots, and foolish women will depart in companies from the prison of the flesh, or that it signifies a copious shedding of human blood.

[Col. 0613A]

### Of Thursday

The clever discoverers, in the fibers of their minds, of an effective and exceedingly prudent science—those who never cease to probe and investigate the omens of things according to sacred philosophy—assert the following, after prudent investigation, concerning the foretellings of thunder on Thursday. For they testify that whenever thunder sounds on Thursday, the thunder foretells a manifold abundance of the fruits of the earth to come, and that the exceedingly fertile and proud multitude of the inhabitants of the sea will multiply and fill all the channels of the rivers in their various groups.

### Of Friday

The noble teachers, who from almost the cradle have been suckled and nourished at the breasts of Mother Philosophy, with their most prudent contemplation and their keen intellects adorned with varied blossoms and the subtlety of philosophy, thus determine concerning the omens of thunder on Friday. They testify that whenever thunder should occur on Friday, the thunder foretells either the killing of a king, or a most violent war and the slaughter of many swiftly impending, or that many cattle will die.

[Col. 0613B; Col. 0614A]

### Of Saturday

The philosophers who, through an artificial science, have attempted to discern subtly the natures and omens of things by intellectual speculation, according to the excessive ardor of their keenest intellect, speak as follows concerning all the foretellings of thunder on Saturday. For if thunder should arise on Saturday and should sound, the thunder indicates that not far thereafter either a great plague of the human race or a most violent war will come.

# THE DIDACTIC WORKS OF THE VENERABLE BEDE, ANGLO-SAXON PRESBYTER: THAT IS, THE FIRST PART OF ALL HIS WORKS. SECTION TWO—DOUBTFUL AND SPURIOUS WORKS

[Col. 0613]

# THE FOUNDATIONS OF DONATUS’S ART OF GRAMMAR, RESTORED BY BEDE

## Preface

[Col. 0613C]

The book of Donatus’s arts has been so corrupted and spoiled by many people—each adding whatever he pleased, whether from other authors or whatever seemed good to him, and inserting declensions, conjugations, and other such material—that, except in ancient manuscripts, it is scarcely found pure and intact as it was issued by him. To prevent the appearance that we too have done this, we have thought it necessary briefly to explain on a small introductory page the reason for which we have arranged the present little work.

Everyone who has acquired a more extensive knowledge of this art than we have knows that the aforementioned grammarian composed his first art for the instruction of children, in the form of questions and answers, according to what he judged sufficient for the abilities and studies of his own time. But because we and those like us are so dull and obtuse that we often do not know what one ought regularly either to ask or to answer, we have compiled this little book according to the smallness of our understanding. It is not at all necessary for the sharper and more capable, but—as we judge—useful for the simpler and less ready.

In it we have preserved the order of the aforesaid grammarian both in asking and in answering; we have also attached, alongside it, certain explanations necessary for children and beginners, as well as other things that such instruction seemed to require. Thus children of good disposition who devote themselves to the study of this art may be able, to some extent, to test for themselves the things about which they are to ask and answer, and, by testing them, discover them more easily. Practiced as if in play and stimulated by exercise, they may thereby become more ready to grasp greater and fuller matters.

# HERE BEGINS THE BOOK

[Col. 0613]

[Col. 0613D]

**How many are the parts of speech?** Eight.

**Which?** Noun, pronoun, verb, adverb, participle, conjunction, preposition, interjection.

**What part of speech is “Donatus”?** A noun.

**What is a noun?** A part of speech with case, signifying a body or thing either specifically or generally.

**How many attributes does a noun have?** Six.

**Which?** Quality, comparison, gender, number, figure, and case.

**Wherein does the quality of nouns consist?** It is divided into two: for either it is the name of one person or thing, and is called a proper noun, or it is the name of many, and is an appellative noun.

**Is this noun proper or appellative?** Proper.

[Col. 0615A]

**How do you prove this?** Because it belongs not to many but to one.

**Is “grammaticus” (“grammarian”) proper or appellative?** Appellative.

**How do you prove this?** Because it belongs not to one but to many by comparison.

**How many degrees are there?** Three.

**Which?** Positive, as *doctus* (“learned”); comparative, as *doctior* (“more learned”); superlative, as *doctissimus* (“most learned”).

**Which nouns are compared?** Appellative nouns alone, when they signify quality or quantity.

**Is “Donatus” compared or not?** No.

**How do you prove this?** Because proper nouns are not compared at all.

**Is “bonus” (“good”) compared or not?** It is compared.

**How do you prove this?** Because it is both appellative and signifies quality.

**How?** *Bonus*, *melior*, *optimus*—“good,” “better,” “best.”

**Is “magnus” (“great”) compared or not?** It is compared.

**How do you prove this?** Because it is both appellative and signifies quantity.

**How?** *Magnus*, *major*, *maximus*—“great,” “greater,” “greatest.”

**Is “stylus” (“stylus”) compared or not?** No.

**Why not?** Because although it is appellative, it signifies neither quality nor quantity.

**How many genders of nouns are there?** Four.

**Which?** Masculine, as *hic magister* (“this teacher”); feminine, as *haec musa* (“this Muse”); neuter, as *hoc scamnum* (“this bench”); common, as *hic et haec sacerdos* (“this male or female priest”). There is also the three-gender category, called “every gender,” as *hic et haec et hoc felix* (“this fortunate man, woman, or thing”). There is also the epicene, that is, promiscuous gender, as *passer* (“sparrow”) and *aquila* (“eagle”).

**What gender is the noun “Donatus”?** Masculine.

**Why?** Because in the singular number and nominative case, the pronoun or article *hic* (“this”) is placed before it.

**How?** *Hic Donatus*—“this Donatus.”

**What gender is the noun “grammatica” (“grammar”)?** Feminine.

**Why?** Because in the singular number and nominative case, the pronoun or article *haec* (“this”) is placed before it.

[Col. 0615C]

**How?** *Haec grammatica*—“this grammar.”

**What gender is “scamnum” (“bench”)?** Neuter.

**Why?** Because in the singular number and nominative case, the pronoun or article *hoc* (“this”) is placed before it.

**How?** *Hoc scamnum*—“this bench.”

**What gender is “sacerdos” (“priest”)?** Common.

**Why?** Because it signifies both a male and a female.

**How?** *Hic et haec sacerdos*—“this male or female priest.”

**What gender is “felix” (“fortunate”)?** Every gender.

**Why?** Because under one meaning it includes three genders.

**How?** *Hic et haec et hoc felix*—“this fortunate man, woman, or thing.”

**What gender is “passer” (“sparrow”)?** Epicene.

**Why?** Because under one meaning it includes male and female.

**How?** *Hic passer*—“this sparrow.”

**Is “stylus” a fixed or mobile noun?** Fixed.

**Why?** Because it cannot be inflected into another gender.

[Col. 0615D]

**Is “sanctus” (“holy”) a fixed or mobile noun?** Mobile.

**Why?** Because it can move through all three genders.

**How?** *Sanctus, sancta, sanctum*—“holy” in the masculine, feminine, and neuter.

**Is “rex” (“king”) wholly fixed or wholly mobile?** Neither wholly fixed nor wholly mobile.

**Why?** Because it can be inflected into another gender, but it cannot move through all three genders.

**How?** *Rex, regina*—“king, queen.”

**How many numbers of nouns are there?** Two.

**Which?** Singular, as *hic magister* (“this teacher”); plural, as *hi magistri* (“these teachers”).

**What number is the noun “Donatus”?** Singular.

**Why?** Because when I say *Donatus*, I signify one, not many. The same answer should be given concerning appellative nouns.

**What number is “artes” (“arts”)?** Plural.

**Why?** Because when I say *artes*, I signify many, not one.

[Col. 0616A]

**How many figures of nouns are there?** Two.

**Which?** Simple, as *decens* (“fitting”), *potens* (“powerful”); compound, as *indecens* (“unfitting”), *impotens* (“powerless”).

**In how many ways are nouns compounded?** Four.

**In what ways?** From two complete forms, as *suburbanus* (“suburban”); from two corrupted forms, as *efficax* (“effective”), *municeps* (“municipal citizen”); from a complete and a corrupted form, as *insulsus* (“insipid”); from a corrupted and a complete form, as *nugigerulus* (“carrying trifles”); sometimes from several forms, as *inexpugnabilis* (“impregnable”), *imperterritus* (“undaunted”).

**Is “Donatus” a simple or compound noun?** Simple.

**Why?** Because it is compounded neither from two complete forms, nor from two corrupted forms, nor from a complete and a corrupted form, nor from a corrupted and a complete form, nor from several forms.

**Is “suburbanus” simple or compound?** Compound.

**How?** From two complete forms.

**Which?** From the preposition *sub* (“under”) and the noun *urbanus* (“urban”); for both remain complete when we say *suburbanus*.

[Col. 0616B]

**Is “municeps” simple or compound?** Compound.

**How?** From two corrupted forms.

**Which?** From the noun *munus* (“office, duty”) and the verb *capio* (“I take”); for both are corrupted when we say *municeps*.

**Is “insulsus” simple or compound?** Compound.

**How?** From a complete and a corrupted form.

**Which?** From the preposition *in* (“in, without”) and the noun *salsus* (“salty”); for *salsus* is corrupted when *insulsus* is said.

**Is “nugigerulus” simple or compound?** Compound.

**How?** From a corrupted and a complete form.

**Which?** From *nugas* (“trifles”) and *gerulus* (“carrying”); for *nugas* is corrupted when we say *nugigerulus*.

**Is “inexpugnabilis” simple or compound?** Compound.

**How?** From several forms.

[Col. 0616C]

**Which?** From the prepositions *in* and *ex*, and the noun *pugnabilis* (“fightable”); all these remain complete when we say *inexpugnabilis*.

**Is “imperterritus” simple or compound?** Compound.

**How?** From several forms.

**Which?** From the prepositions *in* and *per*, and the participle *territus* (“terrified”); but the preposition *in* is corrupted when we say *imperterritus*.

**How many cases of nouns are there?** Six.

**Which?** Nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, vocative, and ablative.

**What case is the noun “Donatus”?** Nominative.

**Why?** Because when I say *Donatus*, I name the person who is so called.

**What case is the noun “grammatica”?** Nominative and vocative.

**Why?** Because when I say *grammatica*, I either simply name the thing so called or address it. This may be said simply; but in sentences and complete discourse the answer concerning all the cases is much easier, where the first and third persons of the verb draw the nominative case, the second draws the vocative, and verbal nouns do likewise. Some are joined with the genitive, some with the dative, some with the accusative, and some with the ablative case, as:

*cano ego Virgilius*—“I, Virgil, sing”;

*canit ille Virgilius*—“that Virgil sings”;

*cane, Virgili*—“sing, Virgil”;

*egeo panis*—“I lack bread”;

*loquor tibi*—“I speak to you”;

*voco te*—“I call you”;

*doceor a te*—“I am taught by you”;

*oratore magistro utor*—“I use the orator as teacher.”

**Are all things declined or not?** No.

**Why?** Because some of them are indeclinable, as *fas* (“what is right”), *nequam* (“worthless”); others are declinable, as *magnus* (“great”), *fortis* (“strong”).

**Are all declinable nouns varied through all the cases or not?** No.

**Why?** Because some are without cases, or *aptota*, as *frugit* and *sinapi* (“mustard”); some have one case, or *monoptota*, as *cornu* (“horn”) and *gelu* (“frost”); some have two cases, or *diptota*, as *hujus tabi, ab hac tabe*—“of this corruption, from this corruption”; *haec sors, ab hac sorte*—“this lot, from this lot”; others have three cases, or *triptota*, as *musa, musae, musam*—“Muse” in the nominative, genitive, and accusative; others have four cases, or *tetraptota*, as *senatus, senatui, senatum, a senatu*—“senate” in the nominative, dative, accusative, and ablative; others, as *docto, doctum, o docte*—“learned” in the dative or ablative, accusative, and vocative; others have six cases, or *hexaptota*, as *unus, unius, uni, unum, o une, ab uno*—“one” in the six cases.

**Is “solus Donatus” (“Donatus alone”) likewise varied through all the cases or not?** No.

**What, then, is it?** A *pentaptotum*, a five-case form.

**Why?** Because it is varied through five cases.

**Which?** Nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, and vocative.

**How?** *Hic Donatus, hujus Donati, huic Donato, hunc Donatum, o Donate*—“this Donatus, of this Donatus, to this Donatus, this Donatus, O Donatus.”

**Why do you not count the ablative?** Because it is like the dative. For just as we say in the dative *huic Donato* (“to this Donatus”), so we now say in the ablative *ab hoc Donato* (“from this Donatus”). The same answer should be given about the others.

**Through how many declensions are declinable nouns inflected?** Five.

**Which?** First, second, third, fourth, and fifth.

**Where is the declension recognized?** In the singular genitive case.

**Into what syllable, then, does the singular genitive of the first declension end?** Into the diphthong *ae*, as *haec musa, hujus musae*—“this Muse, of this Muse.”

The second ends in a long *i*, as *hic Donatus, hujus Donati*—“this Donatus, of this Donatus.”

The third ends in a shortened *is*, as *hic pater, hujus patris*—“this father, of this father.”

The fourth ends in *us* or in a long *u*, as *hic senatus, hujus senatus*—“this senate, of this senate”; *hoc cornu, hujus cornu*—“this horn, of this horn.”

The fifth ends in the divided diphthong *ei*, as *hic dies, hujus diei*—“this day, of this day.”

**Of which declension is this noun?** Of the second.

**Why?** Because its singular genitive ends in a long vowel.

**How is it declined?** Nominative *hic Donatus*; genitive *hujus Donati*; dative *huic Donato*; accusative *hunc Donatum*; vocative *o Donate*; ablative *ab hoc Donato*.

**Why is it not declined in the plural?** Because proper nouns do not admit plurality.

**How is “grammatica” declined?** Nominative *haec grammatica*; genitive *hujus grammaticae*; dative *huic grammaticae*; accusative *hanc grammaticam*; vocative *o grammatica*; ablative *ab hac grammatica*. In the plural: nominative *hae grammaticae*; genitive *harum grammaticarum*; dative *his grammaticis*; accusative *has grammaticas*; vocative *o grammaticae*; ablative *ab his grammaticis*.

**Is it varied through all the cases in the plural or not?** No.

**What, then, is it?** A *tetraptotum*, a four-case form.

**Why?** Because it is varied through four cases.

**Which?** Nominative, genitive, dative, and accusative.

**How?** *Hae grammaticae, harum grammaticarum, his grammaticis, has grammaticas*—“these grammars, of these grammars, to these grammars, these grammars.”

**Why do you not count the vocative?** Because it is like the nominative.

**Why?** For just as we say in the nominative *hae grammaticae* (“these grammars”), so we say in the vocative *o grammaticae* (“O grammars”).

**Why do you not count the ablative?** Because it is like the dative.

**Why?** For just as we say in the dative *his grammaticis* (“to these grammars”), so we now say in the ablative *ab his grammaticis* (“from these grammars”).

[Col. 0617D]

**How is “pax” (“peace”) declined?** Nominative *haec pax*; genitive *hujus pacis*; dative *huic paci*; accusative *hanc pacem*; vocative *o pax*; ablative *ab hac pace*—“this peace, of this peace, to this peace, this peace, O peace, from this peace.”

**Why is it not declined in the plural?** Because its plural is not in use.

**With how many letters is the noun “cantor” (“singer”) written?** Six.

**Which of these are vowels?** *a* and *o*.

**How do you prove this?** Because they are pronounced independently and independently form a syllable.

**Which are consonants?** All the rest.

**Why?** Because they do not sound independently but sound with vowels.

**Which are semivowels?** *n* and *s*.

**Why?** Because they are pronounced independently but do not independently form a syllable.

**Which are mutes?** *d* and *t*.

**Why?** Because they are neither pronounced independently nor independently form a syllable.

**With how many letters is “Iuno” (“Juno”) written?** Four.

[Col. 0618A]

**Which of these are vowels?** *U* and *o*.

**Why?** Because they are pronounced independently and independently form a syllable.

**Why do you not count *I*?** Because it is being used in the place of a consonant.

**How do you prove this?** Because it is joined with another vowel.

**With how many letters is “Venus” written?** Five.

**Which of these are vowels?** *E* and the second *u*.

**Why?** Because they are pronounced independently and independently form a syllable.

**Why do you not count the first *u*?** Because it is being used in the place of a consonant.

**How do you prove this?** Because it is joined with another vowel.

**Of how many syllables does the noun “Donatus” consist?** Of three.

**What is the antepenultimate syllable like?** Long.

**By nature or by position?** By nature.

**Why?** Because only its vowel is lengthened.

**How?** As in the verse:

> *Donatus fama notus in orbe pia.*  
> “Donatus, known by fame throughout the pious world.”

**What is the penultimate syllable like?** Similar [the text appears to use *similis*, “similar,” where the expected term may be uncertain].

[Col. 0618B]

**And what is the final syllable like?** Short.

**Why?** Because it has a shortened vowel and does not end in two consonants, or in one double consonant, or in anything that stands for two consonants.

**Of how many syllables does “aes” (“bronze”) consist?** Of one.

**What kind?** Long.

**By nature or by position?** By nature.

**Why?** Because two vowels are joined in it and form a diphthong.

**Which?** *A* and *e*.

**Of how many syllables does “arcus” (“bow”) consist?** Of two.

**What is the first like?** Long.

**By nature or by position?** By position.

**Why?** Because its shortened vowel ends in two consonants.

**Which?** *R* and *c*.

**Of how many syllables does “axis” (“axle”) consist?** Of two.

**What is the first like?** Long.

**By nature or by position?** By position.

**Why?** Because its shortened vowel ends in one double consonant.

**Which?** *X*.

**Of how many syllables do “adjutor” (“helper”) and “advena” (“newcomer”) consist?** Of three.

**What are their antepenultimate syllables like?** Long.

**By nature or by position?** By position.

**Why?** Because their shortened vowels end in another consonant and another vowel used in the place of a consonant.

**Which?** *D* and *i*, and *d* and *u*.

**Of how many syllables does “major” (“greater”) consist?** Of two.

**What is the first like?** Long.

**By nature or by position?** By position.

**Why?** Because its shortened vowel ends in *i* alone, used in the place of a consonant.

**What foot is “Donatus,” then?** An antibacchius.

**Why?** Because it consists of two long syllables and one short syllable.

**Of how many time-units is it?** Of five.

**Why?** Because that foot occupies the same number of time-units.

**What foot is “Donatianus”?** None.

**Why?** Because it exceeds the number of four syllables.

**What, then, is it?** A *sinzigia* [syzygy, or compound metrical unit].

**From which feet is it made?** From a spondee and an amphibrach.

**Why?** Because the two long syllables placed at the beginning make a spondee. The following three, of which the first and last are short and the middle one long, produce an amphibrach.

**Of how many time-units is it?** Of eight.

**Why?** Because the feet joining together in the *sinzigia* occupy the same number of time-units.

**What foot is “aes”?** None.

**Why?** Because a foot is never made from one syllable.

**Of how many time-units is it?** Of two.

[Col. 0619A]

**Why?** Because a long syllable has two time-units.

**With what accent should “Donatus” be pronounced?** With the circumflex.

**Why?** Because in words of three, four, or more syllables, if the final syllable is short but the penultimate is long by nature, the penultimate is circumflexed.

**How?** *Donatus.*

**With what accent should “fax” (“torch”) be pronounced?** With the acute.

**Why?** Because monosyllables with a shortened vowel are pronounced with the acute accent.

**How?** *Fax.*

**With what accent should “res” (“thing”) be pronounced?** With the circumflex.

**Why?** Because monosyllables with a lengthened vowel are pronounced with the circumflex accent.

**How?** *Res.*

**With what accent should “meta” (“boundary”) be pronounced?** With the circumflex.

[Col. 0619B]

**Why?** Because in disyllables whose first syllable is long and whose second is short, the first syllable is circumflexed.

**How?** *Meta.*

**With what accent should “nepos” (“grandson”) be pronounced?** With the acute.

**Why?** Because in disyllables, if the second syllable is long, the first is given the acute, whether the first is short or long.

**How?** *Nepos.*

**With what accent should “bonus” (“good”) be pronounced?** With the acute.

**Why?** Because in disyllables, if both syllables are short, the first syllable is given the acute.

**How?** *Bonus.*

**With what accent should “Tullius” be pronounced?** With the acute.

**Why?** Because in words of three, four, or more syllables, if the penultimate syllable is short, the antepenultimate is given the acute.

**How?** *Tullius.*

**With what accent should “Metellus” be pronounced?** With the acute.

[Col. 0619C]

**Why?** Because in words of three, four, or more syllables, if the penultimate syllable is long by position, that syllable receives the acute and the antepenultimate is pronounced with the grave accent.

**How?** *Metellus.*

**With what accent should “latebrae” (“hiding places”) be pronounced?** With the acute.

**Why?** Because in words of three, four, or more syllables, if the penultimate is long by position through a mute and a liquid, the antepenultimate receives the acute.

**How?** *Latebrae.*

**With what accent should “Micenae” (“Mycenae”) be pronounced?** With the acute.

**Why?** Because in words of three, four, or more syllables, if both the penultimate and the final syllable are long by nature, the penultimate receives the acute.

**How?** *Micenae.*

**What part of speech is “ego” (“I”)?** A pronoun.

**What is a pronoun?** A part of speech that, placed in place of a noun, signifies almost the same thing and sometimes receives person.

**How many attributes does a pronoun have?** Six.

**Which?** Quality, gender, number, figure, person, and case.

**Wherein does the quality of pronouns consist?** It is divided into two: pronouns are either definite or indefinite.

**Which are definite?** Those that receive persons, as *ego* (“I”), *tu* (“you”), *ille* (“that man”).

**Which are indefinite?** Those that do not receive persons, as *quisque* (“each person”).

**Is this pronoun definite or indefinite?** Definite.

**Why?** Because it receives person.

**Is “quis” (“who, someone”) a definite or indefinite pronoun?** Indefinite.

**Why?** Because it does not receive person.

**What are the genders of pronouns?** Almost the same as those of nouns: masculine, as *qui* (“who”); feminine, as *quae* (“who”); neuter, as *quod* (“which”); common, as *qualis* (“of what kind”) and *talis* (“such”); and three-gender, as *ego* (“I”) and *tu* (“you”).

[Col. 0620A]

**What gender is this pronoun?** Every gender.

**Why?** Because it can be placed in the position of a masculine, feminine, or neuter noun.

**What gender is “quis”?** Masculine.

**Why?** Because it can be placed only in the position of a masculine noun.

**What gender is “quae”?** Feminine.

**Why?** Because it can be placed only in the position of a feminine noun.

**What gender is “quid” (“what”)?** Neuter.

**Why?** Because it can be placed only in the position of a neuter noun.

**What gender is “qualis” (“of what kind”)?** Common.

**Why?** Because it can be placed in the masculine or feminine gender of a noun.

**Is “ego” a fixed or mobile pronoun?** Fixed.

**Why?** Because it cannot be inflected into another gender.

**Is “ille” a fixed or mobile pronoun?** Mobile.

**Why?** Because it can move through all three genders.

[Col. 0620B]

**How?** *Ille, illa, illud*—“that man, that woman, that thing.”

**Is “talis” a fixed or mobile pronoun?** Neither wholly fixed nor wholly mobile.

**Why?** Because it can be inflected into another gender, but it cannot move through all three genders.

**How?** *Hic talis et hoc tale*—“this [masculine or feminine] such person and this such thing.”

**How many numbers of pronouns are there?** Two.

**Which?** Singular, as *hic* (“this one”); plural, as *hi* (“these”).

**What number is the pronoun “ego”?** Singular.

**Why?** Because it can be placed only in the position of a singular noun.

**What number is the pronoun “nos” (“we”)?** Plural.

**Why?** Because it can be placed only in the position of a plural noun.

**What number is the pronoun “sui” (“of himself/herself/themselves”)?** Both.

**Why?** Because it can be placed in the position of either a singular or a plural noun.

**How many figures of pronouns are there?** Two.

**Which?** Simple, as *quot* (“how many”); compound, as *quotquot* (“however many”).

[Col. 0620C]

**Is this pronoun simple or compound?** It is simple.

**Why?** Because it is compounded neither from two complete forms, nor from two corrupted forms, nor from a complete and a corrupted form, nor from a corrupted and a complete form, nor from several forms.

**Is “quisque” (“each person”) a simple or compound pronoun?** Compound.

**How?** From two complete forms.

**Which?** From the pronouns *quis* and *que*; for both remain complete when we say *quotquot*. The same answer should be given about the others according to the pattern of nouns. [The example appears internally inconsistent in the supplied text: *quisque* is discussed, but *quotquot* is given in the explanation.]

**How many persons of pronouns are there?** Three.

**Which?** First, as *ego* (“I”); second, as *tu* (“you”); third, as *ille* (“that man”).

**What person is this pronoun?** First.

**Why?** Because when I say *ego*, I signify not you or another, but myself.

[Col. 0620D]

**What person is the pronoun “tu”?** Second.

**How do you prove this?** Because when I say *tu*, I signify not myself or another, but you.

**What person is the pronoun “ille”?** Third.

**Why?** Because when I say *ille*, I signify not myself or you, but another.

**How many cases likewise are there for pronouns?** Six, just as for nouns.

**What case is this pronoun?** Nominative.

**Why?** Because it can be placed only in the position of the nominative case of a noun.

**What case is the pronoun “tu”?** Nominative and vocative.

**Why?** Because it can be placed in the position of either the nominative or vocative case of a noun.

**Are case-forms found among pronouns or not?** They are found.

**Why?** Because some are not [the supplied text reads *non optata*; read here as *monoptota*, “having one case”], as *eccum* and *ellum* (“behold him”); some have three cases, as *sui, sibi, se* (“of himself, to himself, himself”); some have four, as *meus, mei, meae, meum* (“my” in four forms); others have five, as *ille, illius, illi, illum, ab illo* (“that one” in five forms).

**Why do you not count forms with two and six cases?** Because no pronouns of that kind are found.

**What, then, is this pronoun “ego”?** A *tetraptotum*, a four-case form.

**Why?** Because it is varied through four cases.

**Which?** Nominative, genitive, dative, and accusative.

**Why do you not count the ablative?** Because it is like the accusative.

**Why?** Just as we say in the accusative *me* (“me”), so we also say in the ablative *a me* (“from me”). The same answer should be given about the others, as in the case of a noun.

**Through how many declensions are pronouns inflected?** Four.

**Which?** First, second, third, and fourth.

**In how many of them, and in which pronouns, are they recognized?** Two in primitive pronouns and two in derivative pronouns.

**How many primitive pronouns are there?** Seven.

**Which?** *Meus* (“my”), *tuus* (“your”), *suus* (“his/her/their own”), *noster* (“our”), *vester* (“your,” plural), *nostras* (“ours”), and *vestras* (“yours”).

[Col. 0621B]

**What, then, is the first declension of pronouns?** That whose genitive and dative end in *i*, and whose accusative and ablative end in a long *e*.

**How?** *Mei, mihi, me, a me*—“of me, to me, me, from me”; *tui, tibi, te, a te*—“of you, to you, you, from you”; *sui, sibi, se, a se*—“of himself/herself/themselves, to himself/herself/themselves, himself/herself/themselves, from himself/herself/themselves.” No further pronouns of this declension are found.

**What is the second?** That whose genitive ends in *-us* [the text reads *hujus*; the supplied “Forte us” indicates uncertainty], and whose dative ends in the letter *i* for the three genders, except *huic*, which receives *c* in the dative for the sake of distinction, lest, if we said *hui*, it be thought not a pronoun but an interjection.

**How?** *Ille, illius, illi*—“that one, of that one, to that one”; *iste, istius, isti*—“that one, of that one, to that one”; *ipse, ipsius, ipsi*—“that very one, of that very one, to that very one”; *hic, hujus, huic*—“this one, of this one, to this one”; *is, ejus, ei*—“he/that one, of him/that one, to him/that one”; *quis, cujus, cui*—“who, of whom, to whom”; *totus, totius, toti*—“whole, of the whole, to the whole.” No further pronouns of this declension are found.

**What is the third?** That whose genitive in the masculine follows the second declension of nouns, in the feminine the first, and in the neuter likewise the second.

[Col. 0621C]

**How?** As follows: *meus, mei, mea, meae, meum, mei*—“my” in its masculine, feminine, and neuter forms; *tuus, tui, tua, tuae, tuum, tui*—“your”; *suus, sui, sua, suae, suum, sui*—“his/her/their own”; and similarly the rest.

**What is the fourth?** That whose inflection follows the third declension of nouns.

**How?** *Nostras, nostratis*—“ours”; *vestras, vestratis*—“yours”; *cujas, cujatis*—“of what person or place.”

There are three definite pronouns: *ego, tu, ille*—“I, you, that one.” There are seven less-than-definite: *ille, ipse, iste, is, hic, idem, sui*—“that one, that very one, that one, he/that one, this one, the same, of himself/herself/themselves.” There are five indefinite pronouns: *quis, qualis, quantus, quotus, quot*—“who/someone, of what kind, how great, which in order, how many.” The corresponding forms of the indefinite pronouns are *talis, tantus, totus, tot*—“such, so great, whole, so many”; and there are seven less-than-definite forms, which answer to the indefinite pronoun. There are seven possessives: *meus, tuus, suus, noster, vester, nostras,* and *vestras*—“my, your, his/her/their own, our, your [plural], ours, yours.”

All pronouns ending in *a* are feminine and belong both to the second and third declensions, such as *illa, ipsa, ista, ea, quanta, quota, tota, mea, sua, nostra, vestra*—“that woman/thing, that very woman/thing, that one, that woman/thing, however great, which in order, whole, my, his/her/their own, our, your.”

Those ending in *e* are all masculine and belong to the second declension, such as *ille, ipse, iste*—“that one, that very one, that one.” One pronoun ending in *i* is found, *sui*, which is of every gender and belongs to the first declension. One pronoun ending in *u* is found, *tu* (“you”), which is of every gender and belongs to the first declension. Three pronouns ending in *as* are found: *nostras, vestras, cujas*, all of every gender and belonging to the fourth declension.

Of those ending in *e*, four pronouns are found: *is, quis, qualis, talis*—“he/that one, who/someone, of what kind, such.” They belong to the fourth declension; but *is* and *quis* are masculine, while *qualis* and *talis* are common, and the neuter forms end in *e*.

Seven pronouns end in *us*: *quantus, quotus, tantus, totus, meus, tuus, suus*—“how great, which in order, so great, whole, my, your, his/her/their own.” All are masculine and mobile through the three genders. But *quantus, quotus, tantus, meus, tuus,* and *suus* belong to the third declension; *totus* belongs to the second.

One pronoun ending in *c* is found, masculine: *hic* (“this man”); one feminine: *haec* (“this woman”); and one neuter: *hoc* (“this thing”). For the sake of distinction, they receive *c* as a distinguishing mark [the supplied wording is grammatically uncertain].

Four pronouns end in *d*: *illud, istud, id, quod*—“that thing, that thing, it, which”; and they belong to the second declension.

Thirteen pronouns end in *m*: *idem, ipsum, quantum, quotum, tantum, totum, meum, tuum, suum, nostrum, vestrum, eccum, ellum*—“the same, that very thing, however much, which in order, so much, the whole, my, your, his/her/their own, our, your [plural], behold him, behold him.” They belong to the third declension, except *totum*, which belongs to the second, and *eccum* and *ellum*, which are not declined at all and have only the singular and plural accusative [the supplied text is uncertain here].

Two pronouns end in *er*: *noster, vester*—“our, your [plural].” They belong to the third declension.

Two pronouns end in *t*: *quot, tot*—“how many, so many.” They are of every gender and belong to no declension.

Whatever other pronouns are found besides these are compounds formed from them and must follow their rules.
