There is one pronoun of the first person, *ego* (“I”), and one of the second person, *tu* (“you”). The rest are third person, except for the possessives *meus* and *noster*, which belong to the first person, and *tuus* and *vester*, which belong to the second person.

**What part of speech is “doceo” (“I teach”)?** A verb.

**What is a verb?** A part of speech with tense and person, without case, signifying either doing something, undergoing something, or neither.

**How many attributes does a verb have?** Seven.

**Which?** Quality, conjugation, gender, number, figure, tense, and person.

**Wherein does the quality of verbs consist?** In moods and forms.

**Which are the moods?** Indicative, as *lego* (“I read”); imperative, as *lege* (“read!”); optative, as *utinam legerem* (“if only I were reading”); subjunctive, *cum legam* (“when I read”); infinitive, *legere* (“to read”); impersonal, *legitur* (“it is read”).

[Col. 0622B]

**What mood is this verb?** Indicative.

**Why?** Because when I say *doceo* (“I teach”), I indicate that I teach something.

**What mood is “doce” (“teach!”)?** Imperative.

**Why?** Because when I say *doce* (“teach!”), I command you to teach something.

**What mood is “utinam docerem” (“if only I were teaching”)?** Optative.

**Why?** Because when I say *utinam docerem* (“if only I were teaching”), I express the wish to teach something.

**What mood is “cum doceam” (“when I teach”)?** Subjunctive.

**Why?** Because when I say *cum doceam* (“when I teach”), in order to produce a complete sense I must join another mood to this verb.

**How?** As in *cum doceam, discis*—“when I teach, you learn.”

**What mood is “docere” (“to teach”)?** Infinitive.

**Why?** Because when I say *docere* (“to teach”), I define neither number nor person unless I distinguish both by adding another mood, as *docere volo, vis, vult*—“I wish, you wish, he wishes to teach”; *docere volumus, vultis, volunt*—“we wish, you [plural] wish, they wish to teach.”

[Col. 0622C]

**What mood is “docetur” (“it is taught”)?** Impersonal.

**Why?** Because when I say *docetur* (“it is taught”), I do not define by which person something is taught, unless I say it with pronouns added: *docetur a me, a te, ab illo, a nobis, a vobis, ab illis*—“it is taught by me, by you, by that one, by us, by you [plural], by those.” In this way one can easily answer concerning all verbs through the other numbers, persons, and tenses; this has been omitted by us for the sake of brevity.

**How many forms of verbs are there?** Four.

**Which?** Perfect, as *lego* (“I read”); meditative, as *lecturio* (“I intend to read”); frequentative, as *lectito* (“I read repeatedly”); inchoative, as *fervesco* (“I begin to boil”), *calesco* (“I begin to grow warm”).

**What form is this verb “doceo”?** Perfect.

**Why?** Because when I say *doceo* (“I teach”), I signify neither meditation, nor repetition, nor the beginning of an action, but simply a present action.

**What form of verb is “doceor” (“I am taught”)?** Perfect.

**Why?** Because when I say *doceor* (“I am taught”), I signify neither meditation nor the beginning of a state of being acted upon, but a present passive state.

[Col. 0622D]

**What form of verb is “lecturio” (“I intend to read”)?** Meditative.

**Why?** Because it ends in *-urio* and signifies intending a future action.

**What form of verb is “lectito” (“I read repeatedly”)?** Frequentative.

**Why?** Because it ends in *-tito* and signifies repetition of an action.

**What form of verb is “fervesco” (“I begin to boil”)?** Inchoative.

Why is this so? Because it ends in *-sco* and signifies the beginning of fervor. All these distinctions are more easily recognized if the endings of each form are carefully committed to memory. There is therefore only one ending of the meditational form, *-urio*, as in *esurio* (“I am hungry”), *lecturio* (“I am about to read”), and *parturio* (“I am in labor”). The frequentative has four endings: *-to*, as in *clamito* (“I shout repeatedly”); *-so*, as in *merso* (“I plunge repeatedly”); *-xo*, as in *nexo* (“I bind repeatedly”); and *-tito*, as in *lectito* (“I read repeatedly”) and *dictito* (“I say repeatedly”). The inchoative has only one, *-sco*, as in *floresco* (“I begin to flower”) and *uresco* (“I begin to burn”). But whatever verbs lack endings and meanings of this kind are to be pronounced, without any ambiguity, as belonging to the perfect form.

How many conjugations of verbs are there? Three.

Which are they? The first, the second, and the third.

[Col. 0623A] What is the first? That which, in the indicative mood, present tense, singular number, second person, in the active and neuter verb, has a lengthened *a* before the final letter, as in *amo, amas* (“I love, you love”). In the passive, common, and deponent verb, it has a lengthened *a* before the final syllable, as in *amor, amaris* (“I am loved, you are loved”); and its future tense, in the same voice and mood, sends a syllable into *-bo* and *-bor*, as in *amo, amabo* (“I love, I shall love”), and *amor, amabor* (“I am loved, I shall be loved”).

What is the second? That which, in the indicative mood, present tense, singular number, second person, in the active and neuter verb, has a lengthened *e* before the final letter. In the passive, common, and deponent verb, it has a lengthened *e* before the final syllable, as in *doceo, doces* (“I teach, you teach”); *doceor, doceris* (“I am taught, you are taught”); and its future tense, in the same voice and mood, sends a syllable into *-bo* and *-bor*, as in *doceo, docebo* (“I teach, I shall teach”); *doceor, docebor* (“I am taught, I shall be taught”).

What is the third? That which, in the indicative mood, present tense, singular number, second person, in the active and neuter verb, has a shortened or lengthened *i* before the final letter. In the passive, common, and deponent verb, in place of *i* it has a shortened *e*, or a lengthened *i*, before the final syllable, as in *lego, legis* (“I read, you read”); *legor, [Col. 0623B] legeris* (“I am read, you are read”); *audio, audis* (“I hear, you hear”); *audior, audiris* (“I am heard, you are heard”). Its future tense, in the same voice and mood, sends a syllable into *-am* and *-ar*, as in *lego, legam* (“I read, I shall read”); *legor, legar* (“I am read, I shall be read”); *audio, audiam* (“I hear, I shall hear”); *audior, audiar* (“I am heard, I shall be heard”).

Where can it be discerned whether the letter *i* is shortened or lengthened? In the imperative and infinitive.

How? For when the *i* is shortened, it is changed into *e*; but if it is lengthened, it is not changed.

When does the third conjugation send its future tense not only into *-am* but also into *-bo*? Sometimes, when it has an unshortened but lengthened *i*, as in *eo, is, ibo* (“I go, you go, I shall go”); *queo, quis, quibo* (“I can, you can, I shall be able”).

Of which conjugation is this verb? Of the second.

Why is this so? Because, in the indicative mood, present tense, singular number, second person, it has a lengthened *e* before the final letter, as in *doceo, doces* (“I teach, you teach”); and its future tense, in the same mood, sends a syllable into *-bo*, as in *doceo, docebo* (“I teach, I shall teach”).

*Doceor*: of which conjugation is this verb? Of the second.

[Col. 0623C] Why is this so? Because, in the indicative mood, present tense, singular number, second person, it has a lengthened *e* before the final syllable, as in *doceor, doceris* (“I am taught, you are taught”); and its future tense, in the same mood, sends a syllable into *-bor*: *doceor, docebor* (“I am taught, I shall be taught”).

*Clamo*: of which conjugation is this verb? Of the first.

Why is this so? Because, in the indicative mood, present tense, singular number, second person, it has an *a* before the final letter, as in *clamo, clamas* (“I shout, you shout”); and its future tense, in the same mood, sends a syllable into *-bo*, as in *clamo, clamabo* (“I shout, I shall shout”).

*Clamor*: of which conjugation is this verb? The same.

Why is this so? Because, in the indicative mood, present tense, singular number, second person, it has an *a* before the final syllable, as in *clamor, clamaris* (“I am shouted at, you are shouted at”); and its future tense, in the same mood, sends a syllable into *-bor*, as in *clamor, clamabor* (“I am shouted at, I shall be shouted at”).

*Scribo*: of which conjugation is this verb? Of the shortened third.

[Col. 0623D] Why is this so? Because, in the indicative mood, present tense, singular number, second person, it has a shortened *i* before the final letter, as in *scribo, scribis* (“I write, you write”); and its future tense, in the same mood, sends a syllable into *-am*, as in *scribo, scribam* (“I write, I shall write”).

How is it recognized that the letter *i* in this verb is shortened? Because in the imperative and infinitive it changes into *e*, as in *scribe, scribere* (“write, to write”).

*Scribor*: of which conjugation is this verb? The same.

Why is this so? Because, in the indicative mood, present tense, singular number, second person, it has a shortened *e* before the final syllable, as in *scribor, scriberis* (“I am written, you are written”); and its future tense, in the same mood, sends a syllable into *-ar*, as in *scribor, scribar* (“I am written, I shall be written”).

*Nutrio*: of which conjugation is this verb? Of the lengthened third.

Why is this so? Because, in the indicative mood, present tense, singular number, second person, [Col. 0624A] it has a lengthened *i* before the final letter, as in *nutrio, nutris* (“I nourish, you nourish”); and its future tense, in the same mood, sends a syllable not only into *-am* but also into *-bo*, as in *nutriam, nutribo* (“I shall nourish”).

How is it recognized that the letter *i* in this verb is lengthened? Because in the imperative and infinitive it is not changed into a shortened *e*, but remains unchanged, as in *nutri, nutrire* (“nourish, to nourish”).

*Nutrior*: of which conjugation is this verb? The same.

Why is this so? Because, in the indicative mood, present tense, singular number, second person, it has a lengthened *i* before the final syllable, as in *nutrior, nutriris* (“I am nourished, you are nourished”); and its future tense, in the same mood, sends a syllable not only into *-ar* but also into *-bor*, as in *nutriar, nutribor* (“I shall be nourished”).

How many genders of verbs are there? Five.

Which are they? Active, passive, neuter, deponent, and common.

What are active verbs? Those that end in *-o* and, when the letter *r* is accepted, make a passive verb from themselves, as in *lego, legor* (“I read, I am read”).

What are passive verbs? Those that end in *-r* and, when that letter is removed, [Col. 0624B] return to the active, as in *legor, lego* (“I am read, I read”).

What are neuter verbs? Those that end in *-o*, like active verbs, but, when the letter *r* is accepted, are not Latin, as in *sto* (“I stand”) and *curro* (“I run”).

What are deponent verbs? Those that likewise end in *-r*, like passive verbs, but, when that letter is removed, are not Latin, as in *luctor* (“I struggle”) and *loquor* (“I speak”).

What are common verbs? Those that likewise end in the letter *r*, like deponent verbs, but fall into two forms, that of the one affected and that of the agent, as in *osculor* (“I kiss”) and *criminor* (“I accuse”). For we say *osculor te* (“I kiss you”), *osculor a te* (“I am kissed by you”); *criminor te* (“I accuse you”), *criminor a te* (“I am accused by you”).

Of what gender is this verb, *doceo*? Active.

Why is this so? Because it ends in *-o* and, when the letter *r* is accepted, makes a passive from itself: *doceo, doceor* (“I teach, I am taught”).

*Doceor*: of what gender is this verb? Passive.

Why is this so? Because it ends in *-r* and, when that letter is removed, returns to the active, as in *doceor, doceo* (“I am taught, I teach”).

*Sto*: of what gender is this verb? Neuter.

[Col. 0624C] Why is this so? Because it ends in *-o*, like an active verb, but, when the letter *r* is accepted, is not Latin: we say *sto* (“I stand”), but we do not say *stor*.

*Loquor*: of what gender is this verb? Deponent.

Why is this so? Because it ends in *-r*, but, when that letter is removed, is not Latin; for we say *loquor* (“I speak”), but we do not say *loquo*.

*Criminor*: of what gender is this verb? Common.

Why is this so? Because it ends in *-r*, like a deponent, but falls into two forms, that of the one affected and that of the agent, as in *criminor te* (“I accuse you”), *criminor a te* (“I am accused by you”).

How many numbers of verbs are there? Two.

Which? Singular, as in *lego* (“I read”); plural, as in *legimus* (“we read”).

What number is this verb? Singular.

Why is this so? Because when I say *doceo* (“I teach”), I signify that I alone teach something.

*Docemus*: what number is it? Plural.

Why? Because when I say *docemus* (“we teach”), I signify that several of us teach something.

How many figures of verbs are there? Two.

[Col. 0624D] Which? Simple, as in *lego* (“I read”); compound, as in *negligo* (“I neglect”).

In how many ways are verbs compounded? Four.

In what ways? From two unchanged forms, as in *perlego* (“I read through”); from two altered forms, as in *efficio* (“I accomplish”); from an unchanged and an altered form, as in *deficio* (“I fail”); from an altered and an unchanged form, as in *offero* (“I offer”); sometimes from several, as in *derelinquo* (“I abandon”).

Is this verb simple or compound? Simple.

Why is this so? Because it is compounded neither from two unchanged forms, nor from two altered forms, nor from an unchanged and an altered form, nor from an altered and an unchanged form, nor from several forms.

*Perlego*: is it simple or compound? Compound.

How? From two unchanged forms.

Which? From the preposition *per* and the verb *lego*; for both remain unchanged when we say *perlego*. The same answer is to be given in this way concerning the other cases as well.

How many tenses of verbs are there? Three.

[Col. 0625A] Which? Present, as in *lego* (“I read”); past, as in *legi* (“I read”); future, as in *legam* (“I shall read”).

How many tenses are there in the conjugation of verbs? Five.

Which? Present, as in *lego* (“I read”); imperfect past, as in *legebam* (“I was reading”); perfect past, as in *legi* (“I read”); pluperfect past, as in *legeram* (“I had read”); future, as in *legam* (“I shall read”).

Of what tense is this verb? Present.

How do you prove this? Because when I say *doceo* (“I teach”), I signify that I teach something in the present. A suitable answer can also be given concerning the other tenses; but they can more easily be recognized from their own differences and properties.

How many persons of verbs are there? Three.

Which? First, as in *lego* (“I read”); second, as in *legis* (“you read”); third, as in *legit* (“he or she reads”).

Of what person is this verb? First.

How do you prove this? Because when I say *doceo* (“I teach”), I signify that I teach something.

*Doces*: of what person is this verb? Second.

[Col. 0625B] How do you prove this? Because when I say *doces* (“you teach”), I signify that you teach something.

*Docet*: of what person is this verb? Third.

How do you prove this? Because when I say *docet* (“he or she teaches”), I signify that someone other than myself or yourself teaches something. But both this grammatical property and all the others, in this part of speech alone, are much easier to recognize than to explain.

*Prudenter*: what part of speech is it? An adverb.

What is an adverb? A part of speech which, added to a verb, explains and completes its meaning.

How many properties belong to an adverb? Three.

Which? Meaning, comparison, and figure.

In what does the meaning of adverbs consist? In this, that they are adverbs of place, or of time, and so forth, as follows.

Give an adverb of place. For example, *hic* (“here”), or *ibi* (“there”), *intus* (“inside”), or *foris* (“outside”), *illuc* (“to that place”), or *inde* (“from there”).

[Col. 0625C] Give one of time. For example, *heri* (“yesterday”), *hodie* (“today”), *nuper* (“recently”).

Of number. For example, *semel* (“once”), *bis* (“twice”).

Of negation. For example, *non* (“not”).

Of affirmation. For example, *etiam* (“also, yes”), *quidni* (“why not?”).

Of demonstration. For example, *en* (“behold”), *ecce* (“behold”).

Of wishing. For example, *utinam* (“would that”).

Of exhortation. For example, *eia* (“come on”).

Of order. For example, *deinde* (“then, next”).

Of questioning. For example, *cur* (“why”), *quamobrem* (“for what reason”).

Of similarity. For example, *quasi* (“as if”), *ceu* (“as”).

Of quality. For example, *docte* (“learnedly”), *pulchre* (“beautifully”).

Of quantity. For example, *multum* (“much”), *parum* (“little”).

Of doubt. For example, *forsitan* (“perhaps”), *fortasse* (“perhaps”).

Personal. For example, *mecum* (“with me”), *tecum* (“with you”), *nobiscum* (“with us”), *vobiscum* (“with you [plural]”).

Of calling. For example, *heus* (“hey!”).

Of responding. For example, *heu* (“alas!”).

Of separation. For example, *seorsum* (“separately”).

Of swearing. For example, *vere* (“truly”), *veraciter* (“truthfully”).

Of choosing. For example, *potius* (“rather”), *immo* (“indeed, rather”).

Of gathering. For example, *simul* (“together”), *una* (“together”).

[Col. 0625D] Of prohibition. For example, *ne* (“lest, do not”).

Of occurrence. For example, *forte* (“by chance”), *fortuitu* (“accidentally”).

Of comparison. For example, *magis* (“more”), or *tam* (“so, as”).

Of what meaning is this adverb? Of quality.

Why is this so? Because when I say *prudenter* (“wisely”), I certainly signify a quality.

How? As in *prudenter loquitur* (“he speaks wisely”).

*Hic*: of what meaning is it? It is an adverb of place.

Why is this so? Because when I say *hic* (“here”), I certainly signify a place.

How? As in *hic habito* (“I live here”).

How many meanings do adverbs of place have? Four.

Which? In a place, as in *intus* (“inside”), *foris* (“outside”); from a place, as in *de* (“from”), *unde* (“whence”); to a place, as in *huc* (“to here”), *illuc* (“to there”); through a place, as in *hac* (“this way”), *illac* (“that way”).

What does this adverb signify? In a place. The same answer is to be given in this manner for the remaining categories.

*Hodie*: of what meaning is this adverb? Of time.

[Col. 0626A] Why is this so? Because when I say *hodie* (“today”), without doubt I signify time, as in *hodie lego* (“today I read”).

How many distinctions are there among adverbs of time? Three.

Which? They either indicate the present, as *nunc* (“now”); the past, as *heri* (“yesterday”); or the future, as *cras* (“tomorrow”).

Which of these does this adverb signify? The present.

*Non*: of what meaning is this adverb? Of negation.

Why is this so? Because when I say *non* (“not”), I categorically deny something.

How? As in *non feci* (“I did not do”), *non dixi* (“I did not say”), *non volui* (“I did not wish”).

*Quidni*: of what meaning is this adverb? Of affirmation.

Why? Because when I say *quidni* (“why not?”), I certainly affirm something—for example, if someone asks whether I wish to learn grammar and I answer, “Why not?”

*En*: of what meaning is this adverb? Of demonstration.

Why? Because when I say *en* (“behold”), I certainly demonstrate something, as in *en agros* (“behold the fields”).

*Utinam*: of what meaning is this adverb? Of wishing.

[Col. 0626B] Why is this so? Because when I say *utinam* (“would that”), I earnestly wish for something, as in *utinam sapiens sim* (“would that I were wise”), and *utinam pie et benigne vivam* (“would that I might live piously and kindly”).

*Eia*: of what meaning is this adverb? Of exhortation.

Why? Because when I say *eia* (“come on”), I earnestly exhort someone, as in *eia lege* (“come on, read”).

*Deinde*: of what meaning of order is this adverb? Of order.

Why? Because when I say *deinde* (“then, next”), I undoubtedly indicate the sequence of something, as when I say: “First I learned the forms of the letters, then the combinations of syllables, and finally, by reading, I acquired understanding.”

*Cur*: of what meaning is this adverb? Of questioning.

Why? Because when I say *cur* (“why”), I certainly ask something, as in *cur ita agis?* (“Why do you act thus?”), *cur ita loqueris?* (“Why do you speak thus?”).

*Quasi*: of what meaning is this adverb? Of similarity.

[Col. 0626C] Why? Because when I say *quasi* (“as if”), I introduce a certain likeness, as in: “He shines as if he were a torch; he is red as if he were a rose; he is pale as if he were dead; he grows black as if he were pitch.”

*Multum*: of what meaning is this adverb? Of quantity.

Why? Because when I say *multum* (“much”), I certainly signify quantity, as in *multum legit* (“he reads much”), *multum didicit* (“he has learned much”), *multum novit* (“he knows much”).

*Forsitan*: of what meaning is this adverb? Of doubt.

Why? Because when I say *forsitan* (“perhaps”), I show that I doubt something, as in *forsitan melius tempus erit* (“perhaps the time will be better”), *forsitan laetiores dies venturi sunt* (“perhaps happier days are coming”).

*Mecum*: of what meaning is this adverb? Personal.

Why? Because it refers to the first person, as in *mecum legit* (“he reads with me”); similarly *tecum* (“with you”), referring to the second person, as in *tecum habitat* (“he lives with you”); and *secum* (“with himself”), referring to the third person, as in *secum cogitat* (“he thinks with himself”). Likewise, in the plural, it refers to the first person, as in *nobiscum vivit* (“he lives with us”); to the second, as in *nobiscum discit* (“he learns with us”); and to the third, as in *haesitant, et secum quaerunt* (“they hesitate and inquire among themselves”).

[Col. 0626D] *Heus*: of what meaning is this adverb? Of calling.

Why? Because when I say *heus* (“hey!”), I expressly call someone, as in *heus juvenis* (“hey, young man!”), *heus frater* (“hey, brother!”).

*Heu*: of what meaning is this adverb? Of responding.

Why? Because when I use *heu* (“alas!”) adverbially, I answer someone who is calling me.

*Seorsum*: of what meaning is this adverb? Of separation.

Why? Because when I say *seorsum* (“separately”), I show that something is done apart, as in *seorsum oves, seorsum hirci pascuntur* (“the sheep graze separately, the goats separately”).

*Vere*: of what meaning is this adverb? Of swearing.

Why? Because when I say *vere* (“truly”), I affirm something by oath, as in *vere ita est* (“truly it is so”), *vere ita non est* (“truly it is not so”).

*Potius*: of what meaning is this adverb? Of choosing.

Why? Because when I say *potius* (“rather”), I signify that one thing is chosen from two or more, as in: “I prefer a tunic to a cloak,” and, “I desire health rather than riches.”

[Col. 0627A] *Simul*: of what meaning is this adverb? Of gathering.

Why? Because when I say *simul* (“together”), I signify that two or certain things have come together, or are going to come together, as in: “They came together; they are staying together with whomever they are lodging; they are going to depart together.”

*Ne*: of what meaning is this adverb? Of prohibition.

Why is this so? Because when I say *ne* (“lest, do not”), I completely prohibit something, as in *ne dixeris* (“do not say”), *ne loquaris* (“do not talk”).

*Forte*: of what meaning is this adverb? Of occurrence.

Why? Because when I say *forte* (“by chance”), I signify that something has happened, as in: “While the indicative proceeds, by chance it encounters robbers; while he hastens rapidly, by chance he stumbled violently.”

*Magis*: of what meaning is this adverb? Of comparison.

Why is this so? Because when I say *magis* (“more”), I compare certain things with one another, as in: “This man is more learned than that one,” and, “This man is wiser than that one.”

In what does the comparison of adverbs consist? In the three [Col. 0627B] degrees of comparison: positive, comparative, and superlative.

Give an adverb of the positive degree. For example, *docte* (“learnedly”).

Of the comparative degree. For example, *doctius* (“more learnedly”).

Of the superlative. For example, *doctissime* (“most learnedly”).

Which adverbs are compared? Those which either come from a comparative noun or form a comparative noun from themselves, as *docte* (“learnedly”), because it comes from the noun *doctus* (“learned”), makes *doctius* (“more learnedly”) and *doctissime* (“most learnedly”). Moreover, because it makes the comparative noun *ulterior* (“farther”) and the superlative *ultimus* (“farthest”), *ulterior* is compared as *ulterius* (“farther”) and *ultime* (“farthest”).

Is this adverb compared or not? It is compared.

Why is this so? Because it comes from *prudens* (“wise”) through the comparative noun; it is compared as *prudenter, prudentius, prudentissime* (“wisely, more wisely, most wisely”).

Is *ne* compared or not? No.

Why is this so? Because it neither comes from a comparative noun nor forms a comparative noun from itself.

How many figures of adverbs are there? Two.

[Col. 0627C] Which? Simple, as *docte* (“learnedly”), *prudenter* (“wisely”); compound, as *indocte* (“unlearnedly”), *imprudenter* (“unwisely”).

Is this adverb simple or compound? Simple.

Why is this so? Because it is compounded neither from two unchanged forms, nor from two altered forms, and so forth. The same answer is to be given concerning the remaining adverbs, whether compound or simple, according to the pattern established for the other parts of speech.

*Docens* (“teaching”): what part of speech is it? A participle.

What is a participle? A part of speech that takes one part from a noun and one part from a verb; for from the noun it receives genders and cases, and from the verb tenses and meanings; from both it receives number and figure.

How many properties belong to a participle? Six.

Which? Genders, cases, tenses, meanings, numbers, and figures.

How many genders of participles are there? Four.

Which? Masculine, as *hic lectus* (“this [masculine] read thing”); feminine, as *haec lecta* (“this [feminine] read thing”); neuter, as *hoc lectum* (“this [neuter] read thing”); and common to the three genders, as *hic et haec et hoc legens* (“this masculine, feminine, or neuter person or thing [Col. 0627D] reading”).

Of what gender is this participle? Of every gender.

Why is this so? Because all participles ending in *-ens* or *-ans* are regarded as belonging to every gender.

*Doctus* (“learned”): of what gender is this participle? Masculine.

Why is this so? Because all participles ending in *-us* are regarded as masculine.

*Docta* (“learned”): of what gender is this participle? Feminine.

Why? Because all participles ending in *-a* are regarded as feminine.

*Doctum* (“learned”): of what gender is this participle? Neuter.

Why is this so? Because all participles ending in *-um* are regarded as neuter.

*Docens* (“teaching”): is it a fixed or movable participle? Fixed.

Why is this so? Because it cannot be inflected into another gender.

*Lectus* (“read”): is it a fixed or movable participle? Movable.

Why is this so? Because it can be inflected into another gender, as *lectus, lecta, lectum* (“read,” masculine, feminine, neuter), and all participles ending in *-us* are movable.

[Col. 0628A] How many cases of participles are there? Six.

Which? Nominative, as *hic legens* (“this one reading”); genitive, as *huius legentis* (“of this one reading”); dative, as *huic legenti* (“to this one reading”); accusative, as *hunc legentem* (“this one reading”); vocative, as *o legens* (“O one reading”); ablative, as *ab hoc legente* (“by or from this one reading”).

Of what case is this participle? Nominative and vocative.

Why is this so? Because it refers either to the third or to the second person of the verb, as in *docens proficit* (“one who is teaching progresses”), *docens proficis* (“you, teaching, progress”). But in this part too, and in pronouns, just as we stated earlier concerning the noun, the properties of the cases are better demonstrated through the connection of the other parts of speech, in sentences and complete discourse.

How many tenses of participles are there? Three.

Which? Present, as *legens* (“reading”); past, as *lectus* (“read”); future, as *legendus* (“to be read”).

Of what tense is this participle? Present.

Why is this so? Because all participles ending in two consonants are regarded as present tense.

*Doctus* (“learned”): of what tense is this participle? Past.

Why is this so? Because all participles ending in *-tus* are likewise regarded as past tense. Similarly those ending in *-sus* and *-xus*, as *laesus* (“injured”), *nexus* (“bound”).

*Docturus* (“about to teach”): of what tense is this participle? Future.

Why is this so? Because all participles ending in *-rus* are likewise regarded as future tense. Similarly those ending in *-dus*, as *legendus* (“to be read”), *docendus* (“to be taught”).

In what do the meanings of participles consist? An active verb produces two participles, present and future, as *legens* (“reading”), *lecturus* (“about to read”). A passive produces two, past and future, as *lectus* (“read”), *legendus* (“to be read”). A neuter produces two, like the active, present and future, as *stans* (“standing”), *staturus* (“about to stand”). A deponent produces three: present, past, and future, as *loquens* (“speaking”), *locutus* (“having spoken”), *locuturus* (“about to speak”). A common verb produces four: present, past, and two futures, as *criminans* (“accusing”), *criminatus* (“having accused or been accused”), *criminaturus* (“about to accuse”), *criminandus* (“about to be accused”).

Of what meaning is this participle? Active.

Why is this so? Because it is derived from *doceo* (“I teach”), an active verb. The same answer is to be given concerning the remaining meanings. [Col. 0628C]

How many numbers of participles are there? Two.

Which? Singular, as *hic legens* (“this one reading”); plural, as *hi legentes* (“these reading”).

What number is this participle? Singular.

Why is this so? Because when I say *docens* (“teaching”), I signify one who teaches, not several; and when I say *docentes* (“teaching”), I signify several who teach, not one.

How many figures of participles are there? Two.

Which? Simple, as *legens* (“reading”); compound, as *negligens* (“negligent”).

Is this participle simple or compound? Simple.

Why is this so? Because it is compounded neither from two unchanged forms, nor from two altered forms, and so forth, as was demonstrated in the preceding parts.

Are inflected forms found among participles or not? They are found.

Which? Triptotes in all feminine and neuter forms, as *docta, doctae, doctam; docto, doctum* (“learned,” in the various forms). Pentaptotals in all masculine forms, as *lectus, lecti, lecto, lectum, lecte* (“read,” in the five cases); and in the participle of every gender, as *legens, legentis, legenti, [Col. 0628D] legentem, legente* (“reading,” in the five forms). Participles lack the remaining forms.

Through how many declensions are they inflected? Three.

Which? All feminines through the first; masculines and neuters through the second; those of every gender through the third.

Give the declension of the participle, and so forth.

*Ast* (“but”): what part of speech is it? A conjunction.

What is a conjunction? A part of speech that connects and orders a sentence.

How many properties belong to a conjunction? Three.

Which? Force, figure, and order.

How many kinds does the force of conjunctions have? Five.

Which? Copulative, disjunctive, expletive, causal, and rational.

Give copulative conjunctions. *Et, -que, at, atque, ac, ast* (“and, and, but, and, and, but”).

Give disjunctive conjunctions. *Aut, -ve, vel, -ne, nec, neque* (“or, or, or, whether, nor, neither”).

Give expletive conjunctions. *Quidem, equidem, saltem, videlicet, [Col. 0629A] quamquam, quamvis, quoque, aut, porro, porro autem, tamen* (“indeed, for my part, at least, namely, although, however much, also, or, moreover, moreover indeed, nevertheless”).

Give causal conjunctions. *Si, etsi, etiamsi, siquidem, quando, quandoquidem, quin, quinetiam, quatenus, sin, seu, sive, nam, namque, ni, nisi, nisi si, si enim, etenim, ne, sed, interea, licet, quamobrem, praesertim, item, itemque, caeterum, alioquin, praeterea* (“if, even if, even if, if indeed, when, since, why not, and even, insofar as, but if, or if, or whether, for, for indeed, if not, unless, unless if, for if, and indeed, lest, but, meanwhile, although, for which reason, especially, likewise, likewise also, moreover, otherwise, besides”).

Give rational conjunctions. *Ita, itaque, enim, enimvero, quia, quapropter, quoniam, quoniam quidem, quippe, ergo, ideo, igitur, scilicet, videlicet, propterea* (“thus, and so, for, indeed, because, wherefore, since, since indeed, inasmuch as, therefore, for that reason, therefore, namely, namely, for that reason”).

Of what kind is this conjunction? Copulative.

Why is this so? Because it joins both words and meaning.

*Aut*: of what kind of conjunction is it? Disjunctive.

Why is this so? Because it separates the meaning, although it joins and connects the words.

*Quidem*: of what kind of conjunction is it? Expletive.

Why is this so? Because it is inserted to fill out either the meaning or the ornamentation of a sentence.

*Si*: of what kind of conjunction is it? Causal.

Why is this so? Because it signifies a preceding cause.

[Col. 0629B] *Enim*: of what kind of conjunction is it? Rational.

Why is this so? Because it gives the reason for what precedes.

How many figures of conjunctions are there? Two.

Which? Simple, as *nam* (“for”); compound, as *namque* (“for indeed”).

Is this conjunction simple or compound? Simple.

Why is this so? Because it is compounded neither from two unchanged forms, nor from two altered forms, and so forth, as was demonstrated in the other parts.

In what does the order of conjunctions consist? In this, that conjunctions are either prepositive, as *at, ast* (“but”); postpositive, as *-que* (“and”), *aut* (“or”); or common, as *et* (“and”), *igitur* (“therefore”).

Of what order is this conjunction? Prepositive.

Why is this so? Because it is always placed before the rest of the sentence.

*-Que*: of what order is this conjunction? Postpositive.

Why is this so? Because it is always appended in the sentence.

*Igitur*: of what order is this conjunction? Common.

Why is this so? Because, according to each person’s preference, it is always placed either before or after the rest of the sentence.

It should be known that there are three copulative conjunctions of prepositive [Col. 0629C] order: *at, ac, ast*. Of postpositive order, one: *-que*. Of common order, *et, atque*. Of the disjunctives, two are of prepositive order: *aut, -ne*; one is postpositive: *-ve*; and three are common: *que, ne, ve*. Of the expletives, one is prepositive: *porro autem*; three are postpositive: *quidem, quoque, autem*; and seven are common: *equidem, saltem, videlicet, quamquam, quamvis, porro, tamen*. Of the causal conjunctions, fourteen are prepositive: *etsi, etiamsi, quin, sin, seu, sive, ni, nisi si, si enim, quamobrem, praesertim, itemque, caeterum, alioquin*. Fourteen are common: *siquidem, quandoquidem, quinetiam, quatenus, nam, namque, nisi, etenim, ne, sed, interea, licet, item, praeterea*. Of the rational conjunctions, one is prepositive: *enimvero*. Fourteen are common: *itaque, enim, quia, quapropter, quoniam, quoniam quidem, quippe, ergo, ideo, igitur, scilicet, videlicet, propter, idcirco*.

*Ad* (“to”): what part of speech is it? A preposition.

What is a preposition? A part of speech which, placed before other parts of speech, either completes, changes, or diminishes [Col. 0629D] their meaning.

What property belongs to a preposition? One.

What is it? Case alone.

How many cases? Two.

Which? Accusative and ablative.

Give prepositions governing the accusative. *Ad, apud, ante, adversum, cis, citra, circum, circa, contra, erga, extra, inter, intra, infra, juxta, ob, pone, per, prope, secundum, post, trans, ultra, praeter, propter, supra, usque, penes* (“to, at, before, against, on this side of, on this side of, around, around, against, toward, outside, between, within, below, beside, on account of, behind, through, near, according to, after, across, beyond, except, because of, above, as far as, in the possession of”).

How? For we say: *ad patrem* (“to the father”), *apud villam* (“at the farmhouse”), *ante aedes* (“before the house”), *adversum inimicos* (“against the enemies”), *cis Rhenum* (“on this side of the Rhine”), *citra forum* (“on this side of the forum”), *circum vicinos* (“around the neighbors”), *circa templum* (“around the temple”), *contra hostem* (“against the enemy”), *erga propinquos* (“toward relatives”), *extra terminos* (“outside the boundaries”), *inter naves* (“between the ships”), *intra moenia* (“within the walls”), *infra tectum* (“below the roof”), *juxta macellum* (“beside the market”), *ob augurium* (“on account of the omen”), *pone tribunal* (“behind the tribunal”), *per parietem* (“through the wall”), *prope fenestram* (“near the window”), *secundum fores* (“along the doors”), *post tergum* (“behind the back”), *trans ripam* (“across the bank”), *ultra fines* (“beyond the boundaries”), *praeter officium* (“besides the duty”), *propter rem* (“because of the matter”), *supra coelum* (“above the sky”), *usque oceanum* (“as far as the ocean”), *penes arbitros* (“in the possession of the arbitrators”).

[Col. 0630A] Give prepositions governing the ablative. *A, ab, abs, cum, coram, clam, de, e, ex, pro, prae, palam, sine, absque, tenus* (“from, from, from, with, in the presence of, secretly from, from, out of, out of, on behalf of, because of, openly before, without, without, as far as”).

How? For we say: *a domo* (“from the house”), *ab homine* (“from a person”), *abs quolibet* (“from anyone”), *cum exercitu* (“with the army”), *coram testibus* (“in the presence of witnesses”), *clam custodibus* (“secretly from the guards”), *de foro* (“from the forum”), *e jure* (“from the law”), *ex praefectura* (“from the prefecture”), *pro clientibus* (“on behalf of the clients”), *prae timore* (“because of fear”), *palam omnibus* (“openly before everyone”), *sine labore* (“without labor”), *absque injuria* (“without injury”), *tenus pube* (“as far as the pubic region”), which we call *pubetenus*.

Give prepositions governing both cases. *In, sub, super, subter* (“in, under, above, beneath”).

When are *in* and *sub* joined with the accusative? When we signify that either we or anyone else is going, has gone, or will go into a place.

When with the ablative? When we signify that either we or anyone else is, has been, or will be in a place.

Give examples of this. With the accusative: *Itur in antiquam silvam* (“One goes into the ancient forest”). With the ablative: *Stans celsa in puppi* (“Standing high on the stern”). With the accusative after *sub*: *Postesque sub ipsos nituntur gradibus* (“And they lean by steps beneath the very doorposts”). With the ablative after *sub*:

*Arma sub adversa posuit radiantia quercu.*

“He placed the gleaming arms beneath the opposing oak.”

[Col. 0630B] What force does *super* have? When it signifies place, it generally serves the accusative rather than the ablative; when we make mention of something, it takes only the ablative.

How does it serve the accusative when signifying place? As in *saeva sedens super arma* (“sitting fiercely above the weapons”).

When does it take the ablative?

*Sedibus optatis gemina super arbore sidunt.*

“They settle on their desired seats, upon the twin tree.”

And:

*Flore super viridi. Sunt nobis mitia poma.*

“Upon the green flower. We have mellow apples.”

How does it take the ablative? When we make mention of something, as in:

*Multa super Priamo rogitans, super Hectore multa.*

“Asking many things about Priam, many about Hector.”

What force does *in* have? It also serves the accusative when it means “against,” as in *in alterum* (“against the other”), *in desertorem* (“against the deserter”).

What force does *subter* have? The same as the preceding [Col. 0630C] prepositions when they signify motion to a place and position in a place.

How does it serve the accusative when signifying motion to a place? As in:

*Fluminaque antiquos subter labentia muros.*

“And the rivers gliding beneath the ancient walls.”

How does it serve the ablative when signifying position in a place? As in:

*Ferre jubet subter densa testudine casus.*

“He orders them to endure the blows beneath the dense tortoise formation.”

Of what case is this preposition? Accusative.

Why is this so? Because it is always placed before the accusative in a sentence.

How? As in *ad patrem* (“to the father”). The same answer is to be given concerning the other prepositions governing the accusative.

*Ab*: of what case is this preposition? Ablative.

Why is this so? Because it is always placed before the ablative in a sentence.

How? As in *ab homine* (“from a person”). The same answer is to be given concerning the other prepositions governing the ablative.

*In*: of what case is this preposition? Of both.

Why is this so? Because it is always placed before both the accusative and the ablative [Col. 0630D] in a sentence.

How with the accusative? As in *itur in antiquam silvam* (“one goes into the ancient forest”).

How with the ablative? As in *stans celsa in puppi* (“standing high on the stern”).

Of which case is *in* in this passage? Of one or the other. The same answer is to be given concerning the other prepositions governing both cases.

Which prepositions serve words and cannot be separated from them? *Di, dis, re, se, am, con*.

How? For we say *diduco* (“I lead apart”), *distraho* (“I draw apart”), *recipio* (“I receive”), *servabo* (“I shall preserve”), *amplector* (“I embrace”), *congredior* (“I meet”).

Does this preposition have any association with those words, or not? No.

Why? Because it can be separated.

How? As in *ad patrem* (“to the father”).

Which are the prepositions that cannot be joined? *Apud* and *penes*.

Does this preposition have any association with those words, or not? No.

Why is this so? Because it can be joined.

How? As in *addo* (“I add”).

[Col. 0631A] Which are joined and separated? Nearly all the others.

Does this preposition have any association with those words, or not? It certainly does.

Why is this so? Because, as was answered above, it is both joined and separated. It should be known, however, that there are eleven accusative prepositions that can be joined: *ad*, as in *admoneo* (“I admonish”); *ante*, as in *antecedo* (“I precede”); *circum*, as in *circumeo* (“I go around”); *circa*, as in *circumcirca* (“around”); *contra*, as in *contradico* (“I contradict”); *inter*, as in *interdico* (“I prohibit”); *ob*, as in *oberro* (“I wander about”); *per*, as in *permitto* (“I permit”); *post*, as in *postpono* (“I postpone”); *trans*, as in *transfero* (“I transfer”); *praeter*, as in *praeterfluo* (“I flow past”).

Which cannot be joined? Fifteen: *apud, adversum, cis, citra, erga, extra, infra, juxta, prope, secundum, ultra, propter, supra, usque, penes*. But of these Donatus assigns only two, *apud* and *penes*; he seems to have omitted the others for this reason: they are more properly adverbs. Hence most of them also admit comparison, and, added to verbs, are used without cases. For they admit comparison, as *citra, citerius, citime* (“on this side, farther on this side, farthest on this side”); from these the nouns *citerior, citimus* (“farther, farthest on this side”) are also derived. [Col. 0631B] Likewise *extra, exterius, extime* (“outside, farther outside, farthest outside”); hence the nouns *exterior, extimus*, or *extremus* (“outer, farthest out, extreme”) are derived. Likewise *supra, superius, supreme* (“above, higher, highest”); hence the nouns *superior, supremus* (“higher, highest”) are also derived.

They are properly joined to verbs adverbially, as in *citra habitat* (“he lives on this side”), *extra jacet* (“he lies outside”), *infra latet* (“he lies hidden below”), *juxta sedet* (“he sits nearby”), *prope incedit* (“he proceeds nearby”), *ultra progreditur* (“he advances beyond”), *supra conscendit* (“he climbs above”), and *jubet usque morari* (“he orders [him] to remain continually”), and *usque ambo defessi simus* (“may we both be utterly exhausted”).

Finally, *adversum* (“against”) and *secundum* (“along, according to”) are clearly recognized as nouns placed in the position of adverbs or prepositions. There appears to be a very close resemblance and a certain kinship among these parts of speech, since prepositions very frequently pass into adverbs and adverbs into prepositions.

Likewise, of the ablative prepositions, [Col. 0631C] those that can be joined are eight: *a*, as in *amitto* (“I send away”); *ab*, as in [Col. 0632A] *abnego* (“I deny”); *abs*, as in *abstraho* (“I draw away”); *de*, as in *demulceo* (“I soothe”); *e*, as in *emitto* (“I send out”); *ex*, as in *exeo* (“I go out”); *pro*, as in *protego* (“I protect”); *prae*, as in *praefero* (“I prefer”). Those that cannot be joined are seven: *cum, coram, clam, palam, sine, absque, tenus*. If anyone wishes to know how close these are to adverbs, let him read Priscian’s treatises on the preposition.

Likewise, all the prepositions governing both cases can be joined: *in*, as in *incolo* (“I inhabit”); *sub*, as in *subsisto* (“I stand beneath”); *super*, as in *superpono* (“I place above”); *subter*, as in *subterjaceo* (“I lie beneath”).

*Evax* (“hurrah!”): what part of speech is it? An interjection.

What is an interjection? A part of speech signifying an emotion of the mind through an inarticulate sound.

What property belongs to an interjection? Meaning alone.

In what does the meaning of an interjection consist? In this, that we signify either joy, as *evax* (“hurrah!”); or grief, as *heu* (“alas!”); or wonder, as *pape* (“ah!”); or fear, as *atat* (“oh!”); and there are other similar forms.

Of what meaning is this interjection? Of rejoicing.

[Col. 0632B] Why is this so? Because when we say *evax* (“hurrah!”), we clearly signify that we are rejoicing.

*Heu*: of what meaning is this interjection? Of grieving.

Why is this so? Because when we say *heu* (“alas!”), we plainly signify that we grieve.

*Pape*: of what meaning is it? It is an interjection of wonder.

Why is this so? Because when we say *pape* (“ah!”), we certainly express wonder at something.

*Atat*: of what meaning is this interjection? Of fearing.

Why is this so? Because when we say *atat* (“oh!”), we signify that we fear something. There are also many other meanings of interjections, but they are recognized as flowing, so to speak, from these four sources of emotional disturbance.

[Col. 0631]

## A Little Book on the Eight Parts of Speech
[Col. 0631C] There are eight parts of speech: noun, pronoun, verb, adverb, participle, conjunction, preposition, and interjection. Of these, two are the principal parts of speech: the noun and the verb. The Latins do not count the article; the Greeks do not count the interjection. Many think that there are more parts of speech, and many fewer; but among all these there are three that are inflected through the six cases: the noun, the pronoun, and the participle.

A noun is a part of speech signifying, with case, a body or a thing either specifically or generally: specifically, as *Roma* (“Rome”), *Tiberis* (“the Tiber”); generally, as *urbs* (“city”), *flumen* (“river”). A noun has six accidents: quality, comparison, gender, number, form, and case.

A noun is the designation of one name, a word for many things; but now we use *nomina* generally for names. The quality of nouns is twofold: they are either proper names or common nouns. According to the Latins, proper names have four kinds: praenomen, nomen, cognomen, and agnomen, as in *Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus*. Common praenomina are marked either by single letters, as *C. Caesar*, *L. Catilina*; by two letters, as *Gn. Pompeius*; or by three, as *Sex. Roscius*.

Common nouns have many kinds. Some are abstract, such as *pietas* (“piety”), *justitia* (“justice”), *dignitas* (“rank, dignity”); some are of first formation, such as *mons* (“mountain”), *schola* (“school”); some are derivative, such as *Montanus*, *scholasticus*; some are diminutives, such as *monticulus* (“little mountain”).

Diminutive nouns have three degrees; as their form becomes more reduced, the number of their syllables often increases. There are also certain diminutives whose origin is not apparent, such as *fabula*, *macula*, *tabula*, *vinculum*. Some nouns are wholly of Greek declension, such as *Temesto*, *Calypso*, *Pan*. Some are wholly converted to the Latin pattern: *Polydectes*, *Pollux*, *Odysseus*, *Ulysses*. Some stand between Greek and Latin form; these are called *netha*, such as *Achilles*, *Agamemnon*.

There are other nouns that signify several things under a single designation, such as *nepos*, *acies*, *aries*. There are also synonyms, or polyonymous words, such as *terra*, *humus*, *tellus* (“earth”); *ensis*, *mucro*, *gladius* (“sword”). Others are patronymics, such as *Pelides*, *Atrides*. These are often formed from names of grandfathers as well as fathers.

In words that are Greek, whether masculine or feminine, we shall preserve the Greek pattern as far as possible. Some masculine forms end in *-des*, such as *Atrides*, from *Atreus*; some in *-lius*, such as *Pelius*, from *Peleus*; and some in *-ion*, such as *Nereion*, from *Nereus*. Feminine forms end in *-is*, such as *Atreis*; in *-as*, such as *Pelias*; or in *-ne*, such as *Nerine*.

There are other words called *thetics*, that is, possessives, which end in *-ius*, such as *Evandrius ensis* (“Evander’s sword”), *Agamemnoniae Mycenae* (“Agamemnon’s Mycenae”). Others have an intermediate signification and are added to nouns, such as *magnus* (“great”), *fortis* (“brave”): we say *magnus vir* (“a great man”), *fortis exercitus* (“a brave army”). These are also called epithets.

Others express quality, such as *bonus* (“good”), *malus* (“bad”); others quantity, such as *magnus* (“large”), *parvus* (“small”); others nationality, such as *Graecus* (“Greek”), *Hispanus* (“Spanish”); others origin or homeland, such as *Thebanus* (“Theban”), *Romanus* (“Roman”); others number, such as *unus* (“one”), *duo* (“two”); others order, such as *primus* (“first”), *secundus* (“second”).

*Primus* is used of many; of two, *prior* (“earlier, former”) is used. Likewise, of two we say *alter* (“the other”), but of many, *alius* (“another”). Some words are spoken in relation to something, such as *pater* (“father”), *frater* (“brother”); others stand in a certain relation to something, such as *dexter* (“right”), *sinister* (“left”). These also admit a comparative degree: *dexterior*, *sinisterior* (“more right,” “more left”).

Some nouns are general, such as *corpus* (“body”); others specific, such as *lapis* (“stone”), *homo* (“human being”), *lignum* (“wood”). Some are formed from verbs, such as *doctor* (“teacher”), *factor* (“maker”), *lector* (“reader”); some resemble participles, such as *demens* (“insane”), *sapiens* (“wise”), *potens* (“powerful”); others resemble verbs, such as *comedo* (“I eat”), *palpo* (“I flatter”), *contemplator* (“he contemplates”), *speculator* (“he observes”).

[Col. 0633A] There are three degrees of comparison: positive, comparative, and superlative. The positive is *fortis* (“brave”); the comparative, *fortior* (“braver”); the superlative, *fortissimus* (“bravest”). The comparative degree, however, is always common in gender.

Nouns that signify either quality or quantity are compared, but not all nouns are found in all degrees. Sometimes only the positive is found, as *mediocris* (“moderate”); sometimes only the positive and comparative, as *senex*, *senior* (“old,” “older”), *juvenis*, *juvenior* (“young,” “younger”); sometimes the positive and superlative, as *pius*, *piissimus* (“dutiful,” “most dutiful”). For the second degree, the adverb *magis* (“more”) is used, as *magis pius* (“more dutiful”).

Sometimes only the comparative and superlative occur, as *ulterior* (“farther”), *ultimus* (“farthest, last”); sometimes only the superlative, as *novissimus* (“latest, last”). Some words fall outside this pattern, such as *bonus*, *malus*, and *magnus*. We say *bonus, melior, optimus* (“good, better, best”); *malus, pejor, pessimus* (“bad, worse, worst”); *magnus, major, maximus* (“great, greater, greatest”).

Strictly speaking, comparison of nouns is established in the comparative and superlative degrees, for the positive is complete and absolute. The comparative degree, however, is often placed before the superlative, as *stultior stultissimo* (“more foolish than the most foolish”), and *major maximo* (“greater than the greatest”). Often the comparative signifies less than the positive, although it admits comparison, as in “the Pontic Sea is sweeter than the other seas.” Often the same word, used in place of the positive, signifies less than the positive and is compared with no one, as:

[Col. 0633B] “Now older, but for the god an old age still fresh and vigorous.”

Some nouns are diminutive in signification but comparative in sense, such as *grandiusculus* (“rather large”), *majusculus* (“rather great”), *minusculus* (“rather small”). The words *tam*, *minus*, *minime*, *magis*, and *maxime* should not be added to the comparative; they are added only to the positive. Thus we say *tam malus* (“so bad”), *minus bonus* (“less good”), *minus malus* (“less bad”), *magis bonus* (“better”), *magis malus* (“worse”), *maxime bonus* (“best”), *maxime malus* (“worst”).

The comparative degree is joined to the ablative case in either number. We use it when we compare someone either with another person’s degree or with his own degree, as: “Hector was braver than Diomedes,” or “more daring than the Trojans”; or we say, “This man is braver than that one.” The superlative, however, is joined only to the plural genitive; we use it when we compare someone with those of his own class, as: “Hector was the bravest of the Trojans.” The superlative is very often used in place of the positive and is compared with no one, as *Jupiter optimus maximus* (“Jupiter, best and greatest”). Sometimes the comparative is joined to the nominative, as “This man is more learned than that one.”

Nouns have four genders: masculine, feminine, neuter, and common. A masculine noun is one to which, in the singular number and nominative case, the pronoun or article *hic* is prefixed, as *hic magister* (“this teacher”). A feminine noun is one to which *haec* is prefixed, as *haec musa* (“this Muse”). A neuter noun is one to which *hoc* is prefixed, as *hoc scamnum* (“this bench”). A common noun signifies both masculine and feminine, as *hic et haec sacerdos* (“this priest, male or female”).

Of these, two are either principal or sole genders: masculine and feminine, for the neuter arises from both. There is also a common noun of three genders, called *omne*, such as *hic et haec et hoc felix* (“this fortunate man, woman, or thing”). There is also the epicene, that is, the promiscuous noun, which under a single signification includes male and female, such as *passer* (“sparrow”) and *aquila* (“eagle”).

Furthermore, some nouns are masculine in sound but feminine in meaning, such as *Eunuchus* (the comedy), *Orestes* (the tragedy), and *Centauris* (the ship); others are feminine in sound but masculine in meaning, such as *Fenestella* (“writer”), *Aquila* (“orator”); others are neuter in sound but feminine in meaning, such as *Phronesium*, [Col. 0633D] *Glycerium*, *Sophronium*, which are women; others are feminine in sound but neuter in meaning, such as *poema* (“poem”), *stemma* (“garland, lineage”); others are masculine in sound but neuter in meaning, such as *pelagus* (“sea”), *vulgus* (“common people”).

There are also nouns that have one gender in the singular and another in the plural, such as *balneum*, *tartarus*, *coelum*, *porrum*, *caepe*, *formanium*. There are likewise nouns of uncertain gender between masculine and feminine, such as *cortex* (“bark”), *radix* (“root”), *silex* (“flint”), *finis* (“end”), *stirps* (“stock, stem”), *pinus* (“pine”), *pampinus* (“vine leaf”), *dies* (“day”).

There are nouns of uncertain gender between masculine and neuter, such as *frenus*, *clypeus* (“shield”), *vulgus* (“common people”), *specus* (“cave”). There are nouns of uncertain gender between feminine and neuter, such as *buxus* (“box tree”), *pyrus* (“pear tree”), *prunus* (“plum tree”), *malus* (“apple tree”); but we often say the fruit in the neuter gender and the trees themselves in the feminine.

Some genders of nouns are fixed, others variable. Fixed nouns are those that cannot be inflected into another gender, such as *pater*, *mater*, *frater*, *soror* (“father,” “mother,” “brother,” “sister”). Variable nouns are either proper names, which form two genders from themselves, such as *Caius, Caia*, *Martius, Martia*; or common nouns, which form three genders, such as *bonus, bona, bonum* (“good”), *malus, mala, malum* (“bad”).

There are also nouns that belong neither among the fixed nor among the variable, such as *draco, dracaena* (“dragon”), *leo, leaena* (“lion”), *gallus, gallina* (“cock, hen”), *rex, regina* (“king, queen”). There are diminutives that do not preserve the genders they received from their nouns of first formation, such as *scutum, scutella* (“shield, little shield”), *pistrinum, pistrilla* (“mill, little mill”), *canis, canicula* (“dog, little dog”), *rana, ranunculus* (“frog, little frog”), *statua, statiuncula* (“statue, little statue”).

A noun ending in the vowel *a* in the singular nominative is either masculine, such as *Agrippa*; feminine, such as *Martia*; neuter, such as *toreuma*, though this is Greek; common, such as *advena* (“newcomer”); or epicene, such as *aquila* (“eagle”). A noun ending in *e* in the singular nominative is either feminine, such as *Euterpe*, or neuter, such as *sedile* (“seat”). A noun ending in *i* in the singular nominative is either a neuter Greek noun, such as *gummi* (“gum”), *sinapi* (“mustard”); or of three genders, such as *abdolon*, *frugi*, *nihili*. A noun ending in *o* in the singular nominative is either masculine, such as *Scipio*; feminine, such as *Juno*; or common, such as *pumilio* (“dwarf”). A noun ending in *u* in the singular nominative is neuter only, such as *cornu* (“horn”), *genu* (“knee”), *gelu* (“frost”).

But these nouns, and those ending in consonants, have different and numerous rules.

There are two numbers: singular and plural. The singular is *hic sapiens* (“this wise man”); the plural, *hi sapientes* (“these wise men”). There is also a dual number, which cannot be expressed in the singular: *hi ambo* (“both of these”), *hi duo* (“these two”). There are also nouns common in number, such as *res* (“thing”), *nubes* (“cloud”), *dies* (“day”).

Some are always singular and masculine, such as *Publius*, *sanguis* (“blood”). Some are always plural, such as *manes* (“the spirits of the dead”), *Quirites* (“Roman citizens”). Some are always singular and feminine, such as *pax* (“peace”), *lux* (“light”). Some are always plural, such as *Kalendae* (“Calends”), *nundinae* (“market days”), *feriae* (“holidays”), *nuptiae* (“wedding”), *quadrigae* (“four-horse chariot”).

Some are always singular and neuter, such as *pus* (“pus”), *virus* (“poison”), *aurum* (“gold”), *argentum* (“silver”), *oleum* (“oil”), *ferrum* (“iron”), *triticum* (“wheat”); and nearly all other things that refer to measure or weight. Through common usage, however, *arma* (“arms”), *Florialia* (“the Floralia”), and *Saturnalia* (“the Saturnalia”) are also treated in this way. Some are singular in form but plural in meaning, such as *populus* (“people”), *concio* (“assembly”), *plebs* (“common people”). Some are plural in form but singular in meaning, such as *Athenae*, *Thebae*, *Cumae*.

Nouns have two forms: simple and compound. A simple noun is *doctus* (“learned”), *potens* (“powerful”); a compound is *indoctus* (“unlearned”), *impotens* (“powerless”). Nouns are compounded in four ways: from two complete forms, as *suburbanus* (“suburban”); from two altered forms, as *efficax* (“effective”), *municeps* (“municipal citizen”); from a complete and an altered form, as *ineptus* (“unsuitable”), *insulsus* (“insipid”); from an altered and a complete form, as *nugigerulus* (“bearing trifles”).

They are also compounded from several elements, as *inexpugnabilis* (“unconquerable”), *imperterritus* (“undaunted”). In the declension of compound nouns, we must observe that those compounded from two nominatives can be declined through all the cases from both parts, as *eques Romanus*, *praetor urbanus* (“Roman knight,” “urban praetor”). Those compounded from a nominative and any other case are declined only in the part that is in the nominative, as *praefectus equitum* (“commander of the cavalry”) and *senatus consultum* (“decree of the Senate”).

Care must be taken not to compound nouns that are already compound or that cannot be compounded at all.

Nouns have six cases: nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, vocative, and ablative. Of these, two are called straight cases, the nominative and vocative; the others are oblique. The Greeks do not have the ablative; some call it Latin, others the sixth case.

The forms are: nominative, *hic Cato* (“this Cato”); genitive, *hujus Catonis* (“of this Cato”); dative, *huic Catoni* (“to this Cato”); accusative, *hunc Catonem* (“this Cato”); vocative, *o Cato* (“O Cato”); ablative, *ab hoc Catone* (“from this Cato”).

Some also posit a seventh case, which resembles the ablative but is used without a preposition. Thus *ab oratore venio* (“I come from the orator”) is an ablative, whereas *oratore magistro utor* (“I use the orator as a teacher”) has a seventh case.

There are six case forms, from which some nouns are monoptotic, some diptotic, some triptotic, some tetraptotic, some pentaptotic, and some hexaptotic. There are also these indeclinable nouns, which are declined neither through cases nor numbers: *frugi*, *nihili*, *nequam*, *fas*, *nefas*, *nugas*. In this category are also the names of numbers from four through one hundred. For from one through three, the numbers are declined through all the cases; likewise from two hundred onward, except *mille* (“thousand”).

There are nouns whose nominative is not in use, as when someone says *hunc laterem* (“this brick”), [lacuna] or from this expression. In many nouns the other cases are likewise defective, such as *sponte* (“of one’s own accord”), *tabo* (“with gore”).

[Col. 0635A] Furthermore, some nouns govern the genitive, such as *ignarus belli* (“ignorant of war”), *securus armorum* (“secure from weapons”); some the dative, such as *inimicus malis* (“hostile to evils”), *congruus paribus* (“fitting for equals”); some the accusative, but figuratively, such as *exosus bella* (“hating wars”), *praescius futura* (“foreknowing future things”); some the ablative, such as *secundus a Romulo* (“second after Romulus”), *alter a Sylla* (“the other after Sulla”); some the seventh case, such as *dignus munere* (“worthy of office”), *mactus virtute* (“honored for virtue”).

All nouns in the singular ablative end in one of the five vowel letters, but only those that are not indeclinable; in the indeclinables this rule does not hold. Whatever nouns end in a vowel in the singular ablative form their plural genitive with the syllable *-rum*, and their plural dative and ablative with *-is*, as: *ab hac musa*, *harum musarum*, *his musis* (“from this Muse, of these Muses, to/from these Muses”).

The following must be declined contrary to this rule because their genders are distinguished: *ab hac dea*, *harum dearum*, *his et ab his deabus* (“from this goddess, of these goddesses, to and from these goddesses”), lest, if we say *diis*, we seem to signify gods rather than goddesses.

Whatever nouns end in the letter *e*, shortened, in the singular ablative form their plural genitive with the syllable *-um*, and their plural dative and ablative with *-bus*, as: *ab hoc pariete*, *horum parietum*, *ab his parietibus* (“from this wall, of these walls, to/from these walls”).

Contrary to this rule we find *ab hoc vase*, *horum vasorum*, *his vasis* (“from this vessel, of these vessels, to/from these vessels”). If they end in a lengthened *e*, they form the plural genitive with *-rum*, and the plural dative and ablative with *-bus*, as *ab hac re*, *harum rerum*, *his et ab his rebus* (“from this thing, of these things, to and from these things”). This rule is considered feminine.

Whatever nouns end in the letter *i* in the singular ablative form their plural genitive with *-ium*, and their plural dative and ablative with *-bus*, as *ab hac puppi*, *harum puppium*, *his et ab his puppibus* (“from this stern, of these sterns, to and from these sterns”).

For the sake of distinction, such nouns end their plural accusative more properly in *-is* than in *-es*: *has puppis, navis, clavis*; singular *puppim, navim, clavim*, not *puppem, navem, clavem*. Among these nouns that can end their plural genitive in *-ium*, there are three rules.

The first concerns those whose singular nominative ends in the letters *-ns*, as *mons, montium* (“mountain, of mountains”). The second concerns those that end in shortened *e* in the singular ablative and are feminine, as *ab hac caede*, *harum caedium*, *his et ab his caedibus* (“from this slaughter, of these slaughters, to and from these slaughters”). The third concerns those that end in the letter *i* in the singular ablative, as *ab hac resti*, *harum restium*, *his et ab his restibus* (“from this rope, of these ropes, to and from these ropes”).

This rule also sometimes gives the singular accusative the ending *-im*, as *hanc restim* (“this rope”) and *hanc puppim* (“this stern”). In many of these nouns, however, usage has altered the forms.

Whatever nouns end in the letter *o* in the singular ablative form their plural genitive with *-rum*, and their plural dative and ablative with *-is*, as *ab hoc docto*, *horum doctorum*, *his et ab his doctis* (“from this learned man, of these learned men, to and from these learned men”).

Contrary to this rule we find *ab hac domo*, *harum domorum*, *his et ab his domibus* (“from this house, of these houses, to and from these houses”); and *ab hoc jugere*, *horum jugerum*, *his et ab his jugeribus* (“from this acre, of these acres, to and from these acres”). We must know, however, that some of the ancients declined them differently: *ab hac domu*, *harum domuum*, *his et ab his domibus*; and *ab hoc jugere*, *horum jugerum*, *his et ab his jugeribus*.

Let us remember, however, that euphony in words sometimes has greater force than analogy or the rules of teachers.

Whatever nouns end in the letter *u* in the singular ablative form their plural genitive with *-um*; with the *u* doubled, they form their plural dative and ablative with *-bus*, as *ab hoc fluctu*, *horum fluctuum*, *his et ab his fluctibus* (“from this wave, of these waves, to and from these waves”). There is no need to retain the letter *u* and say *fluctubus*, since necessity makes us say *artubus*, lest anyone think that we intend *artes* (“arts”) rather than *artus* (“limbs”).

As stated, indeclinable nouns do not fall under this rule, such as *fas*, *nefas*, *nihili*; nor do nouns that are only plural, such as *Saturnalia*, *Vulcanalia*, *compedalia*; nor words borrowed from the Greeks, such as *emblema*, *epigramma*, *stemma*, *poema*. For the ancients also declined nouns of this form in the feminine gender. In these matters, analogy is recognized either by comparison with established nouns or by diminutive forms.

Let us remember that these Greek nouns are declined according to the Greek pattern, although some strive to inflect them according to Latin cases.

All Latin nouns in the singular nominative end in twelve letters: five vowels, six semivowels, and one mute: *a, e, i, o, u, l, m, n, r, s, x, t*. Thus: *a*, as *tabula* (“table”); *e*, as *sedile* (“seat”); *i*, as *frugi*; *o*, as *ratio* (“reason”); *u*, as *genu* (“knee”); *l*, as *mel* (“honey”); *m*, as *scamnum* (“bench”); *n*, as *flumen* (“river”); *r*, as *arbor* (“tree”); *s*, as *flos* (“flower”); *x*, as *nox* (“night”); *t*, as *caput* (“head”). Some add *c*, as *lac* (“milk”), *halec* (“salted fish”).

A pronoun is a part of speech that, being placed in place of a noun, signifies almost the same thing and sometimes receives person. A pronoun has six accidents: quality, gender, number, form, person, and case.

The quality of pronouns is twofold: they are either definite or indefinite. Definite pronouns receive persons, such as *ego* (“I”), *tu* (“you”), *ille* (“that man”); indefinite pronouns do not receive persons, such as *quis*, *quae*, *quod* (“someone, something”). There are also pronouns less than definite, such as *ipse* (“himself”), *iste* (“that one”).

Some are prepositive, such as *quis*, *hic*; some subjunctive, such as *is*, *idem*. Some indicate nationality, such as *cujas*, *nostras*, *cujatis*, *nostratis* (“of what nation,” “ours,” “of what country,” “our countryman”); some order, such as *quotus*, *totus* (“which in order,” “the whole”); some number, such as *quot*, *tot* (“how many,” “so many”).

Some indefinite pronouns are spoken in relation to something, such as *cujus, cuja, cujum* (“whose”); others are definite, such as *meus, tuus, suus* (“my,” “your,” “his or her own”). These are also called possessives. Some express quality, such as *qualis*, *talis* (“of what kind,” “of such a kind”); others quantity, such as *quantus*, *tantus* (“how great,” “so great”).

Some are demonstrative, indicating a present thing, such as *hic*, *haec*, *hoc* (“this”); others relative, signifying an absent thing, such as *is*, *ea*, *id* (“that, he, she, it”). Some are more emphatically demonstrative, such as *eccum*, *eccam*, *ellum*, *ellam* (“here he is,” “here she is”).

Pronouns have all the genders that nouns have: masculine, such as *quis*; feminine, such as *quae*; neuter, such as *quod*; common, such as *qualis*, *talis*. Some are of all three genders, such as *ego*, *tu*, *ille*.

Both numbers belong to pronouns: singular, such as *iste* (“that one”); plural, such as *ista* (“those”). Some are common in number, such as *qui* and *quae*. We say *qui vir* (“which man”), *qui viri* (“which men”); *quae mulier* (“which woman”), *quae mulieres* (“which women”).

Some pronouns are entirely singular, such as *meus*, *tuus*; others entirely plural, such as *noster*, *vester* (“our,” “your”).

Pronouns also have two forms: they are either simple, such as *quis*; or compound, such as *quisquis* (“whoever”). Compound pronouns are declined according to the form of the noun in that part by which the pronoun ends in the nominative case. Examples are *quisquis*, *quispiam*, *aliquis*, *quisnam* (“whoever,” “someone,” “someone,” “who, then?”).

*Idem*, which consists of two altered forms, is a masculine pronoun when its first syllable is lengthened, but an adverb of place when it is shortened.

Definite pronouns have three persons: first, such as *ego* (“I”); second, such as *tu* (“you”); third, such as *ille* (“he, that man”). The first and second persons are common in gender. The first person, in the singular number, has no nominative case in this pronoun, but it has one in the plural.

Pronouns likewise have six cases, just as nouns do: nominative, *hic* (“this”); genitive, *hujus* (“of this”); dative, *huic* (“to this”); accusative, *hunc* (“this”); vocative, *o* (“O”); ablative, *ab hoc* (“from this”).

Some pronouns are not declined through all the cases, such as *eccum*, *ecca*, *ellum*, and *cujus, cuja, cujum, cujatis, nostratis*. Some lack the nominative and vocative, such as *sui, sibi, se, a se* (“of himself, to himself, himself, from himself”); these are not common in number. Others lack the nominative, such as *ego, mei* or *mis, mihi, me, a me* (“I, of me, to me, me, from me”).

No pronoun admits comparison, although pronouns signify quality and quantity.

The difference between pronouns and articles is that those are considered pronouns which, when standing alone, fulfill the function of a noun, such as *quis*, *ille*, *iste*. Articles, however, are joined to pronouns, nouns, or participles, as *hic, hujus, huic, hunc, o, ab hoc*; and in the plural, *hi, horum, his, hos, ab his*.

These same pronouns are also used as articles and for demonstration, as *neuter*, *uter*, *omnis*, *alter*, *nullus*, *alius*, *ambo*, *uterque* (“neither,” “which of two,” “all,” “the other,” “no,” “another,” “both,” “each of two”). Some consider them nouns, others pronouns, because articles do not need to be added in declension.

A verb is a part of speech that signifies, with tense and person but without case, either doing something, undergoing something, or neither. A verb has seven accidents: quality, conjugation, gender, number, form, tense, and person.

The quality of verbs is found in moods and forms. According to many, there are seven moods: the indicative, which is declarative, as *lego* (“I read”); the imperative, as *lege* (“read!”); the promissive, as *legam* (“I shall read”), though we do not accept this as a mood; the optative, as *utinam legerem* (“would that I were reading”); the subjunctive, as *cum legam* (“when I read”); the infinitive, as *legere* (“to read”); and the impersonal, as *legitur* (“it is read”). Some, however, regard the impersonal as a gender and signification of the verb.

Impersonal verbs end either in *-tur*, *-it*, or *-et*. Those ending in *-tur* and *-it* arise from the indicative, as *lego, legitur* (“I read, it is read”), *contingo, contigit* (“I happen, it happened”). Those ending in *-et* have two forms: some arise from the indicative, as *misereor, miseret* (“I pity, it is pitied”); others arise independently, as *taedet*, *pudet*, *poenitet* (“it wearies,” “it shames,” “it repents”), although the ancients said *pudeo* and *taedeo*.

The quality of verbs is also established in their forms, which some confuse with the genders of verbs, that is, their significations. Latin forms are therefore four, since Greek likewise lacks these distinctions: perfect, meditative, inchoative, and frequentative. The perfect is *lego* (“I read”); the meditative, *lecturio* (“I desire to read”); the frequentative, *lectito* (“I read repeatedly”); the inchoative, *fervesco*, *calesco* (“I begin to boil,” “I begin to grow warm”).

Frequentatives are always of the first conjugation. Inchoative verbs are not declined through all tenses, because what begins does not have a past tense; they arise from neuter verbs. There are also frequentatives derived from nouns, such as *patricat* (“he acts like a patrician”), *crocitat* (“he croaks”). There are quasi-diminutives derived from the perfect form, such as *sorbillo*, *sigillo*. Others lack a perfect form as their source, such as *potisso*, *vacillo*.

Frequentatives often lead a verb through three degrees, as *curro, curso, cursito* (“I run, I run about, I run repeatedly”); often through only two, as *nolo, nolito* (“I do not wish, do not wish!”). There are verbs resembling inchoatives which we know not to be inchoative by their tense, such as *compesco, compescui* (“I restrain, I restrained”). There are also inchoatives derived from perfect forms, such as *horreo, horresco* (“I shudder, I begin to shudder”). Some have no source, such as *consuesco*, *quiesco* (“I become accustomed,” “I rest”).

Verbs have three conjugations: the first in *a*, the second in *e*, and the third in *i*.

The first is that which, in the indicative mood, present tense, singular number, second person, in an active or neuter verb, loves a lengthened *a*; or, in a passive, common, or deponent verb, has the final letter or final syllable in the relevant form. Examples are *voco, vocas, vocor, vocaris* (“I call, you call, I am called, you are called”). Its future tense in the same forms ends in the syllables *-bo* and *-bor*: *voco, vocabo, vocor, vocabor* (“I call, I shall call, I am called, I shall be called”).

The second is that which, in the indicative mood, present tense, singular number, second person, in an active or neuter verb, has a lengthened *e*; or, in a passive, common, or deponent verb, has the final letter or final syllable in the relevant form. Examples are *moneo, mones, moneor, moneris* (“I warn, you warn, I am warned, you are warned”). Its future tense in the same forms ends in *-bo* and *-bor*: *moneo, monebo, moneor, monebor* (“I warn, I shall warn, I am warned, I shall be warned”).

The third is that which, in the indicative mood, present tense, singular number, second person, in an active or neuter verb, sometimes has the letter *i* lengthened and sometimes shortened; or, in a passive, common, or deponent verb, has a shortened final *e*, a lengthened *i*, or the final syllable. Examples are *lego, legis, legor, legeris* (“I read, you read, I am read, you are read”); *audio, audis, audior, audiris* (“I hear, you hear, I am heard, you are heard”).

Its future tense in the same forms ends in *-am* or *-ar*: *lego, legam, legor, legar* (“I read, I shall read, I am read, I shall be read”); *audio, audiam, audior, audiar* (“I hear, I shall hear, I am heard, I shall be heard”).

There is another species of the third conjugation, pronounced with a lengthened *i*, which some consider a fourth conjugation. Its future properly ends in *-am* and *-bo*, and in *-ar* and *-bor*: *servio, serviam, servibo* (“I serve, I shall serve”); *vincio, vincis, vinciam, vincibo, vincior, vinciris, vinciar, vincibor* (“I bind, you bind, I shall bind, I shall bind, I am bound, you are bound, I shall be bound, I shall be bound”).

Some who reject this deny that the third conjugation can properly end in *-bo* and *-bor*, except in a verb whose first-person singular present indicative has *e* or *o*, such as *eo, queo, eam, queam, ibo, quibo* (“I go, I can, I shall go, I shall be able, I shall go, I shall be able”); and in the passive, *queor, quear, quibor*. The same applies to any similar forms.

The genders of verbs, which others call their significations, are five: active, passive, neuter, common, and deponent.

Active verbs end in the letter *o* and, upon receiving *r*, form passives from themselves, as *lego, legor* (“I read, I am read”). Passive verbs end in *r* and, when this is removed, return to the active, as *legor, lego* (“I am read, I read”). Neuter verbs end in *o* and, upon receiving *r*, are not Latin, as *sto, curro* (“I stand, I run”).

There are also neuter verbs that end in *i*, such as *odi*, *novi*, *coepi*, *memini* (“I hate,” “I know,” “I began,” “I remember”). Others end in the syllable *-um*, such as *sum*, *prosum* (“I am,” “I am useful”); others end in *-et* and are called impersonal, such as *pudet*, *poenitet*, *taedet* (“it shames,” “it repents,” “it wearies”). These and similar forms should be considered defective.
