There are also neuter-passive verbs, such as *audeo, ausus sum* (“I dare, I have dared”), *gaudeo, gavisus sum* (“I rejoice, I have rejoiced”), *soleo, solitus sum* (“I am accustomed, I have been accustomed”).

Deponent verbs end in *r* and, when this is removed, are not Latin, such as *conficior*, *convertor* (“I am completed,” “I am turned”). Common verbs end in *r* and fall into two forms, active and passive, such as *scrutor*, *criminor*. We say *scrutor te* (“I examine you”) and *scrutor a te* (“I am examined by you”); *criminor te* (“I accuse you”) and *criminor a te* (“I am accused by you”).

There are verbs outside this rule, called irregular, such as *soleo*, *facio*, *fio*, *fido*, *audeo*, *gaudeo*, *vescor*, *feror*, *medeor*, *edo*, *volo*, *nolo* (“I am accustomed,” “I do,” “I become,” “I trust,” “I dare,” “I rejoice,” “I feed,” “I am carried,” “I heal,” “I eat,” “I wish,” “I do not wish”).

Some cannot be properly declined, such as *cedo*, *ave*, *faxo*, *is*, *infit*, *inquam*, *quaeso*, *aio* (“tell me,” “hail,” “I shall do,” “he goes,” “he begins,” “I say,” “I ask,” “I say”). There are also monosyllables that are lengthened contrary to the rule, such as *sto*, *do*, *flo* (“I stand,” “I give,” “I blow”).

Similarly, there are verbs of uncertain signification, such as *tondeo*, *lavo*, *fabrico*, *punio*, *numero*, *munio*, *partior*, *populor*, *assentior*, *adulor*, *luctor*, *auguror* (“I shear,” “I wash,” “I fashion,” “I punish,” “I count,” “I fortify,” “I divide,” “I ravage,” “I agree,” “I flatter,” “I wrestle,” “I practice augury”). All these verbs end in the letters *o* and *r*, and nearly all the tenses of participles belong to them.

There are also verbs that can be compounded, such as *pono*, *traho*, *repono*, *retraho* (“I place,” “I draw,” “I replace,” “I draw back”). There are some that cannot, such as *aio*, *quaeso*.

Verbs have two numbers: singular and plural. The singular is *lego* (“I read”); the plural, *legimus* (“we read”). According to some, there is also a dual, such as *legere*.

Verbs have two forms: they are either simple, such as *scribo* (“I write”); or compound, such as *describo* (“I describe”). Verbs are compounded in four ways, like the other parts of speech: *repono*, *sufficio*, *reficio*, *incipio*, *suspendo* (“I replace,” “I supply,” “I restore,” “I begin,” “I suspend”).

Some compound verbs can be made simple, such as *repono*, *distraho*; others cannot, such as *suspicior*, *compleo*.

Verbs have three tenses: present, past, and future. The present is *lego* (“I read”); the past, *legi* (“I read, I have read”); the future, *legam* (“I shall read”). The past tense, however, has three distinctions: imperfect, perfect, and pluperfect. The imperfect is *legebam* (“I was reading”); the perfect, *legi* (“I read, I have read”); the pluperfect, *legeram* (“I had read”).

Thus, in the declension of verbs, we count the present, imperfect past, perfect past, pluperfect past, and future.

Verbs have three persons: first, second, and third. The first is the person who speaks, as *lego* (“I read”). The second is the person addressed, as *legis* (“you read”). The third is the person spoken of, as *legit* (“he reads”).

[Col. 0638C] The first person does not require a case, but it usually admits the nominative, as *verberor innocens* (“I am beaten, though innocent”), *servio liber* (“I serve, though free”). The second person draws the nominative, as *verberaris innocens* (“you are beaten, though innocent”), *servis liber* (“you serve, though free”). The third person likewise draws the nominative, as *verberatur innocens* (“he is beaten, though innocent”), *servit liber* (“he serves, though free”).

Moreover, impersonal verbs ending in *-tur* govern the dative and ablative cases, as *geritur a te* (“it is done by you”) or *illi* (“for him”); *licetur mihi, tibi, illi* (“it is permitted to me, to you, to him”). Those ending in *-it* govern the dative, as *contingit mihi, tibi, illi* (“it happens to me, to you, to him”). Those ending in *-et* govern either the dative or accusative, as *libet mihi, tibi, illi* (“it pleases me, you, him”); *decet me, te, illum* (“it is fitting for me, you, him”).

There are also verbs, some of which follow the construction of the genitive, such as *misereor mei, tui, sui* (“I pity myself, you, himself”), *reminiscor mei, tui, sui* (“I remember myself, you, himself”); others the dative, such as *maledico tibi*, *suadeo tibi* (“I curse you,” “I advise you”); others the accusative, such as *accuso illum*, *invoco istum* (“I accuse him,” “I invoke that man”); others the ablative, such as *discedo ab illo*, *avertar ab illo* (“I depart from him,” “I shall be turned away from him”); others the seventh case, such as *fruor te*, *potior auro* (“I enjoy you,” “I obtain possession of gold”).

Common verbs in the first person of the indicative have one of the vowels *e*, *i*, *u*, or *o*. If they do not have a vowel or the letter *o*, then, except for *f*, *k*, and *q*, they take all the remaining Latin consonants: *e*, as *sedeo* (“I sit”); *i*, as *inanio* (“I empty”); *u*, as *ruo* (“I rush”); *b*, *bibo* (“I drink”); *c*, *voco* (“I call”); *d*, *vado* (“I go”); *g*, *lego* (“I read”); *h*, *traho* (“I draw”); *l*, *pello* (“I drive”); *m*, *amo* (“I love”); *n*, *cano* (“I sing”); *p*, *scalpo* (“I carve”); *r*, *curro* (“I run”); *s*, *lasso* (“I weary”); *t*, *plecto* (“I strike”); *x*, *nexo* (“I bind”).

In these forms, *i* and *u* sometimes occur as consonants, as in *adjuvo* (“I help”); for *triumpho* (“I triumph”) is written with *p* and *h*. The letter *k* cannot be prefixed. Likewise, *q*, *f*, *m*, *n*, and *o* cannot be prefixed.

Some verbs are defective in moods, such as *cedo*; others in forms, such as *facesso*; others in conjugation, such as *adsum*; others in genders, such as *audeo*; others in numbers, such as *saxo*; others in forms, such as *impleo*; others in tenses, such as *sero*; others in persons, such as *cedo*, *edo*, *facesso*, *adsum*, *soleo*, *faxo*. Even among impersonal verbs, although they can be declined through all the moods, some are found to be defective, such as *libet* and *miseret*.

An adverb is a part of speech which, when added to a verb, either completes or diminishes its signification, as *jam faciam* (“now I shall do it”) or *non faciam* (“I shall not do it”).

Adverbs either arise independently, such as *heri* (“yesterday”), *hodie* (“today”), or come from other parts of speech. They arise from a common noun, such as *doctus, docte* (“learned, learnedly”); from a proper noun, such as *Tullianus, Tulliane* (“Ciceronian, in Ciceronian fashion”); from a pronoun, such as *meatim, tuatim* (“in my manner, in your manner”); from a verb, such as *cursim, strictim* (“at a run, briefly”); from a noun and a verb, such as *pedetentim* (“step by step”); from a participle, such as *indulgens, indulgenter* (“indulgent, indulgently”).

Adverbs derived from nouns end either in *-a*, as *una* (“together”); in lengthened *-e*, as *docte* (“learnedly”); in shortened *-e*, as *rite* (“properly”); in *-i*, as *vesperi* (“in the evening”); in lengthened *-o*, as *falso* (“falsely”); in shortened *-o*, as *modo* (“just now, only”); in *-u*, as *noctu* (“by night”); in *-el*, as *semel* (“once”); in *-m*, as *strictim* (“briefly”); in *-r*, as *breviter* (“briefly”); or in *-s*, as *funditus* (“thoroughly”).

Adverbs ending in *-e* should be lengthened, except those that either are not compared, such as *rite*; do not follow the rule of comparison, such as *bene* and *male*, which form *bene, melius, optime* (“well, better, best”) and *male, pejus, pessime* (“badly, worse, worst”); or derive from a noun or verb, such as *impune*, *saepe*, *caeterum*, *facile*, and *difficile* (“with impunity,” “often,” “otherwise,” “easily,” “with difficulty”).

Some adverbs are placed in such a way that they ought rather to be called nouns used as adverbs, as in *torvum clamat* (“he cries fiercely”), *horrendum resonat* (“it resounds horribly”).

[Col. 0639B] Thus, adverbs ending in lengthened *-e* derive from a noun whose dative ends in the letter *o*, as *huic docto, docte* (“to this learned man, learnedly”). Those ending in *-r* derive from a noun whose dative ends in the letter *i*, as *huic agili, agiliter* (“to this agile person, nimbly”).

Authority often uses many forms contrary to this rule. For, as we have said, some retain the dative form and make adverbs, such as *falso*, *sedulo* (“falsely,” “diligently”); others do much contrary to the rule, such as *huic duro*, not *dure*, but *duriter* (“to this harsh man, harshly”).

An adverb has three accidents: signification, comparison, and form. The signification of adverbs is recognized as follows: some are adverbs of place, such as *hic* (“here”); of time, such as *hodie*, *nuper* (“today,” “recently”); of number, such as *semel*, *bis* (“once,” “twice”); of negation, such as *non* (“not”); of affirmation, such as *etiam*, *quin* (“also,” “indeed”); of demonstration, such as *en*, *ecce* (“behold,” “look”); of wishing, such as *utinam* (“would that”); of exhortation, such as *eia* (“come on”); of order, such as *deinde* (“then”); of questioning, such as *cur*, *quamobrem* (“why,” “for what reason”); of likeness, such as *quasi*, *ceu* (“as if,” “just as”); of quality, such as *docte*, *pulchre* (“learnedly,” “beautifully”); of quantity, such as *parum*, *multum* (“little,” “much”); of doubt, such as *forsitan*, *fortasse* (“perhaps”); personal, such as *mecum*, *tecum*, *nobiscum*, *vobiscum* (“with me, with you, with us, with you all”); of calling, such as *heus* (“hey!”); of responding, such as *hem* (“there!”); of separation, such as *seorsum* (“apart”); of swearing, such as *aedepol*, *Castor*, *hercle*, *medius fidius* (“by Pollux,” “by Castor,” “by Hercules,” “by the god of faith”); of choosing, such as *potius*, *imo* (“rather,” “nay”); of gathering, such as *simul*, *una*, *pariter* (“together,” “together,” “equally”); of prohibition, such as *ne* (“lest, do not”); of outcome, such as *forte*, *fortuitu* (“by chance,” “accidentally”); and of comparison, such as *magis*, *tam* (“more,” “so”).

There are also indefinite adverbs, such as *ubi* (“where”); and some definite ones, such as *hic* (“here”), *modo* (“just now, only”).

Adverbs of place have two forms: “in a place” and “to a place.” “In a place” is expressed by *intus*, *foris* (“inside,” “outside”); “to a place” by *intro*, *foras* (“inward,” “outward”). We say *intus sum* (“I am inside”), *foris sum* (“I am outside”), *intro eo* (“I go in”).

Some add “from a place,” as *intus exeo* (“I go out from inside”), *foris venio* (“I come from outside”). Some also add “through or by a place,” as *hac*, *illac*, *istac* (“this way,” “that way,” “that way”); and *heus* and *heu* (“hey!” and “alas!”).

Many have not considered interjections to be adverbs, because they are not always followed by a verb.

Comparison belongs to the adverb because here too there are three degrees of comparison: positive, such as *docte* (“learnedly”); comparative, such as *doctius* (“more learnedly”); superlative, such as *doctissime* (“most learnedly”). Since there are also adverbs that cannot pass through all the degrees, we join *magis* and *maxime* to them in place of the comparative and superlative in order to increase their signification; to diminish it, we use *minus* and *minime*.

[Col. 0639D] Just as adverbs are compared, so they are also diminished from the positive, as *primum, primule* (“first, rather first”); from the comparative, as *melius, meliuscule* (“better, rather better”), *longiuscule* (“rather farther”). There are either no examples or only rare ones from the superlative.

Adverbs have two forms: they are either simple, such as *docte*, *prudenter* (“learnedly,” “prudently”); or compound, such as *indocte*, *imprudenter* (“unlearnedly,” “imprudently”). Adverbs are also compounded in four ways.

There are many words whose classification is uncertain between adverb and noun, pronoun, verb, participle, conjunction, or preposition, such as *falso*, *quo*, *pone*, *profecto*, *cum*, *propter*, *heu* (“falsely,” “where/to which,” “behind,” “certainly,” “with/when,” “because of,” “alas”). Some of these we distinguish by accent, others by sense.

There are adverbs of place that the unwary think are nouns: “in a place,” as *Romae sum* (“I am at Rome”); “from a place,” as *Roma venio* (“I come from Rome”); “to a place,” as *Romam vado* (“I go to Rome”). No preposition is added to these, although prepositions are usually added to provinces, places, or regions. This is because they do not depart from the signification of a noun, as *de Africa venio* (“I come from Africa”), *Siciliam pergo* (“I proceed to Sicily”), *in Italia sum* (“I am in Italy”).

A preposition is placed separately before adverbs and is not joined to them, although we read *derepente*, *desursum*, *desubito*, *exinde*, *abusque*, and *dehinc* (“suddenly,” “from above,” “suddenly,” “from there,” “all the way from,” “from then on”). These, however, we shall pronounce as though they were one part of speech under a single accent.

A participle is a part of speech so called because it shares partly in the noun and partly in the verb. For it receives genders and cases from the noun, tenses and meanings from the verb, and number and form from both. A participle has six attributes: gender, case, tense, meaning, number, and form.

Participles have four genders: masculine, as *lectus* (“read”); feminine, as *lecta*; neuter, as *lectum*; and common, as *legens* (“reading”). Participles have as many cases as nouns, for participles too are declined through all the cases.

Participles have three tenses: present, past, and future, as *luctans* (“struggling”), *luctatus* (“having struggled”), and *luctaturus* (“about to struggle”). The meanings of participles are derived from the classes of verbs. From an active verb come two participles, present and future, as *legens* (“reading”) and *lecturus* (“about to read”). From a passive verb come two, past and future, as *lectus* (“read”) and *legendus* (“to be read”). From a neuter verb come two, present and future, as *stans* (“standing”) and *staturus* (“about to stand”). From a deponent verb come three, present, past, and future, as *luctans*, *luctatus*, and *luctaturus*. From a common verb come four, present, past, and two futures, as *criminans* (“accusing”), *criminatus* (“having accused”), *criminaturus* (“about to accuse”), and *criminandus* (“to be accused”).

Inchoative participles exist only in the present tense, as *horrescens* (“growing fearful”), *calescens* (“growing hot”), and *tepescens* (“growing warm”). Defective verbs sometimes have a participle of one particular tense, as *soleo, soles, solitus* (“I am accustomed, you are accustomed, accustomed”); sometimes they have none, as in the case of the verb *memini* (“I remember”), from which no participle is found. Sometimes a defective participle comes from a non-defective verb, as from *studeo* (“I am eager”), whose participle *studens* (“being eager”) has no future tense. Participles do not come from an impersonal verb unless they have been established by usage.

Participles have both numbers: singular, as *hic legens* (“this man reading”); plural, as *hi legentes* (“these men reading”). Likewise, participles have two forms: they are either simple, as *scribens* (“writing”), or compound, as *describens* (“describing”). Participles too can be compounded in four ways.

There are nouns that have the appearance of participles, such as *comatus* (“long-haired”) and *galeatus* (“helmeted”); because they do not come from a verb, they must not be classified as participles. Among these are also words that seem to be participles but have been deprived of verbal meaning, such as *pransus* (“having dined”), *coenatus* (“having supped”), *placita* (“pleasing”), *nupta* (“married”), *triumphata* (“triumphing over”), and *regnata* (“having ruled”); for the verbs *prandeor, coenor, placeor, nubor, triumphor,* and *regnor* are not used.

There are other participles which, after receiving a preposition, depart both from verbs and from participles, as *innocens* (“innocent”); for *noceo* (“I harm”) is used, but *innoceo* is not. There are also defective participles that cannot occur through all the tenses and that come from verbs, such as *ceptus* (“begun”) and *arguendus* (“to be accused”). There are forms resembling participles that come from verbs but, because they have no tense, are judged nouns rather than participles, such as *furibundus* (“raging”), *ludibundus* (“playing”), and *moribundus* (“dying”).

Many participles are also nouns, such as *passus* (“suffering” or “a pace”), *visus* (“seen” or “sight”), *cultus* (“cultivated” or “cultivation”), *sapiens* (“wise person”), and *indulgens* (“indulgent person”). They are nevertheless distinguished by their cases, recognized by their tenses, and changed through comparison. There are participles that become nouns when comparison is applied to them, such as *acceptus* (“acceptable”), *incensus* (“kindled”), *acceptior* (“more acceptable”), and *incensior* (“more kindled”).

Some deny that adverbs can be formed from participles, but the authority of extensive reading refutes them with numerous examples.

[Col. 0640B–D]

A conjunction is a part of speech that links and orders a sentence. A conjunction has three attributes: force, form, and order.

The force of conjunctions is divided into five classes: copulative, disjunctive, expletive, causal, and rational.

The copulative conjunctions are *et, que, ac, atque, at,* and *ast* (“and,” “and,” “and,” “and,” “but,” “but”).

The disjunctive conjunctions are *ne, vel, nec, an,* and *neque* (“or,” “or,” “nor,” “or,” “nor”).

The expletive conjunctions are *quidem, equidem, saltem, videlicet, quanquam, quamvis, quoque, autem, porro, licet,* and *tamen* (“indeed,” “indeed,” “at least,” “namely,” “although,” “however much,” “also,” “but,” “moreover,” “although,” “nevertheless”).

The causal conjunctions are *si, etsi, etiamsi, siquidem, cum, quandoquidem, quinetiam, quamvis, sin, seu, sive, nam, neque, si, nisi, si enim, enim ne, sed, interea, quamobrem, praesertim, item, itemque, caeterum, alioquin,* and *praeterea* (“if,” “even if,” “even if,” “since,” “when,” “since indeed,” “indeed,” “although,” “but if,” “or,” “or if,” “for,” “nor,” “if,” “unless,” “if indeed,” “for not,” “but,” “meanwhile,” “wherefore,” “especially,” “likewise,” “and likewise,” “besides,” “otherwise,” “moreover”).

The rational conjunctions are *ita, itaque, enimvero, quare, quia, quapropter, quoniam, quoniam quidem, quippe, ergo, ideo, igitur, scilicet,* and *propterea* (“thus,” “therefore,” “indeed,” “wherefore,” “because,” “for which reason,” “since,” “since indeed,” “inasmuch as,” “therefore,” “for that reason,” “therefore,” “namely,” “on that account”).

Conjunctions have two forms: simple, as *nam* (“for”); and compound, as *namque* (“for indeed”). Conjunctions have order because they are either prepositive, as *at* and *ast* (“but”); subjunctive, as *quae* (“which”); or common, as *ergo* and *igitur* (“therefore”).

There are also words concerning which it is uncertain whether they should be called conjunctions, prepositions, or adverbs; nevertheless, all are easily distinguished by their meaning. Conjunctions are also found standing in place of other conjunctions, with their force altered.

[Col. 0641A]

A preposition is a part of speech which, placed before other parts of speech, either completes, changes, or diminishes their meaning. It is placed before a noun, as in *invalidus* (“weak”); before a pronoun, as in *per me* (“through me”); or after it, as in *mecum, tecum, nobiscum, vobiscum* (“with me, with you, with us, with you [plural]”). It precedes a verb, as in *praefero* (“I prefer”); an adverb, as in *expresse* (“expressly”); a participle, as in *praecedens* (“preceding”); a conjunction, as in *absque* (“without”); or itself, as in *circumcirca* (“all around”).

Prepositions either serve particular cases or forms of speech, or are combined with both cases and forms of speech, as *di, dis, re, se, an,* and *con*. We say *diduco* (“I lead apart”), *distraho* (“I draw away”), *recipio* (“I receive”), *secubo* (“I lie apart”), *amplector* (“I embrace”), and *congredior* (“I meet”). They are separated, as *apud* (“at”) and *penes* (“in the possession of”). All the rest are both joined and separated. Among them, the prepositions *in* and *con*, when compounded in such a way that the letter *s* or *f* immediately follows them, are generally lengthened, as *insula* (“island”), *insula* [the same form as printed], *consilium* (“counsel”), and *confessio* (“confession”).

[Col. 0641B]

A preposition has only cases as its attribute. There are two cases associated with prepositions: the accusative and the ablative. Some prepositions govern the accusative, some the ablative, and some either case.

The prepositions governing the accusative are: *ad, apud, adversum, cis, circa, citra, circum, contra, erga, extra, intra, inter, infra, juxta, ob, pone, per, prope, propter, secundum, post, trans, ultra, praeter, supra, usque,* and *penes*.

Thus we say: *ad patrem* (“to the father”), *apud villam* (“at the estate”), *ante aedes* (“before the house”), *adversum inimicos* (“against enemies”), *cis Rhenum* (“this side of the Rhine”), *citra forum* (“on this side of the forum”), *circum vicinos* (“around the neighbors”), *circa templum* (“around the temple”), *contra hostem* (“against the enemy”), *erga propinquos* (“toward relatives”), *extra terminos* (“outside the boundaries”), *inter naves* (“among the ships”), *intra moenia* (“within the walls”), *infra tectum* (“beneath the roof”), *juxta macellum* (“beside the market”), *ob augurium* (“on account of the omen”), *pone tribunal* (“behind the tribunal”), *per parietem* (“through the wall”), *prope fenestram* (“near the window”), *propter amnem* (“beside the river”), *secundum fores* (“along the doors”), *post tergum* (“behind the back”), *trans ripam* (“across the bank”), *ultra fines* (“beyond the boundaries”), *praeter officium* (“beside the duty”), *supra coelum* (“above the sky”), *usque Oceanum* (“as far as the Ocean”), and *penes arbitros* (“in the possession of the arbitrators”).

Of these, *ad* and *apud*, although they govern only one case, are used in different ways. We say: *Ad amicum vado* (“I go to a friend”), *apud amicum sum* (“I am with a friend”); for it is not correctly said: *Apud amicum vado* (“I go at a friend”) or *ad amicum sum* (“I am to a friend”).

The preposition *usque* does not seem to many to be a preposition, because it is not ordinarily expressed without another preposition; hence it is joined to either case, according to the preposition with which it is combined, as *usque ad* (“as far as, up to”) and *usque ab* (“all the way from”).

The prepositions governing the ablative are: *a, ab, abs, cum, coram, clam, de, e, ex, pro, prae, palam, sine, absque,* and *tenus*.

Thus we say: *a domo* (“from the house”), *ab homine* (“from a person”), *abs quolibet* (“from anyone”), *cum exercitu* (“with the army”), *coram testibus* (“in the presence of witnesses”), *clam custodibus* (“secretly from the guards”), *de foro* (“from the forum”), *e jure* (“from the law”), *ex praefectura* (“from the prefecture”), *pro clientibus* (“on behalf of the clients”), *prae timore* (“from fear”), *palam omnibus* (“openly before everyone”), *sine labore* (“without effort”), *absque injuria* (“without injustice”), and *tenus pube* (“as far as the pubic hair”). This last preposition is placed after the noun for euphony and produces *pubetinus*.

The preposition *clam* serves both cases.

The prepositions governing either case are *in, sub, super,* and *subter*. Of these, *in* and *sub* govern the accusative when they mean “against” or “before,” as *ibat in Eurialum* (“he was going against Euryalus”) and *sub ipsum Arcturum* (“directly before Arcturus itself”), that is, “before” (*ante*; the printed *a te* is an evident OCR corruption). They govern the ablative when they retain their proper force and are not used in place of accusative prepositions.

They also govern the accusative when we signify movement toward a place or toward ourselves or others, or the act of going, having gone, or being about to go. Examples are these:

*In*, with the accusative: *itur in antiquam silvam*—“one goes into the ancient forest.”

*In*, with the ablative: *Stans celsa in puppi*—“Standing upon the lofty stern.”

*Sub*, with the accusative: *Postesque sub ipsos / Nituntur gradibus*—“And they press upon the very doorposts with their steps.”

*Sub*, with the ablative:

*Arma sub adversa posuit radiantia quercu*—“He placed the shining arms beneath the opposing oak.”

But *subter* and *super* are naturally placed with the accusative, and are then generally joined to the ablative, as:

*Gemina sub arbore sidunt*—“They settle beneath a twin tree.”

And:

*Ferre juvat subter densa testudine casus*—“It is pleasant to endure misfortunes beneath a dense testudo.”

But many do not think that there are more than two ambiguous prepositions, *in* and *sub*. The others, *super* and *subter*, when they signify place, are joined figuratively with the ablative.

Apart from this usage, the preposition *super*, when it means “about”—that is, when it attempts to introduce mention of someone or something—takes only the ablative, as:

*Multa super Priamo rogitans, super Hectore multa*—“Asking much about Priam, much about Hector.”

[Col. 0642B]

Separated prepositions are accented when joined to cases or forms of speech, often changing their own nature and becoming common forms. Prepositions themselves may corrupt verbs, as *conficio* (“I complete”); they may themselves be corrupted, as *suffero* (“I endure”); or they may both corrupt and be corrupted, as *suscipio* (“I undertake”).

The ancients also joined prepositions with the genitive, as *curruum tenus* or *currum tenus* (“as far as the chariots”). Likewise, we find *post*, *ante*, and *circum* joined with both cases.

We should understand, however, that prepositions retain their force when they are placed before a word; when placed after it, they possess neither their own meaning, nor the force of a noun, nor their proper rule. Separated prepositions do not cohere with other separated prepositions and become adverbs whenever they are not followed by a case.

Some think that form and order also belong among the attributes of a preposition: form, because prepositions are either simple, as *ab* (“from”), or compound, as *absque* (“without”); order, because they are either prepositive, as *sine* (“without”), or subjunctive, as *tenus* (“as far as”). But we count these and similar matters among those called irregular.

[Col. 0642C]

An interjection is a part of speech inserted among other parts of speech to express emotions: fear, as *hei* (“ah!”); desire, as *o* (“O!”); grief, as *heu* (“alas!”); or joy, as *evax* (“hurrah!”). The Greeks attach this category to adverbs, but the Latins do not, because a verb does not immediately follow such expressions. Other individual parts of speech, or several together, may also be used in place of an interjection, as *nefas* (“wrong!”) and *pronefas* (“utterly wrong!”).

The accents of interjections cannot be fixed, just as with other words that we find irregular.

End of the little book on the eight parts of speech.

[Col. 0641]

# BOOK ON ARITHMETICAL NUMBERS

## I. On Numbers

[Col. 0641D]

A number is a multitude constituted from units; for unity, occurring once, cannot be a number. Arithmetic, moreover, is the discipline of numbers. The Greeks call number *ῥυθμός* (*rhythmos*). Among the Greeks, Pythagoras is said to have first written down the discipline of numbers, and afterward Nicomachus arranged it more extensively. Among the Latins, Apuleius first translated it, and Boethius afterward.

The word *nummus* (“coin”) gave *numerus* (“number”) its name and, from the frequency of its use, bestowed the term upon it. *Unus* (“one”) derives its name from Greek, for the Greeks call one *ἕνα* (*hena*). Likewise *duo* and *tres* (“two” and “three”), which they call *δύο* (*duo*) and *τρία* (*tria*). *Quatuor* (“four”), however, takes its name from the square figure; and the remaining names of numbers likewise derive their etymology from the Greek language.

We too have been granted, in some measure, to stand within the discipline of numbers, since through it we learn to reckon the hours and discuss the cycles of the months. Through it we also recognize the span of the returning year: indeed, we are instructed by number so that we do not confuse it. Remove number from things, and everything perishes. Take reckoning away from the world, and all things will be enveloped in blind ignorance; those who do not know the method of calculation cannot be distinguished from the other animals.

The division of numbers concerns even and odd numbers. Number is divided into even and odd. An even number is divided as follows: evenly even, evenly odd, and oddly even. An odd number is divided as follows: first and simple, second and composite, and third, intermediate, which is in a certain way both first and composite. But let us examine the order and form of numbers.

[Col. 0643]

[Col. 0643A]

There is a difference between sixfold and one-and-a-half-fold. The sixfold belongs to the multiple class, in which the lesser is contained six times in the greater. The one-and-a-half-fold belongs to the superparticular class, in which the lesser is contained in the greater once together with its own half.

## II. On the Various Kinds of Numbers

A number therefore has many kinds, although all arise from one origin. They are:

Either cardinal numbers, as we have already said, such as one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, and the rest in this order;

or ordinal numbers, such as first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and the rest;

or adverbial numbers, such as once, twice, three times, four times, five times, six times, seven times, eight times, nine times, and the rest;

or distributive numbers, such as single, two each, three each, four each, five each, six each, seven each, eight each, and the rest;

or ponderal numbers, such as single, double, triple, quadruple, quintuple, and the rest;

or declarative numbers, such as alone, the other, or another.

There are also multiplicative numbers, such as single, double, triple, quadruple, quintuple, sextuple, septuple, octuple, and the rest.

There are also forms expressed adverbially, such as simply, doubly, triply, quadruply, fivefoldly, sixfoldly, and the rest.

There are also other kinds of derived numbers, derived from the foregoing, such as singular, dual, ternary, quaternary, quinary, senary, septenary, octonary, novenary, denary, elevenfold, twelvefold, and others similar to these. This method of counting can also be extended to adjectives, for example: *ternaria ternarium* (“threefold feminine, threefold neuter”), *quaternaria quaternarium* (“fourfold feminine, fourfold neuter”), *quinaria quinarium* (“fivefold feminine, fivefold neuter”), *senaria senarium* (“sixfold feminine, sixfold neuter”), *septenaria septenarium* (“sevenfold feminine, sevenfold neuter”), *octonaria octonarium* (“eightfold feminine, eightfold neuter”), *novenaria novenarium* (“ninefold feminine, ninefold neuter”), *denaria denarium* (“tenfold feminine, tenfold neuter”), *undenaria undenarium* (“elevenfold feminine, elevenfold neuter”), *duodenaria duodenarium* (“twelvefold feminine, twelvefold neuter”), and the rest in this manner.

Likewise, there are forms compounded with *as* (“unit of currency”): *assis*; the rare *dussis*, or *dipondius* (“two asses”); *tressis* (“three asses”), *quadrassis*, *quinquassis*, *sexis*, *septussis*, *octussis*, *nonussis*, *desses* or *decussis*, *vigessis*, *trigessis*, *quadragessis*, *quinquagessis*, *sexagessis*, *septuagessis*, *octuagessis*, *nonagessis*, and *centussis*. After this number, according to Varro, numbers are no longer compounded with *as*.

Likewise, there are names for ounces: *deunx*, *dextans*, *dodrans*, *bessis* or *besse*, *septunx*, *quinqunx* or *quincunx*, *triens*, *quadrans*, *sextans*, *sexcunx*, *sextula*, and *libra*.

Likewise, forms compounded from *libra* (“pound”), such as *bilibris*, *trilibris*, *quadrilibris*, and other similar forms.

Likewise, forms derived from *annus* (“year”), such as *anniculus* or *annuus* (“one-year-old” or “annual”), *biennis* (“of two years”), *triennis* (“of three years”), *quadriennis* (“of four years”), *quinquennis* (“of five years”), and similar forms.

Likewise, forms compounded from *mensis* (“month”): *bimus* (“two-month”), *trimus* (“three-month”), *quadrimus* (“four-month”), and so on; *bimulus* and so on; *bimestre* (“two-month period”), *trimestre* (“three-month period”), *quadrimestre* (“four-month period”), and so on.

Likewise, forms compounded from *pes* (“foot”): *bipes* (“two-footed”), *tripes* (“three-footed”), *quadripes* or *quadrupes* (“four-footed”), and so on; *bidepalia*, *tridepalia*, *quadrupedalia*, and so on; *novempedalia*, *decempedalia*, *centipedalia*, and so on.

Likewise, forms compounded from *caput* (“head”): *biceps* (“two-headed”), *triceps* (“three-headed”), *quatriceps* (“four-headed”), *centiceps* (“hundred-headed”), and so on.

Likewise, forms compounded from *faria* (“kind” or “manner”), such as *bifaria*, *trifaria*, *quadrifaria*, *quinquefaria*, and so on; *multifaria* (“of many kinds”), and so on. Also *bifariam*, *trifariam*, *quadrifariam*, *quinquefariam*, and so on; *multifariam*, and similar forms.

Likewise, forms compounded from *dies* (“day”): *biduum* (“two days”), *triduum* (“three days”), *quatriduum* (“four days”), and similar forms.

Likewise, forms compounded from *corpus* (“body”): *bicorpor* (“two-bodied”), *tricorpor* (“three-bodied”), and similar forms.

Likewise, forms compounded from *patens* (“open”): *bipatens* (“open in two ways”), *tripatens* (“open in three ways”), and other similar forms.

Likewise, forms compounded from *pars* (“part”): *bipartiens* (“dividing into two parts”), *tripartiens*, *quadripartiens*, *quinquepartiens*, and so on. Also *bipartitus, bipartita, bipartitum* (“divided into two parts,” masculine, feminine, neuter); *tripartitus, tripartita, tripartitum* (“divided into three parts”); *quadripartitus, quadripartita, quadripartitum* (“divided into four parts”); *quinquepartitus, quinquepartita, quinquepartitum* (“divided into five parts”); and similar forms.

Likewise, forms compounded from *lingua* (“tongue”): *bilinguis* (“two-tongued”), *trilinguis* (“three-tongued”), *quadrilinguis* (“four-tongued”), *quinquelinguis* (“five-tongued”), *centilinguis* (“hundred-tongued”), and similar forms.

Likewise, forms compounded from *via* (“way”): *bivium* (“two-way passage”), *trivium* (“three-way passage”), *quadrivium* (“four-way passage”), *multivium* (“many-way passage”), and so on.

Likewise, forms compounded from *fides* (“faith” or “trust”): *bifidum* (“split in two”), *trifidum* (“split in three”), *quadrifidum* (“split in four”), and similar forms. Also *bifidus, bifida* (“split in two,” masculine and feminine); *trifidus, trifida* (“split in three”); *quadrifidus, quadrifida* (“split in four”); and similar forms.

Likewise, forms compounded from *sulcus* (“furrow”): *bisulcus* (“two-furrowed”), *trisulcus* (“three-furrowed”), and similar forms. Likewise, forms compounded from *geminus* (“twin”): *geminus*, *tergeminus* (“threefold”), *centigeminus* (“hundredfold”), and so on.

Likewise, forms compounded from *manus* (“hand”): *unimanus* (“one-handed”), *centimanus* (“hundred-handed”), and similar forms. Likewise, forms compounded from *digitus* (“finger”): *bidigitus* (“two-fingered”), *tridigitus* (“three-fingered”), *sedigitus* (“six-fingered”), and similar forms.

Likewise, forms compounded from *oculus* (“eye”): *monoculus* (“one-eyed”), *binoculus* (“two-eyed”), *centoculus* (“hundred-eyed”), *milloculus* (“thousand-eyed”), and similar forms. Likewise, forms compounded from *forma* (“form”): *uniformis* (“of one form”), *biformis* (“of two forms”), *triformis* (“of three forms”), *quadriformis* (“of four forms”), and similar forms.

Likewise, forms compounded from *vir* (“man”): *duumvir* (“one of two men”), *triumvir* (“one of three men”), *quinquevir* (“one of five men”), *sextumvir* (“one of six men”), *septemvir* (“one of seven men”), *decemvir* (“one of ten men”), *centumvir* (“one of a hundred men”), and similar forms. These designate a particular rank among men who serve the state. Also in the plural: *duumviri, triumviri, sextumviri, decemviri*, and the rest.

Likewise, forms compounded from *angulus* (“angle”): *triangulum* (“triangle”), *quadrangulum* (“quadrangle”), *quinquangulum* (“pentagon”), *sexangulum* (“hexagon”), and similar forms. Likewise: *dinummus* (“two-coin”), *trinummus* (“three-coin”), and so on. Likewise: *diobolaris* (“worth two obols”), *triobolaris* (“worth three obols”), and so on. Likewise: *bigae* (“two-horse team”), *trigae* (“three-horse team”), *quadrigae* (“four-horse team”), and similar forms. Likewise: *bijugus* and *bigatinum* (“two-yoked”), *trijugum* (“three-yoked”), *quadrijugum* (“four-yoked”), and similar forms. Likewise: *bigamus* (“twice-married”), *trigamus* (“thrice-married”), and similar forms.

## III. The Pythagorean Table, or the Counting Abacus

[Col. 0645]

## IV. Numerical Letters

[Col. 0647]

There are seven letters in the alphabet that serve for reckoning, namely:

**I V X C L D M**

or these, which amount to the same thing:

**i v x c l d m**

The value of these letters is as follows:

| Letter | Value |
|---|---:|
| I or i | One — 1 |
| V | Five — 5 |
| X | Ten — 10 |
| L | Fifty — 50 |
| C | One hundred — 100 |
| D | Five hundred — 500 |
| M | One thousand — 1000 |

These letters signify not only units, tens, and hundreds, as you see here, but also thousands, when a line is placed above them, as follows:

| Letter | Value |
|---|---:|
| I | One thousand — 1,000 |
| V | Five thousand — 5,000 |
| X | Ten thousand — 10,000 |
| L | Fifty thousand — 50,000 |
| C | One hundred thousand — 100,000 |
| D | Five hundred thousand — 500,000 |
| M | One thousand thousand — 1,000,000 |

For this reason some represented the same number in this way: **MM**.

Thus, from these seven letters, anyone can extend reckoning discretely to infinity.

[Col. 0647]

# DIALOGUE ON CALCULATION (C)*

[Col. 0647]

Augustine spoke of the four divisions of Scripture: “There are four necessities in the Church of God: the divine Canon, in which the future life is narrated and proclaimed; History, in which deeds and events are recounted; Number, in which future events and divine solemnities are reckoned; and Grammar, in which knowledge of words is understood. Therefore there are four parts of Scripture: the divine Canon, History, Number, and Grammar.” These divisions are, as it were, the four foundations of Scripture.

Isidore says in praise of calculation: “The science of numbers must not be despised. In many places in the holy Scriptures, its great mystery shines forth. For it was not without reason that it was said in praise of God: ‘You have made all things according to measure and number and weight.’ The number six, being perfect through its parts, declares the perfection of the world by a certain significance of its number. Likewise, the forty days during which Moses, Elijah, and the Lord himself fasted cannot be understood without knowledge of numbers. Thus there are also other numbers in the sacred Scriptures, whose figures can be unraveled only by those familiar with the knowledge of this art.”

We too have been granted, in some measure, to stand within the discipline of numbers, since we discuss the courses of the months and recognize through number the span of the returning year. Indeed, we are instructed by number so that we do not become confused. Remove number from all things, and everything perishes. Take reckoning away from the world, and everything is enveloped in blind ignorance. Those who do not know the method of calculation cannot be distinguished from the other animals.

[Col. 0649A]

**PUPIL:** We therefore wish to know from where this science of numbers first arose.

**MASTER:** From God, naturally, because all wisdom and knowledge come from the Lord God, from whom all things were made.

**Pupil:** Tell me, then, when was this science first discovered?

**Master:** From the time when creatures were made, that is, from the beginning of the world. For number first began then, just as we read in Genesis: “And there was evening and there was morning, one day.” At that point he spoke of night and day when he said “evening,” that is, night, and “morning,” that is, day. He spoke of number when he said “one day,” then “second,” “third,” “fourth,” “fifth,” “sixth,” and “seventh.” Again God spoke of number when he spoke of the sun and moon: “And let them be for signs and seasons and days and years.” For who can understand days, seasons, and years except through number?

Hence Boethius said: “All things constructed by the first nature of things seem to have been formed according to the principle of numbers. For this was the principal model in the mind of the Creator. From it the multitude of the four elements received its pattern; from it we understand the recurring cycles of time, the movements of the stars, and the revolution of the heavens.”

Boethius also says: “By the very nature of numbers, the entire course of the stars and the whole science of astronomy have been established. Thus we gather the risings and settings; thus we observe the slowness and swiftness of the wandering stars; thus we recognize eclipses and the moon’s manifold changes.”

**Pupil:** This art, then—that is, number—what general name does it have?

**Master:** Philosophy, naturally, because all wisdom is called philosophy.

**Pupil:** What is philosophy, and of what language is the word?

**Master:** It is a Greek word and is interpreted as “love of knowledge.” For among the Greeks *Φίλος* (*philos*) is rendered in Latin as *amor*, “love.” *Σοφία* (*sophia*) is interpreted as “wisdom” or “knowledge.”

**Pupil:** How is philosophy defined?

**Master:** Isidore defined it in this way: “Philosophy is knowledge of human and divine things.” This example shows that all wisdom, whether divine or human, is called philosophy.

Another definition of philosophy is: “Philosophy is the probable knowledge of divine and human things, insofar as this is possible.”

Another definition is: “Philosophy is the art of arts and the discipline of disciplines.”

**Pupil:** How many divisions of philosophy are there?

**Master:** Three: physics, ethics, and logic—that is, natural, moral, and rational philosophy. Hence Isidore says: “The species of philosophy is threefold. One is natural, which in Greek is called *φυσική* (*physikē*), that is, physics, in which the investigation of nature is discussed; another is moral, which among the Greeks is called *ἠθική* (*ēthikē*), that is, ethics, in which morals are treated; and the third is rational, which in Greek is called *λογική* (*logikē*), that is, logic, in which, through argument, the manner in which truth itself is sought in the causes of things or in the conduct of life is examined.”

Thus, in physics lies the cause of inquiry; in ethics, the order of discovery; and in logic, the method of understanding.

There are therefore also three parts of philosophy, that is, three divisions of wisdom: Physics, Ethics, and Logic. The divine utterances too are contained in these three kinds of philosophy. For they may discuss nature, as in Genesis and Ecclesiastes, or in Proverbs and the Epistles of the apostle Paul, or in the Song of Songs, the Gospels, and many other books; or they may discuss morals; or the higher heavenly mysteries, that is, logic.

**Pupil:** Who, then, discovered these three parts of philosophy?

**Master:** Thales of Miletus, one of the seven sages of the Greeks, discovered physics. Socrates discovered ethics. The philosopher Plato discovered logic.

**Pupil:** To which of these three parts of philosophy does calculation belong?

**Master:** Without doubt, to physics.

**Pupil:** How many divisions does physics have?

**Master:** Four: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.

**Pupil:** What is arithmetic?

**Master:** The art of counting.

[Col. 0650A]

**Pupil:** What is geometry?

**Master:** The measurement of the earth.

**Pupil:** What is music?

**Master:** Melody.

**Pupil:** What is astronomy?

**Master:** The law of the stars.

**Pupil:** Of these four divisions of physics, that is, of natural science, which should be learned first?

**Master:** Arithmetic, without doubt. It holds, in a certain sense, the position of origin and mother among the others. Arithmetic is prior to all the rest because God, the Creator of this world’s structure, first had it as the model of his reasoning. From it he established everything; that is, he established and ordered all the elements through numbers.

**Pupil:** Who first discovered number among the Hebrews and Egyptians?

**Master:** Abraham first discovered number among the Hebrews, and afterward Moses. Abraham transmitted this science of number to the Egyptians and taught them; afterward came Joseph.

[Col. 0650B]

**Pupil:** Who first possessed this science of number among the Greeks and Latins?

**Master:** Pythagoras among the Greeks; Apuleius and Boethius among the Latins. Hence Isidore says: “Among the Greeks, Pythagoras is first said to have written down the discipline of numbers, and afterward Nicomachus arranged it more extensively; among the Latins, Apuleius and afterward Boethius translated it.”

**Pupil:** What is number called among the Hebrews, Chaldaeans, Syrians, and Macedonians?

**Master:** Among the Hebrews, Chaldaeans, and Syrians it is called *Nonnan*. Among the Macedonians it is called *calculus*. *Calculator* (“calculator”) received its name from *calculus*, that is, from the small pebbles which the ancients held in their hands and used to compose a number. Among other Greeks it is called *cyclus* (“cycle”) or *rhythmus* (“rhythm”); among the Egyptians, *latercus*, from which *laterculus* is formed as a diminutive, and *rima*, from which *rimarii* (“reckoners”) are called.

**Pupil:** Is the word *numerus* (“number”) simple or compound?

**Master:** Compound, formed from two corrupted words. For *nume* comes from the word *nummus* (“coin”), while *rus* is derived from the word *rivus* (“stream”). The word *numerus* received its name from a stream of coins—that is, from the multitude of the revenue that was paid to kings or emperors. Hence Isidore says: “The coin gave number its name, and from its frequent use bestowed the term.”

**Pupil:** From what did *numerus* receive its name?

**Master:** From Numeria. Hence Augustine says: “Number is named from a certain goddess Numeria, whose priests offered with their faces turned backward and, after making their offerings, proceeded backward.”

**Pupil:** How is number defined?

**Master:** Isidore defined it as follows: “A number is a multitude constituted from units.” We say that one is the seed of number, not a number. Another writer likewise says: “One is not a number, but numbers grow from it.”

Donatus, however, also included one among numbers, saying: “Number is singular, as in ‘This is the teacher.’” Augustine likewise says: “Number is a collection of a singular body, voice, and signification.”

Number is also said to derive from counting, as stated above, from the goddess Numeria, whom the ancients said was the goddess of number; or *numerus* is so called as though it were a stream of coins. For the ancients, not knowing how to count, counted their periods and days with pebbles—white ones in prosperity and black ones in adversity. Hence Persius says:

> “Count this day, Macrinus, with the better pebble.”

**Pupil:** How are the numbers from one to one thousand and the myriad named?

**Master:** They are named as follows:

One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten; eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen or six-and-ten, seventeen or ten-and-seven, eighteen, nineteen, twenty; twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three, twenty-four, twenty-five, twenty-six, twenty-seven, twenty-eight, twenty-nine, thirty; thirty-one, thirty-two, thirty-three, thirty-four, thirty-five, thirty-six, thirty-seven, thirty-eight, thirty-nine, forty; forty-one, forty-two, forty-three, forty-four, forty-five, forty-six, forty-seven, forty-eight, forty-nine, fifty; fifty-one, fifty-two, fifty-three, fifty-four, fifty-five, fifty-six, fifty-seven, fifty-eight, fifty-nine, sixty; sixty-one, sixty-two, sixty-three, sixty-four, sixty-five, sixty-six, sixty-seven, sixty-eight, sixty-nine, seventy; seventy-one, seventy-two, seventy-three, seventy-four, seventy-five, seventy-six, seventy-seven, seventy-eight, seventy-nine, eighty; eighty-one, eighty-two, eighty-three, eighty-four, eighty-five, eighty-six, eighty-seven, eighty-eight, eighty-nine, ninety; ninety-one, ninety-two, and so on; one hundred, one hundred and one, one hundred and two, and so on; two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, five hundred, six hundred, seven hundred, eight hundred, nine hundred, one thousand; two thousand, three thousand, four thousand, five thousand, six thousand, seven thousand, eight thousand, nine thousand, ten thousand.

Thus it is established that ten multiplied ten times makes one hundred; one hundred multiplied ten times makes one thousand; and one thousand multiplied ten times makes a myriad. Thus twenty makes two myriads; thirty, three myriads; forty, four myriads; fifty, five myriads; sixty, six myriads; seventy, seven myriads; eighty, eight myriads; ninety, nine myriads; one hundred, ten myriads; two hundred, twenty myriads; three hundred, thirty myriads; four hundred, forty myriads; five hundred, fifty myriads; six hundred, sixty myriads; seven hundred, seventy myriads; eight hundred, eighty myriads; nine hundred, ninety myriads; ten times one hundred thousand, one hundred myriads.

[Col. 0651C]

**Pupil:** By what signs are these names of numbers that we have mentioned represented among the Latins?

**Master:** By these seven signs: **I V X L D C M**.

**Pupil:** How do these signs represent and multiply numbers?

**Master:** They signify either simply, by themselves, or in combination.

**Pupil:** In combination with one another, or multiplied by themselves?

**Master:** They signify simply as follows: **I** by itself means one; **V** alone, five; **X** alone, ten; **L** by itself, fifty; **C** by itself signifies one hundred; **D** alone, five hundred; **M** alone, or with a title above it, signifies one thousand.

**Pupil:** How, then, when multiplied by themselves, do they produce a number?

**Master:** For example, **I** doubled, thus **II**, signifies two; tripled, **III**, three; quadrupled, **IIII**, four.

**Pupil:** Why does **I** signify one?

**Master:** What could be more appropriate than for the letter that is smallest among the letters in its character to signify the number that is smallest among numbers, namely one? No sign among the Latins is multiplied more than four times.

Then after **I** comes **V**, which signifies five.

**Pupil:** Why does **V** signify five?

**Master:** Because it is the fifth vowel in the order of vowels; and what it is in the order of vowels, it is likewise in number. Hence the fifth letter is said to be marked with five strokes; and of the letter **X**, ten. Nor is **V** doubled; rather, when another **V** follows, **I** is placed in the number. If there is one **I**, six results; if two, **VII**, seven; if three, **VIII**, eight; if four, **VIIII**, nine. It does not increase beyond this.

Then comes **X**, which signifies ten.

[Col. 0652A]

**Pupil:** Who demonstrated that **X** signifies ten?

**Master:** Isidore says: “Among the Greeks, the names of letters also combine words and make numbers. The Latins, however, do not combine numbers with letters, except for the letter **X**, which in its form signifies a cross and in number denotes ten.”

When **X** follows, **I** is multiplied up to **XIIII**, which denotes fourteen. Then **V** follows **X**, producing **XV**. When **V** follows, **I** is multiplied four times, making **XVIIII**, that is, nineteen.

**Pupil:** What sign signifies twenty?

**Master:** The letter **X** doubled. For it contains twice ten; thus **XX** is called twenty because it is generated from twice ten. Likewise **XXX** is thirty, generated from three times ten.

**Pupil:** By what sign is thirty represented?

**Master:** By **X** multiplied three times. **X** is not multiplied more than three times.

**Pupil:** By what sign is forty represented?

[Col. 0652B]

**Master:** By **X** and **L**.

**Pupil:** Why is forty so called?

**Master:** That is, generated from four times ten.

Every numerical letter signifying less, when it precedes another, subtracts from the following letter as much as it contains itself. Thus: **I, II, III, IV** for **IIII**; **V, VI, VII, VIII, VIIII** for **IX**; **X, XX, XXX, XL** for **XXXX**, as some wish; **L, LX, LXX, LXXX, LXL** or **XC** for **LXXXX**; **C, CC, CCC, CD** for **CCCC**; **D** for **CCCCC**; **DC, DCC, DCCC, CM** for **DCCCC**; and **M**.

**Pupil:** What sign signifies fifty?

**Master:** The letter **L**.

**Pupil:** Why?

**Master:** Because the principal number in the law of the Lord is fifty. The Jubilee fell under that number, namely in the fiftieth year. It was therefore fitting that the number which holds primacy in the ancient law—that is, fifty—should be represented by the letter **L**, which is the first letter of the word *lex* (“law”).

Sixty is represented by **L** and **X**; seventy by **L** and two **X**s, **LXX**; eighty by **L** and three **X**s, **LXXX**.

**Pupil:** What sign signifies ninety?

**Master:** Two signs signify ninety: either **X** between two **L**s, as **LXL**, or **X** before **C**, as **XC**.

**Pupil:** What sign signifies one hundred?

**Master:** The letter **C**.

**Pupil:** Why?

**Master:** Because it is the first letter of the word *centum* (“one hundred”). It was often the practice among the ancients to signify words by their first letter.

**Pupil:** From what is *centum* derived?

**Master:** From *cantus* (“song”), that is, from a circle or a chorus of singers.

It was customary among the ancients to have one hundred men in a singing chorus. Thus *centum* is said to derive from *cantus* or from a circle. The letter **C**, doubled in this way, **CC**, signifies two hundred; tripled, **CCC**, three hundred; quadrupled, **CCCC**, four hundred.

**Pupil:** What sign signifies five hundred?

[Col. 0652D]

**Master:** The letter **D** itself.

**Pupil:** Why?

M. It was fitting, moreover, that once the number of the preceding letter, namely C, had been completed, the letter that follows in the order of the alphabet—namely D—should hold the next number, that is, five hundred. Then, with C following D, thus DC, it signifies six hundred. With two Cs following D, thus DCC, seven hundred. With C written three times following D, thus DCCC, it becomes eight hundred. With C multiplied four times following D, thus DCCCC, it signifies nine hundred. A thousand, however, is marked by M, as we have already said, since it is the first letter in the word *mille* (“thousand”). A thousand, moreover, proceeds from multiplicity and extends as far as one hundred times one hundred thousand.

[Col. 0653]

# BOOK ON THE DIVISIONS OF TIME (C)*

## I. On the divisions of time

[Col. 0653A]

**STUDENT.** How many are the divisions of time?

**MASTER.** Fourteen.

**S.** Which?

**M.** The atom, the moment, the minute, the point, the hour, the quarter, the day, the week, the month, the threefold season, the year, the cycle, the age, the century, and the world. These fourteen divisions of time are found in the rising and setting of the sun and in the waxing and waning of the moon. They thus increase from smaller numbers to larger ones: that is, from atoms to a moment, from a moment to [Col. 0653B] a minute, from a minute to a point, from a point to an hour, from an hour to a quarter, from a quarter to a day; from a day to a week, from a week to a month, from a month to a season, from a season to a year, from a year to a cycle, from a cycle to an age, from an age to a century, and from a century to the world. Then the world is called the fullness.

Isidore presents these fourteen divisions of time in the fifth book and thirteenth chapter of the *Etymologies*, saying: “Times are so called because they are divided into atoms, moments, minutes, points, hours, days, quarters, weeks, months, seasons, years, lustrums, ages, and centuries—all in the mortal world, so that its cycles may also be regulated.”

**S.** How do larger numbers grow out of smaller ones?

**M.** They grow as follows. Five hundred sixty-four atoms make one moment. Four moments make one minute. Ten minutes make one point. Five points make an hour in the moon. Six hours complete a quarter. Four quarters [Col. 0653C] appear to complete one day. Seven days make a week. Four weeks make one month—but a month of the sort that has twenty-eight days, such as February. Those four months that have thirty days—April, June, September, and November—have four weeks and two days. The other seven months, namely January, March, May, July, August, October, and December, which have thirty-one days, appear to have four weeks and three days. Thus the twelve months are gathered into a year: fifty-two weeks and one day. But when a leap year occurs every fourth year, the year then has fifty-two weeks and two days.

Three months make one season. This season is called threefold because each of the four seasons of the year has three months; they are called spring, summer, autumn, and winter. These four seasons make one year. [Col. 0653D] Four years make a leap cycle, because after four years have been completed, the leap day intervenes. Likewise, fifteen years complete the cycle of the indictions, and nineteen years appear to complete the lunar cycle.

A cycle of epacts runs through nineteen years by an equal number of years; among the Romans it is placed at the beginning of the year, that is, on the Kalends of January. Likewise, by an equal reckoning, another cycle of epacts runs for nineteen years at the beginning of the year among the Hebrews and Greeks, that is, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. The solar cycle is said to complete its course in twenty-eight years. The great cycle, in which the sun and moon come into agreement until they return to themselves after 532 years, returns to itself at the beginning of the third year.

There is true agreement between the sun and moon when, according to the reckoning of the leap year and the leap, the day of the month according to the sun, the day of the week, and the same epacts from which the cycle first began all coincide on one day. We must investigate these fourteen divisions of time that we have mentioned more carefully as we proceed. First, we must inquire about the first division of time that we named: the atom.

## II. On atoms

**S.** What, then, is an atom? Of what language is the word? How is it arranged or defined? Is it a simple or a compound name?

**M.** *Atomus* is a Greek and compound word, and it means “indivisible” or “insecable.” For ἄτομος among the Greeks is translated “a preposition” (sic) [Col. 0654B]; *tomus*, however, means “divided” or “divisible.”

**S.** How is an atom defined?

**M.** Isidore defined it, saying: “Philosophers call atoms certain extremely small parts of the world, so that they are not easily revealed to sight and do not admit of being cut. They are carried here and there, like the finest dust, which, scattered through windows, is driven about by rays of sunlight.”

**S.** How many kinds of atoms are there?

**M.** Five.

**S.** Which?

**M.** The atom in a body, the atom in the sun, the atom in speech, the atom in number, and the atom in time.

**S.** How is an atom present in a body?

**M.** Whatever is smallest in bodies and cannot be cut or divided is called an atom, such as the tiniest grains of sand. As the poet says of a hair:

> No one can split me; many can cut me off.

For there is a hair in the body that can scarcely be divided lengthwise. The atom in the sun is the very fine dust that we mentioned, driven about by the rays of the sun. The atom in speech is, for example, a letter. For you divide any part of speech into syllables, and you divide syllables into letters. You cannot divide a letter. Hence Sergius the Greek says: “All speech is resolved into words; words are again resolved into syllables; syllables are in turn resolved into letters; the letter alone has nothing into which it can be resolved.” Therefore philosophers call it an atom.

**S.** How is an atom present in number?

**M.** In this way: you divide eight into two groups of four; you divide four into two groups of two; you divide two into two; one remains. You cannot divide one; for this reason it is called an atom in number.

**S.** How is an atom present in time?

**M.** It is as follows. You divide a moment into twelve parts; you divide each one of those twelve parts of a moment into forty-seven parts. The forty-seventh part is the five-hundred-sixty-fourth part of a moment. This is the atom in time. If you add together forty-seven twelve times, you will find five hundred sixty-four atoms. That number of atoms makes one moment.

## III. On the moment

**S.** What is a moment, and how is it defined according to sound—that is, according to its surface and according to perception—or according to the substance hidden within the sound?

**M.** A moment is defined according to sound as follows. Isidore says: “A moment is a small and extremely brief period of time, named from the motion of the heavenly bodies, that is, from the motion of the sun and moon. It is the extremity of an hour in brief intervals, when the sun gives way to itself and succeeds itself.”

**S.** How many kinds of moment are there?

**M.** Four.

**S.** Which?

[Col. 0655A]

**M.** The indivisible moment, as Isaiah says: “The nations are reckoned as a moment on the balance.”

**S.** How is a moment recognized?

**M.** Augustine says: “One moment is the sun’s most definite passage through the sky, and forty such moments already make an hour. The second moment is when you throw a stone into water, until the water ceases moving; or a piece of wood that falls, until its branches cease moving. The third moment is indivisible, as Paul says: ‘All things were made in a moment,’ that is, with the greatest speed. The fourth moment is as long as the eyelids remain at rest.” Four moments make one minute.

## IV. On the minute

**S.** From where is the minute so called?

**M.** Isidore says: “It is called a minute from *minuendo* (‘diminishing’), because two moments and two parts of a third moment are diminished from the darkness on each day, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April to the twelfth day before the Kalends of July.”

**S.** How is a minute defined?

**M.** Isidore defined it, saying: “A minute is called, as it were, a lesser moment, because it counts less but completes more.” Two and a half minutes—that is, ten moments—make one point.

## V. On points

**S.** From where is the point so called?

**M.** Isidore explains it when he says: “The point is named from pricking, because on sundials they are marked by certain punctures of definite designation. The point is the work of those who make a sundial. For at the end of the eleventh line they placed a point. *Punctus* is Greek; in Latin, *medium*, because Jerusalem is in the middle of the world; there the sundial was first made with its points.”

A point has three parts. Four points are forty moments and make one hour.

## VI. On the hour

[Col. 0655C]

**S.** From whom did the hour receive its name?

**M.** *Hora* derives its name from *horo*, that is, from the sun.

**S.** Of what language is *hora*, and how is it defined?

**M.** *Hora* is a Greek word, and it means “end” or “time.”

**S.** What is a sundial?

**M.** *Hora* means “end” or “time”; *locus* [perhaps *logos*] is interpreted as “place,” “series,” or “shadow.” Hence *horologium* means a shadow or series of ends and times, because on a sundial times are measured by shadows.

**S.** Who first invented the sundial?

**M.** Ahaz, king of Judah. Some say that a sundial was first erected near the temple of Quirinus. We speak of the shores of the sea and rivers and of garments, meaning their extremities or boundaries. But an hour is the end of time.

**S.** How is the spelling distinguished between the shores of seas and rivers and the edges of garments, and the hour of time?

[Col. 0655D]

**M.** When we speak of the shores of seas and rivers and of garments, the word is pronounced without aspiration; but *hora*, that is, the end of time, is pronounced with aspiration. Six hours make one quarter.

## VII. On the quarter

**S.** What is a quarter, what is it called, and how is it defined among the Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins?

**M.** It is defined as follows. A quarter is named from the fourth part of an ounce; by another name it is called a *sicilicus*, that is, six scruples. The Hebrews call it a quarter, the Greeks a *dodrant*, and the Latins a quarter.

There is also a greater quarter, which has three ounces, that is, the fourth part of an *as*; for an *as* has twelve ounces. In time as well, a quarter consists of six hours, the fourth part of a natural day, because four quarters complete one day, and that day has twenty-four hours.

## VIII. On the day

[Col. 0656A]

**S.** From where did the day receive its name?

**M.** From division, because it divides light from darkness. Alternatively, days are said to have been named from the gods, whose names the Romans consecrated to certain heavenly bodies. The day is also so called because it separates and divides light and darkness; by common usage it is called the leader of works and the absence of darkness. *Ema* in Hebrew, *hemera* in Greek, *dies* in Latin.

**S.** Which was first, day or night?

**M.** Day, certainly, because on the first day God created light, as Isidore says and Augustine confirms.

**S.** Is night before the day or after the day?

**M.** It is assigned to the day, as Jerome disclosed: “Night is the beginning of the day, not the end of the preceding one, because before Christ’s crucifixion day preceded night, whereas now, after the Lord’s resurrection, night precedes day.”

**S.** How many gates of the day are there?

**M.** Four. Among the Chaldeans, from sunrise to sunrise. Among the Egyptians, from sunset to sunset. Among the Hebrews, from the sixth hour to the sixth hour, because the Hebrews did not count the night. Among the Romans, from midnight to midnight.

**S.** How is the day defined?

**M.** Isidore defined it, saying: “The legitimate day consists of twenty-four hours, until day and night, through the revolving motion of the sun, complete the spaces of their course from east to west.”

**S.** In how many ways is the day spoken of?

**M.** In two.

**S.** What are they?

**M.** The natural day and the artificial day.

**S.** What is the natural day?

**M.** The legitimate day, from sunrise until it rises again; that day contains twenty-four hours.

**S.** How many divisions does the natural day have?

[Col. 0656C]

**M.** Two: day and night. Hence Isidore says: “There are two spaces of the natural day: the daytime, namely, and the nighttime.” When he says “daytime space,” he means day; “nighttime space” is night.

**S.** Who, then, shows that day and night together are called a day?

**M.** It is shown in Holy Scripture, where we read: “And there was evening”—that is, night—“and morning, one day.” This shows that night and day together are called a day.

**S.** What, then, is that artificial day?

**M.** From sunrise to sunset is called the artificial day, that is, the presence of the sun above the earth. Hence Isidore says: “Day is the presence of the sun, or the sun above the earth; just as night is called the absence of the sun, that is, the sun beneath the earth.” The definition of the day is divided in two ways: popularly, that is, abusively; and naturally, that is, properly.

**S.** How, then, are the natural day and the artificial day defined together?

[Col. 0656D]

**M.** Isidore defined them, saying: “The day is customarily called by two names: properly, from sunrise until it rises again; abusively, from sunrise until it reaches sunset.”

**S.** How many periods does the artificial day have?

**M.** Three.

**S.** Which?

**M.** Morning, midday, and evening.

**S.** What is morning, how is it defined, and how many hours does it have?

**M.** Morning extends from sunrise until the hour after the third hour; midday extends from the hour after the third until the hour before the ninth; evening extends from the hour before the ninth until sunset.

**S.** How, then, is morning defined?

**M.** Isidore defined it, saying: “Morning is the morning and full light, and *mane* (‘morning’) is so called from *manus*. For the ancients called *manus* ‘good.’ What is better than light? Therefore the ancients called the day *manus*, namely, from purity. Alternatively, morning is said to be named from the *manes*, that is, the gods of the underworld. For the pagans believed that when the sun withdrew, the gods of the underworld had drawn it to themselves.”

**S.** How is midday defined?

**M.** Isidore defined it, saying: “Midday is so called as if it were *purus dies*, ‘pure day.’ For in the whole day nothing is purer than midday. The ancients called what was pure *merum*.”

**S.** Why is evening so called?

**M.** As if from *supprimendo* (“suppressing”). For then the sun inclines toward sunset. These, then, are the three periods of the artificial day, and they are regulated by the course of the sun. Morning is from sunrise until the sun has risen to the height of the sky. Midday is when the sun travels through the middle of the sky, at its height. Evening is when the sun descends from the height of the sky toward sunset.

**S.** How does the day begin among the Hebrews, Chaldeans, Egyptians, Romans, and Persians?

**M.** Among the Hebrews and Athenians, the day begins at the sixth hour of the day, because the Hebrews count according to the moon; thus they reckon as though the moon’s age changes or is renewed at midday. Among the Chaldeans and Persians, the day begins at sunrise, because the Chaldeans worshipped the sun first. Among the Egyptians, the day begins at sunset, when the star Vesper rises, which is also called Lucifer; the Egyptians worshipped that star first. Among the Romans and Persians, the natural day extends from midnight to midnight, on account of Jerome’s statement: “Because the world was made at midnight, and at midnight it will again be destroyed.”

Without doubt, from the beginning of the world until Christ’s resurrection, day preceded night; from Christ’s resurrection until the judgment, night precedes day. Hence Isidore says: “At the beginning of the Lord’s works, the day had its origin in light, to signify man’s fall; now, however, it proceeds from darkness to light, so that day is not obscured into night, but night shines into day, as it is written: ‘He caused light to shine from darkness.’”

Day, therefore, signifies knowledge of the divine law, while night signifies ignorance and blindness of conduct, according to the prophet’s saying: “I have likened your mother to night; my people have become like one without knowledge”—as if he had said, “without light.” Sometimes day signifies prosperity.

## IX. Where the day begins or ends, and where the first day of the age occurred

**S.** Where does the natural day properly receive its beginning and end?

**M.** The natural day is said to begin differently, according to the preference of various peoples.

**S.** How?

**M.** The Hebrews, Chaldeans, and Persians, following the order of the first creation, begin the course of the day in the morning and bring it back to morning, placing the time of shadows after the light. The Egyptians, by contrast, reckon from sunset to sunset. The Romans preferred to count their days from midnight to midnight, and the Athenians from midday to midday.

**S.** In what place, then, did the first day of the age occur?

**M.** On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, the day on which we believe light was first formed. Thus, we believe, those first three days passed without any measurement in hours, since the heavenly bodies had not yet been made. On the fourth day—that is, the twelfth day before the Kalends of April—the sun and the stars were created to serve as signs and for seasons, days, and years.

## X. On the weekday

The weekday (*feria*) received its name from *fari*, “to speak.” It is said to be *faria*, as though it were the name *feria*. It is derived from the second person, *faris*, or because the first person is lacking. *Feria* is used by custom. For *feriae*, *scalae*, *scopae*, *quadrigae*, and *Thebae* occur in the plural.

Thus, since *feria* received its name from *fari*, it can be called the Sabbath. On the Sabbath, in the Old Law, the works of the week were recounted. Alternatively, if *feria* is said to derive from *fieri*, as some think, it is formed from an active verb whose passive could at least be used in this way to name the weekday. For on that day it was first said: “Let there be light.” Therefore, if it is called the first weekday or the first day of the Sabbath, the meaning is the same.

It is also asked what sense is intended when it is said “the first weekday”; that is, the first day in relation to the weekday, as Isidore says. According to Pope Sylvester, *prima feria* means, as it were, “the first day.” Weekdays are called *feriae* from *fari*, “to speak,” because on them we have time for speech, whether by divine judgment or through human duty. All the days of the week, moreover, are called *feriae*.

**S.** Who first arranged and named the week and the days of the week?

**M.** Without doubt, God, who created all creatures in six days and rested on the seventh day. Hence the Lord himself said in the Law: “For six days you shall labor and do all your work; but the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God; you shall do no work on it. For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them, and he rested on the seventh day.”

Since God said on each day, “Let there be light,” the Sabbath in particular is so called because, as we have said, on that day the works of the week were customarily recounted. Among the Hebrews the Sabbath is called a weekday; among the Greeks, rest; among the Latins, *feria*, that is, the Lord’s day, from *fieri* (“to be made”), because on that day God said, “Let there be light.”

Hence Isidore says: “For this is the first day of the age. On that day the elements of the world were formed; on that day the angels were created; on that day also Christ rose from the dead; and on that day the mysteries of Christ and the Church were revealed to John the Evangelist on the island of Patmos, as he said: ‘I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day.’”

## XI. On the night

**S.** What is night?

[Col. 0658C]

**M.** The absence of the sun, the shadow cast over the earth, until it returns from sunset to sunrise.

**S.** From where is night so called?

**M.** Either because sight is harmful, or because it is harmful to human activities, or because thieves and robbers find in it an opportunity to harm others.

**S.** For what reason was night made?

**M.** To moderate human labor, so that bodies might have rest, and so that certain animals unable to endure the sun might have an opportunity to seek food.

## XII. On the increase and decrease of days and nights day by day

It should be known that each day and each night, as they increase, grow by two moments and two parts of a third moment. Likewise, as they decrease, they diminish by the same amount, so that in three days eight moments increase or decrease; in six days, sixteen moments; in nine, twenty-four; in twelve, thirty-two; in fifteen, forty—that is, one complete hour—for forty moments make an hour.

Therefore, if you desire to know how the solar increase causes the days and light to grow, how the night and darkness diminish, and how much grows in each month, this must be investigated carefully and diligently. You will learn that each day, as the sun rises, two and a half moments and a sixth part of a moment are taken from the darkness and added to the light. Likewise, as they decrease, they diminish; thus in three days there are eight moments, in six sixteen, and in twelve thirty-two. Over fifteen days and five hours, as the sun rises, one hour increases. Over thirty days and ten hours, two hours increase—that is, eighty moments.

Thus, in ninety days, one day, and six hours—that is, from the winter solstice to the spring equinox—two hundred forty moments, or six hours, increase. [Col. 0659A] In the same way and with the same increase of moments, two moments and two parts of a moment per day increase during the other three months, from the spring equinox to the summer solstice: two hundred forty moments, that is, another six hours.

Thus, from the winter solstice to the summer solstice, over six months—that is, 182 days and twelve hours, or half a natural day—four hundred eighty moments increase, that is, twelve hours. Add these to the six hours that existed in the winter-solstice day: together they make eighteen hours in the summer-solstice day, and six hours in the night.

## XIII. On the week

A week is the course of seven days, and it received its name from the number seven. For *hebdomada* in Greek is called *septimana* in Latin, because it contains within itself seven mornings, that is, seven days.

## XIV. On the months

[Col. 0659B]

We also read that months were named before the Flood, as Isidore says. Holy Scripture shows that the year had been named as consisting of twelve months before the Flood. For thus we read in Genesis: “The waters were diminishing until the twelfth month; on the first day of the month the tops of the mountains appeared.” The Hebrews counted those months according to the moon, and they have always done so.

**S.** Who first discovered solar months?

**M.** As Isidore says: “Because of the moon’s more rapid course, and so that error would not arise from the speed of the calculation, the Egyptians devised months according to the course of the sun, since the slower motion of the sun could more easily be grasped.”

**S.** Who first devised the month among the Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins?

**M.** Moses among the Hebrews, the Arcadians among the Greeks, and Romulus among the Romans.

**S.** In what number were the months devised among the Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins?

**M.** In the number twelve. The ancients defined a month as the time in which the moon traverses the zodiacal circle. The ancient pagan world gave the months certain names from its gods and certain names from circumstances.

The month is so called from the moon, which is called *mene* in Greek; among the Greeks, months are also called *menes*.
