Likewise, among the Hebrews, as Jerome attests, the moon is called *iare*, and it gave its name to the months. The month pertains both to the sun and to the moon, but more properly to the moon. It should therefore be defined as the circuit and renewal of lunar light, from new moon to new moon.

A solar month is the sun’s passage through one-twelfth of the zodiac—that is, the circle of the signs—and it is completed in thirty days and ten and a half hours, namely, twenty-two and a half hours longer than a lunar month.

Among the Hebrews the moon is called by three names: *iare*, *lavana*, and *mavors*. It is called *iare* from the number of days in the month, *lavana* from its whiteness, and *mavors* from its waning, because it wanes every month.

## XV. On the month of January

In Hebrew, *Thabeth*; among the Egyptians, *Tibi* or *Tidechi*; among the Macedonians, *Etdrimos* or *Ethinios*; in Greek, *Januarios*; in Latin, *Januarius*.

Numa Pompilius named January and established it as the first month of the year, dedicating it to the upper gods. January received its name in two ways: from an idol and from a circumstance.

From an idol: from Janus, the two-faced king of the Epirotes, who, driven out and expelled from his homeland, came to the Romans and became an exile among them. It happened that a large barbarian people besieged Rome. Janus was an ingenious man who advised the Romans how they might free the city from that siege, but only on condition that after his death the Romans would worship him as a god.

After they had promised this, he asked for eight linen cloths soaked and anointed with oil, wax, and water. When this had been done, he told them to wrap themselves in those cloths and set them on fire. He then asked that two heated and burning swords be given to him. Afterwards he climbed onto the wall and told the Romans that, when he had raised himself upon the wall and shouted like a god, they should throw open all the gates, rush upon the enemy, and win the victory.

And so it happened. The Romans secured the victory, killing and putting the enemies to flight. Janus, however, was consumed by fire. After his death the Romans worshipped him as a god and built him a great temple in Rome, which from Janus’s name they called the Janiculum. It had one hundred gates. In that temple they made a bronze image of Janus with two faces. Hence he was called Janus *bifrons*, “two-faced.” Men worshipped him from one side and one face, while women worshipped him from the other face.

For this reason they called the month Janus after the two-headed god, who looked back toward the end of the past year and forward toward the beginning of the coming year. January is also named from a circumstance, because it is the gateway of the year, that is, its beginning: just as a person enters through a doorway, so the years enter through this January.

## XVI. On the month of February

In Hebrew, *Sabath*; among the Egyptians, *Mechir* or *Methi*; among the Macedonians, *Perittios*; in Greek, *Februarios*; in Latin, *Februarius*.

**S.** In what ways did February receive its name?

**M.** In two ways: from an idol and from a circumstance.

From an idol: from the god Februus. Hence Macrobius says: “Numa Pompilius named the second month February and dedicated it to the god Februus, who is also called Pluto and was believed by the pagans to have power over purifications. In that month it was necessary to purify the city of Rome, so that the prescribed rites—that is, sacrifices—might be performed for the spirits of the dead.”

Alternatively, February was named from a circumstance, namely, from the sharp fevers of the Luperci. The Luperci and Lurcones are two peoples in the East who, after the impurities of the entire year, washed their bodies in a certain lake situated among them, became feverish, and, as pagan tradition relates, then changed their forms.

Because they did this in the month of February, washing themselves and then becoming feverish, February was named from washing or bathing. Hence it is written: “The pagans had a certain *februm*, that is, a bath,” and thus this month received its name from a circumstance. February is also named from *febris*, “fever,” that is, from the cold, because of the cold weather of the month.

## XVII. On the month of March

In Hebrew, *Adar*; among the Egyptians, *Phamenoth*; among the Macedonians, *Distros*; in Greek, *Martios*; in Latin, *Martius*.

March received its name in two ways, from an idol and from a circumstance. From an idol: it was named from Mars, the father of Romulus. Hence Macrobius said: “Romulus established and named March as the first month of the year and dedicated it to his father Mars.” That this month was the first among the ancient Romans is shown especially by the fact that Quintilis, Sextilis, and the other following months are numbered in order from it; and in that month the Romans collected taxes.

Isidore likewise says: “It was called March on account of Mars, the founder of the Roman people.” March also received its name from a circumstance, namely, from males; for at that time all the animals of the earth desire males for the pleasure of mating. It is also called the month of new crops.

## XVIII. On the month of April

In Hebrew, *Nisan*; among the Egyptians, *Pharmuthi*; among the Macedonians, *Xanticos*; in Greek, *Aprilios*; in Latin, *Aprilis*.

**S.** In what ways is April named?

**M.** In two ways: from an idol and from a circumstance.

From an idol: from Venus, the mother of Aeneas. For in Greek *Aphron* means “foam,” from which Venus is believed to have arisen; among the Greeks she is called *Aphrilis* or *Aphronis*. Alternatively, April is named from a circumstance, namely, from opening; *Aprilis* is as if it were *aperilis*.

Before the month of April, the sky is gloomy and dark, covered and hidden by clouds; the air is shadowy, and the sea is closed to ships. The earth itself is covered by water, frost, snow, or clouds. All these things are opened in springtime, that is, in the month of April. The clear sky, once the clouds have been driven away, is opened for human use; so too the sea for ships, and the earth and trees open themselves into shoots and flowers.

For all these reasons, it should rightly be believed that the month of April is so called as if it were *aperilis*. At this time everything blossoms.

## XIX. On the month of May

In Hebrew, *Iarus*; among the Egyptians, *Pacho* or *Paon*; among the Macedonians, *Artemisios*; in Greek, *Maios*; in Latin, *Maius*.

**S.** In what ways is May named?

[Col. 0661B]

**M.** In two ways: from an idol and from a circumstance.

From an idol: May was named after the god Maius among the pagans, who was identified as Jupiter. Hence Macrobius says: “Among the Tusculans, the god Maius was called Jupiter; he was so named from greatness and majesty.” Zingius, however, thinks that the month of May was named after Maia, whom he calls the wife of Vulcan, that is, the mother of Mercury.

Therefore, on the Kalends of May they sacrificed to the goddess Maia, and in this month all merchants likewise sacrificed to Maia and Mercury. Mercury is the god of merchants; hence he is also called Mercury, as if *mercium curius*, that is, the procurator of merchandise.

May is also named from a circumstance, namely, from the elders of the Romans. Hence Macrobius says: “Romulus made May the third month. After he had divided the Roman people into two parts, establishing one as the elders and the other as the younger men, so that one part—the elders—might protect the republic by counsel, while the other, the younger men, might protect it [added: *armis*, “by arms”], he named this month of May and the following month of June in honor of both parts.”

## XX. On the month of June

In Hebrew, *Sivari* or *Sivan*; among the Egyptians, *Pauni*; among the Macedonians, *Deseos*; in Greek, *Junios*; in Latin, *Junius*.

**S.** In what ways is June named?

**M.** In two ways: from an idol and from a circumstance.

From an idol: from Juno, the daughter of Saturn, who was worshipped by the pagans as a goddess; they called the month June after her name. Hence Macrobius says: “Among the Latins, June was formerly called *Junonius* and was named after Juno. Later, when certain letters—namely, n and o—had been worn away, *Junonius* became *Junius*.” A temple was also dedicated to Juno on the Kalends of June.

Others thought that the month of June was named after Junius Brutus, who was the first consul elected in the city of Rome. Alternatively, June is named from a circumstance, namely, from the younger men of Rome who defended the republic by arms. Hence Macrobius says: “June follows May and was named from a part of the people.”

## XXI. On the month of July

In Hebrew, *Tamul* or *Tani*; among the Egyptians, *Epiphi*; among the Macedonians, *Panemos*; in Greek, *Julios*; in Latin, *Julius*.

**S.** From where did July receive its name?

**M.** From a certain emperor, namely Julius Caesar. On the fourth day before the Ides of July, Gaius Julius Caesar was born; he was the first to seize imperial power among the Romans. Afterwards, in his honor, the month was called July from his name. Previously it had been called Quintilis.

## XXII. On the month of August

In Hebrew, *Tamni*; among the Egyptians, *Mesor* or *Mesori*; among the Macedonians, *Loos* or *Lor*; in Greek, *Augustos*; in Latin, *Augustus*.

**S.** From where did August receive its name?

[Col. 0662A]

**M.** From the emperor Octavian Caesar Augustus, who on the Kalends of August defeated Antony, who was contending for the kingdom, and Cleopatra, queen of Egypt and Antony’s wife, who was bringing him auxiliary forces and an army.

Caesar Augustus defeated these two on a single day, the Kalends of August, and afterwards held the principate of the entire world. Thus August was named from Augustus, who in that month first entered upon the consulship and brought three triumphs to the city. Afterwards he was called Augustus by the Roman people, and the month was called August in his honor, so that his memory might remain in the calendar.

For among the Romans that month had previously been called Sextilis, because it was the sixth month from March. Macrobius therefore says: “August was formerly called Sextilis, until, by decree of the Senate, it was called August in honor of Augustus.”

## XXIII. On the month of September

In Hebrew, *Elul*; among the Egyptians, *Tooth*; among the Macedonians, *Gorpeos*; in Greek, *Septembrios*; in Latin, *September*.

September received its name from a number, because it is the seventh month from March, since March was once the first month among the Romans, in the time of Romulus. From it the other months are named according to numbers, just as Quintilis is so called because it is the fifth month from March. Thus Sextilis and September are numbered from March.

## XXIV. On the month of October

In Hebrew, *Theseri*; among the Egyptians, *Paopi*; among the Macedonians, *Hyperbereteos*; in Greek, *Octimbrios*; in Latin, *October*.

October is so called because it is the eighth month from March. Among Eastern peoples this month is placed at the beginning of the year.

## XXV. On the month of November
Maresvan in Hebrew, Athir among the Egyptians, Dios among the Macedonians, Novimbrios in Greek, November in Latin. November is so called because it is the ninth month reckoned from March. [Col. 0662C]

XXVI. On the month of December.

Casleu among the Hebrews, Chiachi among the Egyptians, Apileos among the Macedonians, Decembrios in Greek, December in Latin. December received its name from a number, because it is the tenth month reckoned from March. Among the Macedonians, this month is also placed at the beginning of the year.

XXVII. On the three names of days in the annual reckoning: Kalends, Ides, and Nones.

Although Romulus possessed a keen intelligence, he was nevertheless uncultivated. When he was arranging the constitution of his own government, he took the beginning of each month from the day on which the new moon happened to become visible. For it does not always appear on the same day, but, for definite reasons, it is sometimes seen later and sometimes earlier. It therefore happened that, when it appeared later, more days were assigned to the preceding month, or, when it appeared earlier, fewer days were assigned; and the first occurrence prescribed a permanent numerical rule for each month. [Col. 0662D] Thus it came about that some months received thirty-one days, while others received twenty-nine.

It was nevertheless decided that all months should be marked from the day of the Nones—that is, from the ninth day—and that sixteen days should be counted between the Ides and the following Kalends. Therefore the longer month had those two days by which it was increased between its Kalends and Nones; hence, for some months, the fifth day from the Kalends constituted the Nones, while for others the seventh day did so.

In those times this responsibility was assigned to the lesser pontiff: he was to watch for the first appearance of the new moon and, when he had seen it, announce it to the king who performed the sacrifices. Accordingly, after sacrifice had been celebrated by the king and the lesser pontiff, with the people summoned (*calata*, that is, “called”) to the Capitol beside the Calabrian Curia, which was closest to the hut of Romulus, he announced how many days remained from the Kalends to the Nones.

For the fifth-day Nones, whose beginning after the Kalends falls on the fourth day, he announced it by pronouncing the word *Calo* five times; for the seventh-day Nones, whose beginning after the Kalends falls on the sixth day, he proclaimed it [Col. 0663A] by repeating the same word seven times. The word *calo* is Greek, meaning “I call”; and it was decided that the first of these days on which the people were called should be called the Kalends. Hence the curia itself to which they were called received the name *Calabra*, or *Classis*, because all the people were called into it.

The lesser pontiff proclaimed by calling how many days remained until the Nones because, after the ninth moon, on the day of the Nones, the country people who were in the fields had to gather in the city in order to receive from the king of sacred rites the reasons for the festivals and to learn what had to be done during that month. Hence some judge that the Nones were so called as the beginning of observation of the new moon, or because eight days are counted from that day to the Ides.

The Ides, however, is the day that divides the month. For in the Etruscan language *iduare* means “to divide.” Hence *widow* (*vidua*), as though “very divided,” *idua*, that is, “completely separated”; or, as some wish, *vidua*, meaning “separated from a husband.” Others, however, think that the Ides were named by a Greek word, specifically from the form called *idea* among the Greeks, because on that day the moon displays its full form. [Col. 0663B]

Accordingly, Romulus organized the annual reckoning so that the year consisted of ten months and 304 days. He arranged the months so that four of them had thirty-one days, while six had thirty days. But since this number conformed neither to the calculations of the sun nor to those of the moon, it sometimes happened that the cold of the year occurred in the summer months and, conversely, heat occurred in the winter months.

Numa then followed him, as though intending to remove this entire error, and extended the year to 354 days, which he believed were required to complete the twelve courses of the moon. To the fifty days he had added, he added six more, taken from the six months that had thirty days—that is, one from each month—and divided the resulting fifty-six days, in equal proportion, into two new months.

He named the first of these January and wished it to be the first month of the year, like the month of the two-headed god, looking back toward the end of the past [Col. 0663C] year and forward toward the beginnings of the future year. The second he dedicated to the god Februus, who was believed to possess power over purifications; from him he also named February. He decreed that the city should be purified in that month, so that due offerings might be paid to the spirits of the dead.

A little later, in honor of the odd number, he added one day and gave it to January, so that both in the year and in the individual months—apart from February alone—an odd number would be maintained. For since twelve months, if each were counted by either an even or an odd number, would produce an even total, the addition of one to the even number made the entire reckoning odd.

Thus January, April, June, Sextilis, September, November, and December were reckoned as having twenty-nine days. They had fifth-day Nones, and after the Ides they were counted through the seventeenth day before the Kalends.

March, May, Quintilis, and October, however, possessed thirty-one days. Their Nones were on the seventh day; likewise, after the Ides, seventeen days were counted in each of them up to the following Kalends. [Col. 0663D]

February alone retained twenty-eight days, as though both diminution and an even number were appropriate to the infernal regions.

When the year had thus been organized by Numa, some days were still lacking for a complete annual number. After several years, therefore, because of the great neglect of these matters, confusion arose in the reckoning of time. Although they corrected it to some extent by intercalating days in various ways, they transmitted no fixed reckoning of the year to posterity.

It therefore came about that, just as the later Numa destroyed the annual reckoning established by the preceding Romulus, so Gaius Caesar, following Numa, criticized the latter’s still inconsistent and uncertain arrangement and corrected what he had criticized down to the smallest detail.

[Col. 0664A] Gaius Caesar therefore, imitating the Egyptians, endeavored to regulate the year according to the number of the sun, which completes its course in 365¼ days. Accordingly, he added ten days to the old reckoning, so that the year would consist of 365 days, the period in which the sun traverses the zodiac. And so that the quarter-day would not be omitted, he decreed that every fourth year the priests in charge of the months and days should insert one intercalary day in the month and place where the ancients had also intercalated a month—that is, before the final days of February. He decreed that this should be called the bissextile.

The ten days which, as we have said, he added, he distributed as follows.

He inserted two days into January, Sextilis, and December.

Into April, June, September, and November he inserted one day each.

He added no day to February, lest the religious observance associated with the infernal gods be altered.

For March, May, Quintilis, and October he preserved the former arrangement, since they already had a sufficiently full number, namely thirty-one. Therefore they too have seventh-day Nones, as Numa established.

[Col. 0664B] January, Sextilis, and December, to which Caesar added two days, although they began after Caesar to have thirty-one days, have fifth-day Nones; and after the Ides nineteen days are counted up to the following Kalends. Caesar did not wish to insert the days he added either before the Nones or before the Ides, lest he corrupt by a new reckoning the religious observances of the Nones or Ides, which had been fixed for a particular day. Nor did he wish to insert them immediately after the Ides, lest the proclamation of any festivals be violated. Instead, after the festivals of each month had been completed, he made room for the additional days:

- In January, he assigned four days before the Kalends, and three days before the Kalends of February.
- In April, six days before the Kalends of May.
- In June, three days before the Kalends of July.
- In August, four days before the Kalends, and three days before the Kalends of September.
- In September, three days before the Kalends of October.
- In November, three days before the Kalends of December.
- In December, four days before the Kalends, and three days before the Kalends of January.

Thus it happened that, whereas all these months to which he added days had previously counted backward to the seventeenth day before the Kalends of the following month, after the increase caused by the added days, those that received two days counted back to the nineteenth day, while those that received one counted back to the eighteenth day before the Kalends. [Col. 0664C]

As we have said, he had only ten months.

XXIX. The months of Numa.

[Col. 0664D]

| 1 | January. |
|---|---|
| 2 | February. |

Quintilis and Sextilis, although they were no longer the fifth and sixth months but had become the seventh and eighth, nevertheless retained their names improperly. Gaius Caesar called one of them by his own name, namely July; Sextilis continued in its defective state until the emperor Augustus, after whom that month was called August.

[Col. 0665]

ON ARITHMETICAL PROPOSITIONS

[Col. 0665A] Divining a number conceived in someone’s mind.

How the number conceived in anyone’s mind can be discovered. Take any number and triple it. Divide the tripled number into two parts; if both parts turn out equal, triple whichever one you wish again, without distinction. But if they are unequal, triple the larger part. Whenever, after it has been tripled, nines can be found in it, count them. For as many nines as it contains, that many twos must be taken.

It must also be observed that, after the number has been tripled and divided, and the half has again been tripled, when the question is asked about the nines, this too must be added: whether anything remains over one, two, or however many nines there are. For if anything remains, there are seven, and one must be taken from them. [Col. 0665B] When these have been reduced to a total, the number that was first conceived in the mind must be declared.

For example, if two were conceived in the mind, when tripled they make six; six divided into three and three is resolved into those two parts; but three tripled makes only nine, and nothing remains. Therefore the number first grasped in the mind was two. Hence, throughout this entire calculation, nine always signifies two, and six signifies one.

It should be understood that every odd number that is taken and tripled and divided in the manner described above ends in six. An even number ends in nine, because one, tripled and divided according to the method stated above, produces six, whereas two, tripled and divided in the same way, produces nine. These two numbers—one and two—are said to be the principles of evenness and oddness.

[Col. 0665C] Another method.

Take any number and triple it. Triple it, divide it into two parts, and then ask the person who conceived the number whether the division of that number is even. If he answers that both parts are even, take nothing; but if he says that they are odd, take one in this first division, as a reminder for the diviner.

Then, when both parts have been equal, triple one part of the division again without distinction. But if they have been unequal, the larger part must be tripled and divided, as above, into two parts. Again ask whether the division has become equal or unequal. If it has become equal, nothing is to be taken. If it is unequal, two are to be taken in the second division.

And if the division at the halfway point was equal, without any difference between the parts, ask how many nines it contains. But if it was unequal, search in the larger part; however many nines are found in it, the diviner must take that many fours.

For example, if six were conceived in the mind, when tripled they make eighteen; eighteen is divided into nine and nine. [Col. 0665D] Since the division is equal, nothing is taken there. The nine that is again the half of this division, when tripled, makes twenty-seven; twenty-seven is resolved into thirteen and fourteen. Since this is the second division and is unequal, two must be taken. Then, in the larger part of this division—that is, in fourteen—it must be sought how many times nine can be found. Fourteen contains nine once; from those nine, four are to be collected by the diviner. Added to the two collected in the second division, they make six. Therefore the first number conceived in the mind was six.

In this method it must be noted that, if both divisions have yielded even parts, nothing is to be taken from them; if the second division is unequal, two are to be taken, while nine contains the significance of four. This seems to occur differently in this calculation from the preceding one because this one is tripled twice and divided twice, whereas the other is tripled twice and divided once. [Col. 0666A] Therefore, in this method, nine signifies four, while nothing signifies two.

Another method.

How to divine on which day of the week someone did something. Whoever has conceived in his mind the number containing the name of a particular weekday must first double it; then add five to that doubled number; multiply the sum obtained from these by five; then multiply the whole by ten; afterward subtract 250 from the total, and regard what remains as the number of the weekday.

For example, if the first weekday is under consideration, double one, making two; add five to it, making seven; [Col. 0666B] multiply seven by five, making thirty-five; multiply thirty-five by ten, making 350. If 250 is subtracted from the total, carefully observe how many hundreds remain, because, as stated above, one hundred signifies the first weekday; two hundred, the second; three hundred, the third; four hundred, the fourth; five hundred, the fifth; six hundred, the sixth; seven hundred, the seventh.

Likewise, if the second weekday is under consideration, double two, making four. Add five, making nine. Multiply nine by five, making forty-five; multiply by ten, making 450. Subtract 250 from this, leaving 200, which signifies the second weekday.

If the third weekday is under consideration, double three, making six; add five, making eleven; multiply eleven by five, making fifty-five; multiply fifty-five by ten, making 550. Subtract 250, leaving 300, which signifies the third weekday.

If the fourth weekday is sought, double four, making eight; add seven, making fifteen; multiply fifteen by five, making seventy-five; multiply seventy-five by ten, making 750. [Col. 0666C] Subtract 250, leaving 500, which signifies the fifth weekday.

If the sixth weekday is sought, double six, making twelve; add five, making seventeen; multiply seventeen by five, making eighty-five; multiply eighty-five by ten, making 850. Subtract 250, leaving 600, which signifies the sixth weekday.

If the seventh weekday is sought, double seven, making fourteen; add five, making nineteen; multiply nineteen by five, making ninety-five; multiply ninety-five by ten, making 950. Subtract 250, leaving 700, which signifies the seventh weekday.

If you carefully entrust this number to your mind, you will be able to investigate all the weekdays without error.

Another problem.

True combined with true makes true. Minus combined with true makes true. True combined with minus makes minus. Minus combined with minus makes minus. True signifies being; minus signifies nothing. [Col. 0666D]

Place whatever total of a number you wish under the name of “true,” that is, of being; and place another total of whatever number you wish under the name of the adverb called “minus,” which, as I have said, signifies nothing. Then compare those two totals. Whichever is greater overcomes the lesser and consumes it according to the magnitude of its quantity.

For example, if two totals of numbers are joined, one called true, that is, being—say seven—and the other called by the name of the adverb minus—say three—these two totals, of being and non-being, are compared numerically. Since the total of true is greater than that called minus, seven is greater than three minus; if it exceeds by the greater part by which it can overcome it, this amounts to four, for three is minus and seven remain four.

Likewise, if three are called true and seven minus, since the total of nothing is greater than that of being, the non-existent seven overcomes the subsisting three and consumes it by its non-being; four non-existent units remain from it. This is what is meant by: join three and seven minus; they make four minus.

But if three non-existent numbers and likewise seven non-existent numbers are joined—as seven and three true, that is, existent, numbers make ten—then the two totals of non-existent numbers, called three minus and seven minus, make ten minus. For true has the power to make, and minus not to make. Join three minus and seven: they make ten; again join three minus and seven: they make four; join three and seven minus; join three minus and seven minus: they make ten minus.

[Col. 0667]

[Col. 0667A] HERE BEGIN OTHER PROPOSITIONS FOR SHARPENING THE YOUNG

And first, concerning the snail.

A snail was invited by a swallow to lunch one league away. During a single day, however, it could not walk more than one ounce of a foot. Let whoever wishes say in how many years or days the snail traveled to that lunch.

Concerning a man and other men whom he encountered on the road.

A certain man walking along a road saw other men [Col. 0667B] coming toward him and said to them: “Would that you were as many again as you are, and half of half as many, and again half of half as many; then, together with me, you would number one hundred.” Let whoever wishes say how many he first saw.

Concerning two travelers who saw storks.

Two men walking along a road saw some storks and said to each other: “How many are there?” After considering the number, they said: “If there were as many more, and as many more again, and half of a third as many, with two added, there would be one hundred.” Let whoever can say how many there originally were.

Concerning a man and horses grazing in a field.

A certain man saw horses grazing in a field and expressed the wish: “Would that you belonged to me and that there were as many more of you, and half of half as many; then I would certainly boast of one hundred horses.” Let whoever wishes determine how many horses that man first saw grazing.

[Col. 0667C] Concerning a purchaser with one hundred denarii.

A certain merchant said: “I wish to buy one hundred pigs with one hundred denarii, provided that a boar is bought for ten denarii, a sow for five, and two piglets for one denarius.” Let whoever understands say how many boars, how many sows, and how many piglets there must be, so that in neither number nor money there is either excess or deficiency.

Concerning two men conducting a joint business with one hundred solidi.

There were two merchants who had one hundred solidi in common, with which they bought pigs. They bought five pigs for two solidi, intending to fatten them and sell them again at a profit. When they saw that it was not the right season for fattening the pigs, and that they themselves could not feed them during the winter, they tried to make a profit by selling them. But they could not, because they were unable to sell them for more than they had cost—that is, they could receive only two solidi for five pigs.

When they realized this, they said to one another: “Let us divide them.” When they divided and [Col. 0667D] sold them at the same price for which they had bought them, they made a profit. Let whoever can say how many pigs there originally were, and divide and sell them so as to make the profit that they could not make by selling them all together: thirty pounds.

Concerning a disk.

There is a disk weighing thirty pounds, or six hundred solidi, containing gold, silver, brass, and tin. Whatever quantity of gold it has, it has three times as much silver; whatever quantity of silver it has, it has three times as much brass; whatever quantity of brass it has, it has three times as much tin. Let whoever can say how much each substance weighs.

Concerning a vat.

There is a vat filled by one hundred *metretae*, each containing three *modii*. It has three pipes, measured according to the *modius*: through one pipe flows a third and a sixth; through another, a third alone; through the third, a sixth alone. Let whoever wishes say how many *sextarii* would have flowed through each pipe.

[Col. 0668A] Concerning a cloak.

I have a cloak measuring one hundred cubits in length and eighty in width. I wish to make smaller cloaks from it in pieces, so that each piece is five cubits long and four cubits wide. Tell me, wise man, how many small cloaks can be made.

Concerning linen cloth.

I have one piece of linen, sixty cubits long and sixty cubits wide. I wish to make pieces from it so that each piece is six cubits long and four cubits wide, sufficient for sewing a tunic. Let whoever wishes say how many tunics can be made.

Concerning two men who each married the other’s sister.

If two men each take the other’s sister in marriage, tell me, I ask, in what relationship their children are related to each other.

Concerning two men who each married the other’s mother.

If two men likewise each take the other’s mother in marriage, by what relationship are their children joined to one another?

Concerning a father and son who married a mother and her daughter.

If a father and son marry a widow or divorced woman and her daughter, in such a way that the son takes the mother and the father takes the daughter, tell me, I beg, in what relationship the children born from these unions will be related to one another. [Col. 0668C]

Concerning a householder and his three sons.

A certain householder, dying, divided among his three sons thirty glass bottles as an inheritance. Ten of them were full of oil, another ten were half-full, and the remaining ten were empty. Let whoever can divide both the oil and the bottles so that each of the three sons receives an equal share both of the glass and of the oil.

Concerning a king and his army collected from thirty villages.

A certain king ordered his servant to collect an army from thirty villages, in such a way that from each village he took as many men as he had brought there. He himself came to the first village alone; to the second with one other; and to the third three men came. Let whoever can say how many men were collected from all thirty villages.

Concerning an ox.

An ox that plows all day: how many tracks does it make in the final furrow?

Concerning a man.

I ask you to tell me how many furrows a man has made in his field when he has made three plowings from each end of the field.

Concerning two men leading oxen.

Two men were leading oxen along a road. One said to the other: “Give me two oxen, and I shall have as many oxen as you have.” The other replied: “Give me two oxen, and I shall have twice as many as you have.” Let whoever wishes say how many oxen each of them had.

Concerning two brothers who each had a sister.

There were three brothers, each of whom had a sister, and they had to cross a river. Each of them desired the sister of one of the others. When they came to the river, they found only a small boat, which could carry no more than two of them at a time. [Col. 0669A] Let whoever can say how they crossed the river so that not even one of the girls was dishonored by any of them.

Concerning a wolf, a goat, and a bundle of cabbage.

A certain man had to transport across a river a wolf, a bundle of cabbage, and a goat. He could find no other boat except one that could carry only two of them. He had therefore been instructed to transport all these things across entirely unharmed. Let whoever can say how he carried them across unharmed.

Concerning a man and a woman carrying the weight of a loaded wagon.

A man and a woman, each of whom had the weight of a loaded wagon, had two children between them whose combined weight equaled that of a wagon. They had to cross a river and found a boat capable of carrying only the weight of one wagon. Let whoever thinks he can do so arrange their crossing without sinking the boat.

[Col. 0669B] Concerning hedgehogs.

Concerning a male and female hedgehog, having two young and weighing a pound, who wish to cross a river.

Concerning a field and sheep to be placed in it.

There is a field that is two hundred feet long and one hundred feet wide. I wish to place sheep in it, provided that each sheep has five feet of length and four feet of width. Tell me, I ask, whoever can, how many can all be placed there.

Concerning a sloping field.

There is a sloping field that has one hundred *perticae* on one side, one hundred *perticae* on the other side, fifty *perticae* at the front, sixty *perticae* in the middle, and fifty *perticae* at the other front. Let whoever can say how many *aripennes* it ought to enclose.

Concerning a quadrangular field.

[Col. 0669C] There is a four-sided field that has thirty *perticae* on one side, thirty-two *perticae* on the other, thirty-four *perticae* at the front, and thirty-two *perticae* at the other front. Let whoever can say how many *aripennes* should be enclosed in it.

Concerning a triangular field.

There is a triangular field that has thirty *perticae* on one side, thirty *perticae* on the other, and nineteen *perticae* at the front. Let whoever can say how many *aripennes* it ought to enclose.

Concerning a round field.

There is a round field whose circumference measures four hundred *perticae*. Say how many *aripennes* it ought to contain.

Concerning a field, a dog, and a fleeing hare.

There is a field one hundred and fifty feet long. At one end stood a dog and at the other a hare. The dog began to run after the hare; [Col. 0669D] but whenever the dog covered nine feet in one leap, the hare covered seven. Let whoever wishes say how many feet, and how many leaps, both the dog in pursuit and the hare in flight covered before the hare was caught.

Concerning a quadrangular city.

There is a four-sided city that has 1,100 feet on one side, 1,000 feet on the other, 600 feet at the front, and 600 feet at the other front. I wish to place the roofs of houses there so that each house is forty feet long and thirty feet wide. Let whoever wishes say how many houses it can contain.

Concerning a triangular city.

There is a triangular city that has one hundred feet on one side, one hundred on the other, and ninety feet at the front. I wish houses to be built there, provided that each house is twenty feet long and ten feet wide. Let him say how many houses can be accommodated. [Col. 0670A]

Concerning a round city.

There is a round city with a circumference of eight thousand feet. Let whoever can say how many houses it can contain, provided that each house is thirty feet long and twenty feet wide.

Concerning a basilica.

There is a basilica 240 feet long and 120 feet wide. Its paving bricks are as follows: one brick is twenty-three inches long—that is, one foot and eleven inches—and twelve inches wide—that is, one foot. Let whoever wishes say how many bricks are needed to fill it.

Concerning a *cavana*.

There is a *cavana* one hundred feet long and sixty-four feet wide. Let whoever wishes say how many vats it ought to contain, provided that each vat is seven feet long and four feet wide, that one passage is four feet wide, and that each vat has a length of seven feet.

[Col. 0670B] Concerning a certain householder.

A certain householder had twenty dependents and ordered twenty *modii* of grain to be given to them. He ordered that the men receive three *modii* each, the women two each, and the children half a *modius* each. Let whoever can say how many men, how many women, and how many children there were.

Another.

A certain householder had ninety dependents and ordered ninety *modii* of grain to be given to them. He likewise ordered that the men receive three *modii* each, the women two each, and the children half a *modius* each. Let whoever can say how many men, how many women, or how many children there were.

Concerning the death of a certain householder.

A certain householder, dying, left children and [Col. 0670C] 860 solidi among his possessions, as well as a pregnant wife. He ordered that, if a male child were born to him, the child should receive nine ounces from the entire estate and his mother three ounces; but if a daughter were born, she should receive five ounces and her mother likewise five ounces.

It happened that she gave birth to twins, namely a boy and a girl. Let whoever can do so determine how much the mother receives, and how much the son and daughter each receive.

Another.

A certain householder had thirty dependents. He ordered that the men receive three *modii* each, the women two each, and the children half a *modius* each. Let whoever can do so determine how many men, how many women, and how many children there were.

Concerning an old man’s greeting to a boy.

A certain old man greeted a boy and said to him: “May you live, son; live,” he said, “as long as you have lived, and as much again, and three times as much; and may God add to you one of my years, so that you complete one hundred [Col. 0670D] years.” Let whoever can do so determine how old the boy was at that time.

Another.

A certain householder had one hundred dependents, whom he ordered to be given one hundred *modii* of grain. The arrangement was that the men should receive three *modii* each, the women two each, and the children half a *modius* each. Let whoever can say how many men, women, or children there were.

Concerning a certain man building a house.

A certain man wishing to build a house hired six craftsmen, five of whom were master builders and one an apprentice. He and the craftsmen agreed that they would be paid twenty-five denarii per day, provided that the apprentice received half of what one of the masters received. Let whoever can determine how much each of them received per day.

[Col. 0671A] [Note: [Col. 0671] This note is printed at the foot of column 671, but its callout letter, “a,” does not appear in the text.] Here the second problem concerning the man and the other men is solved, and so forth. EDIT.

Concerning animals purchased.

A certain man wished to buy one hundred assorted animals for one hundred solidi, so that a horse would be bought for three solidi, an ox for one solidus, and thirty-three sheep for one solidus. Let whoever can say how many horses, how many oxen, and how many sheep there were.

Another.

A certain man wished to buy one hundred assorted animals in the East for one hundred solidi. He ordered his servant to buy a camel for five solidi, an ass for one solidus, and twenty sheep for one solidus. Let whoever wishes say how many camels, asses, or sheep there were in the transaction involving one hundred solidi.

Concerning a man and grazing sheep.

A certain man saw sheep grazing on a mountain and said: “Would that I had as many, and as many again, and half of half as many, and from this half another half; then, as the hundredth together with them, I would enter my house.” Let whoever can solve it say how many sheep he saw grazing there. [Col. 0671B]

Concerning a *sode* and a sow.

A certain householder established a new quadrangular enclosure. In it he placed a sow, which gave birth to seven piglets in the middle of the *sode*; since, together with their mother, who is the eighth, they were eight in number, each one gave birth to seven in every corner, and she herself again, in the middle of the *sode*, together with all of them collectively, gave birth to seven. Let whoever wishes say how many pigs there were, counting the mothers.

Concerning a ladder with one hundred steps.

There is a ladder with one hundred steps. On the first step sat one dove, on the second two, on the third three, on the fourth four, on the fifth five, and so on at every step up to the hundredth. Let whoever can say how many doves there were altogether.

Concerning pigs.

A certain man had 300 pigs and ordered that pigs should be slaughtered in odd numbers over three days. [Col. 0671C] A similar problem is stated concerning thirty. Let whoever can now say how many odd numbers of pigs—whether out of 300 or out of 30—are to be killed over three days. This problem has been composed as an insoluble one for the purpose of rebuke.

Concerning a boy’s greeting to his father.

A certain boy greeted his father: “Hail, father.” His father replied: “Farewell, son. May you live as long as you have lived; triple the years doubled, and take one of my years, and you will have one hundred years.” Let whoever can determine how old the boy was at that time.

Concerning a dove.

A dove sitting in a tree saw other doves flying and said to them: “Would that there were as many of you again, and as many more still; then, together with me, you would number one hundred.” Let whoever can say how many doves were originally flying.

Concerning a purse.

[Col. 0672A] A certain man walking along a road found a purse containing two talents. Others who saw this said to him: “Brother, give us a share of your find.” He refused and would not give them anything. They then attacked him and seized the purse, and each took fifty solidi. Let whoever wishes say how many men there were.

Concerning a bishop.

A certain bishop ordered twelve loaves to be divided among the clergy. He gave this instruction: each presbyter was to receive two loaves, a deacon half a loaf, and a lector a quarter of a loaf, provided that the number of clerics and the number of loaves should be the same. Let whoever can say how many presbyters, how many deacons, and how many lectors there ought to be.

Concerning a man meeting schoolboys.

A certain man encountered schoolboys and said to them: “How many are you in the school?” One of them replied: “I do not wish to tell you this. Count us twice, multiply that by three, then divide it into four parts. The fourth part of us, if you add me to it, completes the number one hundred.” Let whoever wishes say how many those were whom the man previously encountered walking along the road. [Col. 0672B]

Concerning carpenters.

Seven carpenters made seven wheels. Let whoever wishes say how many carts they made.

Concerning wine in vessels.

There are one hundred *metretae* of wine. Let whoever wishes say how many *sextarii* they contain, or how many *meri* the one hundred *metretae* themselves contain.

Concerning a householder distributing.

A certain head of a household, when dying, divided among his four sons four vessels of wine: in the first vessel were 40 modii, in the second 30, in the third 20, and in the fourth 10. Calling the steward of his household, he said: “Divide these four vessels, with the wine in them, among my four sons, but in such a way that each receives an equal portion both of the wine and of the vessels.” Let whoever understands say how it should be divided so that all may receive an equal share from it.

[Col. 0672C] On the camel.

A certain head of a household had 30 leagues from one of his houses to another. He had a camel which, in three journeys from one house to the other, was to carry 90 modii of grain; and on each league the same camel always ate one modius. Let whoever is able say how many modii remained.

On the steward in a monastery.

A certain abbot had 12 monks. Calling the steward of his household, he gave him 204 eggs and ordered him to give each of them an equal share of all of them. Yet he ordered that among the 5 priests he should distribute 85 eggs, among the 4 deacons 68, and among the 3 others 51. Let whoever is able, I ask, say how many eggs fell to each of them as his portion, so that in no respect would the number be either excessive or deficient, but all, as we said above, would receive an equal share in everything.

[Col. 0671D] In one league there are 1,500 paces, 7,500 feet, and 90 ounces; as many ounces as there were days, making 246 years and 210 days.

Those first seen by him numbered 36; half of half of this number is 18, and half of this number is 9. Say it therefore as follows: 72 and 18 make 90; add 9, making 99; add the speaker, and you will have 100.

Another: 28 and 28, and a third time likewise, make 84; a third of the half makes 14; altogether there are 98. With two added, 100 appear.

Concerning the horses.

[Col. 0672D] There were 40 horses grazing; the others therefore make 80. If half of half of this—namely 20—is added, they make 100.

Concerning the hundred denarii.

Make 9 sows and 1 boar for 55 denarii, and 80 piglets for 40; behold, there are 90 pigs. With the remaining 5 denarii, make 10 piglets, and you will have the number 100 in both respects.

Concerning the common business.

At first there were 250 pigs, purchased for 100 solidi—as stated above, at the rate of 5 pigs for 2 solidi. For whether you say fifty times five or five times fifty, you count 250. When these had been divided, one took 125 and the other likewise 125. One sold the inferior pigs at 3 per solidus, while the other sold the better ones at 2 per solidus. Thus the one who sold the inferior pigs obtained 40 solidi from 120 pigs, while the one who sold the better pigs obtained 60 solidi: for 30 of the inferior pigs were sold for 10 solidi, and 20 of the better pigs for 10 solidi. Five pigs remained to each, from which they could make a profit of 4 solidi and 2 denarii.

Concerning the discus.

Gold weighs 9 ounces; silver weighs three times 9 ounces, that is, 2 pounds and 3 ounces; orichalcum weighs three times 2 pounds and three times 3 ounces, that is, 6 pounds and 9 ounces; tin weighs three times 6 pounds and three times 9 ounces, that is, 20 pounds and 3 ounces. When 9 ounces, 2 pounds with 3 ounces, 6 pounds with 9 ounces, and 20 pounds with 3 ounces are joined together, they make 30 pounds.

Again, in another reckoning, in solidi: gold weighs 15 silver solidi; silver three times 15, that is, 45; orichalcum three times 45, that is, 135; tin three times 135, that is, 405. Add 405, 135, 45, and 15, and you will find 600 solidi, which are 30 pounds.

Concerning the cup.

Through the first pipe 3,600 sextarii flowed; through the second, 1,400; through the third, 1,200.

Concerning the cloak.

Of 400, 80 are a fifth part; and of 100, 4. Therefore, whether you say eighty times five or one hundred times four, you will always find 400; that many cloaks there will be.

A tenth of sixty is 6, and a tenth of forty is 4. Therefore, whether you place a tenth of sixty or a tenth of forty ten times, you will find 100 portions, 6 cubits long and 4 cubits wide.

Concerning the bottles left behind.

There are therefore three sons and 30 bottles; of the bottles, 10 are full, 10 half-full, and 10 empty. Three times ten makes 30; each son receives 10 bottles as his share. Divide them by thirds: give the first son 10 half-full bottles; then give the second 5 full and 5 empty bottles; and similarly you will give them to the third. Thus there will be an equal division among the three brothers, both in the oil and in the glass.

[Col. 0674A] Concerning the tracks of oxen.

The ox makes no track at all in the last furrow, because it goes before the plow, and the plow follows it. For as many tracks as the ox makes by going before it in the cultivated ground, so many are erased by the plow following behind and tilling. Therefore none of its tracks is found at all—that is, no track in the last furrow.

Concerning the furrows made by a man.

From one end of the field there are three, and from the other there are [furrows], making seven turns of the furrows.

Concerning the ox led away.

The first man, who asked that two oxen be given to him, had 4; the one who was asked had 8. The man who was asked gave two to the petitioner, and each then had 6. The one who had received them from the nearer side returned 2 to the first giver, who had 6, and he then had 8, which is double 4; while the other had 4 remaining, which is half of 8.

[Col. 0674B] Concerning the sisters.

First of all, my sister and I entered the boat and crossed to the other side. After crossing the river, I put my sister off the boat and brought the boat back to the bank. Then the sisters of the two men—namely, those who had remained on the shore—entered. After those women had left the boat, my sister, who had crossed first, entered to me and brought the boat back. When she had gone out, the two brothers entered the boat and crossed to the other side. Then one of them, together with his sister, entered the boat and crossed over to us. My sister and I, while his sister remained outside, crossed over with the man who had been sailing. Once we had been carried to the bank, either one of those two women brought the boat back to the other side; my sister having been taken aboard with her, they crossed together to us. Then the man whose sister had remained on the other side entered the boat and brought her back across with him. By such careful and diligent maneuvering the crossing was accomplished, with no contamination of shameful intercourse.

[Col. 0674C] Concerning the wolf and the goat.

In similar fashion I would first take the goat across and leave the wolf and the cabbage outside. Then I would return, take the wolf across, and, leaving the wolf outside, take the goat aboard again and bring it back. Having put the goat ashore, I would carry the cabbage across, and then row back once more and take the goat across. By doing this, the crossing will have been safely completed, without the ravine of tearing apart.

Concerning the weight of the wagon.

In the same order as above, two children should first enter and cross, and one of them should bring the boat back. Then their mother should enter the boat and cross; afterward her son should bring the boat back. Once it had been brought across, his brother should enter the boat, and the two should cross together. Again, the son who had crossed earlier should enter the boat and bring it back to his brother. Once it had been brought back, both should enter and cross. By such skill in rowing the crossing will be completed, perhaps without shipwreck.

Another.

Similarly, two children should first cross, and one of them should bring back the boat. Their father, entering it, should cross to the other side. Then the one child who had previously crossed with his brother should bring the boat back to the bank; his brother, entering it again, should cross with him. One of them should go ashore, and the other should bring the boat back to his mother; she should enter that boat and cross to the other side. When she had gone ashore, her son, who had earlier crossed with his brother, should enter the boat again and bring it across to his brother. Both should enter it and cross, and the safe transportation would be completed, with no fear of the shipwreck of death.

Concerning a field and sheep.

This field is 200 feet long and 100 feet wide. Take twice five from 200, making 40; then divide 100 by 4—one-fourth of 100 is 25. Therefore, whether you multiply 40 by 25 or 25 by 40, they complete the number 1,000. Thus that many sheep can be placed there.

Concerning a sloping field.

The length of this field is 100 poles, and the width of each end is 50; its middle, however, contains 60. Add the number of the two ends to the middle, and they make 160. Take a third of this, that is, 53, and multiply by 100, making 5,300. Then divide into 12 equal parts, and 351 are found; divide these again into 12 parts, and 37 are found. That is the number of aripennia in this field.

Another.

The two lengths of this field make 62; take half of 62, making 31. The two widths of the same field, joined together, make 66; take half of 66, making 33. Multiply 33 by thirty-one, making 1,020. Divide twice by 12, as above: that is, divide 1,020 by 12, making 85; then divide 85 again by 12, making 7. Therefore the number of aripennia in this field is 7.

Another.

Add the two widths of this field; they make 60, and take half of 60, making 30. Since it has 18 feet at the front, take half of 18, making 9. Multiply 30 by 9, making 270. From this perform two divisions by 12: divide 270 by one-twelfth, making 22½; then divide 22½ by one-twelfth, making 2, with 4 remaining, which is one-third of 12. Therefore there are 2 aripennia in this field and three parts of an aripennis; this makes 1 aripennis and 10½ poles.

Another.

One-quarter of this field, which is enclosed by 400 poles, consists of 100. If you multiply these by themselves—that is, if you multiply them by 100—they make 10,000. You must divide these into 12 parts; one-twelfth of 10,000 is 833. When you have divided this again by 12, you will find 69. For that many aripennia this kind of field contains.

Concerning a field, a dog, and a hare.

The length of this field is 150 feet. Take half of 150, making 75. The dog, however, covered 9 feet in a single leap. Thus 75 multiplied by 9 makes 675: so many feet the dog ran in pursuit of the hare until he caught it with his tenacious teeth. But since the hare covered 7 feet in a single leap, multiply 75 by 7, making 526. So many feet the hare covered in fleeing before it was overtaken.

Concerning a rectangular city.

If the two lengths of this city are joined, they make 2,100; likewise, if the two widths are joined, they make 1,200. Take half of 1,200, therefore, making 600; again take half of 2,100, making 1,050. Since each house is 40 feet long and 30 feet wide, take one-fortieth of 1,050, making 26; then take one-thirtieth of 600, making 20. Multiply 26 by 20, therefore, making 520. That is the number of houses the city can contain.

The two sides of this city together make 200. Take half of 200, making 100. But since it has 90 feet at the front, take half of 90, making 45. Since the length of each house is 20 feet and its width 10 feet, take one-twentieth of 100, making 5; and one-tenth of 40 is 4. Multiply 4 by 5, therefore, making 20. That is the number of houses of this kind the city can contain.

Another.

The circuit of this city is reckoned as 8,000 feet, divided in a sesquialteral proportion into 4,800 and 3,200. In the former the length of the houses is represented, and in the latter their width. Subtract half from each total, therefore, and 2,400 remain from the greater and 1,600 from the lesser. Divide the 1,600 into units of twenty, and you find eighty times twenty; likewise divide the greater total, 2,400, by 30, and eighty times thirty are counted. Multiply 80 by 80, making 6,400. That many houses can be built in a city of this kind according to the proposition written above.

Concerning a basilica.

A length of 140 feet contains 126 bricks, and a width of 120 feet contains 120 bricks, since each brick has a width of one foot. Multiply 120 by 126, therefore, and the total becomes 1,512. That many bricks can touch the pavement in a basilica of this kind.

Concerning a cavana.

In 100 there are fourteen sevens, while in 64 there are sixteen fours. Of these, 4 are assigned to the passageway, which is said to extend along the length of the cavana. Since, therefore, in 60 there are fifteen fours, and in 100 fourteen sevens, multiply fifteen by ten, making 210. That many vats, according to the dimensions stated above, can be contained in a cavana of this kind.

Concerning the head of a household.

Multiply three by one, making 3: that is, one man received 3 modii. Likewise, five times two makes 10: that is, 5 women received 10 modii. Multiply seven by two, making 14: that is, 14 children received 7 modii. Add 1, 5, and 14, therefore, making 20; these are 20 members of the household. Then add 3, 7, and 10, making 20; these are 20 modii. Thus there are together 20 members of the household and 20 modii.

Another.

If you multiply 3 by 3, making 9, and multiply 2 by 5, making 10; then multiply 22 by one-half, making 11—that is, 3 men received 9 modii, 5 women received 10, and 22 children received 11 modii—the numbers 3, 5, and 22, joined together, make 30 members of the household. Again, 9, 11, and 10, joined together, make 30 modii. Since there are together 30 members of the household and 30 modii, the total is 36.

Joined together, 6, 20, and 64 make 90 members of the household; and again 18, 60, and 32 make 90 modii. Since these together make 90 members of the household and 90 modii, the total is 37.

Multiply 74 by one-half, making 37—that is, 11 men received 17 [the transmitted text is arithmetically inconsistent here; “17” may be an OCR error]. Joined together, 11, 15, and 74 make 100, which are 100 members of the household. Likewise, 33, 30, and 37 joined together make 100, which are 100 modii. Concerning purchased animals.

Add 9 and 3, making 12; for 12 ounces make a pound. Likewise add 7 and 5, again making 12. Therefore twice 12 makes 24; and 24 ounces make 2 pounds, that is, 40 solidi. Then multiply, because make, etc.
