[Col. 0677]

A SHORT TREATISE ON THE METHOD OF CALCULATION. (C)*

PREFACE.

[Col. 0677A] That unity from which the whole multitude of numbers proceeds, which properly belongs to the discipline of arithmetic, since it is truly simple and does not subsist through any gathering of parts, admits no division at all. As for other things, although something may be such that, because of its wholeness and solidity, it has deserved to be called by the name of unity, nevertheless whatever is composite must necessarily be subject to division. For in the whole nature of things, apart from the unity of numbers just mentioned, nothing can be found to be one that cannot in every respect be distributed by division. This happens because it subsists not through simplicity but through composition. Thus one says: one man, one horse, one day, one hour, one coin, one temple, and innumerable things of this kind. Although they have acquired the name of unity, they are nevertheless divided according to the requirements of circumstance and reason.

For the convenience of this division, the ancients devised the following method of calculation, so that every whole could be divided by it through a rational partition, whether the thing proposed for division were corporeal or incorporeal. In this method the unit is called an *as*, and its parts, according to their proportional relationships, have been defined by their proper names. Signs were also devised for this purpose, by which the same names might be expressed, so that through the distinction of the names and the signs attached to them the nature of each individual part might more easily be recognized.

[Col. 0678A] Concerning the *as* and its parts.

The *as*, which is expressed by the letter I, just as one is ordinarily written in numbers, has twelve parts. If you remove one of them, the remaining eleven parts are called *labus* [term uncertain]. The one you removed, namely the twelfth, is called an ounce.

If you remove two, the ten remaining are called a *dextans*, and what you removed—namely two—is called a *sextans*.

But if you remove three, the nine that remain are called a *dodrans*, and the three removed are called a *quadrans*.

If you wish to remove four, call the eight remaining a *bis* or *bes*, and the four a *triens*.

When five have been removed, it was agreed that the seven remaining should be called a *septunx*, and the five removed a *quincunx* or *quinqunce*.

When the division has been made through the middle, they called each half, consisting of six parts, a *semis*.

An ounce and a half they called a *sescuncia*, *sesquncia*, or *sesquiuncia*.

Finally, half an ounce they called a *semuncia*.

The remaining smaller fractions, whose accumulation makes up half an ounce—such as *sicilici*, *sextulae*, and the rest—are better understood by inspecting the calculation itself.

METHOD OF CALCULATION

[Col. 0677]

[Col. 0677C] This same calculation begins at one thousand and proceeds as far as fifty thousand.

First it grows by doubling, then by tripling, and thereafter by the remaining multiplications, increasing so greatly in number that the total of its quantity extends to infinity.

It is written in lines descending from the upper part to the lower. Above, the lines contain the totals of thousands arising from multiplication; below, they contain the small fractions of the divisions. Nevertheless, when reading, one must begin from these lower lines, and from there read upward until one reaches the sum of the thousands, which gradually increases from that multiplication.

One must begin with half a *sextula* and proceed by doubling up to II, that is, two thousand.

Then again, by tripling, from half a *sextula* up to III, that is, three thousand.

Then from half a *sextula* by quadrupling up to IIII, namely four thousand.

And so onward to the end.

[Col. 0678C] Concerning the consonance of numbers.

The final notes are *lichanos hypaton*, *hypate meson*, *parhypate meson*, and *lichanos meson* [the transmitted text reads *hircanos meson*]. Every mode and its subordinate—namely, the first and second—is governed and brought to its close by *lichanos hypaton*. The second and its subordinate—namely, the third and fourth—are governed and brought to their close by *hypate meson*. The third with its subordinate—namely, the fifth and sixth—is governed and brought to its close by *parhypate meson*. The fourth with its subordinate—namely, the seventh and eighth—is governed and brought to its close by *lichanos meson*. This is the rule for beginning in any mode: they must never begin above the fifth higher position or below the fifth lower position, but must confine their beginnings within those eight notes, or sometimes nine.

It should be noted, however, that between the higher and lower finals there is always, at the fifth position, a certain consonance of this kind, so that [the text breaks off: “etc.”; the remainder is lacking].

[Col. 0681]

A SHORT TREATISE ON THE DIVISION OF NUMBERS.

PREFACE.

To his Constantine.

[Col. 0681A]

The power of friendship turns almost impossible things into possible ones. For how could we have attempted to explain the principles of numbers on the abacus unless you, my sweet solace in labors, Constantine, had encouraged us? Accordingly, although several lustra have now passed since we possessed either a book or practice in these matters, we present some things recalled to memory in the same words, and some in the same sense. Nor should the unlettered philosopher think that these matters are contrary to any art or to himself. For what will he say about digits, place-values, and minutes, if he disdains to be the hearer of his elders? Yet he wishes to appear to know alone what he does not know with me, as Flaccus says. What of the fact that the same number is sometimes simple and sometimes composite, now a digit and now established as a place-value?

You therefore have, diligent investigator of such matters, a path of reasoning—brief in words but extensive in meaning—fully suited both to the collection of intervals and to their distribution in the actual operations of the geometrical ray according to inclination and elevation, and, in both theoretical and practical investigations, to the measurement of heaven and earth.

THE SHORT TREATISE BEGINS

[Col. 0681]

Concerning the simple number.

[Col. 0681B] If you multiply a single number by a single number, you assign to each digit a single number and to every place-value ten, directly and conversely.

If you multiply a single number by a ten, you assign ten to each digit and one hundred to every place-value.

If you multiply a single number by a hundred, you assign one hundred to each digit and one thousand to the place-value.

If you multiply a single number by a thousand, you assign one thousand to the digit and ten thousand to the place-value.

If you multiply a single number by ten thousand, you assign ten thousand to the digit and one hundred thousand to the place-value.

If you multiply a single number by one hundred thousand, you assign one hundred thousand to the digit and one million to the place-value.

Concerning the ten.

If you multiply ten by ten, you assign one hundred to the digit and one thousand to the place-value.

If you multiply ten by one hundred, you assign one thousand to the digit and ten thousand to the place-value.

[Col. 0681C] If you multiply ten by one thousand, you assign ten thousand to the digit and one hundred thousand to the place-value.

If you multiply ten by ten thousand, you assign one hundred thousand to the digit and one million to the place-value.

If you multiply ten by one hundred thousand, you assign one million to the digit and also ten million to each place-value.

Concerning the hundred.

If you multiply one hundred by one hundred, you assign ten thousand to the digit and one hundred thousand to the place-value.

If you multiply one hundred by one thousand, you assign one hundred thousand to the digit and one million to the place-value.

If you multiply one hundred by ten thousand, you assign one million to the digit and ten million to the place-value.

If you multiply one hundred by one hundred thousand, you assign ten million to the digit and one hundred million to the place-value.

Concerning the thousand.

If you multiply one thousand by one thousand, you assign one million to the digit and one billion to the place-value.

[Col. 0681D] If you multiply one thousand by ten thousand, you assign ten million to the digit and one hundred million to the place-value.

If you multiply one thousand by one hundred thousand, you assign one hundred million to the digit and one hundred billion to the place-value.

Concerning ten thousand.

If you multiply ten thousand by ten thousand, you assign one hundred million to the digit and *millios mille millia* [an uncertain transmitted numerical term] to the place-value.

If you multiply ten thousand by one hundred thousand, you assign one billion to the digit and ten billion to the place-value.

Concerning one hundred thousand.

[Col. 0682A]

[Col. 0682B] If you multiply one hundred thousand by one hundred thousand, you assign ten billion to the digit and one hundred billion to the place-value.

How a single number is divided by a single number, or a hundred by a hundred, or a thousand by a thousand.

In the division of numbers on the abacus, just as single numbers relate to single numbers, so in a certain way tens relate to tens, hundreds to hundreds, and thousands to thousands, as follows:

If you wish to divide single numbers by single numbers, or tens by tens, or hundreds by hundreds, or thousands by thousands, you subtract the single numbers from the single numbers according to their designation.

How single numbers measure tens, hundreds, and thousands according to their quantity.

In the division of numbers on the abacus, just as single numbers relate to tens, hundreds, and thousands, so tens relate to hundreds and thousands, hundreds to thousands, and thousands to the higher composite tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands, as follows:

If you wish to divide a ten, a hundred, or a thousand by a single number, whether continuously or with interruptions, you multiply the difference between the divisor’s single place and its ten-place by the full denomination of the dividend. You reduce the place-values according to their proper denomination and the stated difference, but add the digits to the digits. If place-values result as above, reduce them until only digits remain. A thousand has place-values in the thousands, digits in the hundreds, and digits in the tens; a ten has place-values in the tens and digits in the units.

How a ten measures a hundred or a thousand, or a hundred thousand, or a thousand and higher numbers.

If you wish to divide a hundred or a thousand by a ten, or a hundred thousand or higher numbers by a hundred, or subsequent numbers by a thousand, you multiply the difference of the divisor—as a single number is related to a ten—by the full denomination of the dividend. That is, using the terms for single numbers, you reduce the ten place-values and digits to the final divisor, just as happens when single numbers divide any number.

How all the single numbers, by tens, measure tens, hundreds, thousands, either continuously or with interruptions.

If you wish to divide by a number composed of a ten and a single number, or by a simple ten or a number composed with a single number, consider what portion of the divisor the single number occupies. For the second single number has a relation to the second places of the dividend, the third to the third, the fourth to the fourth, the fifth to the fifth, and so on. That is, the difference between the divisor’s single place and its ten-place is multiplied by the denomination of the second, third, fourth, or fifth place. Whatever exceeds the second, third, fourth, or fifth places, you add together; and if they are more numerous than the divisor, they are reduced by the same rule. Likewise, composite single numbers are added to the dividend. You will do the same with hundreds and thousands, except that you distribute one hundred or one thousand among the others—a thing that does not occur with one ten—and the place-values are taken from one hundred or one thousand, while they obtain their positions from several dividends.

Another division of a hundred or a thousand, and thereafter, by the same divisors.

If you wish to divide a hundred or a thousand, and thereafter, by a composite number consisting of a ten and a single number, first divide the hundred as above, taking the difference between the divisor’s single place and its ten-place. Multiply what remains by the denomination of the proposed hundred. If a single number is added to the hundred to form a composite number, or if a ten is combined with a single number, reduce or add as stated above in the tens and units. The first place-values are in the sum nearest to and smaller than the dividends; when increased, they occupy the positions of the other dividends.

How tens joined to hundreds, or hundreds to thousands, measure hundreds, thousands, or higher numbers.

If you wish to divide by a composite number consisting of a hundred and a ten, or by a composite number consisting of a thousand and a hundred, whether a hundred or a thousand, consider what portion of the divisor is represented by five hundred, one hundred, or one thousand, and multiply the divisor’s difference by the denomination of those parts, as you did with single numbers joined to tens.

Another division of a hundred or a thousand, and thereafter, by the same composite and simple divisors.

[Col. 0683C]

If you wish to divide a hundred or a thousand by a ten, or a thousand by a hundred, take the divisor’s difference according to the relation of single numbers to tens, and multiply it. Do this either by the entire denomination of the dividend, if the divisor is a simple ten or hundred, or by the second, third, fourth, or fifth places if the divisor is composite, taking account of what part of the composite divisor is occupied by the ten or hundred.

How two joined extremes, with one middle number omitted, measure the others.

If you wish to divide a hundred or a thousand by a composite hundred or thousand, with one intervening place omitted, take one of the dividends for composing the fractions and compare the greatest divisor with the remaining part. If anything is in excess, set it aside among the remainders. Multiply the fraction by the denomination through which the divisor is made equal to the dividend. In the digits the complete difference is placed. Before the place-values, however, there is another difference, one less, having, as it were, a relation to the adjacent places when there are digits and place-values. A place-value alone, that is, without digits, presents its full difference. A digit alone supposes the full difference; and when the digit stands alone, the full difference is taken from the one set aside for composing the fractions. These differences, and any quantity perhaps set aside from the greatest divisor, indicate what remains from the dividends.

How a hundred with a single number measures a thousand and higher numbers, or a thousand with tens measures tens of thousands and higher numbers.

[Col. 0684A]

If you wish to divide a thousand or higher numbers by a composite number consisting of a hundred and a single number, distribute one thousand among hundreds. Again, set aside one hundred for composing the fractions, and compare the greatest divisor with the remaining part. If anything is set aside, place it among the remainders. Multiply the fraction as in the preceding chapter, and arrange all the remaining quantities, whether those set aside or those used as differences. Again multiply the same differences, and any quantities that may have been set aside, by the denomination of the proposed dividend. Once more, follow the same rule down to the final differences. With thousand-divisors combined with tens, and with tens of thousands and higher numbers, preserve essentially the same method.

How many divisors there are in each dividend.

[Col. 0684B]

If you wish to know how many divisors there are in each dividend, take the place-values from which the denominations of the multiplication arise and apply them to the digits. If place-values result from their increase, return them to the place-values. If they result in equal divisors among the single numbers, add the same number of units to the totals. Thus, in the denominations derived from the whole and from the parts—namely, from the second, third, fourth places, and so on—establish one unit for the final divisor according to the same rule.

And just as, in hundreds and thousands, whatever exceeds one is multiplied by the denomination of the whole sum, so the divisors are multiplied by the denomination of the entire dividend. But in hundreds and thousands alone, a simple ten-divisor of a hundred or a thousand, and the denominations of still higher composites, sends the calculation to the third place: that is, to the third place from the one being divided, in the collection of divisors. A hundred or a thousand, its divisors, and its composites, leaving one place, send their denominations to the outermost digits.

[Col. 0684C] Concerning the extension of certain measurements of land.

The digit is the smallest part of agrarian measures.

An ounce contains three digits.

The palm extends to four digits.

Sixteen digits measure a foot.

A pace has the measure of five feet.

A pole extends to two paces, that is, ten feet.

One hundred and twenty-five paces complete a stadium.

Eight stadia make a mile.

One thousand paces—that is, one and a half miles—make a league, containing 1,500 paces.

Two leagues, or three miles, make a *resta*.

Some read *leucam* for *leuvam*.

The circuit of the whole earth is completed by 252,000 stadia, which make twenty-one Gallic *leuvae*, when those same stadia are divided by twelve; thirty-one miles and five hundred, when those same stadia are divided by fifty. Thirty-one thousand paces and 500 feet result when those same stadia are multiplied by 125; 157 thousand miles and 500 ounces when multiplied by five; 1,800 feet, ninety thousand million, when multiplied by twelve, one million. Digits: five thousand, six hundred and seventy-one thousand; ounces multiplied by three.

[II LIBELLI.]

[Col. 0685]

NOTICE OF THE EDITOR OF THE *PATROLOGIA* CONCERNING THE TWO FOLLOWING SHORT TREATISES.

The following short treatises could already be read above, in chapters one and four of the book *On the Reckoning of Time*. By what authority we assigned these passages to that work was stated in the notice prefixed to the aforementioned book. The reason why we now repeat them must be explained here briefly.

As we were about to publish both treatises, two readings—quite different from one another—presented themselves above all others. The first was the one transmitted by the older editions, enriched with the commentaries of Bridefert and John of Nijmegen; the second was brought forth by Dr. Giles from a collation of numerous manuscripts. We judged it expedient to reprint the latter; but, lest the reader be deprived of the commentaries to which we have alluded, we have also taken care to reproduce them, together with the booklets themselves, in full.

[Col. 0685]

## BOOKLET ON SPEECH BY THE GESTURES OF THE FINGERS AND ON THE COMPUTATION OF TIME

### LETTER OF A CERTAIN LEARNED MAN TO THE READER CONCERNING THE SAME BOOK

[Col. 0685]

[Col. 0685A] Since perhaps, just as a certain new method of computation handed down by the most learned Bede may seem to you a novelty, so something of lesser importance may also easily appear unworthy of you, a man of the highest dignity, I decided that it would be worthwhile to set before you certain testimonies both Greek and Latin, by which you may perceive that this method of counting was in use not only among our own people—and among those older than Bede and Jerome—but even among the Greeks themselves. I therefore confidently hope that our offering will prove as welcome to you as anything could be. Let us now first hear that famous Chaeronean, Plutarch, giving his testimony in Greek.

**Plutarch, near the beginning of the *Apophthegms of Kings and Emperors***

> Orontes, the son-in-law of King Artaxerxes, having fallen into disgrace through anger and having been condemned, said that, just as the fingers of reckoners can now indicate a myriad and now a unit, so also the friends of kings can at one time possess everything and at another the least possible.

[Col. 0685B] That is: Orontes, the son-in-law of King Artaxerxes, when he lay dishonored and condemned on account of the king’s anger, said: “Just as the fingers of reckoners can signify now ten thousand, now one, so likewise the friends of kings can sometimes do everything, sometimes the very least.”

**Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book I**

Hence his likeness is generally represented holding the number 300 in the right hand and 65 in the left, to indicate the measure of the year.

**Pliny, *Natural History*, Book XXXIV, chapter 7**

Janus with two faces, dedicated by King Numa and worshiped as an emblem of peace and war, was represented with his fingers formed in such a way that [Col. 0686A] by signifying 355 days, he might indicate himself to be a god of the year, of time, and of eternity.

But, incidentally correcting both authors, 55 is more correctly written in Pliny than 65 in Macrobius. For surely what measure of the year could a statue established by Numa have represented? Or in what way could it then have indicated a reckoning of the year that Gaius Caesar, as chief pontiff, would establish only many years later? Those two words in Pliny, “by signifying,” should moreover be rejected as interpolated.

**Apuleius, *Apology* 2**

If you had said thirty years instead of ten, you might seem to have erred in the gesture used for counting, since you ought to have opened your curled fingers. But when you add half again to forty—the number more easily signified than the others by an outstretched palm—you cannot have made a mistake in the gesture of the fingers, unless perhaps, reckoning the thirty years of Pudentilla, you counted the consuls of each year in pairs.

[Col. 0686B] **Quintilian, *Institutio Oratoria*, Book I**

Since geometry is divided into numbers and figures, knowledge of numbers is necessary not only to an orator but to anyone at least educated in the elementary arts. In legal cases it is very frequently relevant; and if an advocate hesitates over totals—not to mention if, merely through an uncertain or unbecoming gesture of the fingers, he disagrees with the computation—he is judged unlearned.

**Juvenal, Satire 10**

But why say more about something beyond doubt? As though, excellent reader, I did not already seem to see you playing with your fingers in such a way as to provoke laughter.

## HERE BEGINS THE PREFACE

[Col. 0685] [Note: [Col. 0685C] **BRIDEFERT OF RAMSEY’S GLOSS.**—*Preface*: that is, a preliminary address. *Begins*: this is a compound word, made from an intact and a corrupted element: *in* is the intact part, and *capio* the corrupted one, for *a* is changed into *i* and shortened. *Incipit* means “it begins,” “takes its beginning,” or “takes its origin.” Some say, however, that it is composed of the preposition *in* and the defective verb *coepi*, which has only a past tense, is written with *ae*, and signifies beginning or initiation. Hence we also read: “David began the stronghold of Zion.”]

Formerly I composed two brief booklets, in concise language, on the nature of things and the reckoning of time. Now, intending—with the Lord’s help—to speak at greater length about the reckoning of time, I have judged it necessary first to demonstrate briefly the most useful, [Col. 0686C] and most readily learned skill of bending the fingers, so that, after providing the greatest ease in computation, we may then approach the investigation and clarification of the sequence of time with the readers’ minds better prepared. Nor should this rule be despised or considered of little worth, since nearly all the sacred interpreters of Scripture are shown to have embraced it no less than the forms of letters.

[Note: [Col. 0686C] **GLOSS.**—“On the nature of things,” and so forth. When he said *On the nature of things*, it should not be passed over why he did not also say *On the Nature of Time*, or *On the reckoning of things and the reckoning of time*. To discuss the nature of things is one matter, and to discuss their reckoning another. The nature of things is the very spiritual or corporeal substance of creatures together with their proper qualities. But first one must inquire into the nature of time, so that its reckoning may readily become apparent; for in this passage *reckoning* is not used for *nature*.

The nature of time, therefore, is the motion of mutable things. But since that motion itself is ordered, does not exceed the natural numbers, and was created by God, creation too is ordered. It can be the proper substance of one set of creatures and the quality of other creatures—that is, ordered mutability. Since the motion itself, which is the substance of time, has natural divisions and the fixed, hidden intervals of duration, when something is discussed concerning those divisions or intervals, it is called the reckoning of time.

The author of this book did not therefore discuss the motions of things, but composed a booklet concerning the divisions and fixed intervals of temporal movements. The whole text of this book is completed in the state, course, and end of time. The first part—that is, from the beginning up to the *Chronicles*—contains the state, meaning the natural course, of time. The middle part, namely what is contained in the *Chronicles*, sets forth the course of time, that is, what happened within it. The final part declares the end of time, namely the remainder of the sixth age and the day of judgment.

For although time always seems to be in motion, it nevertheless returns to the state from which it begins. No motion can ever take place which did not at some point begin from a state of rest. As the courses of time glide onward, God will impose an end whenever he wills.

Here one must note that, if the statement means that time itself is to be ended, the question is difficult. Time, created and ordered by God, is a substance. How, then, will a created substance fail—unless perhaps the heavenly signs by whose motions time is produced will become fixed and cease to move? Yet they cannot as yet believe this. For if the heavenly signs continue always to move, time necessarily cannot have an end.

If, however, by “the courses of time gliding onward” he means what takes place in time—human affairs, human beings being born, growing, declining, and dying, and likewise the other animals, trees, and vegetables failing and being renewed—the question is easy. All these things will have an end within the courses of time.

Or the statement must certainly be understood in this way: all time, and all that takes place within it, will have an end; but the things that take place in time will end in such a way that they will no longer exist at all, whereas time itself will end not because its natural intervals cease, but because it will no longer be perceived as running. For when eternity itself appears to the highest human beings, where nothing passes away and nothing is to come, but everything is always the same, then whatever of time flows past is not perceived—just as, when we rest in sleep, we do not perceive the intervals passing by. Hence the Prophet says: “One day in your courts is better than thousands.” And elsewhere: “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house.” For under the name of intoxication the forgetfulness of all mutable things is understood.

But concerning all these matters I bring forward the complete purity of the Hebrew truth, which the most eminent of teachers—Jerome in his books of *Hebrew Questions*, Augustine in his book *The City of God*, and Eusebius himself, the chronicler, in the third book of his *Ecclesiastical History*, and others—[Col. 0687D] have presented.

In the book of *Hebrew Questions* blessed Jerome says:

> It should be known that, up to the Flood, where in our copies someone is said to have begotten a son at 200 years and more, the Hebrew text has 100 years, followed by the remaining years.

And shortly afterward:

> There is a famous question, debated throughout all the churches: according to careful computation, Methuselah is said to have lived fourteen years after the Flood. How, then, is it true that only eight persons were saved in the ark? It remains, therefore, that here too, as in many other places, there is an error in the number.

Again, above, in Book XV of *The City of God*, blessed Augustine says:

> Therefore that diversity of numbers, which are different in the Greek and Latin manuscripts and different again in the Hebrew—where there is no such uniformity continued through so many generations, with one hundred years first added and afterward subtracted—should be attributed neither to the malice of the Jews nor to the diligence or prudence of the Seventy translators, but to the error of the copyist who first received for transcription from King Ptolemy’s library the manuscript from which it was copied. There too, of course, a copyist’s error could have occurred.

Again, in the same book he says:

> For from Adam up to the Flood there are counted, according to our manuscripts, 2,262 years, but according to the Hebrews 1,656.

Again, in Book XVI, chapter 10, blessed Augustine says:

> Thus from the Flood to Abraham there are 1,072 years, according to the commonly received edition of the Seventy translators. But in the Hebrew manuscripts far fewer years are reported to be found. They give either no explanation or a very difficult one, saying that the text had previously been written by several people in a different style—that is, with a different pronunciation, not a different faith, meaning not a different understanding.

Augustine uses this testimony against those who, unable to understand the meaning of his words, said that Augustine had written incorrectly about these questions, whereas other writers had written correctly about them—that is, that one and the same meaning is understood more easily from the words of the other writers than from Augustine’s writings.

He therefore urges them to leave their writings to those who are able to understand them and to return to those from whom they can more easily derive the meaning. For this reason it is necessary for several books to be composed by several authors, differing only in wording but having one and the same meaning, so that whatever is not understood in one author may be understood more easily in another.

For example, Jerome and Augustine held one and the same view concerning one and the same question; but from Augustine’s words I understand what I did not understand from Jerome’s. You, on the other hand, understand Jerome’s meaning where you did not understand Augustine’s.]

[Note: [Col. 0688B]

**SCHOLION OF JOHN OF NIJMEGEN.**—“Intending, with the Lord’s help, to speak about the reckoning of time, we judged it necessary first to demonstrate briefly the most useful and most readily learned skill of bending the fingers.”

Bede indicates that the notation of numbers, made by various gestures of the fingers, is necessary for computations of time. Since the solar and lunar cycles, on which this reckoning of time depends, are worked out in large numbers—numbers which it would be cumbersome to mark with written numerical signs, and whose long sequence it would be difficult to grasp—it is most convenient to have an easy method by which any number may be expressed through the bending of the fingers. Human beings, prompted by nature, seem to have done this first because the fingers are suited to counting.

Since each hand has five fingers, from which the number ten is formed, this number was made perfect, complete, and supreme according to the capacity of the fingers. For beyond ten, proceeding continuously, every nation represents the lesser numbers by repetition. This occurs not only in vocal counting: when we have said ten and proceed further, we do not use a simple word but, repeating one, say eleven—that is, ten and one. The same thing occurs in written signs: ten, and then the sign of the unit repeated, X and I, which together are eleven.

The arithmeticians call every number below ten a *digit*, such as I, II, III, and so forth. Each of these is expressed by one of the fingers: I by the thumb of the left hand, II by its index finger, VI by the right thumb, and so on up to ten.

They also call “articles” those numerical signs that can be divided into ten equal parts, such as X, XX, XXX, XL. These are expressed by the joints of the fingers. Thus the first ten, when counted in natural order, is placed on the upper joint of the thumb, and the second on the lower joint.

This, however, is the very common method of counting, familiar to children. I have included it so that I might indicate to children what the origin of “digits” and “articles” is among arithmeticians.

There is another method of marking numbers, drawn on a board by means of parallel lines, with counters placed upon them. This method too is ancient and has not fallen out of use, except that nowadays coins are used in place of counters. It has been and still is used in commercial forms of counting.

The method still used through Arabic signs—namely 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 0, which they call *ciphers*—appears to be recent and unknown to the ancient Romans and other nations, for no monuments of antiquity bear these little signs engraved upon them.

But I return to Bede. Finally, there is a learned and ingenious method of counting with the fingers, different from these, which Bede teaches here. Several arguments establish that the ancients used it, but through human carelessness and negligence it has fallen out of use.

That it is ancient is apparent from Book XXIV, chapter 7, of Pliny’s *Natural History*, where he says that Janus, dedicated by Numa Pompilius, was represented with his fingers formed so as to show himself a god by signifying 335 days, the annual measure of time and eternity. Marcus Tullius Cicero also repeatedly makes fun of Hortensius’ subtle distribution of action among the fingers.

It is likewise recorded in the history of Artaxerxes that Orontes, the king’s son-in-law, when he had been reduced to an inferior rank by a certain indignation on the part of his father-in-law, used to say that the dispositions of princes seemed very similar to the fingers of arithmeticians. For just as, in counting, they now produce a myriad by the gesture of the fingers and now a unit, so those who depend entirely upon kings are sometimes extremely powerful and sometimes, having fallen from that degree of honor to the lowest, are objects of universal mockery.

Caelius, in his *Ancient Readings*, thinks that the following passage of Fabius in the *Oratorical Institutes* should be referred to the same matter:

> If an advocate—not to mention if he hesitates over totals, but if merely by an unskilled or unbecoming gesture of the fingers he disagrees with the computation—he is judged unlearned.

In this passage, however, Quintilian appears to be referring to the common computation discussed above; the same may be said of Hortensius. For an orator acts before the people, who would often not understand these subtleties.

Elsewhere, however, I find him speaking more clearly about this computation, in Book XI, *On the Formation of Gesture*, where he says:

> For I have not seen, even among rustic people, the gesture of someone asking for a cup, threatening blows, or producing the number five hundred by a bent thumb, although these gestures have been censured by certain writers.

Here he plainly understands this method of counting. The number five hundred is produced—as you also learn here from Bede—with the thumb of the right hand bent toward the palm in the form of the Greek letter Γ, a gesture that would be used in speaking. Some read “fifty,” perhaps because they do not understand the passage; for fifty is expressed by the left hand, but that hand alone does not make the gesture.

There is also a passage in Apuleius, in the second *Defense of Magic*, which cannot be understood without this part of the counting system. The following is also well known:

> “…and now his right hand counts his years,”

said of Nestor, who reached the age of one hundred. One hundred, two hundred, and three hundred are counted on the right hand just as one, two, and three are counted on the left.

Nichardus wittily plays upon an old woman who lived far too long and who, in years, would even surpass the stags:

> An old woman, having outlived a deer,  
> Began to count her old age for a second time on her left hand.

Knowledge of this method of computation is therefore necessary for understanding many things in the ancient writers. For this reason I have treated it at greater length, lest what at first sight does not flatter the reader should immediately be judged frivolous.

Before this book of Bede was published, this method was unknown. In my opinion, this is the only part of antiquity preserved through him; whatever there is of it, therefore, you owe entirely to Bede. Children also have in this matter a not unpleasant exercise for the fingers, for the graceful extension and bending of the fingers also belongs to *cheironomia* (χειρονομία), the art of gesturing with the hands.

“Then with the readers’ minds better prepared.” For chapter 55, which concerns the recurrence of the solar and lunar cycles, is worked out by the numerical method performed through the bending of the fingers.]

Many others besides these, and Jerome himself, the interpreter of sacred history, did not hesitate to employ this aid of the discipline in his exposition of the Gospel passage:

> “The hundredfold, the sixtyfold, and the thirtyfold fruit, although they arise from one soil and from one seed, nevertheless differ greatly in number. Thirty refers to marriage; for the joining of the fingers themselves, embracing and binding one another like a gentle kiss, depicts husband and wife. Sixty refers to widows, because they are placed in hardship and tribulation; hence it is also pressed down upon the upper finger. And the greater the difficulty of abstaining from the enticements of pleasures once experienced, the greater also is the reward.”

[Note: [Col. 0690B] **BRIDEFERT OF RAMSEY’S GLOSS.**—“Many others besides these, and Jerome himself, the interpreter of sacred history, did not hesitate to employ this aid of the discipline in his exposition of the Gospel passage.”

In the thirteenth chapter of Matthew’s Gospel it is written: “But the seed sown on good soil is the one who hears the word, understands it, and bears fruit, producing in one case a hundredfold, in another sixtyfold, and in another thirtyfold.” Blessed Jerome says, in chapter 35 of his commentary on Matthew:

> We must first hear, then understand, and after understanding return the fruits of our teaching: producing either a hundredfold, a sixtyfold, or a thirtyfold fruit.

We spoke more fully of these matters in the book *Against Jovinianus*, and will now touch upon them briefly, assigning the hundredfold fruit to virgins, the sixtyfold to widows and those practicing continence, and the thirtyfold to holy marriage.]

[Col. 0690C] The hundredfold number, then—please attend carefully, reader—is transferred from the left hand to the right, with the same fingers but not the same hand. The same fingers by which married women and widows are signified on the left hand, when made into a circle, express the crown of virginity.

[Note: [Col. 0690C]

**SCHOLION OF JOHN OF NIJMEGEN.**—“And Jerome himself, the interpreter of sacred history.” In Matthew, chapter 13, there is a passage about a farmer who went out to sow. In this passage our Savior establishes three degrees of difference among fruitful soils: from the first he gathered a twentyfold fruit, from the second a sixtyfold, and from the third a hundredfold.

In this parable, Saint Jerome, in Book I of *Against Jovinianus*, refers the greatest number to virgins, the next to widows, and the smallest to marriage. He derives this confirmation from the gesture of the fingers—a festive rather than necessary confirmation—which Bede has explained elegantly here.

Erasmus explained this passage through conjectures, yet in such a way that he did not depart from the truth; at that time he had not yet encountered Bede’s book. Later, however, when he happened to find it somewhere, he treated the matter from the author himself.

Three fingers of the hand are called the little finger, the middle finger, and the “shameless” finger; the other two are the index finger and the thumb.]

## HERE BEGINS THE BOOKLET

[Col. 0689]

First, indication is made on the left hand, in the following manner.

[Col. 0689D] When you say “one,” bend the smallest finger of the left hand and press it into the middle joint of the palm.

When you say “two,” place the second finger from the smallest, bent in the same way, in the same place.

When you say “three,” bend the third finger in the same manner.

[Col. 0690D] When you say “four,” raise the smallest finger in the same way.

When you say “five,” raise the second from the smallest in the same way.

When you say “six,” raise the third as well, leaving only the middle one, called the medical finger, fixed in the center of the palm.

When you say “seven,” place only the smallest finger—while the others remain raised—over the base of the palm. Likewise:

When you say “eight,” [place] the middle finger.

When you say “nine,” arrange the “shameless” finger opposite it.

When you say “ten,” fix the nail of the index finger in the middle joint of the thumb.

When you say “twenty,” insert the tip of the thumb between the middle joints of the index and “shameless” fingers.

When you say “thirty,” join the nails of the index finger and thumb in a gentle embrace.

When you say “forty,” place the inner side of the thumb against the side or back of the index finger, with only those two fingers raised.

When you say “fifty,” bend the thumb at its outer joint in the form of the Greek letter Γ and incline it toward the palm.

[Col. 0691B] When you say “sixty,” carefully encircle the bent thumb, as above, with the bent index finger, enclosing it from the front.

When you say “seventy,” fill the bent index finger, as above, by inserting the thumb into it, with only the thumb’s nail raised across the middle joint of the index finger.

When you say “eighty,” fill the bent index finger, as above, with the thumb extended lengthwise, inserting its nail into the middle joint of the index finger.

When you say “ninety,” press the nail of the bent index finger into the base of the thumb.

Thus far for the left, or sinister, hand.

Second, indication is made on the right hand as follows:

One hundred on the right hand is made as ten on the left.

Two hundred on the right as twenty on the left.

[Col. 0691C] Three hundred on the right as thirty on the left.

Four hundred on the right as forty on the left.

Five hundred on the right as fifty on the left.

Six hundred on the right as sixty on the left.

Seven hundred on the right as seventy on the left.

Eight hundred on the right as eighty on the left.

Nine hundred on the right as ninety on the left.

Likewise, one thousand on the right as one on the left.

Two thousand on the right as two on the left.

[Col. 0691D] Three thousand on the right as three on the left.

Four thousand on the right as four on the left.

Five thousand on the right as five on the left.

Six thousand on the right as six on the left.

Seven thousand on the right as seven on the left.

Eight thousand on the right as eight on the left.

Nine thousand on the right as nine on the left.

For the remaining part of the body, indication is first made with the left hand.

When you say “ten thousand,” place the left hand supine at the middle of the chest, with only the fingers raised toward the neck.

When you say “twenty thousand,” spread the same hand widely across the chest.

When you say “thirty thousand,” place the same hand prone but raised, inserting the thumb into the cartilage at the center of the chest.

When you say “forty thousand,” turn the same hand supine while holding it raised at the navel.

When you say “fifty thousand,” place the thumb of the same hand—that is, the left—prone but raised, on the navel.

When you say “sixty thousand,” grasp the left thigh from above with the same hand, prone.

When you say “seventy thousand,” place the same hand supine upon the thigh.

When you say “eighty thousand,” place the same hand prone upon the thigh.

When you say “ninety thousand,” grasp the loins with the same hand, turning the thumb toward the groin.

Thus far for the left hand; now proceed to the right.

[Col. 0692B] When you say “one hundred thousand,” place the right hand supine at the middle of the chest, with the fingers raised toward the neck.

When you say “two hundred thousand,” spread the same hand widely across the chest.

When you say “three hundred thousand,” place the same hand prone but raised, inserting the thumb into the cartilage at the center of the chest.

When you say “four hundred thousand,” turn the same hand supine while holding it raised at the navel.

When you say “five hundred thousand,” make the gesture with the right hand as for fifty thousand with the left.

[Col. 0692C] When you say “six hundred thousand,” make the gesture with the right hand as for sixty thousand with the left.

When you say “seven hundred thousand,” make the gesture with the right hand as for seventy thousand with the left.

When you say “eight hundred thousand,” make the gesture with the right hand as for eighty thousand with the left.

When you say “nine hundred thousand,” make the gesture with the right hand as for ninety thousand with the left.

When you say “hundred thousands” (that is, a hundred times a hundred, called a *million* by modern writers), you will interlock both hands, inserting the fingers of one into the other.

[Note: [Col. 0692C]

**BRIDEFERT’S GLOSS.**—Here are contained the six complete orders of numbers within the entire method of indication by the fingers.

The first order is that of units.

The second is that of tens.

[Col. 0692D] The third is that of hundreds.

The fourth is that of thousands.

The fifth is that of tens of thousands.

The sixth, and last, is that of hundreds of thousands.

Isidore, in Book XI of the *Etymologies*: “Fingers” are so called either because there are ten of them or because ten joined together exist. For they contain within themselves a complete number and a most fitting order.

The first is called the thumb because it excels the others in strength and power.

The second is called the index, the salutary finger, or the demonstrative finger, because we generally greet or point with it.

The third is called the shameless finger because physicians commonly touch putrefying wounds with it.

The fourth is called the ring finger because a ring is worn on it. It is also called the medicinal finger because physicians use it to gather ground ointments.

[Col. 0693A] The fifth is called the little finger because with it we scratch the ear.

[Col. 0693B] Although the thumb is shorter than the others, it nevertheless excels the others in strength.

The index finger was once also called the saluting and demonstrative finger.

The thumb and index finger of the right hand represent numbers from one hundred through nine hundred.

The other three fingers of the same right hand represent numbers from one thousand through nine thousand.

The left hand will contain numbers through the measured joints of the body, and the right through the joints and arrangements of the limbs.

Thus you have a demonstration of all numbers through characters, or through the bending of the fingers.]

[Note: [Col. 0693C]

**OTHER GLOSSES OF BRIDEFERT.**—“When you say ‘one,’ bend the smallest finger of the left hand and press it into the middle joint of the palm.”

In Book XI of *The City of God*, blessed Augustine says:

> The principle of number should not be despised; for, to those who examine carefully, its great importance is evident in many passages of the holy Scriptures. Nor was it without reason that it was said in praise of God: “You have ordered all things by measure, number, and weight.”

And Eucherius, a most learned man, recalls:

> This number, which is one, refers to the unity of God, as it is written in the Book of Exodus: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one.”

Two refers to the two Testaments. In the Books of Kings: “And he made in the Debir two cherubim, ten cubits in size.”

Three refers to the Holy Trinity. In the Letter of John: “There are three who bear witness: the Spirit, the water, and the blood.”

[Col. 0693D] Four refers to the four Gospels. In Ezekiel: “And from the midst of them came the likeness of four living creatures”; and John, in his Apocalypse: “Four living creatures before the throne of God, full of eyes before and behind.”

Again: the number four is perfect, and when divided into its parts it possesses perfection. For it is divided into one, two, and three. One belongs to God, because there is one God, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all, through all, and in us all. Two refers to the twofold commandment of love or, as was said above, to the two Testaments. Three refers to the holy and indivisible Trinity, namely the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Four refers to the grace of the New Testament or to the four books of the holy Gospel, to which it is especially attributed.

Because a square stone does not waver but lies equally whichever way it is turned, the stability of the saints is rightly signified by the number four: they are not carried about by every wind of doctrine, but, like firm stones, whether in prosperity or adversity, they persevere most steadfastly in good works and faith, considering the saying: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved.”

Five refers to the five books of Moses. Paul says: “In the church I would rather speak five words with my understanding.”

Six refers to the sixth day, on which the Lord made humanity together with all living creatures. In Genesis: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” And: “There was evening and morning, the sixth day.”

Again, blessed Gregory says in Homily 17 on Ezekiel:

> We have often said that the number six signifies the perfection of a good work. We do not follow those who have tried to establish that the number six is perfect because, when counted in its natural order—one, two, and three—it is completed by six, or because it is divided into three parts, namely a sixth, a third, and a half, that is, into one, two, and three. Rather, we say that the number six is perfect because humanity was created on the sixth day and because the Lord is described as having completed his works on that day. Hence the number six is also customarily used for perfection.

[Col. 0694B] Seven refers to the seventh day, on which, after completing everything, the Lord rested. In Genesis: “And he rested on the seventh day from all the work that he had done.”

Again, blessed Gregory says:

> We know with complete certainty that Holy Scripture customarily uses the number seven for perfection. Hence it says that the Lord rested from his works on the seventh day. For this reason the seventh day was also given to human beings for rest, namely as the Sabbath. For this reason the jubilee year, in which complete rest is expressed, is completed after seven weeks.

When one is added to this unit, the sum of our union is fulfilled. These words are therefore written in the first book of the blessed Gregory’s *Moralia*.

Augustine, in Book XI of *The City of God*:

> The number seven is customarily used according to the variety of whatever is being signified. Hence it is said: “The righteous falls seven times and rises again”—that is, however often he falls, he will not perish.

He wished this to be understood not of sins but of tribulations that lead to humility.

And: “Seven times a day I praise you,” which is expressed elsewhere in another way: “His praise shall continually be in my mouth.”

For this reason the Holy Spirit is often signified by this same number, concerning whom the Lord says: “He will teach you all truth.”

Eight refers to the day of resurrection, that is, the eighth day. In the title of the Psalm: “For the end, for the octave.”

Nine refers to the mystery that the Lord gave up his spirit at the ninth hour. In the Gospel: “And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice and gave up his spirit.”

Ten refers to the Decalogue of the Law. In the Psalm: “With the ten-stringed psaltery I will sing to you.”

Twelve refers to the apostles. In the Gospel: “Now the names of the twelve apostles are these.”

Fourteen refers to the mystery of the Lord’s generation. In the Gospel: “From Abraham to David, fourteen generations.”

[Col. 0694D] Fifteen refers to the fifteen steps of the Temple.

Sixteen refers to the number of the prophets.

Twenty-two refers to the mystery of the divine books according to the letters of the Hebrews.

Twenty-four refers to the mystery of the number of elders. In the Apocalypse: “And twenty-four elders seated upon thrones.”

Thirty refers to the fruit of faithful married couples. In the Gospel: “And they will produce fruit, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixtyfold, and in another thirtyfold.”

Thirty-three refers to the mystery of the age during which the Lord lived in the flesh. In the Apostle, as some understand from this passage: “Until we all attain the unity of faith and knowledge of the Son of God, to mature manhood, to the measure of the full stature of Christ.”

Forty refers to the mystery of Lent. In the Gospel: “He was being led by the Spirit in the wilderness for forty days.”

Forty-two refers to the number of the encampments in the wilderness, or to the number of generations from Abraham to Christ.

Fifty refers to Pentecost. In the Acts of the Apostles: “When the day of Pentecost was fulfilled.”

Sixty refers to the fruit owed to widows or those practicing continence. In the Gospel: “And they will produce fruit, in another case sixtyfold.”

Seventy-two refers to the number of presbyters or disciples whom the Lord chose. In the Gospel: “After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them in pairs before his face into every city.”

One hundred refers to the fruit of martyrs or virgins. In the Gospel: “And they will produce fruit, in another case a hundredfold.”]

There is also another method of computation, and so forth, proceeding by divisions. Since this pertains especially to the reckoning of Easter, it will be explained more suitably when we reach that subject in due order.

[Col. 0695B] This computation pertains to the nineteen-year cycle and to the solar cycle. In saying “proceeding by divisions,” he also includes the lunar cycle.

A certain manual speech can also be devised from the method of computation I mentioned above, both for exercising the intellect and for playing a game. By expressing letters one by one, a person may hand over words composed of those same letters to another who also knows this skill, so that the other may read and understand them even from a distance. Through it one may either indicate necessary matters more secretly or, until they discover the meaning by a kind of divination, deceive the uninitiated.

The order of this game or speech is as follows:

When you wish to communicate the first letter of the alphabet, hold one on your hand.

[Col. 0695C] That is, just as you show one on the hand by means of the smallest finger, so you must understand *a* in the very bending of the finger, and likewise with the others.

For the second, two.

For the third, three.

And so, in order, the remaining letters.

For example, if you wish to warn a friend placed among ambushers to act cautiously, show with your fingers:

The third is, in the alphabet, | e |.

The first is, in the alphabet, | a |.

The twentieth is, in the alphabet, | u |.

The nineteenth is, in the alphabet, | t |.

The fifth is, in the alphabet, | e |.

The first is, in the alphabet, | a |.

The seventh is, in the alphabet, | g |.

[Col. 0695D] The fifth is, in the alphabet, | e |.

For the letters of this sequence signify *act cautiously*. It can also be written in this way, if the matter requires greater secrecy.

> **Note: [Col. 0695D]**
>
> There is also another method of reckoning, namely this one, by fingers and joints, proceeding joint by joint—that is, by the joints of the hand, namely the fingers. For it proceeds through the outer segments. “Hold one in your hand”: that is, indicate unity in your hand. By “hand,” namely the left hand, “hold” is meant; that is, just as you display one in your hand by the little finger, so you should understand the letter *a* in the very bending of the fingers. When you signify the second letter, [hold] two, namely, and so with the rest: that is, just as the number of fingers extends successively up to twenty-three, for we have no more letters.
>
> And when you wish to display *k*, which is the tenth letter among us, show it by the same number by which you show ten on your hand. **[Col. 0696A]** Likewise, when you wish to display *l*, show it by *k* and *A*, beginning again from the start, because *l* is the eleventh letter among the Latins. And if you wish to display *x*, which is the twenty-first letter, indicate it by *u*, which is the twentieth, and by *A*, which is the first. And so with the others up to *z*, the final letter.

But this can be learned and practiced more easily together with the Greeks’ reckoning and letters. For, unlike the Latins, who customarily express their numbers with a few letters, repeating the same ones, the Greeks expend the entire character-system of their alphabet upon numerical figures and depict the three numbers that exceed it with individual signs, following almost the same order for forming numbers as for writing the alphabet, in this manner:

> **Note: [Col. 0696C]**
>
> “Following the order of the alphabet for writing, in this manner.” If you wish to display any letter of our alphabet, consider the number naturally assigned to it in the order of our alphabet, and then write the Greek **[Col. 0696D]** letter that does not have the same name but signifies the same number. For example, if you wish to display *g*, which is the seventh letter in the order of our alphabet, you must not therefore write *gamma*, which has the same value among them, because it is third in the order of their alphabet and not seventh; rather, write *zeta*, which represents the number seven among them, just as *g* does among us.
>
> One must also note that when the Greeks express numbers by their elements, they pass from ten to twenty—from *iota*, which means ten, to *kappa*, which signifies twenty. The remaining numbers counted between ten and twenty, however, are not represented by individual characters but by two joined together, as when they wish to display the number eleven: they write *alpha*, which signifies one, and *iota*, which signifies ten. The same applies to the rest; this too must be observed in such a form of expression.

> **[Col. 0697C]** Here you have a definite example with which you can practice in other cases, as in this verse:

> *Insert Greek letters for our numerals.*

Meanwhile, you should know that the letter *x* was taken from the Greeks: although it has the shape of the letter which among them is called *chi*, it nevertheless received its name among them through the reversal or transposition (*anastrophē*) of the Greek letter called *xi*—hence, among the Latins, *ix*. What we write with *c*, or *k*, or *qu*, the Greeks write with *kappa* alone, *k*. Likewise, *v*, which the Greeks do not possess, whenever they wish to express its sound, they represent by joining *omicron* and *upsilon* together.

But this numerical speech and writing for discovering Latin letters—and, that is, the letters of the Greeks—can be learned and practiced more easily together. For the Greeks recognize a number from their letters more easily than we do from ours, because every number has its own particular letter by which it is understood. The Latins, however, do not understand numbers except through a few letters, and these are also repeated.

> **[Col. 0697D]** The Greeks, that is, do not use a few letters like the Latins, but all the letters. The Latins use only a few, namely these seven: **IVXLCDM**.

Four of these are doubled, tripled, and quadrupled according to the requirement of the number, as in **IIII, XXXX, CCCC, MMMM**. The Greeks, for their part, express numbers with all their letters; but, having extended the entire character-system of their alphabet into numerical figures, they depict the three numbers exceeding it with special signs that are not part of the alphabet. The first is **ϛ**, called *episēmon*, and it is the sign for the number six. The second is **η**, called *kopē*, and it has the value ninety. The third is **[sign omitted in the supplied text]**, called *enneacosis*, because it has the value nine hundred: for *ennea* is Greek for “nine,” *enneakonta* for “ninety,” and *enneakosia* for “nine hundred.”

Although these three numerical characters are inserted among the Greek letters, they are not letters but signs for particular numbers. *Episēmon* is placed in the sixth position because it has the form of *semis*, which signifies six ounces, or because it stands beside *epsilon*, signifying five. **[Col. 0698A]** *Cophē* is likewise placed beside the letter *pi*, which has the value ninety. *Enneakosios* is placed at the end because it represents the final number, 900, closing the three series of nine numerical figures, since among the Latins there is no number beyond one thousand. The Greeks, however, mark one thousand with **M**, and indicate it distinctly by a stroke placed above any numerical sign, as with **A̅**, and so forth.

And although these things can be done in the other languages as well, there are nevertheless three principal languages: Hebrew first, Greek second, and Latin third.

Hebrew has twenty-two letters in its alphabet, and five called final letters, as follows:

Thus, in all, the Hebrews have twenty-seven letters, which are divided into three parts, as appears here, and each part has nine letters. **[Col. 0698B]** In the first group there are only units; in the second there are tens, or numbers of ten; and in the last there are hundreds, or thousands. The Greeks have the same arrangement, as was shown above, for they likewise have twenty-seven letters.

The Latin letters follow; there are twenty-three, namely:

There is no need to give any further account here of the Greek number-system, because it has already been written above that they follow almost the same order in forming numbers as in writing their alphabet.

Bede observes that this is easier among the Greeks, who use all the letters and signs of the alphabet in order to signify numbers.

> **[Col. 0698D]** Accordingly, as soon as they have learned to signify numbers with their fingers, without any intervening delay they also know how to place those same signs before letters. But enough of this.

Now let us proceed to explain the divisions of time, insofar as the Lord, the creator and arranger of time, deigns to assist us.

> **Note: [Col. 0698D]**
>
> “To signify numbers with the fingers”: as though he had said, just as they know how to count and read by means of the same letters, so by means of the same fingers they know how to count and display or represent the letters. “Without any intervening delay”: that is, without slowness. “Those same”: namely, numbers or signs. “To place before,” or “to complete.” “They know”: namely, those Greeks; that is, according to the significance of the numbers. “But enough of this”: namely, let what has been said suffice. There has now been enough about indicating with the fingers.

# A LITTLE BOOK ON THE CALCULATION OF OUNCES

> **[Col. 0699A]** To know also the division of ounces—which is no less useful for calculating periods of time and other things than for money—is a respectable discovery. Since both scattered histories and Holy Scripture itself use these divisions, we have taken care to set down their names and signs together in a few words, beginning with the *libra*, which is called so as if from *libera*, “free,” because it freely makes weights equal; for it favors neither friend nor enemy, but only justice.

## Division by ounces

A *libra*, *as*, or *assis*, consists of twelve ounces and is marked thus: **X**, or **Ib**.

A *deunx*, or *labus*, consists of eleven ounces and is marked thus: **[sign]**, or **[sign]**.

A *decunx*, or *dextans*, consists of ten ounces and is marked thus: **[sign]**, or **[sign]**.

> **[Col. 0699B]**

A *dodrans*, or *doras*, consists of nine ounces and is marked thus: **[sign]**, or **[sign]**.

A *bes*, *bisse*, or *besse*, consists of eight ounces and is marked thus: **[sign]**, or **[sign]**.

A *septunx*, or *septuns*, consists of seven ounces and is represented thus: **[sign]**, or **[sign]**.

A *semis*, *semissis*, or *sextus*, consists of six ounces and is marked thus: **[sign]**, or **S**.

A *quinquunx*, or *quincunx*, consists of five ounces and is thus indicated: **[sign]**.

A *triens*, or *treas*, consists of four ounces and is represented thus: **[sign]**.

A *quadrans*, or *quadras*, consists of three ounces and is drawn thus: **[sign]**.

> **[Col. 0699C]** A *sextans*, or *sextas*, consists of two ounces and is marked thus: **[sign]**.

A *sexcunx*, or *sescuncia*, consists of one and a half ounces; it is also called *sesquiuncia* and is marked thus: **[sign]**.

## Division by scruples

An ounce consists of twenty-four scruples and is marked thus: **ξ**, or **[sign]**.

A half-ounce consists of twelve scruples, one third of an ounce, and is indicated thus: **[sign]**.

Two *sextulae* consist of eight scruples and are formed thus: **[sign]**.

A *sicilicus* consists of six scruples and is marked **C**.

A *sextula*, or *sescla*, consists of four scruples and is formed thus: **[sign]**, or **[sign]**, or **[sign]**.

> **[Col. 0699D]** Half a *sextula* consists of two scruples and is depicted thus: **[sign]**.

A *scrupulus*, or *scripulus*, contains six *siliquae* and is marked thus: **[sign]**, or **[sign]**.

The *sicilicus* was first invented in Sicily.

A *siliqua* is a kind of grain.

These, then, are the terms or signs of weights. They apply not only to measuring money but also to measuring any bodies or periods of time.

> **[Col. 0700A]** Hence the practice or convention arose that, in the recitation of computations, children often substitute *as* and *dipondius* for “one” and “two”; likewise, *tressis*, *quartussis*, *quintussis*, *sextussis*, *septussis*, and other such terms are pronounced as though they meant three asses, four asses, and so forth, and similarly with many of the following numbers.

Therefore, whether you wish to divide one hour, a whole day, a month, a year, or some other greater or lesser span of time into twelve parts, the twelfth part itself is an ounce; the remaining eleven are called a *deunx*. If you wish to divide it into six, the sixth part is a *sextans*; the remaining five are called a *dextans*, or, as some say, a *distas*. If into four, the fourth part receives the name *quadrans*; the remaining three receive the name *dodrans*.

The rule of this discipline resolves a matter that confuses many inexperienced people. In his exposition of blessed Job, when describing the heat of the ocean tide as coming twice each day, Philip added that this occurred after three quarters of an equinoctial hour had passed, arriving later without interruption, whether by day or by night.

> **[Col. 0700B]**

If you wish to divide something by three, you will call the third part a *triens* and the two remaining parts a *bes*. If by two, the half is called a *semis*. (The twelfth part of an *as* or *libra* is an ounce; it contains twenty-four scruples, six *sextulae*, and 144 *siliquae*. A *scripulus* is a small stone.) The same applies to the other divisions, which can be learned and taught equally well by the speech of one conversing and by the pen of one writing.

Likewise, if you need to divide physical measures—whether a mile, a *stadium*, a *jugerum*, a *pertica*, or even a cubit, foot, or palm—you should proceed according to the method stated above.

> **[Col. 0700C]**

Finally, in Exodus half a cubit is called a *semis*. Moses relates that the ark of the covenant had a length of two and a half cubits and a height of one cubit and a half.

In the Gospel, the fourth part of the entire body of the world, namely the earth, is mystically designated by the name *quadrans*, when the sinner is told, in reference to being sent into punishment: “You will not go out from there until you have paid the last *quadrans*”—that is, until you have expiated earthly sins—as blessed Augustine explains:

> “For this is what the sinner heard: ‘You are earth, and into earth you shall go.’ The fourth part of the distinct members of this world is found to be the final one, the earth, if you begin with heaven, count the air as the second, water as the third, and earth as the fourth.”

He also remembers this discipline in his exposition of the passage, “It was the preparation day of Passover, about the sixth hour,” saying:

> **[Col. 0700D]**

> “The sixth hour was not yet complete, but it was about the sixth hour: the fifth had been completed, and something of the sixth had begun. Yet they would never say ‘five and a quarter,’ or ‘five and a third,’ or ‘five and a half,’ or anything of this kind, if such divisions were not found to have been customary among the divine authors.”

> **Note: [Col. 0700D]**
>
> ## BRIDFERT’S GLOSS
>
> “These, then”: namely, as I said, he began. “Weights”: **[Col. 0701A]** a weight (*pondus*) is so called from *pendere*, “to hang,” because it hangs balanced on a scale. “Signs”: that is, figures. “Not only”: that is, not merely for money—gold, silver, or any metal. The substance of the ancients consisted almost entirely in livestock; although today it consists in livestock and other things as well, this name is nevertheless not retained.
>
> “Hence the practice or convention”: because these terms of weights apply not only to measuring money but also to other things, the practice arose that they should also be used for names of numbers in the recitation of computations—that is, when they play at dice, which is a kind of game. The recitation of computations occurs when we say “one, two,” and so forth.
>
> Properly, however, *assis* signifies one pound, *dipondius* two, *tressis* three, and *quartussis* four. *Sesfertius* formerly meant a *dipondius* or *dupondius* and a half, as though “the third half”; *tressis* means three asses, and so forth. Very many subsequent names are pronounced, up to *centussis*, that is, one hundred asses.
>
> “Philip”: he was a disciple of the blessed Jerome.

> **[Col. 0701B]** “Whether, therefore, an hour”: if you wish to divide a greater period of time into twelve parts, the twelfth part itself will be an ounce; a greater period is, for example, a nineteen-year cycle. A smaller period of time is, for example, a moment; its twelfth part is likewise an ounce. Whatever you wish to divide into twenty-four parts:

| Part | Is called |
|---|---|
| Part 24 | A scruple |
| Part 12 | A *semis* |
| Part 2 | A *triens* |
| Part 16 | A *bes* |
| Part 6 | A *quadrans* |
| Part 18 | A *dodrans* |
| Part 4 | A *sextans* |
| Part 20 | A *dextans* |

> **[Col. 0702A]**

If you wish to divide an hour, a day, or something similar into forty parts, that fortieth part itself bears the name *moment*.

| Part | Is called |
|---|---|
| Part 20 | A *semis* |
| Part 10 | A *quadrans* |
| Part 30 | A *dodrans* |

Whatever you wish to divide into ten parts: all ten parts together receive the name *decunx*. Similarly:

| Part | Is called |
|---|---|
| Part 10 | A *decunx* |
| Part 9 | A *dodrans* |
| Part 8 | A *besse*, and so forth |

Similarly, whatever you wish to divide into nine parts: all the parts together bear the name *dodrans*. When the ninth part is removed, the eight remaining parts are called a *bes*. Whatever you wish to divide into eight parts: all of them together are called a *bes*. Remove one, and the seven that remain are called a *septunx*.

> **[Col. 0702B]**

Thus, by customary usage, eight hours, eight days, eight points, eight moments, and whatever is taken eight times are called a *bes*. Likewise, nine are always called a *dodrans*, ten a *decunx*, eleven a *deunx*, seven a *septunx*, six a *sextans* or *semis*, five a *quincunx*, four a *triens*, and so forth, as in the following.
