# A LITTLE BOOK ON THE ARGUMENTS OF THE MOON

> **[Col. 0701C]** An *argumentum* is a swift confirmation of universal matters, which establishes the credibility of a doubtful matter. It is called *argumentum* as though it were an indication of an ingenious mind, or as though it were ingeniously discovered. *Argumentum* and *argumentatio* differ from one another. An *argumentum* is what briefly sets forth the subject at the beginning of a book; *argumentatio* is what establishes the credibility of assertions in a disputation. Or *argumentum* is so called because it “argues” or reveals the mind. *Argumenta* are ingenious devices that give credibility to a doubtful matter. An *argumentum* occurs when something is confirmed from what has already been said.

## To find the weekday on the Kalends of the months

If you wish to know the weekday—that is, the day of the week—on the Kalends of the months, know how many regulars each month has, beginning with March, because the world was made in that month and it was the beginning of the year among the ancient Romans in the time of Romulus. In that month the solar epacts run, that is, the weekdays that recur, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, in the cycle of twenty-eight years.

March therefore has five regulars, April one, and so forth. February has six. When these regulars have been added to the concurrents of the year in question throughout the twenty-eight-year cycle—for at that point the solar cycle returns upon itself—and the entire sum has been divided by eight, the number remaining will be the weekday for the Kalends of the twelve months.

But if you divide the entire number by seven, the Kalends of the month in question will fall on Saturday. If the number of regulars and concurrents together has not reached seven, whatever that number is, that will be the weekday on the Kalends of each month throughout the year.

## To find the weekday by the days of the month

If you wish to know what weekday each day is, count the days from the beginning of whichever month you wish, and always subtract one—that is, the first day of the month—because when you say, “Add the weekday that occurred at the beginning of this month,” you are including the first day itself, which you must not count twice.

The same is to be understood concerning the moon where it says, **[Col. 0702C]** “Add the age of the moon that occurred on the Kalends of this year and month.” Also add the number indicating which weekday occurred on the Kalends of that month. For example, if the Kalends of that month fell on the first weekday, add one to the elapsed days. If they fell on the second weekday, add two; if on the third, three; and so on up to seven.

Whenever necessary, divide by a seventh part—that is, remove seven as many times as possible. Whatever remains after the sevens have been removed will be the weekday. If nothing remains, it is a weekday [the source’s designation is incomplete].

## To find the weekday by the days of the year

If you wish to know what weekday any day of the year is, count the days from the Kalends of January up to the day about which you are asking. When you know the number, add the weekday that occurred on the Kalends of January; and if it is a leap year, remember also to reckon the leap day after it has passed. Divide everything by seven. Whatever remains will be the weekday. If nothing remains, it is the seventh weekday.

## To find the weekday on the Kalends of January by the years of the Lord

> **[Col. 0702D]**

If you wish to know what weekday falls on the Kalends of January, take the years from the Incarnation of the Lord, however many there have been; add one fourth of them; subtract one from the result—or two if it is a leap year—and divide the remainder by seven. Whatever remains will be the weekday on the Kalends of January.

## To find the moon on the Kalends of the months

If you suddenly wish to find what lunar day always falls on the Kalends of a month, take the regular of the current month, add the epact of the year in question, and combine them into one. If they reach thirty, the moon on the Kalends is thirty. If they are less than thirty, the lunar day is likewise that number. If they exceed thirty, subtract thirty; what remains is the lunar day on the Kalends of the month.

Take care, however, that if the lunation is thirty, you subtract thirty; if it is twenty-nine, subtract twenty-nine, because from the beginning of the year to its end one lunation is thirty and another twenty-nine. In a leap year the day proceeds together with the moon. For example, if today the moon is calculated as six, it must likewise be calculated as six tomorrow.

> **[Col. 0703A]**

## To find the moon by the days of the month

If you wish to know what lunar day it is on any day you choose, determine what lunar day was found on the Kalends of that month through the epacts and regulars. Retain that number, add the elapsed days of the month, as we said above concerning the weekday, and always subtract one; combine the result into one.

If it reaches thirty, it is lunar day thirty. If it is less than thirty, the lunar day is likewise that number. If it exceeds thirty, subtract thirty; what remains is the lunar day.

## To find the moon by the days of the year

If you wish to know the lunar day on every day, count the days from the Kalends of January up to the day on which you wish to calculate. When you know the number, add the age of the moon that occurred on the Kalends of January. Divide everything by twenty-nine and thirty. If more than thirty remains, subtract thirty and twenty-nine; whatever remains will be the lunar day.

## To find the moon on the Kalends of January

> **[Col. 0703B]**

If you wish to know the age of the moon on the Kalends of January, take the lunar cycle of the present year, whatever year you choose, multiply it by eleven, add one regular, and divide everything by thirty. Whatever remains will be the age of the moon on the Kalends of January.

Remember only this: after cycle 16—namely, in cycles 17, 18, and 19—you must add not one regular but two.

## At what hour and point the moon is kindled by the sun

If you wish to know at what hour and at what point the moon is kindled and changed each day, take the current lunar cycle of any year, multiply it by five, and add the number of days from the Kalends of January up to the present day. Divide the days of the year together with the multiplication of the current lunar cycle by sixty. Whatever remains is the number of points for that day; make hours from them. Five points make one hour.

For example, if five remain, the moon ends at the final point of the first hour, and another begins.

> **[Col. 0703C]**

## To find the age of the moon

If you wish to know the subsequent age of the moon by the same cycle, multiply it by six, and add the number mentioned above, which comes from the days of the year and from multiplying the cycle by five. Add as many regulars as there are sixties contained initially in that multiplication. Divide everything by thirty. Whatever remains is the age of the moon; if nothing remains, it is thirty.

## To find the moon on any given date in the preceding or following year

If you wish to know what the moon was on any given date in the preceding year, take the lunar day of the present year on whatever date you wish to examine in the preceding year, and subtract eleven. Whatever remains, know that this was the lunar day on that date in the preceding year.

> **[Col. 0703D]** If the lunar age is less than eleven, know that where it is now one, it was then twenty; where it is now two, it was then twenty-one. Continue calculating until you reach lunar day twelve, and then subtract eleven. Whatever remains was the lunar day on that date in the preceding year where it is now twelve.

If you likewise wish to determine the moon in the following year, add eleven to the present lunar age. Whatever the result is, know that this will be the lunar age on the same date in the following year. If the number grows beyond thirty, subtract thirty; whatever remains is its age.

## To find the moon in the hundredth year

If you wish to know what lunar day it will be on any day in the hundredth year from the present, multiply the eleven annual [days] by one hundred: the result is 1,100. Add the epact for the present day, from which you begin counting. Add five regulars—that is, five leaps, which are called regulars for this reason.

> **[Col. 0704A]** Combine everything and divide by thirty. Whatever remains will be the age of the moon in the hundredth year.

## By how many points the moon shines

If you wish to know by how many points or hours the moon shines, first determine whether it is waxing or waning. If it is waxing, multiply its age by four. For example, if it is the tenth day, multiply ten by four, producing forty. The moon shines for forty points on day ten, that is, for eight hours.

Likewise, if you wish to know how many points it does not shine, see how many there are from ten to fifteen: plainly five. Multiply five by four, producing twenty points, which make four hours. Thus the moon shines for four hours on the tenth day.

Again, if you wish to know for how many hours the moon shines after the full moon on day twenty, see how many there are from twenty to thirty: plainly ten. Multiply by four, producing forty points, which make eight hours.

Then, if you wish to know how long it does not shine, see how many there are from fifteen to twenty: plainly five. Multiply by four, producing twenty points, which make four hours. Thus the moon does not shine for four hours on day twenty.

Continue in this way to the end. On the thirtieth day the moon shines not at all, because at conjunction it is opposite the sun; that time is called *interlunium*, the dark of the moon.

## In what sign or part of a sign the sun or moon is located

> **[Col. 0704B]**

If you wish to know in what sign or in what part of a sign the sun and moon are located, use this calculation. First determine where the moon’s illumination occurs. The moon’s illumination will be as follows: in the month in which there is a thirtieth lunar day, that day itself is the illumination of that month. Likewise, the month that has the twenty-eighth lunation has its illumination then, and on that day the sun and moon are together.

Next calculate what the age of the moon was and multiply it by twelve, because each day it moves twelve parts away from the sun. Divide that number by thirty, and remember that for however many times you have thirty, you have that many complete signs, because each sign has thirty parts.

You must nevertheless know this: restore the first sign in which the moon was illuminated from the number obtained in the multiplication.

## By how many parts the moon is distant from the sun

> **[Col. 0704C]**

If you wish to know by how many parts the moon is distant from the sun, multiply its age, whatever it may be, by four, and multiply the resulting number again by three. However many you find, by that many parts the moon is distant from the sun.

For example, if you are examining the tenth day, proceed as follows: four times ten is forty; three times forty is 120. Thus, on the tenth day the moon is 120 parts distant from the sun—that is, the moon is located in the part of the sky which the sun will reach after 120 days.

By “parts of the signs” we mean nothing other than how far the sun travels through each sign on each day.

Again, if by the same calculation you wish to find in what sign the moon is, first determine in what sign the sun is and in what part of it—that is, how many days it has completed there—and how many remain until thirty. For the sun remains in each sign for that many days.

Take from the number stated above as many parts as remain out of thirty, and assign them to that sign to complete it. Of the remainder left from that same number, assign thirty to each succeeding sign until you no longer have thirty. In whichever sign thirty is lacking, know that the moon is located there.

To make what we are saying clearer, let us give an example involving one day. In the present year, on the Kalends of August, the moon is fifteen. Multiply by four, producing one hundred; multiply this by three, producing three hundred. On the Kalends of August of this year, therefore, the moon is 300 parts distant from the sun.

The sun, however, is in Leo, in its fifteenth part, because it entered that sign on the fifteenth day before the Kalends. Fifteen days therefore remain for it to complete the sign. Take these fifteen from the 300 and assign them to Leo to complete the sign; 285 remain. From this, assign thirty to the next sign, Virgo; and thirty each to Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces, Aries, and Taurus. Together these amount to 270. Fifteen remain. On that day the moon is in the fifteenth part of Gemini.

The moon completes the zodiac thirteen times in its twelve months. You will find this calculation with glosses in chapter 17. The moon, waxing, moves four points farther from the sun each day.

> **[Col. 0705A]**

If you are unfamiliar with the signs, read these three calculations and investigate their differences carefully.

## What the solar and lunar epacts or regulars are

When you hear of the lunar epacts, understand the age of the moon in each year on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.

When you hear of the solar epacts—that is, the concurrent weekdays—understand on which weekday, in each year, the ninth day before the Kalends of April will fall.

When you hear of lunar regulars, understand the lunar ages of the individual months in that year alone in which the thirtieth lunar day is found on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April; for that is the first year of the nineteen-year cycle.

When you hear of solar regulars, understand on which weekday the Kalends of each month will fall in the year in which the concurrents are seven—that is, in which the ninth day before the Kalends of April is Saturday.

The Kalends are also called “given Kalends,” because in ancient times on them it was announced—that is, reckoned—how many days remained until the Nones. **[Col. 0705B]** From this usage it has continued down to the present day: “how many given days” means how many days have passed from the Kalends of the month, or how many days remain until the Kalends of the following month.

Read Book II, *On Times*, chapter 13; there you will find more about the Kalends, Nones, and Ides.

## On the epacts on the Kalends of the months

If you wish to know the epacts on the Kalends of the twelve months, know how many regulars each month has, beginning with September, because that is the beginning of the year and the beginning of the months among the Egyptians. At the beginning of September the Egyptians change their epacts, and the first epacts that the Egyptians have at the beginning of the cycle are the regulars that we have on the Kalends of the twelve months.

For example: September five, October five, and so forth, up to August fourteen. When these regulars have been added to whatever epacts occur on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April in a given year, you will find the epacts on the Kalends of the twelve months.

## Epacts

> **Note: [Col. 0705]** In Migne, the numbers in square brackets are printed above the words they follow.

None: **11 22 3 14 25 6 17 28 9 20 1 12 23 4 15 26 7 18.**

In the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, in which there are no epacts, you will find the moon on each set of Kalends in this way. In the other years, add the epacts, and in this way you will find the lunar day on each set of Kalends.

Why, however, in the eighth, eleventh, and eighteenth years of the nineteen-year cycle this calculation does not preserve the consistency of its pattern on certain Kalends can be found fully in Book II, *On Times*, chapter 20.

## Where the regulars used for finding the weekday originate

If you wish to know where the regulars counted according to the sun originate—that is, the five for March—count, in the calculation, as many numbers as there are months in the year for which you are seeking the regulars: namely, 365. Divide these by twelve: twelve times thirty makes 360, leaving five; this is the five for March.

March has thirty-one days. Add its five regulars, which you have found, producing thirty-six. Divide these by seven: five times seven is thirty-five, leaving one—the one for April.

April has thirty days. Add the one regular you have found, producing thirty-one. Divide by seven: four times seven is twenty-eight, leaving three—the three for May.

Proceed in this way with the remaining months to the end. Pay close attention, and you will not be mistaken.

## Where the lunar regulars originate

If you wish to know where the lunar regulars originate, take 365 days and divide by thirty. Ten times thirty makes 300, and twice thirty makes sixty, leaving five. This is the five for September.

September has thirty days. Add the five regulars you have found, producing thirty-five. Subtract thirty, leaving five—the five for October.

October has thirty-one days. Add the five regulars you have found, producing thirty-six. Subtract twenty-nine, leaving seven—the seven for November.

November has thirty days. Add the seven regulars you have found, producing thirty-seven. Subtract thirty, leaving seven—the seven for December.

Remember only this: one time subtract thirty and the next time twenty-nine, on account of the moon’s illuminations and extinguishings, which occur in this way.

## On the pronunciation of the days of the year according to Victorius, for finding the weekday of the individual Nones, Ides, and Kalends

Likewise, concerning the same according to Dionysius.

## On the pronunciation according to Victorius

> **[Col. 0707A]**
If you wish to know why February is said to be at Kalends 32, and why these readings do not begin with the same month, although both concern the weekday: the first was completed by Victorius of Aquitaine, the second by Dionysius the Greek. The former counts the days of the year; the latter counts the days of the month. Dionysius counts how many elapsed days there are in the month, whereas Victorius counts them in the year. For this reason February is said to be at Kalends 32, because January has 31 days: add the Kalends, and the total is 32. For this reason also he began to count from January, because it is the gateway of the year, and he counts the days of the year. Dionysius, on the other hand, begins from March, because it is the first month, as the Lord said: “This month shall be the first among the months of the year”; and therefore he counts the days of the month.

Victorius counts February at Nones 36. It has four days before the Nones; add them to 32, and the total is 36. At the Ides, 44: it has eight days before the Ides; add them to 36, and the total is 44. March is at Kalends 60, because it has fifteen days [Col. 0707B] after the Ides. Add the Kalends of March, and the total is 16; add 16 to 44, and the total is 60. At Nones, 66, because it has six days before the Nones. Thus always count by complete totals, and you will not go wrong. At the end he says: January is at Kalends 366, because the solar year has 365 days. Add the Kalends, and the total is 366. At Nones, 5, because the days of the year have already been completed; at the Ides, 13.

## The manner of recitation according to Dionysius

If you wish to know why March is said to be at Kalends 29: February lies immediately before March. It has 28 days; add the Kalends of March, and the total is 29. At Nones, 7, because it has six days before the Nones; add the Kalends, and the total is 7. At the Ides, 15, because all the months have eight days before the Ides. Add the 7 which you had at the Nones, and the total is 15. Add the 17 which March has beyond the Nones and Ides, and the total is 32.

April is said to be at Kalends 32, because March has 31 days; add the Kalends, and the total is 32. At Nones, 5, because it has four days before the Nones. At the Ides, 13: add the 5 which you had at the Nones to the eight days before the Ides, and the total is 13. Add 18 to 13, and the total is [Col. 0707C] 31.

May is said to be at Kalends 31. Do the same for each month. Take care only that you always attach the Kalends to the month immediately preceding it, and the Nones to the days that come before them; and if anyone is inexperienced, let him commit this to memory. January, August, and December have four days before the Nones: there you can learn the method completely.

### The same subject

If you wish to know why “once 59” is given, attend to the calculation, and you will find it there. This sequence is relevant to finding the moon, because in one instance the moon rises to 30, and in another to 29. Put them together: the total is 59. And why did he write no more of that calculation in this place than six times 59? Because six times 59 is 354, which is the number of days of the lunar year; for this reason the calculation does not go beyond it.

## Why it is called a *terminus*

The *terminus*, as some maintain, is so called because the stone itself [Col. 0708B] has something less than three feet.

## The greater regular numbers of the nineteen-year cycle according to the Paschal terminus

If you wish to discover the origin of the principal regular numbers in the nineteen-year cycle—that is, “The Nones of April know five; the eighth Kalends draw forth one; the Ides of April also have six,” and so on to the end—always take the Kalends of April as the first weekday. On whatever weekday you find the number mentioned above for the Kalends, that many regular numbers there will be.

For example, take the Kalends of April as the first weekday, and you will find the Nones of April on the fifth weekday. When you have found this, [Col. 0709A] recite: “The Nones of April know five.” In another year do the same, and you will find the eighth day before the Kalends of April on the first weekday. When you have found it, say: “The eighth Kalends draw forth one.” Do this for each year of the nineteen-year cycle, and without error or ambiguity you will find the regular number. Add to it the concurrent number of the year in question, and you will find the weekday on which the fourteenth moon of the Paschal term falls.

Observe also that whenever the terminus occurs before the Kalends of April—namely, on the eighth or eleventh day before the Kalends of April—you must count backward by weekdays and by Kalends in this manner: Kalends of April on the first weekday; second day before the Kalends on the seventh weekday; third day before the Kalends on the sixth weekday; fourth day before the Kalends on the fifth weekday; and so forth until the terminus. When it occurs after the Kalends of April—namely, on the Nones of April or the fourth day before the Nones—you must proceed directly, in regular order, to the terminus.

## By whom these termini were discovered

We read in the letters of the Greeks that, after the martyrdom [Col. 0709B] of the apostles, the holy abbot Pachomius in Egypt, together with his monks, asked the Lord in prayer to show him how Easter ought to be celebrated. The Lord sent through his angel to the aforementioned holy Pachomius the nineteen-year cycle, in this form: “The Nones of April know five; the eighth Kalends draw forth one,” and so forth.

Different computists, however, find the Paschal termini in different ways. It is unnecessary to set out their calculation here; simply read the *quaternion* of Lord Ulperic, chapters 30, 32, 33, 34, and 35. There you will find, in many forms, everything necessary concerning all the termini.

## Likewise

Thus it is read in the letter which the blessed Cyril wrote to Pope Leo:

> “For I shall tell you what Pachomius, that distinguished monk, outstanding through deeds of apostolic grace and founder of the Egyptian monasteries, who also established the monastery called in the Egyptian language [Col. 0709C] Panum, received when the angel dictated the letter, so that he might not fall into error in calculating the Paschal solemnity and might know the moon of the first month in a common year and in an embolismic year.”

## The regular numbers called greater, for finding the fourteenth moon of the first month

[Col. 0709D]

March has 36 greater regular numbers, and April 35, for finding the fourteenth moon. If, therefore, you wish to know the Paschal terminus in March or April, subtract from those regular numbers the epact of the same year, in whichever of the two months you wish to calculate it. If more than 30 remain from those regular numbers, subtract 30; however many remain, that many days into the month will be the Paschal terminus. If one remains, the terminus will be on the first day of the month; if fifteen, on the fifteenth day; if thirty, on the thirtieth day: that is, the fourteenth moon.

## The regular numbers called lesser, for finding the weekday of that moon

March has 4 lesser regular numbers, and April 7, for finding the weekday of the fourteenth moon. If, therefore, you wish to know immediately on which weekday the Paschal, Quadragesimal, or Rogation terminus occurs, take the days left after the epact has been subtracted from the greater regular numbers. Add the concurrents of the present year, and always add 4 regular numbers for March and 7 for April. Add everything together and divide it by seven. The remainder indicates the weekday on which the terminus of Easter—that is, the fourteenth moon—occurs, or the Quadragesimal or Rogation terminus—that is, the second or twentieth moon.

Remember what age the moon had at the Kalends of January in that year, and subtract that many days backward from the end of March. Wherever the day falls, there will be the birth of the moon of the first month. Do this in every year except the three embolisms: the last of the eight-year group, and the first and last of the eleven-year group.

In the last embolism of the eight-year group, the beginning of the first month—that is, the first moon—is found on the Nones of April. In the first embolism of the eleven-year group, the first moon of the first month is found on the fourth day before the Nones of April. In the final [Col. 0710A] embolism of the eleven-year group, the beginning of the first month is found on the second day before the Nones of April. This rule never fails.

In the remaining years always follow the procedure described in March, except in these three cases, when the moon at the Kalends of January is 26, 29, or 27. Once the first moon of the first month has been found, add thirteen days to it, and thus you will find the fourteenth moon of the Paschal terminus.

## Example concerning the years of the Lord’s Incarnation 776 and 936 or 937: how to find the fourteenth moon of the first month and the weekday of that moon with the aforesaid regular numbers

March has 36 greater regular numbers and 4 lesser ones. April has 35 greater regular numbers and 7 lesser ones.

[Col. 0710B]

In the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon is 30 on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April; in that same year the moon is 14 on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, that is, on the Nones of April. Add 5 to 30, and use the result as the regular number for April in the year in which the fourteenth moon falls in April. In the year in which the fourteenth moon falls in March, assign March the regular number 36.

You can easily recognize from the epacts whether the fourteenth moon falls in March or April. If you have more than 15 epacts or fewer than 5, the fourteenth moon is calculated in April. If you have more than 5 and fewer than 15 epacts, the fourteenth moon belongs to March.

Therefore take the regular number 35 for April and always subtract the epacts of the same year. What remains is the day of the fourteenth moon. For example, in the third year of the nineteen-year cycle the epacts will be 22. Subtract 22 from 35; 13 remain. On the thirteenth day of April, that is, on the Ides of April, the fourteenth moon occurs.

If you seek the weekday of the fourteenth moon, add the concurrent number of that year to the number left—as, in the present example, to the 13 remaining in [Col. 0710C] April—and also add 7, the regular number for April. Collect all these numbers and divide by seven; the remainder is the weekday of the fourteenth moon, and thus you will reach the Sunday very easily.

For March, take the regular number 36 and subtract the epacts of that year. For example, in the second year of the nineteen-year cycle the epacts are 11; 25 remain. On the twenty-fifth day of that month, that is, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, the fourteenth moon will be present. If you seek the weekday of that day, add to the stated number the concurrent number of that year and the 4 regular numbers for March. After collecting these, divide by seven; the remainder is the weekday of the fourteenth moon. If nothing remains, it is the seventh weekday.

If, after the epacts have been subtracted, 30 remain, whatever remains is still the day of the month on which you will find the fourteenth moon. Thus, in the year in which the epacts are 4, subtract 4 from 35; 31 remain. Subtract 30; 1 remains. The fourteenth moon occurs on the first day of the month, that is, on the Kalends of April. If, after the epacts have been subtracted, exactly 30 remain, the fourteenth [Col. 0710D] moon occurs on the thirtieth day of the month. This happens once in nineteen years, namely, when 6 epacts are assigned, and the fourteenth moon occurs on the third day before the Kalends of April.

To instruct you by examples in finding the weekday on which the fourteenth moon occurs, take, for example, the year 776 of the Lord’s Incarnation. Take the epacts of this year, 26; subtract them from the 35 regular numbers, and 9 remain. Thus the fourteenth moon will be on the ninth day of the month, that is, on the fifth day before the Ides of April. Add also the concurrent number of the present year, namely 1, to 9; the total is 10. Add 7; the total is 17. Divide these by 7: twice 7 is 14, and 3 remain. The third weekday will be the fourteenth moon; the fifteenth moon will be on the fourth weekday, the sixteenth on the fifth, the seventeenth on the sixth, the eighteenth on the seventh, and the nineteenth on the first weekday, which is Easter. On the fifth day before the Ides is the fourteenth moon; on the fourth day before the Ides, the fifteenth; on the third day before the Ides, the sixteenth; on the second day before the Ides, the seventeenth; on the Ides, the eighteenth; and on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, the nineteenth.

In the second year after this, the number is 7, because it is more than 5 and less than 15. The fourteenth moon belongs to March, which you will seek as follows. Take the regular number for March, 36. Subtract 7; 29 remain. On the twenty-ninth day of March, that is, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, the fourteenth moon occurs.

[Col. 0711A]

To find the weekday, take the same 29 and add the concurrent number of that year, namely 2; the total is 31. Add the 4 regular numbers; the whole sum is 35. Divide by 7: seven times 5 is 35, and nothing remains. Therefore the seventh weekday will be the fourteenth moon, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April; the fifteenth moon will be on the third day before the Kalends of April, which is Easter Sunday.

Thus, in each year of the nineteen-year cycle, by subtracting the annual epacts from the regular numbers in this manner, you will find the fourteenth moon without error. By adding to those regular numbers the stated concurrent number, you will likewise find the weekday of the fourteenth moon without difficulty. When you have calculated the remaining weekdays of that week, assign the increasing age of the moon to each day; then you will very quickly find both the moon’s position and its age.

## The year of the Lord’s Incarnation 936

The Paschal terminus is on the fourth day before the Ides of April.  
**D.** How is this evident?  
**M.** April has 35 regular numbers for finding the fourteenth [Col. 0711B] moon, and this year’s epacts are 25. After subtracting 25 from 35, 10 remain. The Paschal terminus, that is, the fourteenth moon, falls on the tenth day within April.

**D.** On which weekday?  
**M.** April has 7 regular numbers for finding the weekday of the fourteenth moon. If we join to the 10—the number left after the epacts have been subtracted—the concurrent number of this year, which is 5, the total is 15; adding the 7 regular numbers makes 22. Subtracting 21 leaves 1. Therefore the Paschal terminus falls on the first weekday, on the tenth day within April, which is the fourth day before the Ides.

- Fifteenth day before the Kalends of May: Easter, moon 21.
- Kalends of April, sixth day before the Ides, fifth day before the Ides, fourth day before the Ides: Paschal terminus 1, moon 14.
- Sixteenth day before the Kalends of March: Septuagesima, moon 18, because of the leap year.
- Fourth day before the Kalends of February, Nones, eighth day before the Ides, seventh day before the Ides: terminus 70, moon 11.

[Col. 0711C]

- Eleventh day before the Nones of March: Quadragesima, moon 9.
- Eleventh day before the Kalends of March, fifth day before the Kalends, fourth day before the Kalends, third day before the Kalends: terminus 40, second moon.
- Eleventh day before the Kalends of June: Rogations, moon 27.
- Second day before the Nones of May, third day before the Ides, second day before the Ides, Ides: Rogation terminus, moon 20.
- Fourth day before the Nones of June: Pentecost, moon 11.
- Thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, sixth day before the Kalends, fifth day before the Kalends, fourth day before the Kalends: Pentecost terminus, moon 4.

## The year of the Lord’s Incarnation 937

**D.** In which month, or on which day according to the Kalends, will the Paschal terminus fall this year?  
**M.** March has 36 regular numbers for finding the fourteenth moon, and this year’s epacts are 6. After removing the 6 epacts from the 36 regular numbers, 30 remain. On the thirtieth day within March, which is the Kalends of April, the Paschal terminus—that is, the fourteenth moon—occurs.

**D.** On which weekday?  
**M.** March has 4 regular numbers for finding the weekday of the fourteenth moon. If we add to the [Col. 0711D] 30 left after the epacts have been expended the 6 concurrents belonging to this year, the total is immediately 36; adding the 4 regular numbers makes 40. Five times 7 is 35, and 5 remain. These 5 indicate the weekday you seek. It can be found still more easily and quickly in this way: the regular number of this terminus is 6, and the concurrents of the present year are likewise 6, making 12 together. Remove 7; 5 remain, and these signify the aforesaid weekday.

[Col. 0712A]

- Fourth day before the Nones of April: Easter, moon 17.
- Kalends of April, second day before the Kalends, third day before the Kalends: Paschal terminus, moon 14.
- Fourth day before the Kalends of February: Septuagesima, moon 13.
- Fifth day before the Kalends of February, sixth day before the Kalends, seventh day before the Kalends: terminus 70, moon 10.
- Eleventh day before the Kalends of March: Quadragesima, moon 5.
- Twelfth day before the Kalends of March, thirteenth day before the Kalends, fourteenth day before the Kalends: terminus 40, moon 2.
- Nones of May: Rogations, moon 25.
- Second day before the Nones of May, third day before the Nones, fourth day before the Nones: Rogation terminus, twentieth moon.
- Twelfth day before the Kalends of June: Pentecost, moon 7.
- Thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, fourteenth day before the Kalends, fifteenth day before the Kalends: Pentecost terminus, fourth moon.

## Whence the greater regular numbers arise

If you wish to know how the greater regular numbers arise—36 in March and 35 in April—you will find it by this calculation. March has 31 days; if you add to it the five remaining Egyptian days, the total is 36. Similarly, if you add the same five to April, the total is 35. Thus the regular numbers 36 for March and 35 for April arise. They are to be used in determining the fourteenth moon of Easter, so that it may be found on which weekday the moon occurs, whether in March or in April.

## Whence the lesser regular numbers arise

If you wish to know how the lesser regular numbers arise—4 in March and 7 in April—take the days of the year from the Kalends of January to the Kalends of March, namely 60 days, and divide by seven. Eight times seven is [Col. 0712B] 56; four remain. These 4 are the regular numbers for March.

If you likewise wish to find them for April, you will find them by this calculation. The number of days of the year at the Kalends of April is 91. Divide these by 7: ten times 7 is 70, leaving 21. Divide by 7: seven times one is 7, and seven times two is 14; 7 remain. Take these 7 and retain them as the regular numbers for April. Do this for each year, and you will find the aforesaid regular numbers without any possibility of error or ambiguity.

## The Paschal date and the birth of the fourteenth moon

We find it established in the cycle of the Romans that Easter should occur neither before the eleventh day before the Kalends of April nor after the seventh day before the Kalends of May. Nor should the fourteenth Paschal moon be sought before the twelfth day before the Kalends of April or after the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May.

Similarly, the Quadragesimal terminus should occur neither before the seventh day before the Ides of February nor after the Nones of March; the Rogation terminus neither before the seventh day before the Kalends of May nor after the tenth day before the Kalends of June; and Pentecost neither before the seventh day before the Ides of May nor after the eighth day before the Ides of June.

[Col. 0712C]

The bishop Theophilus of Alexandria, also of holy memory, in letters sent to the synod at the city of Nicaea in Bithynia, where 319 bishops assembled, or to the emperor Theodosius, announced that from the eighth day before the Ides of March to the Nones of April—that is, for 29 days—whatever moon may have been born within that intervening period, the beginning of the first month is thereby established; and he wrote that the fourteenth moon is to be carefully sought from the twelfth day before the Kalends of April to the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, and that, even if it falls on a Saturday, Easter is to be celebrated on the following Sunday, that is, on the sixteenth moon.

If the fourteenth moon of that month fell on a Sunday, he wrote that Easter should without doubt be celebrated on the next Sunday, after that week had passed, on the twenty-first moon. The holy synod established that this must be guarded against in every way: no one should seek Easter before the vernal equinox, which is the twelfth day before the Kalends of April; nor should Easter ever be celebrated in the lunation born before the eighth day before the Ides of March, or in the lunation of the ninth of April.

[Col. 0712D]

We admonish everyone in every way not to be deceived in recognizing the first month. From this above all arises the single error that causes disagreement about the feast, when the beginning of the period is misunderstood. The beginning of the year and the basis of the leap year must now be sought at the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the fullness of the world.

## As above

If you wish to find the Paschal terminus, look at the epact corresponding to that Paschal terminus. If you find it to be less than 15, complete it to 15 by counting from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April. On whichever calendar date that number is completed, there without doubt will be the terminus.

If you find an epact of 15, the Paschal terminus will be on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. If the epact is greater than 15, complete it to 45, likewise counting from the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. On whichever calendar date that number is completed, there will be the terminus.

When there is no epact, always count from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April until the [Col. 0713A] number 15 is completed, namely, until the Nones of April.

## As above

If you wish to know the date of Easter after several years from the present—for example, after 100 years—it is sufficient to find only the epacts and the solar concurrents. Divide 100 by 19; 5 remain. Know, therefore, that the epacts in the hundredth year will be as in approximately the fifth year. In the same way, dividing 100 by 28, you will find in the hundredth year the concurrents belonging to approximately the fifteenth solar year.

## As above

We read in the Old Testament that the time of Easter was commanded to be observed according to three judgments of the signs: after the equinox, in the first month, during the third week—that is, from the evening of the fourteenth moon, which is the beginning of the fifteenth, until the evening, that is, the terminus of the twenty-first moon.

[Col. 0713B]

A fourth rule was imposed upon us in this observance from the time of Christ’s resurrection: after the equinox has passed, when we see that the fourteenth moon of the first month has risen in the evening, we should not immediately rush to celebrate Easter. Rather, we should await the Sunday on which the Lord deigned, by rising, to make Easter itself—the passage from death to life, from corruption to incorruption, and from punishment to glory.

## As above

Christian Easter is celebrated in every way from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April to the seventh day before the Kalends of May, on whichever Sunday the regular moon occurs.

## The mystery of the fourteenth day on which the lamb is sacrificed

The fourteenth day demonstrates the faith of Christ to us through the Ten Commandments and the four Gospels. The sacrifice of the lamb appropriately takes place on the fourteenth day, because Mesraim, fourteenth from Adam, first sacrificed blood to idols, up to the twenty-first day—that is, in figures of the two laws and their unity.

The lamb was sacrificed on the fourteenth [Col. 0713C] day, when the moon is full and nothing is lacking from its light, because Christ is sacrificed only in a perfect heart and in full light without darkness.

## Finding the position of the fourteenth moon through nineteen years

It is therefore established that in the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, when no epact is placed at the beginning, the moon is 9 on the Kalends of March and 16 on the eighth day before the Ides of March. Subtract 30 from this and begin the first moon; the fourteenth occurs on the Nones of April, which is the first terminus of the nineteen-year cycle.

Again, take the 16 which you had in the preceding year on the eighth day before the Ides of March and add 11; on that same day the moon is 27. When you subtract 30 from this, the next fourteenth moon occurs on the eighth day of April, which is the second terminus.

Continue in this way through each lunation until the nineteenth year, on the same day—namely, the eighth day before the Ides—always adding 11 to the moon’s age on that day in the preceding year. Whenever the result is below 30, subtract it from 30, [Col. 0713D] and continue subtracting from the following number until 14 is reached. Wherever 14 occurs, there without any ambiguity will be the Paschal terminus.

If 30 should fall on that same day—which happens only once in nineteen years—subtract the following number in the usual manner, and wherever 14 occurs, there will be the terminus. When the first moon occurs on the eighth day before the Ides of March, that day will certainly be Paschal.

Take the utmost care not to count as Paschal a moon born before the eighth day before the Ides of March. Whatever age the moon has on that same day, either retain it as 30 or subtract 30 from it; wherever 14 occurs in the following number, do not doubt that it is Paschal.

This order and method has never been, and never can be, disturbed by anyone from the day on which it was established at the Council of Nicaea. Rather, the one who appears to wish to disturb it will himself be shaken.

When the nineteenth year has been completed, together with the final terminus of that year, if you wish to test again that this method is sound by reason and that this authority stands securely on authority, add 11—the number of the [Col. 0714A] Nones—to the lunar age of the preceding year on the often-mentioned eighth day before the Ides of March, adding it first because of the lunar jump of 12. The moon will again occur at the beginning, on that same day, as 16; and thereafter everything will follow in the same order as before.

## Quadragesimal termini indicating the second moon

| Eighth day before the Kalends of March: 5 regular numbers | The eighth of March began the law of the five books. |
| Fourth day before the Ides of February: 1 regular number | But the Ides of February, threefold, honor the one God. |
| Sixth day before the Nones of March: 6 regular numbers | The six Nones carried six vessels with them. |
| Eleventh day before the Kalends of March: 2 regular numbers | The eleven of March receive two just Kalends. |
| Sixth day before the Ides of February: 5 regular numbers | At the Ides, five lively girls stand in sixes. |
| Third day before the Kalends of March: 3 regular numbers | The three Kalends bring back three signs of gifts. |
| [Col. 0714B] Fourteenth day before the Kalends of March: 6 regular numbers | Four and ten grew to six in days. |
| Nones of March: 4 regular numbers | On the Nones, March created twice two elements. |
| Sixth day before the Kalends of March: 7 regular numbers | The sixth of the Kalends bears seven lamps as its rule. |
| Ides of February: 3 regular numbers | At the Ides of February, threefold power is joined. |
| Fourth day before the Nones of March: 1 regular number | The special Nones bear baptism fourfold. |
| Ninth day before the Kalends of March: 4 regular numbers | By strength we grasp the course of nine, twice two. |
| Fourth day before the Ides of February: 7 regular numbers | Seven ministers honored the Ides fourfold. |
| Kalends of March: 5 regular numbers | With five senses, search out the Kalends of March. |
