Whenever you hear “Ides” in these verses, know that they belong to February; when you read “Kalends” or “Nones” in them, understand that they belong to March. Add the regular numbers of these same verses, beginning with the Nones in question and immediately proceeding into March, to the concurrents.

## The beginning and the moon of Quadragesima and Easter

If you wish to know the beginning of Quadragesima, use this method: however many days after the day before the Ides of April Easter falls, that many days after the Kalends of March will be the beginning of Quadragesima. And however many days before the second day before the Ides of April Easter falls, that many days before the Kalends of March will be the beginning of Quadragesima.

Even if Easter falls on the day before the Ides of April, the beginning of Quadragesima will be on the Kalends of March. Likewise, however many days before the Kalends of April Easter falls, that many days before the twelfth day before the Kalends of March [Col. 0714D] will be the beginning of Quadragesima—unless that year happens to be a leap year; then you will find it one day earlier than the twelfth day before the Kalends of March.

If the moon is 3 at the beginning of Quadragesima, it will be 15 at Easter; if it is 4 at the beginning, 16 at Easter; if 5, 17; if 6, 18; if 7, 19; if 8, 20; if 9, 21. Whatever the age of the Paschal moon, if you subtract 12 from it, you will obtain the age of the moon at the beginning.

From the Ides of February to the second Ides of March there are 34 days, and from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April to the seventh day before the Kalends of May there are 34 days. Thus it has been determined that the beginning of Quadragesima can in no way occur before the sixth day before the Ides of February or after the [Col. 0715A] day before the Ides of March, but only within those 34 days.

Concerning Easter, it has been determined in the council of the holy Fathers that it should occur neither before the eleventh day before the Kalends of April nor after the seventh day before the Kalends of May. The moon at the Quadragesimal terminus is not found at the Paschal terminus as the fourteenth moon.

The Sunday of the Paschal feast is therefore regulated according to the fourteenth moon of the first month; so also the beginning of Quadragesima is regulated and observes the second moon of March. For whichever Sunday follows the fourteenth moon of the first month will without doubt be the Sunday of the Paschal feast. The same applies to Quadragesima.

## Fixed termini

The Paschal terminus is sought from the Kalends of April, and the others take their order from it. Observe this carefully: the Paschal terminus and the solemnity itself are never before the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, because the holy Catholic Fathers decreed that Easter should not be celebrated as long as night exceeds day.

But once [Col. 0715B] day begins to exceed night, when the fourteenth moon arrives, the terminus is observed, and on the following Sunday the solemnity of Easter is immediately celebrated by all the faithful. The moon found at the terminus is always the fourteenth.

## Septuagesima

If you wish to find the terminus of Septuagesima, first see how many days the Paschal terminus is distant from the Kalends of April, whether backward or forward. Count the same number of days from the fifth day before the Kalends of February, likewise either forward or backward, and you will find the terminus of Septuagesima without difficulty. The moon at the terminus of Septuagesima is the tenth, which is completed in the month of February. The moon of each month is the one completed within that month.

Seek the Quadragesimal terminus from the twelfth day before the Kalends of March; beginning in every respect, proceed as we said concerning Septuagesima. It is the second moon of March.

Observe in these two termini that in a leap year you must begin seeking them one day later: [Col. 0715C] seek Septuagesima from the fourth day before the Kalends of February and Quadragesima from the eleventh day before the Kalends of March. You will not do this with the other termini.

You will observe this concerning Septuagesima in every leap year. Concerning Quadragesima, however, do so only when that terminus will occur before the leap day. If it will occur after the leap day, then, even in a leap year, begin seeking it from the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, as in other years.

In a leap year the Quadragesimal terminus sometimes falls on the eleventh moon. I have noted this so that, when it occurs, it will not confuse the calculator.

The Rogation terminus is sought from the second day before the Nones of May, and the same number of days is counted as in the other termini. At that terminus the moon is the twentieth.

[Col. 0716A]

The Pentecost terminus is sought from the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, and the same number of days is counted there as in the other termini. At that terminus the moon is the fourth.

All the termini occur on one and the same weekday. Just as Easter, so these other feasts too are extended to Sunday. As we said concerning Easter, understand the same concerning the others: if a terminus falls on Sunday, defer the feast to the following Sunday.

## As above

Remember that throughout the nineteen years the terminus of Septuagesima revolves with the tenth moon of February; that of Quadragesima with the eleventh moon of March; that of Easter with the fourteenth moon of April; that of Rogations with the twentieth moon of May; and that of Pentecost with the fourth moon of June—except in the eighth and nineteenth years, in which the Septuagesimal terminus is established with the eleventh moon of March and the Quadragesimal terminus with the second moon of the embolismic month.

## The positions of the termini

[Col. 0716B]

- After the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, wherever you find the tenth moon, place the Septuagesimal terminus.
- After the eighth day before the Ides of February, wherever you find the second moon, place the Quadragesimal terminus.
- After the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, wherever you find the fourteenth moon, place the Paschal terminus.
- After the seventh day before the Kalends of May, wherever you find the twentieth moon, place the Rogation terminus.
- After the sixth day before the Ides of May, wherever you find the fourth moon, place the Pentecost terminus.

## How the termini of the following year are found from the present year

You can find the terminus of any year very easily in this way: place the terminus of the preceding year at the first joint of the thumb, then proceed by counting across the remaining joints of that and the other fingers. Wherever you arrive when you return to the same joint, there without doubt will be the terminus.

Take care only that you do not wish to celebrate the [Col. 0716C] terminus before the twelfth day before the Kalends of April or after the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May.

## Likewise concerning the termini

It must be noted that in a leap year the Septuagesimal terminus does not observe the positions of the termini described below, because of the leap day. For this reason the terminus must be carried forward by one day, so that it agrees with the Paschal terminus on the same weekday on which the Paschal terminus occurs in that year.

For example, the terminus prescribed for the present year, the tenth day before the Kalends of February, is transferred to the ninth day before the Kalends of February. The same is to be understood of the Quadragesimal terminus, provided that it occurs before the leap day; in a leap year the moon of February will be 30.

## Explanation of the Reckoning of All the Dates in Each Year of the Nineteen-Year Cycle

### Explanation concerning the keys of the dates

[Col. 0717A]

If anyone wishes to find all the dates in any year of the nineteen-year cycle by means of the written regular numbers, let him always take the date of Septuagesima from 7 January, the date of Lent from 28 January, the date of Easter from 10 March, the date of the Rogations from 15 April, and the date of Pentecost from 29 April; and wherever the number noted for the present year comes to an end, there without doubt he will find the date.

### On the Advent of the Lord

Let it be known to everyone that whoever wishes to celebrate the Advent of the Lord carefully should see to it that he does not pass either before 27 November or after 5 December, but during these seven days, wherever Sunday occurs, there he will certainly be able to celebrate, without any ambiguity or error. For a brief reading is read more eagerly and understood more quickly.

### Finding the years from the beginning of the world, and through them the indiction, solar cycle, leap-year cycle, nineteen-year cycle, and lunar cycle

If you wish to know how many years there are from the origin of the world, multiply 409 by fifteen; the result is 6135. Add 7 regular numbers, and also add to them the indiction of the present year: that is the number of years from the origin of the world. After the indiction has been completed—that is, after the fifteenth—you must multiply not fifteen times 409, as now, but fifteen times 410; and then, after another fifteen years, not fifteen times 410 but fifteen times 411. Again, after another fifteen years, not fifteen times 411 but fifteen times 412.

If you wish to verify from those years what the indiction is, add 8 regular numbers to them and divide these by 15: the remainder will be the indiction. If nothing remains, it will be the fifteenth. The reason 8 regular numbers are added is that, when the world was made, approximately eight years remained in the cycle of indictions—not because there was an indiction before the beginning of the world or at the very beginning of the world, for there was no such thing until the time of the Romans, but because in the year when the indiction was first discovered and began to be reckoned, the years elapsed from the beginning of the world, divided into fifteen-year portions because of the indiction cycle, lacked 7 years of the number of a fifteen-year period, as though 7 indictions had preceded the beginning of the world and 8 remained. This is to be understood not only of the indiction cycle but also of the other solar or lunar cycles, when they are found by dividing the years from the origin of the world according to the number of each cycle.

### Finding the solar cycle

[Col. 0717D]

If you wish to know which solar cycle it is, take however many years there have been from the origin of the world, add 17 regular numbers to them, and divide by 28; the remainder is the solar cycle. If nothing remains, it is 28.

### Finding the concurrent numbers

If you wish to know the concurrent numbers, retain the years from the origin of the world and add to them one quarter of their number; combine the resulting numbers into one total and divide it by 7. The remainder is the concurrent number. If nothing remains, it will be 7.

### Finding the leap year

If you wish to know which year after the leap year it is, take the years from the origin of the world and divide them by 4. The remainder—for example, 1, 2, or 3—indicates the year after the leap year. If nothing remains, it is a leap year.

### Finding the nineteen-year cycle

[Col. 0718A]

If you wish to know which year of the nineteen-year cycle it is, take the years mentioned above, add 7 regular numbers to them, and divide them by 19. The remainder is the year of the nineteen-year cycle. If nothing remains, it is the nineteenth.

### Finding the lunar cycle

If you wish to know which lunar cycle it is, retain the years as stated above, add 4 regular numbers, and divide them by 19. The remainder is the lunar cycle. If nothing remains, it is the nineteenth.

### Finding the epacts

If you wish to know which epact it is, take the years from the beginning of the world, add 6 regular numbers, and divide them by 19. Multiply the remainder by eleven, and divide the result again by 30. The remainder is the epact. If nothing remains, it is 30—that is, the one which at the beginning is called “none.”

### Finding the years from the incarnation of the Lord, and through them the other matters mentioned above

[Col. 0718B]

If you wish to know how many years there are from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus, multiply 62 by fifteen; the result is 930. Add 12 regular numbers, add the indiction of the same year whose number you wish to calculate, and combine them: the total is the number of years from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Be especially careful to remember this: as the years succeed one another, whenever you reach the fifteenth indiction—for example, if you have been calculating fifteen times 62, you must then calculate 63, that is, in the year following the fifteenth indiction. After fifteen years, when the first indiction returns, multiply not 62 by fifteen as before, but 63. When the first indiction returns again, multiply 64; and when it returns once more, multiply 65 by fifteen.

### Finding the indiction

[Col. 0718C]

If you wish to know which indiction it is, take the years from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, add 3 regular numbers to them, and divide by 15. The remainder indicates the indiction; if nothing remains, it is 15.

### Finding the solar cycle

If you wish to know which year of the solar cycle it is, take however many years there have been from the incarnation of the Lord, add 9 regular numbers, and divide the total by 28. The remainder is the solar cycle; if nothing remains, it is 28.

### Likewise

If you wish to know the position within the sequence of the solar cycle, determine how many years of the Lord there have been and subtract 8 from them, because that many years remained in the same solar cycle when the Lord was incarnate. Divide the remainder by 28; the resulting remainder is the year in the sequence of that cycle.

### Finding the concurrent numbers

[Col. 0718D]

If you wish to find the concurrent numbers, take however many years there have been from the incarnation of the Lord, always add one quarter of them, and in addition add 4. Divide the total by 7: the remainder is the concurrent number. If nothing remains, it is 7.

### The leap year

If you wish to know which year from the leap year it is, take the years mentioned above, without adding or subtracting anything. Divide them by 4. The remainder indicates the year after the leap year; if nothing remains, it is a leap year.

### The nineteen-year cycle

If you wish to know which year of the nineteen-year cycle it is, take the years from the incarnation of the Lord and always add 1. Divide them by 19; the remainder is the nineteen-year cycle. If nothing remains, it is 19.

### The lunar cycle

[Col. 0719A]

If you wish to know which lunar cycle it is, take the years as stated above, subtract 2 from them, and divide the remainder by 19. The remainder is the lunar cycle; if nothing remains, it is 19.

### Finding the epacts

If you wish to know how many epacts there are, take the years mentioned above, divide them by 19, multiply the remainder by eleven, and divide the result again by 30. The remainder is the epact.

## Examples of the foregoing calculations, using the years from the origin of the world

If you wish to know how many years there are from the origin of the world, multiply 409 by fifteen; the result is 6135. Add 7 regular numbers, making 6142; also add the indiction of the present year, which is the second, making 6144.

**Disciple.** How?

**Master.** 400, 800, 1200, 1600, 2000, 4000, 6000; 9, 18, 27, 36, 45, 90, 135. Combine [Col. 0719B] them: 6135. Add 7 regular numbers, making 6142; add the second indiction, making 6144. Thus, according to our calculation, there are 6144 years from the beginning of the world to the present year, which is without doubt the 944th year from the incarnation of the Lord, according to the cycle of Dionysius.

### The indiction

Divide 6144 by 15; the remainder is the indiction.

**Disciple.** How?

**Master.** 15, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180, 210, 240, 270, 300, 600, 900, 1200, 1500, 1800, 2100, 2400, 2700, 3000, 6000. The remainder is 152. Divide this by 15: 15, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150; two remain. The second indiction is therefore this year.

### Finding the solar cycle

Divide this by 28; the remainder is the solar cycle.

**Disciple.** How?

**Master.** 28, 56, 112, 224, 448, 896; 28, 56, 112 make 1008; six times 1008 makes 6048; 113 remain. Divide these again by 28: 28, [Col. 0719C] 56, 112; 1 remains. This year is the first in the sequence of the solar cycle.

### Finding the concurrent numbers

Divide this by 7; the remainder is the concurrent number.

**Disciple.** How?

**Master.** Add 1500 to 6000, and 36 to 144, since that is one quarter of the latter; the total is 7680. Divide this by 7.

**Disciple.** How?

**Master.** Fifty times 7 is 350; 700; 1050. Seven times 1050 is 7305; 330 remain. Divide these again by 7: forty times 7 is 280, and 50 remain. Divide these by 7: seven times 7 is 49; 1 remains. The first concurrent number is this year.

### Finding the leap year

Divide this by 4. The remainder—for example, 1, 2, or 3—indicates the year after the leap year.

**Disciple.** How?

**Master.** 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100; ten times 100 is 1000; six times 1000 is 6000, leaving 144. Divide this again by 4: five times 4 is 20; five times 20 is 100, and 44 remain. Divide these by 4: eleven times 4 is 44. Now nothing remains, because this is a leap year.

### Finding the nineteen-year cycle

Divide this by 19; the remainder is the nineteen-year cycle.

**Disciple.** How?

**Master.** 19, 38, 57, 76, 95, 114, 133, 152, 171, 190, 209, 228, 247, 266, 285, 304, 608, 912; 19, 38, 57, 76, 95, which together make 1007. Six times 1007 is 6042; 109 remain. Divide these again by 19: 19, 38, 57, 76, 95; 14 remain. This year is the fourteenth in the sequence of the nineteen-year cycle.

### The lunar cycle

Divide this by 19; the remainder is the lunar cycle.

**Disciple.** How?

**Master.** Divide as above: 106 remain. Divide these again by 19: 19, 38, [Col. 0720A] 57, 76, 95; 11 remain. This year is the eleventh in the sequence of the lunar cycle.

### Finding the epact

Divide this by 19; multiply the remainder by eleven; divide the result again by thirty. The remainder is the epact.

**Disciple.** How?

**Master.** If you divide this whole number by 19, as above, 108 remain. Divide these again by 19: 19, 38, 57, 76, 95; 13 remain. Multiply this by eleven.

**Disciple.** How?

**Master.** Eleven times 10 is 110; eleven times 3 is 33; together they make 144. Divide this by thirty: 30, 60, 90, 120; 23 remain, because there are 23 epacts this year.

## The years of the Lord and the other calculations mentioned above

If you wish to know how many years there are from the incarnation of the Lord, multiply 62 by fifteen.

**Disciple.** How?

**Master.** 60, 120, 180, 240, 300, 600, 900. Twice 15 is 30; add 12 regular numbers, making 942; add the indiction of the present year, [Col. 0720B] which is the second, making 944. Thus, without doubt, there are 944 years from the incarnation of the Lord, according to the cycle of Dionysius.

### The indiction

Divide this by 15; the remainder indicates the indiction.

**Disciple.** How?

**Master.** 15, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180, 210, 240, 270, 300, 600, 900; 47 remain. Divide these again by 15: three times 15 is 45; two remain. The second indiction is therefore this year.

### The solar cycle

Divide the total by 28; the remainder is the solar cycle.

**Disciple.** How?

**Master.** 28, 56, 112, 224, 448, 896; 57 remain. Divide these again by 28: 28, 56; 1 remains. This year is the first in the sequence of the solar cycle.

### The concurrent numbers

Divide this by 7; the remainder is the concurrent number.

**Disciple.** How?

**Master.** Add 225 to 900, and 44[lacuna], since that is one quarter of them, [Col. 0720C] and the total will be [lacuna]84. Divide this by 7.

**Disciple.** How?

**Master.** Fifty times 7 is 350; 700; 1050; 134 remain. Divide these again by 7: ten times 7 is 70, leaving 64. Divide these by 7: nine times 7 is 63; 1 remains. The first concurrent number is this year.

### The leap year

Divide this by 4; the remainder indicates the year after the leap year.

**Disciple.** How?

**Master.** 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 200, 300, 600, 900; 44 remain. Divide these again by 4: eleven times 4 is 44. Now nothing remains, because this is a leap year.

### The nineteen-year cycle

Divide this by 19; the remainder is the nineteen-year cycle.

**Disciple.** How?

**Master.** 19, 38, 57, 76, 95, 114, 133, 152, 171, 190, 209, 228, 247, 266, 285, 304, 608, 912; 33 remain. Set aside 19; [Col. 0720D] 14 remain. This year is the fourteenth in the sequence of the nineteen-year cycle.

### The lunar cycle

Divide the remainder by 19; the remainder is the lunar cycle.

**Disciple.** How?

**Master.** Divide by 19 as above: 30 remain. Set aside 19; 11 remain. This year is the eleventh in the sequence of the lunar cycle.

### Finding the epact

Divide this by 19; multiply the remainder by eleven; divide the result again by 30. The remainder is the epact.

**Disciple.** How?

**Master.** In the same way as above. Set aside 912; 32 remain. From these subtract 19; 13 remain. Multiply this by eleven.

**Disciple.** How?

**Master.** Eleven times 10 is 110; eleven times 3 is 33; together they make 144. Divide this by 30: 30, 60, 90, 120; 23 remain, because there are 23 epacts this year.

[Col. 0721A]

In every calculation that you perform, if nothing remains above, know that the calculation has been completed. For example, if you divide the years of the Lord by 4 and nothing remains, it is a leap year. If you are seeking the indiction and, after the fifteenth, nothing remains from the division, know that the indiction is the fifteenth. Understand the same concerning the other calculations.

### Another example, which we verify from the calculations written above

If you wish to know how many years there are from the incarnation of the Lord, multiply 76 by fifteen; add 4 regular numbers, because 11 years of that indiction had preceded and 4 still remained; moreover, add the indiction of the year whose number you wish to calculate—for example, 8 in the present year—and together they make 972, although according to Dionysius 950 are found this year, as appears in his cycle. After the indiction has been completed, add 1.

### Finding the indiction

If you wish to know which indiction it is, take the years mentioned above, [Col. 0721B] add 11 regular numbers to them—namely, the years that preceded the incarnation itself—and divide by 15. The remainder indicates the indiction.

### Finding the solar cycle

If you wish to know which year of the solar cycle it is, take the years mentioned above, add 15 to them, because that many years of the same cycle had preceded and 13 remained, and divide by 28. The remainder indicates the year of the solar cycle.

### Finding the concurrent numbers

If you wish to know the concurrent numbers, take the years mentioned above and first subtract 2 from them because of the leap year, which at that time occurred in the second year. Then add to the remainder one quarter of the whole number, and divide by 7. The remainder is the number of concurrent numbers.

### The leap year

[Col. 0721C]

If you wish to know whether it is a leap year or which year after it it is, take the years mentioned above and subtract 2 from them because of the leap year, which, as stated above, occurred then in the second year. Divide the remainder by 4: however many remain are the years after the leap year. If nothing remains, it is a leap year.

### Finding the nineteen-year cycle

If you wish to know which year of the nineteen-year cycle it is, take the years mentioned above and subtract 2 from them because that many years still remained in the same cycle; then divide by 19. The remainder indicates the year of the nineteen-year cycle. If nothing remains, it is 19.

### The lunar cycle

If you wish to know which year of the lunar cycle it is, retain the years mentioned above and subtract 5 from them, because that many years still remained in the same cycle; divide [Col. 0721D] by 19. The remainder indicates the year of the lunar cycle.

### Finding the epact

If you wish to know how many epacts there are, take the years mentioned above and subtract 3 from them, so that you may arrive at the second year of the nineteen-year cycle, where the cycle of the epacts begins. Divide the remainder by 19; multiply the remainder by eleven; and if that number remains below 30, know that it is the number of epacts for that year. If it exceeds 30, subtract 30 and regard the remainder as the epacts. Let only the person who can rightly criticize the author of these calculations disregard this method.

## The sequence of the indictions

“Indiction” is so called from *indicere*, “to proclaim” or “impose.” When the Romans ruled all nations, they imposed tribute on everyone, which was always paid in the fifth year: bronze was paid in the first five-year period, silver in the second, and gold in the third; in the fourth the cycle was again begun from the start, [Col. 0722A] that is, with bronze. Thus, by joining three five-year periods, individual indictions of fifteen years were established. It was also decreed that no book and no edict of the ruler should be considered valid unless it carried an indiction. After each five-year census had been completed, it was customary to purify the city, that is, to go around it, as if for its purification. Hence a five-year period is also called a *lustrum*, and we very often say *lustrare*, “to purify.”

### Likewise

We learn that the ancient Roman diligence established indictions to prevent the confusion that might perhaps arise concerning dates. For example, if an emperor died or lost his rule in the middle of a year, it could happen that one historian assigned that year to the reign of that ruler because he had ruled part of it, while another historian thought that the same year ought rather to be assigned to his successor, because the latter too possessed an equal part of it in his reign. But so that error might not grow out of such disagreement concerning dates, they established indictions, by which both writers—and indeed even the common people—could preserve the entire course of time very easily. For ease of calculation they decided that there should be fifteen of them.

## The origin of the concurrent numbers

If you wish to know where the concurrent numbers take their beginning, it is certainly from the seven days through which the world revolves, because the number of concurrent numbers does not go beyond seven, nor does the number of the days of the week.

**Disciple.** From where does the first concurrent number at the beginning take its origin?

**Master.** The solar year has 365 days. Divide these by 7: seven times 52 is 364, leaving 1. From this, the first concurrent number is placed at the beginning. Then, in the second year, add 1; in the third, 2; in the fourth, 3; and in the fifth, the leap year, add 5. Take careful pains in this matter: during the other years of preparation for the leap year, as we said above, always add one after one; in the leap year add two; and take care not to go beyond seven, but always return to one after seven. Continue in this way through 28 lines. Pay close attention, and you will not be mistaken in this matter.

## Points, the quarter-day, and the leap year

One point is a quarter of an hour and makes 10 moments; two points make 20 moments; three, 30; four, 40. These 40 moments make one hour. Six hours in one year make one quarter-day; and four quarter-days in four years make one day and night. This is the day called the leap day, which is read as 6 Kalends of March. For example, if today is read as 6 Kalends of March and tomorrow also as 6 Kalends of March, it is called *bissextus* because 6 Kalends of March is read twice.

### Likewise

It should not be believed, as some think, that the leap day is made because of that day when Joshua prayed for the sun to stand still, since that day existed and passed. Rather, it is called *bissextus* because one point increases in each month. One point is a quarter of an hour. Four points in the course of the sun make one hour, while twelve points unfold three hours. Therefore, in four years the three hours, which are twelve points, make one artificial day, which is added to February when it has reached 6 Kalends of March, so that it may have the same date on the following day. For example, if today is 6 Kalends of March, that day which has been completed in four years is added; nevertheless, the following day is also read as 6 Kalends of March. It is therefore called *bissextus* because February has 6 Kalends of March twice. For this reason the Romans decided that the leap day should be intercalated in February, because February was shorter than the others and was the final month of the year.

### Likewise

The leap year is one day added every four years. For each year a quarter of an *as* increases; when it has completed an *as* in the fourth year, it makes a leap year. It is called *bissextus* because twice six times makes an *as*: this is one day, [Col. 0723A] just as a quarter is so called because it is made by multiplying four times. The leap day that the sun adds to the annual course of the days is inserted from 6 Nones of March until 2 Kalends of January in the course of the moon, and from there it is withdrawn. Intercalary days are so called because they are inserted, so that the reckoning of the moon and sun may correspond. For *calare* means “to place”; *intercalare*, “to insert.”

## Who first discovered the leap year

**Disciple.** Who first discovered the leap year?

**Master.** Julius Caesar discovered it in the forty-eighth year before the birth of Christ and decreed that it should be named.

**Disciple.** Why is it called *bissextus*?

**Master.** Because “twice six”—6 and 6—before one comes to the Kalends of March is intended by one name to signify two days: one natural and the other artificial.

**Disciple.** For what reason is it placed among the days of the year?

**Master.** Each year produces one quarter; when four quarters have been completed, they make a full day, which is called the leap day. It is collected through 1,360 days and is like an arrival and a traveler.

**Disciple.** Why is it called *bissextus*, and what would happen if there were no leap year?

**Master.** The leap year occurs because the solar year does not complete 365 days without the quarter. The quarter is formed throughout the whole year, in each month, and through days and years the moments are gathered.

**Disciple.** How are they gathered?

**Master.** Two portions of a moment are gathered in each day and night. In three days two moments are gathered; likewise, in thirty days and nights twenty moments are gathered. Thus throughout the whole year 240 moments are gathered. These are 24 points, which make six hours—that is, one quarter-day.

## How one year increases through the leap years

In four years, one day; in eight, two; in twelve, three; in sixteen, four; in twenty, five days increase. In twenty-eight years they complete a week; in forty years, thirty days; in 120 years, they prepare one ounce of a year; in 340 years, they show two months; in 480 years, four months are demonstrably present, which is one third of a year. [Col. 0723C] In 960 years, it is clear that there is half a year. In 1460 years, a complete year—that is, 365 days—is established.

## The difference between the nineteen-year cycle and the lunar cycle

It is useful for readers to know what the difference is between the nineteen-year cycle and the lunar cycle. We know that both cycles follow the moon and that both have nineteen years. The nineteen-year cycle was divinely revealed to holy Moses, at the Lord’s command, so that those who lived far away might know to celebrate Passover in the second month; and it varies according to the days of the sun, that is, with respect to the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month.

Next we must investigate who established the lunar cycle, or at what time it was discovered. It is established that it was discovered by the Romans thirty years before the birth of Christ, that is, in the first year of the reign of Herod, son of Antipater the Ascalonite, who was the first foreigner to acquire the kingdom of the Jews from Octavian by gifts, and who reigned for 37 years. And just as the nineteen-year cycle, according to the legal institution of the Hebrews, begins with the fourteenth day of the moon at Passover and ends there, so the Romans established that the lunar cycle should begin at the Kalends of January and end there, and that through each year the age of the moon should be determined, even to the point of identifying each day the hour and point at which it is illuminated or extinguished.

And just as the nineteen-year cycle proceeds through two common years followed by a third embolismic year, so the lunar cycle proceeds in a similar order, except that the fourth year of the nineteen-year cycle is itself the first year of the lunar cycle.

## The origin of the epacts

If you wish to know where the epacts arise—that is, the additions of the moon—take the days of the solar year and of the common lunar year. The solar year has 365 days, the lunar year 354. The solar year has eleven more days than the lunar year. From these are made the epacts, [Col. 0724A] that is, eleven lunar additions at the beginning. Take these eleven as the epacts at the beginning.

Or in another way: take five intercalary days and add six half-moons together; they make eleven, so there are eleven at the beginning. Regard these as the additions from which the others arise in the following manner. Add the eleven you found, and add another eleven: they are 22. Take these as the epact for the next year. Again add eleven to 22: they make 33. Cut off 30; 3 remain, and take these as the epact. Again add 11 to 3: they make 14. The whole of the next epact follows. Proceeding in this way, you will find the epacts very easily. Only remember not to go beyond 30.

At the end of the nineteenth year you will have 18 epacts. Add 11 to 18: they make 29. Add the lunar leap, and they make 30. Here it appears that it does not add but leaps backward by one day. This thirtieth epact is at the beginning. Therefore combine these epacts and the regular numbers—namely, 5 for September, 5 for October, and so on to the end—and if the total exceeds 30, subtract 30. The remainder will be the age of the moon on the Kalends [Col. 0724B] of each month when it is a common year. In embolismic years, therefore, take careful account.

## The great cycle

If you wish to know how the great cycle arises, know this: the solar cycle is 28, and the lunar cycle is 19. Multiplied by one another, they make the great cycle. That is, if you multiply 19 by 28, they make 532 years, which is the great year, in which all the stars of heaven return to their original course.

## The solstices and equinoxes

There are two solstices. The first is the winter solstice, on 8 Kalends of January, the day on which our Lord Jesus Christ was born according to the flesh from the Virgin Mary in Bethlehem. At that time the sun stands still and the days begin to grow longer.

The second is the summer solstice, on 8 Kalends of July, the day on which, in the province of Palestine, in the city of Sebaste, Saint John the Baptist was born, and in Ephesus Saint John the Evangelist; then the sun stands still and the days begin to grow shorter.

[Col. 0724C]

Opposite these are two equinoxes. The first is the spring equinox, on 8 Kalends of April, when the lengthening day is equal to the night. On that day occurred the conception of holy Mary, Mother of God, when she was greeted by the angel; on that same day our Lord Jesus Christ also suffered according to the flesh in Jerusalem.

The other is the autumn equinox, on 8 Kalends of October, when the shortening day is equal to the night. On that day occurred the conception of Saint John the Baptist at the fortress of Machaerus.

From 8 Kalends of April to 8 Kalends of January, 275 days are counted. Therefore, according to the number of days, Christ our Lord was conceived on Sunday, 8 Kalends of April, and was born on Tuesday, 8 Kalends of January. From his birth until the day on which he suffered there are 32 years and 3 months, 12,414 days. Thus, according to the number of days, it is established that he was born on Tuesday and suffered on Friday: born on 8 Kalends of January and suffering on 8 Kalends of April.

From the time our Lord was baptized [Col. 0724D] until the day on which he suffered there are 2 years and 90 days, making 810 days. Thus he was baptized on 8 Ides of January, Monday, and suffered, as I said above, on 8 Kalends of April, Friday. With his own days included, the total is 12,414 days, and from 8 Kalends of January to 8 Kalends of April there are 90 days.

## Various calculations

If you wish to know why you add seven regular numbers in the calculation from the beginning of the world, remember that the Lord made heaven and earth in seven days and ordained that there should be seven future days; for this reason they are used in the calculation.

**Disciple.** And why does he command multiplication by fifteen?

**Master.** Because the indiction cycle has no more than fifteen years.

**Disciple.** Why is the solar cycle divided into 28 parts?

**Master.** Because it completes its course in 28 years.

**Disciple.** Why are 4 regular numbers added in the lunar cycle?

**Master.** Because the moon has a quarter just as the sun does, and for this reason four regular numbers are admitted; or because four regular numbers are used since, earlier in the nineteen-year cycle, the lunar cycle is inserted in the fourth year.

**Disciple.** Why is it divided into nineteen parts?

**Master.** Because it does not rise beyond nineteen years, but is counted first again.

**Disciple.** Why are seven regular numbers also placed in the nineteen-year cycle?

**Master.** If you understand, you will find the answer completely. Pay attention to what he says: in the lunar cycle you take 4 regular numbers. Then count how many years earlier the nineteen-year cycle is: unquestionably 3. Add 3 to 4; they make 7. These 7 are to be taken in the nineteen-year cycle, and divided into nineteen parts.

**Disciple.** Why into those parts?

**Master.** Because it completes its own name. The nineteen-year cycle is so called because it runs through nineteen years, and for this reason it is divided by nineteen.

**Disciple.** Why do you add nothing for the leap year except the years from the beginning of the world?

**Master.** Without doubt because the substance of the leap year has always been prepared from the beginning.

**Disciple.** Why did he also count 12 regular numbers to find the years of the Lord?

**Master.** Because he did not think that a complete indiction could be made from that number unless he had said to add 12.

**Disciple.** Why are three regular numbers used to find the indiction?

**Master.** Because when the incarnation of the Lord took place, three years of that indiction had preceded it.

**Disciple.** Why does he command division into fifteen parts?

**Master.** Because the indiction cycle runs through fifteen years.

**Disciple.** Why are the epacts divided into nineteen parts?

**Master.** Because the cycle of the epacts varies through nineteen years.

**Disciple.** Why does he again command multiplication by eleven?

**Master.** Because eleven additions accrue each year.

**Disciple.** Why does he again command division into thirty parts?

**Master.** Because it does not rise beyond thirty.

**Disciple.** Why does he command the solar cycle to be added for finding the concurrent numbers?

**Master.** Because leap years are counted through the solar cycle.

**Disciple.** Why does he command one quarter to be added, and what is the quarter?

**Master.** The quarter is the leap-year portion from the beginning of the cycle to its end. For this reason he commands that quarter to be added, because the leap year occurs in the fourth year.

**Disciple.** Why does he command division into seven parts?

**Master.** Because the concurrent numbers do not rise beyond seven.

**Disciple.** Why does he command one regular number to be added to the nineteen-year cycle?

**Master.** Because when the incarnation took place, one year of the nineteen-year cycle had preceded it. Observe how: Christ was conceived on 8 Kalends of April; the Nones of April had already passed, and for this reason he adds one.

**Disciple.** Why does he command division by nineteen parts?

**Master.** Because it runs through nineteen years.

**Disciple.** Why does he command two regular numbers to be subtracted from the lunar cycle?

**Master.** Because when the incarnation took place, two years of the lunar cycle remained.

**Disciple.** Why does he command division by nineteen parts?

**Master.** Because it does not rise beyond nineteen.

## When the years, epacts, indictions, and other cycles change

The years from the origin of the world change every year on 18 March. The years from the incarnation of the Lord change on 25 December. The epacts begin, according to the Egyptians, at the Kalends of September, and according to the Romans at the Kalends of January. The indictions begin on 24 September and end there. The lunar cycle [Col. 0725D] begins and ends at the Kalends of January. The concurrent numbers begin at the Kalends of March and end there. The common year, the embolismic year, and the nineteen-year cycle begin with the first moon of the first month—that is, with the moon which indicates the date of Easter—in the year in which the first moon is on 23 March.

## On the weekday and the moon: a dialogue between a child and a child
Question: On what weekday did the Kalends of January fall this year? Answer: On the third day [Tuesday].

—Q. How do you know? A. January has three regular numbers, according to the Egyptians, for determining the weekday at its beginning, and the concurrent numbers were then seven; joined together, they make ten. Removing seven, three remain. Alternatively, January has two regular numbers according to the Romans. If we add to them one concurrent number—namely, the one that follows the seven concurrent numbers mentioned above—we likewise obtain three: the Kalends, the sixth day before the Ides, and the nineteenth, eighteenth, seventeenth, sixteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days before the Kalends of February fall on the sixth day [Friday].

—Q. How do you know this? A. February has six regular numbers; these, together with the seven concurrent numbers, appear to yield thirteen. Removing seven, six remain: the Kalends, the sixth day before the Ides, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, the fifteenth, and the eighth day before the Kalends of March fall on the sixth day [Friday].

—Q. How can you be certain of this? A. The five regular numbers of March and one concurrent number are said to make six: the Kalends, the eighth day before the Ides, the Ides, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, the sixteenth, fifteenth, and eighth day before the Kalends of April fall on the second day [Monday].

—Q. How can you prove this? A. April has one regular number, and we join to it one concurrent number; together they make two: the Kalends, the sixth day before the Ides, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, the seventeenth, sixteenth, fifteenth, and eighth day before the Kalends of May fall on the fourth day [Wednesday].

—Q. How do you know? A. Its three regular numbers and one concurrent number show four: the Kalends, the eighth day before the Ides, the Ides, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June, the sixteenth and fifteenth day before the Kalends of June fall on the seventh day [Sunday].

—Q. How can we know this? A. It has six regular numbers, and we have one concurrent number. Added together, this number is believed to yield seven: the Kalends, the sixth day before the Ides, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July, the seventeenth, sixteenth, fifteenth, and eighth day before the Kalends of July fall on the second day [Monday].

—Q. How does it show this? A. One regular number and one concurrent number make two: the Kalends, the eighth day before the Ides, the Ides, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, the sixteenth and fifteenth day before the Kalends of August fall on the fifth day [Thursday].

—Q. How is this evident? A. August has four regular numbers, and there is now one concurrent number; joined together, this number is seen to make five: the Kalends, the sixth day before the Ides, the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September, the eighteenth, sixteenth, fifteenth, and eighth day before the Kalends of September fall on the first day [Saturday].

—Q. Tell us whether this is so or not. A. September has seven regular numbers. If we join to them the frequently mentioned concurrent number, we shall undoubtedly have eight. Taking away seven, one remains: the Kalends, the sixth day before the Ides, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, the twenty-second [reading uncertain], sixteenth, fifteenth, and eighth day before the Kalends of October fall on the third day [Tuesday].

—Q. Work out that number. A. One and two together make three: the Kalends, the eighth day before the Ides, the Ides, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, the sixteenth and fifteenth day before the Kalends of November fall on the sixth day [Friday].

—Q. By what method can this be seen? A. Five and one make six: the Kalends, the sixth day before the Ides, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of December, the seventeenth, sixteenth, fifteenth, and eighth day before the Kalends of December fall on the first day [Saturday].

—Q. How can we know this? A. One and seven appear to produce eight. Seven being removed, one remains: the Kalends, the sixth day before the Ides, the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January, the eighteenth, sixteenth, fifteenth, and eighth day before the Kalends of January fall on the fourth day [Wednesday].

—Q. Make this clear. A. One and three are believed to yield four.

—Q. What weekday is today? A. The sixth [Friday].

—Q. How do you know? A. May has three regular numbers for determining the weekday, and the concurrent numbers are now three; joined together, they make six. Today is therefore the sixth day.

—Q. What is the age of the moon? A. Twenty.

—Q. How is this evident? A. May has eleven regular numbers for determining the moon’s age, and the epacts are now nine; joined together, they make twenty. We therefore believe that the moon is twenty days old today.

—Q. What weekday is today? A. The seventh [Sunday]. How is this evident? There are now two days of this month; one being subtracted, the other remains. If we join it to the six regular numbers—that is, to the number of the weekday that fell on the Kalends—we clearly see that the total is seven.

—Q. What is the age of the moon? A. Twenty-one.

—Q. How can we recognize this? A. There are, as we said, two days of the month. If we separate one of them and attach twenty to the other, together they are twenty-one; although silently, they disclose the moon’s age.

—Q. What weekday is today? A. The first [Sunday].

—Q. How is this certain? A. Two days of this month have now passed. If we count them together with the six regular numbers, we have eight plainly before us. Seven being set aside, one remains, because it is the first day.

—Q. What is the age of the moon? A. Twenty-two.

—Q. How are you certain of this? A. We know that two days of this month have passed. If we add to them twenty—the moon’s age at the beginning of this month—twenty-two appears, signifying the moon’s present age.

—Q. What weekday is read as today? A. The sixth [Friday].

—Q. How can we know this? A. One hundred and twenty days of the present year have passed. If, therefore, we join to them the number of the weekday that fell at the beginning of this year—namely, four—and also add the leap-day, then divide this total by seven, six remain undivided; these indicate the aforesaid weekday.

—Q. What is the moon’s age today? A. I think, twenty.

—Q. How is this to be believed? A. As we have already said, 120 days of the year have passed. If we count together with them the moon’s age on the Kalends of January, namely eighteen, they make 138 in all. After subtracting 118, which are the days of four lunations, the remainder reveals the moon’s age.

—Q. With how many points does the twentieth-day moon shine? A. Forty; according to Pliny’s reckoning, three moments and one-third of a moment less.

—Q. How many hours? A. Eight.

—Q. How should we investigate this? A. From 20 to 30 there are 10; multiplied by four, these make 40, which are the points of eight hours.

—Q. How many parts is the twentieth-day moon distant from the sun? A. Four times 20 is 80; three times 80 is 240. It is therefore 240 parts distant from the sun, and we believe that after the same number of days it will reach the same sun at the place through which the present moon is passing.

—Q. In what sign was the new moon recently? A. In Aries.

—Q. In what degree? A. In the twenty-sixth.

—Q. On what calendar date? A. On the second day before the Ides of April.

—Q. In what sign is it dwelling today? A. We cannot easily answer this unless we examine the matter from every side. We know that the sun is now dwelling in Taurus, has already completed fourteen days there, and has sixteen still remaining to complete the sign. These sixteen must be supplied to Taurus, so that the sun’s course within it may be completed, from the parts by which we find the moon separated from the sun. Subtracting sixteen from 240, and reckoning the remaining 224 by groups of thirty, fourteen remain; these lead us to infer that the moon is spending that many parts in Capricorn.

—Q. At what hour, or at what point, will the moon today be illuminated by the sun? A. The lunar cycle is now the seventh. If we multiply it by five, obtaining 35, and join this number to the 120 days of the present year and to one, then divide by 60, 36 remain; these are the points of this day. They show that the moon is illuminated by the sun at the first point of the eighth hour. But if we again turn the aforesaid cycle six times, and join together the 36 points that remained, two units for the two sixties, and also the present day, then divide by 30, twenty-one remain undivided; these disclose the age that the moon has entered at the hour of its illumination.

—Q. In what sign was the new moon recently? A. In Aries.

—Q. In what degree? A. In the twenty-sixth.

—Q. On what calendar date? A. On the day before the Ides of April.

—Q. What is the moon’s age? A. Twenty.

—Q. In what sign is it dwelling today? A. Have I not worked this out above as well as I could? Nevertheless, if you wish, we shall repeat it more closely. The present moon was born in the twenty-sixth degree of Aries and afterward retained four degrees, through which it ran; it subtracted twenty and six, which it did not touch. If you wish to prove in what sign the twenty-day moon is today, multiply 20, its age, by four; this gives 80 quadrants. Again multiply one of these quadrants by 6, because there are six hours in each quadrant, and also take six points from the seventy-ninth quadrant. You will have seven hours and one point, which must be assigned to Aries, since the moon ran through that many hours of it when it was new. Finally, take the 78 quadrants that remained and assign nine to Taurus, nine to Gemini, nine to Cancer, nine to Leo, nine to Virgo, nine to Libra, nine to Scorpio, and nine to Sagittarius. Six quadrants then remain, together with four hours and four points—that is, forty hours and four points. Of these four hours, however, two hours must be assigned to the six signs because of their half-hours. There therefore remain 36 hours and four points, through which the moon is now flying in Capricorn.

—Q. In what sign was the new moon recently? A. In Aries.

—Q. In what degree? A. In the twenty-sixth.

—Q. On what calendar date? A. On the second day before the Ides of April.

—Q. What is the moon’s age? A. Twenty-seven.

—Q. In what sign is it dwelling today? A. Do you ask this again and again? See that you do it for the sake of learning rather than for the sake of criticism. We know that the sun is still dwelling in Taurus, has already completed twenty-two days there, and still has eight of the thirty remaining—that is, eight days to complete the sign. These must be supplied to Taurus, so that the sun’s course in it may be completed, from the parts by which we find the moon separated from the sun. Subtracting eight from 324, and reckoning the 316 that remain by groups of thirty, sixteen remain undivided; these designate the moon as being in Aries by sixteen degrees.

—Q. I shall inquire further, so that I may at least discover some distance. In what sign was the new moon recently? A. In Aries.

—Q. In what degree? A. In the twenty-sixth.

—Q. On what calendar date? A. On the day before the Ides of April.

—Q. What is the moon’s age? A. Twenty-seven.

—Q. In what sign is it dwelling today? A. Four times 20 and 7 make 100 and 8 quadrants. Of these quadrants, the first thing to subtract is thirty-six points—that is, seven hours and one point—because the moon retained this amount from Aries when it was new. We must then distribute the remainder, namely 107 quadrants less one hour and one point, among the signs. Eleven times nine is 99. Thus, if I am not mistaken, the moon has traversed eleven signs since it was born: Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces. Seven quadrants remain, together with four hours and four points—that is, 47 hours, excluding one point. Of these hours, twelve half-hours—that is, eight hours—must be removed, so that every three signs may have 27 quadrants and, in addition, two hours. There still remain 38 hours and four points. We therefore say that the moon has now traversed that many hours and points through Aries. But when we immediately add to Aries the eight hours in which the moon customarily remains after twenty-seven days, nothing will be lacking from its eight quadrants, because the first moon traversed Aries in seven hours and one point.

# THE COMMON COMPUTUS, CALLED THE EPHEMERIS, CONCERNING THE WEEKDAY AND THE MOON, AND THOSE THINGS THAT PERTAIN TO THE MOON—THAT IS, EPACTS, MONTHS, SIGNS, TERMS, AND THE YEARS OF THE NINETEEN-YEAR CYCLE

## PROEM

[Col. 0727D] This equilateral square, called a tetragon, advances from 30 to 900. Its division into five groups of six gives the reader an opportunity to exercise himself in each of the mathematical disciplines. For, by connecting the properties of the means of the three arts, such a division displays the following numbers: arithmetic, 6, 12, 18; music, 12, 18, 24; geometry, 6, 12, 24.

The line of the twentieth term of the total is A, which in the lowest space is counted as zero for the epacts. From A, along the same line, each of the Greek letters that should follow in order is separated—whether upward or downward—by the number of the epacts. Thus B, the second in the order of the letters, is here at 12; and C, the third in order, is here at 23. The nineteen-year cycle will likewise be such as the letter holds in its natural order, because I assigned that year to the epacts. Thus B is here in the twelfth position, although it is second in the order of the letters; hence it is clear that this is the second year of the nineteen-year cycle, as shown by the exposition of the first and twelfth lines. This is undoubtedly contained in the preceding explanation.

Finally, because the moon remains in each sign for two and a half days, I assigned alternately two days to some signs and three to others. In line 8 of this table, below the number marked there, let five whole days be held by two complete signs, while what is subtracted from one is assigned alternately. I placed the months opposite this in line 24, so that you may observe in which sign the sun is in each month of the year. For here you see Aries from the capital letter, and April from the other indication; here Taurus, and there May, and so on in the same manner. Therefore, to find in which sign the moon is on any given day, know the day and month, then examine lines 18 and 24. Opposite the new moon, the months and signs will meet: April in line 24 and Aries in line 18. You will always find the terms if you observe the moon on February 10, March 2, April 14, May 20, and June 4.

## ON THE RECURRENCE OF THE CONCURRENT NUMBERS

The following figure concerning the recurrence of the concurrent numbers contains only this information: the calculator is to know, after a number of years from the present, what the future concurrent numbers will be—for example, after 100 years or any of the other numbers inserted in the figure.

The figure therefore contains the concurrent numbers for each of twenty-eight years, with the number placed beneath each indicating after how many years the same concurrent number returns. But since it could not begin with each individual year on the parchment, it was begun with the first year written here, the year of the solar cycle that has concurrent number 1 and is a leap year. Whatever occurs there arises in the same way from each of the years. The year following the leap year will, from this point onward, produce the same numbers in the same order after thirty years. Therefore, whenever you wish to know the concurrent number after a given number of completed years, see how many times it contains 30; and by the doubled portion of 30 you will recognize the correspondence of the years that have turned, whether past or future.

The figure that follows, covering the twenty-eight years of the solar cycle by which the concurrent numbers are computed, indicates on which weekday the Kalends of each month occur. Its beginning is taken where there are twelve months, the first of which is March. The letters placed above each year show the first weekday throughout the year. How the leap year returns every fourth year will appear below, in the recurrence of the solar cycle, through the individual returns of the concurrent numbers. In this figure, the concurrent numbers that belong to the first, second, third, or fourth year of the leap-year sequence are marked, whether they have occurred before or will occur afterward; the numbers of the years have been prefixed.

[Col. 0734A] In the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, when no epact is assigned, the new moon is found on the Kalends of March; in the second, on the twentieth day; in the third, on the first; and in the fourth, on the twelfth. We first placed the moons of these March Kalends, collected over the nineteen-year cycle, in order; then, in the seven orders that follow, we described the reckoning of the weekdays of Easter.

When, therefore, you wish to find the fourteenth moon of the Easter festival, and finally Easter itself with its moon, for any year of the nineteen-year cycle, inspect the moon of the aforesaid Kalends and then follow it until you reach the weekday on which the Kalends of that month occurred. The line you are holding will show you there the day of Easter with its moon. For example, if the Kalends of March fall on the first day [Sunday], you will find the day of Easter with its moon on the first weekday, where we have placed it. If they fall on the second day [Monday], you will likewise find the day and the paschal moon there, as we explained for the first. This inquiry proceeds in the same way through the seventh weekday and is never marked by error; indeed, the method of this calculation proceeds with firm stability for 130 years, which is one quarter of the great year. When it has been carried through to the end, it returns into itself and is unfolded again; once unfolded, it always returns into itself.

Moreover, we arranged this cycle so that at the head of the nineteen-year cycle we have placed, the Kalends of March fall on the first day [Sunday] with concurrent number three, which is assigned to the first year of the preparation for the leap year. But since the twenty-eighth solar cycle is completed through nineteen years of the lunar cycle, the concurrent number we mentioned does not return to the same place until 532 years have been completed—that is, until this cycle has revolved four times. This total is produced by multiplying the two cycles by one another.

It should be understood that this page differs in no respect from the preceding one except that the former contains the moons of the Kalends of January, whereas this one contains those of March; both, however, contain the same system. They also differ in this respect: the Kalends marked below, which correspond to the fifth weekdays of the January lunations, occur on Sunday in the same order beneath the March lunations. Since the lunar weekdays of the Kalends and the calendars of Easter with their lunations are the same on both pages, they differ only in that they run differently. For, as has been said, the calendars marked below that correspond to the fifth weekday of January occur here on Sunday in March, while what is the sixth weekday there is written here under the second [Monday], so that in all other respects there may be agreement. Thus the fourteenth moons, as on the preceding page, are contained here in the ninth line. From these, each set being placed opposite the other in the same row, arise seven calendars, which follow the calendar proper to the fourteenth moon in each year, according to the decree of the Council of Nicaea of the 318 holy Fathers.

The pages that appear below differ scarcely at all from one another in usefulness. Both have the years of the Lord on the reader’s left and the great year on the right. Throughout the page the concurrent numbers are black; leap years are made evident by three dots placed beside them. The yellow color marks the beginning of the solar cycle, which runs through twenty-eight years. The green marks the beginning of the indiction cycle, which revolves through fifteen years.

They also contain the explanations that you see below. Although these are subscribed only to one page, they are joined to all the following pages, depicted by colors and concurrent numbers, in the same manner and order. Among these explanations, note what is entitled “Observation of the New Moon of the First Month,” December 13 [the printed text reads *Id. Jan.*]. Here one must understand that the twelfth moons are marked, as terms according to the order of the lunar cycle, which properly begins for the Romans in the fourth year of the nineteen-year cycle. Thus, as you see above, the twelfth moon that occurs on the Kalends of January is found in the following year on the twelfth day before the Kalends of the same month.

Accordingly, according to the Romans, in the calendars marked below, common and embolismic years are observed in the manner of the paschal term. From the date on which you have the twelfth moon of January in the present year, count backward eleven days, and you will have the eleventh moon if it is a common year. But if it is an embolismic year, count forward nineteen days, and you will have the twelfth moon on the twentieth day. This never fails except in the nineteenth year, because of the leap of the moon; in that year you will count thirteen days.

Since nineteen times seven makes 133, there are that many Sundays of Easter described here. If you multiply these by one quarter—namely, four times one hundred, four times thirty, and four times three—you obtain a total of 532, which is the great year.

Although over 133 years the course of the weekdays in relation to the moon differs because of the reckoning of leap years, after 532 years it returns to the same order. Thus this formula contains, without error, the truth of all the paschal orders of the great year, except at one point only: where in a common year you find the fifteenth moon on Easter Sunday, after many years you will find that it ought to be the sixteenth there once only. This produces no other error.

For example, if the Kalends of March fall on the first weekday [Sunday], you will find the day of Easter with its moon on the first weekday where we have placed it. If they fall on the second, you will likewise find the day and moon marked there, as we explained for the first. This inquiry proceeds in the same way through the seventh weekday and is never marked by error. Indeed, the method of this calculation advances with firm stability for 133 years, which is one quarter of the great year; when it has been carried through to the end, it returns into itself and is unfolded again, and, once unfolded, always returns into itself.

Moreover, we arranged this cycle so that at the head of the nineteen-year cycle we have placed, the Kalends of March fall on the first weekday [Sunday], with concurrent number three, which is assigned to the first year of the preparation for the leap year. But since the solar cycle is completed through nineteen years within twenty-eight cycles, the concurrent number we mentioned does not return to the same place until it has completed 532 years and this cycle has revolved four times; this total is produced by multiplying the two cycles by one another.

## The Twelve Months of the Civil Year, Also Called the Common Year

There are twelve signs of the zodiac; nevertheless, here they do not follow their sequence and position. Otherwise Aries ought to be in the first place, Taurus in the second, and so forth.

[Col. 0755] [Col. 0757]

[Col. 0757A] The common year is also called simple and ordinary. It consists of twelve months, whose order and names now follow here, according to the stars and according to the Hebrews:

1. April | In these first two months is spring.  
2. May |  
3. June | In these three months is summer.  
4. July |  
5. August |  
6. September | In these three months is autumn.  
7. October |  
8. November |  
9. December | In these three final months is winter.  
10. January |  
11. February |  
12. March | Here begins the first part of the four seasons of the year, called spring.

An embolismic year is called a year having a passage, or rather an overstepping, because it exceeds [Col. 0757B] the common year by one lunar month.

The nineteen-year cycle, or course of nineteen years, is that fixed span of years after which all the lunations return to the same hour in which they previously occurred.

An epact is the remainder of days, hours, and minutes that remains from the embolismic year and is reserved for the following year.

Since we have distinguished the entire sequence of the annual circuit, which is contained in twelve months, by means of letters, we have done so only in such a way that the first and second orders comprise twenty-seven days each, while the third comprises one more—namely, the day that accrues from the eight surplus hours when repeated for the third time. For the moon remains in each sign for eleven days, six hours, and two-thirds of an hour. When this half-hour is therefore repeated twelve times, eight hours are produced in the year, that is, in the lunar circuit. From these eight hours, over three years—that is, three lunar circuits—one day grows, provided, however, that this day is not found in the regular page, although in the annual one there is an empty place between *o* and *a* in the third position. From the six hours, however, a day grows in the fourth sign; and for this reason the fourth sign is always multiplied three times. We have placed these alternately, that is, we have made intervals, leaving one of them empty there. For there are more days in the lunar circuit than in the alphabet; but since we have not assigned them to the same work on every day—that is, to the annual booklet—however many letters it contains, so many years, that is, lunar circuits, it also comprises.

[Col. 0757C–0758A]

Why is an empty place not found between *o* and *a* for the third time on the regular page, as it is found in the annual sequence? It is not found there because the moon traverses the zodiac in twenty-seven days and eight hours, and the letter of each day—or the empty place—is on the regular page; moreover, the same alphabet is counted thirteen times in one year. If there had been an empty place, twenty-eight days would be found in each circuit; and from this an enormous error would have arisen if there had been an empty place between *o* and *a*.

It is likewise asked how, on the regular page, the heavenly body signified by the empty place between *o* and *a* in the annual sequence in the third circuit is found, when no empty place is found on that page. We can answer briefly that between *o* and *a* that heavenly body is recognized by analogy with the leap day, for which there is no empty place in the annual sequence but which is inserted between two solar days, namely, between the seventh and sixth days before the Kalends of March.

[Col. 0758B]

It is likewise asked why the fourth heavenly sign is always written three times in the alphabet on the regular page. We can answer as follows: one heavenly sign is written three times because of the complete day that arises from the six hours repeated four times for each heavenly sign. That day is therefore assigned to the sign in which the moon is then staying—that is, always to the fourth sign.

It is likewise asked whether three days are counted in a sign that is not written three times on the regular page. They are indeed counted in the third lunar circuit, where there is an empty place between *o* and *a* in the annual sequence.

It is likewise asked whether four days are counted in a sign. They certainly are counted when one sign is written three times because of the six hours mentioned above. That day is assigned to the heavenly sign which arises from the half-hour—that is, from the eight hours repeated for the third time. Examine the seventh and eighth years, the sixteenth, the seventeenth, and the eighteenth.

[Col. 0758C–0759A]

It is likewise asked why one alphabet is written thirteen times in the annual sequence in a single year, if one alphabet is not repeated thirteen times. This too is resolved as follows: because of the number of solar days through which the sun travels around the zodiac, one alphabet is repeated thirteen times in the annual sequence—that is, in 365¼ days. In twenty-seven days and eight hours, as we said above, it circles around the zodiac. Therefore it is not necessary for the same alphabet to be repeated in order to signify the same days, so that the same signs may be displayed.

It is likewise asked why a different alphabet is not begun for each year on the regular page. The answer is this: if it had always begun with *a*, the sign of Aries would always be signified; and the heavenly sign in which the moon remains in the first year of the nineteen-year cycle, when the ninth moon is on the Kalends of January, would have *a* written beneath it—that is, beneath Aries. Likewise, in the sign in which the moon remains in the second year of the aforementioned cycle, when the twentieth moon is on the Kalends of January—that is, in the sign of Virgo—*a* is written beneath it. The same applies to the others.

It is likewise asked why Aries is written at the end of the year and at the beginning of that same year. This is done for the following reason: the moon passes through the final part of Aries when it is the ninth moon on the Kalends of January. This is also because of the eight hours repeated, since the moon remains in each sign for two days, six hours, and two-thirds of an hour. When this half-hour is therefore repeated twelve times, eight hours are produced in the year. From these eight hours, over three years, one day grows. Yet that day is not found on the regular page, although an empty place is found between *o* and *a* in the third position.

From the six hours, however, a day grows in the fourth sign; and for this reason the fourth sign is always multiplied three times.

If you wish to discover where the signs ought to be tripled, learn that the moon traverses the zodiacal circle in twenty-seven days and eight hours. Double the twelve signs twice: they make twenty-four, and three days remain out of the twenty-seven; this three is one quarter of twelve. The eight hours are omitted, since, by increasing over three years, they produce a complete day. Therefore the signs ought to be tripled in the fourth place.

# JANUARY

[Col. 0759]

The first month of the Romans. It has thirty-one days; the moon, however, has thirty. The night has sixteen hours, and the day only eight.

The tenth month of the Hebrews, Tebeth, occupies a place in this month; and the second month of the Greeks is Eudinios.

## Martyrology

[Col. 0759B]

Now let us weave in verse the course of the month of Janus,

And sing what signs of festivals each day likewise brings.

**[Kal.]** Let us recall what the ancient fathers honored, and what shadow of the future

The holy one born of the Virgin Christ revealed:

The flesh was circumcised—behold, it now makes the Kalends sacred—

And holy Basil shines in the honor of his merits;

Euphrosyna shines together with blessed Almachius.

**[IV n.]** On the fourth day before the Nones, Macarius dedicates his dwelling,

He who, a devout inhabitant of the desert, preserved and taught its way of life.

**[III n.]** The third day before the Nones celebrates Genevieve.

**[II n.]** Then, on the day before the Nones, the returning festival honors the one who increases;

**[Nones.]** From this point the gracious confessor Simeon possesses the Nones,

And Pope Telesphorus likewise shines on the same day.

**[VIII id.]** On the eighth day before the Ides, holy Epiphany is celebrated.

**[VII id.]** The seventh day celebrates Christ, brought back from Egypt,

And the people of Antioch likewise commemorate their Lucian.

**[VI id.]** On the sixth day after the Ides, vows are offered to Eugenianus.

**[V id.]** On the fifth, to Vitalis, Fortunatus, and Revocatus.

**[IV id.]** On the fourth, blessed Melchiades and Paul the hermit

Rejoice, taken up at the end of their lives into the heavenly citadel.

**[III id.]** From this point Salvius consecrates the Ides at Carthage for the third day.

**[II id.]** On the day before the Ides, the people of Itachia commemorate their Cyriacus.

**[Ides.]** On the Ides, Hilary serves the city of Poitiers,

The devoted people honoring the shepherd who strengthens them.

**[XIX k.]** It is established that the nineteenth and ninth day before the Kalends of February

Is adorned by the holy and fortunate confessor.

[Col. 0760B]

**[XVIII k.]** Habakkuk and Micah together honor the eighteenth day.

**[XVII k.]** On the seventeenth day before the Kalends, the martyr Marcellus shines,

As does the supreme pontiff, glorious for his merits and his name.

**[XVI k.]** The sixteenth day is likewise proclaimed through the virtue of Antony;

This day also possesses the honor of two companions,

Whom the people of Langres celebrate, covered by one marble monument.

**[XV k.]** On the fifteenth, the Roman people rejoice in Prisca as a martyr.

**[XIV k.]** On the fourteenth, Nicetas and Hautmar shine.

**[XIII k.]** On the thirteenth, the bishop Fabian flourishes;

Sebastian is joined to him by equal virtue,

Him whom joyful Soissons now honors after his conveyance there.

**[XII k.]** The twelfth belongs to Agnes, honored as virgin and martyr.

**[XI k.]** The sacred Levite Vincent adorns the eleventh,

And noble Anastasius is joined to him by virtue.

**[X k.]** On the tenth, abundant praise shines forth for Emerentiana.

**[IX k.]** On the ninth, the virtue and martyrdom of Babylas shine.

**[VIII k.]** On the eighth, glory honors Paul, converted from the world,

And Auvergne adorns its own Projectus in celebration.

**[VII k.]** Soon the seventh day shines with the blood of Polycarp,

Whom Smyrna truly celebrates, burned for the true King.

The Punic land venerates its own on the sixth day.

**[VI k.]** Sulpitius, Bathildis, and Adelgund also flourish.

**[V k.]** On the fifth, the noble Roman offspring of Agnes commemorate the blessed one.

**[IV k.]** On the fourth, the martyrdom of Papius and Maurus shines.

Then they rejoice in Valerius, bishop of Trier.

**[III k.]** On the third, Hippolytus resounds through the city of Antioch.

**[II k.]** On the day before the Kalends, the splendid trophy of Saturninus and Thyrsus,

And likewise of Victor, now marks out the circuit.

[Col. 0761A]

The tropical Capricorn consecrates the beginning of January.

Numa Pompilius added the months of January and February to the year, assigning twenty-eight days to each. Later he added one day to January, because the unequal number was appropriate to the upper gods, and he named it January after Janus. He wished it to be the first month of the year, as the month of the two-faced god, who looks back upon the end of what has passed and forward upon the beginnings of what is to come. Some think that it was named from the fact that it is the boundary and doorway of the year.

It should be noted that in the eleventh year, on the fourth day before the Nones of January, the moon ends in the embolismic cycle, which is inscribed on the second day before the Nones of December. In the tenth year, the January moon ends on the Kalends of February.

From the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February to the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, whenever the tenth moon occurs, Septuagesima falls on the next Sunday after it.

In January do not let blood. Take a potion against suffocation, and take an electuary; fast and drink a cup full of the best wine, for the infusion of blood. Take ginger and rhubarb.

The first day of January is feared, and the seventh at its end.

That is, usually the first hour of the first day, and also the fifth hour of that seventh day.

# FEBRUARY

[Col. 0761]

The second month of the Romans. It has twenty-eight days; the moon, however, has twenty-nine. The night has fourteen hours, and the day only ten.

The eleventh month of the Hebrews, Shebat, occupies a place in this month; and the third month of the Greeks is Peritios.

## Martyrology

[Col. 0761B]

Now also let us set forth in verse the course of February,

And the signs of the festivals that each day likewise brings.

**[Kal.]** The powerful virgin Brigid consecrates the first Kalends of February to herself,

Celebrated by the Scots with marvelous devotion.

**[IV n.]** On the fourth day before the Nones, let the Lamb, brought into the temple, be commemorated—

When, by God’s purification, the believing people place him in one temple

With devout mind and lay down the tribunal that has received him.

**[III n.]** On the third day before the Nones, festivals are consecrated to Lupicinus;

On these days Celerinus and Celerina also shine with pious blood,

As do the blessed Ignatius and Laurentinus.

**[II n.]** Then, on the day before the Nones, gracious Aquilinus claims the day,

Together with the bishops Phileas and Philoromus.

**[Nones.]** On the Nones, the virtue of the eminent virgin Agatha,
