Celebrated for her beauty, subdues the peoples of Sicily.

**[VIII id.]** On the eighth day before the Ides, the martyr Dorothy shines.

**[VII id.]** [Note: “A faulty verse, and not the only one, as will be clear to the reader.” EDIT.]

Augula, you triumph over the world on the seventh day.

Then also spring first rises at the stars’ ascent.

**[VI id.]** On the sixth, Dionysius and Aemilianus adorn the day.

**[V id.]** On the fifth, pious vows commemorate blessed Ammon.

**[IV id.]** Soter, Irenaeus, and the virgin Scholastica shine on the fourth

With outstanding praise of their merits.

[Col. 0761C]

**[III id.]** From this point Desiderius crowns Lyons on the third,

And Rome shines through Parthenius and Calocerus.

**[II id.]** On the day before the Ides, the festival and blood of Eulalia shine,

The distinguished city of Barcelona rejoicing in that martyr.

**[Ides.]** On the Ides, Julianus ascends to heavenly honor,

His blessed bride joining her exultant spirit to heaven.

**[XVI k.]** Then, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends,

**[Mart.]** The martyr Vitalis and the virgin Felicula shine,

And their deeds commemorate Valentinus as blessed.

[Col. 0762B]

**[XV k.]** From this point, on the fifteenth, the merit of Agape becomes bright;

On this day Brescia venerates famous Faustinus, struck down by bitter punishments,

And holy Jovita.

Here too the sun enters the sign of Pisces.

**[XIV k.]** On the fourteenth, the martyr Juliana shines,

And honors Onesimus, blessed through the teacher Paul.

**[XIII k.]** On the thirteenth, the festival of Polychronius returns,

As do the faith and blood of Donatus, whom the altar also joins.

**[XII h.]** The holy Martial honors the twelfth day.

**[XI h.]** Publius and Julianus together adorn the eleventh.

**[X h.]** Soon the tenth recalls and crowns his praise and fame.

**[IX h.]** On the ninth, the day shines under your name, Victorinus.

**[VIII h.]** On the eighth, the teaching of Peter’s chair shines,

In joyful Antioch, where he first flourished as bishop.

**[VII h.]** The seventh shines with the exceptional honor of Polycarp,

The presbyter who, following Christ’s commands in word and faith,

Was able through martyrdom to preserve the faithful crowd.

**[VI h.]** On the sixth, Matthias radiates apostolic virtue,

And the Baptist has now uncovered this head, long kept hidden.

For this is the leap day, and it is inserted every fourth year.

**[V h.]** On the fifth, the day increases the praise of blessed Crescentius.

**[IV h.]** On the fourth, Nestor rejoices together with his companion Theon.

**[III h.]** On the third, Hesperia flourishes through the bishop Leander.

[Col. 0762C]

**[II h.]** On the day before, gracious Macarius is joined to Rufinus.

Here the light of the month of February is brought to an end.

These three verses, which do not begin in the same order as the others, are separated from the Martyrology.

Every fourth year has a February of twenty-nine days, because of the leap day.

In Numa’s month, the constellation of Aquarius stands in the middle.

[Col. 0763A]

Numa named February after Februus—that is, Pluto, the god of the underworld—who was believed to be the patron [F. parent] of purifications. In that month, the state had to be purified in the manner by which he decreed that due vows should be paid to the spirits of the dead. Therefore he dedicated this month to the infernal gods, to whom an even number was appropriate.

In a leap year February ought to receive a thirtieth moon, because the moon too is proved to have a quarter [of a day]. In all other years it ought always to have twenty-nine. But in the eleventh year, on the Kalends of February, the thirtieth moon occurs; it is assigned not to February but to January.

From the seventh day before the Ides of February to the Nones of March, whenever the second moon occurs, Quadragesima falls on the next Sunday after it.

The solar epacts—that is, the days of the concurrent weeks—are most suitably changed on the Kalends of March. For if you change them according to the Kalends of January, in a leap year you have to change them twice, so that in January and February you use the concurrent days omitted in the solar cycle, while in March and the other months you use those that you find written there from the cycle. To find the concurrent days—that is, [possibly: “the day”]—one is added to the present number so that the following numbers may be found. In every fourth year, two are added because of the leap day, and they never exceed the number seven. After twenty-eight years, one always returns to the beginning.

Reduce blood from the thumb, but first take a preparation of *diagridium* to produce evacuation. When you are going to drink it, enter a hot bath; and when all your limbs have begun to grow warm, drink hot water mixed with wine. Applied to the head, a poultice cures troubled eyes. Do not eat beets, because they contain poison.

The fourth day of February is the one to fear; the third precedes the end.

That is, usually the eighth hour of the fourth day, and the fifth hour of the other day, are to be avoided.

# MARCH

The third month of the Romans. It has thirty-one days; the moon, however, has thirty. The night has thirteen hours, and the day only eleven.

The twelfth month of the Hebrews, Adar, occupies a place in this month; and the fourth month of the Greeks is Distros.

## Martyrology

[Col. 0763B]

At last, concerning March, distinguished by its notable festive season,

We shall briefly say by whose honor it excels.

**[Kal.]** Donatus and Albinus hold the Kalends of March.

Soon, on the sixth day before the Nones, Heraclius and Paul are honored.

**[VI non.]** On the fifth, Magra defends the Nones with pious love.

**[V non.]** On these days Emeterius, Celedonius, and Marinus,

And Asterius, shine illustrious in shed blood.

**[IV non.]** From this point, Pope Lucius shines on the fourth with a precious death,

And a noble throng of eight hundred martyrs glows.

**[III non.]** On the third, the martyr Phocas possesses the day in the name of his merits—

He who conquered death by blood and the dragon by virtue.

**[II non.]** On the day before, Victorinus rejoices, and Victor, released from prison,

They who penetrated the stars in lofty flight.

**[Nones.]** On the Nones, Felicity and Perpetua shine,

Who dedicated a chaste life to Christ through a blessed death.

**[VIII id.]** On the eighth day before the Ides, the martyr Cyril,

And Rogatus, venerable with similar honor, together hold the day.

**[VII id.]** On the seventh, the lesser churches of Armenia commemorate one festival

Under forty soldiers.

**[VI id.]** On the sixth, Gaius and Alexander are honored together;

A band of forty-two is joined to them in blood,

Whom we likewise commemorate as slain in savage Persia.

**[V id.]** From this point, Candidus and Valerius retain the fifth.

[Col. 0764B]

**[IV id.]** On the fourth, your end, gracious Gregory,

Consecrates heaven, to which you sought through eternal praise.

**[III id.]** On the third, the presbyter Macedonius fills the day with honor,

Accompanied by his wife Patricia and his daughter Modesta.

**[II id.]** On the day before, Euphrosius shines together with the martyr Peter.

**[Ides.]** On the Ides, the people of Thessaly preserve the day for the matron and martyr.

**[XVII k.]** On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, according to custom,

The day preceding the Kalends shines with the honor of Cyriacus and Largus,

And also flourishes with the precious blood of Smaragdus.

**[XVI k.]** On the sixteenth, the day is distinguished by your name, Patrick,

You who pitied pagan worship throughout the towns of Scotland;

On this day vows are also paid to blessed Gertrude.

**[XV k.]** On the fifteenth, Bishop Alexander possesses the lofty day three times five;

And the presbyter Pigmenius purifies Rome with blood.

**[XIV k.]** On the fourteenth, the day shines through John, inhabitant of the desert.

**[XIII k.]** On the thirteenth, shining with the praise of Guthbert,

He leads the peoples of the English through mystical joys.

**[XII k.]** Then on the twelfth, the faith and name of Benedict shine,

Through whom the monastic dignity rejoices throughout the world.

**[XI k.]** On the eleventh, the bishop Paul grants holy light,

By whose authority Narbonne exults in its own teacher.

**[X k.]** From this point, on the tenth, Felix, and Theodorus with Julianus,

Adorn the day with exceptional praise of virtues.

**[IX k.]** Romulus and Secundulus likewise fill the ninth.

[Col. 0765A]

**[VIII k.]** On the eighth, the Angel announces the Lamb who is to come,

And the Lamb himself is raised upon the cross for the world’s death.

**[VII k.]** On the seventh, it commemorates Montanus together with his holy wife,

Who also suffered with forty martyrs.

**[VI k.]** On the sixth, the triumph of the rising Lamb shines.

**[V k.]** On the fifth, Priscus, Alexander, and Malchus are honored.

King Guntramnus, migrating from this life, also adorns it.

**[IV k.]** On the fourth, Eustathius shines with the praise of virtue,

And Quirinus with Abbot Columbanus as his teacher.

**[III k.]** On the third, it shines with Domninus and his companion Victor.

**[II k.]** On the day before, blessed Diodolus and Anesius shine.

Here the orbit of March, revolving, marks out the end of the month.

March, holding the sickle, wishes to cut the vine.

Romulus arranged the month of March together with the following nine months, and established it as the first month of the year. He dedicated it to Mars, whose son he wished to be thought, because it is said that Juno gave birth to Mars in Phrygia during this month. Hence it is called March from Mars.

In the eleventh year, the moon that ought to have been the twenty-ninth on the Kalends of March becomes the twenty-eighth, because of the fourth embolism, which is inserted on the second day before the Nones of December in the tenth year. If that year is a leap year, it will be the twenty-ninth. But this moon belongs not to March but to February. The moon of March, however, begins on the fifth day before its Nones.

[Col. 0765B–0766A]

From the twelfth day before the Kalends of April to the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, whenever the fourteenth moon occurs, Easter is properly celebrated on the next Sunday after it.

From the eighth day before the Ides of March to the Nones of April, whatever moon begins its course marks the beginning of Nisan, the first month of the Hebrews.

In March they should eat sweet food while fasting and drink unmixed sweet wine; they should eat cooked *agrestum* [sour greens; uncertain], and prepared radishes. They should use a hot bath; they should not let blood or take a laxative, because the laxative itself generates chills. Their drink should be rue and lovage.

The first day of March kills; its fourth is feared at the point of its spear.

That is, usually the first hour of the first day, and also the second hour of the fourth day, are to be avoided.

# APRIL

[Col. 0765]

The fourth month of the Romans. It has thirty days; the moon, however, has twenty-nine. The night has eleven hours, and the day thirteen.

The first month of the Hebrews, Nisan, occupies a place in this month; and the fifth month of the Greeks is Xanthikos.

## Martyrology

[Col. 0765C]

**[Kal.]** Agape and Chionia, distinguished by a virginal garland,

Rightly consecrate the Kalends of April to themselves.

**[IV n.]** On the fourth day before the Nones, the sacred Nicetas is in the city of Lyons.

**[III n.]** On the third, Evagrius shines, and the martyr Benignus,

And the virgin Theodosia shines with equal radiance.

**[II n.]** On the day before, Ambrose entered heavenly honor.

**[Nones.]** On the Nones, the pious virgin shines after death [*haerent*—the text is uncertain].

**[VIII id.]** On the eighth day before the Ides, Xystus, martyr and holy man,

Excels, having suffered death under the emperor Hadrian.

**[VII id.]** Diogenes and Eleusius are commemorated on the seventh.

**[VI id.]** Maximus and Solutor hold the sixth day before the Ides.

**[V id.]** On the fifth, the radiant flower and beauty of virginity shines

With a lofty brightness, like a lamp, on the Ides.

**[IV id.]** On the fourth, the prophet Ezekiel speaks with holy mouth.

**[III id.]** On the third, with the supreme pontiff Leo shining,

Those who fed Christ’s flock with word and hand shine.

**[II id.]** On the day before, Bishop Julius revisits the Roman walls,

A renowned shepherd on behalf of Catholic doctrine.

**[Ides.]** On the Ides, gracious king Hermenegild, you perceive your raging father,

Reporting the truth and triumph over death.

**[XVIII k.]** On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May,

Valerian rejoices, and his brother Tiburtius;

The soldier Maximus accompanies them, shedding blood.

[Col. 0766C]

**[XVII k.]** On the seventeenth, joined to the tenth, the blessed Olympias is shown,

And another Maximus likewise defends her.

**[XVI k.]** On the sixteenth, Charisius and Callistus shine,

Whom the sea, drowning them with the people, blessed on the seventh day.

**[XV id.]** On the fifteenth, Mappalicus, Hermes, and Peter

Shine together, illustrious in merit, virtue, and blood.

**[XIV k.]** On the fourteenth, Eleutherius and the holy mother Anthia,

Following an excellent life by dying, shine twice sevenfold.

**[XIII k.]** On the thirteenth, with Gaius, Aristonichus, Rufus, Hermogenes, and Galatus,

The day shines with Expeditus [*expedito*, as printed] and the martyr.

**[XII k.]** Marcellinus, Domninus, and Vincentius, equally [F. *aeque*],

Shine in the name of the twelfth;

And the festivals of the blessed martyr Synesius are celebrated in faith and festivity.

**[XI k.]** Then the pontiffs, blessed in tomb, teaching, and death,

Gaius and Simeon are honored together on the eleventh.

**[X k.]** On the tenth, three presbyters crown the day,

And three palms: Parmenius, Elimenes, and Chrysotelus.

Here too, revealed by divine will,

The bodies of the martyrs purify the Church with a threefold martyrdom:

The blessed Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius,

And the sacred Felix, worthy of a double minister.

[Col. 0767A]

**[IX k.]** The ninth teaches that Fortunatus and Achilleus are joined;

On this day also, holy George, who despise the world

Through unconquered blood, you bring innumerable trophies.

**[VIII k.]** The martyr Alexander, rejoicing in thirty martyrs,

And, with a third, on the eighth consecrates the walls of Lyons.

**[VII k.]** Soon blessed Mark thunders with evangelical speech,

On the seventh, by which he receives an exceptional radiance as his crown.

**[VI k.]** On the sixth, the struggles of Pope Cletus are commemorated,

And Richarius shines, a cultivator of blessed life.

**[V k.]** On the fifth, we celebrate Pope Anastasius;

The bishop Anthimus is joined to him by worthy virtue.

**[IV k.]** On the fourth, it commemorates Vitalis, slain for Christ’s name,

Who earned eternal life through death.

**[III k.]** On the third, it venerates the pontiffs dedicated at altar and through merits:

Agapius and likewise Secundinus.

**[II k.]** On the day before the Kalends, Jacob and Marianus,

Having received a similar honor of martyrdom, reap their end in April.

April, which spring consecrates to itself with a purple flower—

We shall say with what festivals it raises its joys.

April moderates the fields by lifting the rake.

Romulus named April as though it were “opening” (*aperilem*), because in it, once the clouds, frosts, and winter storms have been removed, the sky, the earth, the sea, the astrologers, the farmers, and the sailors are opened up. The trees and willows also begin to open into bud, and all living creatures into offspring.

[Col. 0767B–0768A]

The computist ought to know that in the eighth and nineteenth years the April moon ends in May, because of the two embolisms that produce a thirtieth moon: in the second day before the Nones of April in the thirteenth year, and on the third day before the Nones of April in the nineteenth year. Likewise, in the eleventh year, on the Kalends of April, there is a thirtieth moon; that is, this moon is assigned to March.

From the seventh day before the Kalends of May to the tenth day before the Kalends of June, the twentieth moon indicates the limit of the Rogation season.

In April it is good to let blood, to take a potion for evacuation, and to eat fresh meat. Abstain from roots. Reduce subcutaneous blood. Use hot baths. Cleanse stomach pain. Use a *calastic* ointment. Their drink should be betony and pimpernel; they should eat radish, because at that time scabies and dimness of sight arise. Whoever observes these prescriptions will restore natural health.

The tenth day of April is to be feared, and the eleventh and the end.

[Col. 0768B]

That is, usually the first hour of the tenth day, and also the ninth hour of the other day, are to be avoided.

# MAY

[Col. 0767]

The fifth month of the Romans. It has thirty-one days; the moon, however, has thirty. The night has eight hours, and the day sixteen.

The second month of the Hebrews, Iyar, occupies a place in this month; and the sixth month of the Greeks is Artemisios.

## Martyrology

[Col. 0767C]

**[Kal.]** The first Kalends of May are consecrated by Christ’s teaching;

The brothers of the Lord, James and Philip, shine among them,

And Jeremiah, an outstanding prophet, is celebrated together with them;

King Sigismund reigns, having shed his blood.

**[VI n.]** From this point, on the sixth day before the Nones, great Athanasius, you shine,

Through whom the serpent Arius first perished in victory.

**[V n.]** Bishop Alexander and Eventius adorn the fifth,

As does Theodolus, slain likewise for God’s name;

The lofty banners of the cross discovered there also shine.

**[IV n.]** On the fourth, Sylvanus, Antonia, and Florianus

Are encircled by the virtue of their minds.

**[III n.]** On the third, Christ crosses the starry Olympus,

And Arles shines through Hilary, while Vienne is proud of Nicetas.

**[II n.]** On the day before, the Roman temples of God celebrate

The exalted John, who drank in the Word with a full heart.

**[Nones.]** On the Nones, holy Juvenal honors the day through a pious death.

**[VIII n.]** On the eighth day before the Ides, in the city of Milan, shines

The martyr Victor, to be venerated with exceptional love.

**[VII id.]** On the seventh day before the Ides, three hundred shine together,

Their blessed martyrdom adorning the day at last.

[Col. 0768C]

**[VI id.]** On the sixth, Gordianus and Epimachus are struck down

For one praise and one faith of Christ;

Holy Job also honors these through the example of suffering.

**[V id.]** On the fifth, Bishop Mamertus, with exceptional splendor,

Marks the day; he instituted for God the solemn offering

Of fasting beneath the light of three days.

**[IV id.]** On the fourth, virgin Domitilla, we honor your companions:

Nereus, Pancratius, and Achilleus,

Whom the first taught and baptized with the apostolic washing,

Whom Peter joined to the virgin in distinguished Rome.

**[III id.]** On the third, we venerate blessed Servatius on the Ides.

**[II id.]** On the day before, Pachomius and Victor, together with a crown of martyrs,

Shine: the former powerful as a hermit, the latter having followed God

With the shared virtue of blood and martyrdom.

**[Ides.]** On the Ides, seven pontiffs together adorn Hesperia.

**[XVII k.]** On the seventeenth day before the Kalends, joined to the tenth,

The day shines in the name of Timothy,

Whom blessed Paul taught with truthful speech.

**[XVI k.]** On the sixteenth, a pilgrim martyr flourishes.

**[XV k.]** On the fifteenth, the martyr Dioscorus fills the day.

**[XIV k.]** On the fourteenth, Pudentiana shines with a virgin’s honor.

**[XIII k.]** On the thirteenth, Basilla holds and supports the day,

And Baudelius, clothed in blood, flourishes together with her.

[Col. 0769A]

**[XII k.]** On the twelfth, Polius, Eutychius, and Timothy,

The bishop and martyr Valens, venerable to God,

Are led by you, Augia, through joyful celebrations with glad vows.

**[XI k.]** On the eleventh, the sacred Castus and Aemilius dedicated the day.

**[X k.]** On the tenth, Desiderius consecrates the city of Langres,

And the bishop and martyr Donatianus, armed with the honor of God,

Together with Mammes and Rogatianus,

Piously adorn the ninth.

**[IX k.]** On the ninth, he adorns the day through the pious contest of faith.

**[VIII k.]** On the eighth, Urban shines with the stemma of his merits,

Whom the island blessed alike through teaching and blood.

**[VII k.]** Augustine, the seventh commends your name,

Through whom the thousands of the English shine with the milk of the Word,

And under whose leadership the Britons, subdued, recognized Christ.

**[VI k.]** From this point, Julius, soldier and martyr, beautifies the sixth.

**[V k.]** On the fifth, the crowd of Paris honors Germanus;

Then his Rome also celebrates the pontiff John.

**[IV k.]** On the fourth, lofty Trier shines for you, Maximinus.

**[III k.]** The third is dedicated to Pope Hubert and Felix.

**[II k.]** Then, on the day before the Kalends, Petronilla, holy offspring of Peter,

A radiant virgin clothed in the beauty of Christ, shines.

From this point we shall proclaim the vows with which May,

The first month growing warm beneath the summer sun, brings its long days.

[Col. 0769B]

Cantius and Cantianus, together with Cantianilla,

Shine; these solemnities close the month of May.

Here May binds the vines to their stakes in due order.

May is named in honor of the elders, just as June is named in honor of the younger people: Romulus divided the population into these groups and gave them their names. He wished one part to protect the republic by arms and the other by counsel.

Others contend that Maia, the mother of Mercury, gave her name to May, because in this month merchants sacrificed to Maia and Mercury.

In the eighth year, the moon that ought to have been the twenty-eighth on the Kalends of May becomes the twenty-seventh, because of the third embolism, which is inserted on the second day before the Nones of March. Likewise, in the nineteenth year, the moon that ought to have been the twenty-ninth on the Kalends of May is found to be the twenty-eighth, because of the seventh embolism, which begins on the third day before the Nones of March.

From the seventh day before the Ides of May to the eighth day before the Ides of June, whenever the fourth moon occurs, Pentecost is celebrated on the next Sunday after it.

In May they should eat no head-meat at all; they should drink something hot and use hot baths; they should cleanse the head; they should open the hepatic vein and take a potion against suffocation. A poultice applied to the head cures troubled eyes, cleanses itching, and treats urine. [Col. 0770B] They should eat cold vegetables; take *agrimonia*; drink wormwood, fennel, pyrethrum, and *gillan* [plant name uncertain].

On the third day of May there is a wolf; on the seventh, a serpent.

That is, usually the seventh hour of the tenth day, and also the tenth hour of the other day, are to be avoided.

# JUNE

[Col. 0769]

The sixth month of the Romans. It has thirty days; the moon, however, has twenty-nine. The night has six hours, and the day eighteen.

The third month of the Hebrews, Sivan, occupies a place in this month; and the eighth month of the Greeks is Desios.

## Martyrology

[Col. 0769C]

**[Kal.]** The origin of June raises your splendor to the stars,

Pamphilus, teacher venerable for blessed martyrdom;

The day of the martyr Nicomedes adorns this festival.

**[IV non.]** On the fourth day before the Nones, sacred Marcellinus and Peter the exorcist

Share the Nones at a worthy altar of sacrifice;

And Blandina is invoked at Lyons with pious honor,

She who, together with forty-eight of the people,

Wove a shining necklace amid flames and waters.

**[III non.]** On the third, Pergentinus and Laurentinus beautify the day

With the double radiance of blood and lineage,

And the people of Aureliana commemorate their Liphardus.

**[II non.]** On the day before the Nones, the martyr and bishop Quirinus,

Accumulating sacred vows, appeases Christ with his own blood.

**[Nones.]** On the Nones, Bishop Boniface shines, born among the English,

Who drew the children of the Ocean to Christ,

Submitting the necks of the Eresonians to pure baptism.

**[VIII id.]** On the eighth day before the Ides, Bishop Ceratus adorns the day,

He who shone in the city named for the emperor Gratian.

[Col. 0770C]

**[VII id.]** On the seventh, your bishop Paul, in lofty Byzantium.

**[VI id.]** On the sixth, Gildardus and likewise Medardus honor the day,

Whom lineage, pious merit, and altar join together.

**[V id.]** On the fifth, Primus holds the day, with Felicianus joined to him.

**[IV id.]** On the fourth, Basilides and these ten martyrs flourish.

**[III id.]** On the third, the same apostle Barnabas adorns the day.

**[II id.]** On the day before, Cyrinus shines, and Nazarius and Nabor;

We join Basilides to them in the same festival.

**[Ides.]** On the Ides, the virgin Felicula illuminates the day with her blood;

Lac, Petronilla: to you the word and time likewise joined her.

**[XVIII k.]** On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July,

The prophets Elisha and Obadiah shine together;

Here too the day rejoices in the martyrs Valerius and Rufinus.

**[XVII k.]** On the seventeenth, Vitus with the illustrious virgin

Margaret shines with the splendor of martyrdom;

And Modestus and the blessed virgin Crescentia shine on this day.

**[XVI k.]** On the sixteenth, Cyricus and Julitta with his mother

Become illustrious through true devotion and faith in Christ.

[Col. 0771A]

**[XV k.]** On the fifteenth, he sends to the stars a joyful crown

Of two hundred and fifty-seven martyrs.

**[XIV k.]** On the fourteenth, the brothers Marcellianus and Marcus

Consecrated the day with precious blood;

The merit and honor of Balbina also illumine it.

**[XIII k.]** Gervasius and Protasius crown the thirteenth.

**[XII k.]** On the twelfth, Vitalis follows his sons as their father.

**[XI k.]** On the eleventh, the martyr Rufinus and Martia shine.

**[X k.]** On the tenth, Albanus defends the Britons with praise.

And Paulinus purifies Nola through his merits and name.

**[IX k.]** On the ninth, Ediltrude, of English descent, shines.

**[VIII k.]** On the eighth, the Baptist John, born among us, is honored.

**[VII k.]** On the seventh, Luceia adorns Rome with love;

Scampio rejoices in twenty-two martyrs,

Among whom Aceias shines with companionable honor.

**[VI k.]** On the sixth, the martyrs Paul and John share the day,

Brothers in lineage, love, faith, virtue, and blood;

With them Constantia shines in a noble garland,

And the holy Salvius visits the shores of the Scheldt.

**[V k.]** On the fifth, Bishop and martyr Zoilus adorns Hesperia,

Joined to nineteen martyrs.

**[IV k.]** On the fourth, he rejoices through the bishop and teacher Leo.

**[III k.]** On the third, Rome raises to heaven

The blessed martyrdom of Peter and Paul alike.

[Col. 0771B]

**[II k.]** On the day before the Kalends, Martial is honored by the people of Limoges;

With these festivals June marks out the lofty circuit.

June, blazing beneath the summer heat that drives away the rain,

We shall sing the temples that it covers with foliage.

June cleaves the earth with the curved plow.

[Col. 0772A] Phoebus also penetrates the stars of Cancer with his burning presence.

Here the Sun stands at the midpoint of the solstice and shines at its highest point.

June is called *Junius* from the young men (*juniores*) of the Roman people; or, as Cyngius thinks, it was formerly called *Junonius*, from Juno, and afterward, with certain letters worn away, was called *Junius*. For the temple of Juno Moneta was also dedicated on the Kalends of June.

It should be observed that in the eighth year, on the fourth day before the Nones of June, there is a thirtieth lunar day, but this belongs to May. The moon of June, however, ends in July.

Likewise, in the eighteenth year a thirtieth lunar day is found on the Kalends of June, but this is assigned to May. The moon of June ends on the second day before the Kalends of July.

From the preceding Wednesday of March, on which the fast is observed, until the fast of June, there are fourteen weeks; and from that time until the fast of September there are likewise fourteen weeks.

In the month of July they should remain fasting each morning, and drink a full cup of cold water. They should not drink beer or mead, as some call it. They should avoid mustard. [Col. 0772B] Let them eat lettuce. They ought to drink vinegar. From herbs, let them drink sage and savin in little draughts, because at that time the brain is accustomed to produce humors.

June, on the tenth day, greets the fifteenth from the end.

That is, for the most part, the fifth hour of the tenth day, and also the fourth hour of the other day, should be avoided.

## JULY

[Col. 0771]

The seventh month of the Romans. It has thirty-one days, while the moon has thirty. The night has eight hours, and the day sixteen.

The fourth month of the Hebrews, Tammuz, falls within this month, and the eighth month of the Greeks, Phamenoth.

### Martyrology

[Col. 0771C]

Now let us recall in verse the saints whom July, girded about with yellow ears of grain, honors at its altars with humble devotion.

[Kal.] Aaron, who was the first priest of the ancient people and of the Law, the first to offer incense and sacrifice at the altar, begins and sanctifies the Kalends of July. The despiser of the world, Carilephus, also honors them.

[VI n.] The sixth is observed with Processus and Martinianus.

[V n.] On the fifth, radiant with the joyful splendor of martyrdom, the bishops Anatolius and Eulogius shine.

[IV n.] Laurianus, you hold the fourth by the title of your merits, and the bones of Martin adorn the tomb into which they were transferred.

[III n.] Domitius marks the third, and the most illustrious Zoe has increased the blessed company through martyrdom.

[I n.] On the day before, the eminent prophet Esaias shines throughout the world by the strength and voice of his martyrdom.

[Col. 0772C] Tranquillinus, you likewise shine with a double splendor: father of saints, accompanying the saints who have been slain. At that time Goar also is honored as Christ’s servant and sacred minister.

[Nonae.] The merit and faith of Pantemnon shine.

[VIII id.] On the eighth day before the Ides, Cilianus and Procopius excel, having followed Christ with virtue and death.

[VII id.] On the seventh, Audax and likewise Anatolus shine.

Nor does Ephrem, the holy despiser of wealth, stand forth less brightly.

[VI id.] On the sixth, blessed Felicitas dedicates to Christ a crown according to her sisterly lot, through her sevenfold offspring, whom she bore and sent beforehand, pleasing to God, to the altar.

[V id.] On the fifth, Januarius sanctifies the day by martyrdom, and holy Pelagia adorns it with a similar brilliance. Then the high Liger now honors the tomb of the blessed father Benedictus, transferred to the mountains of Beneventum.

[Col. 0773A] [IV id.] On the fourth, Aquileia, in supplication, frequently honors Hermagoras, the bishop who sustains the people and the city by his prayers.

[III id.] On the third, Serapion presents Egypt, and the martyr Attalus gleams with heavenly blossom.

[II id.] On the day before, Phocas, bishop and martyr, seeks heaven.

[Idus.] On the Ides, Cassianus and Syrus shine, and the bishop James is celebrated for his abundant merits.

[XVII k.] With the seventeenth, which marks the tenth month and foretells August, you shine in your excellent feast, Hilarinus the martyr.

[XVI k.] On the sixteenth, Carthage looks toward you with rich vows, joyfully frequenting the twelvefold people of martyrdom; at the same time the Scillitan martyrs shine, those whom their homeland sent to the capital.

[XV k.] On the fifteenth, the mother Symphorosa was dedicated with her seven children, slain together with her pious offspring.

[XIV k.] Arsenius the hermit adorns the fourteenth.

[XIII k.] Holy Philibert also adorns the thirteenth.

[XII k.] On the twelfth, Praxedis, the virgin, shines; and, in the name, end, and faith of the prophet Daniel, on this same day the pious solemn dedication of Peter is celebrated.

[XI k.] On the eleventh, blessed Mary, whom Christ in his mercy freed from seven demons, adorns the day. Her origin is indicated by the surname “Magdalene,” derived from Magdala.

[Col. 0773B] Vandregisilus, on this day the vows of monks return to you.

[X k.] From here the illustrious Apollinaris honors the tenth.

[IX k.] Soon Christina, Aquila, and Nicetas sanctified the ninth.

[VIII k.] On the eighth, James, son of Zebedee, adorns the day—the first who, for the true King, gave apostolic blood. Cucuphas and Christopher follow him.

[VII k.] On the seventh, Adrianus and Aemilius hold the blessed day; Martianus also triumphs with similar virtue.

[VI k.] The presbyter Hermolaus shines as martyr on the sixth.

[V k.] Nazarius with Celsus possesses the fifth, and the martyr Pantaleon sanctifies it with his own honor. The Roman bishop Stephen then consecrates an altar distinguished by the blessed merits of Peter and Paul, which gleams in the jeweled church of Dionysius with the signs, admonitions, visions, and faith of martyrdom.

[IV k.] Felix, Simplicius, Faustinus, and blessed Beatrix, [Col. 0774A] together with Lupus of Troyes, jointly gild the fourth.

[III k.] Abdon and Senen mark the third as saints, Persians whom Rome granted from the stock of its kingdom.

[II k.] On the day before, the pious glory of martyrdom covered Fabius.

July leaves these solemnities behind as it departs from the world.

Thus July cuts the grass and stores the hay.

July was formerly called Quintilis, because, when March was the first month, it was then the fifth month. Later it was called July in honor of Julius Caesar the dictator, by a law proposed by the consul Marcus Antoninus, because Caesar was born in this month, on the fourth day before the Ides of Quintilis.

It should further be known that in the eighth year, on the Kalends of July, there ought by the rule to be a thirtieth lunar day; but because of the third embolism, this is the twenty-ninth lunar day, and it also belongs to July.

Likewise, in the nineteenth year, we who begin the lunar epacts in September omit, because of the leap, the thirtieth lunar day of July on the third day before the Kalends of August, [Col. 0774B] so that on that same day we call the lunar day the first instead of the thirtieth.

Thus on the Kalends of August it is the third lunar day, although according to the rule it ought not to be, so that on the Kalends of September it may become the fifth.

In July they should not use Venus [possibly “venery”; the reading is uncertain]. Blood should not be let in any way. They should not drink a potion. They should use rue and sage; they should drink celery flowers and grape juice. Fasting, they should drink a full cup of water to dissolve choler.

The thirteenth of July diminishes the tenth before the Kalends.

That is, for the most part, the eleventh hour of the thirteenth day, and also the ninth hour of the seventh day, should be avoided.

## AUGUST

[Col. 0773]

The eighth month of the Romans. It has thirty-one days, while the moon has twenty-nine. The night has fourteen hours, and the day ten.

The fifth month of the Hebrews, Ab, falls within this month, and the ninth month of the Greeks, Laos.

### Martyrology

[Col. 0773C]

August, at last filled with ripe grain, let us show in song the saints who bring new sacred offerings.

[Kal.] The Maccabees, whom savage Antiochus compelled to die with their mother, retain the Kalends of August by right; they willingly dedicated their blood to Christ who was to come. Rome celebrates Peter, released from prison and chains, and Vercelli duly frequents its own Eusebius.

[IV n.] On the fourth, Rome piously grants festive joys to the martyr and blessed pope Stephen.

[III n.] On the third, the solemn feast of the discovery of Stephen is celebrated—he was the first to follow Christ’s death by dying. Gamaliel, Nicodemus, and Abibon, likewise discovered, shine in fulfillment of their vow and in everlasting praise.

[II n.] On the day before, Justinus is celebrated with his proper honor: a presbyter slain in a cruel persecution, who adorned tombs.

[Nonae.] On the Nones, Cassianus, Memmius, and Oswald, the pious king of the English, retain their place by merit and virtue.

[VIII id.] On the eighth day before the Ides, Christ’s holy flesh, destined to suffer death and the cross, gave beforehand a heavenly figure. Sixtus, bishop and martyr, is honored at Rome on this day; nearby Felicissimus and Agapitus triumph.

[VII id.] Donatus and Afra likewise bore the seventh through pious death.

[VI id.] On the sixth, Cyriacus penetrates heavenly honor.

[V id.] Romanus, martyr and soldier, shines on the fifth.

[IV id.] On the fourth, Lawrence, you shine with abundant merit; having suffered the fire, you conquer the unjust torturer.

[III id.] On the third, Tiburtius, you seek the stars as a pious flower and glory; blessed Goaricus also possesses this day.

[I id.] On the day before, Euplus, you receive the everlasting palm of martyrdom.

[Idus.] On the Ides, Laurence receives Hippolytus, his companion, among the stars, having suffered for Christ in an equal contest. Then the land, venerating Regina, worthy of honor for her merits, virtue, and faith, frequently visits Radegund, the Aquitanian.

[XIX k.] On the nineteenth before the Kalends of September, Eusebius is sanctified and celebrated as blessed at Rome.

[Col. 0775B] [XVIII k.] On the eighteenth before the Kalends, Mary, the light and flower of the world, seeks heaven as a virgin exalted and accompanied by an angelic choir.

[XVII k.] On the seventeenth, you hold the day, Arnulfus, priest.

[XVI k.] The blessed martyr Mammes shines on the sixteenth.

[XV k.] Agapitus sanctifies the fifteenth through his contest.

[XIV k.] Magnus and Andreas shine on the fourteenth, accompanied by five hundred ninety-seven others, whom two thousand saints likewise follow.

[XIII k.] On the thirteenth, Samuel excels among them, whom his devoted mother consecrated to the Lord from the cradle.

[XII k.] From here the twelfth blossoms through the blood of the martyr Privatus.

[XI k.] On the eleventh, Timothy, who suffered at Rome, honors the day; the people celebrate their own Symphorianus of Autun, whom his mother likewise dedicated to Christ, destined to die.

[X k.] Lucius and Ptolemaeus crown the tenth by their virtue.

[IX k.] Blessed Bartholomew adorns and holds the ninth. Through his teacher, India came to know the honor of God, scarcely rescued from the mad rites of Hercules and Bacchus. Hence, according to the various traditions concerning his tomb, he is said to possess Aeolia, Lapara, Beneventum, and their churches. Rome also shines with the martyr Genesius, and Rouen honors the pious Audoenus.

[Col. 0775C] [VIII k.] From here, holy Genesius, Arles celebrates you on the eighth.

[VII k.] Irenaeus and Abundus adorn the seventh through martyrdom.

[VI k.] Rufus, recalling your triumphs, displays them on the sixth.

[Col. 0776A] [V k.] Hermen proves himself blessed by a fortunate death on the fifth.

Father Augustine, light of the Church and faithful sacred standard of the people, by whose pastoral care and teaching Africa and the world shine, is celebrated on this same feast. His golden churches now preserve him buried in Italy. Saint Santonus shines here with the honor of his Vibianus. The city of the Alamanni, Constance, recalls a saint; here it also honors Pelagius, renowned for his shed blood.

[IV k.] John the Baptist, herald of God, voice of the Word, whom savage commands delivered to a dancing girl, marks the fourth with everlasting praise for his merits. At the same time, Rome again visits the churches of the virgin Sabina.

[III k.] On the third, Adauctus excels together with pious Felix.

[II k.] On the day before, Paulinus illuminates the walls of Trier, a bishop renowned for the true doctrine for which he suffered exile.

At last, August closes its gates with these feasts.

The fervent lion burns August with fire.

Augustus reaps and sends the crops into the granaries.

Here Virgo joins its stars to Phoebus in the constellation of Erigone.

With these signs the season of joyful autumn also rises.

The month of August was formerly called Sextilis, until it was given, by decree of the Senate, to the honor of Caesar Augustus, because on the first day of this month he defeated Antony and Cleopatra and secured the power of the Roman people.

It should be considered that in the sixteenth year, on the second day before the Kalends of September, a thirtieth lunar day is found; but this is not the moon of August, rather it belongs to the sixth embolism, which begins on the fourth day before the Nones of August, and is assigned to no month, since an embolismic moon is surplus to all the months.

Likewise, in the nineteenth year, on the Kalends of August, because of the lunar leap by which the thirtieth lunar day of July is skipped, the third lunar day occurs, although according to the rule it ought to be the second.

In August they should not eat cabbages or mallows; they should eat agrimony; they should drink very little beer and mead. They should not eat beets, because then they are bitter and watery and produce black choler; they should drink *gilganum* [an unidentified plant or preparation].

[Col. 0776C] The scorpion of August drives away the second day at the beginning of the month.

That is, for the most part, the first hour of the first day, and also the seventh hour of the other day, should be avoided.

## SEPTEMBER

[Col. 0775]

The ninth month of the Romans. It has thirty days, and the moon likewise has thirty. The night has twelve hours, and the day also twelve.

The sixth month of the Hebrews, Elul, falls within this month, and the tenth month of the Greeks, Gorpiaeus.

### Martyrology

[Col. 0777A]

September, gently tasting Bacchus’ cups, let us sing and remember those whom it honors by reverence at the altars.

[Kal.] Joshua, the lawgiver’s heir to the honor he left behind, who distinguished the land promised to the people by lot among the stars, regions, high mountains, and cities, holds and begins the Kalends of September. Priscus, clothed in blood, purifies them as a martyr; Bishop Lupus of Sens shines in his lofty church; and the solemnities of holy Verena gleam.

[IV non.] From here Justus honors the fourth day before the Nones at Lyons.

[III non.] On the third, Antoninus, the boy and martyr, triumphs; then Bishop Aristaeus is blessed through death.

[II non.] Moses, bearer, receiver, and author of the divine Law, deemed worthy of frequent converse and vision with God, is buried on the day before on the lofty mountain. No one afterward was permitted to know his tomb. At that time Cabillonum also blossoms through the blood of Marcellus.

[Nonae] On the Nones, Ferreolus shines with Ferrutio; Donatus and Arcontius likewise adorn Capua.

[VIII id.] The prophet Zechariah holds the eighth day before the Ides.

[VII id.] Bishop Evortius keeps the seventh, and Chlodoaldus, a priest distinguished by royal lineage, also shines.

[VI id.] On the sixth, Mary’s birth from the light is celebrated, when God assumed human form from a virgin; the martyr Adrianus also accompanies Rome with his blood.

[V id.] Gorgonius holds the fifth through fame and merits; Gaul now seeks him, suffering at Rome, and worships him.

[IV id.] Sosthenes and Victor are remembered on the fourth, having received and earned the same crown for Christ’s kingdom.

[III id.] Prothus and his brother Hyacinthus honor the third. They taught the sacred Law to Eugenia; Felix likewise dedicated them on this day through a blessed death, together with Regula, joined to them in martyrdom and blessedness.

[II id.] Soon, on the day before, the Syrian martyr Celsus seeks heaven.

[Idus] On the Ides, the abbot Amatus shines in merit and by name.

[XVIII k.] On the eighteenth before the Kalends, which custom calls the coming month October, the standards of the exalted cross shine—the cross which Heraclius victoriously carried back from Persia, rescued from an unworthy land. Cornelius sustains his Rome by virtue and blood; Carthage joyfully shines with Cyprian, its distinguished teacher and martyr, who wrote the sacred teachings of the Church throughout the world. Here also the merit of Bishop Eparchius is celebrated.

[XVII k.] Nicomedes the presbyter adorns the seventeenth.

[Col. 0777C] Petronilla, your virgin companion and blessed martyr, shines. The bishops Leobinus, Aper, and Leo, worthy of honor at the altar for their merits and lives, protect the people of Chartres.

[XVI k.] On the sixteenth, Pope Martin is blessed. We venerate holy Euphemia with pious love. Lucius likewise excels together with Geminianus, and Christ’s laurel jointly adorns those who suffered.

[XV k.] Lantpertus crowns the fifteenth through his virtue; the ever-trembling faction fears him, slain as he was.

[XIV k.] Methodius, bishop in voice and faith, in signs and blood a martyr, honors the fourteenth, worthy of celebration.

[XIII k.] Eustathius triumphs on the thirteenth as an example of the virtue of endurance, and as the form and glory of martyrdom.

[XII k.] The virgin Fausta and Evigilasius adorn the twelfth. He abandoned the world’s profits at Christ’s call.

[XI k.] Matthew sanctified the eleventh with his evangelical voice.

[X k.] Mauritius crowns the tenth with his accompanying legion, which likewise conquered death by shedding its blood.

[Col. 0778A] Emmerammus accompanies him with equal honor, whom distinguished Britain claims by name.

[IX k.] The ninth belongs to Thecla, drenched in rosy blood. Pope Liberius dedicates it throughout the city of Rome, and the deacon Sosius shines with deserved honor.

[VIII k.] John, conceived in a barren womb, holds the eighth. The holy martyr and presbyter Andochius sanctifies it, accompanied by Tyrsus and Felix with equal love.

[VII k.] On the seventh, Bishop Lupus revisits the walls of Lyons, a memorable shepherd of the devoted city; the people of Amiens shine through the martyr Firminus.

[VI k.] On the sixth, Cyprianus exults as a martyr, whom the blessed virgin Justina enabled to know the kingdom of God after he had abandoned his mad arts and frenzies.

[V k.] Cosmas excels on the fifth together with his brother Damianus. Antimus follows them, along with Leontius and Euprepius, who dedicated one crown to you, Christ, through death.

[IV k.] Faustus, Martialis, and Januas adorn the fourth, distinguished alike by the robe and contest of martyrdom.

[III k.] On the third, Michael, powerful through heavenly virtue and prince of the celestial army, consecrated temples to himself.

[II k.] Jerome, approved interpreter of the Law, both old and new, instructor in doctrine and condemner of wicked heresy, closes rejoicing September on the day before the Kalends.

The Sun, with Libra, clings to it while making the day equal.

Here Libra makes the hours of light and sleep equal.

With your constellation, Virgo, September enriches Bacchus.

Here September crushes the gathered vine-shoots with a club.

September is called as though “the seventh rain,” because it is counted as the seventh month from March, once the first month, and is generally darkened by rains or clouds.

It should be considered that in the fifth year, on the fourth day before the Nones of September, the moon of the second embolism begins and ends on the Kalends of October as a thirtieth lunar day, which is assigned neither to September nor to October.

We, following the Egyptians, begin the epacts—that is, the lunar additions—in the month of September, and always take new ones there. But the epacts, according to the most learned authorities, change together with the concurrent days and the lunar cycle on the Kalends of January.

To find the epacts, eleven are always added to those preceding, so that the following ones may be found. Except in the nineteenth year, when we add twelve to the eighteen epacts—not eleven, as in the other years—in order to produce thirty epacts, which we call none.

In September, fasting, they should eat daily little pieces of bread soaked in milk; and they may take any foods, because all kinds of food and fruit are prepared at this season. Let them draw blood from the thumb. Their drink should be agrimony and celery seed. Eat cooked and raw leeks. Drink costus and mastic.

On the third of September, the fox strikes the tenth from the foot.

That is, for the most part, the eleventh hour of the thirteenth day, and also the ninth hour of the other day, should be avoided.

## OCTOBER

[Col. 0777]

The tenth and third-from-last month of the Romans. It has thirty-one days, while the moon has twenty-nine. The night has fourteen hours, and the day ten.

The seventh month of the Hebrews, Tishri, falls within this month, and the eleventh month of the Greeks, Hyperberetaeus.

### Martyrology

[Col. 0779A]

October, laden with foaming must and fruits, let us follow in remembrance those who bring cups and baskets.

[Kal.] Remigius, who first taught and subdued the savage Franks, marks October with his own honor. Germanus, distinguished in teaching and conduct, likewise protects his own Auxerre by his merits. He repelled from the ocean those fleeing the faith and the unspeakable doctrine, and shielded you, painted Britain, with signs. Bavo accompanies these men in virtue and holy honor.

[VI non.] Soon Leodegarius adorns the sixth day before the Nones; the duke and the people, powerful in sedition, killed him.

[V non.] The two Euvalds, equal in lineage, name, altar, and doctrine, have by their merits dedicated the fifth to themselves.

[IV non.] Marcus and Marcianus fill the fourth with their office, brothers in birth, martyrdom, nature, and death.

[III non.] Apollinaris honors the third day before the Nones; Ravenna, whose churches he frequently visits as bishop, crowns him.

[II non.] On the day before, the virgin Faith triumphs through a blessed death.

[Nonis.] On the Nones, the bishops Linus and Marcus retain the day.

[Col. 0779B] [VIII id.] On the eighth day before the Ides, holy Demetrius, you are blessed, having suffered unjust torturers in Christ’s name.

[VII id.] Abraham, first called by the name of the exalted Father, then called Father of the nations by heavenly appointment, the example of obedient faith and saving standard, sanctifies and holds the seventh.

On this day Dionysius also shines in distinguished, threefold martyrdom, together with his companions, whose churches illumine the whole world with their light. Gaul, with Paul as its teacher, made him a blessed doctor and worthy minister; and Italy shines with the martyr Domninus.

[VI id.] Holy Lot adorns the sixth with the title of justice. Cassius, Gereon, Victor, Florentius, and the accompanying people triumph in martyrdom.

[V id.] Tarcus, Probus, and Andronicus crown the fifth; glory makes them equals in virtue and death.

[IV id.] Edistius increases the fourth day before the Ides by his merits; Ravenna is powerful through its celebrated martyr.

[III id.] Marcellus, Faustus, and Januarius fill the third. On this day, too, a temple is consecrated to you, Peter, and to Dionysius; and Tolbiac shines with the altar of Chrysanthus and Daria, with the level plain on which the fortress rises.

[II id.] On the day before, Bishop Callistus, outstanding in triumph and accompanied by a martyr, shines greatly through his trophy.

[Idus.] On the Ides, a crowd of Moors is summoned to you, Agrippina, joyful in spirit and blessed; together they dedicated their service to Christ through virtue and death.

[XVII k.] Gallus the confessor, who marks the coming November with the seventeenth, is honored. At the same time, two hundred and seventeen are remembered, whom unjust fury slaughtered for Christ with equal honor.

[XVI k.] Holy Bishop Florentinus adorns the sixteenth.

[XV k.] On the fifteenth, Luke shows Christ dedicated by his festival and office, speaking through your words, Paul; and Triphonia, who tramples the kingdom, shines nearby.

[XIV k.] Beronicus shines on the fourteenth with fourteen pedagogues; forty-nine likewise accompany them.

[XIII k.] The martyr Caprasius is honored on the thirteenth.

[XII k.] The presbyter Asterius shines on the twelfth with exceptional praise. He taught many saints to overcome the savage wars that threatened pious people everywhere with death. The good inhabitant of the desert, Hilarion, accompanies him. Then, along the many banks of the Rhine, the trophies raised to Christ by virgin companies shine—those belonging to the city of Agrippina, whose impious fury once slaughtered thousands under renowned female leaders.

[Col. 0780A] [XI k.] Bishop Philippus increases the eleventh with his feast. Hermas and blessed Eusebius shine on this same day.

[X k.] Holy Severinus, shining from the summit of the first temple, watches over your settlers on the tenth.

[IX k.] On the ninth, forty-six thousand shine in triumph at Rome, renowned in holy combat.

[VIII k.] Crispinus and Crispinianus hold the eighth. Having suffered the flames, they overcame the savage tyrant. On the same feast let us venerate the twin jewels of martyrdom, Chrysanthus and Daria, whom a new chapel at Rome now beautifies, brought there to their tombs by Christ’s new gift, where the waters of the Rhine give way to lofty forests. Here also Bishop Hilarius shines with great honor.

[VII k.] The seventh truly displays bishops radiant in fame, miracles, and tombs: Amandus by name, and likewise Vedastus, joined to him in merits and time.

[VI k.] From here Vincentius, fighting as a martyr, adorns the sixth. On this day Chrysetes and the virgin Sabina likewise triumph.

[V k.] The fifth excels in the honor of Simon and Judas, whom Persia, rich in God, received when they were sent there. As faithful patrons, they deserved burial through martyrdom and miracles, if afterward she had been a worshipper of the faith.

[Col. 0780B] Born from Caesar, Cyrilla shines here with blessed courage, a virgin to whom Decius was not a father [the reading is uncertain]. Here, too, the matron is honored along the shores of Pharos.

[IV k.] The presbyter Zenobius, retaining the fourth, gilds it.

[III k.] On the third, Marcellus, armed with Christ’s love, consecrated a double century worthy of heaven, accompanied by two hundred and twenty martyrs.

[II k.] On the day before, they celebrate Quintinus as blessed for his deeds. Victorious for Christ in a distinguished and varied contest, he brings falling October to its close in the world.

October sows what it reaps when ripe.

October also makes Libra equal during the season of sowing.

From here Scorpio governs the seasons of joyful autumn.

October, like September, takes its name from its number and its rains: it indicates how many months it is counted from March and that it is more frequently watered by rain.

It should be noted that in the fifth year, on the Kalends of October, there is a thirtieth lunar day, and it belongs to the second embolism; [Col. 0780C] the moon of October ends on the third day before the Kalends of November.

The indictions always begin on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, and end and change there.

Indictions were devised to mark the times of kings—that is, so that no error could arise in the reckoning of times—and, for ease of calculation, they comprise only fifteen years.

In October they should use grape clusters and *framustum* [an uncertain food or preparation], because it heals the body and produces evacuation. They should eat leeks lightly cooked, since raw they contain poison, while cooked they are beneficial as an antidote. Fasting, drink goat’s or lamb’s milk, to sweeten the blood, break up stones, and care for the lungs. Drink clove and pepper preparations.

On the third of October, the sword binds ten in order.

That is, for the most part, the fifth hour of the third day, and also the ninth hour of the tenth day, should be avoided.

## NOVEMBER

[Col. 0781]

The eleventh and penultimate month of the Romans. It has thirty days, while the moon has twenty-nine. The night has sixteen hours, and the day only eight.

The seventh month of the Hebrews, Marcheshvan, falls within this month, and the twelfth month of the Greeks, Dios.

### Martyrology

[Col. 0781A]

Now, while November keeps vigil through the long night, let us bring forth in song the saints whom it celebrates in watchfulness.

[Kal.] Caesarius marks November at its first beginning; Rome rejoices in his outstanding triumph. This month, too, surpassing the others with starry crown, joins all the saints in one honor, those whom heaven’s kingdom alike holds and cherishes.

[V n.] On the fourth, holy Victorinus, the martyr, is blessed; on the Nones, Julianus and Benignus likewise shine, presbyters distinguished by virtue and blood.

[III n.] On the third, Germanus, Vitalis, Caesarius, and Theophilus shine together with equal festival light.

[II n.] From here, on the day before, Amantius the confessor adorns the people of Rodez.

[Nonae] On the Nones, Zacharias, prophet and priest of the temple, excels. He received again, by the ancient custom, the prophet’s voice and office, which his son’s gift had caused to be forgotten. Holy Felix and the monk Eusebius increase this day.

[VIII id.] On the eighth day before the Ides, the martyr Felix is celebrated.

[VII id.] On the seventh, you sanctified Amaranthus through a pious death; Villibrordus also holds the day, under whose leadership many of the people of the Eresones perceived Christ calling them.

[VI id.] Claudius, Castor, Simplicius, Symphorianus, and Nicostratus shine with an equal crown of light, adorning the sixth with merit and blood.

[V id.] Soon, on the fifth, the Ides blossom through the martyr Theodore.

[IV id.] On the fourth, Modestus, Florentia, and Tiberius shine with triple martyrdom, for the threefold name.

[III id.] On the third, the holy confessor and priest rejoices on the sixth, threefold in virtue and faith, renowned through his office and speech. Martinus, a martyr famous throughout the world for his faith, is also invoked on this same day with vows and feast. Domicilla likewise triumphs, having endured exile, scourges, threats, torments, and death for Christ.

[II id.] On the day before, your Chunibertus, Agrippina, excels. The banks of the Seine also recall the saint.

[Idus] On the Ides, your heir, O Martin, holds the day: Brixius, proved by exile, tears, and miracles.

[XIX k.] Clementinus, Theodotus, and Philuminus hold the day.

[XVIII k.] On the eighteenth before the Kalends of December, those who likewise suffered the commands of a cruel torturer are remembered.

[XVII k.] On the seventeenth, Eugenius the martyr shines.

[XVI k.] Eucherius and Gregorius fill the sixteenth; the former is bishop of Lyons, the latter of Neocaesarea.

[XV k.] On the fifteenth, Amanus shines with praise along the banks of the Liger and among festive peoples. By merits, miracles, prayer, and counsel he redeemed his own city from hostile devastation.

[Col. 0782A] [XIV k.] The martyr Hisychius crowns the fourteenth, and the city of Antioch, joyful in its Roman, returns to him [the wording is uncertain].

[XIII k.] On the thirteenth, Felicianus, together with Severinus and Exuperius, sanctifies the day through the contest of faith.

[XII k.] Rome dedicates the twelfth to you, blessed Pontianus; bishop and martyr, he sanctifies it through his service.

[XI k.] The abbot Columbanus keeps the eleventh for himself. From the Ocean he scattered the teachings of holy religion through pious speech and action.

[X k.] Holy Cecilia soon illuminates the tenth with perpetual splendor, ever to be proclaimed for her distinguished trophies. She is a virgin, supported on one side by a kinsman and on the other by a holy husband.

[IX k.] Pope Clement holds the ninth through contest and lofty titles of virtue. Having suffered death in the waters, he found a temple constructed by divine gift. On this day also blessed Felicitas, preeminent with her seven children, shines in a blessed triumph.

Here too Trudo, the despiser of the world, adorns his people.

[VIII k.] Chrysogonus sanctifies the eighth through merits and death.

[VII k.] Bishop and martyr Peter adorns the seventh. Under his leadership, the people of Alexandria, supported by him, despise the crooked and blind paths of error.

[VI k.] On the sixth, you sanctify the day, Linus, pope of rosy blood.

[V k.] Agricola and Vitalis honor the fifth through martyrdom.

[IV k.] On the fourth, your companion, Paul of Silea, increases and adorns the day.

[III k.] On the third, let us dedicate the day to you, Saturninus, and to Maurus.

[II k.] The Apostle Andrew excels on the day before with abundant rays of virtue shining throughout the world, and with titles of honor; by word and miracles he subdued the untamed Achaeans.

These vows of the peoples will close the wintry November.

Scorpio, rushing headlong, commands November to enter winter.

But November always purifies the crops by threshing them.

Here the harsh frosts of winter’s cold begin.

From here the Archer saddens the sky with his icy star.

November, by its name, like the preceding months, indicates how many months it is from March; and it indicates that it has more frequent rains.

It should be known that in the eighteenth year certain people who begin the epacts in January skip the thirtieth lunar day of November on the seventh day before the Kalends of December, placing the lunar leap there, so that on the Kalends of January the ninth lunar day may be found in the first year.

Let this be known to everyone: the first office of Advent of the Lord should begin neither before the fifth day before the Kalends of December nor be postponed beyond the third day before the Nones of that month. Rather, whether on those days or on the days lying between them, whenever the Lord’s Day occurs, it must properly and without doubt be sung.

In November and December it is good to have exercise; let them open the hepatic vein, because at that time all the humors are stirred. Let them abstain from baths and eat no head-meat at all; their drink should be cinnamon.

On the fifth of November, the needle barely remained third in the urn [the wording is obscure].

That is, for the most part, the eighth hour of the fifth day, and also the fourth hour of the other day, should be avoided.

## DECEMBER

[Col. 0783]

The twelfth and final month of the Romans. It has thirty-one days, while the moon has twenty-nine. The night has eighteen hours, and the day only six.

The eighth month of the Hebrews, Kislev, falls within this month, and the first month of the Greeks, Apellaeus.

### Martyrology

[Col. 0783B]

[Kal.] Eligius, bishop of Noyon, marks December for you at its first light with fitting episcopal honor.

[IV non.] On the fourth day before the Nones, Africa offers sacrifice to Verus and Secundus.

[III non.] On the third, it likewise offers sacrifice to Cassianus, the martyr.

[II non.] Then Heraclius excels on the day before, together with Victorius.

[Nonae] The martyr Dalmatius and Crispina keep the Nones.

[VIII id.] Bishop Nicholas adorns the eighth day before the Ides.

[VII id.] Polycarp holds the seventh together with Theodore.

[VI id.] Eutychianus shines on the sixth, and Pope Felix with his blood; Zeno also holds the day with united martyrly honor.

[V id.] We celebrate Sebastianus on the fifth, transferred from the city. Through him the Gallic countryside rejoices in its own patron, with the great church and altar that rise to him, whose pinnacles rival the splendor of antiquity. The virgin Leucadia also sanctifies the day for herself through her merits.

[IV id.] On the fourth, we venerate Eulalia with holy love, the Spaniard of Mérida, whose blood and bones are preserved.

[III id.] On the third, Rome offers the solemnities of Pope Damasus. Victoricus and Fuscianus likewise appear and possess equal splendor of festival and vow.

[Col. 0783C] The fields of Amiens bloom with the blood of Hermogenes and Donatus, who now shine twice over.

[II id.] Then, on the day before, two saints shine, joined by their blood.

[Idus] On the Ides, Syracuse dedicated Lucia to you. Having suffered the tyrant Paschasius for Christ’s name, the Holy Spirit made her immovable before wicked men. Vidoch and the priest Colerius likewise shine; before whom the storms of the Ocean often yield.

[XIX k.] On the nineteenth before the Kalends, Bishop Nicasius, who customarily calls the nineteenth before the Kalends, increases the day with honor; Bishop Spiridion is likewise celebrated on that day.

[XVIII k.] Maximinus holds the eighteenth.

The fertile fields of Aureliana offer him the wine of Bacchus.

[XVII k.] On the seventeenth, the three youths are remembered who despised the impious commands of the Assyrian tyrant. Neither the crackling furnace nor the flame of the raging furnace could terrify their faithful and steadfast spirits.

[Col. 0784B] [XVI k.] Holy Ignatius triumphs on the sixteenth, shepherd and martyr of the city of Antioch, whose living flesh the teeth of wild beasts made into bread. Rufus and Sosinus follow him, having shed their blood for Christ.

[XV k.] The fifteenth blossoms through the blood of Moysitis [reading uncertain].

[XIV k.] Zosimus and Darius crown the fourteenth.

[XIII k.] Bishop Zephyrinus shines on the thirteenth.

[XII k.] The twelfth celebrates the translation of Thomas, through whose building India deserved to know the kingdom of God, accompanied by fearsome signs.

[XI k.] Rome celebrates the eleventh with thirty martyrs.

[X k.] Victoria shines on the tenth, a virgin of Christ.

[IX k.] On the ninth, we prepare gifts for the coming light: lamps, vigilant altars, and temples. Here the forty virgins also shine in heaven, who dedicated worthy lives through vow and virtue.

[VIII k.] On the eighth, the Creator, having deigned to assume the form of a servant, came to recall erring humanity—
Through a virginal birth he clothed himself in mortal limbs,

and then we commemorate Eugenia and Anastasia also,
who followed Christ with like-mindedness and faith.

[VII Kalends] [Col. 0784C] Hence the seventh is made illustrious by Stephen, Levite and first martyr,

who, blessed, followed the King, born and suffering,
in life, faith, struggle, and death.

We shall speak of the final month of the year,
whose festivals he celebrates and reports in brief days.

[VI Kalends] The Lord’s beloved and inspector of the heavenly word,

who deserved continually to draw from the perennial fountain
of Christ’s breast—John sanctifies and marks the sixth.

[V Kalends] Those whom dreadful desire tore from their mothers’ breasts,

while Herod desired to destroy the newborn Christ:
on the fifth we venerate the infants.

[IV Kalends] David, prophet and pious king, the origin of the divine lineage,

marks the fourth with speech and faith,
and the city of Arelas shines, rejoicing in its shepherd Trophimus.

[III Kalends] The gentle Mansuetus and Florentius adorn the third together.

[II Kalends] On the day before the Kalends, Sylvester, pope, throughout the Roman city

subjects the rejoicing peoples to himself with friendly prayers.
He was the first of the pontiffs to deserve to see peaceful times
and to cleanse the rulers of the world by baptism.

[Col. 0785] The virgin Columba likewise received an everlasting palm through her virtue,

following Christ by her own blood;
and Sabinianus, together with Potentianus, appears at the same festival,
equal in altar and triumph—
they who, as its first patrons, instructed the city of the Senones.

These festivals finally close December.

The Archer ends his signs in the middle of December.

From this point the solstice is revealed, as the lofty days return;
from this point Phoebus, turning back, begins to increase the light.

Behold, this man now prepares the December calendars for the pig (*suem*; the sense is uncertain).

December is so called from the number ten and from the rains, like the three preceding months. Romulus arranged these ten months, assigning alternately thirty-one days to one and thirty to the other, and concluding them all in three hundred and four days. Later Numa added fifty-one days in two months and calculated the year almost according to the course of the moon. [Col. 0786] After him, finally, that Julius Caesar added ten days and established the year at three hundred and sixty-five days and six hours, according to the course of the sun—as it is still observed today.

In the thirteenth year, on the Kalends of December, there is a thirtieth moon; but this is assigned to the fifth embolism, which begins on the fourth day before the Nones of November. The moon of December ends on the third day before the Kalends of January. The moon of the first embolism begins on the fourth day before the Nones of December and ends on the second day before the Kalends of January.

In December they should not eat cabbages, because from them blood comes forth, infused with poison from the cabbage: drink Jewish spikenard (*spicum Judaicum*).

The company of seven gives twelve, and then ten, in December.

The first hour of the seventh day, for the most part, and also the eighth hour of the tenth day, are to be avoided.

## DISTRIBUTION OF THE YEAR

[Col. 0785]

In these verses there are as many syllables as there are days in the civil year—namely, three hundred and sixty-five. By means of these syllables you will find on which day the more important festivals fall: each month of the year has two verses.

### Names of the months

Twelve months.

January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December.

### Letters of the week

Seven letters of the days.

The horse snorts at the great weapons,
when it sees the weapons of war.

### On the Advent

This Sunday falls on 26 November.

The Advent of the Lord follows the solemnity of Linus;
Advent always begins on the Sunday before *Barbar.* [an uncertain abbreviation in the source].

### The four parts of the year

19 November, 22 February, 25 May, 24 August.

Elizabeth gives winter; Peter, enthroned, gives spring.
Urbanus burns with summer; Bartholomew gives autumn.

### The four Ember seasons

Lucy, 13 December; the Cross, 14 September; the other two are movable.

The seasonal fasts require Wednesday:
Ash Wednesday, and the Wednesday following Lucy, the Spirit, and the Cross.

### The four temperatures

Summer is dry and hot; autumn dry and cold;
winter is cold and wet; spring is warm, thirsty, and moist.

### The equinoxes

17 September, 24 April.

Lambert and Gregory: night is made equal to day.

### The solstices

15 June, 13 December.

Vitus and Lucy are the two solstices.

[Col. 0787] ## On the leap year

24 February.

The Kalends of March held the sixth day twice;
on the following day the feast of Matthias is celebrated.
If Saturdays fall there, they are celebrated nowhere else.

### The days of the months

April, June, September, and November have thirty days.

The others have one more. February has twenty-eight;
but if it is a leap year, one is added,
and then write the Kalends of March twice on the sixth day.

### The Kalends, Nones, and Ides

May, October, July, and March have six Nones.

The remaining months have four. Every month has eight Ides.

Saturnian Juno claims the Ausonian Kalends.

### The days of the year

The year contains L, X, V, three C’s, and six hours:

these produce the leap year every fourth year.

## COMPUTATION OF THE EMBOLISMS

### JANUARY, THE FIRST MONTH

It must be noted above all that in the eleventh year, on the fourth day before the Nones of January, the moon of the fourth embolism ends. This embolism is inserted on the second day before the Nones of December in the tenth year, and the moon of January ends in February.

[Col. 0788] Four-line poem for this first month.

January loves to run its course on warm nourishment
and often bids us restore ourselves with pleasant drink.
Let no blood sweat from a vein cut for you,
but it is permitted to immerse the body in warm water.

### FEBRUARY, THE SECOND MONTH

[Col. 0787]

[Col. 0789] It must be noted above all that February’s lunar month, without a leap year, is the twenty-ninth; with a leap year it is counted as the thirtieth, whether it is reckoned before or after the Kalends of March. It must also be noted that in the eleventh year the January moon ends on the Kalends of February as the thirtieth moon, and does not belong to February but to January. The February moon ends in March.

[Col. 0790] Four-line poem for this second month.

In February, avoid vegetables and marsh birds as food;
they are customarily feared for their debilitating fever.
Then drink medicines; then open a vein in your thumb,
and warm your limbs abundantly in a hot stream.

### MARCH, THE THIRD MONTH

[Col. 0789]

In the same eleventh year, the moon that ought to have been the twenty-ninth on the Kalends of March will be the twenty-eighth, because of the embolism inserted on the second day before the Nones of December, if it is not a leap year. But if it is a leap year, the twenty-ninth moon falls on the Kalends of March, and the thirtieth on the sixth day before the Nones; this moon is counted not as belonging to that month but to February.

[Col. 0790] Four-line poem for this third month.

March increases the humors of the earth and of the body;
then you must carefully maintain a pure regimen.
Sweet things seasoned with a sharp flavor are beneficial then;
medicines are of no use, and opening a vein is harmful.

### APRIL, THE FOURTH MONTH

[Col. 0789]

[Col. 0791] In this matter, therefore, we urge the reader to observe that in the eighth and nineteenth years of the nineteen-year cycle the April moon is taken in May, because of the two embolisms that produce the thirtieth moon on the second day before the Nones of April and on the third day before the Nones of April. Likewise, in the eleventh year there is a thirtieth moon on the Kalends of April, but it is assigned to March.

[Col. 0792] Four-line poem for this fourth month.

April slowly restores the strength of the earth from the cold;
then the skin is also thin and full of openings.
Then the inner parts are more enlarged, and everything is full;
the belly bids itself be emptied, and the vein opened.

### MAY, THE FIFTH MONTH

[Col. 0791]

In the eighth year, the moon that ought, according to the rule, to be the twenty-eighth on the Kalends of May is the twenty-seventh, because of the embolism inserted on the second day before the Nones of March. And the moon that ought to be the thirtieth on the Kalends of June will be the twenty-ninth.

Likewise, in the nineteenth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the moon that ought to be the twenty-ninth on the Kalends of May will be the twenty-eighth, because of the embolism inserted on the third day before the Nones of March.

Four-line poem for this fifth month.

Now everything is flowering; now the year is most beautiful,
and now everyone wants things to be gentler for himself.
Now enjoy the baths; now take care to take medicines,
and now let your vein flow with blood released.

### JUNE, THE SIXTH MONTH

[Col. 0791]

[Col. 0793] It must be observed that in the eighth year, on the fourth day before the Nones of June, there is a thirtieth moon, but it ought to belong to May. The moon of June ends in July.

Likewise, in the nineteenth year, there is a thirtieth moon on the Kalends of June, and it belongs to May. The moon of June ends on the Kalends of July.

[Col. 0794] Four-line poem for this sixth month.

June delights in coolness and is nourished by life-giving moisture and herbs;
flee what is hostile then.
Let gentle pleasure then refresh the mind,
but let no medicine afflict your body.

### JULY, THE SEVENTH MONTH

[Col. 0793]

It must also be observed that in the eighth year the moon ought to be the thirtieth on the Kalends of July, but it is the twentieth, and belongs to June.

Up to this point extends the disturbance caused by the third embolism, which is inserted on the second day before the Nones of March.

[Col. 0794] Four-line poem for this seventh month.

July intensifies the fiery heats of the air;
in this season, give yourself the shorter rest of sleep.
Avoid the baths, and do not touch the vein with iron;
do not wish to recline in reckless intercourse with your mistress.

### AUGUST, THE EIGHTH MONTH

[Col. 0795]

It must be considered that in the seventeenth year, on the second day before the Kalends of September, the thirtieth moon is found because of the sixth embolism, which begins on the fourth day before the Nones of August; it does not belong to August.

For the embolic moon is assigned to no month, but is, as it were, superfluous.

[Col. 0796] Four-line poem for this eighth month.

August itself restricts sleep and food,
and forbids those eager for love to enjoy its pleasures.
Let no one drink medicines or injure his body with iron;
nor let him delight himself in cold waters.

### SEPTEMBER, THE NINTH MONTH

[Col. 0795]

It must also be considered that in the fifth year the second embolism begins on the fourth day before the Nones of September and ends on the Kalends of October.

[Col. 0796] Four-line poem for this tenth month.

September gives apples and pleasant fruits from the tree;
then also feed on pressed goat’s milk.
Nothing forbids taking medicines then or opening a vein,
nor should your food avoid an external seasoning.

### OCTOBER, THE TENTH MONTH

[Col. 0797]

It must be noted that in the fifth year, on the Kalends of October, thirty is found, and it is an embolic moon. The moon of October ends on the third day before the Kalends of November.

[Col. 0798] Four-line poem for this final month.

In October hunting, wines, and birds are offered;
use them, and do not hesitate not to have kept measure—
but in such a way that you do not burden your chest
with excessive food, while striving not to have kept measure.

### NOVEMBER, THE ELEVENTH MONTH

[Col. 0797]

It must be understood that in the final year of the nineteen-year cycle, on the seventh day before the Kalends of December, the moon ought to be the thirtieth; but there the first is found, because of the leap which the Latins inserted there: the thirtieth moon is divided and skipped there, so that in the first year the ninth moon occurs on the third day before the Kalends of January.

[Col. 0798] Four-line poem for this penultimate month.

Mulled wine is said to be healthful in November,
and ginger, sweet, split, and floating in honey.
Then do not bathe often, nor frequently attend the rites of Venus,
lest you seem prematurely old before your time.

### DECEMBER, THE TWELFTH MONTH

[Col. 0799]

It must be noted that in the thirteenth year, on the Kalends of December, the thirtieth moon is found because of the fifth embolism, which begins on the fourth day before the Nones of November. It does not belong to December; it ends on the third day before the Kalends of January.
