## ON THE CALCULATION OF THE YEAR ESTABLISHED BY JULIUS CAESAR

[Col. 0799]

[Col. 0799A] January, August, and December have four Nones and nineteen days before the Kalends; after the Ides, thirty-one days.

March, May, July, and October have six Nones and seventeen days before the Kalends; after the Ides, thirty-one days.

April, June, September, and November have four Nones and eighteen days before the Kalends; after the Ides, thirty days.

February, however, has four Nones and sixteen days before the Kalends; after the Ides, twenty-eight days.

When it is a leap year, it has twenty-nine days and a thirtieth moon.

All months, however, have eight Ides.

### The places of the embolisms

The first embolism, that is, the superadded month, begins on the fourth day before the Nones of December, when the epacts are twenty-two, and ends on the second day before the Kalends of January.

[Col. 0799B]

The second embolism begins on the fourth day before the Nones of September, when the twenty-five epacts begin, and ends on the Kalends of October.

The third embolism is inserted on the second day before the Nones of March, when there are seventeen epacts; ending on the second day before the Nones of April, it produces the thirtieth moon. Hence on the Kalends of May the moon becomes the twenty-seventh, although according to the rule it ought to be the twenty-eighth; and on the Kalends of July, what ought to be thirty becomes twenty-nine.

The fourth embolism begins on the second day before the Nones of December, when there are twenty epacts; ending on the fourth day before the Nones of January, it produces the thirtieth moon. Therefore on the Kalends of March the moon becomes the twenty-eighth, [Col. 0800A] which according to the rule ought to be the twenty-eighth, if the leap-day addition does not intervene for it.

The fifth embolism is inserted on the fourth day before the Nones of November, when there are twenty-three epacts, and reaches its end on the Kalends of December.

The sixth embolism begins on the fourth day before the Nones of August, when fifteen epacts end, and reaches its end on the second day before the Kalends of September.

The seventh, which is also the final embolism, is inserted on the Nones of May, when there are eighteen epacts. Ending on the third day before the Nones of April, it produces the thirtieth moon. Hence on the Kalends of May the moon is the twenty-eighth, which the rule intended to be the twenty-eighth. Likewise, in that same year, on the third day before the Kalends of August, the lunar leap is suitably placed, so that the thirtieth moon of July is skipped there and the first is called in place of the thirtieth; thus on the Kalends of August it becomes the third, though it ought to be the second, so that on the Kalends of September, when no epacts begin, it can become the fifth.

## On the regular numbers for finding the weekdays and the moon

[Col. 0800B] [Col. 0801A]

The little points raised upward and placed near the numbers here seem to signify halves.

### On the leap year

If you wish to know when a leap year occurs, take the years from the Incarnation of the Lord and divide them by four. If one, two, or three remain, it will not be a leap year. But if nothing remains, that year will be a leap year. Likewise, if you add two to the years from the beginning of the world and then divide them by four, you will find the leap year in the same way.

### On the weekday of the Kalends

If you wish to know the weekday of the Kalends, add the regular numbers given above to the concurrent number of the year. If the result is seven or less, that is the weekday. But if it exceeds seven, subtract seven, and regard what remains as the weekday. If you wish to know any other weekday, count how many elapsed days the month has, not including the present day; add to these the weekday on which the Kalends fell, divide the total by seven, and the remainder will indicate the weekday.

### On finding the epacts

Take the position of the year in the nineteen-year cycle, subtract one, and multiply the remainder by eleven. When you have multiplied it, always subtract thirty; what remains will indicate the epact. Likewise, whatever moon falls each year on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, that is the complete epact for the same year.

### Where the epacts arise

If you wish to know where the epacts— that is, the lunar additions—arise, know that the solar year has three hundred and sixty-five days. The lunar year, that is, twelve lunar months, contains three hundred and fifty-four days. Thus the solar year precedes the lunar year by eleven days. These eleven days produce the epacts.

In the first year of the nineteen-year cycle we have no epacts because nineteen lunar years, with seven embolic months supplying the difference, equal the same number of solar years: they begin together and end together. One solar year, however, precedes one lunar year by eleven days, as we have said. Therefore after having no epacts, we have eleven. Two solar years likewise exceed two lunar years by twice eleven, that is, by twenty-two days. Therefore twenty-two epacts follow eleven. In this order, if you compare equal numbers of solar and lunar years, [Col. 0801D] you will see the reckoning of all the epacts.

### On the regular numbers of the moon

If you wish to know where the regular numbers for finding the moon on the Kalends come from, know that in the year in which there are no epacts, whatever the moon’s position is on the Kalends of each month, each month will have the same regular number in other years, so that, when the epacts of any year are added, the moon on the Kalends can be found.

### What the moon’s age is on each Kalends

If you wish to know the age of the moon on the Kalends, add these regular numbers to the epacts of the year. If the result is thirty or less, that is the moon’s age. If they exceed thirty, subtract thirty; what remains will reveal the moon’s age.

If you wish to know the age of the moon within any month, count how many elapsed days the month has, not including the day about which you ask; add twice the moon’s age on the Kalends, and subtract from this the lunar month of that month. What remains will indicate the moon to you in this way.

## The places of the Paschal term, with their regular numbers

[Col. 0802A]

### On finding the Paschal term

[Col. 0802B]

If you wish to know the Paschal term—that is, the fourteenth moon of the first month—mark the Nones of April in the verses written above. Memorize the five verses, in which the nineteen different places of the fourteenth day of that same moon over the nineteen years are set out according to a fixed reckoning. Each verse reveals to you, for each year, the place of that term without any uncertainty.

To find the weekday of that same term, take the regular numbers of those verses and add to them the concurrent number of any year. If the result is seven or less, that is the weekday. If it exceeds seven, subtract seven and regard what remains as the weekday. If this weekday is Sunday, Easter will be on the following Sunday. If it is another weekday, Easter will be celebrated immediately on the following Sunday.

### On the regular Paschal terms

If you wish to know where these regular numbers themselves arise, count from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, which is the first day of the world, up to the place of the fourteenth Paschal moon. If you find seven or less, you will have that many regular numbers. If there is more, always subtract seven; what remains is the regular number.

Fifteen years of the nineteen-year cycle are placed above with different numbers; below, four are written, which, together with the numbers placed above them, receive one line of vowels positioned below for finding the moon. Its age meets the person searching from the right and from the left.

When, therefore, you ask in which sign the moon is, note in the calendar, on the third line back, which letter is placed before the day. Having noted the year of the nineteen-year cycle, investigate it here; beginning in front and behind, you will find opposite it the sign and the month belonging to that sign.

### Letters of the weekdays

### On the Golden Number

If the number called the Golden Number is six this year, the following year will have seven, and the next year joined to it will have eight; then nine, then ten, and so on up to nineteen. Then one must return to one, afterward to two, then to three, likewise to four, and afterward to five. Thus it always proceeds in a cycle from one through nineteen.

### Explanation of the preceding table or figure

Seven letters of the days, *a b c d e f g*, are placed above this calendar and repeated four times. Each marks all the Kalends, arranged in one order opposite one another, so that the same letter throughout the whole year always corresponds to the same weekday. Since there are fourteen Kalends opposite each letter, it is clear that throughout the year one letter presides over fifty-two Kalends and one weekday corresponds to it.

The alphabet *a b c d e f g h i k*, which here extends at least to ten, was explained above in the preceding figure.

The other alphabet, namely *a b c d e f g h i k l m n o p q r s t u*, with two spaces, extending to twenty, belongs to the following table composed in verse. Although here it is placed in the two lower lines, the same arrangement is found in the first and twelfth lines of the following table. We nevertheless arranged this same material above in the calendar.

The two alphabets have this in common: after the final *u* of this one, both alphabets begin again shortly after one space.

If you ask what the moon is on each day, first learn what the epact of that year is. Having found it, seek in this calendar or in the preceding one the alphabet separated by two spaces, extending to the letter *u*. Having found, in those two lines, the letter or space belonging to the day whose moon you wish to know, investigate the same letter or the same space.

When you have found it, count forward from that place according to the number of epacts of that year. Where that number ends, there the age of the moon on that day is believed to be, since in this figure the points count as numbers.

Thus eight are written first, then two points, which count as ten and eleven. Again twelve are written, followed by two points, which count as thirteen and fourteen. The same is understood in all the other cases.

Once this figure has been carefully and attentively considered, you will have no doubt about how the same arrangement operates in the first and twelfth lines of the table composed in verse.

These two lines also have this noteworthy feature: the moon which begins first in the letters or spaces of the upper line ends on the twenty-eighth in the lower line; conversely, the first moon of the lower line ends on the thirtieth in the upper, except in the third year of the nineteen-year cycle.

To make the rest clear: in the year whose epact is twenty-three on the Kalends of August, the second space is first *a*. When this space is found in the lower line, the moon is shown from it at the twenty-third place as the seventh; it began—that is, in the calendar—in the second space after the letter *k* as the first.

Investigate all these matters in the verses also. In composing them I satisfied my own purpose and consulted not the cleverness of just anyone inexperienced, but that of students. For the less learned will find in the other figures whatever I have usefully arranged here, even for the exercise of the serious-minded.

This reckoning of the nineteen-year cycle, counted nineteen times, extends to 342 years.

## FIRST TABLE OF WEEKDAYS

[Col. 0815] ### Explanation of the preceding table

The first seven letters at the head of this page, *a b c d e f g*, designate the seven weekdays on which the Kalends of January may fall. The letters *d* and *p*, which are placed at the beginning and scattered throughout the page, are prefixed to the Kalends on which, over the nineteen years, the Sunday of each of the two feasts occurs. For it is certain that *d* signifies the day on which Lent begins, and *p* Easter.

The Roman epacts are also written at the side. They are preceded by numbers progressing naturally from one to thirty and admit no number except one found among the epacts. Therefore, if you wish to find the Sunday of the beginning of Lent and of Easter, know on which weekday the Kalends of January fell and what the Roman epacts of that year are. On the front—the side of this page—will appear the weekdays and epacts.

If, then, you wish to know where the Sunday of the beginning of Lent and of Easter falls in any year, know where the epact of that year is opposite it. This is always properly Roman, [Col. 0818A] three lines before the Egyptian epact on the reverse. For the third year of the nineteen-year cycle among the Romans is reckoned as the first among the Egyptians.

Thus, if you add eight to any Egyptian epact, the Roman epact will be given to you, provided that the sum remains below thirty.

If it exceeds thirty, subtract thirty and take what remains as the Roman epact. Having found it, investigate it finally in the other following number; and wherever you find it, proceed along that line toward the letter designating the weekday of the Kalends of January. There you will encounter the beginning of Lent and Easter Sunday with its lunar date.

## Second table of weekdays

### Explanation of the preceding table

The preceding table indicates the beginnings of Lent, Easter, and the Rogation days for each year of the nineteen-year cycle. At its head, the concurrent numbers are prefixed in their order, together with the seven weekday letters marking Sunday; in the margins, on the reader’s left, are the epacts, and on the right the years of the nineteen-year cycle.

If, then, you wish to know in any year of the nineteen-year cycle the beginnings of Lent, Easter, and the Rogation days, which are marked on the page by the letters *q p r*, find the concurrent number of the present year and the epact. Descending from the head of the page along the line of concurrent numbers, and entering inward from left to right across the line of epacts, wherever their perpendicular intersection occurs you will undoubtedly find the Kalends marking those beginnings.

For example: this year there was one concurrent number, immediately before the leap year, while the epact was twenty-five. The beginnings themselves were: *q*, the fifth day before the Nones of March; *p*, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May; *r*, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June.

### Into the first table

This figure shows on which weekday the Kalends fall for each month throughout the twenty-eight years of the solar cycle.

This figure was also made for finding the weekday of any day. It consists of twenty-eight lines, corresponding to the number of years in the solar cycle through which the concurrent numbers are known to proceed.

It has only the first seven letters of the alphabet, because there are the same number of weekdays.

When, therefore, you wish to find the weekday of any day in the whole year, look in the calendar to see which letter is marked beside that day on the reverse; then return to this figure, having found the year of the solar cycle from the number written on the reverse.

On that line, having found the letter of the day, look upward and you will find the weekday you seek written beside it.

### Into the third table
This table, called the Septizodius because it resolves into itself through a cycle of seven years, has seven times seven compartments, that is, forty-nine letters in all. Those in the second row, from the letter *a* through *g*, placed in the individual months, pertain to the reckoning of the leap year and to the reckoning of the weekdays, which revolve through twenty-eight years. This arrangement, just as it is necessary only in leap years, applies from the Kalends of January through the leap day. The alphabets of these figures have the same letter on the last day of the year—that is, on the second day before the Kalends of January—namely, *a*. Therefore, in the fourth year, which is a leap year, when you are about to enter this smaller figure, first seek in the larger one the weekday of the day before the Kalends of January, which is the last day of the preceding year and is certainly found written above. On the following day, which is the first day of the following year, coming to this figure, seek the same *a* on the same weekday. But, leaving that line aside, take the *a* placed beneath it in the following line; looking backward, you will find the weekday of the Kalends of January. Thus, throughout that entire month and through February up to the leap day, proceeding along the same little line—not across it, as in the larger figure, but lengthwise—you will find, as you see the weekdays marked, the weekday of each individual day in the customary manner.

The day six days before the Kalends of March, which, being counted twice, produces the leap day, is described only once in the calendar and bears the letter *f*. Therefore, in this smaller figure you will customarily repeat in reverse the weekday on which the first six days before the Kalends of March are read, at *f*. On the following day, when, because of the leap year, you call it the actual six days before the Kalends of March, return to the larger figure. The line which you are about to enter, marked on one side by the solar cycle and on the other by the leap year, designates the leap day. Seek the same *f*, and, looking upward, you will again find the weekday of that day. And so thereafter you will proceed throughout that year along the same line, and during the following three years along the three following lines, until, in the fourth row, you repeat this process as stated.

[Col. 0821]

## Manfred’s Reckoning of the Embolismic Years (C)*

[Col. 0821A] In the first embolismic year—that is, in the third ogdoad—there are twenty-two epacts. Accordingly, the moon is twenty-seven on the Kalends of September and October, and twenty-nine on the Kalends of November and December. The moon that is twenty-nine on the Kalends of December is the moon of that month, and there it is extinguished. The moon that begins on the fourth day before the Nones of December and ends on the Kalends of January is the thirtieth embolism. The moon that is on the Kalends of January is its first moon, and it too must end at thirty.

In the second embolismic year—that is, in the ogdoad—there are seven epacts. The twenty-fifth moon on the Kalends of September is the thirtieth, and it is extinguished there; it is the moon of that month. The moon that changes on the first day before the fourth day before the Nones of September and ends at thirty on the Kalends of October is the embolism. The moon that begins on the first day before the sixth day before the Nones of October and ends at thirty-nine on the third day before the Kalends of November is the October moon; on the Kalends of November and December it becomes the second moon. On the Kalends of January it is the fourth, as the order requires.

In the third embolismic year—that is, in the final ogdoad—there are seventeen epacts. On the Kalends of September and October the moon is twenty-two; on the Kalends of November and December, twenty-four; on the Kalends of January, twenty-six; on the Kalends of March, twenty-six; on the Kalends of April and May, twenty-seven; on the Kalends of June and July, twenty-nine; on the Kalends of August, and on the Kalends of September, three.

Why do you make one lunar age on the Kalends of April and May? Because nowhere else is this found in the computation. The reason is that the moon which begins on the second day before the Nones of March is first, is twenty-six on the Kalends of April, twenty-eight on the fourth day before the Nones of April, and on the second day before the Nones of April is the thirtieth embolism and is extinguished. The moon which begins on the first day before the ninth of April is the Paschal moon; it reaches fourteen on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May and ends at twenty-nine on the fifth day before the Nones of May. The moon which is first on the fourth day before the Nones of May and ends at thirty on the fourth day before the Nones of July is the May moon. The moon which begins on the fourth day before the Nones of June and ends at twenty-nine on the day before the Kalends of July is the June moon. The moon which begins on the first day before the sixth day before the Nones of July and ends at thirty on the second day before the Kalends of August is the July moon. Afterwards the computation of the moon of the Kalends of August becomes first; on the Kalends of September it is fourth, as the order requires.

For if one lunar age had not been made on the Kalends of April and May, the result at the Paschal limit—which falls on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May—would have been not the fourteenth but the fifteenth moon, and there would have been an error concerning Easter or the lunar ages.

Accordingly, in the first embolismic year—that is, in the hendecad—there are twenty epacts. Therefore the moon is twenty-five on the Kalends of September and October, twenty-seven on the Kalends of November and December, twenty-nine on the Kalends of January, and thirty on the fourth day before the Nones of January, which is the January moon. The second moon, which begins on the fourth day before the Nones of January and is extinguished on the thirtieth day before the Kalends of February, is the embolism. The moon which begins on the fourth day before the Nones of February and ends on the sixth day before the Nones of March is the twenty-ninth moon of February. If that year is a leap year, this same February moon is counted as thirty, as in the other leap years.

The moon which begins on the fifth day before the Nones of that month and ends at thirty on the Kalends of April is the March moon. The moon which begins on the fourth day before the Nones of April and ends at twenty-nine on the second day before the Kalends of May is the April moon. Whatever moon occurs on the Kalends is the first moon of that month. The remaining moons follow their proper order.

In the second embolismic year of the same hendecad there are twenty-three epacts. The moon is twenty-eight on the Kalends of September and October and thirty on the Kalends of November and December. The moon that ends at thirty on the Kalends of November is the moon of that month; the moon that begins on the fourth day before the Nones of November and ends at thirty on the Kalends of December is the embolism. The moon that begins first on the fourth day before the Nones of December becomes the second moon on the Kalends of January and the third on the Kalends of February. The others thereafter follow their proper order.

In the third embolismic year—that is, in the hendecad—there are twenty-six epacts. Nevertheless, you will in no way discover the embolism through these epacts unless you return to the epacts of the preceding common year. In the preceding common year there were fifteen epacts. The moon is twenty-nine on the Kalends of August and ends there because it is the moon of that month. The moon begun on the fourth day before the Nones of August and ending at thirty on the second day before the Kalends of September is the embolism. On the Kalends of September and October, through the twenty-six epacts, it becomes the first moon; the others follow in order.

In the final embolism of the hendecad there are eighteen epacts: on the Kalends of September and October, the moon is twenty-three; on the Kalends of November and December, twenty-five; on the Kalends of January, twenty-seven; on the Kalends of February, twenty-eight; on the Kalends of March, twenty-seven; on the Kalends of April and May, twenty-eight; on the Kalends of June, thirty; on the Kalends of July, one; on the Kalends of August, three, because of the lunar leap; on the Kalends of September, five.

We make one lunar age on the Kalends of April and May because the moon which begins on the third day before the Nones of March is twenty-eight on the Kalends of April, twenty-nine on the fourth day before the Nones of April, and on the third day before the Nones is the thirtieth embolism. The moon which begins on the second day before the Nones of April and extends to the sixth day before the Nones of May is the twenty-ninth moon of April; it is the Paschal moon, reaching fourteen on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May. If this had not been done, the fifteenth moon would have occurred three times at the Paschal limit, and there would have been an error concerning Easter and the lunar ages.

The moon which begins on the fifth day before the Nones of May and ends at thirty on the Kalends of June is the May moon. The June moon begins on the third day before the Nones of that month and ends at twenty-nine on the second day before the Kalends of July. The moon which is first on the third day before the Kalends of July and is extinguished at twenty-nine is the July moon. Although it ought to end at thirty on the third day before the Kalends of August, it loses one day because of the leap in the computations and is counted as the third moon of August on its Kalends, although the reckoning of the argument shows that it should be the second. It ends at twenty-nine on the sixth day before the Kalends of September. The remaining moons follow their order.

March, fifth; April, first; May, third; June, sixth; July, first; August, fourth; September, seventh; October, second; November, fifth; December, seventh; January, third; February, seventh; September, fifth; October, fifth; November, seventh; December, sixth; January, ninth; February, tenth; March, ninth; April, tenth; May, eleventh; June, twelfth; July, thirteenth; August, fourteenth.

For the limit of Septuagesima, count from the seventh day before the Ides of January. For the limit of Lent, count from the fifth day before the Kalends of February. For the limit of Easter, count from the fifth day before the Ides of March. For the limit of the Rogation days, count from the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May. ## Preface of a Certain Diligent Student to the Cycles of the Blessed Cyril and of Dionysius the Roman, and of Bede

[Col. 0823B] Dionysius, an abbot and a Roman by birth, composed the Paschal cycles with remarkable concision, being distinguished by his knowledge of both languages. As he himself says, he began them with the year 248 of Diocletian, whom he called a tyrant rather than a prince. But, deciding to commemorate the Lord’s Incarnation rather than that tyrant, he published five nineteen-year cycles, in which he marked the years of Christ. For the holy Cyril had encompassed the Paschal observance up to the time of Dionysius in five nineteen-year cycles. Dionysius placed Cyril’s fifth cycle before his own five; thus, beginning with the year 532 of the Lord’s Incarnation, he carried his arrangement through to 722.

But since these cycles, once completed, could in no way return into themselves—and the cycles comprised by Saint Cyril over ninety-five years were likewise unable to do so, just as those which Dionysius himself arranged over the same span of time were unable to do so—for, as he himself admits, the complete computation of the sun and moon is never found again in its entirety without some confusion unless the great year has been completed, he therefore orders that, after the six years remaining at that time from the fifth cycle of blessed Cyril have been completed, the sober reader should not repeat them, but should understand that he must begin from Dionysius’s first cycle, which is headed by the year 532.

To his five nineteen-year cycles, twenty-three others were added, and together they completed the great year, which is accomplished in 532 years and consists of twenty-eight nineteen-year cycles. This year revolves through its own traces without any confusion because the solar cycle is completed in twenty-eight years and the lunar cycle in nineteen years, and both end with the same sequence with which they began. The great year of 532 years is repeated so that the Paschal computation pertaining to the sun and moon may be repeated without error.

Thus, while there are twenty-eight nineteen-year, or lunar, cycles in it, there are also nineteen solar cycles. The solar cycle begins in these cycles of Dionysius in the ninth year of its own cycle and ends in the eighth. The clearly marked nineteen-year cycle governs the entire reckoning of the moon. Accordingly, it is certain beyond doubt that nineteen times twenty-eight, or twenty-eight times nineteen, amounts to 532.

By this number of years the great year, which is called Paschal, is completed, as has been said. For in the epacts, the concurrents, the nineteen-year or lunar cycle, the Paschal limit, and Easter Sunday together with the moon of that day, what the year 532 of the Lord’s Incarnation was, such will be the year 1064. What the first year of the Incarnate Word was, and the year 533 after it, such will also be the year 1615; and thereafter, in the same order, through the end, this agreement is preserved everywhere by three series of the Lord’s years. The first of these has entirely passed; the second, as though it were a second great year, still lies ahead; how much of the third remains in the future—although I have included it in these cycles—God alone knows.

Since this is so, the question arises concerning the year of the Lord’s Passion, which, being the thirty-fourth from the Nativity, causes the Paschal limit, namely the fourteenth moon—the moon on which God is handed over for sacrifice—to coincide through the concurrents and regulars of the same line, although the Catholic faith holds that he was handed over after the supper on Thursday and crucified on Friday, the fifteenth moon.

In the obscurity of this question, the Lord Bede, though greatly attentive, shed no light, except that he preferred the authority of the Evangelical faith to that of this man, who seems in a certain way to have followed blessed Theophilus. Theophilus says that the Lord was handed over on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, although the aforementioned man adds one day and writes that it was on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April and that the fourteenth moon was then present. He also differs from all ecclesiastical teachers in showing that the Lord was crucified under the nineteenth moon. For Theophilus, like the others, asserts that he was crucified under the fifteenth moon, since he reports that he rose from the dead on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, after many matters which he had discussed with his fellow bishops concerning the origin of the world.

Thus later generations forgave this one error of so great a man in such a way that they followed him in all the Churches. But another point has occurred to me, which I must not consign to oblivion. In the year 529 from the Incarnation of the Lord, under the emperor Justin, the most holy father of the monks, Benedict, shone in Italy through his virtues, as Victor, bishop of Capua, or Paul, the monk of Cassino, testifies; and he was a contemporary of this Dionysius. This Father Benedict, namely, departed from this life on Holy Saturday of Easter, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, as is read in the most truthful accounts.

[Note: [Col. 0823] He died in the year 543, as Leo of Ostia asserts, in solar cycle 20, on 21 March, on Saturday.]

If one seeks in the cycles frequently mentioned by Dionysius a year in which Holy Saturday falls on the aforesaid Kalends, it can be found three times in the entire great year, namely in only three nineteen-year cycles: 4, 22, and 27. But since Father Benedict, after the year 529 of the Lord, continued to shine through his miracles while living at Cassino, it is clear that he did not depart from this world in either cycle 22 or cycle 27. Gregory, Pope, the remarkable narrator of his life, died in the year 605 from the Lord’s Incarnation; it is certain that Benedict did not die in cycle 4 either, For Benedict’s monastery had already been overrun by the Lombards when Gregory died.

Therefore, unless the reliability of the accounts were absolute, the cycle just mentioned would bring a charge of falsehood concerning the departure of both the Lord and the servant. Provoked by this charge, I began to investigate what this controversy involved, and first turned from the years of the Lord to the statements of the chronicles—especially those of Eusebius of Caesarea and Jerome, interpreter of the divine law—in order to determine how many years there were from Christ’s Incarnation to the reign of Diocletian, since from that point to the first year of Dionysius’s cycles I had found 248 years.

After investigating for a long time, I discovered a span of 286 years, or 287, from the birth of one to the rule of the other, since Christ was born in the third year of the 194th Olympiad, while Diocletian seized the imperial power in the second year of the 266th Olympiad. Since seventy-one Olympiads had elapsed in between, making 284 years, two or three years are collected from the two outer Olympiads. Taken together, all the years from the Lord’s Incarnation to the first of Dionysius’s cycles—whether before or after Diocletian’s rule—amount to 534, or rather 535.

In saying this I do not prejudge or condemn the opinions of others. Rather, investigating the truth from authoritative books, I affirm, in accordance with the faith of the Council of Nicaea, that no year of any nineteen-year cycle corresponds to the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection unless it has thirteen as its fourteenth moon on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

A year of the kind sought in connection with the departure of Father Benedict never occurs except in the sixteenth year of that same cycle, having its fourteenth moon on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. For the former Paschal limit to fall on Thursday, five concurrents join with seven regulars; for the latter to fall on Holy Saturday, three concurrents appear with four regulars.

From the Lord’s Passion to the departure of holy Father Benedict, 497 years elapsed. Dividing these by thirty, and doubling the thirtieth part, it becomes clear that, apart from the third, no concurrent could occur in the 497th year from the Lord’s Passion. Whoever wishes to know this rule of division more fully should read chapter 55 of Lord Bede concerning the return of the concurrents. The same holy priest ought to have taken this into account when adding to his cycles; thus he could have avoided another’s negligence. Although he touched upon this matter, he leaves it to those who come later to solve, while they think that no point of calculation escaped him. For this reason they value his authority so highly, preserved through so many passing years, that it can scarcely be corrected, with so many considerations opposing correction.

Nevertheless, beneath all these twenty-eight nineteen-year cycles we have placed two, so that we may make evident to the diligence of the reader what we have said Dionysius ought to have done. Once these have been examined, the skilled calculator will have no doubt about the remaining matters throughout the great year—provided that he is willing at least to entertain doubt.

Finally, it should be known that in these cycles of Dionysius the years of the Lord proceed in their own sequence and, after fifteen years have elapsed, the indiction returns. They pertain neither to the sun nor to the moon, and therefore, when the year is completed, they do not return in the manner in which they began.

### Joannes of Nijmegen to the diligent reader, with greetings

Bede wrote eighty-four nineteen-year cycles of the years from the birth of Christ through 1595, or, if you prefer—and it amounts to the same thing—twenty-eight cycles repeated three times. Some of these have been corrupted, partly through the damage of time and partly through the ignorance of copyists; others have perished entirely. We have restored them elsewhere as far as we could, and elsewhere corrected them, so that they might remain complete through 1595. A later age, when the endpoint of these years arrives, will add more.

It should nevertheless be known that these eighty-four cycles can be reduced to twenty-eight, each of which consists of a threefold series of years, since everything returns to the same state in the 531st year as well. The great cycle consists of the same number of years; once they have elapsed, because of the courses of the sun and moon, everything that belongs to the nineteen-year cycles must return in the same order and manner, except for the indictions and the Sunday letters.

Farewell, and judge our work favorably.

## [On the Paschal Cycle]

### Preface of the Presbyter Bede on the Paschal Cycle

[Col. 0857D] The same Paschal cycle is enclosed by eight lines. The first row contains the years from the Lord’s Incarnation, increasing by one each year. The second contains the Roman indictions, which always revolve within themselves in a course of fifteen years. The third contains the eleven lunar epacts, which increase with each solar year according to the course of the moon and are always added when the moon of the Kalends is sought; they are placed at the eleventh day before the Kalends of April.

The fourth contains the weekday concurrents, which, being placed at the ninth day before the Kalends of April because of the loss caused by the leap year, necessarily complete twenty-eight years. Their reckoning requires twenty-eight nineteen-year cycles to be written, so that each concurrent may begin one cycle and the entire sum of the Paschal computation may be unfolded in 532 years.

The fifth contains the lunar cycle, which the nineteen-year cycle precedes by three years, and which is itself also included. The sixth contains the fourteenth moon, with which the ancients celebrated Easter. It wanders at various intervals from the twelfth day before the Kalends of April to the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, taking its beginning from the seventh day before the Ides of March through the Nones of April. From the fourteenth moon to the fourteenth of the following year there are 354 days if it is a common year, and 384 if it is an embolismic year.

The seventh gives the Sundays of Easter, extended freely from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April to the seventh day before the Kalends of May because of the reckoning of the embolisms. Finally, the last gives the moon of the Paschal feast, varying from the fifteenth to the twenty-first because of the Sunday. For the leap removes a night but adds a lunar age, which has grown throughout the entire cycle. It removes a night in the sense that the moon falls short before it is thought to do so. In nature, however, that night itself remains; it is the beginning of the coming year and the opening of the cycle that is beginning.

For this reason, the final year, which then retains eighteen epacts, assigns to the first year not eleven days, as ordinarily happens in the other years, but twelve. And because they revolve at the end of thirty days, no zero epact is placed at the beginning of the cycle.

### A Poem on the Same Subject

The first line, Christ, contains your years,

And the second holds the indiction established by the cycle.

The third will preserve the fixed numbers of the epacts.

The fourth counts the seven days of the leap year.

The fifth computes for you the years of the lunar cycle.

The sixth now marks the fourteenth moons.

The seventh shows the time and day of Easter.

The last row displays the moon’s age.

### The Cycles of the Presbyter Bede for Discovering the Paschal Moons of Each Year, from Year 1 through the Year of Christ 1595

## Canons of the Nineteen-Year Lunar Cycles

If you wish to know which year it is according to the Greeks alone, multiply 15 by 418; the result is 6270. Add the indictions of whatever year you wish—those of the present year are shown to be 2—and the result is 6272.

If you wish to know which indiction it is, take the years from Adam that you have and divide them by 15. As many as remain, that is the indiction; if nothing remains, it is 15.

If you wish to know which solar cycle it is, take the years just mentioned and divide them by 28. As many as remain, that is the solar cycle.

If you wish to know what the concurrent is, take the solar cycle, which is now shown to be 28, add a quarter of that same number to it, divide by seven, and as many as remain, that is the concurrent on the ninth day before the Kalends of April.

[Col. 0878] If you wish to know which lunar cycle it is, take the years from Adam and divide them by 19. As many as remain, that is the cycle.

If you wish to know what the epact is, take however many nineteen-year cycles there have been, always subtract one from them, multiply the remainder by 11, and then divide by 30. As many as remain, that is the epact.

If you wish to know which year it is from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, determine how many indictional series there have been—for example, in the fifth year of the reign of Tiberius, 46. Multiply these by 15, making 690. Add the regulars, 12, because according to Dionysius the Lord was born in the fourth indiction, and add the indiction of the year you want—for example, one for the present year. The total is 703. These are the years from the Nativity of the Lord.

[Col. 0879A] If you wish to know which indiction it is, take the years from the Lord’s Incarnation, namely 775. Always add 3; the result is 778. Divide these by 15; 13 remains. The thirteenth is the indiction of the present year; if nothing remains, it is 15.

If you wish to know which lunar cycle it is, take the years of the Lord—for example, 774—and always subtract 2, leaving 762. Divide these by 19; 2 remains. The second is the nineteen-year lunar cycle; whenever nothing remains, it is 19.

If you wish to know what the epacts are, count from the first nineteen-year year through the day you want—for example, to the fifth year. Always omit 1; 4 remains. Multiply by the eleven epacts of four years, making four times eleven, or 44. The epact in the second nineteen-year cycle is 14. In this abbreviated manner you will compute through all the nineteen years.

If you wish to know the additions—that is, the weekday concurrents—take the years from the Lord’s Incarnation, however many there have been—for example, 764 in the second indiction—and always add a quarter of the years, namely 190 and 1. Together they make 955. Add the regulars, 4, making 959. Divide these by 7; 7 remains. Seven are the solar epacts, that is, the weekday concurrents, under the aforementioned indiction 2.

If you wish to know which year of the nineteen-year cycle it is, take the years of the Lord, for example 764, and always add 1, making 765. Divide these by 19; 5 remains. The fifth is the year of the nineteen-year cycle; if nothing remains, it is 19.

If you wish to know which indiction it is, take the year of the Lord and add 3. Divide by 15; what remains is the indiction of the present year.

If you wish to know what the lunar epacts are, divide the years of the Lord by 19, multiply what remains by 11, then divide again by 30; the remainder is the epact.

If you wish to know the weekday concurrents, take the year of the Lord and always add a quarter of those same years to the year of the Lord. Add 4 to these as well, because there were five concurrents at the Nativity of the Lord. Divide the total by 7; the remainder is the solar epact.

[Col. 0879D] If you wish to know which year of the nineteen-year cycle it is, take the year of the Lord and add 1, because he was born in its second year; divide by 19, and what remains is the year of the nineteen-year cycle.

If you wish to know which lunar cycle it is, take the years of the Lord and add 1; divide by 9, and what remains is the year of the lunar cycle.

If you wish to know the leap year, divide the year of the Lord by 4. Whatever remains is the number of years from the leap year.

If you wish to know how many points of light each moon shines according to the Romans, take the days from January—for example, 66 on the Nones of March. See which lunar cycle it is—for example, 6. Multiply that lunar cycle by five, making 75. Add this to the days, 200, of January, making 115. Take 60 twice, making 120. Six remains. These are the points of the moon that has shone on that day, namely, one hour and a point of the second hour.

If you wish to find the moon itself, remember the total you had before dividing by 40. Whenever you have subtracted 40, add that many *asses* to the same total. Then multiply your lunar cycle by six, add it to the total, and divide by 30; you will find the moon of that day.

If you wish to know the beginning of Lent when it is a common year, count from Easter up to the Ides of April how many days you find there; count that same number of days backward from the Kalends of March—this will be the beginning of Lent. But when it is an embolismic year, [Col. 0880B] count from the day before the Ides of April up to Easter; then count backward from the Kalends of March as many days as you have found there, and this will be the beginning of Lent. And I do not want you to be misled in this, because in common years Easter always falls before the day preceding the Ides of April. An embolism always extends farther back.

If you wish to know what the epact is in whatever year you choose, calculate what the moon is on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, and that moon-number will be the epact. For example: if the moon is 9 on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, it will have epact 9; or whatever number you find for the moon, that same number will be its epact. In whatever position or conjunction in that year you have the epact, in that same position you will retain the paschal term and the lunar cycle.

If you wish to know what the moon is at the beginning of Lent, [Col. 0880C] calculate, for whatever year you choose, on what weekday the paschal term falls; begin on that weekday, and count from the second lunar day through each successive weekday up to Sunday. Whatever lunar day you find there will be the moon at the beginning of Lent. Similarly, calculate the moon for Rogationtide: on that weekday count from the twenty-first day up to the Monday after Sunday, and whatever lunar day you find there will be the moon of Rogationtide. If on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April the moon is 15, or 14, or 13, or less, you may celebrate Easter in that lunation. But if on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April the moon is 16, or 17, or more, you can in no way celebrate Easter in that lunation; only after that lunation has ended, with the following one, may you celebrate Easter without any uncertainty. But if the moon is born on the eighth day before the Ides of March, or from the seventh day before the Ides of March up to the Nones of April, you shall by no means celebrate Easter in that lunation.

If you wish to know what the moon is at the beginning of Lent, take the Paschal moon of whatever year you choose and always subtract 12 from it; whatever remains is the full moon-number at the beginning of Lent. For example: if the Paschal moon is 15, subtract 12; 3 remain. It will be the third lunar day at the beginning of Lent.

If you wish to know when the leap day occurs, take the year of the Lord—for example, the present year, 688. Divide it by 4. If nothing remains, it is a leap year. But if 1, 3, or 2 remains, it is not a leap year. And so that perhaps no obscurity of error may arise for you throughout any calculation you undertake, if nothing remains, know that the divisor itself is the number by which you are calculating: for example, if you calculate by 10 and 9 and nothing remains, know that the numbers are 10 and 9; if by 15, 15; if by 7, 7.

The fourteenth lunar day must be sought from the eighth day before the Ides of March through the Nones of April; it displays the beginning of the new moons of the first month. From the twelfth day before the Kalends of April up to the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, on whichever day the fourteenth moon occurs, it will lead you to the celebration of holy Easter. But if the fourteenth moon occurs before the twelfth day before the Kalends of April—that is, on the thirteenth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day before the Kalends of April—know that it is not the paschal moon. Rather, when you have extended that same lunation to thirty days and another moon has been born, you may cautiously celebrate holy Easter in that lunation. Likewise, be careful that the fourteenth moon does not pass beyond the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, either to the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May or to the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May. For you will begin to be led into great error. Christian Easter, however, is celebrated in every way from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April up to the seventh day before the Kalends of May, on whatever Sunday the moon occurs. If the moon occurs before the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, or after the seventh day before the Kalends of May, you shall not celebrate Easter at all.

The leap day is therefore inserted in three places: first, on the sixth day before the Ides of February; second, where it is most often placed, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March; third, on the Nones of March.

[Col. 0882A]

“Cycle” in Greek, “circle” in Latin; an ogdoas (ὀγδοάς) is 8 years, a hendicas (ἑνδεκάς) is 11. Hen (ἕν) in Greek means 1 in Latin; decas (δεκάς) means 10. The computation is from the Nativity of the Lord to the Nativity, that is, the lunar cycle. There is also another computation from Easter to Easter, where the first moon is in January of the present year. There again, in the second year, the moon 11 will be in the same place. A common year is one that has 12 lunations. An embolismic year is one that has 13 lunations. “Nineteen-year cycle” (*decemnovennalis*) is composed from corrupted forms, from 10 and 9, and from “year.” In one month the leap day adds 20 moments; in two months, an hour; in a year, six hours. It is therefore called *bissextus* because it has two Kalends of March. The lunar saltus increases each year by an hour, 10 moments, half a moment, and one nineteenth part of half a moment. To complete the lunar saltus annually, as we have said, an hour, a point, and one nineteenth part of a point are added. The moon’s rising is therefore not observed at the same temporal positions or under the same celestial climates, but always somewhat earlier than in the preceding month, so that in the nineteenth year the eleventh day occurs, while the tenth day is skipped. The eighth day before the Kalends of July, the longest day and shortest night of the whole year, makes the summer solstice. The eighth day before the Kalends of January, the longest night and shortest day of the whole year, makes the winter solstice.

[Col. 0881]

BOOK OF THE PRIEST BEDE ON THE CONSTITUTION OF THE CELESTIAL AND TERRESTRIAL WORLD

[Col. 0881C]

This perceptible world consists of the four elements, and of them in their entirety, so that no part of them is left outside the world. Therefore nothing comes to the world from elsewhere, and nothing otherwise departs from it. I say that the world consists of them in their entirety in contrast with human beings and other bodies, which, because they do not consist of all the elements in their entirety, have something added to them and removed from them. Likewise, in trees and grasses a certain sap is added from the earth through the roots; when it has been diffused through all their parts and hardened by a kind of natural heat, it passes into woody strength. When something is added to or removed from a human being, if this happens in the proper proportional order, the person remains whole; if otherwise, the person is corrupted.

Humors

[Col. 0881D]

There are four humors in a human being, which imitate the different elements, increase at different times, and rule at different ages. Blood imitates air: it increases in spring and rules in childhood. Yellow bile imitates fire: it increases in summer and rules in adolescence. Melancholy imitates earth: it increases in autumn and rules at maturity. Phlegm imitates water: it increases in winter and rules in old age. When these abound neither more nor less than is right, a person flourishes. As for the fact that something is added to or removed from a person, these natural instruments of influx are responsible for it, namely, the mouth and the lower parts. There are also certain subtle openings, which we call pores, through which wind entering from below makes the face swell; these are detected more clearly through the outflow of sweat. We have not said that the world is accidental, on account of its perfect composition, but rather that the reconstitution of its parts is the restoration of the whole, according to different authorities. For condensed fire passes into air, condensed air into water, and water, when thickened, into earth. Conversely, through recontraction, earth is diluted into water, water is thinned into air, and air passes into fire. Each of the elements of which the world consists takes its own place according to its nature: fire, by its lightness, occupies the highest place; earth, by its weight, the lowest; water is poured around the latter; and air around these two. Above the firmament, according to the divine authorities, are supercelestial waters, and above them [Col. 0882D] are spiritual heavens in which the angelic powers are contained. Earth has placed itself centrally in such a way that it is equally distant from the firmament on every side, apart from the elevations of mountains and the depressions of valleys. An intellectual line passes through its center from the Arctic to the Antarctic Pole; it is also bound by the air surrounding it, so that it never deviates.

Form of the Earth

Now let us discuss the form of the earth. Anaxagoras held it to be round and flat, in the form of a shield. Others wanted the elevations of its outer parts and its cavernous interior to be in the form of a dish, so that whatever fell would be received there. But many absurdities would follow from this view: the changes of the sun and moon would then appear equally to everyone, and everyone would always have an equinox, because all would see half of all the parallels. Thus neither nights nor days would become shorter, and everyone would have the same east, the same west, and the same south. It remains, therefore, to say that the earth is round, and that because of the sloping position of human beings, they view the regions of the sky in different ways; for the sloping regions truly conceal them. Of the winter tropic we see one part, while three lie hidden; of the summer tropic we see three, while one lies hidden. When the sun is in those regions, we see it for as long a period as those circles appear to us. We also have different risings, settings, and meridians according to the revolution of the firmament and the spherical form of the earth. For when it is midday for those in the East, it is sunrise for those in the South; and when it is sunset for those in the East, it is sunrise for those in the West.

Zones

[Col. 0883B]

The earth is also divided into zones. The middle zone is scorched by the frequent presence of the sun and of the other planets, according to those who attribute heat to them as well. The two outermost zones lack the benefit of heat; the other two are tempered, on one side by heat and on the other by cold. If you wish to consider the magnitude of their breadth, understand that a circle extends from the North into the South, both in the lower and in the upper hemisphere. Divide this into groups of sixty and assign six to the neighboring cold zone, five to the temperate zone, eight to the scorched zone, five to the farther temperate zone, and six to the cold zone. Behold: in the proportion that these numbers bear to one another, the dimensions of the zones likewise bear that proportion.

Climates

[Col. 0883C]

It must be understood that anyone situated in the middle of the scorched zone would have such a disposition that he would always have an equinox; for he would see all the parallels as halves and both poles at the end of his horizon. But the closer he came to the North, the more those northern parts would be raised for him and the southern parts depressed, according to the different climates—that is, inclinations. There are eight, according to some authorities seven; but those who preferred eight included some parts of both the scorched and the cold zones. The more common usage preferred eight, though only three of these are inhabited.

The first is between Meroë and Syene. In it the longest day is thirteen hours and the shortest eleven, so that two hours make the difference. Next comes the climate of the rays, where the longest day is fifteen hours and the shortest eight; there the difference is six hours. The last climate of our habitation is called Borestenicum, from the lake, mountain, or city of Borestene in Armenia. There, according to Bede’s *On Times*, the longest days are eighteen hours; [the following reading is incomplete or corrupt: “where six”]; there the difference is seven hours. If astrologers describe it differently, perhaps they also arrange the climates differently.

If anyone proceeded so far that he had the pole directly above his head, he would see only half of the zodiac and the entire equinoctial parallel; hence he would have continuous day for half the year and continuous night for the other half. It should be observed that in the first climate a third is added in each of the six months, and as much is subtracted in the other six months. [Col. 0884A] In the climate of Rhodes, a whole hour is added in each of the six months, and a whole hour is subtracted in each of the other months. In Borestenicum, two hours are added in each of the six months, and the same amount is subtracted in the others. This division of climates was made according to the computists, but there is also another division according to the philosophers, who consider nature itself, as has been established in the climate of Rhodes. In the first of the six months, one twelfth is added—that is, half an hour; in the second, one eleventh; in the third, a quarter and a half; in the fourth, a quarter; in the fifth, a sixth; in the sixth, a twelfth.

Earthquakes

The earth also moves, and this is what we call an earthquake; hence conjectures are offered. The earth, in imitation of the arteries through which the spirit circulates in a human being, has caverns, openings, and channels through which winds and rivers circulate. All rivers enter the sea, yet it does not overflow, because they return to their own channels through the channels. Certain winds also enter the caverns and openings; while seeking to burst out, they rush with such force that the parts of the earth adjoining them are shaken. Others say that the earth is hollow in the form of a furnace, or of two hemispheres, and that when the mass of the mountains sometimes collapses, the earth is shaken as a result. Others say that the earth is situated above the abyss; when the abyss moves, the earth moves. Others say that the animal Leviathan embraces the earth and holds its tail in its customary manner; when it is sometimes scorched by the sun, it tries to seize the sun, and thus, through the movement of its indignation, the earth also is shaken. At times it also draws in immense quantities [Col. 0884C] of waves, so that all the seas feel it when they return the flood, and the earth is shaken as a result.

After the distinctive properties of the earth, let us discuss the common properties of earth and water. These two elements are mixed with each other, so that it may become plainly evident which of them is above the other. For we see waters on the surface of the earth, and we find them by digging in its veins. Physicists, however, say that the true and inland Ocean was placed in the middle of the scorched zone so that it might be tempered with the fire of the sun and of the other planets by means of its waters. For heat attracts moisture and is nourished by it.

Recessions

That true and inland Ocean makes two withdrawals: one from the East toward the South, and another toward the North; another from the West, likewise toward the South and the North. According to some authorities, there is no knowledge of those two that turn toward the South. Those that converge toward the North, however, meet with such force that by their impact they produce that famous advance and retreat, alternately covering and uncovering the earth. Just as the sun is accustomed to draw up the waters of the Ocean with its flames, and when they cannot long be sustained in the air, they fall back by their weight, so that, when a flood occurs, the earth is sometimes overwhelmed. Others say that winds drive the waters and thus overwhelm the lands; when they release them, the waters return to their channel. Others say that our inhabited regions are near the mouth of Leviathan: when it draws in the waves, the earth appears; when it releases them, the earth is covered.

Tidal Surges

[Col. 0885A]

There are also lesser surges, namely, *malinae* and *ledones*. *Ledones* begin on the fifth lunar day and likewise on the twentieth; for as many hours as they advance, they recede. *Malinae* are greater: they begin on the thirteenth and twenty-seventh lunar days, last six days and fifteen hours, and are swifter in advancing and slower in retreating. The sea also surges three times between day and night: twice during a summer day and once during the night; twice during a winter night and once during the day. It lasts for three quarters and one twenty-fourth of an hour. Whether the waves surge or are driven by the wind, they are arranged successively, and the tenth is the greatest.

The sea also increases and decreases according to the moon’s waxing and waning. When the moon begins to wax, the sea rises for seven days and decreases for the following seven. Then it rises again during the next seven days, up to the twenty-first day; from there the land decreases until the twenty-eighth day. It should be noted that, although it increases in this way, it does not return to its proper state until after eight years. The farther the moon reaches into the northern regions, the more the sea increases; it increases less when the moon occupies the South more fully. Physicists say that the lunar body has certain inflows and outflows, arising especially from fresh waters, whereas the solar influence arises from salt waters. Besides these withdrawals there are other withdrawals of withdrawals, said to have been produced by Hercules. When he saw that our inhabited region nevertheless possessed fresh waters, he broke through the roots of two mountains, namely Adamantis and Calpes. One of them—that is, Atlas—remained in Mauretania, and Calpes in Spain.

The Inland Sea

Between these mountains, Calpes and Adamantis, the strait that enters has a width of five miles and divides Africa from Europe. It forms famous gulfs. It makes the Galician gulf in the region of Narbonne, at Mount Pessulanus; it forms the island of Corsica and is called the Tyrrhenian Sea in the territory of Italy. The part facing Carthage, namely, between Italy and Sicily, is called the Ionian Sea. Around Sicily it is called the Adriatic, which washes Italy on the east. It forms many coastal regions of Greece toward the South, as well as Cyprus, Rhodes, and Carpathus. Where it ceases to provide a boundary between Africa [Col. 0885D] and Asia, the Nile begins toward the North and is called the Hellespont between Sestus and Abydos; farther on it is the Pontus, then the Propontis, then the Bosporus, and there it ceases to provide a boundary.

Between Europe and Asia stands the Tanais, which rises in the Riphaean Mountains and forms the stagnant Maeotian marshes. Likewise, in the East the Caspian Sea bursts forth from the Erythraean Sea, which is also called the Red Sea, for it washes the Red Shore; hence the marine waters are colored, and it carries precious stones there. Asia possesses the combined size of Europe and Africa. It begins at the gardens of Eden, that is, the gardens of delights; in the East and South it is bounded by the Nile, and in the North by the Tanais. Africa has, in its corners, the city of Cyrene and Catabathmus toward the South and West. Toward the North are Mauretania and Atlas, and the famous cities Adrumetum, “eight thousand” [context uncertain], and Hippo. Europe has Spain and Calpes toward the West, the Maeotian marsh toward the North, and Greece toward the South.

Mists

These two elements are mixed with each other. For the earth would vanish unless it were cemented together by the moisture of the waters. When it sometimes exhales moisture, the ascending vapors are called mists; when they open the face of the sky, they are clouds; when they are compressed by the force of the winds or fall as rain through the heat of the sun, they are called rains. Rains are called *pluviae* when they are continuous and gentle; they become showers (*imbres*) when they come beneficially, as in spring when they produce grasses; they are storms (*nimbi*) when they come suddenly and destructively.

Snow

[Col. 0886B]

When the moisture of mists rises, if it is overtaken by terrestrial cold, it is converted into snow. Snow usually falls more heavily on mountains than on level places, either because the height of the mountains more greatly obstructs it, or because the outlets of cold are more abundant there. There are two kinds: one falls in mild air, as large flakes that melt immediately; the other consists of small flakes that fall in the sharpness of the cold and penetrate the openings of roofs. Snow also does not fall on the open sea, but near the shore. For salt water is warm, and terrestrial cold prevents it from reaching the air above it. Hence also the view is supported that the sun feeds on the warm waters of the sea, whereas the moon feeds only on fresh and cold waters, since it lacks both heat of its own and light. Others say that all celestial bodies feed on fresh waters, for fresh waters entering the sea are carried along its surface; hence the planets are said to draw the sea toward themselves.

A question arises: since the water is warm, why does a person become colder by touching it than by touching earth? The answer is that this occurs only with fresh waters, not with salt waters. Or it may occur with both salt and fresh waters, and a person becomes colder through it because water is more cohesive and adheres to a person more than earth does when placed upon him. Therefore you should attribute this to the subtlety of water, which penetrates the pores more deeply or attaches itself to them.

A further question arises: if mists come from salt waters, why do fresh rains descend upon us? You may attribute this either to the immense stretches of air or to the heat of the sun. We see what great power fire has in bitter herbs, which it cooks until the taste becomes bearable, or in sweet air, where bitter moisture loses its bitterness, just as fresh waters fall into the sea and then return fresh through certain channels to their own beds. You can test this. For if you filter fresh waters through seaweed from the sea, they will become bitter.

Hail

Clouds, as we have said, are dissolved by the force of winds or by the heat of the sun, and rain is produced. If, while falling, the rain is overtaken by terrestrial cold, it changes into hail and becomes white. There are two kinds. One, mixed with fine snow, comes during cold weather. The other comes on spring and summer days, and more often by day than by night. The higher the clouds are lifted, the more they begin to thin and disperse through the air. When the sun cannot incorporate into itself the waters it has drawn up and allows immense quantities of water to fall, they fall more frequently into the sea; thus God spares the earth. We call it *manubia*, a compound of *manus* (“hand,” which is good) and *nubes* (“cloud”) by antithesis, as though it meant “the least good of clouds.”

Air

After speaking of earth and water, let us next discuss the neighboring element, air, whose movement is said to be caused by water: when water moves, it naturally moves the air. When it moves from the East, it is called Eurus; from the West, Zephyrus; from the South, Auster; from the North, Aquilo.

If it is asked why we say that water, rather than earth, is moved naturally, I answer: because we see water being moved continually, but not air always. If someone insists, saying, “Wherever there is an efficient cause of something, there must be an effect,” I answer that the movement of water is near it—or you may say that it is not moved everywhere, but only in some place. Others say that a light ripple of air, which on land we call a breeze and at sea an offshore wind, is obstructed by the mountains; there it becomes turbulent and increases. Others say that the firmament moves with rational motion, and that the planets beneath it stir the lower air and drive it with every kind of movement: upward, downward, rightward, leftward, forward, and backward; and in a circle, which alone is rational, although it does not persist in that movement for long. We sometimes detect this also in a whirlwind.

It does not cause confusion that I said the planets move irrationally: I meant this in comparison with the firmament, which never ceases from the same course. The planets, however, glide along different paths.

On Lightning

Finally, the three cardinal winds converge and drive the clouds with such force that from their collision there arises a sound and a certain brightness. What offends the hearing is thunder; what offends the sight is a flash or lightning-flare; that which strikes is called a thunderbolt.

A certain stone is also produced there. This may be attributed to excessive compression, excessive heat, or excessive cold, since pressure might bring it about. It is sufficiently evident where milky moisture coagulates; heat, which softens or consolidates things in different ways, is apparent in mud. That cold produces hardness is visible in molten metals, including iron: it makes stones split apart, cleaves wood, and constricts water.

Others say that a certain thick wind is contained in the clouds; when it bursts out, it produces a sound. The wind enclosed in a bladder provides proof of this, since when the bladder bursts it thunders violently. Others say that atoms of moisture rise in vaporous fashion and fires descend in heat-producing fashion; at their meeting that sound is born. A certain likeness is offered by a smith plunging hot iron into water.

On Dew

Dew also sweats out in the air. It is attributed to the moon because the moon is a sieve of the celestial bodies. Others attribute it to Venus, which produces it both in the evening and in the morning. If dew is overtaken by cold, it becomes frost. A thick hot vapor also forms; frost falls in the greatest sharpness of cold and clings to hedges and the branches of trees.

Another substance flies about in autumn. Children call it “summer”; spiders use it to make webs. It is the dregs of air dried by the sun. Moreover, when winds are impending, this lower air collides with the upper air; sparks leap forth from it, imitating the falling of stars. In reality, however, none of the fixed or wandering stars falls; rather, the sparks, meeting moist air, are extinguished, and when found in fields they resemble phlegm. They are poisonous substances.

On the Rainbow

An arc is also formed in the air, occupying the region opposite the sun. According to the physicists, the sun reflects from watery, concave clouds that are not very dense; hence the colors of the world arise in them, though they cannot be clearly distinguished in fluid form from a short distance. Bede, however, says that there are four different colors, imitating the four elements: green imitates the green surface of the earth; bluish-gray, water; hyacinth-colored, air; and red, ethereal fire.

Sometimes there are also two arcs, because the moon similarly makes an arc, although it is full, since it is not the Rainbow itself. It usually appears when winds or rains are impending. Sailors also observe it. For from the side on which it first dissolves, they anticipate that winds or rains are coming.

On the Aether

The aether hangs above this neighboring air, and the moon occupies the place nearest to their boundary. Physicists have called the moon “aetherial earth,” perhaps for this reason: just as earth is named from *terere*, “to wear down,” so one who is worn down by the purification of the celestial bodies is received into the moon. It is also set opposite the sun so that it may reflect the sun’s light, like a mirror.

There are many lunar beings: souls ascending or descending, which leave behind in each sphere whatever transformation they had acquired, or take something up there; or they are evil spirits (*cacodaemones*). As for the dark features that appear to be in the middle of the moon, these may be attributed to the causes mentioned above.

On the Moon’s Dark Surface

The moon consists of the four elements, but three of those elements are well mixed and smoothed together. For they are naturally transparent and give back light from themselves. Earth, however, is not well mixed with the others in that region, does not pour forth light from itself, and is rough there. A rough surface is one covered with rust or left insufficiently smoothed.

It has seven forms. The first is *monoeidēs* (μονοειδής), named from unity, when the moon is new. The second is *dichotomos* (διχότομος), or *dyatomos* (διατομος), when it is halfway; for *dyas* (δυάς) means “two,” and *tomos* (τομός) means “section.” Then comes *amphikyrtos* (ἀμφίκυρτος), “rounded on both sides.” The full moon occurs while it is waning; it is likewise *amphikyrtos*, after *dichotomos*, and then *monoeidēs*.

On the Eclipse of the Sun and Moon

The moon is always a full sphere. On the side by which it faces the sun, it is always full; but sometimes it is obscured wholly or partially when it is on the fourteenth or fifteenth day, if it is on the ecliptic line and opposite the sun across the diameter. A diameter is a line that sometimes divides something into two halves; *dyas* means “a pair,” and *metron* means “measure.” For then, with the earth placed in the middle, it prevents the sun’s light from being poured onto the moon, and its shadow extends as far as the moon. This is a lunar eclipse, which we call a darkening.

It occurs both in the lower and in the upper hemisphere, and both in the East and in the West. It does not, however, always occur when the moon is on the fourteenth or fifteenth day, but always after six months. When it occurs in the same sign and in the same month, it happens only after nineteen years. When it occurs in the same sign, month, and part of the sign, it occurs only after 55 years. When it occurs in the same sign, month, and part, with all the planets restored to their proper places, it occurs only after fifteen months of years.

A solar eclipse occurs on the thirtieth lunar day: the sun undergoes an eclipse. For it declines either toward the South or toward the North. When it occurs in the same sign and likewise in the same month, it occurs after 55 years; but when it occurs in the same sign, month, and part, with all the stars restored to their former place, that is, after 15,000 years.

On the Order of the Planets

Now let us discuss their order. Plato, following the Egyptians who persuaded him of this, placed the sun in the region immediately beyond the moon, for the following reason. The moon lacks light of its own because it borrows it from the sun. For if Venus and Mercury were placed between the sun and the moon, they would sometimes intercept the sun’s light. The argument is rather weak, since the shadow of a smaller body, covered by a greater light, is diminished and does not extend far; thus these two bodies would obstruct nothing for the moon.

Tully follows the Chaldaeans, saying that the sun is intermediate among the planets in number, not in distance, for it has withdrawn farther from the firmament than from the earth. We do not, however, deny that Venus and Mercury are sometimes higher than the sun; historical accounts also prove this. For it is recorded in the history of Charles that Mercury appeared for nine days in the sun like a spot. When it entered or departed, clouds were said to make it visible. Roman history likewise says that when Augustus Caesar was conducting funeral rites for his adoptive father Julius, Venus shone, and he considered it that man’s star.

When these two are below the sun, they are clearly visible at midday. The reason is that they are nearer to the earth and appear larger, and the sun does not obscure them. But when they are above the sun, its brightness prevents them from being seen, as though they were now smaller. When the sun also reflects its light directly upon them, whether they are in front of it or behind it, they are seen either only slightly or not at all.

On the Obscurity in the Middle of the Moon

The following conjecture is also made about the moon: that a certain little cloud is placed between us and the moon, partially preventing us from seeing the moon’s brightness. For the moon itself is the administrator of corporeality both for superior and inferior things, and certain atoms are sifted there. Their more liquid parts give corporeality upward; their dirtier parts are poured into these lower and perishable things, where they evaporate. It also withdraws the moon from our sight in that part, just as a mist, when it exhales from the mountains, hides it from our eyes there.

On Epicycles and Intersections

When Venus and Mercury are visible or invisible because of their proximity to or remoteness from the sun: Mercury is visible like the moon when it has reached the twelfth part; Venus, when it has withdrawn seven degrees of the sign from the sun, appears as though it were already larger. The moon too would be visible there if it possessed light of its own.

That the planets are carried above and below the sun is shown by conjectures in three ways: either through the intersection of circles; or because they are epicycles—that is, “super-circles,” having no center on the earth, and making the sun, as it were, the center of their course; or because they measure the sun’s altitude through obtuse or acute bends, just as the planets escape the breadth of the zodiac. The illustration placed below demonstrates this to the eyes. But since we have mentioned how they traverse the zodiac, let us discuss that more fully.

On the Lines of the Zodiac

[Col. 0890B]

When Venus and the moon have been carried to the extremities of the zodiac, they reach twelve lines into which it has been divided. Venus nevertheless exceeds them by two moments; Mercury traverses eight of its lines.
