The sun keeps to the two middle lines and exceeds them only in Libra, whence Ovid writes: “The horses stray beyond their bounds.” Mars traverses four; Jupiter, five. These too, however, frequently become anomalous. Saturn traverses only three.

Although there is doubt about the order of the sun, Mercury, and Venus, there is none about the rest. For they have withdrawn so far from the sun and from one another that what the sun completes in one year Mars completes in two, Jupiter in twelve, and Saturn in thirty.

On the Transitory Planets
## [Col. 0890C] On the Transitory, Stationary, Retrograde, and Irregular Planets

Among the planets themselves, some are *hippolitic*—that is, transitory—some stationary, some retrograde, and others irregular. The hippolitic, or transitory, planets are those that proceed from a preceding sign to a succeeding one. Since all the others do this, the sun and moon do so especially; for these two proceed from the earlier signs to the later ones in such a way that they never stand still and never move backward.

If someone objects that the sun does stand still because it remains longer in Gemini than in Sagittarius, say that this remaining is not standing still, but rather that it has a greater distance to complete there than in the other signs, where its axis is not so high. This is evident from its eccentricity.

The stationary planets are those that appear near some fixed star for a longer time than they ordinarily do. They do not in fact stand still, but according to the configuration of their course they either ascend or descend, and do not advance very far along their natural course. There are, however, proper limits within which they appear stationary: namely, when they are three or four signs distant from the sun. This occurs by a triangle or quadrangle—that is, in a trigon or tetragon, or a *tricetum* or *quadricetum*.

The cause of this station is said to be the sun. There is a morning station and an evening station. The morning station occurs when a planet is stationary before sunrise. It should be noted that retrograde motion occurs only at the evening station.

For example, if Jupiter proceeds from Gemini into Cancer and then returns to Gemini, although some planets do this only once in certain signs, Saturn nevertheless always returns twice to each sign, and sometimes reaches the same sign a third time. According to some, this produces a delay in its course; according to others, the cause is the size of its circle.

Pythagoras, however, said that no planet moves retrograde, stands still, or is irregular, but that all complete the distances between places equally over unequal periods of time. The figure shows how they appear retrograde or stationary although they are not.

The irregular planets are those that remain either longer or less long than usual, or that rise or appear at a place other than their customary one. Although this also happens with the others, it happens especially with Mars, which in the latter two years never observes the rule of the preceding ones.

Venus and Mars are never regularly distant from the sun by a *tricetum* or *quadricetum*, nor do they rise or set at their chronological rising, because Venus is no more than one and a half signs distant from the sun, and Mars one sign and two parts of another. It is there that they undergo their stationary and retrograde movements.

They can sometimes appear nearer, both above and below, at the same time retrograde or in advance. Hence we seem to have two Morning Stars and likewise two Evening Stars. When Mercury is in advance, however, it claims for itself the name Morning Star.

Venus is the name of the nature—that is, the natural name: wherever this star is, it is called Venus. When it precedes the sun at rising, it is called Lucifer; when it appears after the sun has set, it is called Hesperus or Vesper. These are names of office.

Aristotle and the Peripatetics also say that the planets revolve in their natural course together with the firmament, but that they are all overtaken by the firmament’s speed. Saturn contends with its speed so closely that within two and a half years it advances ahead of the firmament by the length of only one sign.

## On Rising

### [Col. 0891C]

It should also be noted that one rising is morning and another evening. A morning rising occurs when some star precedes the sun’s rising after midnight; an evening rising, when some star appears after sunset.

There is also a mundane rising, a heliacal rising, and an achronic rising. A mundane rising occurs when a star emerges from the lower hemisphere into the upper. A heliacal rising occurs when the sun, moving away from a star, permits it to be seen. An achronic rising occurs when a star or constellation sets and its opposite rises diametrically. *Chronos* means “time.”

## On Setting

There is likewise a mundane, heliacal, and achronic setting. A mundane setting occurs when any star descends from the upper hemisphere into the lower.

### [Col. 0891D]

A heliacal setting occurs when the sun, approaching a star, prevents it from being seen. An achronic setting occurs when some star or sign sets and its opposite rises diametrically.

## On the Concealment of the Stars

When stars are concealed, either by the sun or by their apses, they are not all concealed for equal periods. Saturn is concealed for as many as 170 days and for as few as only 10. Jupiter for as many as 36 days and for as few as 10, likewise. Mars is irregular; hence in the *Deeds of Charles* it is said to remain hidden for an entire year.

Venus is concealed for as many as 58 days and for as few as 52. Mercury for as many as 16 days and for as few as 12. When the moon approaches the sun within one twelfth of a sign, it begins to grow dark; when it recedes within one twelfth, it becomes illuminated, and it remains hidden for only two days.

## On the Apses

At the intersections, moreover, apses are either certain routes so called, or breaks through the spirals along which stellar bodies proceed. Thirty or more fixed [stars] are concealed, but the smaller ones remain concealed longer; for the larger ones become visible sooner.

They begin to grow dark when the sun is left by the earth more than fifteen parts away from any one of them. This course is completed in fifteen days, and, as it recedes from it, it darkens it for fifteen days.

## On the Concord of the Planets

### [Col. 0892B]

As we said above, when the sun looks upon the planets in a *tricetum* or *quadricetum*, they become stationary or retrograde; and when they look upon one another, they also provide one another with a great concord.

For when a beneficial planet looks upon a beneficial one, beneficial influence is increased; if an adverse one looks upon an adverse one, adversity is increased; if a beneficial one looks upon an adverse one, or the reverse, the effect of both is diminished.

Mercury, however, because it is indifferent, though more good than evil, always becomes such as the planet is that it regards, and of the same color. If it regards an adverse planet, it increases and accelerates its height; but if it regards a favorable one, it increases and accelerates its adversity. Nevertheless, it is more inclined toward favorable influence.

## On the Domiciles

If individual planets enter their individual domiciles, they serve one another greatly. I call the principal domicile of each planet that in which each planet was found at the origin of the world. The moon and sun each have one domicile, but each of the remaining five has two, one of them secondary.

At the beginning of the world, therefore, the moon was in Cancer. Since it always foretells good together with its constellation, it does so especially in Cancer. If it has the sun with it, it pours increase and bodily abundance especially into things, as is evident in the flourishing summer.

The sun, however, was found in Leo, where it especially displays its powers through dryness and heat. Hence the dog days are hotter than other days, since the sun is then in its own domicile. The dog days are so called from the Dog Star, which the sun then enters.

Mercury, being the weakest of all, obtained the first choice. From the preceding signs it chose the Dog (*Canem*) and Gemini, and from the succeeding signs Leo and Virgo, so that it might principally display whatever it wished there. Nevertheless, if another planet entered there as a guest, it said that it wished to serve that planet in color and effect.

Venus, being next in position, made the next choice. From the preceding signs it chose Taurus, and from the succeeding signs Libra, for the same reason: so that it might display its effects there. If an evil planet entered there, however, it would oppose it and diminish its powers through its own prosperity. If Mercury were especially present, it would accelerate favorable outcomes.

Although Venus chiefly signifies good through its constellation, it brings above all the most delightful pledge of a happy marriage.

For the same reason Mars chose Aries and Scorpio, so that it might foretell the greatest adversity and especially indicate burning heat. Jupiter chose Pisces and Sagittarius; it is moderated by adverse influences and increased by favorable ones. When it hastens together with Mars toward indications of its own goodness, it disposes things toward the fortunate outcome of kingdoms.

Saturn obtained two contiguous signs, namely Aquarius and Capricorn. With good influences it is milder, with evil ones more savage, and with Mercury swifter in cruelty. Among its evil indications it abounds in cold and excessive harshness.

## On the Coldness of Saturn

### [Col. 0893B]

Among all the planets, Saturn is the coldest. Several explanations are given for this in the form of fables, since he was indeed an old man. Old men are of a cold nature, and phlegm therefore abounds in them, increasing in winter.

He is also said to be cold because he is farthest from the sun, or because, when the sun is situated in Saturn’s domiciles, it is farthest from us, and we are then oppressed by cold.

When Saturn is situated with the sun in its own domiciles, it produces the most severe burning cold. It is not otherwise cold except by its effect: through its evil constellation it kills human beings, and the dead are cold. Or again, it is cold because it is nearest to the waters above the heavens, and therefore becomes cold.

Many conjectures are offered concerning these waters, and concerning how they can remain round and in perpetual motion.

## On the Waters Above the Heavens

The first conjecture is that there are projecting and hollowed-out places on the outer surface of heaven, just as there are on the surface of the earth, and that water is held in them. They revolve with such speed that the water does not spill. This can be demonstrated by any full vessel: the more vigorously it is whirled by hand, the less it spills.

### [Col. 0893C]

The second conjecture is that the waters are contained there in vaporous form, just as clouds hang here. The third is that, because of the sun’s remoteness—for from it the chief heat is supplied—the hardened, icy heaven holds them fast. Hence Saturn is called the coldest of the planets, because it is nearest to those waters.

There is also a fourth conjecture: that the firmament does not revolve as a fixed body, but that the stars attached to it, though not fixed, move; and they are uncertain whether it is square or round.

Finally, the question is resolved by divine power: the waters are held there according to God’s will, although the manner is hidden from human beings. God has reserved them there for divine purposes, either for use or to temper the fire of heaven. Above these are the spiritual heavens, in which the angelic powers are contained. According to others, there is nothing there except emptiness.

## The Time in Which the Planets Complete Their Courses

### [Col. 0893D]

Saturn, because of the size of its circle, its retrograde motion, its stationarity, and its declination either toward the south or toward the north, and because of its apparent movement or visibility, completes its year only in thirty years; it passes through one sign in two and a half years.

Jupiter does so in twelve years, and therefore traverses one sign each solar year. Mars does so in two years, and therefore traverses six signs in one year, unless it becomes irregular. The *Deeds of Charles* report that it was not seen for an entire year.

The sun completes its course within 365¼ days. The quarter-day is not counted in the first, second, or third year; in the fourth, however, the intercalary day is inserted. This is called the bissextile day because it is counted twice at the sixth day before the Ides of March; hence the bissextile year.

Let us explain how this is to be understood. Suppose that the sun is at the beginning of Aries. After 365 days it will be so near that same part of Aries that, if six hours still remained, it would reach that same part. Consider the remainder carefully.

In its entire circuit, as we said, it covers only this distance. Let us therefore first see, by equal computation, how much it covers in each sign. According to the computists, in each sign it spends thirty days, ten hours, and half an hour. From these figures you will arrive again at the same total: twelve times thirty makes 360; twelve times ten hours makes five days; and twelve times a half-hour makes a quarter-day. Thus the total is the same.

### [Col. 0894B]

Philosophers, however, observing the truth of the matter, discovered that the sun remains longer in one sign and less long in another. Thus in Gemini it remains two days beyond thirty days and ten and a half hours. Conversely, in Sagittarius it spends two days fewer than thirty. This happens because its axis is eccentric: it is nearest to the firmament in Gemini and farthest from the earth, and the reverse is true in Sagittarius.

If you wish to return to the same total, you can understand it in this way. In Gemini it remains two days beyond thirty; therefore in the next sign it diminishes ten hours, and so, diminishing continually until Sagittarius, it leaves two days fewer than thirty. Then, ascending again, it takes sixteen hours in each sign until Gemini.

They discovered this either because the apse of Gemini contains more space between the rays that serve or terminate it, or because the sun, ascending higher there, has a longer distance to travel in that sign than in another.

### [Col. 0894C]

It does not therefore make longer days, because the higher it is, the more strongly it is driven by the revolution of the firmament from east to west.

The same occurs with the other planets. Saturn is nearest to the firmament in Scorpio, the moon in Taurus, and Jupiter in Virgo. If Venus is with Saturn, this signifies a good marriage for someone in the future. Hence Venus is said to have appeared to Aeneas in the form of a huntress, signifying to him that a good marriage would come about.

Mars is in Leo; if the sun is with it, it signifies the burning of spirits and of the air. The sun, as has been said, is near the firmament in Gemini, Venus in Sagittarius, and Mars in Capricorn. In the opposite signs they are nearest to the earth.

Venus completes its course in 349 days. Mars, because it is swifter, does so in nine fewer days; but since they more frequently become retrograde, they can take longer.

The moon, according to Macrobius, traverses the zodiac in twenty-eight days. He says this, however, to support the number seven, which, multiplied four times, makes twenty-eight. In truth, it traverses the entire zodiac in fewer than twenty-seven days and about eight hours, but it is not illuminated during that period.

For example, if the sun and moon are together at the beginning of Aries, the moon, proceeding for twenty-seven days and about eight hours, reaches the same point. But it does not find the sun there, because the sun itself has already proceeded according to its own law to approximately the end of Aries. To reach it, the moon then spends two days and four hours; at that point it is illuminated again by the sun.

### [Col. 0895A]

There are not, therefore, twenty-nine days and twelve hours between one illumination and the next; these hours are not counted in the first month. Hence that month has only twenty-nine days. In the second month they are counted, and when added to the others they make the month have thirty days, except in the nineteen-year cycle, when one day is subtracted.

## On the Leap of the Moon

For this reason we give the moon more time each month than it actually consumes. The excess is so small that it is difficult to calculate month by month. In the entire year, however, it amounts to only one hour, one point, and one nineteenth of a point. Collected each year, this makes one full day in the nineteenth year; by omitting that day, we remove it, counting three lunations as only twenty-nine days.

A point is one quarter of a lunar hour, but one fifth of a solar hour.

What we have said applies to those who say that the firmament revolves with rational motion from east to west and again toward the east, while the planets move from west to east and again toward the west. This is the view maintained by the Platonists.

Aristotle and the Peripatetics, however, say that the planets revolve with rational motion together with the firmament, but that the firmament overtakes them by its speed, so that they appear to move backward. According to this view, the higher they are, the faster they are, so that Saturn, the swiftest, contends with the firmament by such speed that in two and a half years it passes beyond the firmament by no more than one sign.

The moon, being the lowest of all, is the slowest. If it is seen today at the beginning of Aries, tomorrow, when Aries rises, you will not find the moon there; instead, it rises in the twelfth part of that sign.

The sun likewise, if it is in the first part of Aries today, will not appear there tomorrow. Rather, after fifteen parts of a natural hour, it rises on the following day in the second part of the same sign. These authorities say that the earth is immobile and that everything revolves equally around it.

Tullius agrees with this view. He says that the sharpest sleep is produced by the excessive speed of the firmament, but the heaviest sleep by the moon, because of the excessive slowness of its revolution.

The firmament revolves above all things equally through five zones, which are divided from one another by parallels running from east to west. They are said to be equally distant—not because all are separated by equal intervals, but because each pair is equally distant from one another, so that nowhere are they closer or farther apart.

Of these, two are the shortest, namely the outermost. The middle one is the equinoctial; the greatest is the one that appears half-sized to everyone except those who live beneath the pole. Those people can see the whole of it, since it terminates their horizon.

The tropics are intermediate. The Arctic is so called because it contains both Bears; opposite it is the Antarctic.

The summer tropic, or boundary, cuts Cancer in the middle according to one arrangement, or, according to Hyginus, in the eighth part. When the sun reaches it, it turns back; this is called the summer solstice. According to others, it marks the boundary of Cancer and the zodiac.

The other tropic is the winter tropic, from which the sun turns back toward us; it lies in the eighth part of Capricorn.

There are also two colures. One divides the equinoctial signs, which are called imperfect with respect to our sight because we do not see them; the other divides all the solstitial signs.

### [Col. 0896A]

They are, as I believe, complete and possess a distinction among their stars. If there are any people there, it is uncertain whether they are carried from south to north or outside, from sign to sign. These matters must be discussed because the colures divide both the zones and the parallels into four parts.

## On the Milky Circle

There is also a Milky Circle, visible in clear weather. Both mythical and physical explanations are given for it.

Juno nursed her stepson Mars, born from Maia, and, to commemorate this deed, sprinkled the heavens with that milk. Others say that Hercules, taking an excess of milk from several nurses, finally vomited it there.

The physicists say that God made two hemispheres, and that when they were joined together a greater brightness was produced. Others say that there are short stars there, packed closely together, and that their proximity produces that radiance while obscuring their distinction from one another.

Others say that the stars of the zodiac shine there, and that near the tropics the sun extends the benefits of its light and fire toward both poles.

## On the Zodiac

The zodiac is bounded by two outer lines and intersected by a middle line called the ecliptic, in which an eclipse usually occurs.

Moreover, the zodiac is divided into twelve signs, each of which is divided into thirty parts. The sun passes through one part each day, and therefore through one sign in a single month, except that enough is removed from each month for the natural day to be made up in a bissextile year.

### [Col. 0896C]

Anyone who remained beneath that parallel which I said cuts the torrid zone would always have an equinox and four solstices. I call the solstice the nearest approach and the greatest withdrawal.

Such a person would have two solstices from proximity, in Aries and Libra, and two from remoteness, in Cancer and Capricorn. The reason why someone positioned in the middle of the torrid zone would always have an equinox is that he would see both poles and all the parallels as half-circles, as well as the entire path of the sun from rising to setting.

Following the likeness of the firmament, the sun’s sphere is broader in some places and narrower in others: it is broader beneath the equinoctial circle and narrower beneath the tropics. Otherwise the sun’s circle would have to be nearer to the firmament in the tropics than in the equinoctial circle, if it were not broadened convexly in the likeness of the firmament and contracted in the tropics.

### [Col. 0896D] Objection

If the sun’s circle is narrower in the tropics, it produces shorter days there, where its path is shorter. At the equinoctial circle, where its circle is more open and its path longer, it produces longer days. Thus it necessarily does not always produce an equinox there.

### Solution

Whatever departs from the middle swelling of the firmament is driven less by its force. Thus the sun, positioned in the tropics, is driven less than beneath the equinoctial circle; and the greater violence of the motion compensates for the greater breadth of the circle by means of greater speed.

When Macrobius says that the speed of the planets is equal, he says this because they strive equally, not because they are advanced equally—just as swimmers moving against a current may exert equal strength without advancing equally, since the force of the current impedes them differently.

So the planets are sometimes stationary and sometimes retrograde, their equal advance being hindered at times by the height of their circles.

Anyone beneath the middle of the torrid zone would therefore always have an equinox and four solstices. The farther someone moved from the middle of the torrid zone toward the northern region, the more that region would be elevated for him and the southern region depressed. For every sixty degrees the northern region gained, the southern would lose the same amount.

He would immediately acquire inequality between days and nights, until, finally positioned beneath the pole, he would see the entire equinoctial circle. In the summer signs he would have continuous daylight for half the year, and in the winter signs continuous night for half the year; he would see the upper hemisphere as a half-circle and the lower hemisphere likewise.

## On the Meridian Circle

### [Col. 0897B]

There are also two circles, the meridian and the horizon. Each people makes its own meridian. It passes over their heads from north to south and changes at every step. Hence, when it is noon for us, it is sunrise for those in the west, and midnight for those who are in the middle of the lower hemisphere. Calculate the sequence in this way.

## On the Horizon

The horizon, considered over a level surface of water or land, terminates in the forward direction at 120 stadia and the same distance behind, if you wish to comprehend its circumference.

Triple its diameter, with the addition of one seventh of the diameter, and you will have the length of its circumference. The horizon is properly called the terminating circle.

## On the Constellations

There are also certain stars that rise after a long interval of time and indicate diseases, such as the Dog Star, which rises after four years, though not in the same places, because in the meantime it completes part of its course.

Nor does it continually signify evil, for it is moderated by the good signs or planets adjacent to it, in whose domiciles it either is or toward which it looks. Its domicile is said to be in the mouth of Leo; when the sun comes there, the days are called dog days. They last fifteen days, from the beginning of Leo to its midpoint.

If the Dog Star is with the sun, it signifies heat.

In Greek it is called Sirius, and its year is the cynic year, from *kynos*, which means “dog”: 1,160 years.

The Egyptians also call *Abus* a certain star that rises after the same interval of time and whose adversity they fear. They see certain stars that are not seen by us because the swelling of the earth intervenes, such as Canopus at the beginning of Egypt.

There is also another star that appeared once, as I believe, and perhaps will never appear again: namely, the one that announced the Incarnation to the three Magi.

## On the Order and Signification of the Planets

The size or quality of the circles is usually discovered from the length of time taken by the planets. The more time a planet consumes in its circuit, the larger its circle is thought to be, although this does not seem so to some, since the size of the circle is not the only cause; stationarity and retrograde motion also contribute.

Saturn, according to Macrobius, takes thirty years because of the size of its circle. The moon, because of the shortness of its circle, takes only a month.

Whatever planet possessed half of Saturn’s path would be midway in distance, because Jupiter makes a path nearer to the others. It is therefore nearly midway in distance, though not in number.

The sun, according to Tullius and the Chaldeans, is midway by number rather than by distance between the three upper and the three lower planets.

Mars, positioned at the center of the world, if it looks upon Saturn by a tetragon, and if Mercury, situated immediately after Saturn, together with the full moon touches the same center, those who are born under that daytime nativity become murderers, destined to fall by the sword, bloodthirsty in counsel or deed, lustful, drunkards, possessed by demons, investigators of secrets, necromancers, sorcerers, and sacrilegious persons—especially if no favorable influence intervenes.

This is the effect of Mars in any sign, but it is especially powerful in its own domiciles, and most of all if Mars, placed in the middle of its domiciles, touches the center.

By “center” I now mean the meridian circle. When the sun is in it, I say that the sun is at the center. It is equally distant from east and west, but rarely equally distant from south and north, except at the two equinoxes.

When Venus and the moon are with Saturn in Saturn’s domiciles, namely Capricorn and Aquarius, whatever women are born under that daytime nativity will be masculine women, ready for agriculture, war, and the construction of houses. They will neglect the things of women and desire perfumes, footwear, and clothing common to men, and they will not be reproved by their husbands.

Mars prevents this indication, whether it is in those same domiciles or looks upon them by a *tricetum* or square.

When Venus is placed with Mars in Mars’s domicile, namely Aries, and looks upon Saturn by a tetragon, the men born at that time will be effeminate, neglectful of manly pursuits, and indulgent toward women.

If Mars looks upon Venus by a tetragon, and no beneficial influence intervenes, those who are born under that nativity will be adulterers, especially joining themselves in marriage to mothers, daughters, or sisters.

For this reason Mars is imagined to have committed adultery with Venus.

The spheres have the earth as their center, but the apses are eccentric. The apses are circles in which the divergences of the spirals occur and where stations and retrograde motions are marked.

In some places the apses are nearer to the earth, and in others nearer to the firmament. Evening itself also possesses a certain contiguous space having three dimensions: length, breadth, and height.

Note that just as the stars make bends because of latitude, so they also make them because of altitude.

## On the Different Equinoxes

### [Col. 0899A]

Those who are in the middle of the torrid zone always have the same equinox, because they always see both poles and all the parallels as half-circles. Those who are removed from that region do not see them as halves; likewise, they do not correctly divide the equinoctial circle in half. If this is so, we never have an equinox.

### Solution

The roundness of the earth and the convexity of the firmament ensure that half of the equinoctial line is always visible to people in every position, except those who live directly beneath the poles. They see the whole equinoctial circle on their horizon and also have an equinox in this way: six signs, that is, half a year, provide continuous day, while the remaining six signs, that is, the other half of the year, provide continuous night.

## Why the Stars Are Seen

When the sun has set, and the fifteenth part of a sign has also set after it, the sun has nevertheless already descended, as the good things of the earth begin to be raised, by whose agency we see the signs. If these did not exist, we would never see the stars, since the sun's daylight obstructs our eyes.

At night the sun withdraws this light from us, but it nonetheless directs it no less toward the stars and the things above.

The philosophers’ position is that souls separated from the body wish, ought, and are able to be embodied again.

They wish to be embodied because, after drinking the water of Lethe, they have forgotten the past; and, seeing the reward set before them if they have deserved well in the body, they desire embodiment.

They are able to do so because they are immortal. They ought to do so by necessity, because new bodies are created each day, whereas souls were all created once, at the beginning. Those that were embodied earlier must therefore be embodied again.

Since Anchises, according to Virgil, ought to show this to Aeneas, he begins at a higher level, namely with what the Greeks call *to pan*, “the All,” which is contained under the number five.

There are four elements—fire, air, water, and earth—and God. The world cannot be called the All unless the divine spirit, which we call the soul, has first been infused into it. From the elements and the soul infused into them, all things are generated.

Since we possess a twofold nature, we must consider what we derive in a certain way from nourishment. The philosophers discovered that we had received our spirit from God because it is invisible; hence God is the highest author, from whom it derives its origin, whereas the body comes from the elements. For just as the elements are visible, so are our bodies; and just as the elements change from one state to another through their composition and recomposition, so our bodies are altered in various ways.

Again, the rational soul is like God, from whom it derives its origin. The body, however, is irrational, like the elements apart from the benefit of the soul.

The soul is simple and unchangeable in its nature, like its author; hence it also preserves eternity. The body, however, is composite and corruptible.

Anchises’ intention concerns these matters, so that the immortality of souls may be demonstrated. Since various objections arise against this, the different errors of the philosophers must be examined. They all erred, but not in the same way.

Some said that souls were created at the beginning of the world and placed in corresponding stars as in vehicles, so that they might learn the rational motion of the firmament. Others said that there was only one world-soul, which fills, penetrates, and gives life to everything. Others said that there were human souls in addition to the world-soul.

Some think that, when the sun is positioned in Cancer, the sun sets beyond them. The same is said of the moon when it moves westward in Cancer, so that, on this side, the moon too is beyond them. But they are mistaken, for they do not correctly call these regions east or west.

## On the Names of the Sun’s Horses

According to the poets, the sun is said to ride in a chariot drawn by horses. According to Fulgentius, their names are these:

The first is Erythros, that is, “red,” because the sun is red in the morning.

The second is Acteon, that is, “shining,” because it shines more brightly around the third hour.

The third is Lampon, that is, “burning,” for at midday it is most intensely hot.

The fourth is Philoges, that is, “loving the earth,” because, as it sets, it seems to approach us.

According to Ovid, however, they have other names: Eous, that is, “rising” or “ascending”; Aethon, that is, “raised up”; Pyrois, that is, “fiery”; and Phlegon, that is, “sloping downward.” For first the sun rises, then it is elevated, afterward it burns, and at the end of the day it declines toward the west.

## On the Human Soul
Those, however, who assert that souls were created at the beginning of the world say that they were placed in corresponding stars, so that they might learn the rational movement of the firmament and, when they were embodied with hope and desire for supreme blessedness, might rationally govern bodies according to the movement of the firmament. Once placed there, they possess complete knowledge of present, past, and future things; but when the desire to become embodied comes upon them, they immediately begin to grow heavy and are drawn downward toward bodies. Their descent is from Cancer, just as their ascent is through Capricorn. As they descend through the first crater of Bacchus, they drink there forgetfulness of their former state; thereafter, as they glide downward, certain ethereal and aerial envelopments meet them, and they draw something from each sphere: in the first, that of Saturn, correlation, that is, the collection of similar things, so that through one similar thing they may know how to approve another—for example, if I wish to show something white, I say, “It is whiter than snow.” There they also receive a certain torpor; in Jupiter, knowledge and the desire to reign and command others; in Mars, the passionate force of ardor; in the sun, the power of perception through the five senses; in Venus, the desire of fervor; in Mercury, the power of discussion; in the moon, the power of increasing and decreasing. The soul also receives there the power and knowledge of all these things, although it does not exercise them before the envelopment of the flesh. After the envelopments of the planets, it is buffeted in the lower air by various disturbances—namely, hail, snow, rain, and winds—and finally is wrapped in the darkness of the body and remembers none of what it knew. It is so weighed down by the watery mass of the body that this is evident in the foolishness of children, who are deceived when they are harmed by glowing coal. [Col. 0900C]

The question is raised whether souls are embodied in the envelopments of the ether or not; and some say that they are embodied in them, while others say that they are not. Those who say that they are not embodied in them assert that their brightness is merely obscured in them, as an image is obscured by smoke. Others, however, assert that souls are united with and embodied in them because, according to Macrobius, souls returning from the body bring back there the same envelopments from which they had taken them. Hence it is understood that they had carried those envelopments with them into bodies, and therefore souls had been embodied in them.

An objection is raised: Therefore, if the soul is embodied in those revolutions, it was an animal before it reached this mortal body, since the soul joined with a body makes an animal. But this is not necessary: when the soul is joined to a finger, it does not thereby make an animal, because besides body and soul many things contribute to the constitution of an animal, such as sensuality and so forth. [Col. 0900D]

When souls are embodied, two powers are given to them, anger and desire, which are improperly called their portions. Anger is given so that they may become angry with evil things; desire, so that they may always desire good things. When the soul uses these powers rationally, human life is just; but when the soul follows contrary paths—becoming angry with good things and desiring evil ones—it degenerates from the origin of its nature.

But again, instruction is given to the soul in order to reilluminate reason, so that by learning and rereading what it has neglected it may return to its former knowledge. Hence what is called “reading” among us is called among the Greeks “repeated knowledge” (*repetita cognitio*). Yet even when reason has been reilluminated, it is sometimes unable to do what it knows to be necessary and useful. In order that it may be able to do so, virtue is added to it. The etymology of this word is as follows: *virtus* (“virtue”) is so called as if it were “relying on its own powers” against vices. It is defined in this way: virtue is a disposition of the soul, in the manner of nature, consonant with reason; that is, it agrees with the soul concerning that for which it was born—namely, the good—and in this it assists the soul.

Since these souls are to be proved immortal, several questions arise, of which this is the first. If souls are immortal and all are of the same dignity in their nature, why does one possess greater power than another? Virgil resolves this by saying: “As much as innocent bodies impede”—that is, the soul exercises its powers according to the suitability of its bodies. A lion shut up in a cage possesses all its powers there, but does not exercise them in the cage as powerfully as in the forest. [Col. 0901A]

The following objection is again raised: Why is the soul, which is more worthy in its own nature, subjected to a less worthy body?

The answer is that the soul is indeed more worthy in its own nature, but in the fact that it is contained it is less worthy than the body that contains it; and according to this dignity it is subjected to the body.

Another objection is raised: If the soul is compressed in the body so that it cannot exercise its powers, then it is corrupted and becomes unworthy, which is not right.

The answer is that it is not corrupted in its own nature, because it preserves its natural brightness, although, shut up in the body, it cannot shine so brightly—as a lamp placed beneath a bushel does not thereby possess less brightness in itself, although it appears less bright. [Col. 0901B]

Again the objection is raised: If souls admit nothing filthy into themselves, why are they punished in hell?

The answer is: Because they know that, after being stripped from their bodies, they still possess stains that clung to them from bodily and earthly things. In order that these stains may be removed, they require purification for a time, just as a gem, when it is lifted from mud, may still be known to have dirt clinging to it and therefore requires purification.

## On the Origin of Souls

Concerning this origin of souls, there are different opinions among different people. Some said that the soul was formed from atoms of fire, imitating Anaxagoras and Heraclitus, who wished fire to be the origin of all things. Some said that it was the blood of the heart, imitating Thales of Miletus, who asserted that everything consists of moisture. The Stoics said that it was a certain natural spirit, which they proved by the following syllogism: “That by whose departure from a human being the human being ceases to be an animal is the soul; but when the natural spirit departs, the human being ceases to be an animal; therefore the natural spirit is the soul.”

Plato, however, said that human souls were composed from the remains of the world-soul. Aristotle called it *entelecheia*, that is, the form of an animated body; and by this they wished it to be an accident. But Plato, whose authority carries greater weight and whom Macrobius chiefly follows, says that the soul is an incorporeal substance moving itself. In this he opposed others: Aristotle, who said that it was an accident and that the first cause was a substance; and others, who said that it was corporeal and that the first cause was incorporeal. [Col. 0902A]

The question is then, according to which view, whether the incorporeal substance—the soul—is generated or ungenerated. Plato asserts both of these concerning it, though from different perspectives. He wants it to be understood as generated in the *Timaeus*, where he says: “The most excellent was made by the most excellent,” or: “In the second [book], I shall sow the seed of the universe.” But he indicates that it is ungenerated in the *Phaedrus*, when he says: “The soul is neither born, and therefore is eternal.”

Yet lest he should later appear to contradict himself in this matter, he calls the soul ungenerated because it follows the law of generated things—namely, that it be dissolved actually or naturally. For all generated things, except the world and divine things, are dissolved actually; the world, however, is dissolved naturally. Although it will never be dissolved, nevertheless, if the Creator wished it, nature would suffer dissolution. For whatever is composed of parts naturally tends to be dissolved; but it is not natural for the simple and uncompounded soul to be dissolved. Hence it is called ungenerated.

Plato indicates that it is generated because, according to many, it had pre-existent matter, or *hyle*. Although Plato nowhere bears witness to this, he nowhere contradicts it. Hyle, considered in its pure state, does not differ from the matter of the soul—considered in its pure state, that is, without reason, anger, and desire, by which it is formed, that is, which are poured into it.

## On the World-Soul

[Col. 0902D]

Some also say that there is only one soul, namely the world-soul, which supplies all things with mind and with powers suited to each thing according to its capacity. Thus it infused reason into the stars, and into human beings—whom it found amid transitory things—with a spherical head and an upright face, it also infused reason and sensuality, as in divine bodies, although, because of their excessive contemplation, divine animals do not exercise sensuality. To the other living beings it gave sensation and growth; to trees and herbs, growth alone.

Just as one face appears in many mirrors and many faces appear in one mirror, so one soul exists in many things. It possesses all its powers everywhere, although it exercises them differently according to the suitability of bodies. [Col. 0903A]

According to this opinion, no human being seems to be worse than another, because one and the same good and immaculate soul in its nature exists in all bodies. Yet it is said to degenerate more in one than in another—for example, because consentuality dominates reason. For whatever body it inhabits, that body is the hell of the soul.

According to this opinion also, no human being dies in the sense of suffering separation of soul, although [the body] is separated from the four elements and they are resolved into all bodies. Rather, a person is said to die when the soul abandons in them the exercise of its former powers.

Furthermore, some say that the same world-soul exists equally with the human soul in a human being, and that worms are given life by it in the human being; thus they assert that a human being has two souls.

## The Same: On the Origin of Souls According to Others

[Col. 0903B]

But the question is whether, if the human soul is generated—that is, created—its author created all souls equally at the first establishment of the world, or made new ones every day. If, as the philosophers testify, all were made equally at the beginning of the world and placed in corresponding stars as in a vehicle, then they descend daily, driven by the desire to become embodied.

To this is added the Hebrew truth, which says: “Behold, the voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the earth”—that is, the souls that were to be embodied in those born from Abel’s blood. They cried out for this reason: because they wished to attain perfect blessedness in bodies. But God does nothing superfluous; therefore this opinion is frivolous.

## Again, On the Origin of Souls According to Others

[Col. 0903C]

Others say that the soul is a part of the divine essence, deriving this from the passage: “And he breathed into his face the breath of life.” This little portion did not return again; thus it is united with God, and yet it can sin. These people act as though God were situated in a place.

Others assert that souls are born from angelic substances. Still others say that souls are born from the earth, guided by seed; and just as the son’s body is divided from the substance of the father, so the son’s soul comes from the father’s soul. They draw their argument from the similarity of character.

## On the Certain Origin of the Soul

It is, however, an article of unquestioned faith that souls are neither born from this source, nor created, nor brought from elsewhere, but are born together with the body itself. There is a particular fixed time after the conception of the seed, when it is transformed into a human body, at which the soul is born together with the body. [Col. 0903D]

The soul has two powers: one higher and the other lower. The higher adheres to heavenly and incorruptible things; the other desires, and is called rationality, spirit, the ruling mind, or *animus*. The lower is the power that consents to the pleasures of the body; it is called sensuality, animality, or the servant mind. The higher ought to govern the lower; but sometimes, through the negligence of the higher, the lower prevails and leads the higher astray. This also is represented by the figures of Adam and Eve. For if Adam, the higher, had governed himself rightly, the lower, Eve, would not have led him astray.

There are also, according to the differences among souls, three kinds of spirit: one that is never united with a body, although it sometimes assumes an aerial or ethereal body, as angels or demons do; another that is never without a body, such as the spirit of brute animals, which arises and perishes with them; and a third that is sometimes in a body and sometimes outside the body, such as the spirit that gives human beings life, that is, the soul. [Col. 0904A]

As for what is said—“The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters”—I think that this was said either of this air of the earth and the surrounding water, or of a subtler substance, namely the ether; or of the Spirit of the Trinity. If it refers to the latter, it indicates the salvation that would come through water.

Note the three figures depicted in the composition of the soul, arriving at almost the same conclusion. For since the intervals in the first figure were to be filled with harmonic consonances, and the proportions themselves could not be distinguished, the figure was made with such small numbers that what could not be shown with smaller numbers might be demonstrated with larger ones. Thus the place of unity is assigned the sixth position, the place of the binary the seventh, and so mark the others in the same way.

But because numbers were still lacking by which the semitones could be distinguished, a third figure was discovered. Yet, for the completion of the half-tones, insofar as they are not displayed there individually, they are displayed in the consonances—the fourth and the fifth—whose proportional numbers are clearly found there.

The world is so called from those sensible things, as if they had been cleansed and separated from the confusion in which they previously existed in hyle. Hence Augustine: “O unclean world!”

It should be known that whenever two epogdoi are established in any epitrite, whatever remains is a *limma*, that is, a lesser semitone. As was discovered by the careful investigation of the art of calculation, it is exceeded by one-third of the lesser semitone itself and by one hundred and fourth part of its third part. [Col. 0904B]

If you wish to know how a lesser semitone can be made from the whole, take the eighth part by which the sesquioctave proportion exceeds the subsesquioctave, and divide it into nine equal parts. Then, leaving five ninths aside, divide the three ninths equally into twenty-seven parts. Once one twenty-seventh part has been removed from these, there will unquestionably remain for you a *limma*, that is, a lesser half-tone.

This should not be overlooked: when the lesser half-tone is placed together with the sesquioctave proportion of that sesquioctave, from which it is diminished by a ninth part, it contains the whole of that sesquioctave, and in addition its twenty-fourth part, its fourth part, its eighth part, and seven eighty-first parts of its eighth part.

For example, let us put forward the following numbers, in which what is being said may become clear: 243, 253, and 273, with a third and a half-ounce; 243 is subsesquioctave to 273, with a third and a half-ounce. For the latter is sesquioctave to the former: it contains the whole of it, its eighth part, which is 30, and a third and a half-ounce, and also a complete tone in relation to it.

But 253, which is the number that is less than a semitone and is compared with 243, is rightly said to be diminished by a ninth part of 278, with a third and a half-ounce. Besides the whole, this can also contain a ninth part of its eighth part, namely 263, to which it corresponds in the way a sesquioctave does. For it does not exceed it except by thirteen, yet it contains the whole of it and its twenty-fourth part, which is also 10 asses and 5; and in addition it contains the twenty-fourth part of that twenty-fourth part, which is also two asses. It further contains an eighth part of this fourth part, which is also a quarter, 50, 9. §§. c. 9. And after the foregoing it contains an eighty-first part of the species of this eighth part, which is a scruple and a pebble.

Therefore the lesser semitone, compared with the subsesquioctave proportion of that sesquioctave from which it is diminished by a ninth part, contains the whole of that subsesquioctave, its twenty-fourth part, a fourth of its twenty-fourth part, an eighth of that fourth, and seven eighty-first parts of that eighth. [Col. 0905A]

If you wish to find this in whole numbers, you will not be able to find it in smaller numbers than between 57,208 and 65,536. So that the proof may become clearer, let an epitrite and a subepitrite number be proposed, where after two tones a semitone remains for you, and where it may be proved that the quarter is exact. Thus let 49,155 be arranged, with its eighth parts: 6,100, 11, 4, 50, 5, 200, 10, 100, 6; its eighth part is 7,700, 76, 65,536.

This, therefore, contains the whole of the former and its twenty-fourth part, which is 648, and an eighth part of this fourth part, which is 80; and in addition it contains seven eighty-first parts of this eighth part.

Between three and four a semitone, left over from two epogdoi, can be found in this way: the eighth part of three is a third and a half-ounce, a sixth, an obol, a pebble, and a half—three, a lesser semitone.

[Col. 0905B]

A lesser semitone is found between these two numbers: 4,800,60,4 and 4,500,100,17. If, therefore, you wish to know how the greater number in every lesser semitone relates to the lesser, retain firmly everywhere the sum of these two numbers.

For in this sum the greater number, 4,800,604, contains the entire lesser number, namely 4,500,100,18, and in addition its nineteenth part, which is 1,200,10,50,3; also an eighty-first part of that nineteenth part, 1,3; and further it contains an eighty-first part, which is unity.

## One, Two

Therefore this book begins with the smallest number, because the Creator of the human structure wished to have a numerical pattern in all his works. Here too the perfection of the work is noted: from one, that is, from God, because he is the one maker of all things that exist; and from two and three, because these deal with every form of otherness that descends from one, that is, from God, just as every otherness in the world derives from the monad.

For this reason the number four is subtracted, so that the perfect number six may remain, because these three are noted as perfect in the science of natural justice. If it were not subtracted, ten would remain, which is known to be perfect, because when divided it is not restored, whereas the imperfect number six is resolved through parts that, when heaped together, make an imperfect number, namely six.

What remains, then? The sophists now defend their own arguments and attack those of others, and conversely. [Col. 0906A] Hence they cannot attain the character of good men, who use certain and probable arguments.

It occurs through the interval of B. He says this by an envelopment and covering, as though at some time the axes of heaven were to move in threes and make the sphere of the world’s body sink down; thus heat would dominate moisture, and a flood would arise through fire, and conversely. In this way he calls the revolution a transition and retransition of the elements: when fire is not condensed into air, air into water, water into earth, or conversely, heat then departs, or moisture becomes a flood, either through fire or through water.

He calls another revolution the convolution of the seven planets, from whose nature excessive heat or moisture arises. There is an even greater cause when it is extremely hot: if moisture then remains too long, the stars poured around the sun send forth heat from themselves around the sun, and consequently diminish; the sun sends heat to the earth, and then they perish by fire.

Or relate “exorbitation” to the sun’s chariot, for it seems to go out of its course in summer, when it rises higher; and then it is turned more toward us than in winter. Or say that by “a long interval” he means the great year, which is 15,000 years.

Some philosophers also say that the sun is of such a nature that it draws into itself the fire of all the stars. To temper it, it draws to itself the moisture of that element, namely water; then water, and especially the seas, contract. When it relaxes, the sea spreads out again, though at some times more than at others.

Hence Lucan:

“Or does the fire-bearing Titan, that he may drink up the nourishing waters,  
Raise Ocean and lift its waves to the stars?”

Note that he says that the prior number is the surface. For no accident is prior to its subject, and he says “bodily surface” because of its perpetual conjunction with the body, which it never abandons, although by its nature it is incorporeal. Thus the corporeal and incorporeal properly tolerate one another in this respect: the corporeal as belonging to the body, and the incorporeal as belonging entirely to the soul are opposed, and do not tolerate one another at all in the same thing.

He says that hyle, impressed by ideas, strengthens the body, and that the divine consists of its most excellent part. This does not appear to be so. For hyle is an unformed thing and does not truly possess a part in its own nature; therefore nothing consists of a part of it, nor does anything consist of its limit. If hyle were to pass wholly into some one thing, then all other things would no longer consist of hyle as matter. This is also contrary to authority, since hyle would consist neither of the whole nor of a part. [Col. 0906D]

It must therefore be said that form comes to hyle, first into some part of it, so that something may be said to come into being; then another form comes into another part of it, and so on individually.

Physicists teach that certain bodies are proportioned according to the suitability of the elemental bodies, in imitation of numbers, so that they may be fit to receive life from the soul. They say that, while this universal composition preserves its proper order, the nature of the animal remains solid and tranquil, insofar as it can remain according to its nature. But if discord in the composition arises in some part from excessive or diminished moisture, illness occurs; if the composition perishes, dissolution follows, and the human being dies.

Hence the book says, “while they remain in the world,” and so forth. But when they fail, the secret power is immediately dissolved, because, insofar as it belongs to the nature of the soul, it is always ready to animate unless the body prevents it. Hence it adds: “the soul itself does not fail,” and so forth. When there can still be an addition.

I do not mean that, with regard to the effect of his works, he is assessed according to the quantity of love; rather, the person is removed at that moment by the justice of God, through which a human being is perfected by an increase of virtues and rots in the filth of vices.

From earth and fire, because it gives life to what is most dense and most subtle. From earth and water, because they are most dense; from air and fire, because they are most fine.

The horizon divides this. This is not true. For the horizon has 360 stadia in length, and it is established by this measure that the earth is longer. But what this book says is to be understood of the horizon of heaven, which is a hemisphere beneath which half of the earth is contained.

“A large part beyond.” “On this side,” because it does not contain the whole; or “beyond and on this side,” that is, from both sides.

“Then because of floods and conflagrations.” Plato bears witness to this, saying: “After a long interval, there occurs an exorbitation of the world’s revolution, which must be followed by the devastation of inflammation. For time produces nothing other than the course of the sun.”

The course of the sun does not produce time, since some days are reported to have existed before the origin of the sun. But the sun is said to produce time because time is distinguished through it. For time is the perpetual course of things, marked by the sun. [Col. 0907C]

Or by spherical motion. That which revolves by spherical motion never abandons the whole place that it occupies in itself, but always remains wholly within the same circuit; through its parts, however, it assumes different places as it revolves. But what moves along a line sometimes completely abandons its former place and is transferred to another; sometimes, without abandoning its former place, it extends farther, as a tree does when growing.

“Let us beware of illusions.” Just as in illusions something appears to exist when nothing exists, so with the words of one who acts sophistically, although there is no truth in them.

Understanding is that by which the mind clearly perceives things that exist.

Providence is that by which something future is seen before it happens.

Magnanimity is the understanding of great and exalted things with a broad and splendid conception of the soul.

Magnificence is the same thing in its effect.

Confidence is that by which the soul places great confidence in itself, with certain hope, in great and honorable matters.

Endurance is the voluntary and daily bearing of difficult and arduous things for the sake of honor or usefulness.

Constancy, or perseverance, is a stable and perpetual abiding in a reason that has been carefully considered.

Modesty is that by which honorable shame acquires a dear and lasting authority.

Friendship is the will for good things, on behalf of the very person whom one loves, to suffer something contrary to that person’s will.

Philosophy is the comprehension of truth. It is divided into three parts: ethics, logic, and physics.

Ethics is moral science, clearly demonstrating the order of life. Three things are subordinated to it: *animus*, soul, and human being.

The *animus* is a thing that takes care of itself.

The soul is that which undertakes care of the commonwealth.

The human being is a domestic entity that arranges its duties; or, according to the dialecticians, a rational animal.

Four things are subordinated to the soul: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance.

Prudence is the perfection of true praise.

Justice is a disposition of the soul.

Wisdom is that which sees all things, or a disposition of the soul preserved for the common good.

Fortitude is a certain rising of oneself always toward better things after abandoning vices; or fortitude is the undertaking of dangers and the endurance of evils.

Temperance is that which establishes each thing according to the gravity of love.

Logic is the diligent method of reasoning and the teacher of judgment. In a strict sense it is defined as comprising rhetoric and dialectic. In a broad sense it is described as follows: logic is the science of discourse, divided into three parts—dialectic, rhetoric, and grammar.

Dialectic is keenness of intellect and a mediator against foolishness. Four things are subordinated to dialectic: proof, assumption, confirmation, and conclusion.

Rhetoric is the instructress of honorable combination and graceful, skillful eloquence. Three things are subordinated to it: nature, instruction, and practice.

Grammar is expertise in speaking.

Physics is the science of natural power, correctly recalling its cause. Physics is of one kind intellectual, as with angels; of another intelligible, as with God; and of another natural, as with substance.

Natural science is divided into six parts: arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy, astrology, and medicine.

Arithmetic is the science of multitude, which is concerned with calculation for its own sake. The following are subordinated to arithmetic: perfection, imperfection, and superperfection.

Geometry is the doctrine that weighs or measures immobile magnitude. It possesses lines, intervals, magnitudes, figures, dimensions, and numbers.

Music is the careful art of melody and its instruments. Music is of three kinds: harmonic, rhythmic, and metric.

Astronomy is the acquired contemplation of mobile magnitude.

Astrology is the expertise that considers the rotation of the heavens through its turning. One kind is natural, the other superstitious. It is natural when it investigates the course of the sun and moon, of the stars, and the fixed stations of times. It is superstitious when it is followed by astrologers who foretell things from the stars.

This, then, is the difference between astronomy and astrology: astronomy contains the revolutions, risings, settings, and movements of the heavenly bodies, and explains why they are called thus. Astrology, however, is partly natural and partly superstitious.

Medicine is the art that treats diseases and the health of bodies. It is of three kinds: methodical, empirical, and logical.

Aristotle asks whether God exists. He deserves punishment, because it is more fitting for a wise person to worship than to inquire.

Alexander to Didymus: “There is one soul, stable in itself, from which all souls are restored.”

Hermogenes: “If God does not exist, whence come good things? If he exists, whence come evil things?”

[Col. 0909]

# Theoretical Music of the Priest Bede (C, S)*

It should be noted that every art is contained in reason. Music too consists in and is concerned with the reason of numbers. That which is produced from instruments of tones is changeable.

There are five senses. Of these senses, two are taken in relation to the body: sight and hearing; and two are within: taste and touch—or rather, smell. It is doubtful whether it senses within or without. Sense is the bond between body and soul.

Some things are incorporeal and invisible, such as the soul; some are corporeal and visible, such as bodies; and some are invisible and corporeal, such as bodily senses. They are corporeal because they are administered to the body, and invisible because that which they serve, as in the case of an inanimate thing or sight, cannot be seen.

Hence it happens that, although the five bodily senses perceive other external things, they do not perceive themselves. Sight does not see itself; taste does not taste itself—for if it did, it would never be fasting—and so it is with the others.

It must therefore be considered that, although we apply the bodily senses without difficulty to sensible things that are to be perceived, it cannot easily be explained and defined by them what the nature of those five senses or of the body is, or what the property of the sensible things perceived may be. If the nature of the senses is sought and defined, they are corporeal and invisible, as hearing is corporeal and invisible.

The sensible thing, however, because it is perceived by hearing—that is, the voice—has properties: it is air made suitable and struck by a certain blow. This too is corporeal and invisible. For things that are nearer penetrate sight more easily than those that are farther away.

If, with our eyes closed, we perceive nothing corporeal, Augustine says in Book XI of *On the Holy Trinity*: “Vision is therefore begotten from a visible thing, but not from that thing alone, unless it is present and seen.”

Accordingly, vision is begotten from the visible thing and the one who sees, in such a way that from the seer comes the sense of the eyes and the attention of the one who looks and gazes. Yet that formation of the sense which is called vision is formed only by the body that is seen—that is, by some visible thing. Once that thing is removed, no form remains that had been present in the sense while what was seen was present. [Col. 0909C]

The sense itself nevertheless remains, just as it existed before anything was sensed, like a footprint in water, which remains as long as the body by which it is impressed is present. Once that body is removed, no footprint remains, although the water remains, as it existed before it received the form of the body.

Therefore we cannot say that the visible thing generates the sense. Yet it does generate the form, or rather its likeness, which exists in the sense when we perceive something by seeing.

If the form of the body that we see and the form produced by it in the sense of the seer are not distinguished by that same sense, this is because their conjunction is so great that there is no evident opportunity for distinguishing them. But by reason we conclude that we could in no way have sensed unless some likeness of the body seen had existed in our sense.

For when a ring is impressed upon wax, an image has not failed to be made merely because it cannot be distinguished until the ring has been separated. Rather, since what was made remains after the wax has been separated, it can be seen. It is therefore easily persuaded that the form impressed from the ring was already present in the wax before it was separated from the ring. [Col. 0910A]

But if a ring were applied to a liquid, once it was removed nothing more would appear. Nevertheless, reason should not therefore deny that, before the ring was removed, the form of the ring made by the ring existed in that liquid. This form must be distinguished from the form that exists in the ring, from which the former was made. Once the ring is removed, the former will not remain, although the latter remains in the ring, from which the former was made.

Similarly, the sense of the eyes does not lack an image of the body that is seen merely because the image does not remain once the body has been removed. For this reason it is extremely difficult to persuade slower minds that an image of the visible thing is formed in our sense when we see it, and that this same form is vision. [Col. 0910B]

If some people have noticed what I am about to mention, they will not labor so greatly in this inquiry. When we have gazed for some time at lights and then closed our eyes, certain luminous colors seem to move before our sight, communicating themselves to one another in various ways and becoming progressively less bright until they cease altogether. We should understand these to be remnants of that form which had been made in the sense when the luminous body was seen; as they gradually and, in a way, step by step fade, they change.

Indeed, the bars of latticed windows, if we happened to be looking at them, often appeared in those colors, so that it is clear that this affection was impressed upon our sense by the thing that was seen. Thus it existed even while we were looking, and at that time it was brighter and more distinct because it was closely joined to the appearance of the thing that was perceived, so that it could not be distinguished at all; and that itself was vision.

Moreover, when the little flame of a lamp is somehow divided by the rays of the eyes, as though doubled, two visions are produced, although the thing seen is one. For the same rays emanating separately from each eye produce separate effects, while they do not terminate in and converge upon the body being viewed together and jointly so as to make one vision from both acts of looking. Therefore, if we close one eye, we see not a doubled flame but one flame, as it actually is. If the left eye is closed, the appearance that belonged to the right eye ceases to be seen; and conversely, if the right eye is closed, the appearance that belonged to the left eye fades away.

Adverbially. For just as, when the day increases or decreases, this is not immediately presented but only over many days, so music also, when it increases and decreases by semitones, or days when they are not continuous, is not perceived until those parts have grown beyond one another.

Since heavenly music is composed of the subtler [elements], it is received as extremely sonorous without any incongruity; for it is secretly poured down from the higher regions to the lower, even though, through habit, we do not perceive it. Although earthly music pleases us, nevertheless, because it is produced from more corporeal elements, it is scarcely found without some incongruity. It should also be noted that, just as the soul performs many actions without knowing it—such as the growth of hair and nails—so many things also occur in its hearing that remain hidden from it through habit, such as the sound of the planets. The multiple ratio (*multiplex*) therefore retains greater power for consonances because it resembles a discrete quantity increasing through growth. And why is this so? Because arithmetic, which exists in itself, and music, which demonstrates consonances, belong to discrete quantity.

[Col. 0911D] Geometry and astrology, however, belong to continuous quantity. Since the superparticular ratio resembles continuous quantity in its decreasing parts, it does not retain the same power for consonances as the multiple ratio, although, on account of the individuality of its parts, it is admitted in second place. The superparticular ratio produces only consonances, whereas the multiple ratio produces not so much consonances as equal-sounding intervals.

According to the Pythagoreans and Ptolemy, nature, according to Aristoxenus, is in quality. Therefore “superparticularity” is written continuously, because it is divided by parts. [Col. 0912A]

Every multiple symphony follows the property of discrete quantity, not, however, infinitely, but through only three degrees: the double, the triple, and the quadruple. Every superparticular symphony, on the other hand, preserves the nature of continuous quantity, not indeed infinitely, but only through three degrees: the sesquialter, the sesquitertian, and the sesquioctave.

For the superparticular ratio doubles its own ratio, whatever it may be, and designates it by a binary number; it begins from the binary and is reduced to it, but does not reach unity. Thus it preserves the proportion of continuous quantity.

In all these there lies hidden the *epogdoos*, that is, the sesquioctave ratio; for this reason it will not be counted specifically among the symphonies. The others are composed from it, since it is the common measure of them all.

The same occurs in voices: three to one is triple, and it contains within itself two consonances, namely 3 to 2, the diapente, and 2 to 4, the diapason.

That one is excessively sharp and is not brought back toward the grave so as to suit it; and the one who is less grave does not wish to be raised. For he recognized the differences between the consonances.

To the ear, and not to reason. For there is much difference between sense and reason.

They are carried along a middle path, because they do not assign discrimination wholly to the ears, nor wholly to reason. Rather, they assign the sound—namely, whether it is acute or grave—to the ear, but the differences between the consonances to reason.

The moments or movements of the arts and of life have been extended: these are things that must be discerned. First they affect the senses, then they are perceived through sensation, and finally they are distinguished by reason.
