For *echō* (ἔχω) means “I have”; hence *synechō* (συνέχω), “I continue.” *Diastēma* (διάστημα) means “interval” or “space”; hence διάστημαπκη [reading uncertain], “spaces” or “intervals.”

Here note the *aisthētērion* (αἰσθητήριον), that is, the guardian of all the senses. It is first held commonly in the heart, and from there is produced specifically for all the bodily senses: in the eyes there is something luminous, having a fiery nature; in the ears, something mobile, airy, and clear, which receives colored forms—whatever things are produced from the higher fiery element, through a very subtle air; the sense of smell in the nostrils is formed from lower and thicker air; taste belongs to water; touch belongs to earth. For no kind of music is found before that discipline of the tetrachords—that is, how the number of strings came to plurality, in which it is not found. [Col. 0913A]

## What a Tone Is

A tone occurs when one little voice (*vocula*) surpasses another by its entire quantity and, in addition, by an eighth part of the voice that has been surpassed, whether in the intensification of its pitch or in the relaxation of its gravity. A semitone occurs when a tone is divided into two parts that are not equal but unequal. [Col. 0913B] They preferred to call one semitone the greater and the other the lesser. A diesis is the lesser semitone divided into two parts; that is, musicians called the lesser semitone a diesis.

Melody (*melodia*) is what is also older, although somewhat harsher, when a consonance is completed from two tones and a semitone, or from a semitone and two tones. Chromatic [music] is what is also later and, by its variety, pleasantly charms the minds for the delight of the ears; it is said to proceed in excessively fine divisions, and consists of a tone and three semitones, or of three semitones and a tone. Enharmonic [music] possesses the whole harmony and surpasses the others in its dignity; it consists of two dieses and two tones, or of two tones and two dieses.

The diatessaron consonance occurs when one little voice, by the intensification of its pitch, entirely possesses another little voice in the relaxation of its gravity, and in addition possesses a third part of the voice that has been surpassed. The diapente consonance occurs when one little voice surpasses another by its entire quantity—namely, by the whole of the surpassed voice and, in addition, by half of it—whether in the intensification of pitch or in the relaxation of gravity.

The diapason is not a consonance but an equal-sounding relation (*aequisonantia*). It occurs whenever one little voice, by its pitch when intensified or by its gravity when relaxed, occupies twice the entire quantity of the surpassed voice.

To understand clearly what intensification and relaxation are—something that must be observed in all consonances—proceed as follows. When you have emitted the first sound from your mouth, your heart, or some material of an instrument, fix a limit. Whatever, through that first sound, rises upward—whether a tone, diapason, diapente, or diatessaron—you should know that all those consonances are produced through intensification of pitch. Whatever, however, flows downward from that first sound, at the point where we said that the boundary must be fixed—whether a tone, diatessaron, or any other interval—you should know that all those consonances are produced through relaxation of gravity.

If you wish to know the sound of a tone, diatessaron, or the other consonances, adopt the following calculation. Take a wooden rule shaped by the master’s hands. Prepare three joints or little bridges, equally balanced and hollowed on every side. Stretch a string over the rule, across two points resting beneath the bridges. Without cutting the string, but in order to measure it, divide the entire string into three equal parts. [Col. 0914A] At the point where the third part ends, place a bridge; strike the third part of the string, then strike the other part, and you will see the consonance of the diapason. For the third part is higher in pitch than the two parts, and the two parts are twice as grave in sound.

For the diapente consonance, next divide the entire string into five equal parts. At the point where three parts have been completed, place a bridge and strike both parts. One part will be graver by the whole quantity of the lesser part and, in addition, by half of it; the other part will be sharper by the whole quantity of the greater part and, in addition, by half of it.

The diatessaron consonance will occur if you divide the entire string into seven parts, place a bridge, and strike both parts. Likewise divide the string into seven, that is, ten parts; where the ninth part ends, place a bridge and strike both parts. You will find the lesser part one tone sharper and the greater part one tone flatter in its entirety. [Col. 0914B]

It is asked why he first placed the diapason, diapente, and diatessaron, and now begins differently in turning the order of those consonances around. The answer is that, insofar as this pertains to arithmetical proportionality, the double precedes the sesquialter, and the sesquialter precedes the sesquitertian, which is placed last. Conversely, musical consonance looks backward. For the first consonance in the art of music is the sesquitertian, that is, the diatessaron; from it one arrives at the sesquialter, that is, the diapente; and from there at the double, which is the diapason.

*Nicos* means “victor,” *machia* “battle,” *orea* in Greek “beautiful,” and *phonē* “voice”; hence Orpheus is said to have a beautiful voice. The names are similar in all cases, but there is a difference in the lichanos of the hypate—chromatic, enharmonic, and diatonic. The same applies to the lichanos of the meson, the paranete of the synemmenon, and the paranete of the hyperboleon. For although there are eighteen strings in the diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic genera, the remaining strings are likewise the same, except for five. Thus five are unlike in the chromatic and five in the enharmonic; when those in the diatonic are added to eighteen, they become ten and eight [the transmitted numerical statement is corrupt].

Ambrose, in his exposition of Psalm 118, chapter 2, says this:

> “I think that Pythagoras, a philosopher who imitated the prophets, established a school so that his disciples, by not speaking for five years, might learn to speak through such silence.”

Axioms—that is, things worthy of admiration—which are also called propositions (*proloquia*), that is, statements subject to truth or falsity. The sesquialter is named from the double, the sesquitertian from the triple, and the others according to their order.

That designation is contrary to sense insofar as, in the primitive ratios, it indicates increase, whereas in the derivative ratios it indicates diminution. For in multiple ratios, the greater the number, the greater the ratio. In superparticular ratios, however, as the number increases, the ratios decrease.

It is asked how the ratio between fifty-three and fifty-eight is smaller than that between fifty and fifty-five, and how, again, the ratio between forty-eight and fifty-three is greater than that between fifty and fifty-five. The answer should be this: if that philologist Boethius were to add two to fifty-three, the result would be fifty-five, and the number five would measure it eleven times. If he were to add another two to fifty-eight, the result would be sixty, and the same number would measure it twelve times. There would then be a sesqui-eleventh ratio—namely, fifty-five to sixty—which is smaller than a sesqui-tenth.

Although that ratio is not reached in 53 and 58, it is nevertheless apparent from this that the ratio is smaller in the larger numbers and greater in the smaller numbers. Likewise, if three were subtracted from forty-eight, the result would be forty-five, and five would measure it nine times. Similarly, if three were taken from fifty-three, fifty would rightly remain, and five would measure it ten times. There would be a sesqui-ninth ratio, which is greater than a sesqui-tenth; and the number 48 and 53 is intermediate between the greater and the smaller.

[Col. 0915B] Here again it is asked why he adds three to the quantity of each number so as to produce larger numbers, and why he subtracts two from the same quantity so as to produce smaller numbers. The solution is that he divided the quantity of five, which is the difference between the aforementioned numbers, into two parts—namely, three and two. He added the greater part to the given quantity so that the numbers would be larger and the ratio smaller; he subtracted the lesser part from the same quantity so that the numbers would be smaller and the ratio greater.

Twelve is sesquialter to eight and sesquitertian to nine. But if you subtract the twelve that is sesquitertian to nine, nine remains, in sesquioctave proportion to eight. From this it follows that the sesquioctave is not half of the sesquitertian that was subtracted. For if you seek two successive sesquioctaves, as in the numbers 192, 216, and 243, the third term—243—cannot be sesquitertian to the first; rather, it would have to be 256, which is greater than the second sesquioctave.

What if the simple sesquioctave were half of the sesquitertian? Doubled, it would certainly restore the whole.

Twenty is sesquitertian to fifteen and sesquiquartile to thirteen. But if you subtract the same number 20, which is sesquiquartile to 16, sixteen remains, in a sesqui-fifteenth ratio to fifteen. That this is not half of the sesquiquartile subtracted is shown by the fact that, if you find two successive sesqui-fifteenths, as in these numbers—9, 10, 23 [the numerical sequence is evidently corrupt]—the third term, namely twenty-four, cannot be sesquiquartile to the first. For if you take a quarter of 900, which is 225, and add it to the same number, the result will be 1125, plainly greater than 1024 by a second sesqui-fifteenth.

But if the simple sesqui-fifteenth were half of the sesquiquartile, doubling it would undoubtedly restore the whole. The same occurs henceforth with all superparticular ratios: if the smaller ratio is subtracted from a continuous ratio, what remains cannot constitute half of the ratio subtracted.

Twelve retains a sesquialter ratio to eight and a double ratio to six. But if you subtract the lesser continuous ratio, or the sesquialter, eight remains, in a sesquitertian relation to six. It follows that this is more than half of the sesquialter subtracted, because if you find two sesquitertians, as in the numbers 18, 24, and 32, they are greater than 27, the number that is sesquialter to 18.

Where it was stated that only multiple and superparticular ratios can have a common measure: four is double two, while six is triple two. Subtract two, to which six is triple; six remains, in sesquialter proportion to four. Two sesquialter ratios are 6 to 4 and 8 to 6, but 4 is double 8—[the text here is evidently corrupt]—smaller, namely 9, than the second sesquialter. The difference between 59,049 and 62,208 is 3,159, which arose from 243 multiplied thirteen times, and it contains less than an eighteenth part of the smaller [number]. Similarly, the difference between 62,208 and 65,536 is 3,328, which arose from 256 multiplied thirteen times; it contains less than an eighteenth part but more than a nineteenth part of 62,208.

An eighth of 59,049 is 7,381 and one eighth of a unit. Added to the same 59,049, this produces 66,430 and one eighth, which exceed 65,536 by 894 and one eighth of a unit.

If an eighth of 243 is required, it is 30 and three eighths of a unit. Added to the same number, this produces 273 and three eighths. Thus, in the proportion of the semitone, there are 256 to 244 [the printed “ducentos 44” is likely corrupt], whose difference is 13; it contains less than an eighteenth part of the smaller and more than a nineteenth part.

For if you multiply 13 by eighteen, you obtain 234, which is four less than 243. In the proportion of the apotome there are 273 and three eighths to 256. Their difference is 17 and three eighths; it contains less than a fourteenth part of the smaller but more than a fifteenth part, because if you multiply 17 by fourteen, the result is 238. If you multiply three eighths of a unit by fourteen, the result is five and one quarter units; added to 238, this gives 243, and these are less than 256 by twelve units and three quarters of a unit.

But if you multiply 17 by fifteen, the result is 256. If, however, you multiply three eighths of a unit by fifteen, they produce five units and five eighths; add these to 255, and you obtain 260 and five eighths, which exceed 256 by four units and five eighths.

Therefore, if you wish to see all these matters in whole numbers—both the terms written above [Col. 0917A] and the differences—count by eights, and you will be glad to find nothing troublesome. Multiply 243 by eight: the result is 1,944; 256 by eight gives 2,048; 273 by eight gives 2,184. Eight times three eighths produces three whole units; add these to 2,183, and you have a sesquioctave relation to 1,944. Their difference is 243, which has arisen from the distance between 243 and 273—namely, 30 and three eighths—multiplied by eight. Eight times three eighths is three whole units. Thus the total difference is 243.

In the relation of the lesser semitone, 2,048 stands to 1,944; their difference is 104, produced by multiplying the difference 13 between 243 and 256 by eight. It contains less than an eighteenth and more than a nineteenth, because 104 multiplied by eighteen is 1,872, produced from 234 multiplied by eight; and this is 72 units less than 1,944. Those 72 units arose from the excess of 243 over 234—nine—multiplied by eight. But if you increase 104 by multiplying it by nineteen, you obtain 1,976, produced from 248 multiplied by eight; this is greater than 1,944 by 32 units. Those 32 arose from four—the amount by which 247 exceeded 243—multiplied by eight.

In the apotome ratio, 2,187 stands to 2,048, and their difference is 139, produced from 17 and three eighths of a unit in this way: eight times 17 is 136; eight times three eighths is three whole units; added to 136, these yield 139. It contains less than a fourteenth and more than a fifteenth, because if you multiply 139 by fourteen, you obtain 1,946, produced from 243 and one quarter of a unit after 243 has been multiplied by eight. A quarter multiplied by eight produces two whole units; add these to 1,944, and you have 1,946. This is less than 2,048 by 102 units, which arose from the distance between 260 and 256—twelve and three quarters—multiplied by eight: eight times twelve is 96, and eight times three quarters is six; together they make 102.

But if you multiply 139 by fifteen, the result is 2,085, produced from 260 and five eighths multiplied by eight: eight times 260 is 2,080; eight times five eighths produces five whole units; add these to the preceding number, and you have 2,085 [the printed “2805” is evidently an OCR error]. These exceed 2,048 by 37 units, which arose from the excess of 260 over 256—four and five eighths—multiplied by eight: eight times four is 32, and eight times five eighths is five; together they make 37.

If anyone wishes to examine the ratios in whole numbers, he ought to consider them in this way. If 16 is multiplied by itself, the result is 256. If it is multiplied by 17, the result is 272. If 17 is multiplied by itself, the result is 289. Thus there will be two sesqui-sixteenth ratios—256, 272, 289—which clearly exceed the sesquioctave, because if an eighth of 256 is sought, it is 32 units; added to 256, this produces 288, which is exceeded by 289 by one unit.

Again, if 17 is multiplied by itself, the result is 289. If 17 is multiplied by 18, the result is 306. If 18 is multiplied by itself, the result is 324. These two sesqui-seventeenth ratios—namely, 289, 306, and 324—do not complete a sesquioctave, because if an eighth of 289 is sought, it is 36 units and one eighth; when this is joined to the number of which it is the eighth, the result is 325 and one eighth, which exceed 324 by one unit and one eighth. [Col. 0918A]

If this eighth of a unit should perhaps seem troublesome, let the preceding numbers be multiplied by eight, and ten ratios will be found in perfectly whole numbers. Thus, when 256 is multiplied by eight, it becomes 2,048; 272 multiplied by eight gives 2,176; similarly, 289 multiplied by eight gives 2,312. These are again two sesqui-sixteenth ratios—2,048, 2,176, and 2,312—which are shown to exceed the sesquioctave, because if an eighth of 2,048, namely 256, is added to it, the result is 2,304, which is exceeded by 2,312 by eight units.

Again, 289 multiplied by eight gives 2,312; 306 multiplied by eight gives 2,448; and 324 multiplied by eight gives 2,592. These are again two sesqui-seventeenth ratios: 2,312, 2,448, and 2,592. They are shown not to complete the sesquioctave because, if an eighth of 2,312—namely 289—is added, the result is 2,601, which certainly exceeds 2,592 by eight units.

In the earlier numbers, therefore, unity constituted the difference between the sesquioctave and the sesqui-sixteenth ratios. In the later numbers, that difference increased by eight units, the same number by which the totals whose difference it was had been increased. Similarly, between the sesquioctave and the sesqui-seventeenth ratios, unity and one eighth of a unit constituted the difference. When multiplied by eight, unity, like those totals whose difference had been multiplied in the later numbers, grew to eight units. The eighth part of a unit, multiplied by the same eight, became one whole unit. Therefore, in the later terms, eight is the difference between the sesquioctave and the sesqui-sixteenth ratios, while nine is the difference between the sesqui-seventeenth ratios and the sesquioctave. The third part of 262,144 is 87,381 and one third of a unit. If you take a ninth part of the *nete diazeugmenon*, or a ninth part of the *paramese*, or a ninth part of either *hypate*, you will be able to have the most exact measure of either *paranete chromaticē* or either *lichanos chromaticē* on the monochord; there, too, the apotome will by no means escape measurement. Between 234 and 247 there is a sesqui-eighteenth ratio, because their difference, 13, is contained eighteen times in the smaller number and nineteen times in the larger. If you add four to these, they become 247 and 260, between which there is a sesqui-ninth ratio, the ratio by which the musicians’ semitone is greater.

The difference by which the lesser semitone exceeds three commas is 5,165; the difference by which it is exceeded by four commas is 1,988. Joined together, these produce 7,154, that is, the ratio of the comma. The apotome exceeds four commas by the same difference by which the lesser semitone exceeds three, and it is exceeded by five commas by the same difference by which the lesser semitone is exceeded by four.

The difference by which the tone exceeds eight commas is 1,925; the difference by which it is exceeded by nine is 5,328. Joined together, these produce a comma, that is, 7,253 [the printed “7153” is likely corrupt]. Thus the sesquioctave ratios are to be investigated beginning from the sixth multiple.

If you take the letter *h* of the *trites synemmenon*, it will be the species that he describes, namely, bounded by movable notes, since between the *parhypate meson* and the *paramese* there is more than a diatessaron, while the *paramese* is by no means movable. [Col. 0919A]

The diagram begins with the *proslambanomenos* of the hypermixolydian and ends at the *nete hyperboleon* of the hypodorian. But the consideration of the notes of the diatonic genus—which arises from the *nete hyperboleon* of the hypodorian through a diatessaron, a tone, and another tone together with a semitone—ends at the *proslambanomenos* of the hypermixolydian. In a remarkable way, the relation by which the strings of the individual modes differ from one another in the length of the diagram is the same relation by which the strings of the tones are distinguished in their order. Here one must observe carefully that he does not say that the *mese* is consonant with the *nete diezeugmenon* because it maintains with it the diapente interval, but because, through the diapason consonance, the *hypate meson* sounds the same as the *nete diezeugmenon*. The *mese* likewise sounds the same as the *nete hyperboleon* through the diapason. The *nete hyperboleon*, however, produces a diatessaron symphony with the *nete diezeugmenon*. The *mese*, since through the diapason it sounds the same as the *nete hyperboleon*, is also consonant by a diatessaron with the *nete diezeugmenon*. The same argument should be made where he says that the *paramese* is consonant with the *hypate meson* on the lower side. He does not say this on account of the diapente, but because, through the diapason, the *paramese* sounds the same as the *hypate hypaton*; therefore the *paramese* is consonant by a diatessaron with the *hypate meson*, just as the *hypate hypaton* is. # THE SQUARE OR MEASURED MUSIC OF BEDE THE PRIEST

[Col. 0919B] Since we propose to discuss certain matters necessary for the benefit of singers concerning the art of music, it is necessary that, in accordance with the author’s intention, we earnestly strive to understand the exceedingly subtle rules set forth below. Since human nature naturally desires to know everything, and since, from the sin of the first man, there are four evils that hinder human nature—namely, ignorance, vice, inability to speak, and need—four corresponding goods have nevertheless been set against them: wisdom against ignorance, virtue against vice, eloquence against inability to speak, and necessity against need. Therefore divine clemency granted philosophers skill in discovering the arts, so that through it each person might be able to grasp the goods mentioned above and, by putting them into practice, raise fallen nature to a better condition.

Since learning one thing is very difficult, there is no doubt that learning many things is almost impossible. [Col. 0919C] Nevertheless, in all matters we recognize far more through our own sense than we learn from a teacher. For just as in a tree nature planted one power as a propagating branch capable of governing many others, so in human beings reason has taught us to discover many things from knowledge of one.

Here too one must observe that every art and every discipline naturally possesses a more honorable rational principle than the craft exercised by hand and labor. For it is much greater and more suitable to know what one is doing than to accomplish the very thing one knows. The bodily craft serves as an attendant; reason, however, commands as mistress. Unless the hand operates according to what reason dictates, the work is done in vain.

Thus the knowledge of music in the apprehension of reason is so much more distinguished than in the work and act of producing it as the mind surpasses the body—which, being without reason, lives without reason. Reason commands and leads the work toward what is right; unless its command is obeyed, a work deprived of reason will stumble. Hence it follows that rational contemplation does not need the actual performance, whereas the works of the hands are nothing unless they are guided by reason. [Col. 0920B–C]

The extent of its glory and the abundance of reason can already be understood from this: other, so to speak, bodily craftsmen have taken their names not from the discipline but rather from the instruments themselves. Thus the *citharoedus* is named from the *cithara*, the *tibicen* or *auloedus* from the *tibia*, and others from the names of their respective instruments. Reason, however, wished teachers of music to be named not from instruments but from contemplation and knowledge.

Therefore, if anyone learns singing spontaneously and wishes to distinguish qualities and quantities, likenesses and differences, the proportions of different sounds, time and measure, as well as the distinctions between long, short, and semibreve figures, let him draw from the fountain of this science’s rejoicing, and he will experience its sweetness. For one who has learned how to plant a vineyard, graft a single sapling, or load a single donkey will not doubt that he can do the same—or do it better—in one case as in all.

At the beginning of this science, we think it necessary to know what music is, who a musician is, and from what the name is derived; what its genus, matter, parts, species, instrument, usefulness, and function are. We must therefore know that music is a liberal [Col. 0921A] science that supplies the skilled capacity for singing.

It is divided, however, because one kind is instrumental, another human, and another rhythmic. Instrumental music is assigned to recognizing and distinguishing songs. It too is divided, because one kind is harmonic, another rhythmic, and another metric.

Harmonic music is that which distinguishes between grave and acute sounds. Or harmonic music is that which consists in numbers and measures in two ways: one spatial, according to the proportion of sounds and voices; the other temporal, according to the proportion of long and short figures.

Another definition of harmonic music is that it is the science of distinguishing melody and the variety of singing, an easy path toward perfection in singing, and above all the proportional consonance of unlike things; it is also the science of number related to sound. [Col. 0921B]

Rhythmic music is that which, in the scanning of words, asks whether the diction coheres well or badly, since in singing one must avoid errors just as in reading.

Metric music is that which demonstrates the measure of different meters by a plausible method, as is evident in heroic, iambic, and elegiac meter.

A musician is one who, with deliberate reason, supplies the science of singing not only through the service of performance but also through the authority of contemplation. If we observe the same principle in the construction of buildings and in warfare, the names are assigned in the opposite way: buildings are inscribed with, or called by, the names of those by whose command and reason they were established, not of those by whose labor and service they were completed. Hence the definition of metric music follows.

There is a great difference between musicians and singers. The latter sing; the former know what music composes. For one who sings what he does not understand is defined as a beast. Hence the verse:

> A beast, not a singer, is one who sings not by art but by use.  
> Art does not make a true singer, but instruction.

Music is called *musica* from the Muses, who according to the fable are said to be the daughters of Jupiter. It has a twofold consideration: according to measure and according to non-measure.

According to measure, as it is understood here, it is the length or brevity of a song, which, as far as we are concerned, is generally called an instrument (*organum*) according to a determinate measure, whose invention we now presuppose. According to non-measure, it is taken either relatively, as where no property of the matter has been discovered. [Col. 0921D]

The genus of this science is skill in harmonic melody, which is accomplished either from the concordance of many sounds or from the composition of long and short figures.

Its matter is sound ordered according to measure. “Sound” is taken for the difference of melody and concord; “ordered” refers to the numbers of the times contained in the figures before a perfect pause; “according to measure” refers to the quantity of long and short figures, which consists in the accent and sustained duration of the voice.

Its parts are divided differently in theory and in practice. The practical parts are three: the science of the grave sound, the science of the middle sound, and the science of the acute sound. It treats these by showing their uses and their comparisons with one another, and how *motelli*, or *conducti*, or *organa*, are composed from these six. [Col. 0922A]

The theoretical parts are three: the dispositions of this art for discovering *neumes*; recognizing their numbers; determining how many species they have; declaring the proportions of some to others; demonstrating all these matters; and teaching the species of their orders and positions, by which they are prepared, so that one may take from them what one wishes and compose harmonies from them.

The species of this art are also the diversities of the subjects from which neumes are made; for sometimes they are performed by the voice, sometimes by breath, and sometimes by touch. By the voice, as with the human voice; by breath, as with the flute; by touch, as with the psaltery or cithara, and similar instruments.

[Col. 0922B] Instruments, moreover, are one thing in practice and another in theory. The instrument of theory is the investigation and demonstration of the proportions of sounds and voices. In practice, one instrument is natural and another artificial. The natural instrument is the lung, throat, tongue, palate, and so forth. The spiritual members, properly speaking, are principally those of the voice and the epiglottis. The artificial instrument is the organ, viol, cithara, atola, psaltery, and so forth.

Its usefulness is great, wondrous, and exceedingly virtuous, since it has dared to enter the doors of the Church. For no science has dared to enter the doors of the Church except music alone. [Col. 0922C] Through it we ought to praise and bless the maker of the world, singing to him a new song, just as our holy fathers the prophets taught. For through it the divine offices, by which we are summoned to everlasting glory, are celebrated daily. And, as Boethius testifies, music holds the foremost place among the seven liberal arts; nothing remains without it. Indeed, the world itself is said to have been constituted by a certain harmony of sounds, and heaven itself to revolve according to the modulation of harmony.

Among all the sciences, it is proved to be the more praiseworthy, courtly, delightful, joyful, and lovable; for it makes a person liberal, delightful, courtly, joyful, and lovable. It moves human emotions and calls forth different dispositions, as in battles. Indeed, the harmony of trumpets inflames combatants, because the more vehement the blast, the [Col. 0922D] quicker the spirit becomes for battle. Why say more? Music truly urges mortals to endure labors and consoles the weariness of individual tasks through the measure of the voice. Music refreshes troubled minds, since it removes headache and sadness; it drives away unclean spirits, evil humors, and illnesses. Hence it is found useful for the health of body and soul, because at times the body becomes infirm when the soul languishes, and it is hindered when the soul itself is hindered. Thus the cause and condition of the body is often brought about through the healing of the soul, through the adaptation of its powers, and through the tempering of its substance by suitable agents in suitable places. Thus we read of David, who relieved King Saul from the evil spirit by the art of modulation.

[Col. 0923A] Music also consoles reptiles, aquatic creatures, and birds by its sweetness; indeed, whatever we say, and whatever is stirred by the pulsations of the veins, is shown to be harmony, joined with useful things.

Practice has one function, theory another. Practice is to compose harmonies and an art capable of moving human emotions. Theory, on the other hand, is to comprehend in summary the knowledge of the species of harmonies, that from which they are composed, that for which they are composed, and how they are composed. Its function is also to know, preserve, and regularly describe long and short figures, as well as their bodies and measures, the qualities and quantities, the similarities and dissimilarities, of proportions, sounds, and voices, and orthography, so that through it every kind of song, however diversified, may be suitably explained.

[Col. 0923B] Since these and many other matters are explained in order in this art, it must first be seen and understood specifically that there are only three genera through which all measured music proceeds: namely, discant, hocket, and organum.

Discant is the song of two or three voices of different kinds, in which consonance—namely, the diatessaron, diapente, and diapason—remains naturally proportioned through the composition of long and short figures according to sweet measure. Hence it must be noted that there are three most general species through which all modes—that is, all songs in which the material consists—are recognized and distinguished, [Col. 0923C] and are also regulated by figure, time, and measure.

Since this discant is explained in various chapters through the said composition under a definite measure of time or times, we shall first examine the representation and form of simple figures; second, figures similarly and equally ligated or joined, in which each figure contains within itself the times belonging to it; and also the plicas, properties, and distinctions of these figures, and how the length or brevity of a song is indicated through them. Next we shall consider what time and measure are.

The representation of figures is that of a sound according to its mode and according to the equivalence of its equivalent. Such figures are sometimes placed with a letter and sometimes without one. With a letter, as in motets and similar works; without a letter, as in the neumes of conducti and similar works.

[Col. 0923D] Between figures that occur with a letter and those that occur without one there is this difference: those without a letter ought, as far as possible, to be more extensively ligated with one another. This property is sometimes omitted above the letter associated with the figures. The properties of these figures, both those associated with letters and those not so associated, are assigned the divisions and rules that follow.

Therefore, in order to learn everything that has been set forth, we must know that only six figures have been devised. They are always related in pairs; each pair is similar in form and quantity, but differs in power, art, rule, and nature.

The first of them, the fountain and origin of the whole science and its end, is called the perfect long *minuta* (diminished). [Col. 0924A] It derives something from perfection with respect to equality, because within a fixed dimension of the length of one [unit], through the duration of the voice, it remains proportionately equal in its prolongation. Dividing and diminishing itself into nine parts in two ways, its form becomes quadrangular, with a tail always fixed to its right side. Through this it also deserves to bear the name of length, as is clear in the present example.

The second is the imperfect long, which is at times also called simply “not perfect.” It is called imperfect because it contains only two times, while retaining the affinity in form and property of the perfect figure, as is evident.

[Col. 0924B]

The third is called the recta brevis, because it contains within itself one complete and undivided time, dividing itself into two unequal parts, or into only three equal and indivisible parts. Its form is quadrangular and lacks every property, as here:

The fourth is called the altera brevis, because it contains two rectae breves and always occupies the position of the other, retaining the affinity of the recta brevis in form, property, and association, as here:

[Col. 0924C]

The fifth is called the major semibreve. It has beside it a lesser major, which is also imperfect, and a brevis, because the imperfect figure is both a brevis and a major: it retains the greater part of the recta brevis, as stated above. Its form is as follows:

The sixth, the minor semibreve, is named similarly, but as the lesser, because it contains within itself the lesser part of the recta brevis, retaining the preceding figure’s affinity in form and quantity, as here:

[Col. 0924D] Since the perfect figure, remaining in unity, is the fountain and origin of this science and its end—because every song proceeds from it and is repeated in it—and since it consists in numbers, times, and measures, containing within itself a threefold equality, it follows that it appears to be prior to the others. For God, the creator of the world, established all things in number, weight, and measure, and this was the principal exemplar in the Creator’s mind. Whatever was formed from the primordial origin of the universe was constituted universally according to the principle of number.

Therefore number naturally precedes every creature, and the ternary is found in each individual thing, because it does not essentially depart from the ineffable Trinity, which created all things. Hence one reads in the authorities how God rejoices in ruling by the ternary; so this number is present in all things. Its principle is unity, which in Greek is called *monos*. Unity itself, however, is not a number, but the fountain and origin of numbers, the beginning and end of all things. It is therefore not improperly referred to the highest Trinity, because every natural thing is acknowledged to consist of three things in the likeness of the divine nature.

In voices and sounds, and in all things, there exists only a threefold consonance: namely, diatessaron, diapente, and diapason. [Col. 0925A] All naturally formed things therefore follow this Trinity, since one must necessarily believe that it was naturally inherent in all things from their first origin and was present in the highest and first craftsman. For nothing is made unless it first exists in the craftsman as the power to make, nor [does he act] wisely without wisdom, and so forth; he needs nothing, and nothing is made by him except through grace.

Since all things are made by him, it is of the greatest importance to the wise that these three things—wisdom, power, and grace—are in the divine Church, because nothing more is necessary for the highest and perfect good. Thus the first principles of all things are only three: the immovable principle, God, the principle of principles; and the movable, heavenly principle, through whose motion all things are moved.

To speak briefly: every measured song proceeds from this figure, is divided, and is repeated into it; and all subsequent figures return to it in order to preserve equivalence. Its rule and nature are such that, whenever it is found before a long, it always contains three times. For example:

[Col. 0925C]

Its related figure, which is made similar to it in form, follows. Its rule and nature are such that it must always stand before a brevis or after one; it is said to be collateral to it. For example:

In this case only two times are held in common by virtue of the collateral figure, which is taken from the ending portion. Hence the verse:

> Before a long, the diminished longs make [three times].  
> If a brevis is added, the long deserves two times.

Hence it must be noted that whenever a single brevis occurs between two longs, it is always reduced to the preceding imperfect long; and, since it is produced from that long, the reverse occurs in a similar manner. One must therefore consider how a perfect figure cannot be made except by means of a following or preceding brevis, since a long and a brevis, and conversely, always make one perfection.

If someone asks whether a natural pattern or song can be made entirely from imperfect figures, as it is made entirely from perfect figures, the answer, with proof, is no, since no one can pronounce pure imperfect figures. Nevertheless, some writers in their arts state that the perfect figure possesses perfection through ultrameasure, and that certain modes, such as the first and fourth, are ultrametrical—that is, do not possess a regular measure. This is impossible, because if it were true, a natural song could be made entirely from imperfect figures, since they call the imperfect perfect.

[Col. 0926A] Just as every natural thing is found to consist of three things in the likeness of the divine nature, and as there is only a threefold consonance in voices and sounds, so every measured song is found to consist of three things in the likeness of the divine nature. Its proof is evident in measure, where the ternary number is reduced to perfection.

And, so that we do not proceed into ambiguity, it must be known that the perfect figure is recognized by several rules. The first is as the verses quoted above sing. The second is whenever two breves lacking every property occur between two longs, having no affinity in form. For example:

[Col. 0926B]

“O Mary, blessed mother,” etc.

The first produces one time and is called the recta brevis; the second produces two and is called the altera brevis, being taken from the ending portion of the preceding figure. Since three times are found to remain in such a binary, any of the aforementioned longs deserves to retain perfection from God, except when the first long is preceded only by a brevis, as is clear from this clause:

[Col. 0926C]

Then it will contain two times. Thus perfection before the joined or separated progression can never be diminished, because a perfect long cannot have perfection except through some following perfection.

Third, if three [breves] are sometimes found between the aforesaid figures and are similar in form, as here:

And although it preserves one time, nevertheless none of the longs will lose the power or grace of its perfection, except as stated above.

Fourth, if four occur between the aforesaid figures, all are considered breves and equal, but the last arises from the following [figure]. Also, a small stroke in the form and length of a semisuspirium should visibly extend from the preceding long beside its side; this indicates the difference of modes or perfections, as here:

Then the following long will contain [its] times, unless it held two. This also follows the order of the fourth and fifth imperfect modes. For if that stroke were absent, the first of the breves would proceed from the preceding figure according to the order of the second imperfect mode. For example:

[Col. 0927A]

Fifth, if figures similar in form should occur, the first three will produce one perfect [figure], and the following unequal binary one [perfect figure]; each of the longs will retain its value, as stated above. For example:

[Col. 0927B] If more should occur according to an odd number, the same arrangement does not take place. Thus anyone can easily distinguish between a perfect and an imperfect long, if the matter is carefully considered.

It must therefore be noted that the perfect figure sometimes appears doubled within one body. Its width then exceeds its length, thus: O. This does not pertain to the origin of other figures except by grace, since it would never be doubled unless plain music were to be broken in the composition or ordering of the tenor. Upon this all motets and all organum are founded.

The recta brevis, or the figure that was repeatedly designated above by several names, is still described in its proper form in the following way:

[Col. 0927C] It contains one time within itself, dividing itself into two unequal parts or into only three equal and indivisible parts. Of the two parts, the first is called the minor semibreve and the second the major; conversely, three equal and indivisible semibreves are called minor semibreves. Hence it must be noted that no semibreve is ever found alone, since by itself it cannot signify anything. Rather, they must be counted in pairs, unequal, as here:

Or in threes, equal, as here:

[Col. 0927D] Thus an unequal binary or an equal ternary of semibreve figures must always be equivalent to a recta brevis. A recta brevis is equivalent to an imperfect long, or to an imperfect altera brevis with a brevis; and a brevis together with an altera brevis is equivalent to a perfect long.

We have now discussed simple figures. We must next discuss those ligated or joined together, and how they differ among themselves. Beginning again from unity, we shall indicate length and brevity according to the way in which they are multiplied.

It must therefore be noted that there are certain species by which every song of euphony is sung. These are divided into five parts, each division containing many different distinctions. The first difference of the first part is a certain figure commonly called a plica.

[Col. 0928A] A plica is nothing other than a sign dividing a sound into a different sound by various intervals of voices, both ascending and descending: namely, by a semitone and tone, by a semiditone and ditone, and by a diatessaron and diapente. This plica is explained through four differences: one is called perfect, another imperfect; one is the recta brevis, and another the altera brevis.

The first difference of the plica, descending perfectly, is a figure having strokes, the last of which is longer [Col. 0928B] than the first, as is evident:

When ascending, however, it retains only one stroke, as is evident:

Since it possesses every power, rule, and nature, it is almost a perfect figure, except that if it precedes a long in the body, it will contain two times; the remainder is in the limbs. In the voice, a plica is made through the composition of the epiglottis with a subtly enclosed reverberation of the throat.

The second difference is the imperfect plica, which also retains a form similar to that of the preceding property, but follows the rule and nature of the imperfect figure: namely, one time in the body and the remainder in the limbs, as is evident in descending:

It is also evident in ascending, as follows:

[Col. 0928C]

The third difference is that which has two strokes, the first of which is longer than the last when descending, as is evident:

[Col. 0928D] When ascending, however, it has two different strokes: one on the right side, ascending and signifying one plica; the other on the left side, descending and signifying brevity, as here:

Thus they observe the power, rule, and nature of the recta brevis and of that which is called the altera brevis.

The second division, of the second part, is a ligature of two figures, also called a binary. It has four differences, each of which has a double form, namely ascending and descending.

It must therefore be noted that if any of these has a property when descending, it will lack it when ascending, and conversely, except in the case of the semibreves. Ascending is understood to occur when the second figure of a ligature is higher than the first; descending is the reverse.

The first difference is this: whenever two figures are found ligated together, descending with property or ascending without property, as here:

[Col. 0929A]

The first recta brevis becomes an imperfect long, as is plainly evident in the fourth, fifth, and sixth modes, both above a letter and without a letter. In the second [Col. 0929B], third, and seventh modes, however, all such figures become equal only above a letter, according to usage.

The second difference, both ascending and descending, is constituted by the contrary of the first difference, as here, both in proportion and in property.

The third difference, both ascending and descending, follows in the form given below, and is pronounced according to equality:

[Col. 0929C] It must be noted that such a ligature is called “equality,” because it produces equality. All the others, whose first figure is longer or shorter, are unequal.

The fourth difference, both ascending and descending, retains a non-proper proportion in the following form:

These are called semibreves, and they too are pronounced unequally, as stated above: two semibreves, of which the first is the minor, and conversely, constitute one long, and are sometimes placed in the position of an altera brevis.

The third division, of the third part, is a ligature of three figures. The conjunction of three figures has nine differences, each of which occurs in two forms, ascending and descending.

The first difference, both without a letter and with a letter, is this: whenever a ternary ligature is found descending with property or ascending without property, in the first grade of a following binary ligature,

[Col. 0930A] the first becomes an imperfect long, the second a recta brevis, and the third a brevis. If the first follows a long, it then gives three times.

The second difference, both in proportion and in property, rules entirely contrary to the first difference, both above a letter and without a letter, as here:

The third difference, both above a letter and without one, is this: whenever ternary ligatures are contained together, whether a long precedes or follows, as here, both ascending and descending:

[Col. 0930B]

The first produces one time, the second two, and the third three. This follows the order of the fourth mode, provided that the long stands in the first grade.

The fourth difference is this: whenever a binary ligature precedes a ternary, the first binary produces one time, and the second [figure of the] ternary produces two, as is contained above in the preceding example. For example:

[Col. 0930C] This follows the order of the fifth mode.

The fifth difference ascends and descends, both above a letter and without one, and is as follows: whenever a ternary ligature made with equality is found, as here:

All are pronounced equally, according to the arrangement of the seventh mode.

The sixth difference, both above a letter and without one, is this: whenever ternary ligatures containing non-proper properties are found, both ascending and descending, as here:

[Col. 0930D]

The first two are made semibreves; the last is pronounced as a long of two times if a brevis follows; if a long precedes, it gives three times.

The seventh difference, ascending and descending, both above a letter and without one, is this: whenever a ternary is found either joined or ligated, as here:

The first two are made semibreves. The last produces one time if a brevis follows; but if a long follows, it gives two times.

[Col. 0931A] The eighth difference, both ascending and descending, holds entirely the opposite of the preceding arrangement, both in writing and in property:

The ninth difference, both ascending and descending, is this: whenever ternary ligatures are found both joined and composed:

All the semibreves are pronounced equal and indivisible in the third position of the fourth mode, where an altera brevis is found. For just as the altera brevis retains affinity with the recta brevis, so these figures retain affinity among themselves, both in form and property.

The fourth division, of the fourth part, is a ligature or conjunction of four figures. It has nine differences, each of which has two forms, descending and ascending. It must be noted, however, that more forms are found in descent than in ascent, because ascent is difficult, since descending is easier than ascending.

The first difference is this: whenever a junction descends or a ligature ascends, four figures are found in some place, and the properties of the first figure touch the length of the following three figures. For example:

[Col. 0931C]

The first will be a perfect long; the first two of the following figures will be semibreves, and the last must contain two times.

The second difference is of the following kind: if the length of the aforesaid property is shortened to the distance of the second figure among those four following figures. For example:

The first gives two times; the remaining semibreves are indivisible and equal.

[Col. 0931D] The third difference is this: if such figures are extended, the first having property by itself and the others being composed together with property, the first will be an imperfect long, the first two following figures semibreves, and the last will give two times if a brevis follows; if a long follows, it gives three times. For example:

The fourth difference is this: if [the property occurs] at the beginning of the first of the four descending figures, or at the beginning of the second of the ascending figures. For example:

[Col. 0932A]

The first gives one time, the two middle figures are made semibreves, and the last gives one time.

The fifth difference is this: if the property occurs at the beginning of the first figure of four joined figures, as here:

The first three are made equal semibreves; the last is a brevis if a brevis follows; but if a long follows, it gives two times.

The sixth difference is this: if the first is made quadrangular and the others are syncopated. For example:

[Col. 0932B]

The first is a recta brevis, and the remaining figures become semibreves.

The seventh difference is that of a fourfold ligature, both by reason of descent and property and by reason of ascending doctrine, as here:

The first three are equal breves; the fourth is an imperfect long if a brevis follows; but if a long follows, it will be perfect.

[Col. 0932C] The eighth difference among these is this: if the last wishes to be shortened, it is varied in the following manner:

The ninth difference is this: if the first two wish to be made semibreves, they must have the property of semibreves.

If the last is a long, then the penultimate figure will contain two times. For example:

[Col. 0932D]

The fifth division, of the fifth part, is a ligature of five figures. It has two differences, each of which has two forms, namely ascending and descending.

The first difference, both ascending and descending, is as follows: as though the property occurred at the beginning of the first fivefold ligature. For example:

[Col. 0933A] The first two are made unequal semibreves, the following two equal breves, and the last a long. If an imperfect long follows, it will be imperfect; but if a long follows, it will be perfect.

The second difference is this: if a sixth figure is added and has a similar property, as here:

The first three are made equal semibreves, the following two equal breves, and the last a long, as has been explained.

Since we have discussed figures or ligatures and joined figures, and how they differ among themselves, we must now discuss the plicas existing in these figures. For just as in every speculative science there are certain matters that must be presupposed, so in this science it is necessary that different times be designated by different figurations and that plicas vary according to the variation of time and measure.

Since the individual plicas were first explained in the first division of the first part, where they are still plainly represented,

[Col. 0933B] a question could arise as to what time is. The answer is that time, as it is understood here, is a certain just proportion in which the recta brevis has its figure in such a proportion that it can be divided into two unequal parts, or only into three equal and indivisible parts, so that the voice cannot take the value of another within the time of the divisions.

It must also be known that time has a threefold figure. Sometimes it is expressed by a recta voice, sometimes by a hollow voice, and sometimes by a lowered voice. A recta voice is the human voice proceeding from the lung. A hollow voice is a sound, not a voice—that is, an unarticulated voice—made by means of some instrument. It is therefore called hollow, because nature is not said here to be fabricated. A small, unaltered voice is also called hollow, because together with a recta voice it cannot produce a proper concordance.

[Col. 0933C] A lowered voice is that proportion or duration by which each of the figures named above, according to greater and lesser values, proportionally has a figure, silently imagining a recta measure, according to what each figure contains in itself as its own portion.

Hence it must be noted that this silent measure is represented by five long and short strokes, of which there are five differences. The first is called the perfect pause. It contains five lines in length and, from top to bottom, possesses all the power, rule, and measure of the perfect long.

The second pause is called imperfect. It contains the height of four lines and has the power of the imperfect figure and of that which is called the altera brevis.

The third is called the short sigh. It contains the height of three lines and stands for the recta brevis.

The fourth is the major semisuspirium. It contains the height of two lines and stands for the major semibreve.

The fifth is the minor semisuspirium, which occupies the middle between two lines and stands for the minor semibreve, which is indivisible. Their relative sizes are clear from the formulae.

[Col. 0934A] It must also be noted that the perfect pause is never placed except in an even position after a minor figure and a perfect one, when the song is natural, and it is placed according to the same principles. The little pause is placed in the position of the perfect figure. The sigh is placed in the position of the brevis, as is proved in *O quam sancta* and in the other hymns or in other compositions.

It produces time within time by the equivalence granted, because it cannot retain its proper quantity afterward; for although the voice is silenced, time nevertheless is not. Hence the verse:

> Times pass away like flowing water.

What follows concerns measure, which occupies a necessary place throughout music and is found extremely useful not only in music but in all things. Hence the verse:

> Just as it is useful to place music in everything that exists,  
> so without measure everything that exists perishes.

[Col. 0934B] It must therefore be seen that measure is contained in this art in two ways: namely, locally and temporally. This is also why the art is called measured music, in contrast with complete music. Complete music is measured only by local measure, which concerns the distance of voices to be measured; for this art, local measure alone is not sufficient, but it also requires temporal measure.

Temporal measure, as understood here, is the change of two, three, or more figures according to their numerical relation to some perfection or equality. Thus, if someone desires to know a certain just proportion, or the consonance of two singers or of three different voices, in a designated place, he should carefully count from some known point to the appointed place through three times, or by equivalence, or should always refer it to the perfect figure.

Hence it must be noted that all modes derive their origin from this measure in different ways.

[Col. 0934C] Since all kinds of figures, times, measures, and plicas have been explained above, and since a mode or manner nevertheless remains, with mode consisting in the modulation of sounds and the distinction of voices, we must now say what a mode is, how many there are, and how all numbers appear to consist from the principal figure.

Mode, or manner, as it is understood here, is whatever proceeds temporally through the proper measure of long, short, and semibreve figures.

It must therefore be noted that we assign nine modes to the constitution of natural instruments. To distinguish their knowledge and destroy the errors of many, three more eminent modes are set apart: the first, fourth, and seventh. From each of these the other six arise in pairs, as dependents, and each of them is called either perfect or imperfect.

A perfect mode is one that has a figure completed by proper regulation, and with such quantity, number, and measure as it possesses in quality at its beginning. An imperfect mode is one that varies in different places.

The first mode is said to be composed solely of perfect figures:

[Col. 0935A] “May the Holy Spirit be present,” etc.

From this it is evident that this mode is never composed in ligatures, but is freely set apart. It alone never suffers pressure; it rules and is not ruled, and in commanding it does not make use of the law of the others.

This is called the first mode, and it is rightly placed before those that follow. For every mode made from figures is reduced to it and resolved into it. In this mode, if pauses are to be made, long pauses will be assigned at the places indicated by the figures; otherwise there will be error, and what is necessary will be greatly syncopated and deprived of its proper character.

The second mode follows. In it an imperfect long is placed first, immediately followed by a recta brevis taken from it.

[Col. 0935B]

“If this is ligated, it is first assigned to it; a ternary is added: ‘Come, Holy Spirit,’ etc. A collection which duality will accompany.”

The third mode is completed; it is more easily learned through its force. From this it is argued that it comes after the first. The second is here joined; the third opposes the preceding arrangement. From this it is called the third, for the reason stated: to it a brevis is first given, followed by a long, and a brevis immediately accompanies it:

[Col. 0935C] “To the proclamation of Mary, devotion,” etc.

This mode is ligated: a binary is joined to the preceding ligature, and a ternary to the ending one.

[Col. 0936A] The fourth holds a quaternary of figures, and for this reason is placed after the third. Its beginning and end are perfect; the middle figures are neighboring and not equal:

“O Mary, blessed Mother,” etc.

Some figures stand by themselves, and there should always be a beginning of perfect figures. Here it will take one ligature after another; everything will be clear.

[Col. 0936B]

The fifth mode is so called because it is gathered from five figures and completed through voices. Its first figure is shortened, and the figure is prolonged from two times; therefore let it be shortened. The fourth is called shorter, not one of the determinate breves; the fifth is assigned three times, and therefore let it be held as a long in every respect:

“Bringing great joy,” etc. [Old French: *Demenant grand’ioye*].

This mode is ligated: first a binary ligature is proposed in two voices, and a ternary is placed after it; two pairs follow it, and a ternary is also placed after those preceding figures.

[Col. 0936C]

The sixth mode does not lack a senary of figures. Two of them are perfect, without doubt, and four of them are placed in the middle. I make the first two of these semibreves whenever I announce a recta brevis among those that follow.

“Suaut voile dont tans und,” etc. [The surviving vernacular wording is materially uncertain.]

At the beginning of such ligatures, place the perfect figure by itself, the one belonging to the group; four ligated figures should follow at the boundary, as is also noted in the collection of writings.

[Col. 0936D]

The seventh mode is composed of seven voices and also of recta breves; let it therefore be placed here:

[Col. 0937A]

“O Mary, virgin daughter of David,” etc.

Four figures join themselves together; let the binary be ligated with the two that run together, and let this be brought to an end. At their endings a plica must always be supplied:

And thus this is rightly called the seventh mode.

The eighth mode will always tolerate two unequal semibreves:

[Col. 0937B]

[Col. 0938A] Let it be joined to two notes occurring together with their proper characteristics:

The ninth mode is completed with three equal semibreves, as follows.

“Lord, Lord, King of glory,” etc. Of these three, one equal duration is taken from all of them.

[Col. 0937]

## OF THE CIRCLES OF THE SPHERE AND THE POLES, BY THE PRIEST BEDE

[Col. 0937]

[Col. 0937D] A sphere is a certain form fashioned in a round shape, appearing equal on every side; from it the other circles are bounded. Its end and beginning cannot be determined, because in a round figure every point of contact can signify both beginnings and ends.

The center is the point from which the circumference of the sphere is drawn and at which the position of the earth is established and indicated.

The dimension by which the whole sphere is displayed is made when straight lines and a rod are drawn from both sides of it to the outermost circumference. This dimension has been called the axis by many. Its extremities, on which the sphere chiefly rests, are called the poles. Of these, the one facing the north is called the Boreal Pole; the opposite one is called the Austral Pole, also named Notus. [Col. 0938D]

### What their designations are

Certain features of the circumference of the sphere are called circles. Among them are the circles called parallels, which are bounded at the same pole. The greatest circles are those contained by the same center as the sphere. The horizon is the circle that bounds those things that cannot be observed or seen. Its definition is uncertain, since it is perceived variously according as the sphere is positioned: sometimes subject to the pole and to the circles called parallels, sometimes resting upon two extreme and equal points, and sometimes joined to other parts of the earth.

[Col. 0939A] The pole called Boreal can always be seen; the Austral Pole, however, is unlike it and is always remote from sight. The natural position of the world is physically said to be bounded at the Boreal Pole, so that all things seem to rise on the right-hand side and set on the left. Rising is a sudden appearance presented to our sight; setting, for the corresponding reason, is the disappearance of something seen, as though removed from the eyes at the boundary of the world.

There are five parallel circles on which the whole system of the sphere depends, apart from the one called the zodiac. Since this does not, like the other circles, end at a fixed dimension but appears inclined to them, it is called *loxos*—“oblique”—by the Greeks.

The five circles mentioned above are measured in the sphere as follows. From the supreme beginning at the pole called Boreal to the pole called Notus and Antarctic, each hemisphere is divided into thirty parts, so that the dimension appears to indicate that the whole sphere is divided into sixty parts. Then, taking six parts from each boundary beginning at the same Boreal point, a circle is drawn whose center is the pole itself. It is called the Arctic Circle because within it the figures of the *Arcturus* appear enclosed. Our people, representing these signs in the form of bears, call them the Septentrions.

After taking five further parts from this circle, a circle is drawn with the same center mentioned above. It is called the *therinos tropicos*, the summer tropic, because when the sun reaches this circle it produces summer for those living in the northern regions, but winter for those whom we previously said are exposed to the blasts of the south. Since the sun does not pass beyond this circle [Col. 0939C] but immediately turns back, it is called the tropic.

From the designation of this circle, four of the remaining parts are taken, and the equinoctial circle is drawn. The Greeks call it *isemerinos*, “equinoctial,” because when the sun reaches this orbit it produces the equinox. Once this circle has been made, half the sphere is seen to have been established.

Conversely, in a similar manner, six parts are taken from the Notus Pole, as was said above concerning the Boreal Pole, and the circle drawn is called Antarctic, because it is opposite to the Arctic Circle defined above. In accordance with this definition of the sphere, and with the Notus Pole as its center, five parts are taken and the *imerinos tropicos* is established. We call it the winter tropic; some also call it the brumal tropic, because when the sun reaches that circle it produces winter for those who face toward the north, but summer for those who have established their dwellings in the southern regions. When it is farther away from those living in the northern regions, they suffer a greater winter, while those to whom the sun appears nearer have summer. Thus the Ethiopians necessarily lie under both orbits.

From this circle to the equinoctial circle there remain four parts, so that the sun appears to travel through eight parts of the sphere.

The zodiacal circle may be defined most accurately in this way: after the signs have been established, as we shall later explain, a circle is drawn through them in order. The circle called the Milky Way, being opposite the equinoctial circle, should be positioned so that it appears to divide it in the middle and to reach it twice—once at the place where Aquilo is established, and again at the region of the sign called Procyon.

The twelve signs are divided as follows. The five circles mentioned above are bounded so that each is divided into twelve parts. From their points, lines are then drawn to indicate the circles thus formed, on which the twelve signs are described.

Some less knowledgeable people ask why the circles are not bounded in equal parts—that is, why the thirty parts are not divided into five parts each and the circles then drawn in the same proportion. We are confident that this can very easily be defended. For when the middle of the sphere has been divided, no circle can be equal to another; although one may approach another closely, it nevertheless appears smaller.

Therefore, when those who first made the sphere wished the proportions of all the circles to be equal, they intended them to be represented proportionally: the farther one moved away from the pole, the smaller the number of parts assigned in measuring the circles, since a larger circle necessarily had to be defined there. This can also be understood from the sphere itself: the farther one moves from the pole, the larger the circles become, and for that reason a smaller number is assigned, so that their effects may appear equal. Even if each hemisphere is divided not into thirty parts but into any other number of divisions, the same principle still applies as if thirty parts had been used.

[Col. 0940B] The zodiacal circle, lying beneath the three circles mentioned above, touches the summer and winter circles at certain points, and divides the equinoctial circle through its middle. Thus, as the sun travels through the zodiacal circle without passing outside it, it necessarily reaches the orbits mentioned above together with the signs on which it appears to rest while completing its course, and in this way defines the four seasons.

Beginning with Aries, it displays spring; passing through Taurus and Gemini, it signifies the same. At the heads of Gemini it appears already to touch the summer circle. Passing through Cancer, Leo, and Virgo, it produces summer. Again, from the farthest part of Virgo it is seen to pass to the equinoctial circle. In Libra it produces the equinox and begins to signify autumn. From that sign it passes to Scorpio and Sagittarius; then it immediately enters the winter circle and spends the winter in Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces. It is therefore shown not to travel through those three circles themselves, but to reach them by passing through the zodiac.

[Col. 0940D] Likewise:

Once the *colures* have been found in the round sphere, and the sphere itself divided into sixty parts, the procedure for finding our *almucantarat* is as follows. From the center of the Arctic Circle, on the meridian colure, take seven sixtieths; there establish the summit of our [instrument or sphere—text uncertain]. With one foot of a compass placed at that summit, take fifteen sixtieths before you with the other foot and draw around the first *almucantarat*, that is, our fixed horizon. Then set it inward at fourteen and draw around it again. Then at thirteen, and so place and draw it around at each successive inner sixtieth until you reach the summit.

To erect the round sphere, proceed as follows. Beneath the Arctic Circle, take two sixtieths toward our habitable region [Col. 0941A] and raise it at that point upon the top of the vessel’s support, which takes the place of the earth. Do this with the one [point or pole], otherwise it will happen that you will not see many of the signs that have risen, while you will see many others that have sunk below. This position is taught by the position found at the equinox.

An eclipse of the sun and moon is of the following nature. Those who observe them again establish that both travel in the region of the zodiac, but not equally. The sun never deviates from the ecliptic, which is the middle line. The moon, however, is not in that same middle of the zodiac, but on one side or the other.

[Col. 0941B] Consequently, when both are on the ecliptic—which is called so because of eclipses—each is obscured by the other, with the earth’s shadow intervening, so that the eclipse of either is not then hidden from us. [Col. 0942A] Nor is this surprising. Since both, as has been said, are on the same line, but one is above the earth and the other below it, it happens that the upper body is deprived of light by the lower, and conversely the lower by the upper, through the earth’s shadow. Thus the defect of the upper body is observed, while that of the lower remains unknown.

The reason why the height of our climate is forty-eight is that the pole is raised above the earth here by that many degrees. [Col. 0942B] For this reason we also raise it thus in the sphere.

[Col. 0941]

## OF THE NATURE OF THE PLANETS AND SIGNS, BY THE PRIEST BEDE

[Col. 0941]

[Col. 0943B] ### Several investigations concerning the planets

If you wish to know in which sign Saturn remains, divide the years from the beginning of the world by thirty, taking Libra as the starting point. Whatever remains below thirty, divide by two years and a half, assigning that amount to each sign. Saturn truly remains in the sign lacking two and a half years.

If you wish to know without doubt in which sign Jupiter remains, divide the aforesaid years by twelve, taking Aries as the beginning, and assign one year to each sign. Jupiter establishes himself in the sign lacking a year.

If you carefully inquire in which sign Mars is situated, divide the aforesaid years by one year and a half, taking Capricorn as the starting point. Divide what remains among the signs, assigning forty-five days to each. Mars is to be found in the sign lacking forty-five days.

If anyone wishes to know in which sign radiant Venus revolves, let him calculate as follows. By a now skillful investigation, the very long reckoning, entangled in much error, has been abbreviated. Let him repeatedly subtract eight from the years from the beginning of the world until he reaches a number below eight; divide whatever remains by three hundred days; wherever this number is lacking, add forty, distribute twenty-five to each sign, and begin from Libra. In the sign lacking this number, he should recognize that Venus establishes herself.

He should also know that Venus is always near the Sun, in such a way that she never withdraws from him into a more distant region by more than four or three signs, whether she precedes him or follows him.

Concerning Mercury, since the question is not considered difficult, I have not thought it necessary to append a lengthy description. He is always seen and found so near the Sun that he can readily be discovered either in the preceding sign, in the following sign, or certainly in the same sign, without ever preceding or following it by a great distance.

### The same subject by another method

Let the total of the years from the beginning of the world be measured by thirty as many times as possible. When the number has been exceeded, recognize the months that remain; from these begin with Capricorn. Then let the other signs receive thirty each, wherever they come to rest. Some think that Saturn is to be determined in this way; wherever thirty are lacking, there Saturn is said to remain.

After separating the years from the beginning of the world by eighteen, divide the months of the years in excess once again by eighteen. Assign the first eighteen to Sagittarius and the same number to the remaining signs; this will indicate where Jupiter has his dwelling. For they say that Jupiter remains in whichever sign lacks the eighteen assigned to it.

After dividing the years from the beginning of the world by six, and likewise separating by six the months belonging to the years in excess, assign six to each sign, beginning only from Scorpio; in this way Mars is said to be revealed. They say that Mars is to be found in the sign lacking six parts.

We are instructed to separate the years from the beginning of the world by twenty-four and then apply to the signs the observed months of the years that do not fit the total, beginning from Libra, so that each sign always receives twenty-four. When this has been reckoned, it reveals Venus’s position.

The frequently mentioned years, separated by a twelfth part, together with the known months of the surplus years, are to be assigned twelve at a time to the remaining signs, beginning with Virgo. They will determine where Mercury begins. Those who investigate such matters suppose that Mercury remains in whichever sign lacks the twelve assigned to it. But if the first division is completed in a multiple of twelve, they always think that the planet in question is found in Virgo.

[Col. 0944C] The planets—that is, the Wanderers—are exactly seven in number. Although they correspond to the seven days, or weekdays, of the whole week, they by no means preserve the same order. Here the Sun is considered fourth, but in our week he is first, for the day is called both the day of the Sun and the Lord’s Day. The Moon is here last and seventh, but in the week she occupies the second day. Mars alone agrees both in his position in the sky and in the weekly number. Mercury is here considered sixth, but among us he is the fourth day of the week. Jupiter, also called Jove, is here second. Old, club-footed Saturn is here first, but among us he is last.

Thus earthly and human matters differ greatly from heavenly and celestial matters. It is not within human power to know, state, or write everything above according to an infallible and exact standard. Let each person therefore be wise with moderation, and let him fear.

[Col. 0943]

## ORDER OF THE PLANETS ACCORDING TO THEIR NATURE AND NUMBER, ACCORDING TO THE HEBREWS

[Col. 0943D] The Sun, called *hama* by the Hebrews, is the first of the planets. Second is Venus, called *Noga*. Third is Mercury, that is, *Cocaph*. Fourth is the Moon, also called *Libala*. Fifth is Saturn, namely *Sabbai*. Sixth is Jupiter, that is, *Sedech*. Seventh is Mars, also called *Madei*.

According to this order, they take possession of the hours of the days and nights of the whole week: beginning with the first hour of the day of the first weekday, the Sun—whence it is called the Sun’s day—the second hour belongs to Venus, the third to Mercury, the fourth to the Moon, the fifth to Saturn, the sixth to Jupiter, the seventh to Mars, and the eighth again to the Sun, and so in the order given.

Hence, according to the names of the planets that rule the first hours of the individual days, the days themselves receive their names: the day of the Sun, the day of the Moon, the day of Mars, the day of Mercury, the day of Jupiter, the day of Venus, and the day of Saturn.

The following planets preside over the first hours of the nights throughout the week.
