Jupiter presides over the first hour of the night following the first weekday; Venus over the second; Saturn over the third; the Sun over the fourth; the Moon over the fifth; Mars over the sixth; and Mercury over the seventh. [Col. 0944D]

The Sun was created in the fifteenth part of Leo, and the Moon in the fifteenth part of Cancer.

Mars was created in the fifteenth part of Scorpio, ninety parts removed from the Sun.

Mercury was created in the seventh part of Virgo, twenty-two parts removed from the Sun.

[Col. 0945A] Jupiter was created in the fifth part of Sagittarius, one hundred and twenty parts removed from the Sun.

Venus was created in the fourteenth part of Libra, fifty-nine parts removed from the Sun.

Saturn was created in the fifteenth part of Capricorn, one hundred and fifty parts removed from the Sun. This is the opinion of all the Egyptians. The Israelites and Chaldaeans, however, think otherwise. They say that the Sun was created in the first part of Aries; Saturn in the first part of Capricorn, ninety parts removed from the Sun; Jupiter in the first part of Sagittarius, one hundred and twenty parts removed from the Sun; Mars in the first part of Scorpio, one hundred and fifty parts removed from the Sun; and Venus in the first part of Taurus, thirty parts removed from the Sun.

The highest point of Saturn’s apsis is in Libra, of Jupiter’s in Cancer, of Mars’s in Capricorn, of the Sun’s in Aries, of Venus’s in Pisces, of Mercury’s in Virgo, and of the Moon’s in Taurus.

The Sun rises in Aries and sets in Libra. Saturn rises in Libra and sets in Aries. Mercury rises in Virgo and sets in Pisces. Venus rises in Pisces and sets in Virgo. Mars rises in Capricorn and sets in Cancer. Jupiter rises in Cancer and sets in Capricorn. The Moon rises in Taurus and sets in Scorpio.

The Sun presides over heat, Mercury over dryness, Jupiter over winds, Venus over rains, and the Moon over cold. Saturn possesses the greater coldness; Mars, the excessive heat of the Sun.

The Sun is of a hot nature and golden color. The Moon is of a cold nature and silver color. Jupiter is of a cold nature and the color of electrum. Mars is of a hot nature and bronze-colored. Venus is of a temperate nature and tin-colored. Mercury is of a dry nature and lead-colored. Saturn is of a cold nature and iron-colored.

### Of the rising and setting of the twelve signs

The intervals of time in which the twelve signs rise or set must be considered. Those that rise obliquely and set directly have quicker risings than settings; conversely, those that rise directly and set obliquely rise more slowly and set more quickly.

Cancer, which rises directly, becomes inclined and sinks, rises in two hours and one twelfth of an hour; it sets in one hour and eleven twelfths of an hour. Leo rises in two hours and one third of an hour; it sets in half an hour and one sixth of an hour. Virgo rises in two and a half hours and one sixth of an hour; Libra likewise rises, and sets in one hour and one third of an hour. Scorpio rises in two hours and one third of an hour. Sagittarius rises in two hours and one twelfth of an hour; it sets in one hour and eleven twelfths of an hour.

Conversely, those that rise obliquely and set directly occupy shorter risings than settings. Among these is Capricorn, which rises in one hour and eleven twelfths of an hour and sets in two hours and one twelfth of an hour. Each of the signs that follow has its opposite counterpart in setting.

These signs have the following correspondences:

Aries agrees with Libra in rising and setting.

Taurus with Scorpio; Gemini with Sagittarius; Cancer with Capricorn; Aquarius with Leo; Pisces with Virgo.

[Col. 0945]

## OF THE SIGNS OF THE SKY

[Col. 0945B] Helice, that is, the Great Bear, has seven faint stars in its head, one in each ear, one above the breast, one on the shoulder, one on the foot, one on the back, two on the front leg, and three above that same leg: eighteen in all.

Cynosura, or Phoenix, also called the Little Bear and by some the Dog’s Tail, has one bright star at each angle, and three in the tail. Between the two Bears there are twenty-four stars. There remain ten other stars that precede them, called the Dancers, and one very small star called the Pole, where they say that the whole world revolves.

Draco, which contains both Bears, coils above Helice’s head and encircles Phoenix’s tail. It has three bright stars in its head and twelve throughout its body, separated from one another: fifteen in all.

Hercules, who is represented standing and bending his knee, has one star in his head, one bright star in each shoulder, one in the left forearm [the printed *cito* is uncertain], two in the right thigh, one in the right knee, one in the same shin, one in the right hand, and one in the club held by that same hand; one in the left knee and one in the same shin: twelve in all.

The Crown has nine stars arranged in a circle, [Col. 0945D] three of which are brighter, toward the head of the Serpent of the Bear.

The Serpent-Bearer, also called Asclepius, stands above Scorpio and holds a serpent in his hands. He has one bright star in his head, three in his left hand, four in his right, and one bright star in each shoulder. He has one in each hip, one in each knee, one in the right shin, and one in each foot: seventeen in all. The Serpent that he holds has two stars in its head and four throughout the rest of its body, making twenty-three together.

Scorpio has two stars on its two lips. Of these, the first are large and the second faint. On its forehead there are three, the middle one brighter than the others. There are three bright stars along its spine, two on its belly, five in its tail, and two above its sting: nineteen in all.

Arcas, also called Boötes, is said to be the guardian of the wagon. He has four stars in his right hand that never set; one bright star in his head; one in each shoulder; one in each breast; four in the right elbow; one in the left; and one in each knee: sixteen in all. [Col. 0946B]

Virgo, also called Justice, has one very faint star in her head, two in each wing, one in each shoulder, one in each elbow, one in each hand, six in the skirt of her garment, and one in each foot.

Of the Gemini, the first, which extends beyond Cancer, has one bright star in its head and one bright star in each shoulder: five in all. The other has a bright star in its head, one in the left shoulder, one in each thigh, and three on its back: seven in all. Together they have twelve.

Cancer has four bright stars on its shell; one on each right leg; two on the first left leg, one on the third left leg, and one on the fourth; one in its mouth; three on its right lip; and two on its left: eighteen in all.

Leo has three stars in its head, two in its neck, one in its breast, three on its back, one bright star at the tip of its tail, two beneath its breast, and one bright star on its foreleg: thirteen in all. [Col. 0946D]

The Charioteer has one star in its head, one in each shoulder—the one in the left shoulder being brighter—one in each elbow, one in the right hand, two at the top of the left hand, two above that same arm in the kids, and one star in each kid: ten in all.

Taurus has one star in each horn, two on its forehead, one in each eye, and one in its nostril. These stars are called the Pleiades, Virgiliae, and also the *subuculae*. It has one in each knee, two in the dewlap, two in the neck, three on its back, of which the last is bright, one in its belly, and one in its breast: eighteen in all.

Cepheus has two bright stars in its head, one bright star in its right hand, one in each shoulder, three in its belt, seven crosswise on its right side above the thigh, two in its left knee, and four at the tips of its feet: twenty-one in all. He is positioned in the cleft of the Septentrion, midway between the middle of the northern circle and the summer solstice.

[Col. 0947A] Cassiopeia has one bright star in her head, one bright star in each shoulder, one bright star on the right side of her breast, one in the right elbow, one bright star at the top of both hands, one bright and large star in her navel, two in her left thigh, one bright star in her knee, and one at each angle at the top of her little seat: thirteen in all.

Andromeda has one bright star in her head, one in each shoulder, one in the right elbow, one in the left, one bright star at the top of her hand, two bright stars at the top of her feet, three in her belt, four above the belt, one bright star in each knee, two in the right foot, and one in the left: twenty-one in all.

The Horse, called the source of wars and Bellerophon, has two faint stars in its muzzle, one bright star in its head, one in its jaw, one bright star in each ear, four in its neck, one in its shoulder, one in its breast, one on its spine, one bright star in its navel, one in each knee, and one in each front hoof: nineteen in all.

[Col. 0947B] Aries has one star in its head, three in its nostril, two in its neck, one at the top of its foreleg, four on its back, one in its tail, three in its belly, one in its loin, and one at the top of its foot: seventeen in all.

The Triangle, which lies above the head of Aries, has one bright star at each angle, one of them brighter than the others.

The Northern Fish has twelve stars and the Southern Fish fifteen. The band containing them has three stars toward the north, three toward the west, three toward the east, and three at the joining: thirty-nine in all.

Perseus, who is said to hold the head of the Gorgon, has one bright star in each shoulder, one at the top of his right hand, one in that elbow, one at the top of his left hand, one in his belly, one bright star in his right loin, one bright star in his right thigh, one in each knee, and two in his shin. The Gorgon is said to have one star in its head and three in its hair: sixteen in all.

The Lyre has one star in each side of its frame, one in each foot, one in its body, one in each shoulder, one in its yoke, and one bright and white star in its drum: nine in all.

The Swan has one bright star in its head, one bright star in its neck, five in its right wing—one of them bright, near the neck—and five in its left wing; one in its body and one large star in its genital region: fourteen in all.

Aquarius has two faint stars in its head, one bright star in each shoulder, one at the top of each hand, one at each breast, one beneath each breast, one in its left loin, one in each knee, one in its right shin, and one in each foot: eighteen in all. The outpouring is made to the right and left; it contains two bright stars, while the others are faint.

Capricorn has two stars in its two horns, one bright star in its nostrils, two in its head, one bright star in its neck, two in its breast, one in its foreleg, one at the top of that foot, seven on its back, five in its belly, and two in its tail: twenty-six in all.

[Col. 0947D] Sagittarius has two stars in its head, one bright star in its shoulder, three on its back, two in its tail, one in its fore-knee, one in each foot, two in its bow, and four in its arrow—one at the top, another in the middle, faint, and two in the feathers of the arrow, one of them brighter: nineteen in all.

The Eagle has one star in its foot, one faint star in the middle of its body, one in its upper beak, and one in its lower beak: four in all.

The Dolphin, which passes somewhat above Capricorn, has one star in its mouth, two in its head, three in the wing beside its belly, one above its back, and two in its tail: nine in all.

Orion, indeed oblique to Taurus, has three bright stars in its head, one of them brighter than the others. It has one bright star in each shoulder, one faint star in its elbow, one at the top of its hand, three in its belt, three faint stars in its cloak, one in each knee, and one in each foot: seventeen in all.

[Col. 0948A] The Hare has one star in each ear, two in its body, one bright star on its back, and one in each hind foot: seven in all.

The Little Dog, which rises after Orion, has one bright star in its tongue, which the Syrians call the intensely red Dog and say changes color at intervals. It has one faint star in each shoulder, two in its breast, three in its left foreleg, one in its right, three above its back, three in its belly, one in its left loin, one in its left hind foot, and one at the tip of its tail: seventeen in all.

The Ship, called Argo among the Argives, has four stars in the forward part of the ship, four in the stern, five in each shoulder, three in the sail, and five along the side: twenty-one in all.

The Whale, which moves beneath Aries and Pisces, has two faint stars in its tail, six from the tail to the rump, and six in its belly: fourteen in all.

Eurus, also called Eridanus and by some the Nile, which is also called Geon, begins in the southern regions and extends toward Orion’s foot. Beneath it lies the star called Canopus, which shines and touches the rudder. The extent of the Ship appears small because it seems to lie around the earth. It has three stars in the first row, three in the second, three in the third, and so on up to the last six.

The Great Fish, also called the South Wind, extends in length from Capricorn as far as Pisces; it lies beneath Aquarius and receives his outpouring. It has twelve stars, of which some are said to be beneath Aquarius’s feet, and three in its fins; these are known to be brighter than the others.

The Shrine, also understood as the Temple, follows the tail of the Great Scorpio, surrounds the Septentrion, and one part of it is duller than Arcturus, while another quickly disappears beneath the west. It has two stars above the grate and two in the vessel: four in all.

The Centaur is said to hold a beast in his hand beside the Shrine, where he appears to be offering it. He has three faint stars in his head, one bright star in each shoulder, [Col. 0948C] one in his left elbow, one at the top of his hand, one in the middle of his breast, two on his spine, two bright stars in his belly, one bright star in his loin, three in his tail, two on his bent knees, one on each arm, and one on each forefoot: twenty-four in all.

As indicated above, he is said to hold weapons and a hare in his left hand, and a beast in his right. Some call the latter a vinegar jar, which has two stars in its tail, one bright star at the top of its forefoot, one bright star on its spine, one bright star on its forefoot, one beneath that foot, and three in its head: nine in all, or thirty-three altogether.

The Serpent is said to have the Crow sitting on its tail, while others place the vessel in its middle. They say that its head extends to the top of Cancer and its tail toward the Centaur. It has three stars, one in its neck, one in its breast, and one in its belly.

The Crow has three stars, one in its beak, one in its wing, and one in its genital region. The Vessel has three faint stars in the middle of its lips: ten in all. Some depict it differently: namely, as a serpent lying on its back, carrying a vessel on its back, with the crow biting the serpent’s tail.

Anticanis is said to appear clearly beneath Gemini. It has three stars, one of them brighter than the others; hence it is called Anticanis, because it is opposite the Dog.

There is among the constellations a circle of white color, which some have said to be the Milky Way. Eratosthenes says that Juno, unaware that Mercury was an infant child, gave him milk; but after learning that he was the son of Maia, she rejected him. Thus the radiance of the spilled milk appeared among the stars.

Others said that Hercules was placed beside the sleeping Juno, and that when she awoke she did what we have described above to him. Others say that Hercules, because of his excessive appetite, desired a great quantity of milk but could not contain it in his mouth; what spilled from his mouth marked out the circle.

Others say that when Ops brought Saturn a stone in place of the child, she ordered him to give it milk; and when she pressed her breast, the milk poured out and formed the circle we mentioned above. This is what Hyginus says.

In the Arrow there is one star of the fourth magnitude, three of the fifth, and one of the sixth.

The Arrow, placed between the summer and equinoctial circles and superimposed upon the sign of the Eagle, is divided by that circle which, subject to both poles, reaches Cancer and Capricorn. Its point faces the region of the *Equipedus* [text uncertain]; the other part extends toward the shoulders of Ophiuchus. It sets at the rising of Virgo and rises with Scorpio.

It has four stars altogether. One appears at the beginning of the object, another in the middle, and two at the place where the iron is usually attached; they appear distinct. This is what Hyginus says.

## SIGNS OF THE MONTHS

[Col. 0949]

[Col. 0949A] 1. JANUARY—“I drink.”

[Col. 0949B] 2. FEBRUARY—“I burn wood.”

[Col. 0949C] 3. MARCH—“I remove what is superfluous from the vine.”

4. APRIL—“I give a welcome shoot.”

[Col. 0949D] 5. MAY—“The flower serves me.”

[Col. 0950A] 6. JUNE—“The meadow is mine.”

[Col. 0950B] 7. JULY—“I bend the ears of grain.”

[Col. 0950C] 8. AUGUST—“I reap the harvests.”

9. SEPTEMBER—“I offer wine.”

[Col. 0950D] 10. OCTOBER—“I cast the seed upon the ground.”

[Col. 0951A] 11. NOVEMBER—“I feed pigs for myself.”

[Col. 0952A] 12. DECEMBER—“I slaughter for myself.”

[Col. 0951]

## BEDE THE PRIEST’S FORECASTS OF THE WEATHER

[Col. 0951B] If the Kalends of January fall on the first weekday, the winter will be good, the spring windy, the summer dry, and the vintage good. Cattle will increase, honey will abound, old women will die, and there will be abundance and peace.

If on the second weekday, the winter will be changeable, the spring good, the summer dry, and the weather windy; the vintage will not be good, human health will suffer, bees will die, and there will be portents that God will give to human beings.

If on the third weekday, the winter will be cloudy, the spring stormy, windy, and rainy, and the summer dry. The vintage will suffer and will be seen [reading uncertain]; women will die, ships will be endangered, and kings will perish.

If on the fourth weekday, the winter will be harsh and severe, the spring bad and windy, the summer good, the vintage good but laborious, and the grain good. Young men will die, and those who sail will suffer greatly.

If on the fifth weekday, the winter will be good, the spring windy, the summer dry, and the vintage good. There will be abundance, and princes or kings will perish.

[Col. 0951C] If on the sixth weekday, the winter will be changeable, the spring good, and the summer dry and good. There will be pain in the eyes, a good vintage, and great abundance; sheep will perish.

If on the seventh weekday, the winter will be stormy, the spring windy, and the crops difficult. Sheep will perish, old men will die, and houses will be burned.

## ON FOREKNOWING FUTURE ABUNDANCE OR POVERTY
If there is anyone who does not know whether the coming year will bring abundance or poverty, let him observe the first night of January, which is proved to be the head of the whole year, and inspect the first hour of that month’s first night. If the hour of the Sun prevails, there will be drought in the land during that year. But if it is the hour of Venus, great strife among men will reign that year, together with a plague among women; six months will be temperate with rain, and the remaining six hot. But if the hour of Mercury first shines forth, there will be four rainy months, especially April and May.

But if the Moon rises in the first hour of January [Col. 0951D], and in the head of Aries, the rains will prevail; floods of rain will uproot the crops; it will rain for six months; there will be various disturbances of wars; merchants’ goods will lose their value; and there will be a great slaughter of people. But if it is found in the belly of Aries [Col. 0952B], sailors will be endangered, and they will fight in the West; Cordova will fight within itself, and will mourn for six months.

But if, in the first hour of January, it is found in the head of Taurus, the crops will flourish with great abundance, there will be no famine for seven years, and kings will die. But if, on the first night of January, the Moon appears in the belly of Taurus, the eastern region will be afflicted by much rain, and there will be a plague among kings. But if it is found in the tail of Taurus, the year will be average.

But if it is found in the head of Gemini, the Cordovan plague will reign in Zaragoza and on this side of it. But if, on that same night, it appears in the tail of Gemini, there will be famine in the central land, and a deadly persecution will prevail against its rulers for nine months.

But if it is in the head of Cancer, there will be rains and abundant crops. And if it is in the belly or tail of Cancer, it will be a peaceful year with great abundance for six years.

But if it is in Leo during the first hour of January’s night, there will be disturbance among the judges, the ravages of robbers will multiply, and the year will be average. But if it is found in the belly of Leo, there will be a great mortality among human beings [Col. 0952C]. But if it is in the tail of Leo, the death of quadrupeds and children will reign that year, and the poor will become rich.

But when it appears in Virgo, Cordova will perish from famine. But if it is at the end of Virgo, there will be an abundance of crops that year. But if it shines in the head of Libra, scarcity will return again. But when it is in the belly of Libra, there will be mutual disturbance among kings.

But if, on the first night of January, it is in the head of Scorpio, there will be great tumult among people. But if it is in the belly of Scorpio, the rain will not cease for forty days. But if it is in the tail, there will be an abundance of all good things.

But if, in the first hour of January, the Moon enters the head of Sagittarius, the disturbance of kings will return again, and famine will prevail for nine years. But if it shines in the tail of Sagittarius, a plague will reign especially among Christians, and famine will visit the land of the Saracens.

But if it occurs in the head or tail of Capricorn, there will be famine throughout the whole land. But if it is in the head of Aquarius, there will be drought in the East; if it is in the belly, there will be persecution by the sword; but if it is in the tail, there will be disturbance [Col. 0952D] in that year.

But if the Moon is in the head of Pisces, wickedness will prevail. But if the Moon is in the tail during the first hour of the night on the Kalends of January, many will perish from famine.

[Col. 0951]

# THE LITTLE BOOK OF THE PRIEST BEDE ON THE MEASUREMENT OF THE CLOCK

[Col. 0951D] If anyone takes pleasure in constructing a clock, whether of metal or wood, which appears to be formed in the likeness of a perpendicular instrument, except that the former is round whereas the latter has six sides, on which the sequence of the hours of the whole year is marked by pairs of months: its length is believed to be sufficient at five digits, more or less. Its thickness also, if each side is sufficient for the gnomon and the inscription of the Calendar dates, seems adequate.

Let the first line, which is assigned to the twelfth day before the Kalends of January and July, have its beginning wherever one wishes. Nevertheless, let the space itself be divided into six equal spaces, or portions, from the first point located in one region as far as the center.

The second line, assigned to the twelfth day before the Kalends of August and May, shall take its endpoint from the middle of the sixth-hour space of the first series.

The third, assigned to the Kalends of April and September on those same dates, as titled above, leaves a three-quarter interval of the penultimate hour of the second series and takes its beginning from the remaining quarter.

The fourth claims one third of the penultimate space of the third series.

The fifth seizes one fifth of the penultimate space of the fourth series.

The endpoint of the sixth line is made equal to the boundary of the fourth hour of the fifth series.

## Finding noon

Draw a circle on a flat board. In its exact center fix a gnomon of such a length that its shadow extends beyond the circle. Carefully observe when the aforesaid shadow begins to retreat within the circumference of the circle, and mark with the greatest care the traces of that contracting shadow by points. With similar observation, see when it again leaves the boundary of the circle—which will happen after noon, when the shadow, once more declining, has receded toward the lower regions—and mark points there in the same way.

Afterward, divide by a straight line through the center the space lying between these points. On the following day, as a test, watch carefully when the shadow of the gnomon covers the aforesaid line; then you may be certain that it is noon.

To carry this out more cautiously, obtain a carefully polished stone tablet and place it in a secluded spot suitable for this work. Once this has been done, do not cease weighing and leveling the same tablet with such a balance and such care until water poured over it either lies evenly upon it or extends equally beyond its circumference on every side.

# ON THE SIGNS AND HOURS OF THE TWELVE MONTHS

[Col. 0955]

## On the three dangerous days

[Col. 0955C]

There are three days in the year that must be observed in every respect: the eighth day before the Ides of April; that day of the Moon at the beginning of August; and that day of the Moon at the end of December. They must be observed because on them all the veins in human beings and animals are full.

Anyone who strikes a person or an animal on these days will either die immediately or on the third day, or will be in danger on the seventh day. And if he takes a potion, he will die within fifteen days. And if a male or female is born on these days, they will die a bad death. And if anyone eats goose on these days, he will die within fifteen or forty days.

## On the Egyptian days

If “darkness” is called *Aegyptus* in the Greek language,

we rightly call the days of death “dark.”

Twice ten and two days are recorded in the year,

on which mortals are accustomed to fear a single hour:

each month possesses two captives of these days,

but do not join them together, lest people be slaughtered by plague.

The first day of January, and the seventh at its end, are feared.

But February has the fourth; the third precedes its end.

The first of March kills; its fourth is thus marked by a spear-point.

April has the tenth; it is feared with the eleventh at its end.

The third belongs to May, the wolf; the seventh is the serpent.

June greets the tenth, with the fifteenth at its end.

The thirteenth of July points to the tenth before the Kalends.

August’s scorpion is first and drives away the second from the end.

The fox strikes the third of September; the tenth is at its foot.

The third of October, the sword, joins ten in order.

The fifth of November, the needle, scarcely remained third in the urn.

The troop of twelve gives seven and ten to December.

Beware of these, lest you remove anything from your own blood.

Begin no undertaking, unless perhaps it is directed toward rejoicing.

Keep both the beginning and the end of the month in your heart,

lest you fall at the middle’s lowest point, but live brightly through the heavens.

[Col. 0955]

# THE LITTLE BOOK OF THE PRIEST BEDE ON THE ASTROLABE

[Col. 0955D] In the construction of the astrolabe, three circles are first drawn. The first and largest is that of Capricorn, the second that of Libra and the Ram, and the third that of Cancer. The sages first found their middle and divided it into four parts, drawing lines that they called *alcotum*, from a to c and from b to d, assigning ninety degrees to each part and dividing the entire circle into 360.

Afterward, from c to b—that is, from the ninety divisions—they subtracted twenty-four, which is c–e; and from that endpoint, namely e, they drew an even line to d. As it passed across the *alcotum*, it cut it on the side of c, where i is located. Having done this, they placed the compass on h–i and, drawing it around, traced the lower circle, namely i–k–l–m.

Next, on the side c–d, they likewise subtracted twenty-four, which is c–f; and from that endpoint i–f they drew an equal line to d–c, extending the *alcotum* from c to g, where they joined the *alcotum* and the line. Then, placing the compass on h–q, they constructed the rear circle g–n–o–p.

They constructed the circle of the houses, namely o–d–i–b, dividing the *alcotum* l–o in the middle, where k is located; placing the point of the compass at the midpoint, they drew it around through o and l.

Having constructed these things, they first undertook to construct the *almucantarat*. They took the circle a–b–c–d, which is divided into 360 degrees, and from the side b–a subtracted the latitude of the climate for which they sought to construct the astrolabe. Thus, for climate 6, in which [Col. 0957A] Rome and Germany are situated, they subtracted forty-two degrees, whose endpoint is g; from g they drew a line through h to i, and from c they drew a line through l.

They extended the *almerez* h–d and the line c–i outside the circles together until the two lines joined in a perfectly straight manner, at the point where k stands. They also drew another straight line from c to g, which, as it passed through, divided the *almerez* where l is located.

Afterward, they divided the line l–k, which is the *almerez*, in the middle; its midpoint is d. They placed the *aldebit*, that is, the compass, on d–l and drew it around. Behold, the first *almucantarat*, from n through c–l–a to m.

Construct the remaining *almucantarats* through each division of the 360 parts, rotating the rule and beginning from the altitude of the land, as if from c–d–e–f, with the rule lying immobile at point z, until you reach the point outside the astrolabe where the lines join.

For example, place the rule at c, on the outer or inner circle, and extend it to z; wherever the rule touches the middle line, make a mark. Then place the rule at d, without moving it at z, and again make a mark on the middle line. Continue in this way. Through these marks, without the *aldebit*, draw lines and construct the *almucantarat*.

If you wish to construct the entire astrolabe [Col. 0957B], leave out of the 360 divisions, if you wish, four degrees for a quarter division; if a fifth division, five degrees. Do the same on the other side of the astrolabe. If you also seek the innermost *almucantarat*, if it is an *orum* astrolabe, one remains bound in the middle circle. If a quarter division, four points; if five, five points.

## Finding the circles on the astrolabe

Let the figure for finding the circles—the middle one, called the equinoctial—be made according to the craftsman’s judgment. Divide this same circle into four equal parts by two transverse lines drawn through the center. Mark these parts with the four letters a, b, c, d, and extend the line passing from a through c beyond the circle, far outward on both sides.

Having arranged these things, divide one quarter, namely a–d, into ninety parts. When this is done, place the letter i at the twenty-fourth part toward a. Without moving one foot of the compass, turn it toward the other side of a, and where it touches the circle place the letter e.

Then draw a line from d to l, and carefully observe where it touches the same diameter that runs from a to c; place a mark there. With one foot of the compass placed at the center, which is f, and the other at the point where the line touches, turn it around, and you will have the smaller circle.

Again draw a line from d through e until it touches the diameter, and impress a point there. As before, place one foot of the compass at the aforesaid center and the other where the line touches; by drawing it around, you will have the larger circle.

## On the arrangement of the climates

If you wish to arrange our climate, divide c–b into ninety parts, and place the letter e at the forty-ninth degree. On the other side, which is a–b, remove the same amount of space and place h there. Then divide into eighteen parts the space between h and e.

In making this division, observe carefully that one end of the rule always remains fixed at a; move the other from mark to mark, which we have inscribed on the middle circle. Wherever it touches the meridian line, place a point, until the last line, beginning at a and passing through the middle of h, touches the aforesaid meridian line far outside the greatest circle.

When you have these things before your eyes, divide in the middle the space between the two outermost points. Fixing one foot of the compass at the middle and rotating the other below the circles, you will rejoice to have found the first *almucantarat*.

When you seek to find another, do the same with the points placed on the opposite side beneath the outermost points. If you carry this out carefully with all the points [Col. 0957D], you will see that all the *almucantarats* follow correctly.

After this, divide into twelve rows the space between the greatest and smallest circles that lies above the first *almucantarat*. Extend the compass to the measure of the first *almucantarat*, place one foot of it somewhere, and move that same foot from place to place until the other foot touches the first of the twelve points on the greatest and smallest circles.

As you do this, turning the compass from point to point, you will find the first hour. Keeping the same measurement of the compass and drawing a line from point to point [Col. 0958A], you will find the twelve hours.

## On the measurement of the rete

[Col. 0958D]

It remains to speak about the measurement of the rete, which is exceedingly difficult to carry out in writing. You will find the zodiac as follows. Looking at the figure above, divide the meridian line from n to o through the middle. Place one foot of the compass at this midpoint; as you draw the other around, you will have the line of the zodiac. Divide this same zodiacal line [Col. 0959A] into twelve parts—not by itself, but by means of the outer boss—and divide those parts, at times [Col. 0960A], according to the intervals divided into five parts that you see engraved on the bronze tablet.

[Col. 0959]

# THE LITTLE BOOK OF THE PRIEST BEDE ON THE BIRTH OF INFANTS

[Col. 0959A] One who is born in seven months, if male, is formed in thirty days and begins to move at forty. A female is formed in thirty-five days, begins to move at seventy, and is completed in 210 days.

A male of ten months is formed in forty-five days and begins to move at ninety. A female is formed in fifty days, begins to move at one hundred, and is born at three hundred.

A male of nine months is formed in forty days and begins to move at eighty. A female takes shape in forty-five days, begins to move at ninety, and is to be born after 270 days. The male is completed sooner because the semen from which he is born is stronger and hotter.

## On the bones

All the bones of the body number 241: seven of the head; four pairs; fourteen jawbones; sixteen teeth; one of the palate; two of the chin; sixteen of the teeth themselves; twenty-four vertebrae; three of the hips; three of the anus; twenty-three ribs; eight cartilages; two shoulder blades; two heads of the shoulder blades; two collarbones (*ferculae*); two of the arms; two upper elbow bones; two lower ones; sixteen bones of the hands; eight comb-like bones in the hands; thirty fingers; two ankle-bones; two heels; two navicular bones; ten bones of the feet; eight comb-like bones in the feet; thirty toes.

## On the nerves and teeth

All the nerves, paired and unpaired, number thirty. [Col. 0960A] The teeth are, as it were, certain plantings set into the bones and the chin; they number thirty-two. Sixteen are placed in the jaws, of which four in the front are called paired and quadruple, broad and sharp, and are called incisors by physicians. They are necessary for cutting every kind of food.

Two are called canine teeth, alongside the quadruple teeth; they are sharp at the top and broad at the root, suitable for grinding hard foods. There are also ten others, five on each side, alongside the quadruple teeth, broad and thick. These are called molars, for they are necessary for grinding and breaking food.

This same number of teeth is to be understood in the chin [Col. 0960B]. All of these are forked, but some differ among them: some have four branches, others three, others two, and some have a fork. The quadruple and paired teeth—the molars—are three; the farther ones are four; the first molars placed below have two branches, the last three.

There are three days and nights on which, if a man is born, his body undoubtedly remains whole until Judgment Day: the sixth day before the Kalends of February, the third day before the Kalends, and the Ides of February. Their mystery is exceedingly marvelous.

Whoever is born on Sunday, whether during the day or at night, will be great and splendid. On Monday he will be strong. On Tuesday he will be desirous and will die by iron. On Wednesday he will be an administrator of the kingdom. On Thursday he will be affable and honorable. On Friday he will be a rival and exceedingly lustful. On Saturday he will rarely be useful.

[Col. 0959]

# ON THE LESSENING OF BLOOD, OR PHLEBOTOMY

[Col. 0959C] At any time, day or night, if necessity presses, in acute illnesses phlebotomy ought to be employed. Especially from the eighth day before the Kalends of April until the seventh day before the Kalends of June, it is beneficial to draw blood, because at that time the blood increases.

Afterward, however, the qualities of the seasons and the course of the Moon must be observed: namely, the fifth, tenth, fifteenth, twentieth, twenty-fifth, and thirtieth lunar days. On these days phlebotomy ought not to be performed, because many physicians affirm that on these days an innumerable number of people have died through this negligence, by failing to observe the qualities of the seasons and the course of the Moon.

For the entire period from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August until the Nones of September, which are called the dog days, must be observed: phlebotomy must not be performed, nor may a purgative be taken, because all the humors are then mixed. Unless, as we have already said, an injury occurs amid acute illnesses—in which case nothing else can be done except that it be struck and the excess or imbalance of the blood evaporate.

[Col. 0959D] As for a purgative, however, there is one suitable period: from the eighth day before the Kalends of October until the eighth day before the Kalends of December. What the body contracted during winter and summer into bile and phlegm can then be purged. If it is carefully purged, one can be safe from bile.

Only the observance of food and drink should be maintained, so that one uses what is appropriate and abstains from what can harm him.

What is phlebotomy except a proper incision of a vein? At what places do we perform phlebotomy, for which illnesses, or which vein ought we to cut?

The arterial veins at the back of the head, for a complaint of the head and the condition of mania, as far as the bone, at a distance of four fingers from the ear. From both temples we make incisions, for eye discharge. Beneath the tongue, two, for rheum of the gums, disorders of the mouth, or toothache. On the forehead, three, for headache and alienation into frenzy. At the nostrils, two, for heaviness of the head and eyes. At the neck, two, for moisture in the head.

At the arm, three, which return blood throughout the whole body: the cephalic, the basilic, and the median veins. At the hand, two: one above the thumb, for swelling of the lung, and the other at the little finger, for swelling of the spleen. Beneath the ankle, below it, for gouty, frenzied, sciatic, or lumbar conditions, and for women whose menstruation does not come and who do not conceive. On the outside, two, for kidney pain. On top of the great toe, two, for swelling or pain of the testicles.

There are many Egyptian days on which, in no way and under no necessity, is it permissible to lessen the blood of a person or animal, or to administer a potion. Of these three are to be observed above all: the eighth day before the Ides of April; that lunar day at the beginning of August; and that lunar day at the end of December. They must be observed with great care because all the veins are then full.

[Col. 0960D] Anyone who cuts a person or animal on these days will either die immediately, or on that very day or the third day, or will not reach the seventh day. And if anyone takes a potion, he will die on the fifteenth day. And if a male or woman is born on these days, they will die a bad [Col. 0961A] death. And if anyone eats goose on those days, he will die on the fifteenth day.

In January, on the first day at the beginning and the seventh day at the end of the month, and on the first, fourth, fifth, eighth, and fifteenth lunar days of that month, one must abstain from the phlebotomist, purgation, and every kind of incision.

In February, on the eighth day at the beginning and the seventh day at the end of the month, and on the seventeenth, nineteenth, and twenty-fifth lunar days of that month;

In March, on the third day at the beginning and the seventh day at the end of the month, and on the fifteenth, sixteenth, seventeenth, and eighteenth lunar days of that month;

In April, on the tenth day at the beginning and the eleventh day at the end of the month, and on the ninth, seventh, and twentieth lunar days of that month;

In May, on the fourth day at the beginning and the seventh day at the end of the month, and on the fifth, twelfth, and sixteenth lunar days of that month;

In June, on the eighth day at the beginning and the fifth day at the end of the month, and on the fifth, sixth, and seventh lunar days of that month [Col. 0961B];

In July, on the seventeenth day at the beginning and the tenth day at the end of the month, and on the sixteenth, seventeenth, eighteenth, and twenty-seventh lunar days of that month;

In August, on the fifth day at the beginning and the fifteenth day at the end of the month, and on the nineteenth, twentieth, and twenty-first lunar days of that month;

In September, on the ninth day at the beginning and the ninth day at the end of the month, and on the fifth, fifteenth, and twenty-fifth lunar days of that month;

In October, on the ninth day at the beginning and the tenth day at the end of the month, and on the sixth and seventh lunar days of that month;

In November, on the fifth day at the beginning and the sixth day at the end of the month, and on the fourteenth and twenty-fifth lunar days of that month;

In December, on the fifteenth day at the beginning and the eighth day at the end of the month; and on the first, fifteenth, and seventeenth lunar days of that month.

Moreover, in every month, the first, fifth, ninth, and fifteenth lunar days, together with the three days at the beginning and the three before the aforesaid period ends, are to be observed as days of abstinence.

The first lunar day is good all day.

[Col. 0962A] The second lunar day is not good.

The third lunar day is good.

The fourth lunar day is good in the morning.

The fifth lunar day is not good.

The sixth lunar day is not good.

The seventh lunar day is good all day.

The eighth lunar day is good from the ninth hour until evening.

The ninth lunar day is not good.

The tenth lunar day is good.

The eleventh lunar day is not good.

The twelfth lunar day is good.

The thirteenth lunar day is good until the ninth hour.

The fourteenth lunar day is good.

The fifteenth lunar day is not good.

The sixteenth lunar day is useless.

The seventeenth lunar day is good all day.

The eighteenth lunar day is not good.

The nineteenth lunar day is better.

The twentieth lunar day is good all day.

The twenty-first lunar day is good in the morning.

[Col. 0962B] The twenty-second lunar day is good from the sixth hour.

The twenty-third lunar day is good from the eighth hour.

The twenty-eighth lunar day is not good.

The twenty-ninth lunar day is not good.

The thirtieth lunar day is not good.

On the fifth, fifteenth, twentieth, twenty-fifth, and thirtieth days, it forbids phlebotomy. From the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August until the Nones of September, the days are called the dog days; during them neither is a phlebotomy performed nor is a potion given. A potion, however, is beneficial from the eighth day before the Kalends of October until the eighth day before the Kalends of December.

At any time, if necessity presses, phlebotomy should be employed. But from the eighth day before the Kalends of April until the eighth day before the Kalends of June is the most beneficial time for drawing blood [Col. 0962C], because at that time the blood grows in a human being. Afterward, the observance of the seasons and the course of the Moon must be maintained.

[Col. 0961]

# THE SEVEN WONDERS OF THE WORLD

[Col. 0961C] I. On the seven wonders of the world made by human hands. The first is the Capitol at Rome, the salvation of its citizens, greater than the city itself. There were statues of peoples captured by the Romans, or images of their gods; on the chests of the statues were written the names of the peoples who had been captured by the Romans, and bells were hung upon their necks.

Priests or watchmen, taking turns by day and night, devoted themselves to guarding them. If any one of them moved, the bell immediately made a sound, so that they would know which people was rebelling against the Romans. Once this was discovered, they reported it by word or writing to the Roman rulers, so that they would know against which people they ought at once to send an army for its suppression.

II. The Pharos of Alexandria was founded beneath the sea upon four glass crabs, twenty paces down. The marvel is how such enormous crabs could have been made, or how they could have been transported without breaking; how cement foundations could have clung above them; how cement could remain under water; why the crabs are not broken; and why the foundations thrown upon them do not slip.

III. On the island of Rhodes, an image of the Colossus, cast in bronze, was made 136 feet high. The marvel is how so immense a mass could have been cast, raised, and made to stand.

IV. The fourth wonder is an iron statue of Bellerophon with his horse, suspended at the highest point of the city and standing in the air. It is not hung by chains, nor supported from above by any prop; rather, great stones of magnet are held in the arches, and it is drawn from both sides by means of supports, remaining in a balanced position. Its weight is estimated at approximately five thousand pounds of iron.

V. The fifth wonder is the theater at Heraclea. It is carved from a single marble in such a way that all its chambers and dwellings, walls, and dens of wild beasts are made from one solid stone. It hangs supported upon seven crabs carved from the same stone. No one in the circuit of the building can speak so secretly, whether alone or with someone else, that those standing around the circuit of the building do not hear him.

VI. The sixth wonder is a bathhouse which Apollonius of Tyana, by lighting a single consecration candle, made hot with an everlasting fire without any tending.

VII. The seventh wonder is the temple of Diana. Its first foundations were struck upon four columns by means of arches; then, rising gradually, stones more elevated than the earlier arches were placed upon four arches. Upon these four were placed eight columns and eight arches. From there, in a third order, rising in equal balance through four divisions, still more elevated stones were placed. Upon the eight, sixteen were founded; upon the sixteen, thirty-two. This is the fourth stage; in the fifth order, sixty-four columns complete the end of this wonderfully constructed building.

[Col. 0963]

# ON THE DIVINATION OF DEATH AND LIFE: THE LETTER OF PETOSIRIS TO NECEPSUS, KING OF EGYPT

[Col. 0963]

[Col. 0963D] Of the things that I have discovered for the protection of human life, I have not been reluctant to send each one to you. It remains for you, through the wisdom divinely inspired in you, to devote labor to applying them, confident that, in the circumstances of the bedridden, fugitives, single combatants, or others of this kind, you will be able to obtain a trustworthy foreknowledge.

If you carefully inspect the arithmetical rule that I have appended to this writing, proceed as follows when you wish to consult it. Take the name of the sick person, the fugitive, the person about to fight, or anyone else about whom you are inquiring, and add up its numerical value. Then consider the Moon: what day it is on the day when the sick person took to bed or the fugitive escaped, or what day it will be when the gladiator is going to fight, and so forth in similar cases. Add to the number of the name the arithmetical number assigned to that lunar day.

Then divide the total produced by these numbers by twenty-nine, and take the number that remains. Having inspected the diagram, find in which place that same number is situated. If you find it in ζωὴ μεγάλη (*zōē megalē*, “great life”), and the matter concerns a sick person, he will quickly recover; if it concerns a fugitive, he will quickly return; if it concerns a gladiator, he will win.

But if it is in μέση ζωή (*mesē zōē*, “middle life”), all these things will occur with greater difficulty. But if it is in ζωή μικρά (*zōē mikra*, “small life”), the outcome will be favorable, yet difficult. But if it is in the place inscribed θάνατος μεγάλη (*thanatos megalē*, “great death”), the sick person will die after a long illness; the fugitive, though long sought, will not be found; but the gladiator will be defeated only with difficulty.

The same things will happen more quickly in μέσος θάνατος (*mesos thanatos*, “middle death”), and most quickly in μικρός θάνατος (*mikros thanatos*, “small death”).

Let the example be the battle of Hector and Achilles. The Moon will be on the seventeenth day, which has the arithmetical number 893. The name “Achilles” has the number 1,276; joined together, these make 2,169. Divide these by twenty-nine, and seek the remainder, namely twenty-three, in the arithmetical diagram. You will find it in the place where ζωὴ μεγάλη (“great life”) is written.

If you do the same for Hector, you will find the remaining number in μικρῷ θανάτῳ (*mikrō thanatō*, “small death”). This position of the numbers signifies without ambiguity that Achilles is the victor and Hector the vanquished.

There is also another method. If the number of the Moon is in ὑπόγειον (*hypogeion*, “below the earth”), and the man’s number is in ὑπέργειον (*hypergeion*, “above the earth”), the man will indeed be endangered, but will escape. Conversely, if the man’s number is in ὑπόγειον and the Moon’s is in ὑπέργειον, adverse things will occur under the appearance of favorable ones.

But if both numbers—that is, both the man’s and the Moon’s—are found above the horizon, they promise favorable things without doubt. If, however, both are found below the horizon, everything adverse will result.

# THE SENTENCES, OR PHILOSOPHICAL AXIOMS, OF THE VENERABLE BEDE, COLLECTED FROM ARISTOTLE AND OTHER EMINENT AUTHORS, TOGETHER WITH CERTAIN BRIEF EXPLANATIONS AND LIMITATIONS

## SECTION ONE. SENTENCES COLLECTED FROM ARISTOTLE

### A

[Col. 0965B]

Heaven and all nature depend upon God (*Metaphysics* XII). This authority is to be understood as saying that heaven and all nature depend upon God both with respect to coming-to-be, or production, and with respect to preservation.

According to Aristotle, however, who falsely supposed that prime matter was coeternal with God and that the world had existed from eternity, it is understood only with respect to preservation, not with respect to coming-to-be. For according to him prime matter was not made, nor was the world; rather, they existed from eternity.

Unless, perhaps, it should be said that according to Aristotle matter and the world were produced by God—not newly and from nothing, for according to him nothing comes from nothing in the first place [*Physics*, texts 33 and 34, and *Metaphysics* VII, text 22], but through a certain simple emanation or a certain natural process such as we most truly believe occurs only in the divine persons.

Act separates and distinguishes (Metaphysics VII and On the Soul III). But sometimes things are distinguished not only by forms but also by matter, for there are proper matters just as there are proper forms. The response is that matter does indeed separate and distinguish through the acts included in it, because matter by its own nature has no activity. Or, better and more briefly: [Col. 0966B] act separates and distinguishes, namely, principally.

Arguing from being to possibility yields a good consequence. This axiom is understood as follows: one must argue affirmatively, without distribution, and without a term that includes negation. Hence it does not follow: “A is the greatest body that exists; therefore A is the greatest body that can exist.” The consequence is invalid, because the antecedent [Col. 0966C] can be true without the consequent.

“White comes from black; a musician comes from a non-musician” (Physics I). It is said there that *from* (*ex*) indicates a circumstance of order. But when one says, “Wood must be composed from its halves,” the word *from* indicates a circumstance of time.

“White, accidentally, is a quantity” (according to the Philosopher in the *Categories*). It is said there that the Philosopher means that the term “white” is placed, accidentally, in the category of quantity. Whiteness in itself is placed in the category of quality; but, by reason of whiteness, that which is white is placed there.

“When the agent and the matter exist in the same way, the effect will be the same” (*Metaphysics* II). This is understood both of principal and instrumental agents: when the agent is entirely the same, and the patient is disposed in the same way, diverse effects are not produced, but only one.

“The appetite of matter is nothing other than motion toward form” [Col. 0967A] (the Commentator, *Physics* I). The response is that the Commentator takes “motion” very broadly, or improperly, namely, for a natural inclination.

“Some natural thing is distinguished from an artificial thing” (*Physics* II, at the beginning). It is said there that the Philosopher speaks indefinitely or particularly, and thus the proposition is true. Or it may be said that he intended only that natural things differ from artificial things in reason, and not in reality, since the thing is the same.

The alchemists say that gold can be made from iron or copper by their art. It is said there that gold or silver is made from iron or copper apparently, but not really. The reason is that by no art can a substantial form be brought into the specific being of another form.

“Art simply makes matter” (*Physics* I). This is said to be understood of second matter, not of prime matter, because prime matter is not made, being ungenerated and incorruptible, as is evident in the same place.

[Col. 0967B] “An accident does not have an accident” (*Physics* IV). This is understood as follows: an accident does not have an accident as its original subject. Thus it is quite possible that whiteness is in a surface, which is itself an accident, and that a line has roundness and corruptibility; but this is not the case with respect to an original subject, because originally these belong to substance.

“An accident is defined through its subject” (*Metaphysics* VII). Thus “white” is a subject possessing sufficient whiteness for its denomination. This is understood as a descriptive definition, not an essential one, because such a definition must be given through a true genus and an essential difference; and such a definition indicates what the being of a thing is, as is clear from the *Topics* I.

“The soul, with respect to its intellectual part, is the act of no body” (*On the Soul* II). That is, it does not depend subjectively on a body. For it depends in this way only with respect to its sensory and vegetative parts.

[Col. 0967C] “An act is incompatible with receiving an act” (Averroes, *On the Substance of the World*). The response is that a substantial act cannot receive another substantial act, but it can receive an accidental act.

“An ark is not wood” (*Metaphysics* IX). The response is that the Philosopher is using an ordinary manner of speaking. Or it may be said that he means that the whole composite is not predicated of its matter. Therefore he means that an ark is not wood as though it were that matter, since otherwise the whole would be its part, and conversely. Or it may be said that the Philosopher means that matter is not predicated of the whole composite in the abstract, though it is predicated in the concrete, as in: “The ark is wooden.”

“Acts belong to supposits” (*Metaphysics* I). The response is that the Philosopher means that acts belong to supposits denominatively; nevertheless, it can properly be maintained that they do not belong to supposits effectively.

“There will be no predication from first substances” (according to the Philosopher in the *Categories*). The response is that this means: there will be no predication from first substances that is the predication of a superior of an inferior, because first substances do not have an inferior—at least not essentially—in true, direct, and affirmative predication.

[Col. 0967D] “An animal is more animate than a plant” (the *Author of the Six Principles*, chapter 3, “On Passion”). This is understood as follows: an animal is more perfectly animated than a plant. Or it is said that an animal has more powers of the soul than a plant, because an animal has vegetative and sensory power, whereas a plant lacks sensory power.

“The vegetative soul is the first of souls” (*On the Soul* I and II). It is said there that the Philosopher is speaking of priority in universality, not priority in perfection; he means that the vegetative soul is found in more things than the sensory or intellectual soul.

[Col. 0968A] “The acts of active powers are in a suitably disposed patient” (*On the Soul* II). This is understood as follows: if something active or an agent is to perform some act or produce some effect in a patient, the patient must be well disposed to receive that act. For just as nothing comes from nothing, so neither does anything whatsoever come from just anything.

“Nothing comes from what is insufficient” (*Physics* I). This is understood to mean: nothing comes from what is insufficient by itself, but when what is superior is added, something can properly come from what is insufficient.

“The soul is abstracted from the body” (the Commentator, *On the Soul* III). The Commentator, Averroes, falsely understands this to mean that the intellectual soul is not the form informing the human being, but merely something assisting it; and that it does not give being, but only operation, namely, intellection. According to the truth, it should be understood as follows: although the intellectual soul is essentially the informing act of the body, nevertheless it depends on the body neither in coming-to-be nor in being—for it is created from nothing and can be separated from the body—nor in its proper operation, namely, intellection. In this operation it does not communicate with the body as with a subject or instrument.

[Col. 0968B] “Accidents contribute greatly to knowing what a thing is” (*On the Soul* I). According to Themistius, this authority is understood of accidents that are essential and proper, because he says: Aristotle does not say, “I know fire through smoke,” but “through heat.” It is also understood of common accidents considered in themselves and combined with one another, as in: “I know Socrates through those accidents taken and combined together: having red hair, being white, having a black head-covering, and wearing a white tunic.”

“There is no demonstrative science of accidents” (*Posterior Analytics* I, chapter 6, text 18). This is true of accidents that are not essential and proper.

[Col. 0968C] “An action does not arise from a proportion of lesser inequality.” It should be noted that there are two kinds of proportion. One is quantitative proportion, by which one extended quantity is proportioned to another. The other is the proportion of action, and the authority is understood of the latter. Thus body and non-body can properly have the second kind of proportion according to some power, as between body and soul. More briefly and better: an action does not arise from a proportion of lesser inequality—namely, no overcoming action arises from it, although a reaction does.

“Art and science are distinguished” (*Nicomachean Ethics* VI). This must be understood by taking “science” strictly for a speculative habit alone, and “art” strictly for a practical habit alone. But if both are taken equally broadly, for practical as well as speculative habits, then they are not distinguished.

“Denomination should be made from the greater” (*Physics* VI). This is understood of positive qualities, especially intensive ones. Denomination need not, however, be made from privative qualities, as darkness denominates something “dark.” The proposition is valid only in the sense that denomination should be made from the greater, that is, from the more worthy.

“Act and potency are the most contrary, or opposed, things” (the Commentator, *On the Soul* I). This axiom is understood to mean that they are the most opposed or contrary, that is, the most universally opposed, because he says that they extend through all the categories; and he does not mean that they are contraries in the strict sense.

[Col. 0968D] “When the subject is corrupted, the science is corrupted” (*Posterior Analytics* I). The response is that this is understood of a subject of inherence, not of attribution. For even if the rose is destroyed in winter, its attributes can still be known scientifically.

“Animal is prior to human being” (according to Porphyry). This is understood in material supposition, as in: “The term *animal* is prior to *human being*”; that is, the term *animal* is more common than *human being*.

“An accident does not have being, but inherence” (*Metaphysics* VII). This is understood most properly by taking “being” strictly, not commonly. For in this way it extends also to inherence.

“An accident does not migrate from subject to subject” (*Metaphysics* VII). This is understood of a subject of inherence, not of attribution or denomination. Or it is said that the proposition is true according to number, but not according to species.

[Col. 0969A] “It is absurd to seek both science and the method of knowing at the same time” (*Metaphysics* II). This authority is understood in two ways. In one way, the words are taken simply as they stand, and thus the proposition is true without qualification. In another way, if “science” means metaphysics and “method of knowing” means logic, then the sense is: it is absurd to acquire metaphysics and logic at the same time, because metaphysics presupposes logic; therefore logic must be known first.

“From a uniform agent there follows a uniform act and effect” (*On the Heavens* I). This is understood provided that the total agent concurs uniformly; then the effect, at least the effect principally intended, remains uniform.

“Different specifically distinct things cannot be produced from the same thing” (*On Generation* II). This is understood to mean that different and specifically distinct things cannot proceed from the same natural being. The case is different with an artificial agent.

“Gold is incorruptible” (according to the alchemists). This is understood as follows: gold is incorruptible, that is, highly enduring among all other metals, because it lasts beyond the span of human arrangements.

[Col. 0969B] “From an ancient will no new action proceeds” (the Commentator, *Physics* VIII). This is understood as follows: from an ancient will, that is, from God, no new action proceeds, that is, no newly willed object, because God does not begin to will anything anew; whatever God willed, he willed from eternity. Hence, even if the world was made in time, God’s will was not changed. For from eternity he willed that the world should be made then.

“For the production of an effect, two things suffice: will and power” (Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, prose 2, book IV). This is not understood absolutely, but with limitation. For example: “I want to read and I can read; therefore I read” is not valid absolutely. But this is valid: “I now want to read and can read for the present; therefore I am now reading.”

“Return from privation to habit is impossible” (according to the Philosopher in the *Categories*). This is understood of a privation that deprives something simultaneously of act and potency, not of one that deprives it of act alone; in the latter case return is indeed possible.

[Col. 0969C] “Action and passion are acts of different powers” (*On the Soul* II). It is said there that different powers have different acts, for powers are distinguished through acts. But because action and passion are acts of different powers, they are distinct. This conflicts with the Philosopher (*Physics* III), who says that every action is passion. The antecedent is evident, because action is the act of an active power, whereas passion is called the act of a passive power. The response is that this authority is understood particularly, not universally: action and passion are materially the same, but formally different.

“From the abstract to the concrete there is a good consequence” (*Topics* II). It is said there that this is true in quidditative and essential predications, but not in accidental predications; and so forth.

“From a cause similar in species, different effects do not proceed” (the Commentator, *Metaphysics* IX). The response is that the term “same” is taken in several ways: for the same in number, in species, or in genus. Thus from a cause similar in species, effects differing in number can indeed proceed, but not effects differing in species or genus.

[Col. 0969D] “Animal is the substance of human being and horse according to a common nature” (the Commentator, *Metaphysics* I). If this is so, then a common nature would have to be posited. It is said there that “is” is taken in signate actuality, so that the term *animal* signifies the substance of human being and horse according to a common nature—that is, under the aspect of genus, or under the common concept corresponding to the term *animal*.

“Water [feeds] fire” (*On the Soul* III). It is said there that “water” is not taken for moisture simply, but for fatty and subtle moisture, because this nourishes fire, as experience shows in butter, fine oil, and burned wine. Moreover, this must be understood of nourishment in an improper sense, because no pure element nourishes.

[Col. 0970A] “Accidents are called beings in relation to something” (*Metaphysics* V). This is understood to mean that accidents do not have being in themselves except in relation to something and to a subject.

“Accidents resemble a shoot” (*Metaphysics* V). This is understood as follows: a shoot is not a tree, but something of the tree from which the tree is derived. Similarly, accidents are not beings, but are of a being—that is, of the substance from which they are propagated and arise (*Metaphysics* V and VII).

“An animal is constituted from body and soul as from ruler and ruled” (*Politics* I). This is understood to mean that in an animal the soul functions as ruler, while the body functions as ruled, because it is the soul’s instrument.

“Tame animals are more worthy than other, untamed animals” (*Politics* I). This is understood insofar as tame animals participate in rule in some way. But if the opposite is found, the case is different.

“Abstinence from food contributes to health in one suffering from fever” (*Nicomachean Ethics* V). The response is that abstinence does so because it is the supreme medicine. This is a common rule among physicians and ordinary people.

[Col. 0970B] “Action and passion are not contained under one another” (*Physics* VI). This is understood to mean that one is not predicated of the other, because the predication “action is passion” is not valid.

“Art imitates nature insofar as it can” (*Physics* II). This authority is likewise true provided that nature is the foundation of that art.

“The art of acquiring food is natural to animals” (*Politics* I). This is understood to mean that nature is concerned to provide food for animals when it first generates them. Or it may be understood as follows: when someone acquires something that nature requires, such acquisition is natural.

“The actions of rulers are not good in themselves” (*Politics* VII). This is understood to mean that they are not good unless the ruler differs from others in natural and acquired goodness to the extent that a man differs from a woman, or a master from a slave.

“Acts of justice are necessary in a state, but are not, in themselves, objects of choice” (*Politics* VII). It is said there that by acts of justice are understood the judgments and punishments of those condemned; these are necessary in a state, yet in themselves they are not objects of choice, but are chosen so that the state may be governed and preserved more effectively.

[Col. 0970C] “Actions concerned with wealth and honors are not simply choiceworthy” (*Nicomachean Ethics* II). The reason is that they are certain dispositions toward the good and toward the performance of good actions, as is clear from *Politics* VII.

All animals other than human beings perform their actions solely through natural intention, as is gathered from the same place. Some small animals perform their actions through habit or habituation, as dogs do. But human beings, among animals, direct their actions according to reason. Accordingly, all other animals act less than they are acted upon for an end, whereas human beings also direct and order themselves and their own actions toward their end.

“The accuser ought to be better than the accused” (*Politics* II). The reason is that the accuser’s duty is to show the grounds of the accusation against the adversary or accused. Also, the accuser functions as agent, while the accused functions as patient. But every agent is superior to its patient.

[Col. 0970D] “The acts of intellect and appetite agree with one another” (*Nicomachean Ethics* IV). The response is: this is true of moral virtues.

“Affirmation and negation are in the mind” (*Nicomachean Ethics* IV). This is understood to mean that affirmation and negation are in the mind—that is, in the practical intellect—whereas pursuit and flight are in the appetite.

“Farmers desire profit more than honors” (*Nicomachean Ethics* VI). This is understood to mean that it is more pleasurable for them to labor and make a profit than to rule and exercise dominion.

“Possession through agriculture is especially natural and just” (*Economics* I). This is so for three reasons. The first is that agriculture is not carried on inhumanely or bestially, or sinfully and violently, that is, with offense against one’s neighbor. Another reason is that nourishment is obtained from agriculture as from matter, and such nourishment is natural. A further reason may be that agriculture contributes to health and expels excessive and harmful humors.

[Col. 0971A] “Love (*amatio*) is generated from a certain habit” (*Nicomachean Ethics* IX). According to Albert, the reason is that love (*amatio*) implies an impetuous inclination of love into the appetite, and this inclination is caused by habit.

“Parental friendship is greater than filial friendship” (*Nicomachean Ethics* VIII). The reason is that parents know more than their children, who are procreated from them, because of the children’s imperfection and the knowledge of them which the parents had when the children were born.

“Marital friendship exists not only for the generation of children, but also for virtue” (*Nicomachean Ethics* VIII). This means that marital friendship exists not only for the generation of children, but also for true virtue, if both spouses are virtuous, because according to Aristotle true friendship exists only between virtuous people.

“A friend is another self” (*Nicomachean Ethics* IX). This is true not with respect to essence, but with respect to the goods that a person wills for himself and for his friend. Or it is true because, in the effect of love, one person sometimes represents another: a person grieves with his friend in adversity and rejoices in prosperity as in his own.

[Col. 0971B] “A friend should hold fast to a friend as the knee does to the shin” (*Nicomachean Ethics* IX). This is true insofar as the word “as” indicates a certain customary relationship.

“Among friends all things are common” (*Nicomachean Ethics* IX and *Politics* II). This is true by consent and goodwill, but not by right. Or otherwise: “Among friends all things are common” means that things are common only when necessity requires it, taking “all things” distributively. This amounts to saying that whatever common useful thing exists is common to the person placed in necessity, so that one friend cannot forbid it to him. Or the statement is understood of useful food, with respect to what is sufficient, not with respect to another use.

“Through erotic love it is impossible for one person to love several women intensely” (*Nicomachean Ethics* VIII). This is true of love directed toward intercourse, but it is not true of genuine love of affection.

“The love of riches increases without limit” (*Politics* I). This is true with respect to the manifestation of the act; or it is true of disordered love, but not of ordered love.

[Col. 0971C] “Act is better and more honorable than potency” (*Metaphysics* IX, text and commentary 19). This axiom is to be understood of good things, for among evil things it can happen that act is worse than potency.

“A wakeful animal is always laboring” (*Nicomachean Ethics* VII). This is understood of some activity, without considering whether that activity is great or small, good or bad.

“When both are friends—namely, truth and a human being—it is sacred to honor truth first” (*Nicomachean Ethics* I). This is understood of true and special friendship: “Friend Plato, friend Socrates, but the greater friend is truth.”

“An accident and its subject are numerically the same” (*Nicomachean Ethics* X). This is understood of a real accident of denomination, not of inherence.

“White signifies quality alone” (according to the Philosopher in the *Categories*). This is true in formal signification, but not in material signification, because taken materially it signifies substance and connotes quality.

[Col. 0971D] “There is no definition of an accident” (*Metaphysics* VII and *Topics* VI). The sense of this proposition must be taken from another axiom found in the same book VII of the *Metaphysics*: accidents have some quiddity, but not quiddity simply speaking. Hence they have a definition in one respect and do not have one in another. For, says Averroes, if by “definition” one understands that which gives the quiddity proper to a thing and belongs to it without qualification, then there is definition only of substances. If, however, definition is taken generally, namely, as a manifestation suited to the nature of a thing—whether that thing exists in itself and can be fully defined without qualification, or not—then accidents too have a definition, not merely descriptive but also essential, as when one says: “Whiteness is a color that disperses sight,” and so forth.

[Col. 0972A] “The miser and the just person are concerned with goods that are simply good” (*Nicomachean Ethics* V). The response is that in this passage the word “simply” signifies nothing other than that these external goods are good in themselves. This does not prevent us from abusing them so that they become evil for us; but they are not evil in themselves, as stated, but accidentally, namely, by reason of our abuse.

“The action of nature always acts in the same way” (*Physics* II). Thus it appears that the senses are never deceived concerning their proper sensible, since sensation is an operation of nature. It is said there that the Philosopher distinguishes between natural and accidental operation. A natural action is said always to occur in the same way; this means that nature, acting upon the same species, produces the same effect when other conditions are equal. But an accidental action occurs now in one way and now in another. Hence it can properly happen that sight sometimes errs when all the requirements for correct seeing are not present.

[Col. 0972B] “Some soul is the act of no body” (*On the Soul* II, treatise 1). This is understood in one way to mean that the soul is the act of no body that is educed from the potency of matter; in this sense it is true of the intellectual soul. Or it means that it is the act of no body as its proper instrument, because the intellect does not require a proper instrument or bodily organ. Or it may mean that it is the act of no body according to inherence.

“Agent and patient must communicate in matter” (*On Generation* II). This is understood of a proper agent and a proper patient. The intellect, however, does not properly undergo passion, but only improperly, because it undergoes a perfective or preservative passion, as they say, and not an altering or corruptive passion. Moreover, this axiom is understood of things that undergo passion in reality through acting. Thus, although the sun and the other stars truly act upon lower things, because they do not in reality undergo passion through acting, it is not necessary to say that they communicate in matter with these lower things.

[Col. 0972C] “There is no reason for principles” (the Commentator, *Topics* II). This should be understood of mediated principles; or, for principles, there is no a priori reason that approves them, although there can properly be an a posteriori reason.

“White is not a substance, but a quality” (*Topics* IV). It is said that this is true: white is not a substance, that is, it is not a substantial term with respect to its formal signification, though it is so with respect to its material signification.

“Two opposites do not follow from the same thing” (*Prior Analytics* I). This is understood to mean that two opposites do not follow from the same contingent thing, though they can follow from the same impossible thing. The authority must also be supplemented by “copulatively” or “conjunctively,” because two opposites can properly follow from one proposition disjunctively, as in: “A human being runs; therefore, a human being runs or does not run.”

[Col. 0972D] “From several terms taken simply to several terms, according to greater and lesser commonality, there is a good consequence” (*Topics* II).
