From this authority the following is elicited: as the simple is to the simple, so the greater is to the greater, and the proximate to the proximate. This is understood to mean that one must argue from terms taken simply to terms taken in a lesser way according to greater and lesser commonality, so that the antecedent and consequent are categorical propositions. Thus it properly follows: “The just person is virtuous; therefore the more just person is more virtuous, and the most just person is most virtuous.”

This rule is valid with seven added conditions. First, the terms taken simply must be the same two extremes in the consequent; hence it does not follow: “White is sweet; therefore, more white is sweeter.” Second, each extreme must be predicable according to greater and lesser degrees; hence it does not follow: “A human being is an animal; therefore, a greater human being is a greater animal.” Third, the antecedent must contain an essential predication; hence it does not follow: “Drinking is good; therefore, more drinking is better.” Fourth, there must be a predication of a proper attribute of its subject. Fifth, the predication must be direct in both cases. Sixth, the subject must be taken as constant. Seventh, [Col. 0973A] precisely the same copula must occur in the antecedent and consequent, and the predicate of the antecedent must be restricted by the subject of the consequent or by something proportionate to it.

“Arguing from an affirmative proposition with a finite predicate to a negative proposition with an infinite predicate yields a valid consequence” (*On Interpretation* II, περὶ Ἑρμηνείας). For example: “Socrates is white; therefore it is not the case that Socrates is non-white.” This is understood materially; formally it is not valid, because it argues from the undistributed to the distributed. If the argument is to be valid according to the rule, a singular term must always be placed on the side of the subject, or the term in the consequent must be restricted to one supposit. Thus the consequence is invalid: “A human being is white; therefore a human being is not non-white,” because the opposite of the consequent is not incompatible with the antecedent, but can be true together with it.

[Col. 0973B] “Arguing from a negative proposition with a finite predicate to an affirmative proposition with an infinite predicate yields a valid consequence” (*On Interpretation* II, περὶ Ἑρμηνείας). For example: “Socrates is not black; therefore Socrates is non-black.” This rule is true, provided three conditions are preserved. First, the argument must be made in propositions with a third adjacent term. Second, it must not argue from the undistributed to the distributed. Hence it does not follow: “Every animal is not a donkey, and every animal exists; therefore every animal is a non-donkey.” Third, the predicate must always be distributed in the antecedent. Hence it does not follow: “Every animal is not [—]; therefore every animal is a non-animal,” because the predicate is not distributed in the antecedent.

“Arguing from an affirmative proposition with an infinite predicate to a negative proposition with a finite predicate yields a valid consequence” (*On Interpretation* II, περὶ Ἑρμηνείας). For example: “A human being is non-just; therefore a human being is not just.” This rule is true provided three cases are observed. [Col. 0973C] The first is that, in both the affirmative and the negative, the predicate is distributed for every temporal difference. If this were not so, and Socrates were non-white during one half of some hour but white during the other half of that same period, the argument would be: “Socrates is non-white; therefore Socrates is not white.” The consequence would be invalid, because the antecedent belongs to Socrates while the consequent does not. If the argument is to be valid, it must be made according to Marsilius as follows: “Socrates is non-white for every part of the present time; therefore Socrates is not white.”

The second condition is that only the whole predicate be made infinite. Hence it does not follow: “This is predicable non-essentially; therefore it is not predicable essentially,” because the same thing can be predicable essentially and accidentally with respect to different things. This is likewise clear from the fact that all the arguments of the author of the *Consequences* fail with adjectival nouns, and similarly in other cases, as is stated there, because this second condition is always lacking.

[Col. 0973D] The third condition is that the argument be made in categorical propositions concerning actual being, and not in modal propositions. Hence it does not follow: “Socrates cannot be non-white; therefore Socrates cannot be white.” If the negation is postponed to the mode in the second proposition, then the consequence does follow, as in: “Socrates can be non-white; therefore Socrates can be non-white.” In this way it is valid.

“Arguing from divided predicates to a conjunctive predicate yields a valid consequence” (*On Interpretation* II, περὶ Ἑρμηνείας). It should be understood that by the conjunctive term, or conjunctive predicate, one means an aggregate composed of a determination and what is determined, while the divided predicate is one of those elements.

This rule is true provided two conditions are observed. First, the two divided predicates must not be accidents of some term. When one thing accidentally appears to inhere in another, the consequence is invalid. Thus it does not follow: “Socrates is white and Socrates is a monk; therefore Socrates is a white monk.” Nor does it follow: “Socrates is large and Socrates is a monk; therefore Socrates is a large monk,” supposing that he is small in stature but great in knowledge, because the antecedent can be true without the consequent.

[Col. 0974A] Second, one predicate must not include the other, lest a tautology be committed. Hence it does not follow: “Socrates is a human being and Socrates is an animal; therefore Socrates is a human animal.”

“Arguing from a conjunctive predicate to divided predicates yields a valid consequence” (*On Interpretation*, περὶ Ἑρμηνείας). This is true provided four conditions are observed. First, accidental predicates must determine the same thing in the antecedent and consequent; when this is not so, the rule is invalid. Second, one predicate must not be a distracting expression with respect to the other. Hence it does not follow: “Socrates is white as coal; therefore Socrates is white.” Third, when the argument uses an ampliative expression, the amplification must not vary. Hence it does not follow: “A chimera is an ampliated imaginable being; therefore a chimera is a being, and a chimera is ampliable.” The consequent is one conjunctive proposition, one part of which is false; therefore the whole is false. Fourth, when one predicate is equivocal, the consequence is invalid. Thus it does not follow: “This is a barking dog; therefore this is a dog, and this is barking,” because the first part of the consequent is a proposition with multiple meanings.

[Col. 0974B] “The soul is a substance actually existing in a subject” (the Commentator, *Metaphysics* VI). It is said there that by “subject” the Commentator means an organized subject, and by “substance in act” he means an organized subject, because every animal requires an organized subject. An organized subject is one that has parts differently constituted and assigned to perform different functions.

“Magnitude and the being of magnitude, flesh and the being of flesh, are different” (*On the Soul* III). This authority should be understood as follows: the Philosopher wishes to show the mode in which the intellect understands. Thus by “magnitude” and “flesh” he understands the universal, or the common concept insofar as it is such. But by “the being of magnitude” and “the being of flesh” one must understand the singular, namely, these same things under individuating conditions. He therefore means only that one thing is understood universally and another singularly.

[Col. 0974C] This is true, and two metaphysical examples are offered, such as “magnitude” and “the being of magnitude,” as well as natural examples, such as “water being water.” Through sensory cognition we can know the being of water, just as we can know the being of magnitude; but through the intellect we can know only magnitude, which here is taken as the universal.

But one might object: the Philosopher says that flesh and the being of flesh are not the same in some cases, while in other cases they are the same. Yet understanding universally and understanding singularly are never the same. The response is that the Philosopher means that the intellect itself knows not only universally but also particularly, whereas the sense knows only singularly. Therefore sensory cognition belongs only to the intellect joined to matter. When Aristotle says that in some cases flesh and the being of flesh are the same, he means only that they belong to the same power of the intellect.

[Col. 0974D] “Accidents do not have matter” (*Metaphysics* VII). The response is that this is true of matter from which (*materia ex qua*), because accidents do not have that; but they do have matter in which (*materia in qua*), namely, the subject in which they exist.

## A

**Act and potency run through all the categories** (according to the Commentator, *On the Soul* I). This is understood in one way as follows: in each category there are terms verifiable of the first substance by means of the verb “is” or “can be.” Or predicables are posited together with the verbs “is” and “can,” and thus the statement is true: in the category of substance one may say, “A human being is, or can be, an animal,” and similarly in the other categories. In another way, it is understood as follows: in every categorical genus there is something that has the character of act and something that has the character of potency. This too is true, because in every genus there are genera and differences, and thus there are acts and potencies, insofar as they have the character of matter, as is clear from Porphyry; and there is also a form or difference, which is the act that distinguishes and separates, as is clear from the Philosopher (*On the Soul* III). In yet another way: act and potency are found in every category, that is, terms that are more and less common; and in this way the more common has the relation of potency, while the less common has the relation of act. Or it is said that he means only that the terms “act” and “potency,” taken in general, are not in any category, though they are found there in a restricted sense.

**The soul is composed of the agent and possible intellect** (*On the Soul* III). This is correctly understood as follows. Just as sense sometimes contributes actively to intellect and sometimes passively, so intellect sometimes contributes actively—at which point it is called the agent intellect—and sometimes passively, in which case it is called the patient intellect, namely, when it receives those affections or species. This should not be understood as a real composition; rather, it is called an active act when it actually forms the intellect.

**The soul is corruptible** (*On the Soul* III). This is understood not according to its essence, but according to a certain instrumental operation.

**“Soul” is predicated equivocally of souls** (according to the Commentator, *On the Soul* III). This is understood analogically, in the sense that “soul” is first predicated of the intellectual soul—first in dignity—and secondarily of the other souls, namely, the sensitive and nutritive souls. It may also be understood of intelligences according to an analogy of perfection.

**Accidents alone are perceptible** (*On the Soul* II). This means that they alone are perceptible per se and directly, although substances too are perceptible accidentally and indirectly.

**An animal is an animal because of the sense of touch** (*On the Soul* II). This means that the expression “because of” does not indicate an efficient cause, but convertibility: everything that is an animal has the sense of touch, and conversely, everything that has the sense of touch is an animal.

**An animal possessing one sense is the most imperfect** (*Metaphysics* I). This is understood with respect to the species as a whole, not with respect to a particular individual.

**The soul is in the heart as a spider is in its web** (*On Sense and the Sensible*). This means that the soul is seated principally and originally in the heart, and less principally in the other members. If you object, “But a spider is not in every part of its web; therefore the soul is not in every part of the body,” the answer is that the Philosopher is speaking opinionatively of those who said that the soul is located only in the heart and directs its operations through all the members, so that those operations govern the whole body. But that opinion is rejected by the Philosopher in the same place, because no instrumental agent can produce any operation without the principal agent acting together with it. Therefore, no complete similarity between the soul and a spider need be sought here.

**The soul is in the body as a monarch is in a well-ordered city** (the Philosopher, in the book *On the Motions of Natural Things*). [Col. 0975D] This too is understood in an improper sense: the expression “as” signifies not a complete similarity, but an adequate and sufficient one, such that the soul governs the body just as a monarch governs a city.

**Some quality is not active** (*On Generation* II). This does not mean that some quality—namely, dryness and humidity—is active in no way at all, but that it is less active than another, because dryness and humidity are less active qualities than heat and cold.

**It is one thing to see through sight and another to discern** (*On the Soul* II). There the Philosopher does not indicate two external senses of sight, but two senses of sight: one external and the other internal. By saying, “It is one thing to discern through sight,” he indicates the internal sense, namely, the internal common sense; by saying, “It is another thing to see,” he touches upon the external visual sense. This is what the Philosopher means.

[Col. 0976A]

**The soul is the form of forms** (*On the Soul* III). This is understood as follows: the soul is the form of forms, that is, the form of forms, because the most excellent form among lower things is the human soul. Or it may be understood this way: the soul is the form of all species, that is, of all intelligible forms, namely, receptively, because it receives the intelligible species of all things.

**The soul is a place** (*On the Soul* II). It should be said there that “place” is understood in two ways. In one way, properly: the ultimate surface of the thing located is called its place, and thus place is an integral part of something. In another way, “place” is understood as that which contains; in this sense the soul is the place of species, because it contains species within itself, that is, sciences and virtues.

**The being of an accident is to inhere** (*Metaphysics* VII and *Physics* I). The meaning is not that an accident actually inheres in the substance on which it depends, but that by its nature it can and ought to inhere unless prevented by something else.

**It belongs to the philosopher to discover the first principles of medical science** (*On Sense and the Sensible*). It is said there that where the philosopher ends, the physician begins; therefore it is necessary for the physician to be a philosopher.

**Food is contrary to what it nourishes** (*On the Soul* II). This is understood by taking contrariety improperly, namely, as equivalent to dissimilarity. It is also understood at the beginning, not at the end: what is dissimilar at the beginning is similar at the end, for like is nourished and increased by like.

**Bees and dogs are more prudent than the other irrational animals** (*Metaphysics* II). This means that they have greater ingenuity than other irrational animals, because they can discern what is suitable for them and avoid what is unsuitable. If “prudence” is taken properly, as right reason concerning things to be done and as an intellectual habit, it belongs only to human beings, not to bees or dogs.

**The sensitive soul is extended in the body** (*On the Soul* II). This is understood of the rational soul, which contains the sensitive grade—not according to its own substance, but with respect to the organs or dispositions required for the act of sensation—so that it requires extended organs. Of the brute’s sensitive soul it is understood simply, even with respect to the substance of that soul itself. For the brute’s sensitive soul is produced and arises from the power of extended, quantified matter; therefore it too is quantified and extended.

**Some animals have only one sense, and some have three** (*On the Soul* III). It is said there that the Philosopher was speaking of imperfect animals.

**In arguing from the positive to the comparative, the inference is valid** (*Topics* II). This means when arguing negatively, not affirmatively, and when the comparative is taken properly. For I rightly conclude: “Socrates is not white; therefore Socrates is not whiter.” But not correspondingly: “Socrates is white; therefore he is whiter.”

**There is one matter of all things capable of being liquefied** (*Metaphysics* V). The reply there is that “matter” is not taken properly; rather, he means that all liquefiable things agree in some matter, because they agree in humidity.

**The soul lives the life of an animal before it lives the life of a human being**, as the Philosopher says (*On Animals*). This means that the soul first appears to exercise the operations of an animal rather than those of a human being; it does not follow from this that the sensitive soul is more present in a human being than the intellectual soul.

**From one agent there proceeds only one thing** (inferred from Aristotle, *On Generation and Corruption* II, with the commentary, text 56; and *Metaphysics* XII, commentary 44, where Averroes also expressly states the same). Understand it as follows: from one, insofar as it is one, only one thing can proceed, especially immediately and without a certain order. Or, better and more clearly: from what is simply one in essence and in power, only one thing can proceed. But from what is simply one in essence yet multiple in potency and power, several things can proceed immediately.

**To the question asked of the first substance by “what,” species is more appropriately given as the answer than genus** (the Philosopher, in the *Categories*). This is understood insofar as “more appropriately” does not mean “more known,” for then the opposite would follow; rather, it means “more determinately.”

**The active and passive, according to potency, are said relatively** (*Metaphysics* II and V). This means that expressions signifying action and passion include terms on account of which they are ordered relatively, according to their being said in the category of relation, but not according to their being and properly.

**From the comparative to the positive, the inference is valid** (*Topics* II). This is understood provided that no negation or expression having the force of negation intervenes, and provided that the comparative is taken properly.

**Arguing from an interpretation to what is interpreted, and conversely, the inference is valid** (according to the Philosopher, in the *Topics*). It is said there that the Philosopher’s statement is understood negatively, not affirmatively. The inference from the interpreted to what is interpreted is also valid when taken affirmatively, as in the following valid argument: “He is an official; therefore he is placed in the bishop’s stead.”

**The soul is not subject to alteration** (*Physics* VII). It is said there that the soul is not altered by a corruptive alteration, though it is altered by a preservative or perfective alteration, from ignorance to knowledge.

**Act does not differ greatly from potency** (*On the Soul* I and *Metaphysics* IX). It is said there that this is true when “act” is taken for the act of potency. In this way, anything that actually exists is said to be in act of potency, and is called objective act; opposed to this is objective potency. Objective potency is what does not exist but can exist, and in this sense act and potency are maximally opposed.

**Appetite arises from lack** (*Physics* I). Do not understand this to mean that what is desired is always absent. Matter, for example, desires the form that it possesses. Rather, the point is that such appetite ordinarily arises from lack. Or, alternatively, this is true of the appetite of desire, but not of the appetite of complacency: we ordinarily desire what we do not yet possess, while we take pleasure in what we possess.

**There is no motion toward substance** (*Physics* V). The reason is that nothing is contrary to substance, whereas every motion occurs from one contrary to another.

**From experience of particulars we acquire universal knowledge** (*Physics* VII). This means that the truth of the universal is inferred from the truth of particulars.

**The soul understands when it wishes, but does not sense when it wishes** (*On the Soul* II). The reason is the difference between the objects: the object of intellect is in the soul itself, so that the soul can even understand itself. But the object of sense is not in the sense itself, for the sense does not sense itself.

**Large bodies of water flow more at night than during the day** (*Meteorology* III). This is because of the absence of solar moisture.

**The artisan is wiser than the experienced worker, and the architect than the manual artisan** (*Metaphysics* I). It belongs to the wise person to know everything universally, to know difficult things, and to possess knowledge for its own sake rather than for the sake of something else.

**Listening to stories is an impediment to knowledge of the truth** (*Metaphysics* II).

**The ancient philosophers began to philosophize only after acquiring the necessities of life** (*Metaphysics* I).

**The soul is the cause of a living body in three kinds of cause: formal, efficient, and final** (*On the Soul* II).

**The artisan, according to what he possesses, aims to assimilate himself to nature** (the Commentator, *Metaphysics* II).

**Animals grow more while sleeping than while awake** (*On Sleep and Waking*).

**Animals breathe in moisture** (*On Death and Life*).

[Col. 0978A]

**Bees have a king who does not go out except with all the bees** (same work).

**The soul is infused into the body at God’s command** (in the book *On the Properties of the Elements*).

**A city is not governed by women** (*Politics* II).

**The soul is more precious than the body in every possession** (*Politics* VII).

**Art supplies what nature lacks** (same work).

**Love, hatred, and self-interest often cause a judge not to see the truth** (*Rhetoric* I).

**A friend rejoices in the good things of his friend and grieves over his friend’s sorrows** (*Rhetoric* II).

**Those devoted to truth strive to distance themselves from the fervor of lust** (according to Boethius, in the *Discipline of the Schools*).

## B

**It is good to commit adultery with the wife of a tyrant in wartime.** This is understood as follows: during wartime it is useful or expedient to commit adultery with the tyrant’s wife so that she may reveal secrets; thus the act should not be called good with the goodness of morality, since it is not morally good but evil. Rather, it signifies usefulness, as stated. This Aristotelian statement must therefore be read cautiously, lest anyone think that adultery is permissible at any time.

**Good and evil are contraries** (according to the Philosopher, in the *Categories*). This is understood as follows. Insofar as good and evil are differences of an art, they are not contraries but contradictories, because the evil of a being is not a being, whereas the good of a being is a being. To this it is replied that the Philosopher is speaking of moral goodness, not of the goodness of a being.

**Useful good is not better than honorable good** (according to Seneca). This is understood of useful good insofar as it is not honorable good, since the same thing can properly be both useful good and honorable good.

**Good added to good makes it better** (*Ethics* I). This is understood as follows: if infinite good is added to finite good, it makes the latter better, that is, nobler. But if finite good is compared with infinite good, it does not make the latter better, because all goods together with the First Mover, and the whole universe, do not make the First Mover better than the First Mover is by itself, since it is infinite good.

**Twice three is not six** (*Metaphysics* V, text 19). It should be noted that the proposition “twice three is not six” must be distinguished. The expression “twice” is taken in two ways. In one way it is taken copulatively, so that the conjunction included in “twice” causes the proposition to be a copulative hypothetical proposition. In that sense it merely means: “Twice three is not six,” and it is true; the Philosopher takes it in this way. In another way, the conjunction included in “twice,” namely “and,” is understood, and the expression is taken collectively, producing a categorical proposition with a conditional term; then it merely means: “Three and three are not six,” and thus it is false. Alexander of Aphrodisias explains the passage in this way: “If we take six simply, this is a number; but if you take six as twice three, then it will be said with qualification.” [Col. 0978D] See also Fonseca (*Book* VIII, chapter 7, on the fallacy of composition and division), and others.

**The good of the soul is the best good** (*Politics* VII). This is understood comparatively: the good that is the good of a human being is the best in relation to those two goods, namely, useful good and pleasurable good.

**Good is found in every category** (*Topics* I). This is understood of entitative good, not moral good, because moral good is not found in every category.

**A brute is more animate than a tree** (according to the author of the *Six Principles*). This means that an animal has more powers or faculties of soul than a tree. See above, the axiom: “An animal is more animate than a tree.”

**The more common a good is, the more divine it is** (*Ethics* I and *Topics* II). This is true of a good belonging to the same species. Thus, although being married is more common than being religious, the latter is nevertheless more divine than the former. Again, when the common use of some good does not detract from the person who possesses it, it is not thereby more divine: although possessing a horse together with ten companions is more common than possessing one alone, it is not more divine, because it detracts from the possessor.

**A basilisk kills a human being merely by looking at him** (according to the common saying). The answer is that this should not be understood to mean that it kills a human being through its essential act or through a visible species. Rather, it should be understood in this sense: basilisks are watery and moist, and extremely porous; through them emanations arise that infect the air, and the air, when drawn in by a human being, kills him. In a similar way it is said of a menstruating woman that she stains a mirror merely by looking at it.

**Good and evil are in things; truth and falsity are in the mind** (*Metaphysics* VI, text 8; and *On the Soul* III). The meaning is not that good is not also in the soul, but that good does not terminate in the soul in the way truth does. Good has the character of terminating appetite according to the real being it has outside the soul, not according to its known being, which it has in the soul. Truth and falsity, however, are founded on the thing and terminate in the soul because, as the Commentator says (*Destruction of the Destruction*, first disputation, solution of the twenty-second doubt), truth is the conformity of the thing to the intellect. Thus, when a thing presents itself to the intellect as it is, it is said to possess the complete character of truth.

**Goods without sorrow are more choiceworthy than goods with sorrow** (*Topics* III). This is understood of goods without sorrow, provided that superiority in goodness does not belong to the goods accompanied by sorrow. The statement deliberately says “goods,” because living gluttonously is not good; therefore it is not more choiceworthy than living temperately. It also deliberately says “provided that there is superiority,” because living temperately without sorrow is not more choiceworthy than doing justice with sorrow. The answer is that good accompanied by sorrow seeks the force of goodness together with the superiority of what is true; but doing justice with sorrow is a matter of power.

**Good by virtue of circumstances is more choiceworthy than necessary good** (*Topics* III). This means that good by virtue of circumstances, taken as such, is more choiceworthy than necessary good, taken as good of created nature. The word “nature” is added deliberately because moral good too is necessary; “created nature” is then added because of God; and “taken as such” is added because the same thing can be good by virtue of circumstances and good of created nature. Thus living well is good by virtue of circumstances and is also good of nature.

**Good simply speaking is more choiceworthy than particular good** (*Topics* III). This is understood of anything of which it is true to say that it is good without qualification; thus the authority must be understood with reduplication.

**Nobler good is more choiceworthy than less noble good** (*Topics* III). It would then follow that a noble robber is morally better than a good peasant, and likewise that a tyrant is more choiceworthy than a morally good count. [Col. 0979D] The answer is that the statement is understood as follows: everything nobler, insofar as it is in the same species of nobility, is more choiceworthy than what is less noble; or it is more choiceworthy than what is equally noble in other respects, provided that the other does not possess another nobility exceeding it.

**One’s own good is more choiceworthy than the common good** (*Topics* III). It would then follow that one’s own good is more choiceworthy than the highest good, which is false. It should be known that good is twofold. One kind is common good, possession of which is diminished by its commonness; such common good is not better than one’s own good, but the more it is one’s own, the more choiceworthy it is—for example, a horse or a tunic. Another kind is good whose commonness diminishes nothing, such as the brilliance of the sun or of a candle in a house. The more common this good is, the more divine and better it is. The Philosopher’s statement (*Ethics* I) is understood of this latter kind. The present authority, however, is understood of the first common good, with the qualification that other things are equal and that the common good possesses superiority.

**Good and being are convertible** (*Metaphysics* IV). This is understood of the goodness of a being, not of the goodness of an art. Concerning the latter, the Philosopher says (*Ethics* I) that in different arts there is a different good, and thus every art designates something good. Nor should the authority be understood of moral goodness, concerning which he says in the *Ethics* that a good person is to be honored according to virtue. “Good” should not be taken for the goodness of perfection either, so that something would be called good because it perfects another. It is of this latter kind that the Philosopher speaks when he says: “Time is a certain good.”

**The good of the universe consists in order** (*Metaphysics* XII), because all things are ordered to the First Good.

**Voluntary good is what is good simply speaking** (*Ethics* II).

**Benefactors love those who receive their benefits more than they are loved by them** (*Ethics* IX).

**Good fortune is an impulse naturally produced by God, who moves all nature** (the Philosopher, in the book *On Fortune*).

**Perfect knowledge produces a good life** (Seneca, to his disciple Lucilius).

**Good being, or wisdom, is neither lent nor bought; if it were for sale, it would have no buyer, whereas evil being is bought every day** (same work, letter 4).

**The memory of benefits ought not to grow old** (Seneca, *On Benefits*).

**God’s goodness was the cause of the making of the world and of the origin of all things** (Plato, in the *Timaeus*).

**Blessed is the commonwealth ruled by a wise prince** (*Consolation* I; Plato, *Republic* VI).

**It is good to be praised, but it is worthier to be praiseworthy** (Seneca, in the book *On Morals*).

**Good custom ought to shake off what bad custom introduced** (same work).

## C

[Col. 0980C]

**What is suitable comes from what is suitable** (*Metaphysics* VII, commentary 28). Averroes qualifies this (*Metaphysics* XII, commentary 18): the suitability is not the same in every respect, but it must be such that the agent is in potency and power what the effect is in act.

**Contraries cannot exist simultaneously in the same subject** (*Physics* V). This is true in complete and perfect being; nevertheless, they can exist in a broken or diminished mode of being (Averroes, *Physics* V, commentaries 6, 19, and 52).

**What preserves one contrary destroys the other contrary.** This is true of a particular agent, but it fails of a universal agent. For heaven, through motion and light, preserves all the elements by the power of celestial heat.

**The truth of propositions consists in composition and division** (*On Interpretation* I, Greek: *Περὶ Ἑρμηνείας*). This means that truth and falsity concern composition—that is, affirmative and negative propositions—although this is not objective.

**Celestial bodies have no matter** (according to the Commentator, *Physics* I, *On the Heavens* I, and *Metaphysics* VIII). It is said that the Philosopher takes “matter” properly, namely, that heaven does not have matter of the same kind as the matter of lower things, because if it did, heaven would be generable and corruptible. Hence the same Commentator says elsewhere that in celestial matter there is potency only with respect to place, not the potency for contradiction found in lower things.

**Heaven is the simplest body** (*On the Heavens* I). This proposition is understood to mean either that heaven is not composed of matter and form, according to Averroes, but is matter existing in act; or that it is indeed composed of matter and form, but is not composed of another body specifically prior to it, as mixtures are composed with the elemental bodies, and does not admit foreign impressions or corruptive alterations as the elements do. It admits only certain preservative or perfective alterations.

**The quantity of flesh is determined both by greatness and by smallness** (*Physics* I, text 38). Not every whole can indifferently be perfect under any quantity; therefore neither can its parts. For the whole depends on its parts. Thus, just as an animal cannot be perfect under any quantity whatsoever, neither can its parts—bones, flesh, sinews, and so forth. This determination of quantity is especially apparent in heterogeneous wholes and their parts.

**The heart is the first to live and the last to die** (in *On Death and Life*). This is understood with respect to vital operations, which first appear in the heart rather than in the other members.

**The heart, liver, and brain are the intrinsic principles of an animal** (as physicians say). This appears to conflict with the Philosopher, who says that there are only three principles of a natural thing: matter, form, and privation. The answer is that physicians are not speaking properly of simple principles, but rather of principles that are themselves constituted from principles. The Philosopher’s authority is understood of essential and intrinsic principles.

**The intrinsic principles of every natural transformation are contraries** (*Physics* I). This is understood as follows: the defining principles of every natural transformation are contraries, with “contraries” taken broadly. These principles are present in it: the terminus from which and the terminus toward which, privation and possession, potency and act.

**A human being has the most certain sense of touch** (*On the Soul* II). This is understood in two ways. First, with respect to ease of understanding, judging, and apprehending; in this sense a spider has a more reliable manner of touching, or a more reliable sense of touch, than a human being. Second, with respect to the manner of distinguishing differences among tactile things; in this sense a human being has the more reliable sense of touch. Aristotle does not mean that human beings have the most reliable sense of touch in comparison with the other external senses, since we judge more reliably through sight. Rather, he means that we have the most reliable sense of touch in comparison with other brute animals, and this with respect to the manner of distinguishing.

**Color is the proper object of sight** (*On the Soul* II). This is understood in two ways. First, whatever is seen is seen by reason of having colors in itself. Second, the term “color” is taken in its signifying use; thus color is the proper object of sight, that is, “color” signifies the proper and adequate object of sight. Or it is said that the Philosopher intended the proposition “The proper object of sight is color” in such a way that “color” stands only confusedly; thus no determinate color need be given.

**Material and efficient cause never coincide** (*Physics* II). This is true of matter properly so called, which is called “matter from which,” but not of “matter in which,” which is taken improperly.

**Concepts are not equivocal** (*On Interpretation* I, Greek: *Περὶ Ἑρμηνείας*). This means that concepts of things are not equivocal with respect to the things of which they are natural likenesses.

**The convertible does not prove its convertibility** (according to the common rule). This is understood of the less-known convertible, such as the exponents of a proposition being expounded.

**It is impossible to define circularly** (*Posterior Analytics* II). This is understood of absolutes in the same genus of definition; it is not, at least a priori or a posteriori, impossible with respect to relations or in different genera of definition.

**It is possible to know several things, but to understand only one** (*Topics* III). The answer is that total knowledge, which is what is being discussed here, is one habit comprising many demonstrations; but actual understanding, when compared with such a habit, is of one thing, not of many.

**Knowledge and awareness are innate in everyone** (*Posterior Analytics* I). This is understood virtually according to their causes, and because the intellect naturally assents to first principles.

**Contrary causes are causes of contrary effects** (*Meteorology* IV, text and commentary 40). This is understood per se: the same thing will not per se be the cause of contraries for the same thing. Accidentally, however, it is not impossible for the same cause to produce contrary effects; one will be per se, the other accidentally. Heat per se produces heating, but accidentally produces cooling. Thus the same thing will be the cause of contraries, as the Philosopher says (*Physics* II, text and commentary 30). The example is given of a sailor whose presence is the cause of the ship’s safety and whose absence is the cause of its sinking. It is clear, however, that the sailor’s absence is not per se the cause of the ship’s sinking, because a positive effect per se requires a positive cause per se; such causes are the winds. Similarly, the proposition “Contrary causes are causes of contrary effects” is true of immediate and proximate causes, but fails of mediated and remote causes. Thus digestion is, as physicians say, the cause of thinness and thickness in urine, because it is a remote and common cause. Moreover, the motion of heaven and light are causes of everything that exists here below. For (*Physics* VIII) motion is, as it were, the life of all things constituted by nature.

[Col. 0982B]

**Heaven is indivisible and unalterable** (*On the Heavens* I). This is understood according to separation; nevertheless, it is divisible according to the designation of its parts, because different parts can be designated in heaven. There are differences of position, and heaven is alterable by a preservative or perfective alteration, but not by a corruptive alteration.

**When the motion of heaven ceases, the motion of lower things ceases** (*On the Heavens* II). This is understood as follows: when those three things cease—motion, light, and influence—the motion of lower things ceases. Otherwise it could be maintained that influence would flow into lower things even when the motion of heaven had ceased, through its influence, just as the sun acts through its light and the planets through their influences; in that case motion would not entirely cease in lower things, in the manner just described.

**Both contraries ought to be positive** (*Metaphysics* II). This is understood of contraries properly so called, insofar as contrariety is distinguished from privative opposition.

**Heaven is situated between generable and ingenerable things** (*On the Heavens* I). The answer is that the Philosopher is speaking according to Plato’s opinion and asserts it. [Col. 0982C] Alternatively, it is said that the Philosopher is speaking of the containing middle, such that generable and ingenerable beings are beneath heaven, while outside heaven are beings living the best life, as the Philosopher says in the same place.

**The final cause has the character of the best** (*Physics* III). It is said there that in this authority the Philosopher is speaking of the end for which something is done, not of the end for whom it is done. God, for example, is the end for which human beings act, since human beings do everything for his sake. No one, however, is himself the end for whom the enjoyment of such supreme good is sought.

**A cause is that upon whose being another thing follows** (*Physics* II, and the author of *The Book of Causes*, *On Causes*). This is understood of a total and sufficient cause, because once such a cause is posited, the effect follows immediately. It is not so with a partial cause. Unless one wishes to say: “A cause is that upon whose being another thing follows according to the nature of that being.”

**Body is the highest genus under substance** (according to the Commentator, *On the Soul* I). This is understood as meaning that body is the most general genus among all subordinate genera, but not absolutely.

**That whose end is good is itself also good** (*Topics* III). This is understood of moral and particular goodness, as is clear: if something’s particular end, with the proper circumstances, is good, then it too is morally good. Alternatively, it is understood of a universal end and of the goodness of a being, and in that sense it is again true.

**It is impossible to demonstrate a circle** (*Posterior Analytics* I). This is understood of demonstration within the same genus; in different genera it is indeed possible.

**The final cause and the cause are the same** (according to the Commentator, *Metaphysics* I). It is said there that the Philosopher takes “cause” in the most proper or strictest sense only for the final cause, because such a cause is the most powerful of causes, as is clear in the same place.

**Heaven does not receive foreign impressions** (*Meteorology* I). This means that heaven does not receive corruptive qualities, although it can receive preservative qualities, such as light and motion, since heaven moves.

**A cause is superior to its effect** (according to the author of *On Causes*; *Metaphysics* IX and *On the Soul* II). This is understood of subordinate causes, such that the subordinating cause is superior to what is subordinated to it. Or it may be understood in this way: every cause conducts itself in a nobler manner in causing than the effect does in being predicated, although it can happen that dignities or goodnesses belong to the effect that the cause does not possess.

**What is suitable comes from what is suitable** (*Metaphysics* XII). This proposition is verified under three conditions: that it proceeds from an agent rather than an instrument, from a proximate rather than a remote agent, and from an essential rather than an accidental agent. It was explained somewhat earlier as well.

**A cause is nobler or more perfect than what it causes** (*Meteorology* IV). This proposition is false simply speaking, but accidentally it is true. It fails in the case of matter, for (*Metaphysics* VII, text and commentary 7) the composite is more of a being than matter, because the composite is in act while matter is in potency. For more on this axiom, see Scotus, who explains and qualifies it extensively and well in his *Theorems*.

**Cause and caused are simultaneous** (*Physics* II and *Metaphysics* VII). This is understood of a cause in realized being, not in the process of coming-to-be, or of an actual cause, not a potential one.

**When the subject is corrupted, its accident too is corrupted** (the Philosopher, in the *Categories*). But one might say: “If so, then when a human being is corrupted, the human being’s happiness is also corrupted, since happiness is an accident of the human being.” On this point, note that human happiness has two subjects: one total, namely, the human being; and one partial, namely, the soul. Alternatively, it is said that the human being is the subject of the denomination of happiness, since a human being is denominated happy by happiness, whereas the soul is the subject of happiness’s inherence; thus the first is corrupted, while the second truly remains. It is therefore granted that an accident of denomination can pass from one subject to another; this is not impossible, nor is it contrary to the Philosopher (*Metaphysics* VII). Or it is said that the total subject is corrupted while the partial subject, namely the soul, nevertheless remains, as stated.

Efficient cause is the principle of motion and rest (Physics II). This is to be understood as follows: a cause is the principle of motion, namely, with respect to operation, and it is the principle of rest, namely, with respect to the cessation of operation.

That whose effect is good is itself also good (Rule in the Topics). This is to be understood of that whose particular effect is good: the efficient cause itself, that is, the agent, will be good; and the statement concerns both the goodness of a being and moral goodness.

Causes per se are finite, but causes per accidens are infinite (Physics II, text 50). There the Philosopher uses this argument from analogy. Just as causes per accidens are indeterminate, because many things happen to one thing, whereas the cause per se is one, so the effect per se is one and of one nature. Effects per accidens are many; hence, since things of this kind arise by chance, chance effects are indeterminate.

That whose corruption or rejection is more to be avoided, its contrary is more to be chosen (Topics III). If this were so, it would follow that air should be chosen rather than a house, because the corruption of air is more to be avoided. The answer is that “corruption” is taken in two ways. In one way, it means the infection of something, such as air or another thing. In the second and proper sense, it means a change of a thing whereby it is said to pass from being to non-being; it is in this latter sense that the term is taken here. You might object: if this is so, it would follow that prodigality should be chosen rather than thrift. The answer given there is that the statement concerns that whose contrary is good or choiceworthy; but thrift is not good, since it is a vice.

The counsel of women is ἄκυρον, that is, invalid, or little firm and binding (Politics I, chapter 13). Aristotle says this, not because women lack intelligence or keenness of mind—for they are sharp-minded and often see the truth—but because their counsel is impeded by movements of the emotions, to which they are very subject. Hence we commonly say that a piece of advice which suddenly comes into a woman’s mind is excellent, but that when she has obtained time for reflection it changes, in accordance with Virgil’s line: “Woman is ever fickle and changeable.” For they are led away from the truth either by anger, love, hatred, or personal advantage.

The final cause is that for the sake of which something comes to be, and it is the end of the other causes, being the most important of the causes (Physics II). This is to be understood as follows: the final cause is that for the sake of which something comes to be, that is, for the sake of which the effect comes to be. He then adds one condition and says that the final cause is the most important of the causes, that is, the best, because all the other causes are ordered to it as to an end. But one might object: every cause ought to be a principle; the final cause is not such; therefore it is not a cause. The major premise belongs to the Philosopher (Metaphysics IV). The answer, according to the Commentator, is that the final cause is considered in two ways. In one way, along the path of generation, and thus it is not a principle but the last thing. In another way, along the path of perfection, because the end is more perfect than all the things ordered to the end. In this latter way it is a principle.

Causes are causes of one another (Physics II). This is to be understood to mean that causes can be demonstrated through one another, though not within the same genus of cause, but through different causes.

Of every syllogism, one of the premises ought to be universal (Prior Analytics I). This is true of a syllogism in which the middle term is common in mode and figure.

Things are continuous when their extremities are together (On the Heavens II and Physics III). Distinguish this from contact, even proximate contact. For in that case contiguous and immediately adjacent things could also be called continuous; rather, continuity is distinguished by the sharing of one boundary. Things are continuous when their parts are joined at some common boundary, which is both the end of one part and, at the same time, the beginning of the other.

It is not the composite that understands, but the soul (On the Soul I). The Philosopher does not mean that man does not understand. For since the soul is a part of man, if the soul understands, man also understands. Rather, he means that the soul does not understand according to the body, or in such a way that in its understanding it communicates with the body as with an instrument. Although in understanding it depends objectively upon the body, it does not depend upon it subjectively. For intellection is plainly an inorganic operation, since it is neither produced by any body nor received in any body; rather, it is produced by the soul alone, and received in the soul alone, without any bodily organ.

The corruptible and the incorruptible are contraries (Metaphysics I). This is true if contrariety is taken generally, insofar as it extends to privative opposition.

Contraries are maximally distant (the Philosopher, in the Categories). This is true when speaking of degrees of distance, but not of distance according to perfection or logical order.

The final cause and the agent coincide (Physics VIII). According to some, this is not simply true. According to others, the final cause and the agent coincide in causes per se, but need not coincide in causes per accidens. In another way, it is said that the final cause and the agent are the same without reduplication, but that with reduplication they need not coincide.

Contraries ought to be in the same genus (Metaphysics VII). This is to be understood as referring to the same categorical genus; for otherwise they would not be contraries, as is clear from their definition.

Contrariety is sought in all the categories but found in quality alone (through Boethius). This is to be understood by taking “contrariety” in the strictest sense. If contrariety is taken broadly, however, it also applies to relation, action, and passion. The meaning is that contrariety belongs per se to quality, and per accidens to relation, passion, and also action, namely, insofar as they are ordered to quality.

Physical bodies are most substance-like (On the Soul II). This is to be understood to mean that physical bodies possess more or a greater degree of being than other substances. They are called “most substances,” however, because they are manifest substances. They appear more evidently to our senses to be substances than do other things that are not physical, namely, artificial things; for such things are substances only because of their matter. Physical substances, on the other hand, are substances not only because of their matter but also by reason of their form. The Philosopher says in the same place: “Natural bodies are the principles of artificial things.”

That whose privation is a worse being has a better habit (Topics II). Thus it would follow that the vegetative soul is better than the intellective soul, as is apparent, because the privation of the vegetative soul is worse. The argument is that by the privation of the intellective soul all animals are removed, both human beings and other animals; but by the privation of the vegetative soul all living things are removed, not only human beings but also other animals. The answer is that this authority is not universally true. It applies where one power does not presuppose another; but the intellective power presupposes the vegetative power.

There is no further disputing with one who denies principles (Physics I). This means that one should no longer dispute with such a person within the science whose principles are in question. For this reason he also says that no craftsman has the task of establishing his own principles, whereas the metaphysician has the task of establishing them all.

Deliberation is not about the past but about the future (Ethics VI). The reason is that what has been done cannot be undone, since, as the Philosopher says in the same place, the power to make what has been generated not generated is the one power lacking to what has been generated.

The more common things are easier (Physics I). An objection is that the metaphysician considers the purely most common things; therefore metaphysics will be the easiest science, which nevertheless appears false. It may be said that more common things are easier and better known through confused cognition, but not through distinct cognition. Again, metaphysics is concerned not only with those more common things, but also with abstract substances, or intelligences, as the principal part of its object. Since a thing is denominated from what is principal, metaphysics is rightly called the most difficult science.

Logic and metaphysics deal with the same subject (Metaphysics IV). This is to be understood to mean that both logic and metaphysics are common sciences with respect to their application.

The causes of contraries are contrary (On Generation II). It is said there that the same particular thing is the cause of opposites. This is not to be understood of the universal agent, because such an agent can be the cause of opposites, as is clear in Physics II and Metaphysics II, in the discussion of causes.

Flesh is the organ of touch (On the Soul II). The answer is that through flesh we sense as through a medium. It is also said that touch is in the flesh as in a medium; or it is said that touch is within the flesh, and this too is stated by the Philosopher (On the Soul II). This accords with the common opinion that the nerve is the organ of touch; according to some, however, flesh itself is also the organ of touch.

That whose use is bad is itself also bad (Rule in the Topics). This is to be understood as follows: that whose use per se is bad is itself also bad.

Deliberation is not about the end but about the things directed to the end (Ethics III).

One ought to act quickly after deliberation, but to deliberate slowly (Ethics VI).

Moral virtue concerns pleasures and pains (Ethics II).

Knowledge of the end is useful in a craft (Ethics I).

Sexual intercourse is the destruction of the body and the shortening of life (Aristotle, in *The Secrets of Secrets*).

You ought to associate with those who will make you better, and not equally with those whom you could make better (Seneca, *To Lucilius, His Disciple*).

Deliberation ought to concern things that can be otherwise (Ethics VI).

[Column 0986A] Promise with consideration, and perform more fully than you promised (same work).

Chance is the occurrence of an uncombined event arising from converging causes among things that come to be (Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy* V).

Habit is a second nature (Ethics VII).

A composite of matter and form is not called one unless its form is one (the Commentator, *On the Soul* II).

A man blind from birth is wiser than one who is deaf and mute (in the book *On Sense and the Sensible*).

Eunuchs live longer than those who are not eunuchs; and therefore, because of the small amount of sexual intercourse, a mule lives longer than a horse (in the book *On Length and Shortness of Life*).

## D

There is knowledge of the infinite (Topics III). There it is said to be true privatively, and through negative and conditional propositions, but not positively and affirmatively.

For one descending from the most general genera to the most specific species, it is necessary to proceed through multiplicity (through Porphyry). There it is said that the authority is false in the divided sense, because it is not necessary for the one descending to proceed through multiplicity; but it must be granted in the composite sense: it is necessary for the one descending from the most general genus to the most specific species to proceed through multiplicity.

The giver of a form gives all that follows upon the form (Physics VIII). This is understood in one way as follows: the giver of a form gives all things necessarily consequent upon the form. Knowledge and the virtues, however, are not necessary to the form, because they belong to the form’s well-being, since they are accidental forms perfecting the intellect itself. In another, better way, it is understood as follows: the giver of a form gives to it, formally or virtually, all things consequent upon the form. For in this way God gives knowledge virtually, because he created an intellective form naturally inclined to acquire knowledge.

God is infinite (same work). This is to be understood to mean that God is infinite in power and perfection, but not extensively, or in quantity.

There is no knowledge of equivocal or multiple things (Posterior Analytics II). There it is said, according to Saint Thomas, that there is no knowledge of equivocal and multiple things remaining equivocal throughout their whole common range. But if something equivocal is taken in a definite signification, then some knowledge of it can rightly be possessed.

There is no knowledge of being per accidens (Metaphysics VI). This means that there is no knowledge of an accidentally true proposition as a proximate object of knowledge, although there can indeed be knowledge of the thing signified by the conclusion.

There is no knowledge of corruptible things and of things capable of being otherwise (Posterior Analytics I). This means that there is no knowledge of singular categorical propositions as proximate objects of knowledge, although it remains true that there is knowledge of such things as signified by the propositions, or as the most remote object of knowledge.

[Column 0986D] Circular demonstration is impossible (same work). This is to be understood within the same genus of demonstration and with respect to the same genus of cause; it does not apply to many demonstrations belonging to the same conclusion and the same genus of cause.

The defined thing is better known than its defining parts (Physics I). There it is said that the Philosopher means that it is easier to possess the concepts of the defined thing than the concepts of the definition, while it nevertheless remains true that the concept expressed by the definition may be better known than the concept that can be defined. Hence, in order to possess the concept of a definition, it is not enough to conceive the concept of the genus or of the difference, as Buridan says. But in order to possess the concept of the defined thing, it is enough to have the concept of the species.

The ten categories are the ten principles of natural things (Porphyry). This is understood of definitional principles standing for natural things, and not of principles of being.

He who says that the species are separate speaks correctly (Metaphysics VII). [Column 0987A] Thus it appears that real universals must be posited if they are separate from singular things. It is said there that the Philosopher compares the universal said in the first way with that said in the second way. Those who posit real universals as separated from singular things therefore speak better and more remarkably than those who say that they are conjoined. He does not thereby mean that such universals should be posited; rather, he means that Plato and his followers spoke better and more remarkably.

God and the virtuous person can do wrong, although they are not of such a character (Topics IV). Aristotle’s intention here is to show that no one is called bad merely because he can do bad things, and he supports this in two ways. First, because the virtuous person and God—whom it is certain are not bad—can do bad things. There is no ambiguity in this with respect to the virtuous person: he can do bad things, in accordance with the saying of John of Damascus, “Everything created is in itself changeable according to choice.” With respect to God, if he is taken as that absolute and immense good, it is impious to hold this, although he can do things that may now appear bad, which, if he were to do them, would be good. Or the proposition can be understood of God conditionally, with an impossible antecedent: for example, “God can do bad things if he wills.” Nothing prevents a conditional from being true when both its antecedent and consequent are impossible. For example: “If a human being is a donkey, he has four feet.” As for the gods of the pagans, however, no one fails to grant this, and Aristotle may perhaps have spoken here according to their custom. Ovid likewise says:

> A great man in war, second to none in piety,  
> Aeneas, oppressed by the hatred of unjust Juno.

There he calls Juno unjust, although she was believed by the peoples to be a goddess. Finally, it can also be said, not without probability, that the term “God” is taken in one way substantively, as it is taken in Metaphysics XII, where it is said that God is the best and eternal animal; it is not taken in that sense here. In another way it is taken adjectivally, in which case it means “divine” and “virtuous,” that is, “possessing virtue”; and in this sense it is taken in the authority cited above and in Politics I.

God is the soul of the world (On the Heavens I; in the same place he similarly calls all the intelligences souls). The answer is that “soul” is taken there improperly, according to a certain likeness. The likeness is this: just as the soul properly so called governs, distinguishes, and moves the body, so an intelligence does the same for its sphere, to which it is assigned.

Definition is in a category (Topics II). The answer is that the Philosopher speaks figuratively there, putting the whole for a part. He means that definition is placed in a category not in its entirety, but only according to its parts.

Difference is taken from form (through Porphyry). This is said of a form insofar as it has the force of a formal or perfectional condition.

Demonstrations are not about things that are per accidens (Posterior Analytics I). This is understood, in accordance with Averroes (*Physics* IV, commentary 20), of things that are per accidens rarely; but it fails with respect to things that are per accidens always. For true, non-essential demonstrations can be made concerning things that are per accidens always; these are called dialectical demonstrations.

Dialectic is not a science (Metaphysics XII and Topics I). It is said there that dialectic is not a special science but a common science; or that the discussion concerns the real sciences, namely, those that treat of things, not of beings of reason and similar objects.

Two contrary habits are not simultaneously in the same thing (Posterior Analytics II). This means that although it is true that they are not actually in the same thing, it nevertheless remains possible for one to be actual and the other potential or dispositional in the same thing at the same time.

God is the best and eternal animal (Metaphysics XII). The answer is that the Philosopher speaks according to the opinion of ordinary people, who said that the gods were animals and universally posited many gods. It is also said that “God” means a celestial body, so that the sense is: God, that is, a celestial body, is the best and eternal animal.

A smallest fire can be given (through the Commentator, Physics VII). The answer is: among actual fires, and in a determinate order, a smallest fire can be given; but relatively speaking, it is not possible to give a smallest fire simply.

The defined thing is better known than the definition (Topics VII). This is understood according to universal concepts apprehended by the intellect, and of imperfect cognition, and with respect to us. It is not true of perfect cognition, as is clear to anyone who considers the matter.

A definition of the whole that applies to a part is not good (Topics VI), for the definition is proportioned to the whole.

Things that endure longer are better (Ethics I). This is understood in one way as follows: some things endure longer by reason of act and potency, and in this sense it is granted that what is good and more enduring is better. If they endure longer by reason of matter, however, the statement is false; for then a stone would be better than a human being, since a stone endures longer than a human being. Or, according to Rupert, it is understood of things belonging to the same species, or at least provided that the less enduring thing does not possess some better accompanying condition. For this reason prime matter need not have a better condition or a more excellent substantial form.

There can be knowledge of defined things, or individuals (Metaphysics XII). This is understood according to universal concepts apprehended by the intellect.

God understands nothing outside himself (Metaphysics XII). Thus it would follow that God does not understand lower things. The answer is that God understands nothing outside himself as through something outside God, while it nevertheless remains true that God understands things outside himself through his bare essence. Or it is said that he does not understand things outside himself through a medium or phantasm, but according to his simple essence. But you might still object: it is said in *On the Soul* III, “Every understanding being must contemplate phantasms.” The answer is that this is understood of the human or dependent intellect, and not of the divine intellect.

[Column 0988C] “As for the parts of the soul, we say …” (On the Soul II). There he appears to wish to say that the soul has parts. The answer is that the Philosopher is speaking of subjective parts, or powers of the soul, and this according to reason, not according to the reality of the thing.

The ultimate differences of things do not admit of more and less (Porphyry and Metaphysics VIII, text and commentary 10). This is true of perfect substantial forms considered in themselves, but it fails in the case of accidents. Thus the Commentator glosses the passage (Metaphysics VIII, text and commentary 10), where he says that a substantial form does not admit of more or less: one human being does not have more humanity than another human being; and if this occurs, it occurs insofar as the form exists in matter. That accidents admit of more and less is clear, as Porphyry and Aristotle also testify in the *Categories*.

There is no knowledge of things per accidens (Metaphysics VII). This is to be understood to mean that there is no knowledge of things that are accidentally or contingently true through categorical propositions expressing actual inherence and present truth.

A demonstration ought to proceed from the first, true, immediate, necessary, and better-known causes of the conclusion (Posterior Analytics I). This is understood of a demonstration of the reason why, which proceeds from first and immediate propositions. Hence the following does not follow: “A demonstration does not proceed from first and immediate principles; therefore it is not a good demonstration.”

Two accidents cannot be in the same subject (Metaphysics XII). This is to be understood of two natural and extended accidents: they cannot be in precisely and adequately the same subject, and in the same part of the subject, although spiritual accidents can be in the same subject.

God is an eternal substance and a simple act, moving as the intelligible and desirable object, as the efficient and final cause of the whole universe; he is supreme delight and supremely good, and wholly immutable, unalterable, incapable of being affected, and incapable of being changed (Metaphysics XII). There the Philosopher means that all perfections that are perfect and contain no imperfection belong to God and are God. For whatever belongs to God is God. This is understood as follows: God is an incorporeal substance, taking “body” in every possible sense, namely, both for a composite body and for a substantial body; and he is eternal, that is, having neither beginning nor end; and he is pure act, containing no potency; simple, that is, not composite; and he moves all movable things as their intelligible and desirable object.

God is a being than which nothing better can be conceived (Physics IV). From this it follows that God is the most perfect being, and this is simply true.

There is no determinate truth concerning future contingents (On Interpretation I, περὶ Ἑρμηνείας). This is said to be true of a future contingent whose truth does not depend upon a proposition that is determinately true at present. But the truth of the proposition “A human being will move” depends upon the truth of the present proposition “A human being is moving.”

[Column 0989B] The richer are generally more faithful to the community in common matters (Politics III). This means that, for the most part, they are more trustworthy—not with respect to procuring the common good, but rather with respect to agreements and pacts. In such matters the rich are trusted more than the poor.

Two bodies are not in the same place (Physics IV and On the Soul II). This is understood of a proper place, not a common place, because a proper place is one that contains only the thing located, as air does. It is also understood naturally; for through supernatural power, several bodies can be penetratively present in the same place.

The dimensions in prime matter are everlasting (through the Commentator). This is according to the opinion of Averroes, who, together with Aristotle, held matter to be eternal and attributed to it certain indeterminate dimensions, which would be delimited and modified by each agent according to the nature of the form to be introduced.

The disposition lying between agent and patient is called action with respect to the agent and passion with respect to the patient (through the Commentator, Metaphysics IX). This is understood as follows: the thing that is called “action” in relation to the agent is called “passion” in relation to the patient. Nevertheless, action and passion are not properly relatives; for reciprocity and denomination are not sufficient to make something properly belong to the category of relation. In addition, it is required that such terms be predicated of one another through the expression “relative to” essentially. This is not the case with “agent” and “patient.”

A definition ought not to be given through opposites (Topics VI). The sense of this axiom is that one opposite is not properly defined through the other unless it is defined precisely as an opposite, since understood in this way it cannot be understood without its opposite. Therefore, since the being of relatives is being toward another—and since their entire concept and whole nature consist in a certain relation or opposition—one such opposite cannot properly be defined except through the other opposite. By contrast, habit should not be defined through privation, heat through cold, or good through evil, because the being of these things does not consist in such a relation. If, however, these are defined insofar as they are opposites, then mention of their opposites should also be made in their definitions. Thus habit may be said to be that which is opposed to privation; heat, that which is opposed to cold; and good, that which is opposed to evil. See more concerning this axiom below under the letter N, at “No good definition …”

Only God is simple (Metaphysics VI). It would therefore seem that a substantial form is not simple. The answer is that “simple” is taken in two ways. In one way it means what lacks composition of parts with one another, though not composition from something else; in this sense the intellective soul is called simple, since it is not composed of parts, although it is equally capable of being composed with matter. In another way, something is called simple when it is neither composed from something else nor capable of being composed with something else. In this latter sense the soul is not simple; God, however, is simple, because he is not composed and is not in any way capable of composition. Moreover, it can be said that God has no composition whatsoever, neither physical nor metaphysical; for he contains no potency or imperfection, but is pure act. All other things, however, possess some such composition, namely, of act and potency, and so forth.

The same judgment applies to equipollent expressions; common rule. This is understood with respect to consequence, namely, from one to another: the consequence is valid. It need not hold in every respect, however, since it need not hold with respect to the mode of signifying, as is clear in the case of “human being” and “capable of laughter.” For “human being” signifies what it signifies absolutely, whereas “capable of laughter” connotes something.

God and nature do nothing in vain (On the Heavens and On the Soul III). This is true according to the whole species, or in most individuals; but nature can do something in vain in a single individual, as when it produces a human being with six or eight fingers.

To doubt about individual matters is not useless (through the Philosopher, in the category of Relation and in Metaphysics). This is understood as doubting by arguments about individual matters that are not self-evident and sufficiently determined; such doubt is not useless. To doubt about things that are manifest and already sufficiently determined is not only useless but also foolish and harmful. Hence theologians rightly say that one who doubts in faith is an unbeliever—namely, one who, seeing the decree of some ecumenical council or the unanimous consent of the holy Fathers concerning some dogma, nevertheless considers himself permitted to doubt that dogma. For the interpreter of Sacred Scripture is sufficiently certain, as is likewise the judgment of such a legitimate and general council, and so forth.

This principle—“It is not useless to have doubted about each thing,” as it is commonly recited—therefore applies especially to matters that are by no means self-evident and that involve much perplexing obscurity. In such matters, those who can argue for both sides easily attain the truth, as is said in the first book of the *Topics*. It is therefore not useless to doubt in matters that are ambiguous in both directions, without adhering wholly and firmly to either side. For, as the common proverb has it, “He who knows nothing doubts nothing,” and so forth.

The same point is expressed in another interpretation: “To doubt about individual matters is not useless” should not be understood as though everything were incomprehensible and nothing could be established or decided as true or false, as the Academics and Pyrrhonists did when they doubted everything and asserted that we could know nothing. They were called ἀπορρητικοί, that is, doubters or those who suspend judgment, as Gellius testifies in Book II, chapter 5. Rather, Aristotle’s meaning is this: to doubt about both sides of a contradiction because of probable reasons compelling one to doubt is highly useful. Accordingly, if someone doubts without reason, the doubt will instead be useless.

[Column 0990D] To abandon sense and follow reason is a weakness of the intellect (Physics II and VIII). This is to be understood as applying when someone knows the testimony of the senses with certainty and yet, on account of the slight notion he has through the intellect, judges otherwise by the intellect. This is indeed a weakness of the intellect, because he judges badly. Otherwise it is certainly true that the judgment of the intellect must not infrequently correct the judgment of the senses, since the senses can be deceived in various ways and for various causes.

Diverse operations indicate diverse forms (through the Commentator, *Metaphysics* XII). This is to be understood of different supposita, but not within the same suppositum.

God does not understand simple things (through Avicenna). This means that God does not understand through species in the same way that we understand.

God is unnameable by any name (through the Commentator, *On Causes*). This means: God is unnameable by any perfect name that conveys or expresses every perfection which a human being can know in him. For this reason many names are attributed to God, such as wisdom, prudence, savior, and the like; hence there are not merely one, but many names.

It is of the nature of contraries to expel one another (Metaphysics I). This means that contraries cannot be in the same subject inherently and formally, though they can be so apprehensively and containingly, because they are contained by the same thing.

The more a thing is capable of being acted upon, the less power it has. This is to be understood of active power. It remains compatible with this that they are mutually passive powers, as is clear in the case of prime matter in *Physics* I.

The transparent is invisible (On the Soul II). This means that it is scarcely and with difficulty visible. The reason is that it is not seen through a proper species, but through an extrinsic species or through color.
