Division ought to be made through opposites (through Boethius). This is to be understood with respect to mediate species, but not immediate species.

Money is the measure of all things, because it is a surety for whatever we need in every necessity (Ethics V).

[Column 0991B] What is worse is always for the sake of what is better (Politics VII).

There are two kinds of right, namely legal and natural. Natural right is that which has the same force among all human beings; legal right is that which has been established by law (Ethics V).

It is difficult to resist habit, because it resembles nature; it is easier to change habit (Ethics VII).

The pleasures of beasts are bad by nature, but those of bad human beings are bad by habit (same work).

Pleasure preserves the agent in its work (Ethics X).

There are two kinds of life, namely contemplative and political; of these the contemplative is better, because it is divine, whereas the other is human (same work).

Deception and ignorance belong more properly to animals than knowledge does (On the Soul II).

There is a twofold appetite in man: the intellective appetite, which is called the will; and the sensitive appetite, which is called the concupiscible appetite (On the Soul III).

[Column 0991C] Teaching naturally proceeds from the teacher according to the operation which teaching has upon the pupil (in Aristotle’s *Poetics*, Book I).

Difference is taken from form (through Porphyry).

The half is prior to the whole in potency, but the whole is prior to the half in act (*Metaphysics* VI, text and commentary 16).

A pupil ought to be teachable, attentive, and well-disposed: teachable in ability, attentive in exercise, and well-disposed in mind for listening (in Boethius, *On the Discipline of Schoolboys*).

God is the highest good, above every substance and every nature; all things seek him, since he is of complete perfection and has less need of society (Plato, *Timaeus*).

Nature has produced us teachable and has given us reason, imperfect indeed, yet capable of being perfected (Seneca, *To Lucilius*).

Learning produces good morals; therefore let each person have the taste imparted to him (Seneca, *On Morals*).

[Column 0991D] Wealth ought to be used, but not abused (Seneca, *On Morals*).

Do not make determinations about doubtful matters, but keep your judgment suspended (Seneca, *On the Formal Life*).

You shall love God, but imitate him in this: be able to benefit all and harm none (same work).

God cannot do evil; but nothing that God cannot do is anything positive; therefore evil is nothing positive (Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy* III).

Divine providence does not impose necessity on things that come to be, because, if everything happened by necessity, rewards for the good and punishments for the bad would perish (same work).

## E

The principles of all the categories are the same (*Metaphysics* XII, text 19). This means that they are the same proportionally: in every category there is something analogous to matter, something analogous to form, and something analogous to privation. Likewise, this is true of remote principles, but false of proximate ones (Averroes, commentary 22, same work).

[Column 0992A] The principles of being and knowing are the same (*Metaphysics* II). The answer is that the Philosopher means that the principles are the same in the same demonstration of the *propter quid* kind: a thing has being through its *propter quid* account just as it has being in demonstration, and it is known in that way as well, as is clear from the *quid nominis* demonstration of the *propter quid*. Or this is understood of intrinsic and essential principles.

From two beings in act one third thing does not come to be (*Metaphysics* VII)—namely, one thing per se, though one per accidens does. But from matter and form one thing comes to be per se, because one is in act and the other in potency.

### E

**Beings do not wish to be badly ordered** (*II Metaphysics*). From that authority it would follow that all natural beings of the whole world or universe were well and most excellently ordered, and thus that there would be no monsters. It should be said that although a monster, considered in itself, is not well ordered, nevertheless, in relation to the beauty of the universe, it is well ordered; and from it the beauty of the universe shines forth. [Col. 0992B]

**Being and unity are convertible** (*IV Metaphysics*). For they are transcendentals, of which the former is related as a subject and the latter as its proper attribute.

**An effect bears a likeness to its cause** (*Through the author of* The Book of Causes). This is understood of particular causes, but not of universal causes—that is, of God and the intelligences—for the rule does not apply to them.

**Metaphysical beings are abstracted from the senses** (*II Physics* and *IV Metaphysics*). There it is said that Aristotle does not mean that they are really distinct, but distinct with respect to the mode of consideration: the metaphysician considers those things that have no relation to motion, whether with respect to matter or to sensible qualities. In this respect the metaphysician’s consideration differs from that of the physicist. This is because, although those transcendentals—being, unity, goodness, truth, and others of the same kind—are found in material and sensible things, they are also found in immaterial and insensible things. Therefore they are said to be abstracted by indifference, and may properly be considered without matter and without a sensible subject. As for the intelligences, which likewise belong to metaphysical consideration, it is clear that, both in reality and according to their concept, they are abstracted from matter and the senses. [Col. 0992C]

**From being and being there does not arise being per se, except accidentally** (*II Physics*). That is, from two beings in act there does not arise one being per se.

**The essences of the categories are unmixed** (*Through Themistius, II* On the Soul). This is understood to mean that a term of one category is not essentially predicated of a term belonging to another category.

**The efficient cause and matter coincide** (*II Physics*). This is understood of the material cause from which something is made; but it does not rule out matter in which something exists—as the subject of a science, namely the intellect—being an efficient cause.

**Nothing comes from nothing** (*I Physics*). This is understood of natural action, for every natural action presupposes a subject. Or otherwise: nothing comes from nothing through a natural agent, but it does come from nothing through a supernatural agent, namely God. For he created this entire universe from nothing, and even today creates each rational soul from nothing. [Col. 0992D]

**Unmoved beings are not a subject of physical consideration** (*II Topics*). This is understood as follows: beings that are not considered under the aspect of motion, either as causes of effects or as principles of things that proceed from principles, are not a subject of physical consideration. The soul, however, is reduced to mobile being as to an efficient cause.

**Goodness is a property of being** (*IV Metaphysics*). This is understood of being outside the soul and of being in act, since goodness belongs first to such being. For in *VI Metaphysics*, in the final commentary, it is said that good and evil are also in things, whereas truth and falsity are in the soul.

**From what is not quantitative, quantity does not arise** (*II On the Heavens*). It is true that a continuous quantity does not arise from what is not quantitative, although a discrete quantity may. And although the three conclusions of grammatical science are not continuous quantity, since they are simple qualities in the soul, they are nevertheless discrete quantity, since they constitute a number. [Col. 0993A]

**From one thing nothing follows** (*II Prior Analytics*). This is understood to mean that nothing follows syllogistically from a single proposition, although something does follow enthymematically from one proposition.

**The same effect does not have diverse causes** (*Through the author of* The Book of Causes). This is understood to mean that the same effect does not have diverse subordinate causes. Therefore it does not follow: “The intellect infers; therefore there are no premises,” since the premises and the intellect are subordinate causes, related respectively as the efficient cause and its instrument.

**Being is neither univocal nor equivocal** (*IV Metaphysics*). This means that being is not equivocal by chance, but is so by design, or by analogy: it belongs primarily to substance and secondarily to accident.

**Being has diverse species** (*I Physics*). This is understood by taking “species” to mean less universal terms, but not by taking “species” for properly so-called habits. For being is not a genus, but an analogical term with respect to its inferiors. [Col. 0993B]

**The equal belongs to the being of quantity** (*I On the Heavens* and *in the Categories*). This is understood of finite quantity, but not of infinite quantity.

**From truth there follows nothing but truth** (*II Prior Analytics*). This is understood to mean that in a good and formal consequence, nothing but truth follows from a true antecedent.

**Nothing is prior to the eternal** (*VIII Physics*). This is true according to time, while nevertheless something may be prior according to nature.

**The same differences are not divisive of a lower and a higher term** (*In the Categories*). This is understood of essential differences, but not of accidental ones; for example, quantity is divided into finite and infinite.

**Eternal things are not in time** (*IV Physics*). This is understood commensurately: an adequate measurement by time does not apply to eternal things.

**The things we know are few in comparison with those we do not know** (*Through Themistius*). It is true that the things we know determinately and in particular, rather than universally or confusedly, are few. For universally we know every being through this proposition: “Every being either is or is not.” [Col. 0993C]

**An excessively powerful sensible object corrupts the sense** (*II On the Soul*). If this is so, then one of the two things is not the other, since one can undergo corruption through being acted upon, while the other cannot. But the sense can undergo corruption through being acted upon, whereas the intellect cannot; therefore sense and intellect would be the same. It is said there that the proposition is understood with respect to disposition, not essence: an excessively powerful sensible object corrupts the sense with respect to its disposition, but not with respect to its essence. Thus it corrupts the matter of the sense, but not the matter of the sense-organ, by reason of the expression used.

**The embryo first lives a vegetative life and afterward a sensitive life.** This means that the operations of the vegetative power appear in the embryo before those of the sensitive power.

**A good furnished with circumstances is more choiceworthy than necessities without circumstances** (The Philosopher, *in the Ethics*). This is understood of the good of generated nature, and not of the good of generating nature. For the former is good without qualification, and the highest good is most choiceworthy. [Col. 0993D]

**Hunger belongs to the hot and dry, and thirst to the cold and moist** (*II On the Soul*). This is understood as follows: hunger is an appetite for hot and dry nourishment, in order to strengthen the natural heat; thirst is an appetite for the cold and moist, in order to restore the radical moisture in which the natural heat operates.

**Echo differs in species from the primary sound** (*Through the Commentator, II On the Soul*). This means that echo and sound differ in species according to their specific account, while nevertheless being one and the same sound in reality. Or it may be said that they differ according to the appearance presented to hearing.

**From what is not a human being there arises a human being** (*I Physics*). It should be understood that “from what is not” does not refer to the circumstance of the material cause, but to the circumstance of time: after what is not a human being, a human being comes to be.

**There ought not to be several principles of the same thing** (*I On the Heavens* and *I Physics*). This is understood within the same genus of causation, but not across different genera. For the first cause is the cause of everything in the genus of efficient or conserving causation; and the form, or soul, is also a cause in the genus of formal causation. [Col. 0994A]

**Being is prior to God** (The Philosopher, *in the Categories*). This means that being is prior with respect to consequence, but not with respect to the nature of existence.

**An effect is not a cause** (*V Metaphysics*). This is understood with reduplication: an effect, precisely as an effect, is not a cause.

**There are not several acts of the same thing** (The Commentator, *On the Substance of the Orb*). This is true of things that are specifically and essentially distinct from one another.

**There are eternal species of things.** This is understood formally or virtually, either in themselves or according to their causes.

**The things we wish to do for our friends are more choiceworthy than those we wish to do for anyone else** (*III Topics*). This is understood of true friendship, that is, friendship formed for the sake of an honorable good. Accordingly, friendship with a beloved woman is not true friendship, since it is not formed for the sake of an honorable good. [Col. 0994B]

**From equality of things known one argues to equality of sciences** (*Through a common conception of the mind*). The reply is that this is not simply true. Rather, from precise equality of the things known and of the modes of knowing, one may equally perfectly argue to equality of sciences. Therefore this consequence is invalid: “The human intellect knows as much as God; therefore it knows in the same way as God.”

**Being outside the soul is divided into the ten categories** (*V Metaphysics*). There it seems to be maintained that no being in the soul belongs to a category, and consequently it seems that grammar, logic, and rhetoric do not belong to a category. It should be said that no being belongs to a category if it exists only objectively and imaginatively in the soul; nevertheless, a being existing in the soul inherentially, such as knowledge, does belong to a category. [Col. 0994C]

**Being and truth are convertible; likewise falsity and non-being** (*VI Metaphysics*). It is said that truth is understood insofar as these are properties of being, but the statement does not hold insofar as they are properties of a proposition.

**It is in the interest of the person being instructed to demand as much certainty in each field as the nature of the subject matter admits** (*Ethics*, chapter II). One seems to expect persuasion from a mathematician and to demand demonstration from an orator; so too, says Boethius, in *I On the Trinity*. It is characteristic of a disciplined person to seek certainty in each field according to what the nature of the subject requires.

**Things are numerically identical when their matter is one** (*V Metaphysics*).

**Examples require not verification but elucidation** (The Commentator, *II On the Soul*).

**It is from the fact that a thing is or is not that an utterance is called true or false** (Through the Philosopher, *in the Categories*).

### F

**The end is the best and better thing in this way—not absolutely, but in relation to each substance** (*II Physics*, text 74). Note that the end is called “best” and “better” not absolutely—that is, in relation to all things—but it should be understood as best and better in relation to the things ordered to the end.

**Something is called futile when what exists for the sake of something else does not come about for the sake of that other thing** (*II Physics*, text 62). The meaning is that an action is called futile when it does not attain the end for which it was performed. Thus, if someone walks for the purpose of purging the bowels but does not purge them, the walking will be called futile, provided that what is done is suited to attaining such an end. Otherwise it is not called futile. If someone washes his hands so that the sun may be eclipsed, and afterward it is not eclipsed, the washing will not for that reason be called futile, since it contributed nothing toward that end.

**Flame is more fire than coal** (Through the Philosopher, *in the Topics*). This means that flame shines more brightly than coal; it is not more perfect, or more truly fire, with respect to essence, but it is more perfect with respect to light. [Col. 0995A]

**The end is the principle in intention and the last thing in execution** (*I Physics*). This is understood of agents acting by purpose and deliberation, but not of agents acting purely naturally, or of the operation of nature. In the latter there is no apprehension of the end.

**Acting belongs to form, while being acted upon belongs to matter** (*I On Generation*). This is true principally; nevertheless, the action of the form, insofar as it is material, subjective, and denominative, also belongs to the whole composite.

**The report that all people proclaim or cry out is not usually altogether empty and false** (*VII Ethics*). Likewise, in *On Sleep and Waking*, what is said by everyone or by most people carries credibility that it is so. It is said that what many proclaim provides credibility. Hence the Commentator says there that it is impossible for a famous statement to be entirely false in itself. This is understood of wise people, wholly worthy of trust. If several wise people were to proclaim and report something, it would provide credibility. For, as Aristotle says in the *Sophistical Refutations*, one ought not to attend to what just anyone says, but to what the wise say, and so forth. [Col. 0995B]

**There is no form of a form** (*VII Metaphysics* and through the author of *The Six Principles*). This means that a form does not have another form essentially and compositionally, such that one form essentially composes another; but it may do so accidentally, as sciences are forms of the soul.

**Form is simple and indivisible** (*II Physics*, text and commentary 31, and through the author of *The Six Principles*). Form is called simple because it is not composed of parts of different kinds that are divisible; and it is called indivisible because it is not divisible into parts of different kinds. For the quiddity of each thing consists in something indivisible, however much that thing may be extended and divisible according to its physical existence.

**The end is better than the things ordered to the end.** This axiom is true of the end *of which* something is the end, but is not universally true of the end *for which* something is done. Thus it applies only to the principal end, not to a secondary end. [Col. 0995C]

**Human happiness is something best, most delightful, and most choiceworthy** (*I Ethics*). This means that human happiness is the best thing among human operations.

**The false is called non-being** (*V and VI Metaphysics*). That is, insofar as it is such. Or it may otherwise be understood by taking “non-being” improperly, namely, for what is not true.

**That power is futile which is not reduced to act** (*I On the Heavens*, text 32, and *III On the Soul*, text 45). This is true of a power that is not reduced to act according to its species; but a power is not thereby called futile even if it is not reduced to act in every individual. A fuller explanation of this axiom may also be found below.

**The end moves the efficient cause** (*II Physics*). It does so in the manner in which such an efficient cause is capable of being moved. Hence, since God is altogether immutable and does indeed effect all things but does so for his own sake as an end, he is said to be moved by the end only entirely metaphorically and improperly. [Col. 0995D]

**Form is prior to matter** (*VII Metaphysics*). If this were so, it would follow that form was ungenerable and incorruptible, which is false and contrary to the Philosopher (*I Physics*), since form is generated. It should be said that the Philosopher means that form is prior to matter in priority of dignity and perfection, but not in priority of nature and generation.

**Form is that which gives being** (*II Physics*). This is understood of substantial form, which is intrinsic and essential to a natural thing and gives the thing its formal being—that is, its mediate being. “Substantial” is said in contrast to accidental form; “of a natural thing” is said in contrast to a thing dependent upon it, namely God; “intrinsic cause” is said in contrast to extrinsic causes, such as the celestial bodies; and “essential” is said in contrast to the primary qualities, which are causes of accidental qualities, such as heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. Form is said to give being to the thing—that is, formal being, by its mediation—in contrast to matter, which belongs to its entitative being. Matter, by its own nature, does not have formal actuality, but only entitative actuality, by which it is an actual being. Nevertheless, it is formless, indeterminate, and wholly potential. [Col. 0996A]

**That power is futile which is not reduced to act** (*I On the Heavens and the World*, text 32). The reason is that, as is said there, God and nature do nothing in vain; the same is asserted in *III On the Soul*, text 45. The reply is that this is true of a power that is not reduced to act according to its species, but it is not called futile even if it is not reduced to act in every individual. For it is not impossible for some power to be frustrated in an individual, since nature can be impeded in acting, as Aristotle proves in *On Sleep and Waking*.

According to others, the reply is different: the proposition is true when that power is principally ordered to the act toward which it is said to be in potency. If it is not principally directed toward that act, however, it need not be a futile power merely because it is not reduced to act. For example, suppose that the quantity of the heavens were in potency to the act of division. If it were never reduced to that act, its power would not be futile, because this possible thing, the quantity of the heavens, is not principally ordered through its power to division. Its power has several objects, but is directed rather toward disposing the heavens for the intelligence, so that through it the heavens may receive qualities suited to their nature and to their proper operations, toward which it is principally ordered. Although it is not reduced to the act of division, its power is not for that reason called futile.

The same applies to the power of division in the smallest natural things. For in *I Physics*, in the *Physics Lecture*, a smallest quantity of flesh is posited, as is clear from text and commentary 36. Although the power of division in such things is not reduced to act, since there is nothing smaller than the smallest thing naturally disposed, that power in the quantity is nevertheless not futile. Its power has several objects and is not principally ordered to this; rather, it is ordered to disposing matter for the form, so that the subject of which it is the subject may receive dispositions suited to its nature for its proper operations, toward which it is principally ordered. These are the points commonly made concerning this matter. See more in Zimara, folio 88. [Col. 0996B–C]

**Fortune is an accidental cause of things that occur outside what is always or frequently the case, to agents possessing a purpose** (*II Physics*, text 52). This means that fortune is a cause with respect to a chance effect, but the effect itself is not a cause and consequently is not fortune. It is called an accidental cause—that is, an indeterminate cause—to indicate that the chance effect does not proceed from determinate causes. Hence the Philosopher says that fortune is an indeterminate and hidden cause.

“Of things that occur,” and so forth, means with respect to unintended effects; intended effects are not fortune. There are two kinds of effects that occur beyond intention. Some are idle in the first instance: these are not good or evil, such as rubbing one’s beard and similar actions. Others occur beyond intention but, by contrast, are not idle; it is in such cases that fortune should be found.

“Always and frequently” means that fortune occurs in contingent effects that happen rarely. Albert the Great says that if someone going to the marketplace were always to happen upon gold, this would not be called fortune, nor would it be said to occur through fortune. Note that something is said to occur outside what is always and frequently the case in two ways. First, because of the rarity of the time, as in a solar eclipse. Second, because of the causes, since it rarely proceeds from determinate causes. The authority is understood in this second sense. Thus it is clear that a solar eclipse is not called fortune, because it does not occur through the rarity of its cause, but through the rarity of the time.

It is said to occur in agents acting by purpose in order to indicate that fortune occurs only in agents acting through deliberation. For this reason, chance is not fortune, since it occurs in things that have no purpose. It is clear from this that infants and brute animals have no fortune, but only chance. [Col. 0996D–0997A]

**The finite is that to which an addition can be made.** The proposition is not universally true, for an addition cannot be made to every finite thing. A circle is a finite figure, yet no addition can be made to it (*I On the Heavens*, commentary 12, and *II On the Heavens*, text and commentary 23). That the circle is a finite figure is clear because it is contained by a single boundary. Moreover, finite beings, considered in their power, cannot receive an addition in reality according to their proper nature, since each being proceeds from its principle according to the capacity naturally given it to proceed, and not otherwise. Thus such things are perfect in their genus, but not absolutely perfect, since absolute perfection belongs only to glorious God, as the Commentator says in *V Metaphysics*, in the chapter on the perfect. Being infinite in power is of this kind.

**The end is the cause of causes** (*II Physics*, text 31). Note that “end” is here taken properly for the principal end, since it is what moves the agent itself. The proposition is understood with respect to form and existence itself, but it fails with respect to privation. Thus, with respect to positive existence, the principal cause is the account of the end, because it necessitates the agent, the agent necessitates the form, and the form necessitates matter. With respect to corruption, therefore, there is no end in itself, but there is an end insofar as something is generated from it; nevertheless, that corruption does not occur without something corrupting. [Col. 0997A–B]

**Form is in a certain way privation** (*II Physics*). This means that there are two kinds of form: positive and privative. Privation may indeed be a privative form, but never a compositive, or positive, form.

**Form is not separable from matter** (*XII Metaphysics*). This is understood of material form. The rational soul, however, is not material, since it is not drawn out of the potency of matter; rather, it is created by God from nothing, incorporeal and indivisible. It can therefore be separated from matter.

**The substantial forms of the elements admit of more and less** (Through the Commentator, *I On the Heavens*). This is understood of accidental forms. Or it may be said that the Commentator spoke according to his own view: the substantial forms of the elements are intermediate, as it were, between accidental forms and other substantial forms. They agree with the latter insofar as they give being, but with the former insofar as they can, like them, be intensified and diminished. [Col. 0997C]

**A figure is that which is enclosed by one boundary or by boundaries** (*I Metaphysics* and *I Euclid*). “Per se” is understood, in order to exclude substance, which is enclosed by a boundary or boundaries accidentally, namely through magnitude, as is clear in *I Meteorology*.

**There is no proportion between the finite and the infinite** (*I On the Heavens*, text 52). This is understood determinately, but it may also be understood indeterminately. Or otherwise, it is understood of a proportion of commensuration, but not of a proportion of order. For example, if the sea were infinite, it could not be drained by a finite sponge; nevertheless, such a sponge could be immersed in it and united with it. Similarly, according to the Catholic faith, two natures are united in Christ: one infinite, namely divinity, and the other finite, namely humanity—not through the commensuration of one nature with the other, but through a certain suitability or order of one nature to the other. Human nature is ordered to the divine as to its cause and complement, and as an image to its exemplar, and so forth. There is therefore nothing surprising in the union of two such natures, even though one is infinite and the other finite. [Col. 0997D]

**The finite and the infinite belong only to quantity** (*III Physics*). Just as quantity is said in two ways—both as quantity of bulk and as quantity of perfection—so “finite” and “infinite” may be said in one way or the other.

**Form is the whole quiddity of a human being** (*VII Metaphysics*). This means that form is the complete quiddity of a human being, and that formal quiddity is more perfect than material quiddity.

**Form is more substance than matter** (*I Physics*). This is understood insofar as “more” signifies perfection. [Col. 0998A]

**Anything comes to be from anything** (*ibid.*). There it is said that the Philosopher is not speaking assertively, but as reporting what had been accepted from the ancients, since Anaxagoras said that forms lay hidden in matter. Or it may be said that the Philosopher means that every natural being that comes to be, or is naturally suited to come to be, comes to be from any other thing—that is, from matter—because the matter is the same in all generable and corruptible things.

**Cold does not enter into the operation of nature** (*IV Metaphysics*; Averroes, *VII Metaphysics*, commentary 3). Averroes limits the proposition in the same place: cold does not operate per se toward form; nevertheless, accidentally, insofar as it tempers heat—which per se gives form—it can, and in fact does, cooperate in the operations of nature in that way. For by tempering heat, cold renders it proportionate to the operations of nature; thus accidentally and with a secondary intention it cooperates. [Col. 0998B]

**Form is something divine, excellent, and desirable** (*I Physics*). This is understood as follows: form is an intrinsic and essential principle that exists in a thing, and it is divine by resemblance, because it resembles the first being. “Divine” is not taken essentially, since in that sense God alone is divine.

**Imagination is an active power** (*II On the Soul*). That is, it is a preserving power of several phantasms, capable of turning back upon them whenever it wishes.

**A simple form is the subject of nothing** (According to Boethius). This is understood of a simply first simple form, such as God, who is the subject of nothing.

**Fortune is hidden and undisclosed to human beings** (*II Physics*, text 53). The reason is that, since a chance effect has no per se cause, but only an accidental one, it can have many causes, because it can be joined to various effects that proceed per se. Thus meeting a magistrate on the road may occur because one had gone out for a walk, or to conduct business, or to make a purchase, or for other reasons. Since this effect therefore has no determinate cause from which it proceeds per se, it is rightly called hidden. [Col. 0998C]

**We can say both that nothing occurs through fortune and that something occurs through fortune, for each statement is said truly and reasonably** (*ibid.*). Nothing occurs per se through fortune; something does occur accidentally through it. But this is to occur only in a qualified sense.

**Fortune is in a certain way a cause, and is not a cause** (*II Physics*, text 54). This is understood as follows: fortune is not a cause simply speaking, but is an accidental cause. Aristotle says there that accidental causes are infinite—that is, indeterminate in number—and illustrates this beautifully in the same place.

**The corporeal form is never separated from matter** (Through the Commentator, *I Physics*). The reply is that Averroes is not there speaking of the corporeal form posited by Avicenna, whom he criticizes under this name in several places. Rather, he is speaking of those indeterminate and perpetual dimensions in matter. Accordingly, for him prime matter is by no means a being in formal substantial act. [Col. 0998D]

**It is easier to do something than to do it rightly** (*VI Topics*, chapter 1).

### G

**Generating what is like oneself is the most natural of the works of living things** (*II On the Soul*, text 34). This is not said because it is more inseparable than certain other operations of the soul—for example, nourishing, sensing, and understanding. Indeed, nourishment, by reason of its inseparability and thus its necessity, is more natural to a living thing than generation. Rather, among the operations of the vegetative soul, this operation is more perfect and more strongly intended by nature. Generation contributes to the preservation of the whole species, whereas nourishment contributes to the preservation of the individual living thing.

**The heaviest of all things is what is in the middle** (*I Meteorology*). Earth is absolutely heavy, since it rests beneath every body, as is clear in *IV On the Heavens and the World*, text and commentary 16. The proposition is understood among the simple bodies, but it fails when comparing them with mixed bodies, since there is a mixed body heavier than earth, such as lead. This is Averroes, *III On the Heavens*, commentary 9. [Col. 0999A]

**There is no generation of generation** (*II On Generation*). Form and the composite are generated through generation, but generation itself is not.

**Let universals rejoice, which, if they exist, are monsters** (*ibid.*). The reply is that Porphyry is speaking ironically and mockingly against Plato, who posits universals as real and distinct from singulars—for example, a common horse and a common human being—from which singulars would derive their being.

**Generation and corruption are contrary motions** (*V Physics*). This is said broadly of motion, so that it signifies nothing other than a certain physical change, whether instantaneous or successive. Or generation and corruption may be taken as aggregates: generation together with the preceding alteration, or corruption together with the preceding alteration. Taken as aggregates in this way, generation and corruption can properly be called contrary motions, on account of the contrary qualities through which one and the same subject is altered toward the generation of one substantial form and the corruption of another substantial form. [Col. 0999B]

**The genus is the matter of the species** (Porphyry). This is understood metaphorically, not properly, because just as prime matter is indifferent to receiving any form, so the genus itself is indifferent to receiving any species.

**The generator does not join together things that are diverse** (Through the Commentator, *XII Metaphysics*). It should be said that this is true when each of the things is a being in act. It does, however, join matter and form, one of which is in potency and the other in act.

**The generator and the generated must be of the same species** (*VII Metaphysics*). This is understood of univocal and particular generation, but not of universal and equivocal generation.

**To generate is the generator** (*I Physics*). The reply is that “to generate” is taken in two ways. In one way, concretely, and then generation is the generator; in another way, abstractly, and then the statement is not true. [Col. 0999C]

**The generation of one thing is the corruption of another** (*I On Generation*). This means that the generation of one is followed by the corruption of another. When a corpse is generated, for example, the animal itself is corrupted. The statement is therefore true of the generation of the elements. The qualification “at least” should be added, because sometimes the generation of one is followed by the generation of many, as is clear in the division of an eel; and such generation of many can occur artificially. Thus the authority should principally be understood of natural generation, not artificial generation. See Toledo, *I Physics*, question 3.

**A heavy body moves in the middle by reason of the middle, as a man moves in a ship** (Through the Commentator, *I On the Heavens*). It is said there that the Philosopher means this correctly: just as a man moves in a ship not per se but through the motion of the ship, so a simple heavy body existing in the middle does not move unless the middle moves along with it. [Col. 0999D]

**A heavy body existing above moves downward because its heaviness is weighed down, or because what remains prevents it** (*ibid.*). The reply is that the meaning is only this: if something were naturally heavy and rested violently above, and then ought to begin moving downward, it is necessary that there be something remaining that prevents this—namely, that its heaviness be impeded—so that after resting the heavy body cannot begin its motion except through something that weighs down its heaviness and something remaining that prevents it. In this sense the authority is true.

**Substantial generation does not have a being in act** (*I On Generation*). That is, not as its subject. For what is changed through alteration is the whole composite. But what is changed through generation, and remains the same under both termini of the change, is prime matter. The composite that existed previously does not remain, while what succeeds it did not previously exist. Therefore neither composite, or being in act, is changed; for what is changed must remain the same under both termini of the change. The subject of generation and corruption is therefore not a being in act, but a being in potency, namely prime matter. [Col. 1000A]

**The generator does not make the form** (*VII Metaphysics*). That is, it does not make it in isolation or as the complete term of generation, for the complete term of generation is the composite itself.

**Generation is production from non-being to being** (*IV Physics*). This accords with Averroes’ statement: “Action does not give plurality but perfection.” That is, action causes things that previously existed in potency afterward to exist in act; it does not cause more things to exist in act than existed in potency—more things in complete being than there were in incomplete or potential being.

**Generation occurs for the sake of form, and not for the sake of matter** (*II Physics*). The reason is that form is more nature than matter, that is, more perfect than matter.

**Gracious physicians begin their consideration with what natural science demonstrates** (*On Sense and the Sensible*). [Col. 1000B]

**The most welcome benefits are those in which there was no delay except the recipient’s modesty** (Seneca, *On Benefits*). In accordance with the common saying: “He who gives quickly gives twice.”

### H

**A human being is above all intellect** (*IX Ethics*). This means that the intellect is the nobler and principal part of the human being. Or it may be said that the person who lives according to reason and intellect is more properly called a human being than one who lives according to sense, and so forth. Hence the Commentator says, in his discussion of the universal, against those who live according to sense: “Woe to you, who have been counted among the number of beasts, while ignoring the divine and excellent thing that is in you.” [Col. 1000C]

**We place the study of the soul among the foremost disciplines** (*I On the Soul*). It is to be placed first among the natural sciences, but not absolutely; for absolutely, among the human sciences, metaphysics is first.

**Human beings for the most part attain the truth** (*I Rhetoric*). This is true of particular facts, but not of universal ones.

**This is a being in the soul; therefore this is a being: the consequence is invalid** (*I Sophistical Refutations*). For example: “This is a human being according to opinion; therefore this is a human being.” The consequence is invalid because to be a human being according to opinion is to be a human being only in a qualified sense.

**A bestial human being is a hundred thousand times worse than a beast** (*VII Ethics*). This means that a human being who lives like a beast according to sense and not according to reason is a hundred thousand times worse than a donkey or some other irrational animal.

Homo est quodammodo finis omnium (II Physics). It is answered that Aristotle there is speaking of things made by art. With respect to such things, he says that man is in a certain way their end, because, in truth, all the arts have been invented for human convenience. This maxim can also be understood without qualification, so that man is in a certain way the end of all natural beings; for all these things were created on account of man. Indeed, even metaphysical or supernatural beings—such as the intelligences—have man as their end by a secondary intention: by their primary intention they act for their own sake, and by their secondary intention for man.

Man is the most certain of all animals (On Respiration).

Very fat men rarely beget children (On the Generation of Animals).

Honor is greater in the person honored than in the person who honors (I Ethics).

Man always needs some pleasure, as a kind of recreation, because of the many labors that confront him (VII Ethics).

People of one nation are naturally more friendly toward one another than toward those of another (VIII Ethics).

[Col. 1001A] The wise or happy man needs external things to some extent, because nature is not sufficient by itself for contemplation; he must have a healthy body, suitable food, and the remaining services. Yet he does not need many things, since it is not necessary for the happy man or philosopher to be lord of land and sea (X Ethics).

A disposition is more perfect than a privation (II On the Heavens).

The wise man is supremely happy (X Ethics).

Man is naturally a political animal (I Politics).

It is an honorable and great kind of revenge to forgive (Seneca, On the Formula of Life).

The moisture of food, coming to the brain and becoming chilled, causes rheum or catarrh in human beings (On Sense and the Sensible).

I

It is impossible for a continuum to be composed of indivisibles (VI Physics and I On the Heavens). This is understood to mean that it is impossible for a continuum to be composed of indivisibles as integral parts. Although there may be some continuum composed of indivisibles, it is nevertheless composed of essential parts, not integral parts.

The infinite, insofar as it is infinite, is unknown (I Physics, text 35; II Metaphysics, text 11; and I Posterior Analytics). This means that if the infinite existed in magnitude or multitude, it would, insofar as it was such, be unknown to us. This is true with respect to knowledge of the thing, not of the name; for as far as the name is concerned, the infinite is known to be that which has no boundaries. It is then said that the proposition is true of the created intellect, which is finite, but not of the intellect of God, which is infinite and possesses infinite comprehension. Such an intellect can, of course, also comprehend the infinite.

In nature there is no thing so base or small that it is not possible to discern in it something divine and worthy of admiration (I On the Parts of Animals, chap. 5). And according to the authority of Hermes, minerals and plants possess properties which, if they were known to human beings, would enable them to do whatever is accomplished by magical arts.

We possess innately a way of knowing and proceeding from what is better known to us to what is better known by nature (I Physics, text 2). That is, the natural order of teaching is for us to proceed from what is better known to us to what is better known by nature. This order is called the order of instruction, not the order of nature. For although it accords with our natural way of knowing, it is not equally conformed either to nature’s way of acting or to the nature of the things themselves. As Aristotle says in the same place, the same things are not better known to us and to nature, or better known without qualification. Hence, according to the order of nature, one often proceeds from what is better known by nature, or better known without qualification, to what is better known to us. These things are better known to us not through distinct but through confused cognition. Thus, although this natural process is the starting point of inquiry, once scientific knowledge has been acquired one can proceed otherwise.

[Col. 1001D] Individuals are infinite in number (Through Porphyry, chap. 3). This is understood not positively but negatively—that is, because their number is not certain and determinate; for there can always be more and more. Or, alternatively, they are infinite not actually but potentially. Species, however, are finite in both ways, actually and potentially, because the species are always the same, although the individuals are not.

There is no alteration in the intellective part of the soul (I Physics). This means that there is no corruptive alteration in the intellective part of the soul, but only perfective alteration. This does not mean that it is perfected in species—for it is altered not only from ignorance to knowledge, but sometimes also from knowledge to ignorance, and not always from evil to good, but sometimes from good to evil—but that it is not corrupted or damaged as some composite or material form is, which can also be corrupted by such alterations.

The intellect understands everything and becomes everything (III On the Soul, text 4). The statement that the intellect in knowledge becomes individual things is understood in two ways. In one way, realistically, and thus it is false. In another way, receptively: the intellect can receive the species of all intelligibles. In this sense the present authority is understood. For just as the pupil is receptive of all colors, so the soul is the species of all intelligibles, because it can receive within itself the species of all intelligibles.

The intellect knows infinitely many intelligibles (ibid.). It is answered that, in a universal proposition, the intellect knows infinitely many intelligibles. Or it may be said that Aristotle is speaking of confused and general cognition, not of distinct and determinate cognition.

Infinites must be left aside by art (Through Porphyry). It is likewise alleged that there is no knowledge of infinite things. It is answered that this can be understood in one way of infinite things according to the aspect by which they are infinite, and in that sense there is no knowledge of them. In another way: there is no knowledge, whether definitional or demonstrative, of infinitely many singulars, because singular terms cannot be defined by a stable and lasting definition.

To understand is to undergo [something] (III On the Soul). This is understood of intellection acquired through phantasms, not through bare essence. God, however, understands in the latter way, because he understands all things through his bare essence.

“This is an affirmative proposition: Socrates may not exist” (II *περὶ Ἑρμηνείας*, *On Interpretation*). This is understood as follows: the proposition has a true affirmative element, namely, concerning its modality, but it is nevertheless negative with respect to what is asserted.

In every good and formal consequence, the opposite of the consequent is incompatible with the antecedent; this is a rule of logic. This is understood of the contradictory opposite, or sometimes even of the contrary opposite; but it is not always true of subcontraries. Or it may be said that the opposites of the consequent are incompatible with the antecedent insofar as they cannot stand together in truth, as is clear to anyone who considers the matter.

The same thing does not follow from either of two contradictories. This is understood with respect to the same contingent matter: two contradictories do not follow conjointly from one another.

In every being that is moved, matter must be conceived (XII Metaphysics). It is answered that “matter” is taken here improperly for the subject of motion, not for the other part of the whole composite.

It is impossible for there to be one principle of a natural thing (I Physics). This is understood exclusively, as meaning that there is only one principle and not several. Otherwise, if there are three, there is certainly also one.

Among eternal things, a plurality of individuals under the same species should not be posited (XII Metaphysics). It would thus follow that there is only one intellect in all individuals of the human species. It is answered that this is understood of eternal things abstracted from matter both in reality and in conception, such as the intelligences, which are without matter or body and can be perfectly defined without reference to a body. Nevertheless, it remains true that there are many intellective souls, and many human intellects corresponding to the multitude of human beings, because the rational soul has an essential order toward the body and does not have complete being unless united to the body. Therefore, even when separated, it is defined by reference to the body. Likewise, although matter is eternal—that is, neither generable nor corruptible—in each supposit there is a different matter numerically, not specifically.

In eternal things, being does not differ from being possible (II Physics). The meaning is that whatever is in that which is truly and properly eternal—and only God can be such—is itself actual. God is pure actuality, in whom there is no potency internally, although external potency may properly be granted: God can do many things that he neither has done nor will do. But this is not internal potency; it is external potency.

All things are in God (XII Metaphysics). This is understood exemplarily, causally, as cause, in an ordering and conserving manner—not inherently, subjectively, or compositively.

[Col. 1003A] The same accident is not in different subjects (IV Metaphysics and I Physics). This is understood in one way as meaning that one simple accident is not in different subjects, neither of which is a part of the other, with respect to the same part and at the same time. In another way, one and the same accident is not in different subjects as inhering in them, although it can be in different subjects as existing in them. For example, knowledge is in a human being denominatively, in the soul inherently, and in a book objectively.

The intellect is a being in pure potency (III On the Soul). It must be known that “intellect” is taken in two ways. In one way, considered in itself and absolutely, it is a being in pure potency and is like a blank tablet on which nothing has been depicted. In another way, it is considered as possessing certain species and notions within itself, and in this sense it is in actuality.

That which is innate to us cannot be taken away from us (II Ethics). It is answered that the Philosopher understands this as follows: what is positively innate to us cannot be taken away, whereas what is privatively innate to us can indeed be removed from us, though with difficulty.

It is impossible for one subject to have several forms (Through the author of *On the Substance of the Orb*). This is understood of substantial and total forms, not accidental or partial forms. Alternatively, if one holds the opinion that several substantial forms exist in the same composite, the authority is understood to mean that it is impossible for several non-subordinated forms to exist in one and the same composite. If that opinion is not held, the authority is, as stated, simply true.

It is impossible for action and passion to proceed from one and the same nature (III On the Soul). It is answered that, in true action and true motion, which are found in bodies or bodily powers, it is impossible for action and passion to proceed per se from one and the same nature. Nevertheless, in equivocally moved things, the same thing can be per se mover and per se movable—that is, per se understanding and understood—in abstract souls or intelligences, with the exception of the material intellect.

To understand is either imagination or not without imagination (I On the Soul, text 13, and III On the Soul, text 35). This is understood of the intellect in the process of coming to be, not of the acquired intellect or habit. Although at the beginning, when the intellect is moved and begins to know, it needs a phantasm, once a thing has been understood and the intelligible species have been preserved, it no longer needs a phantasm. The meaning may also be that the intellect does not understand sensible things without imagination or a phantasm, but understands immaterial things—namely, separate substances—and itself without a phantasm.

Finally, Averroes says in *The Life of Aristotle* that one should hold that the possible intellect of man can gradually be perfected by moral, mathematical, and natural sciences, until at last, through union with the agent intellect as form with matter, it knows God and abstract substances immediately, without any phantasm, and thus intuitively, even in this life. Although Averroes’ conception is false, it is perhaps not wholly foreign to Aristotle’s view. From this it is clear that Alexander of Aphrodisias and his followers reason incorrectly in *The Life of Aristotle* from this text and text 39 of III *On the Soul* against the immortality of the rational soul.

Alexander argues as follows: If the soul does not exist without imagination, it cannot exist without a body, according to texts 12 and 13 of I *On the Soul*. But according to text 39 of III *On the Soul* it cannot understand without a phantasm or imagination; therefore, according to Aristotle, it cannot exist without a body. This argument of Alexander, which some wrongly consider insoluble in *The Life of Aristotle*, can most probably be dissolved by answering the minor premise in one of the three ways just mentioned.

The same thing, remaining in the same condition, is always apt to do the same thing (II On Generation, text 56). This is understood to mean that the same thing, insofar as it is the same and remains in the same condition with respect to the same matter, disposed in the same way and through the same subject, is naturally apt to do the same thing.

In substantial generation no sensible subject ought to pre-exist (II On Generation). This means that the same pre-existing subject should not remain as an actual something constituted by formal and substantial actuality. For generation is a change of the whole into the whole, and therefore terminates in some new composite.

In no genus of causes is there a process to infinity (II Metaphysics). This is true of essentially subordinated causes.

The intellect cannot understand several things simultaneously and at once (II Metaphysics). This is true of distinct and determinate understanding. It can nevertheless understand in a confused manner.

It is impossible for a multitude to be actually infinite (III Physics). This is understood to mean that it is impossible for the multitude of divided beings to be actually infinite; but nothing prevents a continuum from being infinite. A continuum has infinitely many parts, but potentially rather than actually or separately, in such a way that it cannot be divided into so many parts that it could not be divided further. Hence it is customary to say that a continuum has infinitely many parts not categorematically but syncategorematically.

In accidental predications, the thing itself and its being are not the same (VII Metaphysics). Aristotle is said to mean that in accidental predications the thing itself—that is, the material signified for which the term stands—and its being itself—that is, the formal signified which the term connotes—are not the same.

In the sleep of an animal, the sensitive power rests and the vegetative power works (Through the Philosopher, in *On Sleep and Waking*). This should be understood to mean that in the sleep of a perfect animal the sensitive soul rests from the operations that belong to it insofar as it is sensitive, but does not cease from the operations that belong to it insofar as it is vegetative. For in sleep the animal is nourished and grows, indeed usually more than while awake.

In moving things, speed follows the proportion of the power of the mover (VI Physics). A distinction is required here. Movers are of two kinds. Some are natural, and such things act according to the utmost of their power; the authority is understood of these. Other movers are voluntary, and the authority does not concern them. Since the first mover is voluntary and free, it is not necessary for it to move the first mobile with infinite speed, however infinite its power or vigor may be.

In mathematics there is neither good nor an end (III Metaphysics). This means that mathematics does not teach how a human being ought to conduct himself morally, and that it does not demonstrate without qualification, or through a final cause, but only through a material cause. Or it may be said that the mathematician does not consider things under the aspect of the good or of the end, but considers them under the aspect of measure.

The intellect is the actuality of no body (III On the Soul). Some commentators there say that this is understood of the divine agent intellect. More suitably, in accordance with the text, it is said that the intellect is not the actuality of any body as of a subject. It exists mediately in the soul itself, following upon the soul at that prior level which it shares with intelligences or separate substances, but not according to that level which it shares with informing forms. Further, “the actuality of no body” means that intellection is a wholly inorganic operation, very different from vision and similar operations of the soul, which are produced both by the soul itself and by a bodily organ or instrument. For this reason they are also called operations of the whole composite, not merely denominatively but truly elicited by it.

The same thing is not moved by different motions (IV Physics). This is true primarily and per se. Per accidens, however, nothing prevents it, as is clear in the case of a man aboard a ship, who is moved eastward by himself within the ship and westward by the ship itself.

The place of the part and of the whole is the same (II Physics). This is understood of a common natural place, not of a proper place.

[Col. 1005A] It is impossible for the same thing to be in different places (IV Physics). This is understood of the whole thing existing simultaneously and at once, and naturally. Supernaturally, however, nothing prevents the same body from existing in several places through divine omnipotence.

The infinite cannot be traversed (VI Physics). This is understood of the infinite in actuality, not of the infinite in potency. A continuous space of this kind has infinitely many parts potentially, not actually.

In a finite magnitude there is no infinite power (IV Physics). This means that in a finite magnitude there is no infinite power actively and inherently. “Actively” is specified because a finite magnitude can indeed possess infinitely passive potency. “Inherently” is specified because of non-inherent potency, which is the glorious God.

Infinite things accrue to one thing (II Physics). This is understood successively, not as all occurring simultaneously.

It is impossible for there to be only one element (II On the Heavens). This is understood exclusively, as meaning that it is impossible for only one element to exist in such a way that there would not also be several elements.

The same thing does not bring itself from potency to actuality (IV Metaphysics). This is understood of the potency to exist or to be generated. Nothing brings itself—that is, produces or generates itself—from potency to actuality, since this is impossible. Otherwise heated water, whether alone or aided by its surroundings, would certainly restore itself to its former coldness.

A return from privation to disposition is impossible (In the category *Opposites*). This is true of privation that removes a power, but it fails of privation that removes an act. Someone situated in darkness is deprived of the actual exercise of sight, yet when light arrives he passes to seeing the light. But from blindness there can be no transition to seeing, because blindness removes not only the act but also the power, and so forth.

The subject of motion and the term of motion are the same (V Physics). This is understood as follows: the subject and term of motion are the same in prime matter. It is not understood of the proximate term, which is the subject of motion.

[Col. 1005C] The intellect undergoes something from the intelligible (III On the Soul). This is understood of the created intellect, which receives species from the intelligible, and of intelligences that understand through an intellection added to them. The intellect of the first mover, however, does not receive species in order to understand through an added determination. Its intellection is its very essence, and therefore it alone is pure actuality.

The intellect is not a body, nor a power in a body (The Commentator, III On the Soul). The commentators say there that the Commentator is not to be followed with respect to his claim that the soul is not a power in a body. In truth, the intellective soul is an informing form, not an assisting form, as he supposed. Alternatively, it may be said that the intellect is not a power in a body—that is, it is neither a power drawn from the potency of matter nor dependent upon the body in its being, as other informing forms are.

That which is nourished does not undergo anything from nourishment or food, but the reverse (III On the Soul). This authority should be understood to mean that what is nourished does not undergo anything from food per se and primarily. Nevertheless, it can undergo something secondarily and per accidens, because every agent, in acting, is acted upon in return, provided that it shares matter with what it acts upon, as is stated in I *On Generation*. The food is assimilated to what is nourished, not what is nourished to the food. Hence the principal action per se belongs to what is nourished.

In every genus equivocations lie concealed (VII Physics). Aristotle does not mean that genera are properly equivocal, but takes “equivocation” very broadly. He means that in every genus there are species possessing different specific accounts among themselves, though not with respect to the genus. Or he may mean that genera signify their significates more broadly than species do.

In those things in which friends can participate more, they are more choiceworthy than things in which they cannot (II Topics). It would thus follow that one’s friends’ peas are more choiceworthy than other people’s chickens; likewise, that the mechanical arts of one’s friends are more choiceworthy than the liberal sciences of others. The statement is therefore understood, first, of goods that are good per se and honorable, because of the first objection. It is understood with the proviso that other goods do not possess a superiority of goodness, because of the second objection. According to others, however, it is understood with restriction or reduplication: all goods in which friends participate, insofar as friends participate in them, are more choiceworthy. Thus, although the arts, as servile arts, are not absolutely more choiceworthy, insofar as friends participate in them they are more choiceworthy. The same is said concerning the other objection.

In itself, however, the statement remains as given: the liberal arts are more choiceworthy, just as we say that an agent as agent is nobler than a patient. Nevertheless, it can happen that the patient is absolutely nobler than the agent, as occurs when fire acts upon a human being. A human being is unquestionably absolutely nobler than fire.

That which is choiceworthy per se is more choiceworthy than that which is choiceworthy per accidens (V Topics). It is answered there that this is so insofar as it is choiceworthy per se. Absolutely, however, the other thing can sometimes be more choiceworthy.

That thing is better whose privation is worse (III Topics). This authority is not simply true, for there is an objection concerning sensing and understanding. The privation of sensing is worse than the privation of understanding. Yet in truth the disposition of sensing is not better than the disposition of understanding. This is clear because the privation of sense entails the privation of intellect, since nothing is understood unless it was previously in sense. Likewise, the privation of prime matter is worse than that of the composite, yet the disposition of the latter is not better. It is answered that the statement is understood where one does not include the other. But the privation of sense in a human being also includes the privation of intellect in a human being, and the privation of prime matter includes the privation of the composite.

Fire is not visible. The author of *The Sphere*—according to Marsilius—is understood as follows: fire in the first sphere is not visible because, in that condition, it has the greatest transparency and subtlety, as is clear from the fact that the stars of heaven are seen through it. Fire is visible only insofar as it is mixed with earthly matter, as is the fire around us.

The same thing is not both known and opined (II Posterior Analytics). This is true in the same respect. Nevertheless, something can be known in one way and opined in another, namely, because of different means. Insofar as we know something through demonstration, we know it; insofar as we opine that same thing through some probable reasoning, we opine it.

The intellect, the intelligible, and intellection are the same in things abstracted from matter (III On the Soul, text and commentary 19). The statement is simply true only of God. In some way it is also true of intelligences, which in understanding are in no way dependent upon a body, either as an instrument or as a subject. It is not true, however, of our possible intellect, which depends upon phantasms in understanding, since the one who understands must contemplate phantasms, as is said in III *On the Soul*, text and commentary 39.

The same thing does not act toward its own corruption (II Physics). Seed appears to contradict this, because the form of the seed causes the body to be animated; and as soon as the body is animated, the form of the seed ceases to be. Therefore, the seed acts toward its own corruption. It is answered that the authority is understood of its primary and per se action. Nothing prevents the same thing from acting per accidens toward its own corruption. This is clear because the organization of the body is produced by the form of the seed together with the influence of the celestial body; yet when that organization occurs, the form of the seed ceases to exist. Thus the seed acts per accidens toward its own corruption.

The agent that disposes the matter and introduces the form is the same (Averroes, VII Metaphysics, commentary 31). The proposition is true in substantial transmutation produced by nature, and is understood with respect to what immediately disposes the matter. It is possible to dispose matter by altering it, while nature nevertheless introduces the substantial form. Although there are many differences between nature and art, which I do not wish to pursue at present, one of them is this: art cannot immediately produce a substantial form, because all forms introduced by art are accidents, as is clear from the *Physics*, commentary 13.

We do not possess smell (The Commentator, II On the Soul). It therefore appears that we lack a true sense. It is answered that human smell is less perfect than the smell of other animals in perceiving odors, both with respect to distance and with respect to faintness. Other animals perceive faint odors and perceive them at a great distance, as dogs, vultures, and similar animals do. Human beings perceive only odors that are near and intense, but they surpass other animals in perceiving a greater number of differences among odors.

An indivisible cannot be equal (I Physics). It therefore appears that the intellect cannot be informed by sciences and virtues and be equal or unequal to another intellect, since it is indivisible. It is answered that an indivisible cannot be equal with respect to a bodily quality, such as heat or cold, but it can be equal with respect to a spiritual quality; and this is not problematic.

An indivisible, wherever it turns, turns wholly (III On the Soul). This authority is understood in two ways. In one way, it means that an indivisible is not, according to one part, turned toward one thing and, according to another part, toward another; in this sense it is simply true, because an indivisible has no parts. In another way, “wherever it turns” means “according to every part it turns”; in this sense the authority is false, because it presupposes that an indivisible has parts, which is not true. A fuller answer can be taken from the explanation of the following maxim.

When an indivisible or simple thing is reached, it is reached wholly or not at all, because it does not have one part and another part (IX Metaphysics, text 22). The meaning is said to be that it is not reached part by part—for in simple or indivisible things “the whole” cannot be spoken of except by privation of composition and parts—but it does not follow that, if it is reached, it is reached in every way. Thus, even if God is known by man in this life, or is clearly seen in the next, he is indeed known wholly and seen wholly, but not totally or in every way; for in that manner he is known only by himself.

For God is both simple and incomprehensible. Although he is not something, he is nevertheless a certain one, equivalent to infinitely many things. Thus the same reality is hidden and manifest to inspection, but hidden from comprehension. This does not mean that, as in some composite thing, one part is hidden while another appears; rather, that one reality, existing as an absolutely infinite perfection, can be known in infinitely many ways.

The divine intellect contemplates all things (Through Boethius, *On the Consolation*). Consequently, it seems that the divine intellect contemplates phantasms. This consequence is false and contrary to the Philosopher, XII *Metaphysics*, where it is said that the divine intellect is purely active. The authority is understood in two ways: objectively and instrumentally. It is therefore answered that the divine intellect understands phantasms objectively, not instrumentally; this is what Boethius means.

Fire is the principle of growth (II On the Soul). This is understood as follows: fire—that is, natural heat—is the instrumental principle of growth.

The agent and the patient are not the same (IX Metaphysics). This is understood with respect to the same thing.

The intellect is stripped of everything that it understands (III On the Soul). If this is so, it seems that the intellect cannot understand itself. It is answered that the statement is understood while the intellect understands directly through proper and distinct species, and does not yet understand reflexively through reflexive and foreign species. In that way it understands itself.

What has been corrupted cannot return as numerically the same thing (II On Generation, text 70, and II On the Soul). Aristotle asks in that place whether a return occurs according to the same numerical identity, so that what has been corrupted and changed returns numerically the same. The sense of the question is well known: he asks whether water, fire, a lion, a color, or anything of this kind, once corrupted, can again be produced by some natural agent as precisely the same numerically. He resolves the question by saying that in eternal substances the same thing returns numerically: thus the sun returns numerically to Aries. This is because it is not changed in substance but moves locally; and the return of a mobile corresponds to the kind of change it undergoes. Since its substance is not changed, it returns the same.

In corruptible substances, however, which are such that they can fail to exist, it is impossible for the same thing numerically to return after corruption; it returns only in species, and so forth. In truth, what has been corrupted cannot be restored numerically the same by physical or natural power, though not by supernatural power. For God can restore all enduring things that have been corrupted. Thus, although nature does not demonstrate the resurrection of the dead, Scripture does; and although natural power does not accomplish it, divine omnipotence does.

[Col. 1008B] The intellect and the intelligible ought to be proportionate (ibid.). This is true according to assimilation, or according to the intelligible aspect, but not according to the aspect of quantity.

Intelligences are known only through motion (Averroes, VIII and XII Metaphysics). This is understood of physical science. The physicist demonstrates intelligences through motion, saying: “Everything that is moved is moved by another.” Therefore an eternal mobile has an eternal mover. An eternal mover cannot be in a body, because a bodily thing cannot move eternally. Hence there is a bodiless, immaterial, abstract power, subsisting per se and complete without a body. In this way Aristotle and Averroes, positing—though falsely—that the world and motion are eternal, prove the intelligences through motion.

The human intellect has matter (XII Metaphysics). According to Saint Thomas and Buridan, this is understood to mean that it contains within itself a certain receptive power for material species. Or it may be said that by “matter” it understands some operation through which the human intellect differs from the divine intellect. Thus Albert says that all things below God have matter, or something proportionable to matter.

The intellect is separate from the body (III On the Soul). This means that it is not bound to any bodily organ. For the intellect’s being separable signifies that it is not organic, nor dependent in its operation upon the body as a composite, cause, or principle.

Nothing is greater than the infinite (III Physics). This is understood of the infinite with respect to extension, because in that respect nothing can be greater in quantity.

The same thing is not the cause of opposites (II Physics). This is understood of the same particular agent: it is not equally and primarily the cause of specifically distinct opposites, because of a universal agent such as God or the sun. “Equally and primarily” is specified because the same thing can indeed be the cause of one earlier and of the other later, of one per se and of the other per accidens, and so forth. “Specifically distinct” is specified because a father who has a son is the cause of opposites, namely, father and son, since these are relatively opposed.

Fire is corrupted in its own sphere, as Giles says. Although an opposite cannot be formally applied to it, since water does not ascend, an opposite can nevertheless be applied to it virtually: fire can in some way be regarded through a cold constellation. If so, it descends, because a heavy thing moves downward, and through such motion the fire is corrupted. Thus, speaking naturally, fire is not corruptible as a whole, but only according to its parts; nevertheless, through divine power it can be corrupted.

The intellect follows the thing in understanding (III On the Soul). This is understood of understanding something by a simple concept, not discursively.

Once motion is ignored, nature must be ignored (III Physics, text 1). If this is so, how can he say that when motion is ignored nature is ignored, since in II *Physics*, text 6, he says that nature is self-evident? It is answered that nature has two kinds of cognition: whether it exists and what it is. That it exists is self-evident; but what it is is not self-evident and can be unknown. It is of this definitional cognition that he says that whoever is ignorant of what motion is will also be ignorant of what nature is. For nature is defined through motion.

In misfortunes virtue shines forth (I Ethics, chap. 2).

In obscure matters one ought to use clear testimonies (II Ethics, chap. 2).

In a frequently repeated matter, a habit is recognized (III Ethics, chapter 14).

It is impossible for a prudent person not to be good (same work).

In a city there are three classes: the rich, the poor, and those of moderate means. Among these, the best are those of moderate means, because the mean is always best (III Politics).

In great enterprises, one person should be assigned to one task, because care concentrated on one thing is better than care directed toward several [Col. 1009B] (IV Politics).

In speaking, we use examples so that what is said may be more easily understood (Book I of the Poetics).

In a weak person there is continual sadness and inconsolable grief (same work).

In every genus there is some good, even though some things found within it are not good (Commentary on Book I of the Art of Poetry).

That is superfluous in a definition which, once removed, leaves what remains sufficient to make the thing defined clear (Book VI of the Topics, chapter 3).

It is impossible to contemplate the universal except through induction (I Posterior Analytics, text 33).

That demonstration is more worthy which uses more worthy principles (same work, text 43).

An indivisible thing cannot move except accidentally (VI Physics, text 36).

By remaining at rest and sitting, the soul becomes prudent (VI Physics, text 20).

The instant is the beginning of the future and the end of the past (VIII [Col. 1009C] Physics, text 11).

That is better which is closer to what is best (II On the Heavens, text 66).

In divine beings, their action in the first intention is for the sake of their own being; secondarily, it is for the sake of something else (Commentary 17 on II On the Heavens).

Frost does not form in the mountains (Book I of the Meteorology, chapter 4).

Proceeding from what precedes to what follows is more widely accepted (II On the Soul, Commentary 11).

He has the most who desires the least (Seneca, On Morals).
