In all things, both the greatest and the smallest, God’s help should be implored (Plato, in the Timaeus).

Anger should be avoided not for the sake of moderation, but for the sake of health (Seneca, Book II, Letter 18).

It is uncertain in what place death awaits you; but you should await it in every place (the same, Book III, Letter 26).

Each person has the understanding appropriate to what he has learned (the same, On Morals).

[Col. 1009D] It is impossible for a dream to be wholly false (Aristotle, On Dreams).

Among animals, only the human being is ambidextrous (Book II of On Animals).

An individual is not generated essentially except by an individual of the same species (I Metaphysics, commentary 32).

That which is the cause of other things’ being true is most true (II Metaphysics, text 4).

It is impossible for there to be a demonstration of everything (III Metaphysics, text 4).

Among eternal things there is neither corruption, evil, nor sin (IX Metaphysics, text 19).

Among everlasting things there is no potentiality (text 17, same work).

Everything indivisible is without matter (XII Metaphysics, text 5).

It is impossible for two contrary motions to be directed toward the same pole (XII Metaphysics, text and commentary 47).

It is better to be ignorant of vices than to know them (XII Metaphysics, commentary 51).

[Col. 1010A] One who is being weakened takes health to be happiness, while one who has become poor takes wealth to be happiness (Commentary on I Ethics, chapter 4).

In the mean, both extremes are actual, but neither is at its ultimate perfection (Commentary on I Physics, commentary 56).

Anger is an appetite accompanied by sadness, arising from the appearance of an injury to oneself or to one’s own people (II Rhetoric).

Anger produces enmity and hatred (same work).

The weak, those who join together and fight, lovers, those who know, and, universally, those who desire something and fail to attain it, become angry easily (II Rhetoric).

Inferior things are governed by superior things (On the Government of Princes).

He is the most blessed and secure possessor of himself who awaits without anxiety (same work).

He does not take a gift without deserving it who, having asked for it, receives it, because it is best to anticipate the desire of the one who asks (Seneca, On Benefits).

He is ungrateful who denies having received a benefit which he did receive (same work).

In giving benefits, one should choose a man who is simple and upright, mindful, grateful, and self-controlled [Col. 1010B] (Seneca, On Benefits).

In every discussion, it is proper that at the beginning one should consider what the subject under discussion is (Plato, in the Timaeus).

Among animals, the human being and the elephant are the longest-lived (On the Length and Shortness of Life).

Happiness does not consist in external goods, because the happy person needs no external good (VII Politics).

Among all animals, only the human being possesses reason (VII Politics).

Even in the smallest matters, divine help ought to be implored; for the Father of all things must be invoked, and when this is omitted, no beginning is properly established (Boethius, III Consolation of Philosophy).

The intellect is a light which God infuses into the soul (Aristotle, Book III of the Rhetoric).

It is impossible for a body not to move in a body (Author of VI Principles, chapter “On Action”).

Whatever is circumscribed by a place is in that place (the same, [Col. 1010C] chapter “On Where”).

Someone asserts that which has been said by a reputable man (Aristotle, Book I, chapter 2).

He is envious who is saddened by the prosperity of good people (chapter 5, Book II of the Topics).

It is uncertain, when the sun has set, whether it is still above the earth, because we then lose our sense-perception (Book V of the Topics, chapter 9).

In plants there is one soul in actuality, but several in potentiality; therefore even a part of a plant, once cut off, remains alive.

When a genus is destroyed, its species are destroyed (Boethius, Book of Division).

Few people sin in natural appetites (III Ethics, chapter 13).

Anger advances the action of the brave person (Commentary on III Ethics, chapter 10).

To become angry when one ought not, and not to become angry when one ought, is the mark of a fool (IV Ethics, chapter 14).

In misfortunes, there is recourse to friends (VIII Ethics, chapter 1).

In human actions, words are believed less than deeds (X Ethics, [Col. 1010D] chapter 11).

In depraved and badly disposed bodies, the soul is dominated by the body (I Politics).

It is impossible for the servants of a loving lord not to be loving (Book I of the Economics).

J

A boaster is especially deserving of blame (IV Ethics).

Justice is the most illustrious of the virtues (V Ethics). This is understood of perfect justice, not imperfect justice, because perfect justice includes all the virtues within itself.

The just person does not reveal secrets (Seneca, On Justice).

A young person cannot be wise, because prudence requires experience, which requires time (VI Ethics).

Young people must be guarded so that they neither say nor hear anything shameful, because from saying or hearing something shameful it often happens that one proceeds to do it (VII Politics).

[Col. 1011A] It is just to assist the poor (I Rhetoric).

It is just to show favor to one who shows favor (Book II of Aristotle’s Rhetoric).

It is just to assist friends (same work).

A boaster is more blameworthy than a liar (IV Ethics, chapter 14).

L

The place of the whole and the place of the part are the same (I On the Heavens, text and commentary 19 and 77; also II On the Heavens, text 35). The Commentator limits this proposition (in III Physics, commentary 52) to place according to species, not place according to number, because the place of the whole is greater than the place of the part.

Light is not a body (II On the Soul). This is understood to mean that light is not a substantial body, although it can properly be a quantified body in a concrete sense; or that light is not a body separated from the luminous body; or, again, that light is not an extended body, that is, not extended by its own proper extension.

A common place is one that contains everything (IV Physics). [Col. 1011B] This is understood to mean one that contains everything other than itself, except the heavens, which contain everything but not themselves.

Place is not of something that is in a place (same work). That is, it does not belong to the nature of place that it itself be in a place. Or: place is not essentially in a place, but accidentally; for place, insofar as it is place, contains, though accidentally it may itself perhaps be contained by something else.

Place is equal to the thing located (same work). This is true of proper place, but not of common place.

A letter and a syllable lack sense (Priscian, Book I of the Minor Grammar). This means that they lack sense, that is, ultimate signification; it does not mean that they are not perceptible by external sense.

The law forbids anyone to kill himself (Commentary on V Ethics, chapter 15). Understand this not only of human law, but also of natural and divine law.

There are only two natural places: the upper and the lower (III Physics, commentary 55).

The best position in war is the middle. For the brave hold the middle position [Col. 1011C] between the bold and the timid (Aristotle, II On the Art of Poetry).

To praise a person to his face is the mark of a flatterer (the same, Book II).

The Book of Physics is the root and foundation of the whole of natural philosophy (Commentary on Book I of the Physics, in the prologue).

Strife and a day do not possess being as some complete substance, but insofar as they are generated and corrupted (III Physics, text 59).

The middle place is the place of the one who rules (in On Youth and Old Age).

The voracious wolf eats without chewing, and at one time eats enough to sustain it for three days (Book V of the History of Animals).

An animal has a tongue so that it may communicate something to another (III On the Soul).

Praise and thanksgiving are owed to the giver, not to the receiver (IV Ethics).

The place of an eternal thing is eternal (II On the Heavens, commentary 2).

[Col. 1011D] The tongue serves two natural functions: taste and speech, including every kind of vocalization (Book II, text 88).

Milk can also be produced in the hands (Aristotle, On Animals, Book I).

The tongue exists for perceiving flavors and articulating letters (Book XI of On Animals).

Although all the sciences are noble, divine science is nobler, because its subject is nobler (VI Metaphysics, commentary 2).

Profit is an aid to need (VIII Ethics, chapter 10).

Dishonorable laws, although they may be most widely used, may be abolished (II Politics).

Play is undertaken for the sake of rest (VIII Politics).

Reading surely benefits; variety, however, delights (Seneca, Letters, Book, 45).

You should listen more willingly than you speak (the same, On Morals).

M

[Col. 1012A]

Matter is not a being (I Physics). This is understood to mean that prime matter is not a being in formal actuality. Nevertheless, it can properly be called a being in entitative actuality, as the schools express it.

Matter always strives toward the harm of its form (I Physics). This must be understood of the matter of corruptible and generable things, because of its potentiality for contraries. In itself it has no proper form, but it has potentiality for all forms.

Motion and time are infinite (VI Topics). This is understood by taking “infinite” syncategorematically, so that “motion” and “time” are taken confusedly. It is also granted in another way, according to succession and potentiality, so that motion is infinite according to succession.

When we are moved, everything in us is moved (VI Physics and II Topics). This is understood either essentially or accidentally.

[Col. 1012B] Matter is neither a what, nor a quality, nor a quantity (VII Metaphysics). This is understood of prime matter considered in itself. It is not a what—that is, this particular thing, namely, a substance of a definite species. It is not a quality—that is, it does not possess any proper quality; it is not qualified by any quality essentially and properly. It is not a quantity—that is, it does not possess any determinate quantity from itself.

Prime matter is intermediate between being and non-being (I Physics). But this seems false, because it would follow that there is a mean between two contradictories. The answer is that prime matter is understood as intermediate between absolute non-being and being in formal actuality. Now absolute non-being and being in formal actuality are not contradictories. The meaning is this: matter is indeed a substance, but an imperfect one, and thus it is a kind of intermediate between being simply and non-being simply. For it is neither being in every respect—that is, a perfect and specifically determined being—nor is it in no way a being; rather, it is a being subsisting in the nature of things, though in potentiality toward all formal actualities and all natural species.

The motion of a mixed body proceeds from the simple element dominant in it (I On the Heavens, commentary on text 7, and II Meteorology). [Col. 1012C] The proposition is true of a perfect mixture, whose mixture is complete, in which the ingredients have been reduced to one form superadded to the mixture. But it fails in a mixture whose mixture consists only in the juxtaposition of parts. For such motion is not simple, but inflected or composite, as is the motion of whirlwinds (Averroes, IV On the Heavens, commentary 7).

The mathematician considers only the formal cause (Averroes, I Physics, commentary 1). The answer is that the mathematician considers form alone because he does not consider sensible matter, an agent, or an end connected with motion, but only the universal form explaining whatness. For the parts of a definition are called forms, as is clear in II Physics, text 28.

The mover and the thing moved must be together (VII Physics, text and commentary 10). [Col. 1012D] The proposition is true of a mover in the genus of efficient cause, but it fails of a mover in the genus of final cause, especially in generable and corruptible things, in which the mover as efficient cause is different, as Averroes says in the first chapter of the Book on the Substance of the World. This is a gloss by Aristotle himself in VII Physics, text and commentary 9.

Prime matter is generated accidentally (the Commentator, I Physics). “Accidentally” is understood as “in a qualified sense,” namely, with respect to the form which is brought forth from it through generation, and with which it constitutes a new composite.

Prime matter is, in truth, generated (I Physics). The answer is that this is true subjectively, in the sense that it begins to be the subject of a form; but it is not generated as a terminus. It is understood in the sense of the immediately preceding axiom: namely, that it begins to be the subject of a form.

[Col. 1013A] “The evil of a being destroys itself,” and this seems to imply that malice, nominally speaking, is something, which is nevertheless contrary to the same Philosopher (II On the Soul). This is understood in two ways. First, conditionally: if the evil of a being existed, then it would destroy itself; that is, “the evil of a being” signifies the destruction of itself. Second, it is understood that evil destroys itself accidentally. For since evil is a privation, it is found only in a good; therefore, when it strives toward the destruction of the good, it accidentally strives toward its own destruction, because a privation cannot exist without a subject.

It is more fitting for a needy person to become wealthy than to philosophize (III Topics). This does not mean that it is better, but that it is more necessary for someone in need.

Prime matter first receives a universal form, then a less universal form (the Commentator, XII Metaphysics). That is, first the form of an element, then the form of a mixed body, and finally the soul. For these forms have an order among themselves, and some are more or less common than others.

The mover must be together with the motion (VII Physics). Not always through the immediacy of the subject, but always through the immediacy of power.

Matter remains in the thing that has been made, but privation does not (I Physics). This is understood to mean that matter remains in the thing made under the aspect and denomination of matter, whereas privation does not remain under that aspect or denomination. For privation is formally the negation of a form and materially an aptitude for a form. Therefore, when the form is not present, privation clearly no longer remains under the aspect of privation.

Motion in quantity is called increase or decrease (V Physics). This is understood of motion properly directed toward quantity. Hence rarefaction and condensation differ considerably from increase and decrease.

Prime matter is not (I Physics). This is understood as above: prime matter is not in formal actuality, because prime matter is not a form. Nevertheless, prime matter is in actuality of essence and potentiality.

More and less do not diversify a species (II Topics). [Col. 1013C] This is understood of essential species: more and less do not diversify an essential species, although they do diversify an accidental species.

The mean is composed of the extremes (V Physics, text 6). This is understood of a likeness-based composition: the mean resembles one extreme in one respect and the other extreme in another respect. Sometimes, however, it is also really composed of the extremes, as brown is composed of white and black, and lukewarm of hot and cold.

Nothing can be less than the minimum (I Physics). This is understood in the divided sense, not in the composite sense. In the latter sense, something less can indeed be given than such a minimum.

Prime matter is not in potentiality toward a form (through the Commentator and the Philosopher, V Metaphysics). This is understood of active and instrumental potentiality, not passive and essential potentiality.

Magnitude and multitude are not accidents of quantity (V Metaphysics). [Col. 1013D] This is understood when they are taken relatively; then they are not species of quantity. But when they are taken absolutely, they are species of quantity.

The world is eternal (VIII Physics and XII Metaphysics). This is understood according to Aristotle and others, to whom the creation of things from nothing was unknown; it is not understood according to the truth, which teaches that God made the world from nothing in time.

A lesser good joined to another makes it a greater good (I Ethics). It would therefore follow that an animate body is nobler than the soul itself. This is understood provided that one good does not include the other. Thus, no good added to God makes Him a greater good, because He is infinite and already possesses every good.

It is evident that God has neither genus, nor quality, nor quantity (through Avicenna). This is speaking properly of these insofar as they have the nature of categories. For God is at once most perfect and most simple. Improperly, or by a certain likeness, these terms are sometimes also said of God.

Prime matter desires form as a woman desires a man, and as the base desires the good or the beautiful [Col. 1014A] (I Physics, text 81). This is understood of natural appetite, not animal appetite. Or it may be understood as follows: prime matter desires form, that is, it desires to be perfected by form. But lest anyone think that matter is simply base, he adds that this is so accidentally, for example, by reason of privation. Thus it is base, since what is base desires the beautiful or the good; yet baseness and deformity are not essentially in matter, but accidentally, insofar as matter shares in privation. Themistius therefore says that this appetite is in matter because providence placed in the base a desire for nobility, and in the needy a desire for as much wealth as is sufficient.

Motion naturally kindles wood, stones, and iron (II On the Heavens and the World, text and commentary 42, and I Meteorology). [Col. 1014B] Observe that two conditions are required for motion to heat, especially. The first is that it be rapid, so that the heatable body is stretched more than it is stretchable by its own nature—for rarefaction is a disposition toward heat—and thus motion heats the moving body by rarefying it. The second is that the motion occur in a large and nearby mobile body.

Matter is known through negation (X Metaphysics, text and commentary 24). Note that matter is twofold: prime matter and secondary matter. Prime matter is nature, whereas secondary matter is of natures, or possesses a nature. Prime matter is a simple substance, whereas secondary matter is a substance composed of matter and form, whether it serves merely as the matter of alteration or as the matter of alteration and composition together. The proposition therefore applies principally to prime matter. It is known through negation insofar as it is a being, or substance, which in itself is neither a form nor something possessing a form. It is in potentiality toward every form.

Motion is time (IV Physics). [Col. 1014C] The answer is that the Philosopher means that this is not an essential but an accidental predication, because motion, insofar as it is numbered and taken as a measure of the duration of these things and of natural operations, is time. Thus it is accidental to motion that it be time.

Motion which proceeds from an external mover is violent (VII Physics, text and commentary 10). The answer is that motion from an external mover is called violent when the external mover is not always moving, or when the mobile does not have an inclination toward such motion. In this way the proposition must be understood according to the Peripatetic school.

The mean promotes motion itself (III On the Heavens; the Philosopher says the opposite; IV Physics). There he says that the medium is a successive resistance and consequently an impediment to motion. The answer is that the authority from III On the Heavens is understood to mean that when the medium is thin, it accidentally promotes motion, namely, by reason of its thinness and usefulness [Col. 1014D]. But essentially the medium always resists motion, because it strives to remain undivided.

A measure must be the minimum thing (XII Metaphysics). The answer is that this is understood with respect to sufficiency for making something known: it must not fall short of the minimum required to make the measured thing known.

The circular motion of the heavens is the first of motions (VIII Physics). This is understood to mean that it is the first of motions in duration, or, alternatively, the first in perfection.

Metaphysics concerns all beings in the world (I Physics). It concerns them in general, or according to their common notions, not according to the proper whatness of each. For the human being, according to his whatness, belongs not to the metaphysician but to the physicist.

Metaphysics is the noblest and most difficult science (I Metaphysics). [Col. 1015A] This is not understood inclusively, as though only the metaphysician considers the most difficult matters and no other practitioner does; rather, it means that the metaphysician principally considers the most difficult matters. It is noblest by reason of its principal subject, because it treats not only of the transcendentals Being, One, Good, and True, but also of God and the intelligences as its principal object.

A slight deviation from the truth at the beginning becomes ten thousand times greater at the end (I On the Heavens, text 33). The example concerns a traveler who goes astray at the beginning of his journey; the farther he proceeds, the more he persists in error. Thus a small error in principles becomes enormous at the end. For this reason Plato commanded that a lengthy discourse be devoted to principles, as the Commentator says in VIII On the Soul, commentary 4.

The mean is nobler than the extremes (V Physics). [Col. 1015B] Note that the mean is twofold. One is a mean according to magnitude; the other is the mean chosen by nature. The proposition is true of the natural mean, but not of the mean according to magnitude or position, as Aristotle and Averroes gloss it in II On the Heavens, text and commentary 74. It may also be answered that there is another equivocation concerning the mean. Some things are called means because they are composed of extremes, as a color intermediate between white and black; others are called means merely by comparison, as air and water are intermediate between fire and earth. Averroes makes this distinction in IV On the Heavens, commentary 26. The proposition assumed is not universally true in either sense. See Zimara, folio 72. It is true, however, in moral matters, because virtue, which lies in the mean between two extremes that are vices, is nobler than the extremes.

It is better to die than to act against the good of virtue (III Ethics).

Medicines are produced through contraries (II Ethics, chapter 5).

To do evil is easy, but to do good is difficult (same work).

The mean in all things is praiseworthy (II Ethics).

[Col. 1015C] The lesser evil is more eligible than the greater evil (V Ethics).

The greatest of external goods is honor (IV Ethics).

Mothers love their children more than fathers do, because they are more certain of them and undergo more labor on their account (VIII Ethics, chapter 7).

Honor is given to superiors, but profit to inferiors, because honor is a tribute to virtue and beneficence, whereas profit is an aid to need (VIII Ethics).

An equivalent return cannot be made to teachers, gods, or parents (IX Ethics).

We are more obligated to bestow goods on friends than on strangers (same work).

A person bears it much more heavily if deprived of honor than if his goods are taken away (II Economics).

The male sex is naturally more worthy than the female (I Politics).

It is better to judge according to the laws and the written text than according to one’s own knowledge or opinion [Col. 1015D] (II Politics).

Many servants sometimes serve worse than a few (same work).

Avarice is like a monster (Seneca, On Morals).

Believe me, a miser cannot be rich or happy (same work).

It is much more beneficial to retain a few precepts of wisdom and have them ready and in use than to learn many without keeping them in mind (Seneca, On Benefits).

Clemency is rare among slaves (Boethius, On Scholastic Discipline).

It is wretched to be a teacher who has never known himself to be a student (same work).

If males do not mate, they live longer than females, because the male is more intelligent than the female (On the Cause of the Length and Shortness of Life).

[Col. 1016A] Woman possesses greater piety and compassion than man, but also greater envy, contentiousness, and quarrelsomeness; she is more malicious than man and is easily deceived (Book IX of the History of Animals).

Menstruation in women ceases in the fortieth year, and in some remains until the fiftieth; therefore old women of ancient times were bearded (Book IX of the History of Animals).

It is much worse to have given a benefit badly than not to have given one at all (Seneca, On Benefits).

Great is the dignity of wisdom, which makes Socrates equal to the supreme God (Apuleius, On the God of Socrates).

To deny what is evident is irreverence (Book II of the Rhetoric).

The mover and the thing moved are together (VII Physics, text 9). At least in power.

Matter is the cause why beings can be and not be (II On Generation, text 51).

It is better to be than not to be (same work, text 59).

The physician is a mechanical craftsman (Commentary on On the Soul, 17).

[Col. 1016B] Melancholics dream most truly (On Divination).

Death is nothing other than coldness and dryness (On the Length and Shortness of Life).

Death is nothing other than the soul’s departure from the body (the same, On Death).

It is much better to possess a soul endowed with knowledge than to see the habit of the body well dressed (Aristotle, Letter to Alexander).

Woman possesses greater piety than man, but also greater envy, and is more malicious than man and easily deceived (Aristotle, Book IX of On Animals).

We say that the person who knows a thing affirmatively knows it more than the person who knows the same thing negatively (III Metaphysics, text 3).

Death is metaphorically called an end (V Metaphysics, text 21).

It is a greater virtue to do good than not to do what is shameful (IV Ethics, chapter 1).

The passage of much time produces experience (VI Ethics, chapter 7).

There is greater pleasure in rest than in motion [Col. 1016C] (VII Ethics, chapter 14).

A malicious person is good neither in actuality nor in potentiality (VIII Ethics, chapter 8).

A bad king is called a tyrant (VIII Ethics, chapter 7).

Mothers love their children more than fathers do (VIII Ethics, chapter 7).

It is better for a city to be ruled by the best man than by the best law (III Politics).

A moderate possession of external goods is best, because it is easiest for reason to be obeyed (IV Politics).

Inferiors stir up sedition so that they may become equals, while equals do so in order to become superiors (V Politics).

Melody often relieves those who are angry or occupied by other passions, making them cheerful (VIII Politics).

Music has the power to make people joyful (same work).

He serves many who serves the body (Seneca, Book II, Letter 14).

[Col. 1016D] It is characteristic of the magnanimous person to despise great things (the same, Book V, Letter 39).

It is a sign of great strength to disregard the one who injures you (the same, On Morals).

“You will die.” This is human nature, not punishment.

“You will die.” I entered under this condition: that I should leave.

“You will die.” Our life is a journey abroad. When you have walked for a long time, you must return home.

“You will die.” It is foolish to fear what one cannot avoid.

“People speak badly of you.” They do not know how to speak well; for they do not do what I deserve, but what they are accustomed to do.

“A wicked person speaks badly of you.” It would move me if he did this by judgment and not by disease; he is not speaking about me, but about himself.

(All these sayings are from Seneca, On Remedies for Fortune.)

N

Nothing acts beyond the degree of its perfection, or, which is the same thing, nothing acts beyond its species (VII Metaphysics, [Col. 1017A] final text and commentary). The proposition is false if understood absolutely. It is limited in this way: it is true of agents acting through their own proper power. Thus the formative power existing in seed, although it is not actually animate, produces an animate thing from it, because it is an instrument moved by an animate thing, namely, by the heavens. The same proposition also fails in the case of accidents, for the same agent disposes the matter and introduces the form, but not by its own proper power, since it acts as an instrument. It fails in the case of a remote agent. It fails in the case of an accidental and chance agent (see VII Metaphysics, commentary 31, on these points).

You do not say that an animal is a human being (through Porphyry). That authority is understood to mean that the predication “Animal is a human being” is not direct, because the inferior is predicated of its superior.

Transposed nouns and verbs signify the same thing (II On Interpretation, Greek: περὶ Ἑρμηνείας, “On Interpretation”). This authority has two senses. One is that merely through the transposition of terms—namely, nouns and verbs—nouns and verbs do not lose their essential significations, although they do lose their accidental ones, such as case, number, and figure. But it has another sense: that through the transposition of nouns and verbs the truth of a proposition is not changed. If this sense is to be true, however, logical properties—namely, ampliation and restriction—must be preserved.

Non-being is not understood (I Physics). [Col. 1017B] This means that non-being is not understood through affirmative categorical propositions. Nevertheless, it can properly be understood through negative categorical propositions, that is, directly.

It is not necessary to bring things into a disputation, or into the act of disputing; rather, we use terms in place of things (I Sophistical Refutations). This is understood of conditioned necessity. Since we must dispute about things through names and cannot bring the things themselves into the disputation, we must use names in place of things.

Number is infinite through the addition of units (III Physics). This means that number can be multiplied to infinity through the addition of units.

Nature and principle are the subject of natural science (Commentary on III Physics). [Col. 1017C] It should be known that every science considers some subject, its principles, its properties, and its species. Nature and principles can therefore also be called the object of physics insofar as physics considers them. Nevertheless, the proper and adequate subject of physics is mobile body itself, whose principles these are.

Nature is directed by an infallible agent (Commentary on XII Metaphysics). This is understood of nature that produces nature, namely God; or it may be understood of nature that has been produced, although it is usually understood simply of nature that produces nature, namely God.

Nothing is in the intellect unless it was first in the senses (I Physics and II On the Soul). This does not mean that every intellectual cognition of a thing must depend on the sense-perception of that same thing, because we have intellectual knowledge of God and the intelligences, although they are not sensible. It is sufficient that all our intellectual cognition depends on sense-perception of either that thing or another. Thus intellectual knowledge of God is said to be caused by knowledge of effects, through which one immediately arrives at cognition of insensible substances, and this is knowledge a posteriori.

Nature does not fail in what is necessary, nor overflow in what is superfluous (II On the Soul and I On the Heavens). [Col. 1017D] This is understood with respect to the imperfection of the ultimate end: in that respect nature neither fails nor overflows, although it sometimes fails or overflows in determining a certain particular and determinate end. Alternatively, it means that nature neither fails nor overflows with respect to the whole species, although it may do so with respect to a part of the species, that is, with respect to certain individuals; or it may be said that nature neither fails nor overflows in the majority, although it may sometimes do so in a few cases. Suppose, for example, that there were only three human beings in the world and that all were born with six fingers on each hand. Then there would be a monstrosity, and the whole of nature would overflow [Col. 1018A] in superfluities. Likewise, if all three were born with one hand or without hands, the whole of nature would fail in what is necessary. It should be said that the whole of humanity would then be actually monstrous, though not potentially monstrous. For not only the actual species but also the potential species must be considered.

No complex thing is definable (II Topics). The answer is: not by a definition of the thing, though it can be defined by a definition of the name. It is also understood as not definable proximately, though it is definable remotely. The reason is that every proximate definable must be a species. But no complex thing is a species; therefore no complex thing is proximally definable. If the complex is resolved, however, it can properly be defined according to its parts.

The things known to us and the things known simply are not the same (I Physics, text 3; I Posterior Analytics, chapter 2). This should be taken as generally true. In mathematics, the things known to us and the things known simply are the same. It is also true of things as they exist outside the mind: in them we first know what is later according to nature, and afterward what is prior. Otherwise, the more universal things would be better known to us and also better known simply. It is likewise true of the human being insofar as he naturally knows things, but not insofar as he understands while endowed with and trained in the sciences. See Aristotle, VI Topics, chapter 11.

Nothing is known demonstratively and definitively (II Posterior Analytics). [Col. 1018B] This is true, namely, when considered as a whole and adequately. The essence of a thing is known through definition; its property is known through demonstration, namely, through the reason for the property. For insofar as the property also has its own essence, it too has, in its own way, a definition.

It does not happen that the sense is deceived concerning its proper object (II *On the Soul*, commentary on text 93). This is understood provided that the sense is rightly disposed and the object is suitably adapted; but, speaking absolutely or distinctly, Averroes responds (in the text cited above) that the sense does not err, for the most part, concerning its proper sensible object. This is also true with respect to common sensibles, such as motion, magnitude, shape, and so forth, although the sense is deceived less often even in these, it is nevertheless deceived more often in them than in proper sensibles.

No good definition should be given through opposites, or be elicited from them (V *Topics*). The reason is that the members of a good definition must belong to the thing defined, whereas opposites do not belong to one and the same thing. It must therefore be understood that this authority concerns a quidditative definition, in the sense that such a definition should not be given through opposites taken conjunctively. Nevertheless, it may be given through opposites taken disjunctively, or with a certain order. Thus nature is defined as the principle of motion and rest: that is, it is the principle of motion or also of rest, but with a certain order. For a natural thing moves toward its proper place so that it may rest there. Thus, for example, the earth moves toward the center of the world so that it may come to rest there, as in its natural place, and be preserved. On this axiom, see also what is given above under the letter D.

Nature intends only the species, and not the individual (according to Avicenna). The response is that it is not individual nature but common nature that is meant: thus the heavens intend only the perpetuation of the species, and not that of the individual. Alternatively, it seems that one should say that Avicenna says this while positing universals as things distinct from individuals, in the Platonic manner. Consequently, one need not concern oneself with this statement of his.

Nothing is known except what is true (I *Posterior Analytics*). What is not, is not known; that is, as the Philosopher says, there is no science of the false. Thus there is no science that the diameter is commensurable with the side, because this is false. You may object: How does this follow? Because science concerns truths, and therefore a demonstration must proceed from truths, although truth may be inferred from falsehood—that is, from false premises—so far as concerns the inferential force and the arrangement of the syllogism. But this does not follow so far as concerns probative force, or as proceeding from a cause, because what does not exist cannot be a cause or prove what does exist.

No indivisible thing moves (VI *Physics*). This is understood per se and circumscriptively, from place to place.

No form is composed of parts belonging to different kinds (according to the author of the *Six Principles*). The response is that he is speaking of a simple and non-composite form. It is not impossible, however, for some form to be composed of parts belonging to different kinds, as is a form aggregated from several forms.

We do not know a truth without a cause (II *Metaphysics*). This is understood a priori. Or it may be understood thus: we do not know, without a cause, the truth of why something is so, although we can know that something is so from a posteriori evidence, or by demonstration, without knowing its cause.

Thanks are due not only to those whose opinions one accepts, but also to those who have spoken only superficially (II *Metaphysics*, commentary on text 2). Even the latter contribute something, for they exercised our intellectual disposition. Thus, in XII *Metaphysics*, commentary on text 45, the same Philosopher says: “We ought indeed to love both groups, but to adhere to the more certain.” The meaning is that we owe less to the latter than to the former, but nevertheless owe them something insofar as they aroused and prepared our intellectual faculty to investigate and extract the truth. For, as Aristotle says there, if Phrynis had not existed, we would not have had Timotheus; although Phrynis was less skilled in the art of music than Timotheus, he was nevertheless his teacher and aroused and prepared him to bring this art to greater perfection and become a more excellent musician. See also further discussion in Simplicius on this text.

Nature has to determine only what is a body or an affection of a body (III *On the Soul*). It seems, then, that the natural philosopher should not determine anything concerning the human intellect. The response is that the natural philosopher determines only what is a body, an affection of a body, or something that depends upon a body in its operation; metaphysics, moreover, also determines concerning the intellect.

Blackness is the privation of whiteness (in *On Sense and the Sensible*). The intended meaning is merely that blackness is a less perfect quality than whiteness.

In a demonstration one must believe the principles more than the conclusion; that is, belief or knowledge of the premises must have greater credibility than knowledge of its conclusion (I *Posterior Analytics*, chapter 2). This is understood as conditional necessity: if belief or knowledge of the conclusion is to be possessed on account of the premises, then the premises must be more known and more believed. For we believe more strongly those things on account of which we believe other things. This is explained by the principle: “That on account of which a thing is such is itself more such.” Understand this of axioms and other principles.

Nothing gives what it does not possess (I *Sophistical Refutations*). That is, what it does not possess either formally or virtually. For it must possess it in one of these two ways if it gives it. It may nevertheless happen that an agent gives something which the agent itself does not possess formally. Thus the sun makes these lower things formally hot, although it itself is hot only virtually.

Nothing violent is perpetual (II *On the Heavens and the World*, commentary on text 8). It should be noted that there are two kinds of violence: violence absolutely speaking, and violence in a qualified sense. It is therefore not impossible for something violent in a qualified sense to be perpetual, but not for something violent absolutely speaking. For example, that the air is cold in the middle region of the atmosphere is violent in a qualified sense, but not absolutely, since not all its parts are cold; some part is warm in its natural disposition. This is Buccaferreus on the first book of the *Meteorology*. Thus the philosophers denied that anything violent per se, absolutely, and in its entirety could be perpetuated; yet in a qualified sense and accidentally this can occur. Nor should this seem strange to you, since many propositions that are per se true in natural science are nevertheless accidentally false, as the Commentator says (in VI *Physics*, commentary 15).

Things known per se cannot be proved (II *Physics*, commentary on text 6). The proposition is limited in this way: things known per se cannot be proved absolutely, demonstratively, and precisely as such. Nevertheless, they can be shown to a particular person by arguments leading to an absurdity, as Aristotle did with those who denied first principles (in IV *Metaphysics*).

We do not remember after death (Aristotle, I and III *On the Soul*). This concerns the aspect in which recollection belongs to the sensory faculty, as Aristotle speaks there; that is, insofar as it occurs through turning toward phantasms. Yet recollection also remains after death by reason of intelligible species, or by reason of knowledge which, once received into the intellect, no longer depends upon the contemplation of phantasms—whether, finally, this knowledge concerns singulars or universals.

Knowledge of the first principles is innate in us (I *Posterior Analytics*). It would seem, then, that at the beginning of its creation the intellect is not like a blank tablet on which nothing has been depicted, which contradicts Aristotle (III *On the Soul*). The response is that this means that the soul is naturally inclined to assent to first principles. These are so manifest and certain that they are known without any proof, solely through understanding the terms, as true and certain—for example, “Whatever is, either is or is not,” or “The whole is greater than its part,” and so forth. Principles of this kind are such that, as soon as the terms are understood—for example, what the Latin word *totum* signifies, what the word *pars* signifies, and so on with the others—it is immediately understood that such a proposition is most true.

It is neither matter nor form, but the whole composite (VII *Metaphysics*). This is understood to mean that matter and form are not supposits, but that the whole composite is.

Nothing is known without a cause (X *Metaphysics*). This is understood a priori and as perfect knowledge. Through imperfect and a posteriori knowledge, however, something can indeed be known without its cause—for example, God (VIII *Physics*).

Nothing is seen except color (II *On the Soul*). This is understood by taking “color” concretely, for “colored object,” so that the meaning is: nothing is seen except what is colored, or insofar as it is colored.

Neither voice nor letter teaches, but the true teacher is the one who illuminates the mind (according to the Commentator, I *Physics*). This means that the voice itself does not teach principally, but only instrumentally; the true teacher—that is, the principal teacher—is the one who illuminates the mind.

There is nothing that can escape the notion of being (according to Avicenna). This means that nothing exists which is not contained under the term “being,” or concerning which it is not true to say that it is a being.

Nothing is possessed of time except the now (V *Physics*). This does not mean that the now is a part of time, but that it is something continuous with the parts of time. Time is not a permanent being but a successive being. To say that it exists, it need not have any permanent part—for then it would not be a successive but a permanent being—but it is enough that it have its parts in continuous succession, so that the later is joined and connected to the earlier through the now. Thus we say that it is now Monday, or now the month of November, and we speak correctly according to everyone’s usage, although this now is nothing but a certain instant joining and connecting the past part of this day with the future.

No honorable good admits of addition (according to Seneca). This means that no honorable good admits of addition through the admixture of its contrary, namely wickedness. Nevertheless, it can admit of an addition of degree to degree within the same species.

A natural agent acts in order to assimilate the patient to itself. This means that a natural agent acts for the sake of acquiring the form to be generated, as an end subordinate to a further end, insofar as this is ordered toward preserving the species within the order of the perfection of the universe.

There cannot be a ruler without friends (V *Ethics*). The reason is that the greater one’s fortune, the less secure it is.

When one of two contraries immediately opposed to a subject is denied of it, the other must be affirmed of the subject (according to Peter of Spain, tractate 5). This authority is true subject to two conditions. The first is that the subject must be receptive of both contraries. In that case, if one is denied of the subject, the other must be designated as present in it. Hence it does not follow: “Wood is not sick; therefore wood is healthy.” The second condition is that the contraries be immediate. Hence it does not follow: “Wood is not white; therefore it is black.”

There is no power directed toward the past (I *On the Heavens*). This may be understood in one way as follows: there is no power capable of producing the past. In this sense the proposition is false, because God can destroy Socrates and reproduce him, as we believe by faith. In another way, it means that there is no power directed toward a past that has already become past, such that through it what has passed could be made not to have passed. Thus God cannot make it the case that Socrates, once destroyed, was not destroyed. For this involves a contradiction. Nevertheless, through his omnipotence he can restore and resurrect him after destruction.

We are not masters of our actions from beginning to end (III *Ethics*). This is understood as follows: we are masters—that is, free producers—of our actions, so that even when all the requirements for acting are present, we can refrain from acting. For example, even if someone is extremely hungry, he can nevertheless abstain from food placed before him. Such freedom is not found at all in brute animals.

Not everything acts upon everything; not everything is acted upon by everything; not everything comes to be from everything (I *Physics*, text 43), but a determinate thing comes from a determinate thing. Averroes assumes and explains these three principles of the contrary principles from which all things come to be (in the same place, in Aristotle).

Nothing acts upon itself (I *On Generation*). This is true primarily and per se, but it can occur secondarily and accidentally.

It is necessary that every divided whole be predicated of its dividing members (according to Boethius). This is understood of those members that function as species or differences, and not of those that function as an analogous term in relation to its analogates.

Nature is determined toward one thing (IX *Metaphysics*, commentary on text 3). The proposition does not mean that nature is determined toward one producible thing, but toward one mode of production, since it is not an indeterminate principle with respect to opposites, as the will is. Observe here the reason given for why rational powers are directed toward opposites: the same science concerns contraries. Averroes gives the reason, saying—following the text—that a rational agent acts in two contrary ways because it acts through knowledge, and because it knows two contraries, it therefore acts in two contrary ways. The science of contraries is one—understand this subjectively, since the intellect is the subject of all sciences.

The nobler things are those that require fewer resources (I *On the Heavens*). This is understood with other things being equal; otherwise a king certainly requires more than a citizen or peasant. It may also be said that Aristotle is speaking of those superior bodies, where what is more perfect requires fewer motions to attain its perfection. For example, the primum mobile is more perfect than the lunar sphere and therefore is moved by only one motion, whereas the lunar sphere is moved by two or three. The situation is different among lower things. The human being is certainly the most perfect substance among them all, but he requires many more motions and operations to attain his perfection than anything else.

Nothing acts below its own species (VII *Metaphysics* and II *On the Soul*). This is understood as acting by its own proper power, although something can act below its own species through the power of an agent, and specifically through the power of a nobler agent.

No mixed quality exists in a simple body, in *On Sense and the Sensible*. This means that no quality mixed from contrary qualities exists in a simple body existing in its natural disposition.

No substance comes to be by chance (VII *Metaphysics*). This is understood of a primary, perfect substance, although it remains true that an imperfect and secondary substance should come to be by chance.

There is no falsehood in those who abstract (II *Physics*, text 18). It is as though he said: the intellect does not lie or speak falsely merely because it abstracts things which are not abstracted in reality. Such abstraction is a simple consideration of a thing containing no falsehood. Thus mathematicians, who abstract from sensible matter subject to motion, do not lie intellectually, because they do not assert that mathematical objects exist outside sensible matter. That would indeed be falsehood. Rather, they consider them without considering sensible matter, which can be done without falsehood.

Nature does not make a leap in its operations (IX *On the Nature of Animals*). For it does not proceed from one extreme to the other without an intermediate.

There is no argument for principles (VI *Ethics*, chapter 4).

No one willingly suffers injustice (V *Ethics*).

No one is good or bad through excess (same place).

He is not altogether happy who is most disgraceful in appearance (same place).

No one is blessed or good except willingly (III *Ethics*).

It makes no small difference whether one becomes accustomed to this or that from youth; rather, it makes a great difference (III *Ethics*).

No one who possesses the other goods wishes to live without friends (VIII *Ethics*).

Neither Hesperus nor Lucifer is so admirable as justice, which very often appears the most illustrious of the virtues. We are also accustomed to say proverbially: “Justice contains all the virtues within itself.”

It is not easy to transfer everyone from an old custom to new ways of speaking (X *Ethics*).

Nature does not make one instrument except for one task (I *Politics*).

There is no difference between a child in age and one childish in character (I *Ethics*).

Of all animals, only the human being possesses speech by nature (I *Politics*).

Nature makes all animals for the sake of the human being (I *Politics*).

A good man and a good citizen are not the same thing (III *Politics*).

One cannot rule well if one has never been under a ruler (same place).

It is necessary not only to establish the constitution at the beginning, but also to correct it (IV *Politics*).

Nobility and virtue are found in few people, because the noble and the good are few (V *Politics*).

No one lays a hand upon impossibilities (V *Politics*).

A sober person cannot easily be attacked or easily despised, whereas a drunken person can; nor can one who is awake, whereas one who is asleep can. Therefore rulers, if they are not to be attacked, must greatly avoid drunkenness and sleep (V *Politics*).

It is not easy for a city to persist without laws and customs (VI *Politics*).

Nature is the cause of order for all things (VIII *Physics*, text 15).

There is nothing so worthless and small in nature that it does not permit us to observe something divine and worthy of wonder (in the first book of *On the Parts of Animals*, chapter 5).

It is necessary that the future ruler have previously been a subject (VII *Politics*).

It is impossible for the constitution to be the best without moderate abundance (same place).

Children should be educated not only in a useful and necessary art, but also in the liberal arts (VIII *Politics*).

Do not regret a past matter, because that is characteristic of the weak (Seneca, *On the Government of Princes*).

Excessive familiarity breeds contempt (same work, book II).

The human being is the noblest of animals (same work).

It is not the person who has little who is poor, but the person who desires more (Seneca, *Letters to Lucilius*).

No one is worthy of God except the person who fulfills God’s work (Seneca, *Letters to Lucilius*).

No one is born rich (same work).

No one should glory except in what is his own (same work).

Nature is content with few and very small things (Boethius, book II of *The Consolation*, prose 5).

It does not matter how many books you possess and read, but how good the books are that you possess (Seneca, *Letters to Lucilius*, book VI, letter 45).

No victory is greater than victory over vices (same work).

The soul is not stripped bare by bodily ugliness; rather, the body is adorned by the beauty of the soul (same work).

“We cannot.” This is caused by the fact that no one reflects upon his own life (same work, letter 89).

Do not be swayed by the authority of the speaker, nor attend to who is speaking, but attend to what is said (the same author, *On the Form of Life*, chapter on prudence).

Do not attribute to yourself what you are not, nor wish to appear greater than you are; be what you are (the same author, *On the Formula of Life*, chapter on self-restraint).

No benefit should be given to a negligent person (the same author, *On Benefits*, book I).

It does not matter what or how much is given, but with what intention it is given, because a benefit consists not in what is given but in the intention of the giver (same work).

Virtue is closed to no one; it is open to all, admits all, and invites all—the poor, slaves, kings, and exiles. It chooses neither household nor wealth, but is content with the naked human being (the same author, *On Benefits*, book III).

Golden bridles do not make a horse better (the same author, book V, letter 41).

Happiness does not consist in benefits, nor in the possession of talents, fields, or estates, nor in beauty, reputation, or glory (Boethius, *The Consolation*).

No plague is more effective for causing harm than a familiar enemy (III *The Consolation*).

It is not difficult to show how one absurdity follows from another (Simplicius, I *Physics*). Both Melissus and Parmenides argue contentiously by syllogism, for they accept false premises and do not syllogize properly (I *Physics*, texts 22 and 25).

No one cares how well he lives, but only that he lives long (Seneca, book III, letter 22).

I do not order you always to devote yourself to books or writing tablets. For some interval must be granted to the mind—not so that it may be relaxed entirely, but so that it may be refreshed (the same author, book II, letter 15).

Nobility is a certain praise arising from the merits of one’s parents (Boethius, III *The Consolation*).

Beings do not wish to be badly governed. A plurality of rulers is not good. Therefore, there should be one ruler (XII *Metaphysics*, text 55).

It is not permitted for a human being either to comprehend by intellect all the mechanisms of the divine work or to explain them in speech (Boethius, III *The Consolation*).

There is no rational creature without freedom of choice (V, same work).

No one deserves the sharpness of sweetness who does not know how to be entangled in the burden of bitterness (the same author, *On the Discipline of Scholars*).

Nothing is more harmful to a pupil than the disgraceful life of his teacher (same work, chapter VI).

Nothing has arisen beneath the sun whose legitimate cause did not precede it (same work).

Nothing is more noble and more like God than a perfectly good man, who surpasses other human beings to the same extent that he himself is surpassed by the immortal gods (Apuleius, in the book *On the God of Socrates*).

A master should never be without a guard, and neither should a city (in *Economics*).

No one takes equal care of his own affairs and those of others (same work).

No one is worthy of knowledge who rises up against the teacher of knowledge (Boethius, in the book *On the Discipline of Scholars*).

Do not always be active, but sometimes give your mind rest; and let that rest itself be full of wisdom, study, and good thoughts (same work).

It is not easy for a rich man to become generous (commentary IV, chapter 2).

Nature is content with moderate and very small things. If you try to force its satiety with superfluities, what you pour in will either be unpleasant or harmful (Boethius, II *The Consolation of Philosophy*).

The splendor of clothing, excellence of appearance, and abundance of gold contribute no more to a woman’s praise and virtue than modesty in every action and devotion to living a morally honorable and decorous life (in Aristotle’s *Economics*).

A sane person should not conduct himself just anywhere (same work).

Let nothing remove or draw you away from philosophy—not poverty, nor lack of any particular thing (Seneca, *Letters to Lucilius*, book II, letter 17).

Not to become angry when one ought, and to become angry when one ought not, is the mark of a fool (IV *Ethics*, chapter 9).

Not everything occurs by necessity; many things happen by chance and are capable of being either way (*On Interpretation*, chapter 6).

Not everything that appears probable is probable (I *Topics*, chapter 1).

No one honors wealth for its own sake, but for the sake of something else; friendship, however, is honored in itself (III *Topics*, chapter 2).

Not only is the person who steals secretly a robber, but also the person who wishes to steal openly (VI *Topics*, chapter 20).

Names are finite, but things are infinite; therefore one name signifies several things (I *Sophistical Refutations*, chapter 1).

Negation does not constitute a species (Boethius, *Book of Divisions*).

Nothing desires what it already has in itself, nor what is contrary to it (I *Physics*, text 81).

No change is infinite with respect to its termini, although it may be infinite with respect to time, as is the motion of the heavens (VI *Physics*, text 93).

Nature always desires what is better (*On Generation*, text 59).

Snow and rain have the same place and the same matter (I *Meteorology*, chapter 4).

A dead man is not a human being except equivocally (IV *Meteorology*, text 54).

In defining, the natural philosopher takes matter, whereas the logician takes form (I *On the Soul*, text 16).

Nights are more characterized by silence than days (chapter *On Divination*).

Nothing is better than intellect and knowledge, except God (*Book on Good Fortune*).

It is not only the human being who dreams, but also brute animals (Book IV *On Animals*).

No animal suffers such exceedingly violent pains in childbirth as a woman (Book VI *On Animals*).

Not everything that appears is true (IV *Metaphysics*, commentary 7).

Nothing acts with an action for which it has no power (IX *Metaphysics*, commentary 7).

We investigate not in order to know what virtue is, but in order to become good (Book II *Ethics*, chapter 2).

We ought not merely to state the truth, but also to assign the cause of the falsehood (VII *Ethics*, chapter 14).

Nature desires little, but opinion desires immeasurably much (Seneca, letter 16, book II).

A person who possesses very many things must necessarily need very many things (Boethius, book II of the *Consolation*).

No evil goes unpunished, and no good goes unrewarded (the same author, book IV, *On Providence*, section 1).

## O

Every unity is indivisible (X *Metaphysics*). This is understood with reduplication, as follows: everything, insofar as it is one, is indivisible. For “one” is defined as that which is undivided in itself and divided from everything else.

Everything that exists exists because it is numerically one, according to Boethius. This may be understood in one way as follows: everything that exists exists because it exists outside the soul; but a universal also exists outside the soul. Therefore it need not be numerically one, or singular, since a universal is a term of intention. Alternatively, it may be said that a universal, with respect to its being, is indeed singular, but with respect to its signification or representation it is something common.

Every cause is prior to its effect (according to the Commentator, in *On Causes*). The response is that priority is twofold: priority in time and priority in nature. The authority must therefore be understood of priority in nature, not in time; and “nature” here must have the force of “naturally.”

Every natural concept must be taken from form (VII *Metaphysics*). This is true of substances possessing form. If they are simple and immaterial, such as God and the angels, then their essential concept must be taken from their proper perfection and essence. It is therefore not surprising that the proper concept of prime matter is not taken from its own proper form, since it has none, but either solely from its entitative actuality or by analogy with the forms and perfections toward which it has an essential potency.

Whatever inheres in what is better and nobler is more choiceworthy (II *Topics*). It would then follow that drinking beyond measure and living drunkenly should be more choiceworthy, and that vices should be more choiceworthy because they inhere in better and nobler beings, namely, human beings. For in many respects brute animals live more temperately and more suitably to nature than human beings. On this matter, see the excellent little book by Plutarch, *Whether Brute Animals Possess Reason*. The statement should be understood not of everything that inheres in the better and nobler good—for then the objection concerning brutes would follow—but of a good. Even then it is not absolutely true, since sometimes what inheres in a simply lesser good is better than what inheres in a greater good. But it is true in a qualified sense, or insofar as it is such: insofar as it is such, it has a certain worthier being, or a nobler character, by reason of the subject, through which it surpasses another good that is otherwise equal or even greater but exists in a lesser good.

Every act of understanding is a being acted upon (III *On the Soul*). This is true of received understanding, but false of unreceived understanding, for example, God’s own understanding. God is pure actuality, understanding through the bare essence that understands, not through any potency or any intellection added to his essence. Therefore his understanding cannot in any way be called a kind of being acted upon.

Everything alterable is corruptible (I *On Generation*).

The response is that the passage speaks of corruptive alteration, not preservative or perfective alteration. For example, whatever becomes hot or cold is corruptible; but what is altered through receiving light, such as the moon, or through receiving knowledge, such as the rational soul, is not corruptible.

Every quality denominates its subject (in the *Categories*). This is understood according to the nature and character of each accident. For a relative accident denominates its subject in one way, and an absolute accident in another: the former with reference to another, the latter without such reference. Moreover, the fish called the torpedo, transmitting numbness through the net into the fishermen’s hands, impresses the same quality upon the net and upon the fishermen’s hands. Yet it does not impress and affect them in the same way, nor does it denominate them in the same way. The fisherman’s hand is said to be numb, but the net is not. For this quality is not naturally disposed to affect each subject in the same way as whiteness does.

The principles must always remain (I *Physics*, commentary on text 50). According to Averroes, this means that principles must not be changeable or generated from other things. This is also the Philosopher’s intention (same place).

Everything that comes to be comes to be from something like itself (VII *Metaphysics*). This is understood as follows: everything that comes to be through univocal and particular generation comes, absolutely speaking, from something like itself. The qualification “through univocal generation” excludes worms and similar animals, which exist and are generated from putrefaction through the power of the sun. The qualification “particular” excludes God, who is the universal cause of all things.

The quantity of every thing is determined, both with respect to greatness and with respect to smallness (I *Physics*, texts 36 and 38). The proposition applies especially to living things and their parts. In these, the body is intrinsically bounded by a maximum and a minimum, since it is the instrument of the soul, as is evident from its definition. Every instrument, moreover, is bounded at both extremes, as is taught in I and VII *Politics*. Further, since the growth and diminution of a living thing proceed from the soul and natural heat, whose power is finite, it is necessary that the living thing itself also be finite and determined. Add that nature does nothing randomly and abhors what is indeterminate and undefined, as is stated in II and VIII *Physics*. Therefore the growth and diminution of a living thing must not be indeterminate; the cause of their limitation is the soul, whose instrument is the body. The proposition must also be understood of things existing per se, not of things existing in another, such as the parts of a continuum in the whole. See further Toletus (Book I *Physics*, question 9).

Every principle must be a necessary proposition (I *Physics*). This is understood of a complex principle, and not of the absolutely first principle of some science; it is not understood of an incomplex and absolutely first principle. For such a principle is not a proposition, indeed it is not even always a necessary being, but rather something contingent and corruptible.

Every substance is nobler than an accident (VII *Metaphysics*). This is true with respect to essential nobility, but not accidental nobility, because an accidental accident can be nobler than a substance, as is evident in sciences and virtues, which are accidents nobler than pieces of wood and stones, which nevertheless are substances.

Every difference must be taken from form (according to Porphyry). This is understood as follows: every difference must be taken from form when comparing composite with composite; but when comparing a simple thing with a composite, it must be taken from matter.

All future things will occur necessarily (I *On Interpretation*). This is true in the composite sense, but not in the divided sense. Or it is true hypothetically, but not absolutely. For if future things are going to occur, then they will necessarily occur. It involves a contradiction for things to be going to occur and not to be going to occur. Nevertheless, not everything that is going to occur is going to occur necessarily in an absolute sense, or by some absolute necessity.

Whatever is, when it is, must necessarily be; and whatever is not, when it is not, must necessarily not be (I *On Interpretation*). This is limited in the same way as the preceding proposition.

Every difference must summon the other part of the thing (according to Porphyry). This is understood of things essentially composed, but not of simple things.

The same science concerns opposites (IV *Metaphysics*). The response is that the Philosopher means that contrary and contradictory opposing propositions belong materially to the same science. Thus someone who considers health also considers sickness, and conversely. Again, someone who considers the proposition “Health is a proportion of the four primary qualities suitable to an animal” also considers the proposition “Sickness is a disproportion of the primary qualities unsuitable to an animal.”

Everything prior can exist without what is posterior (according to the author of *On Causes*). This is understood only if one does not depend upon the other; otherwise it is not true.

Objects move the intellect (III *On the Soul*). The response is that objects do not move the intellect per se and immediately, but move it through intelligible species.

Every being has some proper operation (IV *Meteorology* and I *On the Soul*). This is understood of beings existing in formal actuality, because prime matter is passive rather than active. It has no proper formal act, but only an entitative act.

Every agent is more excellent than its patient (II *On the Soul*). This is understood of the principal agent, not of what commonly has the character of an instrument. Or it is understood of an agent as such, but not absolutely. See what was said above concerning this same axiom under the letter A.

Every proposition in which one of the most general genera is denied of another is immediate (II *Posterior Analytics*). This is understood when one of the most general genera is denied of another with reduplication, as in: “No substance, insofar as it is substance, is quantity insofar as it is quantity.”

It belongs to the best to make the best things (II *On the Heavens*). This is understood with respect to essential features. Thus every thing produced by God is produced in the best way with respect to its essential and substantial features. A human being, later assisted by natural gifts, acquires many further natural properties—for example, practical and speculative sciences. Assisted by supernatural gifts, namely, prevenient and cooperating grace, he also acquires many supernatural properties which he did not possess at his creation.

All things capable of transformation into one another have the same matter (I *On Generation*). This is understood with respect to specific identity: matter is specifically the same in all of them. Thus matter is subjectively present in all forms.

Every effect bears a likeness to its efficient cause (the *Author of the Book of Causes*). This is true of a particular cause, but not of the universal cause, namely, God. See the axiom explained shortly before: “Everything that comes to be comes to be from something like itself.”

## O

**Everything in which there is potency is either a body or a potency in a body** (Metaphysics X, Commentary 41, Averroes). This is true of passive physical potency, which, speaking simply, attests [Col. 1027B] imperfection, since it is the potency of matter. It fails, however, of logical potency, and also of a being of reason, for in all intellects below the First there is such logical potency, as Averroes maintains in On the Soul III; yet those intellects are neither bodies nor powers existing in a body.

**Every whole is divided into three** (On the Heavens I). Aristotle is speaking there of a body; that is, every quantitative whole, or body, consists of three dimensions: length, breadth, and depth.

**Every agent naturally undergoes reaction in acting, and every patient naturally reacts in being acted upon** (On Generation I). This is understood as follows: every agent that shares matter with the patient, acts through a real action, exists within the sphere of activity of the patient, and is not of greater power to resist than the patient is to react. Because of the first condition, God and the celestial intelligences do not undergo reaction when acting upon sublunary things, since they do not share matter. Those separate substances [Col. 1027C] have no matter at all, while the heavens do not have matter common with sublunary things but matter of a different kind. Because of the second condition, God and the intelligences do not undergo reaction when enlightening our intellect or inwardly suggesting and inciting it; indeed, neither do the heavens undergo reaction when, objectively, they move our intellect to contemplate them. Because of the third condition, the heavens likewise would not undergo reaction from, for example, the earth, even if they had matter of the same kind as the earth, because the earth’s sphere of activity does not extend so far as the heavens, whereas the sphere of activity of the heavens extends as far as the earth. Because of the fourth condition, a great fire into which a drop of water is thrown does not undergo reaction from it, even though it acts upon the drop by suddenly converting it into fire.

**Every being is either a being in the soul or outside the soul** (Metaphysics VI). The answer is that this is not simply true, because the soul provides a counterexample: the same thing is not in itself and not in itself as in a subject. The Philosopher therefore plainly intends that every being other than the soul [Col. 1027D] is either in the soul or outside the soul.

**Every science is either a posteriori or a priori** (According to the common statement of the logicians). The answer is that this is true of knowledge of a single conclusion, for there is a counterexample in the case of a complete science—for example, the science of the soul, which is partly a posteriori and partly a priori.

**Every cause makes its effect known a priori** (According to the author of On Causes). The answer is that this authority is true of causes per se, but not of causes accidentally so called.

**The object of the will is nothing but the good** (Ethics III). The answer: This is true of the apparent good, but not always of the existing good. The will desires only what appears good to it; but this is not always truly good, and is often merely apparently good.

**Contradictory opposition is the greatest opposition** (Sophistical Refutations I). The answer: This is true of things that are contradictorily opposed, insofar as they are mutually incompossible, namely, with respect to [Col. 1028A] truth and falsity.

**Every change is either rapid or slow** (Physics VI). This is understood of change distinguished from its termini. Or it may be said that it is understood of successive and temporal change; for this statement does not apply to instantaneous change.

**Every science concerns things that are universally perpetual** (Posterior Analytics I). It is understood as follows: every science concerning its proximate object of knowledge must consist of perpetual propositions, that is, propositions of perpetual truth.

**Opposites are in the same genus** (According to Porphyry). With respect to existence, this is true potentially, but not actually. For both contraries are not always actual at the same time.

**Everything that has a contrary admits of more and less** (From the Categories). This is meant in such a way that, for example, one white thing is not only whiter than another white thing, but one and the same thing is at one time white and at another time whiter.

**Every science derives nobility from its subject** (In [Col. 1028B] the Preface to On the Soul). The answer: This is true if “subject” means the designated subject, but not if it means the subject of the sign; that is, the subject of attribution, not the subject of inherence. Otherwise mathematics, physics, and metaphysics would have equal nobility, since they all inhere in the human soul. It is therefore understood of the subject assigned by the intellect, not of the intellect that assigns and receives the science of that designated subject.

**Everything intelligible precedes the act of understanding, or moves it.** This is understood of the principal intelligible, such as things outside the soul, which precede the intelligible itself in the order of nature, though not in time. But the less principal intelligible, namely, the operation, does not precede the intellect; rather, it proceeds from the intellect.

**Everything that is corrupted is corrupted by its contrary** (Ethics V). It is understood as follows: everything that is directly, formally, and per se corrupted is corrupted by its contrary. “Per se” and “directly” are expressly added because of [Col. 1028C] substance. Although substance is corrupted, it is not corrupted per se but accidentally: a quality is first corrupted per se, and the corruption of the substance follows as a consequence; thus the substance is corrupted accidentally.

**Every per se proposition is necessary or impossible** (According to Boethius in the book of the Posterior Analytics). It is understood as follows: every proposition that is per se true is necessary, and every proposition that is per se false is impossible.

**Contrary opposites come to be about the same thing** (Metaphysics VII). Thus it seems that good and evil come to be about the devil himself. This is understood provided that the subject is not determined to only one of the two, or to the other alone. For then contrary opposites do not come to be about the same thing. But the devil determines himself to evil alone and not to good.

**Everything more certain is more choiceworthy than what is uncertain** (Topics III). This is understood, other things being equal.

[Col. 1028D] **Everything perfect is in three** (According to the Commentary on On the Heavens I). This is understood to mean that the true number begins with three; of two, it is not properly said that they constitute a number, but only that they are two.

**Every perfection is in God** (According to the Commentary on Metaphysics V). The answer is that this must be understood to mean that God’s perfection surpasses every perfection of creatures.

**Every natural motion is faster at the end than at the beginning** (On the Heavens I).
