It is understood as follows: every natural motion through the same medium, equally disposed throughout, other things being equal, and produced by the same impulse from the same source, is faster at the end than at the beginning. “Through the same medium” is added because it may happen that a mixed body moves faster in fire than in air. “Equally disposed” is added because, if the medium were thinner at the beginning and denser at the end, the motion would not have to be faster at the end.

**Every question asks about opposites** (Metaphysics I). That authority is not simply or universally true, since one question may ask about only one opposite. [Col. 1029A] It is true, however, in the sense that a problem-question asks between two opposites, as in this question: whether the world is eternal or not.

**Everything that is in God is God himself** (Metaphysics VI). This is understood as follows: everything that is formally and essentially in God is God himself; but this does not apply to what is in God effectively, ordinatively, or conservatively.

**All our cognition proceeds from sensed things** (According to Lincoln, above, on the Posterior Analytics I). This is understood mediately or immediately. The same interpretation applies to the statement: “Nothing is in the intellect unless it was previously in the sense.”

**Every intermediate is an intermediate between contraries** (Physics VI). This is understood of intermediate and secondary qualities. Or it may be understood thus: every intermediate, whether composite or successive, is between contraries; or thus: every intermediate between diverse things, in the commonly accepted sense, is an intermediate between contraries.

**Whoever says anything at all says many things in a certain way** (Topics II). From this the second rule is drawn: whoever states one antecedent states many consequences, formally or virtually; for whoever says “Man exists” [Col. 1029B] virtually says “Animal exists,” “Body exists,” “Substance exists,” and so on for each of them.

**Everything sensible is sensible through matter, and everything intelligible is intelligible through form** (On the Heavens I, text and commentary 92). The answer, according to Averroes’ doctrine in Metaphysics XII, Commentary 14, is that matter which is per se sensible is proximate matter, not remote matter; but form is per se intelligible. Form is not sensed per se, but because of its operation. Therefore form is appropriately called intelligible and matter sensible. This is understood of proximate matter, not remote matter.

**Everything that is from what is prior is more choiceworthy** (Topics III). If this were so, water would be nobler than wine, matter nobler than form, and an old garment nobler than a new one. It must therefore be understood as follows: everything that is good because of what is prior according to perfection is better. But one might object that what is prior is nobler and better. The answer is that everything prior in essential perfection is better than what follows it, in itself and properly speaking. “In itself” is added because, according to our use, it need not follow that a florin is prior and more perfect than knowledge because the former is a substance and the latter an accident. [Col. 1029C] “Essential perfection” is added because of matter, which is not essentially more perfect than form. “Essential” is also added because of priority in nature, as with water in time [uncertain Latin: *aqua temporis*], and with an old garment.

[Col. 1029D] **Every pleasure is evil** (Ethics IV). It should be known that pleasure is twofold: bodily pleasure and pleasure of the soul. Bodily pleasure is twofold: one kind is contrary to the dictate of right reason, and this is always evil; the other is subject to reason, and this is always good. Pleasure of the soul is also twofold: one kind is a desire rightly regulated by reason itself, and this desire is always good; the other follows a private appetite, and this is always evil. The statement is understood of pleasure contrary to the dictate of right reason.

**Everything that is nearer to the good is more choiceworthy and better** (Topics III). If this were so, it would follow that a shirt is better than a tunic. In reply, it should be said that proximity is twofold: one kind is local, while the other is proximity of perfection. The authority is understood of proximity of perfection; otherwise the counterexample would prove the statement true.

**All the passions of the soul disturb the judgment of reason**, according to the common saying. This is confirmed by Sallust’s statement that all who deliberate about doubtful matters ought to be free from anger, hatred, and so forth. The answer is that passions which precede the use of reason disturb our intellect. But those that follow the judgment of reason, and are moderate and subject to reason, do not disturb the judgment of reason; rather, they obey it.

**Everything more difficult is more choiceworthy, and nobler than what is less difficult** (Topics III). If this were so, riches would be nobler and better than sciences and virtues. Likewise, the smith’s art would be more choiceworthy than grammatical knowledge, [Col. 1030A] and necromancy [OCR: “nigromantia”] would be more choiceworthy than logical knowledge. It should be known that something is called more difficult in three ways. First, with respect to preservation; in this sense riches are more difficult than the sciences. Second, with respect to exercise; in this sense the smith’s art is more difficult than grammar, because it is more difficult to forge than to produce a grammatically correct speech. Third, with respect to opposition; the authority must be understood of this difficulty. It is also understood of things belonging to the same species, provided that the less difficult thing does not possess a preeminence of goodness.

**Everything generable is corruptible** (On the Heavens I). The answer: This is true of everything generated as the proper and adequate term of generation, which is the composite itself. Although a human being is generated as such a term through the induction of the rational soul, the soul itself is not generated. Therefore this composite, the human being, is generable and corruptible, but the soul is not. The soul is not something that is generated; rather, it is that through which another thing is generated, namely, the human being.

[Col. 1030B] **The Creator of creatures established the species of all things** (Author of the Book of Six Principles). That is, God does not now create new species, although within one and the same human species he continually creates new souls.

**Given any great thing, it is possible to give a greater** (According to a rule of Metaphysics). This is understood as follows: it is possible to give a greater thing, that is, to imagine one.

**Every motion proceeds from one extreme to another through a medium** (Physics IV). The authority is understood of motion that occurs naturally. Motion occurring in a vacuum is not natural, since nature abhors a vacuum. Similarly, it may be said that motion through a vacuum does not occur through a true medium, but only imaginatively; therefore the authority is true of motion that takes place with resistance from a medium.

**The time of all existing natural things is the same** (Physics IV). This is understood comparatively, not absolutely. The motion of the first mobile measures all things, but according to more and less.

[Col. 1030C] **Everything that moves is divisible** (Physics VIII, texts 40 and 46; Physics VI, text 32; Physics V, text 62). It is understood as follows: everything that moves per se from place to place circumscriptively and commensurately is divisible. “Everything that moves per se” is added because of the intellective soul, which, although it moves with the motion of the body, does not do so per se but accidentally. “Circumscriptively” is added because, although an angel moves per se, it does not move circumscriptively from place to place, but definitively. Yet it is said that the heaven moves per se and nevertheless is not divisible, as is stated in On the Heavens I. The answer is that the statement is true of real division; nevertheless, the heaven is divisible according to the assignment of parts, namely, the eastern and western parts.

**Everything that moves locally describes for itself a space precisely equal to it at the same instant** (From Physics VI). Thus it seems that indivisibles, such as angels, would be divisible. The answer is that the authority is understood of what moves circumscriptively from place to place.

[Col. 1030D] **The best is opposed to the worst** (Ethics VIII, chapter 10). This axiom is not always true. For it is better to be studious than to have a natural inclination toward the study of the virtues. Yet it is worse not to have an inclination toward the study of the virtues than not to be studious; for if you lack that inclination, you are not a human being, since that inclination is implanted in human nature. Thus the worst is not always opposed to the best.

**Everything that moves is partly in the terminus from which it moves and partly in the terminus toward which it moves** (Physics VI). Thus it seems that a moving thing is never in a space precisely equal to it, contrary to the preceding authority. The answer is that this is understood as follows: while it is moving, everything that moves reaches the terminus toward which it moves and the terminus from which it moves in a particular way; that is, it is neither perfectly nor completely in the terminus from which it moves nor in the terminus toward which it moves.

[Col. 1031A] **All distinct acts are such that one can be preserved without the other** (Metaphysics VII). The answer is that this is true where one does not depend for its being upon the other. The acts of Socrates and of God are distinct acts, yet one cannot exist with the other. Likewise, knowledge is in the soul, and vital operations are distinct from the soul, yet one cannot be preserved without the other, as was said earlier.

**Everything that moves is moved by another** (Physics VII). It is said that it is impossible for something to move itself per se, as is stated in On the Soul III, while also being moved; thus it is impossible for anything to be both the total agent and the total mover, since at least God or prime matter must concur.

**Every intellect must be impassible** (According to the Commentary on On the Soul III). Against this stands the Philosopher in the same work at the beginning, where he says that the intellect is a passive power. The answer is that the Commentator means that the intellect must be impassible with respect to corruptive passion, although it can be passible with respect to preservative passion.

[Col. 1031B] **Everything incorruptible is nobler than what is corruptible** (Physics I). This is understood provided that the corruptible thing does not possess some better condition attached to it than the incorruptible thing. For example, matter is incorruptible, yet a corruptible form may be better—not because of its corruptibility, but because of something else.

**Every end is better than what is ordered to the end** (Topics III and Physics II). This is understood of the end for the sake of which something is done, since such an end is always better than what is ordered to it, precisely because it is the end for whose sake that thing exists.

**Every being is either substance or accident** (Metaphysics XII). This is understood of a being that is simply one, not an aggregate. Or the term “being” may be taken nominally, not participially; for an army is one being, that is, one existing thing, yet it is not one substance but several substances.

**Everything that comes to be pre-exists in some part of itself** (Metaphysics VII). [Col. 1031C] Consequently, it is formally in matter before its production, which conflicts with the Philosopher in Physics I. It must therefore be understood as follows: everything that comes to be completely, as a composite, has pre-existing parts, such as matter and form—if not in time, at least in nature. Prime matter precedes the composite in time, whereas form precedes it not in time but only in nature.

**Everything that moves has integral parts** (Physics VI). This is understood of what moves per se and circumscriptively.

**Every motion is from contrary to contrary** (Physics IV). This is understood of natural motion, not violent motion.

**Every being at its natural place rests from motion** (Physics IV and On the Heavens I). This is understood to mean that every being at its natural place rests from local motion. It is not true, however, of other motions, such as alteration and increase.

**All things that subsist by nature, except God—which, according to Empedocles, was heaven—consist of strife and friendship**, Aristotle writes [Col. 1031D] (Metaphysics III, text and commentary 15; On the Heavens and the World I, text and commentary 22; Meteorology I). According to certain philosophers, this had a sound interpretation. For anyone who considers particular cases inductively will see that certain properties run among beings. For example, something may be poison to a healthy person and yet a salutary medicine to someone who is ill. (See Zimara, folio 90.)

**Every body is in a place** (Physics I).

**Every whole is greater than its part** (Common proposition).

**We sense everything through a medium** (On the Soul II, text 114).

**People are deceived only in what they do not know, or in what is not very clearly known** (Metaphysics IV, Commentary 8).

**Everything that comes to be comes to be either by nature, by art, or by chance** (Metaphysics VII, text 22).

[Col. 1032A]

**Every lie is wicked and must be avoided** (Ethics IV).

**A work produced by better people is always better** (Politics I).

**Every household ought to be governed by its eldest member** (The same work).

**Every difference seems to produce sedition** (Politics V).

**The best people are those devoted to cultivating the land** (Politics VI).

**Every excess of things either harms or accomplishes nothing** (Politics VII).

**We love everything, but prizes more** (The same work).

**Everything that labors needs rest** (Politics VIII).

**Everything is alien; only time is ours** (Seneca, Letter 9).

**Every sin is a voluntary action** (The same author, On Morality).

**One ought to learn before teaching** (Boethius, On Discipline, chapter 6).

[Col. 1032B]

**Every artisan loves his own work** (Ethics IX, chapter 8).

**All things desire to be divine, and for the sake of the divine they do whatever they do according to nature** (On the Soul II, text 34, and Physics I).

**Every discourse, if it is shorter than it ought to be, obscures understanding; if longer, it will be difficult to retain and will induce forgetfulness in the student** (Boethius, On the Art of Grammar II).

**Art ought to imitate nature in this respect: that everything it does it should do for the sake of an end** (The same work).

**All things desire the good** (Rhetoric I; Topics III, chapter 1; Ethics I, chapter 1).

**Everything customary is pleasurable** (The same work).

**Forgetfulness is a sign of a slight valuation, and therefore produces anger** (The same work).

**Every affirmation is true or false** (In the Categories, chapter 5).

**To forget what one has shamefully done is characteristic of good people; to remember it, of bad people** (Topics III, chapter 10).

**The learner ought to believe** (Sophistical Refutations I, chapter 2, and [Col. 1032C] Posterior Analytics I, text 5).

**Everything that is corrupted is corrupted by a contrary** (Physics I, text 7).

**Everything that has matter is generable and corruptible** (Physics I, Commentary 89).

**Every agent acts for the sake of an end** (Physics I, text 75).

**Everything that moves must move in time** (Physics IV, text 129).

**Every motion is from something to something** (Physics V, text 3), that is, from the terminus from which it proceeds to the terminus toward which it proceeds.

**Every opinion contradicted by sense is unsound** (Physics VIII, Commentary 27).

**Opposites placed side by side become more evident** (On the Heavens II, text 40).

**Every natural being desires everlasting continuance** (Averroes, Book II, text 34).

**Every united virtue is greater than a multiplied virtue** (Author of On Causes, chapter 6).

**All animals bitten by a rabid dog become rabid, except [Col. 1032D] the human being** (Book VII of On Animals).

**All human beings by nature desire to know** (Metaphysics I, in the prologue).

**All things are corrupted in that out of which they are constituted** (Metaphysics III, text 15).

## P

**That because of which each thing is such is itself always more such** (Posterior Analytics I, chapter 2, and Metaphysics II, text 4). This axiom is restricted in five ways.

First, the attribute involved in the comparison must formally belong to both things being compared. Hence the following does not hold: “He walks because of health; therefore health walks more.” Nor does this: “The drunk man is drunk because of wine; therefore wine is more drunk.”

Second, the attribute involved in the comparison must admit of more and less. Hence it does not follow: “I am capable of laughter because man is capable of laughter; therefore man is more capable of laughter.” Nor does this follow: “Peter is a man because of his father; therefore his father is more a man.”

[Col. 1033A] Third, the cause must be univocal, not equivocal. Hence this does not hold: “The wall is white because of the painter; therefore the painter is whiter.” For even if whiteness belongs formally to both and admits of more and less, the painter of the white wall is not a univocal cause but an equivocal and almost universal cause, like God, who is the cause of all natural things.

Fourth, the comparison must concern positive effects, not privative ones. For it does not follow: “Peter is small because of his father; therefore his father is smaller.” Nor does this follow: “Because of God I do not love the world; therefore I do not love God more.”

Fifth, the things being compared must be genuinely distinct. Hence this does not hold: “I see because of my eyes; therefore my eyes see more.” For seeing by me and seeing by my eyes are not two different things.

**A perfect thing is one that can produce another like itself** (Meteorology IV, text and commentary 19). The proposition is true where another similar thing can be produced. The qualification is added because of God, since he cannot produce another God, as another God is not producible. It is further answered [Col. 1033B] that the proposition is chiefly true of the animals and plants found here. Aristotle is speaking there of seeds, as is clear to anyone examining the words of the text. In accordance with this, Aristotle says in On the Soul II, text and commentary 34: “The most natural work of living things that are perfect and not mutilated, or that possess spontaneous generation, is to produce another such as themselves: an animal, an animal; a plant, a plant.” Hence the proposition is properly true of things possessing a generative power.

**Particulars and singulars always divide into a multitude what is one** (According to Porphyry). The answer is that “particulars and singulars” must there be understood as “the less common.” The meaning is therefore that particulars and singulars—that is, less common things—divide, or contract through division, what is one, namely, the genus. For example, they contract body into animate and inanimate, and animate into sentient and non-sentient.

[Col. 1033C]

**A particular proposition in natural matter is equivalent to its universal** (On Interpretation I). This is understood of a particular proposition taken simply and of an indefinite proposition. Thus “Man is an animal” is equivalent to the universal proposition “Every man is an animal,” when the proposition concerns natural and necessary matter.

**A particular negative proposition is not convertible** (On Interpretation II). This means that a particular negative proposition is not formally convertible into another particular negative proposition, according to the customary manner of speaking. Nevertheless, it can be converted into one according to an unconventional manner of speaking.

**A proper attribute is predicated of only one** (According to Porphyry). This is understood of an adequate subject. Thus, although “capable of laughter” is predicated of John and Paul, and consequently of many others, it is nevertheless said to be predicated of only one insofar as it is predicated of man alone as its adequate subject.

[Col. 1033D] **Privation is not a being per se** (Posterior Analytics I). This means that privation, although it exists in matter, is not a being in formal act per se, but through the form of which it is the privation. Indeed, privation formally signifies a negation, but materially or connotatively it signifies an aptitude for form; hence it is rightly called a non-being.

**The principles must always remain** (Physics I, text 50). That is, they must be found in every change, or must always possess the conditions Aristotle describes there—namely, that they do not come to be from other things or from one another, and so forth.

**It is proper to substance not to be in a subject** (According to the Philosopher, in the Categories). The meaning is that no substance is in a subject as an affection, although it may be in a subject as a part.

**Plato was not wrong in placing sophistical discourse among non-beings** (Metaphysics VI). The answer is that the Philosopher takes “non-being” improperly for a being that bears the likeness of something, although it is not that thing.

[Col. 1034A]

**The penetration of dimensions is impossible** (Meteorology IV). The answer is that dimensions are of two kinds. Some are such that one has the role of act and the other the role of potency, as whiteness and prime matter; penetration is then possible in such dimensions. The same applies when two things have the role of act with respect to a third thing that has the role of potency, as whiteness and sweetness in milk. Other dimensions are such that neither one has the role of potency, or neither of the two has the role of potency; in such a case the penetration of dimensions is impossible.

**An infinite regress is forbidden** (Physics II). This is understood of essentially subordinated predicates.

**Potency is opposed to act** (Metaphysics IX and On the Soul I). It is said that this must be understood as relative opposition.

**The principles do not come to be from one another** (Physics I). This is not simply true, but only insofar as the word “from” indicates the circumstance of a part. For although form comes to be from matter, matter is not a part of form.

[Col. 1034B]

**Potency is accidental to matter** (According to the Commentator, Physics I). This is understood insofar as that common and essential potency of matter is determined, through particular accidental dispositions, to this or that form. Such potency, or such determination, is accidental to matter.

**The common is prior to the proper.** It should be said that the common is prior to the proper if both belong to one genus. But in things belonging to different genera, nothing prevents the proper from being prior to the common.

**It belongs to the political philosopher to consider the soul** (Physics I). Thus it seems that the book On the Soul is not a science. The answer is that the Philosopher in Physics I means that the political philosopher considers the soul practically, whereas in the book On the Soul the soul is considered speculatively.

**Privation and matter differ in concept and species** (Physics I). This means that the terms “privation” and “matter” have different concepts or definitions. Nevertheless, they may have the same numerically identical thing as their signified object or substratum; therefore they are not distinguished by that thing.

[Col. 1034C]

**The principles of sensible things are sensible** (On the Heavens and the World III, text and commentary 16). Averroes glosses this in the same place as referring to proximate principles. As he says, the proposition is not true of remote principles, because the remote principles of sensible things are not sensible, such as first form and prime matter.

**A higher power can do whatever a lower power can do, and in a nobler manner** (On the Soul III). The proposition is true of powers belonging to the same genus in substantiality, in the way in which the vegetative power is contained in the sensitive power, as a triangle is contained in a quadrilateral. The proposition has no place in things that do not belong to the same genus in substantiality. Thus the soul is a higher power than the body, but the soul cannot perform the function of the body; and form is higher than matter, but cannot perform the function of matter. [Col. 1034D] Likewise, when material powers are compared with abstract powers, the proposition does not hold formally speaking. For it does not follow: “Man generates; therefore an intelligence generates.”

**Increase presupposes alteration** (On the Heavens I, Commentary 22). According to Aristotle, in the Categories, this is understood of increase found in physical bodies. It fails, however, of imaginary increase found in mathematical things. It applies to true increase, which occurs in plants and animals, since such increase requires a preceding alteration.

**The principle in cognition is the end in operation, and the principle of operation is the end in cognition** (Physics VI, commentary on text 89, and Metaphysics VII, commentary on text 23). The proposition is true of practical matters, such as actions and productions. (See Aristotle, Ethics III, chapter 6.)

**Children are called blessed because of hope** (Ethics I). This is understood as follows: children are called blessed—that is, are said to be blessed—because of the hope of future blessedness, although they are not actually such. But one might ask why this is so. The answer is that we conceive this hope in them from their natural disposition; or because we see them inclined toward good and fleeing evil; or because they have been begotten by good people.

[Col. 1035A]

**Apart from truth there is neither affirmation nor negation** (On Interpretation II). The reason is that truth stands in a proposition as form; but nothing can exist without form.

**A proposition is wholly false if it has no true singular proposition** (Posterior Analytics I). This can be understood as follows: when the most general genus of one category is predicated of the most general genus of another category, the proposition is wholly false, since it has no true singular proposition. Or it may be understood simply to mean that a universal proposition of which no particular proposition is true is wholly false. For if it is not true in any part, it can certainly be said to be wholly false.

[Col. 1035B] **We are neither blamed nor praised for our passions** (Ethics II). Therefore passions are not worthy of blame or praise. The answer requires a distinction. Passions can be considered in two ways: in themselves, and insofar as they are subject to the command of reason and to the deliberation of the will. In the first respect they are judged worthy neither of praise nor of blame, since they are certain movements of the irrational appetite, which we share with other animals. If they are considered in the second way, they are worthy of praise or blame. For the sensitive appetite is closer to reason than the external limbs; but the acts of the external limbs are good or evil, and are so insofar as they are voluntary. Therefore the movements of the sensitive appetite are also good or evil. Moreover, although the appetite in itself lacks freedom, through its conjunction with reason it possesses freedom; and therefore virtues are located in it, such as courage and temperance. Thus passions, insofar as they are voluntary, deserve praise or blame.

[Col. 1035C]

**More goods are more choiceworthy than fewer goods** (Topics III). This is understood as follows: a greater number of possible goods that can coexist are more choiceworthy than fewer coexisting goods, provided that one of the greater number is not chosen for the sake of another, and provided that the superiority of goodness lies on the side of plurality.

The qualification “provided that one of them is not chosen for the sake of another” is added because becoming healthy and being health-producing are not more choiceworthy than health, since the former is chosen for the sake of the latter. It is also said that the goods must be of the same kind, so that the superiority of goodness does not arise from their matter but only from their plurality. For this reason it does not follow that four groschen would be more choiceworthy than a florin, although they are a greater number of goods.

It is further said: “provided that those goods are capable of coexisting.” Hence it does not follow that being a monk and being married would together be more choiceworthy than being a monk alone. Similarly, living chastely and begetting one’s likeness would be more choiceworthy merely because they are more numerous than living chastely alone. [Col. 1035D] This is false, however, because the goods are incompossible.

Finally, the statement is understood of finite goods, because God, who is an infinite good, infinitely surpasses all other goods, however numerous they may be, although he is one.

The passive intellect is indeed corruptible, because it understands nothing without a phantasm (III *On the Soul*). According to the Commentator, this text may be understood as follows: by “passive intellect” is meant the cogitative power, which is educed from the potentiality of matter; he calls it “intellect” in relation to the other senses, on account of its excellence. Others, however, say that the passive intellect—that is, the phantastic intellect, objectively dependent upon a phantasm—is corruptible. This is specifically on account of phantasy and phantasms, for both are corrupted: phantasy and the phantasms themselves. In another way, this is understood of an intellect that is not informed by intelligible species but is nevertheless apt to be informed, as regards its denomination. [Col. 1036A] For once it has been informed, it ceases to be called the possible intellect and becomes the acquired intellect, or the intellect in habit; and thus, with respect to that denomination, the possible intellect is corrupted.

When the possible is posited as actual, no absurdity follows. The meaning is this: if a proposition about possibility is changed into its proposition about actuality, then its proposition about actuality will not be impossible. For a fuller understanding of this authority, it should further be noted that, when certain possible propositions are posited as actual, three conditions are required. First, if a universal proposition about possibility is to be posited as actual, this should not be done by means of a universal proposition but rather by means of a singular one. Thus, “God can produce everything producible” should not be posited as actual in the form “God produces the producible,” but rather as “God produces this producible,” and similarly in other cases. Second, when the subject and predicate in a proposition about possibility are incompatible, then, in positing it as actual, a demonstrative pronoun [Col. 1036B] must be placed in the position of one of the extremes. Thus, “Everything white can be black” is posited as actual in the form “This is black,” with “this” indicating what was previously white. Third, when certain privative qualifications or terms are included in a proposition about possibility, and these could introduce some incompatibility in the corresponding proposition about actuality, then, when it is posited as actual, such qualifications must be omitted. Thus, “Socrates, who has eyes, can be without eyes” is posited as actual as “Socrates is without eyes.” Likewise, “Socrates can read tomorrow” cannot be posited as actual as “Socrates reads tomorrow,” but rather as “Socrates reads.”

When a substantial form is posited, that of which it is the substantial form is also posited (V *Metaphysics*). This is understood as follows: when an actual substantial form is posited, and is posited in the manner in which it is a form, that of which it is the form is posited as well. Now, after the death of a human being, the soul is no longer its actual form; therefore, at that time, the human being does not exist. He will exist again only when, at the resurrection of the dead, the soul has once more been united by God to the body.

[Col. 1036C] Some principles become known through sense, and others through custom (*Common Philosophical Axiom*). For this reason Aristotle says in VII *Topics*, chapter 4: Those who doubt whether the gods ought to be worshiped, or whether parents ought to be loved, require punishment; but those who doubt whether snow is white do not require sense. The worship of God and the love of parents are principles in the law, strengthened by custom, and therefore legislators have imposed bodily punishment. But that snow is white is known through sense, and that there is motion is likewise evident to the senses. Hence Aristotle says in VIII *Physics*, commentary on text 22, against Zeno, who denied motion: “To say that everything is at rest, and to abandon the senses while seeking a reason for this, is a certain weakness of the intellect.”

What is possible is rather to be chosen than what is impossible (III *Topics*, chapter 1). That is, what is easy rather than what is difficult. For there is no choice concerning things that cannot in any way be done, as is clear from III *Ethics*, chapter 2. This pronouncement is to be understood with the following qualification: provided that other things are equal—a qualification that should be understood in many other similar axioms as well. For this reason, acquiring knowledge through teaching is more to be chosen than acquiring it through discovery. The former is easy in itself, whereas the latter is very laborious. Although virtue is acquired with greater difficulty than knowledge, it is nevertheless more to be chosen because it is better; and the same applies in many other cases.

Principles are like the threshold of a doorway in a house, which no one overlooks (II *Metaphysics*, commentary 1, where the text also plainly says, “For who makes a mistake at the doors?”). Observe that some principles are principles of cognition, while others are principles both of cognition and of being. The proposition therefore applies to principles of cognition—such as first principles and common conceptions of the mind—that is, to the most common principles, which have their evidence solely from knowledge of the most common terms, such as “of everything it is said either to be or not to be,” and so forth. There are also principles that derive their evidence from the testimony of sense itself, such as that there is motion, and so forth. Particular principles, however, which do not possess such evidentness, sometimes require some persuasive support. For some principles of a particular science become known through induction, others through custom, as do the principles of laws and legal sciences, and others through other means, as Aristotle writes in I *Ethics*, chapter 10.

Plants are simple (II *On the Soul*). This is understood relatively, because their organs do not display as much diversity as animals’ parts do.

The sensitive power is opposed to the intellect (I *Ethics*). Not in itself, but accidentally. Each tends toward its own object and its own good. But circumstances of place, time, person, and so forth sometimes arise such that these goods cannot coexist. Moreover, the sensitive appetite is naturally disposed to obey reason, as Aristotle teaches in the same place. Therefore, it is not simply opposed to reason.

The sensory principle is in the heart (II *On the Soul*). [Col. 1037B] The meaning is that the animal and sensory spirits proceed from the heart.

The first motion is in the east (IV *Politics*). The reply is that this is true antonomastically, that is, by way of excellence, because nobler effects shine forth there.

The philosopher is one who knows the principles and causes of substance (IV *Metaphysics*, commentary 2). Here “philosopher” should be understood as the divine philosopher, for divine science is called “first philosophy” by antonomasia, by reason of nature and nobility, although in the order of teaching it comes last.

What is to be chosen is rather that to which a greater good or a lesser evil follows (III *Topics*, chapter 1). For example, preserving the evangelical counsels in this life rather than merely the common precepts, and cutting off a diseased limb rather than preserving it.

Principle and cause are convertible (I *Metaphysics*). This is understood of the principle of being, which is fourfold according to the four causes: efficient, final, formal, and material. If “principle” is taken in this way, then principle and cause are convertible. [Col. 1037C] Otherwise, “principle” has a wider extension than “cause.”

Through participation in the species, several human beings are one human being (*Isagoge* of Porphyry). This is understood as follows: according to St. Thomas, several human beings are one human being through participation in the species, that is, they are one in species. It does not follow: “They are one in species; therefore, they are one,” because everything that is one in species is one only in a qualified sense. Others explain it this way: several human beings are one human being through participation in the species, that is, they continue one human species, and thus the human species is perpetual. It may also be explained logically: several human beings are one human being, that is, several human beings are signified by the term “human being” through participation in the species. In another way, the natural likeness of a human being, or one common concept of the human being, is shared by several human beings.

The perpetual is corruptible. The meaning is that “perpetual” does not signify that something can never be corrupted, but only that it is never corrupted.

[Col. 1037D] A natural power is irrational (II *On Interpretation* and IX *Metaphysics*). The reply is that the proposition is valid with a specification, as in: “A power is natural; therefore, insofar as it is natural, it is irrational,” and so forth. It is not valid simply and without qualification, because a human being acts at one time purely naturally and at another according to the intellect, or according to the judgment of reason.

In perpetual things, being able to be differs in nothing from being (III *Physics*, text 32).

A philosopher ought not to assert anything that he does not at least show by demonstration or induction (VIII *Physics*, commentary on text 15).

Natural propositions become doubtful for two reasons: either because some people, having been brought up in false opinions, cannot assent to the true principles of philosophy; or because some hold something concerning the principles of geometry [the transmitted text is incomplete], against whom Aristotle argues in II *Metaphysics*, commentary on text 16, and the Commentator in I *On the Heavens*, commentary 90.

Because of evil inflicted by enemies, no one is injured and grieved as greatly as by evil inflicted by friends (II *On the Art of Poetry*).

No one is praised on account of bad and perverse customs (II *On the Art of Poetry*).

Those who have recently become rich are worse than those who have long been rich (II *Rhetoric*).

When the possible is posited as actual, no absurdity follows (*Prior Analytics*, chapter 18).

The principles of demonstrations are definitions (II *Posterior Analytics*, text 2, and I *Physics*, text 10).

The perfect is that outside of which there is nothing to take (II *On the Heavens*, text 23).

The soul completes more time in ignorance than in knowledge (II *On the Soul*, text 115).

Probable things, taken as a whole, cannot be false (III *On the Soul*, commentary 5).

Philosophy teaches human beings to know their creator (Aristotle, *On Death*).

The pure and perfect philosopher mortifies the desires of this age, which lead him to the mortification of body and soul (same work).

Because human beings wonder, they now and originally began to philosophize (in the Prologue to the *Metaphysics*).

The perfect is that which lacks nothing; and it is twofold: perfect simply, outside of which there is nothing, and perfect within a genus (V *Metaphysics*, text 21).

Lunch differs from dinner only according to the difference of time (VIII *Metaphysics*, text 5).

Privation and habit are the root of contraries (X *Metaphysics*, commentary 15).

The beginning is more than half (I *Ethics*, chapter 10, and V *Politics*).

Passion is neither virtue nor vice; according to it we are neither praised nor blamed (II *Ethics*, chapter 4).

What is first in generation is last in resolution (Book III, chapter 6).

Small expenses, made frequently, consume one’s substance (V *Politics*).

Concealed hatreds are worse than open ones (Seneca, *On Morality*).

Let hunger, not taste, stimulate your palate (the same author, chapter on self-restraint).

“I have lost money.” “Perhaps he would have lost it.” “O fortunate man, if you had lost your avarice along with her!” (the same author, *Remedies for Fortuitous Misfortunes*).

Philosophy is the teacher of all the virtues (Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy*, Prose 3).

Philosophy is the supreme consolation of weary souls (the same author, Book III, Prose 1).

Good character does not abandon its own rewards (the same author, Book IV, Prose 3).

Constant association produces contempt, whereas rarity wins admiration (Apuleius, *On the God of Socrates*).

The most excellent animal existing on earth is the human being (the same author, same work).

By our affirming or denying, nothing is posited in the thing itself (I *On Interpretation*, chapter 6).

[Col. 1038D] Everyone bears with the greatest difficulty being deprived of his honor (*Book of Economics*).

The reward of the virtues is honor (IV *Ethics*, chapter 9).

## Q

Every day we die, for every day some part of life slips away (Seneca, *To Lucilius, His Disciple*).

To seek a reason and abandon the senses is a certain weakness of the intellect (VIII *Physics*, text 22). This is understood as follows: he who seeks reasons by which to destroy what appears to the senses is weak in discernment and feeble in intellect. He does not know how to distinguish what is known in itself from what is not known in itself. True conclusions are declared only by propositions, propositions by sense, and the test of truths consists only in their agreement with sensible things, not the reverse.

When there are two agents, one stronger and the other weaker, the stronger produces its effect more quickly than the weaker (Common axiom). This is true of agents that eliminate a contrary, because where there is contrariety there is resistance, and where there is resistance there is succession, as the Commentator says in IV *Physics*, commentary 71. It fails, however, in agents without the elimination of a contrary, as is clear in the case of two luminous bodies, one more intense than the other. Both illuminate instantaneously, although the light produced by the more powerful is more intense than that produced by the weaker.

Whatever moves and is not moved no longer belongs to physical consideration (I *Physics*). Thus it seems that there is a science of God, since he is immobile, as is clear from VIII *Physics*. The reply is that the authority means only that beings that move, when considered apart from their relation to motion, do not belong to physical consideration; thus the physicist has nothing to consider about them except by reference to motion, of which nature is the principle. For whatever belongs to physical consideration simply, or quiddatively, must have a principle in itself such that it too is physically moved, rather than merely causing motion. Intelligences, therefore, although they move things physically, are not themselves physically moved. For this reason, according to their quiddity, they do not belong to physics.

Every definition that can be posited can be placed in a category (I *Topics*). This is understood to mean that every definition, according to its parts and reductively, can be placed in a category, but not per se and properly.

What comes to be is not (I *On Interpretation*). This is understood as follows: if some permanent being exists successively, then, while it is coming to be, it is not—that is, it does not possess complete being—but the successive coming-to-be of the thing is its being.

Every reduplicative proposition in which the predicate is reduplicated is false and impossible (I *Prior Analytics*). The reply is that this is true, as is clear in the proposition “A human being is an animal insofar as it is an animal”; that proposition is false and impossible, as is clear in the same place.

Whatever things are the same as one and the same thing are the same among themselves (I *Physics*). This is understood as follows: whatever things, taken separately, are the same as one and the same thing are the same among themselves. For if they are the same as a third thing only when taken collectively, they are not for that reason the same among themselves. It is further understood as follows: whatever things are the same as one singular term are the same among themselves. Thus a species is excluded; although Peter, Paul, and John are the same as the species, they are not the same among themselves. The reason may also suffice to limit this axiom: they are not simply the same in species.

Whatever the first cause can do together with the second cause, it can do by itself (according to the author of *On Causes*). This is understood in the genus of efficient cause and according to the absolute power of the first cause. But the axiom does not apply in the genus of formal or material cause. For although God can make a human being without a human being—for example, by creating a human being from nothing—he cannot make that human being white except through rational whiteness, that is, through some rational form; nor can he make him material or corporeal except through matter and body.

Whenever two things are the same in essence, if one is per se corruptible, so is the other (IV *Metaphysics*). Now we see that matter and the composite are the same thing in essence, and thus it seems that matter would be compossible; the same may be argued of the intellectual form. The reply is that this is true when they are entirely the same and one according to essence. But the matter and form of the composite are diverse essential principles of the composite and diverse essential parts; they cannot be said to be one in essence in the way that the composite is.

Whatever things differ in genus differ in number and in species (V *Metaphysics*). This is understood in two ways. First: whatever things differ really in genus differ really in number and species. Second: whatever things differ categorically in genus differ categorically in number and species. Or it may be said that the authority is understood within the genus of substance, and not within the genus of accidents.

Quantity is not among the active and passive powers in relation to one another (IV *Metaphysics*). The reply is that the Philosopher means that being active and passive are not attributed to quantity, but properly to the species of quality.

What receives being after not-being is generable (IV *Physics*). The reply is that this is true of what receives being from a form, because it is the form that gives being to a thing, as is clear from the Philosopher in I *Physics*. Hence the rational soul is not generable, although it has being after not-being, because it does not have being as a composite from some form. It is also true of formal being, but not of entitative being. Hence prime matter is not generable, because, although it did not always exist but received being from God after not-being, it nevertheless has no formal act but only entitative act; therefore it is not called generated or generable.

A question is a doubtful proposition (according to Boethius). [Col. 1040B] Thus it seems that a question is a proposition, which is nevertheless false. The reply is that “question” is taken in one way for the interrogative sign and the sentence with which one asks; in this sense, a question is not a proposition, and this is what Boethius means. In a second way, it is taken for the reasoning to which an interrogative sign is added; in this sense, a question is a proposition. For example, the sentence “Heaven has matter” is a proposition, to which is added: “Whether heaven has matter.” This is what Boethius means.

Whatever things differ by more than number differ in species (V *Metaphysics*). The reply is that the Philosopher means that whatever things differ essentially by more than number differ in species. Thus a man and a woman need not differ in species, just as Socrates who is white and Plato who is black do not differ in species, since they differ only accidentally in species.

He who does not understand one understands nothing (IV *Metaphysics*). The reply is that this is understood as follows: he who does not understand at least one thing understands nothing. Or, taking *non* as an indefinite term: “He who understands not-one understands nothing”; and this too is true.

Whatever lacks operation lacks essence as well (according to the Commentator, IX *Metaphysics*). The reply is that this authority is not universally true, because prime matter provides a counterexample. It is nevertheless verified if “essence” is taken for specific act or formal being.

What is not cannot be known (I *Posterior Analytics*). This is true as applied to what is near and directly knowable, but not as applied to what is remote. Or the meaning is: what is not cannot be known [the transmitted wording is uncertain]. For as a thing is related to being, so it is related to being known.

The quiddity of a thing is the form of the thing (VII *Metaphysics*). This is true in simple things, but not in composites. For there, according to the common opinion, matter too is part of the quiddity.

Whatever things have a difference in the same subject differ specifically (IV *Metaphysics*). If, therefore, those degrees in properly speaking alteration are acquired successively and have a difference in the same subject, they differ specifically, as the authority maintains; and thus the quality according to which properly speaking alteration occurs would not be simple but would be of different kinds. The reply is that the authority means that intensible and remissible qualities existing in the same subject, without constituting one total quality, differ in species. But if those qualities constitute one total quality, then they do not differ in species. For example, whiteness and blackness are in the same subject and are intensible and remissible, yet they do not constitute one quality in that subject; therefore, they differ specifically.

What is always or for the most part useful is better than what is useful only sometimes (III *Topics*, chapter 2). For example, justice and temperance are better than courage, since we can use the former always or almost always, but courage more rarely.

What is useful for all or for more things is better than what is useful for fewer things (III *Topics*, chapter 3). For example, water is superior to wine because no human being can do without water and its use is more extensive.

What inheres in a better thing is better (III *Topics*, chapter 1). For example, what inheres in the soul is better than what inheres in the body, such as virtue rather than health: virtue inheres in the soul, health in the body. This is not entirely true, however, unless it is understood of goods that are proper to the things in which they inhere.

Some things are better left unseen than seen (XII *Metaphysics*, text 5). This is true in human affairs, but not in divine affairs.

What a prudent person, a good person, a right law, one who excels in some matter insofar as he is such, an expert in any field, the majority, everyone, or everything chooses is superior (III *Topics*, chapter 1). For example, to care more for eternal things than for things that pass away with time; to suffer an injury rather than inflict one; to permit certain lesser evils in the commonwealth so that greater ones may not occur, rather than wish to eradicate everything completely; likewise, what the holy doctors have taught in explaining the divine Scriptures rather than what petty grammarians assert, and so forth.

Whatever is the cause of a cause is the cause of the effect (according to the author of *On Causes*). This is understood to mean that whatever is the cause of a cause, speaking of an essential and positive cause, is the cause of the effect. It is called “positive” because of vices, which are caused privatively. Thus, although God is the cause of a human being, he is not the cause of sin, because sin is a certain privation and defect of the human being. A straight tibia together with a bent tibia is the cause of walking, but not of lameness, because lameness is a certain defect and privation belonging neither to the cause of walking nor to walking itself, but to the deficient tibia.

Whatever things are of the same species: whatever belongs to one belongs to the other. This is a common conception of the mind. This is understood essentially, or of essential predicates, and likewise of proper accidents. It fails greatly in the case of other predicates.

What lasts longer is superior (III *Topics*, chapter 1). At least, understand: provided that other things are equal and that the things compared are good. Thus, the longer a life is spent uniformly in virtuous action throughout its entire duration, the better it is.

What is closer or more similar to a good thing, or more similar to a better thing, is better (III *Topics*, chapter 2). For example, those who imitate the apostolic life or Christ the best and greatest more closely than others do.

He who says that the soul rejoices or grieves says that it weaves and builds (I *On the Soul*). This is understood as follows: he who says that the soul alone rejoices or grieves says that it weaves, whereas the Philosopher means that this belongs not to the soul alone but to the soul insofar as it is joined to the body. Giles gives a more accurate and concise formulation in the same place: “He speaks less properly who says that the soul alone rejoices or grieves, and more properly who says that the human being does so.”

The things whose efficient causes are good are themselves good. Or, as some state it: The things whose causes are good are themselves good (II *Topics*, chapter 3). The truth of this is limited to the respect in which they proceed from good causes. For although some evils arise from good causes—for example, slight sins from good men—they do not proceed from those causes insofar as they are good. Often, too, an effect that would not have been evil if it had arisen from a good cause is corrupted by another evil cause; for example, if someone returns another person’s sword so that a murder may be committed. Indeed, very often, even when all the causes are good, one bad circumstance can make the effect vicious. Therefore, if the cause is good and the effect proceeds from it insofar as it is good, the effect will be good only if it is not corrupted from some other source.

Whatever can do more can do less (I *On the Heavens*). This is understood per se and by its own power, and of things belonging to the same genus. It does not follow: “He can compose a book; therefore, he can cook an ordinary meal,” even though the latter is less, since the two do not belong to the same genus. But it does follow: “He can compose a book; therefore, he can compose a letter, or three or four suitable lines.”

Those whose generations are good are good (II *Topics*). [Col. 1042A] This is understood per se, whether with respect to generation or with respect to the efficient cause. For it can happen that the father is good while the son is not, because of the son’s own will.

Those whose corruptions are good are themselves evil. This is understood of things whose corruptions are per se good; for if their corruptions are good accidentally, the things corrupted are not for that reason bad. For example, the death of the innocent Christ was per se evil, but good insofar as it was offered by him for our redemption. Conversely, the death of the tyrant Herod was per se good. But if the disgraceful slaughter of the nobles that he desired as he approached death and left to his sister, as though by testament, had followed, it would have been accidentally evil.

What truly is is an accident of nothing (I *Physics*, texts 30 and 26). That is, substance is not an accident of anything. The statement concerns substance properly so called, and likewise accident, and also things that are said univocally rather than analogically. For knowledge is substance in God but an accident in a human being. The reason for this proposition is that, as is said in the *Categories*, it is common to every substance not to be in a subject. But this is proper to every accident. Therefore, just as being in a subject and not being in a subject are contradictories, so being a subject and being an accident are contradictories.

What is more useful at every time is more eligible (III *Topics*). It would follow that courage is more eligible than temperance or justice, because courage is useful at every time. The reply is that courage is taken in two ways: first, with respect to the habit; second, with respect to the act. In this latter sense, courage is the operation of courage, and in that way it is not always actually useful, because if we were all just, we would have no need of such courage.

Whatever is in the effect is in the cause (Common proposition in *Metaphysics*). It would follow that every imperfection is in God. It is therefore understood as follows: whatever is perfection in the effect is also in the cause, not formally but virtually or reductively, because every perfection is ultimately ordered to the first cause.

To ask why certain things are appropriated in the same genus to certain beings is the height of folly. Therefore, one should not ask why earth is earth, or fire is fire, or ask, in the case of a simple thing, why a human being is a human being. It is mere trifling (VII *Metaphysics*, commentary 59; likewise IV *Metaphysics*, commentary 3, where it is said that predicating the same thing of itself is nugatory).

Quantity is not in the genus of active things (IV *Physics*). This is understood in one way as meaning that quantity, insofar as it is quantity, is not in the genus of active things; in this sense the proposition is true. But quantity insofar as it is substance is indeed in the genus of active things. In another way it is said that quantity, according to its essence, is not in the genus of active things, although it is so according to its dispositions.

What cannot be otherwise be we call necessary to be so (V *Metaphysics*, text 6). Note the two kinds of necessity that Aristotle presents in the same place: necessity simply speaking, and necessity as what is better and more fitting. Something may be necessary for an end in two ways. First, it is that without which the end cannot exist, as food is necessary for preserving human life. Second, it is that by which the end is reached better and more fittingly, as a horse is necessary for a journey.

When the nobler is generated from the less noble, generation is both simply and in a qualified sense corruption; but when, conversely, the less noble is generated from the nobler, it is simply corruption but in a qualified sense generation (I *On Generation*).

What exists potentially can fail to exist (XII *Metaphysics*, text 30).

What differs little appears to differ as though not at all (II *Physics*, text 56).

Nothing is contrary to quantity.

What a person does not believe does not move him to fear or hope (II *Commentary on the Art of Poetry*).

[Col. 1043A] What is customary is as though innate (I *Rhetoric*).

Whatever is more excessive and greater than it ought to be is evil (same work).

What is shorter is always more pleasurable (II *Rhetoric*).

What has been said cannot be taken again (in the *Categories*, chapter on Quantity).

What is said frequently confuses the hearer (V *Topics*, chapter 4).

Those who are ignorant of the meanings of virtue-names are easily deceived (I *Elencus*, chapter 1).

He who says that nature does not act for an end removes God’s solicitude for these lower things (II *Physics*, commentary 75).

What is not is nowhere (IV *Physics*, text 1).

He who lacks sense lacks the intellect of that class of sensible things (II *On the Soul*, commentary 93).

Whatever things differ in subject differ in being (same work, text 152).

He who senses nothing learns nothing and understands nothing (text 39 of *On the Soul*).

What is in potentiality is the privation of what is in actuality (Commentary on *Sleep and Waking*).

Whatever the secondary cause can do, the primary cause can also do in a nobler and higher manner (author of *On Causes*, chapter 2).

He who seeks philosophy seeks the highest and divine degrees (Book *On Morals*).

He who finds philosophy finds life in both ages (same work).

He who doubts and wonders appears to be ignorant (in the Prologue to the *Metaphysics*).

As each person is, so he lives (IV *Ethics*, chapter 14).

They pray for things that are simply good for human beings (V *Ethics*, chapter 2).

The greater one’s fortune, the less secure it is (VIII *Ethics*, chapter 1).

What is acquired with greater labor is loved more (IX *Ethics*, chapter 8).

Some new things give pleasure, but afterward do not give pleasure in the same way (X *Ethics*, chapter 2).

He who serves another is not sufficient in himself (IV *Politics*).

What is little differs almost not at all from what is nothing (V *Politics*).

Whatever you are about to say, before saying it to others, say it to yourself (Seneca, *On Death*).

## R

Remission occurs through the admixture of a contrary; this is gathered from the Philosopher’s teaching (V *Physics*, commentary on text 9, and II *On the Heavens*, commentary on text 37). The proposition is true of things possessing a contrary; it has no place in things lacking contrariety, for light is intensified and diminished because of the power or weakness of the agent. Even in things possessing a contrary it does not hold universally, for among simple things considered in their purity, one element is remiss in quality with respect to another.

[Col. 1043D] To seek a reason for things evident to the senses is a certain weakness of the intellect (VIII *Physics*, commentary 22). There Themistius says that, where the senses provide assurance, to seek a reason is a very ridiculous act and a certain weakness and dullness of mind—not immediately to perceive what requires a reason. For there are some things more certain and clearer than to demand any reason for them. See this same axiom explained under the letter Q.

It is ridiculous to try to demonstrate nature, because this is known in itself (II *Physics*). The reply is that the authority means that it is ridiculous to wish to demonstrate nature, for example, with respect to what it is and similar matters, because these are known in themselves; but this does not apply with respect to other questions.

The roots in plants are analogous to the mouth in animals (II *On the Soul*). The reason is that, according to the Philosopher in the same place, both root and mouth receive nourishment, through which the thing is preserved in its individual being.

Natural and artificial things are distinct (II *Physics*). [Col. 1044A] This is understood according to denomination: an artificial denomination is posterior to a natural one, and thus they are distinguished according to reason, though not according to the thing itself. Art is related to nature as the mode of a thing is related to the thing; therefore, it is distinguished from nature not really but only formally.

Repetition ought to be used in difficult matters (in the *Categories*, under Relation). Such matters—for Aristotle says this near the end of the chapter—cannot be perfectly clarified unless they have been treated repeatedly. Themistius likewise writes clearly in III *Physics*, in his exposition of the commentary on text 15, where he repeats Aristotle’s definition of motion in other words. He says: “But let us repeat that same point again, not merely a second time but a third and fourth time, and, if it pleases us, even more often, so that the difficulties may become apparent and be disentangled, and so that at least through frequent treatment we may easily grasp them.”

The recipient must be stripped of the nature of what is received, both in real reception and in spiritual reception [Col. 1044B] (II *On the Soul*, commentary 67, and III *On the Soul*, commentary 4). This proposition is understood as referring to the nature of that species, not to the nature of its genus, especially not its most remote genus, and especially not that which is said equivocally.

Relatives are simultaneous by nature (in the *Categories*). It should be observed that two conditions are necessary for things to be simultaneous by nature. First, there must be mutual consequence from one to the other with respect to their existence. Second, neither may be the cause of the other. Because the first condition is lacking, the superior and inferior are not simultaneous by nature. For although “A human being exists; therefore, an animal exists” is valid, “An animal exists; therefore, a human being exists” is not. Because the second condition is lacking, the sun and light are not simultaneous by nature, since the sun is the cause of light; Relations, however, possess both conditions. For the mutual consequence from one to the other is valid, and neither is the cause of the other. These two conditions, however, are verified in them insofar as they are relatives, that is, according to the very form of the relation, but not according to the foundation and subject of the relation. [Col. 1044C] For that human being who is a father is certainly prior to the human being who is his son, and is his cause. Nevertheless, insofar as he is a father, he is not prior to the son, nor does the son depend more upon him according to this relation than he himself depends upon the son; rather, there is a wholly mutual dependence. Therefore, either neither is the cause of the other, as the doctors commonly say, or they are causes of each other, as Simplicius says together with Archytas.

Some things are universal and others particular (I *On Interpretation*, chapter 5).

A rhetorician does not always persuade, nor does a physician always heal (I *Topics*, chapter 22).

Rudity is not knowing for which things one ought to seek a demonstration and for which one ought not (IV Metaphysics, text 9).

Restraints are remedies for pleasures (II Ethics, chapter 3).

A king ought to relate to his subjects as a shepherd does to sheep (VIII Ethics, chapter 8).

The ruler is naturally more worthy than the ruled (I Politics).

[Col. 1044D] Rest is necessarily pleasant, because it is a remedy for sadness, which consists in toil (VIII Politics).

Remedies do no good unless they are allowed time to remain [in effect] (Seneca, Letter 40, Book V).

The effects of things are made clear through the performance of their work (Boethius, chapter 7, On the Discipline).

An answer given to questions expressed equivocally ought to be given with a distinction (VII Metaphysics, commentary 36).

Dew is subtle rain descending at night (I Meteorology, chapter 4).

Faith ought to be given to reason if the things demonstrated agree with those things perceived by the senses (III On the Generation of Animals, chapter 10).

Rest and play appear to be necessary in life (IV Ethics, chapter 15).

Wine taken immoderately disturbs reason, dulls the intellect, weakens the memory, brings on forgetfulness, pours in error, and induces ignorance. Taken moderately, [Col. 1045A] however, it sharpens the mind (Boethius, On the Discipline, chapter 2).

## S

There is always one contrariety in one genus (I Physics, text and commentary 56). This is true of contrariety according to being and nonbeing—that is, according to privation and possession—for in every genus there is one contrariety, namely, privation and form, or according to contrary differences dividing the genus between them.

The division of a genus is always into several species (Porphyry, *Isagoge*). This is understood to mean that every genus is always divisible by logical division, through opposed differences, into several actual species existing potentially in the genus. There must be at least two of those species; nevertheless, this is compatible with there being more.

[Col. 1045B] “Thus the things that are in speech are signs of the passions that are in the soul” (I *On Interpretation* [περὶ Ἑρμηνείας]). In this proposition, by “the things that are in speech” the Philosopher understands vocal signs, and by “passions in the soul” he understands mental terms and concepts. The sense of the authority is therefore that vocal signs are signs—that is, signs of concepts or mental terms. From this authority is gathered the common dictum that words ultimately signify concepts by convention, although the concepts to which they are subordinated signify naturally.

Only the species has a property (Porphyry, *Isagoge*). This is understood to mean that a property is attributed to the species more than to anything else, because a property flows from the essence of a thing, that is, from its species. Alternatively, it is said that he himself commonly takes “species” for any common subject.

The sophist desires more to appear to be wise without actually being wise than to be wise without appearing so (I *Sophistical Refutations*). The meaning is that the Philosopher intends only this: what belongs properly to the sophist is appearance, not reality.

It belongs only to the metaphysician to consider the quiddities of all things (VI Metaphysics). The response is: this is true in general, but not in particular. For the physicist considers human beings, the earth, and other natural things quidditatively.

[Col. 1045C] “If you say the word ‘is’ in isolation, it too is nothing” (I *On Interpretation* [περὶ Ἑρμηνείας]). The meaning is: if you say the word *is* purely, that is, in isolation, it too is nothing—that is, it signifies neither truly nor falsely. Others, however, have the authority in another form: “Nor should you say the word *is* in isolation.” It is then understood as follows: not that, if you say the word *is* in isolation, it signifies nothing in such a way that it signifies nothing at all—for it does signify something—but because it signifies a certain composition, which nevertheless cannot be understood without its extremes, it is rightly said to signify nothing.

Singular things are closer to sense (I *Posterior Analytics*). It is objected that in the same work universals are said to be more knowable than singulars. The answer is that the intellect first cognizes under a singular concept, though one that is more vague or common: thus it first cognizes that something is some animal before it cognizes that it is some human being, and first cognizes that something is a human being before it cognizes that it is this human being.

[Col. 1045D] The agent is always more honorable than the patient, and the principle—that is, the efficient cause—is nobler than matter (III *On the Soul*, text and commentary 19). This is understood of things similar in form, in degree of form, and also in potency. For action follows an abundance of form, and an abundance of form follows an abundance of matter. It is glossed in another way as concerning a patient corresponding to the agent itself. For it is not absolutely necessary that every agent be nobler than every patient. It is certain, for example, that the powers of the sensory soul are passive, as is clear in II *On the Soul*, text and commentary 51, while the powers of the nutritive soul are active; yet we do not say that they are simply nobler than the sensory powers, and so forth.

“But this is separated from that as the perpetual from the corruptible” (II *On the Soul*). This is understood as follows: the intellective power is separated from the other powers as the perpetual from the corruptible. [Col. 1046A] Others say that the Philosopher there compares the intellective power in human beings with the sensory soul in irrational animals and the vegetative soul in plants. In this sense it is true that the intellect is separated from the vegetative and sensory powers as the perpetual from the corruptible; but it is not true insofar as those powers exist in one subject, namely, the human being. Still others understand it as follows: “this,” that is, the divine intellect, is separated from “that,” that is, the human intellect, as the perpetual from the corruptible. Although, in the truth of the matter, the human intellect is incorruptible, perhaps according to Aristotle it is corruptible; his error, however, ought not to trouble us.

Substance does not come to be from non-substances (I Physics, text 22). The reason is that otherwise substance would come to be either from nothing or from an accident, and thus the accident would be prior to substance. See Aristotle, VII Metaphysics, text 4.

If one of two contraries exists in nature, the other must exist (III *On the Heavens*, text 18). [Col. 1046B] The proposition is true of positive contraries that contribute to the perfection of the universe, for the universe is complete and perfect at every moment. Hence all species that contribute to the perfection of the universe always actually exist in the universe. Although for us roses are not present at this moment because it is winter, they are found in another region where at this moment it is spring. But this fails for privatively opposed things, since it does not follow that, if the full exists in nature, the void therefore exists in nature; nor does it follow that, if the finite exists, the infinite will also exist. The statement is otherwise pronounced and restricted in this way:

“If one of two contraries exists in nature, the other will exist.” The response is that this is true of positive things and according to physical consideration, but not according to logical consideration. Similarly, although generation and corruption are contrary to each other, it does not follow conversely that wherever there is contrariety there are generation and corruption. For there is contrariety in the heavens according to the rare and the dense, yet there is neither generation nor corruption there. See Simplicius on this text in II *On the Heavens*, and text 41.

[Col. 1046C] Simply speaking, that is better and more choiceworthy which the better discipline commands us to choose (III *Topics*, chapter 1)—for example, moral philosophy rather than medicine.

Sense is a certain alteration (II *On the Soul*). The response is that sense, or sensation, is a certain preservative alteration.

Metaphysics alone is the common science (I Metaphysics). The response is that the Philosopher there considers science common in terms of its principles or objects. In this respect, relative to the other sciences, metaphysics is indeed common because it considers what is more common.

The sophistic, dialectical, and metaphysical disciplines concern the same thing, since the Commentator says that metaphysics and dialectic agree in subject. The response is that this is true because they agree in natural subject, but they differ in formal subject. Thus metaphysics formally and essentially, or principally, considers being insofar as it is being; whereas sophistic and dialectic [Col. 1046D] consider being of reason essentially and principally, and consequently consider being. In this way they agree in natural subject, and it is not incongruous for the same thing to be considered by several disciplines.

As a thing has being, so it also has cognition (IV Metaphysics). This is understood in one way as follows: as a thing has being through a cause, so it is also known through a cause. But it does not follow conversely that a thing has being in the way it is known. For it is known universally, yet it does not have being universally, since everything that is, is because it is one in number, as Boethius makes clear.

Only the species is defined (according to Boethius in the book *On Definitions*). This is true insofar as the species alone is defined as the proximate definable by a quidditative and essential definition, although genus and individual can be defined as remote definables. This is also said with respect to equivocal things, which, insofar as they are equivocal, do not belong to any species and therefore, insofar as they are such, are not defined.

When any integral part is removed, the whole is removed [Col. 1047A] (a dialectical axiom in the *Topics*). This is true if the word “whole” is taken for the integral whole precisely insofar as it is an integral whole. For if it is taken for the thing to which integrity is attributed, but not insofar as it is integral, it is false. For example, if Socrates’ finger has been cut off, one may conclude that Socrates is not integral; but one may not correctly conclude that Socrates does not exist. For although Socrates is not whole without the finger, he can nevertheless remain in nature without the finger. Therefore, if one wishes to take the word “whole” broadly, one must apply this qualification: the name of an integral part must be taken to mean a necessary part—such as the head or chest in Socrates—not just any part indiscriminately. For when any necessary part is removed, the thing whose life depends on that part is entirely removed. This dissolves the argument: “A certain part of a white human being is not white—for example, the pupil; therefore, a white human being is not white.” One should answer: it is correct to infer that a white human being has some non-white particle; but it is not [Col. 1047B] correct to infer that a white human being is not white. That conclusion could be reached only if the person arguing showed that no greater portion of the white human being is entirely white, whereas it must be entirely white for that person to be white.

Definition belongs only to substance (VII Metaphysics). The response is that quidditative, essential, and proper definition belongs only to substance. The Philosopher did not, however, intend to deny that an accident can be defined by an addition to its substance. For just as an accident does not have its own being, or being per se, in the manner of substance, but has a certain being dependent upon substance, so too it has a definition with an addition.
