Substance is prior to accident in time, nature, and definition (VII Metaphysics, text 4). The reason is that since an accident does not subsist through itself, it necessarily presupposes substance. This is to be understood either of a determinate accident—for according to Averroes, indeterminate quantity precedes every substantial form—or of substance taken broadly. [Col. 1047C] For although indeterminate quantity is prior in nature to form, it is nevertheless posterior in nature to prime matter.

The sense of sight is loved above all the senses (in the prologues to the *Metaphysics*). This is understood with respect to knowledge and according to the representations that the senses make in themselves. Sight is then loved above all the senses because it shows us more differences among things—not only lower bodies but also those higher and celestial bodies. Further, more things are perceptible by sight than by the other senses, both more clearly and at a greater distance. Finally, sight represents things to us with less difficulty than the other senses.

By the sense of touch we distinguish the wise from the foolish (II *On the Soul*). The reason is added in the same place: “We call those who are soft in flesh apt in mind.” Thus the Philosopher does not mean that we are wise according to touch; rather, he means that according to touch, as a sign, we call people disposed and suited to knowledge. This is true of softness arising from a good temperament, or sanguine softness, but not of the phlegmatic softness found in women.

[Col. 1047D] Things are similar whose quality is one (V Metaphysics). It would follow that a vocal term does not signify a written term, since it does not have one quality or any similarity with it. The response is that although a vocal term and a written term are not similar in quality, or even in some real similarity, they are nevertheless similar in the quality or similarity of representation, and in this way one signifies the other. Moreover, the quality in similar things need not be one in number; it is enough that it be one in species.

Science belongs among perpetual things (I *Posterior Analytics*). This means that the truths of which demonstrations and sciences exist never change and cannot change. A triangle will always have three angles equal to two right angles; a composite of the four elements will always be corruptible; and so forth.

[Col. 1048A] Science is divided into that which is sought for the sake of utility and that which is sought for the sake of knowledge. The response is that the Philosopher there distinguishes sciences into speculative and practical sciences. He says that practical sciences have an action as their end, and that speculative sciences have cognition as their end—which does not mean that this cognition too is not good and capable of being ordered toward the good, and therefore useful in that sense, but that it does not have action as its end and does not pertain to the necessities of this common life in the same way as practical science.

The species of things are related as numbers are (VIII Metaphysics). This is understood as follows: just as the number ten is added to another number and a new species of number results—ten added to ten gives twenty, and one added to three gives four—so, in a similar way, when something essential that is not the essence of a given species is added to that species, another species results.

There is no demonstration of the subject (I *Posterior Analytics*). This means that no science demonstrates that its subject exists; it presupposes it. [Col. 1048B] In every science, as is stated in I *Posterior Analytics*, the meaning of the name and whether the thing exists are presupposed concerning the subject, while what the thing is and what kind of thing it is are investigated and shown by demonstration.

Sense is of singulars, whereas intellect is of universals (III *On the Soul*). The response is that this means sense is of singulars, not that the intellect does not also understand singulars, but that only the intellect understands universals and universally. Sense can cognize singulars, but it knows only singulars and does so singularly. More briefly, the axiom may be stated: sense is exclusively of singulars, whereas intellect is not only of singulars but also of universals.

Substance is not the same as accident (I *Topics*). This is understood essentially, because an accident and its subject do indeed constitute one thing in number, but accidentally, as is clear in VII Metaphysics.

If you are handsome, praise nature; if you are rich, praise fortune; if you are wise, praise yourself (Seneca). This maxim [Col. 1048C] is not wholly true; rather, if you are wise, praise nature above all. For, as Victorinus says, nature makes one capable, art makes one skillful, and practice makes one powerful.

Science is divided in the same way as things are (III *On the Soul*, text and commentary 38). This proposition is true of our science, for Aristotle is speaking of it. But it fails of the sciences of God and of the intelligences, because knowledge in God and in the intelligences is not divided according to the division between potency and act, nor between universal and particular. Knowledge in the intelligences is also not divided according to the diversity of sciences, and so forth. God’s knowledge of beings is such that no other intelligence can participate in it, because beings are not something different from God’s knowledge so as to be contained in it; and nowhere is being simply identical in every respect with the intellect of the knower, except in the First Principle.

If the predicate follows the subject, an increase in the predicate follows an increase in the subject. If the predicate does not follow the subject, neither will an increase [Col. 1048D] follow an increase. This is commonly expressed as: as the absolute relates to the absolute, so the greater relates to the greater, and the greatest to the greatest (IV *Topics*, chapter 3). For example, if greater virtue is better and the greatest virtue is best, then virtue is good. The reasoning is parallel. But if greater virtue were not better, or the greatest virtue best, virtue would not be good at all. Likewise, if the morally noble good is good in itself, the more morally noble is better, and the most morally noble is best. And if doing an injustice is evil in itself, doing a greater injustice is worse, and doing the greatest injustice is worst.

The axiom is nevertheless qualified: it is ordinarily understood of predicates said essentially of their subjects. Otherwise it does not hold universally. For one may not correctly say: “Greater use of wine is worse, or the greatest use is worst; therefore, the use of wine is bad.” Nor may one say: “Exercise of the body is good; therefore, more is better and the most is best.” The reason is that greater use of wine is not essentially worse, nor is the greatest use essentially worst. [Col. 1049A] Nor is bodily exercise good essentially or in itself, but accidentally; hence it does not follow that more is better and the most is best. Otherwise every exercise of the body would be good, and every use of wine bad.

If infinitely many points were to converge, they would not make a line (I *On the Heavens*). The response is that the Philosopher is speaking of indivisible points, and means: if infinitely many indivisible points were to converge, they would not make a line. This is true, for the divisible is not composed of indivisibles, although it may be continuous.

The separation of form from matter is its corruption (IV Physics). The response is that the Philosopher is speaking there of a form drawn out of the potency of matter, such as the form of an irrational animal.

Definition belongs only to the incomplex (VI *Topics*). The response is that this is true of the proximate definable, but not of the remote definable.

Like does not suffer from like (I *On Generation*, text 46).

[Col. 1049B] If it is shameful not to be able to defend oneself with the body, it is more shameful not to be able to defend oneself in speech (I *Rhetoric*).

I say “simply” when I say it without addition (II *Topics*, chapter 30).

What is simply known is not what is known by everyone, but what is known by intellects that are well disposed (V *Topics*, chapter 4).

One must always set true things before the learner (VIII *Topics*, chapter 1).

Those who know the universal often fail to know the singular itself (Politics, text 30).

Sensing is of the singular, but sense is universal (II *Posterior Analytics*, text 27).

Of the sciences, one is perfect, namely, that which is through a cause; another is imperfect, namely, that which is without a cause (ibid., commentary 1).

If it were possible for us to exist in an unchangeable state of being (IV Physics, commentary 98).

By sitting and resting, the soul becomes prudent (VII Physics, text 20).

[Col. 1049C] Substance is nobler than accident (II *On the Soul*, commentary 2).

The stars are not seen by day because of the sun’s light (ibid., commentary 72).

Sense always speaks the truth concerning particulars, but not concerning universals; intellect, however, does the converse (ibid., commentary 152).

As probity is a reward for the good, so wickedness is a punishment for the wicked (Boethius, IV *On the Consolation*).

The resolution of doubt is the discovery of truth (VII Ethics, chapter 4).

Rising during the night is exceedingly beneficial for health and for the study of philosophy (the book *Economics*).

## T

[Col. 1049D] We know each thing when we know all its causes (I Physics, text 1; likewise X *Posterior Analytics*, chapter 2, and II *Posterior Analytics*, chapter 11). The proposition is to be understood of knowledge of a thing that is simply perfect, and of its essential causes. The reason is that, as a thing relates to being, so it relates to being known (II Metaphysics, text 40). All causes, both proximate and remote, concur in producing the being of any thing. Hence infer that no thing can be perfectly known through one science alone, but only partially or according to some particular consideration.

Only one thing is opposed to one thing (I *On Interpretation* [περὶ Ἑρμηνείας]). This is understood within the same species of opposition, since it is not incongruous for several things to be opposed to one thing in different species of opposition.

There are only two elements (V Metaphysics). This is understood as follows: there are only two elements—that is, two true first principles—matter and form. There are, however, four so-called elements: air, fire, water, and earth. Certain ancients posited and called these the first principles of things, although they were not first, since they were composed from those first principles, matter and form.

[Col. 1050A] A quality of a certain kind added to its like makes the latter more such (III *Topics*, chapter 9). This is understood of positive and natural qualities, such that a positive quality added to a positive quality in the same subject makes it more such. It says “positive” because this is not true of privative qualities: one negation added to another does not strengthen its force but rather destroys it. It is also understood of something that is not infinite. This qualification is expressly made on account of God’s perfection, which is infinite; consequently, nothing can be added to it that would make it more perfect.

Substance is threefold: form, matter, and the whole composite (II *On the Soul*, and VIII Metaphysics). The Philosopher thus appears to intend that matter and form are distinguished from the whole composite. This seems contrary to what he says in I Physics, where he says that the whole is its part. The response is that the Philosopher distinguishes matter, form, and the whole composite when taken separately, not when taken together. The authority in I Physics [Col. 1050B] is understood to mean that the whole is nothing other than its parts joined together or taken together.

Three is the first multitude (I Physics). It would therefore seem that two is not a multitude. The response is that the Philosopher means that three is the first multitude exceeding another number, and in this sense it is true.

The end of theoretical science is truth, whereas the end of practical science is action (I Metaphysics). The response is that the Philosopher is speaking of action performed externally. Although logic and the other arts also perform an operation while they contemplate, that operation is internal.

Each thing is perfect when it reaches its proper power (VII Physics). The response is that the Philosopher means that each thing is most perfect when it reaches the due degree and ultimate limit of the perfect power appropriate to it.

Time is not motion (IV Physics). The response is that the Philosopher means that this is not an essential predication. Time is motion, but only accidentally and convertibly, because when I say “time is motion,” the subject is predicated [Col. 1050C] of its proper attribute.

Time is everywhere (IV Physics). This is understood commensuratively, because every succession is measured by time.

Time is not the number by which we count (IV Physics). This is true if “number” is taken as the principal counting number, and also as the intrinsic instrument, namely, by virtue of the soul’s distinguishing power. It is nevertheless an extrinsic number—that is, the known thing subject to measurement, according to which the soul arrives at knowledge of the less-known measure.

Time is perceptible by reason of succession, because time is motion, and motion is perceptible; consequently, time is perceptible (II *On the Soul*). According to the Commentator, time has two kinds of being: formal and material. The formal is the soul’s distinguishing conception; the material is motion. The authority is true with respect to material being.

Touch is in the flesh (II *On the Soul*). This is contradicted in [Col. 1050D] II *On the Parts of Animals*, where it is said that the organ of touch is something else existing within. The response is that, according to Aristotle, the complete and adequate organ of touch is threefold: the heart, the nerve, and the flesh. The heart is the first origin of the sensory and tactile faculty; the nerve truly participates in and conveys this faculty; and the flesh participates in it as something that conveys the faculty, although not as directly as the heart. To the passage from II *On the Parts of Animals* Aristotle’s words are therefore said to concern the primary organ, or an organ that conveys rather than participates in the sensory or tactile faculty. In that sense it is true that the flesh is not the organ of touch, but the heart or the nerves.

The earth is a resting thing (according to the Commentator, who says: “Even if all the gods descended, they could not move the earth”). This is understood of the earth as a whole, although it moves in respect of its parts, since every day it is altered in respect of its parts and, indeed, certain parts also move locally.

[Col. 1051A] The earth is in water as in its proper and natural place (IV Physics). The response is that the Philosopher uses there a common manner of speaking, according to which something is said to be in another when its greater part, and each of its parts, is surrounded by the other. In this sense the earth is in water. Nevertheless, it does not have one proper place that would be water alone or sea alone.

The whole is not known when the parts of which it consists are unknown (I Physics, text 35). The reason is that, as a thing relates to being, so it relates to being known. The being of the whole results from its parts. If, therefore, the whole is essential and according to qualities, as Averroes says, its parts must be essential, such as matter and form. But if it is a qualitative whole, its parts must be noncommunicating—that is, distinct and separated in place, with one outside the other.

The whole has the nature of its parts: a common proposition. This is true with respect to what is signified, but not [Col. 1051B] with respect to the mode of signifying.

The whole and the perfect are entirely the same (II Physics and IV Metaphysics). This is understood when “whole” is taken categorematically, not when it is taken syncategorematically.

It is shameful to be ignorant of what everyone ought to know (ibid.).

Sadness corrupts the nature of the one who possesses it (III Ethics, chapter 15).

A large crowd judges better than one person alone (III Politics).

Good is threefold: the good of the soul, the good of the body, and the external good that comes from outside (VII Politics).

Times are distinguished above all by the motion of the sun (Plato, in the *Timaeus*).

It is as sad to be praised by base people as to be praised for base deeds (Seneca, *On Continuation*).

## U

[Col. 1051C] One thing has only one nature (according to the Commentator, I *On the Heavens*). This is understood to mean that one nature is productive of only one motion, and not of motions distinct in species. Nevertheless, one thing can have several natures, one of which is productive of motion, as form, and another of which is the subject of motion, as matter.

The one and the many are opposed (II Metaphysics). It would therefore follow that terms belonging to the category of quantity are contrary to one another, contrary to the Philosopher’s statement that nothing is contrary to quantity. The response is that “opposition” is equivocal here, for it is taken broadly for any incompatibility.

A universal is one in many and one of many (I *Posterior Analytics*). This is understood as follows: a universal is one in many, like a superior in its inferior, or it is one in many significatively. For it signifies many according to one common conception, and it is one of many—that is, it is predicated of several things.

[Col. 1051D] A universal is nothing, or it is posterior to its singulars (II *On the Soul*). This is understood as follows: a universal, in being, according to Plato’s imagination, is nothing. But insofar as it conveys the common concept of one thing as belonging to others, it is posterior to singular things, by which it is caused. For when many individuals are considered by the intellect insofar as they are similar in human nature, not divisible or variable through essential and accidental differences, the universal conception immediately follows upon this consideration with respect to human nature—namely, the conception of species. Just as, if someone turns his face toward a mirror, his likeness naturally appears there, so, when a thing objectively exists in the intellect in the manner described, some such intentional property or being of reason—genus, species, and so forth—naturally follows upon it.

The use of a thing whose use is good is good; and: if the use of some thing is bad, that thing is bad (a topical axiom). This is qualified as true if “the use of a thing” means the use that the thing itself, by itself and by its nature, claims for itself. [Col. 1052A] For example, sophistry is harmful in itself because its use is harmful in itself, since it deceives and deludes people, and so forth. Otherwise, from the bad use of jurisprudence, medicine, or eloquence—many people abuse these to the ruin of others—it would be possible to conclude that these arts are harmful. Conversely, from the good use of injuries, hatred, and enmities—which good people patiently endure—it would be possible to conclude that injuries, hatreds, and enmities are good things, which is utterly absurd. Since the blind heretics of our time do not notice this, from the abuse of the priesthood, the papacy, and the Church’s other sacred ministries and pious practices—abuses with which not a few are marked and reproached—they conclude, as though from the proper use of these things, that these sacred ministries and pious practices ought to be entirely removed. The absurdity and blindness of this cannot be adequately expressed, because, with the sole exception of virtue—which alone no one who possesses it can use badly [Col. 1052B]—there is no thing so good and excellent that wicked people cannot abuse it.

One cause has only one effect (I *Posterior Analytics*). This is understood to mean: one cause, remaining in the same condition with respect to the same effect, has one effect. For a cause that is differently disposed sometimes has several effects, one mediated and another immediate.

Universals are the most difficult to know because they are furthest removed from the senses (in the prologue to the *Metaphysics*). It is commonly glossed as referring to universals in causing, such as God and the intelligences. For such abstract beings, since they are furthest removed from the senses, are the most difficult to know.

A universal is everywhere (I *Posterior Analytics*). This is understood of a universal in causing, and such is the glorious God. Similarly, it is said that a universal in predication is everywhere, insofar as it does not determine itself to a here and now but abstracts from conditions of this kind that individuate.

A universal is the cause of its singulars (I *Posterior Analytics*). [Col. 1052C] The response is that the Philosopher is speaking there according to Plato’s opinion, who said that the universal is the quiddity of singulars.

A universal is eternal and incorruptible (I *Posterior Analytics*). This is understood to mean that a universal proposition in the *Posterior Analytics* expresses an eternal truth; or, alternatively, that a proposition expressing an eternal truth can be constructed from universal terms.

Universals are more knowable than singulars (I Physics). The response is that the Philosopher means this in the following sense: universals—that is, things more confused—are more knowable than singulars—that is, things less confused. See above, under the letter A, the axiom “Proceeding begins from universals.”

Universals exist per se (V Metaphysics). This does not mean that they subsist separately, as the Platonists foolishly imagined, but that, insofar as they are universals, they are not this particular thing and therefore do not receive this or that accident, so that one universal could be called the same as or different from another with respect to accident. [Col. 1052D] For Aristotle is discussing sameness and difference there.

Wherever there is sense, there is appetite (II *On the Soul*). According to Themistius, this is understood of the concupiscible appetite, which is the appetite for what is suitable and pleasant; it is not understood of the irascible or intellectual appetite.

Where there is the greatest intellect, there is the least fortune (according to Boethius). The reason for the authority is that intelligent and wiser people experience fewer fortuitous effects than foolish people, because the wise always act with deliberation and consequently fewer things happen to them contrary to their intention.

One and the same being is natural and artificial (II Physics). This is understood with respect to different aspects.

When one absurdity is granted, others follow (I Physics, texts 21 and 22). That is, from one absurdity given and conceded, many others follow; or from one false premise, many consequences proceed without difficulty.

[Col. 1053A] One thing is said to be contrary to one thing (X Metaphysics, text and commentary 24). Alexander responds by saying that when this is taken simply, one thing is contrary to one thing; but when it is not understood simply, it is not incongruous for one thing to have several contraries. For something can have several contraries according to different aspects, although it is one and the same in number. Thus the same snow, one in number, is white and cold, and has heat and blackness as contraries, with respect to different aspects.

One subject has one form (Averroes, in the book *On the Substance of the World*). The reason is that one thing has one being. The proposition is restricted so that it is understood of substantial form in complete being, because through such a substantial form a thing is this particular thing and actual, as stated in II *On the Soul*, text and commentary 2. Therefore, whatever comes to such an entity already in act is an accident.

Each thing is divided into those things from which it is composed (VI Physics, text 3).

There is only one first ruler (X Metaphysics). It is said there that a plurality of principles is not valid, and the Philosopher adds: “Let there therefore be one first ruler”—that is, [Col. 1053B] one mover or one first cause. According to the faith, however, this is understood as follows: “There is only one first ruler”—that is, there is one God, singular in essence and triune in persons, from whom being and life have been given to all things, more clearly to some and more obscurely to others, as was shown at the beginning of this little book. There it is said: “Upon this being heaven and all nature depend”—upon this being, that is, upon God, who is blessed forever and ever. Amen.

## V
Moral virtue consists in a mean relative to us, determined by reason (Ethics II, ch. 6). This means that the mean of virtue is not a mean belonging to the thing itself, but a mean determined by reason—true causally and effectively, though not essentially, as if the act of reason itself were reduced to the mean. The reason is that moral virtue perfects not the act of reason but the act of the appetitive power. Therefore the act of reason itself is not reduced to the mean through it. For a fuller understanding of this axiom, note that the mean determined by reason, in matters of the virtues, is to perform an action when it ought to be performed and as it ought to be performed, according to the rule prescribed by prudence, so that one neither exceeds nor falls short. Excess consists in performing an action when it ought not to be performed, or in a manner in which it ought not to be performed—where the matter is affirmed but the circumstances are denied. Deficiency consists in denying the matter while affirming the circumstances, as when one does not take pleasure at a time when one ought to take pleasure. The mean belonging to the thing itself is an equality determined in the thing: if you owe one hundred and repay one hundred, you have preserved the mean belonging to the thing, since one hundred is equal to another one hundred. This mean belonging to the thing is of two kinds. The first is arithmetic, consisting in the equality of two quantities. The second is geometric, consisting in equality of proportions; this is always preserved by distributive justice. For distributive justice has the duty of distributing to each according to his own merits. For example, if a commander in war must distribute the spoils won among the soldiers, he ought to observe this proportion: he should give each soldier according to his own merits.

[Col. 1054A] Sight and illumination occur in an instant, and likewise pleasure (On the Soul II and Ethics X). The Philosopher argues to the contrary in the book Meteorology. Reason supports this contrary position, since, when a medium must newly be illuminated, this must occur through the application of the luminous object to the medium, through the generation of a new light, and through the removal of an obstacle; yet these things cannot occur in an instant. The answer, therefore, is that sight, illumination, and pleasure, considered in themselves, are not incompatible with occurring instantaneously. Thus, if the whole medium were applied in an instant—impossibly—light would indeed be produced in it instantaneously. But because the whole medium cannot, by natural power, be applied in an instant, the illumination of the whole medium cannot occur in an instant by natural power. Nevertheless, the illumination of that part of the space or medium which is rightly applied occurs wholly and perfectly in an instant. Heating, or another similar alteration, does not occur in this way, because even if something is properly applied to fire, it is not perfectly heated in an instant, but gradually and successively.

[Col. 1054B] Virtue is a certain perfection. Everything is then most perfect when it has attained its proper virtue, and is most in accordance with nature. Vice, however, is the corruption and removal of these things (Physics VII, text 18). Truly, this is a great praise of virtue. A person is called complete when he possesses virtue; diminished, when he possesses vice.

It happens that moral virtue is concerned with pleasures and pains (Ethics II). This is understood as the disciplining of the appetites’ passions. Note here that the Stoics thought virtue existed when there was no movement of appetite in the senses and no assault of any passion; therefore they called such states “apatheiai” or “impassibilities,” as though virtues arose from such a negation of the passions. The Peripatetics, however, held that virtue existed when the passions and movements of the senses were restrained according to reason. Thus, although they rise up against reason, they are nevertheless overcome by reason, and reason moderates them.

Virtues are stronger on the right side than on the left [Col. 1054C] (according to the Philosopher in the Problems). The explanation of why the soul begins movement on the right side rather than the left is founded upon this problem. It should be said, however, that this statement is to be understood of motive virtues, not cognitive virtues, as is readily evident to everyone.

Virtue is a habit that perfects its possessor and renders his action praiseworthy (Ethics II). The meaning is that virtue makes an action good not principally but dispositionally, because it disposes the will always toward the good, so that it performs the good readily and with pleasure. Nevertheless, the will, through its own power, can also elicit a good action; but it cannot do so as readily and pleasantly as it can when accompanied by virtue.

Virtue consists in what is divisible (Topics II). The answer is that the Philosopher is speaking of perfect virtue.

The virtuous and the happy do not perform hateful or evil actions (Ethics I). The answer is that the Philosopher does not mean that the virtuous person can in no way perform evil or hateful actions; rather, he means that he does so rarely and not easily. For the more he is formed and perfected in virtue, the more rarely and less readily he will do so.

## SECTION TWO. SAYINGS COLLECTED FROM CICERO

[Col. 1053]

### PREFACE

[Col. 1053D] Now that the length and magnitude of the authorities drawn from Aristotle have increased, it is more convenient, in the second treatise of the present little work, to proceed with an exposition of the remaining maxims concerning the blessed life, lest weariness delay the mind. It was not done rashly to add these flowers, by which the image of virtue is placed before the eyes—virtue which alone, as he says, adds eternity to noble lineage:

“Virtue alone is nobility, and the only one. Indeed, virtue is a vigorous and steadfast warfare of the spirit. Roused by the difficult approach, it allows envious minds to penetrate to it; and so it comes about that those born in a humble station rise to the highest dignity, while the most noble, having fallen into some disgrace, turn the light received from their ancestors into darkness.”

And so the work will be hastened, and whatever has been diminished by the undertaking will be made good through diligence, so that, in return for your service toward us and for our devotion to the pursuit of life, this gift may be offered in the fullest measure to your gracious will.

It is immediately apparent that there is this difference between the books of Aristotle and Cicero, both of whom are known to have composed works on the Republic: Aristotle ordered the commonwealth, whereas Cicero described it; the one discussed what it ought to be, the other what it had been established by the ancestors to be. We have given, in the preceding book, excerpts from Aristotle’s works; it is now the purpose of the present book to give excerpts from Cicero, and it would be shameful and an utter disgrace to pass him over. For he was the greatest cultivator of humane studies; educated by his talent from adolescence and extensively trained in speaking, he could easily and without effort commit his thoughts to writing. Relying, therefore, upon this felicity of talent, this gift of nature, and finally this wisdom and learning, he prescribed many things from childhood to the end of his life. Among these are certain works of study and instruction which occupy youth and delight old age; adorn prosperity and provide refuge and consolation in adversity; give pleasure at home and cause no impediment abroad; spend the night with us; make us most like the immortal gods; and, because of their excellence, artistry, and grace, make it seem that we ought altogether to be unable to die. Accordingly, first, from the books of Marcus Tullius Cicero’s *On Duties*, authorities are selected concerning every human duty.

### From the First Book of *On Duties* by Marcus Tullius Cicero

No part of life, whether in public or private affairs, in the courts or at home, whether you are dealing with yourself or entering into an agreement with another, can be free from duty; and the whole moral beauty of life lies in cultivating it, while disgrace lies in neglecting it.

Every inquiry undertaken by reason concerning anything ought to begin from a definition, so that it may be understood what the subject under discussion is.

When usefulness seems to draw one toward itself while moral goodness draws one back in the opposite direction, it happens that the mind is torn in deliberation and is burdened with an uncertain anxiety of thought.

In the beginning, nature has bestowed upon every kind of living creature the disposition to protect itself, its life, and its body; to avoid whatever appears likely to harm it; and to seek and procure everything necessary for living, such as food, hiding places, and other things of that kind.

A desire for union for the purpose of procreation is common to all living creatures, and they also possess a certain care for what has been procreated. But the chief difference between a human being and a beast is this: the beast, moved only insofar as it is affected by sensation, adapts itself solely to what is present and at hand, sensing very little beyond the past or the future. A human being, however, who participates in reason and through it perceives consequences, sees the causes of things, is not ignorant of their developments and, as it were, their antecedents, compares similarities, and joins and connects future things with present ones, readily sees the course of his whole life and prepares the necessities for living it.

By applying a certain measure and order to the matters treated in life, we shall preserve moral beauty and dignity.

We are all drawn and led toward the desire for knowledge and learning, in which we consider excellence beautiful; but to stumble, err, be ignorant, and be deceived we call both evil and disgraceful.

What is devoted to labor and care in honorable and knowledge-worthy matters will rightly be praised.

All the praise of virtue consists in action, though action may be interrupted. Frequent and numerous returns to study are available.

Every thought and movement of the mind will be occupied either in taking counsel concerning honorable matters that pertain to living well and happily, or in the pursuits of knowledge and learning.

[Col. 1056A] Justice is the virtue in which there is the greatest splendor, by which good men are so called; and joined to it is beneficence, which may equally be called kindness or generosity. The first duty of justice is that no one harm anyone unless provoked by injury; the next is that one use common things as common and private things as one’s own.

Plato wrote splendidly: “We were not born for ourselves alone; our country claims a part of our birth, and our friends another part.”

And, as the Stoics hold, everything produced on earth is created for human use, while human beings are created for the sake of human beings, so that they may be able to benefit one another. In this we ought to follow nature as our guide: bring common advantages into the common stock; by exchanging duties, by giving and receiving, bind the fellowship of human beings to one another through skills, labor, and resources. The foundation of all justice, however, is trust— that is, constancy and truthfulness in one’s words and agreements.

[Col. 1056B] There are two kinds of injustice: one consists in those who inflict injury; the other in those who, when they can, do not ward off injury from those upon whom it is inflicted. For whoever makes an unjust attack upon someone, driven by anger or some other disturbance, appears, as it were, to lay hands upon a fellow member of society. But whoever does not defend or resist an injury when he can is as much at fault as if he were to abandon his parents, friends, or country.

We seek wealth both for the necessities of life and for the enjoyment of pleasures.

Magnificent furnishings and a refined and abundant way of life also give pleasure; these things have produced an unlimited desire for money. Yet the enlargement of one’s household resources, provided that it harms no one, is not to be blamed; injustice, however, must always be avoided.

Most people are especially led to forget justice when they fall into a desire for power, honors, and glory. What Ennius says—“There is no sacred fellowship or trust in a kingdom”—has a wider application. For whenever there is something in which several people cannot excel at once, such intense rivalry usually arises that it becomes extremely difficult to preserve a sacred fellowship.

In all justice it makes a great difference whether an injury is committed under some disturbance of the mind, which is usually brief and temporary, or deliberately and after reflection. Those things that occur suddenly and through some impulse are lighter than those inflicted after deliberation and preparation. It is already itself a just thing that an action be done rightly, if it is voluntary.

The care of another person’s affairs is difficult.

Equity shines by itself.

Promises that are useless to those to whom they have been made need not be kept. Nor need one keep a promise if it harms you more than it benefits the person to whom you made it; for it is contrary to duty to prefer a greater loss to a lesser one.

In a republic, the laws of war must above all be preserved. For since there are two ways of contending—one through debate, the other through force—and since the former is proper to human beings while the latter belongs to beasts, one must resort to the latter if it is not possible to use the former. Wars, therefore, should indeed be undertaken for the sake of living in peace without injustice; but once victory has been won, those who were not cruel or savage in war must be spared.

For my part, I have always thought that peace should be sought—a peace that will contain no ambushes.

And those whom you have conquered by force must be cared for; likewise, those who, having laid down their arms, have fled for refuge to the commander’s pledged protection must be received, even if the battering ram has struck the wall.

Even if, at particular times, they have made a sworn promise to the enemy under oath, their faith must be preserved in that very matter.

Let us remember that justice must also be observed toward the lowest. The condition and fortune of slaves, however, is the lowest. Since injury is inflicted in two ways, either by force or by fraud, fraud seems characteristic of the fox and force of the lion; both are utterly alien to a human being.

Of all injustice, none is more deadly than that of those who, precisely when they are deceiving most, act so as to appear good men.

Nothing is more suited by nature to human beings than beneficence and generosity, but they require many precautions. First, one must see that kindness does not harm either those toward whom it appears to be shown or others; next, that kindness does not exceed one’s resources; and finally, that it be bestowed upon each according to his worth, for this is the foundation of justice, to which everything must be referred. For those who gratify someone in a way harmful to the person whom they appear to wish to help are to be judged not beneficent or generous but destructive flatterers. Those who harm some people in order to be generous toward others are guilty of the same injustice as if they converted another’s property to their own use. There are many who desire splendor and glory and take away from some in order to give to others; they think that they will appear beneficent toward their friends if they enrich them by whatever means. This, however, is so far from being a duty that it may rather be contrary to duty. Therefore we must see that we use generosity in a way that benefits friends and harms no one. Those who wish to be more generous than circumstances permit first err in this: they are unjust toward their own neighbors. The resources that ought more fairly to be supplied to and left with these people they transfer to strangers. Such generosity usually contains a desire to seize and take away unjustly, so as to obtain resources for distribution. One can see that most people do many things not from natural generosity but, being led by a certain desire for glory, so that they may appear beneficent; their actions seem to proceed more from display than from goodwill.

Such pretense, however, is more closely allied with vanity than with generosity or moral goodness.

The character of the person upon whom a benefit is bestowed should be considered: his disposition toward us, our commonality and fellowship of life, and the benefits he has conferred upon our interests.

No one at all should be neglected in whom some indication of virtue appears.

The first point of duty is that we love most those by whom we are loved most. But we should judge goodwill not in the manner of adolescents, with a certain ardor of love, but rather by its stability and constancy.

For if we do not hesitate to confer duties upon those whom we hope will be useful to us, what sort of people ought we to be toward those who have already been useful?

Many people do many things with a certain rashness and without judgment, either indiscriminately toward everyone or stirred by some sudden impulse, as though by a gust of wind. Such benefits should not be considered equal to those conferred with deliberate and steady judgment. In bestowing a benefit and returning a kindness, if all other things are equal, the principal duty is to help most especially whoever is most in need of assistance. Most people do the opposite: they serve above all the person from whom they hope for the most, even if he has no need of them. Human fellowship and union will be preserved most effectively if each person shows the greatest kindness to those with whom he is most closely connected.

There is a Greek proverb: “Among friends, all things are common.”

Kinship of blood and goodwill bind human beings together through affection. It is a great bond to possess the same memorials of one’s ancestors, to share the same sacred rites, and to have common burial places.

But of all associations, none is more excellent or firmer than that in which good men, alike in character, are joined in intimacy. Nothing is more lovable or more closely binding than similarity of character among good people. Among those who have the same pursuits and the same wishes, it comes about that each takes as much pleasure in the other as in himself; and what Pythagoras desires in friendship is achieved: that one person be made out of many.

[Col. 1058A] That friendship is most delightful which similarity of character has joined together.

Some duties are owed to some people more than to others. For example, one should help a neighbor sooner in gathering his harvest than one’s brother or close associate; but if there is a lawsuit, one should defend a relative or friend rather than a neighbor.

No one who has attained the glory of courage has acquired praise through ambushes or malice. Therefore we wish brave and magnanimous men to be good and straightforward, friends of truth, and by no means deceitful.

Knowledge that is removed from justice should be called cunning rather than wisdom. When one has desired to excel all others, it is difficult to preserve equity, which belongs especially to justice.

There is no time that ought to be without justice. Therefore those are to be regarded as brave and magnanimous who not inflict injury but ward it off.

For whoever depends upon the mistaken judgment of an unlearned multitude is not to be counted among great men.

[Col. 1058B] Scarcely anyone is found who, after undertaking labors and facing dangers, does not desire glory as though it were the reward of his achievements.

The desire for money must be avoided. Nothing is so narrow-minded and petty as love of riches. Nothing is more honorable and magnificent than to despise money if one does not possess it, and, if one possesses it, to devote it to generosity and freedom.

The desire for glory must also be guarded against. It takes away liberty, for which magnanimous men ought to strive above all. Nor should commands be sought; sometimes they should rather not be accepted, and at other times they should be relinquished.

In every undertaking, before beginning, careful preparation must be employed.

Arms are of little use abroad unless there is a plan at home.

War should be undertaken in such a way that nothing but peace appears to be sought. It is the mark of a brave and steadfast spirit not to be disturbed in difficult circumstances, not to act with a turbulent mind or plan, and not to depart from reason.

To move rashly in the battle line and engage the enemy hand to hand is something savage and like the behavior of beasts. But when time and necessity demand it, one must fight hand to hand, and death must be preferred to slavery and disgrace.

One must also avoid offering oneself to dangers without cause, since nothing can be more foolish.

To wish for a contrary storm in calm weather is madness; but to come to the aid of a storm with whatever courage and by whatever means is wise.

In general, those who govern the republic should hold to two precepts of Plato. The first is that they protect the welfare of the citizens in such a way that whatever they do is directed toward it, forgetting their own advantages. The second is that they care for the whole body of the republic, lest, while protecting one part, they abandon the others. For, just as guardianship, so the administration of the republic must be conducted for the benefit of those entrusted to its care, not for the benefit of those to whom it has been entrusted. Those who care for one part of the citizens and neglect another introduce into the state the most destructive thing of all: sedition and discord. Hence it comes about that some appear to favor the people, others to support the best citizens, while few seem concerned for everyone.

The ambition for offices and the rivalry for honors are altogether wretched. Nothing is more praiseworthy or more worthy of a great and distinguished man than gentleness and clemency. Every act of correction and punishment must be free from insult; it should be directed not toward the advantage of the person who punishes or rebukes someone in words, but toward the advantage of the republic.

One must also take care that the punishment not be greater than the fault, and that some people not be punished for the same causes while others are not even summoned. Above all, anger must be prohibited in punishment. Whoever approaches punishment in a state of great anger will never maintain that moderation which lies between excess and deficiency.

[Col. 1059A] It is desirable that those who govern the republic be like laws, which are led to punish not by anger but by equity. Even in prosperous circumstances and when things are flowing according to our wishes, let us especially avoid pride, haughtiness, and arrogance.

For just as it is frivolous to bear adversity immoderately, so it is frivolous to bear prosperity immoderately. Equanimity throughout life, with the same expression and the same countenance always, is a splendid thing. Those who advise us to conduct ourselves with greater humility the more superior we are appear to give sound instruction.

In the most prosperous circumstances we should especially make use of the counsel of friends and grant them even greater authority than before. At such times we must beware of opening our ears to flatterers and of allowing ourselves to be flattered, for it is easy to be deceived in this matter. We think ourselves to be such as to deserve praise, and from this arise countless faults, when people, puffed up by their opinions, are disgracefully provoked and become involved in the greatest errors.

For to disregard what each person thinks of himself is not only arrogant but altogether irresponsible.

Every action should be free from rashness and negligence, and one should not do anything for which one cannot give a credible reason. The appetites must be made to obey reason; they must neither run ahead of it through rashness nor abandon it through laziness or cowardice. They must be tranquil and free from every disturbance of mind; from this there will shine forth all constancy and moderation.

All the appetites must be restrained and calmed, while attentiveness and diligence must be aroused, so that we do nothing rashly, accidentally, thoughtlessly, or negligently. We were not generated by nature in such a way as to seem made for play and amusement, but rather for seriousness and for certain more weighty and important pursuits. It is permissible to use play and amusement, but only as one uses sleep and other forms of rest, after satisfying serious and weighty concerns. The manner of joking itself ought not to be excessive or immoderate, but refined and witty. Just as we do not grant children complete freedom to play, but only that which is not alien to honorable conduct, so in joking itself some light of a good and cultivated character should shine forth.

There is also a certain measure to be maintained in play, so that we do not pour ourselves out excessively in every direction and, carried away by pleasure, slip into some disgrace.

The human mind is nourished by learning; it is always either investigating or doing something through thought, and it is led on by the pleasure of seeing and hearing.

If someone is somewhat more elevated toward virtue, even though he is captivated by pleasure, he conceals and disguises his desire for pleasure out of modesty. From this it is understood that the bodily will is not sufficiently worthy of human excellence, and ought to be despised and rejected. If, however, there is someone who assigns some value to pleasure, he must carefully preserve moderation in enjoying it. Therefore food, drink, and bodily care should be directed toward health and strength, not pleasure. If we also wish to consider what excellence and dignity human nature possesses, we easily understand how disgraceful it is to dissolve oneself in luxury and live delicately and softly, and how honorable it is to live sparingly, self-controlled, austerely, and temperately.

Just as there are great differences among bodies—for we see some strong in running because of their speed, others in wrestling because of their strength, and likewise some faces possessing dignity and others beauty—so there are also still greater differences among minds.

There is no point in resisting nature or pursuing anything that you cannot attain.

Therefore, as they say, nothing is fitting against Minerva—that is, against nature when it opposes and resists.

Whatever things, then, we are best suited for, we shall chiefly cultivate. But if necessity should at some time force us into pursuits that do not belong to our talents, every care, reflection, and diligence must be employed so that, if we cannot perform them gracefully, we may at least perform them with the least possible disgrace. Yet we should not strive so much to pursue the goods that have not been given to us as to avoid vices.

For kingdoms, commands, noble birth, honors, wealth, resources, and their opposites depend upon chance and are governed and directed by circumstances. But what role we ourselves wish to play proceeds from our own will. Thus some devote themselves to philosophy, others to civil law, others to eloquence; and among the virtues themselves, one person prefers to excel in one, another in another. Those whose fathers or ancestors have excelled in some form of glory generally strive to excel in the same kind of renown.

Above all, we must determine what sort of people we wish to be, and in what way of life. This is the most difficult deliberation of all. At the beginning of adolescence, when the weakness of judgment is greatest, each person chooses the kind of life that he has most loved. Thus he becomes entangled in a definite kind and course of life before he has been able to judge what would be best. We are usually imbued with the instructions of our parents and led into their habits and customs. Others are carried along by the judgment of the multitude and most eagerly desire whatever seems most beautiful to the greater part.

Nature is much firmer and more constant than fortune.

The wise consider that friendships which give less pleasure and are less approved should be gently loosened rather than suddenly severed. When one’s way of life is changed, every effort must be made to ensure that the change appears to have been made with sound judgment.

It is therefore proper for a young person to revere those older than himself and to choose from among them the best and most approved, relying upon their counsel and authority.

Above all, this age must be kept away from lust and trained in labor and endurance of both mind and body, so that its industry may be vigorous in military and civil duties. Even when young people wish to relax their minds and give themselves to amusement, they must avoid excess and remember modesty. This will be easier if, in such matters, they are willing to have older people present.

The physical labors of the elderly should be reduced, while exercises of the mind should be increased. Care should be taken that they assist friends, the young, and especially the republic as much as possible through counsel and prudence. Nothing must be guarded against more carefully in old age than surrendering to weakness and idleness. Luxury, though disgraceful at every age, is most foul in old age. If immoderate lust is added, the evil is doubled: old age itself incurs disgrace, and it makes youth more shameless in its excess.

It is therefore the proper duty of a magistrate to understand that he is representing the state, that he must uphold its dignity and honor, preserve its laws, distribute its rights, and remember the matters entrusted to his good faith.

Nothing is more fitting than to preserve constancy in every matter undertaken and in every decision made.

[Col. 1060D] Two things must above all be avoided: that nothing become effeminate or soft, and that nothing become harsh or rustic.

Since there are two kinds of beauty, one consisting in grace and the other in dignity, we customarily call grace feminine and dignity masculine. Therefore every ornament unworthy of a man must be removed from his appearance, and a similar fault must be avoided in his gestures and movements. The dignity of his form should be preserved by the goodness of his complexion, and his complexion by physical exercise. Cleanliness should also be maintained, but it must not be offensive or excessively elaborate; it should merely avoid rustic and inhuman negligence. The same principle applies to clothing, in which, as in most things, moderation is best. One must beware either of using excessively languid slowness in walking, so that one appears like the bearers of a ceremonial litter, or of adopting excessive speed in haste; when this occurs, breathing is disturbed, the face changes, and the mouth is twisted, all of which clearly indicates a lack of constancy. But one must work still more carefully to ensure that the movements of the mind do not depart from nature. We achieve this if we take care not to fall into disturbances and loss of spirit, and if we keep our attentive minds fixed upon the preservation of dignity. We must see to it that our thoughts are directed toward the best things and that we present our appetites obedient to reason.

Throughout life the soundest instruction is that we avoid disturbances—that is, excessive movements of the mind that do not obey reason.

We must take the greatest care to appear both respectful and affectionate toward those with whom we converse.

Let anger be far away, since nothing can be done rightly or thoughtfully when it is present. For the most part, one may employ gentle correction, joined with seriousness, so that severity is applied while insult is excluded. Actions performed under some disturbance cannot be performed consistently, nor can they be approved by those who are present.

To speak falsely, especially about one’s appearance or oneself, and, to the laughter of the audience, to imitate a boastful soldier.

A household should be adorned with dignity, but dignity should not be sought entirely from the house. The master should not derive his honor from the house; rather, the house should be honored by the master.

Moderation must be transferred to every use and manner of life. In every action undertaken, three things must be observed. First, the appetites must obey reason, since nothing is more suited to preserving one’s duties. Second, one must consider how important the matter is that one wishes to accomplish, and must not undertake more or less care and effort than the matter requires. Third, one must take care that whatever belongs to a liberal appearance and dignity be moderate. Of these three, however, the most important is to make the appetites obey reason.

It is disgraceful and very faulty, in a serious matter, to introduce speech suitable for a banquet or some delicate conversation.

[Col. 1061C] One ought to keep not only one’s hands but also one’s eyes abstinent.

Somehow it also happens that we perceive wrongdoing more clearly in others than in ourselves. Without modesty, nothing can be right or honorable.

Of all the things from which some return is sought, none is better, more fruitful, sweeter, or more worthy of a free person than agriculture.

The duties of justice, which pertain to human welfare—and nothing ought to be more important to a human being—must be placed before studies and the duties of learning.

Greatness of spirit, when removed from human justice, kindness, and fellowship, becomes a kind of savagery and brutality. Every duty that contributes to preserving human union and society must be preferred to the duty concerned with intellectual knowledge and learning.

[Col. 1061D] Considered action follows thought and prudence. Thus it comes about that acting thoughtfully is more valuable than thinking prudently.

The first duties are owed to the immortal gods, the second to one’s country, the third to one’s parents. After these, they are owed in due order to the rest.

### From the Second Book of *On Duties* by Marcus Tullius Cicero

What, by the gods, is more desirable than wisdom, what more excellent, what better, what more worthy of a human being? Those who seek it are called philosophers; and if one wishes to interpret the word, philosophy is nothing other than the pursuit of wisdom.

Those who perceive matters poorly often admire crafty and cunning people and judge malice to be wisdom. Their error must be removed, and their entire opinion must be redirected toward this understanding: they must realize that one can attain one’s aims through honorable counsels and just actions, not through fraud and malice, and must wish to attain them in that way.

[Col. 1062A] Piety and holiness will make the gods favorably disposed.

I maintain that it is proper to virtue to win the minds of human beings and attach them to its own interests.

Prosperity, honors, commands, and victories, although they are matters of fortune, cannot be brought about in either direction without the efforts and zeal of human beings.

The situation is bad when what ought to be achieved through virtue is attempted with money.

People also submit themselves to another’s command and power for many reasons. They are led either by goodwill, or by the magnitude of benefits, or by the excellence of dignity, or by the hope that the arrangement will be useful to them, or by fear that they will be compelled to obey by force, or are captivated by the hope of gifts and promises, or finally are hired for payment. Of all things, nothing is more suitable for preserving and maintaining power than being loved, and nothing is more unsuitable than being feared.

Fear is a bad guardian of lasting power; goodwill, by contrast, is faithful even toward perpetuity.

[Col. 1062B] Since this principle has the widest application and is of the greatest value not only for safety but also for wealth and power, let us embrace it: let fear be absent and affection be maintained. In this way we most easily achieve what we want both in private affairs and in the republic. For those who wish to be feared must necessarily fear the very people by whom they are feared.

Nor is any power of command so great that it can be lasting while fear presses upon it.

Let this therefore be certain, and let it be regarded as both the first and most necessary matter: we must have steadfast friendships with those who love us, are our friends, and admire what is ours.

The love of the multitude, moreover, is powerfully stirred by the very reputation and opinion of generosity, beneficence, justice, trustworthiness, and all those virtues that belong to gentleness and ease of character.

Faith, moreover, can be secured in two ways: if we are thought to have attained prudence joined with justice. For we place our trust in those whom we believe to understand more than we do and whom we think able to foresee the future. We also trust those who, when action is required and matters have reached a crisis, can assess the situation and arrive at a decision on the spot. People regard this as useful and genuine prudence. Just and trustworthy people—that is, good men—are trusted in such a way that there is no suspicion in them of fraud or wrongdoing. Thus we rightly entrust our safety, our fortunes, and our children to them. Of these two qualities, justice has greater power to inspire trust: for justice has sufficient authority even without prudence, whereas prudence without justice contributes nothing to winning confidence. The more crafty and cunning a person proves to be, the more hateful and suspect he will be once the reputation for integrity has been removed.

We must use ordinary and familiar language when we speak of popular opinion.

Not everyone despises those of whom they think badly. Those who are despised are people who, as the saying goes, are useful neither to themselves nor to anyone else—people in whom there is no labor, no industry, and no care. Those are admired who are thought to surpass others in virtue, while being entirely free from disgrace, and especially from those vices against which others cannot easily defend themselves.

No one can be just who fears death, pain, exile, or poverty, or who prefers the things opposed to these over justice.

We admire above all the man who is not moved by money; when this has been clearly observed in someone, we consider him worthy of attention. Every system and ordering of human life requires aids, especially that one should have people with whom one can exchange intimate conversation. This is difficult unless one presents oneself as a good man.

Justice possesses such great power that even those who live by crime and wrongdoing cannot live without some element of justice. If one of a group of robbers steals or forcibly takes something from another of them, he leaves himself no place even within the business of robbery. If, then, justice has such power that it strengthens and increases even the resources of robbers, how great should we suppose its force to be among laws, courts, and civic institutions?

Justice must therefore be cultivated and preserved by every means, both for its own sake—for otherwise it would not be justice—and also for the advancement of honor and glory.

Socrates rightly used to say that the nearest and almost shortest road to glory was for a person to make himself such as he wished to be regarded. Those who think that they can acquire lasting glory through pretense and empty display, through false speech and even a feigned expression, are seriously mistaken. Genuine glory takes root and spreads; everything fictitious quickly falls away like little flowers.

Nothing feigned can be lasting. Whoever wishes to attain genuine glory should perform the duties of justice.

If someone has possessed from early youth a source of distinction and renown—whether inherited from his father, acquired by some circumstance, or bestowed by fortune—all eyes are fixed upon him, and people investigate what he does and how he lives, as though he were moving in the brightest light; none of his words or actions can remain obscure. Those, however, whose early years have passed unnoticed among people because of their lowly and obscure position, as soon as they begin to be young men ought to set their sights upon great things and strive toward them through honorable pursuits. They will do this with firmer resolve because that age is not merely free from envy but is even favored. As in other matters the works of the mind are much greater than those of the body, so the things we pursue through intelligence and reason are more pleasing than those we pursue through physical strength.

Young men are most easily and most favorably judged when they have attached themselves to distinguished and wise men who give good counsel to the state. If they associate frequently with such men, they give the public the impression that they will become like those whom they themselves have chosen as models for imitation.

[Col. 1063C] It is difficult to say how greatly courtesy and affability in conversation win people’s hearts.

There is great admiration for someone who speaks at length and wisely; those who hear him think that he understands and knows more than others. If his speech also contains seriousness blended with modesty, nothing more admirable can be found—and all the more so when these qualities appear in a young man.

This rule of duty must be carefully observed: never summon an innocent person to a capital trial. Nothing of that kind can be done without grave wrongdoing. For what is so inhuman as to turn eloquence, which nature has given for the safety and preservation of human beings, toward the ruin and destruction of the good? Yet just as this must be avoided, so one must not regard it as a religious offense to defend, when necessary, someone who is guilty, even impious and sacrilegious. The multitude demands it, custom permits it, and humanity itself supports it.

It is the judge’s duty always to pursue the truth in cases; the advocate’s, sometimes to defend what is plausible, even if it is less than true. Glory and gratitude are acquired especially through such defenses, and in greater measure when it happens that assistance is given to someone who appears to be surrounded and oppressed by the power of some influential person.

In a certain letter Philip accuses his son Alexander, quite properly, of seeking the goodwill of the Macedonians through generosity:

“What evil in your reasoning,” he says, “has led you to hope that those whom you have corrupted with money would be loyal to you? Are you trying to make the Macedonians think of you not as their king, but as their servant and provider?”

He said that nothing was more degrading for a king—indeed, nothing worse [the reading is slightly corrupt]—than that largesse is corruption. The recipient is made worse and becomes more ready always to expect the same thing again.

Nevertheless, one must sometimes give, and this kind of kindness should not be rejected altogether. It is often appropriate to spend from one’s household resources on deserving people, but carefully and moderately. Many have squandered their inheritances through thoughtless generosity. What, indeed, is more foolish than to take care to make it impossible for you to continue doing for long what you willingly do? Moreover, robbery follows generosity. When such people begin to fall into poverty through giving, they are forced to lay hands on the property of others. Thus, while they intend their gifts to win goodwill, they do not gain as much affection from those to whom they have given as hatred from those from whom they have taken.

For this reason, one must neither close one’s household resources so tightly that kindness cannot open them, nor unlock them so widely that they stand open to everyone. Moderation must be applied, and it must be proportioned to one’s means. We must remember the saying frequently used by our people, which has now become proverbial: “Generosity has no bottom.” Yet suspicion of greed must be avoided. The reason for giving is therefore that it is either necessary or useful; and even in these matters the best rule is moderation. Kindness, however, should be more ready toward the unfortunate, unless they happen to be deserving of their misfortune.

It is appropriate to be generous in giving but not harsh in demanding; and in every transaction—contracting, buying, selling, hiring, letting, and in matters of neighborhood and boundaries—to be fair and accommodating, yielding much of one’s legal right to many people, while shrinking from litigation as far as possible, and perhaps even a little farther than what is strictly possible. For it is not only generous sometimes to withdraw slightly from one’s legal right; it can occasionally be profitable as well. One must take care of one’s household resources, since allowing them to dissipate is disgraceful, but in such a way that there is no suspicion of illiberality or greed.

Theophrastus rightly praised hospitality. For, as it seems to me, it is highly becoming that the homes of distinguished people should be open to distinguished guests. It is also extremely useful to those who wish honorably to possess influence: through their guests they can exercise power and favor among foreign peoples.

For to provide legal protection, to assist with advice, and by this kind of knowledge to benefit many people contributes greatly to increasing both resources and influence. Thus, among the many outstanding achievements of our ancestors, the knowledge and interpretation of civil law were always held in the highest honor and were most excellently established by them.

Although not everyone—not even many people—can be a legal expert or an eloquent speaker, it is nevertheless possible to benefit many through one’s services: by recommending to judges or magistrates someone seeking a favor, by keeping watch on behalf of another’s interests, or by making requests to those who give advice or conduct defenses. Those who do this acquire very great gratitude, and their activity becomes widely known.

One need hardly warn such people of the following, since it is obvious to them: when they wish to help others, they must take care not to offend anyone. They often injure either those whom they ought not to injure or those whom they did not intend to injure. If they do so knowingly, it is recklessness; if unknowingly, negligence. One should also use every possible excuse with those whom one has offended unwillingly: explain that what one did was necessary and that one could not have acted otherwise. I think it better to place a benefit with good men than with fortunate men. Nevertheless, one should make every effort to satisfy everyone in every respect.

[Col. 1064D] But if the matter comes into dispute, we should surely follow the authority of Themistocles. When he was consulted about whether he should marry his daughter to a good but poor man or to a less reputable rich man, he replied: “I would rather have a man who needs money than money that needs a man.”

But morals have been corrupted and depraved by admiration for wealth. The size of another person’s wealth concerns each of us very little; it perhaps helps the person who possesses it—and not always even him.

The final rule concerning benefits and services is that one must not contend against justice or on behalf of wrongdoing. Justice is the foundation of the lasting preservation of reputation and honor; without it nothing can be praiseworthy.

Above all, a person who administers the state must see to it that each person retains what is his and that there is no public diminution of private property.

For it was chiefly for this reason—that people might protect what was their own—that states and cities were established. Human beings were indeed brought together under the guidance of nature; nevertheless, they sought the protection of their cities in the hope of safeguarding their possessions.

Care must be taken that everyone understands that, if they wish to remain safe, they must submit to necessity. Moreover, all who govern the state must see to it that there is an adequate supply of those things that are necessary.

The chief point in every administration of public business and office is to remove even the slightest suspicion of greed. No vice is more repulsive—returning, as it were, to the point from which the discussion began—than greed, especially in leaders who govern the state. To turn the state into a source of profit is not merely disgraceful but criminal and impious.

Those who preside over the state can win the goodwill of the multitude by nothing more easily than by abstinence and self-restraint.

For the person whose property has been taken away is an enemy; the person to whom it has been given, even if he pretends not to have wished to receive it—and especially in the case of loans—conceals his pleasure lest he appear not to have been able to repay. But the person who suffers an injustice both remembers it and displays his pain.

The highest principle and wisdom of a good citizen is not to tear apart the interests of fellow citizens but to hold everyone together in the same spirit of equity.

Those who will protect the state must above all ensure, through fairness in law and the courts, that each person retains what is his; that the weaker are not defrauded because of their lowly position; and that envy does not obstruct the wealthy either in keeping or recovering what belongs to them. Property should be acquired through means free from disgrace, preserved through diligence and thrift, and increased through those same means. This is from Book II of *On Duties*.

From Book III of *On Duties* by Marcus Tullius Cicero.

There can be no doubt that expediency can never conflict with moral honor.

To deprive another person for the sake of one’s own advantage, and to increase one’s own advantage through another person’s misfortune, is more contrary to nature than death, poverty, pain, or all the other things that can befall the body or external possessions. For it is permitted, without opposition from nature, that each person should prefer acquiring for himself what pertains to the necessities of life rather than acquiring it for someone else. Nature, however, does not permit us to increase our means, resources, and wealth through the plunder of others.

This principle has been established not only by nature—that is, by the law of nations—but also in the same way by the laws of peoples, through which the state is maintained within each individual community: no one may harm another for the sake of his own advantage. This is what the laws contemplate; this is what they intend—to preserve the safe association of citizens. Those who break it apart are restrained by death, exile, imprisonment, and fines.

The very order of nature accomplishes this still more forcefully. It is the divine and human law, and anyone who wishes to obey it—and all will obey it who wish to live according to nature—will never allow himself to desire what belongs to another and take for himself what he has taken away from someone else.

For elevation and greatness of spirit, as well as fellowship, justice, and generosity, are much more in accordance with nature than pleasure, greed, and riches. To despise these latter things and consider them worthless when compared with the common advantage is the mark of a great and elevated spirit. It is likewise more in accordance with nature to undertake the greatest labors and hardships, if possible, for the preservation or assistance of all peoples, imitating that Hercules whom the memory of humanity, mindful of his services, placed among the assembly of the gods, than to live in solitude not only free from every hardship but also amid the greatest pleasures, possessing an abundance of everything, and surpassing others even in beauty and strength.

For this reason, every person of the finest and most noble character prefers that former life by far to this latter one. It follows that a person obedient to nature cannot harm another human being.

Those who say that consideration is owed to their fellow citizens but deny it to foreigners destroy the common fellowship of the human race. Once that has been removed, kindness, generosity, goodness, and justice are utterly abolished. Those who abolish these must also be judged impious toward the immortal gods.

For justice alone is the mistress and queen of all the virtues.

Each person ought to bear his own disadvantage rather than diminish another’s advantage.

Nothing is useful that is not also honorable; nothing honorable that is not also useful. Where there is disgrace, there can be no advantage, for we were born for moral honor.

We ought to be thoroughly persuaded—if we have made any progress in philosophy—that even if we could conceal everything from gods and human beings alike, we should nevertheless do nothing greedily, unjustly, lustfully, or without self-control.

For honorable things are sought in secret by good men.

We must not abandon our own interests and hand them over to others when we ourselves need them; rather, each person must serve his own advantage, provided that it is achieved without injury to another.

Chrysippus expressed this cleverly: “A person running a race,” he says, “ought to strain and exert himself as much as he can in order to win, but he must not trip the person with whom he is competing or drive him aside with his hand.” So, in life, it is not wrong for each person to seek what pertains to his own needs; but it is wrong to seize it from another.

A good man will do nothing on behalf of his friend against the appointed time, against an oath, or against his pledged word. For if everything is to be done that friends wish, such relationships should be regarded not as friendships but as conspiracies.
