When what appears useful in friendship is compared with what is honorable, the appearance of utility must fall and honor prevail. When, in friendship, things that are not honorable are demanded, religious obligation and good faith must be placed before justice, as the text has it.

Nothing cruel can be useful. Cruelty is especially hostile to human nature, which we must follow.

It is also wrong to prevent foreigners from using cities and to drive them out. To deny that someone who is not a citizen may stand in place of a citizen is right and permissible; but to prevent foreigners from making use of a city is plainly inhuman.

All pretense and concealment must be removed from life. Therefore every lie must be removed from commercial dealings.

Ennius says that a wise man is wise for nothing if he does not seek to benefit himself. It is the mark of wisdom, however, to do nothing contrary to customs, laws, or institutions, and to take account of one’s household resources. For we wish not only ourselves to be wealthy but also our children, relatives, friends, and especially the state. The resources and means of individuals are the wealth of the state.

No greater danger in life can be found than the pretense of intelligence in malice. To me, even genuine inheritances do not seem honorable if they have been sought through the malicious flatteries of service—not through truth but through pretense. In such matters, one thing that is useful and another that is honorable can sometimes falsely appear to be the case.

The just man whom we recognize as a good man will take nothing away from anyone that can be transferred to himself. Whoever is surprised by this should admit that he does not know what a good man is. But if someone wishes to unfold his confused conception of the matter, let him teach himself that a good man is one who benefits those whom he can and harms no one unless provoked by injustice.

Such a man will therefore dare neither to do nor even to think anything that he could not openly proclaim. It is certainly disgraceful for a philosopher to hesitate over things about which not even peasants hesitate. It follows that it is wholly incompatible with a good man to lie for the sake of profit, bring accusations, rob, or deceive.

Is anything really worth so much, or any advantage so desirable, that you should lose both the splendor and the name of a good man? What can this supposed advantage bring if it has seized the name of a good man and stripped him of trustworthiness and justice? What difference is there between someone’s changing from a human being into a beast and his wearing the form of a human being while bearing the savagery of a beast? If people neglect everything upright and honorable so long as they gain power, do they not bear the savagery of a beast?

What if a father attempts to seize tyranny or betray his country? Will his son remain silent? On the contrary, the son will implore his father not to do it; if he achieves nothing, he will accuse him and finally even threaten him, if the matter concerns the destruction of the country. He will place the safety of his country before the safety of his father.

Pacts and promises must always be kept when they have not been made through force or fraudulent deceit, as praetors commonly say.

Deposits, however, are not always to be returned. If someone deposits a sword with you while in sound mind and later demands it while insane, it would be wrong to return it and a duty not to return it. And if someone who has deposited money with you should make war upon his country, would you return his deposit in accordance with the agreement? I do not think so. You would be acting against the state, which ought to be dearest to you.

Thus many things that seem honorable by nature become dishonorable according to circumstances. Fulfilling promises, standing by agreements, and returning deposits become dishonorable when circumstances have changed their relation to expediency.

People overturn the foundations of nature when they separate expediency from moral honor. We all seek advantage and are drawn toward it; we cannot in any way act otherwise. For who avoids what is useful, or who, rather, does not pursue it with the greatest eagerness? But because we cannot find what is useful except together with praise, propriety, and honor, we therefore regard these as first and supreme.

We consider the name of expediency less splendid than necessary. From this comes the one rule of all things, which I wish to be thoroughly familiar to you: either what appears useful must not be dishonorable, or, if it is dishonorable, it must not appear useful.

An oath is a religious affirmation. Whatever one has promised while affirming it as though God were witness must be kept. Perjury is not merely swearing falsely; rather, when one has sworn what one believes in one’s mind—as it is formulated in the words of our mouth—not to do that is perjury. For our ancestors wished no bond to bind good faith more tightly than an oath. There is also a law of war, and the good faith of an oath must often be observed even with an enemy.

An agreement made under force ought not to be considered binding, as though force could not be applied even to a brave man.

From Cicero’s *On Friendship*.

You must understand that people’s eyes are fixed upon you. They call and regard you as the one wise man, not merely by nature and character but also through study and learning—not in the way the common crowd uses the word, but in the way educated people customarily call someone wise. They believe that your wisdom consists in considering everything of yours to depend upon yourself and in thinking human misfortunes inferior to virtue.

But when you say that I attribute to you so much as I neither acknowledge nor claim for myself, you speak as a friend.

I do not think that anything can happen to a steadfast man that would cause any interruption in his duty.

To be deeply distressed by one’s own misfortunes is the conduct of someone who loves himself, not his friend.

[Col. 1067D] What shall I say about his most approachable character, his devotion to his mother, his freedom and frankness with his sisters, his kindness toward his own people, and his justice toward everyone? All these qualities are known to us.

How dear he was to the state was shown by the grief at his funeral. What, then, could an addition of a few years have done to help him? His life had been such, whether by fortune or by glory, that nothing further could be added to it; and the speed of his death removed the experience of dying.

I can only urge you to place friendship before all human things. Nothing is so suited to nature and so appropriate to both prosperous and adverse circumstances. But I especially maintain that friendship cannot exist except among good people.

We must look to the things that belong to ordinary life and common usage, not to things that are invented or merely wished for.

Let us therefore proceed, as the saying goes, with sound common sense, and regard and call good those men who conduct themselves and live in such a way that their trustworthiness, integrity, evenness, and generosity are approved; who possess no desire, lust, or greed; and who display great steadfastness, since they attain as much as human beings can attain in following the best nature of living well.

For I seem to see that we have been born in such a way that some fellowship exists among all people, but that the closer someone comes to us, the more preferred he is: citizens more than foreigners, relatives more than strangers. Nature itself has produced friendship among relatives, but it does not possess complete firmness. Friendship has this advantage over kinship: goodwill can be removed from kinship, but not from friendship. Once goodwill has been removed, the name of friendship disappears, while kinship remains.

The power of friendship can best be understood from this: from the boundless fellowship of the human race, which nature itself has brought together, the relationship has been contracted and narrowed so that all affection is joined either between two people or among a few.

Friendship is nothing other than agreement in all divine and human matters, accompanied by goodwill and affection. I do not know whether the immortal gods have given human beings anything better than this, except wisdom. Some place wealth first, others good health, others power, honors, or bodily pleasures. The last of these is truly characteristic of beasts; the former things are fragile and uncertain, depending not so much upon our plans as upon the recklessness of fortune.

Those who place the highest good in virtue act nobly; but virtue itself both produces and preserves friendship, because friendship cannot exist in any way without virtue. Among good men, then, friendship possesses such great advantages that I can scarcely describe them.

To begin with, how can life be worth living, as Ennius says, if it does not rest upon the mutual goodwill of a friend? What is sweeter than having someone with whom you dare to speak about everything just as you would speak with yourself? What enjoyment would there be in prosperity unless you had someone who rejoiced in it as much as you yourself? Adversity, on the other hand, would be difficult to bear without someone who bore it even more heavily than you.

Finally, the other desirable things are useful for particular purposes: wealth, so that you may use it; power, so that you may be courted; honors, so that you may be praised; pleasures, so that you may enjoy yourself; health, so that you may be free from pain and perform the functions of the body.

Friendship contains the greatest number of things. Wherever you turn, it is at hand; it is excluded by no means and from no place. It is never untimely and never burdensome. Thus, as the saying goes, we use neither water nor fire in more situations than we use friendship.

I am not speaking of ordinary or moderate friendship, which nevertheless itself gives pleasure and benefit, but of true and perfect friendship, such as belonged to those few who are celebrated by name. Friendship makes prosperity more splendid and makes adversity easier by bearing and sharing it. Although friendship contains very many and very great advantages, it surpasses them all in this: it sheds a bright light of hope upon the future and does not allow the spirit to be weakened or fall. Indeed, the friend who looks upon his friend sees, as it were, a model of himself.

Therefore the absent are present, the needy are rich, and the weak are strong. And, what is more difficult to say, the dead live. Such honor through memory and such longing follow them among their friends that the death of the former seems blessed and the life of the latter honorable.

If you were to remove the union of goodwill from the nature of things, no household or city could stand, and agriculture would not continue. If the power of friendship and concord is not sufficiently understood, it can be perceived from dissensions and disagreements. What household is so stable, what state so firm, that hatred and discord could not utterly overturn it? From this one can judge how much good there is in friendship.

Love—for friendship was named from it—is foremost in joining people through goodwill. Benefits are often received even from those who are cultivated and attended with a pretense of friendship for the sake of the occasion.

But in friendship there is nothing false, nothing feigned; whatever exists is genuine and voluntary. For this reason friendship seems to me to arise from nature rather than from need, from the inclination of the spirit accompanied by a certain feeling of love rather than from calculation of how much advantage the relationship would provide.

Something of this can even be observed in certain animals. They love their offspring for a time, and are loved by them, in such a way that their feelings are readily apparent. In human beings this is much clearer, first in the affection that exists between children and parents, which cannot be broken apart except by a detestable crime. Then a similar feeling of love arises when we find someone whose character and nature are joined to ours, so that we seem to perceive in him something like a light of integrity and virtue.

Nothing is more lovable than virtue, and nothing attracts us more strongly to love. Indeed, because of virtue and integrity we in some way love even those whom we have never seen. If the power of integrity is so great that we love even those whom we have never seen—or, more remarkably still, love it in an enemy—what is surprising about human spirits being moved when they seem to observe the virtue and integrity of people with whom they can be joined through ordinary association?

Love is strengthened, however, by benefits received, by devoted effort, and by the addition of habit. When these things are applied to the first movement of the spirit and of love, a remarkable greatness of goodwill bursts into flame. Those who think that this proceeds from weakness, so that it may provide a way for each person to obtain what he desires, leave friendship with a lowly and least generous origin, if I may put it so; they wish its character to arise from poverty and need.

Just as we are generous and beneficent not in order to demand gratitude—for we do not lend out a benefit at interest—but because we are naturally inclined toward generosity, so we think friendship should be sought not because we have been led on by hope of reward, but because its whole fruit lies in love itself.

For if advantage cemented friendship, the same advantage, once changed, would dissolve it. But because nature cannot be changed, true friendships are everlasting. Scipio used to say that nothing was more difficult than for friendship to last until the final day of life. He also used to say that people’s characters often change, sometimes because of different circumstances, sometimes because of advancing age. He drew an example of this from the similarity of the stages of early life: the strongest loves among children are often laid aside together with the purple-bordered garment or the adult toga.

If they continued farther into adolescence, friendships were sometimes broken apart by rivalry, luxury, social position, or some advantage that both could not obtain. If some had advanced farther in friendship, they could nevertheless often be shaken if they entered into competition for honor. For Scipio used to say that no greater plague existed in friendships than the desire for money among most people, and, among the best, rivalry for honor and glory. From this, he said, the greatest enmities often arose between the closest friends.

He also said that serious disagreements commonly arose when friends demanded something improper, asking others either to serve their lusts or to assist them in wrongdoing. Those who refused, even though they acted honorably, were nevertheless accused by those whom they declined to obey of abandoning the obligations of friendship. But those who dared to demand anything whatsoever from a friend, by the very act of demanding professed that they would do anything for their friend’s sake. Scipio said that their long-standing complaints commonly not only extinguished close relationships but also generated lasting hatred.

There is no excuse for wrongdoing if you have done wrong for the sake of a friend. Since the belief in virtue was what brought friendship together, it is difficult for friendships to endure if you have turned away from virtue. If we were to decide that we should either grant friends whatever they wish or obtain from them whatever we wish, then, provided the matter contained no fault, we would indeed possess perfect wisdom.

Let this law therefore be established in friendship: neither should we ask for dishonorable things, nor do them when asked. It is a disgraceful and wholly unacceptable excuse—among other offenses, and especially so if someone admits that he acted against the state for the sake of a friend.

I care no less about what sort of state there will be after my death than about what sort of state exists today.

Let this, then, be established as the first law of friendship: that we ask our friends for honorable things and do honorable things for the sake of our friends. We should not even wait to be asked; eagerness should always be present and hesitation absent. Let us gladly give honest advice freely. In friendship the authority of friends who give good counsel carries great weight; it should be employed in admonition not only openly but even sharply if circumstances demand it, and when it has been given, it should be obeyed.

Those who remove friendship from life seem to remove the sun from the world; we possess nothing better or more delightful than friendship from the immortal gods.

You may observe the just grieving most deeply over unjust things, the strong over the weak, and the modest over disgraceful things. It is therefore characteristic of a well-ordered spirit both to rejoice in good things and to grieve over their opposites. If emotional distress befalls a wise man—and it certainly does, unless humanity has been uprooted from his spirit—what reason is there for us to remove friendship entirely from life, lest we undertake some hardships on its account?

For what is more absurd than to take pleasure in many empty things—honor, glory, buildings, clothing, and bodily adornment—yet not to take much pleasure in a spirit endowed with virtue and capable of loving or, so to speak, returning love? Nothing is more delightful than the repayment of goodwill and the mutual exchange of devotion and services.

If we add what may rightly be added—that nothing is so attractive and so compelling in any matter as similarity is in friendship—it can certainly be acknowledged as true that good people love good people and summon them to themselves as though joined by kinship and nature.

For who, in the name of gods and human beings, would wish neither to love anyone nor to be loved by anyone, while being surrounded by every resource and living in the greatest poverty amid total abundance?

In the life of tyrants, where there is no trust, no affection, and no stable confidence in goodwill, everything is always suspect and anxious, and there is no place for friendship. Who, after all, would love someone whom he fears, or someone whom he thinks fears him? Such people are nevertheless courted, but only through pretense and for a time. If they should happen to fall—as usually happens—then they understand how destitute of friends they had been.

Fortune itself is not only blind but also usually makes blind those whom it embraces. Thus such people are generally carried away by arrogance and insolence, and nothing is more intolerable than a foolish person favored by fortune.

What, moreover, is more foolish than, while possessing abundant resources, means, and wealth, to acquire all the other things that money can buy—horses, servants, fine clothing, precious vessels—but not to acquire friends, the finest and most beautiful furnishings, so to speak, of life? When they acquire the other things, they do not know for whom they are acquiring them or for whose sake they labor. Each of these things belongs to whoever prevails through strength.

The possession of friendship, however, remains stable and secure for each person. Even if the things that are, as it were, gifts of fortune remain, a life uncultivated and deserted by friends cannot be pleasant.

How many things we would never do for our own sake we do for the sake of friends: plead for an unworthy friend, make supplications, attack and pursue someone with greater harshness than we would consider sufficiently honorable in our own affairs. There are many matters in which good men take much away from their own advantages and allow much to be taken away, so that their friends may enjoy them rather than themselves.

To acquire the goodwill of citizens through flattery and fawning is disgraceful; but virtue, when goodwill follows it, is by no means to be rejected.

Thus those whom we judge suitable for friendship must be firm, steadfast, and consistent; people of this kind are very scarce, and it is certainly difficult to judge them unless they have first been tested. Yet testing must take place within the friendship itself, [Col. 1071A] and so friendship anticipates judgment and removes the opportunity for testing.

Where shall we find people who do not prefer honors, magistracies, commands, powers, wealth, and power to friendship? When these things are set out on one side and the force of friendship on the other, will many prefer the latter? Nature is too weak for despising power. Where will you find someone who puts his friend’s honor before his own? Thus true friendships are found with the greatest difficulty among those engaged in the honors of public life. A person who has shown himself serious, constant, and steadfast in every matter of friendship ought to be judged one of that rare class of human beings, almost divine. The foundation of the steadfastness and constancy that we seek in friendship is trustworthiness: nothing is steadfast that is untrustworthy. Moreover, it is right to choose someone straightforward, open, and like-minded, who is moved by the same things; all these qualities pertain to fidelity. A complex and crooked character cannot be trustworthy.

[Col. 1071B]

Nor can one who is not moved by the same things be in agreement with nature, or be steadfast or trustworthy. We must add to this that a friend should neither take pleasure in bringing accusations nor believe accusations brought against another—qualities that all belong to the constancy I have been discussing. Thus the truth of the saying emerges: friendship cannot exist except among good people.

A good man—whom we may also call wise—must hold to these two principles in friendship. First, let nothing be fabricated or feigned. To love or hate openly is more honorable than to conceal one’s opinion behind an expression. Second, he must not merely repel accusations brought by someone else, but must not himself be suspicious, always imagining that something has been violated by his friend. A certain pleasantness of speech and character must also be added; it is no ordinary seasoning of friendship. Let sadness and excessive severity in every matter be absent. These qualities indeed possess dignity, but friendship ought to be more relaxed, freer, sweeter, and more inclined toward every kind of graciousness [Col. 1071C] and wit.

Friendships should not be like partnerships in other matters. The oldest things, like wines that have endured age, ought to be the sweetest. There is truth in the saying that many bushels of salt must be eaten together before the duty of friendship is fulfilled. New friendships, if they offer a promising appearance—so that, as with plants that are not deceptive, the fruit may be seen—are not to be rejected; nevertheless, age must be preserved in its proper place.

For the power of habit is very great. Even with a horse, if nothing prevents it, no one fails to use more willingly the horse to which he is accustomed than one that is untouched and new. Habit is effective not only in this animal but also in inanimate things, since we take pleasure in places themselves—mountainous and wooded places—in which we have stayed longer.

But in friendship the greatest thing is for the superior to be equal to the inferior.

[Col. 1071D]

For the fruit of intelligence, virtue, and every excellence is gathered most fully when it is bestowed upon each person nearest to us. Therefore, just as those who are superior in the bond of friendship and companionship ought to make themselves equal with their inferiors, so inferiors ought not to grieve that they are surpassed by their friends in intelligence, fortune, or dignity. The class of people who reproach others with their services is truly hateful; the person to whom the services were rendered ought rather to remember them, while the one who rendered them ought not to call them to mind.

Different characters produce different interests, and their dissimilarity separates friendships. Good people and bad people cannot be friends with one another for any other reason than that the distance between their characters and interests is as great as distance can be.

In every matter, one must consider both what one asks of a friend and what one allows oneself to obtain from a friend.

For nothing is more disgraceful than to wage war against someone with whom one has lived in intimacy. Therefore, one must first take care that no disagreement arise among friends; and then one must also beware that friendships do not turn into serious enmities, from which quarrels, [Col. 1072A] curses, and insults are born. If these are bearable, however, they must be endured, and this honor must be paid to an old friendship: the person who inflicts the injury, not the one who suffers it, should be regarded as at fault.

In general, the one precaution and provision against all these faults and troubles is not to begin loving too quickly, and not to love those who are unworthy. Those are worthy of friendship in whom there is, within themselves, a reason why they should be loved. The excellent are rare everywhere, and nothing is more difficult than to find something perfect in every respect within its kind. But most people know nothing to be good in human affairs except what is profitable, and they love friends like livestock, especially those from whom they hope to obtain the greatest benefits.

Thus they lack the most beautiful and most natural friendship, which is to be sought for its own sake and through itself; nor are they themselves examples of it. A true friend, therefore, is never found. Such a friend is, as it were, another self: one who loves himself and acquires another whose spirit he mingles with his own [Col. 1072B] so that, almost, one is made from two.

But most people, perversely—not to say foolishly—want a friend of the kind they themselves cannot be; and the qualities they do not grant to their friends, they expect from their friends. The proper course is first to be a good man oneself, and then to seek another like oneself. Among such people the stability of friendship can be firmly established: joined first by goodwill, they will rule over those desires to which others are enslaved; then they will rejoice in fairness and justice, and each will undertake everything on behalf of the other. Neither will ever ask the other for anything except what is honorable and right; and they will not merely respect and love one another, but also revere one another.

For anyone who removes reverence from friendship removes its greatest ornament. Thus it is a destructive error among those who think that friendship permits license for every lust and wrongdoing. Friendship has been given by nature as an ally of virtue, not as a companion of vices, so that virtue, since it cannot reach the highest things when solitary, might reach them when joined and associated with another [Col. 1072C].

One ought to love after making a judgment, not to judge after falling in love.

Many despise wealth, being pleased with a frugal life and modest surroundings. Honors, however, with desire for which some people burn, how many despise so completely that they regard nothing as less important or more trivial? Likewise, there are many who consider worthless other things that seem admirable to certain people.

About friendship, everyone without exception thinks the same: those who have devoted themselves to public affairs, those who take pleasure in the investigation and study of things, those who conduct their private business in leisure, and finally those who have surrendered themselves entirely to pleasures—all recognize that life is nothing without friendship, provided that they wish to live liberally in any respect.

For friendship creeps through the lives of everyone and allows no manner of passing one’s life to be without it. Indeed, even if someone is so harsh and inhuman by nature that he avoids and hates the company of human beings, he could not endure failing to know someone before whom he might pour out the bitterness of his spirit.

[Col. 1072D]

Nature loves nothing solitary.

The use of friendship is varied and manifold, and many causes of suspicion and offense arise. To wish both to avoid them and to lessen them, and to bear them, is the mark of a wise person. Your offense must be relieved in such a way that both usefulness and trust may be preserved in the friendship.

For friends often must be advised and rebuked; and these things must be received in a friendly spirit when they are done benevolently.

But somehow it is true what my intimate friend said in the *Andria*: “Compliance produces friends; truth produces hatred.” Truth is troublesome if it gives rise to hatred, which is the poison of friendship. Yet compliance is much more troublesome, since, indulging faults, it allows a headlong spirit to rush onward. The greatest fault lies in the person who both rejects the truth and is driven into deception by compliance.

In all this, therefore, [Col. 1073A] care and attention must be exercised: first, so that advice is free from harshness; then, so that rebuke is free from insult.

In compliance, there should be openness and fellowship; the flattery that assists vices must be kept far away, for it is worthy neither of a friend nor even of a free person. One lives differently with a tyrant and differently with a friend. But if someone’s ears are closed to truth, so that he cannot hear the truth from a friend, there is no hope for his welfare.

That saying of Cato is well known: “It is much better to incur the bitter enmity of people over certain matters than to have friends who seem sweet.” The former often speak the truth; the latter never do. It is absurd that, while they are being corrected, people become distressed by the very trouble from which they ought to be free. They are not troubled that they have done wrong, but resent being rebuked—when the opposite ought to be the case.

Thus, just as it belongs to true friendship both to advise and to receive advice—to do the former freely but not harshly, and to accept the latter patiently and without resistance—so we must regard nothing as a greater plague in friendships than flattery, ingratiation, and false compliance.

[Col. 1073B]

Since every kind of pretense is vicious—it destroys one’s judgment of truth and corrupts it—it is especially opposed to friendship. It destroys truth, without which the name of friendship cannot remain. For since the power of friendship consists in making, as it were, one spirit out of several, how can this happen if there is not in each person one spirit, always the same, rather than a variable, changeable, and manifold one?

What could be as flexible and as wayward as the spirit of one who conforms not only to another’s feeling and will but even to his expression and nod? “He denies it, I deny it; he says it, I say it.” Finally, as Terence says, “I ordered myself to agree with everything.”

A flattering friend can be separated and distinguished from a true one by applying as much care as is needed to distinguish all painted and counterfeit things from what is sincere and true.

Although compliance is destructive, it can harm no one except the person who accepts it and takes pleasure [Col. 1073C] in it. Many people do not possess virtue so much as they wish to appear to possess it, and these people enjoy the nourishment of flattery. When speech is adapted to their wishes, they think that empty language is testimony to their praises.

This, then, is not friendship: one person does not want to hear the truth, while the other is ready to lie. Nor would the flattery of parasites in comedies be commended to us as amusing if there were no boastful soldiers. The flatterer always magnifies what the person to whom he speaks wishes to be considered great.

Therefore, although this flattering emptiness has power over those who themselves entice and invite it, even more serious and steadfast people must be warned to take care that they are not caught by cunning flattery. No one fails to see an open flatterer unless he is utterly senseless. The crafty and concealed flatterer must be carefully avoided, lest he insinuate himself; for he is not easily recognized, since even while flattering he often opposes, and, pretending to argue, he ingratiates himself. Finally, he gives in and allows himself to be defeated, so that the person who has been deceived [Col. 1073D] may seem to have won more.

What, however, is more disgraceful than being deceived? We must take greater care that this does not happen.

Virtue both wins friends and preserves them. In virtue there is harmony of things and character; in it there are steadfastness and constancy. When virtue has raised itself up and displayed its light, and has seen and recognized the same light in another, it draws near to it and in turn receives what exists in the other; from this either love or friendship bursts into flame. Both words, in fact, derive from *amare*, “to love.”

To love is nothing other than to value the very person whom one loves, without seeking any advantage. Through this goodwill we, as young men, loved our elders; it shines even more brightly among equals. But since human affairs are fragile and fleeting, everything brief ought always to be regarded as bearable, even when it is great.

I urge you, then, to value virtue so highly that, without it, friendship cannot exist, and that, once virtue is set aside, you consider nothing more valuable than friendship. Let this suffice concerning friendship; what follows concerns old age.

From M. T. Cicero’s book *On Old Age*.

[Col. 1074A]

Philosophy can never be praised worthily enough. Whoever obeys it can pass every period of life without distress. For those who possess within themselves no resources for living well and happily, every age is burdensome.

But for those who seek all good things from themselves, nothing that the necessity of nature brings can seem evil. Old age belongs especially to this category: everyone wishes to attain it, yet once attained, everyone accuses it. Such inconsistency, foolishness, and perversity! They say that it creeps upon them and arrives sooner than they had expected.

“Equals most easily gather with equals,” as the old proverb says.

For moderate and undemanding old men, neither inhuman nor difficult, lead a tolerable old age.

But offensiveness and inhumanity are troublesome at every age.

[Col. 1074B]

Some say that old age seems more tolerable because of wealth, abundance, and dignity. For old age cannot be light in extreme poverty, whether for a wise person or a foolish one; nor, even amid the greatest abundance, can old age be free from burdens. The most suitable weapons of old age are unquestionably the arts and the exercises of virtue. Cultivated throughout every age, they produce remarkable fruits when one has lived long and much—not only because they never abandon us, not even at the final period of life (although that is indeed their greatest benefit), but also because the consciousness of a life well lived and the recollection of many good deeds are extremely pleasurable.

Not everyone can be a Scipio or a Maximus, remembering the capture of cities, battles fought on land or sea, wars waged by themselves, and triumphs. There is also a quiet, pure, and refined life, a peaceful and gentle old age, such as we are told Plato had: he died while writing in his eighty-first year. Isocrates had one like it; he is said to have written the book entitled *Panathenaicus* in his ninety-fourth year [Col. 1074C] and lived for another five years afterward. His teacher, Gorgias of Leontini, completed 107 years and never ceased from his study and work. When he was asked why he wished to remain alive so long, he replied: “I have nothing for which to accuse old age.” A splendid answer, worthy of a learned man. For foolish people lay their own faults and their own blame upon old age.

Ennius, already seventy years old, bore what are thought to be the two greatest burdens—poverty and old age—in such a way that he seemed almost to take pleasure in them.

When I consider the matter in my mind, I find four reasons why old age seems miserable: first, that it removes us from active affairs; second, that it makes the body weaker; third, that it deprives us of almost everything; fourth, that it is not far removed from death.

Old age withdraws us from active affairs—but from what affairs? From those that are carried on in youth and with physical strength? Are there, then, no activities proper to old age, which can be directed by weakened bodies but by the mind [Col. 1074D]?

Those who deny that old age can cease from active work bring forward no argument. They are like people who say that a helmsman does nothing while sailing, when some climb the masts, others run about the decks, and others empty the bilge, while he, holding the tiller in his hand, sits quietly at the stern. He does not do what young men do, but he does many things greater and better. Great matters are not accomplished by physical strength, speed, or bodily swiftness, but by counsel, authority, and judgment. With these, old age is usually not deprived but even strengthened.

For memory remains in the old, provided that interest and diligence remain. Memory declines unless one exercises it.

No one is so old that he does not think he can live another year; yet these same people labor over things they know have absolutely nothing to do with them. They plant trees that will benefit another generation, as our Statius says in the *Senephebi* [title uncertain]. Good heavens, if old age brought no other fault with it when it arrives, this one would be sufficient [Col. 1075A]: by living long, one sees many things one does not wish to see.

Just as wise old men delight young people endowed with good character, and old age becomes lighter for those who have been cultivated and loved from youth, so young people rejoice in the instructions of the old, by which the young are led toward the pursuit of virtue.

We have seen Solon boasting in verse; he says that by learning something every day he grows old.

Nor do I now miss strength. That was the second charge concerning the faults of old age. I miss the strength of youth no more than, when young, I missed the strength of a bull or an elephant. Whatever one has, one ought to use; and whatever one does, one ought to do according to one’s strength.

No teacher of the liberal arts should be considered unhappy merely because his strength has grown old and failed, especially since this very weakening of strength is more often caused by the faults of youth than by those of old age. For a lustful and undisciplined youth hands over to old age an exhausted body.

[Col. 1075B]

There is a fixed course of life and a single path of nature, simple and proper to itself. Each period has been assigned its appropriate season: the weakness of children, the fierceness of the young, and the seriousness of an age that has now become established. In the same way, the maturity of old age naturally possesses what ought to be gathered in its own time.

Exercise and moderation can preserve some of one’s former strength even in old age. Old age has no physical strength, nor is physical strength demanded of old age. Thus both written laws and established practices excuse the elderly from duties and offices that require strength. We are compelled not only to do what we cannot do, but not even to do as much as we can.

Many old people are so weak that they cannot perform any duty or office at all; but that is not a fault peculiar to old age. It is a common condition of ill health and old age.

Why, then, should it be surprising if old people are sometimes weak, when even young people cannot escape weakness? We must resist old age and compensate for its faults [Col. 1075C] through diligence. We must fight against old age just as we fight against illness. Attention must be paid to health; moderate exercise must be used; only as much food and drink should be taken as restores strength rather than overwhelms it.

Nor should help be given only to the body; much more must be given to the mind and spirit. For these too, unless one pours oil into them as into a lamp, are extinguished by old age. Bodies become heavier through the exhaustion of exercise, but spirits are lifted by exercising themselves.

That childish foolishness of old age, which is usually called senility, belongs to frivolous old people, not to everyone. Appius, both old and blind, governed four robust sons, five daughters, so large a household, and so many dependents. He kept his mind taut like a bow and did not grow slack or yield to old age. He retained not only authority but command over his household; the slaves feared him, his children revered him, and everyone held him dear. Ancestral custom and discipline flourished in that household.

[Col. 1075D]

Thus old age is honorable if it defends itself, retains its rights, is free from fault, is enslaved to no one, and rules its own household until its final breath. Just as I approve a young man who possesses something of an old man, so I approve an old man who possesses something of youth. If he follows this course, he may be old in body, but he will never be old in spirit. These are exercises of intelligence, these are the courses of the mind; in these, while pouring himself out and laboring, he has little need of bodily strength. Nor does he notice when old age steals upon him.

Some people criticize old age. This is the third accusation against old age: they say that it is deprived of pleasures. But, oh, what a splendid gift of age, if it takes from us what is most vicious in youth!

Archytas of Tarentum used to say that nature had given human beings no more deadly plague than bodily pleasure, whose allurements incite eager lusts to seek enjoyment recklessly and without restraint. From this, he said, arise betrayals of one’s country; from this, the overthrow of states [Col. 1076A]; from this, secret conversations with enemies. Finally, he said, there is no crime or evil deed to which the desire for pleasure would not drive someone to undertake it. Rapes, adulteries, and every such disgrace, he maintained, are incited by no other enticements than pleasures.

Although nature—or some god—had given human beings nothing more excellent than the mind, nothing was so hostile to this divine gift as pleasure. For where lust is dominant, there is no place for self-control, and virtue cannot possibly remain in the kingdom of pleasure.

To make this more readily understood, he used to instruct us to imagine someone aroused by as much bodily pleasure as could possibly be experienced. No one, he thought, would doubt that, for as long as he rejoiced in this condition, he could neither direct his mind toward anything nor accomplish anything through reason or thought. Therefore nothing is so detestable and so destructive as pleasure, since, when it is greater and more prolonged, it extinguishes all the light of the spirit.

[Col. 1076B]

Pleasure, hostile to reason, obstructs deliberation and, so to speak, blinds the eyes of the mind; it has no association with virtue.

Why, then, so much discussion of pleasure? Because it is not merely no reproach but even the highest praise of old age that it has little desire for such pleasures and is free from banquets, heavily laden tables, and frequent drinking. It is therefore free from drunkenness, indigestion, and sleepless nights.

Although old age is free from excessive banquets, it can still take pleasure in moderate gatherings. Nor should we measure the pleasure of the gatherings themselves by bodily pleasures more than by the company of friends and conversation.

If old age possesses something like nourishment for study and learning, nothing is more pleasant than an old age free for such pursuits.

What pleasures of banquets, games, or prostitutes can be compared with these pleasures—and especially with these studies of learning, which grow together with age in prudent and well-trained people [Col. 1076C]? Certainly no greater pleasure of the mind can exist.

The pleasures of farmers, in which I take the greatest delight, are not hindered by old age, and they seem to me to approach most closely the life of a wise person. For they have to do with the earth, which never returns what it has received without interest. Yet I am delighted not only by its fruits but also by the power and nature of the earth itself.

Country life is made joyful not only by grainfields, meadows, vineyards, and groves, but also by gardens and orchards, by the grazing of livestock, by swarms of bees, and by the variety of every kind of flower. Nothing can be richer in practical use, more beautiful in appearance, or more splendid by nature than a well-cultivated field. Old age does not merely delay us from enjoying it; it invites and delights us in its enjoyment.

In my judgment, I scarcely know whether any life can be happier. The cultivation of fields is beneficial not only because of human labor, but also because of the pleasure, satisfaction, and abundance of all things that belong to human life and even to the worship [Col. 1076D] of the gods. The elderly may enjoy this good fortune, and it does not prevent them from maintaining their interest in other matters as well, right up to the final period of old age.

When the Samnites brought Curio, who was sitting beside his hearth, a great weight of gold, they were rejected. He did not think it splendid to possess gold, but to rule those who possessed gold. Could a spirit so great fail to make old age pleasant?

The final period of life is happier than the middle period because it has more authority and less labor.

The crown of old age is authority. Honored old age in particular possesses such authority that it is worth more than all the pleasures of youth. But throughout this entire discussion, remember that I am praising the old age that has been founded upon the foundations of youth. From this it follows that the old age that must defend itself in speech is miserable. Neither gray hair nor wrinkles can suddenly take away authority; rather, an earlier period honorably lived gathers the final fruits of authority.

[Col. 1077A]

Those very actions that seem light and ordinary are the most honorable: being greeted, sought out, yielded to, risen for, escorted, escorted home, consulted. These practices are observed most carefully both among us and in other states, according as each society is best ordered.

Every injury is offensive in a fragile body.

Just as not every wine turns sour through age, so not every period of life grows sour through the aging of nature.

I do not understand what senile greed is supposed to mean. For can anything be more absurd than to seek more provisions for a journey the less of the road remains? The fourth reason remains—the one that seems most to distress and trouble our age: the approach of death, which cannot be far from old age.

What a miserable old man is one who, after so long a life, has not seen that death ought to be scorned—death which must either be entirely disregarded if it completely extinguishes the spirit, or much more even desired if it leads the spirit somewhere it will be eternal. There is certainly no third [Col. 1077B] possibility.

Why, then, should I fear, if after death I shall either not be miserable or shall even be happy? Yet who is so foolish, so confident in himself, even if young, that he knows he will live until evening? Indeed, that age has many more chances of death than ours. Young people fall ill more easily, suffer more seriously, and are treated more painfully. Thus very few reach old age—which would happen if they lived better and more prudently. For the mind, reason, and judgment belong to the old.

Scipio says that death is common to every age. But the young person hopes that he will live a long time; the old person cannot have the same hope. The young person hopes foolishly. For what is more foolish than to treat uncertain things as certain and false things as true? But the old person does not even have what he hopes for. Yet he is in a better position than the young person, since he has attained what the young person hopes for: the young person wishes to live a long time; the old person has lived a long time.

And yet, good heavens, what in human life is long?

[Col. 1077C]

To me, nothing seems long-lasting if it has an end. When the end arrives, what has passed has flowed away; only as much remains as one has acquired through virtue and good deeds. Hours, days, months, and years yield to one another, and time that has passed never returns. Nor can anyone know what will follow. Each person ought to be content with the amount of time granted to him for living.

A short period of life is long enough for living well and honorably. If one proceeds farther, one should no more grieve than farmers grieve when, after the sweetness of spring has passed, summer and autumn have arrived. Spring, as it were, signifies and displays youth and shows the fruits that will come. The remaining seasons are suited to harvesting and gathering those fruits.

The fruit of old age is the abundance and recollection of the good things previously acquired. Everything that occurs according to nature must be counted among good things. What, then, is more according to nature than for the old to die? The same thing happens to the young [Col. 1077D] in opposition to and resistance from nature.

Thus the young seem to me to die as when the force of a flame is overwhelmed by a great quantity of water. The old die as when a fire, consumed of its own accord and without the application of force, is extinguished. As unripe apples are forcibly torn from trees, while ripe and mature ones fall, so force takes life from the young, but maturity takes it from the old.

This maturity is already so pleasant to me that, the nearer I approach death, I seem to see the land—as though I were at last going to reach port after a long voyage. Old age has no fixed boundary; one rightly lives in it as long as one can perform and maintain one’s duties and safely scorn death. From this it follows that old age is even bolder and stronger than youth.

The best end of life comes when nature itself, with mind intact and senses clear, dissolves the work it constructed. Just as the person who built a ship or a building most easily takes it apart, so the same nature that best arranged the human being [Col. 1078A] dissolves him best.

Every recent joining is difficult to loosen; one that has grown old is loosened with ease. Thus the short remainder of life is neither to be eagerly desired by the old nor postponed without reason. Pythagoras forbids us to leave the guard and station of life without the commander’s order—that is, without God’s order.

The wise Solon’s epitaph is that in which he says he does not wish his death to be free from the grief and lamentations of his friends. But perhaps Ennius expressed it better:

> Let no one honor me with tears or mourn my funeral;  
> Let him make it so that, while alive, I fly through the mouths of men.

He does not think that death should be mourned if immortality follows it.

This must be anticipated from youth onward: we must disregard death. Without such reflection, no one can possess a tranquil spirit. It is certain that we must die, but it is uncertain whether we shall die on this very day. If someone fears death hanging over him every hour, who can stand with a secure spirit?

[Col. 1078B]

While we are enclosed within these structures of the body, we perform a certain task imposed by necessity, and a burdensome labor. The heavenly spirit has been lowered from its highest dwelling and, as it were, submerged in earth, occupying a place contrary to divine nature and eternity.

But I believe that the immortal gods scattered spirits into human bodies so that there would be beings to care for the earth and, contemplating the order of the heavens, to imitate it in the manner and constancy of their lives. Reason alone did not compel me to believe this; so too did the arguments and authority of the ancient and noble philosophers, especially Pythagoras, who demonstrated that we possess spirits drawn from the universal divine mind.

There is also the authority of Socrates, who on the final day of his life discussed the immortality of spirits. Why say more? I have convinced myself of this and feel it thus: since there is such brilliance of intellect, such memory of the past, such foresight of the future, so many arts, so much [Col. 1078C] knowledge, and so many discoveries, the nature that contains such great things cannot be mortal.

Our Plato, too, said the following while dying, according to Xenophon:

> Do not suppose, dearest sons, that when I have departed from you I shall be nowhere or nothing. For while I was with you, you did not see the spirit that governed these limbs; you understood that it existed from the things I did. Believe, then, that it will remain the same even if you see none of it.

I could never be persuaded that spirits, while living in mortal bodies, die when they have departed from those bodies. Nor could I believe that the spirit is foolish once it has escaped from a foolish body; rather, when it has been freed from the mixture of the body and has begun to be pure and whole, then it becomes wise.

Moreover, when human nature is dissolved by death, it is clear whither each of the other things departs. Everything goes away to the place from which it arose. But the spirit alone is not visible, either when it arrives or when it departs.

You see, furthermore, that nothing is more like death than sleep [Col. 1078D], and the spirits of sleeping people most clearly reveal their divinity. From this it is easy to understand what they will be like when they have completely released themselves from the bonds of their bodies.

Many outstanding men—there is no need to enumerate them—would not have undertaken such great efforts for the memory of posterity unless they had judged that their spirits would continue to exist after the body’s death. Would it not have been much better to pass a life of leisure and quiet without any great labor or struggle? Yet unless spirits were immortal, the spirit of every good person would not strive so earnestly for the glory of immortality.

What of the fact that every wise person dies with the most even temper, while every foolish person dies with the most agitated? Does it not seem to you that the person who sees more and farther knows that he is proceeding toward better things, while the one whose vision is duller does not see this?

I do not wish to lament life, as many uneducated people have often done; nor do I regret having lived, since I have lived in such a way that I do not think I was born [Col. 1079A] in vain. I am departing from life as though from an inn, not as though from my home. Nature has given us a temporary lodging for staying, not a permanent dwelling.

Oh, glorious day, when I shall depart for that assembly and gathering of divine spirits! And if some god were to grant me the opportunity to become young again, I would not wish, as though I had completed the course, to be called back from the finish to the starting barriers.

For what advantage does life possess? What does it not possess of toil? Old age is light, not only free from trouble but even pleasant. If, however, we are not destined to be immortal, it is nevertheless desirable for a human being to be extinguished at the proper time. Nature has established a limit for living, as it has for all other things.

Old age is the completion of life, as of a drama; we ought to escape the fatigue of that drama, especially when companionship is added.

This concludes the discussion of old age. May we reach it, so that we may be able to approve by experience what has been said. What follows concerns the *Paradoxes* of that same Marcus Tullius Cicero.

From M. T. Cicero’s book *Paradoxes*.

[Col. 1079B]

Nothing is so incredible that it cannot be made probable by speaking; nothing so dreadful, nothing so uncultivated, that speech cannot make it shine.

By Hercules, I have never considered money, magnificent houses, wealth, commands, or pleasures to be among the good things that should be sought.

Can what is good for one person be bad for another, or can anyone be good while surrounded by an abundance of good things?

If anyone wishes to mock me, let him; sound reasoning will carry more weight with me than popular opinion. Nor will I ever say that a man has lost his goods if he has lost livestock or household furnishings. I shall often praise that wise man Bias, too. When the enemy had captured his homeland, Priene, and the other inhabitants were fleeing in such a way as to carry away many of their possessions with them, someone warned him to do the same. “Indeed,” he replied, “that is what I am doing. For I carry all my possessions with me.” He considered these toys of Fortune not even his own—things that we nevertheless call “goods.”

## [Col. 1079C]

“What, then,” someone will ask, “is good?” If something is done rightly, honorably, and virtuously, that alone, I think, is good. Some cling firmly to the view, and defend it carefully, that pleasure is the highest good. That word, however, seems to me to belong to animals, not to human beings. When either God or Nature—the mother, so to speak, of all things—has given you a mind, than which nothing is more excellent or more divine, will you so cast yourself down and abase yourself that you think there is no difference between yourself and a four-footed animal? For the more each person shares in the good, the more praiseworthy he is. Nor is there any good of which its possessor cannot honorably boast. What of these qualities is found in pleasure? Does it make a man better or more worthy of praise? Or can anyone boast proudly and exalt himself in proclaiming that he has obtained pleasures?

And if pleasure—which is defended by the strongest advocates—is not to be counted among good things, and the greater it is, the more it dislodges the mind from its proper seat and condition, then surely living well and happily is nothing other than living honorably and rightly.

No one can fail to be supremely happy if he places all his possessions within himself alone. But for the man whose every hope, plan, and thought depends upon Fortune, nothing can be certain, and nothing can remain assured for even a single day.

Death is terrible for those whose entire existence perishes with their life, but not for those whose praise cannot die. Exile is terrible for those whose place of residence has, as it were, been marked out for them, but not for those who say that the whole world is a single city.

Sins are to be measured not by the outcome of events but by the vices of human beings.

What force could restrain people more from every kind of wrongdoing than the realization that there is no distinction among offenses?

## [Col. 1080A]

We cannot determine the limits of material things, but we can keep the mind within its proper bounds.

Nothing is either mine or anyone else’s that can be taken away, seized, or lost.

How, then, and over whom, will this man rule as a free person, when he cannot rule his own desires? Let him first restrain his lusts, despise pleasures, control his anger, curb his greed, and drive away the other stains of his mind. He will then begin to rule others when he has ceased to obey, to his dishonor and disgrace, the worst of masters within himself. So long as he obeys these masters, he should be regarded not merely as no commander but as not free at all.

The most learned men have declared that no one is free except the wise man. For what is freedom other than the power to live as one wishes? Who, then, lives as he wishes except the man who follows what is right, who takes pleasure in his duties, whose way of life has been considered and planned in advance, who obeys the laws not out of fear but follows them, and removes what he judges to be most conducive to his well-being; who does, says, and finally thinks nothing except willingly and freely; whose plans and every undertaking proceed from himself and are directed toward the same end? Nothing has greater power over him than his own will and judgment. Even Fortune herself, reputed to possess the greatest power, yields to him.

As the wise poet says: “Each person is fashioned by his own character.” Thus only to the wise man does it belong to do nothing unwillingly, nothing with grief, nothing under compulsion. Hence that brief conclusion must be acknowledged: no one is free unless he has been formed in this way.

All wicked men, therefore, are slaves—and this is not so much unexpected and astonishing in reality as it is in words. They are not called slaves in the sense of chattels, which become the property of their masters through legal bond or some civil-law right; rather, slavery is understood as the obedience of a broken and degraded spirit, deprived of its own judgment.

Who could deny that all kings—if they are frivolous, greedy, and finally wicked—are slaves? Does that man seem free to me over whom a woman rules, to whom she lays down laws, prescribes, forbids, and commands whatever she pleases; who can refuse nothing to one who commands and dares reject nothing? If she asks, it must be given; if she calls, he must come. She drives him out when he is leaving and threatens him with things he must fear. I think such a man should be called not merely a slave but the most contemptible of slaves, even if he was born into the most distinguished household.

Is there any doubt, too, about the slavery of those who, out of greed for a legacy, refuse no condition of the harshest servitude? What injustice in serving will a man not endure when he has hope of an inheritance, or what nod of a wealthy and childless person will he fail to observe? He speaks according to that person’s wishes; whatever is announced, he does; he agrees, sits beside him, and invites him. What in all this belongs to a free man, or even to a slave who is not utterly inert?

And what of that greed which appears to be directed toward the more respectable objects of honor and provincial command? How harsh a mistress it is, how imperious, how violent! Consider also the judge: how much authority he possesses, and with what fear he afflicts the guilty. Is not every kind of fear a form of slavery? Every weakness of mind, every humiliation, every broken timidity is slavery.

## [Col. 1080D]

No one owes anything except what it would be disgraceful not to repay. For whom do we understand to be rich—and in what person do we place this word? I think, in the person who possesses enough that he can live generously with ease. Your mind, not human speech or your possessions, ought to judge you rich: if you think nothing is lacking to you and care for nothing further, you are satisfied—or, if you are content even with money, I concede that you are rich.

But if, because of greed for money, you think no profit-making dishonorable, although no form of such business can truly be honorable for your class; if every day you defraud, deceive, demand, bargain, take away, and seize; if you strip your associates and plunder the treasury; if you await your friends’ wills and even put yourself forward for them—are these signs of abundance or of want?

It is the human spirit, not the strongbox, that is customarily called rich. However full the strongbox may be, if I see that you are empty, I shall not consider you rich. People measure the extent of wealth by how much is enough for each person.

Someone has one daughter: he needs money. Two: he needs more. If there are more, still more. But if, as they say, someone had the fifty daughters of Danaus, those many dowries would require a great deal of money. The measure of wealth is adjusted to whatever each person needs, as I said before.

How, then, shall I call rich the man who has not more daughters but countless desires, capable of exhausting great resources in a short time, when he himself feels that he is in need? The fruit of wealth lies in abundance, and abundance is revealed by satisfaction with one’s possessions and by plenty.

If, then, a person is to be considered richer in proportion as he possesses what is of greatest value, who could doubt that wealth lies in virtue, since no possession and no power of gold or silver should be valued more highly than virtue?

## [Col. 1081A]

Immortal gods! People do not understand how great a revenue saving can yield. Which man is richer: the one who lacks something or the one who has more than enough; the one who is in need or the one who abounds; the one whose greater possessions require ever more to maintain them, or the one who supports himself by his own strength?

The measure of money is determined not by the valuation of one’s estate but by one’s way of life and expenditure. To be free from greed for money, not to cling to revenue, and to be content with one’s own possessions—these are the greatest and most certain riches.

These shrewd valuers of things place a high value on meadows and building plots because that kind of possession can scarcely be damaged. How highly, then, should virtue be valued? It can neither be snatched away nor secretly stolen; it is not lost through shipwreck or fire, nor changed by the disturbance of storms or times. Those who possess it are the only rich people, for they alone possess things both fruitful and everlasting. They alone possess the characteristic proper to wealth: they are content with their own possessions. They consider what exists sufficient; they desire nothing, need nothing, feel that nothing is lacking to them, and demand nothing.

But wicked and greedy people, because they possess things uncertain and dependent on chance, always desire more. No one among them has yet been found for whom what he possesses is enough. They must be judged not merely as not prosperous and rich, but even as needy and poor.

This concludes the material on the *Paradoxes*. We now proceed to the *Tusculan Disputations*.

## From the First Book of Marcus Tullius Cicero’s *Tusculan Disputations*

It is easy to defeat those who do not resist. Honor nourishes the arts, and we are all kindled toward the pursuit of glory and praise; those pursuits always lie idle among those who disapprove of them.

It is characteristic of an intemperate person to abuse both leisure and learning.

Everyone must die. What pleasure can life hold for us if we must think day and night that we are on the point of dying? The more closely antiquity stood to the beginning and divine origin of things, the better, perhaps, it discerned what was true.

There is no race so savage, no human being so brutish, that the belief in gods has not imbued his mind. Many hold mistaken views about the gods. This usually results from corrupt custom. All believe that divine power and nature exist; nor is this belief produced by a mob or by human agreement, nor has the opinion been confirmed by institutions or laws. In every matter, however, the agreement of all nations should be regarded as a law of nature.

What nature is better in human beings than that of those who believe they were born to help, protect, and preserve other human beings? Hercules went to the gods; he would never have gone there unless, while among human beings, he had prepared that path for himself.

No one will ever offer himself to die for his country without a great hope of immortality.

It is the mark of a great intellect to recall the mind from the senses and withdraw thought from habitual patterns.

Let each person practice the art he knows.

Nothing is swifter than the mind; no speed can compete with the speed of the mind. If the mind remains uncorrupted and true to itself, it must move in such a way as to penetrate and divide the whole heaven. Philosophy has driven darkness from this mind as from the eyes, so that we may see all things above, below, at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end. This divine power seems to me to accomplish things both so numerous and so great.

Nor can the God whom we understand be understood in any other way than as a kind of mind released and free, separated from every mortal mixture.

Socrates, when he already almost held in his hand that deadly cup, spoke in such a way that he seemed not to be driven toward death but to be ascending into heaven. For he held, and argued, that there are two paths and two courses for souls departing from the body.

Those who had contaminated themselves with human vices and given themselves wholly to lust—those who, blinded by these passions, had polluted themselves either with private vices and crimes or had conceived unforgivable deceptions in violating the commonwealth—had a certain byway cut off from the assembly of the gods.

But those who had kept themselves whole and pure, who had had as little contact as possible with bodies, who had continually withdrawn themselves from them, and who, while living in human bodies, had imitated the life of the gods—those people would have an easy return to the gods from whom they had come.

Cato departed from life in such a way that he rejoiced to have found a reason for dying. For the entire life of philosophers is a meditation on death. What else are we doing when we withdraw the mind from pleasure—that is, from the body—from household property, which is the body’s servant and attendant; from public affairs; and from every business? What, I ask, are we then doing except calling the mind back to itself, forcing it to be with itself, and separating it as far as possible from the body?

To separate the mind from the body is nothing other than learning how to die. Let us therefore meditate on this, believe me, and separate ourselves from our bodies—that is, let us accustom ourselves to die. While we remain on earth, this will resemble the life in heaven; and when we are released from these bonds and carried there, the course of our souls will be less impeded. When we have reached that place, then at last we shall live. For this present life is death—a death you might lament, if you wished.

## [Col. 1082C]

Such is our love for our country that we measure it not by our own feeling but by its welfare. Therefore death does not deter the wise man—death, which daily threatens him because of uncertain accidents and can never be far away because of the brevity of life—from caring for the commonwealth and his own people for all time, and from considering even posterity, whose experience he will not share, to belong to him.

Nature is so constituted that, just as our birth brings us the beginning of all things, so death brings us their end. As we had no relation to anything before birth, so nothing after death will have any relation to us.

What age is long, or what is long for a human being at all? Has not old age overtaken us, pursuing us from behind as we run—now as children, now as young men—without our expecting it? But because we have nothing beyond it, we call this long. All these periods are called long or short according to the portion of life allotted to each person.

If, while we wait and long, our minds hang suspended, are tormented, and are distressed, immortal gods, how desirable must that journey be which, once completed, will leave no further care or anxiety!

A distinguished man does not die miserably. Nothing evil can ever befall a good man, whether alive or dead, nor will his affairs ever be neglected by the immortal gods. Let us hold firmly to this: nothing is evil that nature has given to all, and let us understand that, if death is evil, it is an everlasting evil. For death seems to be the end of a miserable life. But if death itself is miserable, there can be no end.

Although sensation has departed, the dead will nevertheless not lack the highest and proper goods of praise and glory, even though they do not perceive them.

## [Col. 1083A]

For no accumulation of goods can be as pleasant as departure from them is painful.

Let people either begin to desire death or cease to fear it. If that final day brings not extinction but a change of place, what could be more desirable? But if it destroys and annihilates everything completely, what is better than to fall asleep amid the labors of life and thus be lulled into everlasting sleep?

If this is so, Ennius’s speech is better than Solon’s. Here is our Ennius:

> Let no one honor me with tears—he says—  
> nor make the funeral rites with weeping.

But the wise Solon says:

> May my death not lack tears; let us leave my friends  
> grief, so that they may celebrate my funeral with lamentation.

But if something should happen to us that seems to have been announced by God, let us leave life joyfully, give thanks, and obey; let us think that we are being released from confinement and freed from our bonds, so that we may either return, as if rowing back, to our eternal and truly native home, or be deprived of all sensation and distress.

But if no such announcement is made, let us nevertheless be disposed to regard that dreadful day as fortunate for us, and let us count nothing among evils that has been ordained either by the immortal gods or by nature, the mother of all things.

For we were not made and created rashly or by chance. Let us therefore consider that a harbor and refuge have been prepared for us, to which, if only we may reach it with full sails. If we are driven back by contrary winds, nevertheless we must be carried back to the same place, only somewhat later. But what is necessary for everyone—how can that be miserable for one person?

Let us pursue above all those things that bring relief from grief, fear, and desire; for this is the richest fruit of all philosophy.

## From the Second Book of Marcus Tullius Cicero’s *Tusculan Disputations*

## [Col. 1083C]

It is difficult for a person to know only a few things in philosophy if he does not know either most things or everything. For no one can select a few things except from among many, and whoever has grasped a few will pursue the remainder with the same zeal.

Whoever fears what cannot be avoided can in no way live with a tranquil mind. But whoever does not fear death—not merely because it is necessary to die, but also because death contains nothing dreadful—acquires for himself a great defense of a happy life.

The effect of eloquence is the approval of its listeners.

This is what philosophy accomplishes: it heals the mind, removes empty anxieties, frees us from desires, and drives away fears. For the brave, not only Fortune, as the old proverb says, but reason helps even more; reason strengthens the power of courage with certain precepts.

For just as a field, however fertile, cannot be fruitful without cultivation, so the mind cannot be fruitful without instruction. The cultivation of the mind is philosophy. It uproots falsehoods, prepares minds to receive seeds, entrusts those seeds to them, and, so to speak, sows them—seeds that, when mature, will bear the richest fruits.

The mind must be strengthened to endure pain.

Without prudence, no virtue can even be understood, much less exist.

Temperance will not allow you to do anything immoderately.

Habit in labor makes the endurance of pain easier. Habit teaches us to bear toil and despise wounds. The power of habit is great. Those who have been well trained prefer to receive a blow rather than avoid it dishonorably.

Virtue is named from *vir*, “man”; and the chief characteristic of a man is courage, whose two greatest functions are contempt for death and contempt for pain. We must therefore use these qualities if we wish to possess virtue—or rather, if we wish to be men—since virtue has borrowed its name from men.

Nature has nothing more excellent, nothing that she desires more, than honor, praise, dignity, and distinction.

If our foot hurts, or our tooth, we cannot bear it; but imagine that the entire body hurts. We cannot endure it. This is a certain effeminate and shallow opinion, no more so in pain than in pleasure. In pain above all we must take care that we do nothing abjectly, fearfully, cowardly, servilely, or womanishly.

A man may sometimes groan, and even that rarely; wailing is permitted not even to a woman. The brave and wise man never groans unless perhaps to gather himself for endurance, as runners in the stadium shout as loudly as they can. Athletes do the same during training. Boxers groan even when they strike an opponent while wielding the boxing gloves—not because their spirit suffers pain or because they are yielding, but because the whole body is strained by the force of the voice, and the blow becomes more powerful.

But since the pain is not diminished, why do we wish to be disgraceful for no reason? What is more disgraceful for a man than womanly weeping?

Many people have bravely received and endured wounds either from desire for victory, love of glory, or even in order to maintain their rights and freedom. Yet these same people, once they have abandoned the contest, cannot endure the pain of illness. They did not endure the pain they had borne so easily by reason or wisdom, but rather through ambition and glory.

If we do everything for the sake of avoiding disgrace and attaining honor, let us despise not only the goads of pain but also the thunderbolts of Fortune.

## From the Third Book of Marcus Tullius Cicero’s *Tusculan Disputations*

## [Col. 1084C]

There are innate seeds of virtue in our minds; if they were permitted to mature, nature herself would lead us to a happy life. But as soon as we are born into the light and taken into care, we are immediately surrounded by every kind of depravity and the greatest perversity of opinion, so that we seem almost to have imbibed error with our nurse’s milk. When we are returned to our parents and then handed over to teachers, we are so imbued with various errors that nature herself yields to vanity and to firmly established opinion.

“A sick mind,” as Ennius says, “is always wandering; it can neither endure nor suffer through.” It never ceases to desire. Philosophy is truly the medicine of the mind. But not everyone who allows himself to be treated immediately recovers. Minds that have wished to be healed and have obeyed the instructions of wise parents are healed without any doubt. And unless the mind has been healed—which cannot happen without philosophy—there is no end to misery.

The function of the mind is to use reason well; and the mind of the wise man is always so disposed that it uses reason in the best possible way.

Everything sudden seems more serious.

## [Col. 1084D]

Forethought about future evils lessens their arrival: when you have seen them coming from far off, they are less severe.

They say that when Anaxagoras was informed of his son’s death, he said: “I knew that I had begotten a mortal.” These words show that such events are bitter to those who had not thought about them beforehand.

It is therefore beyond doubt that everything regarded as evil seems more serious when it is unexpected. Forethought and preparation of mind can do much to diminish pain.
