Nothing blunts and lightens grief so much as the continual thought throughout life that nothing can occur that cannot occur; as meditation on the human condition; as reflection on the law of life and practice in submitting to it.

This does not cause us always to grieve, but prevents us from grieving at all. For the person who considers the nature of things, the changes of life, and the weakness of the human race does not grieve while considering them; rather, he bears more easily what occurs because he has long considered that it could occur. This one reflection above all weakens and dissolves every trouble.

## [Col. 1085A]

What is more despicable or disgraceful than an effeminate man?

The sudden arrival of enemies sometimes disturbs people more than an expected attack, and a sudden storm at sea frightens sailors more violently than one foreseen. Most things are like this. But when you carefully consider the nature of unexpected events, you will discover nothing other than that everything sudden appears greater.

Pain diminishes gradually and little by little as time advances—not because the thing itself is ordinarily changed or can be changed, but because experience teaches what reason ought to have taught: that things which appeared greater are actually less serious.

A person will endure a misfortune more tolerably when he knows that such a thing must happen to a human being.

We were born under this law: no one can remain forever free from evil. For no mortal exists whom pain and illness do not touch.

A life honorably and splendidly lived brings such great consolation that grief either does not touch those who have lived in this way or the pain of the mind pricks them only lightly.

Mothers and teachers commonly chastise children who, during a domestic mourning, have done or said something too cheerfully; they compel them to weep, not merely with words but also with blows.

They say that Theophrastus, as he was dying, accused nature because she had given deer and crows—creatures for whom it mattered nothing—a long life, while giving human beings, for whom it mattered most, such a short one. If human life could have been longer, he said, it would have happened that human existence would be educated by all perfected arts and every branch of learning. He complained that he was then beginning to see these things just as he was being extinguished.

That is an excellent principle, and, if you ask, a right and true one as well: we should love those who ought to be dearest to us as much as we love ourselves. But it is impossible for this to go further. In friendship it is not even desirable that my friend love me more than himself, or that I love him more than myself. If it were so, the disturbance of life and of all duties would follow.

It is characteristic of folly to notice the faults of others and forget one’s own.

The duties of those who offer consolation are to remove grief completely, calm it, diminish it as much as possible, suppress it, prevent it from spreading further, or redirect it toward other objects. Time must be applied to diseases of the mind no less than to diseases of the body.

What is admirable that is not also difficult? These points are from the third book of the *Tusculan Disputations*; what follows is from the fourth.

## From the Fourth Book of Marcus Tullius Cicero’s *Tusculan Disputations*

Just as we naturally desire good things, so by nature we turn away from evils. They say that the source of all disturbances is intemperance, which is a falling away from the whole mind and from right reason. For just as temperance calms all desires, makes them obey right reason, and consumes them through the considered judgments of the mind, so intemperance, its enemy, inflames, disorders, and agitates the entire condition of the mind. Thus grief, fear, and all the other disturbances arise from it.

For all those whose minds recoil from reason are always threatened—some by pain, others by terror. The upright man does everything correctly.

What could seem great to a person who knows all eternity and the vastness of the entire universe? What could seem great to the wise man in human pursuits or in so short a span of life, when he is always so alert in mind that nothing can happen to him unexpectedly, nothing unforeseen, nothing wholly new?

He also directs his keenest attention in every direction, so that he always sees for himself a place and position in which he may live without annoyance or distress, and so that he may bear calmly and appropriately whatever event Fortune brings. If he does this, he will be free not only from grief but also from all the other disturbances. A mind free from these things makes a person perfectly and completely happy; a mind agitated and drawn away from sound and steadfast reason loses not only constancy but also health.

Those who endure disgrace and infamy without pain seem to have been granted impunity for their sins. It is better to be gnawed by conscience.

In almost every matter they consider moderation to be best.

There is no courage that lacks reason. Human affairs must be despised, death disregarded, and labors and pains considered bearable. Once these principles have been established by judgment and firm conviction, courage becomes strong and steadfast.

It is useful to employ the movement of the mind when it cannot employ reason.

We ought not to take grief upon ourselves on behalf of others, but, if we can, to relieve others of their grief.

When reason is applied, it discerns what is best; when neglected, it becomes entangled in many errors.

For persuasion that what has occurred both can and ought to be endured, it is useful to enumerate those who have endured such things.

Let the things commonly considered good—honors, riches, pleasures, and the rest—be good indeed. Even so, an exultant and frenzied joy in possessing those very things is disgraceful. Just as laughter may be permitted, yet excessive guffawing is censured, so the mind’s outpouring in joy is the same fault as its contraction in pain. The desire involved in seeking is the same frivolity as the joy involved in enjoying.

And just as people are rightly judged frivolous when excessively oppressed by distress, so those whose minds are elated by joy are judged frivolous. Just as those who exalt themselves in joy while indulging in sexual pleasures are disgraceful, so those who desire those pleasures with an inflamed mind are criminal.

This is from the fourth book; what follows is now from the fifth and final book.

## From the Fifth Book of Marcus Tullius Cicero’s *Tusculan Disputations*

## [Col. 1086C]

All correction of our vices and sins must be sought from philosophy. When, from the earliest period of our lives, she had drawn our will and zeal into her embrace, we now flee to the same harbor from which we had set out, driven by a great storm and battered by these grave misfortunes.

O philosophy, guide of life, investigator of virtue, expeller of vices! What could human life—not merely our own lives but human life altogether—have been without you? You gave birth to cities; you summoned scattered human beings into the fellowship of life; you first joined them through dwellings, then through marriages, and finally through the sharing of letters and speech. You were the inventor of laws and the teacher of morals and discipline.

We take refuge with you; from you we seek aid; to you, as before, we now surrender ourselves, for the greater part of us—and now wholly and completely. A single day lived well and according to your precepts is almost preferable to all immortality.

From whose resources, then, should we draw rather than yours? You have granted us tranquility of life and removed the fear of death. Do not think that any saying has ever been uttered more clearly in philosophy, or that any promise of philosophy is richer or greater, than this: virtue is sufficient for living happily.

Turbulent movements and agitations of the mind, aroused and lifted up by unconsidered impulse, drive away reason entirely and leave no part of a happy life. For who can fail to be miserable while fearing death or pain, one of which is always present and the other always impending?

If such a person also fears poverty, disgrace, infamy; weakness, blindness; or, finally, slavery, which often befalls not merely individuals but powerful peoples, can anyone who fears these things be happy? What if he not only fears things to come but also bears and endures them in the present? Add exile, mourning, and bereavement; if he is broken by these things and overwhelmed by grief, can he finally be anything other than utterly miserable?

What of the man whom we see inflamed and raging with lust, desiring everything greedily and, the more abundantly he drains pleasures from every side, the more heavily and ardently thirsting? Would you not rightly call him utterly miserable?

What of the man lifted up by frivolity and empty joy, exulting and senselessly celebrating? Is he not all the more miserable the happier he appears to himself?

Thus, just as these people are miserable, so, on the contrary, those are happy whom no fears terrify, no griefs consume, no lusts drive, and no empty joys melt away in exultant, languid pleasures.

If there is someone who considers Fortune’s power and all human experiences that can befall each person to be bearable, so that neither fear nor distress touches him; and if he desires nothing and is carried away by no empty pleasure of the mind—why should he not be happy? And if these qualities are produced by virtue, why should virtue itself not make people happy through its own nature?

Lust never finds an end.

## [Col. 1087B]

The mark of an acute reasoner is to see not what each person says but what ought to be said to each person.

We call those equipped and adorned with every virtue both wise and good men.

Philosophers must not be judged by individual expressions but by continuity and consistency.

The matter itself, I think, ought to be considered, not the words.

For the man who possesses within himself everything suited to living happily, whose happiness does not hang upon the good fortune or misfortune of others and is not compelled to wander according to events affecting another person—that man has an excellent way of life prepared for him. The person who always places all his hope in himself will never rejoice or grieve excessively.

The human mind, plucked from the divine mind, can be compared with nothing except God himself, if it is permissible to say so. If this mind has been cultivated, and its vision has been so cared for that it is not blinded by errors, it becomes perfect mind—that is, complete reason—which is the same thing as virtue.

If everything is happy that lacks nothing, and if whatever is complete and filled out within its own kind possesses this quality, and if this is characteristic of virtue, then surely all who possess virtue are happy.

What can be lacking for living well and happily to the person who trusts in his own goods? Or how can anyone be happy who distrusts them? We want the happy person to be secure, unconquerable, surrounded and fortified—not merely to possess little fear but to possess none.

Things cannot be called or considered good if it is possible to abound in them and yet be utterly miserable. Do you doubt that a man distinguished by health, strength, beauty, the keenest and soundest senses—and, if you wish, agility and speed as well—if you give him riches, honors, commands, power, and glory, would be utterly miserable if he were unjust, intemperate, fearful, dull-witted, and utterly without understanding? Would you hesitate to call him miserable?

Thus that leading philosopher argued: as each person's disposition is, so is the person; as the person himself is, so is his speech; his actions resemble his speech, and his life resembles his actions. The dispositions of the mind in a good man are praiseworthy; therefore the life of a good and honorable man is also praiseworthy. From this it follows that the life of the good is happy.

Is the temperate, steadfast man, without fear, without grief, without any excitement, without lust, not happy? A happy life is praiseworthy, and nothing is praiseworthy without virtue. Therefore a happy life is achieved through virtue.

For just as folly, even when it has obtained what it desired, never thinks it has obtained enough, so wisdom is always content with what is present and never regrets itself. This is how things stand: your possessions delight you; mine delight me.

Custom never conquers nature; nature is always unconquered.

It is characteristic of the wise man to do nothing that he might regret and nothing unwillingly; to do everything splendidly, steadfastly, seriously, and honorably; to expect nothing as though it were certain to happen; and, when something occurs, not to marvel as though it had happened unexpectedly or as something new; to refer everything to his own judgment and stand by his own decisions. I cannot imagine anything happier than this.

We cannot even use our minds when filled with too much food and drink, and I have never approved of becoming full twice in a single day.

How can life be pleasant when prudence and moderation are absent?

The day would fail me if I wished to defend the case of poverty. The matter is obvious, and nature herself reminds us every day how few, how small, and how cheap the things are that we need.

Will obscurity, low social standing, or even popular hostility prevent the wise man from being happy? Take care lest popularity and the glory that is sought have more annoyance than pleasure.

Do flute players and those who use the lyre regulate their songs and rhythms according to their own judgment rather than that of the crowd? The wise man, endowed with far greater skill, will not inquire what the crowd wants but what is most true.

Leave behind, by fleeing from them, the injuries of Fortune that you cannot bear.

These points from the *Tusculan Disputations* of Marcus Tullius Cicero are sufficient.

## From the Sixth Book of Marcus Tullius Cicero’s *On the Republic*
It often happens that our thoughts and conversations give birth to something in sleep, as Ennius writes concerning Homer: while awake, he used to think and speak about him very frequently.

For all who have preserved, aided, and enlarged their native country, there is, he declares, a definite place appointed in heaven, where they may enjoy blessedness throughout eternity. For nothing is more acceptable to that sovereign God who rules the whole universe than the councils and assemblies of human beings joined together by law, which are called states. Their rulers and preservers have set out from here and return here.

Those live who have flown out of the bonds of their bodies as from a prison; but what you call your life is death.

For unless God—the God whose temple is all that you see—sets you free from these bodily confinements, you cannot gain access to this place. Human beings were created under this law: to watch over that sphere which you see placed at the center of this temple, and which is called the earth. Their souls were taken from those everlasting fires that you call stars and constellations; these, round and spherical, animated by divine minds, complete their circles and orbits with marvelous speed. Therefore, Publius, and all the pious, must keep the soul in the custody of the body, nor may one depart from human life without the command of him from whom that soul was given to us, lest you seem to have evaded the human task assigned by God. But, Scipio, practice justice and piety—for piety toward parents and relatives is great, but toward one’s country greatest of all—and that life is the road to heaven.

Always contemplate these heavenly things; despise those that are human. For you see how little renown from human speech, and how little of the glory that people seek, you can attain: the inhabited regions are few and narrow, and even within those inhabited places there are immense deserts between them, as though they were spots; and those who inhabit them are not merely so separated that nothing can pass among them from one people to another, but some stand obliquely, some transversely, and some entirely opposite to you. From them, certainly, you can obtain no glory.

We cannot attain glory that is eternal—or even glory that lasts long.

Therefore, if you wish to look upward and contemplate this dwelling-place and eternal home, do not surrender yourself to the talk of the crowd, nor place your hopes for your affairs in human rewards. Let virtue itself draw you by its allurements toward true honor. What others say about you, let them see to it themselves; nevertheless, they will speak. For all that speech is enclosed within the narrow boundaries of the regions that you see. No one’s renown has ever been everlasting: it is overwhelmed by the death of human beings and extinguished by the forgetfulness of posterity.

Since, then, it is evident that what moves itself is eternal, who can deny that this nature has been granted to souls? Everything that is inanimate—or lifeless—is moved by an external impulse. For whatever is living is stirred by an inward motion of its own. This, then, is the soul’s distinctive nature and power; and if it alone among all things moves itself, it certainly was not born and is eternal. Exercise it in the noblest pursuits. The noblest are concern for the safety of one’s country. Stirred and trained by these, the soul will fly more swiftly to this, its own dwelling and home. It will do so even more quickly if, while still enclosed in the body, it projects itself outward, so that, contemplating what lies beyond, it withdraws itself as far as possible from the body. For the souls of those who have surrendered themselves to bodily pleasures, made themselves almost their servants, and, driven by desires obedient to pleasure, have violated the laws of gods and human beings, after escaping from their bodies, circle and roll around the earth itself. They do not return to this place until they have been tormented for many ages.

## How terrible the death of Marcus Tullius Cicero was

Valerius Maximus, in *On the Ungrateful*, shows in these words how terrible the death of Marcus Tullius Cicero was.

Marcus Cicero defended Gnaeus Pompilius Lena, of the Picene region, at the request of Marcus Caelius, with no less care than eloquence; and, though the case was extremely doubtful, he sent him safely back to his household gods. Later, Pompilius—though Cicero had injured him neither in deed nor in word—voluntarily asked Mark Antony that he be sent to pursue and slaughter the proscribed man. Having obtained the assignment of that detestable service, he ran joyfully to Caieta and ordered the man—leaving aside the fact that he was a person of the highest dignity, and certainly one whom, for his wholesome zeal and distinguished service, he ought privately to have revered—to expose his throat. Immediately, in the midst of the most secure and undisturbed leisure, he cut off the head of Roman eloquence and the most illustrious right hand of peace, and returned joyfully to Rome bearing it as though it were rich spoils. Nor, while carrying that criminal burden, did it occur to him that he was carrying the very head for which Cicero had once pleaded. Literature is too weak to brand this monster adequately; therefore no second Cicero exists who could lament Cicero’s fate with sufficient dignity.

### Epitaph of Marcus Tullius Cicero, inscribed around his statue in the temple of great Jupiter near the monument of the Tullii

Here lies the Arpinate, buried by the hands of a friend,  
who was a supreme and outstanding orator.  
A citizen and an enemy slaughtered him by a cruel death.  
You accomplish nothing, Antony: his eloquent writings remain.  
With a single wound, indeed, you destroy Cicero;  
but Tullius tears you apart with everlasting wounds.

The body of great Cicero, buried in this tomb,  
is covered here—he who was renowned for his brilliant talent,  
who was a burden to the wicked and a protector of the good,  
through whom Rome, almost undeservedly, perished as consul.  
But, by vigilant care, after exposing the enemies  
and delivering them to punishment, he preserved the city unharmed.  
The prince of eloquence, marvelous in his great achievements,  
Tullius dies, struck down by an undeserved slaughter;  
yet he filled all lands with his illustrious name.  
His talent, though his body was slain, is untouched by death.  
He lives, and throughout the world his genius possesses power,  
though his limbs lie buried in this tomb.

[Col. 1089]

# The Book of Proverbs of the Venerable Priest Bede

## Prologue

When I had recently read the sayings called the *Proverbs of Seneca*, arranged in alphabetical order, I was initially astonished that so much wisdom could exist in any unbeliever as is found in some of those proverbial sayings. Then I was greatly moved to imitate him with some similar zeal, by collecting, from both secular and sacred writings, and also from our own writings, certain proverbs suitable for the edification of the faithful.

For if Seneca, who possessed neither faith nor hope of obtaining eternal life, but delighted only in moral uprightness in this present life, made an effort both to correct himself and to instruct others toward correction, how much more should I—who believe that God is present everywhere and promises eternal life to those who love him, and who know that it has been said to everyone, “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’”; and, “Cry out without ceasing”; and, “Declare to my people their crimes”; and who, according to the Gospel parable, have received from the master of the household the charge that to some five talents were given for investment, to others two, and to others one, while he said, “Conduct business until I come”—how much more must I draw certain people toward edification through the gifts of knowledge granted to them!

And how pleasant and sweet it ought to seem to everyone to keep continually in mind and memory some very brief little saying through which one may be corrected, since we know that the criminal thief obtained forgiveness for all his sins by supplicating the Lord in a few words and saying, “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom”! Who could not be taught, when asking God for the gift of understanding, how to obtain it, if he frequently turns over in his mind that little verse: “Understanding is good for all who practice it”? Certainly, if he knows only the meaning of those words and believes that the truth is contained in them, they can be sufficient for his salvation. For they teach him that, if he does the good which he now understands, greater understanding will come to him. Is not such teaching and promise to be embraced in every way?

Similar teaching can also be found in many of the sayings that I have placed here. But I explained the aforementioned little saying only in this prologue, in order to encourage the reader’s mind to read not only what I have collected here, but also all the sayings of sacred Scripture. For no one is saved merely by hearing or reading sacred words without intention of heart. Hence our Lord also frequently admonishes his hearers in the Gospel, saying: “Let the one who has ears to hear, hear.” It is as though he were saying: “Let the one who has the will and intention to obey the divine commands and do the good that he understands listen to me, who am teaching. Otherwise, hearing my words profits him nothing.”

The sayings of the proverbs collected here may, if anyone so wishes, suitably instruct schoolboys after the reading of the Psalter. For they are much shorter and clearer in meaning than those proverbial sayings of the fabulist Aesop; and they are also more useful than certain sayings of Cato. Nearly all teachers customarily read both collections as the first lessons for children, without considering that sacred rather than pagan elementary instruction ought first to be offered to the little ones as well as to elderly believers in Christ, so that, instructed to some extent in these matters, they may afterward learn secular literature appropriate to the art of grammar with greater security.

For although children are less capable of distinguishing between good and evil, evil nevertheless generally takes hold of them more easily and more firmly than good. Therefore those who wish to be diligent for the beneficial outcome of instructing children should also take pains concerning the beneficial beginning of their instruction, and should know that it is extremely difficult for a person to depart from the evil that he has acquired through long habit.

Moreover, one must observe that when God looks down upon the children of human beings, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God, he also sees what care or intention teachers have in instructing their pupils: whether they teach them for the sake of seeking worldly glory or spiritual glory. Take note of this, you pupils, and likewise you teachers.

## Proverbs

[Col. 1091]

### A

Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.

The Lord raises up all who fall, and lifts up all who are crushed.

A man’s steps are directed by the Lord, and he will desire his way.

With the Lord there is mercy, and with him abundant redemption.

Embrace discipline, lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the right path.

Narrow and confined is the way that leads to life.

The soul that sins shall itself die.

The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.

The wise person who listens will become wiser.

The turning away of the little ones will kill them, and the prosperity of fools will destroy them.

Chosen silver is the tongue of the righteous.

A companion of fools will become like them.

One who walks on the straight path and fears God is despised by him who walks on a disgraceful road.

To follow the Lamb wherever he goes is especially fitting for virginity.

The greedy person is not filled with money, and the one who loves riches gains no fruit from them.

When you approach the service of God, stand in justice and the fear of Christ, and prepare your soul for temptation.

Before ruin the heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled.

Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law.

The natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God.

The one whom Cain’s wickedness does not exercise refuses to be Abel.

The love of God is never idle.

The one who casts discipline aside will quickly feel ruin.

A friend is proved in adversity.

Love of the world is contempt for God.

Love of the world stores up treasure for death.

One kind of striking is used to correct a sinner; another is used to condemn him.

No one can reach great joys except through great labors.

The one who quickly judges anyone is hastening toward death.

To love is characteristic of sons; to fear, of servants.

Among human beings, the heart is weighed from words; with God, words are weighed from the heart.

Water is changed for us into wine when sacred history is transformed for us into spiritual understanding.

The greedy person is properly the cause of his own misery, imposing upon himself the thirst of greed.

Prosperity prepares a friend; adversity tests one.

The greedy person does nothing rightly except die.

The greedy person lacks as much what he has as what he does not have.

Greed always makes people hateful; generosity makes them renowned.

Greed is not extinguished by the riches one desires, but increased by them.

Before conversion comes a throng of sins; after conversion follows a throng of temptations.

Every virtue needs the help of another virtue.

You will not be able to love what is right unless you humble yourself for Christ.

You cannot attain humility without great contrition of both the outward and inward person.

Arduous faith demands sturdy years.

The impulses of the flesh, unless they are removed by the authority of the mind, lead every person to destruction.

It is a very arduous thing to serve after having held power.

All good things must be asked entirely from the Lord.

The practice of virtues consists in perfection of character.

Before God’s countenance, nothing wicked remains unpunished.

The way of life is conveyed more clearly and better through deeds than through words.

Ambition has compelled many mortals to become false.

### B

Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered.

Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, who alone does wonders.

Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor; on the evil day God will deliver him.

Blessed is the one who will seize his little ones and dash them against the rock.

The arms of sinners will be broken, but God strengthens the righteous.

The good shepherd gives his life for his sheep.

Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.

Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his confidence.

Blessed is the man who has been found without blemish, who does not pursue gold, and who has placed no hope in money or treasures.

Blessed is the person who is always fearful; but the one who is hard-hearted will fall into evil.

The one who seeks good rises early to good purpose.

It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth.

The Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him.

Every wickedness is brief compared with the wickedness of a woman.

Blessed is the one who has a share in the first resurrection.

Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life.

To speak well and live badly is nothing other than condemning oneself.

The one who does what he rightly understands possesses good understanding.

The one who does not know how to give a benefit asks unjustly.

The more the minds of good people endure hardships for the sake of truth, the more confidently they hope for the rewards of eternity.

It is more blessed to give than to receive.

If you cannot do good, nevertheless do not condemn or hinder it.

A good conscience retains its own brightness in darkness.

The brevity of the present life must be considered by everyone.

The best battle is waged when the spirit opposes the flesh.

The strongest warrior is the one who can conquer himself.

The one who quickly returns what he owes gives twice as pleasingly.

Be gentle toward the meek and strict toward the proud.

The heart of a wicked woman is a cruel beast.

No one is permitted to drink and eat in order to satisfy gluttony, but only to restrain hunger and thirst.

No one is good whom the wickedness of evil people has not tested.

### C

Charity is not to be extorted from anyone, but sought through acts of kindness.

Charity is patient; it is kind.

Charity covers a multitude of sins.

No one ought to place his loved ones before Christ.

The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands.

With the chosen you will be chosen, and with the perverse you will become perverse.

God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart.

The sinner watches the righteous and seeks to put him to death.

In the Lord’s hand is a cup of pure wine, full of mixed wine.

Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever.

When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord.

God guards all who love him, and he will destroy all sinners.

When you give alms, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing.

Heaven and earth will pass away, but the words of God will not pass away.

If a blind man gives guidance to a blind man, both will fall into a pit.

The thought of the human heart is inclined toward evil from its youth.

Correction causes even the greatest sins to cease.

When the ways of a person please the Lord, even his enemies will be turned toward peace.

The thoughts of the righteous are judgments.

The king’s heart is in the hand of God; wherever he wishes, he inclines it.

Consider the works of God: no one can correct the person whom he has rejected.

A beautiful and foolish woman is like a gold ring in her nostrils.

The heart of a person plans his way, but it belongs to the Lord to direct his steps.

The heart of the wise is where there is sadness, and the heart of fools where there is joy.

The heart that knows the bitterness of its own soul will not admit a stranger into its joy.

Turn to the Lord and abandon your sins.

Gray hairs are a person’s understanding, and an unstained life is the maturity of old age.

From the one to whom much is given, much is required.

Be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might.

With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.

The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh.

The body that is corrupted weighs down the soul and depresses the mind that thinks of many things.

Bad conversations corrupt good morals.

Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another so that you may be saved.

Although God can do all things, he cannot do evil, because evil is nothing.

The one who believes that God can accomplish all things more quickly deserves to obtain what he has asked.

No counsel against God is either great or small.

A cause that is not foreseen does not allow anyone to advance toward better things.

God does not seek forced service.

The virtue of humility is the guardian of chastity.

The one who treats small matters as nothing quickly falls into greater crimes.

Discord begins when someone strives to make common things his own.

Continence is a virtue not of the body but of the mind.

Counsel is needed before action.

Through harmony small things grow; through discord great things fall apart.

Whatever advantages people possess seem small, but when they are absent, how great they were becomes apparent.

Although bodily virginity is a heavenly virtue, it benefits no one without virginity of mind.

A bad habit is scarcely, or never, overcome.

Those who cross the sea change the sky, not their spirit.

Love of money grows as money itself grows.

Give whatever help you can to the wretched and the needy.

The abundance of virtues forms one body, as it were.

The one who slanders another and the one who willingly listens to the slander commit an equal crime.

Things that cannot be lightly healed must be cut away with pain.

Everyone is called the child of the one whose works he does.

If anyone wishes to be called a child of God, let him revere God as Father by doing his will.

The greatest captivity is where souls are led captive.

The one who falls has open eyes: he knows how to speak rightly, but despises living rightly.

If someone wishes to recognize how great God’s grace is toward him, let him look at others. Whatever more he perceives himself to possess in health, understanding, or possession of some good, by that much he should know himself to be richer in the grace of God.

A common disease must be driven out by common means.

Correct yourself first, since you are the ruler of others.

It is fitting for everyone to consider what is appropriate.

No one feels compassion for another who does not know how to show mercy to himself.

When the head is sick, the whole body suffers with it.

### D

The Lord looks down from heaven upon the children of human beings, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God.

The Lord questions the righteous and the wicked; but the one who loves iniquity hates his own soul.

The Lord will give a word to those who proclaim the Gospel with great power.

The Lord will give strength to his people; the Lord blesses his people with peace.

The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, for they are empty.

The Lord is sweet and upright; therefore he will give law to sinners on the way.

God is a just, strong, and patient judge.

The Lord of hosts himself is the King of glory.

God will come openly, and he will not keep silent.

The rich have become poor and hungry, but those who seek the Lord will lack no good thing.

Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the requests of your heart.

Turn away from evil and do good.

Give, and it will be given to you.

Forgive, and you will be forgiven.

God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.

The laborer is worthy of his wages.

You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and your neighbor as yourself.

God is faithful and without any iniquity.

The Lord makes poor and makes rich; he humbles and exalts.

He puts to death and gives life; he leads down to the underworld and brings back.

Fear God and observe his commandments; this is the whole human being.

Do not reject the discipline of the Lord, nor grow faint when you are corrected by him.

Love righteousness, you who judge the earth.

The riches of salvation are wisdom and knowledge.

A man’s learning is recognized through patience.

God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.

God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him.

No one has ever seen God.

Love of one’s neighbor works no evil.

The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.

For those who love God, all things work together for good.

While we have time, let us do good to everyone, especially to those who belong to the household of faith.

The one who seeks God seeks joy.

Discernment is the mother of virtues.

Discipline or mercy is greatly weakened if one is held without the other.

Wickedness that someone conceives in childhood is difficult to correct.

No evil is to be attributed to God, since he makes use even of evil for good.

It is difficult for anyone to recognize the gift of health except through the discipline of illness.

Delicacies and variety of dishes are fuel for luxury.

The one who does not share another’s grief cannot console the grieving person.

The one who both commits wickedness in himself and corrupts others by his wickedness is bound by a double guilt.

The one who lies long in sins will also, if he wishes to convert, endure for a long time the troubles of the devil’s temptation.

God is therefore said to create evils because he also sends scourges on account of our sins.

The divine word exercises the wise through its mysteries, and in its surface meaning refreshes the simple.

The person who offers God pure hands is more pleasing to him than the one who offers full hands.

We find it more difficult to do without arrogance than without gold and gems.

There is a double guilt of sin: not being holy when one is believed to be holy, and pretending to be holy.

While the unjust rage, the just are purified.

It is exceedingly difficult for a person to conquer himself.

Long repose supplies nourishment to vices.

A generous and open-handed person pleases all mortals.

Do not call the halfway point of an undertaking completed.

The one who wishes to imitate Christ always has something to learn.

Words of instruction benefit few without deeds.

Do not quarrel in words about uncertain matters.

Call back those who are at odds; press on as a supporter of those who deserve help.

True riches are all the good things of the virtues.

A person should be called rich when he has little need.

### E

The Lord is exalted above all nations, and his glory above the heavens.

Wait for the Lord; act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened; wait for the Lord.

Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity.

The mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart.

Be wise as serpents and simple as doves.

Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.

By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.

With the same measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you.

Rescue those who are being led to death, and do not cease to free those who are being dragged to destruction.

The worship of God is an abomination to the sinner.

Poverty and disgrace belong to the one who abandons discipline, but the one who accepts correction will be glorified.

There is a way that seems right to a person, but its end leads to death.

A horse is prepared for battle, but victory is given by the Lord.

A child is recognized by his pursuits.

There is a shame that leads to sin, and there is a shame that leads to glory.

“Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life,” says almighty God.

Let us amend for the better what we have sinned through ignorance.

Drunkenness and gluttony are to be detested by every Christian.

An abundance of food inflames the flesh toward harmful desires.

God detests almsgiving that is offered from robbery.

To be ashamed of evil is wisdom; to be ashamed of good is folly.

The one who does not care how he may proceed more rightly errs most easily.

The person who does not have enough and the person for whom no abundance suffices are equally needy.

To desire and reject the same things: that, at last, is firm friendship.

A person begins to be evil at the moment when he is able to become good.

A wise person corrects and reforms himself through another’s danger.

Efficacy is granted to prayers for the life of the petitioner.

An excellent teacher is one who does the good that he himself teaches.

Holy speech becomes more precious than gold.

All must rightly know that being is proper to God alone.

The one without instruction will suffer darkness everywhere.

Few are chosen, but many are called.

A person without care for souls is like an empty vessel.

### F

The Lord is faithful in all his words and holy in all his works.

The Lord is a support for those who fear him.

The river of God is filled with waters.

The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a redemption for many.

The children of this age are wiser in their generation than the children of light.

Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings.

It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.

The thief comes only to steal, slaughter, and destroy.

Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy and homeless into your house.

The net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures.

The lips of a prostitute are a dripping honeycomb, and her throat is smoother than oil; but her end is bitter as wormwood.

Grace is deceptive and beauty vain; the woman who fears God is the one who will be praised.

God chastises every son whom he receives.

The one who has mercy on the poor lends to the Lord.

The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous, confident like a lion, will be without fear.

Those who give alms will have great confidence before God.

No one can lay another foundation besides the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.

The saying is faithful and worthy of complete acceptance: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners.

Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen.

Faith without works is dead.

God will judge fornicators and adulterers.

If a brother helps his brother, both will be comforted.

The fever of the body is heat; the fever of the soul is greed and lust.

The strongest fast is bread and water.

The scourge of God then cancels guilt when it changes a person’s life.

The one who abandons the purpose of spiritual life and returns to the world seems to defraud God.

To foresee future things belongs especially to those entrusted with care over others.

Cold and hunger can be driven away with simple clothing and food.

For the faithful, night is changed into day; for the unfaithful, even light itself becomes darkness.

The bodily eye desires a woman’s form before the mind does.

Those who could not be overcome by adversity are often overcome by prosperity.

The strength of the righteous is to conquer the flesh and extinguish delight in the present life.

The strength of the reprobate is to love what passes away without ceasing and to endure the Creator’s scourges without feeling.

The devil should not be feared, since he can do nothing except by permission.

To struggle in vain and, by exhausting oneself, seek nothing but hatred is the height of madness.

It is useless to labor for bodily health unless the soul’s salvation is obtained.

We renounce our purses more easily than we renounce ourselves.

The service rendered from love rather than fear is more faithful and more pleasing.

Lust subdues iron minds.

The one who here neglected to extinguish the fires of his greed and wickedness will eventually be handed over to an unquenchable flame.

Forgiveness should readily be granted to the one who does not sin deliberately.

The one who subdues desires is stronger than the one who subdues enemies.

A fierce and restless person who continually exercises his tongue in quarrels is compared to a dog.

We commit fornication against the Lord when we turn away from his chaste love through adulterous thoughts.

The person devoted to foul and unclean lust imitates the pleasure of a filthy sow.

The one who desires to please not the best but the worst gives offense easily.

Do not quickly display the great deeds of your life.

Blessed is the one who can attain everlasting rest.

Blessed are the eyes that behold the joys of heaven.

An iron mind is frequently overcome by wicked words.

Every tree is known by its own fruits.

The end of the commandment consists in the love of Christ.

### G

Taste and see that the Lord is sweet; blessed is the person who hopes in him.

Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God.

The Lord will give grace and glory.

The generation of the upright will be blessed.

There will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous people who do not need repentance.

A stone is heavy and sand burdensome, but the anger of a fool is heavier than either.

A wise son is the glory of his father.

Glory, honor, and peace to everyone who does good—to the Jew first and also to the Greek.

This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience.

Twofold love makes human beings near to God.

It is a great offense to refuse to appease the person whom you have offended.

The neglect of provision for monasteries is a great destruction of the Church.

The disposition of the mind is shown by the movement of the body.

The word of God is a sword sharp on both sides, penetrating soul and body.

The gravest kind of enmity is to bless with the lips and curse with the heart.

To boast and grow proud because of temporary advantages is a sign of a foolish mind.

It is more glorious to endure an injury in silence than to avenge it by replying.

Perfect joys are nowhere on earth.

The person devoted to gluttony and luxury is compared to senseless beasts of burden.

What is freely given by God must also be freely given to human beings.

A serious mind does not have a doubtful judgment.

That sin is serious from which someone takes an example for sinning.

No one should make common advantages his private possessions.

The one who breaks wicked vows brings acceptable gifts to God.

The one who rejoices in the Lord tastes the sweetest honey.

A great crime must be overcome with great zeal.

Worldly glory is not to be loved at all.

The grace of God alone makes those whom it wishes worthy of attaining high things.

### H

A human being is like grass; his days are like the flower of the field.

When a human being was in honor, he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them.

A human being has become like vanity; his days pass away like a shadow.

Trust in the Lord with all your heart.

A human being sees the face, but God looks upon the heart.

An inheritance toward which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end.

Honor the Lord from your substance, and give to the poor from the first fruits of your crops.

Humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the time of visitation.

God loves a cheerful giver.

It is already time for us to rise from sleep.

A human being is born for labor, a bird for flight.

After one and a second admonition, avoid a heretical person.

It is dreadful to fall into the hands of God.

To sin is human; to persevere in sin is diabolical.

Everyone should turn toward good with the same zeal with which he practiced evil.

The one who clung continually to evil should, after conversion, do the same in good.

Honesty and sobriety are to be sought in all things.

Honor shown to God makes those who show it worthy of eternal glory.

If you wish to have honor and power, I will give you a great command: rule yourself.

To honor one’s parents concerns all human beings.

The mysteries of divine law are open to the humble and faithful, but hidden from the proud and unfaithful.

To depart completely from evil is no longer to wish to sin out of love for God.

To fear human beings more than God is not part of the Christian religion.

A spiritual friend is an heir and a relative.

Very often the last become first.

Remember to appease quickly those whom you have injured.

The one who despises the treaties of peace wages terrible wars.

Bear the Lord as an enemy, but love him as a dear one in yourself.

Alas! How rarely faith is now found among all people.

### I

The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.

Understanding is good for all who practice it.

The wicked walk about on every side.

In God we shall perform mighty deeds, and he himself will bring our enemies to nothing.

He sends the angels of the Lord around those who fear him, and he will deliver them.

The righteous will be remembered forever; he will not fear an evil report.

By your patience you will possess your souls.

When the wicked has entered the depth of sins, he will despise them.

Wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins.

Through the devil’s envy, death entered the world.

Hell and destruction are before the Lord; how much more the hearts of the children of human beings.

Among the proud there are always quarrels, but those who do everything with counsel are governed by wisdom.

In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin.

At the end of a person, his works are laid bare.

On a day of good things, do not forget evil things.

The beginning of every sin is pride.

Every idle person is in his desires.

In much speaking sin will not be absent.

In every place the eyes of the Lord contemplate the good and the wicked.

In all things let us present ourselves as God’s ministers.

In this very thing a person sins: that he would wish to sin if he could do so with impunity.

Earnest supplication forbids the pure heart to sleep.

God must be invoked continually, so that he may graciously grant us both the will and the ability to act well.

We are permitted to suffer all the troubles of the devil’s temptation so that we may learn to sympathize and grieve with all who suffer the same troubles.

Those undertaking a long journey need greater foresight than those traveling nearby.

So also monks, serving God continually, need to be provided for more carefully than others who live freely.

However great the labor, no matter how great, can be compared with infinite labor.

The invisible things of God are perceived and understood through the things that have been made.

[Col. 1099C] God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong.

The beginning of good things is confession of evil things.

The flesh is afflicted in vain if the mind does not resist pleasures.

True innocence is that which harms neither itself nor others.

When an angry man has ceased to be angry, then he is most angry with himself.

Even if an angry man raises the dead, he pleases no one.

The wicked are more unhappy when they have accomplished what they desired than if they had been unable to fulfill their desires.

Those who inflict injury are more unhappy than those who suffer it.

The longer the fire of carnal desire is allowed to burn, the more difficult it is to extinguish.

One ungrateful person harms many wretched people.

He who gives promptly gives the needy person a benefit twice over.

Poverty lacks little; avarice lacks everything.

To love one’s enemies is indeed a difficult commandment, but it brings a great reward.

[Col. 1099D] The imprudent soldier boasts in peacetime that he is brave.

The smallest sins are forgiven those who have wept bitterly over greater sins.

In evils, no one but the innocent is accustomed to hope for good things.

He labors in vain in many things who strives more to offer his possessions to God than himself.

He labors in vain who honors a blind man.

He does great injury to the Creator who loves any creature more than Him.

Money, once collected, commands or serves each person.

The envious man withers at another’s flourishing prosperity.

Anger prevents the mind from being able to perceive the truth.

He who diligently pursues impious things cannot be prudent in Christ.

The poor man is plainly full of envy above all others.

To harden God means nothing other than not to show mercy.

A fattened body rarely tastes heavenly things.

Chastity is difficult to preserve amid feasts.

[Col. 1100A] Almost all weak people want to be tolerated by others, but themselves refuse to tolerate others.

If the weakness of the flesh is endured patiently, it is like a cleansing fire.

Glory awaits those who undertake arduous struggles.

J

The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit.

Cast your care upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you.

The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves.

The righteous will flourish like a palm tree; he will be multiplied like a cedar of Lebanon.

You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right.

The path of the righteous proceeds like a shining light and increases until the perfect day.

The strictest judgment will be imposed on those who rule.

The righteous person lives by faith.

He does not lose the name of “righteous” who, through repentance, continually [Col. 1100B] rises again.

Fasting is not perfect virtue, but the foundation of many virtues.

Human justice is so fragile that it consists more in the remission of sins than in the perfection of virtues.

One must continually consider how great God’s grace is with us.

L

Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice.

The law of the Lord is immaculate, restoring souls.

The righteous will rejoice in the Lord and hope in the Lord, and all the upright in heart will be praised.

Light has arisen for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart.

The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.

Because you will eat the labors of your hands, you are blessed, and it will be well with you.

[Col. 1100C] Broad and spacious is the way that leads to death.

Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.

Let us lift our hearts with our hands to God.

A roaring and again-hungry lion is an impious ruler over a poor people.

The tongue of the wise adorns knowledge.

A despised lamp is, in the thoughts of the rich, prepared for the appointed time.

A gentle tongue is a tree of life.

The letter kills, but the spirit gives life.

Let another praise you, and not your own mouth.

Speak the truth, each one with his neighbor, because we are members of one another.

If the tongue is not restrained, it does not merely lie where it has fallen, but continually slides toward worse things.

[Col. 1100D] The arrival of a wolf shows with what disposition each shepherd stood watch over his flock.

The eye is the lamp of the body, but spiritual wisdom is the light of the mind.

Tears do not ask for pardon, but they merit it.

He who is greedy for human praise rejects the gift of divine reward.

Persistent labor conquers all things.

Pleasures more than sorrows corrupt certain people.

Assiduous labor suppresses carnal passions.

A person in whom no vice reigns should be called free.

Through long practice one must learn what it is appropriate for each person to say or keep silent about.

Avoid shameful profit as you would loss.

A frivolous and fickle person differs in nothing from birds.

Although many people are pleased with your life, it must not please you.

Profit cannot be made without another’s loss.

[Col. 1101A] The virtue of abstinence drives out the assault of lust.

Nothing restrains hidden pride more than open fault.

A wanton young man needs to be admonished frequently.

Do not dissolve the ancient laws by transgressing them.

He rightly praises God who truly loves Him.

He remains worthy of praise who strives to be kind.

He girds his loins who restrains the desires of the flesh.

An unusual illness also seeks an unusual kind of medicine.

M

Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and there is no measure of his wisdom.

God is wondrous in his saints.

Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised, and there is no end to his greatness.

The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord.

Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his purposes.

[Col. 1101B] The mercy of the Lord is from eternity and to eternity upon those who fear him.

The sinner borrows and does not repay; but the righteous person shows mercy and gives.

God loves mercy and truth.

Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord will deliver them from them all.

Many are the scourges of the sinner, but mercy will surround the one who hopes in the Lord.

God is compassionate and merciful, patient and abundantly merciful.

The death of sinners is most evil; and those who hate the righteous will err.

Better is the little possessed by the righteous than the great riches of sinners.

No one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends.

The hired man sees the wolf coming, abandons the sheep, and flees.

[Col. 1101C] Obedience is better than sacrifices.

The wounds of a lover are better than the deceitful kisses of one who hates.

Better is a patient man than a strong man, and he who rules his spirit than one who captures cities.

Better is a dry morsel with joy than a house full of sacrifices with strife.

Music in mourning is an unwelcome tale.

A man’s wickedness is better than a beneficent woman.

Better to be humbled with the meek than to divide spoils with the proud.

Better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting.

Better to be corrected by a wise man than to be deceived by the flattery of fools.

The memory of the righteous is with praises, but the name of the wicked will rot.

Remember your Creator in the days of your youth.

Human life upon earth is warfare, and his days are like the days [Col. 1101D] of a hired man.

Death and life are in the power of the tongue.

The earnest prayer of a righteous person has great force.

A little leaven corrupts the whole lump.

The world is passing away, and its desire; but he who does the will of God remains forever.

It is better not to have something to give than shamelessly to ask for something you can give.

It is better to be defeated honorably than to conquer dishonorably.

It is better to do beforehand what will happen than afterward to repent of an evil deed.

It is not a lie when we speak mystically of insensible things as though they were sensible.

It is simultaneously astonishing and grievous that many people, abstaining from certain foods as though they were religious, soon strive by every means to do the worst things as though they were criminals.

It is likewise astonishing and grievous that very many, pretending, for forgiveness of sins, [Col. 1102A] to visit distant holy places, become much worse than before when they return.

The character and pursuits of rulers and subjects are discerned by their quality.

Greater crimes should be believed slowly when they are reported, but punished more quickly when they are truly recognized.

It is better to possess holy rusticity than sinful eloquence.

A soft and dissolute person should be called not a man but a woman.

A woman who devotes herself to virtue may be called a man.

It is better to divorce a human being than God.

The hand of the poor is Christ’s treasury.

He celebrates the Sabbath badly who is idle from good works.

A large part of understanding is knowing what you do not know.

It is great security of heart not to desire what belongs to another.

The courage of any soldier is not recognized except in [Col. 1102B] war.

A death preceded by a good life should not be considered evil.

When a bad man pretends to be good, he is at his worst.

By ruling badly, one loses supreme authority.

An evil conscience nowhere rests securely.

Dead to this world, he knows nothing except how to live for Christ.

To conquer the flesh of a young man is a great struggle.

The greatest plague occurs when the shepherd is childish.

A fickle and fragile mind quickly endures the scandals of the flesh.

A mind accustomed to evils will scarcely be torn away from them.

Blind lust should be called death and destruction.

One must seek above all what will always have to be retained.

N

The Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the path of the wicked will perish.

Do not be jealous of one who prospers in his way, of a man who commits injustices.

[Col. 1102C] Do not become like a horse or a mule, which have no understanding.

Do not hope in iniquity, and do not desire acts of plunder.

Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it keeps watch in vain.

A king is not saved by great power.

Do not place your trust in princes, in human beings, in whom there is no salvation.

No one is good except God alone.

A human being does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.

The healthy do not need a physician, but those who are ill.

Unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.

No one can serve two masters.

A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a bad tree bear good fruit.

Scandals must come, but woe to the person [Col. 1102D] through whom the scandal comes.

A disciple is not above his teacher.

Nothing is covered that will not be revealed, and nothing hidden that will not be known.

No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.

Do not delay turning to the Lord.

Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner.

Do not neglect the discipline of the Lord, and do not grow weary when you are reproved by him.

Do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you; rebuke a wise man, and he will love you.

There is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin.

The righteous person knows the souls of his animals, but the entrails of the wicked are cruel.

A friend is not recognized in prosperity, nor is an enemy hidden in adversity.

Nor should you place a stumbling block before the blind.

[Col. 1103A] God does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.

Nothing happens on earth without a cause.

The Lord knows those who are his.

Not only are those who do evil guilty, but also those who consent to those doing it.

No one will be crowned except the one who has competed lawfully.

Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good.

Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world.

Do not be surprised if the world hates you.

No one should seek what is his own, but only what belongs to another.

Let us not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth.

God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation anyone who fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him.

Nothing is more unhappy than the happiness of sinners.

[Col. 1103B] A shining skin reveals a sordid mind.

It is not a secure joy to know many things in the divine books, but to keep what one has learned.

To know and be able to do good things previously unknown and impossible demonstrates the gifts of heavenly grace.

Nothing is so easy that it does not become difficult if you do it unwillingly.

No one first sins against another without sinning against himself.

God never abandons a mind that truly acknowledges its sins.

He scarcely knows what labor is who has never striven against spiritual wickedness.

Negligence and idleness drag a person to destruction.

Unless someone is founded in faith and hope, he does not rise to the practice of true love.

Nothing happens to anyone, whether badly or well, solely for his own sake, but so that others may simultaneously be corrected or consoled through him.

The devil’s wickedness, such as is reported to have been in Job, will be in all people if it is permitted to go that far.

[Col. 1103C] No one harms the Church more than the person who acts perversely while holding authority.

It is not the multitude of sins but impiety that leads a person to despair.

A person’s life is not in his own power.

It will profit no one to be considered holy when he is not.

Ask for nothing that you intend to refuse.

It is a presumption greatly to be lamented that Christians presume to do the evils that pagans abhor.

For Christians destroy the monasteries of their God and their saints, whereas pagans venerate their own idols.

Do not live one way in solitude and another way in public.

To know or care about nothing is to live as one dead.

He denies himself when he asks for what is difficult.

Impose on no one what you cannot yourself endure.

No one sins more dangerously than the person who defends sins.

No one is noble except the one whom virtue ennobles.

Unless someone continually sets the fear and love of God before himself [Col. 1103D], he quickly falls into some sin.

No one can measure himself adequately unless he considers another person.

Nothing is great in human affairs except a spirit that despises great things.

Neither a human being nor gold can give anything that can make one blessed; the life of the blessed rests on God’s power.

The eyes do not sin if the mind wishes to rule them.

It cannot be said how great the enemy’s skill is.

Consider nothing accomplished while anything remains to be done.

It is of no benefit to have learned what is good unless you do it.

Do not wish to delay if you can convert someone.

The person who knows many things is not to be praised, but the one who lives well.

The effort of fools always loves companions of its own kind.

O

The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are attentive to their prayers.

[Col. 1104A] The mouth of the righteous will meditate wisdom, and his tongue will speak judgment.

The sinner will watch the righteous and gnash his teeth at him.

Whatever the Lord wished, he made in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses.

Every kingdom divided against itself will be desolated.

Every planting that the heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted.

Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.

Everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.

Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.

To everyone who has, it will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away.

Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people [Col. 1104B], but blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven.

Pray that your flight may not occur in winter or on the Sabbath.

All things are possible for the one who believes.

Bless God at all times, and ask him to direct your ways.

Guard your heart with all vigilance, because from it life proceeds.

There is a time and an opportunity for every undertaking.

Do everything with counsel, and afterward you will not repent.

All wisdom is from the Lord God, and it has always been with him.

Hatred stirs up quarrels, but love covers all offenses.

One and the same Spirit accomplishes all things, distributing to each as he wills.

Whatever you do in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.

Be all of one mind in prayer, compassionate, [Col. 1104C] loving the brotherhood, merciful, modest, and humble.

Count it all joy when you fall into various temptations.

Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer.

One must obey God rather than human beings.

Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights.

Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him.

All things are clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean.

All things are lawful, but not all things are beneficial.

Every life of unbelievers is sin.

Idleness is an enemy of the soul.

Every day should be treated as though it were the last.

An idle word is one that lacks either the reason of just necessity or the purpose of useful intention.

[Col. 1104D] Compliance produces friends, but truth produces hatred.

Opportunities cannot be lacking for those who are perishing.

He is altogether mistaken who thinks he can attain triumph through peace and ease.

Every divine stroke is either a purification of the present life or the beginning of a punishment to come.

Vices are overcome by continual prayer.

God is praised and proclaimed better by deeds than by words.

Bold eyes are the betrayers of a lustful heart.

Hidden faults continually perpetrated deserve that perverse kings and shepherds be appointed.

All arguments for faith must be drawn from past events.

Everything that is just can rightly be called one.

One must always pray lest we be led astray by the enemy.

Be subject to every prelate as though to Christ.

O, how many cares the mind needs at every hour!

A mouth that lies is said to slaughter the soul.

P

[Col. 1105A]

The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth.

Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.

Keep your tongue from evil, and let your lips not speak deceit.

The patience of the poor will not perish forever.

Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.

Everyone will be perfect if he is like his teacher.

God is able from stones to raise up children of Abraham.

Strike your son with a rod, and you will deliver his soul from death.

Correction benefits the prudent more than a hundred blows benefit a fool.

The perverse are difficult to correct.

[Col. 1105B] A ruler who willingly listens to lying words has all wicked ministers.

By the things through which someone sins, by those same things he is tormented.

A weight and a weight, a measure and a measure—both are abominable before God.

Proven virtue rebukes the foolish.

Because of the sins of the people, the Lord makes a hypocrite reign.

A sinner, even a hundred-year-old child, will be accursed.

The whole world will fight against the senseless.

Do not follow your desires.

Test the spirits, whether they are from God.

The wisdom of the flesh is death, but the wisdom of the spirit is life and peace.

You ask, and you do not receive, because you ask wrongly.

Love is the fullness of the law.

Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.

Let sinners be rebuked before everyone, so that the others [Col. 1105C] may have fear.

Those placed amid pleasures cannot attend to how great eternal punishment is.

Peace should truly be called peace when spirit and flesh agree in every way.

A peaceful person deserves to be called a son of God.

Parents are to be loved and honored insofar as they are subject to the supreme Father.

A person disobedient to his prelates and elders deserves either, if he himself has been set over others, to suffer the same treatment from them.

Every shepherd flees when he withdraws consolation from his subjects or, seeing injustice, does not oppose it.

Those who have sinned together will undergo equal punishment.

True repentance is both to mourn the evils committed and not to commit again the evils that ought to be mourned.

A public fault also requires public repentance.

Those who [Col. 1105D] refuse to endure small scourges for their crimes will sometimes suffer the most severe punishments.

A full belly easily disputes about fasts.

Perfect hatred is hatred that lacks neither justice nor reason.

Sin is added to sin when what was wickedly done is also wickedly defended.

The proof of good will is refusing to sin when you are able to do so.

All who leave lawful things for the love of God must take care lest, by living lukewarmly, they fall into unlawful things.

The speech of teachers must be shaped according to the quality of their hearers.

The life of the good is always burdensome to those of depraved character.

Some sins pollute the soul, while others extinguish it.

Deliberate before you promise, lest after your promises have not been fulfilled you be called a liar.

Danger is never overcome without danger.

Prudence measures the outcomes of things.

[Col. 1106A] Those who do good are more worthy of praise than those who bless.

Money becomes precious when, transferred to others for the love of God, it ceases to be possessed.

Very many fear disgrace, but few fear the guilt of conscience.

Keep peace with human beings and war with vices.

One must rule money, not serve it.

Poverty of soul is greater than poverty of body.

Let the person who sins daily strive immediately to restore himself.

A perfect soldier very often weighs his strength.

For a perverse mind, its own fault is the greatest punishment.

One who is quick to laughter is also said to be quick to anger.

Do not be ready or prone to laughter’s antics.

The more things one attends to, the less perception one has for each individual thing.

The present life is brief, but the future life is everlasting.

Q

[Col. 1106B] How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart!

Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face continually.

Seek the Lord, and your soul will live.

You who fear the Lord, praise him.

You who love the Lord, hate evil.

As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him, for he himself knows our formation.

The one who has not received his soul in vain and has not sworn deceitfully to his neighbor—this person will receive blessing from the Lord.

Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high and regards the lowly in heaven and on earth?

Those who sow in tears will reap in exultation.

Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.

The one who perseveres to the end will be saved.

[Col. 1106C] The things that are impossible with human beings are possible with God.

The one who is from God hears the words of God.

What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?

What will a person give in exchange for his soul?

Whoever says to his brother, “Fool,” will be liable to the fire of Gehenna.

Whoever hates his life in this world preserves it for eternal life.

What God has joined, let no human being separate.

The one who is unfaithful in the least is also unfaithful in greater things.

To refuse to obey God is like the crime of idolatry.

Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near.

The one who follows righteousness is loved by the Lord.

The one who hides his crimes will not prosper, but whoever confesses and abandons them will obtain [Col. 1106D] mercy.

The one who loves discipline also loves wisdom.

The one who offers a sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son in the presence of his father.

The one who turns away his ear so as not to hear the law—his prayer will be abominable.

Like a storm, the wicked person passes away.

What you do not gather in youth, how will you be able to have in old age?

The one who is inclined to mercy will be blessed.

Whoever prepares a pit for his brother will fall into it himself.

Whoever despises small things will gradually fall.

If someone is wicked toward himself, toward whom will he be good?

Whatever your hand can do, do it diligently, because there will be neither work nor reason nor wisdom in the underworld, where you are hastening.

Whoever spares the rod hates his son.

Those who fear God will not be incredulous toward his word.

[Col. 1107A] The one who is soft and dissolute in his work is the brother of the person who dissipates his own work.

What the wicked person fears will come upon him.

As is the ruler of a city, so are its inhabitants.

The one who guards his mouth also guards his soul.

Whoever hardens his ear to the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be heard.

The one who teaches a fool is like someone who glues together a potsherd.

Those who instruct many in righteousness are like stars for everlasting eternities.

The one who offends in one thing loses many good things.

The greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things.

The one who fears frost will have snow come upon him.

Those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the prize.

Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world makes himself an enemy of God.

The one who thinks he stands should beware lest he fall.

Whoever has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.

[Col. 1107B] Whoever converts a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death.

The one who does not eat must not judge the one who eats.

Whoever does not care for his own, and especially for members of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.

Whoever is led by the Spirit of God is a son of God.

Whoever sees his brother suffering need and closes his heart against him—how does the love of God remain in him?

The one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly.

The one who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.

The higher the rank, the deeper the fall.

What you do not want done to you, do not do to another.

The one who does not know will be unknown.

The arriving wolf shows what sort of shepherd each one is.

An insult inflicted tests how each person is secretly disposed within himself.

What praise will we deserve for the pallor of fasting if [Col. 1107C] we are livid with envy?

What virtue is there in not drinking wine while becoming drunk with anger and hatred?

What does it profit to thin the body through abstinence if the mind swells with pride?

Like someone putting his possessions into a pierced purse is the person who does some good things but nevertheless does not abandon his customary pursuits of depravity.

The person who remembers having committed many unlawful acts ought, as penance, also to abstain from lawful things.

Whoever considers what he should vow to God should vow himself and render himself.

How great a good health is shows itself in illness.

If someone can rescue a person who is perishing and does not rescue him, he will be guilty of that person’s death.

The one who can be corrected by gentle words should not be exasperated by rebuke.

Those who persevere in chastity and virginity become equal to the angels of God.

[Col. 1107D] Whoever continually considers how to do some good prays without ceasing.

Whatever exceeds measure is suggested by demons.
