To the extent that someone progresses in humility and chastity, to that extent he will draw near to God.

What must be endured in every way, endure patiently.

What is shameful to do is also shameful to say.

To the extent that the mind becomes divided among many tasks, it becomes less capable in each one.

Whatever each person reads now, that is what he will have; whether good or evil, he will always have it.

As long as a person is not displeased with the evils he has done, vices reign in him.

Whoever has never learned to be subject cannot properly rule anyone.

What is more unhappy than to be affected by the observed happiness of others?

[Col. 1108A] Whatever a person has not experienced in himself, he scarcely believes in another.

Who is rich? The one who desires nothing. And who is poor? The avaricious person.

Whoever receives what is enough should desire nothing more.

What is characteristic of a fool? To be unable to harm and yet wish to harm.

What is the work of the prudent? When able, not to wish to harm.

How close the shore is, yet what a labyrinth lies in the heart of the sea!

The more you are able, the more humble yourself before Christ.

The one who gives you much also asks the same from you.

How good the Lord is to all who seek him!

How dark is the love by which the author of light is despised!

R

Your kingdom, O Lord, is the kingdom of all ages.

[Col. 1108B] Praise befits the upright.

The Lord will redeem the souls of his servants, and all who hope in him will not offend.

Reveal your way to the Lord, hope in him, and he himself will act.

Judge rightly, children of men.

The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.

Laughter is mixed with sorrow, and mourning occupies the end of joy.

A gentle answer breaks anger.

When the wicked rule, there will be the ruin of human beings.

A king who sits on the throne of judgment disperses every evil by his mere gaze.

A king who judges the poor in truth will have his throne established forever.

A righteous king raises up the land; an avaricious man will destroy it.

A kingdom is transferred from one nation to another because of injustices.

[Col. 1108C] Be renewed in the spirit of your mind and put on the new person, who has been created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth.

Pure and undefiled religion before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their tribulation.

The root of all evils is greed.

A religious person, if he becomes angry quickly, is also easily moved to repentance.

He whose conscience of his own innocence provides no rule of judgment cannot rightly judge the merits of others.

Humble married people follow the Lamb more rightly than proud virgins.

Those who are strong in body, unless they devoutly serve God, from whom they have their strength, will suffer punishments for this.

Whatever more a person has than the animals must be ascribed to divine mercy.

The kingdom of God is worth as much as you possess.

[Col. 1108D] The ruin of the people is evil priests.

As often as human reason resists perverse thoughts, so many heavenly crowns does it merit.

The governance of souls is the art of arts.

Those who seize the property of others will themselves someday be seized for destruction.

Sudden fury admits no reason.

Those who rebel against divine mercy will be handed over to the devil’s power.

Every obscure matter should be explained through comparison.

Excessive remission and leniency are reckoned before God as great cruelty.

The reprobate are wearied in this age by desires and in the next by torments.

A rustic tongue belonging to a man who keeps a gentle heart is more pleasing to the Lord than the skilled tongue of a proud man.

Sadly, faith should rarely be granted to any person.

A pious and just king strives to be what he is said to be.

[Col. 1109A] For the name “king” admonishes him to govern what has been entrusted to him.

In adverse circumstances, do not be so shaken that you lose your resolve.

S

Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling.

A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit.

May the glory of the Lord be forever and ever.

May the name of the Lord be blessed from this time forth and forever.

The salvation of the righteous is from the Lord, and he is their protector in time of tribulation.

The Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works.

The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes.

God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.

[Col. 1109B] If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you.

God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.

If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone.

The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and it withdraws from thoughts that lack understanding.

The eyes of the wise are in his head.

Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart.

A fool is not corrected by words.

The wise and understanding heart abstains from sins.

Folly is bound up in the heart of a child, and the rod of discipline will drive it away.

A deceitful balance is an abomination before God, but an accurate weight is his will.

The wise person remains like the sun, but the fool changes like the moon [Col. 1109C].

God speaks once and does not repeat it a second time.

The wise person seeks out the wisdom of all the ancients.

Hidden wisdom and an unseen treasure—what use are either of them?

The wise person makes himself known by few words.

The righteous falls seven times and will rise again; but the wicked will fall into evil.

A harsh word arouses fury.

Dreams exalt the imprudent.

A secure mind is like a continual banquet.

To conceal a king’s secrets is good, but to reveal the great deeds of God is honorable.

A fool raises his voice in laughter.

If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love is perfected in us.

If someone says, “I love God,” and hates his brother, he is a liar.

The spiritual person judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one.

[Col. 1109D] As all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ.

The wisdom of this world is foolishness before God.

The gifts and calling of God are without repentance.

Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.

If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit.

Whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s.

People are to be loved in such a way that their errors are not loved.

A watchman stands above, observing us, who sees our acts every day.

For God to know is to approve; not to know is to reject.

Before God, the highest nobility is to be distinguished by virtues.

The vices of subjects are sometimes to be concealed, but afterward they must be disclosed because they were concealed.

To escape the devil’s snares depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy.

[Col. 1110A] Hypocrites and schemers provoke God’s anger.

The person who wishes to live with the innocent seeks solitude.

Comparisons drawn from various things should continually be offered for our edification.

As a dog returns to its vomit, so the imprudent person repeats his folly.

As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin.

To bear the name of holiness without works benefits no one.

The wise person is the one who teaches others more by deeds than by words.

The salvation of the rich is to assist the needs of the poor.

The virtue of patience repels the arrows of insult.

Those may be called scorpions who do not resist good people to their faces but slander them as soon as they have gone away.

[Col. 1110B] The person who denies himself, abandoning the person of carnal life, puts on the spiritual and new person, that is, Christ.

It is exceedingly foolish if we seek to please those whom we know do not please God.

Each person should argue or dictate sufficiently that he may be understood.

Excess, both of words and of things, must be avoided.

As honey is gathered from various flowers, so every virtue should be gathered from various people.

A person intent on secular literature cannot grasp the mysteries of Sacred Scripture.

When reading Sacred Scripture, one must attend to what is said mystically or according to the letter, and what is said in part or for the whole.

Meditation on Sacred Scripture draws the mind away from harmful thoughts.

As many foods are useless without salt, so [Col. 1110C] are all virtues without love.

As a pipe produces no sound without someone blowing into it, so the human heart receives no good without divine inspiration.

As the course of any horse is tested in an open place, so the will of a person is tested in the freedom that has been granted.

As everyone’s eyes are in the head, so every intention of the faithful must also be fixed in Christ.

He deserves to be tormented without end who sets no end to sinning in his heart.

The ministers of the supreme Prince must be provided for above all.

Forgive others as you wish them to forgive you when you sin.

Blood touches blood when sins are added to sins.

Pride alone corrupts all good things.

Foolish vows must be broken.

Without instruction, life is, as it were, an image of death.

If you love being called father and prince, preserve the name with honor and fulfill it in your conduct.

Often the great pine is shaken by the winds, and lofty towers fall with a heavier crash.

Equal concern must be maintained for those standing and those fallen: for the former, lest I fall back; for the latter, so that they may rise quickly.

Speech is given to many, wisdom of mind to few.

If you cannot help more people, at least take care of yourself.

If you have vowed anything to the Lord, do not delay in fulfilling it.

It belongs to the Lord alone to bring good out of evil.

The miser is always in need; no amount of money fills him.

If you wish to be saved, prefer nothing to this salvation.

The spirit is life; the death of the flesh is philosophy.

## T

[Col. 1110D] You are worthy of praise, O God, in Zion, and the vow shall be paid to you in Jerusalem.

The testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to the simple.

[Col. 1111A] To you, Lord, the poor man is abandoned; you will be the helper of the orphan.

Fear the Lord, all his saints, for there is no want for those who fear him.

Store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal.

The fear of the Lord drives out sin.

The fool pours out all his spirit, but the wise person delays and stores it up for the future.

There is a time for every matter under heaven.

The name of the Lord is a most fortified tower; the righteous person runs to it and is exalted.

A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise.

It will be well for the one who fears God at the end.

A threefold cord is not easily broken.

A false witness will not go unpunished.

Fear is not in love, but perfect love casts out fear.

[Col. 1111B] It is shameful that one who does not know how to govern his own life should become a judge of another’s.

The more truly the brightness of light illuminates someone, the more subtly that person judges matters of darkness.

The tempter, ever watchful, strikes with sharper snares those whom he sees most abstaining from sins.

The excessively grasping person and the excessively extravagant person both converge in the single vice of excess.

He whose power is over all is to be feared above everyone.

Minds that are excessively tender must be formed by harsher disciplines.

Everything done in due season is acceptable both to God and to human beings.

The torments of some benefit others by correcting them.

Each person bears his neighbor only as much as he loves him.

Vices are worse in proportion as they are concealed beneath the appearance of virtues.

[Col. 1111C] A person errs in faith for as long as he distrusts that all things are observed and governed by God.

Hidden hatreds are worse than open ones.

Such is the nature of vices that, unless what has passed is erased by swift repentance, other vices arise from it.

Let us be inwardly such as we show ourselves outwardly.

Who does not know how to be silent does not know how to speak either.

It is difficult to help those who remain silent, but those who confess the nature of their illness receive healing more easily.

It is shameful for a teacher when he reproves a fault that convicts him himself.

Fear that you will fall when you see another falling.

The person who suffers from suspicion will never be secure.

Those whose hope is fixed on low things are easily saddened.

The indignation of a king is a great storm.

A truthful witness remains suitable for a true king.

He who remains wholly present everywhere is to be worshiped with all one’s strength.

The fear of God and continual prayer make a person fly toward heavenly things.

[Col. 1111D] We bear the evils of the world more tolerably if we are armed against them with the shield of foreknowledge.

Christians who live lukewarmly are corrected with greater difficulty than pagans.

## U

All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth for those who seek his covenant and his testimonies.

Where your treasure is, there is your heart also.

Every tree is known by its fruit.

Where pride is, there will also be disgrace.

One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all.

Each person will receive his own reward according to his labor.

To each person the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good.

Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.

[Col. 1112A] Where charity and love are, there is the assembly of the saints.

Each virtue is lesser in proportion as the others are lacking.

Where there is no fear of God, there the reign of sin is found.

From the source of the good person’s advancement, the envious person wastes away.

As kings wish, so laws prevail.

Those are excessively delicate who are unwilling to endure any adversity.

Love of usefulness quickly advises what ought to be done.

Great usefulness lies hidden even in small things.

Every human being is like a stone unless he is softened from above.

## V

The face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth.

The Lord will require truth and will repay abundantly those who act proudly.

By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host.

A voice of rejoicing and salvation is in the tents of the righteous.

Human help is vain.

Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord.

Men of blood and deceit will not live out half their days.

A talkative person will not prosper on earth.

Evils will seize an unjust man unto destruction.

Woe to you who tithe mint and dill and cumin, while abandoning the weightier matters—that is, mercy and judgment.

Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation.

Watch at all times, praying that you may be considered worthy to escape the things that are to come.

The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deep.

All human beings are vain in whom there is no knowledge of God.

The voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; there the strong man will be afflicted.

Wine makes even the wise apostatize.

Woe to the city whose king is young and whose princes eat in the morning.

An irascible person provokes quarrels, but the patient person calms those that have been stirred up.

Woe to the one who is alone, for when he falls he has no one to lift him up.

Woe to those who call good evil and evil good.

Anger kills the foolish person, and envy slays the simple.

The way of the wicked is dark; they do not know where they may stumble.

Health of heart is life to the flesh; envy is the rottenness of the bones.

The way of life belongs to the one who guards discipline, but whoever abandons reproof goes astray.

The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people.

[Col. 1112D] A gracious word multiplies friends and softens enemies.

Power is perfected in weakness.

A good word is better than an excellent gift.

A person double-minded is unstable in all his ways.

An upright will to do good will be reckoned by God as the work of a good deed.

True discernment is acquired only through true humility.

Every pleasure, like bees, after pouring out its welcome honey, wounds the heart with its sting.

Fever of the mind is more severe than fever of the body.

The wise person places the fruit of virtue in his conscience; the less perfect person places it in glory.

The one who keeps the eyes of his mind open to the sight of the true light is watchful.

Overcome by any one vice, a person quickly slips into another.

Virtue is always exposed to envy.

[Col. 1113A] The pursuer of empty glory resembles one who entrusts his seeds to the wind to be scattered.

The person able to retain health should despise or ridicule no one’s infirmity.

Pride must be avoided: it deceived even the angels and destroys all virtues.

Vices must first be uprooted in a person; then virtues must be planted.

Virgins and monks should moderate their fasting so that they may always be strong for God’s service.

Pleasure has punishment, and necessity brings a crown.

[Col. 1114A] Those devoted to vices cannot be enriched with virtues.

That physician is very inexperienced who knows how to give no medicines except mild ones.

The person who casts away modesty has cast away all the virtues at once.

Hardly anyone passes into good except from evil.

Leisure makes the mind changeable.

Silver is cheaper than gold, and gold than virtues.

If you do not know how to live rightly, yield to those who do.

Various virtues can dwell together.

It is a great virtue to bless in return for curses.

Great strength of spirit lies in being moved by no one’s praise.

[Col. 1113]

# BOOK OF THE VENERABLE PRIEST BEDE, ON SUBSTANCES

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1113B] Wishing to offer some small gift to Holy Church, but finding nothing in my hand except a modest knowledge of dictation and writing, I wish to adapt this very thing to her service, insofar as the Lord deigns to help me. For I desire to write as an admonition to all the faithful, or rather to those who need admonition, dividing them into two groups, clergy and laity, and selecting for each group appropriate exhortations by which they may lift their minds from carnal things to spiritual things, from visible things to invisible things, and contemplate what is above, just as the Apostle also says: “For the invisible things of God are perceived and understood through the things that have been made.”

I ask that the offering of this effort not seem unworthy to anyone, because, as we read, even among the distinguished and most precious gifts once offered to the temple of the Lord there were also common goat hairs; and the two small coins [Col. 1114B] offered to God by the poor widow are approved by the testimony of the Lord himself, our Lord Jesus Christ.

I also ask that, if anyone thinks better about what I shall say, or is able to express the same things more suitably, he should not therefore hastily criticize the little words of my rusticity, because, as a certain wise man says: “We cannot all do everything.” For if that person could express the same thought better than I according to the powers of his intellect, perhaps someone else wiser than he would know how to express it more excellently.

Let each person, therefore, abound in his own judgment, giving greater thanks to God in proportion as he has received from him the talent of more excellent knowledge; and let him likewise observe that the rustic sayings of the humble please God more than the splendid verbosity of the arrogant and of those who glory in the pomp of secular learning.

# ON SUBSTANCES

[Col. 1113]

[Col. 1113C] The substance, therefore, which is able to subsist by itself without the assistance of anything is God alone. But that substance whose entire being consists in the power of another is plainly proved to be a creature. Yet just as the divine substance consists in three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—so also every creature is distinguished in three ways.

For it is either rational, such as angelic spirits and human beings; or animal, such as all things that possess life-giving breath without reason; or neither, possessing only existence, such as trees and stones.

Hence it is altogether clear that every creature ought to submit itself to God, from whom it has everything that it is. The reason and observance of this submission plainly pertain only to rational creatures, that is, to angels and human beings. For just as these alone were created more excellent than the other creatures, so also submission and worship of God are required from them alone; and they are either rewarded for the devotion of their submission or punished for resistance and pride.

But because this judgment has already taken place among the angelic spirits—for some of them, on account of the merits of their obedience, have been assigned to eternal blessedness in such a way that they can will nothing other than good, while others, on account of their pride, have been cast into eternal punishments and can bend their reason toward nothing except evils—[Col. 1114C] only human beings remain, who are still able to turn the faculty of reason and free choice in either direction.

Therefore they alone must still be instructed and admonished, so that, continually setting both kinds before themselves—namely, good and evil spirits—they may choose rather to follow the merits of the good by obeying the divine commands than to be joined to the punishments of the evil by resisting him without whom no one can be saved.

This, then, is the first matter that we urge all human beings to consider with the greatest attention. For it ought to be sufficient for a sound mind and an undamaged reason, even if it knew no other examples of the terrifying judgment.

But because our adversary the devil continually goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour, and because, alas, among so many thousands of human beings more are now found fragile than strong against this same adversary, it is necessary for all the faithful, as they themselves go about seeking how to resist so great an adversary, to instruct and admonish one another in various ways, lest the holy Church, well founded and supported in the periods of the past, be utterly destroyed [Col. 1114D] in our own times, in which, after the thousand years have been completed according to the prophecy foretold in the Apocalypse, Satan appears to have been released.

[Col. 1115A] For he no longer deceives people only by hidden snares as before, but also breaks forth openly, overthrowing the most skilled and inciting them to every kind of wickedness.

What, I ask, could be worse than that monasteries, built by ancient rulers for the praise of God and the reverent remembrance of his saints, should now be destroyed because of the insatiable greed of certain people?

For what faithful and religious person, observing how great a destruction of monasteries is now taking place, though all the divine commandments and miracles and the teachings of the holy Fathers are very well known to many—not only through laypeople eagerly seizing and plundering their estates, but also through clerics and the abbots themselves voluntarily offering up, as though they were saleable goods entrusted to them, the possessions from which not only the monks but also the dependents, the poor, and visiting travelers were to be fed—could fail at once to infer that this is the destruction of Holy Church, or fail at once to grieve that the ancient enemy has been able to exercise such wickedness and persecution against Christians through other [Col. 1115B] Christians, and especially through those who have been appointed pastors of the Church?

For if such destruction of holy places were carried out by barbarians, they would have to be restrained by Christian force if they could not otherwise be corrected. But, alas, such peace and harmony prevail in this wickedness that, with very few exceptions, no one is found who cares about the misery of so great a persecution—as though they were ignorant of the Christian religion and had forgotten that all the monasteries were built for the honor of Christ and his saints.

What I say is indeed pitiable to say, but much more pitiable in deed, since those who were specially chosen to live in monasteries under religious and spiritual discipline, to serve God, and continually to intercede for the salvation of those who are still unable to restrain themselves from worldly pomp, are deprived of the substance they need for their daily food and clothing.

For the more someone has renounced his own possessions for the love of God, the more he needs the necessities to be given to him from the common resources of the monastery to which he has fled; [Col. 1115C] because, as long as he remains in this present life, no human being can lack daily food and clothing.

Therefore whoever takes from monks the estates by which they are to be maintained is proved to be a destroyer both of divine service and of the whole monastic religion.

He also becomes guilty for this reason: he has taken away the means by which the poor, travelers, and guests visiting holy places were to be refreshed according to the rule of Saint Benedict—or rather, according to the command of the Lord himself, who says: “Give alms, and everything will be clean for you.”

He himself will also say at the final judgment to those who now receive him in the poor and in guests: “I was a guest, and you received me.”

I have thus briefly recalled that single sin which is committed in the destruction of monasteries. But if anyone wishes to consider carefully the other ordinances of the Christian religion, he will find that very many of them have likewise been destroyed through the persecution of Christians.

For what place now exists without robbery or war? Where are the rights of Christian law, and the protection of the king who ought to be feared? [Col. 1115D] Where, I ask, are the pastors and defenders of the Churches who resist the despoilers of the poor and widows?

Indeed, those who are called pastors and defenders, and who ought to lay down their lives for the sheep entrusted to them, have themselves become persecutors, sparing no one, provided only that they live in luxury and abound in riches.

Are not these and similar things activities of persecution?

Hearing and grieving continually over this pitiable persecution, I, the least of all, since I could not correct certain people by ordinary speech, considered admonishing them in writings of such a kind that both laity and clergy might understand their meaning.

Do not all people recognize that the sun and the other elements can be apprehended in some way and understand together what function they perform? Indeed, a person deprived of bodily sight cannot excuse himself from knowing the sun. For if he cannot perceive its brightness, he can at least feel its warmth.

Moreover, when he hears someone speaking about the immeasurable brilliance of the sun, he can certainly take notice through inward [Col. 1116A] sight and hearing together. For he cannot be deprived of these by any human being, provided that no wickedness obstructs such sight and hearing.

Hence our Lord also admonishes his hearers, saying: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.” And John says in the Apocalypse: “Whoever has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.”

We preface these words in the manner of a prologue so that, since in writing we wish to gather spiritual things from carnal things and invisible things from visible things, we may rouse the spiritual ears of readers and hearers somewhat to attend to them.

First, therefore, we must say what we ought first to believe and know above all: namely, in which element we may contemplate the mystery of the holy Trinity and unity.

Finally, as it seems to me, nowhere in Scripture can we be taught more clearly than through the sun how we ought to attend to the faith of the holy Trinity.

For we know that three inseparable things exist in the sun: namely, the body itself or wheel of the sun, and [Col. 1116B] its brightness and its heat.

In its wheel, which we know to have been placed always in the firmament of heaven, I understand the person of the Father; in its brightness, the person of the Son, because the Apostle also says of Christ, the Son of God: “Who, being the brightness of glory,” and so forth; and in its heat, I believe the person of the Holy Spirit is signified.

I shall immediately add why I believe these things.

Just as we have never seen or heard of the wheel of the sun being brought down from heaven to earth, but know that its brightness, which is in it and is always emitted from it at its rising, is sent down over the whole earth; and just as we know that the heat, which proceeds both from the wheel of the sun itself and from its brightness, although we do not feel it equally in every place and season, nevertheless proceeds equally from both and burns more intensely in some provinces and less intensely in others because of some hidden arrangement of divine judgment—so I believe the same concerning each person of the holy Trinity.

Concerning God the Father, I believe that he has never been sent to come to earth, but that he sends his brightness, that is, the Son, to illuminate various people.

Concerning God [Col. 1116C] the Son of God, I believe that just as the brightness of the sun is sent upon any physical things and becomes visible, so he too, having been made incarnate, appeared visibly, and the radiance of his teaching shone over the whole earth, as it is written of him: “Light has risen in the darkness for the upright.”

Concerning the Holy Spirit, I believe that just as earth illuminated only by the brightness of the sun, but not penetrated by its heat, usually produces no fruit, so also, even if someone has been illuminated by knowledge of the divine word and has learned all the miracles of God either by reading or by hearing, unless he receives heat—that is, the love of doing good—from the Spirit’s gift, he enjoys the light of all knowledge in vain.

That this is truly so can be perceived not only by faith but also proved by experience itself. For we frequently see certain people who are wise and thoroughly instructed in divine law, in whose actions we can scarcely discern whether they possess any knowledge of divine learning or whether they believe anything about eternal joys and punishments.

[Col. 1116D] What, then, should be thought about such people except that they have indeed been sufficiently illuminated by the brightness, that is, by the word of our Lord, but have felt none of the heat of the Holy Spirit? For if spiritual heat had come to them together with the brightness, it would certainly not have left them so lukewarm and negligent.

But to approve the mystery of such great heat not merely by my own conjecture but also by the testimony of Holy Scripture: is it not read that the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles in fire and kindled them with such ardor that they feared neither any power of the world nor any tortures of human savagery?

I believe that the Lord spoke of this same heat and fire when he said: “I have come to cast fire, and what do I desire except that it burn?”

We can also mystically contemplate, in every human being surrounded by the sun’s brightness, what the Lord says: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock,” and so forth.

For just as the brightness of the sun repels no one who comes into the rays of its light but illuminates everyone, so our Savior receives all who come to him [Col. 1117A] mercifully. Hence he urges them to come to him, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.”

Again, just as the brightness of the sun, illuminating the exterior walls of any house on every side, cannot send its light into those who are shut inside, but immediately pours it over them when the door is opened, so also our Lord, by the power of his divinity, continually looks upon the children of human beings to see whether there is anyone understanding or seeking God, and seeks, as though knocking, someone who will open the door of his heart to him.

The door of the heart is the mind. Therefore, when our Lord finds the door closed—that is, a mind unbelieving and lacking devotion to the pursuit of the whole religion—he departs from it grieving; grieving, that is, in the humanity he assumed, just as it is also read in the Gospel that, when he drew near to Jerusalem, he wept over it. For no grief affects the divinity.

But when he finds the door open—that is, a mind faithful and devoted to fulfilling the commandments of divine instruction—he immediately enters, and dines with the inhabitant of that dwelling. He pours [Col. 1117B] into him, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, remorse and repentance for his sins, or reveals to him the mysteries of Holy Scripture; or, because his food is to do the will of his Father, he dines with him by making him despise all things that perish and desire only the joys of eternal life.

The Lord holds such a banquet with us whenever we permit him to enter our heart.

Through the same mystery of the sun we can also contemplate to some extent what the Lord says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.”

For wherever the brightness of the sun appears, the sun itself remains shining there together with it, because the activity of both is indivisible.

Moreover, if the heat proceeding from both—which, without its coming, anyone is illuminated in vain—is also felt to be present at the same time, then three things are found together in one activity. I believe that this can likewise be understood in the Lord’s words just mentioned.

[Col. 1117C] For if two persons are understood in the Father and the Son, who come, the third person, as it seems to me, can be understood in the co-worker of the one who loves, and in the one who, like a preceding incentive, moves him to love.

Finally, this is found in many passages of Holy Scripture: we can neither do certain good things nor even speak a good word without the gift of the Holy Spirit. Such is the saying: “No one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit”; and: “It is one and the same Spirit who accomplishes all things, distributing to each as he wills.”

But so that the depth of so great a mystery may be understood more easily, let us seek its likeness still further in the sun.

We all know that in summer, when the sun’s heat usually occupies the earth intensely, we very often feel such heat proceeding from both—not only during the day, when the sun and its brightness are seen together, but also at night, when neither appears—that we can scarcely endure it.

Therefore, because such great heat is felt long before the sun [Col. 1117D] and its brightness themselves appear, it can be said to precede them, although it never departs from them.

The same can be perceived concerning the fragrant sweetness of any spices. Wherever frankincense, myrrh, or another substance of this kind is burned, the sweet smell reaches the noses of those who are far away before it reaches their sight; yet it does not depart from the substance that has been burned.

If, then, the force of both heat and fragrance is so great that, preceding the arrival of those from which they proceed and delighting the senses of those into whom they enter, they do not abandon their own substance, why should we not believe much more that the power of the Holy Spirit illuminates various people and, preceding them, prepares their hearts for the divine coming, yet never departs from his own essence?

For he who is wholly everywhere cannot be absent from any place, except where he is driven away by the darkness of wickedness and ignorance, as it is written: “For the holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and withdraws from thoughts that are without [Col. 1118A] understanding, and is rebuked by the iniquity that comes upon it.”

The Lord indicates through the prophet where this same Spirit rests, saying: “Upon whom does my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at my words?”

Let us ascend further through the mystery of the sun proposed above and consider those Gospel words: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

For all who have clear sight can in some way observe, as far as vision dazzled by the brightness permits, that the brightness of the sun itself, which surrounds the whole earth, never leaves the sun but is always in it—a light shining from light.

If such a property can be seen in a creature by bodily eyes, it must be believed to exist much more in the Creator and almighty God.

For just as the brightness of the sun is always in the same sun, and wherever it tends by shining, it always remains with it, so “in the beginning”—that is, in the Father—was the Word, and the Word was with God: namely, the Son of God always remaining in the [Col. 1118B] Father, always God from God, light shining from light.

But the sun’s own rounded form also seems not to be without mystery. For everything round has neither an end nor a beginning.

We are taught to believe the same concerning almighty God, because, since nothing is found above him, below him, or wider than him, he is enclosed by no boundary.

Having brought forth, therefore, what is found in the sun alone concerning the mystery of the holy Trinity, let us bring forth two further examples, so that those who cannot understand the more subtle things said or written concerning faith in the holy Trinity may be taught to investigate the same faith in certain elements.

In water, therefore, which we are accustomed to designate by three persons, saying “that spring, that stream, and that pool,” a trinity is shown to exist, but the substance of one element.

Although the persons differ as spring, stream, and pool, they nevertheless agree in one substance.

Here too something can be found resembling what I said about the sun.

No stream, finally, flows without the substance of its spring, so long as the spring [Col. 1118C] continues to bubble forth. But if the spring dries up, the stream too is deprived of the person of its source.

The pool also corresponds sufficiently to the person of the Holy Spirit, because just as the spring and the stream, flowing together into the pool, possess the substance of one element, so the Father and the Son, meeting in the unity of the Holy Spirit, are one and constitute one substance.

The same mystery of the holy Trinity can also, I think, be found in a lighted candle. For since a burning candle consists of three elements—wick, wax, and fire—it bears the figure of the three persons, but is one substance.

And just as a candle has no usefulness in the making of its wick and wax without being lit, so also faith will profit nothing in the case of one who believes in the Father and the Son but separates the fire of the Holy Spirit from them.

Having offered these examples concerning the holy Trinity, which, as I think, are clear to everyone, I now wish to gather here and there other examples pertaining to moral understanding.

First, from certain parables that are read as spoken in the Gospel [Col. 1118D] by the mouth of our Lord himself, admonishing clergy especially through them to withdraw their minds to some extent from worldly allurements and pomp when reading or hearing such words of teaching.

Then from various things that can be perceived in this world through sight or hearing by both laity and clergy: the gathering of flowers by bees in different places; the immeasurable brilliance of the sun; the adornment and beauty of creation; the very lowliness that belongs to human nature; the ability and difficulty of working in certain seasons; the necessity of daily eating; and the abundance or scarcity of food supplies.

From all these things, therefore, I decide that the laity especially must be admonished, because, once it has been revealed to them what these things signify, they will afterward have no excuse before God on the ground of ignorance of letters, since every day they are instructed by the things they possess and among which they live to know the Creator.

But, leaving these matters aside for the moment, I shall address first the clergy, whom I have determined to instruct through the [Col. 1119A] most holy Scripture of the Gospel reading.

For the Apostle says: “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction.” These words apply especially to those who possess knowledge of letters and are therefore continually able to recognize how they ought to govern those entrusted to them.

Hence clergy also need, paying the utmost attention to what is written—“To whom more is entrusted, from him more is required”—to strive not to bury the talent of knowledge they have received in the ground, that is, to spend it on earthly concerns, but to devote it to the service of him from whom it is established that they received it.

Let them also recall that, in proportion as they have been enriched with greater knowledge, they are, by divine judgment, permitted to be attacked by more wicked spirits.

For, as we read, the devil’s food is the chosen; by this it is signified that, attacking the skilled and the holy above all, he strives to devour them in the belly of his wickedness.

Such an attack must [Col. 1119B] continually be forestalled by reading those books in which the enemy’s deceptions are exposed, and especially the Gospel, where each vice and virtue is foretold by the Lord through parables.

Therefore I wish here to make a brief admonition from the Gospel reading, so that it may be readily known which reading ought to be set against each vice.

When, therefore, continual negligence of divine instruction is perceived in the mind of a teacher, let him read that parable: “A sower went out to sow his seed.” For in that passage, as the Lord himself explains it—and thereby instructs all teachers in the interpretation of the other parables as well—all the causes from which negligence of the divine word arises are recalled.

That many people believe for a time and withdraw at the time of temptation; that they are choked by the cares, riches, and pleasures of this life; or that they are hindered in any way from bearing the fruit of the divine word—this arises especially from that negligence by which, despising the fear and love of God, they believe that they can obtain temporal and [Col. 1119C] eternal goods through one and the same kind of love.

Or it arises because, although they know for certain that the two must be distinguished in love, they set before themselves the expectation of a long life and the divine mercy, which promises pardon to all who turn to it, even if late.

Abusing this promise—believing, that is, that whenever they wish they can quickly convert, as though the time of conversion were in their own power—they devote themselves meanwhile with all their effort solely to earthly concerns and pleasures.

As the time of conversion is postponed from day to day, month to month, and year to year, they either convert at last only with difficulty, or, as though chained by their worst habit, die without conversion.

For, as a punishment for sin—which they have deserved by delaying conversion for so long—it eventually appears impossible to them that which once seemed easy.

To drive out such dangerous and terrifying negligence, it is very helpful to read the parable just mentioned and its interpretation frequently and attentively, provided that earnest care and continual prayer are present at the same time, so that it may be expelled.

[Col. 1119D] For the devil, greatly fearing the reading and attentive consideration of the divine words, flees from those who read and meditate upon divine things.

Again, if anyone feels himself burdened by excessive stinginess and an immoderate appetite for costly clothing or food, let him continually attend to the parable of the rich man who, because he was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day, and because he was unwilling to give the beggar Lazarus even the crumbs fallen from his table, was buried in hell; and, without doubt, by refraining to some extent from this vice, he will be reformed.

But so that he may be compassionate toward anyone who has fallen and may be a discerning teacher concerning their amendment, let him attend to the parable about the man who, going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, fell among robbers and, wounded by them, was left half dead. Since some passersby did not visit him at all, a certain Samaritan, traveling along, took him up to be healed; and, pouring in oil and wine, restored him to health. For the pouring in of oil and wine [Col. 1120A] signifies the necessary mingling of mercy and severity, without which no one full of the wounds of sin can be healed. Hence all teachers can be sufficiently instructed: in treating sinners, neither mercy without severity nor severity without mercy is to be maintained.

That it is necessary for all the faithful who possess earthly substance to purchase and seek eternal joys with temporal goods is sufficiently indicated by that parable: “A certain man was rich, who had a steward”; for at the end of its reading the Lord makes clear why he put it forward, saying: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity,” and so forth. In this parable also, by drawing an argument from the contrary—from the steward’s fraud—the Lord suggests to us that examples for edification can be proposed both from contrary things and from consequential ones. Fraud is contrary to every Christian, and therefore no one is permitted to commit it; nevertheless, we can in some way be edified by it, observing that if one of the worldly [Col. 1120B] has looked after his future advantage through fraud, much more ought we to provide, through almsgiving acquired justly, for what benefits us in the future life.

A similar example is found when a religious person, seeing a prostitute adorned in every way for her lovers, immediately exclaims: “Would that I were as diligent in pleasing Christ as this prostitute is diligent in pleasing the world!” Or when a spiritual teacher admonishes his disciples, saying: “Just as many are zealous to obtain carnal prudence, so you too should strive to obtain spiritual prudence,” even though neither the prostitute nor worldly prudence is good. From these examples it is gathered that even the worst things can be appropriated for edification.

Again, lest anyone be overcome by the desire for human praise, impelled by certain good works, let him attend to that parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field,” and so forth. For unless a good action is sometimes concealed, it is carried off by evil spirits, as money displayed is carried off by robbers.

Likewise, lest he be harsh and unfeeling [Col. 1120C] toward those who in some way sin against him, let him attend to that parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants,” and so forth. In it it is shown clearly enough how we ought to be merciful toward our debtors, if we wish our own debts to be remitted by the Lord.

Pride also, which strives to destroy all virtues, lest it rule in anyone, should attend to those two comparisons. One is: “Two men went up into the temple to pray”; the other: “When you are invited to a wedding, recline in the lowest place.” From both, therefore, everyone can learn how great a ruin or disgrace ordinarily follows pride. Both likewise end with one and the same statement: namely, that everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

Likewise, lest we use permitted and lawful things immoderately, or rely upon them more than is lawful, that parable should be continually considered: “A certain man made a great dinner and invited many.” For the fact [Col. 1120D] that a great dinner is said to have been prepared and many invited, but that some excused themselves from coming because they had bought a country estate, some because they wished to inspect fields they had purchased, and others because they had recently taken a wife, signifies that a very great multitude of the faithful is invited by the Lord to the joys above; yet, while very many are found to be excessively ambitious to acquire possessions and many others are immoderately devoted to a lawful marriage, few are those who, obeying the divine call, reach the kingdoms of heaven.

Nevertheless, the judgment of this parable is to be feared all the more because it is feared by so few. Every day people try to excuse themselves from the divine call not only because of excessive ambition to acquire country estates and fields at a fair price, and because of immoderate love of a wife, but also because of those fields which they strive by some fraud to acquire or seize from holy places or from the poor, and because of the enticement of a prostitute.

If those who use possessions acquired justly and granted by God [Col. 1121A] immoderately are excluded from the heavenly kingdom, what is to be believed about those who, seizing what belongs to others by force or fraud and joining themselves to prostitutes, persist in these things to the end of their lives? Here let each person believe what he wishes. I believe that “heaven and earth will pass away, but the divine words will not pass away, except so that they may be fulfilled as they were foretold.”

I have therefore decided to offer these few words of exhortation to the clergy from the most holy book of the Gospels, because such a book is known to almost all clerics, since it is frequently read and heard by them.

Clerics who are diligent can also be sufficiently instructed from the various writings of both the Old and the New Testament, and can be edified not only by good examples but also by bad ones. If they take care to consider Abel’s justice; Job’s patience; the venerable blessing made by God to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; David’s humility; the steadfastness of Daniel and the Three Young Men; Susanna’s chastity; the religious devotion of both Tobiahs—that is, father and son—and the perfection of the other fathers in the Old Testament, they can be edified in every way by such men’s examples.

Again, if they wish to review [Col. 1121B] the deeds of the wicked—how much evil Cain inflicted upon his brother; for what sins the Sodomites were overthrown; how the pride of Nebuchadnezzar and Holofernes was crushed; in how many ways the murmuring children of Israel were afflicted; what the sinning sons of the priest Eli endured; how Solomon, wisest of men, fell; what a ruin Absalom and the two judges raging against Susanna deserved; how vainly the deceit of Herod and the Jews raged against Christ; and with what great wickedness Simon Magus, blinded, perished—what else is suggested by so many evils except that those who hear may fear, and those who fear may take care not to fall into similar things?

For unless very many people were compelled by fear, [Col. 1121C] they would in no way be drawn to salvation. It is therefore evident that we can be edified through evils as well as through good things, if we weigh them as they are ordered by the Lord. We are drawn to love God through good things; but we are compelled to fear him through certain evils.

Therefore, I ask that both what I have already presented and other similar things written in the Gospels be read with the utmost attention, and that from their reading we discern, at least to some extent, what we ought to do.

Next, in exhorting the laity, I do not lead them to read any Scripture, since it is unknown to them; rather, I beg that certain likenesses known through daily experience be explained to them by the clergy. Let them be told: “Do not think that, because you do not know letters, you have any excuse before God. We point out to you certain things in which, as though reading them daily in books, you can recognize what you ought to do.”

Just as bees customarily gather the liquid of honey in various places and from various flowers, so you too ought to gather the sweetness of every virtue. From one person humility is to be gathered, from another charity, from another faith, from another patience, from another generosity, from another chastity, from another discernment, from another zeal for almsgiving and care for the poor, and from another any other virtue. When these things, gathered in this way, enter the mind of one person, honeys extracted from various flowers are heaped together, as it were, in a single hive.

You ought to gather the honey of virtues not only from human beings but also [Col. 1121D] from every kind of creature but also from every kind of creature that you see or hear each day, and from things that you perceive in some way. For you ought first to gather and place in the hive of your heart faith, which is the foundation of all virtues: namely, believing that God almighty is present everywhere and observes everything that we do or even think.

You ought to gather this faith in the following way. Consider the sun: although it surrounds the whole world and illuminates it with its radiance, nevertheless, because it is a creature—and every creature is exceedingly inferior to the Creator—you can easily learn from this that the sun shines far less brightly than the Creator. The sun can shine only as much as is permitted [Col. 1122A] by the obstruction of the earth or of some other thing. The Creator’s splendor, however, is incomprehensible, and his invisible gaze comprehends all past, present, and future things simultaneously, as though in a single glance of the eye. By it he also looks upon the children of men, “to see if there is anyone who understands or seeks God.”

This splendor can be believed in or recognized only with the full devotion of the heart. Each person will be capable of that light in proportion as he progresses in faith and love of God, and as hunger and thirst for his righteousness set him aflame. Concerning these three things the Lord says in the Gospel: concerning faith, “All things are possible for the one who believes”; concerning love, “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him”; concerning hunger and thirst, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied.”

You can also gather something similar from daily experiences. What farmer would practice agriculture unless he hoped and believed that it would be profitable for him to some extent? Or how can any pursuit be undertaken [Col. 1122B] unless it has begun to be loved? Or who can receive bodily food, necessary for all living things, without weariness, unless some hunger and thirst impel him to it? Even sleep itself is not received unless with some pleasure.

Since you know that all these things exist bodily in this way, ask the Lord with deep attention to grant you to imitate them spiritually: first, to believe rightly in him; then, to love him with your whole strength and your whole mind; finally, to maintain continually a hunger and thirst for the divine word, without which no one can love righteousness.

But whoever does not love righteousness has no hope of salvation for his soul, just as there is no hope of bodily health for one who suffers an aversion to bodily food. For concerning both spiritual and bodily food the Lord says: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God.”

If, therefore, by imitating bodily hunger and thirst you also obtain spiritual hunger and thirst, [Col. 1122C] you will never be empty of good will, gathering everywhere, like bees, the honey of some virtue and wisdom—just as we have said that from the sun’s immense radiance, which we are discussing for the moment, the immensity of the divine presence is to be gathered.

Therefore, whenever you look upon that same immense radiance of the sun, immediately, remembering the divine presence and knowledge, invoke the Lord with the whole devotion of your mind, that he may deign to pour some light of his wisdom into your hearts.

Having heard these things about the sun—which, although it appears to be a single flower, nevertheless yields honey of various virtues to be gathered from it—you must also hear how you ought to gather the same honey from elsewhere. For those meadows and flowers are never suitable sources from which such honey can be gathered unless there are people to gather it.

Consider, then, generally the adornment of the whole world: how all things harmonize and are tempered with one another—hot things with cold, cold things with hot; the daylight seasons with the nighttime ones, summer with winter. Then consider each thing individually [Col. 1122D], namely the adornment of heaven and earth: of heaven through the sun, moon, and stars; of earth through its various lovely flowers, herbs, trees, and fruits, from which the human race receives food; the beauty of precious stones; the various pictures delightfully woven both into cloaks and into other costly fabrics; the various colors with which they are made; the sweet music of strings and organs; the brightness of gold, silver, and every other metal; the lovely courses of waters, which are necessary both for carrying ships and for setting up mills; myrrh; the fragrance of spices; and finally the handsome faces of certain human beings.

When you have looked outwardly upon all these things, composed with a wondrous and ineffable adornment, consider also how great an adornment they possess inwardly—that is, spiritually—and what they admonish us through their symbolism. For they signify certain important things from which you can gather the honey of great virtue and wisdom.

In short, all the adornment and beauty of creation [Col. 1123A] that serves us in the present life teaches and admonishes us to observe this: if temporal goods are so delightful in sight and sound, eternal things are proven to be much more delightful and beautiful.

There is another matter that we ought to consider in the beauty of temporal goods. Since every person must be tested in this life as to whether he loves God more than a beautiful creature, or prefers eternal goods to temporal ones, some beautiful and delightful appearance—whether of women, clothing, metals, or other things—is continually set before him, so that, tested by them, he may learn through experience what his fear and love of God are like.

No one can be certain of what he is unless he has been tested in such a temptation. You can recognize a very familiar example of this in every soldier. The skill and courage [Col. 1123B] of any soldier are recognized only in war. If he acts cautiously there, fortifying himself while striking down his adversaries, only then is he deservedly praised and proclaimed a brave soldier.

That conflict which we must continually wage against the devil, who envies our salvation, is also not inappropriately called a war. He never ceases to entice us by tempting us to love temporal goods more than eternal ones and to place our hope solely in perishable things. But, mindful of eternal life, for which we were created, redeemed, and invited, we ought to resist the allurements and desires that he casts into our hearts, considering what is written: “Do not follow your desires.” Another passage of Scripture likewise indicates what a crown results from the struggle of temptation, saying: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life.”

If, then, you carefully recall and reflect [Col. 1123C] upon these two points that we have just mentioned concerning the beauty of temporal and visible things—namely, how through it we ought to consider the quality of eternal goods, and that through it we are tested as to whether we love God more than all beautiful carnal things—if, I say, you diligently recall and contemplate both points, you will be able to gather a great sweetness of various virtues, sweeter than every bodily honey.

Furthermore, this must be known and stored up as spiritual honey in the little vessels of your hearts: whatever adversity exists in creatures, and whatever lowliness is found in human nature itself, arose from the transgression of the first human beings.

After they had despised the divine command, they immediately deserved to have things contrary to themselves both within themselves and throughout all creation: within themselves, because they had been stripped of that most honorable glory of blessed immortality in which they themselves were created and which all the elect will one day receive, and they felt within themselves dishonorable signs of shameful flesh, so that they were ashamed to find themselves naked; in creatures, because there are as many adversities as there are creatures.

Indeed, no creature is found that cannot in some way oppose sinful humanity with adversity. [Col. 1123D] Yet almighty God turns all these things toward some useful purpose. Through them he either chastises human beings so that they may turn from their wickedness—as often happens through foul weather, pestilence, famine, and other scourges—or in them he gives each person an opportunity to show what his character is, as often happens through those who abuse wealth and power. Or he displays the devil’s malice through the ferocity of certain beasts, as in the lion and the wolf.

Is there not great usefulness in all the adversities just mentioned? Will it not be useful for people corrupted by prosperity to be corrected through some adversity? Will it not be useful that hidden enemies of the Church are permitted to rule after receiving power, so that both what they are like may become apparent and so that, through their persecution, they may make others tested like gold in a furnace? Will it not be useful that the ferocity and malice of the invisible enemy are displayed through certain fierce beasts?

Just as a lion and a wolf visibly lie in wait [Col. 1124A] for herds of animals, so the devil, seeking someone to devour and draw to destruction, invisibly lies in wait for all the faithful. And how could you, who do not know books, recognize the malice of the invisible devil in any other way unless you were taught through some visible creature known to you?

Believing such things about the adversity of all the elements, “think of the Lord in goodness,” as it is written: he who determines that all adversities as well as prosperities should occur in the world according to a disposition directed toward some usefulness or mercy.

Whatever lowliness of human nature arose from our first parents has been turned by God into such a great good that by it every disease of pride—which could arise in human beings in imitation of angelic nature—might be suppressed.

In the end, every preceding work indicates to its maker how he ought to make what follows. Thus, when a work of angelic dignity partly fell through pride and, falling to the earth like a potter’s vessel, was thereby broken, it showed God almighty that another vessel should be fashioned in another way—not as though he were unaware of so great a fracture, but so that what had been done might become known to us.

For he, who foreknows everything before it happens, teaches us through preceding events [Col. 1124B] how we ought to weigh future ones. The fact that he permitted certain angels and our first parents to fall, he did for our caution, so that, instructed by this, we would presume nothing about ourselves.

God therefore acted toward fallen humanity as a highly skilled physician is accustomed to act toward a sick person. If, recognizing the nature of the illness, he hopes that the patient can be healed, he takes him in hand for treatment. Then, if the illness requires it, he applies plasters, sometimes made from exceedingly base material, to the extent that they are mixed with the dung of animals or birds, and even made with the flesh of dogs, vultures, or snakes. Moreover, if necessary, the physician adds cauterization. Although this medicine is perceived to be most useful for the health of the flesh, as those who have experienced it testify, it is nevertheless concealed because of its stench and baseness.

By this we are also mystically instructed [Col. 1124C] to conceal in the same way all the lowliness by which we are surrounded, because not everything useful is honorable. Thus each bodily medicine—the plaster and the cauterization—although it may appear exceedingly base, nevertheless contains within itself a great demonstration of spiritual medicine, from which you can gather the necessary honey of moral imitation.

For, as Scripture says, nothing happens on earth without a cause; and things that appear carnally base are precious in their significance. If bodies are healed by a filthy or foul-smelling medicine, and it is not the quality of the medicine but the health proceeding from it that is weighed, why should it seem strange or incongruous if almighty God, who foreknows all future things and is the physician and savior of all who believe in him, has done something similar for diseased souls—healing them, or rather preventing their sickness, just as wise physicians act with some humble antidote?

Nevertheless, we ought to conceal this, [Col. 1124D] just as our first parents are read to have done when they were ashamed to find themselves naked, lest we appear either to bring shame upon ourselves or to do an injury to our Creator, who decided to humble us through such lowliness, and thereby accuse him in the secret of our thoughts of having permitted us to become so base more through his power than through justice.

To think such things about God is, to some extent, to be proud against him. Whatever it was that permitted our first parents to sin, or that surrounded us with some lowliness through their transgression, all of it must be believed to have been done for the sake of our salvation.

And although the depth of divine wisdom cannot be wholly investigated in this matter, we must nevertheless seek certain signs from visible things by which our understanding may be taught to agree with that same divine wisdom. Hence we have taken what we have already said about a very base kind of treatment as an illustration of this point.

If some bodily health can be acquired through a base medicine [Col. 1125A], spiritual health must likewise be believed to arise in the same way. For all carnal beauty easily entices human hearts toward exaltation, while lowliness restrains them toward humility. Therefore it pleased God to lead the human being who, because of the beauty of his condition, had fallen into the greatest illness of pride toward the health of humility by imposing upon him some lowliness as a remedy.

Spiritual health is acquired only through the remedy of humility, and human humility is obtained only through some form of contrition.

From all these things you can plainly understand that, as it is written, “the Lord is faithful in all his words and holy in all his works.” He foresaw that human pride had to be restrained by such remedies, and he teaches that spiritual remedies, unknown to many, are to be sought through bodily figures and examples that are known to almost everyone.

But enough has been said about this. Let us now proceed further, to the matters that we have decided should next be discussed.

For the proposed order requires us [Col. 1125B] now to tell you what the variety of seasons signifies: sometimes they are suitable for carrying out various activities, such as spring, summer, and autumn; at other times they are unsuitable, such as winter. The first three seasons, in which we can work more easily, signify the whole period of the present life granted for obtaining forgiveness. Concerning this the Apostle also says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.”

Winter, which is especially unsuitable for working, signifies the time of the final judgment, during which no works of fruitful repentance can be performed. Hence the Lord also warns in the Gospel, saying: “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath.” It is as though he were saying: “Be always vigilant, lest, having squandered the time granted for forgiveness, you then seek it in vain when there is no opportunity for forgiveness.”

Elsewhere he expresses the same meaning more clearly, saying: “Therefore keep watch, praying at all times, that you may be counted worthy to escape the things that are to come.” The prophet Isaiah urges that care be taken concerning this same time, saying: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near.” For he will be far away when he hears the prayers of no sinner.

The Sabbath, which is added to winter [Col. 1125C] because among the Jews it is a feast day on which people are accustomed to rejoice greatly, signifies any useless idleness or a time of inappropriate joy. Therefore the Lord warns that our flight should not be on the Sabbath—that is, lest, placed amid the delights of the present life, we put off future joys.

Since, then, you have heard that through winter a time of the final judgment unsuitable for certain labors is foreshadowed, consider what must now be done by you while you are able to do good and possess the light of life. You have no remaining excuse on account of ignorance of letters, since even in winter you are able to read the well-known things that must be done by you.

Next, it remains to say what the necessity of daily eating suggests that you should do. Everywhere you have flowers from which you can gather the honey of some edification. The fact, therefore, that we are compelled [Col. 1125D] to restore our bodies daily so that we may be stronger for every bodily activity signifies to us that we need daily to be restored by spiritual food—that is, heavenly teaching—lest we fail in the labor that we must continually endure both for divine service and for the forgiveness of our sins.

For unless almighty God wished spiritual restoration to be signified by bodily nourishment, he would certainly have decreed that the same condition should exist in the present life as in the future. There, no one is found who is nourished by the restoration provided by bodily food.

It remains also to say [Col. 1126A] what the abundance and scarcity of bodily substance signify. Through both, great and necessary instruction is shown to everyone. Abundance teaches this: just as it increases the joy of the present life and diminishes anxiety, so spiritual riches—that is, the virtues of the soul—diminish all anxiety about future calamity and misery and increase the joys of eternal blessedness.

Scarcity, on the other hand, indicates this: just as it brings manifold sorrow to those who suffer it, since they do not know where to seek the food without which they cannot live, so the losses of spiritual life foreshadow the lamentations of eternal condemnation.

Since, then, dearest brothers, it has been explained to you in various ways how, without letters, you can seek and walk in the path of a religious life, continually attend to each of the things we have said, and diligently reflect upon them in your hearts.

So that you may recall these things more easily [Col. 1126B] and that they may cling more firmly to your hearts, I wish to repeat them briefly. First, we told you how you ought to imitate the diligence of bees, gathering from various people or things, as from flowers, the sweetness of virtues.

Next, we explained what the immense radiance of the sun signifies. Then we spoke of the threefold understanding to be retained in visible things. The first teaches us, from the beauty of temporal goods, to consider how beautiful eternal goods are. The second suggests that from the same beauty people are to be tested as to whether they love God more than any earthly thing. The third indicates that the adversity of all creation, and the lowliness of human nature itself, arose from the transgression of our first parents, but that God turned this same adversity and lowliness toward some human benefit.

Then we also explained what the winter season, unsuitable for certain works, signifies, and what the necessity of daily eating, as well as the abundance and scarcity of bodily substance, signify. Since all these things can be very familiar to you through daily experience, continually consider how much edification you can derive from them, imitating the work of bees in gathering virtues.

No excuse on account of ignorance of letters now remains for you, [Col. 1126C] since in the things you see or hear every day, or perceive in some way, you can recognize knowledge of religious truth as though in books.

These admonitions are addressed especially to the laity. Then, exhorting both clergy and laity, I beg you to consider the continual disorder of the weather which, because our sins demanded it, had threatened for many years, so that either immense cold, or immense rain, or immoderate drought, destroying the fruits of the earth, produced pitiable famine. Fear lest the earth, corrupted by iniquity, wholly refuse to provide necessary food, or even swallow up some people, as is said—alas!—to have recently happened in certain places.

Let them therefore refrain [Col. 1126D] to some extent from their customary avarice and robbery, as well as from wantonness and the many foolish practices that certain utterly senseless people have brought from foreign nations into these regions through unconventional shaving and monstrous clothing. Unless this kind of folly is abandoned, divine punishment will fall not only upon those who practice it but also upon those who consent to it.

[Col. 1127]

THE FOUR BOOKS OF THE VENERABLE Bede THE PRIEST, *ON TEACHINGS* [Greek: ΠΕΡΙ ΔΙΔΑΞΕΩΝ], OR THE ELEMENTS OF PHILOSOPHY.

[BOOK ONE.]

PREFACE.

[Col. 1127A] Cicero also says in the Prologue to his *Rhetoric*: “Eloquence without wisdom is harmful; wisdom without eloquence, although of little benefit, nevertheless benefits to some extent; but wisdom together with eloquence is of the greatest advantage.” They are mistaken who, setting aside what benefits and does no harm, cling to what harms and does not benefit. To do this is to dissolve the marriage of Mercury and Philology, sought with such care by Virtue and Apollo and approved by the entire assembly of the gods. It is also like continually sharpening a sword but never striking with it in war.

Nevertheless, many who usurp the title of teacher not only do this but also swear to others that they should act in the same way. Knowing nothing about philosophy, yet ashamed to confess that they do not know something, or seeking consolation for their ignorance, they praise more dearly what they do not know as being of little use.

But since, as Terence says, “It is no wonder if a prostitute behaves shamelessly,” setting aside their shamelessness, I have decided to say something about philosophy, so that I may perfect it as diligently as I can—not by stirring the diligent to diligence, but by stirring those who are not diligent to diligence.

Beginning, therefore, with the first creation of things, we shall continue as far as humanity, saying many things in our treatment of the human being. Before beginning the discourse, I ask this: if anything imperfect is found in this work, let them attribute it to human imperfection and therefore not condemn whatever in it is useful. For good things should not be condemned because of one badly expressed statement, nor bad things praised because of one well-expressed statement. Sometimes Thersites keeps watch while Ulysses sleeps, and in a long work it is permissible for sleep to creep in.

As we begin to treat philosophy, let us say what philosophy is.

CATALOGUE OF BOOK ONE.

[Col. 1127]

[Col. 1127B] What philosophy is. Things that exist and are not seen. Things that exist and are seen. By what arguments it may be proved that God exists. Why divine power is called the Father. Why wisdom is the Son. Why will is the Holy Spirit. Whether they are bodies or spirits. How the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. Why certain works are attributed to one of the persons, although one does nothing without the other. Why incarnation is attributed to the Son.

[Col. 1128B] What it means to know something and to know it perfectly. What it means to be perfectly ignorant. Concerning demons. Why forgiveness of sins is attributed to the Holy Spirit. Concerning the soul of the world. What a heavenly animal is. What is ethereal. What is aerial. What is moist. How the Son is begotten from the Father and yet coeternal with him. Concerning the elements.

HERE BEGINS BOOK ONE.

[Col. 1127]

[Col. 1127C] Philosophy is the true comprehension of things that are and are not seen, and of things that are seen. Things that exist but are not seen are incorporeal. For the senses can perceive nothing apart from material substance. Things that exist and are seen are corporeal, whether they possess a divine or a perishable body, since bodies are subject to the senses.

Since philosophy therefore consists in knowledge of both kinds of things, let us discuss both, beginning with those that exist but are not seen. These are the Creator, the soul of the world, demons, and human souls. Since the Creator is prior to all of them—for everything has existence from him, while he has it from no one—let us begin with him.

But because the saints say that God cannot be perfectly known in this life, let us explain what it is to know something perfectly, so that it may become clear why the Creator cannot be perfectly known in this life. Eleven things are asked concerning anything: whether it exists, what it is, how great it is, what it is for, what kind of thing it is, what it does, what is done to it, where it is, how it is situated in place, when it exists, and what it possesses. To know something perfectly, then, is to know these eleven things about it.

Although we know that God exists, we nevertheless do not comprehend perfectly what he is. His quantity—for he fills all things—exceeds the narrowness of our breast; human wisdom is not sufficient to explain his relation; it does not comprehend his qualities; and no finite tongue is sufficient to recount his actions. No one can perfectly explain what is done to him—not by the power of the one acting, but by the permission of the one who suffers; where he is, who is wholly and entire above all things and below all things; how he is in a place, though he is not local; his relation to time, since he exists before all time; or what he possesses, since he holds all things in the span of his hand.

We therefore neither entirely fail to know him, since we know that he exists, nor do we know him perfectly, since we are ignorant of all these things concerning him. We have said that in this life God can be known to exist; let us now set out the arguments by which this can also be demonstrated to unbelievers, namely, through the creation of the world and its daily ordering.
