[Col. 1129A] Since the world was made from contrary elements—hot, cold, moist, and dry—which were joined together in the composition of the world, this must have occurred either through nature at work, by chance, or through some craftsman. But it is proper to nature to flee what is contrary and desire what is similar. Nature therefore did not join the contrary elements; nor were they joined by chance.

For if chance had produced the world, why would it not also produce a house, or something of that kind, which is easier? Again, if it had produced the world, some causes would have preceded it, whose concurrence would have produced chance. Chance is an unexpected outcome arising from converging causes. Since therefore nothing preceded the world except the Creator, it was not made by chance; consequently, it was made by some craftsman.

That craftsman was either a human being, an angel, or God. But the world was made before the human being, while the angel came into existence with the world. Therefore God alone created the world.

This is demonstrated through its daily ordering as follows: Things that are ordered are ordered wisely; therefore there is some wisdom, since nothing is ordered wisely without wisdom. There is therefore a wisdom by which all things are ordered. That wisdom is either human, angelic, or divine.

It is not human wisdom, for it makes things live and speak. Although human wisdom produces its form—namely, that of a human being or another animal—it cannot confer movement and life upon it. As for angelic wisdom, how could it order the angels themselves? It is therefore divine wisdom that accomplishes this.

Every wisdom, however, is someone’s wisdom. There is therefore one whose wisdom it is; and that one is neither a human being nor an angel. It is therefore God. Thus, through the daily ordering of things, one arrives at divine wisdom, and through wisdom at the divine substance.

Hence divine wisdom is called the seal and image of divinity. In this divinity, which creates all things and governs all things, philosophers said that there are the power to act, wisdom, and will. For if he could not act and did not know, how did he make something so beautiful? If, again, he made it but did not will to do so, he acted either in ignorance or under compulsion. But what could he have been ignorant of, since he even knows human thoughts? And who could compel him, since he can do all things?

[Col. 1129C] There is therefore in the divinity power, wisdom, and will. The saints call these three persons, transferring their names from common usage by a certain affinity: they call divine power the Father, wisdom the Son, and will the Holy Spirit.

Power is called the Father because by it he creates all things and orders them with paternal affection. Wisdom is called the Son because he was begotten by the Father before the ages and yet is coeternal with him. For just as the Son is temporally from the Father, so wisdom is eternally and consubstantially from power.

But we have said that the Son is begotten by the Father and yet is coeternal with him. Let us say something about that begetting, first asking that the words, “Who shall declare his generation?” not be thought to work against us. This was said not because it is impossible, but because it is difficult.

The Father therefore begot the Son—that is, divine power begot wisdom—when he foresaw how he would create things and order what had been created. Since he foresaw this before the ages, he begot the Son—that is, wisdom—before the ages, and from himself, not from another. For he came to know this neither through anyone’s teaching nor through the experience of practice, but from his own nature.

Since he has existed—from eternity, if it is permissible to speak in this way—he has known these things from eternity; there was never a time when he did not know them. If he is therefore eternal, his wisdom is eternal also. The Father thus begot the Son, coeternal and consubstantial with himself.

Divine will is called the Spirit. Properly speaking, a spirit is breath, in which a person’s will is often discerned. One breathes differently when joyful and differently when angry. Therefore they called the divine will, metaphorically, the Spirit, and, by antonomasia, the Holy Spirit.

This Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, because divine will is goodness: the fact that God is so powerful and wise is shown in its effect. For the Holy Spirit’s proceeding from the Father and the Son means nothing other than that the divine will extends from power and wisdom to the creation and governance of things.

[Col. 1130A] This goodness and will are coeternal with the Father and with the Son. For he was never powerful and wise without also being good and willing to create. In God, being and being good are one and the same; and before time he willed what he made, since there is no changeability in him. The aforementioned divine will and goodness are therefore coeternal.

Thus there is a trinity of persons, but a unity of essence. For divine power, wisdom, and goodness are one substance. Although this trinity cooperates in everything—for it never acts powerfully without wisdom and goodness, nor wisely without power and goodness, nor benevolently without wisdom and power—certain works are nevertheless attributed to power, and thus to the Father; certain works to wisdom, and thus to the Son; and certain works to goodness and will, and thus to the Holy Spirit.

The sending of the Son is attributed to power, that is, to the Father, although it was also accomplished by wisdom and will. The incarnation is attributed to wisdom, that is, to the Son, although it was also accomplished by power and will.

And rightly it is attributed to wisdom. Although he was so powerful that by his will alone he could free the human race from the devil’s power, he nevertheless preferred to unite divinity with humanity, so that the one who reconciled God and humanity in himself might possess what belongs both to the human being and to God.

If he had been God alone, the devil would never have laid hands upon him—for how could a servant lay hands upon the son of a powerful master whom he recognized? Hence it is written: “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Son of God.” If, again, he had been merely human, how could one captive free another captive? For all have sinned and lack the grace of God.

Our Redeemer was therefore both God and human, and still is, so that through his divinity he might be able to save, while through his humanity he might remain hidden from the devil. Thus, when the devil attacked an innocent person contrary to right and justice, he might justly admit the power over the guilty that had been entrusted to him by God.

The remission of sins is attributed to the divine will and goodness because, through goodness and will, God forgives what he could have punished just as swiftly through power and wisdom.

But since, while speaking about divinity, we have gone beyond the limits of our knowledge, let us now be silent about it and proceed to what remains, praying that, if something is found here that is not written elsewhere, it not be judged heretical. For something is not heretical merely because it is not written, but only if it is contrary to the faith.

In the preceding division we placed first among things that exist but are not seen the Creator, and then the soul of the world. Having completed our treatment of the Creator, let us speak of the soul of the world.

The soul of the world, according to some, is the Holy Spirit. For by the divine will and goodness—which, as we have said, is the Holy Spirit—all things that live in the world live.

Others say that the soul of the world is a natural power implanted in things by God, by which some things merely live, some live without sensation, and some live, perceive, and discern. For there is nothing that lives and perceives, or discerns, in which that natural power is not present.

A third group says that the soul of the world is a certain incorporeal substance that is wholly present in individual bodies. Yet, because of the sluggishness of certain bodies, it does not perform the same function in all of them. Virgil, wishing to express this, says: “So far as harmful bodies do not retard.”

If someone concludes that there are therefore two souls in a human being—the human soul and the soul of the world—we reply that we do not call the soul of the world a soul, just as we do not call the head of the world a head.

Plato says that this soul was devised from divine and indivisible substance, from the same nature and from a different one. Anyone who wishes to know how this is to be explained will find it in our other writings.

We have said that the third class among things that exist but are not seen is demons. As we begin to discuss them, let us say how many orders there are of them and why they are called demons.

Plato therefore held that there are three orders of demons, from the highest to the lowest, affirming that nothing exists without a rational creature. He says that in the firmament there is a certain rational animal, which he defines as follows: “A rational, celestial, immortal, impassible animal”—namely, the stars, about which we shall speak in their proper place, for they belong among things that exist and are seen.

Next, he said that in the ether there is a certain kind of invisible animal, extending from the firmament to the moon, the first order of demons, which is defined as follows: “A rational, immortal, passible, ethereal animal.” Its duty, he says, is to devote itself exclusively to divine contemplation and to rejoice in that contemplation.

In the lower region, namely around the upper part of the air near the moon, he says that there is another kind, defined as follows: “A rational, immortal, passible animal, extending care to all.” According to him, its duty is to convey prayers to the human being, not to God, and to convey God’s will to human beings, whether through dreams, signs, inward inspiration, or vocal admonition.

It is called passible because it loves good people, rejoices with their prosperity, and suffers with their adversity.

The third order is in this moist part of the air. It is defined as follows: “A moist, rational, immortal, passible animal.” Its duty is to envy humanity and, out of envy, to plot against it, because humanity ascended through humility from the place from which this order descended through pride.

It is also so lustful that it sometimes has intercourse with women and begets children. Hence they are called incubi, because they lie with women in this way.

They differ from the other demons because the first two orders are called cacodaemons, that is, “knowers of good”: καλόν (*kalon*) means “good,” and δαίμων (*daimōn*) means “knower.” These, however, are called cacodaemons, that is, “knowers of evil”; κακόν (*kakon*) means “evil.”

Do not be troubled by the commonality of the name, by which both those beings and these are called demons, as though they were “knowers,” since both the former and the latter are also called angels. Hence Scripture speaks of an evil angel.

The human being inhabits the lower part of the world, namely the earth: a rational, mortal animal, about whom we shall speak in his proper place.

Concerning the demons mentioned above, the question is whether they have bodies or not, since they are animals and every animal is said to have a body, or whether they are spirits, as the prophet says: “Who makes his angels spirits.”

Some therefore say that they are bodies, but so subtle that they cannot be perceived by the senses. Thus, in comparison with our bodies, which are dense and gross, they are called spirits, just as air, although it is a body, is nevertheless called spirit because of its subtlety.

Blessed Gregory confirms this. Speaking of angels in the *Moralia*, he says: “In comparison with our bodies they are spirits, but in comparison with that highest and uncircumscribed Spirit they must be called bodies.”

They prove this again by the authority of blessed Augustine, who in the *Enchiridion* includes a chapter concerning what kind of bodies angels have.

Others say that they are not bodies but spirits, specifically because they are not everywhere: they move from place to place, in contrast with the supreme Spirit, who is wholly and entirely everywhere.

Blessed Gregory called them bodies, but it does not follow from this that they are bodies, just as in the statement, “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.” This does not mean that God regards the wisdom of this world as foolishness, but that, in comparison with divine wisdom, it is foolishness; nor does it follow that it is actually foolishness.

Regarding that chapter of blessed Augustine on what kind of bodies angels have, they say that blessed Augustine is speaking there of the bodies they assume when they appear to human beings—whether those are real bodies or not—and nevertheless does not say that the angels themselves are bodies.

We, however, grant more to the opinion of those who say that they are spirits. Nor should it seem unreasonable that Plato says there are two kinds of cacodaemons, while divine Scripture says there are nine orders of angels. Plato divided them according to places, whereas the divine page divides them according to functions. Thus those nine orders are contained within the two kinds, and conversely.

[Col. 1132B] After treating the Creator, the soul of the world, and the demons, it remains to treat the human soul. But since we have spoken about the human being up to this point, let us postpone speaking about his soul, so that the treatment of the human being may be one continuous discussion.

Up to now our discourse has dealt with things that exist but are not seen. Now let our pen turn to things that are seen. But before we begin to speak about them, we ask that, if in speaking about visible things we say something probable but not necessary, or present something necessary but not probable, we not be criticized for it.

For as physicists we put forward only what is probable; as philosophers, however, we add what is probable, even if it is not necessary. Let it nevertheless be considered whether any of the writers of our own time have discussed the matter in a more probable way.

Since we are about to discuss things that exist and are seen—namely, that they are bodies and that all bodies consist of elements—let us take our beginning from the elements, showing what an element is, why there are four elements and not fewer, what the chaos of the elements was, and how it was dissolved.

An element, as philosophers define it, is the simple and smallest particle of some body: “simple” with respect to quality, and “smallest” with respect to quantity.

An example is this: “An element is a simple part,” that is, a part whose qualities are not contrary. But because this definition appears to include bones and similar things, to exclude them he adds “smallest,” meaning that it is a part of something in such a way that nothing is a part of it.

Letters are similarly called elements because they are parts so simple that nothing is a part of them.

Philosophers hold that the four humors consist of elements; that from the humors arise both homoeomerous parts—that is, uniform parts, such as flesh and bones—and organic parts—that is, functional parts, such as hands and feet, and so forth; and that human bodies consist of both kinds of parts.

Therefore, according to him, none of these four visible things, which some have regarded as elements, is a simple element: neither earth, nor water, nor air, nor fire. None of them is simple in quality or smallest in quantity.

In earth, for example, there is something hot, something cold, something dry, and something moist. Since this is evident to everyone, let us omit its proof. Things that are plainly true or plainly false do not need to be proved; what requires proof is what is subject to some doubt.

Earth is therefore not simple in quality or smallest in quantity, since it consists of such large parts. For it has four parts, or five zones. It is therefore not an element. The same can be proved concerning water, fire, and air.

The elements, then, are the simple and smallest particles of which the four things that we see consist. These elements are never seen, but are understood through division.

To express the matter figuratively, the human body is divided into organic parts, such as hands and so forth; the organic parts into homoeomerous, or uniform, parts, namely parts of flesh and bones; the homoeomerous parts into humors, such as melancholy; and the humors into elements, that is, simple and smallest particles.

Some stages of this division can be carried out in actuality, while others can be carried out only in reason and thought. The human body can be divided in actuality into limbs, and the limbs into homoeomerous parts; but only the intellect can divide homoeomerous parts into humors and humors into elements. For, as Boethius says in his commentary on Porphyry, “It is the power of the intellect to join together what has been divided and to divide what has been joined.”

Someone may ask where the elements are. We say that they are in the composition of the human body and of other bodies, just as a letter is in the composition of a syllable, even if it does not exist separately.

There are, however, some people—rustics, for example—who think that nothing exists unless they can apprehend it with their senses. An animal does not perceive things that are spirits, whereas a wise person ought to investigate things imperceptible to the senses even more than things perceptible to them.

Since the elements are simple and smallest particles, those that are cold and dry are called earth; those that are cold and moist, water; those that are hot and moist, air; and those that are hot and dry, fire.

Since the four visible things are composed of these particles, that among them in which cold and dry particles predominate is called earth after those particles; that in which cold and moist particles predominate is called water; that in which hot and moist particles predominate is called air; and that in which hot and dry particles predominate is called fire.

If, then, we wish to give the aforementioned particles names appropriate to them, let us call these four visible things elements.

Some people have never read either the writings of the philosophers or those of the physicists. Out of pride they disdain learning from anyone; in their arrogance, they touch upon matters they do not understand and appear to say something. They say that these four visible things are qualities: heat, coldness, moisture, and dryness.

But to those who, as though tearing physics apart limb by limb, make this claim, Plato answers in the same voice, calling the elements material substances, since no quality can be the matter of anything. Matter is that which, after receiving a form, passes into another form.

The philosopher also answers them in his *Isagoge*, where he says that the elements are one thing and their combinations another—namely, hot and dry, and likewise for the others.

Macrobius answers them as well, saying: “Since there were different qualities in each of the individual elements, he gave each one such a quality that in the element to which it is attached it would find something related and similar: water finds coldness in common with earth, air moisture in common with water, and fire heat in common with air.”

Observe that he said that the elements are not qualities, but that qualities are in the elements. If, therefore, what is present in something differs from the thing in which it is present, it is not identical with that thing.

Others say that these visible things are elements, proving this by the authority of Juvenal, who says of gluttons: “They seek taste through all the elements: game on land, fish in water, birds in air.”

Since this opinion is true and not contrary to the opinion of the philosophers, I shall explain how it can stand together with it.

The philosopher, treating as a physicist of the natures of bodies, called their simple and smallest particles “elements,” as it were their first principles. Philosophers, however, when discussing the creation of the world rather than the natures of individual bodies, said that these four visible things are the elements of the world, since the world consists of them.

They were created first; then all other things were made from them as from elements, as will be shown below. There is therefore no disagreement between them.

But they object: None of these is an element, because none of them is not made from the four elements.

They prove this as follows. In earth there is something of water, since we see some moisture emerging from it. In the same earth there is something of air, as vapor rising from it proves, and something of heat, which we perceive by touch. They prove the same thing concerning the others, citing Plato’s authority: “Since earth passes into water and water into earth, why should one be called water rather than earth?”

We reply that there is something of the others in each one of them, but that they are not thereby made from the others, because the others are present in them accidentally, not substantially.

Since earth is porous and surrounded by water, some moisture from the water penetrates into it, as does some air. Since earth is at the center of the world and fire is equally distant from the earth on every side, what is surprising if it receives some heat from it? These things are present in earth accidentally, not naturally, and earth does not consist of them.

The same may be proved concerning the others. But because we pursue brevity in this work, let us leave it to the ingenuity of others to investigate what each of the others contains and how this occurs in them. The beginning should indeed come from the teacher, but perfection ought to come from ingenuity and study.

Since they again say that Plato asked why water should rather be called water than earth, or conversely, when it is dissolved in this way, we understand him to be speaking not of elements that are dissolved in this way. For an element is never dissolved in its entirety.

He says that what is dissolved is not earth but “earthy”—that is, a part of earth—whereas what remains and retains the property of earth he calls earth and an element. God granting us life, we shall speak sufficiently about this.

The elements, then, are the particles of the aforementioned bodies, as the philosophers say. The visible things, however, are the elements of the world, as the philosophers say. These are the subject of the treatment that follows.

Why each thing was made; why there are four, and not fewer.

Since an opinion that makes use of the authority of a wise man is more secure, let us say what Plato thought about this. “The principle of divine beauty,” he says, “required that the world be made such that it could be seen and touched.”

As if he were saying: Since God created the world solely out of goodness, not from need—for he is the perfect and supreme good—he wanted it to be made in such a way that it could be seen and touched. Thus the human being, perceiving divine power and goodness through his eyes in the creation and governance of things, would fear the power, revere the wisdom, and imitate the goodness.

He then adds: “Nothing could be seen except through the benefit of fire; nothing could be touched without something solid; and nothing could be solid without earth.”

We shall show, in speaking about the bodily senses, how sight cannot exist without fire, nor touch without earth.

Afterward he adds: “For this reason God laid down fire and earth as foundations, so to speak.”

But since these contain contrary qualities—for earth is corporeal, dull, and immobile, while fire is subtle, sharp, and mobile—God saw that they could not be joined without an intermediary. Therefore he created an intermediary between them.

Since we have mentioned their conjunction, let us explain what the conjunction and mixture of contraries are.

The mixture of contraries occurs when two things become one in such a way that neither remains what it was before. For example, when something extremely hot is mixed with something extremely cold, it becomes lukewarm, with neither the extremely cold nor the extremely hot remaining.

The conjunction of contraries, however, occurs when two things become one in such a way that both remain what they were before. Such a conjunction cannot exist without an intermediary between contraries possessing active qualities, namely heat and coldness. But why this is so, we shall explain in speaking about the human being.

If one is placed against the other, they resist each other, and one is dissolved by the other. For them to endure, therefore, there must be an intermediary.

If the intermediary is such that it is more inclined toward one than toward the other, it will gradually pass into the one toward which it is more inclined, and the conjunction will consequently be dissolved. For example, if something more inclined toward heat than toward cold is placed between something extremely hot and something extremely cold, it will pass into the nature of heat and the coldness will perish; thus the conjunction will be dissolved.

But if the intermediary is such that it is equally related to both, passing no more into the nature of one than of the other, it will preserve their conjunction.

Therefore, wishing the aforementioned two elements to be mixed but joined, so that each would remain what it is, God created an intermediary between them—not one, but two: water and air.

For if he had placed only water between them, it would have been more akin to earth than to fire. It shares corporeality and dullness with earth, and mobility with fire; the conjunction would not endure.

Similarly, if he had placed only air between them, air shares subtlety and mobility with fire, and dullness with earth.

But someone may say: Even if one of these is not sufficient, God could nevertheless have made something else that would have been sufficient.

To this we reply that we are not setting a limit to divine power. We say only that none of the things that exist could have sufficed, nor could there be, according to the nature of things, anything that would have sufficed.

Having shown that one of these alone would not suffice, and that no other thing capable of sufficing for this could exist, let us explain the matter.

When two contrary qualities exist between two things, since a pair cannot be divided into two equal parts, something can be placed between them that receives one property from each and thereby suffices between them.

Thus earth and air have two contrary qualities. Earth is cold and dry, while air is hot and moist. Water, sharing coldness with earth and moisture with air, suffices by itself between them.

Similarly, fire and water have contrary qualities. Fire is hot and dry, while water is cold and moist. But since air shares moisture with water and heat with fire, it alone suffices between the two.

If, however, there are three contrary qualities between two things, then, just as a three cannot be divided into two equal parts, no intermediary equally related to both can be found. It would have to receive one quality from one and two from the other, since a three cannot be divided into whole parts in any other way.

[Col. 1135C] Quality, however, is not divided by intermediates; therefore there cannot be an intermediate between them unless it participates in one quality from one side and two from the other. Someone may object again: “If, according to this pairing involving three qualities, there could not be one middle that received one quality from each side, perhaps according to the pairing that occurs in two qualities they could have had such a middle. For if air lies between fire and water, participating in one quality of the one and another of the other, why could there not be between fire and earth, in a pairing of two qualities, one middle that received one quality from each? Fire is hot and dry, while earth is cold and dry.”

We reply that, even on this account, no middle was necessary, since they agree in one respect; but such a middle could not exist with respect to dryness. For if there were some such middle, receiving something from each, it would either receive heat from fire and dryness from earth, and thus be identical with fire; or it would receive dryness from earth and—[the same would be] identical with fire; or it would receive coldness from earth and dryness from fire, and thus be identical with earth; or it would receive heat from fire and coldness from earth. Beyond these alternatives, as I think, nothing can be contrived. But it is impossible for anything to be both hot and cold.

Since there are four elements and four combinations of their qualities, six combinations result, of which four are possible and two impossible. The four possible combinations are hot and dry, hot and wet, [Col. 1136A] cold and wet, and cold and dry. The two impossible ones are hot and cold, and wet and dry.

The Creator therefore placed two elements in the middle, because one would not have sufficed for the reasons stated above. The arrangement of the elements is as follows: earth occupies the lowest position; next comes water; then air; and fire is higher than all. For if anything lower than earth existed, earth, being naturally heavy, would tend toward it, since heavy things naturally tend downward. If anything existed above fire, fire, because of its lightness, would tend toward it and strive to separate itself from the others.

Water is placed next to earth because it is naturally heavy, even if not as heavy as earth, and therefore ought to occupy the next position. Then comes air, heavier than fire and lighter than water; appropriately, it is placed between the two.

And since we have explained what an element is, how many there are, why there are not more, and have indicated the reason for their arrangement, let us speak of the chaos that existed at the beginning of the world. We shall first present the common opinion, then refute it, and finally confirm our own view with arguments. Nearly everyone says that, at the first creation, the elements did not occupy definite places but were mixed together into a single mass, in which heavy and light things were present and which at one moment rose and at another descended. They also add an explanation of why there would have been such a great confusion of things unless God, by his power, wisdom, and goodness, had arranged them.

They then support this with the authority of Plato, who says in the *Timaeus* that God brought the elements from disorderly agitation into order. We, however, say that the opinion they put forward is false, that the explanation they introduce is unsuitable, and that the authority they invoke has not been properly understood. Let us first prove that the opinion is false, then that the explanation is unsuitable, and finally that the authority has not been properly understood.

Tell me, then, whoever maintains this: Was that mass, which consisted of the four elements, greater than, smaller than, or equal to the elements that now exist? If it was greater, then not everything corporeal is contained in the four elements, or some portion of it perished. If it was smaller, then the Creator subsequently created some new matter from which he enlarged the elements. If it was equal, it filled all the space that the elements now fill; therefore it had no place toward which it could rise or descend. The opinion is therefore false.

The explanation they introduce is unsuitable—namely, that God did this in order to show how great the confusion of things would have been unless his goodness had arranged them. To whom would he have shown it? To an angel? But an angel knows the natures of things by nature and grace. To a human being? But humanity did not yet exist; and if it had been made in order to be shown to human beings, it would have been preserved until humanity existed. Yet the elements were arranged before the creation of humanity.

Plato’s authority has not been correctly understood by them. When Plato says that God brought the elements from disorderly agitation into order, he does not mean that they had ever actually been agitated disorderly—for what place would have been left for disorder when God was arranging all things? Rather, he means that they would be in disorder unless they were ordered by God as they now are. Since earth naturally tends downward and fire upward, unless earth occupied the lower place and fire the higher, earth would continually seek a lower position and fire a higher one; thus there would be disorderly agitation.

The Creator brought this into order by assigning earth its place, namely the lower position, and fire the higher position, so that earth would have nowhere to descend and fire nowhere to ascend. God therefore brought the elements from disorderly agitation—not agitation that had existed, but agitation that could have existed—into order. It is as when, upon the advice of one of our friends, we avoid something that would otherwise occur: we say, “He delivered us from this evil,” not because the evil had previously existed and he afterward delivered us from it, but because, had he not been there, it would have happened to us.

Thus, at the first creation, the elements were where they now are, but they were not as they now are. Earth was entirely covered by water; water was denser than it is now and was raised over a large part of the air; air was denser and darker than it is now, since neither the sun, nor the moon, nor the other stars yet existed to illuminate it. Fire likewise was denser than it is now.

Because earth was entirely covered by water, was illuminated by no light, was not marked out by buildings, and was not filled with its own animals; because water and air were dense and dark; and because the stars above did not appear, they called this “chaos,” that is, the confusion of the elements. Hence Moses says: “The earth was formless and empty, and darkness was upon the face of the abyss.”

This chaos was dissolved in the following manner. Water had been raised as far as the greatest part of the air; the air was dense; and fire likewise was dense. Within that density there was a quantity of earthy and watery substance which, coagulated and hardened by the heat of fire and the dryness [of fire], created the visible and luminous bodies of the stars.

That the composition of the stars contains elements both from below and from above, though the highest element predominates, can be proved from the fact that they are visible, bright, and mobile. Whatever is visible derives its visibility from something invisible or visible; but nothing visible can arise from what is invisible. Hence Lucretius says: “Do not believe that the sensible is born from the insensible.” And Macrobius says: “Every quality, when doubled, increases; it never produces its contrary.”

The stars therefore do not derive their visibility from fire or air, for these are invisible; they derive it from what is visible, namely earth and water. Likewise, they do not derive their brightness and mobility from what is dark and immobile; therefore they derive them from what is bright and mobile, namely air and fire.

They were therefore made from the four elements. Of the lower elements, water predominates in them; of the higher elements, fire predominates. This can be proved by their effects: they impart heat to the earth and draw moisture toward themselves for their nourishment. Like things, after all, rejoice in like things.

Someone may object: “Since air contains denser moisture than fire, and heat, though not as great as fire’s, why were the bodies of the stars not made in air?”

We reply that, although air is hot, it is also wet. It therefore could not become dense by drying and thereby create a luminous and visible body. It is as when dense water is placed over fire: it becomes thicker and often passes into a stony substance. But if something hot and wet is placed over another hot and wet substance, such as boiling water, so that it receives heat from that alone, it will not become dense.

Or, according to Constantine: “When one of these four elements possesses two qualities, it has one individually from itself and the other from another element. Fire is hot from itself, but dry through motion or from earth. Air is wet from itself, but hot from fire. Water is wet from air, but cold from itself. Earth is dry from itself, but cold from water. Whatever exists in each element from itself is stronger in it than what it receives from another.”

Since moisture in air is from itself, while its heat is from fire, moisture prevailed in it, and it could not dry out and create the bodies of the stars.

Moreover, and more importantly, it was not the divine will that the stars should exist in air. Since air is near earth, if the stars had been in it, they would have set the earth on fire by their proximity, and nothing could have lived upon it.

Once the bodies of the stars had been created in this way, because they are fiery in nature they began to move, and through their motion they heated the air below them. Through it the water was heated; and from heated and thickened water various kinds of animals were created. Those that possessed more of the higher elements are birds. Hence birds are sometimes in the air because of the lightness of the higher elements, and sometimes descend to earth because of the heaviness of the lower ones.

Others, which possessed more water, are fish; hence they can live only in this one element. Thus birds and fish were created from water. Therefore it is written: “God of great power, who from the waters brings forth living creatures, sending some back to the depths and raising others into the air.”

After these creatures had been created from water through the effects of the higher elements, wherever the water was thinner it was dried by the heat and by the creation of the beings mentioned above. Patches then appeared upon the earth, in which human beings and other animals lived.

But since the earth, with water placed over it, was muddy and boiling from the heat, it created various kinds of animals from itself. If fire predominated in some part of the earth, choleric animals were born there, such as the lion; if earth predominated, melancholic animals, such as the ox and the ass; if water predominated, phlegmatic animals, such as the pig.

From a certain part in which the qualities of the elements came together equally, the human body was made. This is what the divine page says when it states that God made humanity from the clay of the earth. We do not believe that the soul, which is spirit, light, and pure, was made from clay, but that it was breathed into the human being by God. Hence Scripture says: “God formed the human being from the clay of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life.”

Although various melancholic animals were created, and countless phlegmatic and choleric ones, only one human being was created, because, as Boethius says: “Every equality is rare and finite, whereas inequality is numerous and manifold.”

But since woman is close to the tempered constitution, and although less so, is nevertheless somewhat temperate, some people think it plausible that the body of woman was created from nearby clay. For this reason woman is neither entirely the same as man nor entirely different from him, and she is not equally tempered, since the hottest woman is colder than the coldest man.

This is what the page of Scripture means when it says that God made woman from Adam’s side. We do not wish to say literally that God made the first human being from a rib.

Someone may object: “By the same reasoning, more men and women could then have been created, and could still be created now.”

We reply that this is true, if it were the divine will. For, whenever something comes into being through the operation of nature, it is necessary that the divine will precede it.

The objector will reply again that saying that the human being was made in this way detracts from divine power. To this we answer, on the contrary, that it enhances divine power, since we attribute to God both the giving of such a nature to things and the creation, through the operation of nature, of a body possessing moisture. For in what way do we contradict divine Scripture if we explain how something that it says was made came to be?

If one wise person now says that something has been made but does not explain how, while another says the same thing and explains it, what contradiction is there between them?

But since these people do not know the powers of nature, they do not want anyone to investigate them, so that they may have everyone as a companion in their ignorance. They want us to believe like peasants and not to seek a reason, so that the prophetic saying may already be fulfilled among us: “The priest shall be like the people.”

We, however, say that a reason must be sought in everything, if it can be found. If someone lacks the capacity to grasp what the divine page affirms, the matter must be entrusted to the Holy Spirit and to faith.

For Moses does not say: “If the lamb cannot be eaten, let it immediately be burned in the fire.” Rather, he says that one should first summon a neighbor who is joined to one’s household, and if even then there are not enough people to eat the lamb, only afterward should it be burned in the fire. Thus, when we inquire into something concerning divinity, if we are not sufficient to comprehend it, we should summon a neighbor joined to our household—that is, we should seek out someone who remains in the same catholic faith. But if neither we nor he are sufficient to comprehend it, then we should burn the matter in the fire of faith.

These people, however, though they have many neighbors joined to their household, refuse out of pride to summon anyone. They prefer ignorance to asking another, and if they know of someone who is investigating, they cry out that he is a heretic, placing more confidence in their own hood than in their wisdom.

But, I ask, do not trust their clothing. For the saying of the satirist has already been fulfilled in them:

> Trust no face, for what street is not filled  
> with gloomy obscenities?

And again:

> That speech is rare, and the desire to be silent is great.

And:

> His hair is shorter than his raised eyebrow.

Since we have mentioned the first creation of things, which different people say occurred at different times, let us explain at what time and for what reasons they say it occurred.

The Hebrews and the Latins therefore say that the beginning of the world was in spring. Hence Virgil, speaking of the days of spring, says:

> No other days, at the first origin of the world,  
> shone forth, nor did they possess another course.

He then adds:

> It was that spring; it was the season of spring.

Their reasoning is as follows: whatever is created is created with equality of proportions; but no season except spring is temperate. Therefore the creation of the world took place in spring.

The Egyptians, however, say that it took place in July. Macrobius, following them, says that on the birthday of the world the moon occupied Cancer and the sun Leo. Their reasoning is this: at the first creation there was so much moisture that the earth was surrounded by water; but such an amount of moisture could not be tempered without a corresponding mixture of heat. Therefore the creation of the world took place in the season of the year in which heat is greatest, namely summer.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 1139]

## PROEM

[Col. 1139A] In the preceding part we briefly touched, insofar as the smallness of our intellect allowed, upon those things that exist and are not seen, and upon the elements, which some have taught to be visible and others invisible. Now we shall endeavor to speak of each one and of its adornment.

Although we know that many seek verbal ornament and few recognize the truth of knowledge, we do not boast of the multitude; rather, relying upon the integrity of the few, we labor solely for the truth. For we preferred to set forth naked truth rather than falsity clothed in ornament.

But who would find the dryness of our speech displeasing, if he knew the occupations of our mind and did not seek verbal adornment, but instead marveled at what we are doing? What room could there be for ornament when we must consider what and how we are to read; then, through reading, explain it; in disputations, declaim against falsehoods; judge the discoveries of others; and sharpen our tongue against the slanders of the envious?

Thus the saying about the children of Israel has already been fulfilled in us: while rebuilding the temple, they held a sword in one hand and a stone in the other.

But enough of this. Let us now speak of each of the elements and of the adornment of each one, beginning with the highest—that is, with fire.

[Col. 1139]

## BOOK TWO BEGINS

[Col. 1139]

[Col. 1139C] Fire is the space extending upward from the moon; this same space is called the ether. Its adornment consists of everything seen above the moon, namely both the fixed and the wandering stars.

Someone may ask: “Is there anything above the moon except the ether, the stars, and the spirits mentioned above? Or are there frozen waters there, above which there are still other waters?”

Some say that above the ether there are frozen waters, which appear to our eyes stretched out like a skin, and that above them there are other waters. They confirm this by the authority of the divine page, which says: “God placed the firmament in the midst of the waters,” and again: “He separated the waters that were beneath the firmament from those that are above the firmament.”

But since this is contrary to reason, let us show why it cannot be so, and how the divine page is to be understood in the passages cited.

If there are frozen waters there, they are consequently something weighty and heavy. But the proper place of weighty and heavy things is earth. If, again, frozen waters are there, they are either joined to fire or they are not.

If they are joined to fire, then, since fire is hot and dry while frozen water is cold and wet, contrary is joined directly to contrary, without an intermediate. There would therefore never be harmony there, but rather an even greater opposition of contraries.

If frozen water is joined to fire, it is either dissolved by the fire or extinguishes the fire. Since the fire and the firmament remain, the frozen waters are not joined to fire.

If they are not joined to fire, something lies between them and the fire. But what could it be? An element. Yet no element made from the elements exists above fire. It would therefore be visible. Why, then, are they not seen? It follows that there are no frozen waters there.

But I know what they will say: “We do not know how this is so, but we know that God can do it.”

Wretched people—what could be more wretched than to say that this exists because God can make it, while neither showing the reason why it exists nor the purpose for which it exists? For God does not do everything that he can do. To use the language of a peasant: “God is able to make a calf from a tree.” Has he ever done so? Let them therefore either show the reason why this exists, or the purpose for which it exists, or cease to judge that it does exist.

If, then, there are neither frozen waters there nor other waters above them, when the divine page says, “He separated the waters beneath the firmament from those that were above the firmament,” it called the air the firmament because the air strengthens and tempers earthly things. Above the air are waters suspended in the form of vapor, in clouds, as will be shown below; these are different from the waters beneath the air.

The statement “He placed the firmament in the midst of the waters” should be explained similarly, although we believe that it was said more allegorically than literally.

Someone may ask again: “What is the dense, watery-colored thing that we see there? It is not fire.”

If air cannot be seen because of its extreme subtlety, fire, which is more subtle still, can be seen even less; moreover, such a color does not belong to fiery things.

To this we reply that nothing is seen there; rather, sight fails there, and from the failure of sight a human being imagines something dense to be present. When that inner ray which produces vision is directed upward, and there is no obstacle there from which it may be reflected, it fails; and, by failing, becomes dense.

But since it passes through the eye, in which there is watery humor, and through the crystalline [lens]—as we shall show when discussing the composition of the eye—when it fails, and no other color presents itself to it, it imagines such a color for itself, namely one resembling water.

They will add: “If nothing is seen there—indeed, if sight fails there—how has it been said that heaven covers everything, that the stars are fixed in the firmament, that there are eleven circles in it, and that in one of them there are twelve signs?”

Let us answer them slowly.

Authority speaks of the things above in three ways: fabulously, astrologically, and astronomically.

It speaks fabulously through Nemroth, Hyginus, and Aratus, when they say that Taurus was transferred there and changed into a sign, and likewise with the other signs. This mode of treatment is especially necessary. For we do not know of each sign in what part of heaven it is, how many stars it contains, or how they are arranged.

To treat astrologically is to speak of the things that appear above, whether they are actually so or not. For many things appear there that do not exist, because sight is deceived. This is how Marcianus and Hipparchus treat the subject.

Julius Firmicus and Ptolemy treat it astronomically.

When it is said, “Heaven covers everything,” this is astrological, because that is how it appears; or the ether is called heaven because it is adorned with stars of various kinds.

It is called the firmament because, through the effect and heat of the stars that are in it, it strengthens and tempers the things beneath it. Heaven therefore covers everything because everything is contained in the ether and beneath the ether.

The stars are said to be fixed in it—not like a jewel in gold, but because, existing within it, they always appear in the same part of it.

Since we have mentioned fixed stars, let us ask whether they move or are entirely without motion; and, if they move, how they move.

Some maintain that they do not move, but that they are carried from east to west and west to east by the firmament, fixed in it. Others say that they move by their own motion, because they are fiery in nature and nothing in the ether or air can be sustained without motion; rather, they always move in the same place and around themselves.

A third group says that they also move from place to place, but that our eyes do not perceive their motion because they traverse so much space in the course of their circles that human life, which is short, is not long enough to comprehend even a small portion of such a slow advance.

Although we agree with the view that they move from place to place, we propose another reason why their motion is not perceived. It is this: every motion is discerned by means of what is immobile or less mobile.

When something moves, if something immobile or less mobile is seen, then, as we see one thing pass by or approach, we perceive motion. But if something moves and nothing outside it appears either immobile or less mobile, its motion is not perceived.

This can be proved by the example of a ship moving across the sea. The motion of the stars would therefore be perceived by means of something immobile or less mobile placed above them—if anything were placed above them. We distinguish the motion of the planets by means of the signs, since they appear now beneath one sign and now beneath another.

Above the stars mentioned earlier, however, there is nothing visible, and therefore there is nothing by which their motion can be distinguished. They move, then, but are called fixed because their motion is not perceived.

They said that there are eleven circles in the same firmament, two of them visible and the others invisible. Let us discuss the visible ones first and then the invisible ones.

The two visible circles are the Milky Way, that is, the milk-colored circle, and the zodiac.

The Milky Way begins near the North, on the eastern side, and, passing obliquely through Cancer and Capricorn, returns to the same starting point. It is called this because of its notable brightness. If anyone wishes to know why that remarkable brightness exists in that part of heaven, let him read Macrobius.

The zodiac rises from Capricorn through Aries to Cancer, and from Cancer descends through Libra to Capricorn. Here “descending” and “ascending” are to be understood according to our position.

It is divided, as Macrobius relates, by the flow of water into twelve equal parts, each of which is called a sign, because by means of them we indicate in what part of heaven the sun and the other planets are, toward which point they have gone out, and toward which they ought to proceed.

Since these signs have been given the names of animals—Aries, Taurus, and so forth—the circle containing them is called the zodiac. For ζωή means “animal.” If anyone seeks the reasons for the names, let him read Helpericus.

The arrangement of the signs is as follows. Cancer is nearest to us, at the boundary between our habitable zone and the torrid zone. Next Leo descends somewhat toward the east, followed by Virgo; then comes Libra, situated in the middle of the torrid zone. Beyond it is Scorpio, then Sagittarius; after Sagittarius comes Capricorn, farthest removed from us. Then, descending obliquely, comes Aquarius, followed by Pisces; then Aries, placed beneath Libra in the middle of the torrid zone; above it is Taurus, then Gemini, and finally Cancer.

[Col. 1141] OF THE APSIDES OF THE PLANETS

[Col. 1143]

[Col. 1143B] We have provided this figure not to indicate the obliquity of the signs, their ascent or descent, their remoteness or proximity, but to display their arrangement and to show which planet’s first, second [sic], or sole domicile each sign is said to be. Which sign belongs to which month, and why, we shall explain when treating of the sun.

The remaining nine circles are invisible, five of which are parallels. One of these is called the equinoctial circle. It passes through the middle of the torrid zone, through Aries and Libra, and divides the heavens into two hemispheres. It is called equinoctial because, when the sun reaches it, either while ascending or descending, it makes day and night equal; we shall explain this below.

The second of the parallels is called the conjunction of our habitable zone and the torrid zone. The third is the conjunction of that same zone and the other frigid zone. The fourth, on the opposite side, is the conjunction of the torrid zone and the other habitable zone. The fifth is the conjunction of that same zone and the frigid zone, as appears here.

Since authority says that there are five zones in heaven, whether they are in the ether or in the air we shall say when treating of air.

These parallel circles, that is, equal and distant circles, are so called because they are equally distant from the middle circle, namely the equinoctial. The conjunction of our habitable zone and the other frigid zone is just as far away.

After these come the two colures. Their beginning is in the middle of the North. One rises from there through Cancer and, descending through Capricorn, returns to the same beginning. The other proceeds from there through the East and returns through the West and Libra to the same beginning. Thus they intersect at the summit of the North and divide the heavens into four quadrants.

They are called colures, as if *colon uri*, that is, “the limb of a wild ox.” For *colon* means “limb,” and *urus* means “wild ox.” They are so called because of their imperfection—not because they are imperfect in themselves, but because that part of the other pole which they intersect is never visible to us.

The two remaining circles are the meridian and the horizon.

The meridian is an intelligible line marking that part of the heavens in which the sun, when present, is equally distant from rising and setting. The horizon is where the sky appears to join the earth; it is called horizon as though it were a boundary.

These last two are not drawn on the sphere, because they vary according to the differences among those who inhabit or observe the world.

The motion of the ether or fire—which, for the reasons given above, is called the firmament or heaven—is as follows. Since fire is naturally in motion, and since there is nothing above it toward which it can ascend, as we have shown, nor could it descend, because that would be contrary to its nature, while all the lower places were occupied by the lower elements, it moves in the way that it can and must move: in a circle.

To move in a circle without occupying different places means to turn its different parts while remaining in the same place. Thus, turning in a circle, it carries with it from east through west and back to east both the wandering and the fixed stars.

Although it rolls in this way above the earth, it does not move in a straight manner but obliquely around our habitable zone, as can be seen from the poles.

A pole is an unmoving star, one at this end and another at the other. The axis is an intelligible line directed from pole to pole through the middle of the earth, around which the firmament revolves.

If the firmament revolved in a straight manner, one pole would be directly above the earth and the other beneath the earth, or at the sides of the earth. Since one pole is between the middle of the heavens and the side on our part, and the other is similarly situated on the opposite side, the line called the axis is oblique, and the firmament revolves obliquely around it.

Since we have sufficiently refuted the false opinion held by some concerning the firmament and have established our own by proof; since we have not been silent about the fixed stars in it, its circles, and its motion; let us begin to speak of the planets. And since we began with the highest of the elements, let us begin with the highest of the planets.

Saturn is therefore said to be the highest of the planets. It spends almost thirty years traversing the zodiac, and for this reason it is represented in the myths as an old man.

This star is said to be cold and harmful. Let us discuss first its coldness and then its harmfulness.

The ancient astrologers proved that this star is cold as follows. They knew that when the sun was in Cancer it scorched the earth, but they observed that in some years this happened less severely. Since they knew that this could not arise from the nature of the sun, they sought to discover which planet was in the same sign as the sun. When they found Saturn, they said that the cause of the coldness lay in him.

Someone may object: “Since the entire body of the stars is fiery in nature, as its motion and brightness prove, how can one star be called cold and another hot?”

We do not accept the explanation given by some who say that this results from proximity to water and earth. We have proved that frozen waters cannot exist above.

Some say instead that fire has several qualities, which are joined together in some bodies and separated in others. Thus, just as there is something fiery but not hot, so there is something bright but not hot.

They say that fiery things are hot only when they are near some dense and moist matter which they can transform into their own substance. Therefore, if a fiery thing lacks the proximity of dense moisture, its heat is absent.

They prove this by the sun, which produces great heat in valleys where the air is denser, but produces no such heat on the highest mountains because of the thinness of the air. The perpetual snows found there bear witness to this; we shall discuss it sufficiently when treating of the position of the earth.

These people also maintain that above the moon there is no heat because of the extreme thinness of the air.

We, however, say that the names of qualities are attributed to things in three ways: because of an effect, as wine is called hot because it produces heat, even though it is felt to be cold; because of sensation, as when we call boiling water hot, although it is naturally cold; or because of a sign, as when we say, “It is healthy to sleep well and to breathe without difficulty.”

When, therefore, a star is called cold, the term should be assigned to its effect. Although it is hot in itself, if it produces cold, it is called cold.

Thus Saturn, when joined with the sun, diminishes its heat; because of this effect he is called cold, even though he is hot in himself.

Someone may object: “If the bodies of the stars are fiery, how does it happen that some of them produce cold?”

We reply that a reason cannot be found for everything in every case, and that with some matters one must have recourse to the Creator. Nevertheless, we can offer this explanation: different fiery bodies heat more or less according to their proximity or distance.

Thus Saturn, because he is farther from us, does not heat the earth; the sun, because it is near the earth, scorches it more intensely.

Or let us say that, although a star may be hot, it contains certain qualities unknown to us because of which its heat cannot descend. But since we have raised the question in the midst of our discussion, and no one can comprehend everything, it will be the task of each person’s intelligence to investigate what he may discover for resolving this question.

This same star is called harmful because of its coldness, especially when it is retrograde. For this reason it is said in the myths to carry a sickle. In carrying a sickle, it does more harm while withdrawing than while approaching.

After Saturn comes Jupiter in the traversal of the zodiac, which it completes in twelve years. This star is benevolent, being temperate in its qualities, as has been demonstrated by its conjunction with the sun. But since it is midway between Saturn and Mars, if it is located in the upper or lower apse of its circle, their harmfulness is tempered, though its benevolence is diminished. Hence in the myths Jupiter is said to have expelled his father Saturn from the kingdom, because, having drawn nearer to Saturn, he removes his natural harmfulness. He is also said to have fathered various offspring by committing adultery, because by joining himself to the aforesaid planets he produces various effects in earthly things.

The third is Mars: a star, that is, hot and dry, and therefore harmful, traversing the zodiac in two years. But because it is placed between Jupiter and Venus, which are benevolent stars, it diminishes its harmfulness through their proximity, and likewise diminishes their benevolence.

It is said to rule in battles because it supplies heat and dryness, from which aggressiveness arises; for hot and dry people are aggressive.

The fourth, according to the Platonists, is Venus: a hot and moist star, and therefore benevolent, completing nearly a circuit of the zodiac in a year. She is said to have committed adultery with Mars because, being in the upper apse of her circle and thereby brought near to Mars, she is less benevolent. She is said to be the goddess of lust because she supplies heat and moisture, from which lust arises.

To speak briefly concerning Venus—something we shall explain at greater length when discussing the human being—hot and dry people greatly desire lust because of their heat, but because of their dryness they do not endure its effect. Cold and dry people have neither desire nor capacity, except rarely; and if they do engage in it, it harms them greatly. Cold and moist people, by contrast, desire it badly but do endure the effect; hot and moist people have both desire and capacity, and it is especially beneficial to bodies of that constitution.

This same star is called Lucifer and Hesperus. But Lucifer is seen only in the morning before the sun, whereas Hesperus can sometimes be seen in the evening. Hence the question arises whether Lucifer and Hesperus can occur at the same time of year. Some say that this is impossible. Since Venus has nearly the same speed as the sun and completes its course in nearly the same period of time, how could it follow the sun in the evening and precede it in the morning on one and the same night? Thus at one season of the year it precedes the sun, and then it is Lucifer; at another it follows it, and then it is Hesperus.

Others say that it is seen before sunrise and after sunset, but does not actually precede or follow the sun, for that is impossible. They say that this star is higher than the sun, and therefore remains visible longer in the evening, although it does not follow the sun, and appears earlier in the morning, although it does not precede it. Thus it is called Lucifer and Hesperus at the same season of the year, not because it precedes and follows the sun, but because, by virtue of its greater altitude, it is seen before and after it.

A third group says that Venus and Mercury are nearly alike in color and size and always accompany the sun. When they accompany it in this way, with one preceding and the other following, the one preceding is not visible in the evening because of the sun’s brilliance, whereas the one following appears after the sun has set. In the morning the reverse is the case: the one preceding is visible, while the one following is concealed by the daylight. But because they are alike in color and size, they have been regarded as one and the same star.

The fifth is Mercury, which likewise completes its course in approximately a year. Venus is said to have committed adultery with it because, when Mercury is in the lower apse of its circle, it mingles its qualities with hers.

The sixth is the sun. But before speaking of it, let us explain the position and retrogradation of all the planets mentioned above. Since the Chaldeans and their followers said that the sun is in the middle of the planets, above Venus and Mercury, whereas the Egyptians, whom Plato followed, called it the sixth and placed it below Mercury and Venus, let us first address this matter.

Some say that the sun is of an attractive nature. If those planets precede the sun, then, when they are near, it draws them toward itself; but when they are distant, it at least compels them to remain stationary until it has passed them. They demonstrate this by the analogy of a magnet and iron. Others say that they never stand still, but merely appear to do so, because, being of a fiery nature, they must always be in motion. Nevertheless, they sometimes appear to stand still because of *arsis* and *thesis*—elevation and depression.

All astrologers agree that each of the planets mentioned above sometimes moves farther from the earth than usual, and is then elevated. At other times it descends toward the earth more than usual; this is what we call depression. When they are elevated or depressed, if this occurs in a direct manner, they appear to remain under the same part of a sign while being elevated, and people believe that they stand still. But when this sometimes occurs backward, they appear to move backward.

[Col. 1146D–1147A] The cause of this elevation and depression is the sun. Since it is the source of all heat, it sometimes dries out the upper and lower regions more than usual. Thus, when the bodies of the stars have been dried, they rise because they are lighter than usual. If, on the other hand, they draw in more moisture than usual for their nourishment, they become more moist and heavy than usual, and therefore descend farther than usual.

Thus, when they are said to stand still, this is an astronomical expression, because that is how they appear.

Next we must explain why the Chaldeans call the sun the fourth, whereas the Egyptians and Plato call it the sixth. It is true that the sun is below Venus and Mercury, near the moon. Since the moon is cold and moist, it was necessary that the sun, which is hot and dry, be near it, so that through the sun’s heat the moon’s coldness, and through its dryness its moisture, might be tempered. Otherwise, since the moon is near the earth and consequently more dominant over it, if it came to the earth in an unbalanced condition, it would render the earth unbalanced as well.

Moreover, since the moon lacks its own light, as we have shown, and receives it from the sun, it was necessary that it be subject directly to the source of its light, without an intervening body.

Although this is truly the case, it nevertheless appeared otherwise to the Chaldeans, for the following reason. The sun, Mercury, and Venus are so associated that they complete their courses in nearly the same period of time, namely, a year. Their circles are therefore nearly equal, if the planets spend shorter or longer periods traversing the zodiac according to the size of their circles. Since they are nearly equal, one is not wholly contained within another. Their circles therefore intersect one another in such a way that the circle of Venus, in its lower part, intersects the upper parts of the circles of Mercury and the sun, encompassing more of the Mercurial circle than of the solar.

The circle of Mercury, in its upper part, intersects the Venusian circle and, in its lower part, the solar circle. The circle of the sun, in its upper part, intersects the Mercurial and Venusian circles, intersecting more of the Mercurial and less of the Venusian.

But because this is more easily grasped by the mind when presented to the eyes, we have shown that intersection in the following diagram, adding the circles of the other planets and the zodiac and dividing all of them into twelve parts, so that it may be apparent why, although the signs are of equal size, the sun moves farther in Gemini than in the other signs.

[Col. 1147] **ON THE COURSE OF THE PLANETS THROUGH THE ZODIAC**

[Col. 1147C] Since the circle of the sun is enclosed within the upper parts of those circles, it is rightly called lower than they. But because it sometimes happens that the sun travels through the upper parts of its circle while those stars travel through the lower parts of theirs, they then appear more freely. For the sun does not obscure things beneath it as much as it is considered to be above those things placed over it.

But let us now turn our treatment to the sun. Since the other planets move in the same manner as the sun, let us speak of the sun’s motion, so that similar matters may be understood concerning the others.

The general opinion of nearly all philosophers was that the firmament revolves from east to west, while the sun and the other planets move in the opposite direction, from west to east. They demonstrate this to the eyes by the arrangement of the signs. When Aries is positioned so that, when it is in the middle of the sky, Taurus lies between it and the east, followed by Gemini and then Cancer, while between that same point and the west are Pisces, followed by Aquarius and then Capricorn, as appears in the figure on the following page:

[Col. 1149] If, then, the sun were moving westward, it would pass from Aries into a sign situated toward the west, namely Pisces, and then into the remaining signs. Since, however, the sun passes from Aries into signs situated toward the east, namely Taurus and so forth, it would undoubtedly be moving from west to east.

They also add a reason why this must be so. When the firmament revolves from east to west, if the planets moved in the same manner, the force would be so great that nothing on earth could remain standing or alive. Therefore, in order to oppose the rapid motion of the firmament and temper its force, they were turned into motion contrary to it.

Although they are carried against the firmament, the firmament nevertheless carries them with it toward east and west. Thus, if someone on a ship moves against the direction in which the ship is traveling, the ship carries him wherever he goes, though he does not thereby cease moving in the opposite direction. Therefore, the gradual motion toward the east is natural motion; the daily movement toward east and west results from the force of the firmament.

Some, however, say that this cannot be so. Since the sun is not among the fixed stars in the firmament, how can it be carried by the firmament? If someone is outside a ship, how can the ship carry him?

Concerning their claim that the sun passes into the signs situated toward the west, they say that it appears to do so, but does not actually do so. Since they say that the firmament and the sun move naturally from east to west, when the sun is beneath the first part of Aries, and since the firmament is somewhat faster than the sun, the sun passes along with it into the thirtieth degree of a single sign. When the sun comes into view at sunrise, therefore, it is not the part of the sign that was previously seen above the sun that is now seen, but a later part. Thus, by passing in this way day after day, it appears to move toward the later signs, although it does not actually do so.

This can be demonstrated by the analogy of the moon. Although it is certain that the moon does not move northward, if clouds pass over it, then, as they pass across the moon, the moon appears to move northward against the clouds.

But since the most learned of all philosophers agrees with the former opinion, and since that opinion is true, let us accept it and answer the objection that the sun cannot be carried by the firmament because it is not within it. We may indeed say, according to our own opinion, that it is in the firmament, because we say that the aether is called the firmament. Nevertheless, even if it is not in the firmament, we say that it can be carried by it. To persist with the same example of the ship: if something light is beside the ship, it is carried by the ship’s force even though it is not in the ship. Therefore, since the sun is light and of a fiery nature, it can be carried by the firmament even if it is not within it.

[Col. 1150B] The sun and the other planets therefore move from west to east, not in a straight course but obliquely, sometimes descending toward the south and sometimes ascending toward our inhabited region, according to the arrangement of the signs mentioned above.

But someone may ask: What necessity was there for the sun to revolve obliquely rather than in a straight course?

**Response.** The necessity is great, as we shall show. First, let us explain what variations its oblique course produces, beginning from the more distant point, namely Capricorn.

When the sun enters Capricorn—which occurs in the middle of December, since the sun always enters a sign in the middle of a month and leaves it in the middle of the following month, and the sign is assigned to the month in which the sun enters it—it is then farthest from us, and our inhabited region is constricted by cold. Earth and water are naturally cold unless they are warmed by the sun.

Moreover, since there is no heat by which the air may dry, it thickens into clouds, which dissolve into rain. Hence arises a certain variation of the year called winter.

Winter is cold and moist. It continues until the sun has passed through Aquarius and Pisces, entering the former in the middle of January and the latter in the middle of February. It therefore lasts three months, and the same is true of each of the four seasons.

During this season the pores of the earth’s surface are constricted, and heat cannot evaporate. Remaining within, it nourishes the roots of herbs and trees and takes the place of a pregnant mother, but it does not contribute to growth, because neither heat nor moisture—the sources of growth—can rise on account of the constriction caused by the cold.

Where frost, snow, hail, rain, thunder, and lightning come from, we shall discuss when treating of the air.

Water, phlegm, and old age resemble this season, for all are cold and moist. In it choleric people fare better and phlegmatic people worse; young people fare better and the extremely old worse. The worst illness is one arising from phlegm, such as quotidian fever; the less harmful is one arising from choler, such as tertian fever. During this season it is beneficial to increase one’s food.

The pores of the human body are constricted by the cold, and heat cannot evaporate. Remaining inside, it consumes more; therefore, to counteract the internal digestion, one must supply external nourishment. Hence among the ancients the god of winter was depicted with a fat belly and was called Spurius because of the filth of the marsh. During this season it is good to use hot and dry things.

Then the sun ascends until it reaches Aries, which it enters in the middle of March. It is neither too far from us nor too near, being situated in the middle of the torrid zone. Hence the air of our inhabited region is neither too hot nor cold, neither too moist nor dry, but is tempered among the four qualities.

Because of this tempering, the pores open, and moist vapor evaporates, rising through the roots of herbs and trees and contributing to their growth and vitality. Hence one month of this season is called April, as though *aperilis*, “opening,” because then the earth opens into flowers.

Its characteristic is changeability: sometimes rainy because of its proximity to winter, sometimes dry because of its proximity to summer; sometimes hot for the same reason, sometimes cold. Hence people often fall ill in March, because when human bodies have been opened by heat, they are immediately corrupted by sudden cold.

But if someone could preserve himself during this season with sufficient caution, he would fall ill later in it than in the other seasons.

Someone may object: Why, then, if a person enters winter with some illness, does he not die as often in winter as in spring? Since illnesses arise from bad humors spreading through the limbs, the humors are broken up by the cold of winter and cannot flow outward. Through the heat of spring, however, they are dissolved; as they course through the limbs, the person succumbs and dies.

This temperate season begins with Aries and continues while the sun is in Taurus and Gemini, entering the first in the middle of April and the second in the middle of May.

Air, blood, and childhood resemble this season because they are hot and moist. Melancholic people fare better in it and sanguine people worse; the old fare better and children worse. The worst illness is one arising from blood, such as synochus; the less harmful is one arising from melancholy, such as quartan fever. During this season it is suitable to use cold and dry things.

When the sun ascends as far as Cancer, it burns and dries the earth through its proximity. Hence summer is hot and dry.
