It begins in the middle of June, when the sun enters Cancer, and continues while the sun is in Leo, which it enters in the middle of July, and while it is in Virgo, which it enters in the middle of August.

It is characteristic of this season to dry the roots of herbs and trees. Fire, choler, and youth resemble it, for these are hot and dry. Phlegmatic people fare better in it and choleric people worse; the extremely old fare better and the young worse. The worst illness is one arising from choler, such as tertian fever; the less harmful is one arising from phlegm. During this season it is beneficial to use cold and moist things. Drink should be increased and food reduced.

For the pores of the body are opened by the heat, and natural heat evaporates; consequently food is not digested as well. But because drink quickly passes into the blood, it should be increased.

Here a question arises. Since these variations in the seasons are said to occur through the sun’s nearness and remoteness, while the sun, when in Leo, is as far from our inhabited region as when it is in Gemini, and when in Virgo as when it is in Taurus, and when in Libra as when it is in Aries, why does it produce heat and moisture in those seasons, heat and dryness in two of them, and cold and dryness in the third?

The answer is that, when it is in the three spring signs, because it is near us it produces heat; because of the proximity of the preceding winter, it produces moisture. But when it is in Leo and Virgo, it produces heat because of its proximity. Since, however, the moisture has already been dried up by the heat of spring and summer, there is nothing by which the heat can be tempered, nor is there any source of moisture. Hence the season is hot and dry.

When the sun is in Libra, because the moisture has by then been completely dried up and the heat extinguished, autumn arises, cold and dry. In it, fruits that contain moisture internally, such as grapes, are ripened and gathered through a double dryness, namely, that of autumn.

Autumn begins in the middle of September, when the sun enters Libra, and lasts while the sun is in Scorpio and Sagittarius, entering the former in the middle of October and the latter in the middle of November.

Earth, melancholy, and old age resemble this season because they are cold and dry. Sanguine people fare better in it and melancholic people worse; children fare better and the old worse. The worst illness is one arising from melancholy; the less harmful is one arising from blood.

To speak generally, in every season of the year the worst illness is one produced by a humor resembling the season. The qualities of the season increase the material of the disease. The less harmful is produced by a humor contrary to the season, since the quality of the season diminishes the material of the disease.

During this season it is beneficial to use hot and moist things. This season is unstable because of its proximity to the preceding summer and the following winter. For this reason, and because of the juices of the fruits then abundant, imprudent people are endangered.

Here a question similar to the previous one arises. Since the sun, when in Scorpio, is as far from us as when it is in Pisces, and when in Sagittarius as when it is in Aquarius, why does it sometimes produce one set of qualities in these signs and sometimes another?

The solution is easy. In the former signs, namely Scorpio and Sagittarius, because moisture has been dried up by the summer and the sun has already passed through the middle of the torrid zone, there are cold and dryness. In the other signs it is similarly distant, and therefore there is cold; but because the heat that dries the air has long since weakened, the air gradually thickens into clouds, and the season becomes moist.

Thus, as was stated above, winter is very cold and moist: at its end it is more moist and less cold, while in the middle it is equally cold and moist. Spring at its beginning is more moist and less hot; at its end it is hotter and less moist; in the middle it is equally balanced.

It should be noted, however, that although these are the four seasonal properties as they occur accidentally, they nevertheless vary. If, for example, a hot and dry planet such as Mars is with the sun in the winter signs, the season is hot and dry contrary to nature. Similarly, if a cold and moist planet is with the sun in summer, the season is cold and moist contrary to nature.

Therefore a prudent physician must always consider which sign the sun occupies and which planet is with it in the same sign, so that he may know what kind of summer or other season will follow and may have a remedy ready against the coming quality.

Since the sun produces these variations by ascending and descending obliquely, let us see what evil would follow if it always revolved in a straight course. No one doubts that, if it always revolved as near to us as it is in summer, we would always have heat and nothing could grow. Similarly, if it were always as distant as it is in winter, there would always be the severity of cold, and neither fruits nor herbs would arise from the earth.

But someone may say: If it moved as it does in Aries, so that it always remained equally distant from us, it would always produce the temperate conditions of spring, and no evil would result.

We reply that a very great evil would result. The earth would never conceive anything within itself, as it does in winter; nor would any fruits that might arise proceed to maturity. Without them no living creature could survive.

Since we have said that the elements, the seasons of the year, the humors, the bodily constitutions, and the ages resemble one another, let us show in the accompanying figure what corresponds to what. (See the first figure on the following page.)

Since we have sufficiently explained the sun’s natural motion and what it accomplishes by ascending and descending obliquely, it follows that we should speak of what it accomplishes while being carried by the firmament.

Although the sun strives against the firmament by its natural motion from west to east, it is nevertheless carried daily by the firmament toward the west. When it is above the earth, it produces light, which is called day. When it is beneath the earth, darkness occupies the upper region, and this is called night.

It must be observed that one day is natural and another customary. Let us discuss the natural day first and then the customary day.

A natural day is a period of twenty-four hours containing the customary day and night. Hence we say that there are thirty days in a month, although it contains both days and nights.

The philosophers divided this day into four parts. From the ninth hour of the night to the third hour of the customary day they called it hot and moist; from the third hour of the customary day to the ninth, hot and dry; from the ninth hour of that day to the third hour of the night, cold and dry; and from the third hour of the night to the ninth, cold and moist.

Hence certain illnesses are better or worse during different parts of the same day, according to the reasoning stated above concerning the seasons.

A customary day is the period during which the sun is carried from sunrise to sunset. They divided this natural day into four parts. In the first part the sun is red; then it shines; afterward it gives heat; and finally it descends and is tempered.

Hence in the myths four horses are assigned to Phoebus, bearing names corresponding to these properties. The first is called Erytheus, that is, “red”; the second Actaeus, that is, “shining”; the third Lampas, that is, “burning”; and the fourth Philogeus, that is, “loving the earth.”

Three variations occur in these customary days during the year. Sometimes they are equal to the nights, sometimes longer, and sometimes shorter. The cause of these variations is as follows.

When the sun is in the winter signs, the swelling of the earth—which lies in the middle of the torrid zone between us and the sun—takes the sun away from us so that we do not see it quickly, and this is why it is quickly removed from our eyes. Thus the brightness above the earth is brief for us, and the day is short; the shadow is long, and therefore the night is long.

But when the sun is in Cancer and the other summer signs, because it rises on this side of the swelling, it is seen quickly in the morning and is removed slowly from our eyes. Thus the brightness above the earth is prolonged and the shadow is short.

When it is in Aries or Libra, because it is equally distant from us, it is for equal periods above and below the earth. Hence the brightness is equal and the darkness equal.

Having enumerated the effects of the sun arising both from its natural motion and from its accidental motion, let us speak of its eclipse, explaining how and at what time it occurs.

For clarity, we state that just as the length of the zodiac is divided into twelve parts called signs, so its breadth is divided into twelve parts called *evaginations*. The moon touches these twelve parts of the breadth, while the sun passes through the middle, as the accompanying diagram shows.

[Col. 1153B] Since the sun always travels through the middle of the breadth, if this occurs on the day of conjunction, the moon is in the middle of that same breadth. It is then positioned directly between the earth and the sun; and if a line were drawn from the earth through the middle of the lunar and solar bodies, as in the figure on the following page—

[Col. 1155A] **A USEFUL FIGURE OF THE ECLIPSE OF THE SUN**

[Col. 1155C] If the intervening moon causes the sun’s rays to be eclipsed, they cannot descend to the earth because of the moon’s obstruction. Hence this never occurs except at the thirtieth or twenty-ninth moon, because on no other day is the moon with the sun at the degree of conjunction.

It does not, however, occur at every thirtieth or twenty-ninth moon; rather, whenever it does occur, it occurs on one of those days. For if, at conjunction, the moon is not in the middle of the breadth of the zodiac but on one side or the other—the accompanying diagram does not show this—it cannot deprive us of the sight of the sun or prevent its rays from descending to us.

But since we have discussed the sun as fully as we can, let us now discuss the moon.

[Col. 1155D] Because of its proximity to water and earth, the moon has a denser body than the other stars. Hence it has neither its own light nor its own heat, but is kindled by the sun.

If it possessed its own heat, then, since it is near the earth and each month ascends to Cancer and descends to Capricorn, it would produce in the earth the heat of summer and the cold of winter every month. Nothing could survive amid such continuous variations.

It therefore lacks both light and heat. Nevertheless, it is illuminated by the sun placed above it—not always equally, as far as we are concerned, but sometimes as a new moon, sometimes as a full moon, and sometimes as an interlunium.

Let us see, then, how this occurs.

Some say that when the moon is beneath the sun in the same sign, it is obscured by the sun’s excessive brilliance and cannot appear; but when it moves away from the sun, its light begins to appear on one side. Thus, the farther it moves from the sun, the greater the light that appears in it; the nearer it is to the sun, the less there is.

But if, because it is nearer the sun, less light appears in it, then, the farther away it is, the greater light should first appear on the side opposite the sun. Since it first appears on the side facing the sun, their opinion seems false.

Our own view is that every luminous body, when something dark is placed beneath it, casts a shadow on the side opposite itself and light on its own side. Since the moon, as we stated above, is naturally dark and is placed beneath the sun, the sun places light on its opposite side—that is, toward the earth it casts a shadow. Hence the moon is not visible to us.

But when it moves away from the sun, a little light begins to appear in the shape of a slender horn; it is then called *monoides*. The farther it moves from the sun, the more light descends upon it, so that on the seventh day it appears *dichotomos*, that is, divided through the middle.

It should be noted that as much light as descends, so much shadow rises, and conversely. After the seventh day and until the fourteenth, it is *amphicirtus*, that is, less than full but greater than half.

On the fourteenth day, because it is removed from the sun by a diameter—a fact that can be proved from the circumstance that it rises when the sun sets—the whole shadow has risen and all the light has descended. It is then *panselenos*, that is, a full moon.

Afterward it begins to approach the sun, the shadow to descend, and the light to rise. It first becomes *amphicirtos* as it descends, then *dichotomos*, and finally *monoides*. All these matters will be clearer in a diagram placed before the eyes.

The explanation of a lunar eclipse is as follows. When the sun and moon are positioned on the aforementioned ecliptic line in such a way that the sun is in the lower hemisphere and the moon in the upper, with the earth between them, if a line were drawn from the middle of the lunar body through the middle of the earth and the solar body in the following manner, then the swelling of the intervening earth would direct a shadow to a certain point, namely, as far as the moon itself.

Consequently, the sun’s rays cannot kindle it, and it suffers an eclipse until, by moving, it has passed beyond the swelling; then light begins to appear in it.

Hence the moon does not fail except at the fifteenth or fourteenth moon, because then it is opposite the sun. Yet this does not occur at every fifteenth moon; whenever it occurs, it occurs on one of those days.

Let us explain why it does not occur at every such time. This happens because of the shape of the earth’s shadow. First let us explain the shapes of shadows produced when a round body of a certain size is placed opposite a luminous body of the same size.

Every such shadow of a body is either *cylindroides*, *calathoidēs*, or *conoidēs*.

A cylinder is a long or rounded figure that increases uniformly and does not meet lines at its summit. Hence a shadow is called *cylindroides* when it has the form produced whenever the luminous and dark bodies are of equal size, as follows.

Since the sun and the earth are not equal in size—for the sun is eight times larger than the earth—the earth’s shadow cannot be *cylindroides*.

A *calathus* is a figure extending from a point into a broad form. Hence a shadow of this kind is called *calathoidēs*. It occurs when the luminous body is smaller than the dark body. The earth’s shadow therefore cannot be *calathoidēs*, because, as Macrobius proves, the sun is larger than the earth.

A cone, by contrast, is a figure extending from a broad form to a point, the opposite of a *calathus*. A shadow is called *conoidēs* when it extends from broad to pointed; it occurs when the luminous body is larger than the dark body. In the present case, the earth’s shadow is therefore *conoidēs*.

When the sun and moon are positioned as we have described, the cone of the earth’s shadow extends directly toward the moon, affects it, and prevents it from receiving rays from the sun until it has passed beyond the cone of the earth’s shadow.

But if the fifteenth moon is not positioned in this way, with one body somewhat toward the north and the other toward the south, the cone of the shadow is not directed straight toward the moon and does not affect it, but lies beside it in the following manner.

[Col. 1157A] **ON THE ECLIPSE OF THE MOON**

[Col. 1158A] **ON THE MOON, THE SUN, AND THE EARTH**

[Col. 1159] **ON THE ECLIPSE OF ALL THE PLANETS**

[Col. 1159A] Having seen how a lunar eclipse occurs and why it does not occur every month, let us say what seems to us concerning the shadow that is always seen in its middle.

Although the body of the moon is naturally dark, in some parts it is beaten and polished like a mirror, while in others it is rough and rusty. Wherever it is polished, therefore, it shines from the sun’s rays; but wherever it is rough, it retains its natural darkness.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1159] **PROLOGUE**

[Col. 1159A] Although we are occupied with the work of teaching and have little time for writing, nevertheless, because we recognize that many people have cut off the garments of philosophy and, seizing its scraps, have gone away believing that the whole of it had fallen to their share, we have been roused by the voice of philosophy herself crying out. To prevent her from remaining naked, we sew the pieces that have been cut off together with the pen of our small ability.

We are not unaware that we are subject to the bites of envy, since today it is dangerous both to know and to possess. But, as someone says:

> Nothing is more justly subject to envy than the author himself,  
> whom it immediately gnaws, torturing his mind and limbs [OCR uncertain];  
> the tyrants of Sicily found no greater torment  
> than envy.

Certain of their torment, and not doubting the many bites of venomous men, let us proceed to what follows, pursuing the truth like Cato through the heat of Libya, armed with various arguments as against the tongues of the small-minded.

And since we have sufficiently instructed the reader concerning the aether and its adornment, let us now teach concerning the air joined to and subject beneath it, showing what things occur in it and from what causes.

## CATALOGUE OF BOOK III

[Col. 1159]

[Col. 1159B] Concerning the air.—Why there are five zones in the air and not in the aether.—Why the upper fire is not burning hot.—From where rains come.—Why the sun heats the earth but the upper fire does not.—How it raises moisture upward.—Why it appears that blood rains.—Concerning the rainbow.—From where hail comes.—From where snow comes.—Why snow does not occur in summer, but hail does.—Concerning thunder and lightning.—Why lightning occurs in summer.—Concerning the fact that stars appear to fall.—Concerning comets.—Concerning the position of water.—Concerning the ebb and flow of the ocean.—From where the waves of the sea come.—Concerning the origin of winds.—Why some water is fresh and some salty.—From where springs come.—From where wells come.—Why the water of a well and a spring is cold in summer but not in winter.—From where burning comes.—From where the Flood comes.—Why humors increase during a lunar cycle and decrease.

# BOOK III BEGINS

[Col. 1159]

[Col. 1159C] Air, then, extends from the moon down to the earth; the nearer it is to the earth, the more humid and dense it is, while the farther removed it is, the drier and brighter. Since it lies beneath the sun, it receives heat and light from it. But because the sun never exceeds the boundaries of the torrid zone, it kindles that part of the air through its proximity; the more distant parts, deprived of its heat, become cold through their proximity to water and earth. Those situated between them are tempered on both sides by the contrary extremes. Thus there are five divisions in the air, which the ancients called the five zones—not, as some believe, above the moon. For there everything is [Col. 1160C] unchanging, since there is no contrariety. Since there is the aether there, which is called fire, and the bodies of the stars are fiery, where could cold exist in any part?

But I know that these people have gone astray through the words of the philosophers, who declare that there are five zones in the heavens, as Virgil says: “Five zones hold the heavens.” Against this we have a twofold defense. The first is that air is often called heaven. Hence the expression, “the birds of heaven.” The second is that the five parts of the aether are placed above the five parts of the air, and each part of the aether is called by the name of the part of the air situated beneath it. Thus the part situated above the cold [zone] is called cold, although there is no [Col. 1161A] cold in it; and the part situated above the torrid [zone] is called torrid, not because there is any heat or burning in the aether. For the upper region is so subtle that it cannot kindle anything until it mixes with something humid and dense.

These same divisions exist in the earth beneath the air, for the quality of the air permeates the earth. Thus there are five divisions in the earth and five zones in the air. Let us therefore discuss the air situated above our habitable region, showing what variations occur in it and from what causes, beginning with rain, which is common to every season.

The causes of rain are sometimes different. At times dense vapor evaporates, and as the humid vapor rises, the tiniest drops envelop themselves in it; when these become larger and heavier, they fall, and rain results. At other times the air is thickened by the cold of the earth and water and passes into an aqueous substance, which, dissolved by the sun’s heat like ice by fire, falls in tiny particles. Sometimes the sun draws up moisture to sustain itself, and whatever in it is more fluid passes into a fiery substance, while whatever is heavier falls downward. Hence we see an inundation of rain occurring after extremely intense heat.

A question arises: since it is characteristic of fire to move upward, why do the sun’s rays and heat move toward the earth? To this we reply that the sun is of a fiery nature—not because it consists solely of fire, but because fire predominates in it. For we have already explained that the bodies of the stars are made from the four elements, though fire predominates. Since, then, they consist of the four elements, whatever in the sun comes from water and earth tends toward what is similar to itself, despite the predominance of fire. But because it proceeds from the source of heat, it carries some heat with it, by which earth and water are warmed. And since it is the nature of heat to rise, the heat that had descended in the manner described, returning upward, draws some moisture with it and, by boiling, transforms it into its own substance.

If, therefore, we wish to speak precisely, we shall say that the sun raises moisture upward rather than draws it toward itself. It is therefore called the source of heat, because it warms what lies beneath it, [Col. 1161C] whereas the upper fire does not. Since it is an element not made from the elements, there is nothing in it that can descend toward the lower regions. Hence the part of the air and earth beneath the sun is hot, while the more distant parts are cold, even though they are subject to the aether.

Someone may say: Is not fire hot wherever it is? To this we reply: only when it is mixed with something dense and humid. Although, therefore, there is fire above the moon, it is not like the lower fire. The humid and dense material by which fire is kindled is lacking there; there is neither cold nor darkness, but a single continuous brightness and no changeability.

But they will say that Aristotle declares: “It is impossible for fire not to be hot.” We reply that Aristotle was speaking there of this lower fire, which, always mixed with some dense material, never ceases to be hot. Or we may say that he means that fire is hot not in actuality but by nature.

The fourth cause of rain is wind, which raises moisture from ponds, rivers, and lakes. Hence many people have seen frogs and fish falling from the air. For when, as we said above, water is lifted by the wind, it happens that it raises frogs and fish with it; when these descend because of their natural heaviness, ignorant observers are astonished.

No season of the year, then, is free from rain. In every season either humid vapor evaporates, or the air is thickened by cold, or moisture is raised by heat or wind. Sometimes this rain, becoming denser than usual and inflamed by excessive heat, turns red and thick, like blood. Those who see this and are ignorant of natural philosophy say that blood is raining.

This is the basis of the plausible statement that drops of blood will fall before the end of this age, since the world is destined to end by burning, as Scripture testifies when it says: “Fire will blaze in the presence of …” [the text is incomplete]. For water suspended in the clouds by heat will be thickened by intense heat; when it has been inflamed and made red, it will fall in the likeness of blood.

And since, in rainy weather, a many-colored arc appears in the clouds, let us explain from what cause it arises and why so many colors appear in it. When we say that the sun’s heat raises moisture, or that humid vapor evaporates, water illuminated in the cloud—like water in a glass vessel—shows a red color where it is thinner and warmer through the sun’s radiance; where it is denser, it shows purple or black. This is why that arc shines only on the side opposite the sun. For the air near the sun is so illuminated by its radiance that different colors do not appear in it.

Having considered the causes of rain and the rainbow, let us discuss hail. When moisture is raised in the manner described, it often happens that a cold and dry wind is present in the upper regions. By its dryness and cold it freezes the drops of water and transforms them into a stony substance. Since the drops are round—as can be proved by the round holes they make in stone through the continual falling of water—hail descends round.

Snow is formed when the drops described above are thickened and frozen before they become large. Here someone may object: Since hail often occurs in summer, why does snow never occur during that season around the lower parts of the mountains? To this we reply that in summer moisture is raised by the heat; as it rises, the drops become enclosed, and after becoming larger and being frozen by the cold, they produce hail. In winter, however, there is cold around the earth, and it happens that the drops of water are constricted by the cold of the season before they become large and are transformed into snow. In summer, by contrast, because there is no cold around the earth, they do not freeze until, having risen high, they have become large and dense. Snow therefore never occurs in summer, although hail often does.

Let us discuss thunder and lightning: whence and how they occur. When humid vapor, as we said above, rises to the upper regions and reaches the highest part of the air, the upper air is set in motion by the weight of the moisture. Its particles, meeting one another like waves of water, produce the crash of thunder. Through this movement the air is heated and passes into a fiery substance, producing a flash. Although the flash occurs together with the crash, it reaches us sooner because sight is faster than hearing.

When the aforesaid particles collide, a force is generated. If it rises upward, there is a crash without lightning. If that force is directed downward but is not strong enough to reach an obstruction, there is still no lightning. When it reaches an obstruction, however, it splits whatever blocks its way. But because it is characteristic of the motion of air to move upward, and because no material prevents its exit, it turns back and gathers up the fires that have been scattered.

If, however, there is much moisture in this lower part of the air, the air involved in that force cannot burn; lightning results that splits but does not burn. Lightning, then, is some portion of the air that, driven by a collision, comes with force as far as an obstruction. Thunder, on the other hand, is the differing impact of portions of the air.

Lightning is therefore not a stony substance, as some assert. If it were stony, it would not move back and forth, nor would it return again; and when it struck something, it would crush flesh and bones. This is why lightning more often lays low things that are high: when it descends obliquely, it returns more quickly to the heights.

But since some maintain that a certain kind of lightning is a stony substance, lest we seem through ignorance or envy to have disparaged or concealed their view, we shall state it briefly. They say that when humid vapor rises to the upper regions, some earthly substance is raised with it. Through the sun’s heat this substance is thickened into a stony mass and is held in the hollow of the clouds until the cloud is divided by some force; then, driven out, that stone strikes something high.

Someone may ask: Since humid vapor rises in every season of the year, as we said above, why do thunder and lightning not occur in every season? To this we reply that although they arise from ascending humid vapor, they do not occur until the vapor reaches the highest part of the air. This can be demonstrated by an analogy with the sea. When the seabed is disturbed by the density produced by vapor rising from the earth, the sea cannot yet be driven this way and that. But when that disturbance reaches the surface, the waves are driven back and forth, and a storm arises.

That a storm begins at the bottom of the sea can be proved by the fact that we see seals stirring the waves beforehand. As Pliny says, they are creatures inclined to sleep; nevertheless, when vapor, as we said above, disturbs the seabed, they are roused and rise to the surface. Seeing this, sailors—certain from experience, though uncertain about natural philosophy—predict that a storm is coming, since the storm has already begun at the bottom.

The same is true in the air. While vapor occupies the lower parts of the air, its density prevents it from driving the air back and forth. But when it reaches the highest region, because of the air’s mobility it drives it this way and that, and thunder and lightning arise.

In winter, although the air is dense, there is not enough heat for the dense vapor to be raised all the way to the highest region; nor does this happen in spring. Remaining, therefore, in the upper part of the air, it produces winds and rain. In summer, when the heat is greatest, it rises all the way to the top, and the various parts of the air collide with one another; hence thunder and lightning occur. In autumn, however, because it is cold and dry, there is neither moisture to be raised nor heat to raise it.

[Col. 1163B] In this same air stars appear to fall, although none falls. Since they are fiery by nature, and since their original place is the aether, they never descend to earth. Moreover, since they are enormous—even if they appear small because of their distance—if one of them fell, it would cover the whole earth or most of it.

They do not fall, then, but appear to fall. For there is often wind and disturbance in the upper regions of the air, even when there is none in the lower regions. Through this disturbance, fiery and shining air travels through the air. When it begins to shine near a particular star, it removes from us the sight of that star by its own brightness, and the star seems to have fallen.

Someone may ask: Why, then, do we not see the star itself afterward? To this we reply that the same star is seen by us afterward, but it is not recognized as the same one. For when, as we said above, the fiery air rushes past, denser air follows slowly behind it. Placed between us and that star, it removes the star from our sight. But before this air passes, the star itself has moved on, and the firmament appears—which is always moving toward the setting—and has carried that star farther with it. When the star reappears, because it is seen in a different place from where it was before, it is thought to be another star.

Concerning the comet, which appears at a change of imperial rule, our view is that it is not a star. It is neither one of the fixed stars nor a planet. That it is not one of the fixed stars is shown by the fact that its motion can be perceived. Nor is it a planet, since it is often seen outside the zodiac and does not follow the motion of the planets.

Furthermore, if it were a star, it would be in some hemisphere. When, therefore, the stars of that hemisphere appear, why does this one, which appears larger, not appear? It is not a star, then, but a fire kindled by the Creator’s will in order to signify something.

Since we have passed rapidly over the air and what occurs in the air, in accordance with our deliberate brevity, let us begin to speak of water and its position. Divine Wisdom, perceiving that nothing can live without heat and moisture, and that earth and water are cold, placed the source of all heat—that is, the sun—above the middle of the earth, so that it might warm the earth equally on both sides and allow something to live in it. But since nothing could live by heat alone, Wisdom placed the source of moisture beneath that same source of heat, in its midst; from these two, the earth is tempered on both sides.

The source of moisture therefore surrounds the earth in the middle of the torrid zone, in the manner of the equinoctial circle, and is properly called the sea. When this sea reaches the West, it produces two currents there, one turning toward the South and the other toward the North, following the sides of the earth. It does the same in the East, producing two currents that turn toward the regions mentioned. When the western current turning toward the North and the eastern current likewise turning toward the North meet one another, the sea is driven backward by the rebound and becomes the famous advance and retreat of the Ocean, which is called the sea’s waves. The other two currents meet similarly at the other end of the earth.

There are others who say that the cause of sea waves is the mountains lying beneath the sea. When the sea reaches them, it falls backward and rises, so that the channel behind is filled while the channel in front is emptied; when it returns again, the rear is emptied and the front is filled.

The aforesaid western current, turning toward the North, follows the sides of the earth and, touching Africa, reaches its extremity. Between Calpe and Atlas, as far as Jerusalem, it is called the Mediterranean Sea, receiving different names from different regions. If anyone wishes to know how it rises and falls, and what names it takes from which regions, let him consult a map of the world. But because what is presented to the eyes enters the mind more easily, let us place before the eyes, in the form of a diagram, what we are describing.

The aforesaid western current, turning toward the North, is called the Atlantic Sea from the adjacent Atlas mountain; England and the neighboring islands lie within it. From the eastern current turning toward the North arises the Indian Sea. Likewise, it must be believed that different seas arise from the other currents turning toward the South. But these should not be described on the basis of our own testimony, since, because of the intervening torrid zone, the position of those regions remains unknown to us.

And since it is our view that winds arise from these currents, let us discuss the origin of winds, both the cardinal and the collateral winds. When, as we said above, two currents divide in the West from the source of all moisture, one toward the South and the other toward the North, the air is set in motion by this separation of the waters. But if the impulse is strong enough to reach us, it produces the wind called Zephyr.

The two eastern currents, by their division and movement, produce the wind called Eurus. When the eastern and western currents turning toward the South meet one another in the middle, the air is set in motion and the northern wind, called Boreas, is produced. It is cold because it arises in the cold zone; it is dry because from this angle of the earth it drives the clouds toward the middle. It is therefore rainy near the boundaries of the torrid zone. When it crosses the torrid zone, it becomes warm; and although it is cold for us, it is warm there.

Similarly, when the two currents turning toward the South meet one another in the middle, Auster is generated. Although beyond the torrid zone it is cold and dry, as Boreas is among us, since it arises in the cold zone, nevertheless, because it crosses the torrid zone, it reaches us warmed and hot. By driving the clouds before it toward the corner of the earth in which we live, it produces rain for us. Thus it is hot and humid for us by accident, although in its own region it is cold and dry.

Having seen from where the four cardinal winds arise, let us see from where the four collateral winds arise. If, among the two currents described above that turn toward the North and generate Boreas in the manner explained, the eastern current happens, through some circumstance, to be faster and meets the western current beyond the midpoint of the North, a collateral wind arises between Boreas and Zephyr.

If the western current meets the eastern beyond the midpoint, now from one side and now from the other, it generates two collateral winds: one between Eurus and Auster, the other between Eurus and Zephyr. But since setting a figure before the eyes will lessen our labor, let us make one similar to the preceding, in which the currents do not meet at the midpoint, as they do in the case of the cardinal winds, so that from this figure we may understand the collateral winds. Since we could not show more than two in a single figure, let the others be understood by analogy with these.

Someone may ask: If winds arise from the aforesaid currents, and the currents divide and meet every day—as the daily waves of the sea testify—why do winds not occur every day? To this we reply that although they occur every day, they do not always produce an impulse strong enough to reach us. It often happens that we do not think there is any wind when it is present in other regions or in the higher parts of the air, though it is not felt by us.

There are nevertheless some who say that caves are the cause of winds. When portions of the air enter them because of their mobility, one portion entering strives to force another out, and a conflict arises by which the disturbed air generates wind. Hence Aeolia, a region full of caves, is called the land of winds. Others say that ascending humid vapor, through its weight, disturbs the air and generates wind. We, however, say that the second, the first, and the third are all causes of winds.

After explaining the source of all moisture and the origin of winds, let us explain why some water is salty. By nature, then, the taste of water is insipid; hence natural phlegm is insipid. Through an accidental cause, however, it becomes salty. The explanation is as follows: Since the sea, as we said above, lies beneath the torrid zone, it is thickened by heat and becomes salty. It is certainly established that through boiling water passes into salt.

Someone may object: If all waters are born from this salty source and return to it, as Solomon testifies when he says, “To the places from which the waters issue they return”—for we must not believe that waters are annihilated, but that they return in a circle—why, then, are some waters sweet and others salty?

The solution is this: Since the earth is full of caves, water enters it through its mobility. Passing through cataracts, it is filtered and thinned and loses its salty taste. When it bursts forth onto the surface of the earth, it produces springs and streams of sweet taste.

But there is disagreement about the source from which wells obtain their moisture. If they originated from cataracts, someone may argue, they would fill and flow away. To this we reply that although they originate from cataracts, they are not filled in that way. For it happens that the cataracts do not end there but continue on both sides. Thus the water of a well passes beyond, but does not boil upward. Where there is a spring, however, the cataract ends. There the water of the well, unable to flow farther because of the density of the earth, is forced to boil upward.

Others say that wells do not originate from cataracts but from the sweat of the earth. When the earth contains some moisture and has been pierced, drops of water descend like a person’s sweat; this is the water of a well.

We, however, think that both causes account for wells. That they derive from cataracts is proved by the fact that well water is immediately found near rivers, and by the frequent occurrence that, when one well is made after another, the water is taken away from the first. That they derive from the sweat of the earth is proved by the fact that well water is found in dry and elevated places.

The reason that water from a well or spring is warm in winter and cold in summer is as follows. Since winter is naturally cold, the pores of the earth contract because of the cold, and heat cannot evaporate. Remaining inside, it warms the earth and the water. In summer, however, when the pores at the surface of the earth are opened by heat, vapor evaporates and the heat is diminished; therefore the water emerging from within comes out cold.

Thus well water is coldest in summer; spring water, because it is nearer to the warm air, is less cold; river water is still less cold, and rainwater less cold than that. If sweet water is therefore produced by being filtered through the cataracts of the earth, those waters that issue from the aforesaid source of moisture across the surface of the earth, rather than through cataracts, are dense and salty, and are called seas.

And since it was the common opinion of the philosophers that the earthly world ends sometimes through a flood and sometimes through burning, let us see how each occurs. Since water, as we said above, lies beneath the source of heat, it happens that moisture gradually increases and surpasses heat, until it grows to such a degree that, restrained by no shores, it spreads across the earth and submerges the land.

When this moisture has been dried up by the sun’s heat and by the dryness of the earth, it happens that heat gradually increases and surpasses moisture, until it grows to such a degree that, spreading across the lands, it burns them.

Some say that this occurs through the common elevation or depression of the planets. If all the planets rise together and are farther removed from the earth than usual, they consume less moisture. Hence the increasing moisture spreads across the lands, and a flood results. [Col. 1166B] But if one, two, or three rise without the others, moisture does not increase, since what increases through the elevation of those planets is dried up through the proximity of the others.

If all the planets are depressed together, they burn the lands through their proximity, and burning results, because what the former do more intensely through proximity, the latter do less intensely through remoteness.

It should be noted that one flood is universal and another particular. A universal flood cannot be continuous, but another can; thus temporal things perish alternately. Since, therefore, the world was destroyed by a flood in the time of Noah, this present world will end through burning.

But since, at the end of this volume, an account has been given of the sea, let us consider why its waves diminish during the first seven days of the lunar cycle, increase during the next seven, diminish during the third week, and increase during the fourth.

When there is conjunction of the moon and sun, since all the sun’s radiance that kindles the moon is above the air, it cannot thin what lies beneath or dry up the moisture; the waves are therefore then full. But when the radiance begins to descend, the moon is kindled, dries the air, and diminishes the moisture. The farther the radiance descends, the more the moisture is dried, and this continues until the seventh day.

On the seventh day, however, because the moon is kindled over its entire half, it warms the moisture through the intervening air. The moisture boils and rises upward, and thus the waves increase until the fourteenth day. But because during the third week the heat that raises the moisture in the moon diminishes, the waves of the sea decrease. During the fourth week, however, because the heat fails as the radiance rises, the air becomes dense and the moisture increases; hence the waves of the sea increase until the new moon.

# BOOK FOUR

## PROEM

[Col. 1165D] The sequence of the preceding books flowed from the first cause of things down to the earth, not indulging an itching of the ears but serving the usefulness of readers, and for that reason yielding less to the minds of fools. For the Apostle’s statement has now been fulfilled: “There will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own desires they will heap up teachers for themselves, having itching ears.”

What freedom for study can remain when we recognize that teachers are flatterers of their pupils, pupils judges of their teachers, and both impose a law about what is to be said and what is to be kept silent? In only a few cases will you perceive the teacher’s serious expression, but you will perceive the face and hear the words of a flatterer. And if there is someone who follows the teacher’s strictness, he is avoided by the scholars like a madman by prostitutes, and is called cruel and inhuman, so that he may now use the words of Umbecius [the name is uncertain in the transmitted text].

For this reason no one is a companion to such a man, just as a maimed body is of no use to a dead right hand [the syntax of the transmitted passage is uncertain]. Why, then, ought teachers to be loved? They are avoided, in accordance with Ovid’s words:

“By whom you often seek riches, you drive us away.”

But since it is characteristic of a good person not to bend the mind toward worse things but to conform it to better things, let us turn the mind away from worse things and conform it to better ones, and pass on to what remains. And since, in following brevity, we have said enough about the other elements and their adornment, let us begin to speak of the earth and its adornment.

## CATALOGUE OF BOOK IV

[Col. 1167]

[Col. 1167A] Concerning the land of Africa. Concerning its inhabitants. Concerning the various qualities of the earth. Concerning the boundaries of Asia and Europe. Why some mountains have perpetual snow. What qualities the earth acquires from different winds. Concerning implanted trees. Concerning semen. Concerning the time suitable for intercourse. Concerning the womb. Concerning the cause of sterility. Whether male semen alone is sufficient for conception. Concerning menstruation. Why animals walk as soon as they are born, but humans do not. Where a male is conceived and where a female. Concerning the operations. How a child is nourished in the womb. Concerning birth. Why those born in the seventh month live, but those born in the eighth do not. Concerning infancy. Concerning natural power. [Col. 1167B] Concerning spiritual power. Concerning animal power. [Col. 1168A] From where growth comes. Concerning sleep. From where dreams come. Concerning the head. Concerning the brain. Concerning the eyes. How sight occurs. Concerning looking steadily. Concerning looking at. Concerning looking away. Concerning hearing. What the soul is. Which actions belong to the soul and which likewise to the body. How the soul exists in the composition of the human being. Concerning its powers. Concerning the time of its union with the body. Why a child does not discern and understand. Concerning youth. Concerning old age. Concerning extreme old age. How a teacher should be sought. How a pupil should be sought. What constitution, for what instruction, at what age. [Col. 1168B] What the order of learning is.

## BOOK FOUR BEGINS

[Col. 1167B] The earth is therefore an element placed in the middle of the world and, for that reason, the lowest. For the world is arranged in the likeness of an egg: the earth is in the middle, as the yolk is in the middle of an egg; around it is water, as the white is around the yolk; around the water is air, like the thin membrane enclosing the white. Outside, enclosing all the remaining elements, is fire, in the manner of an eggshell.

This earth, placed in the middle of the world and receiving all the weights from it, is naturally cold and dry in its various regions, but through accidental causes it contains various qualities. One part of it, situated beneath the torrid part of the air, is torrid from the sun’s heat and uninhabitable. Its two extremities, situated beneath the two cold parts, are cold and uninhabitable. The part situated beneath the temperate part of the air is temperate and habitable.

But, as we said above, two parts of the air are temperate; correspondingly, two parts of the earth are temperate and capable of habitation: one on this side of the torrid zone and the other beyond it. Although both are habitable, we believe that only one is inhabited by human beings—and not even all of it. But since philosophers speak of the inhabitants of both regions not because they are actually there but because they could be there, let us speak, through an understanding of philosophical reading, of those whom we believe to exist.

The habitable part of the earth in which we live is divided into two. Since the air is temperate on every side of the earth, on every side a certain part of the earth is temperate and habitable. But because the currents of the Ocean encircle the sides of the earth according to the measure of the horizon, they divide it into two. We inhabit its upper part, and our antipodes the lower; nevertheless, none of us can reach them, nor can any of them reach us.

On the northern side, cold and the currents prevent passage; on the eastern and western sides, the currents alone do so. The other habitable region is likewise divided into two: our antheci inhabit its upper part, and their antipodes the lower.

Thus there are four habitations in the two habitable regions. Their inhabitants coincide with one another at some times and differ at others. We and our antipodes have summer and winter, and the other seasons, at the same time; but when we have day, they have night, and conversely.

If summer results from proximity to the sun and winter from remoteness, while spring and autumn result from an intermediate distance, the signs are equally distant from us and from them, since they preserve the earth’s natural position and complete their course through whatever sign the sun occupies. It will therefore be summer, or winter, or another season for us and for them equally. We rightly have the changes of the seasons at the same time, but not day and night at the same time.

Since day results from the sun’s radiance and night from the earth’s shadow, and since the shadow is always on the side opposite the sun’s radiance, when the radiance of day is in the lower part of the earth, the shadow is in the upper part; and when the radiance is in the upper part, the shadow is in the lower. There is therefore no hour when it is not day in some part of the earth and night in another.

But someone may ask: If we and they have summer and winter at the same time, why, when we have day, do they have night? In summer our days are very long and our nights short; they will therefore have short days and long nights in their summer, which is contrary to the nature of summer.

To this we reply that although we have day while they have night, they do not have night at the very moment when we have day. Indeed, at a certain time day is common to us and to them, but it is evening for one and morning for the other. When the sun is rising for us, it is still setting for them; we have morning and they evening, so that for them it is not yet night around the first hour. Similarly, at sunset, after the sun begins to descend for us and begins to appear for them, it is morning for them and evening for us.

Thus we and they have days of equal length and nights of equal length, though not at the same time. The same applies in winter, but we leave it to the minds of readers to work out how this is so.

We and the antheci have radiance and shadow at the same time, but when the sun is near us, it is distant from them: when we have summer, they have winter, and conversely. Here a question similar to the preceding one arises; anyone who approaches it instructed by what was said above will easily find its solution.

We and the antipodes of the antheci have neither summer nor winter, nor day or night, at the same time. The antheci and their antipodes stand to one another as we stand to our antheci, and our antipodes stand to us as theirs do to them.

Since we have explained enough about the three habitations and their inhabitants, let us begin to speak of our own. Our habitation extends from east to west and from south to north. Although it is called temperate, it is not equally temperate in all its regions. The part nearer the torrid zone—Libya and Ethiopia—is hot and dry; the part near the cold zone is cold and humid; the eastern part is hot and humid; the western part is cold and dry; and the part equally distant from the extremes is equally temperate.

This region has three principal divisions: Asia, Africa, and Europe. Asia begins in the east and extends laterally toward the north and toward the torrid zone; it ends at the Tanais and the Nile and occupies the middle part of the habitable world. Europe and Africa occupy the other two parts.

The boundaries of Africa are the Nile on the eastern side, the torrid zone to the south, the Mediterranean Sea to the north, and the current to the west; the cold zone lies to the north in the following manner.

In this region, then, there are mountains whose summits have perpetual snow, while their valleys have intense heat. But since heat comes from the sun and from the upper regions, and mountains are closer to the sun than their valleys, why is there snow on their heights but not in their valleys? We answer [Col. 1169B] that what we briefly touched on above applies here: although heat comes from the sun—and heat is itself of a hot nature—until it encounters moisture, which it transforms according to its own nature rather than merely mixing with it, it can heat nothing. Thus, in the mountains mentioned above, because the air is thin on account of its remoteness from the earth, it cannot be ignited by the sun; but because of its lightness, being driven here and there, it becomes cold. In the valleys, however, because the air is dense and consequently remains still, it is quickly ignited and becomes hot. This can be demonstrated by the following analogy: if the air in summer is still, it becomes ignited and is hot; but if a wind comes and moves it, it is felt to be cold.

Here a question arises: if the air in the upper regions of the mountains is so thin, how is it thickened into clouds and snow? We answer that it is not itself thickened; rather, moist vapor that rises from the valleys is thickened by the coldness of the upper regions into clouds and is condensed into snow.

This same habitable region, exposed to different winds, acquires different qualities. [Col. 1169C] If some part of it is protected by mountains facing east and is closed off toward the north and west but exposed toward the south, it is hot and dry: suitable for habitation in winter, but very bad in summer. If the arrangement is reversed, it is bad in winter and good in summer. A part exposed toward the east and closed off on the other sides is hot and moist, and therefore good. Conversely, a part that is cold and dry is bad in autumn and good in spring.

What we say about the regions of the earth can be demonstrated by the windows of a house. Southern windows are bad in summer and good in winter; northern windows have the opposite properties. This is why the ancients made spaces between southern and northern thresholds, so that in winter they might recline in the southern one and in summer in the northern one.

And since we have said enough about this element and its parts, it remains for us to speak about herbs and the fruits of trees. But since Macer and Dioscorides teach about them sufficiently and clearly, let us be silent about them, setting out only one question, together with its solution, concerning uncertain matters. It is this: since the trunk is one thing and the shoot another, and since the cause of growth rises from the earth through the roots and trunk, how do they pass over into the nature of the shoot, branches, and fruit? [Col. 1169D]

The solution is as follows. From the earth, hot and moist vapor rises through the pores of the root, drawing with it something of earthly nature and watery substance, and conferring the principle of life and the growth of fruit. It rises through the trunk. The trunk retains what is suited to its own nature and, digesting it by natural heat, transforms it into the pith, the woody trunk, and the bark. What rises toward the shoot it likewise digests into the nature proper to it.

It remains, then, to speak about the earthly animal. Although every such animal is mortal, one kind is rational and another irrational. But since irrational animals are infinite and are not greatly relevant to the reading of philosophers, let us postpone speaking about their natures—why some ruminate and others do not, why some bellow and others do not—and discuss the rational mortal, namely the human being, which is the more worthy subject. The human being consists of two things, soul and body. First, then, let us teach about the human body, which first presents itself to our thought [Col. 1170A], and afterward about the soul and its powers.

But since in the first book we taught about the composition of the first man and woman, and how man was made from the mud of the earth, let us teach about the daily creation, formation, birth, ages, and members of the human being, as well as the functions and uses of the members. Since the conception of a human being takes place from semen, let us say something about semen itself.

Semen, then, is the male seed, composed from the very substance of all the members. That it is composed from the substance of all the members is evident from the fact that all the members are formed from it; and it is the nature of things that like things should arise from like things. Here is another argument for this: if a father has some incurable disease in a particular member, such as gout of the hands or gout of the feet, the son will have the same disease in the same member.

And since we have mentioned semen, which is received in the womb at the time appropriate for intercourse, let us say a little about the womb. [Col. 1170B] The time for intercourse begins at the fourteenth year. But since semen derives its cause from heat and moisture, and childhood is hot and moist, why does intercourse not occur during childhood? We answer that at that age the pores and passages are constricted, serving this purpose, so that semen cannot exit; in other periods they are open and suitable for intercourse. In old age and advanced age, intercourse scarcely occurs because of coldness.

After eating, but before sleep, intercourse is burdensome and this activity is diminished. Natural heat, which ought to digest the food, is diminished. After sleep, however, because the food has been digested into blood, it is the proper time for it. What bodily constitution is suitable for this activity will be sought in the second part.

The womb is a receptacle, a chest for receiving semen, hairy inside so that it may receive the semen more effectively. It has seven chambers, stamped in the shape of a human figure like a coin. Hence a woman can give birth to seven children, and never more, from a single intercourse. And because sterility sometimes arises from the womb [Col. 1170C], let us say something about it.

The cause of sterility is excessive dryness, excessive moisture, excessive heat, or excessive cold. Since semen consists of a balanced mixture—that is, of blood—it requires that something similar to it be present. Sometimes excessive fat is the cause why conception does not occur, for all the little follicles are blocked by it, so that the semen cannot enter. Hence Virgil says that at the time of intercourse mares should be thinned by leanness; then he adds the physiological explanation: “lest a fatter condition clog the furrows that cling together.”

Again, frequent intercourse is a cause of the same condition. For the inside of the womb becomes smeared and, like joined marble, can retain nothing. But if there is no cause of sterility in a woman, and semen suitable for generation enters the womb, the womb is immediately closed, so that Hippocrates says that not even a needle could be inserted: conception has taken place.

We said “suitable for generation” because if the semen is too cold, too hot, too dry, or too moist, it is not fit for generation. But it is asked whether the male semen alone is useful, without the woman’s semen being sufficient for generation. [Col. 1170D]

Some say that the male semen alone is sufficient. Their proof is that often a man has intercourse with a woman who is unwilling, and she sometimes gives birth while weeping, where there could have been no semen from the woman. For the emission of semen does not occur without desire.

We, however, say that the woman’s semen is also present in conception. This can be proved by the disease that a child contracts from its mother in a corresponding member. As for their claim that a child is conceived by a woman who is unwilling, we say that although she is displeased at the beginning, in the end she is pleased because of the weakness of carnal desire.

But since menstruation usually ceases once conception has occurred, let us explain how and why it ceases then. Since every woman is naturally very hot, though colder than the coldest man, she cannot digest food well. Superfluities therefore remain, and these are purged each month; hence they are called menstruation. Once conception has taken place, however, heat is doubled by the fetus. Food is therefore digested better, and fewer superfluities arise. Again, since the fetus is nourished from the mother’s blood [Col. 1171A], it has no need of purgation.

Hence the other animals walk as soon as they are born, but the human being does not walk, because in the womb he is nourished from menstrual blood. But why are women more ardent in sexual desire after conception, whereas irrational animals abstain from it? Thus, although women are colder than men, they are nevertheless more lustful than men.

We had proposed to explain why after intercourse a leprous woman is not harmed, whereas a man who was previously healthy becomes leprous; but lest the hearts of religious people be offended if they should happen to take this work into their hands, by our speaking too long about such a matter, we omit it.

When the semen has been placed in the womb and its mouth has been closed, if it remains on the right side, because the liver is near the womb on the right side, the fetus is nourished by better and warmer blood and becomes male. If it is on the left, which is farther from the source of heat—that is, from the liver—it is female. But if it is not properly on the left, but somewhat toward the right, the woman is masculine.

When the semen has been placed in one of the three regions mentioned above [Col. 1171B], the digestive power begins to operate. By warming it with the heat of the mother, it thickens it; through dryness it creates a follicle containing the conception within itself, so that no superfluities may mingle with it and corrupt it. This follicle grows and develops together with the child.

On the seventh day after conception, as Macrobius reports, drops of blood begin to appear on the surface of the follicle. In the third week they sink into the conception’s fluid; in the fourth, they coagulate into a certain liquid solidity, as though between flesh and blood. In the fifth week, if the child is destined to be born in the seventh month—but otherwise in the ninth week—the formative power begins its work. Its function is to impart the human form.

This is followed by the assimilative power, whose function is to transform what is cold and dry into cold and dry members, such as bones; what is cold and moist into phlegmatic members, such as the lungs; what is hot and dry into choleric members, such as the heart; and what is hot and moist into sanguine members, such as the liver.

Next comes the concavating power. Its function is to hollow out the hands, pierce the nostrils, and so forth. [Col. 1171C] Once the members have been formed, assimilated, and hollowed out, moist vapor begins to pass through the veins and arteries, conferring movement and life.

This movement begins on the seventieth day after conception if the child is destined to be born in the seventh month; if in the ninth month, on the ninetieth day. But since everything that lives in time requires some food, the nutritive power follows last and continues until death.

But it is asked how the child is nourished in the womb. We answer that certain nerves located in the umbilical cord are joined to the womb; through them the child is nourished and grows by pure blood descending from the mother’s liver. Since it receives digested matter, it does not need to discharge superfluity.

The birth that follows these powers has two limits: the seventh month and the ninth. [Col. 1171D] It is asked why a child born before the seventh month cannot live, why one born in the seventh month lives, and why one born in the eighth does not.

Physicians say that before the seventh month the child does not have enough movement for it to live if it were born. In the seventh month it has sufficient movement for life; therefore, if the child has weak nerves by which it is joined to the womb, it breaks them by moving and is born capable of life. In the eighth month, the movement acquired in the seventh has weakened; if it is born then, it cannot live. Once restored, however, it begins to move in part of the ninth month, breaks the nerves suitable for life, and is born capable of living.

And because it has been nourished in a warm and moist environment, when it is born and comes forth into what is unlike that environment, it feels the opposition and emits a wailing cry. Therefore the first human voice is one of pain.

From birth until the seventh year is infancy, because during part of this period the child cannot speak; during the other part, if it speaks, it speaks imperfectly. At this age it can possess sensation, but not reason and understanding. Let us therefore say something about sensation. As for how they cannot possess reason and understanding at such an age, since these are powers, we shall demonstrate it later when speaking about the soul.

And since it has its beginning from the animal power, which is preceded by the natural and spiritual senses, let us first offer a preliminary account of these powers, beginning with the natural power, which comes first.

Since the human being consists of four elements [Col. 1172A], vapor that is moist and hot comes into being from heat and moisture. Diffused through the members and moving them, it performs the three digestions and is called the natural power.

And since mention has been made of three digestions, let us inquire what digestion is, where it occurs, and how it takes place. Digestion is the transformation of something brought about by boiling. The first digestion takes place in the stomach, the second in the liver, and the third in all the members.

Let us therefore speak first about the first digestion. Since the human body requires growth at a certain age, and since in every restoration the inner and outer heat or cold destroy something, it was necessary for food and drink—through which nourishment and growth might be supplied—to enter the body. But because food is coarse, it was necessary for it to be made thin and delicate before it entered the stomach.

For this purpose the teeth are prepared. They are born from phlegm descending through the gums, thickened and hardened by coldness, so that they may crush food. The tongue is present so that, like a miller’s hand, it may turn the food and bring it back under the teeth. It is spongy for this purpose, so that, receiving the juice of the food, it may distinguish its taste.

Thus this crushing is compared to a kind of milling. The food, prepared in this way [Col. 1172B], descends with drink through the esophagus into the stomach through the opening called the “gate,” whose mouth is wider; there it is cooked and transformed into the form of a gruel. This is the first digestion.

Whether the stomach is of a hot nature is a matter of dispute. Some say: it must be of a hot nature, for otherwise it could not digest food. Since it cooks and transforms food, it is hot.

We, however, say that the stomach is naturally cold but accidentally hot. It is of a nervous nature, so that when a person eats more than usual it expands, and when he eats less it contracts. It also had to be of a nervous nature so that, when it received something hard and unchewed, it would not be injured.

Since everything nervous is of a cold nature, the stomach is cold as well. But so that it may retain food better and digest it properly, it is hairy inside. Although it is naturally cold [Col. 1172C], it is nevertheless heated accidentally: it lies beneath the liver, so that it is almost entirely enclosed by it. On its right side is the gall bladder, and on its left the heart; these are hot and dry, and therefore the stomach becomes hot, just as food is cooked when fire is placed beneath it.

If, then, we wish to speak precisely, we should say that food is cooked in the stomach, not by the stomach.

Food, having thus been transformed into the form of gruel, exits through the lower opening called the “gate” and enters the duodenum. It is so called because it has the length of twelve fingers, each of them being of the same measure. Whatever is suited to its nature or nourishment is retained in it; the remainder passes into another intestine called the jejunum, which retains nothing from it.

Certain veins coming from the liver join the jejunum. Through them, what is more fluid passes into the lower regions of the liver; these veins are called meseraic because they send the juice there. What is feculent descends lengthwise—that is, into the bowel—and constitutes the first superfluities of digestion.

The liquid that passes into the lower regions of the liver [Col. 1172D] is digested by its heat. Because it is hot and dry there, it passes into bile and is transmitted through certain veins to the gall bladder; this is the seat of bile. A portion of it then passes into the stomach to strengthen the appetitive power.

What is cold and dry passes into melancholy and descends to the spleen, the seat of melancholy; but a portion ascends to the stomach to strengthen the retentive power.

What is cold and moist is changed into phlegm and passes to the lungs, the seat of phlegm; a portion is transmitted to the stomach by the expulsive power.

What is hot and moist is transformed into blood and remains in the liver, which is the seat of blood. Four humors are therefore generated in the liver, each inhabiting its proper seat: bile in the gall bladder, melancholy in the spleen, blood in the liver, and phlegm in the lungs.

Some, however, say that phlegm has no proper seat, but remains with the blood [Col. 1173A] so that it may circulate more effectively through the members. This is the second digestion.

What is superfluous there descends through the vein called the splenic vein, which lies beside the spleen, to the kidneys. The kidneys retain what is liquid there for their own nourishment and transmit the remainder through the pores of the ureters to the bladder. Exiting through the male member, it is called urine; this is the superfluity of the second digestion.

But because children have constricted ureteral pores, what is thick there passes into a stony substance. At other ages, because the pores are open, a stone is not generated there but around the kidneys. Thus, in children a stone is born in the neck of the bladder, while in old people it is formed around the kidneys.

The blood generated in the liver in the manner described passes through the veins to all the members. Digested by their heat, it is transformed into their likeness. Part of the superfluity exits through sweat; another part returns to the liver, where it is cooked and exits together with urine as it descends. The sediment is called *sedimen*. If it is at the bottom of the urine, it is called *hypostasis*; if in the middle, *encortim*; if at the top, *nephile*.

What these terms signify [Col. 1173B], what they mean when they occur in different places, when the sediment is continuous or dispersed, and what derives from substance and what from heat, is not ours to say. If anyone wishes to know this, let him read Galen’s work *On Urines*.

It is also the function of this natural power to produce growth, which occurs through moisture and heat. What sometimes rises is a property of heat; what thickens is a property of moisture.

But someone may say: if growth comes from what is hot and moist, how do choleric and melancholic people grow so much, when the former are cold and dry and the latter hot and dry?

We answer that no human being is not hot and moist, although some are more so and others less. For example, a human being is naturally hot and moist and balanced among the four qualities. But because nature is corrupted, it happens that these qualities are intensified or diminished in some individual. If heat is intensified in someone and moisture diminished, he is called choleric—that is, hot and dry—but he is not without moisture. If moisture is intensified and heat diminished, he is called phlegmatic. If dryness is intensified and heat diminished, he is called melancholic. [Col. 1173C] If the qualities are present equally, he is called sanguine.

All people are therefore naturally hot and moist, but because different qualities are intensified or diminished, they begin to differ from one another, and the name of the contrary quality is applied to them in a diminished sense.

A person can therefore grow under any bodily constitution, though more under one and less under another, and in one constitution in length, in another in breadth.

Choleric people are slender and tall: tall because of heat, whose property is to rise, and slender because of dryness. Sanguine people are tall because of heat and fat because of moisture. Phlegmatic people are short because of coldness and fat because of moisture. Melancholic people are short because of coldness and slender because of dryness.

Natural properties are nevertheless often altered by accidental causes. Choleric and melancholic people become fat through idleness or eating, while sanguine and phlegmatic people become slender through abstinence and labor. That sanguine and phlegmatic people, and so forth, are unnaturally short results from the smallness of the womb or of the semen. [Col. 1173D]

This natural power has certain principal members, certain members that serve and assist it, certain members that are one thing, and certain that are neither. But since this has been sufficiently discussed by the physician in the *Isagoge*, let us set it aside and proceed to sleep, which belongs to the natural power.

Sleep is the rest of the animal powers, together with the activation of the natural powers. It occurs in this way: as moist vapor rises toward the upper regions, the nerves through which the animal power ordinarily descends become filled. The animal being therefore ceases to see, hear, and so forth, until the natural heat has dried that vapor; then the natural spirit begins to descend, and the animal’s sensation is aroused to some degree.

Dreams arise from remnants of thoughts, from food and drink, from time, from bodily constitution, and from the manner of lying down; they signify nothing. Other dreams arise through the ministry of angels, and others from the cause of the world and the freedom of the soul. We have at hand accounts of the manifestations of all these. But since this has little relevance to our purpose, and we are moving toward the end of the book [Col. 1174A], let us pass it over and proceed to the power of the spleen.

The vapor mentioned above, passing through various openings, reaches the heart in a more refined form and expands it so that it may draw in air and temper the inner heat. To expel superfluities, however, the same power contracts it. It is then called the spiritual power, which is served by the arteries.

But let us come to the animal power. The vapor mentioned above, ascending through the nerves, becomes so subtle through filtration that, when it reaches the brain, it is called spirit. Descending through various instruments, it produces various animal powers, as we shall show.

Let us first speak about what proceeds from the brain itself; then we shall explain how the senses proceed from it. Since the brain is contained in the head, let us begin with the head.

The head is a certain spherical substance, compressed at the front and rear by two fingers’ breadth. [Col. 1174B] It is round so that the brain may move within it more effectively and so that superfluities remaining in its corners may not corrupt it. It is compressed at the front and rear by nerves proceeding from it: the anterior nerves produce sensation, while the posterior nerves produce voluntary bodily movement.

On its exterior surface, hairs adhere to the little skull-bones by means of a membrane, and they are born from vapor that rises and exits through the pores. That vapor, as it exits, is constricted by the coldness of dry air and passes into a corporeal substance. As another vapor exits, it drives the hairs upward, and thus they grow. But because it is natural for heavy things to descend, they bend and fall downward.

Hence, since no age lacks superfluities, neither the hair nor the nails lack growth. The nails are formed from the superfluities of the heart, which exit through the tips of the fingers and, hardened by coldness, become nails.

The hairs of the beard and chest, however, are absent in certain ages, and the beard is absent from the female sex. Since the beard exists in a man through heat, it can arise from the double heat of the heart and testicles. In a woman, because of coldness, it cannot exist unless she is unusually hot by a condition contrary to nature. For the same reason eunuchs do not have beards. In childhood [Col. 1174C] it cannot exist because of the constriction of the pores.

And since the hairs of the head arise from ascending vapor, they contract different colors according to the constitution of each person. Since these matters are sufficiently discussed in physiology, let us proceed to the rest.

Beneath the skull are two membranous coverings called *meninges*. The first, which is harder than the brain, is called the dura mater. The one nearer the brain is thinner, lest it injure the brain, and is called the pia mater.

Beneath these is the brain. Constantine gives the following definition of it: “The brain is a fluid and white substance, without blood.”

It is asked whether the brain is cold or hot. We say that it is naturally cold, so that it may not be dried out by continual movement.

There are three chambers in the head: in the prow, in the middle, and in the stern.
