The first chamber is hot and dry and is called the phantastic chamber—that is, the visual chamber—because in it lies the power of seeing and understanding. It is hot and dry so that it may draw in the forms and colors of things.

The middle chamber is called the logistic chamber—that is, the rational chamber—because in it lies the power of distinguishing. What the phantastic chamber draws in [Col. 1174D] passes into this chamber, where the soul distinguishes it. It is hot and moist so that, in distinguishing, it may conform itself more effectively to the properties of things.

The third chamber is called the memorial chamber because in it lies the power of retaining memory. What has been distinguished in the logistic chamber passes into the memorial chamber through a certain opening, which a small membrane closes until it is opened when we wish to commit something to memory or recall it to memory. This chamber is cold and dry so that it may retain things more effectively, for constriction belongs to what is cold and dry.

But someone may say: how could this ever have been proved? We answer: through wounds received in those regions. When someone had possessed a good memory, reason, and understanding, physicians observed that, after receiving a wound in one of those chambers, he lost the power belonging to that chamber while retaining the powers of the others.

Hence Solinus, in the *Polyhistories*, tells of someone who, after receiving a wound in the back of the head, fell into such ignorance that he did not know that he had ever had a name.

The ancients therefore rightly said that the seat of wisdom is in the head. For in the head reside the things that make a person wise: understanding, reason, and memory.

From the brain [Col. 1175A], nerves proceed to the eyes. Through them the animal spirit exits and produces vision, as we have shown. But first let us say something about the substance of the eyes.

The eye is a certain rounded and clear substance, though somewhat flat on its surface, consisting of three humors and seven tunics. It is rounded so that it can turn this way and that. Its surface is flat so that it may receive the forms of things more effectively. It is luminous and consists of humors so that the visual spirit may penetrate it. It consists of seven tunics so that it may expel superfluities and prevent them from injuring it.

If anyone wishes to know the names of the humors and the arrangement of the tunics, let him read Galen.

Nature made two eyes so that, if one were injured, the other might remain. Let us next speak about vision.

When the animal spirit, proceeding from the brain through the nerves, reaches the eyes, it exits and, having received some external brightness—whether from the sun or from another source [Col. 1175B]—is directed toward an obstacle. When it strikes the obstacle, it spreads through it and is formed by its shapes and colors; it passes through the eyes and through the phantastic chamber into the logistic chamber, and vision is produced.

Hence through vision we distinguish the shapes and colors of things.

The Stoics, however, say that the visual spirit does not reach the thing itself; rather, the eye receives the forms of things within itself, and when that ray reaches them and is similarly formed, it produces vision.

Others say that the visual spirit reaches neither the obstacle nor the eye to be formed by it. Instead, they say that the air between the observer and the obstacle is formed by shapes and colors; when the ray reaches it and, having been formed, returns, it produces vision.

We prefer the view that the visual spirit reaches the thing itself. The proof is that we often contract the same disease from the sight of someone suffering from ophthalmia. How could this happen unless the visual spirit, reaching the corrupted eye [Col. 1175C], were itself corrupted and, when it returned, corrupted our eyes?

The same point can be proved in another way. Since people have contrary constitutions—some cold, some hot, some moist, and some dry—the visual spirit issuing from one person draws those qualities along with it. Diffused over the face of another person whose constitution is contrary, it corrupts him. For contraries are harmed by contraries.

Hence old women are healed by licking the face and spitting: they spit out what is harmful there.

For vision to be produced, three things are necessary: an inner ray, an external brightness, and an obstacle belonging to the object. When these three come together, vision exists; if any one of them is lacking, vision fails.

There are three kinds of vision: *detuitio*, *contuitio*, and *intuitio*.

*Intuitio* occurs when we see something through the appearance of an image that presents itself at the same time. Since we have explained sufficiently how vision is produced, we have said enough about it.

*Contuitio* occurs when we see something on whose surface an image appears.

*Detuitio* occurs when the image appears not on the surface but in the depth, as in water. It is called *detuitio*, as though it were “looking downward.”

It remains, then, to speak about *intuitio* and *tuitio*. [Col. 1175D] Since their cause is the same, let us discuss *intuitio*, so that what we demonstrate about it may be understood also of *tuitio*.

When the visual spirit is directed toward something in order to see it, it is driven here and there by its instability. Having been formed by the shapes of the things surrounding it, if it reaches something dark, it cannot be seen because of its own subtlety. If, however, it reaches something radiant, it appears because of that thing’s brightness.

Aristotle said that no image appears there, but that a person sees himself and what lies behind him in the following way: when the spirit mentioned above encounters something radiant, it is struck back by that thing’s rays and reflected. Returning to the face of the observer, it perceives him and what lies behind him. But because this occurs through the mediation of a mirror, it seems that the image appears in the mirror.

Some say that the air between the person and the mirror is marked by various forms and colors, and that therefore, if something is placed before it, it appears bright, but otherwise it does not.

Hearing occurs as follows. When air, struck by the natural instruments, receives the form of a voice [Col. 1176A], it exits and impresses the same form upon the first portion of air it encounters, and that portion impresses it upon another, until it reaches the ears, in the manner of a dry and hollow drum. As the drum resounds, the animal spirit is aroused. Descending to the ears through certain nerves, it forms itself according to the same shape; and, having thus been formed, it returns to the logistic chamber and produces hearing.

The other senses are produced in a similar way by the same animal spirit descending through the nerves from the brain to their instruments.

Having perceived these matters, it is now time to discuss the soul and its powers.

The soul is a certain spirit joined to the body, conferring the capacity to discern and understand. That discerning and understanding proceed from the soul is proved as follows: when care for the body increases, those powers arise; when bodily care decreases and care for the soul increases, they grow. For if they arose from the nature of the body, they would grow as bodily care increased. When the cause is augmented, its effect is augmented.

Again, since every creature is either corporeal or spirit, it was fitting that the human being should consist of body and spirit, so that he might have some affinity with both. With lifeless bodies he shares existence; with herbs and trees, life; with irrational animals, sensation; with spirits, discernment. Hence it is said in the divine Scripture that the human being is every creature.

Since, then, the human being consists of body and soul, although the soul is dominant—for in it he is like the Creator—it would be inappropriate if the human body possessed its own activities while the soul did not. But someone may say: How shall I distinguish which activities in a human being should be attributed to the soul and which to the body? We say that those activities which a human being shares with an irrational animal or with lifeless bodies, even if the soul performs them in the human being, should not be called activities of the soul but of the body. Those, however, which are found in the human being and cannot exist in any other body belong to the soul. Thus discerning and understanding belong to the soul, while sensation and similar powers belong to the body.

But someone may say: If these activities are not activities of the soul, should they nevertheless be called the soul’s virtues or vices? And why is the soul condemned or rewarded on their account? We reply: Although the activities are not its own, their vices can belong to it. The soul was given to the human being so that it might correct the body’s unlawful impulses; their occurrence is therefore due to the soul’s ignorance or negligence. Just as a disciple or servant may sin through the negligence of his teacher or master, and the teacher or master is not wholly free from blame, so the soul is not wholly free from blame when such things occur, even though the activities are not its own.

Since, then, the human being consists of soul and body, it is asked whether the soul has been placed upon the body, concreted with it, mixed with it, or joined to it. One of these conditions must apply to things that are present in the composition of something.

It has not been placed upon the body, because then the soul would be outside the body and would not move it equally. Everything placed upon something is outside that upon which it has been placed, and it has greater force at the point of contact, as fire placed upon something does.

It has not been concreted with the body. A concrete thing is that which passes from its own substance into the substance of another, as water passes into salt through boiling. Since the soul does not pass into the substance of the body but always remains spirit, it is not concreted with the body.

Nor is it mixed with the body. No component of a mixture retains its own being; body and soul, therefore, are not mixed. They are joined, then, in such a way that the whole soul is present in every part of the body, retaining its own being, wholly and entire.

They will object: If the whole soul is in every part, then, when one part of the body is cut off, the whole soul has been removed from the body. We reply that the soul is not in any part of the body except insofar as it is joined to a body capable of life. When it is separated from one part of the body, therefore, the soul remains in the other parts, in which previously it was wholly present.

Again, it is asked whether soul and body come from the same source or from different sources. We say that the soul has no cause except the Creator alone, who gives being to all things. Hence Plato, the most learned of all philosophers, says that God implanted in the stars created by him and in the spirits the cause of forming the human being, but that God himself made the soul and entrusted it to them. Human bodies exist and grow through the ministry of the spirits and the effect of the stars, but the soul exists solely by the will of the Creator.

Again, it is asked whether the human soul exists before the body, and when it is joined to it. We say that it does not exist beforehand; this can be proved by reason and authority. If it existed beforehand, it would be either in misery or in blessedness, without any preceding merit. This is proved by the authority of blessed Augustine, who says: “Every day God creates new souls, but no one determines the time of their union with the body.”

Nevertheless, it seems to us that the soul is joined to the body after the operation of the formative and concavating power. At that point the natural power can no longer move through the shadow, without which life cannot exist, nor can the soul exist in the body.

The soul has different powers: intelligence, reason, and memory. Intelligence is the soul’s power by which a person perceives bodily things with a certain understanding of why they are so. Reason is a certain power of the soul by which a person perceives what a thing is, in what respect it agrees with other things, and in what respect it differs. Memory is the power by which a person firmly retains what has previously been learned.

But it is asked: If these are properties of the soul, why does an infant, in whom the soul is present, not discern, and so forth? We reply that the human soul, having its beginning from the Creator and being perfect in its own kind, would know whatever can be known by a human being, were it not for the weight of the flesh. This can be proved by the first human being, who, before the corruption of humanity, possessed perfect human knowledge from the time he came to be.

Now, however, humanity having been corrupted, the soul is corrupted from the moment it is joined to what is corrupt; nor can it exercise its properties until, awakened by use and experience or by someone’s teaching, it begins to discern. It is like someone with a keen power of sight who is confined in a dark prison: he cannot see until he becomes accustomed to the darkness or a light is kindled. Hence Virgil:

> “How much our harmful bodies hinder us.”

In the first period of life, experience through use has not preceded, nor is the time suitable for teaching. Since that age is merely hot and moist, it immediately digests and desires food; hence it requires frequent intake and evacuation, and thick vapor is generated. Rising to the brain, in which the power of discerning and understanding resides, this vapor disturbs it.

Youth follows this period; it is hot and dry. The natural moisture that a person contracts from the mother’s womb has been dried up. Consequently, vapor is not generated so thickly, nor is the brain disturbed so greatly. This is an age suitable for learning, especially if the lamp of diligent instruction is kindled.

Old age follows, cold and dry. The natural heat has been extinguished; consequently, memory is vigorous in this age, but the body’s powers fail. Memory arises from dryness and cold, whose function is to constrict. The body’s powers fail as heat, whose function is to produce impulse, diminishes. Extreme old age follows, cold and moist. When the natural heat has been extinguished, cold phlegm increases; hence memory fails in that age and people become childish. Phlegm possesses an expulsive power.

This is followed by the dissolution of soul and body. Once the natural heat has been extinguished, a person cannot live for long.

Since we have said enough about the human being, whose proper condition is to be taught, let us say what sort of people should be sought as teachers, what sort as learners, what bodily constitution is suitable for instruction, at what age instruction should begin and when it should end, and what the order of learning should be.

A person should be sought as a teacher who teaches neither for the sake of praise nor in hope of temporal reward, but solely from love of wisdom. If he loves his own praise, he will never want the pupil to attain his own perfection. He will withhold instruction lest the pupil become his equal or surpass him in what he himself values most.

If, again, he teaches because he has been motivated by hope of temporal advantage, he will not care what he says so long as he extorts as much as possible. Trifles are often more pleasing than useful things. But if he approaches teaching out of love of knowledge, he will not withhold instruction through envy, nor avoid known truth in order to extort something. Even if the number of his companions should diminish, he will not falter; rather, he will become watchful and diligent for the instruction of himself and others.

As a learner, one should seek and cherish a person who is not noisy in his teaching and not proud, lest he appear to be something when he is nothing; one who loves his teacher as a father, or even more than a father. For from the one who gives us greater and more worthy things, we ought to receive greater love. From our father we began as ignorant persons; from our teacher we become wise, which is greater and more worthy.

Good teachers, therefore, should be loved more than parents. Yet it is not right that teachers be loved more; it is useful that the teacher’s words concerning knowledge please us, because even good things often displease us when spoken by someone we do not love, and we avoid them while striving not to imitate those whom we do not love.

Although a sanguine constitution is suited to learning, being well balanced in every respect, anyone can become perfect in any constitution, even if with labor; for, as Pamphilus relates:

> “Difficult labor conquers all things.”

The beginning of instruction is suitably placed in adolescence, because, as Plato says:

> “A person’s age is like wax: if it is too soft, it neither receives a shape nor retains it; and likewise, if it is hard.”

Thus neither an age that is too tender nor one that is too hard is suitable for instruction.

The end of instruction is death. Hence, when a certain wise man was asked, “Where is the end of learning?” he replied, “Where the end of life is.” When a certain philosopher was dying at the age of ninety, one of his pupils asked him whether he was grieved by death. He replied: “Because I was just beginning to learn.”

The order of learning should be as follows. Since all instruction is conveyed through eloquence, students should first be trained in eloquence. It has three parts: writing correctly and pronouncing correctly what has been written; proving what ought to be proved, which dialectic teaches; and adorning words and thoughts, which rhetoric imparts.

We should therefore begin with grammar, then proceed to dialectic, and afterward to rhetoric. Equipped with these as with weapons, we should approach the study of philosophy. Its order is this: first the quadrivium, beginning with arithmetic; second, music; third, geometry; fourth, astronomy; and afterward the divine Scripture, so that through knowledge of the creature we may arrive at knowledge of the Creator.

## The Likeness of Noah’s Ark

Noah’s ark undoubtedly represented the Church, because, just as the ark was carried to and fro, wearied, upon the waves of the Flood, so the Church is shaken in a stormy world by the various tempests and calamities of this age. And just as Noah’s ark contained not only clean but also unclean animals—for it had human beings and it also had serpents—so in the great house, that is, the Church of Christ, there are various vessels, some indeed for honor and others for dishonor.

## Bede the Priest: On the Languages of the Nations

The diversity of languages arose in the building of the tower after the Flood. Before the tower’s pride divided human society into different sounds of signs, there was one language among all nations, called Hebrew, which the patriarchs and prophets used not only in their speech but also in the sacred writings.

At the beginning, however, there were as many languages as there were nations. Later there were more nations than languages, because many nations arose from one language. In this passage “languages” means words; because words are produced by the tongue, they are named from the instrument by which they are produced. Thus “mouth” is sometimes used for words, and “hand” for writing.

There are three sacred languages: Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, which are especially distinguished throughout the whole world. In these three languages Pilate had the charge against the Lord written above the cross. Therefore, because of the obscurity of the sacred Scriptures, knowledge of these three languages is necessary, so that one may have recourse to another whenever the speech of one language introduces uncertainty concerning a name or its interpretation.

The Greek language is regarded as more distinguished than the other languages of the nations. It is more sonorous than Latin and all other languages, and its variety is divided into five forms. The first is called κοινός (*koinos*), that is, “mixed” or “common,” which everyone uses. The second is Attic, namely Athenian, which all the authors of Greece used. The third is Doric, used by the Egyptians and Syrians. The fourth is Ionic. The fifth is Aeolic, in which the Aeolians are said to have spoken. Such distinctions are observed in the Greek language; their speech is divided in this way.

Some have said that there are four Latin languages: the ancient, Latin, Roman, and mixed.

The ancient language is that which the most ancient inhabitants of Italy used under Janus and Saturn: an uncultivated language, such as appears in certain songs.

Latin is the language spoken under Latinus and the kings of Tuscany by the other inhabitants of Latium. In it the Twelve Tables were written.

Roman is the language that arose among the Roman people after the expulsion of the kings. In it the poets Naevius, Plautus, Ennius, and Virgil, and among the orators the Greek Cato, Cicero, and the others, expressed themselves.

Mixed is the language that, after the empire was extended more widely, burst into the Roman state together with foreign customs and peoples, corrupting the integrity of speech through solecisms and barbarisms.

All the peoples of the East strike their language and words in the throat, as do the Hebrews and Syrians. All the peoples of the Mediterranean strike their speech against the palate, as do the Greeks and Asians. All western peoples break their words against the teeth, as do the Italians and Spaniards.

Syriac and Chaldean are close to Hebrew in speech, agreeing in many respects and in the sound of their letters. Some, however, think that the language itself was Chaldean because Abraham came from the Chaldeans. If this is accepted, how is it that in Daniel the Hebrew boys are ordered to be taught a language they did not know?

Every human being can acquire any language—whether Greek, Latin, or one of the languages of the other nations—either by hearing it or by receiving it through reading from a teacher. Although knowledge of every language is difficult for anyone, no one is so negligent that, living among his own people, he does not know the language of his own people. For what else should he be considered but worse than irrational animals? They utter the cry of their own species, whereas he is worse who lacks knowledge of his own language.

What language God spoke at the beginning of the world when he said, “Let there be light,” is difficult to determine, for languages did not yet exist. Likewise, it is asked in what language he afterward sounded in the external ears of human beings when speaking to the first man, or to the prophets, or when the voice of God physically sounded, saying, “You are my beloved Son.” Some believe that it was that one and only language which existed before the division of languages.

It is believed among the various nations that God speaks to them in the same language that the people themselves use, so that they may understand him. God speaks to human beings not through his invisible substance but through a bodily creature, through which he also wished to appear to human beings when he spoke.

The Apostle says: “If I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels.” Here it is asked in what language angels speak. It is not that angels have some languages of their own; rather, this is said by way of exaggeration and accumulation.

It is also asked in what language human beings will speak in the future. This is never discovered, for the Apostle says: “Whether languages will cease.”

## Interpretation of the Sibylline Words

(This interpretation of the Sibylline words has also been attributed by some to Bede; we have placed it here so that it would not be missing.)

In general, all prophetesses are called Sibyls. By divine will they were accustomed to interpret everything and announce future events.

The most learned authors report that there were ten Sibyls. The first was Persian; the second, Libyan; the third, Delphic, who prophesied before the Trojan wars; the fourth, Cumaean, in Italy; the fifth, Erythraean, born in Babylonia and called Erythraean after the island in which her songs were composed; the sixth, Samian, named from the Samian river at Beneventum; the seventh, Amalthean, or Cumaean; the eighth, Hellespontine; the ninth, Phrygian; and the tenth, called Tiburtine in Greek and Albunea in Latin. Her songs contain many things written concerning God and Christ.

This Sibyl was the daughter of King Priam and was born of Hecuba. In Greek she was called Tiburtine, in Latin Albunea, or Cassandra. Traveling through various provinces and regions of the world, she proclaimed in Asia, Macedonia, Erostachia, Agagusdea, Cilicia, Pamphylia, and Galatia. After filling the regions of the world with her prophecies, she went from there to Egypt, Ethiopia, Bragada, Babylonia, Africa, Libya, Pentapolis, Mauretania, and Palarinum. She preached throughout all these provinces, and, filled with the spirit of prophecy, foretold good things for the good and evil things for the wicked.

We know what she announced in her proclamations and what she predicted would come in the last days. When the Romans heard of her fame, they immediately reported it before the senators. The senators sent ambassadors to her and had her brought to Rome with great honor.

One night, one hundred men from the Roman Senate each saw a dream. Each saw what seemed to be nine suns in the sky, divided individually, with different figures within them. The first sun was bright and shining over the whole earth. The second was brighter and larger, possessing an ethereal radiance. The third was fiery, terrible, and blood-colored, yet in the end very bright. The fourth sun is the fourth generation, in the time of Christ. The fifth sun was dark, blood-colored, and like a lamp in a dark thunderstorm. The sixth sun was exceedingly dark and had the sharp, stinging point of a scorpion. The seventh sun was terrible and again had a bloody sword in its midst. The eighth sun was poured out and had a blood-colored hue in its midst. The ninth sun was exceedingly dark, but had one shining ray.

When the Sibyl entered Rome, the Roman citizens saw her and admired her extraordinary beauty. She was pleasing in appearance, beautiful in face, eloquent in speech, and, by the beauty given by God, very well formed; she offered sweet eloquence to her hearers.

The men who had seen the dreams came to her and said: “Teacher and lady, your body is of such great beauty as we have never seen in any woman except you. We ask you to reveal what the dream we all saw in one night signifies for the future.”

The Sibyl answered them: “It is not proper to disclose the mystery of this vision in a place full of refuse and polluted by various contaminations. But come, let us ascend Mount Apennine, and there I shall announce to you what will come upon the Roman citizens.”

They did as she said. She questioned them, and they recounted the vision they had seen. Then she said to them: “The nine suns that you saw signify all the generations that are to come. Because you saw them differing from one another, the life of the children of human beings will also differ.

“The first sun is the first generation. The people will be simple and distinguished, lovers of liberty, truthful, gentle, exceedingly kind, lovers of comforting the poor, and sufficiently wise.

“The second sun is the second generation. The people will live splendidly, increase greatly, worship God, and conduct themselves on earth without malice.

“The third sun is the third generation. Nation will rise against nation, and there will be many battles in Rome.

“The fourth sun is the fourth generation. The people will deny what is true. In those days a woman of Hebrew descent, named Mary, will arise. She will have a husband named Joseph, and from her, without intercourse with a man, they will bring forth, through the Holy Spirit, one named Jesus. She will be a virgin before giving birth and a virgin after giving birth. Therefore, the one who is born from her will be true man, as all the prophets foretold. He will fulfill the law of the Hebrews and add his own things to it, and his kingdom will endure forever and ever.

“When he is born, armies of angels will be on his right and on his left, saying: ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.’ A voice will come over him, saying: ‘This is my beloved Son; listen to him.’

“Some of the Hebrew priests were there. When they heard these words, they were indignant and said to her: ‘These are terrifying words. Let this queen be silent.’

“The Sibyl answered them: ‘O Jews, these things must happen, but you will not believe in him.’

“They said: ‘We will not believe, because God gave a word and covenant to our fathers, and he will not withdraw his hand from us.’

“She answered them again: ‘The God of heaven will beget a Son for himself, as it is written. He will be like his Father, and afterward he will grow through the stages of infancy as a child. Kings and rulers of the earth will rise against him.

“In those days the name of Caesar Augustus will be renowned. He will reign in Rome and subject the whole earth to himself. There are not many gods or few gods, nor three nor two gods, but one God, alone and immeasurable, who made heaven, the sun, the stars, and the moon, the fruit-bearing earth, and the sea. Those who honor him will inherit eternal life and the everlasting paradise that they themselves will inherit.

“There will also be a simultaneous resurrection of the dead. The lame will run with great speed; the deaf will hear; the blind will see; those who do not speak will speak. From five loaves he will satisfy five thousand people, and the fragments will be gathered into twelve baskets; from them they will fill the likeness of peoples. By his word he will restrain the winds, tread upon the sea, walk upon the waves, and release everyone from sickness. He will raise the dead and drive away many pains; and the living will be satisfied from one loaf of bread.

“But when everything I have said has been accomplished, the whole law will be dissolved in him, and afterward he will encounter the impious hands of unbelievers. After this the Hebrew priests will assemble against Jesus, because he will perform many signs. They will seize him, strike God with unclean hands, and spit poisonous spittle upon his sacred face. He will simply offer his holy back to the blows and receive their slaps. He will remain silent, so that no one may recognize from where the Word came. He will be crowned with a crown of thorns. For food they will give him gall, and for thirst vinegar. They will hang him on a tree and kill him.

“The veil of the temple will be torn in the middle. The day will be dark for six hours. He will bring the lot of death to an end by accepting sleep for three days, and then, returning from the underworld, he will come into the light. They will achieve nothing against him, for on the third day he will rise again, show himself to his disciples, and, while they watch, ascend into heaven; his kingdom will have no end.

“The Jews call me a mad and lying Sibyl. But when all these things have happened, then at last they will remember me, and no one afterward will call me mad, but the great Sibyl of God.”

Then she said to the Roman leaders:

“The fifth sun is the fifth generation. Jesus will choose two fishermen from Galilee and teach them his laws, saying: ‘Go, and teach all nations the doctrine you have received from me.’ Through seventy-two languages all nations will be subjected.

“The sixth sun is the sixth generation. They will conquer this city for three years and six months.

“The seventh sun is the seventh generation. Two kings will arise and inflict many persecutions in the land of the Hebrews on account of the Lord.

“The eighth sun will be the eighth generation. Rome will be abandoned, and those waging war will howl amid tribulations and sorrows, saying: ‘Do you suppose that we shall perish?’

“The ninth sun is the ninth generation. Roman rulers will arise for the destruction of many.

“Then two kings will arise from Syria, with an army countless as the sand of the sea. They will seize the cities and territories of the Romans as far as Chalcedon, and then there will be much bloodshed. When all these things are remembered, the city and nation will tremble because of them, and they will destroy the peoples of the East.

“After this two kings will arise from Egypt. They will conquer four kings, kill them and their entire army, and reign for three years and six months.

“After them another king will arise, designated by the letter C, powerful in battle. He will reign for thirty years, build a temple to God, fulfill the law, and administer judgment on God’s behalf during that time.

“After him another king will arise, who will reign for a short time; they will attack and kill him.

“After this there will be a king designated by B. From B will proceed King Audon; from Audon will proceed A; from A another A will proceed; and from this one yet another A will be born. This second A will be exceedingly warlike and a fighter.

“From this A a king designated by R will be born; from R will be born L, who will have power over nineteen kings.

“After this a Salic king from France will arise, designated by K. He will be great and most pious, powerful and merciful, and will administer justice to the poor. Such will be the grace of virtue in him that, as he walks along the road, the treetops will bend toward him. Water flowing toward him will in no way delay its course. No king like him has previously existed in the Roman empire, nor will one exist after him.

“After him a king designated by L will come; after this L will reign, and after L, thirty; from L will proceed A. This A will be exceedingly warlike and strong in battle, and he will be numerous throughout the land and across the waters. He will not be delivered into the hands of his enemies; he will die in exile outside his kingdom, and his soul will be in the hand of God.

“Then a king designated by V will arise. On one side he will be Salic and on the other Lombard; he will possess power on earth against his opponents and against all his enemies.

“In those days a king designated by O will appear. He will be most powerful, strong, and good; he will administer justice to the poor and judge rightly. From him another most powerful O will proceed. Under him there will be battles between pagans and Christians, and the blood of the Greeks will be shed. His heart will be in the hand of God, and he will reign for seven years.

“From that woman a king designated by O will be born. He will be bloodthirsty and criminal, without faith or truth. Through him there will be much wickedness on earth and much bloodshed, and the churches will be destroyed under his power. In other regions there will be many tribulations and battles.

“Then nation will rise against nation in Cappadocia, and they will take Pamphylia captive at that time, because he did not enter through the door into the sheepfold. This king will reign for four years.

“After him a king designated by H will arise. In his days there will be many battles; they will conquer Syria and take Pentapolis captive. This king will be of Lombard descent.

“Then another Salic king, designated by C, will arise. He will conquer the Lombards, and there will be battles and struggles. This Salic king will be strong and powerful, but his kingdom will last only a short time.

“Then the Hagarenes and tyrants will arise. They will take Tarentum and Barro captive, and many cities will be plundered. They will also wish to come to Rome, and no one will resist them except the God of gods and Lord of lords.

“Then the Armenians will come and devastate Persia, so that the cities they plunder will not be recovered. They will hasten to the East and dig trenches there; they will attack the Romans and obtain peace for a little while.

“The king of the Greeks, a warrior, will enter Aepolis and destroy the temples of idols. Locusts and caterpillars will come and eat all the fruits of Cappadocia and Cilicia; the people will be tormented by hunger, and afterward he will be no more.

“Another Salic king will arise, namely H, a strong man and warrior. Many neighbors and relatives will become angry against him. In those days a brother will betray his brother, and a man will have intercourse with his sister. There will be many shameful acts among human beings on earth. Old men will lie with virgins, and wicked priests with deceived girls. Bishops will be followers of criminals, blood will be shed on earth, and they will pollute the temples of the saints.

“Among the people there will be fornications, impurities, and the crime of sodomy, so that the sight of them will appear as a reproach to him [referent uncertain]. People will be plunderers, abusive, haters of justice, and lovers of falsehood, and the judges of Rome will be changed. If they are admitted to judge today, they will be changed on another day for the sake of accepting money, and they will not judge rightly but falsely.

“In those days there will be rapacious, greedy, and perjured people, lovers of falsehood. Law and truth will be destroyed. Earthquakes will occur in various places; island cities and regions will be submerged. In various places there will be plagues among human beings, and the land will be laid waste by enemies. The vanity of the gods will not prevail to console them.

“Afterward a king designated by L will arise. Under him there will be wars, and he will reign for twelve years.

“After this a king designated by F will arise. He will come and prevail, reign for some time, then come to Rome and take it captive. His life will never be ended by death at the hands of his enemies. He will be good and great, administer justice to the poor, and live for a long time.

“After this another king designated by H will arise. From this H twelve H’s will proceed. He will be of Lombard and Teutonic descent, and they will reign for one hundred years.

“Then after him a king named H will arise, a Salic king from France. Then will begin sorrows such as have not existed since the beginning of the world. In his days there will be many battles, the tribulations of many people, and bloodshed; earthquakes will occur throughout cities and regions; many lands will be taken captive, and there will be no one to resist the enemies, because the Lord will be angry with the earth.

“Rome will be attacked in persecution and by the sword and will be seized into the hand of that king. There will be rapacious and greedy people, tyrants who hate the poor, oppress the innocent, and save the guilty. They will be unjust and utterly wicked, and the rulers who destroy others will be taken captive. There will be no one on earth to resist on their behalf or rescue them, because of their wickedness and greed.

“Then a king named H, steadfast in spirit, will arise. This same steadfast H will be king of the Romans and the Greeks. He will be tall in stature, handsome in appearance, radiant in face, and well formed in every feature of his limbs. His reign will end after 122 years.

“In those days there will be great riches, and the earth will abundantly yield its fruit, so that a measure of wheat will be sold for one denarius, a measure of wine for one denarius, and a measure of oil for one denarius.

“This king will keep before his eyes the Scripture which says: ‘The king of the Romans claims the whole kingdom of the Christians for himself.’ He will devastate all the islands and cities of the pagans, destroy all the temples of idols, and summon all pagans to baptism. Throughout every temple the cross of Christ Jesus will be erected.

“Then Egypt will precede Ethiopia in offering a gift to God. Those who do not worship the cross of Jesus Christ will be punished by the sword. When the 122 years have been completed, the Jews will be converted to the Lord, and his tomb will be glorious in the sight of all. In those days Israel will be saved and will dwell securely.

“At that time the prince of iniquity will arise from the tribe of Dan. He will be called Antichrist. He will be the son of perdition, the head of pride, the teacher of error, and the fullness of wickedness. He will overturn the world and perform great wonders and signs through false imitations. By magical art he will deceive many, so that fire will appear to descend from heaven.

“Years will be shortened into months, months into weeks, weeks into days, and days into hours.

“From the north will arise the most filthy nations whom King Alexander confined: namely Gog and Magog. These are twelve kingdoms, whose number is like the sand of the sea.

“When the Roman king hears of this, he will summon an army, defeat them in battle, and strike them down to complete destruction.

“Afterward the king will come to Jerusalem. There he will lay down the diadem of his head and all royal attire, and he will leave the kingdom of the Christians to God the Father and to his Son Jesus Christ.

“When the Roman empire has ceased, Antichrist will then be openly revealed and will sit in the house of the Lord in Jerusalem. During his reign two most renowned men, Elijah and Enoch, will go forth to announce the coming of the Lord. Antichrist will kill them, and after three days they will be raised by the Lord.

“Then there will be a great persecution such as has never occurred before and will never follow afterward. But on account of the elect the Lord will shorten those days, and Antichrist will be killed by the power of the Lord through the archangel Michael on the Mount of Olives.”

When the Sibyl had foretold these and many other future events to the Romans, including the signs by which the Lord would come to judge, she thundered out the following verses in prophecy:

## Sibylline Verses Concerning Christ

The sign of judgment: the earth will grow wet with sweat.

From heaven the king who is to come through the ages will arrive,

Present in the flesh, plainly, to judge the world.

Then the unbelieving and the faithful alike will see God,

The Most High, together with the saints; the end now stands in him.

Then souls will be present together with the flesh, whom he himself judges.

When the world lies uncultivated amid dense brambles,

People will cast away their idols and all their wealth together.

Fire will burn the lands, the sea, and the heavens.

Seeking the gloomy gates, he will shatter the doors of Tartarus.

For a free light will belong to all the flesh of the saints,

While the springs will be surrendered and eternal flame will burn them.

Each person will speak, making his hidden deeds known;

God will open the secret hearts to the light.

Then there will also be mourning, and everyone will gnash his teeth.

The sun’s radiance will be snatched away, and the chorus of stars will perish.

The heavens will be rolled up; the moon’s brightness will disappear.

He will cast down the hills and raise the valleys from below.

There will no longer be anything lofty or high among human things.

The mountains will now be level with the plains and the blue depths of the sea.

All things will cease; the shattered earth will perish.

Thus together the springs and rivers will burn with fire.

But the trumpet will, with mournful sound, send forth from on high,

and the earth, opening, will reveal to the world the wretched race, its crime, and its varied labours,

and Tartarean chaos.

[Col. 1186C] And before this Lord the kings will be brought forward, every one of them,

and fire and a stream of sulfur will fall from heaven.

Then the Lord will judge according to each person’s work, and the wicked will go into the fire of eternal Gehenna; but the just will receive the reward of eternal life; and there will be a new heaven and a new earth, and the sea will no longer exist. And the Lord will reign with the saints forever and ever. Amen.

# Appendix to the Spurious Works of the Venerable Bede

## The *Hisperica Famina*, or a Little Work of Unusual or Secret Latin, by an Unknown Author

Edited by Angelo Mai according to an ancient Vatican manuscript. (*Classical Authors*, vol. V.)

[Col. 1185]

## Mai’s Preface

[Col. 1185C] 1. This work of unheard-of Latin had long been observed by me in the Vatican Codex of Queen Christina of Sweden, of the tenth or eleventh century, which once belonged to the French senator [Col. 1186C] Petavius. I was awaiting a suitable opportunity to publish it, and the grammarian Virgilius has now provided one. To that teacher of singular Latin this little book comes as a not inappropriate companion; its author can scarcely be doubted to have been Scottish by nation, since the word *Scottigena* indicates this twice, on pp. 488 and 489.

When we say “Scottish,” however, we may equally understand “Irish,” for it is well established that the name “Scotland” was once common both to Ireland and to the land now properly called Scotland. Yet someone may ask: Why does a Scottish man call his poem *Hisperica Famina*, when among the ancients the word *Hesperia* meant either Italy or Spain?

I confess that I cannot sufficiently resolve this difficulty. In any case, the author says that he speaks not in the Ausonian manner but in the Hisperic sound, § 2:

> “I have sounded forth to seize the Hisperic scepter; therefore I strike out a rough speech. But if an Ausonian chain had bound me, a sonorous utterance would have spread its draught through my throat.”

And again, § 11:

> “No Ausonian chain fetters me; therefore it does not tear away the Scottish-born encomium.”

Italy having thus been excluded, we are left to think of Spain. Nevertheless, when the tenor of the whole work is considered, the author again appears rather Irish or Scottish: he praises *articorhetors*, devotes himself to voyages by sea, hunting, the tending of herds, and meat-laden banquets and salted foods, which he says are smeared with Scottish oil. This brings to mind Jerome’s remark about Jovinianus, that he was “weighed down by the porridge of the Scots” (Jerome, prologue to the *Commentary on Jeremiah*).

Either, then, *Hisperica* means “Irish,” or Irish things are called Hisperic because Ireland lies in the western region of the European world. For this reason the Greeks called Italy “Hesperia,” while the Italians in turn designated Spain by the name “Hesperia.” On this matter I await the judgments of learned men.

2. The author himself mentions twelve kinds of Latin, p. 483. Among these he seems to call two especially defective: the barbaric, by which name I understand Celtic, Frankish, and all northern words; and the Hisperic, which he himself uses. He says that this latter kind arose from a “glory-bearing land”; but I again hesitate as to which region he means, whether Spain or rather Scotland.

The style of the work is inflated, abnormal, extravagant, obscure, and often impossible to unravel. I am therefore reminded again of Jerome, who, speaking of the expression of Jovinianus—whose son Pelagius Orosius calls Scottish-born (*On Free Will*, Leiden edition, p. 613), although others interpret the statement differently—says:

> “There is such barbarism in his writings, and speech so foully confused with so many faults, that I could not understand what he was saying; everything swells, everything collapses” (Jerome, *Against Jovinianus*, book I, beginning).

And below:

> “What are these monstrosities of words? What disgrace of description?”

Yet although the language of the Hisperic utterances is far worse than that of Jovinianus, it will nevertheless be much more useful and advantageous for enlarging the history of Latin and recounting its fortunes.

3. The subject matter of the little work is as follows. After an inflated opening, in which the author discusses in his own fashion his eloquence, apparently the studies of his own people, and the various kinds of dialect, he writes a certain prose poem. In its first section he elaborately sets out the course of the day—that is, human activities from early morning until late evening.

In the following sections he presents, as it were, a natural history of the sky, the sea, fire, and winds. Then he speaks of clothing, a small chest, writing tablets, a sacred chapel, and prayer to God. He crowns the work with descriptions of hunting and feasting, as well as a battle against hostile brigands.

[Col. 1187]

[Note: [Col. 1187D] The grammarian Virgilius speaks more than once of this secret, mystical, or unusual kind of Latin, and supplies brief examples from various authors in his second epistles and epitomes. I have wished to enrich Virgilius’s teaching with this extensive specimen of such Latin; it will be useful to compare it with the *Polyptych* of Atto of Vercelli, of nearly the same kind, which I published in the sixth volume of the Vatican collection of ancient writers. Lovers of elegant Latin will rightly condemn this work with every curse; nevertheless, those who examine the history of the Latin language more learnedly will be grateful to me, its editor. Georg Walch, the historian of Latin, would certainly have found here a new opportunity for discussion, had he known the matter.]

# The *Hisperica Famina* (C)

[Col. 1187C] 1. A broad opening rouses the cavern of my breast; from my grieving lung I draw forth a mournful sound, but within my breast I confine a joy-flowing storm in the chambers of my lungs. As distinguished observers of wisdom, the *articorhetors*, pour an excellent draught of urbane style into their throats and fashion serpentine syllogisms of literature, while a flower-bearing host of *articorhetors* bends the reins of the triangular world of earth—do they bring forth fabulous treasures from their mouths?

Are quarrels of dispute growing among youthful offspring? Or are peaceful children withdrawing the scepters? Does a savage band of warriors [Note: Manuscript: *amatorum*, “lovers.”] collapse, poisoned by the contest in battle, so that white garments are drenched with streams of thieves’ oyster-blood? Or has the foaming wave of the woolly sea overwhelmed idle rowers in shipwreck? Or has a dreadful death carried off the inhabitants in a common slaughter? [Note: [Col. 1188D] That is, the inhabitants.]

What annals do you teach? Which rhetorician do you follow? Against this reader I summon as a skilled challenger one who eagerly fashioned a learned arena. I have already fought three athletes, slain idle combatants, punished strong contemporaries, and struck down in battle mightier Cyclopes.

Hence no equal escapes me. While savage little spears wound me, at once I draw my pliable sword, with which I slaughter noble statues. I seize a wooden Idumaean shield [Note: [Col. 1188D] Gloss: that is, by hand.] which shines with fleshly protection for the legs. I brandish an iron dagger, whose cave-like, projecting point hardens the beaked weapons, the *cidones*, against all my contemporary opponents in the contest.

2. This polished scattering of expressions shines, so that it heaps no faulty mound of words, but compresses healthy strength within a well-balanced reading and, with evenly fashioned form, scatters honey-sweet speech through the mouths of the people in an Ausonian sprinkling.

As countless swarms of bees move through hollow beehives, sip honey-bearing streams in their combs, and cut out their customary honeycombs with their mouths, so here a polished company of rhetoricians appears. During the elapsed stages of time we have not grown an equal phalanx, nor shall we behold in the villages of the temporal world a company of equally radiant renown in the future.

But a dreadful water-snake stands ready, which will wound such a crowd with a viper’s stroke unless they summon the ruler of the vast heavens, who will release the flower-bearing host by a lawful distinction.

In the new cycle of the temporal world I have sounded forth to seize the Hisperic scepter; therefore I strike out a rough speech, and a small stream creeps through the mouths. But if an Ausonian chain had bound me in the broad course of temporal life, a sonorous utterance would have ravaged the draught through my throat, and an immense flood of urbane style would have flowed from my mouth.

What kind of distinctive performance are you fashioning? Are you splitting noble trees with axes so that you may cut out an urbane speech in a four-sided chariot among dense boards? Or are you bringing forth golden crescents, cooked in a flame-bearing bronze furnace, with solid hammers? Or are you raising a slender song on stretched strings? Perhaps you are blowing hollow reeds in sonorous harmonies?

3. But I do not stand forth with an intelligible sharpness of mind. You observe wool-bearing flocks of two-toothed sheep through fragrant pastures; you pursue the councils of rhetoricians by a tiresome route; and with twin shoulders you play a swanlike, curved, ruddy whiteness, compressing it with reed-like, dripping shafts, while you embrace a combed, fleshy, leg-bearing chimney.

You do not listen to learned mysteries with ingenious intellectual sharpness, but with exhausted effort you follow the learned companies of historians. Hence, with ingenious judgment, you have obtained a wondrous counsel from the stake: to rush into the native soil of your ancestral land, so that with a strong rural gesture you may fashion your proper rites, and all things stand seized at the gates of the hot passageways. [Note: [Col. 1189D] From Greek *panta*, “all things,” as becomes clear below.]

Growing herds graze the crops; the sorrowful mother moistens her cheeks with tearful drops; the infant mutters and cries; and the flower-bearing countryside resounds with a trumpet blast. The foreign, land-producing mother removes the male and celebrates peaceful marriages in gentle chambers. These “all things” testify that the rites of birth have reached their limit.

4. As a mountainous torrent crosses the rugged land, destruction uproots leafy alders through muddy waves; it rolls out broken things with a murmur, strikes the muddy bank in the riverbed, and tears up compacted gravel in its whirlpool. In the same way it makes an Ausonian river overflow with luxuriant growth.

As the rose-colored fire of a summer hearth consumes old logs with rust-colored embers, and a small flame diminishes strong wood into speaking heaps, so a smoky furnace breathes out a burning belch, bends flame-bearing tongues across the ceilings, and with equal learned heat roasts the companies of historians.

As a savage cattle-butcher terrifies herds and kills a fat young bull with a drawn weapon, so the entrails bind together a horrible maw with fat; with bloody jaws it swallows a slaughtered stream. In the same way I disturb the speech of historians with painful fear.

Although you may have touched the glassy summit of the open sky, although the twin stars of the chief white light have traversed the northern boundaries of the sevenfold Olympus, although you have counted the sandy grains of the shore-dwelling planet, and although the colonists of the world have deemed the living breath of the sea a starry seedbed at its boundary, you will not pour out a Hisperic flood from your eager throat.

As far as the East is distant from the western boundary, the northern, fiery star surpasses the ploughing bear with a greater radiance; the discordant clash of contending soldiers surpasses the honeyed buzzing of bees; and the raging Bear surpasses the tender two-toothed creature. To that extent the powers of our talkative style are separated from one another.

5. I examine twelve *vechri* [Note: [Col. 1189D] That is, twelve kinds of Latin, about which the grammarian Virgilius speaks in the *Epitome*, book V. Of these twelve kinds he says that two are the worst, which especially stain the gold of Ausonian or Latin speech: the barbaric kind of speech, and the Hisperic, which is the subject matter of this little work.] that tear apart the Ausonian palate.

Among these are two offenses that wound the verbal structure with a viper’s touch. One, by barbaric growth, infects the path of speech, fixes it in a double pattern, and joins four examples; it adds the distinguished letters of continuous literature; it removes the established writing through poisonous damage; it moves the literal characters [Note: [Col. 1190D] Gloss: or reed pens.] of urban eloquence; and with a poisonous barrier changes the stable tenor of writing.

The other *vechrus* has arisen from a glory-bearing soil; by a lawful stroke it violates the Hisperic encomium and corrodes the intelligible houses of the several parts. The remaining offenses are noted: they wound the golden Ausonian speech of the reader. From these the offense of a distinctive, talkative style is attached to this assertion.

[Note: [Col. 1190D] The author means by the law of the day the arrangement of the day’s activities.]

# Here Begins the Law of the Day

[Col. 1190A]

6. The sun-colored plough cuts through the heavenly panel, illuminates the sea with its vapor, follows the upper sky with a flame-vomiting flash, and climbs the noble chamber of the firmament.

Phoebus stifles the pale Mene [Note: [Col. 1190D] Gloss: the moon.] with a thoroughly reddened light; the waxen Pleiades do not emit their radiance; the sun-flowing path draws out the sea-colored stain; the fire of Phaethon unravels dense sweat; the dewdrops dry with rusty heat; nor does the olive-colored cloud shade leafy woods; rain divides the hay-bearing grapes; the fire, red as urine, warms small hollows; and the worldly radiance scorches the circuit.

The winged, peaceful court echoes with harmony; slender songs murmur through open mouths; they refresh the hollow hills of the ears with sweetness; the leaf-haired flock robs the bird-filled hiding places; they sharpen the bell-like clods; the worms swallow fragments of pitch; the foul-smelling places sting; and they fill the hungry bellies with food-bearing juices.

The cattle company surveys vast pastures; the *calastres* move by kicking; the country estates sow various gatherings; within, they fill their entrails with pale serpents; with toothless movements they chew leafy fodder; the innocent sheep separate their folds; they cross wooden bridges on foot; wool-bearing herds enter the bridled lambs; and with their teeth they crop grassy grapes.

The shaggy company of swine has left its whirlpools; with their snouts they dig into the earth; they swallow the roots of stable ferns and taste the vegetable juice.

The wooden stalls deprive the fiery hoofed horses of food [Note: [Col. 1190D] The manuscript has *aes suum*, “their bronze,” rather than *esuum*, “of foods.”]; with rough movements they traverse worn paths; the riders loosen the iron shackles from their legs; and with toothless movements they fill their hollow chests.

The mad troop of wild offspring treads the noble hills, wraps the harshest brushwood in its steps, and eagerly surveys the humped natives from a rugged height.

The monstrous dolphins sweep the foaming sea; through open gates of their throats they swallow salty waters; and they devour the scaly whirlpools.

7. [Note: [Col. 1190D] Greek *pantes*, “all.”] All the others perform the customary rural rites. Some fashion earthen trenches with sharp trowels; they thicken enclosures with thorny hedges and heap stone walls with masses of rock. Others drive many kinds of herds into pastures; they resound with sonorous cries [Note: [Col. 1190D] *Oche*, “joy,” in Atto, *Polyptych*, p. 44.] [Note: [Col. 1190D] The letter *r* is written above *re*.] and disturb the savage country with melodious lowing.

Countless companies of leafy things frequently approach the woodland. They strike noble trees with axes, twist branches torn out with axes, cut down the appointed alders with sharp tools, and carry away heavily loaded wagons on strong yokes.

Here a sonorous tumult rouses us from sleep in our resting chambers to wakefulness and to gather clothing in bodily heaps.

Then tighten the soft beams with leg coverings; gird white shirts of rough linen with leathern belts; fasten silver crescents upon yellow garments; unroll the pleasing movable coverings; and arrange soft carpets in a woolly embrace.

8. Cut out a learned settlement and observe the literary letters. Some celebrate a trophy for the rhetorician: if he has taken healthy sleep within his breast’s enclosure, unless the rising Phoebus has torn the dream’s pleasure from his eyelids, and unless he has fitted a worn blanket to his loins, he is to produce a reader’s industry.

Why do you overwhelm us with the thunderous blast of your speech and disturb the inner caverns of our ears with swelling language? We have allotted the whole course of the nocturnal toil to the reader’s watches; you have indulged your legs in sleepy decay. Therefore the sleepy touch now does not spur us.

Let some servant approach this learned frozen mass with foaming liquid, so that he may pour a glassy draught from heated waters and wipe away the night’s uncleanness with a fountain wave.

Release the woven coverings from their hollow frames and listen to learned industry. Let applause rise murmuring in the air, and let verbal sound resound, if the whole united company stands in the hall. Therefore separate such a cohort. Let the others go to sunny houses; some should explore the leafy woods, and others settle in this spacious hut.

9. The sun cuts through the upper center of the sky and approaches the middle span of the day. Hence the breast burns with hungry flame. Therefore let us visit the territories continually, so that the feast may have supplied fragrant fodder.

Who will lead the beautiful company through the crossroads? I have often explored these secret hot passageways and penetrated the distant estates of this northern region. I examine the handsome inhabitants who feed the wandering choirs of rhetoricians.

Condense the route into a narrow passage; set the goads in the star-bearing furrow; let the cruel ones have pierced the savage obstacles with Nepithean spears. Such are not the crossroads guarded by viperous brigands: they strip the many kinds of travelers’ companies with spears, seize the plunder they have collected, and slaughter armed bands with swords.

Therefore let us rush through the difficult places in a close wedge; let us tread with our feet the harsh estates that heap stony statues into a burning mass and give birth to thorny brambles. These flower-bearing fields emit their crops and heap up purple [Note: [Col. 1191D] Perhaps *callhas*.] plants. Nor do they compress broken stones; rather, they join together the leafy bunches of herbs.

10. A dog’s urban sound murmurs among the woods. Perhaps a foreign brigand is clinging to the walls, or the ears of those exploring have caught the noise of a troop.

Two slaps raise a sonorous bray, so that the steward, rejoicing, turns the wandering company toward the lodging place.

Draw out the seal with hooked nails. This hollow hall contains a swept floor, which is continually cleaned with birch bundles, and no dust gathers there.

This muddy floor lies beneath the open air; it holds compacted grains of dirt, and leafy brooms do not remove the waste from the vestibule.

Fill a sturdy basin with watery moisture; wash the filthy foundations with flowing water; and wipe the muddy feet with glassy liquid.

Fasten wooden curved supports into the wall and set a straight course with neatly arranged frames, so that it may provide a spacious spectacle for the country people.

Cover the seats with leather mats; place the rose-colored furnace of the wood-burning fire in the little courtyard; heap small pieces of dry grass, so that the flame-vomiting fire may belch forth, distribute its heat, and drive out the cold hearth.

Who will ask for such servants, so that they may grant a honey-sweet abundance?

11. No Ausonian chain binds me [Note: [Col. 1191D] The author seems to say that he is not restrained by Latin strictness. The Scottish-born encomium or language that he adds may perhaps demonstrate the author’s homeland. Indeed, the word *Scottigena* recurs below.]; therefore I do not tear away the Scottish-born encomium. But I will strike down the raging ones with an intimate companion.

The handsome inhabitants excuse themselves from embracing scant provisions under divine authority. Split these granted foods with sharp knives and load the wooden food-bearing tables with a heap.

Separate the learned choir into four rhythms. Wash the watery skins with soda, so that the cleansed vessels may become visible.

Strengthen the pleasant, food-bearing harmony into abundance [Note: [Col. 1192D] The manuscript has *contentum*, “content.”], so that it may pour a healthy juice into the inner organs.

Warm the food with flame-bearing hair, so that it may pour a sweeter taste into the throats. Hide the fragments of crumbs in hollow baskets.

Ask the noble lord of heaven that the inhabitants may not rush into the food-bearing bag of Cocytus, but may approach the summit of the sevenfold upper heaven.

Those who granted the sweet heaps of food—let each exacting person ask for a polished female server, so that salty stones may dance through the ashes and the crackling, salt-bearing foam may bubble over the watery meat.

Let us approach the appointed town, where we have fixed a dense agreement among those reclining together. What sweeter comforts have you swallowed? With toothless movements we gnawed crusts of meal, smeared with the Scottish-born seasoning of oil; with pressed teeth we chewed flesh-bearing legs; a milky draught spread through us; and with thirsty mouths we tasted the joy-flowing ale.

12. The sun-colored plough shines over the western sea and bends its rose-colored rays beneath the sphere. It brings forth the lunar star from the vast sky; the radiance of the Pleiades varies the sights of the heavens [Note: [Col. 1192D] Greek: *ouranon*, “heaven.”]. A nocturnal, heavy, serpentine cloud darkens the world; it makes the leafy vapors olive-colored, and gloomy darkness shades the worldly circuit.

Uncounted herds move through the cattle-yards and rush into the bovine enclosures; they climb the quadrangular halls of the sheepfolds; shaggy swine inspect the worn pigsties; charioteers fasten the iron seals of the hoofed horses to their supports; and countless companies of country people release the customary bond of labor from the carts and rest in sunny halls beneath their customary coverings.

Therefore let us approach the walls of the noble city of the world, ready to seek the gracious hospitality of its inhabitants. Let us signal the entrance with a sonorous bray, so that this learned company may gather in the lodging.

Set out seats covered with leather mats; feed the burning chimney; light a radiant lamp at the hearth; pour out a glassy fruit in a wooden vessel; wash the filthy supports; and distribute the service of the meal among the customary company.

Let the others rush with a swift turn up the wooded hill and tear away the grasses with tightened ropes [Note: [Col. 1192D] “Let them tear away the grasses?”]. Let others approach the watery height and carry away a full water jar on their shoulders. Let others cook the canine meat and fashion meal-bearing wheels.

Split the established heaps of food with knives; load the wooden tables with an abundance of food; and heap honey-sweet fragments in combed baskets.

13. I withdraw into the hiding places of my hollow breast, so that the inhabitants who have bestowed honey-sweet abundance and granted the sweet heaps of food may have prolonged an honorable lodging.

Light torches dipped in seasoning at the furnace and examine the reader’s industry according to the annals. The eyelids compress the weight of sleep.

Therefore cover the cattle-beds with soft mats and spread out rough movable carpets; fold soft cushions beneath the projecting supports.

Cover the charcoal embers with an ashen mound, lest the nearby dust catch fire and burn in the broad blaze of the fiery furnace.

Close the four-sided royal door with a tight bar, lest savage robbers burst in to steal hidden treasures.

Let the others listen to learned wisdom with the sharpness of their minds. Let some withdraw the dream-filled warmth from their legs. Let others keep the nightly watches, until the rose-colored Phoebus of the East has shone forth.

# Concerning the Sky

14. From this broad firmament of Olympus I shall bring forth, in a slow murmur, structures of speech.

This heavenly sphere was fashioned in a compact arrangement; with its wandering covering it encloses shadow-bearing regions and embraces the fire-haired stars in its vast mass.

It grazes the twin ploughs of the burning white light. The sun-colored Orion shines over the boundaries of day. Pale darkness illuminates the evening [Note: [Col. 1192D] The manuscript has *promerium*, apparently for *pomerium*, “evening.”].

The glassy heaven compresses five belts [Note: [Col. 1192D] Gloss: “the sky.”]. The remaining zones contain warmth and cook the regions with worldly heat. Others breathe out a cold belch, unfold snowy spray, scatter freezing winters with dreadful rushing, and blow forth stormy motion in a whirlwind.

The many-formed rainbow is made visible by the rays through the fine vapor of the sun-flowing clouds. The heavenly circuit twists itself into a revolving whirl; the fixed poles run around the axis.

Olympus supports the angelic companies as a throne and encloses the splendid chamber with a pale mark. Physicists assert that the heaven has a sevenfold cycle. Countless forms stand at the summit of the sky, which I do not undertake to explain in the language of time.

# Concerning the Sea

15. Of this broad brightness of Amphitrite I strive to fashion a word-filled account.

This foaming sea surrounds the world’s shores; with ancient waves it strikes the earth’s edges; with watery masses it rushes upon the rocky places; with a roaring whirlpool it stirs the lowest gravel; it scatters foam through the star-bearing channel; it is often shaken by sonorous winds; and the chattering South Wind wearies the waves.

The sea sprinkles the heavenly circuit with drops; the leafy, pale-haired ocean beats upon the cattle-tracks; it destroys ships in danger by shipwreck.

At other times the sea forms a calm surface and emits no dreadful sighing of stormy murmurs, but its chattering waves melt away in tranquil warmth.

A double rhythm of Neptune’s wave is established. At once it prevails upon the shores with foaming approach and folds back its returning retreat into its ancient womb. It bends its customary movement into a twofold course; the muddy wave plucks at the sunken boundary; it draws out the marginal limits with growing matter; with a vast swelling it floods the straits; it bends wooden alders from the earth into the fields; it continually heaps shoreweed into its bosom; it tears broad mussels from the rocks; it pulls out shells smeared with crimson; it unfolds at the harbor sandy images of many-formed shellfish; the wave-wandering waters waver into the hot passageways; and the foam roars with swelling.

Sometimes it grazes the swelling wave more gently and does not travel along the customary boundaries of the marginal land. It supports beaked keels with harsh waves; with resounding waves it drives wooden ships through the watery sea; it carries immense boats across the marble-colored whirlpool; and huge Liburnian ships sail through the bosom of the sea.

A school of dolphins plays beneath the pale waves. Monstrous whales contend through the deep; they chew painful whirlpools [Note: [Col. 1193D] Gloss: “fish”]; they suck the glassy sea through their throats; and they swallow little fish.

Neptune’s sea-blue waters are swept by foaming, saw-toothed creatures; the wave of the sea troubles those who taste the flavor of salt-bearing things.

If all the inhabitants of the world [Note: [Col. 1193D] Greek: *pantes*, “all.”] were to look into the inner womb of the sea [Note: [Col. 1193D] “Inhabitants.”], they would rush into the sudden, deadly enclosure of the abyss.

# Concerning Fire

16. Here a rose-colored fire crackles in the wood-burning furnace. It breathes forth burning heat; it folds flame-bearing swords in ruddy embers; it roasts twisted branches in a flame-bearing fire; it attacks the fuel-bearing logs; the swift pyre vomits smoking vapor; it scatters ashen sparks in the heat; and the food-bearing heat fashions countless services.

At once it roasts meal-bearing crusts in charcoal warmth; it cooks raw, trembling things in hollow cauldrons; it softens silver metals in the furnace; and golden masses melt redly in the chimney.

It warms all the green lamps with fuel [Note: [Col. 1193D] Greek *panta*, “all things.”], and slowly brings forth the native vigour of the flame-vomiting hearth.

Already it had grown hard within the womb of the flint; the fire-kindler, with skillful effort, struck the iron fire-steel. A spark flashed brightly upon the dry tinder; the fire-lighter bent the gathered flax and, with mutual whirling, the small spark [Note: [Col. 1193D] Greek *mikron*, “small.”] belched out smoke.

He heaped dry splinters into a torch, and the immense pyre grew with swelling flames.

The furnace draws out coverings from shadowy, hidden tiles; with flame-bearing heat it drives away hostile cold and wraps everything in burning fires.

At least, all the inhabitants should cut the tree trunk, and the hearth should burn it with its urine-colored belch.

Here a flowering woodland shines in broad brilliance; it embraces the urban walls of the immense world, in which huts stand with towered, many-formed construction.

The high country establishes its enclosures. It brings forth mature crops beneath a fruit-bearing covering; it heaps fragrant vineyards, which join swift little grapes to their branches.

Countrywomen sweep the estate cleared of thorns; watery rivers irrigate its muddy veins; the earth belches forth liquids in bursting springs; and rose-colored fields abound in hay-bearing crops [Note: [Col. 1194D] Perhaps *calthis*]. They join delicate fruits.

It produces blue serpents that satisfy the herds. Lofty hills surround the cleared woodland [Note: [Col. 1194D] Perhaps “hills”]; and at the outer boundaries it trims the woods [Note: [Col. 1194D] So the manuscript, in a second hand. The first hand has “in the fields.”].

It gathers countless growths of foliage, which support different fruits on spreading branches. Deep furrows separate the vegetable-bearing fields, which hold grassy grapes upon pale handles.

The earth-bound region feeds countless herds; an immense foundation bears the rocks of the earth; and the fertile countryside joins together abundant structures.

These things I do not strive to explain in a verbal course, lest I burden the learned veins of the rhetoricians.

# Concerning Wind

[Col. 1194B]

17. Here the sonorous west wind strikes the noble trees; it folds ancient holm oaks into the furrows of the earth; with strong gusts it strips towered huts; it rubs the upper ceilings of the heights; it bends the sea-blue waters toward the earth; and it lifts sea-foam into the stars.

The South Wind troubles the pale-haired Tithonus. Physicists report twelve west winds and examine four east winds. These cling to the alternating blast of the South Wind and, like wings placed beneath, cast them into shadow.

They blow the worldly mass into a vast air-filled skin. The murmuring South Wind grazes three trophies: it carried away the foaming flood in a swelling skin, thundered as it bore off a powerful measure, and struck bodily forms with its touch.

Nor can the whistling storm be looked upon; and the lofty ruler of heaven will judge that the speech of the humped winds has been cast forth from murmuring wings.

# Concerning Many Things

18. This distinguished company shines with flowering pomp. It freezes yellow coverings on the outside and joins heaps of clothing with many kinds of labor.

Some hold purple cloaks tightly; others trim swanlike stoles with soft coverings; others pack hyacinth-colored garments around their bodily legs; many roll up garments in a bodily assemblage; they adorn oyster-coloured armlets; they wear yellow mitres upon their crowns; they settle curly locks; they join together loose braids; and they wear shining curved ornaments around their necks.

Countless people seize quadrangular shields with shield-like handles, brandish iron daggers from their water-skins, and heap up other creations, which I do not express in the language of time.

# Concerning the Tavern

19. This white tavern shines forth; it compresses thick bristles under a rather short covering.

Its quadrangular structure is made from a sewn piece; a single upper opening embraces it. That opening is closed by a cover with tightly fitted wheels [Note: [Col. 1194D] The manuscript has “many-sided wheels.”], and is fastened with twelve cords. The burden is carried with curved supports upon the necks of the rhetoricians.

I shall describe the construction of this curved object. A butcher had previously covered fattened legs of cattle; with a sharp knife he stripped the hairy hide, stretched it densely against a wall among the rods, and dried it in fiery smoke. The craftsman, rejoicing, tore away the prepared framework; with tightened leather thongs he trimmed the hide-covered roof; he fashioned four corners and completed the cupboard with a leather covering serving as a door.

I do not explain the remaining forms in speech, lest I arouse weariness in the learned camps.

# Concerning the Table

20. This wooden table has been fashioned for reading boards. From one side it joins a waxed surface [Col. 1195A]; by means of a wooden partition it connects columns to *Defidas*, upon which fine engraving has played.

The other side, already wooden, supports a surface with a larger construction, varied with painted decoration, and compresses polished edges.

This wood once grew among the pale-haired trees of the land. A craftsman cut the growing trunk with an iron axe, shaped its quadrangular growth with a wooden tool, removed a small border with a hatchet, and completed the decorated table.

It is carried in the right hand of historians and heaps learned mysteries upon waxen tablets.

Now I withdraw the verbal path with a swift turn, lest I burden the ingenious houses of the rhetoricians.

# Concerning the Oratory

21. This wooden oratory has been fashioned from panelled boards. Its quadrangular sides are compressed by paired double joints; the foundations of the temple provide a stable support.

What dense ceiling grew with a globular covering? It joins an upper chamber; quadrangular panels are placed upon a polished roof.

It joins an altar in its bosom, at which the priests celebrate the collected Mass [Note: [Col. 1195B] In the Christian inscriptions edited by me, *vates* means bishops. Here I understand priests.].

A single door occupies the western boundary; the wooden royal gate is closed by tight fastenings. An extended, panelled portico supports a gathering-place. The summit joins four pinnacles.

It gathers countless constructions, which I do not undertake to explain in a word-filled account.

# Concerning Prayer

22. I ask the supreme Lord of the vast heaven, who created the world’s mass by his gracious power, who encloses the earthly foundation with a sea-colored boundary, who restores human beings through a worthy renewal, who covers the leafy fields with a pale-haired heap, who nourishes flower-bearing stalks from the earth, and who places the rewards of the gracious throne among the troops of the *gibrae*:

grant me, as I sail across the summer sea, a sturdy ship, so that I may escape its raging dangers. [Note: [Col. 1195B] Perhaps “stormy.”]

# Concerning the Deed Itself
23. Once the stages of a long-enduring abyss had elapsed, as the glowing dawn of Phoebus’ rising shone [Col. 1196A], a certain frenzied armed marauder reached the outer boundaries of a hostile land. Then, traversing the hills by a swift path, the blue-haired [Note: [Col. 1196B] “Of the hills”?] scouts observed among the manes a bristling herd of porcine nature in the woods.

Thereupon a certain powerful tyrant pierced the shaggy flanks of a savage boar with a fierce axe. Then, with a broad and skillful movement, he twisted the dewy corpse, dripping with purple blood, around his neck. The slaughterers cut up the vast carcass with swords, strike the flint with iron metal, and spread a pyre with sunny branches; and the flame-vomiting furnace of the hearth smokes through the leafy forest.

Next, a four-cornered gridiron, fitted with spits, is set up; they roast the bristling haunches in rosy flames and fasten the raw legs upon wooden spits. Drops of bloody fat fall between the fires; the armed men taste pieces of roasted flesh, and swallow the porcine food with their throats.

Thereupon the inhabitants of that land, descendants of this people, continually guarded the outer borders of their native soil, lest a hostile danger prevail in their ancestral furrows [Col. 1196B]. And now, as they surveyed the final circuit of the globe by its accustomed winding paths, they saw the marauder proclaimed among the woodland oaks.

Then, as the leafy band rushed upon them, it shattered the forest glades; and the insolent company immediately shouted that, after the cruel slaughter, no survivors would escape from the ranks, nor would savage claws carry them through the air to the heavens.

Thereupon the frenzied tyrants thicken their close battle line and carry forward beaked weapons of war. A white metal covering is scattered across the bronze furrow; fierce axes pierce with reciprocal force, and the arrows, having been discharged, bore through the fleshy haunches; slaughter-bearing streams of purple blood creep along the sides.

The unarmed giants fall into the contest and loose their great masses with swords, while the poisonous marauder, striking with the strength of battle, breaks the advancing phalanx. They strip the corpses of their deadly heap of clothing, and amid the dreadful, cruel tumult they rejoice.

Then, returning by the path that led back to their ancestral land, the inhabitants set forth a fabulous *soria* (“heap, mass”) [Note: [Col. 1196D] Gloss: “heap, mass.”].
